title: Arab conspiracy theorists blame Israel for Jordanian strikes on Syria, attack on Jordan church
body: Conspiracy theorists and prominent Arab voices alike have sought to blame Israel for last week's attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan's Karak governorate and Monday's Jordanian strikes on Syria, alleging either that Israel orchestrated a “false flag attack” or that Amman was the target of Israeli disinformation intended to sow discord between the two countries.Jordan carried out airstrikes in southern Syria on Monday evening, saying it had targeted hideouts linked to Friday's deadly attack and claiming the strikes were coordinated with Damascus, which denied any such coordination.Five civilians, including women and children, were killed as a result of the Jordanian strikes, a health official told state news agency SANA.Palestinian journalist suggests Israeli intelligence used in Jordanian strikesPalestinian journalist Maher Chawich, who has primarily written for Qatari media and is the former editor-in-chief of the Palestinian Al-Awda magazine, questioned on X/Twitter if Amman had relied on Israeli intelligence to carry out the strikes on Syria, and whether Israel had attempted to “exploit Jordan's security concerns to push Amman toward a confrontation with Damascus.”“Are we facing a security escalation imposed by real circumstances, or a regional trap that recalls what happened in Sweida, aimed at creating tension between Damascus and Amman? The danger of the repercussions calls for clarification of the sources of information, the nature of the targeted objectives, and the extent of their verification before carrying out the operation,” he wrote. “For the question is not only who was targeted in southern Syria, but also who provided the information on which the targeting decision was based, and who benefits from straining relations between the two countries?”هل وقع الأردن في فخ استخباراتي شبيه بما شهدته السويداء؟ ما جرى في الجنوب السوري يطرح تساؤلاً حساساً حول مصدر المعلومات الاستخباراتية التي استند إليها #الأردن في تنفيذ غاراته. هل اعتمدت عمّان على معلومات استخباراتية إسرائيلية قد تكون مضللة أو غير دقيقة؟ وهل يمكن أن تكون #إسرائيل قد سعت إلى توظيف المخاوف الأمنية الأردنية لدفع #عمّان نحو مواجهة مع #دمشق؟ نحن أمام اختبار مبكر للعلاقات السورية الأردنية، في منطقة تتشابك فيها الحسابات الأمنية مع المصالح الإقليمية. فهل نحن أمام تصعيد أمني فرضته معطيات حقيقية، أم أمام #فخ إقليمي يعيد إلى الأذهان ما جرى في #السويداء، ويهدف إلى إحداث التوتر بين دمشق وعمّان؟ خطورة التداعيات تستدعي #توضيح مصادر المعلومات، وطبيعة الأهداف المستهدفة، ومدى التحقق منها قبل تنفيذ العملية. فالسؤال ليس فقط من استُهدف في #الجنوب_السوري، بل أيضاً من قدّم المعلومات التي بُني عليها قرار الاستهداف، ومن المستفيد من توتير العلاقات بين البلدين؟ #أطفالنا_ليسوا_إرهابا— Maher Chawich  (@ChawichMaher) October 26, 2026Jordan strikes not new developmentDespite presenting the Jordanian strikes as a new development, Amman has repeatedly struck southern Syria, alleging in May that it had targeted weapons depots and drug manufacturing facilities in the Druze-majority Syrian province of Sweida.@DiplomaticQatar, an account just short of 120,000 followers, also shared the claim that Israeli misinformation had been behind Jordan's attack.“Every incident that occurred from the Jordanian military airstrike on the Syrian border of Daraa and the killing of women and children... is in favor of Israel,” he wrote in a post that has been viewed over 10,000 times. “I wonder who provided the false intelligence information about this location. Is it Israeli intelligence information that wants to strike the Jordanian-Syrian relations?”كل ماحدث من هجوم الطيران العسكري الأردني على حدود درعا السورية ومقتل نساء واطفال . هو لصالح اسرائيل . ياترى من ادلى بالمعلومات الاستخباراتية الخاطئة بهذا المكان هل هي معلومة استخباراتية اسرائيلية تريد ضرب العلاقات الاردنية السورية .—  دبلوماسي قطري قديم (@Diplomaticqatar) October 27, 2026Ahmad Alhmidan, a Qatar-based media producer and founder of the Ghiras digital youth initiative, claimed both that Amman's attacks had been the result of misinformation and that the terror attack in Jordan was “carried out by an entity linked to [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu and to Israeli agents inside Jordan, with an Arab state behind the operation, while Iran was directly involved as the principal contractor.”“Netanyahu wants to sabotage the trilateral security framework, which focuses on restoring the Syrian state's control over Sweida, returning Syrian territory, and preventing the Great Storm Project.”“Any successful Jordanian-Syrian understanding in the south narrows the space in which Israel can operate under the pretexts of protecting the Druze, securing the border, or preventing threats. Any confrontation between Damascus and Amman therefore serves to weaken this framework before it is completed,” he wrote. “Iran's interests run parallel to this: igniting southern Syria, obstructing any stable security arrangements, and recreating the chaos that allows it to remain an indispensable player. At the same time, this incident serves Netanyahu's interests, creating an overlap between the two sides' interests even if they do not have a direct alliance. Iran benefits by diverting the threat of war away from itself and shifting tensions to another arena, while Netanyahu benefits from disrupting arrangements that restrict Israel's room for maneuver in southern Syria.”لا ينبغي قراءة حادثة كنيسة حمود في الكرك، ثم القصف الأردني على جنوب سوريا، كحادثتين منفصلتين؛ فالمشهد كله يبدو كأنه سلسلة واحدة صُممت لتبدأ بحدث أمني داخل الأردن، ثم تنتهي بدفع الأردن إلى رد عسكري مبني على معلومات استخباراتية غير صحيحة، والغاية النهائية هي فتح شرخ بين الأردن وسوريا. حادثة الكرك، بحسب هذه المعطيات، لا علاقة لتنظيم داعش بها، وإنما نفذتها جهة مرتبطة بنتنياهو ومرتبطة بعملاء لإسرائيل داخل الأردن، مع وجود دولة عربية خلف العملية، بينما كان المتعهد الرئيسي إيران بصورة مباشرة. وهذا يعني أن العملية لم تكن غايتها مجرد إحداث ضرر أمني داخل الأردن، وإنما صناعة حدث يمكن البناء عليه سياسيًا وعسكريًا في المرحلة التالية. المرحلة التالية كانت القصف الأردني. ووفق هذه المعلومات، الأردن لم يتحرك بناءً على تقدير صحيح للمشهد، وإنما جرى تضليله بمعلومات استخباراتية خاطئة جعلته يضرب أهدافًا داخل سوريا، ليجد نفسه بعد ذلك أمام أزمة مع دمشق وسقوط ضحايا مدنيين. أي إن الهدف لم يكن أن يضرب الأردن سوريا لمجرد الضرب، بل أن يُدفع الأردن إلى فعل يمكن بعده إشعال الشارع السوري ضده، وإشعال الشارع الأردني ضد سوريا، وتحويل العلاقة بين بلدين يفترض أنهما يتحركان في مسار أمني متقارب إلى حالة من الشك والخصومة. وهنا تظهر المصلحة الإسرائيلية بصورة أوضح. نتنياهو يريد إفشال الخارطة الأمنية الثلاثية التي تركز على استعادة الدولة السورية للسويداء، وإعادة الأراضي السورية، ومنع "سوفا 53". وكل تفاهم أردني-سوري ناجح في الجنوب يضيّق المساحة التي تستطيع إسرائيل التحرك فيها تحت عناوين حماية الدروز أو ضبط الحدود أو منع التهديدات. لذلك فإن أي صدام بين دمشق وعمّان يخدم إضعاف هذه الخارطة قبل أن تكتمل. أما إيران، فمصلحتها تسير في اتجاه موازٍ: إشعال الجنوب السوري، تعطيل أي تفاهمات أمنية مستقرة، وإعادة خلق الفوضى التي تسمح لها بالبقاء لاعبًا لا يمكن تجاوزه. وفي الوقت نفسه، فإن هذه الحادثة تخدم نتنياهو، وهذا يخلق بين الطرفين تقاطع مصالح حتى لو لم يكن بينهما تحالف مباشر؛ فإيران تستفيد من إبعاد شبح الحرب عنها عبر نقل التوتر إلى ساحة أخرى، ونتنياهو يستفيد من تعطيل الترتيبات التي تضيق المجال الإسرائيلي في الجنوب السوري. لهذا فإن أخطر ما يمكن أن يحدث الآن هو أن يقع الأردن وسوريا في الفخ مرة ثانية بعد أن وقع الأردن في المرة الأولى بسبب المعلومات الاستخباراتية الخاطئة. المطلوب من الأردن أن يخرج بخطاب رسمي واضح يعترف بخطأ القصف ويعتذر عنه، لأن الاعتذار هنا لا يضعف الدولة، بل يسحب أهم ورقة من يد من يريد تحويل الحادثة إلى خصومة شعبية وسياسية طويلة. والمطلوب من الجانب السوري في المقابل أن يتعامل مع الحادثة باعتبارها ملفًا بين دولتين حليفتين، وأن يتجنب التصعيد الذي يحول الخطأ إلى قطيعة. لأن من خطط للحادثة لا يريد مجرد قتلى في الكرك أو ضحايا في درعا؛ هو يريد نتيجة أبعد: أن يصبح الأردني خصم السوري، والسوري خصم الأردني، وأن تنهار الخارطة الأمنية التي بدأ الطرفان ببنائها أصلًا لمواجهة الفوضى في الجنوب. ولهذا فإن النجاح الحقيقي الآن ليس في الرد الأسرع، بل في منع الخصم من الحصول على النتيجة التي صنع الحادثة من أجلها. إذا كان المقصود توريط الأردن وسوريا في صراع، فإن إفشال العملية يبدأ من هنا: الاعتراف بالخطأ، حفظ حقوق الضحايا، التحقيق في مصدر المعلومات الاستخباراتية، ثم إغلاق الباب نهائيًا أمام تحويل حادثة أمنية إلى صراع بين دولتين وشعبين. لا تقعوا في الفخ مرتين.— Ahmad Alhmidan أحمد الحميدان (@afalhmidan) October 27, 2026Anonymous accounts, with substantially fewer followers than @DiplomaticQatar, have pushed that the attack in Karak was a “false flag” operation and that the attack on Syria had been a Jordanian gift to Israel, allowing Jerusalem to validate “its occupation of southern Syria and getting Syrians and Jordanians to fight each other.”Israel carries out a false flag terrorist attack on a church in Jordan. The Jordanian king's response? Bomb Syrian children and call them terrorists. Gifting Israel by validating its occupation of southern Syria and getting Syrians and Jordanians to fight each other— Moey  (@MoeyNotBlake) October 27, 2026

title: Eisenkot is hoping to beat Netanyahu, but what does the Yashar leader stand for? - explainer
body: Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot hopes to beat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and his bloc of political allies to get the first chance to form the next government.However, due to the size of the Israeli-Arab parties, which are not specifically affiliated with a bloc, Eisenkot is not expected to be able to easily form the next government even if he wins more votes than the Netanyahu right-wing bloc.Instead, he is expected to need to undertake complex negotiations with his coalition partners, especially Yisrael Beytenu's Avigdor Liberman, to convince them to form some kind of government or minority-voting bloc arrangement with the Israeli-Arab parties.Eisenkot's campaign on Tuesday started early in the morning at Ofakim and Nir Oz in the Gaza Strip corridor, calling attention to the failures of the past government in preventing Hamas's October 7 invasion.He then traveled further north to Ashdod, with other stops along the way, before voting in Herzliya at 1:45 p.m. and eventually reaching his election-night headquarters at the National Sports Complex in Tel Aviv.The former IDF chief also went with his wife, Hana, to visit the grave of his son, Gal Eisenkot, who died in Gaza in late 2023.Already by late morning, Yashar had filed complaints with the Israeli Election Commission complaining of alleged systematic vandalism and destruction of ballots carrying the party's name at various voting sites.Eisenkot's largest support comes from voters who blame Netanyahu for October 7 or who blame him and his bloc for failing to draft the haredi sector into the IDF even after over 1,000 Israeli soldiers died in recent years.What are his views on other issues?Iran: Eisenkot less willing to take risk in attackingThere are few major differences between Netanyahu and Eisenkot here, though some nuances remain. Both would oppose a "bad deal" if US President Donald Trump's administration opts for one.In that sense, the main difference is how they would address such a bad deal.Unlike Netanyahu, Eisenkot would likely keep his opposition private in order to try to improve the deal quietly, while viewing American public opinion as something he has less control over.Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot would be ready to attack Iran in some circumstances, but most would agree that, at this stage, Netanyahu would be willing to take on more risk and might interpret the point of no return as earlier than Eisenkot.Gaza: Eisenkot has no real plan except Trump'sNeither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a real plan for Gaza. Both have promised to eliminate Hamas's control of the Strip, Eisenkot within 18 months, and Netanyahu by the end of Trump's term, but neither has a clear path for doing so.Eisenkot has no clear plan of his own, but unlike Netanyahu, is willing to push forward with Trump's ceasefire plan without significant resistance, including empowering Palestinian Authority-linked technocratic leaders and police, and international peacekeepers in Gaza.He would likely be ready to allow partial rebuilding for partial Hamas disarming, if for no other reason than to pause and maybe even push back the diplomatic tsunami which is already threatening Israeli national security and economic stability.These differences could have implications over the next year and years, but Eisenkot has made it clear he will not move toward a Palestinian state, certainly not in any first term.West Bank: Eisenkot harsher on Jewish extremism, settlement expansionIf there are strong commonalities between Netanyahu and Eisenkot on Iran and Gaza and the differences are more in the nuances, they are night and day on the West Bank.The only thing they both have in common is a strong commitment to fight Palestinian terror as the number one issue.But on fighting Jewish extremism and on expansion of the Israeli settlements, the number two and three issues, they are far apart.Eisenkot would immediately reinstitute administrative detention of Jewish extremists, which Defense Minister Israel Katz suspended in January 2025, and which Netanyahu has allowed to remain suspended for nearly two years despite losing control of Jewish extremists.In addition, Eisenkot will clean house at the police, injecting officers who will come down hard on the Jewish extremists.He will likely also fire Shin Bet Director David Zini and replace him with a new chief who will crack down more on Jewish extremists.Regarding the over 100 new "farms" which Netanyahu's government expanded under Bezalel Smotrich's authority within the defense ministry, Eisenkot will likely clear most or all of them.He will certainly freeze new settlement building or limit it to the "natural" expansion of existing settlements.Collectively, these actions would help pause or even roll back the diplomatic tsunami which has started to engulf Israel's national security and economic stability.However, Eisenkot has no vision for how to resolve the standoff with the West Bank Palestinians, which has lasted since 1967. Once again, he opposes a two-state solution in the near and medium term.Lebanon: Netanyahu, Eisenkot alignedThere seem to be no major differences between Eisenkot and Netanyahu on Lebanon.Both would maintain a security zone. Both are open to partial withdrawals in exchange for the Lebanese army partially clearing Hezbollah from the security zone, and neither trusts that the Lebanese army will do its job sufficiently.Under light pressure from Trump (heavier pressure will be on Gaza and likely the West Bank), might Eisenkot agree to partial withdrawals faster than Netanyahu? Maybe.But Eisenkot has said he would draw a line at eight kilometers so that Hezbollah cannot fire anti-tank missiles into Israel.The only major nuanced difference might be that Eisenkot will try to return France to a productive role, hoping to score some diplomatic points with them on other fronts, whereas Netanyahu now relishes public conflicts with Paris.At the headquarters of Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, the energy begins to build ahead of the polls closing at 10 p.m. Israel time. (Credit: Yonah Jeremy Bob)Syria: Eisenkot to keep security zone, has trouble trusting al-SharaaNetanyahu and Eisenkot also likely differ little on Syria.Once again, both want to keep a security zone, and both have dropped hints at times that they might agree to partial withdrawals, but both have strong doubts about trusting Syrian leader Ahmad al-Sharaa because of his al-Qaeda past.Diplomatic relations: Eisenkot to improve European tiesEisenkot would heavily improve relations with Europe.He might reach some new understandings with Middle Eastern countries who once liked, but now loathe, Netanyahu.All of those diplomatic wins could help on various national security and economic stability issues.But the most crucial prize is the US.Despite Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu, if Eisenkot wins and is more compliant with some of Washington's demands in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, and Syria, they will likely figure out how to get along.More importantly, Eisenkot will not give up on the Democratic party, which has turned more against Israel than in any time in decades.He will try to hit "restart" post-Netanyahu.The bad news is that he has no clear plan for doing this, and the gulf between Israeli and American expectations about the Middle East really is large, even if Netanyahu exists stage left.   Whether Eisenkot could bridge that gulf would be one of the key challenges and uncertainties of his premiership.

title: Iran threatens 'legal action' against South Korean shipping company in Strait of Hormuz
body: Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a body set up by Tehran to manage passage requests in the Strait of Hormuz, said on Tuesday that all vessels belonging to South Korean shipping company Sinokor would face "legal action" starting on November 1.Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the strategic waterway by attacking shipping there since ​US and Israeli ⁠airstrikes on Iran on February 28.It has restricted transit to gain leverage over Washington while disrupting oil flows from Arab Gulf producers, especially to customers in Asia.The authority said on X/Twitter that Sinokor vessels had committed the most crossing violations in the strait over the past three months, and that it had taken "appropriate actions" against at least seven of them.Sinokor did not immediately comment on the authority's statement.Ships owned by Sinokor were previously included on a list issued by Iran in August of 45 tankers that it said had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz.US imposes naval blockade against Iran-linked shipsIn response to Iranian attacks, the United States also imposed a naval blockade ​against ships linked to the Islamic Republic in the strait.While the blockade has all but choked off Iranian exports, Gulf producers have adapted to attacks on shipping by relying on so-called dark transits, switching off tankers' tracking systems to evade detection, to protect the oil flows that underpin their economies.

title: 'Don't feel like waiting': Voters complain of long lines at polling stations amid historic turnout
body: Voters are facing long waits at polling stations, including in small communities along the Gaza border."Well, I don't feel like waiting. I'll come back in the evening," said A., who waited 45 minutes before leaving the polling station."One at a time," a security guard at a polling station in Ofakim told a group that appeared to be members of the same family."Dad, can I come with you?" asked a girl of about eight as she stood in line."No," her father replied. "You have to go into the voting booth alone."Election Day has drawn tens of thousands of people to polling stations, shopping centers, and entertainment centers.At the new shopping center in Ofakim, home to the Rachela restaurant that made headlines after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his entourage visited, every business is open and packed with customers.The supermarket, part of a major chain, is bustling, as are the electrical appliance store, the nuts and sweets shop and the baby products store. Residents are making the most of Election Day, both to cast their ballots for the Knesset and to shop for groceries, electrical appliances and baby cribs.The corner café, which also operates a bakery, is packed with customers. The usually short line at the cashier stretches as shoppers clutch bags filled with baked goods, cakes, yeast pastries and colorful cookies.Around midday, a family with three children enters the café. Their political allegiance is immediately apparent: The children's shirts feature a ballot slip bearing their preferred party's letters.At a small table in the outdoor seating area, another family sits close together as the father explains the meaning of democracy to his daughter.Political discussions can be heard at almost every table, with conversations covering a range of topics, including the conduct of outgoing ministers and Knesset members."I'm waiting for a call to drive someone to a polling station," said one of those seated at a table."Are rides to polling stations still a thing?" someone asked."Apparently so," the driver replied.Bribing others to vote for certain partiesMeanwhile, updates about events in communities across the region are circulating through every available channel, including WhatsApp, text messages, email and social media.One woman shared an unusual account from Yeruham, along with a phone number. When contacted, the woman on the other end of the line spoke with an accent suggesting she was originally from one of the former Soviet republics."Before we went into the polling station, I was offered 500 shekels to vote for a certain party. Of course I didn't agree."Near a polling station next to a high school, a woman with a megaphone makes a final effort to convince passersby to vote for her preferred party.In her view, it is the only party worth supporting. She considers the others to be people who understand nothing and undermine efforts to manage affairs properly.The polling station itself, in the meantime, is packed with voters.

title: Iran security chief meets Supreme Leader Khamenei after talks with Mecca pact countries
body: Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei on Tuesday met Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since succeeding his slain father in March, a day after holding talks with representatives of Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan.State media said Khamenei had stressed the importance of pursuing Iran's interests and maintaining its conditions for ending the war.Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan visited Tehran on Monday hoping to help de-escalate the Middle East conflict, begun when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.The talks were the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations - which signed the Mecca mutual defense pact in August - since the war pulled Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement into direct conflict.Iran's state media said on Tuesday that "safeguarding national and regional security by maintaining control over the Strait of Hormuz and strengthening bilateral relations with neighboring countries" were among the topics Khamenei and Rezaei had discussed.Iran did not engage in discussion of nuclear programAn Iranian official told Reuters on Monday that there would be no discussion of Iran's nuclear program at Monday's meeting with the Mecca pact countries, and the issue would not be addressed until Tehran's demands for ending the war were met.Iran rejects Western concerns that the program is military in nature.Iran's conditions include an end to a US blockade of Iranian ports and US sanctions on Iranian oil exports. US Vice President JD Vance said three weeks ago that Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment to end the war.

title: Israeli forces likely to withdraw from Hebron after Election Day, officers assess
body: According to assessments by officers in the IDF Central Command, Israeli forces will withdraw from Hebron after the elections because the operation has run its course and is generating tensions that serve as "fuel" for incitement and copycat terrorist attacks.The officers explained that military activity over the past 24 hours has been pointless and is undermining the legitimacy of IDF operations in the area, particularly given the failure to locate weapons or terrorists in the neighborhood.As previously reported, Walla revealed on Monday that a disagreement had emerged between IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth, and 98th Division commander Brig.-Gen. Meni Liberty on one side, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz on the other, over whether to continue the operation in Hebron.As part of the operation, IDF forces evacuated hundreds of Palestinian families from the neighborhood where the terrorists responsible for Friday's deadly attack at a temporary IDF checkpoint in Hebron had originated.In addition, IDF forces took control of buildings and searched hundreds of structures but failed to locate weapons, military equipment, ammunition, explosives laboratories, or weapons manufacturing facilities.Senior IDF officials call for withdrawal from HebronConsequently, senior IDF officials insisted on withdrawing from the neighborhood, arguing that the operation had achieved all it could. However, the prime minister and defense minister insisted that IDF forces remain in place.Security officials explained on Tuesday morning that Operation "Roar of Judah" in Hebron represents "the difference between strategic security thinking and routine security thinking, even when the latter is carried out professionally and effectively by the IDF."The officials said a similar dispute had arisen before the takeover of the refugee camps in Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nur Shams, between Defense Minister Israel Katz, representing the political leadership, and senior IDF commanders.Ultimately, the various operations went ahead, involving the evacuation of Palestinian residents, the takeover of the camps, the elimination of terrorists and seizure of weapons, extensive destruction of physical infrastructure, including homes, and the widening of roads through narrow streets.Security officials say IDF presence prevents PA from gaining footholdSecurity officials further argued in favor of the continued IDF presence in the camps, preventing residents from returning, and denying the Palestinian Authority a foothold in the camps, maintaining that the PA is neither willing nor capable of combating Palestinian terrorism.The investigation has also revealed that a substantial Hamas network operating in Hebron was uncovered during the operation and is run by local operatives. Authorities are also examining whether the network received instructions from abroad, including from Hamas operatives in Turkey.According to security officials, the decision to evacuate residents from hundreds of buildings is unprecedented. However, they argued that the small quantity of weapons discovered so far indicates that the operation has not yet exhausted its potential.

title: Arab voting may be deliberately disrupted by 'unusual delays,' Israeli civil rights watchdog warns
body: Voting may be deliberately obstructed in polling stations across Arab sector towns, the Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) warned on Tuesday, urgently appealing to Central Elections Committee (CEC) Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg to dispatch inspectors to polling stations following reports of significant and unexplained delays in the voting process.According to reports received by ACRI, voters were being processed unusually slowly, with long queues forming at numerous polling stations. The association expressed concern that the delays may not be accidental and could undermine Israeli Arab citizens' ability to exercise their right to vote in Tuesday's election.Reports came from numerous localities, including Rahat, Tel Sheva, Laqiya, Segev Shalom, Abu Tulul, Umm Batin, Iksal, Jaljulya, Kafr Kara, Jisr e-Zarka, Kafr Manda, Ar'ara BaNegev, Tamra, Kafr Kanna, Tira, and Daburiya.Ra'am said that police, coordinating with Otzma Yehudit representatives, had been preventing voters from entering polling stationsRa'am says Israeli police coordinating with Otzma Yehudit representatives, prevent voters entering polling stationsRa'am released footage it said showed police officers coordinating and cooperating with representatives of the Otzma Yehudit party at a polling station in the Bedouin town of Hura in the Negev.According to the party, the Right had been conducting a systematic campaign against Ra'am, fearing that it could secure eight Knesset seats, a result it said could enable the formation of an alternative coalition of 61 MKs and bring down the Right.Ra'am added that police had taken control of polling stations in Ar'ara BaNegev following a power outage at the site and were preventing voters from entering.Israeli officers reportedly delay Arab voting in Segev ShalomOne incident was reported at Segev Shalom High School, where large numbers of police officers and Border Police's National Guard personnel were reportedly preventing voters from entering the polling station compound, citing the need to manage overcrowding.However, according to the report, only a small number of voters were inside the compound, while approximately 200 people had been waiting outside the school for an extended period as officers blocked their entry.ACRI warned that without immediate intervention, the delays could prevent large numbers of Arab voters from exercising their right to vote.The Adalah Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel also issued an appeal to the CEC on Tuesday, demanding that Arabic-language ballot slips be urgently delivered to polling stations following reports of a lack of Arab-language ballot slips at various polling stations.Segev Shalom and Ar'ara BaNegev residents arrested for briberyOn Monday, the eve of Election Day, three Bedouin residents from the Segev Shalom and Ar'ara BaNegev communities were arrested for allegedly attempting to bribe voters to choose Ra'am.The case was transferred to Lahav 433 on Tuesday.“Three suspects were arrested in possession of envelopes containing cash, along with ballots for [Ra'am party leader] Mansour Abbas,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said, calling for a formal investigation into the incident.Suspects transferred to Southern District Fraud Unit ahead of court hearingThe suspects were transferred to the Southern District's Fraud Unit for questioning and are expected to be brought before a court today.Reportedly, the suspects were detained just hours before the polls opened. Israel Police said it had seized, from their homes, envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash, notes, and additional items likely connected to the investigation.In response, Ra'am said in a statement, “We categorically reject attempts by elements within the police to link Ra'am to the compromising of electoral integrity.”

title: Sheikh Abdullah discusses regional developments with Australian and Latvian foreign ministers
body: Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, discussed regional developments with the foreign ministers of Australia and Latvia. title: India capitalizes on Europe’s growing demand for ammunition
body: NEW DELHI — India’s defense exports to Europe have surged, driven largely by demand for ammunition and artillery shells as European countries ramp up military spending amid Russia’s war in Ukraine. The rising exports could pave the way for deeper industrial cooperation between the two sides. Indian Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said that demand linked to the European Union’s “ReArm Europe” initiative, combined with India’s expanding defense manufacturing base, is boosting exports. He spoke Oct 23. at an event in New Delhi. Singh cited a Bloomberg report that found a sharp increase in India’s exports of ammunition and related products to Europe. India exported at least $872 million worth of ammunition in the four years since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, a more than 1,600% increase compared with the preceding four-year period, according to the report , which cited data from Trade Data Monitor. Central and East European countries including Romania, Slovenia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Croatia, and Poland were among the biggest customers. Ammunition exports have risen sharply since 2024 as European countries replenish stocks and strengthen defense capabilities following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, analysts say. The exports include artillery shells, small-caliber ammunition, mortars, propellants and explosives. European destinations accounted for 40% of Indian global exports of arms and ammunition in the last financial year, according to Samuel Rajiv, Research Fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses in New Delhi. He said this surge could translate into a long-term trend. “There will be greater opportunities for India due to Europe’s greater focus on defense, which will result in a lot of money going into the transformation of its defense industrial base,” said Rajiv. “At the same time, Indian exports will gain momentum not just because of Europe’s requirements but the steps India is taking to expand its own defense manufacturing base.” Indian exports could also get a fillip as tariffs on arms and ammunition from India become lower when a free trade agreement concluded between India and the European Union takes effect in the coming year. New Delhi is also seeking a broader role in Europe’s defense market through industrial partnerships. Defense Secretary Singh said India wants to establish joint ventures with European companies in India, while Indian companies would seek partnerships in Europe to gain access to government defense procurement programs. Russia is not an option for Europe, that is over. Dinakar Peri, Carnegie India Analysts say although it remains to be seen whether India and the EU can build more sustained defense industrial ties, partnering with each other is emerging as a viable option for both sides as Europe seeks to diversify its supply chains. “India offers that scale, size and ecosystem as well as trust as Europe tries to build resilience from the United States. Russia is not an option for Europe, that is over. China has its own red flags in many ways in strategic areas and critical domains. So that leaves very few options available,” says Dinakar Peri, Fellow in the Security Studies Program at Carnegie India. At the same time, India has also been working to diversify its defense relationships given its longstanding dependence on foreign suppliers, including the United States. “So a closer partnership with Europe also works for India,” he said. Pointing out that several American, French, and Israeli contractors have already integrated Indian vendors into their supply chains, analysts say the EU can make India its sourcing hub for a range of items. However New Delhi’s longstanding military ties with Russia could raise concerns in some European capitals as India eyes deeper defense partnerships with the EU. “It remains to be seen whether this will become an obstacle to deeper defense industrial ties with the EU,” according to Peri. “Bilaterally, India already has strong defense relationships with countries such as France, but it is unclear how the EU as a bloc will view India’s military ties with Moscow.”

title: Spot gas prices surge twofold — GECF
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. International spot gas prices surged twofold since February due to the drop in liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports in Europe and Asia, Secretary General of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) said.
"LNG imports in major Asian and European markets have declined, spot prices have more than doubled since February, and pressures on storage, power markets, and consumers have intensified," he said.
The inevitable normalization of LNG supplies together with new gas liquefaction facilities can ease pressure on the market, while longer supply disruptions will have broader implications for energy security and economic stability," the secretary general added.

title: Poverty normal globally, not created by Tinubu, says APC spokesperson, Morka
body: By Emmanuel Okogba Spokesperson of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Felix Morka, has defended President Bola Tinubu against criticism over poverty and hunger in Nigeria, arguing that successive administrations have failed to eradicate poverty. Morka made the remarks during a RIGHT OF REPLY on ARISE TV, Tuesday, while responding to questions about whether Tinubu was evading responsibility for the country’s economic challenges by describing poverty as a longstanding problem. “Poverty is something that is, you know, a feature of many societies around the globe. Poverty has been with us for a very long time,” he said. The APC spokesman cited the eight years former President Olusegun Obasanjo and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar spent in office together, arguing that they had also failed to eliminate poverty. “Now, in the historical context, Atiku Abubakar was vice president of the Federal Republic for eight years with the former president Olusegun Obasanjo. Now, between the two of them, they had eight years to eradicate poverty, assuming that poverty was that easy to snap your finger and eradicate. Now, let me quickly say that, you know, they didn’t eradicate poverty,” Morka said. He argued that other administrations had similarly failed to eliminate poverty, adding that the challenge could not be resolved simply by political declarations. “All of the other presidents who have come before them did not eradicate poverty, even if we were to suggest that they had a constitutional obligation to eradicate poverty, they didn’t. They couldn’t eradicate poverty,” he said. Morka maintained that Tinubu was therefore correct to refer to the historical context of poverty in Nigeria, rejecting suggestions that the president was using previous administrations to avoid accountability. “So when this president says poverty has been, and, you know, these individuals in their own term of office could have, you know, completely extinguished poverty, take it out. They didn’t. You know, he was saying something that was completely true and not controversial,” he said. He added that opposition figures, including Atiku, were wrong to criticise the president for referring to the past. “So it is only people who simply want to, you know, evade responsibility, like Atiku Abubakar, who will in fact say, you know, why are you referring to the past? Talk about the present,” Morka said. Defending Tinubu’s position, he added: “Listen, there’s no present without the past. The present is only the present because there’s a past, which this president was referring to. So that is not, you know, evading responsibility.” Morka also accused previous administrations of selling off Nigeria’s assets and leaving millions of citizens in poverty, although he did not provide specific details to substantiate the allegation in the interview excerpt. He argued that Tinubu had not promised to eradicate poverty within a specified period. “The president never told you that in the first month or 100 days of my government, or in the first two years or three years, I’m gonna eradicate poverty.” Morka added. He argued that the constitutional provision allowing a president to seek re-election gave administrations an opportunity to develop and implement policies over two terms. “There’s a reason the constitution gave every elected president the possibility of a re-election. Four years in the first instance, and a possibility, if the citizens, the electorate decide to re-elect that president, to serve another four years. There’s a reason for that,” he said. According to Morka, a president’s first term provides time to understand the country’s challenges, establish priorities and begin implementing policies before seeking another mandate. “It’s because four years, first of all, it’s a period to profile, understand, create your pathfinders to what you’re doing. And then to do that in the second, I mean, people agree with you that you have started,” he said. The post Poverty normal globally, not created by Tinubu, says APC spokesperson, Morka appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: ‘We bear the consequences’: Diaspora Jews fear fallout from Israel’s election - interview
body: As Israelis head to the polls, Diaspora Jews are watching with a stake in an election they cannot vote in, fearing its consequences will follow them home.From Norway to Mexico to the US, several prominent Diaspora Jews told The Jerusalem Post they are “terrified” that the outcome could deepen the conflation of Israel's government with Jews worldwide, leaving them to bear the fallout of decisions they did not make.Robert Hercz, the head of B'nai B'rith Norway, told the Post that he has been closely following the elections and is “terrified: not only for the future of Israel, but also for how the election will affect Jewry worldwide.”“The world - and especially the European countries - are disproportionately [pre]occupied with Israeli politics - and much of what we get served in the media is oversimplified and polarized. And governments and politicians need to feed their Israel-bashing voter bases.”This means that if Netanyahu wins, Hercz continued, “the politicians and the media in our parts of the world will go crazy, which in turn will have extremely negative consequences for us Jews living outside Israel.”Israel-Norway relations will not improve while Netanyahu in officeRegarding Norway, Hercz opined that Israel-Norway relations will not improve as long as Netanyahu is in office.“Not necessarily because of the politics in Israel, but because the Norwegian government and institutions are so over-invested in anti-Netanyahu rhetoric that they will not be able to move over to a different relationship and policy until Netanyahu is no longer in office,” he added.Mark Freedman has spent 43 years working as a Jewish communal professional. He has also served as North American board chair of the Pardes Institute of Jewish Studies, and chairs the board of Amiti, a US-based nonprofit that works primarily in Israel to help CEOs of Israeli NGOs.He told the Post that “The sands have shifted beneath our feet.”“In the past, lay leadership primarily took a neutral role in how it viewed the Israeli government and the elections that created that government.”“I think the main change now is the emergence of an old form of antisemitism that has renewed itself, the one that deems Jews in North America to somehow have collective responsibility for the actions of the Israeli government.”“So that naturally makes one feel that [Diaspora Jews] have more of a stake in the outcome of the elections.”He gave examples of how Israeli domestic politics filters into the Diaspora.“A lot of it plays out in local elections, where you see discussions about Israel that you've never seen before. Local municipalities are now adopting resolutions that are criticizing Israel as racist and genocidal. That would have been unheard of 15, 20 years ago.”“So naturally this filters down to the local level.”Freedman does believe that the outcome of the elections could have an impact on global antisemitism, and that a new government could lead to an “incremental shift” in a positive direction.“If there's a government in Israel that is willing to align itself with what we view as traditional values in terms of law enforcement, in terms of equal participation in society, that would have an impact certainly on American views.”He added that, on a personal level, “it's really heartbreaking,” to see the divisions and issues inside Israel.“There is so much positive about Israel, as a Jewish state and beyond that as a democratic state, and that's at risk right now,” Freedman told the Post.“I think that people in the United States who follow Israeli politics and who care about Israel as a Jewish homeland are just deeply concerned. So tomorrow's election will have a great deal of impact on the way that the perception will be formed going forward.”Netanyahu's international image is 'permanent flashpoint'Arielle Shturman Waiss is a physician from Mexico City and the founder of ConCiencia Project, a science-based sexual and reproductive health education initiative. She leads health programming in the humanitarian aid sector and is active in Jewish communal life in Mexico and the international Jewish world.She told the Post that Netanyahu's international image is a “permanent flashpoint” and that “regardless of context, he ends up embodying everything perceived as wrong with Israeli political leadership.”This perception, by immediate extension, attaches to Jews in the Diaspora, Shturman Waiss added, “because the ability to distinguish between what is Israeli, what is Jewish, and what is legitimate criticism of a government keeps eroding in public debate.”“For those of us living in the Diaspora, the problem is more specific: his electoral victory imposes a presumption of consensus on us. It is assumed that we endorse his actions and his radical style of leadership, and that we do so by choice. Because he reached power through a democratic process, that presumption becomes nearly impossible to dismantle; any nuance we try to introduce reads as an excuse.”“But a citizenry's vote in a complex parliamentary structure is not a mandate over the identity of an entire people,” she stressed.Israel events affect Diaspora Jews more since October 7“Whatever happens in Israel reaches us in Jewish communities worldwide,” Venezuelan national and founder of Tikkun Talks, Deborah Apeloig, told the Post.“That has always been true, but since October 8, 2023, we have seen it and felt it with a different intensity.”Apeloig spoke of October 8 deliberately, as she says this day marked the moment the narrative “began shifting against Israel, even as we were still trying to comprehend the massacre.”She added that, as a Venezuelan Jew working across Latin America, she has felt “how quickly events in Israel become judgments about Jews everywhere.”“Too often, the Israel presented to the world is reduced to black and white. Its complexity, humanity and diversity disappear behind headlines, political statements and social media narratives better known as “TikTok University”. Through Tikkun Talks, I work to reach beyond our echo chamber, build bridges and repair the world, one conversation at a time.”Apeloig told the Post she has received hundreds and thousands of meaningful messages from non-Jewish people whose perspectives have shifted, alongside comments “demonizing Netanyahu or using inflammatory statements by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich to condemn an entire country and Jews collectively.”Echoing the words of Shturman Waiss, she said it can feel like we take one step forward in building bridges, and a “radical politician's words send us 10 steps backward.”“Those politicians are responsible for their words; the people spreading antisemitism are responsible for theirs. But we in the Diaspora live with the consequences of both.”Because of this, she said the elections are of great importance to her, even though she cannot vote.“The decisions belong to Israeli citizens, but their impact reaches far beyond Israel's borders.”“I'm hopeful as I watch Israeli democracy unfold, and I hope the outcome brings leadership that strengthens Israel, helps heal its divisions, and builds a brighter future for the Jewish people worldwide,” she concluded.

title: Abu Dhabi announces Dh872 million project linking Ramhan and Jubail Islands to E12 motorway
body: Abu Dhabi has announced a Dh872 million ($237 million) project that will link Ramhan and Jubail Islands to the Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed (E12) motorway. With seven bridges and three tunnels, the development across 166,000 square metres is expected to be completed in 2027. It includes a network of ramps, roads, and utility corridors to improve road accessibility and capacity and support smoother traffic flow in the area. Eisa Al Mazrouei, director general of Infrastructure Development at the Department of Municipalities and Transport, said the project formed a key part of Abu Dhabi's expanding transportation network. "This sophisticated construction project represents an important part of Abu Dhabi's evolving transportation network, facilitating access to Ramhan and Jubail Islands while unlocking new development zones and economic opportunities," Mr Al Mazrouei said. The DMT announced that advanced works are underway and the project is part of the department’s efforts to enhance mobility links across the capital. It also supports the DMT's broader plan to develop integrated communities and help bolster the emirate's urban and economic growth. The project's design incorporates sustainability through environmentally conscious elements. It will use energy-efficient LED lighting throughout to reduce energy consumption and light pollution, and will recycle approximately 90 per cent of construction waste, equivalent to more than 2,200 tonnes. Ramhan and Jubail islands , off Abu Dhabi's coast, are earmarked for significant residential and commercial development, making improved road connectivity a priority in the emirate's long-term planning. Ramhan Island by Eagle Hills spans 400 hectares, with more than half of it developable. Construction is under way and, when it opens, the island will be home to about 1,800 stand-alone villas, 900 marina residences, a luxury hotel, and a retail promenade. Jubail Island is surrounded by kilometres of protected mangroves, waterways and forested trails, all of which make it “the place to be” for families wanting more than just a place to live. Conceptualised and developed by Lead Development, the 4,000-hectare waterfront master-planned community is redefining what it means to live well at “human speed”. It is surrounded by nature, with space to grow for generations to come, the company says.

title: We’ve had touchscreen laptops for years. Can Apple make them better?
body:
A fridge is about to be merged with a toaster. Dogs and cats are soon to be living together. But it’s not mass hysteria; Apple is expected to finally announce a touchscreen MacBook tomorrow at its “Pro and Tell” event.
A laptop with a touchscreen should be no big deal — we’ve had them for ages. But Apple took a hardline stance against them. In addition to Tim Cook’s infamous 2012 quote equating it to combining kitchen appliances, Steve Jobs emphatically dismissed touchscreen laptops as “ergonomically terrible” back in 2010, saying, “Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical.”
The closest Apple got was the MacBook Pro Touch Bar, from 2016 to 2023, but that horizontal landing strip for your fingers on the keyboard deck mostly amounted to unrealized potential. It sacrificed physical function keys (and for a while, the escape key) in favor of a non-deterministic UI. A touchscreen on a laptop is an established idea we already know can be useful for taking direct action on things around your screen — whether with an occasional tap and flick or through prolonged stylus use.
So how is Apple going to do it exactly? How will the company that puts the word “magic” in some of its product names bring the magic to a touchscreen MacBook?
For starters, rumors indicate this touch-enabled MacBook Pro will have a new OLED display. That sounds great, because OLEDs are awesome for deep blacks and vivid color contrast, though it’s likely to make them even more expensive. They’re rumored to use the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips and come in 14- and 16-inch sizes like their contemporaries. In our current RAMageddon world, the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro currently starts at $2,499. Now add a pricier OLED touch panel to it. Woof.
[Image: The ill-fated Touch Bar is the only bit of touchscreen we’ve gotten on a MacBook thus far. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/7462669/jbareham_161111_1263_0050.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The screen is also speculated to have a Dynamic Island cutout for the webcam instead of a notch. While I don’t love the notch, I’m firmly in the “It’s fine — you stop noticing it when you use it for a while” camp. The Dynamic Island should be a small aesthetic improvement, and if it operates as it does on iPhones, then it could also offer some touch-based multitasking with timers and music apps tucking info into it.
The touchscreen MacBook is also rumored to have a thinner and lighter chassis design. The MacBook Pros got thicker and heavier with the M1 Pro / M1 Max generation after years of chasing thinness — that pursuit brought us worse thermals and the dreaded butterfly keyboards. Frankly, this rumor makes me the most nervous, because I don’t want a MacBook Pro that once again risks performance compromises for the sake of thinness. Not now, not ever again. Can Apple make its high-end MacBooks thinner again without compromising raw performance, battery, or quality of life?
And what will the new MacBook’s touchscreen setup be like? How will you interact with it? Will it remain a conventional clamshell design, or will Apple give its hinge any added flexibility to allow new ways to use it via touch? I recently wrote about how fun I find 2-in-1 convertible laptops like Lenovo’s Yoga line, which has a hinge that folds all the way around and includes a stylus for mounting to the chassis. It’d be great to see Apple showcase something boldly exciting as it “pros and tells,” but I won’t be surprised if the first touchscreen MacBook keeps things safe with a standard clamshell.
[Image: I don’t mind the slight chunkiness of current MacBook Pros, but lightening their load could be nice. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/25718386/247372_MacBook_Pro_M4_ADiBenedetto_0025.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Whether it’s a clamshell or a convertible, will this MacBook work with an Apple Pencil, or will it be touch-only? I hope Apple Pencil support is included, along with magnetic charging like on iPads, since it seems like a no-brainer for designers to use a precision tool for drawing on a touch-friendly Mac. But even if it works with an Apple Pencil, this will still be a Mac through and through — not an iPad. Apple is expected to introduce a revised macOS 27 Golden Gate with touch-friendly enhancements just for this new MacBook, while keeping it a full-blown desktop OS. Since this MacBook is unlikely to replace current models in Apple’s lineup (the MacBook Pros with Pro and Max-level chips were just updated earlier this year), this is likely to be an offshoot of macOS.
MacBook Pros have mostly been about chip bumps and modest feature improvements since the M1 Pro and M1 Max generation revitalized the line in 2021. An OLED touchscreen model represents a major shakeup, and like the iPhone Duo there’s room for messiness or weird new quirks due to Apple design decisions. We’ll learn tomorrow what Apple deems is the “right” way for a touchscreen to work on a Mac.

title: Patriot missile service hub in Poland. Negotiations are reaching the final stage
body:
Prime Minister Donald Tusk has suggested that an announcement regarding the location of a service centre for Patriot system missiles could be made as early as today. Although nothing has been officially confirmed, „much indicates” that Poland has been selected as the location for the centre.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk was most likely referring to the service centre for the PAC-3 family of missiles, used in Patriot systems. The initiative for such a centre was announced at the NATO summit in Ankara, as part of a Letter of Intent between Lockheed Martin and four nations: Poland, Germany, Sweden, and the Netherlands.
NA ŻYWO | Wypowiedź Premiera Donalda Tuska przed posiedzeniem Rady Ministrów https://t.co/xpmuRLjszX
The head of government noted that there is no official communique yet, but there are many indications that positive information from Poland’s perspective will be shared within a few hours.
PAC-3 , currently produced in the modernised PAC-3 MSE version, is an actively radar-guided missile used for defence against the most complex threats (ballistic and cruise missiles, aircraft). PAC-3 MSE constitutes the primary armament for newer configurations of Patriot systems, including the Polish Wisła system. During the war in Ukraine, it has been used to engage Iskander and Kinzhal aero-ballistic missiles, which are considered the greatest threat to critical infrastructure.
Poland was chosen as the country where the service centre for PAC-3 missiles for the Patriot systems will be located, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, the Secretary of State in the Ministry of National Defence, announced.

title: In His Reporting, Japanese Journalist Yuki Imai Revealed a Fascination With Russia. Then He Was Arrested.
body:
In his last dispatch from Russia, the recently arrested Japanese journalist Yuki Imai reflects on the rising number of North Korean laborers in the country’s Far East. On the street, one asks him for a cigarette, while he sees others singing Soviet-era songs at a restaurant and buying jewelry in a shopping mall.
“Japan has no diplomatic relations with North Korea, but here on Sakhalin, I find myself catching glimpses of a people who otherwise remain entirely out of reach,” he writes , referring to the large, far-flung Russian island where he did the bulk of his reporting.
North Korean workers are some of the biggest victims of labor abuses in Russia, to say nothing of the isolated country’s shadowy involvement in the Ukraine war.
While the report makes no mention of those issues, the recollected encounters show how Imai, 34, didn’t shy away from the kinds of politically sensitive topics that have landed other foreign correspondents in trouble with the Russian authorities.
At some point, that reporting may have angered the wrong people.
Two weeks ago, a group of masked men broke into Imai’s hotel room in Sakhalin’s largest city, Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, and wrestled him to the floor. They were Federal Security Service (FSB) agents, arresting Imai on espionage charges likely related to his journalistic work. He is now awaiting trial in Moscow’s notorious Lefortovo Prison, where he faces up to 20 years in prison.
In Japan, his case is enveloped in secrecy. Few who knew Imai — including his employer, the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper — are willing to talk publicly about his background, the kind of journalist he is and what motivated him to report on the ground in a contentious region, despite the mounting risks for foreign correspondents.
But a review of his limited online presence and published articles reveals a picture of someone who was deeply fascinated by Russian culture, had family connections to the Far East and was committed to explaining the complexities of his home country’s relations with Russia.
The Hokkaido Shimbun declined to comment for this story, saying that it was still “gathering information” about the criminal charges against its journalist. In an open letter signed by Editor-in-Chief Takeshi Yamamoto, the newspaper said it was “responding with our highest priority on ensuring our reporter’s safety.”
Foreign correspondents are often criticized for parachuting into unfamiliar territory, firing off a quick report and leaving without ever developing a deeper understanding of their subject. Imai wasn’t that kind of journalist.
An acquaintance of his told the exiled news outlet IStories that Imai first came to Russia in 2014 for Russian language studies at St. Petersburg State University. According to the report, he also took an interest in Russian politics and literature.
It doesn’t appear that interest waned, even after Imai reportedly returned to Japan to continue his studies.
In recent years, Imai channeled his curiosities through journalism. He started reporting for the Hokkaido Shimbun, a daily newspaper located in the capital of Japan’s immense northern island of the same name. Owing to its proximity to both the Russian mainland and the disputed Kuril Islands, the newspaper publishes a robust section focused on Russian affairs, with a particular emphasis on bilateral relations.
The Far East is a geopolitically complicated region. Both Russia and Japan claimed and contested large areas of territory there during the 19th and 20th centuries before World War II largely sealed the matter, handing the Soviets control over most of it.
The enduring disagreement over ownership of the four southernmost Kuril Islands, which are controlled by Russia, has prevented the two countries from formally signing a peace treaty to end World War II.
Imai’s articles interrogated the conflict’s legacy and Japan’s absence from the islands that were once its territory, reporting on everything from the construction of a controversial war monument to the recent demolition of a disused Japanese government-funded medical clinic.
He also covered developments in politics and defense, from Russia’s recent parliamentary elections and relations with North Korea to the rise in military drone production on Sakhalin.
It’s unclear if any of these stories were the reason for Imai’s arrest, but it’s easy to see how officials might have felt his coverage was prodding at delicate topics, even if it wasn’t particularly intrusive.
For Imai, Russia and Japan’s fractured relationship was not merely a subject of professional fascination. He had roots in Russia’s Far East, noting in an article published this summer that his grandfather had lived in the Sakhalin town of Kholmsk — then called Maoka — before World War II, something that drew Imai to the same place a decade ago.
“My grandfather had lived in Maoka before the war,” he wrote, “and I wanted to see the remnants of Japan that remained in the town.”
The “remnants” he referred to are the long-abandoned buildings of a former Japanese paper factory. In the same article, Imai writes about the melancholic experience of walking past this area in August of this year after the factory was demolished. Gazing at the lot where the factory used to stand, he felt “as if a part of the town’s history had been lost.”
Outside of his social media account and articles for the Hokkaido Shimbun, details about Imai’s background are scarce. That may come as a surprise to outsiders who remember the blitz of news coverage surrounding the arrest of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich in Russia on spying accusations in spring 2023.
In Imai’s case, there has so far been no public outcry and no media campaign spearheaded by colleagues or family, as happened with Gershkovich and other foreigners arrested in Russia on dubious charges in recent years.
Aleksandra Bielakowska, the advocacy manager of Reporters Without Borders’ Asia-Pacific Bureau, said this is a common tack the government and families take when a Japanese reporter is arrested overseas.
“Usually how it works in Japan is that the Japanese government takes the lead, and they very rarely allow anyone else to intervene with any type of engagement,” Bielakowska said. “They will be very strict about not sharing any information or insight into what’s going on.”
In the past, that’s extended to even naming the individual, she added. The only reason the Japanese public knows Imai’s name in this case is because it was released by the Russian side. Publicly, Japanese officials have still not acknowledged that he was the person arrested.
In a statement to The Moscow Times last week that did not name Imai as the detained individual, Japan’s Foreign Affairs Ministry called on the Russian government to release the journalist and treat him in a “humane, fair and impartial manner.” On Tuesday, the Hokkaido Shimbun announced that officials from the Japanese embassy had finally met with Imai after nearly two weeks of no contact.
Part of the reason for this secrecy comes down to deeply rooted cultural norms.
“It’s just sort of the Japanese way of doing everything. They always prefer to avoid any sort of loud confrontation. They always prefer to deal with things behind the scenes,” said James D.J. Brown, a professor of international relations at Temple University, Japan Campus.
But that quiet approach could backfire by encouraging Russia to target others, Brown argued.
“This poor guy is being locked up, and most of the population doesn’t know his name. I also feel that if you don’t publicize it, there’s more risk of other people falling into the same danger,” he told The Moscow Times.
The biggest unanswered question is what Russia wants from Japan. Japan doesn’t hold any Russian prisoners that the Kremlin would like to see returned home. Still, Brown speculated that Imai could end up as part of a multinational prisoner swap, similar to the 26-person exchange in 2024 that freed Gershkovich.
However, Brown thinks Russia may care less about a prisoner swap and more about punishing Japan over larger policy issues.
Authorities in Tokyo have made a series of recent decisions that have unsettled the Kremlin about security in the Far East, including hosting American Typhon intermediate-range missiles.
Japan has also helped pay for weapons for Ukraine through a NATO initiative, while Japanese companies, like the drone manufacturer Terra Drone, have started doing business with the Ukrainian military.
“I think that, for all of that, Russia has decided that they want to apply pressure on Japan,” Brown said. “And frankly they regard Japan as likely to concede, so they feel they probably have a good chance of forcing some concessions.”
“It’s almost certain they will,” he said, referring to Japan giving in to at least some of Russia’s demands, whatever those may end up being. “That also explains the low-key approach. They want to perhaps have the freedom away from the public eye to cut a deal.”

These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.

title: Meta, Google, Microsoft to support INEC in tackling false claims ahead of 2027 elections
body:
Big Tech companies, including Meta, Google and Microsoft, have promised to support Nigeria’s electoral commission, INEC , to tackle false information and AI-generated manipulations during the 2027 general elections.
Speaking at different fora in recent weeks, the companies said they are working with INEC and other stakeholders to promote reliable electoral information and address the risks posed by AI-generated images, videos and other misleading content.
Nigeria’s 2027 election is scheduled to begin on 16 January 2027 with the presidential and National Assembly elections, while the governorship and state Houses of Assembly elections are on 6 February 2027.
The electoral commission has expressed concern over the rise of AI-generated contents, particularly during the elections, but maintained that AI won’t determine the outcome of the elections.
Microsoft said their generative AI tools from creating unrealistic images of political candidates ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general election.
Speaking at the AI and Democracy Forum (AIDF) in Abuja, Microsoft’s Senior Director of Global Elections, Dave Liechtman, said the company would load INEC’s final list of candidates into its system to prevent generative AI from creating unrealistic images of the candidates.
Mr Liechtman said the initiative was part of the companies’ commitment to preventing the unauthorised use of candidates’ likenesses on their platforms.
“I offered to INEC at their offices this week that, – I think you just finalised the candidate list this weekend – we’re going to load that candidates’ list into our system to make sure that generative AI cannot be used to generate unrealistic images of candidates,” he had said.
Google has also opened SynthID Detector, its artificial intelligence watermark-detection platform, to the public as concerns grow about manipulated images, videos and audio ahead of the general elections.
SynthID Detector allows users to upload media files and check whether they contain invisible watermarks placed by supported AI-generation systems.
It can currently identify SynthID watermarks in content created using tools operated by Google and participating companies, including OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao.
Google said the platform was designed for everyday users, including journalists, fact-checkers and members of the public who need additional information when examining suspicious online content.
Speaking at the launch of #AI4Elections Hackathon organised by Rise Networks, in collaboration with INEC, Meta’s head of public policy for Anglophone West Africa, Sade Dada, said the mother company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp would work with INEC to promote trustworthy election information and tackle false claims, including fabricated images and videos generated using artificial intelligence.
The Artifical Intelligence Hackathon was launched to develop technology solutions to electoral challenges ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections. It will bring together Nigerian developers, researchers, university students, electoral experts, and civil society organisations to develop practical, responsible AI tools to support electoral processes.
The initiative also have the International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR), the Centre for Information Technology and Development (CITAD), the International Press Centre and other civil society and academic institutions as partners.
Ms Dada highlighted Meta’s “Remove, Reduce and Inform” approach to content moderation, which involves removing content that violates its policies, reducing the distribution of certain harmful content and providing people with information to help them assess what they see online.
She also cited GovGuide Nigeria, an AI-powered chatbot that provides government information in English, Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba, as an example of how AI can be used to improve public access to information.
Ms Dada stressed that AI tools used during elections must remain politically neutral and subject to human oversight.
She said Nigeria’s experience with trustworthy election information could provide lessons for other countries, noting that the credibility of the 2027 elections would have implications beyond the country.

title: South Korean Burger Chain Mom’s Touch to Open 50 Outlets in Kazakhstan
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – South Korean burger chain Mom’s Touch plans to open at least 50 outlets in Kazakhstan over the next decade as it expands into Central Asia through a franchise agreement with local food group Shin-Line, The Korea Herald reported Oct. 26. An aerial view of Shin-Line Group’s headquarters and production facility in Kazakhstan (Mom’s Touch). Photo credit: The Korean Herald The first outlet is expected to open in the first half of 2027. The agreement also covers the Kyrgyz Republic, while the company plans to expand into major Kazakh cities, including Astana. “We are preparing to open our first store in the first half of next year and develop Kazakhstan into a key base for our Central Asian operations,” a Mom’s Touch official said in a comment to The Korean Herald. Mom’s Touch plans to introduce its signature chicken burgers made with whole chicken-thigh fillets, along with fried chicken and pizza. Its local partner, Shin-Line Group, has a cold-chain logistics network serving about 10 countries and operates more than 70 outlets of a South Korean convenience store chain, mainly in Almaty. The expansion follows Mom’s Touch’s entry into Uzbekistan in 2025. Founded in South Korea in 2004, Mom’s Touch built its brand around chicken burgers made with whole chicken-thigh fillets rather than ground meat. Its signature Thigh Burger has helped establish the chain as a major domestic competitor to international fast-food brands.
