title: Parties sidestep app ban inside polling stations, asking voters outside to identify themselves
body: Parties barred from using voter-tracking apps inside polling stations found other ways on Tuesday to track which of their supporters turned out to vote.Under this election's rules, parties may not use voter-management apps such as Elector inside polling stations. The restriction aims to stop party systems from collecting voter information inside polling stations and to protect voters' privacy and the integrity of the vote.Parties, including Likud and United Torah Judaism, have apparently found a workaround. Representatives and activists stationed outside polling stations are reportedly asking voters to identify themselves, then logging in to party systems to record that those voters have cast their ballots. Voters can choose to do this freely, within the limits of the law.WhatsApp allegedly being used to track voteWhatsApp is also allegedly being used to track the vote. When contacted, Likud's Elector operation said its system was working normally and that it was encouraging supporters of the “national camp,” as the right-wing bloc calls itself, to vote.The instructions sent over WhatsApp were detailed: open the app, go to the “Contacts” tab and mark supporters. A follow-up message asked recipients to use the app to message all their supporters.So while the app has been kept out of polling stations, parties are still running a digital operation just outside them, updating voter information, reaching supporters, and managing their Election Day effort.

title: Tinubu directs security agencies to arrest killers of Sheikh Yahaya Masussuka
body: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA — PRESIDENT Bola Tinubu has directed the Nigeria Police and other relevant security agencies to move swiftly and ensure that those behind the murder of prominent Islamic preacher Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka and his friend, Adamu Abubakar, in Dutsin-Ma, Katsina State, are apprehended and brought to justice. President Tinubu also condemned the dastardly act, describing it as heinous and an assault on the values of peace and the sanctity of human life. The gunmen killed the two men in a drive-by shooting on Monday evening. A statement by the presidential spokesman, Bayo Onanuga, said: “The President, who was deeply saddened by the news of the killing, described the act as heinous and an assault on the values of peace and the sanctity of human life.” He extended his heartfelt condolences to the families of the deceased, their followers, and the government and people of Katsina State over the tragic loss. According to the statement: “The President has directed the Nigeria Police Force and other relevant security agencies to move swiftly, intensify efforts already underway by the Katsina State Police Command, and ensure the perpetrators are tracked down, apprehended, and brought to justice. “President Tinubu prays for the repose of the souls of the departed and for comfort for all those who mourn their deaths.” The post Tinubu directs security agencies to arrest killers of Sheikh Yahaya Masussuka appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: General Rezaei meets with Yemeni ambassador in Tehran
body:

In the meeting, the latest situation on the conflict fronts in Yemen was reviewed by General Rezaei and the ambassdor.

title: Apple Pay and Google Pay Begin Rollout in Uzbekistan
body: Apple Pay and Google Pay began rolling out in Uzbekistan on October 27, allowing customers of local banks to add eligible Visa and Mastercard cards to their digital wallets to make contactless payments. The launch marks another step in Uzbekistan’s efforts to integrate its banking system with international payment services, following changes to the country’s data protection laws and months of negotiations with Apple and Google. Which Banks and Cards Are Supported? According to Spot , Apple Wallet initially supports cards from eight banks and financial institutions: Uzum Bank, Orient Finans Bank, the National Bank of Uzbekistan, Kapitalbank, Hamkorbank, Ipak Yuli Bank, TBC Bank, and Octobank. Uzum Bank and Hamkorbank currently support Visa cards only, while the other six institutions are listed as supporting both Visa and Mastercard. Google Wallet, meanwhile, lists nine participating banks , including seven of those supporting Apple Pay, alongside AVO Bank and Aloqabank. Customers can add eligible cards through Apple Wallet or Google Wallet, with payments authorized using their phone’s security features. Once activated, the services allow customers to pay at compatible contactless terminals without using a physical bank card. However, the rollout is still in its early stages. Some banks are continuing to test Apple Pay, and not all eligible cards can yet be added successfully. As of October 27, Uzbekistan was also absent from Apple’s published list of countries where Apple Pay is supported. Google Pay’s launch was announced on October 19 by Marcin Krasuski, Google Cloud’s director of government affairs and public policy for Central and Eastern Europe, during an event in Samarkand. Support for locally issued bank cards became available on October 27. Changes to Data Protection Laws The rollout follows changes to Uzbekistan’s personal data legislation in March 2026, which relaxed restrictions on storing certain types of personal data outside the country. The previous rules had been an obstacle to the introduction of international digital payment services. As The Times of Central Asia reported in July, the Central Bank subsequently began negotiations with Apple and Google, while commercial banks and the national payment systems Humo and Uzcard worked on the technical requirements. For now, support is limited to eligible Visa and Mastercard cards. The Central Bank is also working to make cards issued through Humo and Uzcard compatible with the international digital wallets. Click Adds Apple Pay to Online Payments Local payment companies are also adapting to the new services. On October 27, Uzbek payment provider Click announced that it had added Apple Pay to its online payment processing system, allowing retailers using Click’s payment page to accept Apple Pay without a separate technical integration. “We wanted to make enabling Apple Pay as simple as possible for both users and businesses. Our partners don’t need to turn the launch of a new payment method into a separate technical project – Click takes care of that part,” said Ulugbek Rustamov, CEO and co-founder of Click. Merchants can request activation of the service from Click, which will handle payment processing, settlements, reporting, and refunds. Click describes itself as Uzbekistan’s first nonbank payment organization to enable Apple Pay acceptance through its own infrastructure. Octobank had previously introduced Apple Pay and Google Pay for its online acquiring partners, including Uzbekistan Airways and Centrum Air, in September.

title: Interview: Alina Mustafina on Her New Book and Freedom in Filmmaking
body: Kazakh filmmaker and writer Alina Mustafina moved from Almaty to Dubai before relocating to Barcelona with her husband. There, she studied film directing after working as a journalist, a career change she recounts in her second book, Between Heaven and Cinema: When a Dream Changes the Route . Her debut feature documentary, Gingerbread for Her Dad , premiered at the Busan International Film Festival in 2024 and competed at the Torino Film Festival later that year. Those screenings give her firsthand experience of taking a film made in Kazakhstan to international audiences. The Times of Central Asia spoke with Mustafina about her new book and the prospects for Kazakh filmmakers abroad . She discusses life in a Spanish film school and the challenge of explaining Central Asian humor to foreign collaborators. TCA: How did the idea for Between Heaven and Cinema come about? Alina Mustafina: This is my second book. It’s about how my husband and I decided to change our lives when we were already in our thirties. We moved from the Emirates to Spain. I retrained as a filmmaker after working as a journalist, and he went from being an engineer to a pilot. I describe the book as “a story about a pilot’s wife and a filmmaker’s husband.” I started writing it back in 2021, still excited about the publication of my first book, How to Move to Dubai and Stay There , which had become quite popular. In about seven months, I wrote the section about Spain, then put the manuscript aside. I no longer had time for books, and it sat there for several years. TCA: What prompted you to return to the manuscript? Alina: The book is dedicated to my son Ander, who, sadly, passed away last year. In it, I write about the time when we found out we were going to become parents and have a son. That happened in Spain. It was important for me to reflect on that difficult period in my life. I decided to contact the same editor I’d worked with on How to Move to Dubai . I sent him the manuscript and suggested that if the publisher was interested, I would finish the book and we could publish it. If not, I wanted them to tell me right away. I decided that a positive response would give me the push to finally finish what I’d started. It would also give me a firm deadline. TCA: Was working on the book therapeutic for you in some way? Alina: In a sense, probably, yes. At the very least, it helped me look back at my journey in detail, feel grateful for it, and see how much my husband and I had been through together and how we’d supported each other. Besides, the book had been hanging over me as unfinished business all those years. I kept thinking about what I’d written, sitting in a drawer somewhere. If the publisher had turned it down, the manuscript would have stayed there. I wouldn’t have had the resolve to do anything with it. But they said yes, and after that I got back to work quite quickly. TCA: What was the initial print run of the new book, and what do you know about sales so far? Alina: The first print run was 2,000 copies. We’ll see how sales go, and if there’s demand, we’ll print more. I don’t have sales figures yet. Publishers usually provide reports once a quarter, and my book has only just reached stores. But there is interest. From the tags I see on Instagram Stories, I can tell that quite a few of my followers are buying it. TCA: How did your first book about moving to Dubai find its way into print? Alina: I initially published it myself, with a print run of just 500 copies. They all sold through Meloman, Flip.kz, and other outlets. After that, I approached the Kazakh blogger Beibit Alibekov , who helped me publish a second print run. I think it was 1,000 or 1,500 copies; I don’t remember exactly. Then I approached a Russian publisher, and to my surprise, they agreed to publish the book, even though it would be the third print run. They produced a proper hardcover edition with illustrations. In 2021, the book became a bestseller in Kazakhstan. I remember seeing it on a bookstore shelf between a book about Elon Musk and Bill Gates’s book about climate change. That really amused me, and I even used it in the publicity: my book is between Musk and Gates! TCA: In your documentary Gingerbread for Her Dad , three generations of women in your family travel from Kazakhstan to Poland to find the grave of your great-grandfather, who died during World War II. But you’re also a journalist and a writer. How do you introduce yourself these days? Alina: I’m a filmmaker. I used to introduce myself as a writer and journalist. If you’d asked me in 2016 or 2017, when the first print edition of my book came out, that’s what I would have said. But now I see myself primarily as a filmmaker. For me, books are more a way of reflecting on my life in writing. Much of the new book had been written a long time ago: the chapters on Spain and Qatar were already finished. I just needed to update them to reflect what had happened in my life over the past few years, including in film. It took me a couple of months to finish the manuscript. Right now, I don’t have the time, ideas, or energy for more books. But I wouldn’t rule them out someday. For now, I’m focused on filmmaking. TCA: How has living in Europe and the Middle East changed your outlook? Alina: I think it’s changed it quite a bit. First, I’ve grown older. I left Almaty as a young woman, and now I’m a mature adult. Second, meeting people from all over the world has made me much more easygoing about people. I’ve learned to accept them with all their quirks. That doesn’t mean I’m ready to be friends with everyone or let people cross my personal boundaries. I simply understand that one person is a certain way, and someone else is completely different. We may not have much in common, but at least I won’t get upset because someone doesn’t match my idea of who they should be. I’ve always been interested in people whose life experiences are different from mine. TCA: Which cultural differences surprised you most? Alina: There were a lot. Spanish people, for example, discuss their private lives quite openly. They might ask very personal questions even of someone they’ve known for only a couple of weeks. Sometimes they deliberately try to embarrass you and see how you react. Coming from an Asian culture, I found that a little strange, but I got used to it. They also use slang all the time, including some pretty crude expressions. For them, it’s perfectly normal. For example, you can casually say “fuck” or its Spanish equivalents when talking to a teacher, and no one will think anything of it. TCA: So the formal hierarchy between teachers and students that we’re used to is almost absent? Alina: Almost entirely. You can go out for a beer or coffee with your instructor, go to a club together, or just call and ask how they’re doing. You can talk completely freely, without worrying about the fact that they’re the teacher and you’re the student. TCA: Did you like that approach? Alina: Very much! At first, it was a little strange and even intimidating. But I liked that no one paid much attention to age or status. Whether you were a teacher or a student, you could interact as equals. I thought that was really cool. In Doha, where I live now, it’s a little different. Of course, a lot depends on where the teacher comes from. If the mentor is European, the relationship with students can be quite informal, too. But if they’re from the Arab world, there are certain boundaries. For example, you wouldn’t use profanity in conversation, especially if the teacher is a woman. There’s much more restraint about what you say and how you say it. TCA: What subjects interested your classmates in Spain? Alina: There were lots of coming-of-age stories. LGBTQ themes came up often. None of the students in our group were LGBTQ, but they still made films on the subject. There were also many stories about relationships between parents and children. I think that’s a universal theme in cinema, wherever you are. But there were also completely different films: bold, brash works that seemed to defy every rule of dramatic storytelling. The filmmaker’s attitude was simply: I don’t care about your rules; I want to make a film to have fun. To my surprise, those were the films I liked best. They were distinctive and unexpected, and you could feel the freedom in them. TCA: Are they less afraid to experiment? Alina: Absolutely. No one was afraid to experiment with style. You didn’t get everyone trying to make films like iconic directors, as tends to happen among our film students. Someone made a short about a girl who pops a pimple, photographs it, and posts it on Instagram. That’s it – the end! And that short won lots of awards. Essentially, it was just a joke, but they made a film out of it. TCA: Do you think young Spanish filmmakers’ work is lighter, while emerging Kazakh directors more often make social dramas? Alina: That’s partly true. A lot probably depended on who was studying filmmaking. Almost all my classmates had their tuition paid by their parents. There were just three exceptions: a woman over fifty, a man of about thirty whose company had sent him to study, and a young man who’d earned the money himself. Everyone else came from fairly comfortable families, mostly middle-class. Some were very wealthy, though. For example, my editor’s family owned an entire section of an apartment building in Barcelona. Imagine, about ten apartments in one building, all belonging to the same family! That’s an enormous amount of wealth, given what property costs in Barcelona. TCA: Were they not interested in socially engaged films? Alina: No, we explored social issues, too. The focus was just different. Homelessness and migration, for example, are always relevant subjects. When I lived there, the crisis was only beginning. People were gradually losing their jobs, the economy was getting worse, and taxes were high. My husband Emre and I ran into this even when looking for a place to live. Landlords didn’t want to rent to us unless we paid six months in advance. They saw us as potentially troublesome immigrant tenants who might stop paying and occupy the property illegally. But overall, I had the impression that before the 2008 crisis, Spanish people had lived quite comfortably. They had a good education and a fairly high standard of living. Then things gradually began to deteriorate. TCA: Do you think young people there are interested in different kinds of films now? Alina: Judging by France today and the protests that have broken out, I think so. When you go to Europe now, you notice far more homeless people, higher taxes, and people with a fraction of the money they used to have. You can feel that people are cutting back. Apparently, that breeds discontent. But when we were studying there and traveling around Spain, I was struck by how carefree the young people were. It seemed that all they dreamed about was partying harder, getting drunk, and going to clubs. Emre and I found that strange. We’d come from another country, we were already adults and had worked, while they continued to live without a care, even though the country’s economy was far from ideal. TCA: In the book, you say your classmates nicknamed you “Kazakita.” What impression of Kazakhstan do you think they got from knowing you? Alina: Oh, I have no idea! Maybe I embarrassed the whole nation! [Laughs.] Or maybe they now think: we knew one Kazakita, and she was so cool! Everyone liked me, so I hope it was the latter. I certainly didn’t showcase any particular traditions. I was just myself: open, cheerful, and interacting with them as equals. In other words, just like them. People often complimented my looks, so perhaps they at least came away thinking Kazakh women are beautiful. If so, that’s something! [Laughs.] TCA: Not all your classmates became film directors. Some make commercials; others moved into different fields. Is it harder to break into the film industry in Spain than in Kazakhstan? Alina: There’s enormous competition there. And I think we Kazakh filmmakers actually have an advantage in some ways. Kazakh cinema isn’t all that well known internationally. When it comes to arthouse cinema, it’s mostly the films of Darezhan Omirbayev or Adilkhan Yerzhanov. When a film from Kazakhstan appears at an international festival, that alone can spark curiosity: imagine, a film from a country we know almost nothing about! In Spain, things are completely different. It has an established film industry, Netflix operates in Madrid, films are being made all the time, and huge numbers of directors are trying to get their projects off the ground. So it’s much harder to stand out. TCA: Does that mean it’s easier for a young director to start a career in Kazakhstan? Alina: No, I actually think it’s much harder to get started at home. But then, if you’ve somehow managed to make a film, it’s easier to get into an international festival. It doesn’t matter whether you made it against the odds, received financing from a fund, or found some other way. Spain, however, offers much better conditions for professional growth. There are more opportunities to study, develop, read, and immerse yourself in art. The surroundings themselves encourage it; the architecture, history, museums, libraries, and cultural institutions. People are generally very well educated. There are also huge numbers of labs, workshops, training programs, and regional funds that can provide financing for films. TCA: You’ve taken part in international film labs and worked with foreign mentors. Have you had to explain aspects of Kazakh culture to them? Alina: Of course, all the time! You have to explain the context in great detail. For example, when we discuss my series about women in Central Asia, I explain to the mentors how life works in our patriarchal society and how important marriage, family, and the role of men are. I explain why a particular situation or line would be funny specifically to our audience. In France, for example, that humor might not register at all. Someone looks at a situation and doesn’t understand what’s funny about it. Then, once you explain the cultural context, they suddenly say: “Oh, now I get it! Yes, that really is funny!” It’s a very useful experience. You learn to see your own culture from the outside and explain things that seem obvious to you. Along the way, you also come to understand better what makes your story unique. TCA: Let’s return to the book. Your husband said it’s about hope. I think it’s also about the courage to give up a comfortable life and start over. Did you want to inspire readers to make changes? Alina: No, it isn’t meant as a motivational book. It tells the story of our lives. It all happened naturally, because that’s how we actually lived. Readers decide for themselves what to do with that story and how to live their lives. Sooner or later, everyone faces a choice: leave things as they are, or take a risk and try something new. A few years after my first book, How to Move to Dubai and Stay There , came out, readers started writing to me: “Alina, we moved to Dubai because of you,” or “Your book gave me the courage to change my life.” I remember thinking: wow, it turns out I’ve somehow influenced other people’s lives! TCA: Is that responsibility frightening? Alina: Yes, but everyone makes the final decision for themselves. Personally, I’m always in favor of giving it a try. Even if it doesn’t work out, you can give up the idea and go back to where you started. That’s much better than spending the rest of your life regretting that you never dared, never took the risk, never seized the opportunity. There will be difficulties whichever path you choose. I’ve never written my books to say, “Everyone, do what we did!” I simply described what we did, and everyone is free to draw their own conclusions. TCA: The book is an easy read, but your life has hardly been trouble-free. Alina: Yes, we live like everyone else, there are joys and difficulties. For example, we’re living in Qatar now, although I personally don’t like it very much. I’d happily move to Paris. But right now, we can’t simply change everything. So even we, with all our love of adventure and change, sometimes find ourselves in circumstances where we have to stay put. TCA: What are your plans? Alina: As grand as it may sound, to live. And, along the way, to keep writing, making films, and looking for the money to do it. I’m currently working on a new documentary series and writing a series through an international film lab. I hope to find funding for that series in Kazakhstan.

title: Tinubu Seeks National Assembly’s Approval for $20.5bn, €1.04bn External Loans
body: * President cites infrastructure deficit, economic growth, security, agriculture, healthcare, education as priorities * Senate refers supplementary borrowing plan to debt committee, gives one week to report Sunday Aborisade in Abuja President Bola Tinubu has asked the National Assembly to approve a supplementary external borrowing plan of $20.52 billion and €1.045 billion to finance projects and programmes across critical sectors of the economy. Tinubu, in a letter read by Senate President Godswill Akpabio at plenary on Tuesday, said the proposed facilities were intended to address the country’s infrastructure deficit, accelerate economic growth, generate employment and improve the living conditions of Nigerians. The president urged the National Assembly to consider and approve the supplementary external borrowing plan for 2026–2027 to enable the Federal Government to implement its projects and programmes without delay. He said the proposed borrowing plan covered infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare, education, water supply, security, employment generation and financial management reforms, among other sectors. Tinubu said: “The 2026–2027 Supplementary External Borrowing Plan cuts across all sectors, with specific emphasis on infrastructure, agriculture, health, education, water supply, growth, security and employment generation, as well as financial management reforms, amongst others.” Explaining the rationale for the request, the president said the need to sustain economic growth following the implementation of his administration’s reforms had made additional external financing necessary. “In light of the critical reforms of my administration, the need to accelerate growth of the national economy provides support for the External Borrowing Plan, which amounts to $20,517,755,901 and €1,045,083,643,” he said. He added that the projects and programmes covered by the plan had undergone technical and economic assessments to establish their potential contributions to national development. “I want to emphasise that the projects and programmes included in the Borrowing Plan were selected based on thorough technical and economic evaluation, as well as their anticipated contribution to the socio-economic development of the country,” Tinubu said. According to him, the proposed interventions are expected to stimulate economic activities, create jobs, promote skills acquisition, encourage entrepreneurship, reduce poverty and strengthen food security. “These initiatives aim to generate employment, promote skills acquisition, foster entrepreneurship, reduce poverty and enhance food security, all of which improve the livelihood of the Nigerian child,” he said. The president disclosed that most of the projects and programmes would be implemented across the 36 states of the federation and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), underscoring the nationwide scope of the proposed investments. He said the scale of the country’s infrastructure needs and the financial resources required to address them had made broader external borrowing necessary to bridge the funding gap. “The majority of these projects and programmes will be implemented across all the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory,” he said. “In light of the need for significant infrastructure investment in the country and the vast financial resources needed to address this gap, it has become essential to pursue broader external borrowings to close the financing shortfall.” He said the funds would be channelled primarily into critical infrastructure, particularly power, transportation and healthcare, while other sectors would also benefit from the proposed financing arrangement. “These funds will primarily be directed towards critical infrastructure projects in various sectors, including power, transportation and healthcare, amongst others,” the president said. Tinubu urged the Senate and the House of Representatives to give the proposal urgent consideration, arguing that prompt approval would facilitate timely disbursement and effective implementation of the projects. The president said: “Given the urgent nature of these needs and the importance of stabilising the country, it is crucial to seek the consideration and approval of the National Assembly leadership and the entire National Assembly for the 2026–2027 Supplementary External Borrowing Plan. “This will enable the government to fulfil its obligations to the Nigerian people through timely disbursements and effective project implementation.” Following the presentation of the letter, Akpabio referred the request to the Senate Committee on Local and Foreign Debts for consideration and directed it to report back to the chamber within one week. The committee is expected to undertake the initial legislative review of the proposal, with possible collaboration with the Senate Committee on Appropriations and other relevant committees. The request will require legislative scrutiny before the proposed external financing can proceed. The letter did not provide, in the material presented to the Senate, a project-by-project breakdown of the proposed facilities, the individual financing terms or the allocation of the funds among the beneficiary sectors. The proposed borrowing plan comes as the Federal Government seeks additional resources to finance infrastructure and development programmes amid competing demands on public finances. Its implementation will depend on the National Assembly’s consideration of the proposal and the details of the projects to be financed under the plan.

title: Global gas prices increase dramatically — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. International gas prices increased dramatically amid global political developments, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum.
"The world gas industry has found itself in the situation of uncertainty. Traditional business ties were undermined. Prices increased dramatically, but we all understand that they can also roll back sharply, return to the previous level," the head of state said.
The industry experiences serious shocks, including aggravation of the situation in the Middle East - one of global gas production centers, explosions at Nord Stream pipelines, disruptions of traditional logistical chains and supply routes, and international barriers against purchases of relevant equipment and technologies, Putin added.

title: Moscow calls on Tokyo to drop its unfriendly policies — Foreign Ministry
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russia calls on Japan to rethink its unfriendly policies if it wants to restore dialogue with Moscow, the Russian Foreign Ministry said after a meeting between Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko and Japanese Ambassador to Russia Akira Muto.
"The Russian side shared its views on a range of issues regarding Russian-Japanese relations. It was stressed that in order to restore a comprehensive interstate dialogue, the current Japanese authorities should abandon their unfriendly course toward Russia," it said.

title: Kazakhstan Targets Domestic Drone Industry Development by 2029
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan aims to develop its domestic drone industry by 2029, focusing on local manufacturing, digital flight management, workforce training and the use of unmanned systems across key economic sectors, the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development reported on Oct. 27. Eighteen government bodies, including the ministries of transport, defense and internal affairs, will coordinate efforts to establish common regulations, develop infrastructure and expand the use of drones while addressing public safety concerns. Photo credit: AI-generated image/ The Astana Times Domestic production and digital infrastructure Kazakhstan plans to introduce a unified digital platform for unmanned aircraft systems and automated traffic management (UTM). The service will bring aircraft registration, applications and flight route approvals into one electronic system. To support local manufacturing, the government proposes incentives, public procurement preferences and long-term offtake contracts for companies registered with Astana Hub. Support will target production of critical hardware, communications systems and secure software, rather than basic assembly alone. The country also aims to establish at least two research and development centers in partnership with universities and international technology companies and train at least 1,000 specialists, including engineers, drone operators, software developers and cybersecurity experts. From classrooms to industry Drone education is expected to expand from schools to technical colleges and universities. Planned measures include aeromodelling classrooms, specialized equipment for science and technology education, updated university curricula and annual student competitions in unmanned technologies. The government also wants to expand drone use in agriculture, energy, mining, logistics, municipal services, emergency monitoring and environmental protection. Relevant agencies will identify practical applications and develop guidelines and incentives for businesses and public institutions. Supporting infrastructure will include vertiports, drone ports, automated charging stations, radio frequencies and satellite communication channels. A pilot project to test autonomous freight transportation is scheduled for 2027-2028. Safety and regulation The government is considering transferring some oversight of drone operations to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, introducing mandatory liability insurance for drone owners, and setting cybersecurity requirements for communications. Operator certificates would be issued through specialized public service centers. The ministry has invited domestic entrepreneurs, developers and engineers to submit projects with export potential and proposals for implementing the initiative. The broader objective is to build a domestic industry that can supply Kazakhstan’s economy and compete in international markets. title: Idris Elba launches free AI filmmaking programme for African creatives
body: African creatives in Ghana and four other countries can apply for a free artificial intelligence (AI) filmmaking programme launched by actor Idris Elba’s Akuna Group in partnership with Google. The initiative, titled From Script to Screen with AI , aims to equip aspiring and emerging filmmakers with skills in AI-assisted storytelling, alongside mentorship and film production opportunities. Applications opened on Monday, 26 October 2026, and close on 15 November 2026. Supported by US$1 million in funding from Google.org, the programme’s curriculum was developed by AI filmmaking training company Curious Refuge. It is open to eligible applicants in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone and South Africa. Participants will undergo a 12-week online academy from February to April 2027, covering the fundamentals of AI filmmaking before choosing a specialist area. The available pathways are fiction, documentary, animation, advertising and screenwriting, allowing participants to develop their skills across different aspects of visual storytelling. Following the training, graduates will be invited to submit one-page film ideas. Those shortlisted will form teams and receive four weeks of mentorship from industry professionals and subject experts before pitching their projects to panels comprising representatives from Akuna, Google and the wider film industry. Selected teams will receive funding to produce their films between July and October 2027, with the completed projects scheduled to be showcased in October 2027. Sir Idris Elba, chairman of The Akuna Group, said the initiative was intended to widen access to training and enable African creators to tell their own stories. “For me, this is about learning. This is about access to courses that help educate creators across the continent to tell their stories. Through Akuna Learning, we’re partnering with Google and Curious Refuge on ‘From Script to Screen with AI’, a remarkable training and mentorship programme teaching African filmmakers to use AI tools. Selected projects will receive production funding, and creators will retain control of their work. I’m looking forward to seeing the stories they choose, and how the education leads to employment and self-momentum, but helps shape the narrative of Africa,” he said. Khaled Gad, chief executive officer of The Akuna Group, said the programme was designed to take participants beyond training and provide a pathway towards producing finished films. “Training on its own does not build an industry. Creators need a route from the classroom to the screen, and this programme carries them all the way, from their first application to a finished, funded film. It opens on the same day and runs to the same standard in all five countries. You do not need a film school background or any experience with AI to apply. You need finished work that shows what you can do, and your application in by 15 November,” he said. The programme targets a broad range of visual storytellers, including filmmakers, screenwriters, animators, digital content creators, photographers, designers, editors and visual artists. Applicants must be at least 18 years old, live in one of the five participating countries and have access to a laptop, reliable internet and consistent electricity. They must also be available for the full 12-week academy and subsequent stages if selected to progress. No film school qualification or previous AI experience is required. However, applicants must submit existing creative work that demonstrates their talent and commitment. Women are particularly encouraged to apply. Applications are free, and successful applicants will not pay to participate. Creators will also retain control of their work, with neither the programme nor its partners claiming ownership rights over the films produced. Interested applicants can submit their applications through Akuna Learning before the 15th November deadline.

Apple is updating the iMac with M6 chips. The new iMac generation was introduced today, giving Apple’s all-in-one desktop computer a performance boost via the same chipset Apple launched with the Mac Mini in August . Prices start from $1,499, and the design otherwise appears largely unchanged. The update was announced ahead of Apple’s “Pro and Tell” event that’s scheduled to take place on Wednesday.
This refresh comes two years after Apple gave the iMac an overhaul with M4 chips , meaning we’re skipping the M5 series entirely on this hardware. That should make this upgrade more meaningful. The M6 is Apple’s first 2nm chip and includes a dual 16-core Neural Engine that can boost performance when running on-device AI tasks. According to Apple’s press release, the M6-powered iMac “delivers up to 5x faster on-device AI performance” compared with the M4 model.
The M6 configurations start from a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU for $1,499, which is the same price as the 8-core CPU-equipped M4 iMac. There’s also a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU starting at $1,699. Preorders will launch at 1:10PM ET on October 28th, and it’ll be fully available starting November 6th.
Besides the chip upgrade, the new iMac isn’t getting much in the way of a hardware refresh. It now has Apple’s N1 wireless networking chip, alongside Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 on the base model instead of just the higher-spec variant. It still carries over the same Thunderbolt limitations as the M4 iMac, however — you get only two ports on the 10-core version, and four on the 12-core upgrade.
There are also some new restrictions and fees included in the configuration options. If you want to customize the iMac with a Magic Trackpad instead of a Magic Mouse, it’ll cost you an extra $50, despite this being a free switch on the previous iMac. Ethernet has been upgraded from 1 gigabit to 2.5 gigabit, but that’s now a $30 premium upgrade compared with sticking with a Wi-Fi only configuration. Apple also won’t let you configure the M6 iMac with a Magic Keyboard that has Touch ID but not a numeric keypad — despite showing an image of that on the new iMac announcement page.
If you were hoping for some new color options then, hard luck. Apple is offering the exact same color variants as it did with the M4, to the point where it’s just reused some of the marketing imagery and updated them to display more up-to-date content. The M6 chip provides a nice performance boost, but otherwise this is a small spec bump for Apple’s colorful all-in-one.

title: Attempts to exclude Russian from gas market have serious consequences
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Any attempts to exclude Russia from global gas market players have serious consequences, President Vladimir Putin said at the summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum.
"Any attempts to exclude Russia from participants of the global gas market and restrict development of this sector in our country have serious consequences. Above all, these are growing exorbitant costs for foreign end consumers of gas, companies, businesses and households," Putin said.
Russian gas companies faced certain difficulties in recent years, including restrictions from the side of certain countries, the head of state added.

Apple is giving its entry-level MacBook Pro a spec bump. After upgrading the entry-level MacBook Pro with its M5 chip a year ago, Apple is refreshing the laptop today with the M6 chip, which the company launched in August as part of recent upgrades to the new Mac Mini.
Last year’s entry-level MacBook Pro update brought minimal changes from the M4 model that debuted a year prior, including the same design, port layout, webcam, and speakers. The most notable updates, aside from the then-new M5 processor, was faster storage and the option to upgrade its capacity to a hefty 4TB for an extra $1,200.
It’s a similar story for 2026. Announced this morning through a press release , the new 14-inch MacBook Pro features three Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports that all support charging and DisplayPort connectivity, a MagSafe 3 charging port, full-size HDMI, and an SDXC memory card slot accommodating photographers. It carries forward the same 12MP Center Stage camera and Liquid Retina XDR display with a nano-texture option, but this year the 14-inch MacBook Pro is getting an upgrade to both Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 through the Apple N1 wireless networking chip that was previously only included on MacBook Pro configurations with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.
Pricing for the new M6 version of the 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 with 16GB of memory, the same as last year’s M5 model. Bumping that to 24GB increases the price to $2,199, while 32GB is $2,399. Included storage starts at 1TB, but increasing that is now more expensive as a result of the current memory shortage . Bumping that to 2TB is an extra $500, while 4TB is now an extra $1,500. Preorders start on October 28th and shipping is expected to begin on November 6th.
The new M6 processor is Apple’s first 2nm chip with a bump to a 12-core CPU, up from 10 cores in the M5, and the company says it offers up to 1.2x faster multithreaded performance when compared to its predecessor. The M6 also features a Dual 16-core Neural Engine to handle heavy on-device AI tasks, plus an upgraded 12-core GPU with a Neural Accelerator in each core. In addition to performance improvements, Apple says its M6 processor is more power efficient.

title: Ghanaian veterinarian leads campaign against proposed African battery cage standard
body: A prominent Ghanaian veterinarian is leading a continent-wide campaign against a proposed standard from the African Organisation for Standardisation (ARSO) that would approve battery cages for egg-laying hens. Dr. Daniel Baba Abiliba, founder of the Animal Welfare League (AWL) and a graduate student at the Yale School of the Environment, is speaking out against ARSO’s draft standard, CD-ARS 1241:2025(E), which would formally accept the worst form of battery cages as a housing system for laying hens. “The battery cage system ARSO is endorsing is horrible, and it runs contrary to African ideals,” Dr. Abiliba said. “Most Africans interact with animals in one way or another, in our homes, on our farms and in our communities. Also, a large number of us know that chickens are sentient beings; they can feel pain, fear, and distress. The battery cage system has been found to contribute a lot of pain and suffering to chickens. This standard does not reflect who we are.” The Pan-African Campaign Together with coalition partners, AWL launched a campaign in March 2026 at stoparsobatterycages.org . It calls on all 44 African national standards bodies to reject the draft by signing the petition. “Treating animals well is not at odds with productivity,” Dr. Abiliba said. “Ghanaian farmers know that healthy, well-kept animals are productive animals. We don’t have to choose between caring for animals and feeding our people.” Ghana’s Leadership in Animal Welfare Ghana has demonstrated strong leadership in establishing national poultry welfare standards through the creation of GS 1404:2026 (Farm Animal Welfare – Requirements for Poultry). Dr. Abiliba contributed directly to this effort as part of the technical committee that drafted the standard alongside the Ghana Standards Authority (GSA), the Veterinary Services Directorate (VSD), and other key stakeholders. The GSA has officially adopted both the standard and its accompanying inspection manual as national benchmarks. In line with this, the VSD is currently piloting implementation across over 100 farms nationwide. “Good animal husbandry has always been part of the African farming tradition. This standard simply puts it into writing and GS 1404 builds on what our farmers already know. ARSO should be learning from Ghana, not moving in the opposite direction,” Dr Abiliba said. A veterinarian with a global record Dr. Abiliba is currently pursuing a Master of Environmental Management at the Yale School of the Environment in the United States. He earned his Doctor of Veterinary Medicine degree from the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST). He was the first Ghanaian to win the MSD/World Veterinary Association Veterinary Student Scholarship and his exemplary work in rabies prevention has been recognised by the World Health Organization. The future of animal welfare in Africa depends on collective action. Readers, farmers, and organizations are urged to join the campaign against battery cages by visiting stoparsobatterycages.org and calling on African national standards bodies to reject draft standard CD-ARS 1241:2025(E).

title: Okpebholo Charges Permanent Secretaries On Accountability, Performance
body: Edo State Governor, Monday Okpebholo, has urged permanent secretaries to uphold accountability, transparency, and professionalism as the state works to improve governance and service delivery. The governor gave the charge on Monday while declaring open a two-day Strategic Leadership and Orientation Retreat for Permanent Secretaries, organised to strengthen leadership and institutional performance in the Edo State Civil Service. He asked the officials to resist corruption, cut unnecessary bureaucracy, embrace innovation, and make sure government policies translate into measurable benefits for Edo residents. Okpebholo described permanent secretaries as the accounting officers of their Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs), responsible for financial discipline. “This is not merely a title; it is a clear duty for accountability, due process, proper record keeping, and ensuring that every expenditure delivers real value to the Edo people,” he said. He also cautioned them against acting on instructions simply because someone claims, “the governor said.” “Verify it. Confirm its authenticity. Ensure it complies with the law, financial regulations, and established procedures,” he added. The governor reminded the participants that governments come and go, but the civil service remains the custodian of institutional memory and continuity. He urged them to ensure timely decisions, faster movement of files, effective project monitoring, and responsive public services. Okpebholo said his administration had introduced several reforms in less than two years to reposition the civil service as an engine of effective governance. These include prompt payment of salaries, continuation of the 13th-month salary, and an increase in the minimum wage from N70,000 to N75,000. He added that promotion arrears had been eliminated, promotions were now timely, and thousands of workers had been recruited or regularised. The governor also highlighted EDO-PREP, designed to strengthen performance and capacity development, and EdoCloud, which supports the state’s paperless governance initiative. According to him, merit, inclusion, and institutional accountability have become central to the reforms, and he urged participants to exchange ideas and commit to better service delivery across Edo. Earlier, the Head of Service, Dr Anthony Okungbowa, commended the governor for prioritising workers’ welfare and strengthening the civil service. Okungbowa recalled that shortly after assuming office in November 2024, Okpebholo directed that salaries be paid by the 26th of every month. He also noted the introduction of the 13th-month salary in December 2024 and the later increase in the minimum wage. He thanked the governor for approving 20 brand-new permanent secretaries, describing the gesture as support for better administrative performance. The head of service urged the participants to use the retreat to reflect on their responsibilities and develop practical strategies for improving service delivery. He said the success of the SHINE Agenda depends largely on how effective the MDAs are and challenged them to identify measurable outcomes their offices could deliver within three and six months. Okungbowa described public office as a position of trust, insisting that permanent secretaries must show discipline, integrity, and professionalism in managing public resources. He also welcomed the newly appointed permanent secretaries and urged them to uphold the values of the civil service. Among those present at the event were the Secretary to the State Government, Barr. Musa Ikhilor, and the Chief of Staff to the Governor, Alhaji Yakubu Musa. The post Okpebholo Charges Permanent Secretaries On Accountability, Performance appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Anduril expanding into laptop manufacturing in partnership with Qualcomm
body: Defense technology company Anduril, best known for building drones and AI-enabled software for the military, is branching out into a new product manufacturing business: laptops. The company on Tuesday announced the launch of a computer initiative, dubbed BlueChip, in partnership with wireless tech giant Qualcomm. Anduril has already developed “functional prototypes” of the laptops, according to a press release. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Series will provide the core computing capabilities for the devices, including “general-purpose processing, graphics, and on-device AI.” The companies plan to begin taking orders next year. The firms touted BlueChip as an effort to boost manufacturing in America and reduce the nation’s reliance on foreign supply chains. “The United States pioneered personal computing and continues to lead the world in designing advanced technology, but decades of offshoring have left America dependent on foreign manufacturers for the computers and components that power everything from personal devices to critical government infrastructure. This dependence creates a national security vulnerability. Conflict or disruptions to overseas supply chains could limit access to essential computing hardware and undermine America’s ability to sustain production when it matters most,” company officials wrote in the press release. The organizations plan to market the tech to government and military customers, among other potential buyers. “It might sound crazy for a company like Anduril to be doing something like this,” Anduril co-founder and leader Palmer Luckey told reporters ahead of the official announcement. However, he suggested that the BlueChip product line isn’t far outside of Anduril’s wheelhouse. “What we’ve been doing at Anduril, including with Qualcomm, is not actually very different from building a computer. You look at any of our autonomous drones, we’ve got a CPU, a GPU, memory, storage, mainboard, battery, sensors, wireless radios. It’s basically all the same stuff you’d have in any computer. The only difference is the shape and that it has a screen and a keyboard. Even on the display side, actually, we have a number of drones that have status screens, so it’s really not all that different,” he said. During a call with reporters ahead of the announcement, Luckey declined to say what the production targets are for the new laptops. “We’re not sharing any quantities yet. We’re gonna have a lot more to announce next year. I think it’s really, really tough right now to announce these things. To be totally candid, we’re in an unprecedented time, as it were, for building computers given … the AI explosion, and so we’re not going into full-rate production until next year. We’re in very early prototyping production. Like, we have a very small line put together, very small quantities of these right now to build out the manufacturing process. But I’m not going to know quantities until we have a little more clarity on the manufacturing side, the vendor supply chain side. There’s a lot of moving pieces,” he said. Anduril plans to use its Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio — where it’s also building autonomous drones for the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program — for BlueChip manufacturing. Cristiano Amon, president and CEO of Qualcomm, told reporters during the call that chips for the laptops will be made at a TSMC facility in Arizona. Luckey added that the companies also have “some stuff going on” in California related to the effort, though he didn’t provide details. “There’s certainly going to end up being other facilities. This is another one of those things where it’s still in flux, exactly which facility is going to do which step. So, I can’t get into as much detail as I’d like,” he said. Luckey noted that, while the laptop will be the first product in the BlueChip line, the companies’ vision is to expand the offerings and it’s “very likely” that some of those will be made at other facilities. Currently, the laptop’s bill of materials is about 90% from the U.S. and allies, according to Luckey. The aim is to eventually get that number up to 100%. Regarding the workforce, the Anduril boss said he’s been “diverting some of our best people to this project for quite some time,” including those who worked on some of the other offerings that the company is better known for, such as attack drones. The U.S. government has not yet provided any subsidies or contracts to Anduril and Qualcomm to develop the laptops, according to Luckey, who noted that the companies have been putting their own R&D dollars into the initiative. He did not disclose how much money is being invested in the effort to get to full-rate production. “I’d say the worst case here is that this is going to be a low-volume laptop for critical industries and government … that desperately need something like this to exist. That is a healthy business for Android to run, even if it doesn’t get bigger. I happen to believe it’s going to be much, much, much bigger,” he told reporters. Amon noted the AI boom that’s unfolding across the economy. “I think when you look at how AI is evolving, computers are also becoming token machines,” he said. “In addition to what you do with a laptop, it’s going to run models, it’s going to be part of this entire compute fabric that’s going to be running AI. And you’re going to have different ecosystems and needs for [the tech] across different industries. It’s very possible that you’re going to have certain industries … in addition to the federal government, that will want devices. They have different kinds of requirements and compliance with security and across the supply chain. … So, I think this could create an interesting opportunity when you think about the addressable market. It’s just a different world going forward when you think about the role of PCs.” Luckey added that the chips in the new laptop are “extremely good” for AI inference. “Maybe not training large models, but on the inference side, they’re fantastic. And so, I’ve been using my BlueChip laptop to do a whole bunch of local model work where … I don’t want to — and actually am not allowed to — send certain information out into the cloud. And so having devices that can do a really good job of onboard AI inference running local models is actually really, really important,” he told reporters. The BlueChip systems are designed for potential military customers. “This is aimed squarely at the defense side of things as the pace-setting element of the design because it’s the most stringent part of the design. So basically I have to design for the military users because they’re the ones that are going to be beating these things up the most. They have the most stringent security requirements, the most stringent environmental requirements, shock and vibration, all of that,” Luckey said. For the average individual consumer, the price tag for the extra-rugged devices might not be cost competitive with other laptop offerings on the market, he suggested. Anduril has been testing out the BlueChip tech with multiple operating systems, Luckey noted. “As of right now, we have it running Windows and two particular flavors of Linux that are very popular with the U.S. military to make sure that all the drivers work, make sure that all the applications work,” he said. One of the applications that has been integrated into the BlueChip system is Anduril’s Lattice software platform that serves as the backbone for some of the military’s high-priority modernization initiatives, such as Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2). “It’s critical that we be able to run Lattice, both the version that processes locally and the version that commands and controls systems that are processing at the edge with Lattice,” Luckey said. The post Anduril expanding into laptop manufacturing in partnership with Qualcomm appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: Palmer Luckey’s Anduril is getting into laptops — and claims they’ll be American-made
body:
Anduril and Qualcomm are partnering on a new line of laptops called BlueChip, launching in early 2027. The first prototype is a ruggedized model using Arm-based Snapdragon X series chips and aimed at the US military, but the ultimate focus of the joint venture is to make laptops entirely in the US. Eventually.
At launch BlueChip will still use foreign components from “allies around the world,” according to Anduril founder Palmer Luckey. The first BlueChip laptops will be “designed and assembled in the United States” with a “long-term goal of building a fully domestic supply chain,” per Anduril’s official press release. Circuitboard assembly is planned to be done at Anduril’s Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio.
Anduril and Qualcomm aren’t sharing many details on how they’re going to build enough manufacturing in the US for a laptop that’s 100-percent domestically made. During a virtual Q&A session with media that included The Verge, Luckey and Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon laid out the motivations for American-made (or at least, American-assembled) laptops. It’s the talking points you’d expect: keeping US money in the US, the potential for creating domestic jobs, minimizing technological / economic reliance on other countries, and reducing national security vulnerabilities.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/2026-BlueChip-Engraving-2-Web.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/2026-BlueChip-Manufacturing-15-Web.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
When asked what percentage of the BlueChip laptop’s components will be made in the US once it launches in 2027, Luckey specified the display glass, the frame around the display, and parts of the ribbon component. In a post on X after this story was published, Luckey said he had been responding to “a specific question about the display modules in the current prototype vs the final product. As I explicitly said, BlueChip has American chips, batteries, metallics, plastics, glass, etc, and we have a clear technical roadmap to 100% American components.”
[Media: https://twitter.com/palmerluckey/status/2115244217127858416]
Here’s the exchange from the call:
> The Verge: When it arrives in 2027, what percent of the components in the BlueChip laptop will be made in the US?
> Luckey: TBD. I’m doing my very, very best. It’s gonna be a whole mix of things based on when do certain memory fabs come online? When do certain CPU, GPU fabs come online? There’s a whole— Like, am I able to get a display line here or not? Do I have to do that after launch? I’m being totally open kimono with you here. Those questions are not settled. It is not clear if I will be able. I know the glass is gonna be made in the US, I know the frame is gonna be made in the US around that display. I know that parts of the ribbon component are gonna be made in the U.S. I don’t know if I will have successfully pulled that component in or a dozen other components. So it’s a little up in the air. I’m doing my very, very best. I think most likely the thing that we ship is not going to be 100-percent American. I think it’ll be a blend of US and allies around the world, mostly US, probably a few things from some allies, and then that’ll be in the context of conversations with those allies about bringing those components into production in the United States, and I’m being honest with the government on this too. I mean, I’ve had conversations where I’ve said, listen. I would love to give you guys an American, 100-percent American laptop right off the bat, but that is not the environment the US government has created or US industry has created. I can’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good.”
When asked whether BlueChip’s first laptop will meet the 65-percent requirement to count as American-made under federal procurement rules, Anduril spokesperson Stephanie Davis told The Verge via email, “For the prototype today, approximately 32% is U.S.-origin by component procurement cost, and more than 90% is sourced from the United States and allied countries combined. We’re working to expand domestic sourcing and production ahead of planned availability in 2027, with the goal of eliminating foreign content and ultimately establishing an end-to-end American supply chain. The final domestic-content percentage at launch remains unsettled, so we can’t confirm above or below 65% today.”
During the briefing, Luckey said that Anduril’s goal is to have a 100 percent American supply chain:
> We are not just barely meeting the bar for Made in America. We are going hard to make this an all-American play, and not even the Buy American Act requires requires what we’re trying. We’re trying to do the ultimate version of this because I know that the law, actually, in my opinion, doesn’t go far enough.
A day after this story’s publication, Anduril’s communications VP, Shannon Prior, followed up with a clarification to say that the earlier statement was inaccurate and the laptop will exceed the 65 percent target at launch:
> Our previous response to The Verge was incorrect. The BlueChip laptop is indeed being developed to exceed the 65% U.S. domestic-content threshold at launch in 2027. Meeting that threshold is a fundamental objective of the program. The precise domestic-content percentage of the final product is still being determined as we finalize suppliers and work through prototypes, and we look forward to sharing more next year.
As for the chips in BlueChip, Qualcomm’s Amon told The Verge it intends to manufacture processors for this laptop at TSMC Arizona. When The Verge followed up to ask how much money Qualcomm is investing into that, Qualcomm communications rep Yelena Tebcherani said, “We don’t have any more details to share at the moment.”
Anduril’s first potential customer for BlueChip laptops is the same as its drones: the US military. The prototype is a ruggedized computer aimed at military personnel, complete with a rifle strap-style carrying handle — presumably so a soldier can slam the laptop shut, quickly grab it, and get on the move. It will run Windows or two undisclosed versions of Linux.
[Image: The BlueChip laptop’s tan, rugged exterior. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/2026-BlueChip-InField-5-Web.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
During the Q&A, Luckey indicated that BlueChip is funded entirely by Anduril and Qualcomm, not government subsidies. He mentioned that Anduril is starting with a military laptop to first service users with the most stringent hardware needs and software security demands. It’s also likely for pursuing those valuable government contracts that could call for large quantities of expensive computers. After the government and defense sectors, Anduril’s next target will be first responders and public safety, before eventually getting to consumer-level laptops — the lowest on the priority list. Luckey mentioned offhandedly, “I’d say the worst case here is that this is going to be a low volume laptop for critical industries and government needs that desperately need something like this to exist.”
Palmer Luckey is of course a controversial figure. Anduril is better known for making drones and autonomous weapons, while Luckey continues making consumer-facing products like Game Boy clones — often polarizing the communities they’re meant to serve. Bringing a supply chain for computers back to the US and one day manufacturing a fully American-made laptop sounds a tall order. It’s complicated even further once you consider the person and company behind it.
Correction, October 27th: This story originally mischaracterized Luckey’s political spending in 2016; he donated to a “pro-Trump troll group dedicated to ‘shitposting in real life,’” which only ever produced “a single billboard,“ according to Tablet Magazine; he did not “[fuel] right wing troll farms,” as this story initially stated. This story also misstated Luckey’s position at Anduril. He is Anduril’s founder, not CEO.
This story has also been updated with Luckey’s response and additional comments on which components will be made in the US.
Update, October 28th: Added a new statement from Anduril committing to exceeding the 65 percent standard.

title: Ford’s sub-$30K electric truck puts the home backup inverter right inside the vehicle
body:
We’re still a few months away from the official reveal of the Ford Fathom, the automaker’s first next-generation electric vehicle. While we wait, Ford has been whetting our appetite with news about the sub-$30,000 pickup — including today’s announcement about the Fathom’s bidirectional charging capabilities.
With an increasing number of EVs coming out with bidirectional vehicle-to-home (V2H) or vehicle-to-load (V2L) charging capabilities, Ford is trying to position the Fathom as a key entrant — and one that simplifies the system by making it an everyday reality rather than a $10,000 luxury perk. Unlike the discontinued F-150 Lightning, which required a massive, expensive external DC-to-AC wall inverter, the Fathom packs the inverter directly into its onboard “E-box” to pump out over 10 kW of AC power natively.
The Fathom’s built-in inverter converts its battery power into standard household electricity to run appliances, back up a home during an outage, or feed energy back into the grid.
[Image: The Ford Fathom’s E-box supplies up to 10kW of power. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/E-box.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Taking advantage of these features will require additional hardware, though Ford aims to make it significantly cheaper than current options. To send power back to the grid, owners will need the Ford Home Power Station. Ford is targeting a 50 percent discount compared to the existing $1,310 Ford Charge Station Pro. For whole-home backup power during a blackout, owners must pair that station with a backup panel. While that combination typically runs around $5,205, Ford is aiming for an estimated $3,123 — a roughly 40 percent reduction — though finalized pricing for both packages is still pending.
The Fathom, a $28,000 electric pickup truck, will be the first vehicle on Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, an innovative new system designed to maximize aerodynamic range while also reducing production costs so Ford can make a profitable EV. For over a year, the company has been hyping it as its “Model T moment” that will revolutionize nearly everything at the 123-year-old company.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Ford-Home-Power-Station_1538x1024.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Ford-Home-Power-Station_Ford-Home-Backup-Panel_.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Ford-Home-Power-Station_Ford-Home-Backup-Panel_1920x1080.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Another barrier to V2H or V2L charging is red tape from public utilities. Ford’s solution was to team up with five of North America’s biggest power companies — Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E); American Electric Power (AEP); BC Hydro; Consumers Energy; and Exelon — which collectively cover millions of customers in the US and Canada. Ford theorized that whatever rules they agree on will likely become the standard everyone else follows. They agreed to cut the paperwork for basic storm backup, use common plugs and software, and make grid programs automatic.
Cutting the cost of the Ford Home Power Station and Backup Panel is certainly helpful, but homeowners will still face additional costs related to permitting, electrician labor, and heavy-gauge wiring. These could conspire to keep these bidirectional charging features out of reach for some customers.
Still, Ford is intent on keeping the costs low for its new electric truck. With supply chain constraints and trade upheaval, that will remain a central challenge for the automaker as it gets closer to one of the most important vehicle debuts in Ford’s history.
Images by Ford

Twelve South has announced a new version of its Airfly dongle that simplifies the pairing process when connecting wireless headphones to devices that don’t natively support Bluetooth. Instead of having to decode flashing or color-changing LEDs, the new Airfly View adds a built-in screen that displays instructions for each step of the pairing process in one of 24 different languages including Japanese, Arabic, Portuguese, and Polish.
The Airfly View is available starting today for $79.99 and includes a carrying case and an adapter for connecting the dongle’s short 3.5mm headphone cable to an airplane’s split headphone jack. That makes it one of Twelve South’s most expensive versions of the Airfly, but the screen is useful for more than just letting you toss the user manual.
The display has a battery level indicator so you can estimate how much of the Airfly View’s estimated 16 hours of battery life remains, and it shows the name of which wireless headphones or earbuds are connected based on how they identify themselves over Bluetooth. That could be useful if you’re juggling a family of flyers who are all traveling with their own headphones.
You can stream audio from a single Airfly View dongle to two connected pairs of wireless headphones simultaneously, but Twelve South also says it “supports Auracast broadcast audio, so it is ready for the next generation of Bluetooth headphones.” That will further expand how many devices can receive audio from a single dongle but is dependent on wireless headphones fully supporting that Auracast feature, and not many currently do.
