title: International delegation barred by Israel from entering West Bank to support olive harvest
body: An international group of MPs and campaigners say they have been prevented from entering the occupied West Bank by the Israeli military, as they travelled to support Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest. Three British MPs and one member of the Spanish Senate were among those refused entry as they tried to enter the West Bank from the Allenby/King Hussein Bridge crossing from Jordan. They had planned to support olive growers facing escalating violence during the harvest. The delegation of 23 people, organised by Progressive International, also planned to meet Palestinian students at Ramallah’s Birzeit University , as well as civil society leaders. Delegates also came from France, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Greece, the Netherlands and the US. “Today I was denied entry into the West Bank, alongside other parliamentary colleagues from across Europe,” said Scottish National Party MP Lara Bird. “We were held for eight hours, interrogated and ultimately prevented from crossing the border,” she wrote on X. Mr Bird said they had not been told by the Israeli military why they were barred from entering. “I came to stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land. Instead, we were turned away, with no reason given,” she said. British Labour MP Clive Lewis said he was also detained for more than eight hours, interrogated, and “made to feel as though we had done something wrong”. “We went to show our support for the Palestinian people and highlight the terrible injustice and violence being perpetrated against them,” he wrote on X. Scottish Greens MSP Kate Nevens and former Labour MP Sam Tarry were also denied entry, along with Josu Estarrona Elizondo, a representative of the Basque EH Bildu party in the Spanish senate. The delegation was barred as settler violence in the West Bank escalates, with attacks by Israeli forces on Palestinian olive farmers and journalists and activists who have come to support them. There were at least 160 settler attacks on Palestinian growers in the first two weeks of October, according to the UN. European diplomats and a French mayor were attacked in the West Bank this month as they went to support farmers. Brad Lander , a Democrat candidate for Congress in the mid terms in New York, was among dozens of people detained for supporting olive farmers last week. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz is reported to have instructed officials to pursue exclusion orders against activists travelling to support the Palestinian olive harvest, according to Israeli media.

title: Kyiv condo gets solar plant with 135 kW battery - Klitschko
body:
One of the residential complexes on the left bank of Kyiv, which combines three buildings with a total area of more than 30,000 square meters, has been equipped with a solar power plant with a 135 kW battery that keeps the elevators, individual heat substations, control systems and lighting of common areas running for at least 15 hours straight, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Under city programs, the condominium association installed three individual heat substations, a 9 kW generator and a solar power plant that includes three inverters, a 135 kW battery and 108 solar panels, he said.
"This building is an example of a systemic approach and professional management. It enabled people to actually renovate their homes and make them more energy resilient, economical and comfortable," Klitschko wrote on Telegram.
According to him, the individual heat substations ensure an even distribution of heat among apartments and save at least 20% of heat energy.
The windows and doors in the buildings were also replaced, the networks were overhauled and insulated, all six elevators were replaced and the lighting system was modernized with motion sensors.
About 70% of the cost of the work was paid by the city or by grants under state programs, Klitschko said.
He also said applications are now being accepted for a competition under the 70/30% co-financing program. The head of this condominium association plans to apply for facade insulation and to get a loan from a revolving fund.

title: Alleged N582m Fraud: Judge Threatens Arrest Of NNPC Coop Society’s Ex-President, Ogunbayo Over Absence In Court
body: Justice Lesley Wike of the Federal Capital Territory High Court, Abuja, has threatened to order the arrest of a former President of the Nigeria National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Staff Multi-Purpose Cooperative Society, Olalekan Ogunbayo, over his failure to appear in court and take his plea in an alleged N582 million fraud charge. Justice Wike issued the threat following complaints by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) that Monday’s proceedings were the third time Ogunbayo refused to appear in court for arraignment on the alleged financial misappropriation of the society’s funds. When the matter was called, prosecution counsel, R. U. Adagba, informed the judge that only the 2nd defendant, Abolade Nurudeen, was in court. The lawyer complained that Ogunbayo was granted administrative bail but jumped bail and that all efforts to locate him for service of the charge have been unsuccessful. The EFCC stated that Ogunbayo had stalled the arraignment twice due to his absence in court and applied that a bench warrant be issued against him to facilitate his arrest and production in court. Adagba cited Sections 35, 113, 114 of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act (ACJA) 2015, arguing that the court has the power to order the arrest of the defendant. However, counsel to the defendants, Innocent Adoo, opposed the arrest warrant application, arguing that arraignment in a criminal trial could not proceed without proper service of the charge on the defendant. He submitted that a defendant must be informed of the allegations against him and given adequate opportunity to prepare his defence, adding that service could not be waived by any party. Adoo told the court that Ogunbayo was still on administrative bail and was unaware of the scheduled arraignment. He explained the defence had used the information available to it to communicate with Ogunbayo, who was said to be in Warri and unable to secure a flight to Abuja for today’s proceedings. The defence counsel consequently urged the court to adjourn the matter to enable both defendants to appear and take their pleas in the interest of justice. Reacting, Justice Wike held that, in the interest of justice, the matter be adjourned to enable the first defendant to make himself available for arraignment. The judge, however, warned the court would take the necessary steps if Ogunbayo fails to appear on the next adjourned date. She subsequently adjourned until November 23 for arraignment. The anti-graft agency had filed an eight-count criminal charge bordering on alleged criminal misappropriation, abuse of office, corrupt practices and obtaining money by false pretence over the sale of the cooperative society’s property at Plot 50, Karsana North, Abuja. BuyMaps The prosecution alleged that Ogunbayo, the society’s president, and Nurudeen, who operates under the name and style of Abolade Nurudeen & Co., conspired in January 2024 to misappropriate proceeds from the transaction. In one of the counts, the defendants were accused of dishonestly misappropriating N582 million realised from the sale of the property. Ogunbayo was also accused of allegedly receiving N100 million, N10 million and N50 million through different bank accounts in connection with the transaction. The prosecution further alleged that Nurudeen received N180 million into an account belonging to his firm after representing that the property had been sold for N1 billion. Both defendants were also accused of involvement in an alleged N160 million corrupt transaction The post Alleged N582m Fraud: Judge Threatens Arrest Of NNPC Coop Society’s Ex-President, Ogunbayo Over Absence In Court appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Bayern praise ‘humble’ Kane after Ballon d’Or win
body: Bayern Munich assistant coach Aaron Danks on Tuesday praised Harry Kane after his Ballon d’Or win, saying the striker will already be focused on scoring his “next goal”. Kane, 33, was awarded the prestigious honour in his hometown of London on Monday evening, breaking through to win the award for the first time. Englishman Danks, who is in the dugout while head coach Vincent Kompany recovers in hospital from a virus, said receiving the game’s highest individual award would not change the England captain’s mindset. “I’m really happy for him and proud of what he’s achieved. I know Harry and his full focus will now be on his next goal, his next performances, his next games,” Danks said at a press conference on Tuesday. “He’ll be straight back into that professional, humble mindset that got him to this level.” Kane had won several goalscoring honours and was runner-up in the Premier League and Champions League with Tottenham but did not break through for a first team trophy until after he moved to Bayern in 2023. Since arriving in Munich, Kane has won two Bundesliga titles and the German Cup, along with making the Champions League semi-finals in two of three seasons at Bayern. Danks said the former Spurs striker was finally getting the recognition he deserves. “I remember years ago when he was back home in England and everybody spoke about him not winning trophies, but if you looked at his career and what he was achieving, he was having a fantastic career. “He was taking the England team to European finals, he was taking Tottenham to Champions League finals. “Maybe he wasn’t getting the recognition in terms of trophies that he deserved, but those things are coming now for him.” Kane and the remaining Bayern contingent who went to London for the ceremony will return to Munich later on Tuesday ahead of Wednesday’s German Cup match against second-tier Magdeburg. “They’re due back at lunchtime today. He’ll train, practice this afternoon and be available for tomorrow… Our full focus is on the game tomorrow,” Danks said. Danks also said he had visited Kompany in hospital and revealed the manager, who was rushed to hospital on Friday after collapsing on the training pitch, was improving. “He’s in good spirits. It looks like every day he’s getting better. There’s no major updates in terms of diagnosis or a return to work, it’s very calm, let him rest, let him recover.” After seven games, Bayern sit top of the Bundesliga, level on points but ahead on goal difference from Borussia Dortmund, with the two sides facing off in Munich on Saturday. AFP The post Bayern praise ‘humble’ Kane after Ballon d’Or win appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: South Korea’s Foreign Ministry recalls eight diplomats from Ukraine
body:
SEOUL, October 27. /TASS/. South Korea’s Foreign Ministry has recalled eight employees of its embassy in Kiev amid escalating tensions with Ukraine. Foreign Minister Cho Hyun announced the decision during parliamentary hearings, saying it was prompted by statements from the Ukrainian side, including remarks concerning the situation along the border with North Korea.
"We have no choice but to recall eight diplomatic workers," he said. Seoul announced the withdrawal of some embassy staff on October 20.
Statements made during the hearings indicated that South Korea does not rule out the possibility that the dispute could jeopardize diplomatic relations between the two countries.
An opposition lawmaker said the current situation "essentially borders on a virtual severance of diplomatic relations" or, at the very least, constitutes an "extremely acute diplomatic conflict" on the brink of such an outcome.
"Yes. If the escalation continues, I believe there is such a possibility," Cho replied.
At the same time, the foreign minister said he remained in contact with his Ukrainian counterpart. He added that "key employees" of the South Korean embassy would stay in Ukraine to assist South Korean citizens if necessary.
On October 8, South Korea’s Foreign Ministry announced that the government had decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine. On October 20, ministry spokesman Park Doo-soon confirmed that Seoul had also decided to withdraw some diplomatic staff from the country.

title: Software may be getting worse, but it used to be horrible
body:
Software is degrading all around us, for obvious reasons. I've written about this before. All else equal, if you increase your code production by 10x but you don't reduce your error rate by a factor of 10, then your production app is buggier than it used to be.
I've seen threads where people also have some nostalgia for the past: "software used to be better in the past" or "we've forgotten how to program like we used to" or "software quality has been declining for decades." And as someone who has used computers since 1990, I'm here to disabuse you of this notion. Software was horrible. Everything crashed all the time. Yes, there were great programmers like John Carmack who could keep the entire program in their head and iterate on thoughtful codebases over decades. No, they did not write a majority of the software that we used to use.
Almost everyone in the world was on Windows. Windows peaked around a 95% market share, plus or minus a few percentage points based on your source. Yes, you probably knew someone with an iMac who would tell you that it was way better than a Windows machine, and they could prove it if anyone ever actually released applications for Macs. And yes, there were Linux distros like Debian where people could get real computing done [0] .
But those were exceptions. Almost every computer user had a Windows machine and either an Intel or an AMD processor. And Windows had a lot of problems.
There was one saving grace though: companies only got one chance to ship their software. At a certain point, it was going to be loaded onto a floppy disk or burned onto a CD or a ROM, put into a box, and mailed out. And that version had to work out of the box. So there was some quality floor that you couldn't slip below.
Here's a collection of things that I remember. This isn't linear; it's my collection of memories from 1990 and onward.
Windows had extreme stability issues for most of my childhood.
Let me introduce you to the song of my people, the Blue Screen of Death.
The blue screen of death in Windows XP, Vista and 7, courtesy of Wikipedia
This was Windows' version of a kernel panic. It happened right when you were in the middle of something. Or maybe you were doing nothing. It didn't matter: the blue screen was coming.
Your computer crashed for a lot of reasons. First, device drivers. If you bought some new peripheral like a joystick, it'd come with a floppy disk or CD with device drivers. You'd dutifully install them. The device drivers had the same function as they do today: they help the operating system understand how to interface with the hardware. This might get you thinking, "Oh wow, so they sent out the device drivers on physical media? You can't update a physical disk once you ship it. Surely they took extra care to get everything right." My friend, this could not be further from the truth. I'm sure there were good drivers and bad drivers. But in aggregate, they were buggy, and it only took one marginal device driver to destabilize your computer.
The Windows operating system also had its own code quality issues back then, and would sometimes fail to fully reclaim resources from programs that exited. So your computer would slowly degrade over time until eventually the slow rot would take down your machine.
All in all, your computer would just blink out of existence from time to time. It was a fact of life.
Do you know what pairs really well with a computer that crashes all the time? Applications that don't autosave. Even better, applications with autosave that don't flush buffered writes and corrupt their save files.
It was commonplace to get into the zone and work on a document for hours, and then suddenly you would get either a Blue Screen of Death, or a pop-up saying that your application had a problem and had to exit. And you'd scream and you'd double-click your document over and over, but it was no use. You had to start over. But there was a consolation prize. It was your turn to tell everyone, "I was working on a document for THREE HOURS! And then the computer crashed and I lost everything. It was all gone. I had to redo it." There was always that one asshole that was like "why didn't you save?" But you didn't get mad. You knew that he was 2 weeks from having the same thing happen to him.
When I joined the Google Docs team back in 2010, we instrumented the Ctrl+s keyboard shortcut for fun. It didn't do anything but record a metric saying that it had been pressed. This "save" keyboard shortcut was in the top 5 non-editing user actions, just behind things like "move the cursor with arrow keys." And it did absolutely nothing. Google Docs autosaves. But everyone was so traumatized from years or decades of losing work that they reflexively saved anytime they edited anything.
When my sister and I were little, we loved going into stores with display units. The computers would often have games installed you could play. Worst case, you could always open up MS Paint or Solitaire and mess around for a few minutes.
One time, we were in a store where the display models had password-protected screensavers. My sister was undeterred. She just hit Ctrl+Alt+Del, selected the screensaver application, and clicked "End Task." And we were in. The best minds of Microsoft were nothing next to the hacking talent of a 9-year-old.
And this is the level of security that your computer afforded you. If you used the Internet for long enough, your computer would start to collect a bunch of advertising malware. When you turned your computer on, you would start to see pop-ups and pop-unders with random ads, even when you weren't using browsers. So you'd do another antivirus scan, or later on you could visit websites that could also run the malware scans for you.
And not to mention the viruses that would drop the Internet to its knees once a year by doing trivial things like "adding a macro to a Word document that sends emails."
Any techie can remember going to a nontechnical relative's house. In some dusty corner, they'd have an ancient Windows computer barely hanging on by a thread. It would literally take 20 minutes to turn on.
You'd sigh and say, "let me fix this for you."
You would open two programs. This would take about 5 minutes. The first program emptied cache files and the Recycle Bin. The second was Disk Defragmenter.
Your computer slowly became unusable if you never saw this window.
Back in the day, hard drives in Wintel boxes stored data with spinning magnetic platters. The hard drive had a retractable arm with a little magnetic reader, and it would read data by retracting the arm to the right position and then moving the disk to the start of a sector.
But of course, as you add more and more files, the game of Tetris doesn't work, and the rest of your file doesn't neatly fit onto the disk before the next file's record begins. So your file would end up in two (or more) places on the hard drive. This was called fragmentation. A little bit of fragmentation was unavoidable, but if more and more files became fragmented then your computer became slower and slower until eventually Grandpa's computer took 20 minutes to start.
Many modern filesystems, Windows' included, automatically handle defragmentation in the background nowadays. But Windows did not back then. You needed to periodically manually start the defragmentation process yourself.
By the time I got into college, I discovered that Windows had a scheduler and could run Disk Defragmenter whenever I wanted, so I just left my computer on all the time and let it defragment at 5 in the morning.
Applications were heavily memory constrained, so programmers tried to save bits and bytes everywhere.
This should have been invisible to me, but it wasn't.
At one point I had a crappy video game version of Axis and Allies for the PC, released in 1998 [1] . Imagine Risk but World War 2. And the AI was really bad, and could generally be beaten easily. But the game had a major flaw: If a country had more than 255 units, the whole game would crash. And naturally the AI also loved to turtle, so it was common for the AI to have a territory with over a hundred units that was impossible to wear down. So because of this programming choice, the game was a race to wipe out the enemy before it could force a stalemate by crashing the game.
This kind of thing happened all the time. During my first programming class in my freshman year of high school, one of our lessons was effectively, "here's why you all recognize numbers like 128, 256, and maybe 65536."
Even if the software worked perfectly, you might scratch your game CD and lose the ability to play it. Then you'd start asking your friends if anyone had a spare copy of Red Alert or something, just so that you could finally finish the single-player campaign.
This wasn't unique to CDs. Anything physical could degrade. My half-brother had a NES game called Dragon Warrior or something, but the cartridge was corrupted and there was no way to leave the first room. And even if you kept all of your games in good condition, the contacts inside of the NES that connected the cartridge to the console could rust and fail. This kind of thing happened all the time.
"But Jake, that's hardware and not software." All I'm saying is that y our software was fragile and it needed to be protected and preserved. It's not like you had the option for a physical disk or the online install and you chose the disk. By the nature of distribution, the software itself would degrade and rot away from you.
One of the earliest online games I played was Diablo II, which means that I have seen the true heart of darkness inside of humanity.
Online games have a strange problem: gamers often don't want to be together. They just happen to cohabitate a space. And Diablo II had a lot of design features that lent themselves to chaos:
There were rampant client-side hacks. In PVP servers, people would use hacks to e.g. fire tracking arrows far beyond the range that they should have been able to.
All item drops were equally available to everyone in the server. That means when you got close to killing an act boss, you and your party would transition from allies to rivals and spam click when the boss finally popped.
If you had a corpse on the ground and died again, you'd lose everything you had equipped. People would try to force you to have a full inventory by dropping a bunch of cheap items onto your corpse, hoping that you'd accidentally pick up common items before picking up your corpse. Then you'd try to pick up your corpse. You'd only pick up some of the items. Then they'd kill you a second time and you'd lose everything that you managed to pick up.
The game had a lot of item duping glitches. As you can imagine, this ruined the in-game economy since it became dominated by the duped items. And it enabled a lot of scams. They'd pretend that they just duped an item, and they'd wait for someone to ask how they did it. Then they'd walk the user through step-by-step, but one step would involve dropping your item on the ground and then the scammer would pick up the item.
There was no guild system, but people still ran guilds. This means that there was no trusted way to identify guaranteed friendlies.
Many of these were fixed by the time Diablo III came around. They had extra guards against duplicated items. Bosses gave players individual drops, so there was no competition for items when you killed bosses. And you didn't need to recover items from your corpse in a way that risked you losing items. These were all hard-won lessons.
I started using my family's computer around 1990 when I learned how to read. The computer was a beige 286 that sat on our desk with the monitor perched on top. It had a 5.25" floppy drive. It had a power button. It had a reset button. And it had a TURBO button. The TURBO button was supposed to be ignored most of the time, but you could press it when you needed to slow the computer's processor down.
Why would you need to do that? Because IBM's first desktop computers ran on the 8088 processor at 4.77MHz [2] . It didn't stay this way for long. But there was a problem: many programmers wrote their applications with the assumption that computers had that 4.77MHz processor. Programmers synchronized animations, video game frame rates, and generally relied on the assumption that they were working with a fixed clock speed. If you used one of these applications on a faster processor, they would likely be unusable.
Computer manufacturers devised a simple solution: add a TURBO button that would just slow your CPU down on demand. Whenever you ran into an application that had timing issues, just press that TURBO button and watch it slow down to a comfortable speed.
I never needed to actually press the TURBO button in anger. My understanding is that most of the applications that benefitted from the TURBO button were games, and we only played newer educational games that didn't have these timing issues. When editing this post, I thought about dropping this section a few times. But can you imagine having an "Original iPhone" button on the side of your iPhone so that the Notes app could work? Good grief.
Modern software isn't perfect. It's bloated. It's slow. It was written by too many people. It's too complex. It has too many cooks in the kitchen. And now, we're losing our grasp on how it works under the hood as we delegate more and more to the agents.
But I'd never go back to the way software used to be written. Give me process isolation and online updates. Give me higher-level programming languages that abstract common pitfalls from C and C++. Give me game designers that handle timing using the system clock. Give me Steam and Windows Update. You can keep your old release process that fell by the wayside.
From what I remember from trying to install Debian in my high school years, the most popular app on Linux was anything that could edit XF86Config .
I'm having trouble corroborating this anecdote with information I can find online. The details might not be exactly right. But this is what happened, to the extent that the memory survived 25ish years.
This entry was posted in software-engineering and tagged software-engineering , software-quality , computing-history , windows , nostalgia , pc-gaming on October 27, 2026 by Jake Voytko.

title: U.S. Air Force Moves AGM-183A ARRW Hypersonic Missile Into Production
body: The $694 million contract marks a major reversal for the Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, which the Air Force nearly cancelled in 2023. The U.S. Air Force has announced on Oct. 26, 2026, that it awarded Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract to begin production of the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW). The contract represents a significant turnaround for a program that the service initially sought to cancel in 2023, following a series of unsuccessful flight tests. According to the Department of the Air Force, the contract was awarded on Sept. 29 under the Department of War’s Enterprise-Wide Agile Acquisition Contract framework. Earlier this year, the service added a $345.7 million request in its FY2027 budget which would be used for the weapon’s Increment 2 phase. “This is a turning point in our advanced weapons roadmap,” Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said in the announcement. “By moving ARRW from test to production, we’re providing our combatant commanders with a credible, high-speed strike weapon capable of penetrating the most advanced anti-access and area-denial systems.” The transition to production is intended to provide U.S. combatant commanders with a high-speed, long-range strike capability designed to penetrate advanced air defense systems and strike time-sensitive and high-value targets, says the press release . B-52 Stratofortress crews from the 23rd Expeditionary Bomb Squadron, Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota and the 49th Test and Evaluation Squadron, Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana, participated in hypersonic weapon familiarization training at Andersen Air Force Base, Guam, Feb. 27, 2024. | Source: U.S. Air Force photo by Staff Sgt. Pedro Tenorio “Fielding ARRW enhances our ability to hold targets at risk anywhere around the world,” said Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Ken Wilsbach. “This hypersonic weapon provides the Joint Force a flexible and rapid response option for highly contested environments.” The Air Force has not disclosed the number of missiles ordered or their expected delivery dates, citing operational security concerns. Nevertheless, the contract now confirms that the AGM-183 ARRW will be the U.S. Air Force’s first hypersonic weapon, which could be fielded on both the B-52H Stratofortress and the B-1B Lancer. The AGM-183 ARRW The AGM-183A ARRW is based on hypersonic glide vehicle technology derived from the Air Force and Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Science and Technology (S&T) Demonstration known as Tactical Boost Glide (TBG). A fragmenting glide vehicle is launched from a conventional rocket, or more precisely a Solid-Rocket Motor (SRM) booster, to the upper atmosphere and, once it reaches hypersonic speeds, it separates from the rocket and glides to its target at speeds up to Mach 15. At these speeds, there is no need for a conventional explosive warhead as the kinetic energy alone delivered during impact would be enough to destroy most targets. The Air Force also defined the ARRW as an “operational hypersonic air-launched weapon enabling the U.S. to hold fixed, high value, time-sensitive targets at risk in contested environments from standoff distances.” The missile would have provided a survivable, lethal, long-range strike capability to go after high-end capabilities of a potential adversary, such as deep-inland strike against targets of strategic importance and coastal strike against high-end systems. Initially, the expected introduction in service of the AGM-183 was planned for 2022. A U.S. Air Force B-52H Stratofortress loaded with two AGM-183 ARRW missiles. | Source: Courtesy photo via U.S. Air Force In 2023, the Air Force said it does not currently intend to pursue follow-on procurement of ARRW once the prototyping program concludes, adding that there is inherent benefit to completing the all-up round test flights to garner the learning and test data that will help inform future hypersonic programs. The decision apparently was influenced by the latest test flight of the missile at that time, which ended with another failure . The FY 2025 Budget Request also did not include ARRW. Although the Air Force decided in April 2023 to not pursue the procurement of the weapon , the Director, Operational Test & Evaluation report mentioned in 2024 that the ARRW program has shown preliminary indications that it could become an operationally lethal weapon, however the lack of terminal characterization data to date, due to technical failure of the test range sensor systems in the December 2022 test and the shroud not ejecting in March 2023, does not yet allow for a full assessment. Preliminary info released from the August 2023 test’s data analysis say it achieved nominal conditions. The report continues saying that, given the limited number of planned test events, there is a risk that the test program will not be able to demonstrate the ARRW lethal effects against the required tactical and strategic targets. The survivability assessment estimated the probability that a single ARRW will complete its mission, given the capabilities of various early warning radars, surface-to-air missile systems, and anti-aircraft artillery batteries to detect and engage ARRW in various one-on-one scenarios, indicating that it will meet its survivability requirements. An illustration depicting the boost glide concept applied to the AGM-183A ARRW and its flight profile. | Source: Airman Magazine/U.S. Air Force The test conducted from Guam in 2024, which saw the launch of a live AGM-183 at the Reagan Test Site in the Pacific, was considered to be the last test of the hypersonic weapon. The test was significative as it represented the first time a U.S. hypersonic weapon was seen this close to China, and was supposed to replicate an operational mission where the bomber flies for 4,000 km before launching the hypersonic weapon.

title: [OPINION] Twilight time for the CPP-NPA’s forever war
body: After the split in the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) in 1993, many doubted that the communist insurgency waged by the CPP and its New People’s Army (NPA) would ever recover. But it did, even surpassing the peak armed strength achieved in the 1980s, first in 2005 then again in 2017. Since then, however, the CPP-NPA, reeling from the government’s intense counter-insurgency operations, has fallen into a slump, in fact, into the most serious crisis in its entire 58-year history. Is it twilight time for the CPP-NPA insurgency? From very modest beginnings, the CPP-NPA grew into a powerful nationwide rebel force during the era of President Ferdinand Marcos, Sr. When the NPA launched its Maoist-style “protracted people’s war” in 1969, it started out as a ragtag band of about 60 fighters, nine automatic rifles and 26 single-shot rifles and pistols in Central Luzon. During the period of martial law, the NPA established guerrilla fronts in all of the country’s strategic mountainous areas outside of the Moro areas. NPA guerrillas engaged the Philippine military in tactical offensives, and built up its armed strength. In the early 1980s, some CPP cadres advocated adjustments to the party’s revolutionary strategy, arguing that its Maoist strategy, which involved “encircling the cities from the countryside” was much too weighted in favor of military over political struggle and rural over urban struggles. They put forward such alternative strategies as the Vietnamese version of “protracted people’s war” which regarded both military and political struggles as fundamental and decisive, and the “insurrectional strategy” of the Sandinistas in Nicaragua, which had asserted the primacy of the “insurrectional mass movement” over the military struggle. Because of the CPP’s boycott of the 1986 presidential election, the CPP and the open “national democratic” (ND) movement were left out of the “people power” uprising. But apart from being a tactical mistake, the boycott fiasco also showed up the flaw in the CPP-NPA’s revolutionary strategy. While its forces were still struggling to develop its military struggle along the stipulated stages of Mao’s “protracted people’s war,” the Filipino masses had toppled the Marcos dictatorship through an unarmed insurrection. Peace negotiations between the government of the late president Corazon Aquino and the CPP’s politico-diplomatic arm, the National Democratic Front (NDF) in 1986-87 quickly collapsed. The government had demanded that the CPP-NPA-NDF lay down its arms, while the NDF had insisted that the talks address the roots of the country’s problems. (The NDF conducted peace talks with each of the post-authoritarian administrations, but did not reach a comprehensive political settlement with any of them.) Beginning of a decline For a while after the boycott fiasco, the NPA continued to grow, reaching its highest level in 1987. The NPA was widely reported to have swelled to 25,000 fighters, although CPP founding chair Jose Ma. Sison later belied that the NPA ever reached that number in the 1980s. The CPP-NPA measures its armed strength mainly in terms of high-powered rifles (such as M16, M14, AK-47 and M1 Garand). According to Sison, the NPA’s armed strength “increased to 6,100 automatic rifles in 1986 and still further increased by some hundreds in 1987 ,” its highest level up to that time. Then the decline started. The political fallout from the boycott fiasco started impacting on the CPP-NPA. This was compounded by the revelations about the killings of hundreds of suspected government spies in the CPP-NPA’s anti-infiltration purges in 1982-89. The fall of the socialist states in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union raised questions about the very rectitude of the revolutionary left’s socialist project. Must Read [Vantage Point] What’s left for the Philippines’ Left? Disagreements within the CPP leadership related to revolutionary strategy, analysis of the contemporary situation, alternative social order, intra-party democracy and other major questions reached a boiling point in the early 1990s. Sison wrote up “Reaffirm Our Basic Principles and Rectify the Errors,” in which he lashed out at those critical of the party’s Maoist tenets, accusing them of propagating a line of “military adventurism” and “insurrectionism.” The CPP split into “reaffirmists” and “rejectionists,” with the “reaffirmists” emerging as the legatee CPP. Through most of the 1990s, the CPP-NPA suffered an ebb. At the turn of the millennium, however, the CPP-NPA started to recover. NPA guerrilla attacks picked up in many regions. The CPP-NPA intensified its collection of “revolutionary tax” from mining, agribusiness, telecommunications and construction firms, as well as of “permit-to-campaign” fees from politicians campaigning in or near NPA zones during election periods. In 2005, the NPA armed strength, it was claimed, surpassed the earlier 1987 peak by a few hundred high-powered rifles. Various counterinsurgency measures undertaken during the administration of President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, however, soon took their toll on the CPP-NPA, which then suffered a decline. In 2002, following the 9-11 terrorist attacks in the U.S., the CPP and the NPA had been included in the list of “foreign terrorist organizations” (FTOs) of the US, the European Union and Australia. The next year, as government-NDF peace talks seemed to be going nowhere, President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo added the CPP-NPA to her government’s counter-terrorist Oplan Bantay Laya, which originally targeted the Abu Sayyaf only. The Oplan strategy combined combat, intelligence and civil-military operations, and emphasized the “neutralization” of communists. Scores of open ND leaders and activists were arrested, tortured, disappeared or summarily executed. In 2006, Arroyo declared an “all-out war” against the CPP-NPA and the extrajudicial killings of leftists worsened. NPA armed strength was said to have dropped by 21.6% over 2006-2009. Starting in 2010, however, the CPP-NPA recovered again. NPA guerrilla operations intensified all over the country. In Mindanao, where the NPA was strongest, tactical offensives reportedly increased from 250 in 2010, 350 in 2011, 400 in 2012, more than 400 each in 2013 and 2014, and more than 500 in 2015. The NPA’s arena of operations, it was further claimed, expanded to 110 guerrilla fronts in 73 of the country’s 81 provinces. According to Sison, NPA armed strength “ surpassed the previous 2005 peak by 3 per cent” – that is, to over 7,000 high-powered rifles. Storm clouds But storm clouds were brewing. In late 2018, President Rodrigo Duterte adopted a “whole-of-nation” approach in combating the CPP-NDF insurgency, a year after it had terminated peace talks with the NDF. The approach, which sought to mobilize and synchronize civilian government agencies, local government units, and military forces in counterinsurgency efforts, combined barangay development projects (roads, water systems, other infrastructure, schools, health stations and livelihood assistance) with localized peace engagements (including local integration of former rebels) in conflict-affected areas. To implement such a strategy, Duterte created a multi-agency National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC), headed by the president himself. President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. continued Duterte’s “whole-of-nation” approach. From the government’s viewpoint, the “whole-of-nation” strategy has been a tremendous success. In 2024, Marcos claimed that no NPA guerrilla fronts remained active across the country. The NTF-ELCAC added that the NPA had been reduced to only 785 “remnants.” In the light of many reports of clashes between the military and the NPA over the last two years, the government’s exultant claims are not credible. But the CPP-NPA has indeed suffered grave setbacks. Since the launching of the “whole-of-nation” approach, NPA numbers have dropped considerably, and guerrilla attacks have declined. The International Crisis Group (ICG) estimates that the NPA has shrunk to between 1,200 and 2,000 fighters . The CPP-NPA no longer provides figures of NPA tactical offensives, but the number of clashes between government forces and Red fighters are indicative of the CPP-NPA’s decline. According to the international NGO Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) , only 106 clashes occurred between government forces and the NPA in 2025 versus 273 in 2020 – a 61% decline in five years. Mindanao, as a whole, is no longer the main NPA flash point. The main areas of armed encounters have shifted from Western Visayas and Northern Mindanao to Eastern Visayas and Caraga . Must Read [OPINION] How the Philippine Left lost its way Over the past eight years, many top CPP-NPA leaders have been killed by the military – in combat or through summary execution. Among them are CPP chairman Benito Tiamzon and secretary-general Wilma Tiamzon, as well as Julius Giron, Antonio Cabanatan, Jorge Madlos, Menandro Villanueva, Maria Concepcion Araneta, Eugenia Magpantay, Randall Echanis and Mariano Adlao. Some other top leaders, such as Victor Ladlad and Rey Casambre. have been arrested and incarcerated. The Philippines’ “all-of-nation” approach has been widely criticized for thousands of human rights violations – illegal arrests, detentions, torture, extrajudicial killings and disappearances. Many open, legal progressive activists have become easy targets of government harassment and repression. Obsessed with its counterinsurgency drive, the government has largely ignored the criticisms and denunciations of human rights groups. According to the ICG, the CPP-NPA is at its lowest ebb in decades. Will it be able to recover as it has in the past? Massive losses One factor that will make recovery difficult is that the CPP-NPA has lost many of its most experienced leaders over the past eight years or so. Apart from top leaders killed or arrested and imprisoned by the military, some senior, long-serving leaders have passed away peacefully, among them Sison himself, Jose Luneta, Fidel Agcaoili and Luis Jalandoni. A few other veterans have been incapacitated by health problems. The loss of the likes of Sison, Jalandoni and Madlos has also left a big gap in the CPP-NPA’s public-facing spokespersons. The CPP-NPA may partially recover for a while, but one thing is definite: it will never be able to achieve the total military victory that it has long aspired for. Its fundamental Maoist principles stipulate that before the revolutionary forces can triumph, the “protracted people’s war” has to progress from guerrilla warfare to regular mobile warfare and eventually to positional warfare; and from strategic defensive to strategic stalemate and eventually to strategic offensive. All through nearly six decades of fighting, the NPA has been stuck in guerrilla warfare and the strategic defensive. Endeavoring to extricate the CPP-NPA from its guerrilla warfare rut, NPA chieftain Romulo Kintanar had pushed for the establishment of bigger NPA formations and for “regularization” in the 1980s. Sison accused him of “military adventurism” and had him expelled from the CPP-NPA, then assassinated. Kintanar had established extensive international linkages for the NPA, knowing that only external sources could provide a sizeable and steady supply of arms and ammunition needed for moving up to regular warfare. This international network withered away after the takeover of the NPA by the “reaffirmist” CPP leadership. (It must be noted here that the Moro National Liberation Front and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, during their wars for secession, did manage to secure arms from external sources, but still did not achieve military victory against the government.) The CPP-NPA’s “protracted people’s war” has gone on much longer than any of America’s “forever wars.” As defined by Cambridge Dictionary , a forever war is “a war that never ends because it cannot be won.” It is a prolonged, open-ended armed conflict without a clear, achievable endpoint or decisive victory. The war without end between the government and the CPP-NPA has already claimed between 40,000 to 60,000 lives. Yet, each year, on the NPA’s anniversary on March 29, it celebrates the protraction of its “people’s war.” It’s twilight time for the CPP-NPA’s forever war. Mao’s rural and peasant-based “protracted people’s war,” employed in “semicolonial, semifeudal” China a century ago, simply has been a bad fit for an urbanizing Philippine society with a middle income economy that has shifted away from agriculture and is increasingly dominated by wage labor and the service sector. Communist insurgencies are on the wane worldwide. The CPP-NPA insurgency is one of a handful of major communist insurgencies still surviving in the contemporary world. Two of them, both Maoist, have not fared any better than the CPP-NPA. India’s Naxalites (Communist Party of India – Maoist), who have waged a 59-year-old “people’s war,” are dwindling, reduced to isolated pockets and struggling with recruitment and funding, with a leadership severely degraded. Peru’s Shining Path (Communist Party of Peru), whose founder, Abimael Guzman, was captured in 1992 and died in prison in 2021, has been all but dismantled, with a few splinter groups financing themselves mainly through cocaine trafficking. If the CPP still hopes to come to power, it should work out a comprehensive political settlement with the government and strive to turn its still appreciable mass base into an electoral base. All of the government-NDF peace negotiations have come to naught. The CPP-NPA-NDF has only been interested in eking out tactical gains – propaganda, release of political prisoners, immunity for “NDF negotiators,” so-called “belligerency status” – while still obdurately aiming for total military victory. Protracted negotiations was merely a tactic in its “protracted people’s war.” The CPP could take the cue from the its counterparts in Nepal, the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist, now Maoist Centre) , which signed a peace agreement with the Nepalese government in 2006 and became the ruling party through democratic elections in 2008–2009 and has been in the ruling coalition several times since then. Back in 1991, writing under the pseudonym Omar Tupaz , I commented on the CPP-NPA’s Maoist “protracted people’s war” strategy: “It will be difficult, if not impossible, to win a revolution in the 1990s by continuing to adhere to a basic strategic framework of a bygone era.” Unfortunately for the CPP-NPA, this seems to be coming to pass. – Rappler.com Nathan Gilbert Quimpo authored Contested Democracy and the Left after Marcos and co-authored Subversive Lives: A Family Memoir of the Marcos Years. In the 1980s and 1990s, he penned critiques of the communist party’s revolutionary strategy under the pseudonym Marty Villalobos and Omar Tupaz .

title: Zelenskyy discusses with leaders of Finland and Norway their conversation with Putin
body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that he had discussed with President of Finland Alexander Stubb and Prime Minister of Norway Jonas Gahr Støre their conversation with Vladimir Putin.
“Spoke with President of Finland and Prime Minister of Norway Alexander Stubb and Jonas Gahr Store following their call today with the Russian leader and as a continuation of our discussions in Oslo with representatives of America, Europe, and NATO. I am grateful for the detailed briefing and for their active support for our diplomacy and the peace efforts we are pursuing together with all our partners,” Zelenskyy said on X Tuesday.
According to Zelenskyy, Stubb and Støre made it clear to the Russian leader that concrete steps toward de-escalation are required, specifically regarding Ukraine’s energy sector and infrastructure. The Ukrainian president also noted that, during the conversation, they discussed preparations for a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, the USA, and Russia scheduled for November to be held at the team level.
"Finland and Norway, as countries that border Russia, have a particular interest in sound and reliable security arrangements. We also discussed various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security," he said.
"There must be peace, de-escalation is needed, and Russia must stop dragging out the war. I thank everyone who stands with Ukraine!" the head of the Ukrainian state summed up.
As reported earlier today, the President of Finland and the Prime Minister of Norway initiated a phone call with Putin. According to Stubb, the discussion was "frank and businesslike."

title: Saudi Arabia Launches Avante 2200-class Corvette HMS NEOM in Spain
body:
The Royal Saudi Naval Forces (RSNF ) ha s launched HMS NEOM , the second corvette of Phase II of the Al-Sarawat Project, at Spanish shipbuilder Navantia’s San Fernando shipyard.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defense said the vessel will undergo systems integration, technical testing and sea trials before entering operational service.
The HMS NEOM is an Avante 2200-class multipurpose corvette designed for maritime surveillance, search and rescue, anti-submarine warfare, air defense, surface warfare and electronic warfare. According to published class specifications, the vessel measures 104m in length and 14m in beam, with a fully loaded displacement of approximately 2,670 tons. Its combined diesel-and-diesel (CODAD) propulsion system uses four MTU diesel engines producing 23,600 horsepower, enabling a maximum speed of 27 knots and a range of approximately 4,500 nautical miles at cruising speed. The vessel can accommodate up to 102 personnel.
The class’s combat systems include the HAZEM combat management system, developed through the SAMI-Navantia partnership, Leonardo Kronos NV 3D radar, Thales electro-optical tracking systems, and hull-mounted and variable-depth sonars. Its published armament configuration includes a 76 mm Leonardo Super Rapid main gun, a 35 mm Rheinmetall Oerlikon Millennium close-in weapon system, a 16-cell vertical launch system for Evolved Sea Sparrow Missiles (ESSM), eight Harpoon Block II anti-ship missiles and two triple 324 mm torpedo launchers. A flight deck and hangar support a helicopter in the 10-tonne class. These are class-level specifications and do not independently confirm that every system has been installed or certified aboard HMS NEOM.
Phase II comprises three corvettes and will expand Saudi Arabia’s Avante 2200 fleet to eight ships. HMS Al-Madinah (Hull No. 6), the first vessel of the second phase, was launched on June 18, 2026, and is being completed and commissioned in Spain. HMS Al-Ula (Hull No. 8) remains under block construction and assembly, with its launch expected next. Like HMS NEOM, it is expected to undergo final combat-systems completion in Saudi Arabia.
The program aims to strengthen the Royal Saudi Naval Forces while progressively localizing technical assembly and developing domestic defense expertise under Saudi Vision 2030. Full operational delivery of the three Phase II vessels is targeted for 2029.
