title: Russian Commander Complains NATO Testing Drones on Ukraine’s Front Line
body:
In an interview with Russia’s state news agency TASS on Tuesday, Oct. 27 the commander of Moscow’s Akhmat special forces unit, Lt. Gen. Apti Alaudinov complained that NATO nations were using the war in Ukraine to test drone technology in combat against Russia.
He commented that large numbers of Western manufactured unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) were being encountered: “We see that drones manufactured in all these countries, which are members of the NATO alliance, are being tested against us on the line of engagement.”
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Alaudinov claimed that these included drones of every type, capability and operational ranges. According to him, this not only included first-person view (FPV) drones used to attack Russian forces and equipment on the front line but also included long-range UAVs that were being used to carry out deep strikes against towns, cities and infrastructure inside Russia.
In March 2022, in the earliest days of the war, the US Council on Foreign relations commented on how Ukraine relied on drones sourced from Turkey, the Bayraktar TB2, as a means of disrupting Russian tank columns on their march towards Kyiv. Their appearance on the battlefield seemed at first to be a game changer, but it was not long before their vulnerability was exploited by Moscow’s air defenses.
However, the value of drones in taking the war to the enemy and the need for countermeasures was soon appreciated by both sides which led to the battlefield dominance UAVs currently enjoy.
Recent statements by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense and reports in the Western mainstream and social media seem to partially confirm Alaudinov’s assertions. Ukraine is cooperating with both government and commercial drone-related programs, not only using “attack” and surveillance drones but also to develop counter-drone technology and tactics.
A July report by the Ministry of Defense explained how it was working with NATO’s Allied Command Transformation (ACT) agency using its battlefield experience to support NATO in developing ways to combat drones. The report says this shows that “Ukraine is not only receiving support from its partners but is also actively shaping their approaches to modern warfare.”
On Monday the US publication The Hill reported on comments made by US Air Force Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, SACEUR, at a meeting in Poland. This followed on from an earlier report by Bloomberg on plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced drones to defend the alliance. The general laid out a possible strategy in the event of an attack by Russia , the concept of “blunt, block and break.” The articles suggested that the mass use of UAVs would be key to the success of Grynkewich’s plan and suggested that virtually every military was developing UAV-based concepts supplemented with AI for warfighting.
A week ago, the Wall Street Journal reported on how Ukraine’s “Kill Zone” was being used to test and develop the use of AI in drones. This followed a report in the defense issues website the Defense Post that discussed how Ukraine had been deploying AI tools developed in the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC) to both plan and control its UAV operations and to predict Russian drone activity. It said a prototype system was undergoing real-time validation by Ukrainian forces.
CBS reported in September that Washington and Kyiv were in the process of agreeing on a policy that would allow the two countries to expand the testing and production of Ukrainian defense technology in the US. It was given new impetus by the use of Iranian drones against US forces in the Middle East.
The report cites experts saying the experience gained by Ukraine in developing drone software and operations, as well as the speed with which it could adapt to battlefield changes, were likely to prove invaluable to the use of drones by the US and its allies.
Deborah Fairlamb, partner in a US venture capital firm that is investing in Ukrainian defense technology, told CBS: “The West needs to start understanding better is that it’s not just about having the tech. It’s about how the tech is used. And this is where Ukraine’s knowledge, skills, experience really need to be transmitted.”
In a separate report on its YouTube channel in July, CBS reported on how Ukraine was deploying US drone technology, such as the “Shield AI” V-Bat vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) reconnaissance and targeting UAV, to support long-range strikes into Russia.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: CSTO in No Hurry to Help Tajikistan
body: The authorities in Tajikistan have been ringing the alarm bells over events in neighboring Afghanistan for more than three decades. The Tajik government did so again after violence broke out along a small section of the Tajik-Afghan border in the last months of 2025, and specifically called on the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) for assistance. The CSTO has responded, but the promised aid has yet to arrive as Tajikistan continues to seek stronger border defenses. The Perennial Border Problem There had been unrest in Afghanistan since the late 1970s, long before Tajikistan became independent in late 1991, and the instability along Tajikistan’s approximately 1,360-kilometer border with Afghanistan has continued ever since. Most of the border area is mountainous and sparsely inhabited, making it ideal for narcotics and weapons smuggling. Weapons smuggling was a huge problem during Tajikistan’s 1992-1997 civil war, when weapons were being brought back and forth across the Afghan frontier to fuel civil conflicts in both countries. From the first day of Tajikistan’s independence until June 2005, Russian border guards helped keep watch on Tajikistan’s Afghan frontier. At least several hundred Russian and Tajik border guards, and Tajik and Afghan smugglers and militants have been killed along the Tajik-Afghan border in the last 35 years. Many countries worried about Tajikistan’s border problems with Afghanistan. Neighbors such as China, the other Central Asian states, and not so far away, Russia did not want narcotics or militants from Afghanistan reaching their countries. In the mid- and late-1990s, the Taliban push through Afghanistan to the Central Asian border increased these neighbors’ concerns. After the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks in New York and Washington, the United States and its allies used facilities in Central Asia to support troops in Afghanistan. All these countries, and more, contributed to Tajikistan’s border defenses in some way, either by simply donating housing materials or winter uniforms, or providing security monitoring equipment and weaponry. It has never been enough to totally stem the border problems, but the security aid Tajikistan received is far more than the country could ever have allocated for that purpose from its state coffers. Emomali Rahmon was Tajikistan’s president in the late 1990s when the Taliban first seized power in Afghanistan. Rahmon viewed the Taliban as a threat, and Tajikistan’s policies toward the Afghan militant group reflected that. Rahmon’s opinion of the Taliban did not change when they regained power in 2021, and despite the other Central Asian states establishing a dialogue and trade ties with the Taliban, Tajikistan has been slow to engage the returned rulers of Afghanistan. In June 2024, Rahmon’s eldest son and heir apparent, Rustam Emomali, told a meeting of the CSTO’s Parliamentary Assembly Council that “Afghanistan has once again become a breeding ground for terrorism.” Emomali said more than 1,000 radical madrassahs had been established in Afghanistan, some in areas close to Tajikistan’s border, and that these religious schools were also preparing suicide bombers. A Turbulent End to 2025 In late August 2025, Tajik border guards in the Shamsiddin Shohin district reportedly exchanged gunfire with Taliban fighters on the other side of the Pyanj River that separates the two countries. At least one Taliban fighter was killed and four others wounded . The cause of the shootout was never clear, though suspicions were that it was related to gold-mining operations, legal and illegal, that are being carried out on both sides of the river. This incident was particularly notable because, after the shooting stopped, a group of Tajik border guards crossed into Afghanistan for talks with local officials and Taliban fighters. There were reports of another gun battle happening between Tajik border guards and Taliban troops in late October, not far from where the August shooting occurred. Reports mentioned casualties on both sides, but did not give any figures or provide any details as to the cause. Then in November, on the Tajik side of the border, five Chinese workers were killed and four others wounded in two separate attacks from the Afghan side. The first attack on November 26 included a commercial drone with explosives hitting a gold-mining site in the Shamsiddin Shohin district that killed three Chinese workers and wounded two others. The second occurred in the Darvaz district, which neighbors the Shamsiddin Shohin district to the east. Gunfire from the Afghan side of the border on November 30 killed two Chinese road workers and wounded two others. It caused China to temporarily withdraw its workers from the Tajik border area and prompted the Tajik government to call on the CSTO for help. Threat Assessment Tajikistan is a CSTO member along with Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Russia. Rahmon met in Dushanbe with CSTO Secretary General Taalatbek Masadykov on April 10, 2026, where he emphasized the need to implement CSTO decisions on responding to security threats. The organization had already approved a program to strengthen the Tajik-Afghan border in November 2024. In June, the CSTO appeared ready to accelerate assistance to Tajikistan. Viktor Vasilyev, the chairman of the CSTO Permanent Council, said the organization was particularly concerned about gunfire from the Afghan side of the border being directed into Tajikistan. “Despite steps taken by Russia and several Central Asian states to establish contact with the authorities in Kabul, the security situation remains complex,” Vasilyev said . However, Vasilyev also devoted much attention to other CSTO matters , such as increasing indications that Armenia would suspend its membership in the organization, tensions between Belarus and Ukraine, and NATO maneuvers. In late August, Masadykov told TASS in an interview that the first shipment of armaments and military equipment would arrive in Tajikistan in the autumn. On October 21, Masadykov said the first stage of sending military assistance to Tajikistan, which he explained involved customers in Tajikistan selecting suppliers and agreeing on order amounts, was complete. The second stage was already underway, with the first shipments of weapons and equipment expected to arrive in Tajikistan before the end of the year. Masadykov also mentioned the military shipment being sent to Tajikistan would “in no way” be a threat to Afghanistan or its people. He didn’t detail which weapons or military equipment Tajikistan will soon receive, but the pace of assistance may be a disappointment to the Tajik government. The Tajik authorities have long been seeking stronger defenses to deter people on the Afghan side of the border from launching attacks or trying to illegally cross into Tajikistan. There were several more incidents along the Tajik-Afghan border in December 2025 and January 2026, and some border guards were killed. For the Tajik government, accustomed to receiving substantial security aid in response to its concerns, this is probably more than a temporary letdown. The CSTO is a Russian-led organization, and Russia is currently the only country that officially recognizes the Taliban government in Afghanistan. While Russia might be the only country to give official recognition to the Taliban, others are at least doing business with the current government in Afghanistan. Uzbekistan’s National Statistics Committee released figures on October 21 that show Afghanistan is Uzbekistan’s third largest export market , behind Russia and China. The Tajik authorities continue to look at Afghanistan as a security problem, and it is, but perhaps not as much as it has been in the past. Other governments appear less concerned about threats from Afghanistan, and the pace of CSTO military assistance could be a sign that Tajikistan’s worries about its southern neighbor are not shared to the same extent by the international community. The CSTO might continue to hype the potential threat from Afghanistan to help justify its own existence , but the next time Dushanbe needs to strengthen its Afghan border, it might fall more heavily on Tajikistan itself to do whatever needs to be done.

title: Ukrainian strikes kill 50 Russian civilians, including child, last week — envoy
body:
LUGANSK, October 27. /TASS/. Fifty Russian civilians, including a child, were killed last week in attacks by the Ukrainian armed forces, while more than 260 people, including seven minors, were injured, Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik told TASS.
"Over the past week, 313 civilians were affected by Ukrainian shelling: 263 civilians were injured, including seven minors, and 50 people were killed, including a child. <…> The highest number of civilian casualties over the past week was recorded in the Belgorod, Bryansk, Zaporozhye, Kursk, Kherson, and Oryol Regions, as well as in the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics," he said.
Miroshnik specified that 278 people, which is 89% of the total number of casualties, were injured in enemy unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) strikes.
In total, according to the diplomat, over the past seven days, Kiev has fired more than 8,200 various types of munitions into the territory of Russian regions.

title: PAU Alumni President Calls for Stronger Varsity-Industry Partnerships to Drive Nigeria’s Devt
body: The President of the Pan-Atlantic University Alumni Association (PAUAA), Dr. Onyebuchi Odianjo, has called for stronger partnerships between universities and industry to drive Nigeria’s development, strengthen professional networks and create opportunities for sustainable economic growth. Odianjo made the call at the inaugural Pan-Atlantic University Alumni Association International Conference, themed ‘The Advantage: Connecting People, Ideas and Opportunities,’ held at the Ecobank Pan African Centre in Lagos. She reaffirmed the association’s commitment to building a vibrant alumni community that translates shared values and professional relationships into meaningful collaborations, student support and broader economic impact. “Our goal remains clear: to build an alumni community whose values extend beyond shared memories to meaningful relationships, mutual support and collective progress. What began as a conversation about the potential of our alumni network grew into a vision for a platform where people, ideas and industries could connect, relationships could become partnerships, and ideas could become opportunities,” Odianjo said. Delivering the keynote address, MD/CEO, Coleman Technical Industries Limited (Manufacturers of Coleman Wires and Cables), George Olutope Onafowokan, stressed that integrity, character and discipline are fundamental to building sustainable businesses and driving long-term economic development. He identified vision, focus, discipline, integrity and good character as essential principles for professional and corporate success, urging business leaders to prioritise ethical conduct and sustainable business practices. “Integrity is your biggest weighted gold, not your car, not your house, not your land. Build it from the day you start your life. The entitlement mentality is the greatest killer of integrity. When you build character and integrity, you derisk yourself, and doing business or leading people becomes seamless,” Onafowokan asserted. He cautioned business founders against establishing enterprises primarily to finance personal lifestyles, noting that businesses are more likely to survive generational transitions when supported by sound governance, sustainable structures and leadership by example. In her address, the Vice-Chancellor of Pan-Atlantic University, Professor Enase Okonedo, commended the Alumni Association’s executive committee for organising the conference and highlighted the importance of values-driven leadership in national transformation. She noted that the university’s growth over the past 34 years reflects the potential of education to develop leaders capable of making meaningful contributions to Nigeria. “We grew from humble beginnings 34 years ago, starting in a living room in Sierra Leone. Today, we sit across expanded campuses with a collective alumni body of 15,000 between the business school and the university. Think about 15,000 well-formed people who can make a difference in Nigeria. You are the ambassadors, and PAU graduates are beginning to stand out not only for their work ethic, but also for their values,” Okonedo stated. The conference brought together alumni, business leaders and other stakeholders to strengthen professional relationships, foster university-industry collaboration and explore opportunities for innovation, enterprise development and national progress.

title: US Air Force puts once-canceled ARRW hypersonic missile into production
body:
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Lockheed Martin a US$694 million contract to produce and field the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW), reviving a hypersonic missile that the service had decided not to buy just three years ago.
The contract was signed on September 29 but disclosed by the Air Force on October 26. The service said the agreement formally moves ARRW from prototyping and flight testing into production.
The Air Force did not disclose how many missiles will be manufactured or when deliveries will begin, citing operational security.
ARRW is a boost-glide weapon designed for long-range strikes against high-value and time-sensitive targets protected by advanced air defenses. A solid-fuel rocket accelerates the missile beyond Mach 5 before releasing an unpowered hypersonic glide vehicle that can maneuver toward its target.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
The B-52H Stratofortress, which has been extensively used during the ARRW test program, will be the weapon's initial operational platform. The Air Force has also worked on integrating the missile with the B-1B Lancer.
The production contract completes an unusual reversal for a program that appeared to be approaching its end in 2023.
Lockheed Martin began developing ARRW for the Air Force in 2018, and captive-carry testing with the B-52H followed in 2019. The program subsequently suffered a series of test failures, including three unsuccessful launch attempts in 2021.
The first successful booster test came in May 2022, when an ARRW released from a B-52H separated successfully, ignited its rocket motor and exceeded Mach 5.
A complete missile was successfully tested for the first time in December 2022 . Another all-up-round test in March 2023 encountered problems, prompting renewed questions about the future of the program.
Later that month, then-Air Force acquisition chief Andrew Hunter told lawmakers that the service did not intend to proceed with ARRW procurement. The remaining tests would be completed to collect data, while investment shifted toward the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM).
ARRW nevertheless continued flying. Additional testing provided the Air Force with more data on the complete weapon, including a March 2024 launch from a B-52H that demonstrated its ability to engage a land target.
By 2025, the position had changed. Then-Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin told Congress that the service intended to purchase ARRW, and the fiscal year 2026 budget subsequently provided US$362 million to restart production and begin procurement.
The fiscal year 2027 budget request adds another US$452 million for ARRW procurement. Air Force planning documents project annual spending of between US$556 million and US$621 million from 2028 through 2031, although the number of weapons associated with those amounts has not been made public.
The decision creates an unusual outcome for the Air Force's two major air-launched hypersonic weapon programs.
HACM became the service's priority when ARRW procurement was abandoned in 2023, but the Raytheon-developed weapon is still in flight testing. ARRW has now become the first U.S. Air Force hypersonic weapon to enter production.
The two missiles use different approaches to hypersonic flight. ARRW uses a rocket booster and an unpowered glide vehicle, while HACM is a smaller air-breathing cruise missile powered by a scramjet engine.
Their intended employment also differs. ARRW's size favors bombers such as the B-52 and B-1, while HACM is being developed as a more compact weapon that can be carried by tactical aircraft.
The Air Force is also funding development of an improved version of the weapon rather than treating the current AGM-183A as the end of the program.
Its fiscal year 2027 research budget requests US$296 million for ARRW Increment 2, including development of a terminal seeker and data link as well as hardware changes and initiatives intended to reduce production costs.
Those additions would give the weapon a capability absent from the original ARRW: the ability to receive targeting information and locate a target during the final portion of its flight.
That could allow Increment 2 to engage moving targets rather than only predetermined locations, opening the possibility of using the hypersonic weapon against targets such as warships.

title: Airbus awarded contract for two additional Galileo satellites
body:
Ottobrunn, Germany, Oct 27, 2026. The European Space Agency (ESA), acting on behalf of the EU Agency for the Space Programme (EUSPA), under a delegation of the European Commission, has awarded Airbus a contract to build two additional second-generation Galileo satellites. Building on an existing order of six second generation Galileo (G2) satellites, this additional pair will benefit from existing manufacturing capabilities and reaffirms this successful partnership.



“With these contracts, ESA and European industry are safeguarding the continuity of Europe’s satellite navigation services, responding to the evolving needs of users, and strengthening Europe’s strategic autonomy. These contracts represent an investment in Europe’s ability to navigate its own future, independently and with confidence,” said Laurent Jaffart, ESA Director of Resilience, Navigation and Connectivity.

“This latest award for two additional sophisticated Galileo satellites underscores Airbus’ satellite manufacturing expertise. We are committed to delivering these next-generation satellites which are vital to augment navigation capabilities for European security and defence and wider societal benefits,” said Alain Fauré, Head of Space Systems at Airbus.

The G2 satellites will incorporate enhanced navigation antennas to enhance the accuracy of the flagship European Global Navigation Satellite System. The spacecraft will be equipped with higher-strength navigation antennas as well as fully digital payloads which are reconfigurable in orbit, enabling them to actively respond to evolving user needs with novel signals and services. Airbus will draw on its coordinated production programme to leverage spacecraft manufacturing, integration, and testing expertise across Airbus sites including Backnang (near Stuttgart), Friedrichshafen, Getafe (near Madrid), Ottobrunn and Toulouse.



Each satellite will incorporate an enhanced atomic clock configuration as well as inter-satellite links to communicate and cross-check data. They will also feature advanced anti-jamming and anti-spoofing capabilities to safeguard Galileo’s signals. The spacecraft will each weigh more than two tonnes and will operate in orbit for 15 years.

A flagship programme of the EU, Galileo is funded by the European Union and managed by the European Commission. Since its inception, ESA leads the design, development and qualification of the space and ground systems, as well as procuring launches. ESA is also entrusted with research and development activities for the future of Galileo within the EU programme Horizon Europe. The EU Agency for the Space Programme (EUSPA) acts as the service provider, oversees the service operations and deployment of the Galileo system, including launch services, and ensures it meets market and user needs.“Galileo” is registered as a trademark in the database of the European Union Intellectual Property Office (n° 002742237).

title: ‘Delays Directly Assist Russia’: Zelensky Slams Slow Delivery of Interceptors
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized delays in the delivery of air defense interceptors for Patriot and NASAMS systems on Tuesday, Oct. 27, saying they directly help Russia carry out its attacks.
“The artificial and prolonged delays in the delivery of interceptor packages for Patriot and NASAMS systems – which have unfortunately been occurring recently – directly assist Russia in achieving the goals of its terrorist campaign,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Every such delay results in another Russian strike hitting a target. Sadly, these attacks happen every single day,” he added, calling for stronger pressure on Moscow and timely military assistance to Kyiv.
The overnight attack hit Kyiv, including the Pivdennyi (South) Bridge, as well as energy, logistics, and civilian infrastructure in multiple regions.
At the time, Zelensky said the number of people injured in the Russian strike on a university campus and surrounding area had risen to 12, including five university students and staff. However, per updated reports, the overnight assault resulted in one person killed and 15 others injured.
“While emergency services were assisting people and addressing the aftermath of the initial strike, the Russians launched ballistic missiles again,” Zelensky wrote.
He said Russia had fired 16 ballistic missiles overnight, along with more than 280 drones.
According to Zelensky, Russian strikes were reported in Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, Kherson, and the Chernivtsi regions.
“In almost every instance, the Russian targets were energy infrastructure, logistics, and civilian urban infrastructure,” he said.
Zelensky stressed that pressure on Russia and concrete support for Ukraine were necessary to change the situation. He thanked those who support Ukraine’s defense and understand the importance of ensuring that military aid arrives on time.
“We must bring peace closer and save lives,” he said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or neutralized two Russian Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 255 drones during an overnight attack primarily targeting Kyiv, the Air Force reported.
Impacts were recorded at 25 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at 16 locations.
The attack prompted the closure of Kyiv’s South (Pivdennyi) Bridge and disruptions on the Green Line metro. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko released the first photos showing damage to the bridge, which remains closed as specialists assess the damage.
Authorities have not announced when traffic or normal metro service will resume.
In Kyiv, strikes also damaged an administrative building in the Podilskyi district and other non-residential buildings.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has asked the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland to provide 10% of their existing stocks of Patriot and IRIS-T interceptor missiles to help defend against Russian attacks.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Kyiv proposed exchanging the missiles for ammunition already contracted for future delivery. Ukraine also needs additional man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS).
Following talks in Paris, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said European partners had prepared winter aid packages for Ukraine and were working with Kyiv to develop an air defense system.
On Monday, Oct. 26, Zelensky said Ukraine had waited nearly a month for US approval of Patriot and NASAMS missiles and would raise the issue with Washington again.
He said Ukraine received only 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over 90 days, despite needing around 350 per month, and has sought 300 interceptors from European partners for winter.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Chinese visitor numbers to Georgia rise by 23% in nine months, setting a record
body: Between January and September 2026, Georgia received 119,081 visitors from China. According to the Georgian National Tourism Administration, this represents a 23.6% increase on the same period last year. The figure for the first nine months of 2026 marks a 15-year record. Excluding 2025 and 2024, the number of Chinese visitors in those nine months alone exceeds the annual total for every other year since 2011, when the authorities began collecting these statistics. ‘Georgia and China are entering a new phase in their relationship’ — Kobakhidze briefing Georgian tea with Chinese twist: Why are entrepreneurs from China so interested in Georgia? Opinion: ‘Georgian Dream is telling US: We do not want relations with you, we prefer China’ According to data from the Georgian National Tourism Administration, the number of visitors arriving in Georgia from China over the past several years has been as follows: 2025 — 127,895 visitors; 2024 — 88,583 visitors; 2023 — 48,304 visitors; 2022 — 7,380 visitors; 2021 — 3,468 visitors; 2020 — 4,363 visitors; 2019 — 48,071 visitors; 2018 — 31,855 visitors; 2017 — 18,179 visitors; 2016 — 10,847 visitors; 2015 — 6,849 visitors; 2014 — 5,919 visitors; 2013 — 6,641 visitors; 2012 — 7,633 visitors; 2011 — 4,848 visitors. The figures show that the number of visitors from China nearly doubled in 2024 compared with 2023, and continued to grow in 2025. The total for the first nine months of 2026 has already approached the full-year figure for 2025. Despite the increase in visitors from China, the overall number of visits by international travellers to Georgia remained virtually unchanged in the first nine months of 2026. According to the tourism administration, Georgia recorded 6,112,078 visits by international travellers between January and September. This was just 0.04% higher than in the same period in 2025. The figures therefore show that the number of visitors from China is growing, while the overall number of international travellers remains almost unchanged. Background The rise in visitors from China comes amid deepening ties between Georgia and China. China is gradually becoming a key strategic partner for Georgia. In July 2023, following a visit to China by former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili , the two countries announced a strategic partnership. On 10 April 2024, they signed an agreement introducing visa-free travel for holders of ordinary passports. The agreement came into force on 28 May that year. It allows citizens of both countries to stay in the other country without a visa for up to 30 days. Opinion: 'China gets more from Georgia than Georgia gets from China' Conflict analyst Giorgi Koberidze argues that economic and political relations between Georgia and China should be clearly distinguished In July 2025, representatives of the Georgian and Chinese foreign ministries held political consultations in Beijing. In June 2026, the presidents of Georgia and China, Mikheil Kavelashvili and Xi Jinping , exchanged messages to mark the 34th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries. During this exchange, they agreed to elevate bilateral ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership. According to the Georgian Foreign Ministry, co-operation with China covers areas including the economy, trade, investment, transport, culture and humanitarian ties. Many experts, however, take a sceptical view of such close ties and the strategic partnership with China. Giorgi Koberidze , head of the Centre for Political Research at GIPA (the Georgian Institute of Public Affairs) and an expert on conflict issues, argues that although economic co-operation between Georgia and China is significant, Tbilisi is not achieving the political results one would expect from a strategic partnership. Another conflict expert, Paata Zakareishvili , notes , that China has never voted in Georgia’s favour. He argues that China effectively attaches little importance to its relations with Georgia, and that the Georgian Dream party is trying to mislead voters by building this partnership. title: Putin briefs Stubb, Store on launch of humanitarian operation in Alyoshki
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin briefed Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store on the beginning of a US-mediated humanitarian operation in the city of Alyoshki, the Kremlin press service said after their phone call.
"The Russian president briefed them on the launch of a US-brokered humanitarian operation in the area around the Russian settlement of Alyoshki and the establishment of a localized ceasefire in the Kherson sector for this purpose," it said.
Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov on September 21 described the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki as critical as food and medicines could not be delivered to the city amid Ukrainian shelling and drone attacks. During a phone call with US leader Donald Trump on October 9, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that regarding the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki, it was agreed that Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova would remain in regular contact with Melania Trump’s staff.
Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Army Valery Gerasimov announced on October 23 that Russian forces will enforce a localized ceasefire at 1:00 a.m. GMT on October 27 to allow for a humanitarian operation near Alyoshki. He said that to ensure the security of people and delivery of vital social supplies, engineering reconnaissance will be carried out and a safe passage of humanitarian aid to the locality of Alyoshki will be provided.
Peskov pointed out on October 26 that the agreement to conduct a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki could set a precedent for similar missions in other areas. He particularly highlighted the United States’ direct and constructive role in coordinating the process. Peskov added that Russia hoped Ukraine would honor all agreements concerning the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.

title: AI promised less work. I've never worked more
body:
The pitch was that AI would give us our time back. Write less boilerplate, delegate the boring parts, go home earlier.
I am not complaining about the tools. I use agents for all of my engineering work now, and I wrote about how that setup evolved and why I still read the code . I can investigate and ship things that would not have been worth starting two years ago.
But somewhere this year I noticed that I am working more than I ever have, and that it feels heavier than it used to. Not because any single task is harder. Because there are so many more of them, all at once.
This post is me trying to understand that, with some data from my own GitHub history.
As a full-stack engineer, a normal week for me meant two or three serious tasks. A feature, a tricky bug, maybe a migration. Each one needed real focus, but I could hold one of them in my head at a time, finish it, and move to the next.
Today my week looks completely different. I have several agents running in parallel: one implementing a change, one investigating a production question, one working through a review, another doing research I will need later. None of them needs me all the time. Every one of them needs me sometimes .
Each agent eventually comes back with a question, a plan to approve, a diff to read or a result to make sense of. Responding means switching contexts: reloading a different problem, a different repository and a different set of decisions.
Two or three serious tasks a week was tiring in a familiar way. Working with many agents is tiring in a new way. My attention is spread across more problems, and I find moving between them much more mentally draining.
I pulled my GitHub contribution calendar for every month from January 2019 to today and marked my roles at Bold.org , which I joined in January 2020: Full Stack Engineer until August 2022, Principal Engineer until August 2025, and Vice President of Technology since then. These are GitHub’s contribution counts, including private work, so they mix commits, pull requests, reviews and issues. It is a rough signal of activity, not a measure of value. 2019 is an incomplete baseline: my job before Bold.org used a self-hosted GitLab, so GitHub only shows what I did outside it. But the shape is hard to ignore.
The first part of the curve is what I expected:
As a Principal Engineer, more of my work went into architecture, deep dives into concepts, setting up projects and planning, rather than fixing bugs or iterating on features. Becoming VP of Technology continued that shift, with even less feature work expected. At least until AI came along.
Almost all of this is private work. The dashed line in the chart is public contributions only: it was near zero from 2021 to 2025 and came back this year, with 191 so far, but that is still less than a tenth of 2026.
The twist is the role. In 2020 I was a full-stack engineer doing feature work full time, and this is roughly what that looked like on GitHub. Today I lead engineering at Bold.org and do far less feature work than I used to. On paper my graph should look like my Principal Engineer years, or lower. Instead it is back where it was when writing code was my whole job.
What changed is how much work feels worth taking on. When coding is cheap, I can fix bugs I would previously have left alone, improve patterns across the codebase, take on new projects and turn more ideas into something real. Much of this is work I would never have considered before. Agents did not just make my existing workload faster to finish. They made it easy to give myself a much bigger one.
Looking at the monthly totals, 2026 is not one steady climb. It is a series of bursts.
January and February were the first clear burst, with 277 and 233 contributions. This is when I started working seriously with agents, and when the observability experiment that became our internal company agent took off. Every week revealed something new I could suddenly delegate, and I wanted to try all of it.
March to June generally winds down, from 203 contributions in March to 77 in June. But April was a smaller burst along the way, another month when I had ideas and acted on them. I think improvements in the models were part of that renewed energy. Its monthly total of 187 is below January to March, but it includes a 29-contribution day and 68 public contributions, my highest public total of the year.
August is the biggest burst of all. Coming back from my summer break, the calendar shows a full week of zero contributions in early August. Then every weekday from August 10 to August 27 was between 14 and 43. August ended at 427 contributions, the busiest month in the whole timeline. September stayed high at 301.
Every cycle starts the same way. A new model or a new workflow makes something possible that was not possible last month, and my head fills with ideas. Because implementation is now cheap, there is no natural friction stopping me from pursuing all of them at once. So I do. I start more agents, open more threads and say yes to more experiments.
That works for a few weeks. Then the reviewing and context switching catch up with me, and I pull back to a more stable flow. I stay there until something exciting comes along, or until a holiday recharges me enough that I go straight back into another burst.
I count three of these cycles since January.
At the end of a burst, I feel tired of AI. I do not want to start another agent or think of more ideas. I do my normal work, but I stop chasing the extra projects and possibilities because I do not have the mental bandwidth for them.
The part that surprised me most is not the peaks. It is how much I am doing between them.
March did not feel like the bursts in January, February or August, but I was still doing substantial work. It had 203 contributions, against my Principal Engineer average of 114 a month. I was still acting on ideas, but that level of activity no longer felt like an exceptional push. Even when I think I am taking it easy, there are still agent results to work through, reviews to finish and small things that are now “just a quick prompt”.
June was genuinely low, with 77 contributions, comparable to my quieter Principal Engineer months. Maybe that was when all the tiredness caught up with me. Not every quiet month is higher than before. But outside the bursts, I still find myself taking on more work than I used to. That is what I mean by the low season not feeling low anymore.
AI made room for work I would never have considered before. I like being able to fix more things and turn more ideas into something real. But the capacity to implement those ideas has grown much faster than my capacity to think about them. Eventually I stop wanting to start another agent and go back to just doing my normal work. I have not figured out a balance. For now, I am noticing that being able to do more keeps turning into doing more. And I am tired.
A note on how this article was written: AI helped me pull and analyze my GitHub contribution data, build the chart and draft this article. The experience, decisions and opinions are mine.

title: Aliyev says all risks to Azerbaijan originate from outside borders
body: Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has warned against foreign interference in the country’s internal affairs, claiming that all potential risks to Azerbaijan originate beyond its borders. Speaking at the opening of the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue in Baku on Tuesday, Aliyev said Azerbaijan had no internal risks and must remain vigilant against ideological threats. He also accused the international community of applying double standards towards Azerbaijan and criticised attempts by foreign actors to dictate how the country should be governed. Aliyev also called on Azerbaijanis to ‘protect our identity, statehood, independence, and way of life’. He added that Azerbaijan had preserved and strengthened its traditions and way of life since regaining independence in 1991, arguing that society demonstrated unity on all issues. Aliyev also warned against what he described as attempts by foreign actors to dictate how Azerbaijan should be governed. ‘Any sign of disrespect towards us, any manifestation of an unjustified sense of superiority, any unfounded idea that someone can dictate something to us has been met with resistance and will continue to be met with a firm stance’, he said. Aliyev accuses international community of double standards During his speech, Aliyev also criticised what he described as double standards in the international community, referring to Armenia’s occupation of Azerbaijani territory during the conflict over Nagorno-Karabakh. He said that Armenia had occupied approximately 20% of Azerbaijan’s internationally recognised territory, displaced one million Azerbaijanis through ethnic cleansing, and destroyed religious and historical monuments, including 65 mosques in Nagorno-Karabakh. Aliyev added that Armenia had not faced sanctions or punishment for these actions. He then extended his criticism to what he described as attempts by other countries to tell Azerbaijan how to live. ‘Before taking such a step, one should look in the mirror and ask oneself: do I have the moral right to teach someone, to explain to an independent country how it should live, what it should and should not do?’ Aliyev said. He claimed that Azerbaijan did not interfere in the internal affairs of other countries and expected the same treatment in return. However, France has repeatedly accused Azerbaijan of meddling in its domestic affairs, including in recent weeks — specifically by inciting unrest and promoting pro-independence narratives in overseas territories like New Caledonia Aliyev argued that respecting these principles in international relations would lead to fewer conflicts and problems and greater cooperation. He also said Azerbaijan’s independent foreign policy had earned the country international respect and that its role in the global energy and transport markets had grown significantly. ‘In many cases, Azerbaijan is perceived as a guarantor of stability in an unstable region’, he said.

title: Evzones Make Historic First Visit to the Greek Embassy in Canberra After 80 Years
body: CANBERRA, Tuesday 27 October 2026 — Six Evzones of the Hellenic Presidential Guard visited the Greek Embassy in Canberra on Tuesday, the first time the Guard has been to the embassy in its 80 years. The Evzones’ visit to the Greek Embassy in Canberra is also their first to the city. Guests at the Greek Embassy in Canberra Ambassador of Greece to Australia, Stavros Venizelos, hosted the guests at the Embassy. title: Norway and Finland are talking to Russia. Should others follow?
body:
The Norwegian government has announced that Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb held a telephone conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The call was reportedly a Norwegian and Finnish initiative following consultations with Ukraine.
This was essentially a continuation of efforts initiated last week, when the two Nordic leaders met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff prior to his visit to the Russian President in Saint Petersburg. The purpose of the Nordic leaders’ conversation with Putin was to convey a position regarding future negotiations aimed at ending the war.
“This war entails enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will affect future generations. During the conversation, we emphasised the importance of actions leading to the de-escalation of the war,” Støre stated.
The Finnish President described the conversation as direct and substantive. “ We are Russia’s neighbours. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our security and the security of Europe . This necessitates dialogue to bring about an end to the war,” Stubb emphasised in an official statement.
The leaders also reportedly discussed a meeting between representatives of Ukraine, Russia, and the US scheduled for November in Abu Dhabi. Støre and Stubb noted that they were acting as representatives of their own respective nations, rather than the whole of Europe.
For Russia-bordering states, it should come as no surprise that Finland and Norway want to partake in the negotiation process. It is, however, worth noting that both leaders were acting as representatives of their own respective nations and not on behalf of the whole of Europe. Europe seems to be falling behind when it comes to the negotiation process. Other Russia-bordering states like Poland and the Baltics are yet to engage in talks with Vladimir Putin. If they do not follow in Norway’s and Finland’s footsteps, they will be left behind.

title: Activists urge voters returning to Israel to save emergency hotline numbers in case of arrest
body: The Detainee Support Network (Ma'arach Otef Atzurim), a group identified with Israel's protest movement, has circulated a message urging Israelis flying in from abroad to vote to save the numbers of a special emergency hotline in case police arrest or detain them when they land.“Coming to Israel to vote? Save these numbers,” read the message, which was shared in WhatsApp groups. It went on to instruct travelers to print out the phone numbers and keep them in their passports in case police take their phones.“Were you detained or arrested by the border police or the Israel Police at Ben-Gurion Airport, on landing, at the polling station on Election Day, or even after the election? Contact the Detainee Support Network immediately,” the message said.Citizens fear police may arrest prospective voters 'because they can'We spoke with a representative of the network to understand what is behind the unusual concern. Asked why police would arrest citizens coming to vote, she replied: “Because they can. It hasn't happened in elections so far, but we want to be on the safe side.”Asked on what grounds voters could be arrested, she said: “It could be all sorts of things – a post you wrote. They're not happy with all the people coming back to the country. They can detain you and take you to the station. Such things have been known to happen.”She said the concern is that travelers could be arrested or detained because they plan to vote for parties in the opposition. However, she acknowledged that there have been no unusual incidents so far: “Everything has gone smoothly in recent days, and I assume it will continue to go smoothly.”The group stresses that this is advance preparation for any possible scenario. “We've prepared for every scenario. Everything is fine. I'm sure the police will do their job properly,” the representative said.

title: German prosecutors reject motion to dismiss case on Nord Stream pipeline sabotage
body:
HAMBURG, October 27. /TASS/. The German Federal Prosecutor’s Office has rejected a motion to dismiss the case against Ukrainian citizen Sergey Kuznetsov, who is accused of participating in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
"The defense’s motion cannot be granted," a TASS correspondent quoted senior public prosecutor Stefan Schmidt as saying at a hearing of the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg. The prosecutor rejected the arguments of Kuznetsov’s defense that it was allegedly impossible to ensure the defendant’s "effective defense" because he is a Ukrainian special forces officer and is prohibited by Ukrainian law from disclosing military secrets.
The trial on the merits began in Hamburg on October 27 in the case involving the sabotage of the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines. The first court hearing took place on October 14. At that hearing, the defense requested that the case be dismissed. According to the defense, a fair trial cannot be guaranteed because the defendant is a former military officer who allegedly has no right to disclose the contents of orders, who issued them, or other information - not even to his own defense attorneys. Neither the prosecution nor the defense has questioned his involvement in the sabotage during the trial.
The German Federal Prosecutor’s Office charged Kuznetsov with war crimes, including carrying out explosions, destroying buildings, and disrupting public utility operations. Investigators believe he and his accomplices devised a plan to blow up pipelines on behalf of the Ukrainian government. Another Ukrainian was recently detained in Croatia. Prosecutors assume that the saboteurs used forged documents to rent a sailboat from a German company to transport explosives to the Nord Stream pipelines. Kuznetsov was detained in Italy in August 2022 and extradited to Germany.
On September 27, 2022, Nord Stream AG reported "unprecedented damage" on three strings of the offshore gas pipelines of the Nord Stream system. Later, Swedish seismologists said they had identified two explosions on the route of the Nord Stream pipelines on September 26, 2022. Following the incident, the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office initiated a criminal case on charges of international terrorism. Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev stated that all of Moscow’s initiatives to investigate the sabotage of the gas pipelines are being ignored, and numerous requests essentially remain unanswered.

title: 2027 Election: CJN Urges Judges To Be Vigilant, Cautious In Handling Political Cases
body: As the nation approaches another election season, the Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN), Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, has urged judges, particularly heads of courts, to be vigilant against practices that undermine the integrity of judicial proceedings. Justice Kekere-Ekun identified such practices to include forum shopping, concealment of related proceedings and attempts to obtain conflicting orders from courts of coordinate jurisdiction. She spoke during the opening session of the 2026 roundtable for heads of courts, in Abuja. The CJN said the issues require particular attention as the country approaches another election season, noting that election-related disputes often attract intense public interest and considerable pressure on the courts. She added: “The Judiciary must be prepared to discharge its constitutional responsibilities with impartiality, courage and fidelity to the law. “Political sensitivity, public sentiment or the urgency with which a matter is presented must never displace the careful application of the Constitution, the Electoral Act and the applicable rules of court. “Judicial officers must be reminded of the need to scrutinise applications carefully, insist on full and frank disclosure of relevant facts, pay due regard to related proceedings and resist any attempt to use urgent applications or ex-parte orders to secure an improper advantage. “The integrity of judicial proceedings must not be compromised by competing political interests or pressure from any quarter. “Forum shopping is particularly damaging because it undermines consistency, encourages abuse of process and exposes the Judiciary to avoidable public controversy. “Your lordships must therefore ensure that existing procedural safeguards are observed and that appropriate steps are taken whenever attempts to circumvent established judicial processes come to light. “No litigant should be permitted to manipulate the judicial system in search of a favourable decision. Public confidence in the Judiciary will be tested during this period,” she said. The CJN reminded the heads of courts that they are expected to provide the leadership necessary to ensure that election-related cases are handled competently, expeditiously and strictly in accordance with the law. She said the objective is to ensure that the courts remain impartial arbiters of disputes, free from political influence and guided solely by the facts, the applicable law and the demands of justice. Justice Kekere-Ekun spoke about the need for judges to always ensure prompt determination of cases, noting that the timely determination of cases remains one of the most pressing challenges confronting the Judiciary. She said delay imposes financial and emotional burdens on litigants, diminishes the practical value of judicial remedies and weakens public confidence in the justice system. The CJN added: “While some causes of delay arise from inadequate funding, infrastructure and judicial manpower, others can be addressed through effective administration. “Inefficient docket management, repeated adjournments, poor scheduling and failure to monitor inactive cases can prolong proceedings unnecessarily. “Every Head of Court should have a clear understanding of the condition of the court’s docket, including the number of pending cases, their age, the categories experiencing the greatest delays and the reasons for their continued pendency. “This information should inform realistic strategies for reducing backlog, improving the allocation of hearing dates and ensuring that concluded matters are promptly removed from the active docket. “Efficiency, however, must not be measured solely by the number of cases disposed of. It requires cases to be determined fairly, competently and within a reasonable time, with the right to fair hearing fully protected,” she said. The CJN stressed the need to preserve the integrity of judicial appointments through a fair, transparent and merit-based selection process. She asked the heads of courts to “strongly and courageously resist pressure from external interests and ensure that appointments are guided by objective criteria, competence, character and suitability for judicial office. “Your lordships also have an important role in promoting professional standards, supporting the development of judicial officers and fostering an institutional culture that upholds impartiality and accountability.” The CJN directed heads of courts to put in place mechanisms to ensure judges sit on time, notify litigants and lawyers promptly when sittings are cancelled, and treat court users with dignity. Justice Kekere-Ekun described as unacceptable the situation where counsel and parties travel long distances at great expense, only to learn on arrival that the court will not sit. She asked heads of courts to ensure registries have dependable procedures naming the officers responsible for notifications, the channels to be used and how to confirm that affected parties have been informed. On courtroom conduct, she said judicial authority is best exercised with “fairness, composure and respect. “Every litigant, regardless of social status, financial means or education, deserves dignity, while lawyers are entitled to courteous treatment. Firmness and courtesy are entirely compatible. A judge can control proceedings without humiliating counsel or a litigant,” she said. She also directed heads of courts to ensure that courts remain professional workplaces free from bullying and harassment. The CJN called for sustained investment in court staff, including registrars, research staff, administrative officers and IT personnel. She urged all jurisdictions to adopt structured mentorship under which newly appointed judges are attached to experienced judicial officers for a defined period before sitting independently. Speaking earlier, the Administrator of the NJI, retired Justice Babatunde Adejumo, said the Judiciary, as custodian of justice and guardian of the rule of law, is under constant public scrutiny, placing a heavy responsibility on those steering its affairs to safeguard its image and shape positive public perceptions. He added that the programme was deliberately designed with minimal external intervention so that the Heads of Courts would direct discussions and determine outcomes. . title: High-Profile Rape Trial Of Ex-Prosecutor Resumes In Japan
body: The trial of a Japanese former senior prosecutor accused of rape in one of the country’s most high-profile cases of alleged sexual assault restarted on Tuesday after a two-year pause. Few women in Japan speak out about sexual assault, but a former prosecutor, who uses the pseudonym Hikari, came forward in 2024 to accuse her boss of raping her six years earlier. The trial first began in October 2024 but was halted after Kentaro Kitagawa — who served as head of the Osaka District Public Prosecutor’s Office at the time of the alleged rape — withdrew his initial admission of guilt and said the sex was consensual. On Tuesday Kitagawa told the court that sex took place but repeated his not guilty plea and “denied that she was unable to resist”, according to public broadcaster NHK. Following his plea change, the court, prosecution and defence spent two years in closed-door proceedings clarifying the points at issue. Hikari, who has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), has previously said she was not used to drinking strong alcohol and lost her memory halfway through an office gathering in 2018. The next thing she knew, she said, she was in Kitagawa’s home and was being raped. “It was like I was having a terrible nightmare,” Hikari said in a 2025 interview with AFP. “I couldn’t resist because I was terrified that I could be killed.” Hikari kept quiet after it happened as Kitagawa had pleaded with her not to go public, saying it would be a damaging scandal for the organisation and threatening to harm himself, she said. Hikari said her condition worsened after she learned in 2024 that people close to Kitagawa, especially an assistant prosecutor — who Hikari says is his lover — had spread malicious rumours about her. Hikari has repeatedly requested an independent probe into harassment within prosecutor’s offices across the country. Officials have rejected that request and instead announced the launch in June of their own internal investigation. Her request for measures to ensure a safe working environment was also rejected, prompting her to officially resign in August. title: U.S. Navy says USS Colorado maintenance visit supports AUKUS preparations in Australia
body: More than 30 trained and certified ASC technicians will work alongside specialists from Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility. The Royal Navy will also participate, making the visit a joint test of the workforce and infrastructure needed to support American and British submarines. “This maintenance period brings us closer to establishing SRF-West,” said Rear Adm. Doug Adams, the U.S. Navy’s director of AUKUS, International & Systems. “Our Lead Maintenance Activity, Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility, is doing a great job ensuring the Australian personnel trained in Hawaii are ready and able to support our submarines.” Submarine Rotational Force–West is projected to host up to four U.S. and one British submarine at HMAS Stirling on a rotational basis. The three AUKUS partners announced Colorado’s selection for the force on October 26. The rotations are intended to prepare Australia to operate, maintain and sustain its own conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines. They will also expand regional maintenance options for allied submarines, supporting deterrence and operational flexibility. The current maintenance period will use upgrades to Diamantina Pier and an Australian-built safety walkway around the submarine’s sail. Other locally developed equipment includes a pure water plant, high-pressure air compressor and dehumidifier validated during earlier visits. “Operating as a single team, we are testing our infrastructure, validating our nuclear stewardship processes, and substantially upskilling our naval and civilian workforces,” said Rear Adm. David Mann, head of the Australian Submarine Agency’s Virginia Division. “These maintenance periods have been critical to Australia being on track to start SRF-West in 2027.” This is Western Australia’s fourth submarine maintenance period since AUKUS was established. Colorado is the third nuclear-powered attack submarine to undergo maintenance in Australia in the past 12 months. “As we approach the establishment of SRF-West, we must remember that our trilateral efforts are being driven by the challenging strategic environment in the Pacific and our collective desire to deter aggression and ensure peace through strength,” said Rear Adm. Chris Cavanaugh, commander of Submarine Force, U.S. Pacific Fleet. He said AUKUS was strengthening integration and interoperability among the three submarine forces.

title: The Curator: Is the Endy Elevate Hybrid mattress worth it? My honest review
body:
The Curator independently decides what topics and products we feature. When you purchase an item through our links, we may earn a commission. Promotions and products are subject to availability and retailer terms.
There are purchases you spend years thinking about while continuing to make do with what you have. For me, a new mattress was one of them. I could happily research bedding, admire beautiful bed frames and imagine my future bedroom–but the mattress itself? Somehow, that upgrade kept getting pushed down the list.
Then I started thinking about the home my fiancé and I will eventually share. Suddenly, choosing a mattress became a decision for two. I’m a side-sleeper. He cycles through what feels like every sleeping position available. We both like support, but we also want that delicious, cancel-your-plans-and-get-back-into-bed cloud feeling.
Enter the Endy Elevate Hybrid Mattress .
I’d wanted to try Endy for years, and its newest hybrid felt like the right place to start. With cooling-focused materials, pressure-relieving foam and targeted support, it checked the boxes on my mattress wish list. And the fact that it’s proudly made in Canada? That made my decision even easier.
Read on for my Endy Elevate Hybrid Mattress review, including what makes this Canadian-made upgrade worth investing in.
The Elevate is an evolution of Endy’s best-selling Hybrid, with an added focus on cooler sleep. The medium-firm model I chose is a 12-inch hybrid with five layers designed to balance cushioning comfort with responsive support. Here’s what’s behind the bedtime upgrade:
A cooling cover that works from the surface
The AirDrift™ Cooling Cover with CoolWeave™ Technology feels cool to the touch and wicks away moisture. As a hot sleeper, this was a major selling point–I wanted a mattress that could help keep me comfortable all night, rather than feel cool only when I first climbed into bed.
Both the Endy Cooling Comfort Foam and Pressure-Relief Foam contain HeatDiffuse™ Gel, designed to draw heat away as you sleep. The breathable, open-cell foam construction also keeps air moving throughout the mattress, helping release heat for consistent comfort.
Underneath those cushioning layers sits a seven-inch layer of zoned steel pocket coils , with up to 1,088 coils , depending on the mattress size. Why does this matter? They provide targeted lumbar support while adding airflow, durability and responsiveness. The reinforced construction supports up to 600 pounds.
The mattress is also designed to isolate motion–a particularly appealing feature when your fiancé likes to cycle through every sleeping position while you’re happily settled on your side.
If never wanting to leave bed is wrong, I don’t want to be right. This is easily the best mattress I’ve owned.
I’d wanted to upgrade my mattress for years, and with my fiancé and I moving in together, I wanted something that would suit us both. My wish list was pretty specific: supportive, cloud-like and–because I’m a hot sleeper–capable of keeping me cool throughout the night. A tall order? Perhaps. But the Elevate delivers.
First, the setup deserves a moment. After putting off a mattress upgrade for so long, actually getting this one onto my bed was a cinch. The bed-in-a-box delivery is convenient: unbox it, position it on your bed frame, carefully remove the wrapping and let it expand. Voilà–bedroom upgraded. For something that felt like such a big decision, the setup was refreshingly uncomplicated.
We chose medium-firm because we both like a little more support without sacrificing that soft, inviting feeling that makes getting into bed the best part of the day. I’m a side-sleeper, while my fiancé sleeps in all different positions, so Endy’s most popular feel seemed like a natural fit.
And I’ll admit it: I do a lot of work from bed. Writing, editing, answering emails–my mattress gets more time with me than I probably should admit. So when your bed also doubles as your office, how comfortable it feels is a pretty big deal.
For me, the cooling is a standout. I needed a mattress that could keep me cool all night long, and this one does just that. The AirDrift cover with CoolWeave Technology deserves a special mention–it brings that cool-to-the-touch feeling I appreciate as soon as I get into bed. Paired with the gel-infused foam and breathable construction underneath, it makes the Elevate feel particularly well suited to someone who sleeps warm.
The biggest difference, though, is how I feel in the morning. I’m waking up feeling more refreshed after a good night’s sleep. As much as I love a beautiful bedroom, actually feeling well rested is the part of this upgrade I appreciate most.
Choosing a mattress for two people feels a little like choosing a restaurant when you’re both hungry: you need something that makes everyone happy.
For us, that meant support with a generous helping of softness. Neither of us wanted to feel swallowed by the bed, but we weren’t looking for an overly rigid sleep surface, either. I wanted that cloud-like comfort without giving up the support underneath.
I went with medium-firm, Endy’s most popular feel, which the brand describes as offering balanced comfort for every sleep position. There are also firm and plush options, so you have some room to choose based on how you like your bed to feel.
As a side-sleeper shopping with a combination sleeper in mind, medium-firm felt like the most sensible starting point. Shared mattress, shared priorities.
Bonus: The Elevate also comes with a 365-night risk-free trial and a 15-year warranty . A mattress is a personal purchase, and most people would appreciate having time to figure out how it fits into real life. A quick lie-down can tell you something; your usual bedtime routine tells you much more.
The Elevate brought together several things I was looking for in one long-overdue decision. Here’s what stands out to me:
Starting at $1,195, the Elevate is an investment–and the final price depends on the size and feel you choose. If you’re furnishing an entire bedroom, that’s worth factoring into the budget alongside your bed frame, bedding and everything else that somehow ends up in the cart.
Firmness is also personal. Medium-firm made sense for our preferences, but that doesn’t mean it will be everyone’s perfect match. Endy offers firm and plush options for a reason. If you have the opportunity to try the different feels in-store, I’d make that part of the shopping process.
And while motion isolation and cooling technology are appealing features, I’d keep expectations grounded. A mattress can be thoughtfully designed without guaranteeing uninterrupted sleep every night. Luckily, the size of our king mattress coupled with this unique feature has kept my fiancé and I happy.
For me, though, finally making the upgrade has been worth it. After years of thinking about an Endy, I now have a Canadian-made mattress I’m happy to build our bedroom around.
