title: Global Breast Cancer Awareness Drive Puts Early Detection in Focus in Kazakhstan
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ALMATY – Kazakhstan is holding free breast cancer consultations and diagnostic examinations throughout October as part of an annual Pink October awareness campaign, encouraging women to undergo regular screening and seek medical attention if they notice changes in their breasts. Kazakhstan is holding free consultations and diagnostic examinations throughout October as part of its annual Pink October breast cancer awareness campaign. Photo credit: Regional Communications Service Breast cancer remains the most common cancer among women in Kazakhstan. In 2025, the country registered 5,743 new cases, according to figures provided by the Ministry of Healthcare. Breast cancer also remains a major global health challenge. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), an estimated 2.4 million women were diagnosed with breast cancer worldwide in 2024, and 694,000 died from the disease. Breast cancer occurs in every country and can affect women at any age after puberty, with rates increasing in later life. Since Kazakhstan launched its national breast cancer screening program in 2008, 19,018 cases have been identified, including 17,186 detected at Stages 1 and 2, when treatment is generally more effective. The number of Stage 3 and 4 cases detected through screening fell from 66 in 2011 to 16 in 2025, according to the ministry. The Pink October campaign includes open days at oncology centers, consultations with oncologists and mammologists, mammography and breast ultrasound examinations. Organizers aim to raise awareness of breast cancer prevention and the importance of early diagnosis. Breast cancer statistics in Kazakhstan National figures highlight the importance of early detection. Since the launch of the screening program, thousands of cases have been identified at earlier stages, giving patients a better opportunity to receive timely treatment. Pink ribbons and other awareness activities highlight the importance of early breast cancer detection during Pink October in Kazakhstan. Photo credit: prohealth.kz. In Almaty, breast cancer is also the most common cancer among women. According to the Almaty Oncology Center, 659 new cases were identified in the city during the first eight months of 2026. A total of 9,520 patients are registered with the disease at the center. Speaking at a briefing organized by the Regional Communications Service in Almaty, oncologists said the growing number of recorded cases is partly associated with expanded screening and greater attention to women’s health. However, specialists stressed that the disease can also affect younger people. “Unfortunately, breast cancer is getting younger every year. The youngest patient we registered at the Almaty Oncology Center this year is 21 years old. She is currently receiving comprehensive treatment, and we are seeing a good response to therapy,” said Akerke Orazbayeva, an oncologist and head of the center’s specialized consultation and diagnostic department. The oldest breast cancer patient observed at the center was 93, Orazbayeva told The Astana Times. “The disease can develop not only in women – around 20 men are registered with this diagnosis at the Almaty Oncology Center. Of course, it occurs much less frequently in men, but the risk cannot be ruled out,” said Akbota Adilova, head of the center’s consultation and diagnostic department. During the first eight months of 2026, doctors in Almaty detected breast cancer at Stage 0 in five women, Stage 1 in 305, Stage 2 in 312, Stage 3 in 20 and Stage 4 in 70. Who can receive free screening? The Ministry of Healthcare encourages women to undergo regular cancer screening at their local polyclinics. Kazakhstan currently offers three types of screening: breast cancer screening for women aged 40 to 76 once every two years, cervical cancer screening for women aged 30 to 70 once every four years, and colorectal cancer screening for men and women aged 50 to 70 once every two years. Photo credit: Regional Communications Service Mammography can identify suspicious changes before symptoms appear. Specialists emphasize that ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be used as additional diagnostic methods when medically indicated but do not replace screening mammography. The WHO also stresses that awareness of symptoms, timely diagnosis and access to treatment are essential to improving breast cancer outcomes. In places where mammography screening is not practical or widely available, public education can still encourage women to seek medical attention when they first notice symptoms. Risk factors and common misconceptions Most women diagnosed with breast cancer have no known family history of the disease, and the absence of other obvious risk factors does not necessarily mean they are at low risk. According to the World Health Organization, approximately 80% of breast cancers occur in women with no specific risk factors other than sex and age. Risk increases with age, while other contributing factors include certain inherited genetic mutations, excess weight, particularly after menopause, alcohol consumption, hormonal and reproductive factors, dense breast tissue and previous exposure to high levels of radiation. Having one or more risk factors does not mean a person will necessarily develop cancer. Specialists say the disease can develop through a combination of factors, and regular screening remains important. Speaking at the briefing, doctors also sought to dispel common misconceptions that may discourage women from seeking medical care. One widespread myth is that breast cancer can always be detected by feeling a lump. Adilova said small tumors may not be noticeable through self-examination, which is why regular screening and attention to changes in breast shape and skin are important. Doctors also addressed concerns about deodorants, antiperspirants and biopsies. Research has not established a link between underarm deodorant or antiperspirant use and breast cancer. Doctors also stress that ultrasound alone is not sufficient to replace mammography as a screening method. Women who notice unusual changes or have concerns about their breast health are advised to consult a medical professional. Preventive surgery and genetic risk Oncologists in Almaty also perform bilateral preventive mastectomy in selected cases involving women with a high hereditary risk of breast cancer. Kaisar Nakipbekov, an oncologist, mammologist and oncosurgeon at the Almaty Oncology Center, said the procedure may be considered when a patient has a genetic mutation associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. In some cases, it may also be performed at the patient’s request following medical consultation. Certain inherited genetic mutations, including those affecting the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, can substantially increase breast cancer risk. The WHO says women with high-risk genetic mutations may consider risk-reduction strategies, including medication or preventive surgery, in consultation with medical specialists. Preventive mastectomy involves removing both breasts to substantially reduce the risk of developing breast cancer. The procedure became more widely known after actress Angelina Jolie disclosed in 2013 that she had undergone the surgery after learning she carried an inherited mutation associated with a high risk of the disease. Pink October events across Kazakhstan Oncology centers across Kazakhstan are offering free breast cancer consultations and examinations as part of Pink October, an annual campaign to raise awareness of the disease and encourage early detection. A nationwide open day is scheduled for Oct. 31, including at the Kazakh Research Institute of Oncology and Radiology in Almaty, where women can consult an oncologist-mammologist free of charge. Visitors are advised to confirm appointment times, registration requirements and available examinations with their local medical facilities. In 2025, more than 8,400 women took part in examinations organized as part of the campaign. Various breast conditions were identified in 3,337 women, including 144 cases of breast cancer. The campaign also invites people to support awareness efforts by wearing a pink ribbon, scarf or another pink accessory, sharing information and using the hashtag Pink October Kazakhstan. Breast cancer screening and treatment are also available through Kazakhstan’s state-guaranteed health care system. Treatment for malignant cancers is covered regardless of a patient’s mandatory social health insurance status. Patients with suspected cancer can access consultations and initial diagnostic examinations through the Green Corridor, which provides expedited pathways within 18 working days. Globally, the WHO is working to reduce breast cancer deaths through its Global Breast Cancer Initiative, established in 2021. The initiative aims to reduce global breast cancer mortality by 2.5% annually and avert 2.5 million deaths by 2040. Its three pillars are health promotion for early detection, timely diagnosis and comprehensive breast cancer management. As organization reminds, improving outcomes requires not only awareness and early detection but also reliable referral pathways and access to effective treatment. title: The Curator: Is Emirates business class worth it? I flew 13 hours to find out (plus 8 travel products that helped me along the way)
body:
The Curator independently decides what topics and products we feature. When you purchase an item through our links, we may earn a commission. Promotions and products are subject to availability and retailer terms.
I finally booked the coveted Emirates business class seat everyone talks about, and here’s an honest look at what Emirates’ A380 business class offers from Toronto to Dubai, what’s worth knowing before you book, and some product picks to help you on your long-haul travel journey.
The Emirates business class experience begins before you even reach the airport. Eligible business class fares come with a complimentary chauffeur service which you can easily book within minutes online. My advice: it’s worth arranging right when you book your ticket so it’s in the system.
Then came a pleasant surprise: my companions flying economy rode along with me. The service was tied to my ticket, but wasn’t limited to only me when I had booked, which turned out to be very handy. And the same chauffeur service waits on the other end in Dubai when you land.
At Toronto Pearson, my business class ticket opened the door to the Air Canada Maple Leaf Lounge, a nice start to a long travel day. Then, boarding the Emirates Airbus A380-800 was a seamless experience, I headed up to the upper deck, where business class is laid out in a 1-2-1 pattern. This is one thing I appreciated; every seat had direct aisle access giving passengers privacy and space.
My first thought was “wow, this is spacious ”. There was room to settle in without feeling hemmed in, and extra storage that kept my handbag within reach.
Then the Emirates experience I had heard so much about began to unfold. Within minutes of settling in, I had a welcome drink, a dish of warm nuts and a hot towel in hand. The Emirates crew followed with handing out pajamas and the full in-flight menu. From the moment I sat down, I was so well taken care of, for a moment I forgot I was boarding a flight.
tomtoc Electronic Organizer Travel Case – $35
WANDF Carry-On Foldable Duffel Bag – $18
Neutrogena All-in-One Makeup Removing Cleansing Wipe – $10
Let’s get to the question everyone asks about Emirates business class: is the seat worth it? On a 13-hour flight from Toronto to Dubai, it’s the part of the trip that mattered most.
At between 70 to 79 inches long (depending on your seat choice), the bed has enough room for travellers to comfortably stretch out. The seat is built for long-haul and the difference shows up in the small adjustments. A control unit lets you shift between three main points: upright, relaxed recline, and fully flat. Beyond the recline, the seat has headrest and footrest, plus a reading light, and a side table beside the seat to hold any items such as laptop or food. Everything you need is within reach including a mini bar stocked with water and snacks.
The best moment came when it was time to sleep. While you slip into the soft pajamas Emirates provides, a crew member prepares the bed with a mattress. While the mattress was more like a topper, it was still nice to have additional cushioning along with a soft pillow and comforter.
There was so much space that I was able to do my skin care routine which helped against the dry cabin air.
On a long-haul flight, meals matter more, and Emirates seems to know it.The 13-hour flight was divided into distinct scheduled main meal services; lunch, breakfast and light bites plus a dedicated light bites and drinks menu you could order from whenever you wanted in between.
Before each meal, a crew member sets a tablecloth over the table which truly feels like sitting down at a restaurant more than anything except you’re cozied up in your seat. What made the dining experience feel more special was the crew behind it who go above and beyond with the service.
Lunch offered choices from steak, bass to arabic mezze, and breakfast had omelettes, paneer and pancakes as the main course along with other small bite and drink options in between to choose from.
What stood out was the freedom in between. If you want a change of scenery and a snack or drink, head to the onboard lounge at the back of the cabin. The spread is casual: cold sandwiches, hot snacks, savoury snacks and small desserts, with a crew member serving drinks at the bar while you socialize.
Packing for a long flight usually means a carry-on full of “just in case” items. On Emirates business class, much of that list is already waiting at your seat. You get pajamas, slippers, an eye mask, and a Bvlgari toiletry kit. Let’s just say, the Bvlgari bag didn’t disappoint. It had the Bvlgari Omnia Crystalline body lotion, face emulsion, perfume, lip balm, deodorant, comb, dental kit, tissues, and a compact mirror—a full set for a long-haul flight.
Tip: don’t overpack your personal toiletries kit because the Bvlgari bag is filled with great useful items.
Entertainment is just as easy. The 23-inch screen makes a movie or show feel closer to a home setup than a seatback. You get noise-canceling headphones and complimentary wifi helping you stay connected throughout. On a long flight, having both options to use the in-flight screen or your own device is great to switch anytime without feeling stuck.
Dubai’s airport is home to Emirates’ very own business class lounge exclusively reserved for passengers flying business. It has plenty of seating so it’s easy to find a spot. The showers are a great perk to freshen up before a flight in comfort. For a caffeine fix, there’s a Costa Coffee shop inside with complimentary drinks and bites.
The food was the highlight. Alongside multiple buffet stations spread across the lounge with different cuisines served—Arabic, Western, Mediterranean, Asian, fresh food is served live, there is an array of drinks, extensive dessert options and when I saw the gourmet ice cream stand, I was sold on sight.
Between the food, the showers and the space to unwind, it’s a lounge that makes the wait time feel like a perk. If a stopover has to happen somewhere, this is a very good place for it.

title: Nvidia backs Indian startup helping companies run AI models with fewer GPUs
body:
As the AI boom strains computing capacity, Nvidia has backed Indian startup Simplismart in a $14 million funding round, betting on software that helps companies run AI models more efficiently and, in some cases, with fewer GPUs.
Nvidia participated in the all-primary Series B round alongside Accel, Shastra VC, and Micromax, with Dallas Venture Capital leading the investment. The deal values the four-year-old startup at about $100 million, including the new funding.
Companies are nowadays spending heavily on GPUs to power AI applications, but running those models reliably and economically at scale remains a challenge. Different workloads demand distinct trade-offs between speed, cost, and performance. Deploying and operating AI models to meet business requirements often also requires complex adjustments. Simplismart says its software automates much of that work, tailoring how models run on existing computing infrastructure instead of requiring customers to manage those configurations themselves.
“Nobody actually needs the fastest or the cheapest inference,” Amritanshu Jain (pictured above, left), co-founder and CEO of Simplismart, said in an interview. He added that companies instead need to run AI models at speeds and costs that make sense for their specific applications.
Simplismart’s software sits between AI models and the computing infrastructure they run on and adjusts how models are deployed and managed to meet customers’ requirements. It says it can optimize factors such as how quickly a model responds, how many requests it handles, and how much computing power it consumes, helping companies get more out of their existing GPU stack.
The Bengaluru-based startup offers companies a way to deploy and run AI models through its own platform or within their existing cloud and on-premises infrastructure. It also provides tools to fine-tune models, automatically scale computing resources as demand changes, and monitor performance. Additionally, Simplismart allows cloud providers to build and operate their own AI inference services on GPU infrastructure using its software.
Simplismart says it helped AI video-generation platform InVideo cut its GPU serving costs by 56% using its software. The startup also works with AI video companies HeyGen and Higgsfield, as well as enterprise AI startup Ema, among others. Moreover, Indian cloud provider Yotta uses Simplismart’s technology to power the serverless AI inference service within its Shakti Studio platform.
Simplismart’s annualized revenue run rate has grown 14-fold over the past six months to an eight-figure sum, Jain told TechCrunch. The figure is based on recent customer usage rather than contracted recurring revenue and excludes revenue passed through to infrastructure providers, the company said. He did not disclose the exact figure.
More than half of Simplismart’s revenue comes from the U.S., despite the startup having more customers in India, Jain said.
Alongside its investment, Nvidia has been working with Simplismart on technical integrations, including around its Dynamo inference software, Jain told TechCrunch. The collaboration involves Simplismart’s engineers and Nvidia’s solutions architects, while Nvidia has also helped introduce the startup to potential customers and partners, Jain stated.
Interestingly, the investment presents an apparent paradox as Nvidia, the dominant supplier of AI chips, is backing software that can help companies run some workloads with fewer GPUs. Jain, however, argued that making AI inference more efficient could ultimately benefit Nvidia by making its hardware more attractive to customers and encouraging wider adoption of AI applications.
Simplismart is serving customers in an increasingly crowded market for AI inference software, competing with offerings from Nvidia itself, as well as major cloud providers and hyperscalers including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. A growing number of startups are also developing tools to make AI models faster and cheaper to run as there is growing demand in this segment, driven by rising demand for AI applications and the need to make better use of expensive GPU resources.
“Where we tend to win is where people have to be more stringent on their SLAs [service-level agreements] and TCO [total cost of ownership],” Jain said, referring to demanding performance requirements and tight cost constraints. Unlike rivals that offer preset options for faster or cheaper inference, Simplismart aims to find a balance tailored to each customer’s needs, he said.
Founded in 2022 by former Oracle engineer Jain and former Google engineer Devansh Ghatak (pictured above, right), Simplismart grew out of the pair’s experience building and deploying machine-learning systems. The two met while studying at BITS Pilani, and the startup now employs 58 people, Jain said.
Simplismart plans to use the new funding to expand its presence in the U.S., grow its team, and invest further in developing its inference software. Jain told TechCrunch that the U.S. remains a key market for the startup as it looks to build on its existing customer base there.
The funding announcement follows a report by Indian English daily The Economic Times that Simplismart was in talks to raise $40 million to $50 million at a valuation of $300 million to $400 million. Asked about the report, Jain declined to comment, saying the startup was not actively fundraising. He added that the Series B was closed and would not be extended.

title: Who is Retrina Fuentes, the judge behind arrest orders vs Duterte critics?
body: Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested on Saturday, October 24, over a cyber libel case filed by an unidentified complainant at the time. It was Davao City Presiding Judge Retrina Espe Fuentes who issued the warrant of arrest. On Monday, October 26, Lustre’s lawyer, Dino de Leon, told Rappler that it was lawyer Mans Carpio — husband of Vice President Sara Duterte — who was the complainant in Lustre’s case. Based on the Supreme Court’s (SC) tracker, Fuentes is currently the presiding judge of Davao City Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 10. The court is located in Benigno Aquino Hall of Justice, in Matina, Davao City. Fuentes was Davao City’s 1st vice executive judge in 2016, according to the Philippine Judicial Academy Bulletin. At the time, Presiding Judge Emmanuel Carpio was sitting as executive judge. Presiding Judge Carpio is the uncle of Mans Carpio. In her 2024 Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth, Vice President Duterte listed Emmanuel Carpio as her uncle-in-law. At the time of Fuentes’ appointment as 1st vice executive judge, Rodrigo Duterte was president, while his daughter Sara was Davao City mayor during that period. Based on SC Office of the Court Administrator’s Administrative Order No. 231-2022 , Fuentes became Davao City’s executive judge on November 1, 2022 under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. The Fraternal Order of Saint Thomas More in Davao City posted a congratulatory message after Fuentes’ appointment. She held the position from 2022 to 2024, according to SC spokesperson Camille Sue Mae Ting. “Davao Regional Trial Court Executive Judge is now Judge Rowena M. Apao Adlawan,” said Ting. According to the SC’s AM No. 03-8-02-SC , the Court may appoint executive judges and vice executive judges in stations where there are more than two RTC branches. Their appointment will be based on their administrative qualifications, experience, and seniority, among others. “The Executive Judge shall take charge of the administrative work of the Supreme Court in all first and second level courts. The Executive Judge derives his/her powers and prerogatives through delegation by the Supreme Court,” said the order. Lustre’s arrest Lustre, the 72-year-old veteran journalist was attending the Saturday News Forum event in Quezon City when Quezon City police from the Quezon City Police District arrested him. After nearly a day in detention, he was able to post a P48,000-bail at past midnight on Sunday, October 25. Lustre is the author of the book, “ Kill, Kill, Kill : Extrajudicial Killings in the Philippines .” It’s about former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs that killed nearly 30,000 people, according to several human rights groups. Duterte is now detained in The Hague, Netherlands over his crimes against humanity case that stemmed from the said campaign. After his release from temporary detention, Lustre said he is scheduled to release a new book titled, “MISFIT SARA Life and Times of Vice President Sara Duterte-Carpio; The Impeachment Trial of a Filipino Vice President.” The Vice President is currently in the middle of her impeachment trial that could remove her from the position and bar her from running for president in 2028. The information sheet against Lustre reads: “The above-named accused, with deliberate intent, willfully, unlawfully, and feloniously, through his Facebook account under the name ‘Philip Jr. Lustre,’ published and posted written statements, thereby making an imputation of a crime against Atty. Manases R. Carpio, a private individual and on the said date, was actually residing in Davao City, through the internet using the social networking platform called ‘Facebook.com,’ by saying: ‘Sumuka si Mans Carpio ng P300-M sa operasyon ng Marines: P150M kay Mike; P50M kay Levi; at P5M sa bawat isa sa 18 Marines? ‘ which published statement, taken in its plain, natural, and ordinary meaning, directly imputes upon Atty. Manases R. Carpio, the commission of a crime, specifically bribery or corrupt.” Must Read Philip Lustre Jr.’s arrest a ‘warning’ for journalists – lawyer Bello’s case Fuentes was also the judge who signed the warrant of arrest against another Duterte critic and former vice presidential candidate, Walden Bello. In 2022, at the height of the campaign season, former Davao City public information officer Jefry Tupas filed a cyber libel complaint against Bello. Tupas was seeking P10 million in damages after being allegedly accused by Bello on social media of being a drug addict and dealer. Duterte’s aide was embroiled in a controversy in 2021 after attending a beach party in Mabini, Davao de Oro that was later raided by anti-narcotics agents. The operation supposedly happened an hour after Tupas and companions had left the party. On August 8, 2022, QCPD personnel arrested Bello over a warrant issued by Fuentes for two counts of cyber libel. He was later freed after posting a P48,000-bail for each of the counts. Bello, at the time, labeled Tupas’ case as “clearly a politically-motivated move.” The following year, Bello filed a petition with the SC seeking to decriminalize libel in the Philippines. In February this year, the former vice presidential bet issued an apology to Tupas, saying his statements were “unfounded.” Other cases handled In 2019, Fuentes was the judge who ordered the arrest of Italian Lorenzo Marchesi , who was 57 years old at the time. He was ordered arrested over alleged possession of child sexual abuse and exploitation materials. Marchesi was arrested after a search of his electronic devices allegedly revealed a collection of illegal materials. Last September, Fuentes was the same judge who issued a warrant of arrest against a man wanted for rape. She issued the warrant on September 2, 2026. “The accused, identified only by the alias ‘Abdul,’ was properly informed of the cause of his arrest and apprised of his constitutional rights, including his rights under Republic Act No. 9745, or the Anti-Torture Act of 2009, in a language or dialect known to and understood by him,” said the PNP. “The arrested person was identified as a top 3 most wanted person, municipal level, under the PNP e-warrant system,” it added. – Rappler.com https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=955067143549974

title: Sterling Anderson doesn’t think humanoid robots should be building cars
body:
At a splashy event in New York City last week, General Motors unveiled its new tech roadmap centered on AI-driven vehicle development, advanced battery tech, high-powered car computers, and autonomous driving.
Some of this was old news: We already knew the automaker was developing hands-free, eyes-off driving automation and had been prototyping new battery chemistries. In a sense, the real purpose of the event was to showcase how all these pieces fit together. With its new “intelligence-defined vehicle” paradigm, GM is banking on artificial intelligence, centralized computing, and virtualized engineering to cut vehicle development timelines in half, aiming to compress a typical four- to five-year process down to just over two.
Yet, this high-tech overhaul arrives against a backdrop of steep industry headwinds and razor-thin margins for error. GM’s aggressive pivot comes as the automaker faces a wave of hyperefficient Chinese EV makers that are aggressively expanding globally. At the same time, softening EV demand in the US has forced GM to recalibrate its electrification hopes, balancing multibillion-dollar investments in next-generation battery plants with the ongoing costs of software development.
To be sure, for GM to bet its future on unproven software architectures and autonomous technology is a high-stakes gamble: If these complex AI systems falter or if development hits delays, GM risks burning through massive amounts of money while falling further behind agile rivals (like Tesla) that were built as software-first companies from day one.
After the event, I sat down with Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer, to talk about the company’s risky new ventures as well as how he plans to steer a century-old Detroit giant through an increasingly fast, software-driven world.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
So this was quite the massive announcement — just lots of disparate pieces. Is there a unifying theme here, would you say? And if so, what do you think it is?
The car’s getting smarter.
That’s it?
That’s it. I think so. Your vehicle is becoming a trusted, intelligent companion, and we’re doing that in a variety of ways. I think I might be one of the only guys who gets as excited as I do about what we’re doing in the development process and making that faster and better.
I don’t know how many people are going to come away with that takeaway in quite the spirit that I think it merits, but the level of tests and performance optimality that we can achieve when we can spin design decisions hundreds of times — that previously would have accommodated one — is huge. It’s really huge. I’ve been asked now by two folks I’ve met afterwards, “Hey, what about safety, and does speed come at the cost of safety?” The way we are getting speed is by virtualizing tests in a way that allows us to improve safety. Historically, I would have been able to afford X prototypes that I could send to crash tests, and it took me six months. Now, I kick off thousands of tests in the virtual world that give me feedback much quicker. So I get speed, and I get safety, better coverage, and better understanding. There’s a lot of cake being eaten, too, in this process.
"“I kick off thousands of tests in the virtual world that give me feedback much quicker.”" - Sterling Anderson
What kind of AI models are you using? I know you talked about how data is sort of the currency here, so obviously there’s a lot that you’re pulling from your own customers, but there’s a range of products out there. What’s the dividing line between what to look for outside the company versus what to pull from inside?
It’s a good question. It depends on what we’re doing with it. In many cases, the transformer-based foundation models enable some of the generative design stuff I was talking about — we have enough data in-house based on decades of design files, analyses, etc., that we can get a pretty well-trained system to express our data well. But we have access to — and anybody has access in many cases to — a lot of data that informs us. The co-training of these models with data that exists beyond GM’s walls tends to make them better. So we do it with all of them.
You’ve talked about moving from deterministic code to probabilistic AI that learns from the structure of the world and from the data. How are you specifically embedding these models into the vehicles? How much is run locally versus pulling from the cloud?
For any safety-critical functionality, the inference is done onboard because we can’t deal with latency, possible dropouts, or whatever else. Some of these examples you saw from the team earlier today, like the OnStar AI interactions, aren’t safety-critical. You probably noticed, given the latency, that you had some round-tripping happening there because we don’t need to run those all onboard. Now, we’re thinking about distilling them down into onboard models just to deal with the latency, but that’s an on-the-edge user experience element, not a core safety consideration.
You talked a little bit during your presentation about how big GM is, which gives you advantages with data, but also a lot of inertia. Back in 2019, GM President Mark Reuss talked about moving toward the “digital brain” of the vehicle, and in 2021 you talked about Ultifi. Have things sped up now? Are you on the glide path at this point?
Yeah, and a big enabler of it is that common electrical system, including centralized compute. Historically, I know of very few killers to software speed quite like complexity. The moment a software team has a very large set of deployment targets that don’t share a common baseline is the moment you slow that team down enormously.
Rolling this out across our entire portfolio is specifically to enable software speed so we don’t have to continue to support vehicles of various configurations. As that hardware set rolls out, software engineers will suddenly be able to operate like they would if they were in a company with two models in production, which they just haven’t been able to in history.
GM is unique in having this huge portfolio of brands with distinct identities. How do you decide what to standardize across every vehicle versus ensuring a Buick remains a Buick and a GMC Sierra remains unique?
It’s a combination of things. First, the essence of each brand tends to manifest in aesthetics and interaction models. Aesthetics is something you can effectively skin via design, both in digital interfaces and physical sheet metal. We already do a fairly good job of commonizing the under-the-skin componentry because why wouldn’t we? For a given segment of vehicle, there’s a particular ride quality that tends to be best received by everybody.
Our T1-2 platform for our next-generation trucks is common between brands. Where you’ll see us differentiate is in the feature set, the aesthetics, and interaction patterns we effectively skin segment by segment. Sales has dedicated brand channels, but engineering is all one organization. That ensures we don’t ship heterogeneous, suboptimal cars for different brands just because a team that was slightly worse was assigned to one brand or another. I want our engineering team focusing all of their effort on what is the absolute best suspension, powertrain, or drive unit, and then we scale it across the portfolio.
Speaking of autonomy, we have autonomous vehicles on the road today — Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla Cybercabs. What are the challenges GM still needs to solve to get to a point where someone can take their eyes off the road comfortably and safely?
When you say “eyes off,” you mean autonomous?
Autonomously, yes. Hands off, mind off, eyes off. But at the same time, you wouldn’t be recommending people go to sleep in their vehicles yet?
We are designing them such that should they fall asleep, it won’t be unsafe, because we don’t have the luxury of ensuring that they’re paying attention. The reason you won’t hear me use terms like “eyes off” is because I hear people use those terms in reference to nonsensical levels of automation. What do you think your mind is doing when your eyes are on your phone? Where’s your mind? Let’s not draw these nonsensical distinctions. If you believe that your driver assistance system is super capable, you are already at risk of complacency — at risk of treating it like it’s an autonomous system. Our philosophy is: If we’re going to design an autonomous system, we’re going to actually design an autonomous system. The path of incrementalism that we’ll take will work for personal ownership, not the one that worked for robotaxis. Instead of regionally specific, speed-limited settings, we’re going to go toward road-type specific settings and expand outward from there. They both converge in the same place — self-driving everywhere at all times — but take different paths to get there.
With robotaxis today, we see problems around nuisance situations — like blocking intersections or emergency vehicles. Do you feel personal autonomy, as GM defines it, solves some of that because the driver remains an option to fall back on?
The form of the fallback matters. We will not fall back in a safety-critical dynamic situation. It’s just not reasonable to do that. What we can do in a non-safety-critical situation — where the vehicle is stopped and something odd is happening — is hand it back to the driver once we’ve reached a safe place. Having a human in the loop is very useful for that.
How do you structure that handoff to avoid driver complacency?
We’re not handing back dynamically. This is not an exchange of “you drive, now I’ll drive, oops, I don’t recognize this.” This is not Level 3. In the same way you put a robotaxi in a bounded region, we will put personally owned autonomous vehicles on a particular road.
When on that road, we will take the human to their destination and give a graceful countdown — like, “Hey, you’ve got 10 minutes left in this ride.” If they take over preemptively, great. Should they not take over, the system brings the vehicle to a safe state off the off-ramp and says, “I told you 10 minutes ago to take over. We’re stopped, and I’m not going any further.”
You have to operate under the assumption that bad actors will try to abuse the system — sitting in the back seat, like we’ve seen with Tesla users.
I get far more nervous when misuse happens in the context of a driver-assist system that wasn’t designed to handle every situation. If the vehicle accepts control, our system is designed to deal with more situations that can be thrown at it in that circumstance. So my anxiety level declines dramatically.
Features like OnStar AI ask for access to calendars, emails, and personal data. Given past FTC orders regarding GM selling customer data to third-party brokers without permission, how do you ensure customers can trust you with this data?
Privacy has to be designed in. With end-to-end encryption, we don’t see your data; you grant permission to an assistant that performs better with context. Data is only available to us at an aggregate, anonymized level. At an individual level, it is encrypted and under your control.
When you buy a car, going through dozens of terms and conditions leads to “click, click, click” without reading, which does a disservice to trust. We have dramatically simplified these authorizations down to a couple of clear choices that explain why the car needs data — like reading your calendar for smart routing. You can revoke permission, delete your data, or port it out at any time. You alluded to trust, which is foundational. Decisions made in the past by people who no longer work for this company have an overhang, but that’s not the company we are today. We earn that trust back by designing the architecture so that even if someone made a bad decision internally, the system technically wouldn’t allow them to access raw user data.
And the way we do that is by designing it. Look, even if we had someone stupid work for us again and do something like this, they couldn’t. They wouldn’t be able to access it.
AI is cutting vehicle development times, but we’re also seeing hype around factory automation and humanoid robots from companies like Tesla and Rivian. Is GM heading in that direction?
If you want to be perceived as a robotics player these days, it seems you have to have a humanoid robot that does backflips. It’s weird. Advocacy for humanoids often comes from people who historically advocate for first-principles engineering, but humanoids are not born from first principles. They put form over function. The logic assumes the human form factor is optimal for a factory floor, but this form factor evolved to run away from lions on the African savanna! Production environments weren’t built for human forms any more than roads built for horses meant cars should have four legs. The most valuable real estate in a factory is the floor. Having bumbling humanoid robots clamoring in and out of vehicles is not where you start. You start with form factors that look alien — like an octopus hanging from a gantry that reaches into a moving vehicle line. We’re ignoring the “religion” of humanoids and focusing on underlying AI intelligence that can operate various specialized robot form factors for specific tasks.
Is GM building these robotics systems itself?
We already are. We actively work with heavy machinery suppliers like Fanuc, but we are actively developing many of our own solutions.
People are excited about cars getting smarter, but they also want them to be cheaper. How do these announcements lead to more affordable options?
LMR (lithium manganese rich) battery chemistry is a huge part of this. It delivers a range close to high-nickel packs at a cost closer to LFP. On a per-range basis, a customer will be able to buy a fourth-gen GM EV for less money than a competitor’s profitable model without relying on subsidies.
Additionally, commonizing our electrical architecture reduces wiring length and vehicle mass dramatically, making cars inherently more affordable. Virtualizing development cuts prototype costs, allowing vehicle business cases to clear at lower retail prices. This applies to ICE vehicles and hybrids as well, not just EVs.
Will this intelligence lead to higher subscriptions and paywalls?
Capability advances inevitably over time without raising financial costs — the device in your lap does far more than computers years ago for less money. Regarding subscriptions: I’m here to build great products. If customers like paying for services like a lease, let them; if not, don’t force them.
[GM spokesperson Chaiti Sen: For immediate features like OnStar AI, it will be included in our basic package. We aren’t going to paywall core baseline experiences or hand customers a bare “tin shell.”]
For your sensor suite, you’re using cameras, radar, and lidar. Do you see that remaining in perpetuity, or could you eventually scale back to a vision-only approach like Tesla?
If you scale back to vision-only, physics suggests you’ll be in trouble in certain situations. Radar is so cheap that dropping it doesn’t make sense — dropping it is a weird religious stance that ignores physics. Lidar operates on a similar wavelength to visible light and helps co-train camera systems to get better faster. Cameras can’t see through dense fog or measure instantaneous velocity like radar can. Having a multisensor suite provides obvious safety advantages that physics simply demands.

title: AI Agents Are Media’s New Favorite Audience
body:
Chattiana’s briefing lists Seo’s agenda and to-do list, and plucks water-cooler topics from the headlines in her various newsletters along with links to the sources.
“I’m kind of challenging myself as an introvert to start more conversations,” Seo, a San Diego-based public relations consultant, tells WIRED. The newsletter, she says, gives her a sense of the daily news and options for filling an awkward silence on a Zoom call.
Seo is far from the first person to consume her news with an AI assist. In fact, the trend has become so common that some news outlets are starting to produce content that treats AI agents—not human readers—as the intended audience. This can look like anything from feeds optimized for AI to pieces structured to allow agents to create personalized articles.
“We believe that the media ecosystem is changing,” says Axios chief revenue officer Jacquelyn Cameron. “We see this with open web deteriorating. We see that search is shrinking. We see that hyperpersonalization is surging, that LLMs are becoming more important in the way that people are consuming” their news.
Major publishers have responded to that change in a variety of ways. Many, including WIRED’s parent company Condé Nast, have signed deals to allow AI platforms to surface their content. Outlets are grappling with “generative engine optimization,” or GEO, strategies to ensure articles appear in responses to AI prompts. Last year, AIOSEO, a SEO plug-in for WordPress sites, launched a feature that provides websites with LLM.txt files, which help AI discover and interpret sites’ content.
Others have taken a more defensive posture: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally trained models on reporting. That case is still ongoing.
What Axios and a handful of others are trying, though, represents a more foundational shift in how the media operates—and who its stories are for.
“We have always said,” Cameron says, “that we want to be where the audience is.”
“We do believe that a significant portion of news consumption will move into AI systems, LLMs, and devices,” Cameron says. She describes the feeds as a more efficient way for agents to access Axios content, cutting back on narrative to prioritize structured data—more similar to a Bloomberg terminal than a series of articles.
The two initial Direct feeds are aimed at corporate clients. The first, which launched this fall, gives the AI agents of Axios Pro Deals subscribers access to merger and acquisition content. The second feed will act as a source to train in-house large language models, and will launch next year.
Starting with feeds aimed at businesses makes sense. Corporate budgets tend to have more tolerance than individual subscribers for experiments, especially if these unproven concepts could offer even a slight business advantage. But the third Axios Direct feed, which the company plans to develop next year, will be consumer-facing—a way for individual subscribers to have Axios’ reporting sent directly to their agent. All three feeds will look similar to RSS feeds—not aesthetically pleasing, as they aren’t intended for the human eye, but instead taking the form of standardized lines of text.
While Axios is trimming its (already brief) content to satisfy AI, Every is taking a different approach. The six-year-old tech media and software company, which announced a $2 million funding round from investors including LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman last year, expects its subscribers to treat AI as almost an extension of themselves.
Every’s founder Dan Shipper says the most common way Every’s content differs from a typical article is that its writers include prompts in pieces whenever possible, allowing readers to test concepts themselves. An article about a new model, for example, includes a series of prompts the reader can copy-paste into AI, demonstrating how the model answers questions and evaluates input.
Certain types of articles—such as guides—also include buttons that readers can press to “Read With Claude” or “Read With ChatGPT.” Clicking pulls up a prompt, instructing AI to “Start with a tight summary: one paragraph, bulleted. Then offer to go deeper.” Writers pack stories with details without worrying about losing readers’ attention, knowing agents will pick out the most relevant bits.
Two years ago, the outlet launched its first “extendable” article: a long-form feature accompanied by a database of reporting, from interview recordings to news articles to YouTube videos. Readers could query a chatbot, which would fetch additional details from the database.
Recently, Every published a 8,000-word article about Codex that subscribers can consume in even more forms. Drawing from the database, subscribers’ agents can tailor a new piece—be it an article, podcast, or video—to suit their interests. One reader might want a bulleted summary, while another could request a short film of interview bits.
“As a writer, you have to make choices about what goes into the story you’re telling,” Shipper says. “And there’s always a question about, are those the right choices? Or, are those the right choices for a particular reader?” With AI, journalists no longer choose.
“People are gonna do crazy, crazy stuff with this,” Shipper adds.
Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, a professor of communication at the University of Copenhagen, says that while the market of publishing for agents is “emerging,” it remains immature and “extremely uneven.” Major questions remain, he says, about price points and how AI agents will interact with content in the future.
Cameron and Allison Murphy, Axios’ chief operating officer, are optimistic about AI as an audience proxy. According to the executives, Axios’s short-form, highly structured style has already made the publisher a favorite for AI to pull from, when responding to prompts. “Time is money for crawlers,” Murphy says. “They don’t want to have to go three quarters down the page to find the main point. So, that’s something that’s already benefiting us.”
But does AI crawling its content actually benefit Axios’ bottom line? Even if readers don’t actually visit the Axios homepage, the brand visibility in and of itself can be positive, Nielsen says. It’s not unlike publishers making content for social platforms like TikTok and Instagram that rarely bring viewers back to their websites.
Publications in general are grappling with how difficult it has become to monetize certain types of content when a chatbot can offer up answers on a silver platter. People only want to pay for information that other publications—and LLMs—don’t have. At Every, that means in-the-weeds guidance on AI and how to use it; at Axios Pro Deals, it’s speedy access to information that could move the market. An all-access Axios Pro Deals subscription costs $2,499 a year, while an annual Every subscription costs $288.
Shipper sees that $288 as a subscription for a human reader, along with their agents. “I may not want to read all of your stuff every month,” Shipper says. But if his subscription can include his agent, “I may want my agent to know it so that it can tell me, ‘Hey, this thing is important.’”
Murphy says that Axios’ starting point is one of acceptance: People are already using AI to absorb information, and that more people will be doing so in the near future.
“I also try to make it a little less existentially terrifying by thinking, this isn’t the first time this has happened in media,” Murphy says. People get their news via social media, via short-form video, via podcasts. “It isn’t really AI as the audience,” Murphy adds. “It’s AI as a tool that helps us reach our audience.”

title: UK and Poland strengthen defences on Europe's Eastern flank
body:
Britain will be more secure as a result of a new defence agreement with Poland designed to deter Russian threats.
The Warsaw Defence Plan comes as Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and his counterpart Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz today meet in Warsaw. Under the agreement, the two nations will work together across sea, land, air, cyber and industry to strengthen security and deterrence across Europe’s Eastern Flank.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said:
Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies - from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century.
The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.
From collaborating on NATO exercises that deter our adversaries to working together to support Ukraine in its fight for freedom, we are committed to standing together for European security whilst boosting our economies with stronger defence industries.
The agreement sets out the first phase of defence cooperation under the new UK-Poland Security and Defence Partnership Treaty and demonstrates the UK stepping up on European security to build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.
It will strengthen joint work on defence between the UK and Poland across a number of key areas, including:
Collaboration on the manufacture and development of the next generation of air defence missiles.
Co-development of drone and counter-drone technologies to deter threats to civilians and critical national infrastructure, as Russia steps up its campaign of drone incursions across the UK and Europe.
Boosting cooperation on cyber security and resilience to help both countries defend defence and civilian sites from hostile threats.
Sharing lessons and experience from developing frigate capabilities, the British Type 31 and Polish Miecznik, which are built from a common design.
Increasing defensive maritime activity in the Baltic Sea through exercises and regional coordination, helping British and Polish forces protect vital lines of communication in the sea.
The UK and Poland will also work together to further strengthen cooperation between their defence industries through closer defence procurement coordination, building on major deals such as Poland’s procurement of its Narew air defence system from MBDA UK.
UK and Polish defence industrial partners BAE Systems and Poland’s PGZ will expand large-calibre ammunition production capacity and capability. More widely, both nations’ defence industries will collaborate to promote defence education, training and workforce mobility to build shared expertise.
Continued UK and Polish participation in large-scale exercises such as Steadfast Defender, Polish Dragon and Joint Warrior will also ensure both nations remain ready to respond to the conflicts of the future, including counter-drone warfare, electronic warfare, and missile defence.
It comes as the UK and Poland plan for a major Coalition of the Wiling exercise in Poland next month, which will see thousands of personnel take part to ensure the Multinational Force Ukraine is ready to support the military training and post-war rebuilding that Ukraine will need.

title: Caritas-Kyiv Charitable Foundation issues recommendations for development of social services in Kyiv region based on new study
body:
Currently, the most in-demand services include social support, home-based care, transportation, and social adaptation. This is according to the findings of a study conducted by the Caritas-Kyiv Charitable Foundation in cooperation with Kyiv Regional State Administration as part of the Seeing the Invisible project. The results were presented at a press conference held at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Tuesday .
"There is plenty of work for everyone: state, municipal, and non-governmental organizations alike. As part of the Seeing the Invisible project, we carried out a comprehensive study. It involved approximately 100 social sector professionals and over 600 residents of Kyiv region," said Vladyslav Zhyliaiev, an advocacy specialist at the Caritas-Kyiv Charitable Foundation.
Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine Photo: Interfax-Ukraine From needs assessment to real solutions: How to make social services in kyiv region communities accessible and person-centered
According to him, the study’s results show that "the needs, as assessed by both residents and professionals, align very closely."
"I always say that if a person’s basic needs aren’t met, if they have nothing to eat, nothing to wear, or no way to pay for housing (which is especially true for internally displaced persons, or IDPs), then, unfortunately, we cannot even begin to discuss anything beyond that. That is why we keep urging the international community to focus on the needs of Kyiv region in particular, as it is in dire need of assistance," emphasized a representative from Caritas Kyiv.
"As the figures show, the region is constantly taking in internally displaced persons. It was one of the first to welcome them, and to this day, it continues to host the largest number. Consequently, while the needs are only set to grow, the available aid is shrinking; yet, we must continue to devote ever-greater attention to these internally displaced persons," he said.
Zhyliaev also noted that special attention should be paid to veterans and their families, families with children facing difficult life circumstances, children with disabilities, people with disabilities, and the elderly.
"What kind of services are needed most? These include social support, in-home care, material assistance, transportation services, social adaptation, supported living, and respite care. We can provide assistance to these families—who are in need—on several occasions, helping them overcome their difficult life circumstances and reach the level of stability they require," he emphasized.
According to the study, Zhyliaev pointed out, "the services that residents feel are most lacking include transportation, respite care, material assistance, social adaptation, and collaborative social work involving the non-governmental sector, municipal institutions, and the public sector."

title: President Stubb, Prime Minister Støre hold phone call with President Putin
body:
This was reported by the Office of the President of Finland , according to Ukrinform.
The office said the call was a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on 20 October and “held in consultation with Ukraine.”
“Stubb and Støre initiated the call to discuss Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe,” the press release said.
According to the office, “the call was related to the upcoming meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi.”
It is emphasized that Stubb and Støre took part in the call as the leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole.
“Norway and Finland have always promoted peace and security in our region. The two countries have a shared interest in stability and predictability in the Baltic Sea region and the High North. This was highlighted in the call,” the press release said.
According to the statement, “Stubb and Støre emphasized that Finland and Norway will continue their longstanding support for Ukraine.”
They also emphasized that the war must end and negotiations resume
“The discussion was frank and substantive. We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions”, President Stubb said.
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation”, Prime Minister Støre said.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this week in Brussels a security meeting involving representatives of the United States, Ukraine, the EU and NATO, at which initiatives to end the war will be discussed.

title: What we know about Putin’s call with Norway’s prime minister, Finland’s president
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store held a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, the Finnish leader’s office said.
Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the report to TASS.
TASS has compiled the main details available so far.
- Stubb and Store held a phone call with Putin on October 27, the Finnish leader’s office said.
- The two leaders took part in the call on behalf of their respective countries, rather than representing Europe as a whole.
- Stubb and Store initiated the conversation with Putin to discuss the situation in Ukraine and an upcoming meeting in Abu Dhabi.
- They also discussed maintaining stability in the Baltic Sea region and the High North.
- Putin discussed efforts to resolve the Ukraine crisis with Stubb and Store, the Kremlin press service said.
- The discussion took into account Putin’s talks with US Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg, as well as Stubb and Store’s contacts with Witkoff and Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo.
- The Russian president gave his assessment of the current situation in the conflict zone in Ukraine and recalled its underlying causes.
- He said peace in Ukraine could be achieved provided that Russia’s interests are fully taken into account.
- Putin, Stubb and Store expressed support for the agreement to resume trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin press service said.
- The Russian president informed the Finnish and Norwegian leaders that a US-mediated humanitarian operation had begun near the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region.
- Putin stressed that the confrontational approach pursued by the EU and NATO is hindering progress toward peace in Ukraine.
- The three leaders also discussed security and stability in the Baltic Sea region and Northern Europe, the Kremlin press service said.
- Stubb and Store "confirmed the importance of respecting international maritime law and the principle of freedom of navigation," the Kremlin said.
- Putin, Stubb and Store agreed to stay in direct telephone contact, the Kremlin press service said.
- Finnish President Alexander Stubb called the conversation frank and substantive, his office reported.
- Stubb stressed that ending the conflict in Ukraine requires continued direct dialogue with Russia.
- Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store stressed the importance of de-escalating the Ukrainian conflict during the call, the country's government press service reported.
- Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Stubb and Store’s phone call with Putin had not been coordinated with their European allies.

title: SITA to acquire Flightscape, CAE’s airline operations software business
body: SITA has agreed to acquire Flightscape, the airline operations software business of Canada’s CAE. The deal expands SITA’s role in airline operations. Flightscape’s software helps airlines plan flights, manage crews, run operations control, coordinate ground activities and deliver in-flight services. According to SITA, more than 90 airlines use it every day. SITA said the acquisition will accelerate its shift from connecting aviation’s systems to helping airlines and their partners make better operational decisions, anticipate disruption and recover faster. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals. Financial terms were not disclosed in the announcement. Bringing operational decisions and industry data together SITA, which is owned by the air transport community, connects airlines, airports and other industry partners through the information they share every day. According to the company, much of that information currently sits outside the systems airlines use to make operational decisions. Flightscape’s software will add that operational core to SITA’s existing products. “Airlines need to make the best possible use of their aircraft, crews and infrastructure while responding to increasingly complex operational challenges,” said David Lavorel, Chief Executive Officer of SITA. “With Flightscape, we will bring together our respective complementary capabilities to strengthen what we offer airlines and connect their operational decisions with insight from across the aviation ecosystem.” SITA pointed to the growing complexity of airline operations. More than 10 billion people a year are expected to fly by 2050, and disruption continues to affect daily operations. Every flight relies on several partners working together, yet each one sees only part of the picture. “The hardest decisions in an operations control center come when plans change and every minute counts,” said Yann Cabaret, CEO of SITA for Aircraft. “Technology and AI can now help airlines and their partners see more of what is happening and respond together.” He added that the aim is to give an airline’s operations team and its industry partners the same information when plans change, “so they can recover as one operation rather than as separate parts.” Building on earlier acquisitions The deal adds to SITA’s recent investments in airline operations technology. In 2021, the company acquired Safety Line, whose technology helps airlines fly more fuel-efficiently. Earlier in 2026, it acquired Big Blue Analytics, whose AI helps airlines build disruption recovery plans in minutes. Both systems work alongside whatever systems an airline already uses. SITA said it will integrate them with Flightscape’s systems in stages, in close consultation with customers. Work on connecting the products will begin only after the transaction closes. What changes for Flightscape customers SITA said Flightscape customers will keep their current service and support across flight operations and in-flight services. The solutions will remain modular and open, so airlines can choose the products they need and connect them to their existing systems. “I believe SITA is a natural home for Flightscape and an excellent strategic fit for the business,” said Carter Copeland, President of Flightscape. “This transaction positions Flightscape within an organization deeply connected to the global air transport industry.” RELATED SITA to acquire Collins Aerospace Airport Solutions in deal set to close in 2027 The post SITA to acquire Flightscape, CAE’s airline operations software business appeared first on AeroTime .

title: Kashagan Arbitration: Tribunal Rejects $12 Billion in Kazakhstan’s Claims
body: An international arbitration tribunal has rejected approximately $12 billion in claims brought by Kazakhstan against investors in the Kashagan oil field, Bloomberg reported on October 22. Citing sources familiar with the confidential proceedings, the report said the claims concerned field development costs incurred between 2011 and 2015 and were filed after the applicable deadline. Claims concerning another $8 billion in disputed costs have been allowed to proceed. Kazakhstan had sought to exclude approximately $20 billion from the costs investors are entitled to recover through oil production. The arbitrators did not examine whether the expenses covered by the rejected claims were justified. The ruling has not been made public. Kashagan is operated by North Caspian Operating Company (NCOC), whose shareholders include KazMunayGas, ExxonMobil, Eni, Shell, TotalEnergies, China National Petroleum Corporation, and INPEX Corporation. The field is located in the northern Caspian Sea. High reservoir pressure and hydrogen sulfide levels drove up construction costs and delayed the project’s launch, with difficult climatic conditions compounding these problems. Production began in 2013 but was suspended shortly afterward because of gas leaks in pipelines. Operations resumed in 2016. Under the 1997 production-sharing agreement, investors recover eligible project costs through a portion of the oil produced. The remaining oil, known as profit oil, is then divided between the state and the project participants. An increase in recognized costs reduces the amount of oil available for distribution as profit. Kazakhstan is challenging costs under contractor agreements, including spending on construction work and equipment. In August, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) reported that the wider arbitration included allegations concerning about a dozen construction contracts worth $10.7 billion , awarded during the 2000s. Kazakhstan alleges that some involved inflated costs or conflicts of interest; it has also alleged bribery. NCOC says its members acted in accordance with their contracts and Kazakh law. In April 2025, ICIJ reported that Kazakhstan had brought claims totaling $160 billion against Kashagan’s investors. The report also cited Kazakhstan’s claim that the consortium receives approximately 98% of oil revenue after priority payments to the state under the production-sharing agreement. According to ICIJ, the proceedings are registered with the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague and could continue until at least 2028. Separately, Kazakhstan is seeking to recover an environmental fine of 2.3 trillion tenge, or approximately $5.2 billion, from Kashagan’s operator. The allegations concern breaches of limits on storing sulfur produced during oil and gas processing. On September 29, the authorities resumed enforcement proceedings to collect the fine. The move followed a three-week suspension while a Kazakh court considered NCOC’s challenge to the enforcement process. NCOC is contesting the fine, and the project’s foreign shareholders have initiated international arbitration , alleging that Kazakhstan violated its investment protection obligations. NCOC says an arbitration tribunal issued an interim order barring collection of the fine while the proceedings continue. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Justice disputes whether the order can prevent the authorities from enforcing a ruling by a Kazakh court.

title: Police confirm man, teenager swept away by flood in Aba
body: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — Abia State Police Command has confirmed that a man who attempted to rescue a teenage girl from a water-filled ditch at Faulks Road, Aba, was swept away alongside the girl during Sunday’s downpour. The Police Public Relations Officer, Maureen Chinaka, disclosed this while responding to Vanguard inquiries, confirming that the incident occurred around the popular Ukwu Mango area of the commercial city. Chinaka said the tragedy happened near an ongoing construction site where an uncovered ditch had filled with rainwater. According to her, the teenage girl was passing through the area when she reportedly hit a stone and fell into the ditch. An adult who witnessed the incident reportedly plunged into the water in an attempt to rescue her, but both were swept away. “Unfortunately, we have not been able to see them. The police are aware, and the matter has been reported. Efforts are in place to see how they can be rescued,” Chinaka said. She confirmed that the two victims had yet to be found as search efforts continued. Asked whether the construction company responsible for the site would face possible charges over negligence, the police spokesperson said investigations were on-going. The tragedy has raised concerns about the safety of construction sites during heavy rainfall, particularly where excavations and drainage channels are left uncovered and become submerged in floodwater. Aba’s flat terrain makes parts of the commercial city vulnerable to flooding during heavy downpours, increasing the risks posed by waterlogged roads, open drains and excavations. The post Police confirm man, teenager swept away by flood in Aba appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Nigeria’s economic crisis predates Tinubu, says ex-minister, Ikoh
body: By Steve Oko Former Minister of State for Science and Technology and Abia State Coordinator of Renewed Hope Ambassadors, Chief Henry Ikechukwu Ikoh, has said Nigeria’s economic crisis predates President Bola Tinubu’s administration, urging Nigerians to assess the government’s reforms against the country’s longstanding structural challenges. Ikoh, who made the submission in a statement by his media aide, Smart Anthony Ogbonna, said Nigeria’s overdependence on crude oil, inadequate industrial diversification, inflation and inconsistent economic policies had contributed to decades of economic difficulties. He noted that Tinubu inherited these challenges in May 2023 and introduced reforms, including petrol subsidy removal and foreign exchange market adjustments, to address fiscal imbalances and establish a more sustainable economy. While acknowledging the hardships caused by the measures, Ikoh argued that their success should ultimately be measured by their impact on employment, food affordability, investment and citizens’ purchasing power. He called for sustained reforms, increased agricultural and industrial production, infrastructure development and effective policy implementation to translate macroeconomic gains into tangible improvements in living standards. The Abia APC chieftain expressed confidence that a second term for Tinubu would consolidate the ongoing reforms, create jobs, attract investment and accelerate economic recovery. He urged Nigerians to support the continuation of the administration’s Renewed Hope Agenda, arguing that policy consistency would provide an opportunity to deepen reforms and expand economic opportunities. The post Nigeria’s economic crisis predates Tinubu, says ex-minister, Ikoh appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Greek Green Bean Salad With Feta and Tomatoes: A Fresh Summer Side
body: A Greek green bean salad with feta and tomatoes turns fresh summer beans into a bright, tangy side dish. Green beans, tomatoes and crumbled feta in a simple vinegar dressing. Photo: Allrecipes What is a Greek green bean salad? In Greek, green beans are called ampelofasolia, so this dish is often known as ampelofasolia salata. Many Greek homes serve the beans warm or at room temperature. They dress them with good olive oil and a splash of vinegar or lemon. Most of us know green beans from fasolakia ladera , the slow summer stew of beans, potatoes and tomato. That dish belongs to the family of ladera , or vegetables cooked in plenty of olive oil. This Greek green bean salad takes a quicker route. You boil the beans until soft, then toss them with raw tomato, herbs and feta while they soak up the dressing. Overall, a Greek green bean salad sits somewhere between a side dish and a meze plate. Like other meze dishes, it works best when shared, and it travels well to a picnic or barbecue. Ingredients for three serves This Greek green bean salad recipe comes from Barbara Sauermann, a recipe developer and Senior Content Producer at Allrecipes. It holds a perfect 5 out of 5 from 20 ratings, and 23 home cooks say they have made it. You need: 1 pound (about 450 g) fresh green beans, trimmed 1/4 US cup (about 60 ml) olive oil 2 US tablespoons (about 30 ml) white balsamic vinegar Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste 1/4 US cup chopped fresh parsley 1 medium shallot, finely chopped Garlic, 1 clove, finely chopped 3 medium tomatoes, chopped 2 ounces (about 55 g) crumbled feta Australian cooks should note that the recipe means a French shallot, or eschalot, rather than a spring onion. A small piece of red onion also works. Choose a good block of feta in brine and crumble it yourself. Our guide on checking one letter on the packet explains how to spot the real thing. How to make the salad Allrecipes lists 20 minutes of preparation, 15 minutes of cooking and 20 minutes of resting. So, the Greek green bean salad takes about 55 minutes from start to finish. First, bring a large pot of lightly salted water to the boil. Add the beans and cook for 10 to 15 minutes, until soft. Drain the beans well and let them steam dry for a minute. Next, whisk the olive oil, vinegar, salt and pepper in a small bowl. Stir the parsley, shallot and garlic into the dressing. Place the beans and tomatoes in a large bowl, pour over the dressing and toss. Fold in the feta. Finally, leave the salad to rest for 20 minutes before serving. The resting time matters for a Greek green bean salad. It lets the warm beans absorb the dressing, while the tomatoes release a little juice into the bowl. Greek cooks like their beans tender rather than squeaky, so taste one before you drain them. If your beans are very fresh and thin, they may need less time. Tips from home cooks Allrecipes shows 13 reviews for this Greek green bean salad, and every rating is five stars. Marsha in Asheville took it to a potluck and wrote, “returned home with an empty bowl!” Cynthia Feldman followed the recipe exactly and called it “DIVINE.” She said it was the first way her husband, who dislikes green beans, would happily eat them. Other cooks made small swaps. Country By Terrilyn had only regular balsamic vinegar, but still found the dish amazing. Marianne left out the shallot and grated the garlic, because she prefers it that way in dressings. One reviewer used red onion instead of shallot, while Samantha had no feta and used Gorgonzola. A Greek cook would stick with feta, but the dressing holds up either way. Momma Mophead had a glut of beans in her garden and wanted something refreshing. She said the salad hit the spot and felt relatively healthy. According to Allrecipes, each serve has about 304 calories, 7 g of protein and 7 g of fibre. Serving ideas for summer Serve the Greek green bean salad with grilled fish, lamb chops or roast chicken. It also makes a light lunch with crusty bread to mop up the dressing. For a full spread, pair it with a crisp lettuce and dill classic and a bowl of olives. If you are torn between summer vegetables, see whether Greeks prefer okra or fasolakia . One cook also said the Greek green bean salad tastes excellent the next day. Keep leftovers in the fridge, then bring them back to room temperature before serving. The full method is in the original recipe on Allrecipes .
