title: Soldiers activated for possible KZN anti-immigrant marches
body:
Parliament, in the form of National Assembly (NA) Speaker, Thoko Didiza, was notified of an activation of 510 soldiers in KwaZulu-Natal by a Presidential edict 12 days after it came into force.
The soldiers, as per a Cyril Ramaphosa signed letter, are “employed for service in co-operation with the SA Police Service (SAPS) in support of Operation Prosper”. The named operation executed and managed by the Joint Operations Division of the SA National Defence Force (SANDF) is termed a safety and security one and sees soldiers and other military personnel activated to assist other government departments and agencies. One – in support of police to curb gangsterism and illegal mining in five provinces – has been underway since April following Ramaphosa making it public in his February State of the Nation Address (SONA).
The Presidential letter, dated 21 October, has it the 510 SANDF personnel will assist police in maintaining law and order in KwaZulu-Natal during planned marches against illegal immigrants. The marches are said to result from misinformation regarding Constitutional Court judgements.
The provincial “employment”, as per the letter to Didiza, started on 9 October and will end on 30 November at an expected cost of R34 082 720.
The other Operation Prosper deployment currently underway sees 2 200 military personnel, the majority on the strength of SA Army regular and reserve units, in the Eastern Cape, Free State, Gauteng, North West and Western Cape provinces. The deployment cost of R823 million was approved by Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana during his Medium Term Budget Policy Speech (MTBS) last Wednesday (21 October).
The latest SANDF deployment follows renewed unrest in Durban in early October, after KwaZulu-Natal Premier Thami Ntuli requested military assistance. On 22 October, a Ugandan national was beaten to death during a protest march in central Durban, intensifying concerns over attacks on foreign nationals. Police arrested five men in connection with the murder and attempted murder of foreign nationals.
In the last month, dozens of people have been arrested in KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng for public violence, unlawful gathering, obstruction and related offences.
Anti-immigration protests in Durban reignited after Home Affairs issued a directive on 28 September implementing a Constitutional Court ruling that asylum seekers can’t be turned away on technicalities before their claims are heard. Home Affairs withdrew the directive on 9 October.
Government officials clarified that the judgment did not automatically grant refugee status, permanent residence or blanket amnesty to undocumented migrants.
Operation Prosper records success in the Western Cape
While soldiers under Operation Prosper are deployed across multiple provinces, significant successes have been recorded in the Western Cape. Earlier this month it was reported close to four thousand nine hundred operations were executed in the first 183 days of the Operation Prosper deployment there.
NATJOINTS (the National Joint Operational and Intelligence Structure) leadership, including co-chair SA Police Service (SAPS) Deputy National Commissioner, Lieutenant General Tebello Mosikili, heard during on-site visits to affected areas of the Cape Flats police and soldiers were responsible for 4 898 operations in that time which equates to more than 26 a day.
The purpose of the visit was to review operational output and refine tactics, Joint Operations Division staffer Lieutenant Colonel Mpho Mathebula reported.
In a review of Western Cape actions since April, the NATJOINTS contingent heard 2 470 arrests were made with 1 755 criminal dockets registered and 142 finalised cases with 140 guilty verdicts and two acquittals. Confiscations included 94 illegal firearms, 2 173 rounds of ammunition and what is listed only as “various drugs” with an estimated street value of R10 million.
The current Op Prosper activation in Western Cape is aimed specifically at curbing gang violence and organised crime by way of crime intelligence assessment followed by a five pillar strategy concentrating on identified areas. Execution on the ground sees targeted cordon and search operations, roadblocks, targeting suspects, countering narcotics distribution and what Mathebula has as “disruption of illegal liquor establishments operating without valid licensing” as well as countering narcotics distribution.
The joint military/police offensive in the province has seen a 12% reduction in murders and a 15% drop in attempted murder since the beginning of April in identified police precincts on the Cape Flats. While results to date are encouraging, she reports, the work will continue apace with the emphasis on improving intelligence to support actions.

title: Blue Box, cannabis, deficit on Ford government’s agenda after 21-week break
body:
Fixing the Blue Box recycling program, speeding up archaeological approvals and enforcing existing cannabis laws are among some of the top legislative items the Ford government plans to focus on as MPPs return to Queen’s Park after an extended summer break.
Premier Doug Ford delayed the return of the legislature until Oct. 27 to avoid pulling focus, the government claimed, from the province-wide municipal election campaigns.
While the hiatus allowed the government to avoid scrutiny during question period, opposition parties say a number of issues have built up over the summer and fall, giving political critics plenty of issues to grill the Progressive Conservatives on.
That includes the government’s suspension of the OSAP program for all private career college students, as the province investigates whether a handful of schools defrauded the student aid program.
Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser suggested his party would focus on the government’s handling of the file and its impact on students.
“But it’s your fault. So we’re gonna make you pay. So if we don’t actually get education right from start to finish, it’s gonna make our economy weaker, and Doug Ford doesn’t understand that.”
NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the current state of the economy, along with affordability, would be her party’s top priority.
While Ford and Prime Minister Mark Carney announced an $8.7 billion funding plan to support the steel, auto and critical mineral industries — critics say it only deals with the fallout of Trump’s tariffs, rather than offer a mitigation strategy.
“What’s missing is an action plan and a strategy that meets the moment we are in,” Stiles said on Focus Ontario.
“When you look at this government returning to the legislature for only five weeks after Doug Ford took a 21 week vacation, it tells me that they don’t have a legislative agenda that’s meeting the moment that we’re in and that’s gonna save a single job.”
The centrepiece of the government’s first week back in the legislature will be the Fall Economic Statement, set to be delivered by Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy on Oct. 29.
Bethlenfalvy warned the government will need to increase the size of the deficit, to deal with a sluggish economy, possibly boosting it beyond $13.8 billion that was projected in the 2026-27 budget.
“The slower economy has impacted our deficit, which was $13 billion last year and is projected to be higher this year,” Bethlenfalvy said during a recent speech.
While the finance minister promised the government wouldn’t raise taxes or implement cuts to health care, he said the province would look to shrink spending, while keeping fiscal capacity available for the tariff fight.
Opposition parties, however, say the government hasn’t been spending enough on tariff impacted communities. During a legislative committee, the Ministry of Finance revealed the province had only spent $140 million of its $1 billion protect Ontario fund, leading to criticism.
“The government spent just about as much money on their Protect Ontario commercials as they’ve spent in the Protect Ontario fund,” said Fraser.
“It’s a sad irony. It’s the government that’s eight years in, it’s failing people, it failing workers who’ve lost their jobs.”
The Ford government is slated to table an omnibus bill during this session of the legislature that it said will “cut red tape, reduce permitting wait times and give businesses the confidence to invest and create jobs in Ontario.”
The government plans to speed up archaeological assessments that are typically required by municipalities for land development.
Minister of Citizenship and Multiculturalism Graham McGregor said the process, which can currently take up to 64 months, would be sped up by 80 per cent once the legislation is passed.
The government said it would also try to curtail the illicit cannabis market by giving the Alcohol and Gaming Commission additional powers to conduct inspections, seize illegal products and levy fines.
The most consequential legislative and regulatory changes, however, could involve Ontario’s fraught blue box program.
Environment Minister Todd McCarthy said the province wants to bring more “transparency and accountability” to the system after producers complained of rising costs and surprise fees that, the government acknowledged, could “impact their businesses.”
The legislation would give Queen’s Park the power to regulate the terms of the contract between companies that produce recyclable materials and organizations that oversee the recycling system.
The changes would give producers consistent and fair contract terms and insight into the program’s operations and costs allowing companies to have a better say over the fees they’re required to pay.

title: Press review: Europe seeks role in Ukraine peace talks as Serbia faces political change
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Europe’s prospects of securing a seat at the Ukrainian conflict settlement talks, Serbia’s future following the opposition’s surprise win in the snap elections, and Brazilian President Lula da Silva’s historic election victory, which will require him to work with the opposition. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Europe does not want Russia and the US to reach an agreement on Ukraine without its involvement and is seeking a seat at the negotiating table. Meanwhile, most countries, including those in Northern Europe, are primarily financing and prolonging the conflict. Norway had previously played a leading role in efforts to resolve the crisis. However, Oslo has not yet submitted any peace proposals to Moscow. Experts believe that it will not be possible to exclude the Europeans entirely, but for now, their position is more likely to hinder the process. While Brussels is seeking to participate in the negotiations, Russia and Ukraine, with US mediation, have agreed on a ceasefire in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region.
Europe is not monolithic; however, the actions of most countries, including those in Northern Europe, are primarily aimed at financing and prolonging the conflict, Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik told Izvestia. "If they put forward any statements or proposals, they resembled ultimatums and were not regarded as mechanisms for seeking a peaceful settlement," he noted.
In turn, the Russian embassy in Oslo said in a comment to Izvestia that the involvement of biased parties -- that is, those that consistently pursue an anti-Russian agenda and unconditionally support Kiev -- in the talks is unlikely to facilitate mutually acceptable agreements. Diplomats emphasized that such steps cannot be regarded as impartial peacemaking initiatives. "No proposals for a settlement of the Ukrainian crisis have been received from the Norwegian side, which has consistently advanced Kiev’s interests throughout the conflict," the embassy pointed out.
According to Valdai Club expert Andrey Kortunov, Europe’s current position is more likely to impede a settlement: European countries are not putting forward constructive proposals during the negotiations, so neither Moscow nor Washington is considering bringing them into the current format. However, it is impossible to establish a new European security architecture without their participation. At a certain stage, their involvement will become not merely desirable but necessary, the expert stressed. To achieve this, Europe will have to take a more flexible stance, he said.
In turn, St. Petersburg State University professor Natalya Yeremina emphasized that local ceasefires like the one in Alyoshki are possible only with the involvement of a third party capable of exerting pressure on Kiev. This case demonstrates how the parties can swiftly reach an agreement under limited and verifiable conditions when the timeframe and specific area are clearly defined, and a mediator and observers are present. Yeremina noted that a global settlement does not yet have a comparable practical framework. The wider peace deal would require extensive security guarantees, she stressed.
The Student List opposition bloc, formed just a month and a half before the vote, unexpectedly won Serbia’s snap elections. With nearly 100% of the ballots counted, it secured more than 52% of the vote and is expected to claim 140 seats in the 250-seat National Assembly, the country’s unicameral parliament. This gives the opposition the opportunity to establish a single-party government. The Serbian Progressive Party, which has been in power since 2012, garnered 39% of the vote, an estimated 103 seats.
The campaign in Serbia took the form of a referendum, as voters chose between the incumbent government and a protest movement, Balkans studies expert Oleg Bondarenko told Vedomosti . According to him, the opposition’s victory will not bring about rapid changes in the country. "Of course, we shouldn’t expect Belgrade to introduce sanctions against Russia anytime soon. However, much will depend on who assumes the roles of prime minister and president," Bondarenko pointed out.
Serbia is entering a new, turbulent period of transformation in both domestic and foreign policy, political scientist Darko Todorovski emphasized. "The Student List bloc is not a political party in the traditional sense, but rather a movement that has attracted everyone dissatisfied with Vucic’s policies. It remains unclear whether it will be able to preserve its unity, given the ideological diversity of its members," he added. According to the expert, Serbia’s foreign policy direction under the new government will not see significant changes in the first year. On the one hand, Belgrade will maintain its policy of balancing between centers of power, albeit with some nuances, and will preserve good relations with Moscow. On the other hand, the government will continue to seek closer ties with the EU without compromising Serbian interests, the political scientist said.
Meanwhile, commenting on cooperation between Moscow and Belgrade, Russian National Energy Security Fund Deputy Director Alexey Grivach told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that the price of Russian gas supplied to Serbia is currently two to three times lower than the European spot market price. However, the long-term contract between Russia and Serbia expired some time ago and is extended every three to six months. "This was done once again in September and will remain in effect until the end of the year. Serbia’s new government will have to address this issue in the middle of winter, likely amid a severe energy crisis in Europe and around the world. Given that gas transit to Hungary and Slovakia passes through Serbia, the situation poses a significant threat to regional energy security," he stressed.
As for possible Serbian restrictions on the Russian economy, they will have a very limited impact, expert Alexander Firanchuk noted. According to him, Serbia’s share of Russian exports and imports stands at nearly 0.3%. "The imposition of sanctions against Russia is unlikely to become a top priority on Serbia’s agenda. The economic consequences of such decisions should be assessed objectively, based on the actual scale of trade ties," the expert said.
After trailing in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election, incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva managed to take the lead and win the second round with 51.79% of the vote, compared to 48.21% for his main rival, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro (2019-2021), Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. The latter told reporters that it was "impossible" for him to concede the election results. Although Lula won by a margin of more than four million votes, his defeated opponent is reluctant to accept the results and intends to contest them.
Lula has secured a historic victory, as since the country became a republic, no president who lost in the first round has ever won in the second, let alone been elected four times, political consultant Pavel Dubravsky told Vedomosti. According to him, the second debate strengthened Lula’s standing, not least because of Bolsonaro’s attempts to belittle the incumbent head of state. For example, the right-wing candidate pointed out that Lula was missing a finger, his little finger on his left hand, which he lost at age 19 in a workplace injury while working at a steel mill. "And Lula da Silva’s campaign team made full use of this to show Bolsonaro’s disconnect from ordinary working people," Dubravsky pointed out. He emphasized that this contrast was the central strategy behind Lula’s victory. "Lula portrayed himself as a defender of the working class. And during the debates, he appeared as a dignified statesman," the political consultant said. Meanwhile, Bolsonaro’s remarks about his opponent came close to foul play, which didn’t win him any points, Dubravsky stressed.
The election demonstrated that in a democracy, the outcome is never a foregone conclusion, Viktor Heifets, editor-in-chief of Russia’s Latin America magazine, emphasized. According to him, Lula achieved the main goal of his campaign by rallying voters who had not supported him in the first round. "For example, he won over some of the voters who had supported presidential candidate Augusto Cury, who was knocked out in the first round [after receiving 2.89% of the vote]," the expert noted. Lula managed to better mobilize his core voters for the second round and capitalize on people’s fears over a potential Bolsonaro victory. The senator himself, on the other hand, lowered his guard too early and failed to build on his success in the first round, Heifets pointed out.
Despite an unprecedented result in Brazilian history, Lula will have to work with a Congress where the influence of right-wing opposition forces, led by Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party, has grown considerably following the election. The party won 121 seats, 24 more than in the current session. Overall, right-wing and center-right parties will hold 341 of the 513 seats.
Slovakia intends to continue buying fuel from Russia for its nuclear power plants. Bratislava is also interested in preserving gas imports from Russia for as long as EU legislation allows. Meanwhile, Brussels has decided to fully eliminate Russian natural gas supplies by September 30, 2027. Despite EU pressure, Robert Fico’s government was the first among EU member states to restart the activities of the intergovernmental commission on economic, scientific, and technical cooperation with Moscow. The large Slovak delegation was headed by Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar, who was making his first visit to Russia. Moreover, during his October 26 trip to Moscow, the top Slovak diplomat not only discussed opportunities for cooperation with Russia but also shared assessments with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov on the situation in Ukraine and the crisis between Russia and the EU. Thus, Slovakia remains one of the most pragmatic European countries, pursuing a balanced approach toward both Russia and the settlement in Ukraine.
In its relations with Slovakia, Russia should prioritize short-term projects for now, Vadim Trukhachev, an associate professor at the Russian Financial University, told Izvestia. According to him, parliamentary elections will take place in Slovakia next year, the results of which could change the country's political direction. The expert noted that if the opposition takes power, the work of the intergovernmental commission could be suspended again. However, current Prime Minister Robert Fico has demonstrated his readiness to expand cooperation with Moscow despite Brussels’ disapproval. Overall, Slovakia is behaving as though it were the only sensible country in the EU that defends its own interests, Trukhachev emphasized.
Slovakia intends to buy Russian gas as long as it is legally permissible, Economy Ministry’s State Secretary Vladimir Simonak, who participated in the meeting, told Izvestia. "We comply with all restrictions arising from EU law. At the moment, the legal status is what it is. As long as the law allows us to purchase Russian gas, we will be happy to continue doing so. As for the future, that is a matter for negotiations. We are trying to protect our interests, including within the EU," he stressed.
Bratislava also intends to keep buying nuclear fuel from Russia. There are two nuclear power plants in the country: the Bohunice Nuclear Power Plant in the west and the Mochovce Nuclear Power Plant in the central part. Both facilities were built with the involvement of Soviet and Russian specialists. "We plan to continue purchasing fuel. The existing partnership is long-term and, in my opinion, is being maintained reliably. Nuclear fuel is not subject to sanctions, either those currently in force or those planned. Therefore, in this regard, we plan to maintain this cooperation," Simonak noted.
"Our position on sanctions is that we must ensure they do not damage our interests as much as they have in the past. As you know, the Slovak government believes that there is no military solution to the conflict in Ukraine. And we would prefer a rapid, peaceful resolution to the conflict in Ukraine rather than a further tightening of sanctions, which would restrict opportunities for cooperation," the state secretary pointed out.
After a slight decline in mid-October, diesel fuel prices in the US and Europe resumed their upward trend last week. In the US, diesel prices neared the record highs recorded in late September, while in some European countries they surpassed those levels. The mid-month drop in diesel prices was apparently triggered by reports that Russia was resuming diesel exports and the US was lifting restrictions on such shipments. However, the market later responded to broader global factors, such as rising oil prices and a persistent supply shortage.
Interestingly, Russian National Energy Security Fund head Konstantin Simonov told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that the volumes of diesel that Russia committed to supplying to the global market in October and November (300,000 and 500,000 metric tons, respectively) could not have a substantial effect on global price dynamics. According to DA Consulting CEO Daniil Tyun's estimate, the cumulative disruption to diesel supplies reached 1.3 million barrels per day in September. Meanwhile, the initially announced Russian shipments of 300,000 metric tons amount to 2.2 million barrels, or just 73,000-75,000 barrels per day when distributed over a month. This accounts for less than 6% of the reported supply disruptions.
Nevertheless, it would be a mistake to downplay the resumption of diesel exports from Russia, Simonov emphasized. In 2025, Russia accounted for 9.5% of the global diesel market. Its shipments reached 3.5 million metric tons per month, or about 800,000 barrels per day. And Russia aims to return to this level by taking advantage of favorable market conditions, such as the temporary lifting of US sanctions on its diesel exports and high prices in overseas markets. Russian supplies at 2025 levels could push global prices lower. However, while the resumption of diesel exports benefits Moscow, a resolution to the global energy crisis might not. After all, the US would quickly reimpose all the sanctions it had lifted against Russia, the expert stressed.
At the same time, experts agree that overcoming the global diesel crisis and securing a sustained price decline is possible only if Russian fuel exports resume alongside the restoration of oil and petroleum product supplies from Persian Gulf countries -- that is, after the conflict in the Middle East ends.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

title: Data center backlash is uniting America
body:
If there’s one issue that seems to activate all kinds of voters in 2026, it’s data centers. The rapid buildout of these massive server storage facilities — and the infrastructure construction and expenses that come with them — has sparked local opposition in communities across the country and become a major issue in many congressional and gubernatorial campaigns.
At the same time, tech money has been pouring into many of these races. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, has already spent $45 million in a year. And Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed group that says it supports AI safeguards, says it’s raised $80 million. Both have funded Democratic and Republican-aligned groups. Other super PACs see an opportunity to push for stricter AI policies, like the recently created Tomorrow Together, which launched $4 million in ads for battleground House races, with messages about data center development and AI safety.
All sorts of candidates appear to be distancing themselves from data centers and taking steps to assuage voters’ concerns about unconstrained buildouts in their backyards. How far they’re willing to go — including by backing an outright moratorium on development — varies. While many Democratic candidates seem likelier to back a pause, that’s not always the case. And though some Republicans have leaned on party messaging about putting development in local control, rather than supporting a ban, others say a pause is exactly what the moment calls for.
Texas gubernatorial and Senate races
Deep red Texas has the second-highest number of planned data center projects in the country after Virginia, and across multiple races, data centers have emerged as a key wedge issue. Democratic and Republican candidates are all trying to look tough on data centers but emphasize different messages in their plans. For example, in the Senate race, Democratic candidate and State Rep. James Talarico includes references to environmental impact and sharing corporate profit with the public, while Republican candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton discusses the need to keep Chinese technology out of US data centers. Both, however, want data centers to bear their own energy infrastructure-related costs and want to do away with certain tax exemptions for them.
In July, Talarico unveiled his “Hold Data Centers Accountable Plan,” which would end state sales tax incentives, give communities more of a say in data center development, require a closed-loop water system in new data centers to limit consumption, and create federal standards to protect the energy grid and environment. Talarico has also proposed an “AI Dividend” for Americans that would be funded by a tax on “AI-attributable profits.”
For his part, Paxton’s “Texas First Data Center Plan,” unveiled in August, would support Gov. Greg Abbott’s state-level policies, including repealing sales tax exemptions for data centers, requiring them to pay for electricity they use and add to state capacity, and preventing AI data centers from building in rural parts of the state. On the federal level, Paxton says he would co-sponsor an existing bill making it easier for data centers to connect to off-grid power systems, introduce new legislation prohibiting the use of Chinese technology to power US data centers or infrastructure, and hold data center companies criminally liable if the facility “empowers AI chatbots that undermine children’s safety.”
In the race for the governor’s office, Democratic challenger and State Rep. Gina Hinojosa has accused Abbott, the Republican incumbent, of “flip-flopping” on data centers. Abbott’s office put out a press release last year celebrating a $40 billion Google investment that would include three new data center campuses, but in August 2026, with campaign season heating up, he announced an audit that could slow new facilities connecting to the state energy grid. Hinojosa, who has recently called for a statewide moratorium on data center development, pounced on the perceived inconsistency. “Greg Abbott has zero credibility here. Nobody believes that the arsonist is about to put out the fire,” she said in a social media video.
The outcome of these races remains highly uncertain. Cook Political Report changed its rating for the governor’s race earlier this month from a likely Republican win to one that leans Republican. It says the open field for the Senate race is a toss-up.
Florida gubernatorial race
In Florida, there’s a clash over whether large-scale data centers can be reined in with the right policies or if they should be outright barred in the state. Democratic candidate and former congressman David Jolly has pledged to install a one-year ban on hyperscale data centers on his first day in office, and hasn’t ruled out a permanent extension. In one ad, Jolly puts data centers in the same breath as crime in a list of things he doesn’t want in Florida.
His Republican opponent, Congressman Byron Donalds, has previously supported data center development in the state and said Florida is “wide open” to build without destroying the state’s beauty. He’s more recently changed his tune though, and while he still doesn’t want to outright ban data centers, he’s tried to assure voters that he’d support policies protecting them from associated risks like higher energy costs. In July, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would require data center developers to fund the energy and water needed to run their operations. He’s also supported a state law with some similar requirements and environmental guardrails. “In my Florida, if you don’t protect our pocketbooks and our people, you won’t build data centers, period,” he assures voters in one ad. Energy experts have warned, however, that Donalds’ pledge to lean on nuclear and natural gas could actually raise costs for consumers.
Despite these efforts, he’s been branded as “Data Center Donalds” by opponents, and polling suggests he may have to fight for conservative voters who also strongly oppose data center development. An October NBC6/Telemundo Station Group poll found that 45 percent of likely voter respondents opposed data centers in Florida, with 38 percent in support and 17 percent undecided. A higher percentage opposed data centers in their own communities, at 59 percent. Still, the poll found Donalds has a lead of 48 percent to Jolly’s 41 percent, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percent. Ten percent of respondents were still undecided.
Pennsylvania gubernatorial race
In one of the country’s relatively few purple states, both candidates for governor have accused each other of changing their rhetoric on data centers just to get votes. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity each appear to have hardened their stances amid the widespread backlash to data center development, even though they previously touted opportunity in such projects.
Shapiro proudly announced a $20 billion investment from Amazon last year that would bring new data centers to the state, and credited Pennsylvania’s new fast track permitting program in helping lure the investment. But this year, Shapiro has tempered his enthusiasm, signing an executive order in August prohibiting nondisclosure agreements for data center developers and taking AI data center proposals off of the fast track. Shapiro has said his views evolved based on community feedback.
But Garrity, too, has seemed to turn against data centers as the election has drawn closer. In a radio interview last year, she said rural parts of the state would be “perfect places to put data centers,” and they’d be largely welcomed based on the economic opportunity they’d bring. She also praised the Amazon investment Shapiro secured at the time, though it’s now a target of some of her attack ads. This year, she has said data center developers must engage the community rather than “jam it down their throats,” and she supports a pause on development lasting no more than three years, according to Spotlight PA.
An early October Quinnipiac University poll of likely Pennsylvania voters found 64 percent believed AI data centers in the state would do more harm than good, with a plus or minus 3.9 percent margin of error. But a far larger portion of Democratic respondents were wary of them, with 80 percent saying they’d do more harm than good. That suggests it may be even more essential for Shapiro to shore up his position for his base, though the poll had him leading 59 percent to Garrity’s 34 percent.
Ohio Senate race
In the battle for Ohio’s Senate seat, data centers are both “the new ingredient (and the new problem),” according to a leaked National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) memo. Republican incumbent Jon Husted and Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown, who’s fighting to win back his former seat, “are in a dead heat,” the NRSC warned in August. And data centers, the group added, “are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”
As the NRSC identified, Brown has made his opposition to data centers a central tenet of his campaign, labeling Husted “the face of data centers” in the state. Brown has hammered Husted over his past support for data centers as lieutenant governor, where he helped install tax breaks. Husted has said he believes local communities should be able to decide whether to bring in data centers, and that some may find the revenue useful.
At least as of August, the NRSC still believed voters favored that approach over sweeping bans but acknowledged that current perception is negative. The group warned that losing the Ohio Senate seat could endanger future support for data centers. “If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one,” the memo says.
Husted introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would require large load customers like data centers to cover their own energy costs and the infrastructure upgrades needed to accommodate them. The bill passed the House and was seen as a potential life raft for Husted, but narrowly failed to pass the Senate, even with a handful of Democrats voting in favor. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up, and a RealClear Polling average of recent surveys shows Brown with a slight edge.
Michigan Senate race
Data centers are a hot topic across two key races in Michigan with razor-thin margins. The state is handling dozens of new data center proposals, and both candidates for Michigan’s open Senate seat support a moratorium. Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers supports a one-year pause but opposes a federal ban, while Democratic candidate and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed says there should be “no more data centers until we can do it safely and with federal protections.” Rogers’ moratorium support came days after The Lever reported on his investments that reportedly stand to gain from the buildout.
El-Sayed put his stake in the ground on data centers relatively early, compared to other Democrats across the country. In February, Politico wrote that “underdogs” like El-Sayed were centering data centers in their primary campaigns, raising what’s now a common topic in campaign ads. El-Sayed is also now locked in what the Cook Political Report rates as a dead heat with Rogers, in a race that could determine the balance of power in Congress. Rogers and El-Sayed are competing for a seat currently held by Democrat Gary Peters, who isn’t seeking another term.
In another toss-up race, Democratic organizer William Lawrence is challenging Republican incumbent Tom Barrett for his House seat. Lawrence called for a year-long federal moratorium on new data center construction during his primary campaign, and when he won the nomination, his supporters reportedly chanted, “data centers lost.” In the general election, data centers have continued to be a central theme. Barrett introduced two bills this summer that would strengthen local decision-making on data center development and bar federal lawmakers from signing non-disclosure agreements about data centers. Lawrence’s data center plan includes environmental standards, worker protections, and “zoning buffers” for data center development.
Wisconsin gubernatorial race
Wisconsin is another state where both gubernatorial candidates have backed away from previous support for data centers, but neither has gone as far as to call for a moratorium. Democratic nominee and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, for example, set himself apart from his progressive primary opponent Francesca Hong by declining to oppose a development moratorium that she supported.
Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee, similarly opposes a moratorium in favor of data center guardrails, and voted for a bill allowing faster permitting for data center projects. But Tiffany has still tried to label his opponent as “data center David Crowley,” pointing to past comments he made saying the state shouldn’t “automatically roll back all data center tax incentives.” More recently, Crowley has said he would sign a bill repealing tax subsidies for the facilities. Cook Political Report says the race is a dead heat.
Nevada gubernatorial race
Nevada’s Democratic Party created an entire website branding Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo “data center Joe,” highlighting his past supportive comments about data centers and money his campaign took from AI-connected donors. Lombardo, locked in a tight race to keep his seat, has fought the accusations. He introduced an executive order last month that ties tax incentives to developers covering power costs and meeting water use standards, empowering the state to claw back money from those who violate it. But Democratic challenger and attorney general Aaron Ford has said he’d go further, pausing tax breaks entirely for new data centers.
At the same time, Ford has been criticized for championing a 2015 bill enshrining data center tax breaks. Ford said his thinking has evolved with new information, and that “the data centers of 11 years ago are not the data centers of 2026.” The issue is particularly salient in a state that’s experiencing significant water issues. The Cook Political Report says the race is a toss-up.
Georgia gubernatorial race
Swing state Georgia has been called “one of the nation’s most attractive markets for AI, hyperscale cloud and enterprise data center development,” and its gubernatorial candidates — Democratic nominee and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican nominee and healthcare executive Rick Jackson — have sparred over each other’s data center records. Bottoms supports a pause on development to evaluate environmental and cost effects, while Jackson says it should be up to local communities to decide whether to bring a data center in.
At a recent debate in the toss-up race, Bottoms said her opponent “cannot be trusted” on the topic based on his investment in a Texas data center. Jackson shot back that Bottoms approved and gave tax breaks to multiple data centers as mayor, which Bottoms denied, saying she only approved one non-hyperscale data center that wasn’t near a residential community. While Bottoms led the Invest Atlanta board in 2018, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported, the group approved up to $440 million in bonds for a mixed-use project at Georgia Tech that included a data center. This was not a “direct financing mechanism” but did help the project get tax abatement, the AJC wrote, and its data center was far smaller than those mainly at issue today.
Arizona gubernatorial and AG races
In dry Arizona where concerns about water are a top issue for many voters, the most interesting conflict is within parties, not across them. Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs and Attorney General Kris Mayes are both locked in close races with their respective Republican challengers, Rep. Andy Biggs and state legislator Warren Petersen. But the two Democrats are split over how to regulate data centers: Mayes supports a statewide pause on development, while Hobbs opposes one.
Mayes says the state should “take a beat” to evaluate water and energy needs, a move Petersen has criticized in a rare outright defense of data centers, saying, “If you like your tech and your phone and your computer and the stuff you can use that for, you probably think data centers are important.” Hobbs, meanwhile, says data centers are here to stay, and the state should instead figure out how to best make them work for communities. That puts her significantly closer to her Republican opponent, who similarly opposes a moratorium.
Iowa gubernatorial race
Iowa’s open governor’s seat is another close race where data centers are taking center stage. The state economic development authority says Iowa’s wind energy and low construction and business costs have attracted developers there, but their growth has also brought concerns to local communities.
Democratic nominee and state auditor Rob Sand has not supported a blanket moratorium but says he would end tax breaks for data centers, make them cover their own costs, and keep NDAs from shielding deals from communities. Republican nominee and businessman Zach Lahn called for a moratorium on new development and eliminating tax incentives for them.

title: Joseph Enemona Crowned Olimene Ata Igala, Hosts Davido
body: A businessman and economist, Dr. Joseph Onuche Enemona, has been coronated as the Olimene Ata Igala by the Ata Igala, His Royal Majesty, Dr. Alaji Opaluwa Mathew Akpa. The coronation ceremony was held on Thursday, October 22, 2026, at the Ata’s Palace in Idah, Kogi State. Enemona hosted Afrobeats super star, David Adeleke (Davido), at the Ogugu Centre, at the ceremony marking his coronation and the inauguration of his new country home in Ogugu, Olamaboro Local Government Area of Kogi State. While thanking God for the conferment of the prestigious chieftaincy title on him by the Ata Igala, Enemona described the recognition as ineffable and a great privilege beyond expression. He thanked the Ata Igala for considering him worthy for such an honour. He said the award of the Olimene Ata chieftaincy title had transformed him from an iconoclast to a protégé of the Ata Igala Kingdom. Enemona said it was a double celebration for him as he also formally opened his new country home in Ogugu, Olamaboro Local Government Area of Kogi State. immediately after his coronation. The ceremony attracted eminent personalities, including Afrobeats star, David Adeleke (Davido) and his team; former Deputy Governor of Kogi State, Chief Dr. Edward David Onoja; representatives of the Ata of Igala Kingdom; former President of National Association of Scrap and Waste Dealers Employers of Nigeria (NASWDEN), Mr. John Egaji Obeh, while the current President of NASWDEN was represented by the Public Relations Officer of the association. Others in attendance were renowned Igala musician, Alhaji Umaja; Iyeoja Ochogwu, Chief Mrs. Ojoma Cecilia Lawson; CEO of Ojoma Heart of Gold Humanitarian Foundation, and other dignitaries. Enemona expressed gratitude to everyone who supported him in making the event successful, colourful and memorable, praying that celebration will not cease in their households and wishing all his guests journey mercies to their respective destinations.

title: Meta gets $3 billion from Nvidia and plans to spend more on Nvidia chips
body:
Nvidia is buying into its customer Meta, which plans to run more of its AI agents on Nvidia hardware. Nvidia is investing $3 billion in Meta's planned equity offering , the Wall Street Journal reports. In the same announcement, the two companies said they would expand their partnership around Meta's AI product Muse . Meta plans to use more Nvidia infrastructure for its next generation of AI agents, including Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs.
Meta wants to raise up to $95 billion through stock offerings to pay for its AI infrastructure buildout. According to CNBC, AMD and Broadcom also signaled nonbinding interest in buying up to $5 billion in Meta shares combined.
The deal fits a pattern investors have been arguing about for months. Nvidia gives money to customers like OpenAI, which then use it to build data centers packed with Nvidia chips. Critics call this circular financing and warn that it could hide how much real demand exists. Ad Ad

title: Africa needs to be more self-reliant and strengthen its security capabilities – Tinubu
body:
Africa needs to become more self-reliant and create partnerships that develop African strategic resilience, Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu told the inaugural Africa International Defence Exhibition (Afridex) in Lagos.
He was represented by Nigerian Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who delivered this message at the opening ceremony at Eko Atlantic on Monday 26 October.
“Afridex 2026 must become a meeting point where military experience informs innovation, strengthens national capabilities, and partnerships, and delivers practical solutions. Our purpose here is very clear. We have to build an Africa capable of defending its people and securing the peace upon which progress depends,” the message from the President read.
Akpabio spoke to a packed auditorium filled with delegates from African and international militaries, representatives from defence businesses, and diplomatic representatives.
A brass band played traditional African music to welcome the guests with particular emphasis on Nigerian hymns. The audience was filled with high-ranking officers and many people dressed in traditional Nigerian clothes made of Ankara cloth and agbada.
“We gather with a shared responsibility to secure our nations in Africa, protect our people, and safeguard Africa’s future. From the Gulf of Guinea to the Sahel, from our territorial borders to the cyberspace and outer space, the threats confronting us are becoming more complex and much more interconnected. They threaten lives, livelihoods, and disrupt trade. They even weaken the foundations of development of many African countries. Africa’s security must also command our collective attention because there can be no enduring prosperity when fear governs daily life. Nigeria speaks from experience. We know the cause of insecurity, the lives that are lost on a daily basis, the communities that are displaced, the livelihoods that are interrupted, and the opportunities that are denied.”
The President’s address did not ignore the real hardships faced by frontline troops.
“Our armed forces have confronted terrorism, insurgency, banditry, piracy, and other transnational threats with courage and sacrifice, almost on a daily basis. We honour their services and remember those who have paid a supreme sacrifice and their souls rest in peace. Their sacrifices place an obligation upon us to provide the leadership, to provide the equipment, the training, and the support that our current men and women in the field need. We have also learned that lasting security requires strong institutions, public trust, reliable partnership, and the industrial capacity to sustain our defence capabilities.
“Our defence partnership must therefore deliver value. Long after equipment has been supplied, every major acquisition should help develop skills, transfer knowledge, strengthen local industries, deepen our capacity to maintain what we operate. The measure of a successful partnership is the capability it leaves behind. African engineers must gain expertise. African enterprises must grow.
“African institutions must become stronger. Self-determination must guide our support for African-led peace operations. The courage to respond to crises must be matched by predictable resources. Adequate equipment, rigorous training, sustained institutional support. Those we send to keep the peace must have the means to keep the peace. We must also secure the seas that connect our economies to one another and to the rest of the world.”
Present day realities, particularly of rapidly advancing battlefield technologies were significant points in the President’s address.
“At the same time, we must prepare for the changing character of conflict in the global society. Cyber capabilities, space technologies, artificial intelligence, and autonomous systems are transforming the security environment.
“Africa must invest in the knowledge and institutions required to understand these technologies, use them responsibly, and develop solutions of our own, particularly for the purposes of maintenance. Our young people have the talents. Our responsibility is to create the opportunities for them. Nigeria is advancing indigenous defence production, strengthening cooperation with trusted partners, and developing capabilities suited to evolving threats. We will continue to support these efforts with a very clear objective.”
The importance of international partnerships that benefit Africa and shared collective defence for the region was a key aspect of his speech.
“Our defence partnership must therefore deliver value. Long after equipment has been supplied, every major acquisition should help develop skills, transfer language, transfer knowledge, strengthen local industries, deepen our capacity to maintain what we operate.”
This emphasis on mutually beneficial international partnerships and collective African security was echoed by an earlier speaker, General Birame Diop, President of the ECOWAS (Economic Community of West African States) Commission, who praised President Tinubu for his leadership in regional security.
“His support for initiatives that promote African self-reliance, defence cooperation, and collective security continues to inspire our collective efforts toward a safer, more secure, and more prosperous West Africa. Nigeria has consistently demonstrated leadership in advancing peace and security across Africa, from the immense sacrifices it made in restoring peace in Liberia and Sierra Leone, to its pivotal role in the operationalisation and deployment of the ECOWAS Standby Force today. This exhibition is yet another testament to Nigeria’s enduring leadership and commitment to regional stability, collective security, and defence cooperation on the continent. By convening Afridex, Nigeria has once again demonstrated visionary leadership, affirming that Africa’s future security lies not in dependence on others, but in our collective ability to design, develop, and provide our own security solutions.”
Diop, too, reiterated the changing nature of 21st century warfare as it pertains to Africa.
“The current security landscape across our continent remains complex and challenging. Terrorist attacks, transnational organised crime, banditry, piracy, and other illicit activities at sea, unconstitutional changes of government, cyber-attacks, and mis- and disinformation continue to threaten peace, stability, and development. These threats are asymmetric, transnational, and deeply interconnected, requiring equally coordinated and innovative responses. At the same time, the geopolitical environment in which we operate is changing rapidly. The world is becoming increasingly multipolar, characterised by growing primacy of national interests, geopolitical competition, shifting alliances, and uncertainty about the future. We must also acknowledge the realities that access to defence equipment, critical technologies, and military capabilities can at times be constrained by the interests and priorities of external powers. Leaders do not wait for crisis to emerge before taking action. They prepare for that. If the future is uncertain, our response must be rooted in readiness, resilience, and self-reliance. This makes initiatives such as Afridex both timely and necessary.”
Nigerian Defence Minister Christopher Gwabin Musa spoke earlier in the ceremony to place Nigerian defence needs firmly within an African and global context, especially as it relates to Afridex.
“We are all aware of the challenges of insecurity confronting not only Nigeria, but indeed, the entire world. And we need for us to continue to work together for the good of humanity. This gathering offers us that platform and opportunity to engage meaningfully in the pursuit of a safer and more secure world. Afridex started as a strategic mission, and I’m glad to see that today the ideas have come to fruition. The world is faced with tumult and uncertainties that challenge our peaceful existence. The threats we encounter are hybrid in nature and fast evolving across all domains of warfare. The challenge before us is to ensure that our defence policies and institutions remain responsive to these challenges and their realities. We must continue to prepare for the changing character of warfare and develop the requisite capacities to deal with them decisively. The contemporary global realities therefore reinforce the importance of collective security.”

title: HSL raises ticket prices and introduces a fare cap for contactless payments
body:
The Helsinki region's public transport fares will rise by an average of 1.8 percent in early 2027.
Helsinki Regional Transport (HSL) is introducing a price cap for contactless payments. The change is meant to make it easier for passengers to choose between a single ticket and a day ticket. The change takes effect on Monday, 2 November.
The cap is calculated starting from the first ticket purchase. The system then adds up the prices of all tickets bought with the same payment method.
However, HSL notes that a physical payment card and mobile payments linked to the same card are treated as different payment methods.
Once the combined total reaches the price of a day ticket, no further charges are made for additional journeys.
The fare cap depends on the zones you travel in during the 24 hours. A two-zone 24-hour ticket is €10.60.
In a press release , HSL said the cap means passengers no longer have to estimate how many trips they will make during the day.
The fare cap applies only to adult single tickets paid with contactless payment — it doesn't cover tickets bought through the HSL app or with an HSL card.
The HSL board meanwhile decided on Tuesday to raise ticket prices by an average of 1.8 percent at the beginning of 2027. In the most popular AB zone, the price of an adult single ticket will go up by 1.5 percent, from €3.30 to €3.35.
Children's single tickets and single tickets in the 50 percent discount group will stay the same in all zones.

title: Proforce highlights PF Terminator at Afridex
body:
Proforce Limited is one of Nigeria’s leading armoured vehicle manufacturers and this week it is showing its capabilities and products at Afridex 2026 in Lagos, including the new PF Terminator 4×4 MRAP (mine-resistant ambush-protected) vehicle.
The company, incorporated in 2008 as a subsidiary of O’la-Kleen Holdings, comprises several subsidiaries, notably Proforce Land Systems, Proforce Intelligence Systems, Deto Shipyards, Proforce Air Systems, WMO Gadgets and Proforce Galaxies.
Its air systems subsidiary makes use of strategic partnerships to offer turnkey solutions and competencies, providing aerial platforms for ISR (intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance). These include unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), trainer aircraft and other ancillary equipment for air defence operations.
In turn, Proforce Intelligence Systems seeks to address threats by means of sophisticated technology. This unit develops and produces various systems for homeland security, cyber security, border control and law enforcement.
WMO Gadgets provides high-quality tactical body armour for police, law enforcement and the military. Its body armour helmets and vests offer B3 and B4 level protection.
“With three facilities located in Nigeria, Dubai and India, Proforce leverages research and deep technical know-how to produce and develop products for the domestic and international markets, including the governments of Chad and Rwanda,” the company stated. “We have recently provided cash-in-transit vehicles to Ghana, which incorporate the latest in materials and technologies. These include ballistic resistance, run-flat tyre systems, advanced suspension, and secure communications.”
Besides its well-known PF Viper armoured personnel carrier (APC) and the PF Hulk 4×4 APC, as well as the larger PF Ara (Thunder) MRAP, Proforce Land Systems recently revealed the PF Terminator MRAP. It was on display in August at the Nigerian Army’s CSS Training Week after its launch at the late June/early July Nigerian Army Day Celebration. Also on display was the command and control variant Proforce said was adopted by the Nigerian Army.
The PF Terminator all-wheel drive vehicle has a gross weight of 15 000 kg and is able to carry 12 personnel and 7 000 kg of payload. It boasts STANAG 4569 Level 2 protection against ballistic projectiles, improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and artillery fragments. With a Kamaz 667.310-310 inline six diesel engine producing 301 horsepower and 937 Nm torque, it has a top speed of 90 km/h. The vehicle is also fitted with a CTIS (central tyre inflation system), enabling it to traverse the toughest terrain for counter-terrorism and special operations. A 420 litre dual-fuel tank gives extended range.
Visitors to Afridex 2026 will be able to inspect the vehicle at close quarters, while Proforce also indicated that it will be taken through its paces during live demonstrations.
The Nigerian military has been investing heavily in indigenous armoured vehicles, to the extent that it had acquired a 15% stake in Proforce. At the same time, Proforce Land Systems has developed a large portfolio of domestic and international clients, including all divisions of the Nigerian military, police force, foreign embassies in Nigeria, and the United Nations (UN). The company’s PF2 has been exported to Rwanda, the Central African Republic and South Sudan (it is used for United Nations peacekeeping missions in the CAR and South Sudan) while the Ara has been sold to the Nigerian Army and Chad and the Hulk to the Nigerian Army.
Thanks to its years of experience in the design and manufacture of armoured vehicles (including armoured civilian vehicles, buses and trucks), the company operates the Proforce Maintenance Repair and Overhaul (MRO) division to support its vehicles, wherever they operate. This facility extends the productive life and deployment of its vehicles and other defence equipment.

title: Nord Stream Trial Continues as Court Rejects Defence Bid to Halt Proceedings
body:
The Nord Stream sabotage trial resumed in Hamburg on Tuesday, with the court rejecting a defence bid to halt proceedings. The judges ruled that Ukrainian military secrecy obligations did not, in themselves, prevent Serhii Kuznetsov from receiving a fair trial.
The dispute dominated the second day of proceedings against the Ukrainian former military officer, who is accused of helping organise the September 2022 operation that damaged three of the four Nord Stream pipeline strings beneath the Baltic Sea.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The defence supported its position with a sworn statement from Kuznetsov’s superior confirming that he was bound by secrecy obligations. The court nevertheless held that restrictions arising from those obligations did not, in themselves, bar his prosecution in Germany. It also noted that Kuznetsov had not sought an exemption allowing him to disclose protected information.
Serhii Kuznetsov (center) with his German lawyers Lars Brögeler (left) and Jes Meyer-Lohkamp (right) at the Nord Stream sabotage trial in Hamburg, Germany, on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer / Kyiv Post)
Serhii Kuznetsov (center) with his German lawyers Lars Brögeler (left) and Jes Meyer-Lohkamp (right) at the Nord Stream sabotage trial in Hamburg, Germany, on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer / Kyiv Post)
Federal prosecutor Stefan Schmidt had urged the judges to reject the defence’s interpretation of the European Convention on Human Rights. Its protections, he argued, could not be understood to allow a state to prevent a prosecution simply by withholding permission for a defendant to disclose information covered by secrecy obligations.
The court also said it would seek improvements to Kuznetsov’s detention conditions. Proceedings were continuing at the time of writing.
At the trial’s opening on Oct. 14, Kuznetsov’s lawyers sought to have the proceedings discontinued, arguing that his obligations under Ukrainian military secrecy rules left him unable to answer the allegations and mount an effective defence. They also disputed the evidence of his alleged leadership role and challenged the prosecution’s characterisation of the pipelines as civilian infrastructure.
Kuznetsov faces charges including causing an explosion, destroying structures, disrupting public services and committing a war crime involving an attack on civilian objects. He denies involvement.
His lawyers argue that Nord Stream served Russian military and strategic interests, raising a question that extends beyond reconstructing the sabotage itself: how should the pipelines be classified under the laws of war?
The prosecution alleges that the operation was carried out on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities. Ukraine has denied responsibility for the attacks.
Serhii Kuznetsov at the Nord Stream sabotage trial in Hamburg, Germany, on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer / Kyiv Post)
Serhii Kuznetsov at the Nord Stream sabotage trial in Hamburg, Germany, on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer / Kyiv Post)
Tuesday’s ruling allows the trial to proceed despite the defence’s contention that Kuznetsov remains unable to speak freely about information relevant to his case.
The case leaves several central issues to be resolved:
What evidence establishes Kuznetsov’s individual role in the alleged operation?
Were the pipelines civilian objects or a lawful military target?
Can the defence obtain the information and authorisations it says it needs from Ukraine?
The ruling leaves Kuznetsov’s lawyers facing the difficulty at the heart of their application: how to answer the prosecution’s allegations when, they say, their client cannot discuss the information needed to challenge them. The court has declined to treat that constraint as grounds to halt the trial.
In August, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk criticized the trial.
“I will not change my mind here, and I believe that those who built this pipeline should be ashamed, not those who disabled it,” he said .
The Nord Stream pipeline, which carries natural gas from Russia to Germany, was first negotiated in the 1990s, with agreements signed in the 2000s by Russian President Vladimir Putin and then-German Chancellor Gerhard Schröder.
The first Nord Stream pipeline was completed in 2011, while Nord Stream 2 was built a decade later. After leaving office, Schröder, with close ties to Putin, soon joined the board of the Russian state-owned oil conglomerate that negotiated the pipeline.
In mid-October, Washington reportedly talked with Moscow about restarting the pipeline as part of the peace negotiations.
Korbinian Leo Kramer is currently a correspondent for the Kyiv Post, reporting from both Central Europe and the frontline regions of Ukraine. He previously worked as a freelance journalist and photographer across eastern Ukraine, covering the human and social dimensions of Russia’s fullscale invasion. His reporting focuses on resilience, everyday life, and the realities of war.

title: Russian envoy says US increasingly recognizes importance of cooperation with Moscow
body:
PARIS, October 27. /TASS/. Recognition is growing within the US presidential administration that cooperation with Russia is important for US national interests, Special Presidential Envoy for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries and Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev told Le Monde newspaper, commenting on the recent visit of US special envoy Steve Witkoff to Russia.
"Before this meeting in Moscow, we had already spent considerable time in Washington, holding discussions with the Department of the Treasury, the Department of Energy, and other government agencies. The Trump administration increasingly recognizes that cooperation with Russia is vital for the national interests of the United States," he said.
Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner are playing "a decisive role in the search for realistic compromises," Dmitriev added.
A new round of trilateral talks involving Russia, the US and Ukraine may take place in Abu Dhabi, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said earlier.

title: Residents of Russia’s Primorsky Krai warned of delays in social benefits as war strains regional budget
body: Primorsky Krai’s regional Labor Ministry said social payments in the krai could be temporarily delayed. The ministry said the regional budget is currently “operating under increased strain, including due to the need to address nationwide tasks connected to the special military operation.” “Under these conditions, funding for certain social support measures is being disbursed in stages, so the transfer of some payments may be temporarily delayed,” the ministry said, adding that it “understands” how important timely social support is for residents of the krai, and the “concern of those who are now waiting for the funds to be transferred.” Authorities in the Nizhneilimsky district, in the Irkutsk region, plan to cut about 37% of the staff at the district administration and public-sector institutions, said Pavel Berezovsky, head of the district. The first to be let go, he said, will be night watchmen at schools, kindergartens, and community centers, along with employees of the municipal enterprises “Service Center” and “Clean City.” As the news outlet “7×7” notes , the staff cuts come amid problems with the region’s budget. The Irkutsk region legislature increased the budget deficit to 38.7 billion rubles in October, about 15% of the region’s own revenues. Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev attributed the increase to the need to fund socially significant spending. In late July, Rostov region authorities declined to raise public-sector workers’ pay by 4% and gave no explanation. In Sakhalin, authorities froze pay indexation for medical workers, explaining that their salaries had outpaced inflation in previous years. In the Sakha Republic, authorities postponed pay indexation for public-sector employees by two months. title: Oyebanji seeks Ekiti assembly’s approval to reappoint three ex-commissioners, 10 special advisers
body:
Ekiti State Governor, Biodun Oyebanji, has sought the House of Assembly’s approval to reappoint three commissioners and 10 new special advisers as he begins his second term in office.
The request comes after Mr Oyebanji’s swearing-in on 16 October for another four-year term, with the governor pledging to sustain ongoing projects, strengthen service delivery and consolidate its achievements.
In a letter addressed to the speaker of the assembly, Adeoye Aribasoye, on Monday, the governor requested the screening and confirmation of Dayo Apata, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN) as Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Akintunde Oyebode as Commissioner for Finance, and Oyebanji Filani as Commissioner for Health and Human Services.
The governor’s Chief Press Secretary, Olayinka Oyebode, disclosed the requests in a statement on Tuesday.
According to the statement, the proposed appointments are intended to ensure continuity in key areas of governance and enable the administration to settle into its second term.
“The proposed appointments reflect the governor’s intention to constitute key components of his administration early and ensure continuity in critical sectors of governance,” the statement read.
It added that the justice, finance and health portfolios were considered crucial to the effective take-off of the new administration, particularly amid prevailing developments in the country.
Mr Oyebanji also sought the assembly’s approval to appoint 10 new special advisers to support the day-to-day administration of the state. The statement did not disclose their names or specify the portfolios they would oversee.
The requests follow the governor’s recent appointments in the power, road infrastructure and transportation sectors, which were announced last week as part of efforts to organise his second-term administration.
The governor appointed Philip Atere as technical advisor for power infrastructure, Tope Fatukasi as technical advisor for road infrastructure, Sunday Makinde as technical advisor for airport, and Tajudeen Alingbolu as the Director -General, Ekiti State Transport Agency.

title: Serbia’s student movement toppled a political giant. Can it now govern the country?
body: BELGRADE, Serbia – By unseating longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday’s election on October 25, Serbia’s student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of. Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing — something neither the students nor their handpicked candidates have any experience of. Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country to celebrate when Vucic conceded defeat late on Sunday in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests. But as the jubilant crowd lit flares and fireworks, sang and danced, questions lingered: who will emerge from this leaderless movement as prime minister, what exactly will their policies be, and can a bunch of political unknowns with no previous affiliation stick together to shore up the economy, root out graft and juggle complex international relations? The answers will determine the political stability of Serbia, the largest economy in the Western Balkans, and its relations with China, Russia, and its largest trading partner, the European Union. The students’ victory “is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centered on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement’s limited governing experience could make the transition challenging,” Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday, October 26. Winners, but can they stick together? The protest movement began after 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in the northern city of Novi Sad in 2024, and the student-led demonstrations called for accountability and an end to corruption. Despite not having a figurehead, the students won widespread support before choosing 250 academics, lawyers, doctors, actors, farmers and musicians to represent them in the election. The movement and some of the top candidates on its list have given some idea of what it stands for, promising a domestic anti-corruption program centered on institutional overhauls. It does not recognise Kosovo, Serbia’s former southern province which declared independence in 2008, but wants to hold a referendum on Serbia’s accession to the EU, with which relations have frayed in recent years. Prominent figures include the head of the students’ candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory. But there is no certainty that any of them will hold a ministerial post, and it remains to be seen whether the candidates can form a cohesive government that can agree on policy long enough to use their comfortable parliamentary majority to enact change. “(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia’s culture; we will just have to see if it lasts,” said Katarina Popovic, also a professor at the University of Belgrade. “We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system.” Reforming public institutions Under Serbia’s constitution, the students’ candidates have 90 days to form a government once parliament is convened after the announcement of final results by the state election commission. Time matters, especially with a budget to pass before year-end amid growing public and private debt levels, while any attempt to end corruption will require an overhaul of the police and intelligence services and judicial reform. State institutions require “detoxification” after 14 years of Vucic, said Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior. Prelevic warned that Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), will pose a strong opposition, and that the new government would have to fight its corner. Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption. International relations In Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic, but stopped short of congratulating the students. “We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector,” Student List representative Jovo Bakic, a sociologist and a university lecturer, told Russia’s RT Balkan TV, adding that there would be no change in Serbia’s foreign policy towards Russia, including not introducing sanctions against Moscow. Also closely watching is Ukraine, which has been an indirect beneficiary of Serbian weapons in its fight to repel Russia’s four-year-long invasion. European officials congratulated the students and said they stood ready to help the country in its fight against corruption. “I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing — someone who will have the privilege, but also the immense responsibility, to lead Serbia through these reforms,” said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement. – Rappler.com

title: Stubb, Støre hold phone call with Putin
body:
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre talked to the Russian leader on Tuesday.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb spoke by phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday, Stubb's office said .
Stubb made the call from Helsinki together with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre . Finland and Norway both share borders with Russia.
According to Stubb's office, the aim was to give Putin a direct message about upcoming negotiations to help end the war. The call was linked to peace talks to be held in Abu Dhabi, where Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators are set to meet in early November.
Stubb and Støre made the call as leaders of their respective countries, not on behalf of Europe as a whole. The call comes after the two leaders met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo last week .
At a press conference on Tuesday afternoon, President Stubb told reporters that the conversation with Putin lasted about an hour and a half, and that Ukrainian President Zelensky was briefed about the contents of the call after it ended.
"Finland never talks about Ukraine over Ukraine's head," Stubb said.
He reiterated that the aim of the conversation was to keep the peace efforts on track, noting that an end to the war "will not be achieved through silence".
"We tried to help ensure that Russia would come earnestly to the negotiating table," Stubb said.
