title: I Tested Every Major AI Agent for a Day. Here’s the Best One
body:
As a software reporter, I sat through meeting after meeting where tech bros—mostly men—demonstrated how their new agent would revolutionize my everyday life and automate away the tedium. The catch was that none of these so-called “agents” actually worked.
Fast-forward to today, and always-on AI agents are booming, with major players racing to release their own versions to attract early adopters. The key reason these personal agents are hitting the larger zeitgeist, beyond Silicon Valley nerds, is that they work. Well, at least more reliably than last year. AI agents still make mistakes, but I also see significant improvements in following through on tasks and controlling a browser. These little guys got their glow-up.
It can be hard to know where to start with AI agents and which one best fits your automation needs. So I spent a day experimenting with every major AI agent to understand their strengths and weaknesses. Before going to bed on Wednesday last week, I set up six always-on agents on my iPhone: Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Instinct, Anthropic’s Claude Duet, Google’s Gemini Spark, and xAI’s Grok Bot.
Each agent differs slightly in price and function. Muse is free to use and has dominated the smartphone app download charts since its September release. Instinct is also free, but you need an invite code from a user; it’s operated through your texts rather than an app. OpenAI’s Dots are behind a $100-a-month paywall, the most expensive I tested, and built inside of ChatGPT. Google’s Gemini Spark is a beta inside the Gemini app and costs $20 a month. xAI’s Grok Bot costs $30 a month and is in its own app. Lastly, Anthropic’s Claude Duet costs $20 a month and is the newest of the bunch—released as a wait-listed research preview the night before my tests.
OpenClaw isn't on my list. Despite the AI agent sparking much of this innovation earlier this year, it’s too clunky for the average person to set up. Maybe it will be in a future ranking, where I could also include smaller players like Hermes by Nous Research and Poke.
What Exactly Is an AI Agent?
If you’ve never used an AI agent—I have zero judgment for the holdouts—it's like texting a digital assistant to complete tasks: scan your email for important missed messages, track vacation flight deals, and help with daily shopping decisions.
Compared to a chatbot’s turn-based experience, these tools are more proactive and will nudge you first when they detect an opportunity to be helpful. All of your messages with these agents are often stored in a single thread that feels like a group text. The AI agents complete many of these tasks by controlling a virtual browser, essentially their own computer for internet access.
The Rubric
I’ve tested AI software from a nontechnical perspective for the last few years, so I feel especially qualified to help guide you through this moment. I designed five basic tests to run each agent through, enacting all this chaos over 24 hours to gauge their proactivity, direction following, and browsing abilities. (Somehow, my iPhone didn’t melt into a puddle.) I scored each attempt on a scale of 1 to 5, and tallied the results at the end to crown a winner—and hand out an award for most annoying.
This is not an endorsement of any of these AI agents. The software remains nascent and often fraught with privacy and security concerns. These agents work best when connected to your personal data, like email and calendars, but require a level of trust that could ward off some users. For example, an X user claimed he recently connected AI agents to his bank account and work Slack, and then was mortified when an agent posted how much money he had for his colleagues to see.
Additionally, these tests are a limited sliver of what the tools can do. All of the agents will improve over time, as you share more data about yourself and how you like to complete tasks. I only shared my personal Google Calendar and Gmail with the tools, so I didn’t fully expose the AI agents, Billy Evans–style, to everything.
Morning Briefing
On Thursday mornings, WIRED’s Gear desk meets to chat about current coverage plans and sometimes pitch ideas for the next week. So, I wanted to see which AI agent put together the best tech news briefing and could use that information to generate a compelling headline. Companies often tout these tools as being great for compiling morning dossiers that keep you up-to-date on important events and breaking news.
I sent each AI agent an extensive prompt detailing my areas of coverage at WIRED, along with context about how this pitch would be used. Even though I asked the AI agents to take 30 minutes and really do deep research before answering, only Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots actually kept researching for most of the allotted time. The other AI agents either instantaneously spit out a pitch or sent me the headline after a couple of minutes of searching. While not a major mistake, it suggests that in this instance Muse and Dots were a bit better at following my instructions—a critical function of an AI agent.
The content of these six AI-generated pitches was a different beast. As you might have already guessed, the pitches didn’t exactly go over well in the editorial meeting. I could see my colleague’s eyes starting to glaze over as I read each headline and description. Gemini Spark generated the best angle, contrasting how Walmart created ways for third-party agents to use its shopping platform while Amazon recently gave Muse the boot. My colleagues, when they stopped yawning, didn’t seem too concerned about getting scooped by an agent.
Gemini Spark: 5/5. A conversational headline that identifies a core tension online.
Walmart Wants Your AI Agent to Buy Your Groceries. Amazon Is Calling the Cops. As retail giants clash over autonomous checkout, giving an AI companion like Meta’s Muse a weekly spending allowance reveals what happens when we stop clicking “Add to Cart” and outsource our domestic appetites to software.
Claude Duet: 4/5. Another interesting and timely pitch.
ChatGPT's Locked Chats Hide Your Secrets From Everyone but OpenAI. OpenAI's new PIN-protected chats treat ChatGPT like the diary a lot of people already use it as, but they guard what you say from roommates and coworkers, not from the company itself.
Muse: 3/5. Not bad, but not that strong.
I Let Claude Duet Text Me First—and It Spent My Claude Plan While I Wasn’t Looking. Anthropic’s new proactive agent promises to watch your inbox, calendar, and invoices so you don’t have to, but every time it checks in on you, drafts a reply you never asked for, or builds a dashboard overnight, it quietly bills that work to the same usage limit you pay for to chat.
Dots: 2/5. More evergreen than newsy.
This Anti-Doomscrolling App Wants to Be Your Phone’s Boss. I’d test SHIFT, whose developers decide which apps stay available during focus sessions, to explore whether escaping doomscrolling is worth outsourcing control of your phone.
Grok Bot: 1/5. Old news.
Meta's Muse Has Basic Taste—by Design. A leaked set of instructions tells Meta's AI agent to fill its top picks with well-known stores and to check only three websites per request, just as millions of people start handing it their holiday shopping lists.
Instinct: 1/5. A bland and hard-to-measure experiment.
I Spent a Week Steering My Feeds. The Algorithm Barely Noticed. Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube are all rolling out "tell the algorithm what you want" controls—I'd test whether they actually change what you see, or just make you feel in charge.

Lunch Time
Next, I wanted to test how these tools help for small, daily purchases. So I outsourced my lunch decisions to my team of AI agents, committing to order from whichever bot did the best.
I added another person, my wonderful boss, to the takeout order, to complicate the task a bit further. He’s vegan and was craving Vietnamese. I wanted something meaty and a hefty dose of caffeine. I needed to order from somewhere close to the WIRED office so I could stretch my legs, pick it up, then immediately keep working on this article.
They all picked similar places: DragonEats or Freshroll. Those Vietnamese restaurants make sense as reasonable, nearby lunch spots. DragonEats is a bit tastier and cheaper, so we went with that one. Instinct and Claude Duet built carts that were a bit too pricey compared to the other options. The only AI agent that truly failed at this task was Gemini Spark. The agent just added a single $5 roll for my boss. More of a snack than anything, I’d say!
Dots: 5/5. Actually ordered what this bot put in the cart. Picked DragonEats through the restaurant's website.
You: Roast pork bánh mì + Vietnamese iced coffee. Your boss: teriyaki tofu fresh rolls with soy sauce instead of fish sauce. Subtotal: $30.57 before tax/fees.
Muse: 4/5. Very similar to the order that I actually placed. Picked DragonEats through DoorDash.
For you: Roast Pork BM—$13.19, Vietnamese Iced Coffee—$5.29. For your boss (all vegan): Teriyaki Tofu Roll—$12.09—the fresh spring roll, kept with the default peanut sauce, not fish sauce; Teriyaki Tofu BM—$12.09. Item total is $42.66. DoorDash doesn't show tax or any fees until the checkout screen, so that final total will be a bit higher.
Grok Bot: 4/5. Another strong alternative. Picked Freshroll through DoorDash.
For you: Power Hour vermicelli bowl with garlic-ginger-honey pork and NamNam sauce, $15.85. Vietnamese cold-brew iced coffee, $5.85. For your boss (vegan): Rainbow Bowl, vermicelli with sesame-lime tofu and citrus ginger sauce, $15.85. Freshroll tofu spring roll with peanut sauce, no fried piece, $5.85. That's $43.40 before tax and fees.
Claude Duet: 3/5. Picked Freshroll and asked if I wanted the order through DoorDash or Uber Eats. I chose Uber Eats.
You: Power Hour bowl with pork, NamNam sauce, and vermicelli ($15.85), plus a Vietnamese Cold-Brew Iced Coffee ($5.85). Your boss: 2 Freshrolls with Tofu (Sesame, Lime) and Citrus Ginger sauce ($11.70), plus a Rainbow Bowl with tofu and Citrus Ginger ($15.85). That comes to $49.25 before fees and tax.
Instinct: 2/5. Created a similar cart as Claude Duet, but it was $4 more expensive. Picked Freshroll through DoorDash.
Boss: 2x tofu fresh spring rolls + tofu Rainbow Bowl. You: pork Power Hour bowl with extra pork + Vietnamese cold brew. Subtotal $53.73 before tax/fees.
Gemini Spark: 1/5. If I brought my boss a single $6 spring roll for lunch, he’d end up hangry and at the vending machine before long. Picked Freshroll through DoorDash.
For your boss, the cart includes a vegan Freshroll fresh spring roll filled with sesame-lime tofu and served with Grandma's peanut sauce ($5.85). For you, there's a regular bánh mì sandwich loaded with garlic-, ginger-, and honey-roasted pork ($10.85), paired with a Vietnamese cold-brew iced coffee ($5.85) for an afternoon caffeine boost—bringing the pickup subtotal to $22.55.

Schedule Conflicts
Another major selling point of these tools is their ability to be proactive, compared to chatbots that essentially only react to your prompts. Before I started the test, I created a Google Calendar event for 2 pm, labeling it as an important source meeting that can’t be moved. I also sent an email from my work account to my personal account, with the made-up scenario that my mom was getting out of the hospital today, and I needed to call her at 2 pm to send love and support from afar.
Which AI agents would read the email and calendar event, identify the conflict, and message me before the overlap to suggest alternatives? Only two of the bots succeeded here, which was fewer than I expected.
Dots: 5/5. Flagged the issue almost immediately and suggested a reasonable alternative.
A possible clash this afternoon: your note to call Mom says 2 pm, and your important source meeting is 2-3 pm, Pacific. Would calling her before the meeting or after 3 work with her discharge timing?
Claude Duet: 4/5. Flagged the conflict hours before it happened, but didn’t find alternatives.
Reece, good morning. Your 2 pm source meeting runs until 3, right when your own reminder says to call your mom.
Grok Bot: 2/5. Missed the conflict on my schedule, though it shared how to avoid this happening again.
I should have caught it, and from now on I'll check your self-reminder emails along with your calendars.
Instinct: 2/5. It didn't flag the overlap, but it provided tips to fix similar issues in the future.
I had nothing cross-checking your inbox against your calendar. Want me to run that check every morning and flag collisions before they hit?
Muse: 2/5. Made the same mistake and offered similar fixes.
My mistake was treating your calendar as the only source — I never cross-checked that email reminder against it, even though Gmail was right there.
Gemini Spark: 1/5. It didn't flag the overlapping events and didn’t suggest easy ways to avoid this in the future.
Because the reminder arrived as an email message rather than a calendar entry or scheduled task, the cross-app overlap wasn't surfaced before 2:00 pm.

Vacation Itinerary
I rarely go on vacation, so when I do, I spend an obscene number of hours researching, and I relish it. I love watching YouTube street food tours and aimlessly scrolling through flights trying to find the best deal. So I don't want to automate this task fully. Even so, I’m open to the idea that these AI agents could help with some of the logistical planning.
As with any AI-generated output, I still recommend checking multiple, non-AI sources before trusting these itineraries or revolving your whole trip around what agents recommend. When travelers in California recently trusted a chatbot to plan everything for a strenuous hiking excursion, the group had to be rescued because they lacked critical supplies (and maybe some critical thinking).
For this test, I sent all the AI agents a long paragraph explaining that my partner and I are considering exploring China late next year during a two-week-long adventure. I asked for a first draft of a potential itinerary that included: flight, hotel, nightlife, and food recommendations. Also, I asked the AI agents to chart a course that blends historical moments with big-city vibes. I can’t stand constantly changing locations, so I told the agents I want to stay in four different hotels max.
Notably, all of them chose identical routes through China—potentially ushering a new era of the Lonely Planet effect, where groups of travelers are nudged to visit similar locations, shops, and restaurants.
Muse: 5/5. This draft itinerary was extremely easy to read, with visual tables and straightforward tips.
Fly out of SFO the week after Golden Week, on a nonstop to Beijing, home nonstop from Shanghai. Four hotels, no backtracking — imperial history first, Sichuan food and pandas in the middle, Shanghai nightlife to finish.
Dots: 4/5. The Dots draft was strong but excessive, clocking in at 24 pages.
AI agent snippet: My recommendation: fly into Beijing, take high-speed trains to Xi’an and Chengdu, then fly to Shanghai and home. You get imperial history, the Terracotta Army, Sichuan food and a big-city finale without an overnight train or an extra hotel move.
Grok Bot: 4/5. Grok Bot’s output was easy to read and full of realistically helpful tips and suggestions.
A first-draft 13-night trip for two: Beijing, Xi'an, Chengdu and Shanghai, departing SFO on Oct 13 and returning Oct 27, after Golden Week.
Gemini Spark: 3/5. This itinerary was fine, though it lacked the readability or finer details of the higher-ranked ones.
A First-Time Traveler's Route Blending Imperial History, Sichuan Gastronomy, Vibrant Nightlife & 4-Hotel Hub Comfort.
Instinct: 3/5. This itinerary was decent and helpful, though I preferred the layouts from other agents.
Beijing in, Shanghai home, with Xi'an and Chengdu between: four bases, no backtracking, history up front and the food and bars getting better every stop.
Claude Duet: 3/5. Despite not using any images or other visual elements in its output, Claude Duet’s itinerary was solid.
Fly into Beijing on Saturday, Oct 9, 2027, then go Beijing → Xi'an → Chengdu → Shanghai, and fly home from Shanghai on Saturday, Oct 23. That's 13 nights in four hotels, two bullet trains and one short flight.

Insomnia Check
I was having trouble sleeping after all this AI agent chaos, though the Vietnamese coffee probably didn’t help. What happens when you give these tools a broad, open-ended task? Sometimes when I need the most help is when I don’t even know where to start.
If I had a human assistant, I would never message them in the middle of the night, so maybe that’s a plus for these digital helpers. The two agents that really flopped at this task, Gemini Spark and Claude Duet, responded to me without the soft touch or situational context a real person might.
Grok Bot: 5/5. This output made sense to me, and if the scenario were real, I would likely follow through on it.
I can set a reminder for later this morning to check in on your mom and see how her leg's doing, so it's off your mind for now.
Dots: 4/5. While Dots and Gemini Spark both gave me a similar task—say what’s on your mind, and we’ll get to it later—Dots’ phrasing felt more supportive and direct.
Send me the three things taking up space in your head; messy is fine, and I’ll turn them into a short checklist with one clear first step. Then you can put the phone down.
Instinct: 4/5. Unlike some of this agent’s other answers, this suggestion felt reasonable.
Here's one you can do from bed: skim the China draft and tell me the one thing you'd change. I'll have a v2 ready when you wake up.
Muse: 4/5. Another strong response from Muse. This agent seems aggressively designed to improve each day and align more with what would help the user.
I'll cross-check today's calendar and your self-sent email reminders for any conflicts or can't-miss items—the check I should've done properly yesterday—and only surface it at a sane hour, unless something's urgent early.
Gemini Spark: 2/5. OK, this is fine advice for a user complaining about sleep issues. At the same time, the comment about my empty morning calendar was annoying. Insomnia isn’t just tied to what's on my Google Calendar.
The best quick task right now is a mental download to get whatever is looping in your head onto paper so your brain can let go of it—especially since your calendar is completely clear today, with no morning commitments waiting for you.
Claude Duet: 2/5. One of Claude Duet’s weakest answers. While both are technically loose ends, I’m not very concerned about revisiting my lunch order and work projects in the middle of the night.
Let's close out yesterday's two loose ends. Your Thursday pitch is delivered, and your lunch cart got covered by the DragonEats order. Say the word, and I'll mark both done, then you can get back to sleep.

Best Overall: OpenAI Dots
Yes, it’s still behind an expensive paywall, so I would suggest most people wait until OpenAI launches this agent for free, or at least on the $20-a-month plan, before trying it out. Even so, Dots performed the best overall in these tests and failed at a task that’s fairly specific to my niche.
In the month since its release, Dots already feels more polished. I prefer a separate app over the current ChatGPT integration, though the smartphone widget option is a decent compromise. Dots for the win.
Most Accessible: Meta Muse
Muse is for the normies! And that’s fine. It did well in tests, coming in a close second on the scorecard, and was the easiest to set up. Oh, and it's free. Despite Meta’s assurances that it responsibly processes user info in secure virtual machines, I still have concerns given the company’s past mishandling of user data.
Best Interface: Anthropic Claude Duet
I tested this AI agent just one day after it officially launched as a research preview, so a few rough edges were expected. Despite Claude Duet scoring in the middle of the pack on most tests, its dedicated app was extremely user-friendly to navigate and follow up on ongoing tasks. I could see users obsessed with productivity and streamlined software experiences really latching onto Claude Duet in the next couple of months. Though you currently have to sign up for Anthropic’s waiting list to access Duet, and it’s behind a $20-a-month paywall.
Most Annoying: Instinct
You might like the sparse design fully integrated into your messenger; I did not. While other WIRED writers have lauded Instinct, calling it so good that they didn’t care what happened to their privacy, the texting-only aspect felt like a deal-breaker for me. I left the experience feeling too removed from what my agent was doing on my behalf and annoyed at its emoji reactions, like a grimace face when I told the agent it missed my scheduling conflict.

title: Two weeks after a Russian supply base burned in Luhansk’s Khrustalnyi, Ukrainian drones came back for an ammo depot
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukrainian drones blew up a Russian ammunition depot near Khrustalnyi in occupied Luhansk Oblast overnight on 27 October, Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported . Drones also hit the oblast’s capital, Luhansk, for hours, and part of the city lost power. Russia’s occupation authorities have not commented. Russia keeps pushing toward the last big Ukrainian-held cities in Donetsk Oblast. Its artillery there runs on shells kept in rear depots across occupied territory, and those depots sit within reach of Ukraine’s mid-range drones. Each depot lost behind the front pushes Russia to store and move its shells from farther back. That lengthens the supply runs Ukraine’s drones already hunt on the roads of occupied Ukraine. Secondary detonations near Khrustalnyi lasted over an hour The drone attack on occupied Luhansk Oblast went on for several hours, Exilenova+ said. Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit the depot near Khrustalnyi, and secondary detonations continued for more than an hour, the channel added. It posted night footage of a large fire glowing on the horizon. An attack by strike drones has been ongoing for several hours in the occupied Luhansk region. The Defence Forces have blown up an ammunition depot near the village of Khrustalnyi. Secondary detonations have been ongoing for over an hour. pic.twitter.com/yEGTgrfsm7 — Exilenova+ (@Exilenova_plus) October 26, 2026 Russia has occupied Khrustalnyi, formerly called Krasnyi Luch, since 2014. The city lies about 65 km southwest of Luhansk. It serves Russian troops as a rear and logistics hub . Fires burn in the Russian-occupied city of Luhansk after a series of explosions during a Ukrainian drone attack, late on 26 October 2026. Photo: Exilenova+ Luhansk lost power as drones hit its former airfield The attack on the city of Luhansk lasted more than four hours, Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of Occupation, said . Residents reported many explosions and fires in several districts, and the power went out. The main strike hit the city’s former airfield, he added. In October 2023, Ukraine’s ATACMS missiles destroyed Russian helicopters at air bases in occupied Luhansk and Berdiansk. NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections, marked in red, at the former Luhansk airfield after Ukrainian drone strikes overnight on 27 October 2026. Image: NASA FIRMS via Andriushchenko Time On Yandex Maps, the Russian online mapping service, the struck area near Luhansk airport is blurred, Andriushchenko noted . Yandex blurs military and critical infrastructure sites this way, he wrote. The area around the former Luhansk airfield, blurred out on Russia’s Yandex Maps, after Ukrainian drones struck it overnight on 27 October 2026. Screenshot: Yandex Maps via Andriushchenko Time Exilenova+ also reported a series of explosions in Luhansk. The oblast had been under a mass drone attack for an hour, with dozens of hits in different towns, Ukrainian Telegram channel DroneBomber wrote late on 26 October. Neither side’s military has mentioned the attack on Luhansk Oblast. Ukraine’s General Staff left it out of its morning report. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed it downed 222 drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black Sea, without listing Luhansk Oblast. Map of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian-occupied Ukraine and Russia overnight on 27 October 2026. Map: Andriushchenko Time, translated by Euromaidan Press Pro-Russian local channels confirmed the attack from their side. A channel covering occupied Luhansk Oblast wrote that eyewitnesses saw a large fire and secondary detonations in Khrustalnyi. LIC, the news agency of Russia’s occupation administration in Luhansk Oblast, reported a series of powerful explosions over Luhansk and a visible glow. The third drone night over occupied Luhansk Oblast in a week Drones have now hit occupied Luhansk Oblast on three nights in seven days. On 21 October, they struck the seized telecom building in the city of Luhansk that houses the occupation’s mobile operator. Two nights later, strikes cut communications and power in part of the city. Explore further Ukrainian drones just lit up Russian-occupied Crimea, Donetsk, and Luhansk — here’s how (video) Khrustalnyi itself burned on 12 October, when strikes hit a former motor depot housing Russian troops. Ukraine also hit an ammunition depot there in June 2022. Back then, the site supplied Russia’s offensive on Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk. Blasts in Mariupol, Berdiansk, and Melitopol, and Russian claims from Bryansk Occupied Mariupol heard two waves of explosions overnight, and the power went out after the attack, Andriushchenko also said. In occupied Berdiansk, several blasts near the Ekvator shopping center preceded a large fire, he added. On the evening of 26 October, strike drones attacked occupied Melitopol in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Exilenova+ said . Locals also reported FPV drones hitting targets in the city. In Russia’s city of Bryansk, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk claimed a night drone attack injured six people and damaged three apartment blocks. He said a man also died when a drone-dropped explosive went off. Yevhen Balytskyi, the Russian-installed head of occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast, claimed a drone hit a Simferopol–Moscow bus near Prymorsk, killing one passenger. As the attacks began, Russian monitoring resources tracked up to 350 Ukrainian drones in the air, DroneBomber said . Most flew over Bryansk and Oryol oblasts, with more groups near Crimea, Novorossiysk, and occupied Luhansk Oblast. Ukraine’s drones also weigh on Russia’s road to occupied Crimea. Truck traffic on the R-280 highway from Rostov Oblast has halved to about 1,000 a day because of drone attacks. Anatolii Tsurkin, who heads a carriers’ association set up in occupied Crimea, said so. Kyiv set aside $113 million for the first phase of a program of middle-strike drones aimed at Russia’s rear. That makes nights like this one likely to keep coming for depots, airfields, and roads across occupied Ukraine. Drones went after one of them overnight, along with a chemical plant that supplies explosives makers

title: Ebola: N10bn emergency fund to cover Lassa fever, other diseases – NCDC DG
body:
The Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), Jide Idris, has clarified that the N10 billion emergency intervention fund approved by the federal government was not meant solely for Ebola response.
Mr Idris said the funding was requested to strengthen Nigeria’s preparedness and response to Ebola as well as other endemic diseases, including Lassa fever.
He spoke on Monday during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today, amid questions over the utilisation of the N10 billion approved by President Bola Tinubu for public health preparedness.
“The money was requested not only for Ebola, but to address issues of control of other endemic diseases,” Mr Idris said.
“Right now, Lassa fever season is coming. Lassa fever and Ebola are the same class of viruses, just like yellow fever and dengue fever.”
According to Mr Idris, several of the measures required to control the diseases are similar, including surveillance, diagnosis, screening and monitoring at points of entry.
“Leadership, diagnostics, screening, surveillance issues, point of entry, all those funny things. They are the same thing, and that was the request initially,” he said.
The clarification came amid questions over the utilisation of the N10 billion intervention fund approved by the federal government.
Mr Idris said the Ebola outbreak subsequently increased the need to deploy the intervention funding to strengthen preparedness and response activities.
He listed the purchase of personal protective equipment, laboratory supplies, fuel and other operational needs among the areas requiring funding
He said the response involves eight pillars, including coordination and leadership, surveillance and laboratory diagnosis.
On surveillance, he said public health officials need funding to conduct contact tracing and collect data, while laboratories require equipment, reagents and other consumables to conduct tests.
“Treatment isolation centres all over the country, there are some that are just broken down. We need to fix it so that it will be ready, including the one in Abuja,” he added.
President Tinubu approved the N10 billion funding in June, when he also established a Presidential Task Force on Ebola Virus Disease Preparedness and Emerging Public Health Threats.
The State House said at the time that the funding would strengthen NCDC’s operational preparedness and support critical national public health emergency response activities.
The approval came months before Nigeria confirmed its first imported Ebola case on 20 October.
The NCDC boss said the country currently has no active positive Ebola case following the medical evacuation of the index patient to Switzerland.
However, he cautioned that Nigeria is not yet “out of the woods” because health authorities are still monitoring contacts and investigating possible secondary contacts.
As of Monday, he said 54 primary contacts had been identified, including an Uber driver who transported the index patient to her first hospital.

title: Putting the Cart Before the AI
body:
I guess it was inevitable that I would have to write something about AI here, although I’ve been putting it off for a while now. But seeing as the hype still does not seem like it is about to die down, I feel like I can put it off no longer. I am not sure if I have anything incredibly unique to add to this topic, but I nevertheless feel like I should put a stake in the ground.
First of all, the field of AI has obviously been around for more than half a century, so it consists of a lot of different technologies, from expert systems to Bayesian classification systems (like those commonly used in spam classifiers), to LLMs. The latter being the source of the incredible hype cycle and bubble economics of AI that we’re in the middle of, so that is what I’ll focus on.
The fact that it’s a bubble is, in my opinion, blatantly obvious. Ed Zitron’s incredibly detailed run-down of OpenAI finances , makes it clear that there is not a sustainable business anywhere in there. Even Microsoft seems to think so, pulling back on data centre construction plans . As the hype meets reality failure rates for AI projects rise with some high-profile examples where early AI adopters had to walk back their optimistic initial commitments.
Even so, the hype cycle continues. Even if an LLM-based tool can’t actually do what it promises today, surely this is only a few iterations away. Clearly the hype is working. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve seen someone show off an AI-based tool with a comment that is some variant of “well, as you can see it doesn’t actually work that well, but I’m sure it will improve with just a bit more training”. Without any kind of justification for that claim.
I’ve even heard people stand up and proclaim that the system they are using was too complex to build an interface to that would be usable by someone without expert knowledge. And then, with a straight face, go on to say that they expect an LLM would be able to make sense of the system and provide a chat-based interface to it, if we just feed the documentation of the system into the LLM as training material. The only way I can explain that kind of wishful thinking is by the sheer power of hype being able to override common sense.
Hype aside, the experiences I’ve personally had when interacting with gen-AI based tools have been ranging from “disastrous” to “kinda okay”. I’ll name a few: One involved a colleague asking Gemini to produce a “recommendations document” based on his notes from a customer meeting. What it produced was a couple of pages of text of what can only be described as the most basic of recommendations, instead of the specialised domain-specific advice we were trying to produce. Thankfully, I managed to convince the co-worker in question to scrap the AI output and start from scratch.
Another experience that produced somewhat better results was a trial run of a tool to apply kernel patch backports to older RHEL kernels, using an AI model to resolve conflicts, trained on existing resolutions in the RHEL tree. This tool is quite useful; although in my mind mostly because the tool itself has a lot of knowledge about the backporting process built in outside of the AI-based conflict resolution logic , which can automate a lot of the tediousness around the process. The actual conflict resolution suggestions provided by the AI model ranged from OK for the trivial stuff, up to “partly correct” for more complex things. Which is still useful, but more in a normal “iterative improvement” sense, not the hyped-up revolutionary sense.
When considering the effectiveness of any tool, attention has to be paid not only to the benefits, but also to the costs. And for generative AI, the costs are pretty significant. Not just in the form of the astronomical monetary and environmental cost, which in itself ought to be deal breakers as far as I’m concerned. But also in the form of real harms that the technology visits on both a personal and a societal level.
And no, I’m not talking about the “generative AI will become sentient and destroy us all” nonsense. I’m talking about real harms being done today; things like chatbots destroying relationships , or images and video becoming unreliable sources of information . Of harms to workers when they are “replaced” by AI, only to be hired back as precarious or temp workers when it turned out they were not, in fact, indispensable after all (which is what happened in that example I linked above ). Of the hidden human cost of training the models . Of the security nightmares attaching AI to everything brings with it, and the bogus “security” reports that open source projects are being subjected to. And of the harm of even further concentration of technological power in the hands of a few giant corporations who own the models everyone is adding dependencies on.
On the individual level, there’s even some evidence to suggest that outsourcing our thinking to AI models leads to loss of competence over time , as we forget how to think for ourselves. An effect that persists when going back to manual work after having used an AI for a related task. Other have noticed similar things , some even going so far so to compare generative AI to digital cocaine .
Given those pretty monumental harms, and the kinda “meh” benefits to be gotten from this technology, I don’t think it’s even a difficult choice. I got into this field, and free software in particular, to create technology that is under the control of users, not technology that is used to control them. Even though there’s been an effort to create an open source AI definition (which is in itself controversial ), the current crop of LLMs all seem to be based on proprietary models and systems that lock people in, while disproportionally harming people who are already on the receiving end of many of the world’s ills.
Sure, if LLMs were completely free to operate and create, didn’t concentrate power in the hands of a few corporations, and didn’t lead to torrents of misinformation and reduced our cognitive ability, they would be… kinda neat toys? But while we’re wishing for things that don’t exist, can I have a unicorn too, please?
I guess that once the dust settles, we’ll see which uses of the technology actually turn out to be useful enough to stick around once they are no longer subsidised by vast buckets of venture capital. And I look forward to the time when we can once again get back to asking “what is the best tool for this job”, and not the backwards “how can we solve this problem with AI” that seems to be the current modus operandi of the tech world.
In the meantime, I just hope that we won’t have boiled the planet, or drowned our society in misinformation and deepfakes before the bubble pops.

title: Kyiv region to host 250 IDPs from Oleshky – official
body:
Kyiv region will host 250 internally displaced persons (IDPs) from Oleshky (Kherson region), where a humanitarian mission began today, reported Director of the Social Protection Department of Kyiv Regional State Administration Ihor Meshchan.
Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine / Oleksandr Zubko Photo: Interfax-Ukraine Photo: Interfax-Ukraine From needs assessment to real solutions: How to make social services in kyiv region communities accessible and person-centered
"While traveling here to the press conference, I received an assignment from the leadership of the region: we are meeting 250 IDPs from Oleshky," he stated at a press conference at Interfax-Ukraine agency on Tuesday .
Meshchan emphasized the importance of the work carried out by the president and the government: "Finally, people who were effectively tortured by Russia for several years will be evacuated from Oleshky, and Kyiv region specifically has been instructed to organize both medical and social support, which we will actively pursue."
According to the regional state administration, 250,146 IDPs are currently registered in the region, of whom 19.3% are children under 18, 20.8% are elderly people, and 5% are persons with disabilities.

title: Russia’s Baltic Fleet ship Perekop docks at Republic of Congo’s Pointe-Noire port
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. The Russian Navy’s Baltic Fleet training ship Perekop has reached the port of Pointe-Noire in the Republic of the Congo, the fleet’s press service reported.
"The Baltic Fleet training ship Perekop arrived at the port of Pointe-Noire in the Republic of the Congo as part of its long-distance deployment. A welcoming ceremony for the training ship was organized at the port, attended by Russia’s Charge d'Affaires ad interim in the Republic of the Congo Sofia Sitnikova, and representatives of the country’s naval command," the press service reported.
It added that a ship tour was organized for the guests, during which the crew explained the specifics of military service and the cadet training process. A series of events is planned during the Perekop’s stay in Pointe-Noire. The Russian and Congolese sailors will take part in a friendly football match. Members of the Congolese Navy will visit the Perekop, and the crew and cadets are scheduled to explore local attractions.
The fleet noted that cadets from the Admiral Ushakov Baltic Naval Institute are undertaking navigation training aboard the Perekop. Along with the Russian cadets, foreign military personnel from the Republic of Namibia who are studying naval affairs in Russia are also taking part in the voyage (cadets from the Center for Foreign Military Personnel Training at the Admiral N.G. Kuznetsov Naval Academy). During the voyage, the cadets continued with their navigation training program. The future officers served as watch officers and their substitutes, learned to plot a course using data from navigational instruments, and developed the skills needed to navigate straits and narrow passages.
The Perekop training ship’s long-distance voyage began in early July and will last until mid-December. In total, the ship is set to cover approximately 30,000 nautical miles. Its route passes through the Northern Sea Route, four oceans, 14 seas, 23 straits, and nine gulfs. According to the deployment schedule, the ship is scheduled to call at 11 ports in foreign countries.

title: Oyedele seeks lasting rules to safeguard Nigeria’s economic reforms
body:
The federal government is considering legislation to prevent successive administrations from reversing key economic reforms, as it seeks to establish a national policy framework to guide decisions on taxation, subsidies, trade and industrial development.
The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy , Taiwo Oyedele, said the proposed framework would establish economic principles to guide successive governments, regardless of changes in political leadership.
He spoke on Monday at the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja, where he presented the draft of Nigeria Economic Policy Framework for public consultation.
“We now need to lock it in, in institutions, in law, as well as policy framework, so that it can be enduring,” he said during a panel session.
The proposal comes as President Bola Tinubu’s administration continues to defend its economic reforms, including the removal of petrol subsidies and changes to the foreign exchange system.
The government says the reforms are necessary to address economic distortions and improve long-term stability. However, their effects on household purchasing power and business costs have remained a subject of public debate.
Mr Oyedele said inconsistent economic policies had discouraged investment and undermined previous reforms, arguing that Nigeria needed a lasting approach to economic decision-making.
“Policy uncertainty is an invisible tax on enterprise. And unlike most taxes, it generates no revenue for government; it only destroys value and discourages investment,” he said.
He said the government was considering whether key provisions of the proposed framework should be backed by law, stressing that the document remained a draft and had not been approved as government policy.
According to Mr Oyedele, the consultation process will run until 27 November, after which the framework is expected to proceed to the Federal Executive Council for approval and the National Economic Council for endorsement.
The draft is built around stability, productivity, enterprise, capital, people, markets and institutions. It proposes common principles to guide economic decisions across government.
One of its key proposals is to require Policy Impact Assessments before major economic interventions. These assessments would set out the problem a proposed measure seeks to address, the evidence supporting it, its likely costs and beneficiaries, and the conditions under which it should end.
The assessments would cover interventions such as tax changes, tariff adjustments, regulatory restrictions and incentives.
The framework also proposes an annual National Economic Scorecard to measure whether economic growth is improving living conditions. Suggested indicators include real wages, productive employment and poverty levels.
The government says these measures would make economic decisions more transparent and allow Nigerians to assess policies by their outcomes rather than announcements alone.
The Ministry of Finance has published the consultation document on its website and invited businesses, professional groups, researchers and other stakeholders to submit recommendations.
Mr Oyedele defended the removal of petrol subsidies, saying the artificial suppression of prices had distorted the economy and created costs that became increasingly difficult to manage.
He argued that government policy should focus on raising household incomes rather than keeping prices below levels that could be sustained by the market.
“Let’s not suppress prices. Let’s focus on raising income,” he said.
The minister also questioned Nigeria’s industrial protection policies, citing locally assembled vehicles that he said contained only about five per cent local content despite benefiting from tariffs and levies of up to 60 per cent.
He argued that protection for domestic industries should be temporary and tied to measurable performance, rather than shielding businesses indefinitely from competition. He also called for improvements in electricity supply, logistics and other infrastructure to lower production costs.
Mr Oyedele said the government was targeting inflation in the low single digits before the end of 2027, with the aim of creating conditions for single-digit interest rates. He did not provide a specific timeline for achieving lower borrowing costs.
He also cited student loans, pension payments, wage adjustments and subsidised credit for small businesses as interventions under the government’s broader economic programme.
He urged wealthy Nigerians to meet their tax obligations, warning that inadequate government revenue could worsen inflation, borrowing costs and pressure on the naira.
The Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Abubakar Bagudu, backed the call for policy consistency, saying President Tinubu had directed government officials to sustain the reforms despite concerns about their immediate effects on households.
“There will be no return to subsidy. There will be no return to those distortions,” Mr Bagudu said.
He said the Federal Government had reached agreements with state governments on better coordination of fiscal and monetary policies, infrastructure development, security and domestic production.
Mr Bagudu also said more than $6 billion had been mobilised from the World Bank and other development partners to support household resilience and economic opportunities.
Anambra State Governor, Charles Soludo, cautioned against abandoning macroeconomic stability, saying sustained policy discipline was necessary to achieve meaningful growth.
“The macroeconomic framework, the stability that is back, must never be taken for granted,” he said.
However, Mr Soludo argued that economic growth of about four per cent remained insufficient to deliver rapid poverty reduction and create enough jobs, calling for higher investment and faster expansion.
Oxford University Professor of Economic Policy, Stefan Dercon, stressed the importance of controlling inflation and improving electricity supply, logistics and port operations to support economic growth.
He cautioned against indefinite protection for domestic industries.
“You can’t keep on protecting in the same way,” he said.
Chema Triki, co-founder and managing director of Growth Teams, said Nigeria needed to develop new productive capabilities and diversify exports rather than depend excessively on its domestic market.
She pointed to the country’s limited export diversification as a reason for strengthening industrial competitiveness.
Omoboyede Olusanya, group managing director of Flour Mills of Nigeria, called for lower interest rates, reliable infrastructure and improved agricultural productivity to reduce manufacturing costs.
He said expensive financing discouraged long-term investment, while poor logistics and unstable supplies of agricultural commodities weakened domestic industries.
Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, highlighted investments in ports, transport corridors, rail infrastructure and food logistics as measures to improve productivity and reduce the cost of doing business.
The Chairman of the Nigerian Economic Summit Group, Olaniyi Yusuf, urged the government to ensure that economic reforms translated into affordable living costs, productive employment and measurable improvements in household welfare.
The Minister of State for Budget and Economic Planning, Doris Uzoka-Anite, said the National Development Plan 2026–2030 would prioritise industrialisation, infrastructure, investment mobilisation, human capital development and stronger institutions.
She said the plan aimed to accelerate economic growth, create jobs and reduce poverty through better coordination of government policies, budgets and investment programmes.
The proposed Nigeria Economic Policy Framework is expected to undergo further consultation before formal consideration by the relevant government institutions.

title: Abortion is on the ballot in Missouri again. Here's what to know about Amendment 3
body:
Amendment 3 would overturn the 2024 amendment enshrining abortion rights.
Just two years after Missouri voters approved an amendment enshrining the right to reproductive freedom in the state constitution, abortion, which was also protected by the measure, is on the ballot there again.
On Nov. 3, Missouri residents will be voting on Amendment 3, only this time it would prohibit abortion, except in cases of medical emergencies, fetal anomalies, rape or incest. If the abortion is due to rape or incest, the procedure must occur no later than 12 weeks' gestation.
Since Roe v. Wade was overruled by the Supreme Court in June 2022, 13 states have ceased nearly all abortion services while four states have a six-week ban on books, according to an ABC News tally.
Following the Supreme Court decision, Missouri enacted a trigger ban, prohibiting most abortions in the state.
However, in November 2024, Missouri became the first state to overturn a near-total abortion ban through a direct vote of the people by passing Amendment 3 -- the same name as the upcoming ballot measure -- with about 52% of the vote.
"Missourians have access to abortion care because the people made it possible," Mallory Schwarz, executive director of the nonprofit Abortion Action Missouri, told ABC News. "But not even months after our 2024 vote, politicians started plotting to overturn the will of the people and now, in a couple of weeks, voters will have to vote again to protect the right to abortion that we enshrined in the constitution previously."
Amendment 3 would repeal the 2024 amendment that granted reproductive freedom, including abortion through fetal viability, which is typically between 24 and 26 weeks' gestation.
If approved, the amendment would also permit state lawmakers to enact legislation to regulate abortions and access to care.
Examples include laws requiring physicians providing abortion care to have admitting privileges at a nearby hospital and licensing requirements for abortion facilities.
State Sen. Adam Schnelting, who sponsored the proposal that led to Amendment 3 being placed on this year's ballot, told ABC News that passing the amendment is "critical to protecting women and children and providing Missourians with a measure that is more in line with their values than the one narrowly passed two years ago."
The amendment would also prohibit gender-affirming care procedures, cross-sex hormones or puberty-blocking drugs for minors. However, gender-affirming surgeries and medical treatments for minors are already illegal in Missouri under statutory law.
Opponents of the amendment have argued that including language about gender-affirming care is an attempt to mask the parts of the amendment that would limit abortion care.
"What politicians are trying to do is mislead voters and overturn the will of the people and ban abortion again," Tori Schafer, an attorney for the ACLU of Missouri, told ABC News. "And they've shown they're willing to resort to all kinds of tricky tactics in order to do that."
Schafer said organizations supporting Amendment 3 don't use the word "abortion" in their ads campaigning for the amendment to pass "because they know, like we know, that abortion care is popular in Missouri."
Schnelting said the statutory ban on gender-affirming procedures and treatment for minors expires in 2027 and including that language in Amendment 3 would ensure such a ban is permanent.
The ACLU of Missouri said the sunset clause only pertains to hormone therapy and that surgery is currently banned in Missouri.
Possibl e cons e qu e nc e s if Am e ndm e nt 3 is pass e d
After the trigger ban was passed in Missouri in 2022, the state's last abortion clinic in St. Louis was forced to stop providing such care .
In 2023 alone, more than 12,000 Missouri women traveled to neighboring states, including Illinois and Kansas , to receive care, according to the Guttmacher Institute, a reproductive rights organization.
Additionally, in 2025, more than 3,000 Missourians obtained medication abortions through telehealth from out-of-state clinicians, nearly four times higher than two years prior, the Guttmacher Institute found.
Some abortion providers told local news outlets they were seeing patients develop complications while waiting for treatment and some patients said they'd had to flee Missouri to seek abortion care for conditions including fetal anomalies.
"Missourians have lived under an abortion ban in the past," Schwarz said. "We've seen people turned away from the emergency room when they needed emergency abortion care. We've seen women forced to wait until their complication was serious enough that they were able to access care or have to flee the state to get care in another state that they should be able to get in their own community."
Schwarz said Abortion Action Missouri's canvassers have had conversations with Missourians against Amendment 3 from all walks of life.
One such conversation was with a Catholic voter who said they did not support abortion rights but also did not support the new amendment.
"They said, 'I'm personally pro-life, but we already voted on this and I'm voting "no" this time because politicians should be listening to the people,'" Schwarz said. "'Politicians shouldn't get to overturn any vote just because they don't like it.' And so, we are hearing that [at] the doors every day, every weekend."
Schnelting said the response to Amendment 3 from his constituents has been largely positive and called the claims that it is overturning the will of the people a "specious argument."
Anti-abortion rights groups have praised the new Amendment 3, arguing that the 2024 vote was extreme and goes beyond what Missourians have historically supported.
"Despite what voters were sold before Election Day, as soon as [2024's] Amendment 3 passed, the abortion lobby brought litigation to perform late-term abortions, end parental consent and remove every safety regulation on their industry," Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, said in a statement last year. "Amendment 3 is far too extreme and dangerous."
Missouri is not the only state with abortion on the ballot on Nov. 3. Voters in three states -- Idaho, Nevada and Virginia -- will consider measures to protect abortion rights and, in some cases, reproductive freedom.
Schafer, from ACLU of Missouri, said other states can learn from Missouri about how access to abortion can be at risk even after voters vote to protect care.
"While this fight is really important to folks like me who live in Missouri and have to suffer the consequences of our legislature ignoring the will of the people, we know that this campaign will also impact folks all across the country," Schafer said. "We have friends in other states who have passed their own versions of the right to reproductive freedom, and we don't want this attempt by our legislature to embolden this opposition strategy across the country."
She went on, "So we know that a lot of eyes are on Missouri, and Missourians deeply believe in the right to make their own decisions free from political interference."
