title: Gunmen kill seven in Plateau community
body: By Golok Nanmwa, Jos Gunmen on Monday night stormed Georo community in Jos South Local Government Area of Plateau State, killing seven persons in an attack that threw residents into panic. The attackers, who invaded the community at about 10:20pm, reportedly opened fire sporadically, killing some persons in their shops and others at a local restaurant. A member of the community, Mr Bot Silas, who confirmed the incident, said, “The gunmen stormed the community at about 10:20pm and started shooting sporadically.” Silas said, “Some of the victims were killed in their shops, while others were attacked at a local restaurant where food was being prepared.” He added, “Seven persons were killed in the attack, and the incident caused serious panic among residents of the community.” Silas said, “The attackers came at night and started shooting, forcing residents to scamper for safety.” Reacting to the incident, spokesman of the Berom Youth Moulders Association, BYM, Rwang Tengwong, condemned the attack and described it as unacceptable. Tengwong said, “The killing of innocent people in Georo is condemnable and must not be allowed to continue.” “I call on the relevant security agencies to intensify efforts to protect communities and apprehend those responsible for the attack.” Tengwong added, “We call on the relevant security agencies to investigate the incident, bring the perpetrators to justice and ensure that residents can live and carry out their legitimate activities without fear.” The post Gunmen kill seven in Plateau community appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Savannah Regional Minister backs EPA’s Styrofoam ban campaign ahead of January 2027 deadline
body: Savannah Regional Minister Salisu Be-Awuribe Issifu has thrown his weight behind the Environmental Protection Authority’s (EPA) campaign to enforce Ghana’s nationwide ban on Styrofoam products, describing the policy as a necessary intervention to protect public health and the environment. He has called on religious leaders, traditional authorities and community leaders to mobilise public support for the ban, urging Ghanaians to abandon the use of polystyrene food containers and embrace safer, environmentally friendly alternatives ahead of the January 1, 2027, implementation date. The minister made the call in Damongo on Monday, October 26, 2026, during the launch of the EPA’s week-long public awareness campaign across northern Ghana. The campaign seeks to intensify public education and secure widespread compliance ahead of the ban, with the EPA taking its message directly to traders, food vendors, consumers and other stakeholders. Addressing a gathering of traditional authorities, market representatives, religious leaders and officials from various public institutions at the Damongo Community Centre, Mr Be-Awuribe Issifu described the ban as a policy that deserves collective support rather than political controversy. He argued that the environmental and health risks associated with Styrofoam products make the intervention necessary and said its implementation should not be delayed. “I am in full support of this Styrofoam ban. For me, the ban should have even been implemented like yesterday. The ban is no doubt a policy that will help address the health and environmental challenges associated with its use, and I am happy that the EPA has brought its first public awareness campaign in the north to the Savannah Region,” he said. The minister stressed that the success of the policy would depend largely on public understanding and a willingness to change long-established consumption habits. He therefore appealed to imams, pastors, reverend ministers and queen mothers to use their influence within their communities to educate the public on the dangers associated with continued reliance on polystyrene food packaging. “Imams seated here, pastors and reverend ministers seated in this hall today, and you the queen mothers, use your platforms to propagate the Styrofoam ban message. Educate your followers to appreciate the dangers of the continued use of Styrofoam,” he urged. On her part, Chief Executive Officer of the Environmental Protection Authority, Professor Nana Ama Browne Klutse, who led a high-powered delegation from Accra, called for a return to traditional food-packaging practices that reduce dependence on single-use plastic foam products. She urged Ghanaians to revive the practice of carrying their own food containers when purchasing meals from vendors, describing it as a practical step towards reducing exposure to potentially harmful substances and limiting environmental pollution. “Let’s go back to the olden days when we used to go out to buy food with our own bowls. This is one of the most sustainable ways to avoid eating chemicals into your system,” she said. Professor Browne Klutse also encouraged consumers and food vendors to explore plant-based packaging materials, including plantain leaves, as alternatives to polystyrene products. “You can use plantain leaves and other plant-based packaging materials that do not have adverse impacts on your health. That is the message from the EPA,” she added. The EPA chief executive is leading a coordinated campaign involving regional directors and other officials across the northern belt to strengthen public education, engage key stakeholders and build support for the impending ban. The authority is targeting communities, markets and institutions to ensure that the January 1, 2027, deadline is widely understood and that consumers and businesses have sufficient awareness to prepare for the transition. The Damongo engagement followed a massive public awareness float through the principal streets of the regional capital on Monday morning. EPA officials visited lorry stations, markets and other busy public spaces, interacting with traders, food vendors and consumers to explain the objectives of the ban and the need for collective action. The exercise culminated in a stakeholder durbar at the Damongo Community Centre, where representatives of the Ghana Police Service, Ghana Health Service, Ghana Education Service, market associations and traditional authorities joined the EPA to discuss the policy and its implications. Several speakers at the gathering expressed support for the ban and pledged to help promote the behavioural changes needed to reduce the use of polystyrene products. The stakeholders emphasised the importance of sustained public education in ensuring that the policy translates into practical changes in how food is packaged, sold and consumed across communities. Wa campaign Following the Damongo engagement, the EPA delegation is scheduled to move to Wa on Tuesday, October 27, to continue the awareness campaign in the Upper West Region. The programme will include a courtesy visit to traditional authorities, an engagement with the regional minister, interactions with market vendors and a grand durbar to deepen public understanding of the ban. The northern campaign forms part of the EPA’s broader effort to mobilise nationwide support and prepare businesses, consumers and other stakeholders for the January 1, 2027, implementation deadline. With the deadline approaching, the authority is stepping up its engagement with communities to ensure that the transition away from polystyrene food packaging is understood not merely as a regulatory requirement, but as a collective responsibility to safeguard public health and the environment.

title: “Be The First Confidence Builders”: UN Deputy Chief Amina Mohammed Urges Nigerians To Own Development Narrative
body: The United Nations Deputy Secretary-General, Amina Mohammed, has challenged Nigerians to adopt a more confident, evidence-based approach when communicating the country’s economic reforms and development potential to the international community. Speaking during a fireside chat titled “Africa’s Next Development Frontier: Inclusive Growth, Resilience, and Human Dignity” at the 2026 Nigerian Economic Summit (NES) in Abuja, the UN chief underscored the direct link between domestic self-perception and international investor confidence. Acknowledging widespread public cynicism surrounding decades of policy debates, Ms. Mohammed addressed the recurring frustration among citizens regarding economic promises versus tangible outcomes. “We have also had the feeling that we’ve been here before—that in Nigeria, we have been talking about these things for decades,” Ms. Mohammed said. “Everyone is asking: ‘So, what’s different? How much more grammar are we going to talk?’ I believe that we also have to ask ourselves: ‘What are we getting wrong? What is it that is not enabling us to reach those potentials that we say we have?'” Reframing The Economic Narrative Despite acknowledging the structural bottlenecks hindering accelerated growth, the former Nigerian Environment Minister made a passionate plea for citizens and business leaders to highlight incremental progress, describing internal skepticism as a key barrier to foreign direct investment. “Let us consistently talk about the glass that is partially full,” she emphasized. “We might disagree on whether it is half-full, a quarter-full, or whatever it may be, but it has been filled, and we must continue to work towards filling it completely.” She observed that while international markets are closely watching Nigeria’s ongoing fiscal and structural reform efforts, negative messaging driven domestically often undermines economic prospects. “Why is that? Because we Nigerians are the greatest critics of ourselves,” Ms. Mohammed noted. “The narrative and the signals that we send outside of this room are important. If we don’t have belief and confidence in ourselves—in spite of the things that may not be right—then the markets are not going to have confidence either. We have to be the first confidence-builders of this nation.” Building Resilience For Sustainable Growth The UN Deputy Chief highlighted that sustainable development must be grounded in inclusive growth, resilience, and human dignity, urging policymakers to pair market-driven reforms with robust social safety nets. As the annual summit convenes public sector leaders, private investors, and policy experts, her remarks reinforce the growing consensus that domestic narrative management and structural accountability are equally critical to positioning Nigeria as Africa’s primary investment hub. The post “Be The First Confidence Builders”: UN Deputy Chief Amina Mohammed Urges Nigerians To Own Development Narrative appeared first on Channels Television .

title: No government will use Ebola as political weapon —NCDC DG
body:
The Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), Jide Idris, has said no government would use the Ebola outbreak as a political weapon.
Mr Idris made the statement on Monday during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today, amid concerns and claims that the Ebola outbreak could be exploited by the government to influence political activities ahead of the 2027 general elections.
“We in the health sector will not use disease issues as a political weapon,” Mr Idris said.
PREMIUM TIMES had earlier reported how some Nigerians linked the Ebola case to the government’s 2027 election plans, with some alleging that restrictions could be imposed under the guise of containing the disease.
Responding to a question on whether the Ebola situation could lead to the postponement of the 2027 elections, Mr Idris said the decision is beyond his authority.
He said there is currently no reason to postpone the elections, but acknowledged that a widespread outbreak could raise public health concerns.
“We hope not, because if the thing gets wide enough, there might be concern. As of now, there is no need for that,” he said.
He said health authorities had been monitoring the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for months and had anticipated that population movement and international flights could lead to an imported case in Nigeria.
“So no government will use Ebola as a political weapon,” he said.
The comments come against the backdrop of growing political activity ahead of the 2027 elections, with President Bola Tinubu seeking re-election and opposition candidates, including former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, already campaigning.
The Independent National Electoral Commission has fixed 16 January 2027 for the presidential and National Assembly elections.
The Ebola response has also become part of the political debate.
Mr Atiku, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), had questioned the government’s handling of the outbreak and demanded an account of the N10 billion approved for Ebola preparedness.
His comments prompted the APC Presidential Campaign Council to accuse him of politicising the health emergency and to say the fund remained untouched.
The State House had announced in June that President Tinubu approved N10 billion in emergency intervention funding to strengthen NCDC preparedness and support public health emergency response activities.
Mr Idris emphasised that the Ebola response is not being driven by electoral considerations.
He said Nigeria had been preparing for the possibility of an imported case because of the outbreak in the DRC and the movement of people between countries.
The NCDC boss also cautioned that Nigeria is not yet Ebola free, despite the evacuation of the index patient to Switzerland.
“We don’t have an active positive case,” he said. “But the contacts, we have contacts. We need to follow up.”
He said health authorities will continue to monitor contacts and investigate additional suspected exposures.

title: Second SA military heritage symposium underway in Cape Town
body:
SA National Defence Force (SANDF) Chief, General Rudzani Maphwanya, officially started proceedings at the second South African military heritage symposium in the Castle of Good Hope, widely seen as South Africa’s oldest and still in use building, on Tuesday 27 October.
As with the first symposium at the same venue last October, the second edition is again championed by Department of Defence (DoD) Chief Logistics (C Log) Vice Admiral David Mkhonto.
In keeping with its overall Battle of Cuito Cuanavale theme, presentations will recognise experiences of all who served, while preserving the lessons and legacy associated with what is accepted as the main siege action of the Bush War involving the then South African Defence Force (SADF) and Unita (União Nacional para a Independência Total de Angola) against Cuba, by way of the Caribbean nation’s armed forces – FAR (Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias) and FAPLA (Forças Armadas Populares de Libertação de Angola).
Maphwanya’s address is titled “Nothing will be forgotten, nobody will be forgotten: military heritage as a national responsibility”.
The general’s thoughts will be expanded on in the first session moderated by Captain (SAN) Graeme Plint, an academic researcher specialising in military history, defence and national security. The subject up for discussion is developing a national military heritage policy for sustainable preservation and governance challenges in managing military heritage in the form of museums, memorials and battlefield. Panellists include Mamakomoreng Nkhasi-Lesaoana, Executive Officer for Heritage Resources Management at the SA Heritage Resources Agency (SAHRA); Dr Saths Cooper, arrested by the then government in 1974 for what are termed “anti-apartheid activities”; senior Stellenbosch University research professional Dr Hendrik Snyders whose PhD focusses on history, and retired rear admiral Asiel Kubu, a previous chief of the DoD Human Resources Division.
Session three, after a reflection on the first symposium, will be a Cuito Cuanavale case study to be moderated by Lieutenant Colonel Jean Pierre Scherman of the Stellenbosch University Faculty of Military Science. Marius Fransman – a former deputy minister of international relations and co-operation – is the only named panellist. The final day one session is titled “story-telling and book launches” with retired major general turned publisher Andre Kruger; Brigadier General Graham Jacobs (Cape Corps and legacy) and Africa Sun Media Managing Director Nirod Bramdaw the named panellists.
Day two starts with perspectives on military heritage led by Stellenbosch University, Faculty of Military Science Professor Evert Kleynhans and Flint with Snyders in the moderator’s chair. They will explore military heritage, women and nation building as well as the need for digital archives.
Military family histories and community memory along with an interactive session titled “From the family vault, artefacts tell the story” lead into the closing plenary – the future of military heritage. Mkhonto will wrap up the symposium presenting and seeking adoption of the “Nothing will be forgotten, nobody will be forgotten” military heritage preservation declaration.

title: Zelensky on overnight attack: Russia targeted energy, logistics, and urban infrastructure almost everywhere
body:
According to Ukrinform, the head of state said this in a Facebook post.
“Artificial and prolonged delays in deliveries of interceptors for Patriot and NASAMS systems, which have unfortunately been occurring recently, directly help Russia achieve the objectives of its terrorist campaign. Each such delay results in another Russian strike hitting a target. Unfortunately, attacks occur daily. Russia is constantly taking new escalatory steps. Pressure on Russia and tangible support for Ukraine are needed to change the situation,” Zelensky said.
He noted that the number of people injured in a Russian strike on a university campus and the surrounding area the previous evening had risen to 12, five of them students or university staff.
“While emergency services were helping people and dealing with the aftermath of the first strike, the Russians launched another ballistic missile attack. A total of 16 ballistic missiles were launched overnight, along with more than 280 drones. Unfortunately, there have been casualties, and targets in Kyiv were hit, including the Southern Bridge. This is a serious escalation in Russia’s campaign targeting our logistics,” the President said.
He added that strikes had also targeted the Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, and Kherson regions, as well as Chernivtsi region. In almost every region, Zelensky said, Russia’s targets were energy facilities, logistics, and civilian urban infrastructure.
As Ukrinform previously reported, President Volodymyr Zelensky said the previous day that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on the supply of missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems.

title: Zaluzhny urges West to develop new military doctrine based on lessons from war in Ukraine
body:
Ukraine’s Ambassador to the United Kingdom and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024), Valeriy Zaluzhny, believes that the war in Ukraine persists due to the weakness of the Western world and its security system—a system that requires a new military doctrine reflecting the realities of modern warfare.
"The West needs to step out of its comfort zone and into the reality of what war looks like in 2026; it must shed the illusion that outdated guarantees and doctrines can truly protect it and its children," Zaluzhny wrote in a Facebook post.
According to him, the Western security system remains rooted in a World War II-era doctrine, merely supplemented by expensive, high-precision weaponry whereas modern conditions demand a comprehensive overhaul of approaches to combat operations.
Zaluzhny emphasized that for the West to ensure its own security, it is not enough to simply procure new weapons or adjust tactics to account for the use of drones.
"The West needs a new doctrine to defend itself. For us in the military, a doctrine is a 'Bible of war'—it integrates all components of the armed forces—weaponry, tactics, structure, training, and funding—into a unified system," he noted.
Zaluzhny stated that such a doctrine would enable the assessment of the impact of new technologies, adaptation to change, and the planning of joint operations. "A relevant, up-to-date doctrine means security for your children and for your state. No other commitments will save you," he wrote.
He added that the West still possesses sophisticated and costly technologies that could help build a new security system; however, the key factor remains the willingness to step out of one’s comfort zone and take collective action. According to Zaluzhny, only by working together can the war for the future of our children be won.
Zaluzhny also mentioned that he addressed officers from various nations at the Joint Services Command and Staff College of the UK Defence Academy, where they are preparing for senior command roles, and noted the participation of Ukrainian military personnel with firsthand combat experience in the training program. Among them is a Hero of Ukraine, Lieutenant Colonel Serhiy Roschin, a squadron commander who has been defending the Ukrainian skies since 2022.

title: Ngiraiwet challenges second impeachment, seeks halt to Ngardmau special election
body: By: L.N. Reklai KOROR, Palau (Oct. 26, 2026) — Former Ngardmau Gov. Jennifer Ngiraiwet is challenging the legality of her second impeachment, arguing that the Ngardmau Legislature failed to provide the notice and opportunity to be heard required by the courts, and asking that the Nov. 13 special gubernatorial election be stopped until the dispute is resolved. Ngiraiwet filed a complaint Oct. 19 against the 11th Kelulul Ngardmau, represented by Speaker Terrence Miozawa, and the Palau Election Commission, represented by Chairperson Bisayang Luii. She is asking the court to declare the legislature’s second impeachment resolution “unconstitutional and without legal effect.” The complaint argues that the second impeachment did not comply with the Appellate Court’s decision in Ngiraiwet v. Eleventh Kelulul Ngardmau (2026), which requires adequate notice of an impeachment or removal action and a meaningful opportunity for the governor to attend the session where the action is considered. The court’s earlier decision is central to Ngiraiwet’s challenge, which seeks to prevent the latest impeachment from proceeding without the constitutional protections the appellate court said must be followed. Ngiraiwet said she is not asking the court to determine whether the allegations against her are true or to question the constitutional authority of the Kelulul Ngardmau to impeach a governor. Instead, she said her complaint seeks to enforce the constitutional protections required by the Appellate Division. She maintains that the second impeachment resolution is unlawful because it was adopted without proper notice and an opportunity for her to be heard. The complaint contends that the legislature’s action failed to meet the requirements established in the appellate court’s decision, making the second impeachment legally invalid. Ngiraiwet also asked the court to prevent the Palau Election Commission from conducting the special gubernatorial election scheduled for Nov. 13 while the court considers the legality of the second impeachment resolution. Her request seeks to halt the election until the court issues a ruling on the impeachment challenge. The dispute follows a prolonged series of legal and political developments surrounding the 11th Ngardmau government’s effort to impeach Ngiraiwet. Meanwhile, a separate petition was submitted to the Palau Election Commission on Oct. 19 seeking the recall of Speaker Miozawa and Floor Leader Neil Fisher. The petition adds another development to the continuing dispute over Ngardmau’s government and leadership. body:

title: Nigerian Navy for the People: Lessons in Soft Power
body: Musa Ilallah When Nigerians think of their Navy, the images that come to mind are usually warships on patrol in the Gulf of Guinea, special forces boarding a hijacked tanker, or operations against crude oil thieves in the creeks of the Niger Delta. It is important work, which has helped keep Nigeria off the global maritime piracy list for more than 1,600 unbroken days. Operation DELTA SENTINEL, launched in January 2026, equally shows what that work looks like on the ground, in communities across the Niger Delta. Since its commencement, the Navy has recovered more than 7.48 million litres of suspected stolen crude oil and illegally refined petroleum products, disrupted over 241 illegal refining sites and networks, and arrested more than 230 suspects. The momentum has risen steadily through the year, from more than 183 operations in the first quarter to over 580 intelligence-driven operations in the second. In the third quarter alone, the Navy recovered over 2.25 million litres of petroleum products, including more than 1.55 million litres of crude oil, and rescued 24 kidnapped persons. The results are increasingly visible in Nigeria’s national accounts: provisional Central Bank of Nigeria data show crude oil export earnings rising from $8.11 billion in the first quarter of 2026 to $9.39 billion in the second, an increase of almost 16 per cent. Arrests are also translating into accountability, with the Federal High Court in Uyo recently convicting nine crude oil thieves. These milestones have been recorded under the leadership of the Chief of the Naval Staff, Vice Admiral Idi Abbas, who marks his first year in office this week. He took command with a vision of building “a modern, agile and professional naval force” working in synergy with other security agencies. As well as launching Operation DELTA SENTINEL on 13 January 2026, barely two and a half months after taking office, he has pushed for technology transfer to expand indigenous shipbuilding and kept a sustained focus on personnel welfare. He has also consistently charged officers and ratings to build and maintain cordial relationships with civilians, reflecting his conviction that the Navy’s standing rests as much on how it treats citizens as on the firepower it commands. Beyond that firepower, there is another, less familiar side to the Nigerian Navy: a rapidly expanding footprint of people-focused impact in communities across the country. This is the Navy’s soft power in the 21st century, and it is proving just as important to national security as any anti-theft operation or patrol frigate. Soft power, a term coined by the Harvard scholar Joseph Nye, describes the ability to shape outcomes through attraction and persuasion rather than force. For a military institution, it means winning trust, building goodwill and earning the cooperation of the people it exists to protect. There is a growing consensus in Nigeria that security cannot be achieved by firepower alone. It depends to a significant extent on communities that share information, support operations and see the armed forces as partners rather than strangers. All the guns, warships and drones in the world can only go so far in communities that are hostile to, or distrustful of, security personnel. Nigeria saw the power of community collaboration first-hand a few months ago, in the operation that freed the abducted victims of Oriire in Oyo State, which featured the active involvement of the Navy’s special forces, the SBS. The Nigerian Navy’s Quick Impact Projects (QIPs) are perhaps the clearest expression of this thinking. Modest in scale but significant in impact, they deliver tangible benefits directly to communities: boreholes, electrification projects, clinics and dispensaries, classrooms, sports facilities and more. They stretch across all six geopolitical zones, reaching dozens of communities including Balanga in Adamawa, Irepodun in Kwara, Manga in Plateau, Takum in Taraba, Gwale in Kano, Bagudo in Kebbi, Nkanu East and West in Enugu, Umuahia in Abia, Ikot Abasi in Akwa Ibom, Obudu in Cross River, Epe in Lagos and Ogbomosho in Oyo. Complementing the QIPs are free medical outreaches. A recent one by the Nigerian Navy College of Accounts and Finance (NNCAF) benefited residents of Umuochala and surrounding communities in Owerrinta, Abia State, with Umuochala community leader, Chief Kenneth Nzeoma, conveying the beneficiaries’ deep gratitude. Similar outreaches have taken place in Imo, Ondo, Delta, Lagos and the FCT in the last six months. What stands out is the geography of these interventions. They are not limited to the coastal or riverine communities where one might expect naval projects to be sited. Many are hundreds of kilometres from the sea, in places where people may never before have seen a naval uniform or vessel. For the Nigerian Navy, “Onward Together” is no longer just an internal slogan; it has come to mean carrying communities and people along. These efforts reflect a modern understanding of what a navy is for: a navy that builds schools and brings water and electricity is a navy that Nigerians are more likely to trust, support, share intelligence with, and join. There is, of course, room to do more. Documenting the impact of QIPs over time would multiply their value, as would involving communities in choosing projects and sharing these stories more widely. The Nigerian Navy began 2026 rated as having Africa’s strongest fleet. That position is set to strengthen, with recent and forthcoming inductions of new vessels, backed by President Tinubu’s commitment to the welfare and capacity of the Armed Forces. The Navy will continue to project power across the seas. But it is equally making its presence felt in homes, classrooms, clinics and sports facilities in communities across Nigeria, quietly winning hearts in the nation it serves. * Musa Ilallah is a public affairs analyst based in Abuja. He can be reached at musahk123@yahoo.com .

title: The case of ex-DA chief Leonardo Montemayor: What we know so far
body: MANILA, Philippines – Former agriculture chief Leonardo Montemayor’s surrender on Monday, October 26 is the latest development in the dispute between farmers’ groups and Planters Products Inc., an agricultural firm recently implicated in illegal rice imports from Vietnam. The Makati Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 148 issued the warrant against Montemayor for cyber libel and oral defamation, based on a case filed by Planters Products Inc. “May pulis na pumunta sa bahay ko, pero tumuloy ako sa Makati para sumuko sa RTC at magpost ng bail,” Montemayor told Rappler on Tuesday, October 27. (There were policemen who came to my house, but I went to Makati to surrender to the RTC and post bail.) Montemayor said he posted bail amounting to P84,000, donated by members of his group, the Federation of Free Farmers (FFF), and political party Magsasaka. The RTC scheduled the arraignment on November 24. A long-running criticism Montemayor, FFF, and Magsasaka have been critical of Planters Products Inc.’s rice imports, particularly its impact on local prices and farmers’ income. They described Planters Products Inc. as a government-owned and -controlled corporation (GOCC), a claim that the company refuted. On March 18, the farmers’ groups questioned the legality of Planters Products Inc. and Food Terminal Inc.’s rice imports and sales. In response, Planters Products Inc. filed last May a cyber libel and slander complaint against the Federation of Free Farmers and Magsasaka. The FFF said then that it was ready to refute the complaint. The animosity between the parties boiled over in October following the rice import controversy involving Planters Products Inc. Over 12,000 metric tons of rice from Vietnam had arrived off Davao past the contract deadline. Department of Agriculture (DA) Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. serves as ex officio chairman of Planters Foundation Inc., the firm that holds majority of Planters Products Inc.’s outstanding shares. This link provided easy fodder for criticism as well as calls for Tiu Laurel to step down even if only temporarily. Before the import controversy erupted, the Food Terminal Inc., a GOCC, also filed a cyber libel complaint last July against the FFF. The FFF criticized the move saying, “FTI’s recent legal action highlights a deeply concerning pattern wherein individuals and organizations questioning government actions are increasingly facing criminal complaints.” ‘Planters Products is sui generis’ The DA secretary’s link to the Planters Foundation Inc. is nothing new. Montemayor said that all DA secretaries, including himself, also served as chairman of Planters Foundation Inc. This has been the practice since the first Marcos government, and it was Ferdinand E. Marcos who issued the letters of instructions that created this arrangement. Must Read Tiu Laurel alleges smear campaign by rice smugglers amid import controversy Tiu Laurel denied that Planters Products Inc. is a GOCC, during the Senate hearing on the DA’s proposed 2027 budget . “Planters Products is sui generis,” said Tiu Laurel. “It is unique on its own.” The list from the Governance Commission for GOCCs as of June 30 includes both Planters Products Inc. and Planters Foundation Inc. These firms are classified under the trade, area development and tourism sector. The DA chief refuted claims that he had a role in the rice importation, reiterating that he was the one who ordered the cancellation of import permits. – Rappler.com

title: Police arrest 3 suspects over man’s murder in Yei
body: The police in Yei River County, Central Equatoria State, are holding three young men in connection with the alleged murder of John Hakim, 23, along Yei Town’s Kinji Street over the weekend. Major General Yoasa Lujang Kamba, the head of the police in Yei, told Radio Tamazuj Monday that the victim was rushed to a health facility but succumbed to his injuries before receiving treatment. The suspects, aged between 21 and 22, remain in police custody pending court arraignment. “On 23 October at around 6 p.m., we received a report from the Peace suburb near the Sea Hotel that a man named John Hakim Joseph, 23, was beaten by three men who then rushed him to the hospital, but he died before receiving medical attention,” he explained. “The three suspects, aged between 21 and 22, are in our custody and will appear in court after investigations.” “Mob justice is illegal, and I want to urge young men to stop such behavior,” Gen. Lujang added. For her part, Rejoice Keji Angilo, the deceased’s aunt, said her nephew was allegedly beaten by three men before being taken to a health facility, where he later died. She called on authorities to ensure justice for the family. “They were fighting with some boys, but I have not seen them up to today. The second guy allegedly slapped the late man and twisted his neck, and he fell unconscious. The other boys panicked and decided to take him to the hospital,” she narrated. “They took the boy to the hospital where they were told to bring Police Form 8. However, when they returned from the police, the boy had already died. We have left the case in the hands of the authorities, and we want to see justice done.” A picture of John Hakim, 23, who was beaten to death in Yei. (Courtesy photo) Meanwhile, David Lodongo Peter, Sub-Chief of Rumojju Sub-Boma, condemned the killing and urged residents to remain calm as police investigations continue. He urged collective community action to address gang activities. “I condemn the killing. We should act before such negative things and loss of life happen,” he stated. “There are gangs in the area where this man died in Kinji. It is a dangerous place, and I urge the government to look into such matters because perpetrators are usually arrested and released without any information.” Major General Lujang urged parents to guide young people away from violence and encouraged residents to report suspected criminal activities to the authorities. “We want to urge the area chiefs and parents to see to it that when your child joins a gang, you better come and report to us so that we put some discipline in them so that they become better people,” he advised. “When they are in our custody, they will not have access to the drugs they take.” Yei River County has seen a rise in gang-related crime lately, creating fear among residents. The post Police arrest 3 suspects over man’s murder in Yei appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Education Minister to meet teacher unions today over payment of promotion arrears for 28,000 teachers
body: The Education Minister, Haruna Iddrisu, says his office will meet the leadership of teacher unions today, Tuesday, October 27, to resolve outstanding validation issues affecting 28,000 teachers awaiting payment of their promotion salary arrears. The meeting is expected to address concerns that have prevented the affected teachers from successfully completing the validation process and receiving their payments. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Tuesday, October 27, the Minister said the government is committed to resolving the issues to enable the remaining teachers to receive their arrears. “I am compelled to invite the teacher unions to an emergency meeting this morning. I have reached out to them,” he said. He urged the teachers not to resume their strike, assuring them that the planned engagement with their leadership would help determine the way forward. The Minister said the government had already paid the arrears of 52,000 teachers who successfully completed the validation process out of about 80,000 who had been demanding payment. “The 52,000 promotion arrears on the new grade were honoured by the government and paid by the government by October 16. What is outstanding is around 28,000, which includes some non-teachers; they may not be able to get payment because the validation process has not been completed,” he explained. READ ALSO: Gov’t pays 52,000 teachers’ promotion arrears, 28,000 pending He said the outstanding payments could be processed again, with the government targeting payment by mid-November or the end of November. The Minister also indicated that the government could consider a supplementary allocation for October as an alternative to facilitate payment to the affected teachers. The planned meeting follows the suspension of industrial action by teachers over delays in the payment of their promotion salary arrears.

title: Bicycles bring joy, healthier habits and new opportunities to Angaur schoolchildren
body: By: L.N. Reklai ANGAUR, Palau (Oct. 24, 2026) — “You don’t know how many years I have been dreaming of a bike and finally my dream has come true,” one Angaur Elementary School student wrote in a thank-you letter after receiving a donated bicycle Saturday, Oct. 24. The student was among 21 recipients of bicycles donated by private sponsors in Palau and abroad to students, teachers and a cook at Angaur Elementary School. The donation brought excitement to the island’s nine elementary school students and nine students taking high school classes online. The school also has five teachers and one cook. For the students, the bicycles represent more than a gift. They offer a way to get to school faster, run errands for their families, enjoy outdoor activities and spend less time on their phones. The bicycles arrived at the school a week before the handover and were stored in a classroom. Every day, students peered through the classroom windows, eagerly waiting to see the bicycles they would soon receive. On Saturday, the students gathered outside the classroom before being called inside one by one to collect a bicycle with their name on it. Their excitement was evident in the smiles and expressions of amazement as each child received a bicycle. Boys and girls of different ages appeared to find the bicycles they had hoped for. One young student, Aliang, smiled when asked whether she knew how to ride a bicycle. She said she did not know how yet, but she would learn. Another student, Skky, received a light purple bicycle and said she loved it. A high school student said the bicycle would help him get to school on time and allow him to run errands. The students also wrote heartfelt thank-you letters to their sponsors, expressing appreciation for the gifts and explaining what the bicycles would mean to their daily lives. One student wrote: “You don’t know how many years I have been dreaming of a bike and finally my dream has come true. This will help me get to school faster when I am running out of time. Also, when my grandma needs something at the store, I can ride my bike there. Thank you for working so hard to make money just to buy a bike meant for me.” The donation was organized by Marvin Ngirutang, who said the idea came from school principal Tiffany Kasiano. Kasiano had told him that the students needed healthier activities. Bicycles, she said, could help ensure students arrive at school on time while encouraging physical activity instead of spending too much time on their phones. Ngirutang said the bicycles were intended to support both school attendance and healthier habits among the students. Hilo Belau Ohana, one of the sponsors from outside Palau, said the bicycles could encourage students to stay active beyond the school day. “When they bike to and from school or even biking outside of school hours like to swim, it promotes good physical and mental health,” the sponsor said. “We hope this will contribute to the young students continuing to be part of their community.” President Surangel Whipps Jr., also one of the sponsors, said the donation was intended to encourage exercise and healthier lifestyles. “The bikes are to promote exercise. Healthy islands are wealthy islands,” Whipps said. The 21 bicycles were donated by private sponsors both in Palau and overseas. The recipients included students in grades one through 12, teachers and the school’s cook. For the children, the handover marked the fulfillment of a long-awaited wish. Their letters showed how the bicycles could make everyday tasks easier, from getting to school on time to helping grandparents with errands. The donation also reflected the sponsors’ hope that the bicycles would encourage students to remain active, participate in their community and develop healthier habits. The post Bicycles bring joy, healthier habits and new opportunities to Angaur schoolchildren appeared first on Island Times News .

title: 2026 U17 WWC: Black Maidens to face Argentina in last 16 on October 28
body: Ghana will return to U-17 Women’s World Cup action on Wednesday, October 28, when they fight for a spot in the quarterfinal stage of the competition. The Black Maidens will face Argentina in the round of 16 following their progression into the next phase of the tournament being played in Morocco. Nana Joe Adarkwa’s side advanced into the next phase of the competition following their 2-0 victory over Canada in their final group game, with two substitutes, Linda Achiaa and Christiana Ashiaku, scoring the goals. Having finished second, the Black Maidens will face Argentina, who also finished second in Group C. Unlike Ghana, Argentina won two out of their three games in the group phase, beating Morocco and New Zealand while losing to Germany. The Argentines scored nine goals in three group games while conceding three goals in that period. Comparing that to Ghana, they were the better side in terms of goals scored and goals conceded, as Ghana scored five goals and conceded six goals. For the Black Maidens, this is the first time they are making the last 16 stage since the 2018 edition, which was also their last appearance in the competition prior to qualifying for the 2026 tournament. Aregntina, on the other hand, are playing in the competition for the very first time and will look to upset Ghana on Wednesday to advance into the last eight. The game is scheduled for an 18:00 GMT kickoff in Rabat.

title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
body: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade. As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure. Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity. These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid. The grid’s backbone Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat. How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost. So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down. Consider, for example, your local solar plant. For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant. Enter transformers. In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines. Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer. Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood. If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home. Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire. The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel. Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core. The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down. When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core. That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage. This process is called magnetic induction. Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University. In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them. That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety. The problem is that today’s transformers are big and bulky, and they’re also difficult and expensive to replace, Lukic says. A solid option Solid-state transformers essentially add so-called power electronics—semiconductors that convert and control electricity to the typical blueprint of today’s transformers. While a conventional transformer operates at the frequency of the part of the grid it’s connected to, a solid-state transformer actually controls the frequency of the current. Typically, a solid-state transformer first converts incoming AC power from the grid to DC power, and then to a higher-frequency AC power using switches made of a semiconductor like silicon carbide. From there, a magnetic component changes the voltage. Because the advanced semiconductors allow transformers to exert so much control over the frequency and stability of the current, the magnetic core can be much smaller than in a conventional transformer. Some come in at roughly one-tenth the size but have the same capacity, Lukic says. Finally, additional power electronics convert the electricity from high-frequency AC to its required form—generally back to DC power and finally to lower-frequency AC. Today, stepping voltage up and down is many transformers’ only job. But solid-state transformers can do much more. They absorb the jobs of devices like rectifiers and inverters (which convert AC to DC power and vice versa), shrinking the total footprint of the electrical equipment and potentially cutting the amount of power lost in the system. In August, the New York Power Authority and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) tested a one-megawatt solid-state transformer under realistic utility conditions at EPRI’s test site. The device was built in Lukic’s lab, and it was the first such test for a transformer of that capacity, he says. The prototype was roughly 98% efficient—meaning it lost only 2% of the energy fed in. An equivalent conventional transformer and rectifier, by comparison, would be about 96% efficient together, Lukic says. A difference of 2% might seem small, but it is significant, since it means the solid-state transformer could cut power losses from conventional equipment in half, Lukic says. One major goal of the project was to help utilities gain more confidence in these new components, Lukic says. That’s crucial, since these devices could be used on the power grid in the future. In the near term, solid-state transformers could be used within data centers to provide electricity for server racks. The prototype is still a relatively low-voltage system, operating at about 15,000 volts. Industrial facilities like larger data centers often require higher-voltage connections, and transmission lines typically operate at hundreds of thousands of volts. Adapting solid-state transformers to these higher voltages will require further engineering development. But the test was a successful demonstration that solid-state transformers can work under real conditions, Lukic says. Companies developing solid-state transformers are largely focused on data centers right now, Lukic says. There’s an influx of money to support developing the new technology, and the voltage requirements aren’t as high as they will be for larger transformers that will be needed for long-distance transmission. In February, Heron Power raised $140 million to commercialize its solid-state transformer, which the company calls the Heron Link. The technology could be used in data centers, solar power arrays, and grid batteries, says Drew Baglino, the founder and CEO. The company is starting to test its technology at larger scales now, Baglino says. Ten megawatt-hours’ worth of batteries at Heron’s headquarters in Scotts Valley, California, will soon undergo testing with Heron transformers. The company is also planning a pilot with a nearby solar farm, Baglino says. One challenge for solid-state transformers is that their power electronics have more failure modes than conventional transformers. In a traditional device, a failure means that the entire device will typically be taken offline, resulting in power interruptions. But Heron designs with that in mind, Baglino says: The company uses a modular design, with many small devices that work together. If one fails, the rest of the system keeps working until the affected bit can be replaced, which doesn’t require shutting the whole thing down. Heron Power is currently building a $100 million factory in California to make advanced transformers. The facility should begin production in 2027 and reach its full production rate of 40 gigawatts’ worth of transformers per year in 2029. The future of the grid In recent years, companies that make grid equipment have put $1.7 billion into the US supply chain for power transformers, which are used in high-voltage transmission, says Benjamin Boucher, a supply chain analyst at Wood Mackenzie. There’s been an additional $1.3 billion invested for distribution transformers, the smaller devices that help transform power for homes and businesses, he adds. But even this investment isn’t keeping pace with the rapid growth of the grid. Wait times for large conventional transformers—the kind needed to connect new power plants, long-distance transmission, and high-demand sites like data centers—are stretching as long as five years. “Transformers have become one of the biggest bottlenecks for utilities, generation developers, and even data centers,” Boucher says. The big challenge is that it’s difficult to get new transformer manufacturing up and running, because it’s a quite technical process that requires a lot of specialized labor. So even facilities announced years ago are still years from opening, Boucher says. Solid-state transformers could help ease some of that pressure. But high-voltage devices needed for power plant connections and transmission lines are the holy grail for solid-state transformers, Lukic says. Existing solid-state technology can’t be used for those applications yet, so the industry will need to develop new materials and designs to support high voltages and handle electricity safely in a compact device. “We’re facing a big risk related to grid infrastructure,” Boucher says. “Without the transformers, you don’t really have an electrical grid.”

title: [Rear View] The 2028 battle is with Dutertismo, not just Sara
body: The results of the latest presidential preference surveys bear the qualifier “hypothetical,” a word that has now become standard fare in pollster disclaimers. It’s a reminder to partisans not to get too excited or too depressed. Partisans ignore it anyway. Impeached Vice President Sara Duterte is leading in these hypothetical match-ups, with voter support hardening in Mindanao, the family’s bailiwick (Pulse Asia pegged it at 96% in a head-to-head with Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo) and holding firm in Central Visayas. Sleepless nights for sure at the Palace and in the war rooms of the liberal pinks and the aimless Left, since a Sara presidency would mean payback for all who wronged her and her family, legal niceties be damned. Her conviction by the Senate impeachment court thus becomes more urgent. The prosecution has dropped three of four articles, and the case now rests on a single charge of unexplained wealth. The defense takes the floor on November 9. Political observers say a verdict is likely before the Christmas holidays, even as senator-judges insist they will not be pressured into prematurely revealing their votes or abandoning their impartiality, real or feigned. Every political player with a stake in 2028 knows that allowing the proceedings to spill into the first quarter of 2027 would be a dangerous gamble. Must Read IN DATA: The fates of early election survey front-runners It would allow the Sara campaign to reframe the trial as election-related, play the underdog card, and possibly convert a segment of the undecided. Her spokesperson has already called the withdrawal of the three articles an admission that the charges never had basis, and that is how her camp wants the trial remembered. Coalition: A must Efforts to consolidate the anti-Duterte ranks (the pinks, the left, the Marcos base) behind a single candidate in a winner-take-all brawl against the Vice President need to proceed with greater purpose and energy. Such a coalition needs to agree that the only objective is to defeat her and prevent a Duterte restoration, purity checks sidelined in favor of winnability. Old grudges between Liberals and the Marcos coalition, the “ pinklawan ” and the Left, will have to be shelved, at least until the canvassing is done. The coalition must also anticipate shifts in the political environment. Right now, opposition groups are planning for the “Us versus Sara” scenario. But what if the Vice President is found guilty, removed, and disqualified from public office, including the presidency? What then? The Duterte camp will surely file a petition before the Supreme Court, and the legal limbo could stretch into September 2027, when the filing of certificates of candidacy (CoC) opens. The Commission on Elections had said it will accept her CoC regardless. The uncertainty allows the Duterte camp to keep its options open while the opposition coalition could only wait. Must Read Who will be VP if Sara Duterte is convicted? The worst case in a presidential election without Sara Duterte on the ballot is for the incipient coalition to fragment, with each group or party retreating into its purity cocoon and fielding its own candidate. The resulting free-for-all could still favor a Duterte candidate. Not necessarily a member of the family, but someone perceived or packaged as heir and protector of the Duterte legacy, one who is embraced, like the former president, as champion of the poor and dispossessed, the same voters dismissed by elitists as society’s dregs and “ bobotante .” If we read surveys as quarterly referendums on the incumbent, then voters are in a foul mood. Angry and betrayed by a President who promised them liberation from poverty but will leave, after six years in the Palace, with a legacy of corruption, greed, and incompetence. The 2028 presidential election goes to the candidate who is seen as the incumbent’s opposite. The Vice President’s conviction looms as increasingly likely. Yet it may lead to an unintended consequence, one that is worse than our current predicament. Sara may be out, but not Dutertismo. – Rappler.com Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay .

title: Polymarket has investigated 'dozens' of election-related cases
body:
Prediction markets, like Polymarket and its main rival, Kalshi, have flourished in Trump's second term. Gabby Jones/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Polymarket has investigated "dozens" of bets on its prediction markets related to the midterm election, according to the company's head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista.
At least two of these Polymarket investigations have been referred to its regulator, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, according to a person who is familiar with the probes, but not authorized to speak publicly about them.
These investigations into election insider trading and manipulation come as prediction market Polymarket — and its chief competitor Kalshi — have exploded in popularity over the past year. But the fast-growing industry also faces significant legal challenges from states and political pushback from lawmakers who argue betting on the outcome of elections poses serious risks to the democratic process.
In April, Kalshi banned and fined a handful of political candidates from betting on themselves. A month later, NPR reported that campaign staffers had made "thousands" using insider polling information to bet on their own candidates on platforms like Polymarket and PredictIt.
Polymarket's Bautista — a former FBI official and cryptocurrency analyst — told NPR her team of 16 and a new election surveillance system are actively policing election bets ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.
"If you have information that you have a duty to protect, don't trade on it," Bautista said. "It's explicitly against our terms of use on both platforms, but also is against the law. If you decide that you are smarter and can do it, we will find you."
Bautista joined Polymarket in June. She oversees information gathered from both the U.S.-regulated version of Polymarket, which requires users to provide their real identities, and its bigger brother, Polymarket International, which is essentially unregulated and where trading can be done anonymously and with cryptocurrency. Despite this, Bautista said crypto trades are rarely completely anonymous.
"There's never been a case that we work where we haven't been able to identify, potentially, who these people are," Bautista said.
She said her election surveillance system pulls in "gigabytes" of data on each user from social media, Federal Election Commission data, cryptocurrency companies, banking partners, statistical models and other public information sources. If a user hits a certain number of internally-defined red flags, Bautista gets an alert on her phone.
"We're getting hundreds of alerts a day," Bautista said.
When asked about the specific detection criteria and thresholds, Bautista did not comment citing system security. But she said insider trading and market manipulation all look the same regardless of the financial market.
"We're looking at threat vectors and risk areas that have existed for decades in traditional markets," Bautista said. "But we recognize, too, that when it comes to prediction markets, we're seeing some of the old tried and known tactics, but being applied to a new vector through prediction markets."
Back in May, Kalshi, Polymarket's top rival, announced its own election surveillance system that also uses FEC data. Their system purportedly blocks any campaign staffer listed by the FEC from betting on an election. In July, Kalshi said it had blocked "dozens" of staffers from trading on elections, though at least one staffer told NPR they got around this. The staffer shared records of their recent trades and spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity for fear of consequences for their future employment.
Prediction markets for elections are uniquely vulnerable to market manipulation and insider trading, said Rajiv Sethi, an economics professor at Barnard College at Columbia University, who has studied prediction markets for decades.
"[Election prediction markets] have the possibility of being a self-fulfilling prophecy," Sethi said. "Elections have the property that what one believes is going to happen can actually affect what happens if a candidate is thought to be losing momentum or the campaign is flagging."
Bautista said her Polymarket team and surveillance system is learning from past cases and putting their feet in the shoes of would-be insider traders and market manipulators.
"If I was worried about somebody trying to materially move an election market to make it look like one option was more likely to happen than the other and I identify a pattern where they're opening several different accounts and they're doing that in short bursts and I see device IDs consistent across different trades placed in short succession with new wallets across five or four different accounts," Bautista said. "If I were to work that case and then action that, the findings of that tactic go back into the process to create the detections."
As prediction markets have exploded in popularity over the last two years, the industry's federal regulator, the CFTC, has done little to police these new financial markets, largely leaving that work to the companies themselves.

title: Democrats still poised to make gains, but poll shows warning signs for just how many
body:
A member of the League of Women Voters of Greater Cleveland helps hold the flag during the national anthem before a basketball game on Oct. 26, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. Jason Miller/Getty Images hide caption
📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App
Democrats retain significant midterm electoral advantages, with key data pointing to them being the favorites to win control of the U.S. House. But, there are indications of why a potential wave could be limited, a new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds.
The poll also sheds light on the issues driving voters across the ideological spectrum. The cost of living continues to be top of mind overall with a third of people saying they've experienced financial hardship in the past year and 4 in 10 saying their personal finances have gotten worse.
"The economy is at the top of my list right now," said Shun Maurice, a 47-year-old from Arizona who participated in the poll. He's an independent who leans toward Democrats and said high food and gas prices are a strain.
"They're too expensive for everybody, no matter who you voted for," he said. "They're just too expensive for the American people in general, and I don't like that."
Preserving democracy also continues to resonate with Democrats and independents, while immigration is the biggest concern for self-described MAGA supporters.
The poll of 1,289 registered voters was conducted Oct. 19-20. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points.
This was the first survey this cycle that Marist applied a likely voter screen, and on multiple questions, likely voters were — within the margin of error — slightly less likely than registered voters to disapprove of the president. Likely voters overall were also slightly less likely to want Democrats to run Congress.
Likely voters are something of a special sauce in polling. Survey researchers apply various metrics — like levels of enthusiasm, past voting history and how important voting is to different respondents — to try to identify the subsample of people who are most likely to vote.
In this survey, just 38% of registered voters approved of the job President Trump is doing, with 61% disapproving (-23). Likely voters gave him a 40% to 59% rating (-19), still not very good, but even a slight margin can make a difference in how significant the gains either party might make in the election are.
That said, an equal share — 53% — of registered and likely voters said they "strongly disapprove" of the job Trump is doing, tied with last month as the highest ever in the poll.
Trump's favorability rating is even lower — just 37% of likely voters have a favorable impression of Trump, while 59% have a negative one.
Democrats also had a strong advantage on which party's candidate people said they are more likely to vote for in their district if the election were held today, known as the generic congressional ballot. Among registered voters, it was a 10-point advantage. With likely voters, it was 8 points, still indicative of Democratic gains.
When Democrats have had that kind of lead on the congressional ballot, they have historically done very well. On average, it was +7 in 2018 and +12 in 2006. In both years, Democrats won the House with at least 30 seats flipped.
But that was before the 2020 Census and ensuing regular redistricting — and the rare, mid-decade redistricting in the last year and a half after Trump asked Republican states to redraw their maps to potentially give Republicans more seats. Though Democrats followed suit, both redistricting periods have tilted congressional seats in Republicans' direction and given them a relative advantage nationally.
Perhaps because of some of those structural disadvantages and past performance, there is a notable degree of nervousness among Democrats.
While 98% of Democratic likely voters said they would vote for a Democrat, just 81% thought the Democrat would win, a 17-point difference. Republicans were only 10 points less likely to believe their candidate would win. Notably, among independents, a higher share thought the Democratic candidate would win.
Working in Democrats' favor — and against incumbents: 55% of likely voters said it's more important in this election to vote for candidates with new ideas who will bring about change. (It was a tick higher with registered voters at 57%.)
Chris Agan, a 43-year-old Democrat in Tyler, Texas, who participated in the survey, never saw himself as an impassioned midterm voter, until this year.
"This year is different. This year, it feels like every opportunity to vote is a referendum against the party in power," said Agan, who's backing Democrat James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton in the race for U.S. Senate.
"We've been seeing a very slow decline in the standard of living in this state, and it's becoming apparently evident to more people at this time," he added. "I think Talarico embodies that realization that there needs to be change."
Double the percentage of likely voters also said their vote would be one against Trump (44%) as opposed to one for him (21%). In the 2024 presidential election, 55% of those who voted for Trump said their vote was for their candidate, according to exit polls .
Trump is not on the ballot, but he has asked voters to "pretend" he is.
Though Trump's unpopularity poses challenges for Republicans, it may not directly translate to more votes for Democrats. Some swing voters don't like the lurch in some corners of the Democratic Party toward democratic socialism.
Matthew Schroder is a 38-year-old independent living in Charlotte, N.C., who was part of the poll. He backed Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2024. Now, he says that while he's unhappy with Trump's job performance, it isn't what's driving his vote this year.
"What I have seen on the left-hand side is a little bit more of an embrace of democratic socialism, which I just oppose completely," said Schroder, who's supporting Republican Michael Whatley over Democrat Roy Cooper in the state's closely watched race for U.S. Senate.
"I know Roy Cooper is considered a moderate, but the fact that the Democratic Party is even letting some of these voices be heard a little bit more … is not something I'm interested in in the least," he added. "It's not a vote of 'yes for Trump' as much as a vote of, Democrats need to completely reject [democratic socialism] and go a completely different direction."
Democratic likely voters are 10 points more likely to say they are "very enthusiastic" about voting (71% vs. 61%). That's actually wider than the difference between Democratic and Republican registered voters in the poll.
The caution for Democrats, though, is that several of their key pillar groups are not very enthusiastic to vote, and Republicans have closed the gap on who is following the election "very closely."
Just 42% of likely voters under 45, 53% of non-white voters and 56% of white women with college degrees said they are "very enthusiastic" to vote. All of those groups disapproved of the job Trump is doing.
Compare that to pro-Trump groups — MAGA voters (68%), white women without degrees (66%) and white evangelical voters (61%).
For independents, 48% report being very enthusiastic to vote.
Traditionally, younger, as well as Black and Latino voters turn out at disproportionately lower rates in midterm elections. But with the realignment under Trump, more white, college-educated voters are voting Democratic and, as a group, they turn out at the highest rates.
When it comes to paying close attention, last month just 34% of registered Republicans said they're following the election very closely, compared to 42% of Democrats.
Now, they're even – 46% of Democrats and 45% of Republicans said they're paying very close attention. When it comes to likely voters, there's no difference either – 51% of Democrats to 50% of Republicans.
On the positive side for Democrats: those who voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 are 15 points more likely than Trump 2024 voters to say they are very enthusiastic. And Democrats overall have an 8-point advantage over Republicans when it comes to who cares a "great deal" about who controls Congress.
Three-quarters of likely voters are confident that their state and local governments will run a fair and accurate election.
That includes solid majorities of Democrats (88%), Republicans (68%) and independents (75%), but Republicans were 20 points less likely than Democrats to think they would be run well. MAGA supporters were almost 30 points less likely.
Large majorities also said their preferred candidate should accept the results of the election. That included 70% of Republicans, but again, they were 20 points less likely than Democrats to say they should accept the results. A quarter of Republicans said their candidate should probably or definitely challenge the results.
There was also a sharp divide between those who identified as democratic socialists and MAGA supporters — 86% of democratic socialists but only 65% of MAGA supporters said their preferred candidate should accept the result. MAGA supporters were twice as likely to say they should challenge.
Methodology: This NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll was conducted from Oct. 19-20 and surveyed a national sample of 1,289 registered voters. They were reached through a multi-mode design: by phone, text or online. To create a likely voter sample, Marist applied a likely voter weight to all registered voters. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points. That means results fall within a range of roughly eight points – about four points lower or higher.
A previous version of a chart in this story incorrectly said that one of the possible responses to a question was "government is almost always wasteful and efficient." The possible response was "government is almost always wasteful and inefficient."
