title: Havelsan expanding partnership with Nigeria
body:
With an eye on building upon its existing partnerships with Nigeria, the Turkish Armed Forces Foundation company Havelsan is at Afridex 2026 this week.
Şevket Ünal, Havelsan Vice President for International Business Development and Marketing, is scheduled to address the panel ‘From Partnership to Production – Advancing Türkiye–Nigeria Defence Industry Cooperation’ on Wednesday, 28 October, at 09:45.
“Havelsan is here at Afridex 2026 to meet military delegations, government representatives and industry partners to discuss operational requirements and opportunities for cooperation across Nigeria and Africa,” the company said in a statement. “Our expertise spans command and control, simulation and training, autonomous unmanned systems, information and communication technologies, and cybersecurity.”
Established in 1982, Havelsan develops software-intensive technologies for defence, public institutions and the private sector. A central capability is the integration of platforms, sensors and systems from different suppliers, helping customers to build on existing investments.
Havelsan’s relationship with Nigeria includes exports of the company’s ADVENT Combat Management System (CMS), developed in conjunction with the Turkish Navy, which supports coordinated operations across different domains. It connects multiple platforms through a common operational picture, rather than serving as a combat management system for a single ship.
“This system was developed to meet the evolving requirements of customers and effectively address the challenges of modern naval operations. ADVENT CMS is a unique and pioneering solution that addresses the demands of force-oriented, network-centric naval operations, as opposed to traditional single ship-centric approaches,” STM said.
Importantly, its scalable architecture accommodates different platform sizes and operational requirements, while integrated tactical data links support information sharing and coordination during joint missions. The ADVENT CMS has been fitted to the two 76 metre offshore patrol vessels built by Turkish shipyard Dearsan for the Nigerian Navy. Havelsan also supplied its GVDS ship data distribution system for these vessels.
Havelsan also provided the BAHA autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and shooting simulators to Nigeria, having delivered two 10-lane shooting simulator systems to the Nigerian Army and BAHA UAVs as part of a border security initiative.
The company designates it ‘Digital Troops’, the portfolio that includes the BAHA autonomous UAV, BARKAN unmanned ground vehicle and SANCAR armed unmanned surface vehicle. These platforms support missions across air, land and maritime environments, including reconnaissance, surveillance and protection. Their autonomy and integration capabilities support coordinated operations involving manned and unmanned assets.
While the Digital Troops concept brings together autonomous and mission-management capabilities to support unmanned aerial, ground and maritime platforms operating together, Havelsan’s training portfolio covers shooting, sniper, tank, armoured vehicle, parachute and urban operations training, alongside electronic warfare test and training ranges and wargaming solutions.
The company has also provided Nigeria with simulation and training solutions. Its Shooting Simulator enables individual and team exercises using realistic scenarios that provide repeatable weapons training in a controlled environment without live ammunition.
“Integrated border security is a key focus for discussions in Nigeria,” Havelsan said. “Our Integrated Border Security System uses DOOB command-and-control capabilities to provide a comprehensive operational picture. Our critical facility security solutions address the protection of infrastructure such as oil and gas pipelines and related facilities.”
The DOOB joint command and control system integrates information from UAVs, sensors, cameras, and communication devices, offering a real-time overview of the border area. It empowers border security forces to make informed decisions and take timely actions.
Whilst this software enables Havelsan to combine surveillance, detection and response coordination in support of border protection and critical infrastructure security, its wider digital portfolio includes biometric identification, smart city applications, digital transformation and cybersecurity solutions.
Havelsan’s MATRA digital maritime solution supports coastal surveillance, vessel traffic management and port management. By combining information from radar, Automatic Identification Systems, cameras and other sources, it provides a real-time view of vessel movements. Tracking, identification and decision-support capabilities help maritime authorities monitor their areas of responsibility and identify potential risks.
In essence, Havelsan’s extensive portfolio supports coordination across land, maritime and air operations. Its Nigeria partnerships provide a foundation for further cooperation in naval operations, reconnaissance and surveillance, and personnel training. “Discussions with local industry will also explore joint production, technology sharing and long-term support arrangements tailored to customer requirements,” Havelsan concluded.
More Afridex news can be found in the show daily magazine here .

title: Kacha, Mastercard Ink Deal to Expand Card Issuance in Ethiopia
body: Kacha Digital Financial Service SC has signed a landmark five-year agreement with Mastercard to issue payment cards directly to its customers and enable card-issuing services for eligible financial institutions across Ethiopia. Under the partnership, Kacha will offer card issuance capabilities to banks, microfinance institutions, and fintech companies, pending regulatory approvals and individual program arrangements. This agreement builds upon recent strides in Ethiopia’s cross-border payment landscape. In February 2024, Awash Bank partnered with Mastercard Payment Gateway Services (MPGS) to launch international physical and virtual prepaid cards for e-commerce. This was followed in March 2025 by the state-owned Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE), which similarly introduced Mastercard-enabled physical and virtual payment cards to broaden cross-border access. While those initial rollouts were driven by individual banks, Kacha’s new agreement uniquely positions it as an enabler for other financial institutions seeking to offer card services, alongside serving its own customer base. “The agreement expands our service offerings and strengthens our capacity to serve both customers and partner institutions,” said Abreham Tilahun, CEO of Kacha. As Ethiopia’s first privately owned payment instrument issuer licensed by the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE), Kacha announced it will immediately begin engaging financial institutions interested in leveraging its card-issuance platform. The partnership arrives amid broader modernization efforts within Ethiopia’s national payment infrastructure. EthSwitch, the country’s national payment switch, continues to drive interoperability among participating systems. Its National Payment Gateway—designed to connect various payment channels and facilitate seamless online transactions—was launched in July 2023 and successfully completed its pilot phase in November of that year.

title: The hidden GOP fundraising weakness is getting worse
body: Republicans’ small-dollar donor base has contracted in recent years, leaving the party more dependent on a tiny group of wealthy megadonors for support. The GOP has had a cash advantage all year thanks to a relatively small group of large donors who have funded super PACs — Elon Musk alone has given nearly half a billion dollars this cycle. But the campaigns themselves have raised relatively little, and there’s one major reason: Other than President Donald Trump, who is still the party’s biggest fundraiser, Republicans still haven’t figured out how to raise money online. New campaign finance filings reveal just how deep the problem goes. While Republicans have long struggled to grow their grassroots donor base, they’ve moved in the wrong direction in recent years. The number of federal donors giving through WinRed, the major GOP online fundraising platform, is down, with roughly 1.5 million donors so far this cycle compared to 2.2 million at this time in 2022. Meanwhile the number of donors has increased by about one third on ActBlue, from 4.9 million to roughly 6.6 million. The contrast is stark: A single Democratic candidate, James Talarico in Texas, has had roughly the same number of donors on ActBlue this cycle as all Republican candidates and committees combined had on WinRed, according to a POLITICO analysis of reports ActBlue and WinRed submitted to the Federal Election Commission. Republican digital strategists who have been sounding the alarm for years say lagging donations are a product of fatigue, driven by years of urgent messages to the same set of potential donors. “We beat the absolute hell out of low-dollar donors with texts and emails without expanding our [donor lists], and now no one pays attention,” said Wesley Donehue, a South Carolina-based GOP digital strategist. Republicans’ online fundraising struggles have put their House and Senate candidates at a particular disadvantage, as candidates — unlike super PACs — face strict contribution limits and need a far larger pool of donors from which to raise money. Poor candidate fundraising has major campaign implications: Democrats’ cash advantage on that front has helped them run nearly as many ads as Republicans despite having less money overall, because candidates and parties get better rates than super PACs on broadcast TV. Democrats’ grassroots fundraising strength is in part because of how decentralized the party is, with individual campaigns and groups building their own donor lists and fundraising operations. Virtually all of the the top Democratic fundraisers online this year are Senate candidates in competitive races. But Republicans’ online fundraising, like so much of the party, is still centered around Trump and the official party committees. Unlike on the Democratic side, few individual Republicans have managed to break out. Republicans’ fundraising troubles have left them more reliant on Trump: The president’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., is among the biggest midterm spenders . The group and its affiliates have now spent $296 million — after facing pressure for much of the cycle from some in the GOP who wished it would have gotten involved sooner . “Candidates are not investing the time and resources in programs that grow the donor lists and attract their supporters into the ecosystem. Instead, they just barrage previous donors with ongoing requests for donation,” said Eric Wilson, a longtime Republican digital strategist and executive director of the Center for Campaign Innovation. “Credit to the Trump team — they brought new people into the ecosystem, and those people continue to give to them.” Trump has continued to fundraise since returning to the White House, including through his Never Surrender leadership PAC, which was formed out of his 2024 campaign committee, and two joint fundraising committees from his previous presidential runs. Of the nearly 1.5 million donors who have given on WinRed this cycle, 324,000 of them — a bit over 22% — have given only to Trump’s groups through the platform but not any other candidate or committee, POLITICO’s analysis found. Another 39% of WinRed donors have given to both Trump and another Republican. Overall, that means about 3 in 5 WinRed donors this cycle have given to Trump, when he is neither on the ballot nor able to run for president again. That’s left non-Trump GOP donors in the clear minority just as the party begins to look for a new standard bearer ahead of 2028. WinRed isn’t the only online GOP fundraising platform, but it is by far the largest and features all of the major party committees along with prominent House and Senate candidates across the map. Its FEC reports include only federal candidates and committees, not those in state-level races or nonprofits that use the platform. Republicans once saw their online fundraising disadvantages as a matter of technology. ActBlue, which has been around since the 2000s, gave Democrats a major fundraising advantage in the late 2010s, at a time when Republicans had no similar centralized platform. WinRed, which launched in 2019, aimed to counter that. Now strategists say the GOP’s infrastructure has come a long way, but the party’s tactics still lag behind. Democratic candidates eyeing higher office often maintain large fundraising operations, which they can use to raise money on behalf of candidates in battleground races while also building their own lists. Among the top 20 ActBlue fundraisers this cycle are former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg’s leadership PAC and Sen. Mark Kelly’s (D-Ariz.) campaign committee. Kelly leveraged GOP attacks on his military service earlier this cycle to boost both his own fundraising and help Democrats across the map . Wilson, the GOP strategist, credited out-of-cycle Democrats for building strong lists that they could use to shore up other candidates. The Republican side, he said, lacks similar coordination. “Any time a Democrat announces they're running for reelection, that week every Democrat in the Senate is sending a message to their list raising money for that person,” he said. About the analysis: Donation totals and number of donors are based on ActBlue and WinRed receipts from all reports this cycle, covering Jan. 1, 2025, through Oct. 14, 2026. Donations that were later refunded are still included. POLITICO’s analysis identifies unique donors based on matching full names and zip codes.

title: Zelenskyy: injured in Kyiv's Desnianskyi district rises to 12, Russia fires 16 ballistic missiles overnight
body:
The number of people injured due to a Russian strike on the evening of October 26 on the area around Kyoto Park and Lisova metro station in Kyiv's Desniansky district has risen to 12 people, five of whom are students and staff of the State University of Trade and Economics, reported President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"The number of injured following the Russian strike on the university campus and surrounding area yesterday evening has risen to 12, five of them being university students and staff," Zelenskyy wrote on his Telegram channel on Tuesday.
According to him, while emergency services were helping people and eliminating the consequences of the first strike, the Russians used ballistics again.
"In total, there were 16 ballistic missiles overnight. Plus more than 280 drones. Unfortunately, there are casualties, there were hits in Kyiv, particularly on the Pivdenny Bridge. A serious escalation in the Russian operation against our logistics. There were also strikes in Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhia, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, Kherson, and Chernivtsi regions. Almost everywhere, Russian targets are energy, logistics, and ordinary urban infrastructure," Zelenskyy said.
The President of Ukraine emphasized that "artificial and prolonged delays in the supply of interceptor packages for 'Patriots' and 'NASAMS', which unfortunately have occurred recently, directly help Russia achieve the goals of its terror campaign. Every such delay means a new Russian hit on one facility or another."
As Zelenskyy noted, "unfortunately, strikes occur every day. Russia constantly takes new escalatory steps. Pressure on Russia and real support for Ukraine are needed for the situation to change. Thank you to everyone who truly supports our defense of life and understands the value of support packages arriving on time. We must bring peace closer and save lives."

title: 28,000 teachers’ promotion arrears may require supplementary funding – Haruna Iddrisu
body: The government may consider a supplementary allocation to pay the outstanding promotion salary arrears of about 28,000 teachers and other staff whose claims have not yet been validated. Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu said the government was considering the option alongside fresh processing of the claims, with the aim of paying the affected staff by mid-November or the end of November. “What is outstanding is around twenty-eight thousand, which includes some non-teachers, who may not be able to get those payments beginning tomorrow (October 28) because (their) validation process has not been completed,” he said on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Tuesday, October 27. “We cannot delay payment of salary across the country to validate them, so we may require a supplementary midway in November or just do it by the end of November,” he added. Mr Iddrisu said the government had paid the promotion salary arrears of 52,000 teachers who successfully completed the validation process, out of approximately 80,000 people seeking payment. He said his office would meet teacher union leaders by the close of Tuesday to discuss the outstanding payments and agree on the way forward. The minister urged the affected teachers not to resume their strike, assuring them that the government was working to address their concerns. The possible supplementary allocation is one of the options being considered to facilitate payment to those whose claims remain outstanding, while the government also considers reprocessing their claims to meet the proposed timeline. The development follows the suspension of industrial action by teachers over delays in paying their promotion salary arrears.

title: French students vow more protests despite concessions from Macron government
body: French student ⁠leaders vowed to carry out further protests despite government concessions on education, keeping pressure on ⁠ President Emmanuel Macron as the movement spreads to unions and other activists, ​stokes unrest and increases the economic damage. The government measures included a commitment to cap the size of some high school classes, €4 billion ($4.5 billion) of loans ⁠for renovating schools and the replacement by 2028 of a university admissions system that students consider socially unfair. Speaking to broadcaster France 2 on Tuesday, Louis Letoublon, a representative of high school pupils, said protest leaders were unsatisfied with proposals made by government officials at a meeting in Paris. "If we don’t see concrete changes in the lives of high school students, we will call for mobilisation. We are expecting new proposals from the government," Mr Letoublon said. In another proposal aimed at quelling the protests, Philippe Baptiste , Minister of Higher Education, vowed that the university admissions system would become "more transparent". Students have expressed frustration about failing to obtain a university spot, with little explanation on the platform. 'Right to study' Asked whether he expected further sit-in protests in schools and universities on Monday, Mr Baptiste said: "I also believe there is a right to study." "What I want now is for everyone to get back to work," he added. The protests, which have broadened beyond education to draw in trade unions and so-called yellow vest ​activists, known ⁠for their high-visibility jackets, pose a test for Mr Macron's ‌minority government. The government has little room to spend its way out of the unrest, with national debt approaching 120 per cent of GDP, while ​the turmoil has boosted support for far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen before next year's presidential election. The package of concessions also included €1 billion of investment in university campuses, a move to increase student grants with inflation and the opening of a further 15,000 higher education places. "It's clear we have to ease the pressure being felt in the education system," Education Minister Edouard Geffray said. There was no overall figure announced for how much funding the package would require. High borrowing needs are already complicating efforts to agree on a budget for next year. The protests, initially caused by student discontent, have shown little sign of ending, after violence nine days ago engulfed dozens of cities in France, leading to fears the state had lost control of the streets. Earlier, Mr Macron acknowledged it was probable that there would be more unrest this weekend, before a nationwide day of demonstrations on November 5. During a tour to survey the damage in Marseille and to thank emergency services after protests on Saturday, he said he would keep security measures in place and work to move demonstrations outside city centres. Ms Le Pen has benefitted from the unrest and perceptions that authorities are struggling to keep ‌the peace. An opinion poll published on Sunday put ⁠her at 32 per cent to 33.5 per cent, well ahead of her nearest rival, ​hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who was on 17 per cent. Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Mr Melenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to ​be held in early ‌May. Confrontations Interior Minister Laurent Nunez earlier said that 1,435 people were arrested across the country during demonstrations on Saturday. He added that police also ⁠reported a new phenomenon, with organised far-right gangs confronting far-left activists in several cities. "We knew there had been calls from ⁠numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out, officially, to defend businesses," he said. "In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organised formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement." A sell-off in French government bonds was paused on Monday after rating agency Moody's on Friday refrained from downgrading the country's sovereign debt. But business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage. Alain Di ​Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers remained closed as a precaution after the violence of October 17, leading to a sharp drop in sales. "We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralised, and we are killing local commerce," he told Radio Classique. Agencies contributed to this report

title: Police Pulling People over Because AI Deems Their Driving Patterns Suspicious
body:
In September 2025, Grace Knowles, a 20-something from northern Virginia, was between jobs and decided to take a road trip. Her trip included driving through Oregon, Texas, and Louisiana. On her way to Florida, she was pulled over by a police officer and had an encounter that a growing number of Americans can expect to experience if the use of AI by law enforcement is allowed to grow. Grace (who has never shared her story publicly until now) told me,
I’d left New Orleans that morning, and I noticed there was a cop car behind me at some point. I know I was going a normal speed, but he pulled me over anyway. And he made up some excuse — that I’d been in the left lane too long.
He started asking me what I was doing, where I was coming from and going. “I’m just a girl doing a road trip,” I said, and told him I’d come from New Orleans. Then he started asking for proof that I’d been there. I showed him a pamphlet from a whiskey museum I’d visited and said “here’s my proof.” Then he got more relaxed, and told me, “I just had to be sure because I’m not a regular cop, I’m part of the FBI, and when I scanned your plate I could see you had suspicious travel patterns,” I think is how he worded it.
The real reason the officer had pulled Knowles over was because some surveillance system he was using had access to automated license plate reader (ALPR) data on where she’d been driving, and had decided that her travel pattern was “suspicious.” In a particularly spooky detail, Knowles told me that “he said he thought I was lying about being in New Orleans because he didn’t show any hits there.”
I was shaken up. He could tell that maybe I didn’t believe him, so he actually invited me to come into his car, so he could show me what he was seeing — showing me everywhere I’d been. I still don’t know why he invited me to see it. But it was cool because I could see the software that he pulled up . It was basically a heat map of the US, and I could see different circles where I’d been, and when he clicked on it, it was a photo of my license plate.
He definitely said he was FBI. Not initially — he waited. He said he was a special agent. I don’t know if he said he was contracted for this project — investigating people for human trafficking or drug trafficking. He was telling me stories of people he and his team had caught carrying large sums of money.
I asked him “how are you even seeing my license plates,” and he said, “Well they’re just everywhere.” He said they’re in the road signs on top of highways — they’re often on the back of those, and people don’t even see them.
The growth of AI license plate surveillance from Flock and other companies means that more and more innocent people may be stopped in this way — though most probably won’t get a demonstration from an officer as to what is going on.
I first noticed Flock touting their ability to use AI algorithms in this way in July 2025. The company boasted that it could not only alert law enforcement of drivers whose travel patterns were “suspicious,” but also track people’s associations by analyzing which vehicles were frequently seen with other vehicles. As I explained at the time, this represented a significant leap from using ALPR data to investigate suspicious vehicles to generating suspicion where none previously existed. A year later, Wired obtained detailed files describing Flock’s next-generation AI system , already in use by some police, which revealed the capability for wide-ranging, open-ended AI queries of license plate data — and not only license plate readings, but also a variety of other data including arrest records, case files, and databases from the shady commercial data broker industry, which are packed with personal information on nearly all of us.
It’s now become clear that this approach to law enforcement is spreading and that Knowles’s experience is part of a larger trend. Stories from across the country are emerging of police using “pretextual stops” to pull people over based on analysis of where they’ve been. In a pretextual stop, someone is pulled over for a claimed, often invented minor infraction (such as drifting out of a lane or failing to use a turn signal) as cover for the real reason, which might be unconstitutional or which they otherwise want to hide. Police even have names for these abusive detentions, which they call “whisper stops” or “intel stops.”
Even before license plate readers and AI, pretext stops were unfortunately quite common as a police strategy, which is why the ACLU has fought to ban them for years. But what we’re seeing now is an enormous departure from how police have always operated — police can now use technology to track all of us all the time, then rely on AI to churn through the resulting oceans of data to suggest suspects, who are then detained under false pretenses. This approach to law enforcement means that:
The seductive yet deeply problematic ability of AI to suggest suspects for law enforcement is yet another reason to put a stop to license plate surveillance, location tracking of any kind, and mass surveillance in general.

title: NCDC: 2027 elections may be postponed if Ebola spreads
body: The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has said the 2027 general election could be postponed if the Ebola outbreak in the country spreads to a level that makes such a decision necessary to protect public health. Dr Jide Idris, Director-General of the NCDC, stated this during an interview on Channels Television. According to him, the severity and geographical spread of the outbreak would determine whether postponing the election should be considered. Idris, however, stressed that there was currently no reason to contemplate such a move, expressing optimism that the outbreak would be contained without disrupting the electoral timetable. “We hope the election will not be postponed, but if the thing (Ebola) gets wide enough, that might be considered. As of now, there is no need for that,” he said. The 2027 general election is expected to begin in January, with political parties and aspirants already making preparations ahead of the polls. The NCDC chief’s remarks come amid concerns about the potential implications of the Ebola outbreak for public gatherings and other activities that could increase the risk of disease transmission if the situation deteriorates. He maintained that any decision to postpone the election would be guided by public health considerations rather than political interests. Addressing suggestions that the government might exploit the outbreak for political purposes, Idris insisted that health officials had no intention of using disease outbreaks as a political instrument. “We in the health sector will not use disease issues as a political weapon. No government will use Ebola as a political weapon,” he said. The NCDC director-general explained that Nigeria had been closely monitoring developments in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where the outbreak originated, and had anticipated the possibility of the virus reaching the country. According to him, population movements, international air travel and activities at the country’s ports of entry were among the factors that made the possibility of importing the disease a concern for public health authorities. He said surveillance efforts had been informed by the developments in the DRC, although the possibility of the virus reaching Nigeria could not be completely ruled out. “This Ebola thing started in DRC a couple of months ago and we were tracking. They said for you to track again there is a possibility that it may get here due to our population movement, flight into this country, and ports of entry, yet it came. No government will use Ebola as a political weapon,” he said.

title: Over 250 participants from eight countries to practice Mars space mission at Skolkovo
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. More than 250 students and young faculty members from eight countries will conduct an autonomous space mission at newly built Martian research stations as part of the first International Space Games, being held at the Skolkovo Innovation Center, the Skolkovo Foundation’s press service reported.
“Skolkovo was established specifically to support innovative projects, including those in education and workforce training, so the choice of venue for the first International Space Games was deliberate. For over 15 years, an environment has been taking shape here where universities, startups, and technology companies work alongside one another. <…> If new solutions and projects result from these Games, we are ready to support them.
Our space technology cluster already comprises more than 50 companies, and new teams will have partners to work with here,” Natalia Kravchenko, advisor to the chairman of the Skolkovo Foundation’s board, noted.
The first expedition will start on October 27, and the Space Games will end on November 1. Teams from Russia, Pakistan, Mexico, and Uzbekistan will spend 48 hours working completely autonomously while tackling engineering and technological challenges. Participants from China, India, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan will then resume the mission. The main objective of the competition is to ensure the continuous functioning of an autonomous settlement on another planet through collaborative efforts.
The Games are being held under the Talent for Space federal project. The Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics is the event’s organizer, while the Skolkovo Foundation serves as the partner and host. The Russian Science and Higher Education Ministry and Roscosmos are coordinating the Games.

title: AI slop is the new TLDR
body:
It is hard to get through a day online at the moment without someone dismissing something as "AI slop". A pull request, a library, a whole project, all written off with two words. When the thing being dismissed is code, I have started to notice that the label usually arrives well before anyone could have actually read the code in question.
That has led me to a slightly uncomfortable conclusion. In a lot of cases, calling AI generated code slop is just a new way of saying TLDR (too long, didn't read). It isn't really a measure of whether the code is good or bad. It says more about the willingness of the person saying it to sit down and learn what the code does.
There is even slang emerging for the general version of this. Posts that are obviously AI generated are now getting the response AI;DR , as in "AI, didn't read". At least that is honest about what is going on. Slop dresses the same reaction up as a judgement of quality.
I should say up front that some AI generated code really is slop. Open source maintainers in particular are being buried under pull requests and bug reports where the person submitting them clearly has no idea what they are submitting. Generating that stuff costs the submitter almost nothing, while reviewing it costs the maintainer real time, and that imbalance is a legitimate thing to be angry about.
Look closely at those cases though and the failure is the same one. The person who generated the code didn't read it either. They asked for something, got something back, and passed it on without understanding it. So the TLDR problem exists on both sides. There is the person who produces code without reading it, and there is the person who dismisses code without reading it. Neither has actually engaged with what is in front of them.
One working definition I came across describes slop as code you can't work with , that is, a codebase that nobody understands well enough to work with effectively. I think that is about right, but notice what the definition hinges on. It is about understanding, and understanding is not purely a property of the code. It also depends on whether anyone has put in the effort to acquire it.
A simple test I now apply to myself is to ask whether I would have said the same thing if a new colleague had written the code. If the answer is that I would have sat down, read through it, and given proper feedback, then reaching for "slop" instead is a sign I am taking a shortcut.
So why would people take that shortcut? I don't think it is simply laziness, or at least not only laziness. I think it is fatigue, and it is worth being honest about where that fatigue comes from.
Think back to the first few weeks of starting at a new organisation. You arrive and there is an existing body of software that you didn't write and don't understand. Before you can do anything meaningful you have to learn what it does, then how it does it, and then why it was built that way. It is a steep learning curve for anything you didn't already know, and it is mentally exhausting. Most people I know come home from their first week in a new job completely wiped out.
Working with AI generated code can feel a lot like that, except it doesn't stop after a few weeks. Every day there is another pile of code you didn't write, built on decisions you didn't personally make. In some respects every day becomes your first day.
It has always been harder to read code than to write it. When you write code yourself, the understanding builds up as you go, almost as a side effect. When you read someone else's code, you have to reconstruct that understanding after the fact, from whatever clues they left behind. With AI doing much of the writing, more of the job has shifted to the harder of those two activities.
There is also an old observation from the study of automation that applies here. When you automate the routine part of a job, the human is left with the part that is harder, which is monitoring what the automation is doing and stepping in when it goes wrong. And because the human is no longer doing the routine work, the hands-on skill needed to step in can quietly fade away. Supervising an AI that writes code is a textbook case of this.
The gap that builds up has been given a name, comprehension debt , meaning the growing difference between how much code exists in a system and how much of it any human actually understands. Like any debt it accumulates quietly, until the day something breaks and nobody knows where to start.
Faced with all that, it is much easier to throw your hands up and declare the whole thing slop than to admit that you can't keep up, or that you haven't been willing to put in the time to learn it properly. I get the temptation. I just don't think it is an honest answer.
What all this points to is that what it means to be a software developer has changed. The term that seems to be sticking for the new way of working is agentic engineering , the idea being that you are mostly no longer writing the code directly, but orchestrating AI agents that do, and providing the oversight.
The analogy I keep coming back to is a conductor of an orchestra. A conductor isn't playing every instrument, but no one would suggest a conductor can get away without a deep grounding in music theory. They have to read the full score, know what each instrument is capable of, hear when a section is out of tune, and know how to fix it. For a developer working with AI, the equivalent of music theory is the fundamentals of software development, architecture and design. You may not be writing every line, but you still need to know what good looks like and recognise when something is wrong.
The analogy does break down in one telling way though. A real orchestra rehearses the same piece over and over before a performance, and the conductor builds up an intimate knowledge of it. With AI the orchestra is effectively playing a new piece every day, with no rehearsal. Which brings us right back to the onboarding problem.
It is also worth noting that reviewing and steering code you didn't write was always part of the job of a senior or lead engineer. People generally grew into that role over many years. What has changed is that everyone is now being put in that position, from day one, often without the experience to back it up. That raises an awkward question about how people new to the industry are meant to learn the music theory if they never get to play an instrument.
I don't want to give the impression I am lecturing from on high here. I now lean on AI quite heavily for some new projects, and I struggle to keep up with the constant flow of new code and new information as much as anyone.
I have tried different approaches. For a while I used Obsidian as a knowledge base, a sort of second brain, to track design decisions and how things fitted together. For some projects that worked well. For others I got so deep into the design, and then into directing the AI to write the code, that going back to get it all into Obsidian felt like more work than it was worth. The end result was that I was back to flying by the seat of my pants and trying to keep it all in my head.
Looking back, I think the reason it failed is that the note taking was a separate chore. Anything that sits outside the actual work is the first thing to get dropped when you are in the flow of things. Whatever approach works has to be a by-product of something you would be doing anyway.
The approach that has worked best for me so far, at least for projects that I expect other people to use, is to have the AI generate workshops.
The process goes something like this. I have the AI build the software, and keep directing it until what it has produced matches the idea I had in my head. At that point I have it generate a set of hands-on workshops teaching how to use it, which run on my Educates training platform or in the JupyterLab workshop extension I wrote. Then I sit down and work through those workshops myself.
In other words, I deliberately put myself through the new employee onboarding. Rather than trying to absorb the code in bits and pieces as it flies past, I get a structured path through what the software does and how to use it, at a pace where I can actually take it in.
What I didn't expect was how good this is at exposing problems. When you work through a workshop as a user, you very quickly see where the design falls short, where the experience is clumsy, or where things just don't work. The AI also contributes here. If, when generating the workshop, I tell it to highlight problems, it will report when it couldn't get something to work, when it ran into what looks like a bug, or when the documentation doesn't match what the code actually does. So the AI generating the workshop is acting as a QA and user experience tester, and so am I when I work through it.
Because the workshops are interactive and the steps are actually executed, they also behave a bit like tests. If a step in the workshop fails, that is a real problem with the software, not just a typo in some documentation nobody will read.
And then there is the secondary benefit, which is that the workshops exist afterwards for other people. A number of them are available in the workshops area of this site. My hope is that they can also encourage people to get past the mental block of TLDR, or AI slop, or whatever they want to call it, and be prepared to sit down and learn something properly. That seems more important than ever at a time when most people will feel it is easier to just ask an AI to do it for them.
I still don't have a workflow I would call good for using AI and keeping on top of what it is doing. I regard myself as fairly conservative when it comes to tools. I don't go chasing every new fad, because to be frank that usually ends up being a complete waste of time. I suspect most people are similar, and adapting is a slow, incremental process of personal experimentation to see what works for them.
The AI tools themselves, including the tooling from the AI vendors, have certainly made it easier to do a lot of this without reaching for other tools. It is still a matter of finding what works for you, though, and right now things are moving too quickly for anything to settle.
One principle I am trying to hold myself to in the meantime is to not let the AI get too far ahead of my own understanding. A new employee is given time to ramp up, and nobody expects them to be onboarding forever. If the code is arriving faster than I can understand it, the answer is to slow down and make time to learn it, not to stop reading and call it slop.
Hopefully one day I will have it sorted out. Fingers crossed.

title: Ngiwal youth softball team rebounds with doubleheader sweep at UN Day Games
body: By: Laurel Marewibuel AIRAI, Palau (October 25, 2026) — Ngiwal’s 14-and-under youth softball team overcame a Saturday loss to close the United Nations Day Games, sponsored by Ngermid Empowered, with two decisive victories, keeping its championship hopes alive at Yelch Baseball Field. The Ngiwal Kidz opened the weekend tournament Friday with a victory over Ngaraard. The team returned Saturday to face Airai, but dropped a hard-fought game in one of the tournament’s toughest matchups. Rather than let the loss end its momentum, Ngiwal held a team meeting Sunday morning to refocus. The adjustment paid off quickly. In the 10 a.m. opener, Ngiwal defeated Melekeok 13-2. The team then carried its momentum into the second game of the doubleheader, beating Ngerchemai 15-6 to finish the weekend on a strong note. The victories showcased the young squad’s resilience, discipline and ability to recover under pressure. Coaches, families and supporters accompanied the players throughout the three-day tournament, which featured youth teams from across Palau. “These games give our kids better options than staying home, stuck to their phones. The games are not only great exercise but also give them opportunity to network with their peers and build good relationships,” said a young mom from Ngermid who was watching and cheering with many parents from Koror and Babeldaob states. The championship games were rescheduled for November because of upcoming community events. Ngiwal, Melekeok and Ngeremlengui are among the teams expected to travel to Peleliu State from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1 for the Palau Evangelical Church Youth Conference. The youth teams participating in the UN Day Baseball Tournaments include teams from Ngerchemai, Ngaraard, Melekeok, Ngeremlengui, Ngiwal, and Airai. The tournament has 2 divisions: ages 7-13 and ages 14-16. The 7-13 division has 6 teams, and the 14-16 division has 4 teams. Ngermid Youth Empowered, a Ngermid youth group and sponsor of the UN Day Baseball Games for youths, was formed to increase youth participation in positive, drug-free community activities. Ngermid Youth Empowered organized these events through a grant from the 2026 Palau-Taiwan Small Grants Program. title: US midterms: Five issues shaping the vote
body: Americans voting in the November 3 midterm elections will decide who controls Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency, along with dozens of governorships and thousands of state offices. The campaign is playing out against an unusually combustible mix of economic anxiety, war, immigration battles, corruption concerns and unease over rapidly expanding artificial intelligence. Polls asking voters about priorities use different methodologies, but they broadly agree on the dominance of pocketbook concerns. An October Pew survey found economic issues easily topped voters’ worries, while a September Emerson poll put the Iran war, jobs, tariffs, gas prices, immigration and AI regulation among the most important factors in voting decisions. Here are five issues shaping the midterms: – It’s the economy – Affordability remains issue number one. Inflation was running at 3.7 percent in September, but the political problem goes beyond the headline rate, with voters paying more for gasoline, housing, electricity, groceries and borrowing. Pew found that 65 percent of Americans see Trump’s economic policies as hurtful to the economy. Another survey, from the Joseph Rainey Center for Public Policy, found 57 percent placing groceries, gas or utilities among their top three issues. Trump’s tariffs feed directly into the debate, with opponents blaming them for higher costs while the administration argues they protect American industry and raise revenue. – Iran war – A foreign war has become a domestic pocketbook issue. The conflict with Iran, underway since February, has driven energy costs higher and become deeply unpopular. Emerson’s September survey rated the Iran war the single most important issue among those it tested, while Reuters/Ipsos found only 34 percent approving of Trump’s handling of the conflict. Republican candidates in several competitive races have called for the fighting to end, and four Republican senators joined Democrats in a September vote seeking to rein it in. – Immigration – The strength of Trump’s signature political talking point has become more complicated. The president returned to office promising mass deportations, but support has eroded following controversy over deaths during arrests and detention, and aggressive ICE operations. Reuters/Ipsos found 55 percent disapproved of Trump’s handling of immigration. Marist, meanwhile, found Democrats and Republicans essentially level on which party voters trusted more on the issue — a striking change from the clear Republican advantage of 2024. The shift is particularly notable among Latinos. A survey across competitive House districts found 62 percent of Latino voters disapproved of the administration’s deportation and immigration enforcement. – Trump, money and power – The president himself is an issue — including how he uses the office. Trump has explicitly asked voters to behave as though he were on the ballot, making the election partly a referendum on his second term. Government ethics ranked second behind the economy in Pew’s open-ended survey, cited by nine percent of voters. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll found 97 percent of Americans believed there was at least some corruption in the federal government. And 66 percent said they had little or no trust in Trump to avoid using the presidency to benefit his family’s businesses. Democrats have promised investigations of Trump family business dealings if they win congressional subpoena power, although Republicans dismiss many such allegations as partisan attacks. – AI comes to town – Artificial intelligence has jumped out of the laptop and onto the campaign trail. Voters worry about job losses, safety and regulation — but increasingly also about the giant data centers needed to power AI. Half of Americans told Pew they were very concerned about AI’s role in the economy, while 59 percent said they disliked political leaders supporting data centers in the respondents’ localities. AI regulation scored surprisingly highly in Emerson’s September survey, just behind immigration and gas prices. Data centers themselves ranked lower nationally, but have become major campaign issues in states including Ohio as communities battle over electricity, water and construction. Congress even spent some of its final pre-election days arguing over who should pay the electricity costs created by them — proof that, in 2026, even the server farm has become political. – Other fault lines – Not every familiar American culture-war issue has dominated the 2026 campaign, but several remain potent dividing lines. Transgender rights continue to produce fierce arguments over participation in women’s sports. Health care is also a perennial election concern, encompassing the cost of insurance and medicines, and access to coverage. These issues have not necessarily driven the national midterm campaign as strongly as affordability, Iran or immigration, but they remain powerful mobilizers for parts of both parties’ coalitions. The post US midterms: Five issues shaping the vote appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Diwali 2026: When is the Festival of Lights and how is it celebrated?
body: Diwali or Deepawali is one of the biggest festivals in South Asia. In countries such as India and Nepal, where the festival of lights is a major holiday, many splash out on big purchases such as jewellery, televisions, cars and property. Some even choose to take possession of new homes at this time. Symbolising the triumph of good over evil and light over darkness, Diwali usually falls in early autumn, coinciding with the new moon, deemed the darkest night of the Hindu lunar calendar. This is why the dates of the festival change every year. This year, celebrations begin with Dhanteras on November 6, with main Diwali falling on November 8. While for many, Diwali honours the Hindu goddess of wealth Lakshmi, with lights and lamps said to welcome her and bring prosperity, for others it celebrates the return of Hindu deity Ram to Ayodhya, having rescued his wife Sita from the clutches of the mythological demon king Ravana. How is Diwali celebrated? Predominantly a Hindu festival, other faiths including Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists also celebrate Diwali. As such, it has become a celebration of positivity and hope, and one that fosters unity and spreads joy among different communities and countries including the UAE (see below for events). On the first day of celebrations, called Dhanteras, Hindus clean their homes and workplaces, symbolising renewal. Diyas or earthen lamps filled with oil are lit for the next five days and homes are decorated with lights and lanterns. Many consider the day auspicious to make major purchases, from cars to gadgets. Jewellery, especially gold to appease goddess Lakshmi, is often bought, with jewellery shops in India and the UAE usually enjoying massive surges in sales on the day. Doorways and entrances to workplaces are also decorated with rangoli, colourful designs made from flower petals, coloured rice or sand, which is meant to attract good luck. On the second day, called chhoti or small Diwali, a variety of Indian sweets are made at home or bought and then exchanged along with gifts among friends and family. The third or main day of Diwali is when those celebrating wear new clothes or their best outfits and light fireworks, although this practice has ebbed over the years as people become more environmentally conscious. Parties and special events are held across communities to mark new beginnings, with “Happy Diwali” being the most common greeting. The fourth day is mostly ritualistic, with many celebrations coinciding with the end of the harvest season. The last day of the festival is called Bhai Dooj, or brothers' day, and marks the bond between sisters and brothers. Similar to Raksha Bandhan , where sisters tie symbolic charms around their brothers' wrists to ward off evil, during Bhai Dooj, brothers often travel to meet their sisters. On this day, sisters feed their brothers with their hands and receive gifts in return. What is the commercial significance of Diwali? Workers often receive bonuses and special gifts ahead of Diwali while sales of gold coins and bars, purchased as investments, surge. In India, the world's biggest gold consumer after China, Diwali is traditionally the time when people buy the most gold as it is considered auspicious. This year, Dubai Festivals and Retail Establishment has launched a Diwali special where shoppers can win gold coins when they shop at any participating malls in the city until October 28. Diwali in the UAE In the UAE, where Indians constitute the largest part of the population, Diwali is celebrated lavishly, with many neighbourhoods lit up for the festival. Dubai Festivals and Retail Establishment will host several events to mark the occasion. Shops and restaurants are also offering special deals and promotions. Here are some ways to celebrate. Global Village, Dubai Global Village will mark the occasion from November 6 to 10 with five days of cultural performances, family activities, shopping and entertainment. A highlight will be a themed drone show on November 8 at 8pm, when 600 drones will light up the sky above the Stunt Arena and Syria Pavilion with formations inspired by the Festival of Lights. The celebrations begin on November 6 with a traditional South Asian musical gathering known as a baithak, taking place on the Main Stage from 8pm to 9pm. Visitors can sing along and interact with performers, while November 7 will feature games and opportunities to win prizes. A festive mela, organised in collaboration with the India Pavilion, will offer traditional decorations, gifts, snacks and sweets. Children can also take part in face painting, diya colouring and rangoli-making activities. Food options include Indian Chef, Grand Dhaba and the Indian Chaat Bazaar, serving dishes such as pani puri, pav bhaji, chole bhature and traditional mithai. All activities are included in the Global Village admission ticket, with prices starting at Dh25. Baps Hindu Mandir, Abu Dhabi Baps Hindu Mandir in Abu Dhabi will mark Diwali from November 6 to 10 with five days of religious ceremonies, cultural performances and family activities. The programme includes traditional pujas and Maha Annakut Darshan, a display of vegetarian food offerings to the deities to mark the Hindu New Year. Visitors can also enjoy cultural performances and other festive experiences. The temple will open specially on Monday, November 9, when it is normally closed. Those unable to attend in person can watch the Dhanteras Pujan ceremony online on November 6 at 8.30pm. Entry is free, but visitors must register in advance online or the Mandir Abu Dhabi app. Walk-ins are not permitted, and visitors must bring a valid Emirates ID or passport. Separate charges may apply for participating in specific religious ceremonies. Noor: Festival of Lights at Al Seef Dubai's Al Seef waterfront will once again host Noor: Festival of Lights on November 7 and 8, with a programme of live music, dance performances and colourful processions. Each evening will begin with a procession of illuminated puppets and traditional dhol drummers winding through the streets, followed by Bollywood dance performances and live music. On November 7, performers will include Ashu Ali and Saif Hayat from indie band The Shams, alongside Punjabi singer Jasbir Jassi. The following evening, live band Jammers and singer-songwriter Sooraj Santhosh will take to the stage. The free event takes place at Souk Al Seef, against the backdrop of Dubai Creek, with festivities running from 6pm to 11pm. Khushiyon Se Bhari Diwali at BurJuman Mall BurJuman Mall is hosting Khushiyon Se Bhari Diwali, a celebration running until November 12. The programme includes festive workshops, musical baithaks – intimate gatherings featuring traditional music – and activities inspired by the Festival of Lights. The mall is also offering opportunities for families and shoppers to take part in the celebrations, with free workshops among the activities. Haldiram's festive hampers Indian sweets brand Haldiram's has launched a gifting collection featuring traditional mithai, savoury snacks, dry fruits and nuts. The range includes boxes of Amritsari Pinni, Kaju Laddoo, Badam Burfi and Motichoor Laddoo, with assorted mithai boxes priced from Dh25 to Dh72. Sweet platters cost between Dh35 and Dh199, while dry fruit and nut gifts range from Dh75 to Dh150. Premium hampers combining sweets, nuts and savoury treats start at Dh110, with customisable gifting options also available on pre-order. The collection is available at Haldiram's branches in Karama, Sheikh Zayed Road and Dubai Silicon Oasis. title: FACT CHECK: No Evidence Tinubu Executed ₦9trn Projects In Kano as Pakistan Claimed
body: Former Chairman of the National Hajj Commission of Nigeria (NAHCON), Professor Abdullahi Saleh Pakistan, says President Bola Tinubu deserves a second term because of projects executed by his administration and what he described as improvement in security. Pakistan made the remarks in a recent interview with DCL Hausa, claiming that the Federal Government had executed projects worth more than ₦9 trillion in Kano State. He made claim to the provision of solar power systems to Northwest University, Kano, which he said cost ₦6 billion, and another solar power system for Radio Kano, which he claimed cost ₦2 billion. He also said that the federal government provided the solar power systems despite Northwest University being owned by the Kano State Government. He said he would continue to support Tinubu’s administration because he believed the president had demonstrated the capacity to govern and deserved another term to complete projects initiated by his government. Pakistan also cited the Kaduna-Abuja highway, saying travellers had faced serious security challenges along the route in the past but that the situation had improved under Tinubu. However, a review by Daily Trust Check of publicly available information, including the GovSpend platform, found no evidence to substantiate the claim that the Tinubu administration had executed projects worth ₦9 trillion in Kano State. The review also found no publicly available reports confirming the commissioning or inauguration of the specific solar power projects Pakistan cited at the stated costs. What we found The Federal Government, through the Tertiary Education Trust Fund (TETFund), earmarked ₦70 billion for a mini-grid solar power project in selected tertiary institutions across the country. President Tinubu approved the project under TETFund’s 2025 intervention cycle. Speaking at TETFund’s first town hall meeting, the Chairman of its Board of Trustees, Aminu Bello Masari, said the initiative would provide renewable and sustainable energy to 12 selected institutions. The institutions include Northwest University, Kano; Nigerian Army University, Biu, Borno State; Ambrose Alli University, Edo State; Alvan Ikoku University of Education, Owerri, Imo State; and Lagos State University. Masari said the project was part of the president’s efforts to address persistent electricity supply challenges affecting teaching, research and innovation in tertiary institutions. He said: “Mr. President is committed to solving the problem of erratic power supply, which remains one of the most critical constraints to teaching, research, and innovation. Therefore, the President approved the implementation of the Mini-Grid Solar Power Project under the 2025 Intervention Cycle, with an allocation of ₦70 billion.” Although the TETFund initiative confirms plans for a solar power project at Northwest University, Kano, the information reviewed does not establish that the institution received a solar power system costing ₦6 billion, as claimed by Pakistan. Similarly, the review found no evidence to confirm his claim that the Federal Government provided a solar power system for Radio Kano at a cost of ₦2 billion. The ₦70 billion allocation covers a solar power initiative involving 12 institutions nationwide. It does not, by itself, substantiate the specific costs Pakistan attributed to the projects in Kano. The review also found no evidence establishing that the Federal Government had executed projects worth more than ₦9 trillion in the state. The absence of publicly available records does not conclusively prove that no such projects exist. However, the claim remains unsupported by the evidence reviewed. Verdict: Unverified. Daily Trust Check found no verifiable evidence to substantiate the claim that President Tinubu’s administration had executed projects worth ₦9 trillion in Kano State. While a Federal Government-backed solar power initiative involving Northwest University, Kano, has been announced, the available information does not confirm the specific project costs cited by Pakistan or establish the broader ₦9 trillion claim.

title: At sea, detecting a drone is only the beginning of the fight
body:
In this guest article, P J Wills, RN (Retd.), outlines how modern threats pose naval command and control challenges.
On October 13, 2026, two commercial vessels, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship HS Dignity and the Ukrainian-owned, Maltese-flagged freighter Chelsea 3, were struck by drones off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast. Bulgarian authorities are investigating the origins of the drones. It is too early to draw conclusions about how the incidents might have been prevented, but they illustrate a challenge facing naval forces across Europe: detecting a potential threat is only the first step. The harder task is understanding what it means and co-ordinating a response in time.
For a navy operating in increasingly contested waters, that distinction matters. A radar track, an intelligence report and a sighting from a nearby vessel may each tell part of the story. The operational challenge is bringing those fragments together quickly enough for commanders to make an informed decision.
This is becoming more difficult as drones, uncrewed surface vessels and other relatively inexpensive systems complicate the maritime threat picture. Naval forces must distinguish potentially hostile activity from legitimate shipping, account for incomplete information and make decisions under pressure. They must do so while protecting their own ships, supporting other forces and maintaining awareness of what is happening across a much wider area.
The answer cannot simply be to buy more sensors or deploy more counter-drone weapons. These capabilities are essential, but their effectiveness depends on how well they work together. Consider a potential drone threat approaching a naval installation or a vessel operating near a busy shipping route. One sensor detects an object, another provides a different track, and intelligence may offer context about activity elsewhere. An individual report might not appear particularly significant. Combined with other information, it could demand immediate attention.
The challenge is not just to display more information on a screen. It is to establish a sufficiently clear picture of events, assess the significance of what is being observed and get the relevant information in a timely way to the people responsible for deciding what happens next.
This is the role of command and control (C2). It connects information, people and capabilities so that commanders can understand a situation, co-ordinate their forces and direct an appropriate response.For naval operations, the implications extend beyond the ship itself. A commanding officer may need to understand what is happening locally while contributing to a wider picture shared with headquarters, other naval units and allied forces. Information that remains isolated within individual platforms or systems can limit the ability to co-ordinate a response across that force.
Interoperability is therefore an operational requirement, not simply a technical specification. NATO allies will continue to operate equipment from different suppliers and national programmes. They do not need identical systems, but they do need to exchange relevant information and establish a shared understanding of events.
That capability must be tested under realistic conditions. It is one thing for two systems to exchange data in a demonstration. It is another for information to remain useful when communications are disrupted or degraded, the operating picture changes rapidly or a commander must make a decision with incomplete evidence.
For disaggregated naval forces operating across dispersed maritime areas, resilience matters as much as connectivity. Systems must support decision-making when information is delayed, links are degraded or units cannot maintain continuous communications. A shared picture is valuable, but commanders must also understand its limitations and retain the ability to act when connections fail.
Artificial intelligence offers ways to help manage the volume of information confronting military personnel. It can support the analysis of historical and near-real-time data, identify patterns and flag anomalies that warrant further investigation. In counter-drone operations, that could help personnel assess activity across multiple sites and sources rather than examining each observation in isolation. But an anomaly is not proof of hostile intent. The value of AI depends on the quality of the information available, the context in which it is assessed and the ability of personnel to interpret the result. AI cannot resolve gaps in information it cannot access. Nor can it compensate for systems that do not share data effectively. Introducing an advanced analytical tool into a fragmented command environment risks adding another layer of complexity rather than improving decisions.
The priority should be to establish the information and command foundations on which these tools depend. That means connecting relevant sources, making information accessible to the right people and ensuring that the resulting picture supports operational decisions.
It also means being clear about the limits of the technology. In a maritime environment, misidentifying a threat or acting on an incomplete picture can have serious consequences. AI should help personnel focus their attention and assess evidence, not turn an uncertain observation into an unquestioned conclusion.
There are signs that European defence procurement is beginning to address this problem. Last week, Denmark’s Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation awarded Systematic a contract to provide an AI-ready command-and-control capability for the country’s counter-drone defence. The programme will connect Systematic’s SitaWare software with existing counter-drone systems across Denmark. SitaWare Headquarters will provide oversight of activity across sites and military domains, while SitaWare Insight will support the analysis of historical and near-real-time data to identify patterns, anomalies and potential threats.
The contract is significant because it focuses on the relationship between existing systems, the information they generate and the people who need to interpret it. Rather than treating counter-drone defence solely as a question of individual sensors or effectors, it addresses the command layer needed to bring information together.
It is the first known contract awarded by a NATO member for a command-and-control capability designed to integrate AI-supported analysis. The programme is at an early stage, however, and its operational impact remains to be demonstrated. It is an example of an approach, not evidence that the wider problem has been solved.
For the UK, this is not simply a question of improving today’s counter-drone defences. The Royal Navy’s future operating environment will increasingly involve crewed and uncrewed platforms working together, dispersed forces sharing information across domains, and commanders making decisions when communications are denied, disrupted or intermittent.
That requires command-and-control software built for these conditions: interoperable with NATO allies, able to integrate different systems and resilient enough to support decision-making when connectivity cannot be guaranteed. The objective is not to create a single, uninterrupted picture of everything happening everywhere, but to ensure commanders have the information they need to act, even when the operating environment is working against them.
Naval power depends on more than the capabilities deployed at sea. It depends on how effectively those capabilities work together. As European navies invest in new sensors, uncrewed systems and AI, they must give equal attention to the command-and-control layer that connects them. Detecting a threat may provide the warning. Turning that warning into a timely, co-ordinated response is what makes it count.

title: FlyArystan Launches Astana-Yining Route, Becomes Xinjiang’s Largest Foreign Airline
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s FlyArystan has launched direct flights between Astana and Yining on Oct. 26, becoming the largest foreign airline operating in China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, Kazinform reported. Photo credit: FlyArystan An Airbus A320 operated flight FS 7989, which departed Astana International Airport at 7:55 a.m. The flight took two hours and 25 minutes. Upon arrival in Yining, the aircraft received a traditional water cannon salute. Regular direct flights on the new route operate three times a week, on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays. FlyArystan President Johan Eidhagen said demand for direct flights to Xinjiang was growing among business travelers, trading companies and tourists discovering the region. “Today, the Kazakh airline has become the largest foreign carrier in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region of China, and we are proud of this,” he said, adding that the airline intends to expand its presence in the region and open new routes. FlyArystan operates four direct routes between Kazakhstan and Xinjiang, connecting Almaty, Astana and Aktau with Urumqi and Yining. The new route comes as Kazakhstan continues to expand its international air connectivity. Air Astana plans to launch seasonal direct flights between Almaty and Malaysia’s Langkawi on Dec. 25, as well as flights between Astana and Bangkok on Dec. 11. Both routes are expected to strengthen tourism and business links. Kazakhstan is also preparing for a possible direct route between Astana and New York in 2027. The launch will depend on the completion of a U.S. aviation safety assessment, the readiness of Air Astana’s Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner aircraft and the required training hours for flight crews and technical staff. The post FlyArystan Launches Astana-Yining Route, Becomes Xinjiang’s Largest Foreign Airline appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Three killed, eight injured in Russian attacks on Kharkiv Region over past day
body:
According to Ukrinform, the head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, Oleh Syniehubov, reported this on Facebook.
In Kharkiv, two men aged 41 and 60 were killed. A 60-year-old woman and a 77-year-old man were injured, while a 61-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl suffered acute stress reactions.
In Shevchenkove, a 74-year-old woman was killed, while a 74-year-old man suffered an acute stress reaction.
In Vilshany, part of the Solonytsivka community, two men, both aged 58, were injured, while a 77-year-old woman suffered an acute stress reaction.
A 43-year-old man was injured when an unidentified device exploded in a forest near the village of Kutuzivka in the Vilkhivka community.
Russian forces attacked Kharkiv’s Shevchenkivskyi, Slobidskyi, Kholodnohirskyi, and Novobavarskyi districts using UAVs and multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS). They also shelled other parts of the region with MLRS and launched one guided glide bomb, four Geran-2 UAVs, three FPV drones, and 111 UAVs whose types are being identified.
In Kharkiv, four apartment buildings, a childcare facility, three businesses, 12 vehicles, an administrative building, and 20 garages were damaged.
In Izium district, warehouses were damaged in Barvinkove, two private houses in the villages of Pisky-Radkivski and Borshchivka, and an administrative building in Izium.
In Kupiansk district, a two-story building, power lines, and a vehicle were damaged in Shevchenkove.
In Kharkiv district, a garage was damaged in Cherkaska Lozova, a vehicle in Dementiivka, a post office and a vehicle in Mala Danylivka, a private house in Bezruky, and a civilian enterprise and private houses in Vilshany.
In Lozova district, a private house was damaged in Myroliubivka, while retail pavilions were damaged in Lozova.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russian forces struck Kharkiv’s Novobavarskyi district on the evening of October 26, killing two people and injuring four.

title: Katsina govt says it invested over ₦4bn in youth craft village as 1,662 trainees graduate
body:
The Katsina State Government says it has invested more than ₦4 billion to renovate and equip its Youth Craft Village, where 1,662 trainees graduated on Monday.
However, the government did not provide a breakdown of the expenditure in its announcement.
Governor Dikko Radda disclosed the investment at the institution’s second graduation ceremony at Muhammadu Dikko Stadium, Katsina, where the graduates received start-up equipment to establish businesses.
The number of graduates rose from 648 at the maiden ceremony to 1,662, an increase of about 156 per cent. However, the government did not indicate how many of the previous graduates had established businesses or were still practising their trades.
In a statement by his Chief Press Secretary, Ibrahim Kaula Mohammed, Mr Radda said the investment covered renovations, facility upgrades and the purchase of modern machines and tools.
The statement did not specify the period covered by the expenditure, the amounts spent on individual projects or the value of the equipment distributed to the graduates.
Mr Radda said the beneficiaries were trained in more than 15 trades, including tailoring, welding and fabrication, carpentry, electrical installation, information and communication technology, catering, cosmetology, plumbing and automobile repairs.
“We do not believe in simply issuing certificates and sending our graduates home without the means to put their training into practice. That is why we are providing them with start-up tools and equipment to enable them to establish their businesses,” he said.
The governor urged the graduates not to sell the equipment, saying they should use it to start businesses and employ others.
He also announced plans to establish additional vocational training centres across the state’s 34 local government areas to train more than 5,000 young people before the end of his administration.
Mr Radda said the government has established an innovation hub and an innovation desk at the craft village.
He further disclosed that the Katsina State Enterprise Development Agency had supported more than 60,000 beneficiaries through various enterprise development programmes, although the statement did not specify the period covered or provide details of the assistance.
Former Governor Ibrahim Shema, who established the Katsina Youth Craft Village during his administration, said the institution was originally intended to equip young people, particularly those from rural communities, with practical skills.
He said the village had attracted trainees from other parts of Nigeria and neighbouring Niger Republic.
Mr Shema also recalled meeting a former trainee who became a head of department in the Federal Capital Territory Administration.
The institution’s coordinator, Kabir Soro, attributed the increase in graduate numbers to the state government’s expansion of the facility.
Also speaking, the Executive Secretary of the National Board for Technical Education, Idris Bugaje, urged other states to establish similar vocational training programmes, including through community and Islamic schools.

title: Ceasefire takes effect in Russian-occupied Oleshky amid humanitarian catastrophe
body: The truce that Russia and Ukraine agreed to for the evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid has begun in Oleshky, in the Kherson region. Both sides confirmed the truce had taken effect. The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said Ukraine introduced the truce in Oleshky at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time (4:00 a.m. Moscow time) to carry out a humanitarian operation. “The truce is being established […] to deliver aid to residents currently in the city and to prepare for the free movement of civilians out of Oleshky,” the statement said. The Russian Defense Ministry said Russian forces ceased fire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time. Residents of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, have lived under Russian occupation since 2022. The situation there has approached a humanitarian catastrophe since the fall of 2026. Constant drone attacks have left residents without food, electricity, or adequate medical care. They cannot safely leave the city and sometimes cannot even bury their dead relatives. The White House announced October 23 that Russia and Ukraine would temporarily halt hostilities in Oleshky to allow residents to leave the city. U.S. First Lady Melania Trump reportedly helped broker the ceasefire agreement. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom.
