title: Dubai Investments seeks to raise $543m from first UAE IPO this year
body: Dubai Investments , a Dubai-listed conglomerate, is seeking to raise Dh2 billion ($543 million) from the 20 per cent sale of its subsidiary DIP Holding in the UAE’s first initial public offering this year. DIP Holding is selling 1.74 billion shares in the Dh1.10 to Dh1.15 per share range, implying a market capitalisation at listing of between Dh9.5 billion and Dh10 billion, the company said in a statement on the Dubai Financial Market on Tuesday. Subscription to offered shares opened on Tuesday and will run until November 3. The company will announce the final pricing for the deal on November 4 through the book building process. The selling shareholder, Dubai Investments, “reserves the right to amend the offering size prior to the end of the subscription period”, the offer document said. Shares of DIP Holding, which operates the mixed-used master development Dubai Investments Park, are expected to start trading on the DFM on November 11. Breaking the lull The deal breaks the lull in the IPO market in the UAE. The Arab world’s second-largest economy was a hotbed for public floats, with the DFM and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange both attracting a steady stream of IPOs over the past few years. The IPO market in the broader Middle East slowed last year, owing to volatility in oil prices and geopolitical unrest. Companies in the region raised $7.1 billion from 61 listings, down from $13 billion a year earlier. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows. The Iran war, which has severely disrupted economic momentum in region, has further dented investor sentiment, forcing companies in the region to hold plans for tapping the equities markets to raise capital. The DIP Holding offering will be a test for investor appetite for new listings, some of which recorded weaker post-listing performance in the past two years. Situated near Al Maktoum International Airport and Jebel Ali Port, Dubai Investments Park is home to 1,000 tenants, 5,700 subtenants and more than 150,000 residents. The district was established in 1997 and hosts warehouses, hotels, retail outlets, schools and medical centres, making it one of the largest mixed-use developments in the emirate. Dividends DIP Holding intends to adopt a semi-annual cash dividend distribution policy. It expects to pay annualised cash dividends of Dh700 million, Dh725 million and Dh750 million for the financial years ending December 2026, 2027 and 2028, respectively. The first post-IPO dividend distribution of Dh350 million, for the full second half of 2026, is expected to be paid in April 2027. “Eligible shareholders will benefit from a dividend relating to the full H2 2026 period, rather than only the period following admission,” the company said. Based on the expected annual dividend of Dh725 million for 2027, the IPO price range implies a dividend yield of about 7.27 per cent at the high end and 7.60 per cent at the low end of the range, it added.

title: Nigeria Could Be Declared Ebola-Free By December — FG
body: If no further confirmed or probable cases are detected and the country meets the conditions stipulated by the World Health Organisation (WHO), the Federal Government has said Nigeria could declare the Ebola outbreak over as early as December 7, 2026. The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, disclosed this on Monday evening in a post on his X handle. He, however, noted that the date would depend on the outcome of contact monitoring and validation of the required 42-day countdown by the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) and the WHO. “If no further confirmed or probable cases are detected, Nigeria could progress towards declaring this outbreak over under WHO criteria, potentially as early as 7 December 2026,” he wrote. Kenya Red Cross personnel doff their Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) during a simulation of the evacuation of remains of an Ebola victim in the Kenyan capital Nairobi on October 22, 2026(Photo by TONY KARUMBA / AFP) Pate, however, stressed that the proposed date was provisional and could change if another case was detected. “This date remains provisional, subject to @NCDCgov and WHO validating the 42-day countdown. Any further case would require a fresh countdown in accordance with those criteria,” he said. The Federal Government confirmed the Ebola case in the FCT on October 20. The patient, according to WHO, recently travelled from Uganda, developed symptoms on October 7 and sought medical attention on October 11 before her infection was confirmed. The NCDC, on Sunday, said it is monitoring 53 primary contacts linked to Nigeria’s confirmed Ebola case. Under the WHO’s criteria, an outbreak can be declared over after 42 consecutive days without a new confirmed case, provided the required conditions for ending transmission are met. The minister said the government’s immediate priority was to monitor identified contacts and strengthen preparedness across health facilities to prevent further transmission. The development follows the medical evacuation of a female Ebola patient and her husband to Switzerland on Monday. The minister said the patient was clinically much improved, stable, conscious and communicating, with her laboratory test results approaching baseline levels. This combo photo shows NCDC officials on duty in Nigeria, and response team members helping to wear protective suits before burying a person suspected of having died from Ebola in Bunia, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, on May 25, 2026. (Channels TV/GLODY MURHABAZI / AFP) In a statement on Monday, the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) said the patient was receiving treatment at Geneva University Hospital (HUG), while her husband, identified as a close contact, had been placed in isolation at Zurich University Hospital (USZ). The Swiss authorities said the case poses no health risk to the country, adding that both hospitals were equipped to manage patients with infectious diseases such as Ebola while protecting healthcare workers and other patients. They added that the facilities have specialised isolation wards and trained medical personnel to manage such infections. “The current situation does not pose any risk to public health in Switzerland,” the FOPH said. According to the statement, the FOPH said it was working closely with the university hospitals in Geneva and Zurich, as well as the relevant cantonal authorities, to manage the situation. Elisabeth Baume-Schneider, Switzerland’s federal councillor, expressed appreciation to Nigeria’s Minister of Health during a telephone conversation. Baume-Schneider thanked the doctors and other healthcare professionals in Nigeria for caring for the two Swiss nationals before their evacuation. The post Nigeria Could Be Declared Ebola-Free By December — FG appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Israeli forces close all entry points to Ramallah in WB
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 27 (MNA) – Israeli forces have closed all entry points to the city of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.
Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that Israeli troops have also set up checkpoints on alternative routes used by residents.
The Israeli forces closed the Ein Siniya and Atara checkpoints, as well as the Rawabi gate north of Ramallah, along with the Nabi Saleh and Aboud gates to the northwest, local sources told Wafa.
A checkpoint was also set up near the Ministry of Education district on the al-Bireh-Jalazone road, while another was erected on the road connecting the village of Yabroud with the town of Silwad, northeast of Ramallah.

title: Putin is taking over Africa. Russia offers missiles, drones and military protection
body:
Russia is preparing another diplomatic and military offensive in Africa. On 28–29 October, Moscow will host the third Russia–Africa Summit, which, together with its accompanying forum, is expected to bring together more than 2,000 participants. This time, the Kremlin is preparing concrete proposals covering air defence, counter-drone systems, military cooperation, nuclear energy and cybersecurity. Despite its war against Ukraine, Russia continues to expand its influence across the African continent. Importantly, Moscow is increasingly combining arms exports with the presence of Russian military personnel and long-term security agreements.
Following the summits in Sochi in 2019 and St Petersburg in 2023, Vladimir Putin will once again welcome African delegations. According to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, most countries have already confirmed their participation. On 28 October, Sergei Lavrov will meet African foreign ministers, while the following day Putin is expected to co-chair the plenary session alongside Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye, the current Chairperson of the African Union. However, the most important discussions will take place during bilateral meetings, where Moscow intends to negotiate further military, energy and economic agreements.
One of the most interesting announcements is Rosoboronexport’s planned presentation of its new Anti-Drone Dome system, designed to protect military facilities, critical infrastructure, transport convoys and government buildings against unmanned aerial vehicles. The solution is intended to integrate radar systems, electronic warfare capabilities, automated command and control, and counter-drone weapons. Russia plans to offer African countries systems including the Pantsir-S1M, Pantsir-SMD-E and Verba man-portable air defence systems, alongside other technologies developed by the Russian defence industry.
This is particularly interesting because many African countries are struggling with terrorism, the activities of armed and rebel groups, and the increasingly frequent use of drones by terrorist organisations. Russia intends to draw on its experience from the war against Ukraine to promote its military technologies. However, it should be remembered that the effectiveness of Russian weaponry remains a subject of debate, particularly given Moscow’s difficulties in protecting its own military bases and energy infrastructure against Ukrainian attacks.
On the other hand, the Kremlin understands very well that African governments need weapons, training, military advisers and solutions that can be deployed relatively quickly. Moreover, if Europe or the United States are unwilling to sell arms to African countries, Russia or Turkey will step in.
The nature of Russia’s military presence in Africa is also changing. Operations previously conducted by the Wagner Group are gradually being taken over by Africa Corps, which is controlled by the Russian Ministry of Defence . Russian military personnel remain present in countries including Mali, Libya and the Central African Republic, providing training, operational support and protection for local authorities.
By March 2026, Russia had concluded nearly 60 military cooperation agreements covering 39 African countries. Between 2020 and 2025, Russian warships made more than 65 port visits to at least 18 African countries. This demonstrates that Russia’s military activities now extend far beyond the Sahel.
Military cooperation is only one part of Russia’s offer. Rosatom has announced that it will be the summit’s title sponsor and plans to sign new documents concerning cooperation in nuclear energy. Moscow is promoting nuclear power plants, floating nuclear reactors and long-term technological cooperation. Such agreements could make African partners dependent on Russia for decades , as they involve not only the construction of infrastructure but also nuclear fuel supplies, specialist training, maintenance and technical support. For the Kremlin, this represents another means of building lasting political and economic influence. After all, Russia is already building a nuclear power plant in Egypt.
The summit’s official programme also includes cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and so-called digital sovereignty. Particularly interesting is a session organised with the participation of Rosoboronexport, focusing on protecting state institutions, countering “colour revolutions” and controlling national information environments.
Russia is offering not only weapons to protect borders and military infrastructure, but also technologies that enable governments to control the flow of information and monitor their populations. For some African governments, including authoritarian ones, this may be an attractive proposition, although it also raises serious concerns about political surveillance – particularly regarding what Russian intelligence services might be able to monitor and control.
Europe, however, possesses far greater economic potential. Trade in goods between the EU and Africa reached almost €355 billion in 2024, while the Global Gateway Africa–Europe Investment Package aims to mobilise up to €150 billion. The seventh European Union–African Union Summit also took place in November 2025. The problem, therefore, is not Europe’s lack of presence in Africa, but its effectiveness in translating economic cooperation into political influence and security partnerships. Russia has considerably fewer financial resources, but concentrates its efforts on selected countries, particularly in the Sahel, military institutions and sectors where it can build long-term relationships.
The third Russia–Africa Summit will not determine the future of the entire continent. African countries have different interests and are developing cooperation not only with Moscow, but also with Beijing, Washington and Europe. Nevertheless, Russia is once again demonstrating that it understands the importance of regular political engagement. Arms deliveries can lead to further training programmes, military advisers can facilitate negotiations over access to bases, and nuclear projects create technological dependencies lasting decades.
Europe will not limit Russian influence in Africa through statements and criticism of the Kremlin alone. It needs competitive offers of military cooperation, training, investment and a direct, regular political presence. What is missing here is Ukraine’s response to this Russian offensive. Moscow is not waiting for the war in Ukraine to end before strengthening its position in Africa. Why should Europe wait?

title: Ghana faces possible US$50 million default judgment at ECOWAS Court over alleged human rights violations
body: The Republic of Ghana faces a possible default judgment at the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice in Abuja, Nigeria, following its alleged failure to file a defence in a US$50 million human rights lawsuit brought by Singaporean businessman and investor, Toh You Kang. The businessman, through his lawyer, Cephas Boyuo, Esq., is seeking the cedi equivalent of US$50 million in compensatory damages over alleged violations of his fundamental human rights, including unlawful arrest and detention, denial of fair hearing, infringement of his freedom of movement, and failure by state institutions to protect his rights. The case arises from a series of events involving Mr You Kang, Emmanuel Nii Ashie Moore, the Greater Accra Regional Chairman of the ruling National Democratic Congress (NDC), and some officers of the Ghana Police Service. According to the originating application filed before the ECOWAS Court, Mr You Kang travelled to Ghana in May 2025 to resolve outstanding business and financial matters arising from transactions involving Mr Moore. Alleged business transactions and financial dispute Court documents indicate that Mr You Kang, an investor and shareholder in Ghanaian-registered NSG Innovation Limited, was introduced to Mr Moore, who allegedly presented himself as a politically connected businessman capable of facilitating government-related business opportunities in Ghana. The applicant alleges that, relying on these representations, he transferred US$100,000 and later provided an additional US$700,000 in connection with purported contracts to supply electrical cables to the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG). He further claims to have supplied approximately US$1.5 million worth of campaign paraphernalia for the 2024 general elections. According to the application, disagreements subsequently arose over the transactions, prompting Mr You Kang to travel to Ghana in May 2025 to seek a resolution. However, what was intended to be a business engagement allegedly took a dramatic turn when he was taken to a private residence, where armed men led by Mr Emmanuel Ashie Moore allegedly demanded US$3 million from him. Mr You Kang alleges that when he refused, he was assaulted before being handed over to the Ghana Police Service, which subsequently arrested and prosecuted him on a charge of defrauding by false pretences. High Court quashes criminal proceedings The applicant contends that the criminal proceedings instituted against him were unlawful because the alleged transactions forming the basis of the charges allegedly occurred outside Ghana. He maintains that the Dansoman Circuit Court lacked jurisdiction to entertain the matter. Following his arraignment on May 30, 2025, the Circuit Court remanded him into custody. He subsequently obtained bail from the High Court but remained subject to restrictions on his movement. On September 4, 2025, the High Court granted an application for certiorari, quashing the proceedings before the Circuit Court and prohibiting that court from continuing with the criminal case. The High Court also made consequential orders concerning personal belongings allegedly retained following his arrest. Mr You Kang argues that the circumstances surrounding his arrest, detention and prosecution constituted violations of his rights guaranteed under international human rights instruments. Allegations against Police and Immigration authorities Beyond the criminal proceedings, Mr You Kang accuses certain officers of the Ghana Police Service of failing to act on complaints he lodged against Mr Moore concerning alleged assault, threats and the retention of his personal property. His application references a report by the Police Professional and Standards Bureau (PPSB), which he contends supports aspects of his allegations concerning the conduct of police officers involved in the matter. He further alleges irregularities in the handling of his travel documents upon his arrival at Kotoka International Airport. According to the court documents, his passport was taken by Mr Ashie Moore without him going through arrival formalities by the Immigration Service of Ghana, and it was subsequently discovered that the document did not bear the required Ghanaian entry stamp. The applicant says correspondence from the Ghana Immigration Service acknowledged the irregularity and sought to rectify it at a time he had already undergone the bad treatment of alleged unlawful detention in Ghana. Mr You Kang eventually departed Ghana for Singapore on September 12, 2025. Ghana allegedly fails to defend US$50 million suit Mr You Kang, acting through his lawyer, Cephas Boyuo, Esq., has filed an application requesting the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice to enter judgment by default against the Republic of Ghana. The application, filed in December 2025, is grounded on Ghana’s alleged failure to respond to the substantive human rights action despite having been duly served. According to an affidavit supporting the application, the originating processes were electronically served on November 13, 2025, on the Attorney-General, Deputy Attorney-General, Solicitor-General and other authorised legal officers of the Republic. The applicant maintains that Ghana failed to file a defence within the period prescribed by the Rules of the ECOWAS Court. The lawyer, Cephas Boyuo, relies on Article 35 of the Court’s Rules of Procedure, which provides for the filing of a defence within 30 days of service. He also invokes Article 90(1), which permits an applicant to seek judgment by default where a respondent, having been duly served, fails to lodge a defence within the prescribed period. The application accordingly invites the Court to enter judgment against Ghana and grant the substantive reliefs sought by Mr You Kang. These include declarations that Ghana violated his fundamental human rights and an order directing the Republic to pay the cedi equivalent of US$50 million in compensatory damages, together with legal costs and fees. Press of ECOWAS Court for hearing date Meanwhile, Mr You Kang’s lawyer, Cephas Boyuo, has formally written to the Registry of the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice requesting that a hearing date be fixed for the pending application for judgment by default. In a letter dated April 13, 2026, counsel drew the Court’s attention to an earlier communication from the Registry dated March 6, 2026, indicating that arrangements were being made for the issuance of a hearing notice. The lawyer expressed concern that approximately one month had elapsed without the issuance of the hearing notice or communication of a hearing date. He consequently urged the Registry to expedite the necessary administrative processes to enable the application to be heard without further delay. Responding in a letter dated April 14, 2026, the Chief Registrar of the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, Yaouza Ouro-Sama, acknowledged receipt of counsel’s correspondence. The Chief Registrar explained that the matter was awaiting a directive from the judges and assured counsel that the process was being monitored. He further indicated that the hearing notice would be communicated to the parties once issued. US$50 million claim awaits judicial determination The legal action raises questions concerning Ghana’s obligations under regional and international human rights instruments, particularly regarding the protection of foreign nationals from arbitrary arrest, unlawful detention and alleged abuses by state officials. Mr You Kang maintains that the actions and omissions of Ghanaian state institutions caused him substantial financial losses, reputational damage, emotional distress and interference with his personal liberty and business interests. Through his lawyer, he is asking the ECOWAS Court to hold the Republic of Ghana accountable for the alleged violations and award the compensation sought.

title: US Air Force explores returning KC-10 tankers to service for North African operator
body:
The United States Air Force (USAF) is exploring the possibility of returning four mothballed KC-10 Extender tankers to service for a ‘partner nation’ in North Africa.
In a Request for Information (RFI) dated 7 October, the Air Force Life Cycle Management Centre noted the request was “issued solely for information and planning purposes” as part of market research.
“The intended purpose is to identify potential sources that may possess the capability to provide for the Air Force’s full requirement. It does not constitute a Request for Proposal (RFP) or a promise to issue an RFP in the future.”
The RFI’s purpose is to identify potential industry sources that possess the capability, expertise, and facilities to execute the regeneration, one-time flight clearance, depot-level return to service, worldwide ferry delivery, in-country Contractor Logistics Support (CLS), and operational/maintenance training for up to four KC-10 Extender aircraft transferred via Excess Defence Articles (EDA) to a partner nation in North Africa. Responses are due by 28 October 2026.
Derived from the McDonnell Douglas DC-10 commercial airliner, the KC-10 Extender entered US Air Force service in 1981, with 60 built by McDonnell Douglas (one was lost in a crash). It carries 160 200 kilograms of fuel and can refuel other aircraft using either a flying boom or a centreline hose-and-drogue system, allowing it to support different types of receivers during the same mission. The KC-10 can also transport up to 75 people and nearly 76 560 kilograms of cargo a distance of about 7 040 kilometres unrefuelled.
The US Air Force began retiring the type on in mid-July 2020 in favour of the new KC-46 Pegasus, when the first KC-10 arrived at the 309th Aerospace Maintenance and Regeneration Group (AMARG) at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona. The final US Air Force KC-10 departed Travis Air Force Base, California, for AMARG in September 2024.
Some retired KC-10s will take to the air again with Omega Aerial Refuelling Services. Ten were put up for auction last year, with Omega successfully bidding for all these airframes.
The first flew out of Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in October this year. Omega currently flies two former Royal Netherlands Air Force KDC-10 tankers, another DC-10 converted into a hose-and-drogue tanker, and two KC-707s.
While the US Air Force did not specify which North African partner nation may receive the KC-10s, it is likely to be either Egypt or Morocco. Both fly large F-16 fleets – the F-16 uses a boom receptacle.

title: Russian attack on Kyiv kills one person and injures 14
body:
According to Ukrinform, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Kychko reported this on Telegram .
Medical personnel hospitalized nine injured people.
According to police, a 46-year-old woman died in the Desnianskyi district. Another 13 people, ranging in age from 19 to 59, were injured. Among the injured were two members of an emergency medical team.
A 22-year-old man was also injured in the Obolon district.
High-rise and private residential buildings, medical facilities, a metro station, a university dormitory, a business center, an administrative building, trams, and cars were damaged.
Investigation and response teams, bomb disposal experts, and other specialized services are working at the sites of the strikes.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russian forces attacked the city with ballistic missiles —damaging medical facilities, a school, the South Bridge , a metro station, a university dormitory, and an apartment building.

title: Opinion| South Sudan and the caretaker legitimacy trap: What happens if elections don’t happen?
body: If South Sudan does not hold elections on 22 December 2026, the caretaker administration may keep state offices running, but it will face a deeper question of legitimacy. The safest path forward is a time-bound, inclusive, legally grounded arrangement that protects civic space and ends with a credible vote. South Sudan has again reached a political deadline with the main promises of its transition still contested. The caretaker administration was presented as an election-period mechanism, not a new political settlement. If the vote is postponed, the country cannot simply behave as though the caretaker mandate has renewed itself. That would turn a short-term arrangement into an open-ended government with concentrated executive authority and reduced institutional checks. The mandate question President Salva Kiir dissolved the Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity, the national legislature and state governments on 22 September 2026, then appointed a caretaker administration ahead of elections scheduled for 22 December. The same decision removed First Vice President Dr. Riek Machar and the other vice-presidents from office. Radio Tamazuj reported that the order relied on the National Elections Act, as amended in 2026, which allows the incumbent president to remain in office until an elected successor is sworn in. That continuity clause may prevent a vacancy in the presidency, but it does not settle the political question created by a failed election. The 2018 peace agreement was built on power-sharing, collegial decision-making and negotiated safeguards among former belligerents. Once those arrangements are dissolved, any prolonged caretaker period requires more than executive interpretation. It requires a lawful and publicly accepted basis, clear limits on authority and a defined end date. The European Union warned on 22 September that a caretaker government should concentrate on routine administration and avoid decisions with major political consequences while checks and balances are weakened. This is the correct standard. A caretaker administration should preserve essential services and public order. It should not use a delayed election to restructure the security sector, entrench appointments, alter electoral rules, or silence political competition. Legality does not create democratic legitimacy The amended election law provides a legal argument for presidential continuity during the electoral period. It does not give the executive an unlimited mandate if the electoral period no longer leads to an election. Parliament passed the amendment on 21 September, one day before the dissolution, and the law preserves the president’s full constitutional powers while requiring the vice-presidents to leave office. That asymmetry has already raised constitutional and political concerns. Former Detainees represented in the peace monitoring system asked the Intergovernmental Authority on Development to clarify whether the 2018 agreement remained applicable after the transitional government was dissolved. Their question remains fundamental. If elections fail, South Sudan will need an agreed bridge between the expired transition and a future elected government. That bridge cannot credibly be designed by one side and imposed on all others. Unresolved political and security questions The continued detention and trial of Dr. Machar is part of the legitimacy problem. A July 2026 report of the UN Secretary-General recorded international calls for his release and for dialogue to restore an inclusive peace process. His case must be handled through transparent due process, independent judicial guarantees, and respect for the peace agreement. Keeping a principal opposition leader in detention while preparing an election would deepen doubts about whether contestants can organize, campaign and challenge state power freely. The same concern applies to civic space. Journalists, civil society organizations, opposition parties and ordinary citizens must be able to debate the country’s future without intimidation, arbitrary detention or restrictions designed to favor incumbents. An election is not credible because ballots are printed. It is credible when citizens can register, obtain information and meet candidates, report abuses and vote without fear. Public confidence is also damaged when state and security institutions are perceived as serving a party, leader or ethnic constituency rather than the republic. Claims about ethnic domination are politically explosive and should be tested against verifiable data, not repeated as slogans. The remedy is institutional: publish recruitment and command structures, enforce merit-based appointments, strengthen civilian oversight and ensure that the army, police and National Security Service act impartially under the law. An election still lacks visible safeguards The National Elections Commission has reported receiving US$25 million from the government and has displayed a voter-registration book, but it had not yet announced the start date for registration when Radio Tamazuj reported on the preparations. Funding is important, but money alone cannot compensate for unresolved legal disputes, insecurity, weak transport and communications, displacement and limited civic space. Millions of South Sudanese remain displaced inside the country or live as refugees abroad. Their right to participate must be addressed through clear procedures, realistic timelines and independent observation. The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan warned in August that renewed political fractures, conflict-related violations and shrinking civic space could reproduce the patterns that preceded earlier violence. If the vote proceeds without minimum safeguards, the result may be challenged. If it is postponed without a negotiated alternative, the caretaker government may lose public acceptance. Both paths carry risks, but indefinite rule without consent is the more dangerous destination. What should happen if the election is postponed? First, the government, opposition parties, civil society, faith leaders, women’s and youth representatives, refugees and internally displaced people should enter a short, independently facilitated dialogue. The purpose should be narrow: determine the legal status of the caretaker administration, agree on the minimum conditions for elections and adopt a schedule that cannot be extended by executive decree alone. Second, the caretaker mandate should be published in full. It should define which decisions are permitted, which require multi-party consent, and which must wait for an elected government. Major security appointments, disposal of public assets, long-term borrowing and changes to electoral institutions should face heightened scrutiny. A small, representative oversight mechanism should publish regular compliance reports. Third, the National Elections Commission should issue a public readiness assessment. It should state what has been completed, what remains outstanding, how much money is available, how displaced citizens will vote, and what operational risks could change the timetable. This assessment should be subject to review by parties, civil society and independent observers. A date without verified milestones is a political promise, not an election plan. Fourth, the authorities should restore the conditions for peaceful competition. Political detainees should receive due process; arbitrary restrictions on assembly, travel and expression should end; and media outlets should be allowed to report without retaliation. The security services must adopt and publish election rules of conduct, with complaints investigated by bodies that are not controlled by the alleged violators. Fifth, regional and international partners should support a credible process rather than a deadline at any cost. Their assistance should be linked to transparent benchmarks: voter registration, civic freedoms, security-sector neutrality, dispute resolution, inclusion of displaced citizens and independent monitoring. External recognition cannot replace domestic consent, but principled mediation can help prevent another unilateral extension. The political choice If elections do not take place, the caretaker administration should not be treated as a permanent government by default. It may continue essential functions temporarily, but its authority must be narrowed, monitored and tied to a new agreement with a fixed electoral endpoint. The question is not whether the country needs an administration the day after a postponement. It plainly does. The question is who authorises that administration, what it may do, and when citizens will finally choose their leaders. South Sudan’s leaders can still prevent a caretaker arrangement from becoming another extension of elite rule. They should replace ambiguity with law, unilateralism with an inclusive agreement, and promises with measurable electoral steps. If they do not, the caretaker government may survive institutionally while losing the consent it needs to govern a divided and exhausted country. The writer is a researcher and writer specializing in humanitarian and development issues in South Sudan, holding a degree in Sociology and Political Science from the Catholic University of Eastern Africa and a Master’s in Peace and Development Studies from the University of Juba. He can be reached via mogtomloyo@yahoo.co.uk . The views expressed in ‘opinion’ articles published by Radio Tamazuj are solely those of the writer. The veracity of any claims made is the responsibility of the author, not Radio Tamazuj. The post Opinion| South Sudan and the caretaker legitimacy trap: What happens if elections don’t happen? appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Fuel Disruptions in Russia Create Opening for Kazakhstan, but Refineries Aren’t Enough
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan is seeking to turn its refining capacity into a competitive advantage in regional fuel markets as disruptions to Russian supplies and tightening global diesel markets create new opportunities and risks for Central Asia’s largest oil producer. Photo credit: Qazaq Expert Club The government aims to fully meet domestic demand for petroleum products and begin exporting finished fuels to neighboring Central Asian countries by 2030. The strategy would allow Kazakhstan to capture more value from its oil resources and diversify its energy revenues beyond crude exports. Dr. Glenn Agung Hole, an institutional economist, associate professor at the University of South-Eastern Norway and nonresident fellow at CFive. Photo credit: Hole’s personal archieve The ambition is realistic, but success will depend on whether Kazakhstan can turn additional refining capacity into a sustainable export industry, said Dr. Glenn Agung Hole, an institutional economist, associate professor at the University of South-Eastern Norway and nonresident fellow at CFive. “I would distinguish between increasing refining capacity and developing a genuinely competitive export industry,” Hole told The Astana Times. According to him, Kazakhstan has substantial oil resources, an established petroleum sector and a favorable geographical position. The government plans to expand the Shymkent refinery’s annual capacity from six million to 12 million metric tons by 2030. Its development strategy also anticipates a potential diesel surplus of 1.8 million tons that year. “However, these are projections, not guaranteed export volumes,” Hole said. Expanding production amid supply pressures Kazakhstan’s export ambitions come as its crude oil production faces pressure. The country produced 69.4 million tons of crude oil between January and September, down 8.3% from the same period in 2025, Deputy Energy Minister Yerlan Akbarov said at an Oct. 13 government meeting Oct. 13. Output at major fields also declined. Tengiz produced 26.7 million tons, equivalent to 88% of its year-earlier output. Kashagan produced 12.8 million tons, while Karachaganak produced 7.5 million tons. The government lowered its 2026 crude oil and condensate production forecast to 96 million tons from 98 million tons, partly because of disruptions to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) infrastructure following drone attacks . The CPC transports around 80% of Kazakhstan’s crude oil exports, leaving the country exposed to disruptions along a major export route. Alternative routes across the Caspian Sea and toward China offer options for diversification, although they can involve higher costs. Despite the decline in crude oil production, petroleum product output has continued to grow. Kazakhstan produced 11.9 million tons of petroleum products in January-September, up 2.4% year over year. Gasoline production increased 3.9% to 4.6 million tons, while diesel output rose 3.3% to 4.8 million tons. Jet fuel production grew 21.8% to 700,000 tons. In 2025, Kazakhstan processed 18.4 million tons of crude oil and produced around 15.5 million tons of petroleum products, meeting more than 90% of domestic demand, according to the Energy Ministry. Alongside the Shymkent expansion, the government plans to increase processing capacity at the Pavlodar refinery and has discussed the possibility of building a fourth refinery. However, greater refining capacity will not automatically translate into higher exports. Kazakhstan must secure sufficient crude supplies, produce fuels that meet the requirements of potential buyers and ensure that additional output can be transported at competitive prices. Hole highlighted that Kazakhstan’s main challenge is not a lack of natural resources but its ability to convert them into productive capital and sustainable industrial development. “Building refineries requires investment. Developing a competitive refining industry requires something more difficult: credible institutions, predictable regulation, functioning markets, access to finance and commercial arrangements that investors can trust over decades,” he said. He added that government targets alone cannot create international competitiveness. Investors must have confidence that commercial conditions will remain predictable, while producers must be able to respond to market demand rather than primarily to administrative decisions. Disruptions open a window for Kazakhstan Disruptions to Russian refinery operations and changes in fuel export restrictions have exposed vulnerabilities in regional supply chains, creating potential opportunities for Kazakhstan to supply neighboring markets. Nurlan Zhumagulov, an executive director of the Energy Monitor Fund, identified the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan and potentially Afghanistan as the most likely destinations for Kazakh fuel exports. Nurlan Zhumagulov, executive director of the Energy Monitor Fund. Photo credit: kazservice.kz “Undoubtedly, our closest neighbors are the most likely export markets. Any surplus Kazakhstan has will most likely go to these countries,” Zhumagulov told The Astana Times. He said regional fuel trade was already shifting as Russian supplies faced disruptions. “The Kyrgyz Republic is having to import gasoline from China, and Tajikistan has also started importing from neighboring countries. Russia previously supplied these markets, but it is now facing problems specifically with gasoline, while Kazakhstan currently has a surplus,” Zhumagulov said. He expects gasoline exports to be partially permitted for certain resource holders in November. The disruptions have affected regional trade. In June, Russian jet fuel exports to Central Asia and Afghanistan fell by more than 92% from May to 3,800 tons, while gasoline deliveries declined 34% to 99,300 tons, Reuters reported . Diesel deliveries, by contrast, rose to 237,700 tons. Hole said Russia’s difficulties reveal a broader vulnerability in Eurasia’s economic geography. “For decades, Russia’s energy infrastructure and industrial capacity have given it considerable influence over neighboring economies. The disruptions affecting Russian refineries demonstrate that established economic relationships can become sources of vulnerability when infrastructure is exposed to military and geopolitical risks,” he said. Kazakhstan could use the situation to strengthen its refining capabilities and position in regional energy markets. However, Hole cautioned against treating Russia’s current difficulties as the basis for a long-term export strategy. “A temporary shortage in Russia does not automatically create a sustainable competitive advantage for Kazakhstan. What matters is whether Kazakhstan uses this period to strengthen its own industrial and institutional capacity,” he said. The opportunity will depend on whether Kazakhstan can establish a reliable supply base and remain competitive when Russian exports recover. Russia partially eased some diesel export restrictions in October, illustrating how quickly market conditions can change. Global market pressures add another dimension. In October, the International Energy Agency warned that diesel shortages could persist well into 2027 amid supply disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East and attacks on energy infrastructure. Tighter global supplies could increase demand for alternative suppliers, but they also create uncertainty over prices and trade flows. For Kazakhstan, the immediate opportunity is likely to be regional rather than global. Proximity to neighboring markets can reduce delivery times and transport costs, while established commercial ties can facilitate trade. “Central Asia offers markets where geographical proximity, established relationships and shorter supply routes may provide genuine advantages,” Hole said. Still, Kazakhstan must compete on price, product quality, reliability and delivery capability, not merely on the availability of crude oil. Hole also warned that Kazakhstan’s dependence on export infrastructure passing through Russia creates strategic vulnerabilities. Disruptions affecting the CPC have demonstrated how external conflicts can constrain Kazakhstan’s economic activity even when the country itself is not directly involved. “If Kazakhstan increases refinery production but remains dependent on a limited number of transport routes, external suppliers or politically vulnerable logistics arrangements, it will have increased production without necessarily increasing its freedom of action,” he said. Hole argued that Kazakhstan should use the current situation to diversify its energy infrastructure, strengthen strategic reserves, improve domestic distribution and negotiate longer-term commercial relationships across Central Asia. Balancing domestic needs with export ambitions Kazakhstan’s ability to become a consistent fuel supplier will also depend on domestic energy policy. The government has repeatedly extended restrictions on gasoline and diesel exports to protect local supplies. Such measures can help prevent shortages, but they create uncertainty for producers and traders seeking to enter foreign markets. If companies cannot predict when exports will be permitted, it becomes harder to sign long-term contracts or make investments based on regional demand. According to Zhumagulov, Kazakhstan also continues to import some Russian diesel and aviation fuel. These imports highlight the complexity of the country’s fuel balance: Kazakhstan may have a surplus of certain products while remaining dependent on foreign supplies of others. Hole noted that Kazakhstan must reconcile its goal of affordable fuel with the commercial conditions needed to sustain investment. “The government understandably wants affordable fuel for households, agriculture and industry. However, if domestic prices are held artificially low for prolonged periods, refining companies may struggle to justify new investments, while differences between domestic and international prices create incentives for arbitrage and informal cross-border trade,” he said. In his view, export restrictions may be justified temporarily to protect domestic supplies, but they cannot become the permanent foundation of an internationally competitive industry. “The state must distinguish between protecting vulnerable consumers and suppressing the economic signals necessary for investment,” Hole said. He advocated a gradual transition toward more commercially sustainable pricing, supported by targeted social measures and a credible domestic energy security framework. The relationship between the state and private capital is equally important. While the government can establish strategic priorities and safeguard national energy security, investors need an environment in which companies can compete fairly, including with state-owned enterprises. The post Fuel Disruptions in Russia Create Opening for Kazakhstan, but Refineries Aren’t Enough appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Israelis head to polls as voting begins in pivotal Knesset election
body: Polls opened across Israel on Tuesday morning as eligible voters head to the polls to elect the country's next Knesset in a pivotal race pitting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his sitting coalition against the opposition bloc seeking to replace him.Within the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party has taken the lead ahead of Netanyahu's Likud in the majority of recent polling, though neither bloc still appears able to secure a 61-seat Knesset majority.Polling stations opened at 7:00 a.m., and exit polls are expected at 10:00 p.m., offering preliminary projections of the election results. The official results will be finalized in the coming days, following the completion of the vote count.Voting at Israeli diplomatic missions abroad concluded on October 16, while voting at some military bases began last week.The fateful elections will be the first to take place since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, with the political landscape and the issues at the forefront of voters' minds having shifted significantly since the previous vote in 2022.IDF manpower crisis, haredi draft, Oct. 7 commission central issues for Israeli votersSome of the central issues include the IDF's severe manpower crisis after three years of war, contentious haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription legislation, and calls for a state commission of inquiry into the government's failures surrounding the attack.Meanwhile, traditional election issues, such as the establishment of a Palestinian state, have moved further to the background as Israel's security outlook has changed, and most parties stand in agreement against Palestinian statehood.Another major issue is the fate of long-serving Netanyahu, who has led Israel for 19 non-consecutive years. Following the October 7 massacre and the ensuing war, the opposition bloc has called for Netanyahu to be held accountable for the attacks, arguing that he should no longer serve as prime minister.There appears to be no clear outcome for the elections, as neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition bloc has been projected as being able to secure a 61-seat majority without the support of the Arab parties.According to the final Channel 12 poll released on Friday before the election, Netanyahu's bloc stood at 50 seats, while the opposition bloc was projected to win 56 seats.The Arab parties, meanwhile, were projected to win a combined 16 seats. Most opposition party leaders have pledged not to form a government with the Arab parties, arguing that such a coalition would not be viable following the October 7 attacks.Netanyahu's Likud party was projected to win 19 seats in the poll, down from the 32 seats it currently holds in the outgoing Knesset.Eisenkot's Yashar party projected to win greatest number of Knesset seatsMeanwhile, Eisenkot's Yashar party was projected to win 22 seats, ahead of both Likud and B'Yachad, led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett, which was projected to receive 14 seats.Voter turnout throughout the day will have a significant impact on the results of the elections. With the electoral threshold set at 3.25% of valid votes, the number of votes a party needs depends on how many people turn out on election day.The Taub Center's updated calculations, prepared by Prof. Alex Weinreb, head of its Demography Area and research director, estimate that at a 70% turnout rate, similar to the 2022 election, a party would need 165,635 votes to cross the threshold.The required vote count rises as turnout increases, meaning smaller parties could face a tougher challenge if more Israelis head to the polls.Several parties are fighting to secure enough votes to enter the Knesset and clear the threshold, including Ofer Winter's People of Israel party and Yoaz Hendel's the Reservists-Economics party. Whether these parties cross the threshold is expected to significantly affect both blocs' ability to form a coalition.For these small parties, even a slight shift in voter support could determine whether they enter the next Knesset or leave their supporters without representation.Meanwhile, police have prepared for the possibility of clashes and public order disruptions on Election Day, particularly in the hours following the release of exit polls.Police announced on Monday that as part of special preparations, approximately 20,000 police officers, Border Police officers, and volunteers would carry out a range of actions throughout the country on Election Day.Forces are expected to be deployed at thousands of polling stations nationwide and in surrounding areas to maintain public order and protect public safety and security, the police stated.This will be done to “safeguard the integrity of the elections, and ensure that the democratic process is conducted properly and in accordance with the law,” the police added.Alex Winston contributed to this report.

title: Ukraine Asks 5 European Allies for Patriot Missiles
body:
Ukraine has asked five European partners to provide 10% of their existing stocks of interceptor missiles for Patriot and IRIS-T air defense systems to help protect the country against Russian attacks, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said.
The request was directed to the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland. Khmara said Ukraine had already signed contracts for future deliveries of interceptor missiles and proposed an exchange that would allow Kyiv to receive ammunition immediately.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Ukraine already has contracts in place for future deliveries of interceptor missiles, so it is proposing an exchange: partners would provide a portion of their current stocks now, in return for the shipments that are scheduled to arrive in Ukraine later,” he said on Telegram .
Ukraine ’s Armed Forces (AFU) also urgently need additional man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS), he added.
“Ukraine is counting on funding for new acquisitions, as well as the transfer of systems from the existing stockpiles of its partners,” Khmara said.
The minister added Ukraine could double its drone production by 2027 if funding arrived on time. Kyiv is proposing not only to increase procurement but also to expand joint production of Ukrainian drones abroad.
“We are proposing not only to increase procurement but also to scale up the joint production of Ukrainian drones in other countries,” Khmara said. He added that the approach would help Ukraine obtain the drones it needs while strengthening the defensive capabilities of partner countries.
Following a meeting in Paris with defense ministers from the UK, France, Italy and Poland, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the participating countries had already prepared winter aid packages for Ukraine.
“Moreover, we will do everything in our power to ensure that the United States continues to support Ukraine – through its own shipments, and, above all, by providing intelligence and satellite data,” Pistorius said.
He added that European countries were working with Kyiv to develop an air defense system.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia was preparing to intensify attacks on major Ukrainian cities.
Senior Ukrainian officials told The Economist that Moscow planned to paralyze Kyiv before the onset of colder weather in an effort to destabilize the political situation. According to the officials, Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered attacks on civilian infrastructure across the capital.
Separately, Ukrainian officials told the Financial Times (FT) that Moscow intended to increase pressure on Kyiv in hopes of forcing Ukraine to accept Russian demands, including surrendering territory in the Donbas, by early 2027.
Ukraine will again raise the issue of delayed air defense missile deliveries with the US, as Kyiv has been waiting nearly a month for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve missiles for Patriot and NASAMS systems, Zelensky said on Monday.
Zelensky added that he had instructed his team to raise the issue with Washington again. Ukraine is also seeking PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors from EU countries and other partners holding existing stocks.
The shortage comes as Ukraine struggles to secure enough ammunition to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks. Zelensky previously said Ukraine had received just 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over 90 days, despite requiring around 350 per month.
He has also asked European partners to provide 300 interceptors for the winter, but efforts to obtain missiles from existing stockpiles have faced resistance, including from Greece.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian Air Force official Yuriy Ihnat said that missiles expended in the Middle East could have sustained Ukraine’s Patriot systems for several years.
He said Ukrainian crews had developed more efficient tactics, typically using one interceptor per target and employing ambushes before quickly relocating systems. By contrast, air defense forces in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight interceptors at a single target, including relatively cheap Shahed drones.
Zelensky also called for faster implementation of decisions expected to support Ukraine’s air defense, as officials prepare for the next Ramstein-format meeting in November. “Every support package is an opportunity to protect people’s lives,” he said.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Ecotutu, Lange and Grant Partner on Cold Storage to Reduce Food Waste
body: Ayodeji Ake Lange and Grant and Ecotutu have partnered to expand access to solar-powered cold storage facilities in Nigeria, unveiling a joint showroom in Lagos to help farmers, traders and businesses preserve perishable goods, reduce post-harvest losses and improve food security. Speaking at the Lange and Grant–Ecotutu Showroom Launch Event in Lagos, the Chief Executive Officer of Lange and Grant, Tunde Okoya, said the partnership would combine the companies’ expertise to address inadequate cold storage infrastructure and improve the preservation of perishable agricultural produce. “The importance of strategic partnerships cannot be overstated in expanding access to cold storage infrastructure in Nigeria. Our collaboration with Ecotutu is focused on tackling post-harvest losses and improving food preservation,” Okoya said. He explained that Lange and Grant’s expertise in manufacturing structural insulated panels for cold rooms and temperature-controlled facilities complemented Ecotutu’s cooling technology and service capabilities. According to him, the collaboration would ensure that customers receive specialised support in both the construction and operation of cold storage facilities, particularly as refrigeration requires regular maintenance and sustained customer engagement. “Because refrigeration is not Lange and Grant’s core business, this partnership will ensure customers receive specialised support in both constructing and operating cold storage facilities. “Refrigeration requires regular maintenance and continuous client engagement, particularly where farmers and businesses depend on cold rooms to protect valuable produce,” he added. The Chief Executive Officer of Ecotutu, Babajide Oluwase, said the company developed energy-efficient cooling solutions to support different stages of the food value chain, from harvesting and aggregation to market distribution. He explained that the technology was designed to address Nigeria’s energy challenges while enabling farmers, traders and businesses to preserve perishable goods for longer periods. Ecotutu deploys monoblock refrigeration systems adapted to local operating conditions and powered primarily by solar energy. The systems are designed to operate automatically, reducing electricity consumption by entering a hibernation mode when the required temperature is reached and resuming operation when temperatures rise beyond the user’s set range. Oluwase said the solutions could be used to preserve fresh produce such as tomatoes and peppers, frozen products including fish, meat and chicken, as well as temperature-sensitive items such as vaccines. He added that the systems feature remote monitoring capabilities, allowing users to track temperature, humidity and energy consumption through mobile phones or computers. Their mobility also enables deployment in locations where cold storage infrastructure is needed. The Chief Marketing Officer of Ecotutu, Michael Akinsete, said the company had been developing solutions to address post-harvest losses since 2022 and currently operated in 10 states, with plans to expand its operations nationwide and beyond. He noted that inadequate cold storage infrastructure continued to contribute to food waste, reducing farmers’ and traders’ earnings while affecting the availability and affordability of nutritious food. To make its solutions more accessible, Akinsete said Ecotutu offered different payment options, including outright purchases, asset financing, lease-to-own arrangements and cooling-as-a-service. Under the service model, farmers and traders can store their produce at designated facilities for an affordable daily fee, reducing the need for individual investments in cold storage equipment. “We are deploying facilities around farm gates and open markets, including locations around Mile 12 and Ajah in Lagos,” he said. Akinsete also disclosed that eligible businesses could access subsidies of up to 40 per cent through the Rural Electrification Agency’s Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up (DARES) programme, subject to the programme’s applicable eligibility requirements. Beyond cold storage, the companies said they were exploring opportunities to develop additional rural food-processing infrastructure, including mini-abattoirs and community poultry facilities. They said expanding access to preservation and processing facilities could help reduce food losses, improve farmers’ earnings and support more efficient food distribution. By combining solar-powered cooling technology with specialised cold-room construction and maintenance support, the partnership aims to provide farmers, traders and other businesses with practical alternatives for preserving food and reducing losses across Nigeria’s agricultural value chain.

title: Ebola won’t be used as political weapon — NCDC chief
body: By Adegboyega Adeleye The Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), Jide Idris, has dismissed suggestions that the Ebola outbreak could be used as a political weapon, insisting that disease concerns would not be exploited for political purposes. Speaking on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Monday, Idris said the health sector would not use the outbreak for political ends, adding that any decision on a possible election postponement would depend on the situation. “We in the health sector will not use disease issues as a political weapon,” he said. “When it came, when it came, it came and we were not even sure whether it would be out of the budget…..so no government will use Ebola as a political weapon,” Idris added. On whether the Ebola outbreak could lead to a postponement of the election, the NCDC chief said he hoped such a measure would not become necessary, stressing that the decision was not his to make. “That is not my decision, we hope not because if the thing gets wide enough. As at now there is no need for that,” he said. Explaining Nigeria’s preparedness for the outbreak, Idris said health authorities had been monitoring developments in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) and anticipating the possibility of the virus reaching Nigeria through international travel and population movement. He said the authorities had tracked the outbreak and committed resources to preparing for the risk of an imported case. “But again you know this Ebola started in DR Congo a couple of months ago and we were tracking and they said we need to track again, that there is a possibility for many reasons that it can get here. A population movement, flight into this country and that side again, we spent funds on it,” Idris said. The NCDC confirmed Nigeria’s first case of the current outbreak in Abuja on October 20, with 53 contacts identified for monitoring. The confirmed patient was subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland on Monday, while health authorities continued monitoring contacts. Idris also urged Nigerians to observe regular handwashing, describing the practice as an important measure for reducing the spread of infections. “Most of these infections, handwashing alone can reduce the incidence by almost 40%,” he said. The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says handwashing education can reduce diarrhoeal illnesses by 23 to 40 per cent and respiratory illnesses by 16 to 21 per cent. The post Ebola won’t be used as political weapon — NCDC chief appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Creepy Cat in the Hat videos reach Finland
body:
AI-generated videos featuring the children's book character the Cat in the Hat are now spreading in Finland.
Viral images that purport to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character roaming the streets after dark are sparking fear and confusion among children.
The so-called Cat in the Hat phenomenon is spreading on social media. In frightening videos, the black-and-white feline, familiar from 1950s children's books, turns up in various towns and cities.
Over the past few days, the phenomenon has also reached Finland. Police in Oulu told Yle that they have been contacted about it. They said they have searched the streets but have not found anyone sneaking around in a cat costume.
Jyrki Mikkonen , principal of Koivuhaka School in Kokkola, says he is aware that content featuring the hat-wearing feline is circulating on social media. The school learned about it from parents.
"There were posts on social media warning that the figure would show up in this area. According to messages from guardians, this is worrying kids," he says.
The phenomenon centres on videos, shared especially on TikTok, that portray the cat character as menacing and claim it has been 'spotted' in various places or is 'on its way' to a particular town or school.
Kaisa Rissanen , of Someturva, a Finnish service that helps victims of online harassment and bullying, says the pattern is familiar. About ten years ago, people dressed up as clowns sparked similar worry.
"The threat is specific to videos created with AI, not to real dangerous situations," she notes.
But even if the threat isn't real, Rissanen says children's fear is genuine.
She also points out that digital security skills are becoming increasingly important as AI-generated content on social media keeps growing.
"This is a good wake-up call that we need to address these topics more broadly," she says.

title: How Trump’s ‘little detour’ to Iran became a roadblock in the midterm elections
body:
When President Donald Trump launched his war on Iran, he said it would last a matter of weeks
WASHINGTON -- Noor Dubow says he regularly votes for Republican candidates who he believes align with his economic views — even though he's never been a fan of Donald Trump , finding himself repelled by some of the president's dehumanizing rhetoric toward immigrants.
But this year, when Dubow cast his early ballot in the midterm election , he found himself tipping more toward Democrats because of his frustration with Trump's decision to go to war with Iran.
“Where are the Republicans in Congress?” asked Dubow, 44, a dispatcher at a trucking logistics firm in Columbus, Ohio, where he has a bird's eye view of the disruption that surging fuel prices are having on the economy. "Why aren't the Republicans holding Trump accountable?”
The Iran war, which Trump often describes as a “little detour,” has emerged as an unforced liability for the president, who once promised to keep the U.S. out of foreign wars. Republican strategists privately acknowledge that the war is severely damaging the party's push to retain control of Congress for the final two years of Trump's presidency as rising gasoline prices drive up costs across nearly every sector and new hostilities emerge.
High energy costs and voter fatigue over the nearly eight-month-old war — one that Trump predicted at the onset would last a matter of weeks — are weighing heavily on Republican candidates.
Regardless of the outcome of the Nov. 3 elections, an AP-NORC poll published last week found that voters from both major political parties want the next Congress to focus on making life more affordable and end the war in Iran that's had enormous ramifications for the global economy.
The situation has only become more complicated for Republicans making their case to voters. The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen.
Over the weekend, the State Department said it was reducing staffing at four U.S. embassies in the Middle East after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel in the region and elsewhere.
Diesel prices continue to hover near all-time highs in the U.S., creating trouble for Republicans in typically conservative states such as Iowa, Kansas , Ohio and Texas who find themselves knotted in competitive races with Democrats.
Yet, Trump has consistently downplayed the conflict's economic impact as he rallies his supporters to try to keep the GOP's grip on both chambers of Congress.
Trump repeatedly insists that the war's end is near, only to threaten that a new, intensive round of bombing could very well be in the offing once the election passes — often within the same campaign speech or a single exchange with reporters.
He also argues that elevated gas prices are a temporary inconvenience worth paying to defang Iran.
Trump at a weekend rally in Michigan said that he has no regrets about launching the war and even argued that its economic impact has been less severe than he had expected.
“Somebody said, ‘If you had it to do again...’" Trump told the friendly audience. "I said, ‘Are you kidding?’ I thought gas would be double or triple. And it’s a small price to pay for taking a nuclear weapon away from maniacs.”
The president's mixed message on Iran has left Republican candidates in a difficult, if not untenable, position, said Christopher Borick, director of the Lehigh University Opinion Observatory.
“Trump's messaging on the war is resonating with a shrinking portion of the electorate,” Borick said. “For voters disappointed with the direction of the conflict, there's little by way of the president's claims that would change their negative outlook.”
Only a few elected Republicans have parted ways with Trump over the Iran conflict. Trump, for his part, has insisted that the midterm elections would have no bearing on how he approached the conflict.
But some party strategists have been sounding the alarm for months.
Early in the summer, five Republican strategists involved in key races or advising campaign leadership told The Associated Press that they had begun seeing warning signs that the war could hurt their candidates if the conflict did not wind down soon.
In June, after Trump forged an interim ceasefire agreement with Tehran, Trump and White House officials appeared more confident. But the deal unraveled within weeks.
At that point, campaign officials in some battleground races became more forceful during internal conversations that House districts Trump won easily in 2024 looked like they were becoming competitive, said the Republican strategists, who were not authorized to comment publicly on the internal party data and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Oil prices peaked in May, fell in June and surged again in September as Trump threatened to escalate the conflict before backing off and suggesting a deal could be around the corner. The national average has hovered above $4 per gallon since the middle of June.
As the Labor Day holiday passed, strategists said internal polls showed voters were more frequently tying the war to higher grocery prices and travel costs.
Trump has dismissed critics who argue that the war is driving an affordability crisis for Americans as pushing a “hoax” or “scam” invented by Democrats. But internal campaign polling suggests that Trump's argument has not resonated with American voters, the strategists said.
In interviews, even some Republican voters who say they support Trump's decision to launch the war admit gas prices are testing their patience.
Clay Coey, 59, said he sometimes cringes when he fills the tank of his 2010 Chrysler Sebring, even as he says he's willing to temporarily pay higher gas prices to eliminate what he sees as a major security threat to the U.S.
“Do I like it? No, I drive this old beast,” said Coey, an auctioneer from DeWitt, Michigan. “However, there does come a point in time where you have to sit here and say, what is worth the cost?"
Some voters say Trump fumbled by predicting the war would be over in a matter of weeks.
Elizabeth Marlett, 61, of Moville, Iowa, said she wished Trump had avoided setting a timeline for the conflict and wished he would order the U.S. military to act more forcefully to force Tehran to capitulate. Still, she's sticking with Trump.
“We need to support our commander in chief, even if things take longer than expected," said Marlett, a small-herd beef rancher from Iowa's GOP-heavy northwest. “That’s life, and we can’t run from something we’ve started.”
Meanwhile, Trump's decision to start the war has been seen by some supporters as a betrayal of a central tenet of the Republican leader's “America First" campaign pledge: the promise to keep the U.S. out of the sort of “forever wars” that bogged down some of his recent White House predecessors.
Sean O'Brien, 21, a student at Auburn University in Alabama, said Trump's Iran decision left him “very disillusioned.”
O'Brien earlier this year attended the Conservative Political Action Conference , a major gathering for those on the political right. Now, he's rethinking his allegiances.
“At the moment, I expect to vote Democratic,” said O'Brien, who considers himself an independent.
Beaumont reported from Sioux City, Iowa. AP journalists Patrick Aftoora-Orsagos in Columbus, Ohio, and Jacqueline GaNun in DeWitt, Michigan, contributed to this report.
