title: Gunmen kill Islamic cleric Sheikh Masussuka in Katsina
body:
The Katsina State Police Command has confirmed the killing of an Islamic cleric, Sheikh Yahaya Masussuka, who was shot by suspected gunmen outside his residence in Dutsin-Ma Local Government Area on Monday night.
DW Hausa reported that the police confirmed the killing to its correspondent, adding that the attackers were riding a motorcycle when they opened fire on the cleric.
The incident reportedly occurred at about 9 p.m. near the entrance to his residence.
Several local news platforms reported that another person was shot during the attack, although accounts differed over the person’s identity and whether he survived.
Photographs circulating on social media purportedly showed residents gathered outside the cleric’s residence following the shooting. PREMIUM TIMES has not independently verified where or when the images were taken.
The circumstances surrounding the attack and the identities of those responsible remain unclear.
The spokesperson for the Katsina State Police Command, Abubakar Sadiq, acknowledged enquiries from journalists in a police WhatsApp group at 10:44 p.m. on Monday, saying he would respond to their calls as soon as possible.
He had not provided further details to PREMIUM TIMES at the time of filing this report.
Mr Masussuka was an Islamic preacher based in Dutsin-Ma, Katsina State, although he was originally from Bauchi State.
He was known for his Quran-centred teachings, particularly his rejection of certain Hadith traditions, which brought him into disagreement with other Islamic scholars. His sermons also attracted considerable attention on social media.
In April 2024, he established Qur’an TV/Radio and Masussuka International School in Dutsin-Ma. The school was designed to provide both Qur’anic and conventional education.
He also advocated peaceful coexistence between Muslims and Christians . In June 2025, the Network for Good Governance and Transparency honoured him with a Peace Ambassador award at an event in Katsina.
In November 2025, the Katsina State Government summoned the cleric following complaints that some of his teachings contravened Islamic principles.
The government also acknowledged receiving complaints from Masussuka that members of Jama’atu Izalatul Bidia were insulting him and threatening to attack him.
The matter was referred to the Katsina Emirate Council, where both sides were invited for discussions. Governor Dikko Radda subsequently directed the cleric to respond to the allegations before a committee of Islamic scholars.
There is no evidence at this stage linking the earlier religious dispute or the reported threats to Monday’s killing.

title: 2027: APC dismisses NDC’s allegation of blocking venues, billboards for campaign
body: By Omeiza Ajayi, Cynthia Alo & Kafayat Kokumo ABUJA — The Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, has accused the All Progressives Congress, APC, of frustrating its campaign preparations ahead of the 2027 general elections by allegedly denying it access to event venues and billboards. National Publicity Secretary of the NDC, Osa Director, made the allegation during an interview on ARISE TV yesterday, insisting that the party will not be intimidated or prevented from exercising its democratic rights. He said the party had encountered difficulties securing venues despite making payments, adding that its latest venue was the fourth it had attempted to use for its planned activities. “This is the fourth venue we are paying for. We kept this one under wraps until just a few hours ago when we issued the press release, only for us to be called that the political marauders have come and said they are the owners of the land, so we should take back our money,” he said. He added that the party will proceed with its activities, despite the alleged restrictions, insisting that no individual or political party owned the country. “Nigeria belongs to us all. Nobody owns Nigeria. We fought, we used our life and sweat and blood to fight for this democracy we are enjoying today. So who is that person to tell me that I will not have a right to exercise my freedom of speech and freedom of assembly?” he said. The NDC spokesman also alleged that the party had been denied access to billboards but maintained that such restrictions would not prevent it from reaching voters. Speaking on the party’s campaign preparations, Director dismissed suggestions that the NDC was starting late, saying its presidential candidate had already held several town hall meetings across the country. He said the party had held at least four meetings and had nearly completed its engagements across the zones, arguing that its approach differed from campaigns focused on rallies, music and public displays. The party was scheduled to inaugurate its national campaign council, commission its newly acquired national secretariat in Jabi, Abuja, and present certificates of return to its candidates yesterday, the spokesman said the certificates were part of a formal process, adding that the candidates had already been uploaded to the Independent National Electoral Commission’s portal. He also announced that the party would publicly present a statement of its finances and challenged the APC to do the same, saying Nigerians would be surprised by the figures. He defended the party’s anti-defection oath, adding that it was intended to address political defections and what he described as irresponsible politicking. Osa Directoralso said members dissatisfied with the outcome of party primaries had the constitutional right to seek redress in court. Director dismissed allegations that the party’s National Leader, Senator Seriake Dickson, was working for the ruling party, describing the claims as baseless. He further claimed that Peter Obi was the preferred candidate of many Nigerians. And warned that any attempt to restrict the political space could force some democracy advocates to return to the kind of guerrilla journalism practised under military rule. APC rejects NDC’s claim of blocked campaign venues as baseless Reacting to the allegation, the All Progressives Congress, APC, dismissed it, asking whether Nigerians were in kindergarten to be treated to such baseless allegations. The official, who spoke anonymously, said the NDC had not said which state or which ministry was involved. “You want us to be responding to such baseless allegations? The party will not. Are we in kindergarten? Which state? Which ministry denied them the use of facilities?” he queried. The post 2027: APC dismisses NDC’s allegation of blocking venues, billboards for campaign appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Python's experimental JIT to be removed
body:
Welcome to LWN.net The following subscription-only content has been made available to you by an LWN subscriber. Thousands of subscribers depend on LWN for the best news from the Linux and free software communities. If you enjoy this article, please consider accepting the discount offer on the right. Thank you for visiting LWN.net! Special discount offer Subscribe to LWN now at the "professional hacker" level for at least six months, and you will receive a special discount of 25%. By Joe Brockmeier October 26, 2026 Python's experimental just-in-time (JIT) compiler , which was added to CPython in 2024 for the 3.13 release , is on its way out. In June, the Python steering council announced that it was pausing work on the JIT in CPython's main branch until there was an accepted Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) that addressed concerns about maintenance, compatibility, and set clear success metrics as well as a timeline for completion. After creating PEP 836 ("JIT Go Brrr: The Path to a Supported JIT Compiler for CPython") to try to meet the council's request, and after months of discussion, the JIT maintainers have withdrawn the PEP. For now, it appears that development on the once-promising project has come to an end. The JIT was added to CPython by Brandt Bucher in early 2024. Generally, such a major feature would be expected to land only after the council had approved a standards-track PEP . Bucher had given a talk ( YouTube video , slides ) about the JIT at a Python core developer sprint, and announced his intent to merge the feature—but he had not taken the step of authoring or submitting a PEP for its approval. He was prodded into doing so by steering council member Thomas Wouters, who was also serving as the release manager for Python 3.13. Bucher and Savannah Ostrowski drafted PEP 744 ("JIT Compilation"), which was an informational PEP —meaning it only provides information to the Python community and does not represent formal consensus to proceed on a feature or project. LWN covered the discussion of PEP 744 in April 2024, and later covered Bucher's talk on the JIT at PyCon US 2024, as well as the follow-up talk at PyCon US 2025. PEP it up Work on the JIT had been proceeding on the basis of PEP 744 until this June, when the council had put forward its formal request for the JIT maintainers to create a standards-track PEP. One might wonder, as Antoine Pitrou did , why the council had decided that it was time to speak up and ask for a new PEP. Wouters said that there was no " single triggering event for this request ", but that the council had been discussing the topic for a while and indicated that it was looking to ensure the JIT work did not interfere with other projects. " There's been work trying to get the JIT to play nice with instrumentation, debugging, and profiling. There's also external JITs (like CinderX), JIT-adjacent things (like Numba and PyTorch's compile), and discussions about a tier 3 JIT. " The council had waited until after the Python 3.15 beta release " to be clear that we're OK with the status quo for 3.15 ". The council asked for a PEP that would make the case for the JIT " as a supported, non-experimental part of CPython: its guarantees, its maintenance commitments, and its impact on redistributors ". The council set a deadline of six months for the PEP to be submitted and accepted; failing that, the council would require the JIT code to be removed from the CPython main branch. Bucher, Ostrowski, and Ken Jin drafted PEP 836 and published it on the Python forum for community feedback on July 3. It generated quite a bit of discussion, some favorable and some critical. One of the key themes in the comments, such as this one by Wouters, and this comment by Mark Shannon, was that the draft felt like it should be two separate PEPs. Shannon, for example, thought that the PEP should only cover goals for accepting the JIT work and felt that it should leave out implementation details. There were also quite a few calls for additional information. Bucher pushed back a bit on the suggestion that it should be two PEPs, and Ostrowski defended the structure of the PEP as it was. " Outlining goals like we have in the PEP without being able to share the plan and everything we've thought through alongside it would make me uncomfortable. To me, goals without plans behind them aren't really goals at all. " When we last looked at this topic in September, the discussion about the PEP had slowed down without a commitment to develop new PEPs or a formal statement from the council. The last word from the council at that time, in the form of a summary of its August 6 meeting , was that it had met with the PEP authors and was " discussing the state of the PEP and whether it answered the questions the SC asked in its request for a PEP ". Experimentation in main On September 21, Wouters posted a statement from the steering council, minus Ostrowski (who is currently a member of the steering council but did not participate since she is a co-author of the PEP), that summarized its position. The statement said that PEP did answer all of the questions that were highlighted in the council's request, " although perhaps some less convincingly than others ". The council wished to make clear that it was not looking for the criteria that the JIT should meet to be a supported feature, or whether it should be considered such. Instead, the council was evaluating whether the JIT should continue as an experiment in CPython's main branch. Part of the problem with allowing experimentation in main is the lack of unified design, and the uncertainty that core developers, package maintainers and users face as the experimentation changes behaviours and API surfaces. The council said that the PEP was not specific enough about support plans, performance criteria, and too vague or too optimistic about a number of other areas. The statement included a ten-point list of items that the council wanted " to see either spelled out in the PEP, or at least discussed and rejected ". The council's list expressed concerns ranging from memory impact to security. For example, on the topic of platform parity, the council wanted to ensure that the JIT was designed to be easily adopted for new platforms. It wanted assurance that the JIT's design would not be tied to specific platform or require platform-specific knowledge to maintain. Another area that the council called out was user impact. It said that the PEP was " overly optimistic " about user-visible differences with the JIT enabled. There were many cases where users depend on idiosyncrasies in the interpreter design, " as we've seen with other Python implementations or even just between major Python versions ", and it wanted clarification on how those differences would be handled. Would they be considered bugs, how would situations be handled if a difference in behavior was unavoidable, and so on. Security was " an underserved area in the PEP ", according to the council; it suggested that a discussion with the Python security response team was in order and that a security review should be part of the criteria for supported status as well. PEP 836 specified a compatibility review milestone to correspond with the first Python 3.17 release candidate—which would be expected sometime in August 2028—that would involve running the test suites of the top PyPI packages to see if the JIT broke them. The council wanted that timeline moved up significantly. " We think that's way, way too late, and the compatibility review should be an ongoing and continuous process starting as soon as possible ". The council also worried about the JIT's design decisions being made " without critical review by the larger group of developers ultimately responsible for [CPython] development, maintenance and support ". The bottom line, it said, was that PEP 836 " mostly answers the questions we asked " with no missing pieces, but it wanted more discussion on those topics so it could " gauge community support and consensus before we're asked to pronounce on this PEP ". Jin replied a few days later to thank the council for its detailed feedback and said that the group would work on its suggestions. Withdrawn After some consideration, it appears, the PEP's authors have decided not to continue pursing the council's approval. On October 19, Ostrowski (who is also release manager for Python 3.16 and 3.17) announced that the PEP was being withdrawn: The Steering Council rightly sets a high bar for a proposal of this scope, and we don't feel we have the personal bandwidth to carry the current version forward. We continue to believe in the technical direction outlined in the PEP, including free-threaded support and a method-based frontend, and remain optimistic about the JIT's potential in CPython. We'll make the reference implementation available and link it from the withdrawn PEP so others who are interested can explore and build on that. Barry Scott asked if that meant that work on the JIT was stopped. Brett Cannon replied that the work would be stopped in the main repository, but it would be up to the community whether the work would continue elsewhere. Dunc Graham suggested that there might be time for an alternative PEP to be submitted before the council's deadline. Cannon said that was not likely, " as all the people actively driving the JIT were either authors on that PEP or contributors to it ". With the PEP withdrawn, the JIT will likely be removed from CPython main fairly soon to ensure that any problems caused by its removal can be addressed early in the Python 3.16 development cycle . It is unclear whether the original drivers of the JIT work intend to continue working on it at all, or if it will simply be left for others to pick up if there is enough community interest. I have emailed the PEP authors for clarification, but have not yet received a reply. to post comments Seems civil Posted Oct 26, 2026 20:00 UTC (Mon) by jkingweb (subscriber, #113039) [ Link ] (7 responses) This reads to me like everyone was civil and acting in good faith and that a problem of process was acknowledged and addressed without acrimony or drama. That's really nice to see, and speaks well of the Python community. Hopefully this won't be the end of the work, because Python can always benefit from better performance. Seems civil Posted Oct 26, 2026 21:54 UTC (Mon) by ballombe (subscriber, #9523) [ Link ] (6 responses) What was the advantage over pypy ? Seems civil Posted Oct 27, 2026 1:53 UTC (Tue) by acarno (subscriber, #123476) [ Link ] For one thing, pypy only suppports Python 3.12, 3.11 and 2.7. More significantly, pypy isn't CPython - it's an alternative implementation that is mostly compatible but with a few noticeable differences (the pypy website lists these). This would have added a JIT to CPython (the reference implementation) directly, meaning all new Python versions - and all included modules, etc. - get access to JIT compilation. In the PEP 836 authors' own words: Alternative Python implementations, such as PyPy and GraalPy, demonstrate that larger speedups are possible for some Python programs, and we deeply value those projects. By Joe Brockmeier October 26, 2026 Python's experimental just-in-time (JIT) compiler , which was added to CPython in 2024 for the 3.13 release , is on its way out. In June, the Python steering council announced that it was pausing work on the JIT in CPython's main branch until there was an accepted Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) that addressed concerns about maintenance, compatibility, and set clear success metrics as well as a timeline for completion. After creating PEP 836 ("JIT Go Brrr: The Path to a Supported JIT Compiler for CPython") to try to meet the council's request, and after months of discussion, the JIT maintainers have withdrawn the PEP. For now, it appears that development on the once-promising project has come to an end. The JIT was added to CPython by Brandt Bucher in early 2024. Generally, such a major feature would be expected to land only after the council had approved a standards-track PEP . Bucher had given a talk ( YouTube video , slides ) about the JIT at a Python core developer sprint, and announced his intent to merge the feature—but he had not taken the step of authoring or submitting a PEP for its approval. He was prodded into doing so by steering council member Thomas Wouters, who was also serving as the release manager for Python 3.13. Bucher and Savannah Ostrowski drafted PEP 744 ("JIT Compilation"), which was an informational PEP —meaning it only provides information to the Python community and does not represent formal consensus to proceed on a feature or project. LWN covered the discussion of PEP 744 in April 2024, and later covered Bucher's talk on the JIT at PyCon US 2024, as well as the follow-up talk at PyCon US 2025. PEP it up Work on the JIT had been proceeding on the basis of PEP 744 until this June, when the council had put forward its formal request for the JIT maintainers to create a standards-track PEP. One might wonder, as Antoine Pitrou did , why the council had decided that it was time to speak up and ask for a new PEP. Wouters said that there was no " single triggering event for this request ", but that the council had been discussing the topic for a while and indicated that it was looking to ensure the JIT work did not interfere with other projects. " There's been work trying to get the JIT to play nice with instrumentation, debugging, and profiling. There's also external JITs (like CinderX), JIT-adjacent things (like Numba and PyTorch's compile), and discussions about a tier 3 JIT. " The council had waited until after the Python 3.15 beta release " to be clear that we're OK with the status quo for 3.15 ". The council asked for a PEP that would make the case for the JIT " as a supported, non-experimental part of CPython: its guarantees, its maintenance commitments, and its impact on redistributors ". The council set a deadline of six months for the PEP to be submitted and accepted; failing that, the council would require the JIT code to be removed from the CPython main branch. Bucher, Ostrowski, and Ken Jin drafted PEP 836 and published it on the Python forum for community feedback on July 3. It generated quite a bit of discussion, some favorable and some critical. One of the key themes in the comments, such as this one by Wouters, and this comment by Mark Shannon, was that the draft felt like it should be two separate PEPs. Shannon, for example, thought that the PEP should only cover goals for accepting the JIT work and felt that it should leave out implementation details. There were also quite a few calls for additional information. Bucher pushed back a bit on the suggestion that it should be two PEPs, and Ostrowski defended the structure of the PEP as it was. " Outlining goals like we have in the PEP without being able to share the plan and everything we've thought through alongside it would make me uncomfortable. To me, goals without plans behind them aren't really goals at all. " When we last looked at this topic in September, the discussion about the PEP had slowed down without a commitment to develop new PEPs or a formal statement from the council. The last word from the council at that time, in the form of a summary of its August 6 meeting , was that it had met with the PEP authors and was " discussing the state of the PEP and whether it answered the questions the SC asked in its request for a PEP ". Experimentation in main On September 21, Wouters posted a statement from the steering council, minus Ostrowski (who is currently a member of the steering council but did not participate since she is a co-author of the PEP), that summarized its position. The statement said that PEP did answer all of the questions that were highlighted in the council's request, " although perhaps some less convincingly than others ". The council wished to make clear that it was not looking for the criteria that the JIT should meet to be a supported feature, or whether it should be considered such. Instead, the council was evaluating whether the JIT should continue as an experiment in CPython's main branch. Part of the problem with allowing experimentation in main is the lack of unified design, and the uncertainty that core developers, package maintainers and users face as the experimentation changes behaviours and API surfaces. The council said that the PEP was not specific enough about support plans, performance criteria, and too vague or too optimistic about a number of other areas. The statement included a ten-point list of items that the council wanted " to see either spelled out in the PEP, or at least discussed and rejected ". The council's list expressed concerns ranging from memory impact to security. For example, on the topic of platform parity, the council wanted to ensure that the JIT was designed to be easily adopted for new platforms. It wanted assurance that the JIT's design would not be tied to specific platform or require platform-specific knowledge to maintain. Another area that the council called out was user impact. It said that the PEP was " overly optimistic " about user-visible differences with the JIT enabled. There were many cases where users depend on idiosyncrasies in the interpreter design, " as we've seen with other Python implementations or even just between major Python versions ", and it wanted clarification on how those differences would be handled. Would they be considered bugs, how would situations be handled if a difference in behavior was unavoidable, and so on. Security was " an underserved area in the PEP ", according to the council; it suggested that a discussion with the Python security response team was in order and that a security review should be part of the criteria for supported status as well. PEP 836 specified a compatibility review milestone to correspond with the first Python 3.17 release candidate—which would be expected sometime in August 2028—that would involve running the test suites of the top PyPI packages to see if the JIT broke them. The council wanted that timeline moved up significantly. " We think that's way, way too late, and the compatibility review should be an ongoing and continuous process starting as soon as possible ". The council also worried about the JIT's design decisions being made " without critical review by the larger group of developers ultimately responsible for [CPython] development, maintenance and support ". The bottom line, it said, was that PEP 836 " mostly answers the questions we asked " with no missing pieces, but it wanted more discussion on those topics so it could " gauge community support and consensus before we're asked to pronounce on this PEP ". Jin replied a few days later to thank the council for its detailed feedback and said that the group would work on its suggestions. Withdrawn After some consideration, it appears, the PEP's authors have decided not to continue pursing the council's approval. On October 19, Ostrowski (who is also release manager for Python 3.16 and 3.17) announced that the PEP was being withdrawn: The Steering Council rightly sets a high bar for a proposal of this scope, and we don't feel we have the personal bandwidth to carry the current version forward. We continue to believe in the technical direction outlined in the PEP, including free-threaded support and a method-based frontend, and remain optimistic about the JIT's potential in CPython. We'll make the reference implementation available and link it from the withdrawn PEP so others who are interested can explore and build on that. Barry Scott asked if that meant that work on the JIT was stopped. Brett Cannon replied that the work would be stopped in the main repository, but it would be up to the community whether the work would continue elsewhere. Dunc Graham suggested that there might be time for an alternative PEP to be submitted before the council's deadline. Cannon said that was not likely, " as all the people actively driving the JIT were either authors on that PEP or contributors to it ". With the PEP withdrawn, the JIT will likely be removed from CPython main fairly soon to ensure that any problems caused by its removal can be addressed early in the Python 3.16 development cycle . It is unclear whether the original drivers of the JIT work intend to continue working on it at all, or if it will simply be left for others to pick up if there is enough community interest. Python's experimental just-in-time (JIT) compiler , which was added to CPython in 2024 for the 3.13 release , is on its way out. In June, the Python steering council announced that it was pausing work on the JIT in CPython's main branch until there was an accepted Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) that addressed concerns about maintenance, compatibility, and set clear success metrics as well as a timeline for completion. After creating PEP 836 ("JIT Go Brrr: The Path to a Supported JIT Compiler for CPython") to try to meet the council's request, and after months of discussion, the JIT maintainers have withdrawn the PEP. For now, it appears that development on the once-promising project has come to an end.
The JIT was added to CPython by Brandt Bucher in early 2024. Generally, such a major feature would be expected to land only after the council had approved a standards-track PEP . Bucher had given a talk ( YouTube video , slides ) about the JIT at a Python core developer sprint, and announced his intent to merge the feature—but he had not taken the step of authoring or submitting a PEP for its approval. He was prodded into doing so by steering council member Thomas Wouters, who was also serving as the release manager for Python 3.13.
Bucher and Savannah Ostrowski drafted PEP 744 ("JIT Compilation"), which was an informational PEP —meaning it only provides information to the Python community and does not represent formal consensus to proceed on a feature or project. LWN covered the discussion of PEP 744 in April 2024, and later covered Bucher's talk on the JIT at PyCon US 2024, as well as the follow-up talk at PyCon US 2025.
Work on the JIT had been proceeding on the basis of PEP 744 until this June, when the council had put forward its formal request for the JIT maintainers to create a standards-track PEP. One might wonder, as Antoine Pitrou did , why the council had decided that it was time to speak up and ask for a new PEP. Wouters said that there was no " single triggering event for this request ", but that the council had been discussing the topic for a while and indicated that it was looking to ensure the JIT work did not interfere with other projects. " There's been work trying to get the JIT to play nice with instrumentation, debugging, and profiling. There's also external JITs (like CinderX), JIT-adjacent things (like Numba and PyTorch's compile), and discussions about a tier 3 JIT. " The council had waited until after the Python 3.15 beta release " to be clear that we're OK with the status quo for 3.15 ".
The council asked for a PEP that would make the case for the JIT " as a supported, non-experimental part of CPython: its guarantees, its maintenance commitments, and its impact on redistributors ". The council set a deadline of six months for the PEP to be submitted and accepted; failing that, the council would require the JIT code to be removed from the CPython main branch.
Bucher, Ostrowski, and Ken Jin drafted PEP 836 and published it on the Python forum for community feedback on July 3. It generated quite a bit of discussion, some favorable and some critical. One of the key themes in the comments, such as this one by Wouters, and this comment by Mark Shannon, was that the draft felt like it should be two separate PEPs. Shannon, for example, thought that the PEP should only cover goals for accepting the JIT work and felt that it should leave out implementation details. There were also quite a few calls for additional information.
Bucher pushed back a bit on the suggestion that it should be two PEPs, and Ostrowski defended the structure of the PEP as it was. " Outlining goals like we have in the PEP without being able to share the plan and everything we've thought through alongside it would make me uncomfortable. To me, goals without plans behind them aren't really goals at all. "
When we last looked at this topic in September, the discussion about the PEP had slowed down without a commitment to develop new PEPs or a formal statement from the council. The last word from the council at that time, in the form of a summary of its August 6 meeting , was that it had met with the PEP authors and was " discussing the state of the PEP and whether it answered the questions the SC asked in its request for a PEP ".
On September 21, Wouters posted a statement from the steering council, minus Ostrowski (who is currently a member of the steering council but did not participate since she is a co-author of the PEP), that summarized its position. The statement said that PEP did answer all of the questions that were highlighted in the council's request, " although perhaps some less convincingly than others ".
The council wished to make clear that it was not looking for the criteria that the JIT should meet to be a supported feature, or whether it should be considered such. Instead, the council was evaluating whether the JIT should continue as an experiment in CPython's main branch.
The council said that the PEP was not specific enough about support plans, performance criteria, and too vague or too optimistic about a number of other areas. The statement included a ten-point list of items that the council wanted " to see either spelled out in the PEP, or at least discussed and rejected ". The council's list expressed concerns ranging from memory impact to security. For example, on the topic of platform parity, the council wanted to ensure that the JIT was designed to be easily adopted for new platforms. It wanted assurance that the JIT's design would not be tied to specific platform or require platform-specific knowledge to maintain.
Another area that the council called out was user impact. It said that the PEP was " overly optimistic " about user-visible differences with the JIT enabled. There were many cases where users depend on idiosyncrasies in the interpreter design, " as we've seen with other Python implementations or even just between major Python versions ", and it wanted clarification on how those differences would be handled. Would they be considered bugs, how would situations be handled if a difference in behavior was unavoidable, and so on.
Security was " an underserved area in the PEP ", according to the council; it suggested that a discussion with the Python security response team was in order and that a security review should be part of the criteria for supported status as well.
PEP 836 specified a compatibility review milestone to correspond with the first Python 3.17 release candidate—which would be expected sometime in August 2028—that would involve running the test suites of the top PyPI packages to see if the JIT broke them. The council wanted that timeline moved up significantly. " We think that's way, way too late, and the compatibility review should be an ongoing and continuous process starting as soon as possible ". The council also worried about the JIT's design decisions being made " without critical review by the larger group of developers ultimately responsible for [CPython] development, maintenance and support ". The bottom line, it said, was that PEP 836 " mostly answers the questions we asked " with no missing pieces, but it wanted more discussion on those topics so it could " gauge community support and consensus before we're asked to pronounce on this PEP ". Jin replied a few days later to thank the council for its detailed feedback and said that the group would work on its suggestions. Withdrawn After some consideration, it appears, the PEP's authors have decided not to continue pursing the council's approval. On October 19, Ostrowski (who is also release manager for Python 3.16 and 3.17) announced that the PEP was being withdrawn: The Steering Council rightly sets a high bar for a proposal of this scope, and we don't feel we have the personal bandwidth to carry the current version forward. We continue to believe in the technical direction outlined in the PEP, including free-threaded support and a method-based frontend, and remain optimistic about the JIT's potential in CPython. We'll make the reference implementation available and link it from the withdrawn PEP so others who are interested can explore and build on that. Barry Scott asked if that meant that work on the JIT was stopped. Brett Cannon replied that the work would be stopped in the main repository, but it would be up to the community whether the work would continue elsewhere. Dunc Graham suggested that there might be time for an alternative PEP to be submitted before the council's deadline. Cannon said that was not likely, " as all the people actively driving the JIT were either authors on that PEP or contributors to it ". With the PEP withdrawn, the JIT will likely be removed from CPython main fairly soon to ensure that any problems caused by its removal can be addressed early in the Python 3.16 development cycle . It is unclear whether the original drivers of the JIT work intend to continue working on it at all, or if it will simply be left for others to pick up if there is enough community interest. None of the alternate python implementations got enough traction to really replace cPython as "the defacto home/standard bearer", unlike for JS which got V8 (for 'quite the while', yes other JS JIT runtimes now also exist but binary module compat is not kept), and LuaJIT had breaking changes especially around the debug module and such for a long time, etc. Honestly, I don't know if cPython should even bother with JIT/perf that much anymore considering the amount of incomplete efforts, though I know this specific effort is by far the closest (and is likely to return). Since the whole P3K conversion era, there are so many more options for writing "performant psudo code", though I get some people vastly prefer Python so *shrug*.

Yes, absolutely, because of CPython's C API. Instead of using opaque handles, it exposes pointers directly to the interpreter's data structures, plus many other implementation details. Any JIT has to either drop compatibility with the API, resulting in poor adoption; forgo many of the best optimizations like tagged pointers, resulting in disappointing speed gains; or emulate the API on demand, resulting in a very uneven performance profile depending on what extensions are used. There have been attempts to fix the situation, like HPy, but they seem to stall out because it's a chicken-and-egg problem. The C API would have to be redesigned and extensions rewritten first, and the optimization work that relies on opaque handles would only start years later.

title: What Influenced Your AI LLM Policy
body:
Contributions (code, documentation, or issues) assisted or fully-written by AI are not allowed for ethical and quality reasons. See What influenced your AI/LLM policy? for more information.
While not advisable, you are free to use AI/LLMs to help you navigate the source code or help you troubleshoot issues. Be sure to triple-check its output and never share any of it with the project, whether in issues or code.
Failure to comply will result in a warning . A repeated offense will result in a permanent ban .
Congratulations, you have made changes that you would like to get merge in the CI-tron project!
Use of AI/LLM coding assistants : Contributions (code, documentation, or issues) assisted or fully-written by AI are not allowed for ethical and quality reasons. See What influenced your AI/LLM policy? for more information.
Code of conduct : Like all Freedesktop.org project, contributing to this project requires accepting the terms of the Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct .
Commit history : Please split your changes into atomic commits, and write good commit messages motivating the change.
Fork / merge request : This project uses a fork/merge-request workflow:
Push your tree/commit to a branch in your fork;
Open a merge request by following the link GitLab provided during the push ;
Wait for the CI results, then address failures;
Wait for review comments, then address them;
Once the code is deemed ready by a trusted developer, it will be merged.
Due to an influx of spam, Freedesktop.org had to impose restrictions on new accounts.
Please see this wiki page for instructions on how to get full permissions.
Due to serious abuse of Freedesktop’s testing infrastructure ( details ), the use of the GitLab CI on freedesktop.org got restricted. Only group members can trigger pipelines, everyone else needs the pipeline manually triggered by an existing group member. See Freedesktop’s wiki for more details and possible remediation.
You may however use your CI-tron-based gateway to run your tests by exposing it in your fork. This can be achieved by:
Obtaining a runner registration project token ;
Adding it to your /config/mars_db.yaml file ( syntax :);
Setting the following variables in your project’s CI variables :
AARCH64_RUNNER_TAG_ARCH (default: aarch64 ): Leave empty or cpu:arch:aarch64 if you also have an amd64 runner
AARCH64_RUNNER_TAG_EXTRA (default: ‘’): CI-gateway
AMD64_RUNNER_TAG_ARCH (default: ‘’): Leave empty or cpu:arch:x86_64 if you also have an aarch64 runner
AMD64_RUNNER_TAG_EXTRA (default: ‘’): CI-gateway
Disabling the use of shared runners in the project .
The decision was primarily taken on ethical grounds:
Why reward the bad actors who have been consistently DDoS’ing our Freedesktop.org infrastructure?
Why spend our limited time interacting with someone else’s machine when we could be training real people who could become future contributors?
Why give legitimacy to the tools that are breaking the social contracts of the free software movement, as defined by their software licenses, thus allowing LLM users to effectively bypass FOSS usage conditions?
While these are political stances, the pragmatic reason is that AI/LLM contributions are a risk for the future maintainability of the project:
Why risk eroding the core-developers’ understanding of the whole system by outsourcing part of the design?
Why make the the quick-and-easy brute force solution practical when we could take the time to research the problem and find a more maintainable fix?
Why depend on an external service that we have no control over when it can: regress, price us out, revoke our access, or be weaponized to sabotage our project?
Why risk accidentally introducing code released by another open source project using an incompatible license?
We understand that you may not have the time needed to adhere to these ideals. We would thus kindly ask you to open an issue using your own words rather than a merge request: We would rather implement something from scratch rather than reviewing the output of your AI/LLM.

title: Distinctive CC44 number plate fetches Dh6.72 million at lucrative Dubai auction
body: A motoring enthusiast is set to stand out in traffic after snapping up a distinctive CC44 vehicle number plate for Dh6.7 million ($1.8 million) at a lucrative auction in Dubai. The major sale to the unnamed bidder proved to be the biggest of the night, as 60 rare number plates went under the hammer at an event held by the Roads and Transport Authority at Hilton Dubai Al Habtoor City at the weekend. The auction amassed sales of Dh65.7 million, with CC44 leading the way, followed closely by BB18, which fetched Dh6.6 million, BB80, which sold for Dh5.9 million, and BB117, which went for Dh1 million. The open auction – the 121st organised by the RTA – featured three, four and five-digit combinations across the AA, BB, CC, H, U, V, W, X, Y and Z codes. Record bids The success of the event served to highlight the enduring appeal of unique number plates for drivers keen to stand out from the crowd. Bidders have shown they are prepared to dig deep to secure premium plates, with in-demand numbers selling for record prices. In April 2023, an Emirati bidder who paid a record Dh55 million for Dubai's number 7 plate at an auction for the One Billion Meals campaign. That broke a record set in 2008, when businessman Saeed Al Khouri paid 50 times the opening Dh1 million bid for the coveted number 1 plate at a charity auction in Abu Dhabi. Growing demand Dubai's expanding vehicle premium market is poised to welcome the UAE's first escrow-backed online marketplace. The Mazal app will hold buyers’ funds until ownership transfer is confirmed, providing security to a second-hand market that has traditionally relied on social media, independent brokers and manual processes. The platform aligns with RTA regulations , offering a secure marketplace with verified buyers and increasing confidence in high-value auctions. Dubai’s private number plate market is growing by about 20 per cent a year, with single-digit and special-number plates commanding high values. In the past three years, Dubai’s status-symbol vehicle plate market has seen Dh1.7 billion in transactions, Mazal app data analysts have said. Mazal will manage these high-value transactions.

title: JIBWIS disowns viral video preaching violence, religious intolerance; demands probe
body:
The Jama’atu Izalatil Bid’ah Wa Iqamatis Sunnah (JIBWIS) has distanced itself from a viral video of a group in its First Aid Group uniform chanting threats to Christians.
In the video, the leader of the group is heard soliciting assault rifles to carry out mass killings in churches in Enugu and Plateau states.
The National Chairman of JIBWIS, Abdullahi Bala-Lau, condemned the footage and urged the State Security Services (SSS), the Nigeria Police Force, and other security agencies to launch an immediate investigation, unmask those behind the recording, and prosecute anyone found culpable.
Mr Bala-Lau stated that the inciting remarks and calls for violence are entirely foreign to the core values, teachings, and objectives of JIBWIS.
He cautioned that merely wearing the organisation’s First Aid Group uniform or standing among members does not confer official representation or authority to speak on behalf of the body.
Expressing concern about the video’s timing and nature, the cleric noted that the incident might be a calculated effort by external actors to smear the organisation’s image and undermine national peace.
He pointed to JIBWIS’s peacebuilding track record, citing its recent international conference in Abuja, which convened Christian leaders, scholars from Islamic denominations, and international delegates to foster interfaith harmony and religious tolerance.
The National Chairman of Jama’atu Izalatil Bid’ah Wa Iqamatis Sunnah (JIBWIS), Sheikh Abdullahi Bala Lau, has strongly condemned a viral video showing a man dressed in the uniform of the organisation’s First Aid Group, participating in a jogging exercise and chanting provocative statements calling for AK-47 rifles to be given to them to enable them to travel to Enugu on Sunday and carry out an attack.
Reacting to the disturbing development, Sheikh Bala Lau called on the Department of State Services (DSS), the Nigeria Police Force and other relevant security agencies to immediately investigate the incident, identify those responsible and ensure that anyone found culpable is brought to justice in accordance with the law.
The National Chairman categorically dissociated JIBWIS from the inflammatory statements, stressing that such expressions of violence, intimidation and threats against any community are completely alien to the principles, teachings and objectives upon which the organisation was established.
He emphasised that wearing the JIBWIS First Aid Group uniform or appearing among its members does not automatically mean an individual is acting on behalf of the organisation or with its authorisation.
Sheikh Bala Lau further expressed concern that the incident could represent a deliberate attempt by individuals or external interests to misrepresent the organisation and damage its longstanding reputation. He therefore urged security agencies to thoroughly investigate the circumstances surrounding the video, including the identity, affiliation and possible motives of those involved.
The Chairman recalled that JIBWIS recently organised an international conference in Abuja, bringing together Christian leaders, Muslim scholars from different Islamic schools of thought, prominent personalities and participants from different parts of the world, with the central objective of promoting interfaith dialogue, mutual understanding, religious tolerance and peaceful coexistence.
He questioned how an organisation that has consistently invested its resources, leadership and institutional efforts in building bridges across religious and ethnic divides could reasonably be associated with statements advocating violence against fellow Nigerians.
For approximately 48 years since its establishment, JIBWIS has remained committed to the propagation of authentic Islamic teachings, the promotion of the Sunnah of Prophet Muhammad (SAW), moral reformation, education, humanitarian services and the peaceful coexistence of people irrespective of their religious, ethnic or geographical backgrounds.

title: Ifeanyi Okoye emerges 12th President of MAN
body: By Yinka Kolawole The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) has elected Dr. Ifeanyi Okoye, Chief Executive Officer of Juhel Nigeria Limited, as its 12th President . He succeeds Otunba Francis Meshioye, who completed his four-year tenure at the recently-concluded 54th Annual General Meeting of the association held on 7th October 2026 in Lagos. A statement by Director General of MAN, Segun Ajayi-Kadir, noted that Okoye holds a Bachelor’s degree in Pharmacy from the University of Ife (now Obafemi Awolowo University) with a Bachelor’s degree in Pharmacy and an M.Sc. and PhD in Pharmaceutical Technology and Industrial Pharmacy from the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, graduating as the best student in his class. He established JUHEL Nigeria Limited in 1987, a wholly indigenous pharmaceutical manufacturing company with headquarters in Enugu, Enugu State, and moved to its permanent site in Emene, Enugu, in 2001 with facilities expanded to include syrups and capsules. In 2010, JUHEL opened a major parenteral manufacturing facility in Awka, Anambra State. Okoye is a Fellow of the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria and an alumnus of Harvard Business School in Boston, USA. He attended the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies in Kuru, Plateau State, and was conferred the national honour of Officer of the Order of the Federal Republic (OFR) in 2012. He has served on several committees, including the Ministerial Committee on the Establishment of World-Class Hospitals and Diagnostic Centers from 2013 to 2015; Member of the Governing Council of the Standard Organization of Nigeria (SON) – 2009 to 2022. Before he was elected President, Okoye served MAN in various capacities, including as Chairman of the Enugu, Anambra and Ebonyi States Branches from 1998 to 2005, and as Vice President from 2006 to 2010. The post Ifeanyi Okoye emerges 12th President of MAN appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Oil spill in Odidi: Is an end finally in sight?
body: •It’s serious, 216 communities affected — Gov Oborevwori •Orders Health Commissioner to deliver medicare •Says Heritage Energy must keep to October deadline By Jimitota Onoyume, Assistant News Editor Has an end finally come for the nearly nine-month crude oil spill in Odidi community, Warri South-West Local Government Area of Delta State? That is the question on the lips of many residents and natives of the area following Governor Sheriff Oborevwori’s charge to Heritage Energy Operational Services Limited, HEOSL, to ensure that the company keeps its promise to redress the devastating situation this October. General Manager, Operations Integrity, HEOSL, Nelson Wilbert, had assured that the company was committed to bringing the spill to an end, saying it would work with relevant stakeholders to achieve this. Wilbert spoke when Governor Oborevwori visited the community for an on-the-spot assessment of the situation. What the governor said he saw during the visit while addressing the community appeared far worse than the information he had earlier. After touring the affected areas, Oborevwori expressed shock at the magnitude of the pollution and the economic devastation it had caused. He said he had initially been briefed that about 86 communities were affected, only to discover that the pollution had spread to as many as 216 communities along the coastal lines. “We have come here to see and not just to get report in the office. The thing is spreading. When it started, it was 89 communities. Today from your record, you said 216 communities. We believe there are small small villages that are affected and not captured,“ the governor said. Deeply moved by compassion, he immediately directed his Commissioner for Health, Dr. Joseph Onojaemo to provide urgent medicare for residents of the affected communities, stressing that the intervention of his administration would go beyond the distribution of relief materials, given the severity of the situation. “We have to take this matter seriously. Once you see what is happening, you realise that it is a very big issue. We don’t want our people dying at this time. We cannot afford to lose our focus or waste time. We have to act quickly and decisively,” he said. The governor also directed Heritage to provide medical support services in the affected areas, insisting that residents should be medically examined to determine the possible health implications of prolonged exposure to the pollution. He ordered the Commissioner for Health, Dr. Onojaemo to immediately deploy and coordinate medical teams to the affected communities and ensure that necessary medications are made available. Oborevwori further warned that the state government would not sleep over the matter until the company fulfilled its promise to redress the problem this month, instructing his Commissioner for Environment, Hon. Moses Ogodo, to keep his eyes on development in the area . He also called for genuine dialogue between the company and the host communities to resolve the crisis and prevent further tension. For the governor, the crisis goes beyond compensation. It is about restoring the environment, protecting lives and rescuing the livelihoods of people whose economic activities depend largely on the waters. The spill, which according to community folks started in February from the Trans-Forcados Trunkline, has brought economic activities in Odidi and surrounding communities to a near standstill. Long before the governor’s visit, residents who spoke with Vanguard described the situation as a prolonged nightmare, saying their lives had been turned upside down by the heavily polluted waters. Aquatic life, they said, had been severely affected, while farms had also not been spared. Fishermen, women who trade in fishes and other seafood, and others whose livelihoods depend on the waterways said they had been left with little or nothing to do. “The spill has forced us to remain at home in the last nine months. No river to fish or even periwinkle to pick,” Agnes and others told Vanguard. Residents also alleged that a sexagenarian died few months ago after slipping and hitting her head on hard ground while attempting to walk across a surface stained with the crude oil. “We don’t know what we can call this. Our people are dying; we can’t breathe. Recently, we lost one of our aunties. She fell and couldn’t breathe again because of the pollution. We need the federal, state and local governments to come to our aid,” a woman in the area said. “Life has not been the same in the community in the last nine months,” a woman identified as Timi said. Timi said she eventually relocated to Warri in search of something to do after waiting endlessly for the situation to be resolved. Amid the prolonged crisis, residents have also raised concerns over alleged oil theft around the affected oil facilities. Some community members alleged that oil thieves may have taken advantage of the situation to siphon crude, although they admitted that they could not confirm the allegation or identify those allegedly involved. One resident, who spoke on condition of anonymity, alleged that boats sometimes come to the area to evacuate crude under the guise of protecting the environment. “They come there with boats to remove crude oil; where do they take the crude to?” he asked as he gazed into the air as though the answer was visibly there. The allegation, whether eventually established or not, has added another layer of concern to an already troubling situation and heightened calls for greater transparency around activities at the affected facilities. For the people of Odidi and the other affected communities, however, the immediate concern is simple: they want the oil to stop flowing and their lives to begin again. They say Heritage’s promise to end the spill will only become something to celebrate when the pollution is actually stopped, the affected environment is properly remediated and efforts are made to restore the aquatic life on which thousands depend. Now, with October fast coming to an end and the governor demanding action, the question is no longer merely when the promise will be fulfilled. Will October finally bring an end to Odidi’s agonising oil-spill nightmare, or will the month slide away with the promise being yet another chapter in a crisis that has already lasted almost nine months? The post Oil spill in Odidi: Is an end finally in sight? appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Ebola: Patient Arrives Switzerland, Nigeria Continues Contact Tracing, Containment — Pate
body: The Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof Ali Pate, has disclosed that the Swiss authorities have confirmed the safe arrival of Nigeria’s Ebola index patient and her spouse in Switzerland. Pate, in an update on his X handle on Monday evening, noted that the patient is now receiving treatment at Geneva University Hospitals, while her husband has been placed in isolation at University Hospital Zurich. According to him, contact monitoring, investigation of alerts and other containment measures were continuing in Nigeria. “The Swiss authorities have confirmed that the patient and her spouse arrived safely in Switzerland today,” Pate stated. The minister also disclosed that Switzerland had expressed appreciation for the medical care provided by Nigerian health professionals and the cooperation between both countries and the World Health Organisation that facilitated the evacuation. “In our telephone conversation, Federal Councillor Elisabeth Baume-Schneider conveyed Switzerland’s appreciation for the care provided by Nigerian health professionals and the close cooperation between our authorities and WHO that made the evacuation possible,” he said. Kenya Red Cross personnel doff their Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) during a simulation of the evacuation of remains of an Ebola victim in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on October 22, 2026. Photo by TONY KARUMBA / AFP Pate thanked the clinical and public health teams in Nigeria and Switzerland, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health, the Swiss Federal Department of Home Affairs and the WHO for their collaboration. He also wished the patient a continued recovery, while assuring Nigerians that the government’s response to the imported infection remained active. “Here in Nigeria, contact monitoring, investigation of alerts and other containment measures continue, with support from Africa CDC and WHO AFRO. We will provide regular updates through NCDC and the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare,” the minister added. Earlier on Monday, Pate confirmed that the evacuation had been carried out with his approval, explaining that the patient’s condition had improved considerably before she left Abuja. “I confirm that, with my approval, earlier this morning, the index case for Nigeria’s first imported Ebola virus disease departed Abuja for Switzerland,” the minister said. According to him, the patient was stable, conscious and communicating, while her laboratory results were approaching baseline levels. “The index patient was clinically much improved, stable, conscious, communicating, and her clinical laboratory test results closing towards baseline,” he added. The minister cautioned, however, that the patient could still be infectious despite her improved clinical condition, explaining that strict public health protocols were followed during the evacuation. “This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place,” he said. Marie Bakikula, a caregiver at a UNICEF-supported nursery in Mongbwalu, poses for a photograph in Mongbwalu, north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, October 10, 2026(Photo by MARIE RUWET / AFP) The Federal Government confirmed Nigeria’s first imported Ebola virus disease case in the Federal Capital Territory on October 20, following the patient’s recent travel from Uganda. The infection was identified as the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus. Following the confirmation, Nigerian health authorities activated response measures, including contact tracing, surveillance and monitoring of people who might have been exposed. The government initially reported that 44 contacts had been identified, while the WHO’s subsequent update put the number being monitored in Nigeria at 52, in addition to the patient’s husband. Ebola is a severe viral disease transmitted through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated materials. Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal or external bleeding. The incubation period can last up to 21 days, making continued monitoring of exposed individuals important even after the infected patient has been evacuated. The Federal Government has urged Nigerians to remain vigilant and rely on information from credible sources as health authorities continue surveillance and other measures aimed at preventing further transmission. The post Ebola: Patient Arrives Switzerland, Nigeria Continues Contact Tracing, Containment — Pate appeared first on Channels Television .
