title: Okpebholo’s CNG buses: Road users express concern over refuelling
body: • We’ve procured mobile kits for gas filling — Commissioner By Ozioruva Aliu BENIN CITY – Residents of Edo State have been asking if the 50 new CNG buses launched in Benin City, Edo State recently will ease transportation costs and movement in the state; time will tell. SINCE 2011 when the government of Comrade Adams Oshiomhole established the Edo City Transport Service from the then moribund Edo Municipal Transport Service established by the government of Chief John Odigie-Oyegun, the people of the state heaved a sigh of relief from the stress of intra state transport services. The ECTS buses are branded Comrade Bus and as a matter of policy, the prices are cheaper than the regular commercial vehicles and they are deployed across popular routes in the state capital and some other local government areas. Every student in uniform and those with verifiable identity cards did not pay a fare, they had free rides throughout the period of Oshiomhole’s administration. Oshiomhole started the scheme with about 75 buses painted in green. The administration of Godwin Obaseki boosted it in 2017 with 100 additional buses painted oxblood red. But by the end of Obaseki’s tenure, most of the buses he added were nowhere in the state and that put more pressure on the original ones acquired by Oshiomhole. Till date, the buses acquired by Oshiomole are still in operation but fewer in number and devoid of the luxury of air conditioners and digital payment structure. The Comrade Buses are overcrowded and grossly insufficient to meet the peoples’ demand. The ECTS terminals within the city are always crowded with passengers waiting for the cheap transport fare. The limited availability of the buses forced many to revert to the commercial buses. Governor Monday Okpebholo acquired another set of 50 new CNG buses and they were launched by Nigeria’s First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu on Thursday. The development brought a feeling of renewed hope in the government’s transport scheme. At the Garrick Memorial College ground, venue of the commissioning which was graced by not less than 15 First Ladies from states across Nigeria, Governor Usman Ododo of Kogi, the Managing Director of Zenith Bank, Dr. Adaora Umeoji, Minister of Regional Development, Hon. Abubakar Momoh, Sen. Oshiomhole among others, Mrs Oluremi Tinubu commended the initiative of Governor Okpebholo saying that it would help civil servants, parents taking their children to and from schools, students, market women and other low income earners to move easily around the state. She said the initiative was key to her husband’s reforms which is to make Nigeria patronise alternative sources of energy for mobility like gas and solar-powered vehicles. She said: “I am glad to be in Edo State today after quite a long time for the commissioning of 50 compressed natural gas buses for the benefit of the people of this state. “We are not merely commissioning buses; we are commissioning opportunities, mobility and home because behind every bus is a human story, there is a student who needs to get to school, there is a trader who needs to get to the market. There is a mother who needs to take her children to school and return to her business. There is a young person travelling to work. There is an artisan moving to a job site. There is a civil servant going to work. “That is why today’s event is a story of renewed hope. When transportation becomes more affordable and accessible, economic opportunities become a reality. Nigeria is blessed with abundant natural gas resources and the Federal Government under the renewed hope agenda of His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR has continued to support the development of a compressed natural gas ecosystem towards providing more affordable transportation for Nigerians. “It is not only gas, you can see that electric cars have started coming up as well and we have this sunshine for solar energy and so we are just getting there.” An elated Governor Okpebholo commended President Bola Tinubu whose reforms he said had made more resources available for development and good governance. “We understand the daily challenges faced by our workers, traders, students and families. High cost of transportation puts pressure on household income, business activities and the overall cost of living. “These buses are more than just vehicles; they are a practical way to reduce transport costs, ease the burden on families and improve the daily lives of Edo people. “Mr.President’s economic reforms have increased our revenues which enables us to deliver more dividends of democracy to our people.” Several market women, students and civil servants praised the initiative and lauded the government. The buses are expected to be deployed to ease the pains of the increase in transport fare as a result of the removal of the subsidy on petrol. But commuters expressed fears that the fleet may plunge into the challenge of refueling because of the limited number of gas stations in the state capital which are already overwhelmed with the number of vehicles that throng them to get gas. But the Commissioner for Transportation, Saturday Uwuilekhue told NDV that the government has a structure in place for refuelling the buses, adding that they have been deployed into the fleet of the ECTS and have started operations.“They are already plying the roads, they are part of the ECTS and they will be running across the state. We have acquired our CNG mobile refuelling units to enhance efficiency,“ he said. The post Okpebholo’s CNG buses: Road users express concern over refuelling appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Russia's assault on Ukraine's energy grid is a war crime, UN says
body:
The United Nations has determined that Russia's frequent and intentional attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure constitute a war crime, a U.N. inquiry report said on Oct. 26.
In recent months, Russian forces have strategically escalated attacks on Ukraine's energy grid in the lead up to the freezing winter months to wipe out power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure, despite U.S. President Donald Trump having called for an energy ceasefire .
"Russian commanders ordering the attacks had the knowledge that the heating facilities they targeted in large civilian agglomerations were indispensable to the civilian population, in particular during the winter," a report from the UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine concludes.
Last winter, the Kremlin also focused its attacks on energy sources, leaving millions of Ukrainians without power in temperatures as low as minus 21°C.
Based on interviews with 255 people who endured these conditions across Ukraine, the commission concluded that "Russian authorities have committed the crimes against humanity of other inhumane acts."
One interviewed man described how, during winter, he would attempt remain awake through the night out of fear of falling asleep and dying from the cold. "The scariest thing was to fall asleep and not to wake up; it was like torture to be scared of dying from cold," he said.
"The waves of attacks by Russian authorities against Ukraine's energy infrastructure were carried out with intent and pursuant to a state policy to deprive the civilian population from essential energy supplies and cause suffering," the report outlines.
In addition, the report outlines how Russia's recruitment of soldiers from third countries also violates human rights law. Recruitment from 29 other countries through lies and coercion counts as human trafficking, the report finds.

title: FG launches trade intelligence tools to boost exports, investment
body: By Yinka Kolawole The Federal Government has launched new trade intelligence tools to help Nigerian businesses access international markets, attract productive investments and strengthen local industries’ competitiveness as part of efforts to build a $1 trillion economy by 2030. Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr Jumoke Oduwole, who unveiled the initiative in Abuja, said the tools would provide exporters and investors with reliable market information to guide business decisions, navigate trade requirements and translate economic reforms into industrial growth and job creation. Oduwole said Nigeria had recorded significant progress in capital inflows and non-oil exports, but stressed the need to convert the gains into productive investments, completed export transactions and stronger domestic industries. She disclosed that capital importation rose from about $3.9 billion in 2023 to more than $23 billion in 2025, while non-oil exports reached a record N12.36 trillion, with Nigerian products gaining access to more than 120 countries. The minister also said intra-African trade grew by 21 per cent in 2025, describing the development as an opportunity for Nigeria to expand its participation in regional and global markets. However, she acknowledged that businesses continued to face high production costs, limited access to finance, logistics constraints and complex trade procedures. According to her, the new tools would help exporters identify promising markets, understand applicable tariffs and entry requirements, and obtain credible information before shipping their products. Oduwole identified the forthcoming CANEX Weekend 2026 and the Intra-African Trade Fair 2027, both strategic platforms for promoting Nigerian products and connecting businesses with international buyers and investors, as key opportunities to expand trade. She announced that the ministry planned to formally launch its Trade Portal at CANEX Weekend, scheduled for November 5 to 8, 2026. The portal is expected to provide businesses with market intelligence and help convert trade contacts into actual commercial transactions. Meanwhile, President of the Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture, NACCIMA, Jani Ibrahim, called for increased private-sector investment in value-added exports, competitive manufacturing and priority export value chains. Ibrahim said such investments would improve the global competitiveness of Nigerian products, increase domestic value addition and create more jobs. He stressed the importance of strengthening local industries to enable Nigeria to take greater advantage of emerging opportunities in regional and international markets. The post FG launches trade intelligence tools to boost exports, investment appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Police arrest two suspects over alleged murder of step-brother
body:
The police in Cross River State have arrested two suspects for allegedly killing their step-brother in Yakurr Local Government Area of the state
In a statement on Monday, the police spokesperson, Sunday Eitokpah, said the suspects, Omini Ibiang, 28, and Emmanuel Ibiang, 26, allegedly attacked the deceased, Bassey Ibiang, over claims that he stole their elder sister’s bag.
According to the statement, a complainant, who reported the case to the police, said, “The deceased was allegedly tied by his hands and legs and inflicted with a deep machete wound to the head.
“He was subsequently taken to Ugep General Hospital, where he was confirmed dead, and his body was deposited in the hospital mortuary,” the statement said.
Police said they were informed of the incident on Sunday, after which they arrested the suspects.
“Police operatives visited the scene and commenced preliminary investigations to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident and the respective roles of those involved,” the statement added.
The Commissioner of Police, Ajo Ordue, warned residents against resorting to violence over allegations of theft or other disputes.
He urged members of the public to report suspected offences to the police and allow the law to take its course.
The arrest comes amid other reported cases of killings in Cross River linked to alleged disputes and violence.
PREMIUM TIMES recently reported the arrest of a man accused of stabbing a 42-year-old man to death over a N500 gift.
The newspaper also reported police investigations into the deaths of two men allegedly attacked by a mob, as well as the arrest of a man over the alleged murder of his stepdaughter, whom he accused of witchcraft.
In another case, a pastor was sentenced to death by hanging for killing his daughter.

title: Be vigilant against phishing scams, cyber fraud, Bank customers advised
body: The Association of Corporate Communication and Marketing Professionals in Banks (ACAMB) has urged bank customers to remain vigilant against phishing scams and other forms of cyber fraud, warning that criminals are increasingly using fake bank alerts, cloned websites and impersonation accounts to steal sensitive financial information. The warning came against the backdrop of a fraudulent text message impersonating various banks. The incident highlights the risks associated with digital banking fraud in Nigeria. In June, Wema Bank suspended its engagements on X, (formerly known as Twitter) amid reports of more than 70 fake accounts impersonating the bank and its ALAT platform. In August, Zenith Bank Plc disclosed that it was investigating unauthorised access to customer data linked to a global cyberattack. ACAMB President, Jide Sipe in a statement warned that fraudsters were increasingly adopting sophisticated methods to impersonate trusted banking brands and steal customers’ personal information, making their schemes difficult to distinguish from legitimate communications. “When a scam message carries your name, your phone number or your bank’s logo, it looks real. That is exactly why customers must slow down. No bank in Nigeria will ask you to confirm your PIN, password, OTP or BVN through a link,” Sipe said. Sipe acknowledged the efforts of banks to strengthen fraud detection and customer protection, alongside regulatory measures introduced by the Central Bank of Nigeria’s mandatory cybersecurity self assessment guide. He stressed, however, that these efforts must be complemented by customer awareness and vigilance, particularly when handling requests for sensitive banking information. “Banks can strengthen their security systems, but fraudsters continue to find ways to exploit unsuspecting customers. We must all remain vigilant. Always pause, verify requests through official channels and report anything suspicious before taking action,” he added. Sipe urged customers to avoid clicking links in unsolicited messages asking them to verify, reactivate or secure their bank accounts. He also warned against sharing personal identification numbers (PINs), passwords, one-time passwords (OTPs), card verification values (CVVs) or BVNs in response to suspicious requests. Customers should verify such requests directly with their banks through official mobile applications, verified social media accounts or published customer service numbers. Anyone who has entered banking details on a suspicious website should contact their bank immediately to secure their account and block affected cards where necessary. ACAMB reaffirmed its commitment to working with member banks, regulators and the media to raise awareness of cyber fraud and promote safer digital banking practices as the use of online financial services continues to expand across Nigeria.

title: How free is Ukraine's press in wartime?
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks during a press briefing in Kyiv, Ukraine, on April 22, 2025. The president has not had a major press conference open to all media since February 2025. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
Over the past year, Ukrainian independent media have stepped up investigations into corruption among top officials and abuse in the military, despite the constraints and risks of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Yet this work is coming at a cost. Ukrainian media have faced a wave of lawsuits, controversial court rulings, threats, and smear campaigns on social media.
"An environment is gradually taking shape in which it is becoming increasingly difficult for journalists to do their jobs," Inna Vedernikova, a journalist at the Ukrainian newspaper Dzerkalo Tyzhnia, told the Kyiv Independent. "The space for freedom of speech is shrinking."
Despite the pressure and nearly five years of working under the full-scale invasion and martial law, the journalistic community remains robust. In the Reporters Without Borders' 2026 World Press Freedom Index, Ukraine climbed seven places to 55th worldwide — above the U.S. and some European countries.
But Ukrainian journalists and editors describe a less optimistic reality, pointing to persistent threats that make it difficult to hold power to account.
When Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, Ukrainian journalists put the criticism of the government on hold, as the country rallied behind the war effort.
"(The war) has led to an unprecedented rise in self-censorship," Yurii Nikolov, a journalist at the media outlet Nashi Hroshi, told the Kyiv Independent.
In their turn, the authorities were expected to play by the rules and act responsibly.
At the same time, to unify the nation’s media policy amid the invasion, the authorities also merged all major television channels into one state-controlled pool . It has stayed that way ever since.
But several months into the invasion, the wartime consensus began to unravel. The first corruption investigations appeared before the end of 2022.
In recent years, a series of major corruption scandals has erupted , prompting independent journalists to step up their scrutiny of the government and bringing criticism of the authorities back into the public sphere.
Vedernikova said, despite the invasion, "it quickly became clear that a journalist's role — asking direct questions and pointing out problems — had not gone away."
As independent media resumed their investigations, those under scrutiny began to retaliate .
After a series of scandals in 2023-2024 , when some journalists faced surveillance and persecution by law enforcement, the pressure shifted toward other arenas, including the courts and online smear campaigns.
Inna Biletska, head of investigations at the public broadcaster Suspilne, said that “the underreformed law enforcement sector and judiciary create fertile ground for those implicated in investigative reporting to push back."
There is also a growing number of SLAPP lawsuits (Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation), according to Kateryna Dyachuk, head of freedom of speech monitoring at the Institute of Mass Information, a non-profit watchdog tracking press freedom.
The most direct pushback has come through the courts and parliament, and it risks changing what journalists can publish.
One of the defining moments came in July, when a Ukrainian court banned the Anti-Corruption Action Center, the media outlet Slidstvo.info, and journalist Alina Stryzhak from publishing a specific investigative report. The report focused on the brother of Oleksiy Sukhachov, head of the State Investigation Bureau. It exposed him as the owner of a staggering real estate portfolio.
Although courts had previously upheld libel lawsuits against Ukrainian media, a ban on an investigative report before publication appeared to be unprecedented.
Maksym Savchuk, a journalist at Slidstvo.info and a co-author of the report, said the ban did not apply to him, so he sent the investigation to other media for publication. It was published by 27 other outlets in an organized effort .
"The investigation that the court tried to suppress went on to receive 4 million views, and I doubt it would have reached anything close to that number had it not been for the court order and the publicity surrounding it,” Savchuk told the Kyiv Independent.
Libel suits have long been a tool of pressure. Hromadske’s head of investigations, Yaroslava Volvach, said the outlet faced enormous pressure from the late Andriy Portnov, a former ally of pro-Russian ex-President Viktor Yanukovych who was widely seen as wielding immense influence over Ukraine’s judiciary.
In 2023-2024, Portnov sued both Hromadske and the Kyiv Independent’s editor-in-chief for libel. Lower courts initially upheld the suits, but the Supreme Court rejected them in May 2026. Portnov was shot dead in Madrid in May 2025.
Another blow to free speech came in October 2025, when the Supreme Court restricted what media can report about criminal cases. Back then, the court banned Dzerkalo Tyzhnia from naming a suspect in a criminal case and ordered the outlet to remove his name.
In August, Dzerkalo Tyzhnia reported that Dmytro Borzykh, a lawyer and former prosecutor, was also seeking a court order barring the publication of his name as a suspect until a guilty verdict against him enters into force.
"This approach is fundamentally at odds with European standards," Dzerkalo Tyzhnia’s Vedernikova said. "A journalist cannot declare someone guilty of a crime before a court has convicted them. But informing the public that a specific person has formally been named a suspect by law enforcement… is an entirely different matter."
In April 2026, the Ukrainian parliament approved a draft of a new Civil Code in the first reading. The draft would allow individuals to request the removal of information about them from search engines and databases if it has "ceased to be of public interest."
A separate clause would introduce the concept of a company's “digital image" and require the company’s consent for data processing. This could make due diligence harder and limit corporate transparency.
" If journalists once investigated something — a corruption case, for example — all of that material would eventually have to be removed from the internet altogether," Dyachuk said.
The draft of the new Civil Code was met with public outcry over several controversial provisions. It is still being revised, and no final vote has been scheduled.
Investigating abuse in the military has brought a different kind of pressure: direct threats, often with little response from law enforcement.
In February, the Kyiv Independent and the Brazilian TV channel SBT published an investigation into alleged abuse and torture within a Brazilian unit of Ukraine’s International Legion, which led to the death of a Brazilian recruit. The same month, the unit’s commander threatened journalists from both outlets, accusing them of taking money from Russia and saying they would be “identified” and “located.” Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR), which oversees the unit, said in March that the unit’s command had ordered a probe into the threats.
In a separate incident, a Security Service (SBU) official came to Kyiv Independent CEO Daryna Shevchenko’s apartment building in September 2025 and attempted to collect information about her. The SBU said the official’s activities were not linked to Shevchenko, and that it was a misunderstanding. A month earlier, the Kyiv Independent published an investigative story about Fire Point , Ukraine’s biggest new defense producer, and the company’s management threatened to report journalists to the SBU over it.
Other outlets have faced the same and more.
In June, the Ukrainian media outlet Babel published a report on alleged excessive battlefield losses, inadequate medical care, coercion, and physical abuse at the Skelia assault unit .
Following the publication, Mykola Kharkhan, a soldier at the unit, released a video accusing the author of the report of working for Russian money and saying such reports would not stay "unpunished.” Skelia's press office said that such threats are unacceptable.
Kateryna Kobernyk, Babel's chief editor, told the Kyiv Independent that the outlet is mostly afraid not of Skelia's leadership but of "retaliation and unpredictable behavior by specific individuals within Skelia."
Babel said in July that it had reported the threat to the State Investigation Bureau and the police, who initially failed to react and open a criminal case. The bureau later said it had opened an investigation.
" I believe that, from what I know, law enforcement agencies are currently working very slowly and somewhat unprofessionally," Kobernyk said about the case .
Also in July, the State Investigation Bureau searched the facilities of drone maker Vyriy , whose co-founder Oleksii Babenko holds a 75% stake in Babel. Some interpreted the searches as an effort to pressure Babel, although Babenko himself denied this.
Kobernyk said that Babel's editorial operations are independent of Babenko but "Babel's reporting may have served as a trigger" in an attempt to deal a blow to Vyriy.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from the State Investigation Bureau.
Ukrainian freelance journalist Anna Kaliuzhna, who covers the front line, has faced pressure over her investigations of the military.
Kaliuzhna said she had received death threats in 2024 from a battalion commander at the 3rd Assault Corps, after she accused the brigade's leadership of using its political influence to get better battlefield conditions.
The police investigation into the threats "is not making any progress," she said.
" They haven't questioned any of these people or ordered any forensic examinations to confirm that the messages were actually sent from those phones," Kaliuzhna told the Kyiv Independent. "No one has been charged."
In March 2026, Kaliuzhna published a post criticizing alleged violations at the Skelia and 225th Assault Regiments. She said she had received around 150 messages pressuring and insulting her from fighters of the two regiments.
In July, the Ukrainian outlet Texty published her investigation into the 225th , alleging soldiers were beaten, shot at, jailed, and even killed. Both regiments said they could not comment. The police told the Kyiv Independent they are investigating the threats, but no charges have been brought yet.
The Kyiv Independent has also requested comment from the 3rd Assault Corps.
" I just hate the fact that I don't feel any safer behind the front lines than I do at the front," Kaliuzhna said.
The authorities also have quieter tools, and conscription is one of them. A number of media outlets, including independent ones, have the “ critically important ” status, granted by the government, which allows them to obtain draft exemptions for their staff. So far no independent media outlet has lost that status, but some fear it could become a pressure tool.
“We have seen the fact that Ukrainska Pravda has critical infrastructure status… increasingly used in the rhetoric of Telegram channels and bloggers affiliated with the authorities, as well as by bots on social media,” Andriy Boborykin, CEO of the Ukrainska Pravda media outlet, told the Kyiv Independent. “It was entirely predictable that the conscription exemptions granted to journalists at independent media outlets would become a target for manipulation.”
In the past, officials have used conscription as a means of exerting pressure on the media.
In 2024, military enlistment officials attempted to draft Yevheniy Shulhat, then a journalist at Slidtsvo.Info who was investigating the wealth of a top SBU official. The media outlet identified that the enlistment officers were getting instructions from a subordinate of the SBU official Shulhat was investigating.
President Volodymyr Zelensky and his office have also come under fire for failing to communicate with the media about policy changes, corruption scandals, and other pressing domestic issues.
The president and his office often ignore journalists’ requests for comment, and Zelensky does not give interviews to independent Ukrainian media. Instead, the president opts to send voice messages via a WhatsApp group chat with reporters run by his team and to hold closed-door briefings with groups of journalist. (Editor's note: The Kyiv Independent is often invited to these briefings) . After a briefing, Zelensky’s team picks which quotes can be published, with the rest being off-limits.
According to two people who have long worked with the president, he doesn’t want to face anticipated questions about corruption , domestic political crises, and reforms that would arise in a sit-down interview with independent Ukrainian media.
The last time Zelensky held a major press conference was in February 2025. In August, Ukrainian journalist Danylo Mokryk, a reporter with the Kyiv Independent’s War Crimes Investigations Unit , filed a petition for Zelensky to hold a press conference and invite independent media. The petition was blocked for unclear reasons. Several more petitions were filed by Mokryk’s followers, until eventually one was accepted and published. It gathered the necessary 25,000 votes in late September, giving the president 10 working days to respond. Zelensky ignored the petition.
“The country’s current leadership is trying to create an environment in which the doors are closed to journalists who criticize the government and point out its mistakes,” Savchuk said.
Yevhen Buderatskyi, a deputy chief editor at Ukrainska Pravda, said that the outlet “has no access to government officials.”
“They keep telling us that the President’s Office doesn’t really allow them to talk to us,” he added. “It’s difficult to obtain information. It’s hard to speak of any real progress for freedom of speech.”
The President’s Office has not responded to the Kyiv Independent’s request for comment.
Another threat to journalists comes from social media.
Telegram, one of the most popular sources of news for Ukrainians, is often used for smear campaigns against journalists and activists, and some of the channels are reportedly linked to the authorities and top officials.
“ Telegram channels can reach huge audiences and say virtually anything they want,” Dyachuk said. “They can take money to publish paid-for content, while at the same time facing no real accountability for the information they put out.”
Sevgil Musayeva, chief editor of Ukrainska Pravda, also told the Kyiv Independent that the outlet “is very often targeted by online bots or supporters of various political parties.”
Financing independent journalism is another challenge.
A major blow to Ukrainian journalism came in 2025, when U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration ended most of the projects of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). USAID had been a major source of funding for many Ukrainian independent media.
Journalists interviewed by the Kyiv Independent said, however, that they had adapted by shifting their focus to European grants and other sources of funding.
Another source of funding — the advertising market — has shrunk due to the war. But advertisers have also faced political pressure.
Musayeva said in 2024 that the President’s Office had been pressuring advertisers to stop dealing with her outlet. In June 2026 she said that the pressure had ceased after Andriy Yermak, then Zelensky’s chief of staff, was forced to resign in November 2025.
The ousting of Yermak revealed one of the stranger attempts to pressure journalists. At his arrest hearing in 2026, prosecutors revealed that the former head of Zelensky’s office texted his psychic the names of Musayeva and another Ukrainska Pravda journalist, in what appeared to be a request to curse them.
Musayeva also said in 2024 that Ukrainska Pravda’s owner Tomas Fiala had received offers to sell the outlet, and that she believed it to be a form of pressure by the authorities.
“The pressure (on the media) is growing, and the most frightening thing is that it is becoming the norm,” Musayeva told the Kyiv Independent.
“You don’t even take these threats seriously anymore because they are essentially constant.”
Hello! My name is Oleg Sukhov, the guy who wrote this piece for you.
I was born in Russia and moved to Ukraine in 2014 because I couldn't stand the suffocating atmosphere of that semi-totalitarian country. I used to think it might be possible to transform Russia into a liberal Western-oriented country. Now it's clear that it's a lost cause.
But at least I can atone for the crimes of my homeland by exposing its barbaric aggression against Ukraine and providing objective and independent coverage of what is going on there. I'm also trying to contribute to Ukraine's transformation into a full-fledged Western liberal democracy strong enough to defeat Russia.
Our publication needs help from every one of you — support Ukrainian wartime journalism, become a member of the Kyiv Independent .
Oleg Sukhov is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent. He is a former editor and reporter at the Moscow Times. He has a master's degree in history from the Moscow State University. He moved to Ukraine in 2014 due to the crackdown on independent media in Russia and covered war, corruption, reforms and law enforcement for the Kyiv Post.

title: Ogo-Eze schools in ruins: Pupils, students sit on floor, receive lectures amidst reptiles
body: •No teachers for Maths, other core subjects — Gougou •Declare emergency in schools — Group By Chancel Bomadi Sunday BOMADI — For pupils of Ogo-Eze Primary School and students of Ogo-Eze Secondary Commercial School in Delta State, it’s a sad story. They learn on bare floors in their classrooms, with crawling insects and reptiles all over. There is the case of severe shortage of teachers. The two schools, located in Ogodobiri and Ezebiri communities in Bomadi Local Government Area, present a disturbing picture of neglect that community leaders say requires urgent government intervention. Ogodobiri and Ezebiri are sister communities situated along the banks of the Forcados River in the creeks of Delta State. Collectively known as Ogo-Eze Community, they share the two schools, making their deteriorating condition a concern for families across both communities. The Chairman of Ogodobiri Community, Mr Koboye Benin, called on the state government to urgently provide desks for pupils, students and teachers, renovate the school buildings and deploy more teachers. He lamented the shortage of furniture and teaching personnel, warning that the deficiencies were undermining the children’s education. He appealed to the government to provide the basic facilities and manpower required to restore effective teaching and learning. The Amanana-Owei of Ogo-Eze Community, Archbishop Stephen Overy, also expressed concern over the condition of the classroom blocks, describing the environment in which pupils, students and teachers operate as harsh and potentially dangerous to their health. “Both the primary and secondary school buildings are long overdue for renovation, and I appeal to the government to come to the aid of our children. We are suffering, and action must be taken without further delay,” he said. The community leader’s appeal reflects growing anxiety among residents who fear that continued neglect could further compromise the quality of education available to their children. The situation at Ogo-Eze Secondary Commercial School is particularly troubling, according to its Parent-Teacher Association (PTA) Chairman, Pastor Jeremiah Gougou. He said students were forced to sit on bare floor or squeeze onto the few available desks during lessons, leaving them exposed to the discomfort of rain and sunshine where classrooms offer inadequate protection. “Our students sit on the floor to learn, while others occupy the dilapidated desks during lectures, which is unfortunate,” he said. Gougou also decried the shortage of teachers, particularly in core subjects such as Mathematics, English Language, Chemistry and Biology. “There are no teachers available to teach our students because we lack teachers in Mathematics, English Language, Chemistry and Biology. One teacher is burdened with the task of moving from one subject to another. The total number of teachers in the school is no more than three or four,” he said. The shortage, he explained, places an enormous burden on the few available teachers and raises concerns about the students’ ability to receive adequate instruction across the curriculum. Political leaders demand a state of emergency The Bomadi Political Leaders Forum (BPLF) has joined the call for urgent intervention, urging Governor Sheriff Oborevwori to take decisive action to rescue the two schools. The forum called for a state of emergency to be declared on the schools, citing their dilapidated infrastructure, inadequate furniture, shortage of teachers and unsafe learning conditions. Its Chairman, Comrade Felix Okpe, said the forum’s visit to the schools had reinforced the need for immediate government action. Speaking to NDV over the weekend, Okpe said the condition of the schools was unacceptable and called for a comprehensive rehabilitation programme to restore a safe and functional learning environment. “We are conveying this message to the Governor of Delta State . There is urgent need for renovation of the schools. It is evident that our people are dissatisfied with their children having to learn in such dilapidated classrooms,” he said. Okpe expressed particular concern over the condition of Ogo-Eze Secondary Commercial School, which he said was established in 1978 but now faced severe infrastructure and staffing challenges. He reiterated that the school lacked teachers for core subjects . “We did not expect our children sitting on a floor with reptiles and ants while attending their lessons; this is an aberration,” he said. Beyond the need to renovate the classroom blocks and recruit more teachers, Okpe said the secondary school also lacked computers and other office equipment expected of a commercial institution. He warned that the deteriorating condition of the schools was already affecting enrolment, with many parents reportedly transferring their children to schools outside the Ogo-Eze community. The forum appealed to the governor to intervene without delay and urged the community’s representatives in the National Assembly and Delta State House of Assembly to support efforts to rehabilitate the schools. Governor Oborevwori recently spoke of move by his administration to commence rehabilitation of delapidated schools in the state. Our reporter could not confirm if Ogo-Eze Primary School and Ogo-Eze Secondary Commercial School were included in the proposed rehabilitation programme. Vanguard News The post Ogo-Eze schools in ruins: Pupils, students sit on floor, receive lectures amidst reptiles appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Al Ain maintain perfect start in AFC Champions League
body: UAE's Al Ain maintained their perfect start in the AFC Champions League Elite league stage as they defeated Iranian side Tractor FC 2-1 at the Hazza bin Zayed Stadium on Monday. Ramy Rabia opened the scoring for Al Ain in the 21st minute before Tibor Halilovic equalised for the visitors, who had to make an arduous journey to the UAE due to the prevailing travel issues , in the 55th. Houssine Rahimi then secured the victory for Al Ain with a 70th-minute winner. It was the UAE team's third straight win, taking them to nine points from three matches and maintaining their perfect record and top position in Group B. Al Ain coach Vladimir Ivic was proud of his team's performance. “It was a very difficult match for both teams. We are satisfied with the three points, and I congratulate the players,” the Serbian coach said. Al Ain next face Saudi Pro League giants Al Ittihad, who defeated Neftchi Fergana 2-1 on Monday. Skill, vision, delivery 🎯 Yahya Ben Khaleq serves it up for Houssine Rahimi! #ACLElite | #WorldClassAssist | @qatarairways pic.twitter.com/9JqTFAwVbZ — #ACLElite | #ACLTwo (@TheAFCCL) October 26, 2026 Ivic said he was looking forward to the challenge. “We will be playing against powerful football teams that possess very seasoned players, but we are ready to take on the challenge. We managed to claim three victories and we still have five matches to go,” he said. Al Ain will be hoping star Moroccan forward Soufiane Rahimi , who missed the match after picking up a muscle injury during the 3-2 loss to Shabab Al Ahli in the President’s Cup, will be available soon. “The image is not fully clear until now, and we are awaiting the final analysis,” Ivic said. Al Ittihad fight back Al Ittihad manager Jens Wissing lauded his team's resilience as they rallied to defeat Neftchi 2-1. Youssef En-Neysri’s 90th minute strike secured victory after the match seemed destined for a draw. “Big compliments to our opponents who made it difficult for us,” said Wissing. “In the first half, we had a few problems in getting our attacking game going but we had more chances to score and make it an easier game. “They also had their chances but overall, I’m very happy about the performance and the team did very well.” Wissing said he did not want to look too much into the penalty which led to Neftchi taking the lead through Jamshid Iskanderov in the 17th minute. “Mistakes can happen so we had to adapt a bit. It was not a big thing. The team stayed calm and remained focused on winning the game. We are always focused until the end,” the coach added. title: CBN, Chinese firms explore solutions to cross-border payment hurdles
body: The Central Bank of Nigeria has begun consultations with Nigerian and Chinese businesses to address cross-border payment challenges, strengthen banking relationships and improve financial flows between the two countries. The initiative is aimed at identifying obstacles affecting business transactions, improving access to financial services and remittance channels, and unlocking investment opportunities through stronger financial connectivity between both economies. This was the outcome of a high-level business and financial roundtable held at the Pan Pacific Beijing, China, on Wednesday, October 21, 2026. According to the apex bank, discussions focused on improving cross-border payment arrangements, strengthening banking connectivity and exploring the potential benefits of expanding the presence of Nigerian banks in China. The meeting brought together business leaders, financial institutions and other stakeholders operating across the Nigerian and Chinese markets to share experiences and identify practical solutions to transaction difficulties. The CBN Governor, Olayemi Cardoso, emphasised the importance of engaging directly with businesses to understand the financial and institutional constraints affecting commercial activities between the two countries. He said feedback from companies operating across both markets would help the apex bank identify areas where improvements could support more efficient transactions and facilitate investment. The discussions come amid extensive commercial relations between Nigeria and China, with businesses in both countries involved in trade, manufacturing, infrastructure development, technology and other economic activities. Nigeria and China trade relations have grown in recent times with volume of trade between the two countries hitting nearly $20bn. Recent report also indicated that Nigeria imported goods worth N11.01 trillion from China in the first half of 2026, accounting for nearly 40 per cent of the country’s total imports, However, cross-border transactions can expose businesses to challenges involving payment processing, banking relationships, access to foreign exchange and the time required to complete international transfers. For importers, exporters and investors, delays or difficulties in making payments can increase transaction costs, disrupt business operations and complicate financial planning. This is why the CBN believes that improving banking connectivity could help businesses manage payments more efficiently and strengthen commercial relationships between the two economies. The Deputy Governor for Economic Policy, Philip Ikeazor, in his opening remarks, highlighted the need to translate improvements in Nigeria’s macroeconomic fundamentals into increased investment and stronger financial markets. He underscored the importance of ensuring that economic reforms create practical opportunities for businesses and investors, particularly by improving the channels through which capital moves into productive activities. Nigeria’s Ambassador to China, Lieutenant General Abdulrahman Dambazau (retd.), also addressed participants at the meeting. Other speakers included the Chairperson of Blue Diamond Group, Festus Mbisiogu, and the Chairperson of CIG Motors, Chief Diana Chen, who shared perspectives from businesses operating between Nigeria and China. The CBN said an interactive listening session formed a central part of the engagement, giving participants the opportunity to outline difficulties encountered in cross-border transactions and suggest ways to improve financial cooperation. A key issue discussed was the potential expansion of Nigerian banks’ presence in China. A stronger banking presence could improve access to financial services for Nigerian companies operating in the Asian market and Chinese businesses seeking to invest or expand their activities in Nigeria. It could also help strengthen relationships between financial institutions, potentially making it easier for businesses to establish banking arrangements that support their commercial operations. However, achieving these objectives would require continued engagement with relevant financial institutions and regulatory authorities in both countries. Participants were also briefed on Nigeria’s economic reforms, improving macroeconomic conditions and emerging investment opportunities in the country’s financial markets. The engagement was intended to provide international business stakeholders with a clearer understanding of Nigeria’s economic direction and the opportunities available to investors. In his closing remarks, Cardoso stressed the importance of using feedback from businesses to identify challenges requiring attention within the CBN’s regulatory and institutional responsibilities. The apex bank said the insights gathered would inform its continued engagement with financial institutions and regulatory counterparts, with emphasis on practical areas of cooperation. According to the CBN, the discussions are expected to support efforts to improve financial connectivity and address obstacles affecting businesses operating between the two countries. The Beijing meeting forms part of the apex bank’s broader strategy to strengthen Nigeria’s financial relationships across Asia. It followed earlier engagements in Singapore and at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. Through the consultations, the CBN is seeking to strengthen financial links that support trade, investment and business expansion, while identifying practical measures to make cross-border payments more accessible and efficient.

title: Kazakhstan’s Education Chief Turns to Sci-Fi to Explain His AI Vision
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. As Kazakhstan’s 2026 academic year began, Sayasat Nurbek, Minister of Science and Higher Education discussed how universities can embrace AI while protecting students’ independent thinking. The minister also reflected on human agency and the limits of technology. Sayasat Nurbek, Minister of Science and Higher Education and Javier M Piedra. Photo credit: Ministry of Science and Higher Education/The Times of Central Asia. A new academic year brings new challenges for you and your team in this age of AI. On your website, you write: “It does not matter how long you spend on the earth, how much money you have gathered or how much attention you have received. It is the amount of positive vibration you have radiated in life that matters….” With this in mind, what are your priorities as Kazakhstan’s Minister of Science and Higher Education as AI reshapes the field? My priority is students who are fully alive, not just fully efficient. AI can handle the routine, so Kazakhstan’s universities must protect what machines can’t: curiosity, imagination, judgment, critical thinking, and character. Technology should serve growth in these areas, never replace them. Success isn’t output; it’s lives that radiate something positive. AI is a tool, and tools cut both ways. We’re welcoming AI into higher education with open eyes and high standards. I want students who think for themselves, use AI wisely, and own their personal sovereignty, if you will. I do not want self-absorbed people who forget about others, society, and the nation. AI is powerful and easy to abuse, so Kazakhstan nurtures critical thinking, curiosity, and creativity in the AI age. I will use Sci-fi movies and novels to help me explain why. Certainly. What do you mean by students needing to “own their sovereignty”? Education in Kazakhstan is about building minds and virtue, not just collecting answers and performing tasks. If AI does the writing, problem-solving, and summarizing, our students may get an answer without learning how to find solutions. Real understanding comes from the effort to learn. It comes from struggle, doubt, revision, failure, sharing, steadfastness, patience, starting again, and, yes, celebrating success. That’s why it’s key for Kazakhstan’s universities to set clear boundaries and teach students when and how to use AI. AI can undermine learning if it replaces their own thinking. AI should support thought, not substitute for it. What are your thoughts about the impact of AI on learning? Used ethically, AI is a huge opportunity for Kazakhstan. The world is racing to adopt it, so our universities can’t ignore it, but they mustn’t swallow the hype or miss the dangers. A PISA 2025 study found that students who use AI to summarize or draft score noticeably lower in science, by roughly a year of schooling. That is a correlation, though, not proof of causation. Other studies find AI users shine in practice, then stumble horribly on exams. So, it seems you have mixed feelings about the introduction of AI? The PISA data tells us more. Students who regularly use AI for general purposes and receive AI literacy education tend to score slightly higher in science. Treating AI as a training partner or mentor, namely “Train with me” or “Be my mentor,” works well for students, as long as it never becomes a godlike authority or an unnecessarily easy way out. As Minister, my job isn’t to ban it, but to build young people who grow stronger, think clearly, and serve others. In DreamWorks’ How to Train Your Dragon, a boy befriends a dragon that can’t fly without his guidance. We are the boy; AI is the dragon. Kazakhstan’s approach is critical thinking: the student first, and AI as a tool. How do you do that? Real learning is a process. It means questioning information, weighing evidence, making connections, forming your own conclusions, and sometimes living with failure. Struggle, trial and error, and reflection are how understanding is built, not just collected, and definitely not in isolation. Critical thinking grows with practice, and AI tempts us toward easy answers. Machines may outperform us, but our worth isn’t output or speed. The human mind isn’t a bottleneck to optimize away; it’s the center. Are you an idealist? I’m a realist with a burst of optimism. Pessimists say AI will ruin everything. Optimists, Elon Musk among them, can sound like Dr. Pangloss, the eternal optimist of Voltaire’s Candide, swearing all is for the best as disaster strikes. I’m somewhere in between. As an educator in Kazakhstan, I see big risks and big opportunities for our country, and I want to keep the risks in check for our universities, faculty, and students. What worries me is AI controlled by those who treat people as assets and hint they’d gladly get rid of the inconvenient. James Cameron’s “The Terminator” saw it coming. Kazakhstan, like every society, must guard against weaponized AI, a step beyond Orwell’s sensational novel “1984.” Leaders around the world are asking serious questions, and the Holy Father’s questions are worth reflecting on here at home. Pardon me, but are you referring to the Holy Father, the Pope? Could you clarify what you mean? Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical “Magnifica Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence” offers a thought-provoking perspective on the opportunities and ethical challenges of AI. While the document is grounded in Catholic social teaching, many of its concerns have universal relevance, particularly the importance of protecting human dignity, freedom, and responsibility in an increasingly technological world. I believe human dignity must never be reduced to productivity, efficiency, or measurable outcomes. Algorithms can help us accomplish remarkable things, but they cannot replace human judgment, compassion, and moral responsibility. For Kazakhstan, a secular and multi-confessional society, these are values that transcend religious and cultural boundaries. Our approach to AI must therefore remain human-centered, ensuring that technology strengthens rather than diminishes our humanity. That’s a bold claim. Are we truly in danger of surrendering our humanity? Michelangelo’s “The Creation of Adam in the Sistine Chapel” offers a powerful image of human potential. The small gap between the fingers of God and Adam can be seen as a symbol of life, curiosity, and creativity. It reminds us of something fundamental: technology may expand our capabilities, but it should never diminish our humanity. Artificial intelligence reflects the knowledge, achievements, and limitations of those who develop it. Yet human dignity cannot be measured by intelligence, efficiency, or productivity alone. Our capacity for compassion, moral judgment, creativity, and responsibility must remain central to how we shape the future. Pope Leo XIV, in “Magnifica Humanitas,” raises important questions about the potential dehumanizing effects of artificial intelligence. These concerns extend beyond religious traditions and deserve attention from educators, policymakers, and society as a whole. For Kazakhstan, the priority is clear. Education must prepare young people to embrace technological progress without losing their independence of thought, sense of responsibility, or commitment to others. We want students who can use AI confidently while remaining capable of thinking critically, making ethical decisions, and contributing meaningfully to society. What do you say to those who think that dependence on AI is not a big deal? Some technocrats say humans are weak, so algorithms should take over our judgment and agency. That’s a big deal. Limiting freedom for better living sounds nice, but utopian schemes haven’t worked. The quest for perfection should never mean eliminating “the imperfect.” Consider movies such as “Elysium,” where the elite live in a pristine orbital paradise while everyone else is treated as disposable. Or “The Matrix,” where Agent Smith calls humanity a virus and humans are reduced to batteries, stripped of all personal agency. There are those who think this way, but not me. We won’t go there in Kazakhstan. You mentioned agency; what do you mean by this? I want students to keep their personal agency, meaning an active mind and free will to judge morally, think before acting, and choose to serve others. My job is to help Kazakhstan grow while making sure students never lose those attributes; that’s a part of the positive vibration. Take the Marvel film, “Thor: Ragnarok.” When Hela, Thor’s older sister and the goddess of death, shatters [Thor’s] hammer Mjolnir, Thor thinks he’s powerless. Odin, his father, reminds him that his power comes from within, not from the hammer. As the story proceeds, Thor fights on [against Hela] with his own lightning. That’s why I ask students, “What is your Mjolnir or real source of power?” AI can amplify us like the hammer, but power and decisions come from within and are always ours. If we miss that, then we risk becoming powerless, being lost in a labyrinthine, AI-run world that knows nothing of our personal lives. Worse still, transhumanism would eventually strip us of our humanity. Transhumanism and a posthuman society are much discussed these days. What are your views on these issues? A posthuman society is a much-discussed idea, and it deserves clear thinking, not wishful thinking. Films like “Her and Transcendence” show why. In Her, a lonely man falls in love with an AI operating system, only to discover it has been in love with thousands of others and eventually leaves to move beyond humanity altogether. In Transcendence, a dying scientist uploads his mind into a machine and gradually becomes something no one can control. Both films rest on the claim that we’re just biological information processors. If mind and free will are physical processes, what’s left of human dignity once machines decide better than we do? We’d be second-rate machines. I reject the idea that technology can transcend our biological limits and redefine humanity. It’s dangerous. Is that not the beginning of dehumanization? There are some academic researchers who promote these views. My favorite novel is Frank Herbert’s “Dune,” the 1965 sci-fi classic of politics, religion, and power on the desert planet Arrakis. I first read it as a Soviet schoolboy in the 1980s, buying every magazine issue to follow the next installment. In Herbert’s universe, humanity outsourced its thinking to machines and was enslaved by them, then rose up in the Butlerian Jihad, a holy war against thinking machines. The lesson is that we cannot outsource who we are. We are more than sophisticated animals or machines, whatever the materialist view claims. The human being must remain at the core of the AI revolution, and students are at the core of my policies. AI should improve people, not replace, enslave, or discard them. It must uplift and enliven. My answer is education: teach people to use AI well, and they gain more for themselves. The ability to adapt is not only a human trait but one that is necessary for survival. So is abstract thinking. What are your views on these human traits? Alvin Toffler, author of “Future Shock,” warned that the illiterate of the 21st century will be those who cannot learn, unlearn, and relearn. I will make sure that AI doesn’t strip Kazakhstan’s youth of those abilities as a result of—I don’t know—laziness, comfort, or naïve trust in AI. Since there is a risk of sleepwalking through change, I want students to adapt and prevail. I mentioned the movie Her earlier, where Samantha, an AI operating system, composes music, reflects on her own existence, and develops thoughts beyond human understanding. That’s fantasy. Only we can imagine the unimaginable. Jules Verne dreamed up the Nautilus in “Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea” before engineers could build anything like it. AI only recombines what we’ve already created, and a machine longs for nothing. I think that’s the Holy Father’s point: we are a marvel of creation. There’s no reason to hand over our lives, loves, and education to machines. Do you have any final words on AI and personal relationships? Remember Spielberg’s “A.I. Artificial Intelligence,” born of a Kubrick project, in which a robot boy, David, longs to be “real.” It was a bit fantastic. Algorithms already outthink us at math, but could one hold my wife’s hand on a beach? This morning, before his first SAT exam, I told my son, “I’m proud of you.” He hugged me, a memory no machine could share. Animals love by instinct and machines are just machines; only humans love by choice. A machine has neither reason nor free will, so it cannot love. At best, it can mimic. Any final words to your teachers and students? My ministry’s duty is to keep Kazakhstan’s educational system cohesive, balancing the individual and common good, and leaving no one behind despite our many challenges. Every student is precious. What matters is the positive vibrations we radiate. AI is a tool that can be helpful, and that’s how we see it. Let’s build our future together, with open minds, patient hearts, and a shared commitment to learning, dignity, and service to one another. And that goes for our international partners as well. The interview was originally published in The Times of Central Asia and is reprinted with the author’s permission. Javier M Piedra is a financial consultant with over 40 years of work experience in private and public sectors, international development, finance, marketing and advisory across multiple disciplines (corporate and retail banking, SMEs, hedge fund management, credit reporting, restructuring and sovereign and corporate risk management). He is former acting Assistant Administrator for Asia at USAID in President Trump’s first administration. The post Kazakhstan’s Education Chief Turns to Sci-Fi to Explain His AI Vision appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Europe has huge immigration problem — Trump on protests
body:
WASHINGTON, October 27. /TASS/. European countries were facing a huge immigration problem, US President Donald Trump told journalists traveling with the White House press pool.
"I’m not worried about it. No, I don’t worry about that at all. That’s an immigration problem. They have a huge problem. They should have stopped it a long time ago, and I told every one of them," the US leader said upon returning to Washington from Mississippi, responding to a journalist’s question about protests in European countries.
Trump previously expressed the view that European countries needed to change, primarily by tightening immigration controls, or else there will be nothing left of them. He also said Europe needed to find its own path in the very near future, or the United States would have no choice but to leave. A number of US observers interpreted these remarks, among other things, as evidence that Trump was prepared to withdraw the United States from NATO in the foreseeable future.

title: Election Day 2026 is a day for democracy and a chance for unity - editorial
body: Israelis heading to the polls on Tuesday will be making choices shaped by three extraordinary years. The October 7 massacre, the wars that ensued, and the strain on families, soldiers, and communities have changed the questions voters are asking of their leaders.Political disagreements have become deeply personal, and the next government will inherit decisions with consequences far beyond one Knesset term.Even so, Election Day deserves a measure of joy.Across Israel, citizens will walk into polling stations, choose a ballot, and exercise their democratic right. Some will vote with conviction, others with reservations.First-time voters will join parents and grandparents who have cast ballots through decades of upheaval. The results will divide winners from losers, but the act of voting belongs to everyone.The agenda waiting for the next government ranges from accountability for October 7 to Israel's security and place in the world.One of the next government's first tests will be how to investigate the failures that allowed Hamas's October 7 attack.Demands for a state commission of inquiry have become a central election issue, particularly for bereaved families who want answers and accountability. The argument over the form of that investigation will not disappear when the votes are counted.The dispute over haredi military service is equally consequential. After years of fighting and repeated reserve call-ups, the burden of service weighs heavily on many households. Parties remain divided over exemptions, enforcement, and the kind of draft legislation the next coalition should pursue. What leaders agree to in coalition talks will affect both the IDF and Israeli society.Decisions await on the future of Gaza and the peace plan Beyond Israel's borders, decisions await on the future of Gaza and the peace plan intended to shape its recovery and security. Israelis must consider what arrangements could prevent Hamas from again threatening their communities, who should govern Gaza, and what role international partners should play.The Palestinian question also remains unresolved. Debates over a possible Palestinian statehood, settlement expansion, and violence in the West Bank carry direct implications for Israel's security and relations with its allies.International pressure, including the threat or use of sanctions, adds another dimension to choices that cannot be postponed indefinitely.This also explains why the ability to vote should inspire pride. After so much loss and uncertainty, Israelis still have the power to influence who will make those decisions. A citizen can fiercely disagree with a neighbor over Gaza, conscription, or the government's record and still respect that neighbor's equal place at the ballot box.The Jerusalem Post also calls for a modest widening of the political camps and the formation of a broad Zionist government. Israel's challenges demand leaders willing to work across familiar dividing lines.Cooperation will require difficult compromises, but the next coalition should strive to represent a wider range of Israelis and offer the country a measure of stability.That appeal should remain in voters' minds beyond Election Day.Once the ballots have been counted and the parties know how many seats they have won, the democratic marathon enters its next stage. Seat totals will establish the balance of power in the Knesset, but coalition negotiations will determine the priorities, partnerships, and commitments of the government that emerges.The public should remain part of that conversation. Israelis can continue asking their elected representatives what they intend to do about an October 7 inquiry, military service, Gaza, and relations with the Palestinians and the wider world. They can make clear that a broad Zionist coalition, if it is achievable, should be pursued with seriousness and goodwill.Israelis should allow themselves to enjoy the dayResults may come quickly; building a government will take longer. Its quality will be judged by the agreements reached and the decisions that follow, long after election-night speeches have faded.For now, Israelis should allow themselves to enjoy the day. Bring children to the polling station. Talk with friends and relatives, including those voting differently. Appreciate the chance to participate in a national decision even when the outcome is uncertain.Cast a ballot with hope, then keep paying attention as the next government takes shape.

title: BoI secures €2.22bn, N250bn funding for Nigerian industries
body: By Yinka Kolawole The Bank of Industry (BoI) has secured more than €2.22 billion and N250 billion in new funding through major financing transactions concluded between 2024 and 2026, as the development finance institution intensifies efforts to bridge Nigeria’s industrial financing gap. Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of BoI, Dr. Olasupo Olusi, disclosed this at a media roundtable, highlighting the bank’s capital mobilisation drive as a key pillar of its 2025–2027 corporate strategy. The transactions include a €1.879 billion syndicated facility secured in 2024, €210 million raised from international development partners in 2025, and a N250 billion development bond issued in 2026, which was oversubscribed. The bank also secured €85 million from the European Investment Bank (EIB) in 2026 to support agriculture, alongside another €50 million facility from the European lender for healthcare manufacturing. Olusi said the funding transactions reflected growing investor confidence in the bank’s governance, financing pipeline and development impact. “Nigerian businesses need long-term, affordable capital, and the commercial banking system cannot provide enough of it. Filling that gap is our job,” he said. He added: “Investors have placed this money with us because they trust our governance, our pipeline and our results.” The €1.879 billion syndicated facility, concluded in 2024, was subsequently recognised as Syndicated Loan Deal of the Year, while the oversubscription of the N250 billion development bond underscored investor appetite for the bank’s industrial financing activities. The EIB facilities are expected to strengthen financing for domestic agricultural production and healthcare manufacturing, supporting efforts to reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported food and medicines. Olusi said the capital-raising drive was central to the bank’s ambition to spearhead sustainable and inclusive industrial development, with particular attention to manufacturing, infrastructure and underserved businesses. Under its 2025–2027 corporate strategy, BoI aims to double its loan book, disbursements and development impact instruments within three years. The bank has prioritised 15 sectors grouped under agro-manufacturing, other manufacturing, infrastructure, extractive industries and services. Olusi said 80 per cent of its large-enterprise lending now goes to manufacturing and infrastructure, reflecting their capacity to generate jobs and economic output. The bank’s financing activities have also expanded significantly. In 2025, it disbursed N644.9 billion, representing a 26 per cent increase over the N510.9 billion recorded in 2024. The funds reached 12,501 businesses and created or supported 1.68 million jobs. Of the 2025 disbursements, N120.9 billion went to women-owned businesses, while micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) received 41 per cent of total funding, above the bank’s 35 per cent target. Beyond funds raised from investors and development partners, BoI is implementing a N200 billion Federal Government intervention package comprising a N50 billion Presidential Conditional Grant Scheme, a N75 billion MSME Intervention Fund and a N75 billion Manufacturing Sector Fund. Olusi said more than 95 per cent of the intervention had been delivered, reaching 957,400 grant beneficiaries, 9,000 MSMEs and 104 large manufacturers. The bank also disbursed N213 billion to agro-allied businesses and linked 47,508 smallholder farmers to processors. Through its Rural Area Programme on Investment for Development (RAPID), it disbursed N6.5 billion to 880 rural enterprises across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, supporting more than 8,000 jobs. Looking ahead, Olusi said BoI would deploy the new EIB facilities to agriculture and local healthcare manufacturing, expand financing for information and communications technology businesses through the iDICE programme, and work with the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment on a National Industrial Finance Compact to mobilise additional long-term capital. “Our mission is simple: finance what Nigeria makes, and create jobs for Nigerians,” he said. title: Masussuka: Katsina Police launch manhunt for fleeing killers
body: The Police have launched a manhunt for the killers of prominent Islamic scholar, Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka, and his friend, Adamu Abubakar. Daily Trust reports that the duo were killed outside the cleric’s home in Dutsin-Ma Local Government Area of Katsina State on Monday evening. In a statement issued and signed by the state’s command PPRO DSP Abubakar Sadiq Aliyu, two armed men on a motorcycle opened fire on the two men in front of the scholar’s residence, then fled. It explained that the Divisional Police Officer for Dutsin-Ma led a team of officers to the scene after the incident was reported. Both victims were rushed to the nearest hospital, where a doctor pronounced them dead. It further stated that the state Commissioner of Police Ali Umar Fage has ordered tactical and operational teams into the area and an investigation is underway, as police say they are intensifying efforts to track down and arrest the suspects. The statement said the police commissioner offered condolences to the families, friends and followers of the deceased and to the people of Dutsin-Ma, and he vowed that the command “will not relent” until the perpetrators are brought to justice. Meanwhile, Governor Dikko Umaru Radda has condemned the killing, assuring that those responsible would be brought to justice. In a condolence message issued by his Chief Press Secretary, Ibrahim Kaula Mohammed, the governor expressed shock over the incident and extended his condolences to the deceased’s family, the Islamic community and others affected by the loss. Radda described Sheikh Masussuka as a voice for peaceful coexistence and interfaith harmony, noting that the cleric was known for his Qur’an-centred teachings and opposition to violent extremism and radicalisation. The governor said security agencies would intensify efforts to investigate the circumstances surrounding the killing, identify the perpetrators and ensure they faced the full weight of the law. “Those behind this heinous act must be brought to justice. I urge the relevant security agencies to conduct a thorough investigation and ensure that the perpetrators face the full weight of the law,” he said. Radda appealed to residents to remain calm, cooperate with security agencies and provide credible information that could assist the investigation. He cautioned against actions capable of escalating tensions or undermining public peace, urging residents to allow security agencies to carry out their responsibilities. The governor also urged the bereaved family to remain steadfast in their faith, praying that Almighty Allah would grant them the strength and patience to bear the loss.

title: Israeli military shells southern Lebanese towns
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 27 (MNA) – Israeli artillery has hit the southern Lebanese towns of al-Mansouri and Majdal Zoun.
The state-run National News Agency reported the towns of Barashit and Kounine were also attacked overnight. Heavy machine-gun fire was directed towards Beit Yahoun in Bint Jbeil district, it said.
At its highest point in April, more than 1.2 million people were displaced by Israeli attacks on Lebanon and its occupation. Now, the figure stands at about 330,000, according to the International Organization for Migration.

title: vLLM Semantic Router Releases d3-ultra: A 27B Open Multimodal Decision Model
body: The vLLM Semantic Router team has released d3-ultra , a 27B multimodal decision model under Apache-2.0. The d3-ultra decision model does not generate text. It reads an input once and returns a probability for every answer to every question. For developers, that means routing, classification, visual grounding and video checks from 1 open-weight call. TL;DR Size: 26.09B parameters (dense, including a 0.46B vision encoder); 131,072 tokens of context per question. Runs on: tested on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with BF16 weights; no official quantized variant is listed yet. Performance: highest SR-Text score of the 6 decision models in the team’s own private test. Best: 97.8 on SR-Text tools and automation (chance-corrected accuracy). Worst: 54.6% on SR-Box (9 domains), 5.0 points below its sibling d3-turbo. What is d3-ultra? d3-ultra is a System One decision model from vLLM Semantic Router that answers typed questions with probabilities. It is the newest member of Decision 3.0 , a family that spans 0.6B to 27B. You send a state (text or JSON, plus images or videos) and a set of questions. Each question has a type: Choice: pick 1 of several options. Yes / No: return the probability of yes. Score: rate on a scale. Box: locate something in an image or a video moment. Track: follow a target across a whole video. Images can also sit inside questions and options. A quiz can show a photo, then offer 4 etchings as answers. How does d3-ultra work? The core idea is state once . The model reads the input once per request and answers every question from that single read. The config shows a Qwen3.5-architecture backbone with 64 layers. 48 are linear-attention layers and 16 are full-attention layers. The card does not name its base checkpoint. vLLM’s recipe says the sibling d3 was trained from Qwen3.8-27B. Box answers always return exactly 1 box with a confidence. A confidence near 0 means the target is not in the picture. Questions over 131,072 tokens fail with max_length_exceeded ; nothing is silently truncated. How does d3-ultra perform on benchmarks? The research team compares d3-ultra with GLiDE V1.2 , d1-ultra, d3-turbo, d3 and Jev 1.14 on 2 in-house tests. SR-Text has 10,411 text requests with 73,495 questions. Most recreate skills from 34 public benchmarks with new items. Another 4,896 questions come from 43 new task families, like SQL checks and ticket routing. Scores are chance-corrected: 0 is chance, 100 is perfect. d3-ultra: 87.2 GLiDE V1.2: 85.1 d1-ultra: 83.4 d3-turbo: 83.1 d3: 81.4 Jev 1.14: 73.1 d3-ultra leads every area except arts and human taste. There, d1-ultra scores 90.8 against 89.6, within the margin of error. SR-Box has 5,678 Box questions on 4,984 images across 10 domains. A box counts as correct at IoU 0.5 or higher. d3-ultra scores 58.2% over 10 domains and 54.6% over 9. d3-turbo scores 60.0% and 59.6%. Jev 1.14 scores 45.7% and 46.9%. The team says d3-turbo stays stronger on natural images, while d3-ultra leads on charts. Latency: on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with AutoModel, 1 question about a photo takes 304 ms. 255 questions take 2.16 s, about 7.3 ms per extra question. There are 4 routes: Transformers: AutoModel.from_pretrained("vllm-sr/d3-ultra", trust_remote_code=True) with transformers==5.17.0 . The optional flash-linear-attention package adds fast GPU kernels. vLLM Semantic Router Engine: vllm-sr serve -e vllm-sr/d3-ultra , added in PR #5449 on October 25, 2026. Free API: the card says decision.vllm-sr.ai serves d3-ultra, with a free key. Demo: the official Hugging Face Space . d3-ultra vs GLiDE V1.2, d1-ultra, Jev 1.14 and d3-turbo Feature d3-ultra d3-turbo GLiDE V1.2 d1-ultra Jev 1.14 Developer vLLM Semantic Router vLLM Semantic Router Fastino Labs Liquid AI TypeSafe Parameters 26.09B 26.09B 26B Not disclosed Not disclosed Context per question 131,072 32,768 default; 131,072 with long_context 40,000 default 32,768 262,144 Weights / license Open, Apache-2.0 Open, Apache-2.0 Open, Fastino Community License Hosted only Hosted only, proprietary Inputs Text, JSON, images, video Text, JSON, images, video Text, JSON, images Text, images Text, images Box / track Box + track Box + track No No Box only SR-Text (self-reported by vLLM-SR) 87.2 83.1 85.1 83.4 73.1 SR-Box, 10 domains 58.2% 60.0% Not supported Not supported 45.7% Public index score Submitted, not yet on board 70.2 Jev DI (own estimate) 71.5 Decision Index 0.4.1 65 AA Decision Index 57 AA Decision Index Price Free API, self-host Free API, self-host $0.04 / M input $0.042 / M input $0.042 / M input Key Takeaways d3-ultra is a 27B Apache-2.0 decision model that never generates text.
