He said although the reforms of the Tinubu administration might have introduced significant changes to Nigeria’s economic structures, the task before economic experts at the summit and beyond was to ensure stabilisation, rather than seek a reversal of the policies. Also speaking, the Chairman and Founder of BUA Group, AbdulSamad Rabiu, commended the economic reforms of President Bola Tinubu’s administration, saying they had begun to address longstanding challenges confronting Nigerian businesses. Rabiu acknowledged the difficulties experienced by ordinary Nigerians but noted that improvements in access to foreign exchange had created a more predictable environment for businesses. “For many years, one of the greatest challenges facing businesses was access to foreign exchange. You could have all the naira but be unable to obtain the foreign exchange needed to buy raw materials and machinery,” he recalled. Also present at the opening session of the summit were the governors of Anambra and Lagos states, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, and Mr. Babajide Sanwo-Olu, respectively; the Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Senator Abubakar Bagudu; the Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr. Jumoke Oduwole; the Minister of Livestock Development, Idi Mukhtar Maiha; the Minister of State for Budget and Economic Planning, Dr. Doris Uzoka-Anite; and business leaders from across Nigeria and beyond, among others. The post NESG: We’re rewriting Nigeria’s story of under-performance — Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Iran, Russia could build fair energy architecture together
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 27 (MNA) – Iran and Russia have significant potential to shape a fair global energy architecture, Tehran’s Ambassador to Moscow Kazem Jalali says.
Iran and Russia have significant potential to shape a fair global energy architecture, Tehran’s Ambassador to Moscow Kazem Jalali said in an op-ed for TASS dedicated to the the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit.
"The joint presence of Iran and Russia in Moscow highlights the fact that both countries have significant potential to establish a fair architecture in the global energy landscape," he noted.
According to the ambassador, current trends indicate that the future of the global gas market "must be shaped by pluralism, diversified supply sources and respect for suppliers’ sovereignty."

title: Without Iran’s participation Persian Gulf security impossible
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 27 (MNA) – Foreign Minister of the Sultanate of Oman Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi says that the security in the Persian Gulf is impossible without Iran’s participation.
Lashing out at the US policies adopted against Iran, Omani top diplomat emphasized, “The US government undermines efforts to achieve peace by portraying Iran as a security threat.”
Back on Oct. 14, Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi and Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi discussed the latest regional developments, including Yemen, in a phone call.

title: BARMM’s Teduray, Lambangian tribes win ancestral land after 2 decades of struggle
body: MAGUINDANAO DEL SUR, Philippines – Some died before they could see it. Others nearly lost hope. After more than two decades of legal battles, bureaucratic delays and relentless struggle, the Teduray and Lambangian indigenous communities in the Bangsamoro region have secured formal recognition of 117,101 hectares of ancestral land — a hard-won victory that now leaves them with another fight: protecting it for generations to come. The turnover of the Certificate of Ancestral Domain Title (CADT), covering 11 separate parcels, was marked by the traditional Tulak Këgëforor ritual in South Upi, Maguindanao del Sur, where most members of the two communities live. The gathering on Friday, October 23, reaffirmed their shared identity and their resolve to preserve their ancestral homeland. A crowd gathers during the formal rites marking the official recognition of their ancestral land title in the BARMM, on Friday, October 23, 2026. Ferdinandh Cabrera/Rappler The Constitution and the Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act protect indigenous communities’ rights to their ancestral lands, which are held collectively for present and future generations. A CADT formally recognizes these rights. Ancestral domains generally cannot be sold to “outsiders,” and development projects are subject to requirements for free, prior and informed consent from the affected communities, which are collectively have the right over the lands. Timuay Alim Bandara, reflecting on the decades-long journey, emphasized that the achievement belongs to the younger generation. “Dahil sa inyo, itong ginagawa natin… hindi para sa mga matatanda kundi para sa inyo na mga kabataang Teduray at Lambangian,” Bandara said during the gathering, underscoring the duty of safeguarding the document and the physical land for future generations. (What we are doing here is because of you… not for the elders, but for you, the young Teduray and Lambangian people.) Organized in collaboration with the Institute for Autonomy and Governance (IAG), the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), and other relevant government agencies, the event drew together tribal leaders in the region, local executives, and national officials. Two-decade journey The path to recognition officially began on August 26, 2005, when the Teduray, Lambangian, and Dulangan Manobo Ancestral Domain Conference (TLADMADC), represented by Bandara as Timuay Labi and head claimant, filed a petition for recognition, delineation, segregation, and the issuance of a CADT. The original claim covered approximately 201,850 hectares across the municipalities of Upi, South Upi, and southern portions of Datu Odin Sinsuat, Talayan, Guindulungan, Datu Unsay, Shariff Aguak, and Ampatuan in the Maguindanao area. RITES. IP community members watch as their leaders lead rites during a gathering marking the official recognition of their ancestral land in Maguindanao del Sur, on October 23, 2026. Ferdinandh Cabrera/Rappler The road to recognition was far from easy . Bandara traced the formal processing roots back to August 12, 1996, under a Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) administrative order. However, due to administrative bottlenecks, the community shifted its processing efforts to the NCIP through the Mamalo Descendants Organization, officially commencing on January 10, 2005. Jurisdictional complexities and legal overlaps between national laws and the former Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) framework created significant delays. A crucial turning point came with the issuance of Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) Resolution Number 38, which initially posed a cease-and-desist challenge before paving the way for renewed institutional cooperation. Through the NCIP Regional Office XII, the BARMM Ministry of Indigenous Peoples’ Affairs (MIPA), civil society organizations (CSOs), security sectors, and local governments across 11 municipalities, overlapping boundaries were reconciled, clearing the path for the official turnover. Heritage protection and resource management Spanning 117,101 hectares split into 11 parcels, the ancestral domain faces new challenges centered on community organization and resource management. Bandara called on community members and local leaders to foster unity, protect boundary monuments established during the 2016 perimeter surveys, and address pressing issues on the ground, such as land depletion and unauthorized sales. “Ang pinaka-challenge dito, paano natin ma-organize ang mga tao na nakapaligid doon sa mga parcels na ito… dahil ang 117,000 hectares ay nakalat-kalat sa buong claim natin,” said Bandara, emphasizing that unified stewardship remains vital under the new development direction set by MIPA. (The biggest challenge is how to organize the people living around these parcels of land, because the 117,000 hectares are scattered across our entire claim.) Bandara noted that policy issues have now been largely established, with local laws for indigenous peoples in the BARMM ready for implementation. He pointed to the Fusaka Inged Development Office (FIDO) and the Reservation and Arbitration Board (RAB) as established mechanisms to handle development and resolve land disputes. Addressing the need for institutional support, Bandara said the BARMM parliament would need to increase financial allocations for MIPA during budget hearings. “Although we understand that through MIPA there is already an automatic allocation of around P200 million, we think that because this is not the only ancestral domain we are looking at, the budget for developing ancestral domain areas inside the BARMM needs to be increased further,” he added. Bandara also addressed the challenge of strengthening community-level policies to curb unauthorized land transactions. “The only problem left is how to really strengthen it at the community level to prevent it…. [The] excuse before: we had nothing to show as titles. So now, with the issuance of CADT, we truly have a legal basis to take legal action against people who violate the law.” Bandara said governance structures within the Timuay Justice and Governance (TJG) would be strengthened, and communities would be organized for every parcel. He said a higher body may need to keep watch given vastness of the ancestral land. Leaders’ perspectives NCIP Chairperson Nancy Catamco emphasized that with the focus now turning toward development, ancestral lands must be guarded more closely than ever. She pointed out the traditional mindset regarding land titles. “IPs really do not have titles in their consciousness. Because for them, land is not claimed. Land should be used for everyone. That is why the thinking of needing a title came late. Because right now, it’s like waking up one morning and realizing the land is no longer theirs, even though they’ve been there. Then suddenly someone else owns it because they managed to get a title” she narrated. On addressing investors and development projects covering the claimed lands, Catamco pushed for the Exercise of Priority Rights (EPR), emphasizing the true essence of Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC). “It’s more of them exercising their priority rights. Meaning, as long as there is FPIC, what they want to get is their consent to say yes. But the essential function of FPIC is really to safeguard the rights of the ICCs/IPs to their self-determination, not to secure consent from a proponent or a project,” Catamco clarified. BARMM MIPA Minister Guiamal Campong cited the historical significance of the CADT issuance and said coordination is ongoing to ensure the title is legally solid and incorporated with the EPR framework: Campong added that his technical team would coordinate directly with the NCIP to explore the Exercise of Priority Rights (EPR). The NCIP also acknowledged MIPA’s crucial role in championing the rights and welfare of Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples in the Bangsamoro. South Upi Mayor Helen Benito-Padua, herself a decendant of the Teduray-Lambangian indigenous community, was amothional during the gathering. “To my fellow leaders, especially in South Upi, may we continue to stand by and respect our ancestral land. May we not say that ‘that’s just paper, that’s just you.’ May we show true unity and respect the hardship of the people who fought to get this title”, she said. “To my fellow Teduray and Lambangian, let us fight for it. Let us not be ashamed of it, ‘let us not sell it or let money sway us.’ Money can be seen while we are alive, but the respect and this title that we can pass on to our descendants cannot be brought back once we ruin it,” she said. – Rappler.com

title: UNGA First Committee: Weak cyber governance risks global peace and security
body:
By R Anil Kumar 

New York/ Bengaluru, Oct 26, 2026. Discussions over the eighty-first session of the UN General Assembly addressed the implications of malicious ICT activities for international peace and security.



During debates on October 23, 2026 at the eighty-first session of the UN General Assembly, the First Committee (Disarmament and International Security) addressed a central challenge in international cybersecurity: although states have developed a common framework for responsible behaviour in cyberspace, translating agreed principles into consistent practice remains difficult. These discussions addressed the implications of malicious information and communications technology (ICT) activities for international peace and security, including the application of international law, implementation of responsible state behaviour, and the need to strengthen national and collective governance and resilience.

The discussion reflects a growing recognition that cyber incidents cannot be assessed solely as technical disruptions: when they affect essential services, critical infrastructure or government functions, their consequences can extend into diplomatic relations, political stability and international security.

The debate takes place as the United Nations transitions from successive Open-Ended Working Groups (OEWGs) to the Global Mechanism on developments in the field of ICTs in the context of international security and advancing responsible State behaviour. Established following the OEWG’s 2021–2025 work, the mechanism began its first substantive plenary session in July 2026. Its agenda is organised around five pillars: existing and potential threats; norms and principles of responsible state behaviour; international law; confidence-building measures; and capacity-building. This institutional transition is significant because it provides a continuing, inclusive forum for states to discuss practical implementation rather than repeatedly renegotiating the foundations of international cyber diplomacy. The challenge now is to translate accumulated political agreement into concrete measures that reduce risks and strengthen cooperation, which shall be addressed over the dedicated thematic group meetings, scheduled for December 7-11, 2026.

The underlying governance problem concerns the relationship between established international law and the voluntary, non-binding norms developed specifically for state conduct in cyberspace. States have affirmed that international law applies to their use of ICTs, including the UN Charter and, where relevant, international humanitarian law and international human rights law. The framework also includes 11 voluntary norms intended to encourage responsible behaviour, such as protecting critical infrastructure, cooperating to address malicious ICT activity and taking appropriate measures to prevent the use of a state’s territory for internationally wrongful acts involving ICTs.

These norms help articulate expectations of conduct and provide a basis for cooperation. Their effectiveness, however, depends on implementation, transparency and states’ willingness to explain how they interpret and apply these principles. Disagreements persist over sovereignty, due diligence, attribution and the circumstances in which a cyber operation may constitute a prohibited use of force or an armed attack.

Operationally, weak governance can create opportunities for malicious activity to escalate into wider political and security crises. Cyber operations targeting energy networks, telecommunications, financial services, healthcare or public administration can disrupt essential services and generate consequences beyond the initially affected systems. State-sponsored operations, criminal groups and proxy actors further complicate the threat landscape, particularly when governments disagree over attribution or the appropriate response.

The principal obstacle is the difficulty of securing consistent implementation amid geopolitical competition and unequal national capabilities. States differ in their interpretations of responsible behaviour, the role of sovereignty in cyberspace and the appropriate balance between national security and an open, interoperable internet. Moreover, much of the infrastructure involved is owned or operated by private companies, while important technical expertise resides in industry, academia and civil society.

Why does it matter?

The First Committee’s debate highlights a central tension in global cyber governance: international agreement on responsible state behaviour has advanced, but implementation remains uneven in an increasingly contested digital environment. The Global Mechanism provides an institutional opportunity to close this gap by linking international law, voluntary norms, confidence-building and capacity-building within a continuing process.

Cybersecurity is not merely a technical or national-resilience concern; it is also a question of international stability, legal accountability and conflict prevention. Ultimately, responsible state behaviour must become operational practice, supported by functioning communication channels, stronger national capabilities and credible cooperation. Without these elements, cyberspace risks becoming another arena in which strategic rivalry, uncertainty and inadequate safeguards undermine international peace and security.

title: Aldar reports 25% jump in Q3 net profit amid launch of new projects
body: Aldar Properties , Abu Dhabi's biggest listed developer, reported a 25 per cent annual jump in its third-quarter net profit as revenue rose during the period, amid the launch of new projects. Net profit attributable to equity holders of the company for the three months to the end of September climbed to Dh1.9 billion ($517.3 million), the company said in a filing on Tuesday to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares are traded. Revenue and rental income during the quarter increased by 16.4 per cent year-on-year to Dh9.3 billion. Aldar has “held” property prices despite uncertainty sparked by the Iran war, group chief financial and sustainability officer Faisal Falaknaz said when asked if the company was adopting a cautious approach to new launches and considered lowering prices. “This is the new normal that we're living in. We obviously look at sales on a daily basis and the volumes are still looking healthy. It's something that we always monitor,” he said during an online news briefing Aldar has been "pushing prices incrementally on some projects”, Mr Falaknaz said. “Yas [Island], for example, we launched a project back in July where we broke a record for non-branded residences where we sold for over Dh31,000 per square metre, and we almost sold over a billion and a half dirhams,” he added. Aldar’s Dubai project , which is set to be launched in the coming weeks in partnership with Dubai Holding, will have about 7,000 townhouses and up to 5,000 apartments, with a gross development value of Dh30 billion, he added. The master development coming up near Dubai Silicon Oasis is expected to be built in phases, with the overall development to be completed in a span of five to six years. Aldar's group development backlog reached Dh71.6 billion at the end of September, including Dh59.3 billion in the UAE, which is expected to drive the company's revenue recognition over the next two to three years. Group development sales totalled Dh6.8 billion in the third quarter, down 34 per cent year-on-year, with seven projects launched in that period. It brings the number of new launches so far this year to 12. UAE sales for the period fell 45 per cent to Dh5 billion. UAE’s property market, which has boomed in recent years on the back of government initiatives such as residency permits for retired and remote staff and the expansion of the golden visa programme, is showing signs of slowing down amid uncertainty caused by the Iran war. Abu Dhabi’s residential property market was mixed in the third quarter, with transaction volumes falling 7 per cent annually to 6,085, while values rose 32 per cent to Dh21.5 billion, a Savills report found. In Dubai, the volume and value of residential property transactions fell in the third quarter as buyers became “more cautious” amid the regional uncertainty. Dubai recorded home sales worth a total of Dh72.6 billion in the three months to the end of September, down 47 per cent compared with the same period last year. The number of transactions dropped 38 per cent to 34,000, a report by property consultants Cavendish Maxwell said this month. Aldar expansion Aldar, in which Mubadala Investment Company increased its shareholding from 27.01 per cent to 28.03 per cent of the company’s issued share capital in August, is expanding across the UAE with new partnerships. This month, the developer agreed to acquire more than 1,100 homes in Sharjah from Arada for Dh1.1 billion, marking its first investment in the emirate. The deal covers nine buildings within three residential blocks at Aljada, Arada’s flagship mixed-use development, with delivery scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2029. The investment builds on a Dh15 billion development partnership announced last month by Aldar and Arada that includes the development of new projects on the Abu Dhabi-Dubai border.

title: Russian sabotage network behind Romanian arson attack, officials say
body:
A fire that broke out on Sept. 14 near a state-owned arms company in Romania was coordinated by a Russian network, Romanian officials said on Oct. 26.
The fire erupted in Brasov, in central Romania , near CARFIL SA, a subsidiary of the national company ROMARM.
The arson attack is "part of a larger campaign of sabotage operations attributed to the Russian Federation in Europe," according to a news release from Romania's Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism, known as DIICOT, and the Romanian Intelligence Service.
Romanian officials identified three perpetrators who they said were coerced by Russian operatives into carrying out the attack. Two suspects are said to be from Belarus and one from Ukraine.
Two have been arrested, allegedly while preparing to carry out similar attacks in Germany, according to DIICOT.
The third suspect remains at large and is believed to be in Poland. European authorities issued a warrant for his arrest on Monday.
Romanian investigators believe that prior to the Brasov fire, the suspects instigated similar incidents which were also coordinated by Russia.
According to the Romanian Intelligence Service, the sabotage operations aim to intimidate and undermine the defense capabilities of affected states, and weaken their contributions to European and regional security.
The attacks join a string of similar incidents across Europe that authorities believe were instigated by Russian operatives.
Lithuanian forces thwarted Russian attempts to burn down Starlink satellite communications equipment on Oct. 18. A similar incident happened in Poland less than a month prior. In August, an arson attack against a defense contractor in Tallinn was likely caused by Russian sabotage operations, Estonian officials said.
Experts warn that the increase in Russian hybrid attacks is a way for Russia to test how far it can push NATO and Europe — probing the limits of NATO security and sowing chaos without triggering all-out war.
Romania, which borders Ukraine, has also been affected directly by Russia's full-scale invasion, particularly by drone activity in the Black Sea. A civilian cargo ship sank on Oct. 23 after a series of Russian strikes.

title: Cheaper DStv: 4 new packages take effect November 5
body: Canal+ and MultiChoice Ghana have introduced cheaper DStv subscription packages to make pay television more affordable and discourage pirated services and illegal digital boxes. The existing six DStv packages will be replaced with four — Starter, Select, Sports and Ultimate — priced at GH¢50, GH¢100, GH¢250 and GH¢570 a month respectively. Canal+ and MultiChoice Ghana agreed on the new subscription rates after engaging with the government through the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations. It is intended to lower the cost barrier to legitimate television content ahead of a planned government crackdown on piracy, while giving subscribers broader access to entertainment, news, movies and sports at significantly reduced prices. The parties announced details of the agreement at a joint press conference in Accra on Monday, October 26, 2026, where they outlined the new subscription structure and measures to tackle piracy in the pay television ecosystem. Interest of Ghanaians The Minister of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, said the government’s engagement with MultiChoice and Canal+ was driven by the need to protect Ghanaian consumers’ interests by making television content more affordable. “I think that for us, when we began this journey with MultiChoice and now, Canal+, the question had been very simple. How do we put content in the hands or in the homes of Ghanaian families at an affordable price? The Ghanaian consumer is our ultimate interest,” he said. He added that the government was awaiting an opinion from the Attorney-General’s Department before launching a major crackdown on illegal television streaming and ghost boxes. He said the National Communications Authority and the Cyber Security Authority had already reviewed the proposed technical solutions and found them viable for tackling piracy, including measures involving the blocking of IP addresses used for illegal streaming. Mr George said the government wanted to ensure it addressed all legal implications before enforcement began, adding that a committee comprising the ministry, NCA, MultiChoice, National Security, Customs, and other relevant institutions would continue to coordinate the exercise and protect consumers. Not a promo MultiChoice Ghana’s Country Chief Executive Officer, Alex Okyere, said the new structure would simplify DStv’s offerings from six packages to four while expanding the content available to subscribers. He said the GH¢50 Starter package would offer 90 channels, including selected entertainment, movie, children’s and free-to-air channels as well as all La Liga matches, while the GH¢100 Select package would provide 123 channels. The GH¢250 Sports package would carry the company’s entire football offering, including the Premier League and UEFA Champions League, compared with GH¢563 currently required to access the full football offering. Ultimate, which replaces the current GH¢854 Premium package, would cost GH¢570 and include additional premium sports such as Formula One, golf, tennis, MotoGP and rugby. “This is not a promo. These are the new packs, new prices that are here to stay. These are the new packs, new prices that are here to stay. So, I think that answers the question,” Mr Okyere said. Piracy effects The Executive Vice-President of Public Affairs for Rest of Africa at Canal+, Dr Keabetswe Modimoeng, described the agreement as a product of sustained engagement between the company and the government and an example of the benefits expected from the Canal+ and MultiChoice merger. He said piracy remained a major threat to the creative industry because illegal consumption of content deprived people across the production value chain of income, including producers, actors, costume designers and make-up artists. Dr Modimoeng said Canal+ was therefore encouraged to make combating piracy a priority, stressing that protecting content ultimately meant safeguarding livelihoods. He added that the country’s macroeconomic and currency stability also made it easier for the company to run the projections and cost modelling needed for sustainable pricing.

title: Ballon d’Or: Kane, Putellas crowned world’s best footballers in London
body:
Harry Kane has ended England’s 25-year wait for the men’s Ballon d’Or after winning the prestigious individual award at Monday’s ceremony in London.
The Bayern Munich striker became the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 to be named the world’s best male footballer.
The England captain claimed the honour ahead of a strong field of nominees, including France’s Ousmane Dembélé and Kylian Mbappé, Norway’s Erling Haaland, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Argentina’s Lionel Messi and Spain’s teenage sensation Lamine Yamal.
The 2026 ceremony, organised by France Football, recognised outstanding individual and team performances across men’s and women’s football.
The award represents a major milestone for Kane, who has established himself among Europe’s leading forwards through his goalscoring consistency and performances for club and country.
Meanwhile, Spain and Barcelona midfielder Alexia Putellas won the women’s Ballon d’Or for the third time, equalling the record set by her former teammate Aitana Bonmatí.
Putellas was rewarded for an outstanding 2025-26 campaign in which she captained Barcelona to four major trophies: the Spanish Liga F, Copa de la Reina, Spanish Super Cup and UEFA Women’s Champions League.
Her achievements also included playing a key role in Spain’s Nations League triumph.
After receiving the award, Putellas thanked her teammates and acknowledged the quality of the other nominees.
“I think anyone here could have fairly won this trophy and be giving this speech here right now,” she said.
The ceremony also celebrated emerging talents, coaches, goalkeepers and clubs that distinguished themselves during the season.
Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal won the men’s young player award, while Vicky López claimed the corresponding women’s honour.
Barcelona Femeni and Paris Saint-Germain were named the women’s and men’s clubs of the year, respectively.
Spain’s Pere Romeu and Luis de la Fuente received the women’s and men’s coach of the year awards, while goalkeepers Cata Coll and Unai Simon won the corresponding prizes in the women’s and men’s categories.
Kane also claimed the men’s top scorer award, with Mexico’s Charlyn Corral receiving the women’s equivalent.
England forward Bukayo Saka received the Socrates Award, which recognises humanitarian work and social initiatives.
The ceremony brought together leading figures in world football to celebrate individual excellence and achievements across the game.
Tunde Eludini is a graduate of the Obafemi Awolowo University Ile-Ife, Nigeria where he studied International Relations. He is a Senior Correspondent coordinating the sports section for PREMIUM TIMES. Twitter : @tundeyeludini

title: Iran, Russia could build fair energy architecture together — Tehran’s envoy
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Iran and Russia have significant potential to shape a fair global energy architecture, Tehran’s Ambassador to Moscow Kazem Jalali said in an op-ed for TASS dedicated to the the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit.
"The joint presence of Iran and Russia in Moscow highlights the fact that both countries have significant potential to establish a fair architecture in the global energy landscape," he noted.
According to the ambassador, current trends indicate that the future of the global gas market "must be shaped by pluralism, diversified supply sources and respect for suppliers’ sovereignty."

title: UAE's Rashid Al Dhaheri relishes historic Formula 3 chance: 'Next year will be something amazing'
body: Rashid Al Dhaheri says he can't wait to represent the UAE as part of the FIA Formula 3 Championship next season after signing with Dutch team Van Amersfoort Racing. No Emirati has ever reached this level of motorsport before, and Al Dhaheri told The National that joining the F3 grid would be a “proud moment” and that the 2027 season could be “something amazing”. Formula 3 is the third tier of motorsport behind Formula One and Formula Two and races alongside F1 at 10 of the Grand Prix weekends. Van Amersfoort Racing is a respected name in the sport and is famed for nurturing young talent such as F1 superstars Charles Leclerc and four-time world champion Max Verstappen. As a UAE national competing in F3, Al Dhaheri is breaking new ground – something the 18-year-old is ready to take in his stride. “It’s not necessarily a pressure, but an opportunity. And for me, it’s just great emotion to be part of this championship,” he said. “Representing the UAE is always, for me, a proud moment, and the objective is to do it in the best way possible, so we'll have quite a lot of work to do.” Al Dhaheri finished fourth in the 2026 FIA Formula Regional European Championship, the category directly below Formula 3. Driving for French team R-ace GP, he won three races, took eight podiums and managed a fastest lap. He was in contention for the title until the final round. He said it was a rollercoaster of a season. “I would say it was obviously quite a step in the journey,” said Al Dhaheri. “I think a lot of highs, a lot of downs, but definitely a lot of things that I learnt from. I guess it’s just part of the journey. But at the end of the day, I think we can be really happy about the season. We’ve done a lot of great steps, a lot of great improvements, and I can’t wait to get going with the second part of the journey.” At the opening round in Austria in April, he started the second race from 11th and charged up the field, passing the pole-sitter on the penultimate lap. He became the first Emirati to win a race in the championship when the driver who crossed the line first was penalised for a false start. “There was a whole build-up during the preseason and being able to win already from the first round, that was something incredible and a great satisfaction and demonstration that the work that we did was right and we just needed to keep going,” he said. Two podiums at Spa in May made him the first Emirati to lead an FIA championship. He won again at Monza in June despite starting from P8. He won pole and converted it at the Hungaroring in July to go 21 points clear after Round 5. Having demonstrated his strength in recovery drives, he admitted overtaking his way up the grid was perhaps more enjoyable than winning from the front. View this post on Instagram “It was really fun because the last one, in Hungaroring, I started from pole and, relative to the other races, it was kind of boring,” he said. The second half of the season was harder. First-lap contact in the opening races at Marseille's Paul Ricard Circuit in July and at Imola in September left him without points in both races, and he relinquished his lead in the standings. His teammate Emanuele Olivieri went on to win the title, with Al Dhaheri finishing fourth . But those weekends have served to help Al Dhaheri better understand what is required to manage a title challenge. “I think a championship is always tricky to manage because when you're there, you always want to go for the best result possible and then when you finish off the season and you know all the results, then you can think about the ifs and buts,” he said. He stands by the decisions he made in France and Italy, insisting “the intention was the right one”. He added: “Of course you learn from the experiences. You learn that if you’re fighting for a championship, there’s certain risks that you can take and some that you can’t. But I think it's all part of the journey.” View this post on Instagram A Mercedes junior driver since 2025 , Al Dhaheri explained that the German marque played an important role in his move to Van Amersfoort. He said: “Of course, when you’re going to a new championship, it’s quite a big decision to be part of a strong team. I think from Mercedes’ side, they really helped out with making the right decision. From my side, I trusted in Mercedes' judgment and I think so far, it’s going quite well. I’m happy about the environment.” Al Dhaheri revealed the deal was agreed while the 2026 season was still under way and that it was a proud moment. “Once it was done, it was like, 'OK, next year will be something amazing'. It was still during the season, so we still had a lot of work to do,” he explained. “I think the true satisfaction will come next year when I'll be able to drive on the tracks and to compete and to raise that flag.” A Formula 3 weekend has only one practice session before qualifying, which sets the grid for the main Sunday race. Al Dhaheri said he will be focused on adapting before the new season kicks off in Bahrain in March 2027. View this post on Instagram “It will be key to figure out the tracks, learn as much as possible remotely. A lot of sim work, a lot of analysis. But at the same time, it’s super key to actually execute on track, because you have one lap,” he said. Al Dhaheri is especially excited to be returning to the Middle East to race in Bahrain and Jeddah, while the last race in Istanbul also caught his eye, calling it “a really cool track”. In terms of ambitions for next year, Al Dhaheri said he always targets a win, “but I think the main thing is to grow and to develop as a driver”. He tempered expectations when asked if he can pull off something special. “I think it’s possible, but it’s really early. There’s still a lot of practices to go. We just finished the official test, so we have a picture, but not the full picture. But I think it’s possible.” Asked if he was just being diplomatic, Al Dhaheri smiled and said: “I don’t want to jinx it.”

title: Singapore Army reshapes its infantry brigades for drone warfare
body:
The Singapore Army is reorganising its infantry branch under the Next-Generation Infantry Battalion (NGIB) concept, adapting its force structure to the evolving threats and opportunities presented by drone warfare.
Having transitioned to motorised infantry in 2009, the army is now restructuring its battalions into more agile formations capable of conducting multiple tasks concurrently.
Under the previous structure, a motorised infantry company comprised three platoons, each with three seven-man sections. Under the NGIB organisation, a company will now have five platoons, each comprising two six-man sections.
Two general-purpose machine gun operators will be reassigned to form dedicated “steel net” sections specialising in surveillance and attack drone operations. Each company will have two steel net sections, each comprising two three-person teams.
The steel net sections will operate Vantage Robotics Vesper surveillance drones and ST Engineering Artos attack drones.
However, the total personnel strength and the number of Terrex infantry carrier vehicles will remain unchanged, with each section assigned its own vehicle.
Beyond these structural changes, the army is introducing a section-level battlefield management system (BMS) that extends beyond vehicle-mounted systems. Each section will receive a mobile BMS device, giving commanders greater situational awareness. The system will also connect to drones, allowing imagery to be relayed to decision-makers.
The full NGIB concept was trialled for the first time by the 5th Singapore Infantry Regiment during Exercise Wallaby in the Shoalwater Bay Training Area in Australia in October 2026, and it will gradually be introduced across other infantry units.
The army said it would also share NGIB concepts with other formations, adopting best practices and ideas where applicable.
The Defence Science and Technology Agency, which collaborated with the army on the NGIB’s development, said a future objective is to enable troops to control drones directly from vehicles.
Chief Infantry Officer Brigadier General Fairoz bin Hassan said the infantry’s role had evolved from conventional light infantry, which fought primarily with direct-fire weapons, to motorised infantry with greater protection, and now towards a force able to engage targets at greater distances using drones.
“We can now fight at a stand-off position. We can use drones to fly far, see far and be able to strike far in our attack missions to be able to hit them. So those are the things that, in the past, line infantry cannot do,” he said.
The army has also recently introduced the Sigma 155mm truck-mounted howitzer and a “precision land shooter”, with these two platforms expected to contribute to the NGIB’s firepower as the formation becomes more integrated with combined-arms units.
The growing use of drones and future robotic systems also presents logistical challenges, particularly in ensuring sufficient energy supplies for field operations. Fairoz said infantry units could no longer rely solely on conventional electrical batteries, and the service is working with Singapore’s defence technology community to develop new power solutions for field use.
Exercise Wallaby remains a premier Singapore Armed Forces training activity, making use of Australia’s Shoalwater Bay Training Area, which is approximately five times the size of Singapore.
The addition of the Greenvale training area under the Australia-Singapore Military Training Initiative will add 310,000 hectares of training space, and enable up to 14,000 Singaporean personnel to conduct unilateral training for as long as 18 weeks annually over the next 25 years.
The expansive training area allows the army to test tactics, techniques and procedures under demanding conditions, and to conduct live-fire training. For instance, Asian Military Review observed army sniper training involving the Accuracy International AX50 12.7mm anti-materiel rifle, as well as Sako TRG 22 and Colt M110 sniper rifles.
Operating far from its home supply chain, the army’s Forward Support Group also expanded its 3D-printing capabilities at Exercise Wallaby 2026. Three containerised facilities can now produce resin and metal parts (including components for drones), and help sustain logistics readiness during high-tempo exercises.
The training areas also serve as proving grounds for future army vehicles before they enter operational service. Potential candidates include the Terrex S5 (known to the army as the Titan) and ST Engineering’s Rhino 4×4 high-endurance, damage-resistant, protected vehicle.

title: Melania Trump’s chief adviser: Russia pledges to respect Oleshky residents’ evacuation choices
body:
Marc Beckman, senior advisor to U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, made this statement in an interview with Ukrinform.
When asked whether the residents of Oleshky would be able to freely choose their evacuation destination without pressure from the Russian occupation authorities, he noted: “Russia has assured the Ukrainians, as well as the Americans, that it will respect the wishes of the people who live in Oleshky,” he said.
According to Beckman, Ukraine and Russia “worked together to put a series of safeguards.”
“Once they are informed of where individuals and their families would like to go—whether to Ukraine, Russia, or to remain in their homes in Oleshky—those safeguards will hopefully provide enough protection to ensure that everyone’s wishes are respected,” he explained.
The First Lady’s chief advisor emphasized that the leadership of Ukraine and Russia, at both the governmental and military levels, has planned the humanitarian operation down to the day and hour.
He did not rule out extending the ceasefire if both sides conclude that it is necessary to deliver humanitarian aid and prepare for evacuation.
According to Beckman, the start date for the ceasefire was determined after technical and logistical issues were worked out jointly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership.
“The date of October 29 was chosen because both the Ukrainian government and military, as well as the Russian government and military, believe it is the earliest and best date to ensure the safety of all residents of Oleshky, bring in humanitarian aid—including medical personnel, medicine, clean water, food, and more—and begin preparing for the evacuation,” he explained.
Beckman did not disclose details of the guarantees provided by Russia or the mechanisms for responding to possible violations of the ceasefire. According to him, Ukrainian and Russian officials have asked that this information not be made public for the time being.
He also reported that Ukraine and Russia have agreed on the composition of civilian teams that will work with the residents of Oleshky, assess their needs, and assist with the evacuation.
The Ukrainian group will be led by Dmytro Lubinets, the Verkhovna Rada’s Commissioner for Human Rights, who will work on the ground alongside other Ukrainian representatives. The Russian side has also designated its representative and other civilian participants in the operation.
Beckman highly praised Lubinets’ work, calling him a person who is extremely devoted to Ukraine and the Ukrainian people and who makes every effort to overcome obstacles.
As previously reported, U.S. First Lady Melania Trump proposed a ceasefire to deliver humanitarian aid to the residents of Oleshky and prepare for the evacuation of civilians.

title: Netanyahu besieged by failure; An election of life and death
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 27 (MNA) – The Israeli regime's parliamentary election is for Benjamin Netanyahu something beyond the ordinary competition of parties for seats in the Knesset; this election has become a fateful test of his political life.
A prime minister who for years has justified his policy with the promise of providing Israel's security, defeating enemies, and achieving "absolute victory" must now answer a fundamental question: if his strategies have been so successful, why has the Iran file remained one of the most important axes of threat and security propaganda for Israel?
Netanyahu has been placed in a situation where his political defeat could mean the end of a long period of power-seeking and security claims. Although the election result is not yet clear, political evidence and domestic criticisms show that he faces one of the most difficult tests of his political career. The security failure of October 7, 2023 and its consequences have severely called into question the credibility of Israel's security establishment.
From the Promise of Absolute Security to a Crisis of Trust
For years, Netanyahu tried to present himself as a politician who, better than any rival, is capable of confronting security threats. However, the operation of October 7, 2023 showed how vulnerable this claim of comprehensive security was. The surprise of Israel's intelligence and military agencies, the entry of Hamas forces into the areas and settlements around Gaza, and the killing and capture of a large number of Israeli settlers dealt a historic blow to this regime's security image.
Afterward, the Netanyahu cabinet launched extensive operations in Gaza, and the scope of Israel's confrontation with Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran also expanded. Netanyahu tried to present the military achievements of these operations as a sign of the restoration of Israel's deterrence power; but his fundamental problem persists: the power of military destruction is not the same as the realization of strategic objectives.
When the conflict becomes prolonged, human and economic costs increase, and the government still speaks of the necessity of continuing operations to reach final victory, this question becomes more serious: has the chosen strategy been able to create lasting security, or has it merely formed a new cycle of conflict?
Iran; A File Netanyahu Cannot Close with Slogans
Iran has been one of the main axes of Netanyahu's security strategy. He has repeatedly placed confronting Iran's nuclear program, missile capability, and regional influence at the top of his policies and has tried to present this file as evidence of the necessity of continuing his leadership.
However, the result of a military campaign cannot be measured merely by the aggressor side's declaration of victory. The real criterion is the extent to which the declared objectives have been realized, a lasting change in the balance of power, and the ability to prevent the return of the crisis. If, after extensive operations, the possibility of renewed confrontation with Iran is still raised, this situation shows that the issue has not been settled from a strategic perspective.
Channel 12 recent report about the alleged dispute between Netanyahu and Eyal Zamir, the Chief of the General Staff of the military, over the possibility of a new military operation related to Iran has highlighted this very contradiction. According to this report, the proposed action could have led to a broader confrontation with Tehran. Israeli officials have denied or questioned the details of this dispute, but the publication of such a report on the eve of elections reveals the sensitivity of the Iran file.
Yair Lapid, the opposition leader, also criticized the prime minister's performance, saying Israel's security should not be turned into a tool for election propaganda. Referring to Netanyahu's promises about Iran, he stressed that the prime minister has repeatedly spoken of "absolute victory" but has not reached the expected results.
This criticism from within the Israeli regime's political structure is considered a blow to Netanyahu's victory narrative; because it shows that even his domestic rivals do not consider the repetition of Iran threats as equivalent to strategic success.
The Axis of Resistance; The Strategic Costs of a Multi-Front Confrontation
The Iran file is not Netanyahu's only testing ground. Gaza, Lebanon, and other regional arenas have also become parts of his cabinet's security record. On these fronts, Israel has been able to deal heavy military blows to some groups of the Axis of Resistance; but inflicting a military blow alone does not mean eliminating the capacity for resistance or achieving a regional order in accordance with Tel Aviv's wishes.
In Gaza, extensive military operations could not easily realize all of Israel's declared objectives. In Lebanon, too, the weakening of Hezbollah's capability cannot be considered equivalent to the complete elimination of this actor without examining the political and security situation after the conflict. At the regional level as well, the confrontation with Iran has shown that military pressure does not necessarily lead to the opposing side's political surrender.
Therefore, the main issue for Netanyahu is not merely the number of operations carried out or the extent of damage inflicted on the opposing side; the issue is whether these operations have been able to turn the declared strategic objectives into a lasting result or not.
Netanyahu faces a fundamental contradiction: the more he speaks of final victory, the more the continuation of threats and the necessity of new operations highlight the question about the realization of that very victory.
The Election; The Final Test of Netanyahu's Record
Israel's electoral competition is being held under conditions in which none of the main camps, according to published polls, has a definitive and obstacle-free path to forming a cabinet. Achieving a majority of 61 seats out of the Knesset's total of 120 seats will depend on coalition-building and post-election negotiations. Therefore, even the electoral performance of the parties alone does not determine the fate of the future cabinet.
However, Netanyahu's issue is not just the number of seats for the Likud party. He must answer for the security failure of October 7, the costs of prolonged conflicts, the condition of reserve forces, internal disputes, and the gap between promises of victory and actual results. His opponents are trying to turn the election into an opportunity to end his period of leadership; his supporters continue to rely on his political experience and security policies.
Under such circumstances, the election for Netanyahu has a meaning close to political life and death: preserving power can give him the opportunity to continue his narrative of regional developments, but losing power will confront his position and political credibility with a serious challenge.
Ultimately, Netanyahu's record cannot be assessed with election slogans or claims of absolute victory. In realizing the promise of lasting security and converting military operations into a decisive strategic victory, he has faced serious failures. Iran remains at the center of Israel's security calculations, and the fronts associated with the Axis of Resistance, despite heavy military blows, have become unresolved files in Tel Aviv's regional strategy.
This is precisely Netanyahu's main weakness on the eve of the election: he can once again speak of victory, but he cannot eliminate the gap between his promises and strategic results merely by repeating this word. The October 27 election is, more than anything, a test for measuring this very gap and the extent of Zionist society's trust in his leadership.

title: A quick guide to Israel's high-stakes elections
body:
A woman walks past a Likud Party campaign billboard featuring President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with a Hebrew message reading, "We have one opportunity to win," in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Monday. Oded Balilty/AP hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — Israel is holding pivotal elections on Tuesday in what many Israelis call the most consequential vote in their country's history after the last few years of war.
Polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu trailing in the race behind his main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot . But it may take weeks or months before it's clear who will be designated the winner.
That's because voters will not directly choose between Netanyahu and Eisenkot. Instead, they will vote for one of a dozen main parties running for office in the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.
The real contest will begin after election day, when party leaders try to assemble a governing coalition of at least 61 lawmakers.
Here is a guide to the leading candidates, the issues shaping the vote and what could happen next.
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is seeking another term in office.
Netanyahu has led the most right-wing government in Israel's history. His coalition has included Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, leaders of far-right, religious nationalist parties that are also running in this election, as well as two ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.
Netanyahu has led Israel through more than three years of war and regional conflict, from the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza to fighting involving Lebanon, Iran, Syria and Yemen. He is campaigning on Israel's military achievements and his close relationship with President Trump, who recently endorsed him . Netanyahu has also made confronting Iran , and ultimately seeking the fall of its regime, a central part of his campaign.
His principal challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff of the Israeli military who is running for prime minister for the first time as the leader of a new center-right party called Yashar, Hebrew for "Straight" or "Upright."
Eisenkot's son, Gal, an Israeli soldier, was killed in Gaza during the war. Recent polls have shown Eisenkot has the strongest chance of replacing Netanyahu, although no party or political bloc appears assured of winning a parliamentary majority.
Eisenkot's Yashar includes figures from Israel's political center and moderate right. The opposition parties he would partner with range from the right and center to the liberal left. He has pledged not to join a government led by Netanyahu.
Two predominantly Arab parties are also running, including the United Arab List, also known as Ra'am, which made history in 2021 as the first Arab Islamist party to join an Israeli governing coalition . The party says it is willing to work with predominantly Jewish parties in exchange for policies fighting crime and promoting housing, infrastructure and other problems facing Israel's Arab minority community, which makes up about 20 percent of the country's population.
But nearly all the main predominantly Jewish political parties, including Eisenkot's, remain reluctant to rely on Arab parties to form a coalition. That reluctance could leave the anti-Netanyahu camp without the 61 seats it needs for a governing majority.
Accountability for Oct. 7: The Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage, looms over the election . Netanyahu has resisted calls to establish a state commission of inquiry into the political and security failures that preceded the attack. Eisenkot and other opposition leaders say they would establish such a commission soon after taking office.
Who should serve in the military: Nearly three years of fighting across several fronts have placed a heavy burden on Israel's standing army and military reservists. The military says it needs additional personnel, intensifying a decades-old dispute over exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men. Netanyahu, reliant on ultra-Orthodox parties for political support, has resisted enlisting them, while Eisenkot is campaigning to expand military service to more ultra-Orthodox Jews.
Israel's judiciary: Before the Oct. 7 attack, Netanyahu's government pursued a judicial overhaul that would have weakened the supreme court and given the governing coalition greater influence over the appointment of judges. The plan triggered some of the largest protests in Israel's history. Netanyahu's far-right partners are campaigning on renewed efforts to limit the power of the courts, while Eisenkot advocates for an independent and powerful judiciary. Netanyahu remains on trial for corruption, and says the charges are politically motivated.
The wars in Gaza and the region, and Israel's policies in the occupied West Bank, have badly strained its relations with many governments overseas, and public support for Israel in the U.S. has plummeted, worrying many Israeli voters. Netanyahu emphasizes his relationship with Trump and argues that military strength has improved Israel's strategic position. Eisenkot and his allies say continued international isolation threatens Israel's economy, diplomatic relationships and security.
A party does not need to finish first in the race for the party leader to be Israel's next prime minister. What matters is whether he can assemble a coalition with majority support in parliament.
Most recent polls suggest that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to a majority. That leaves several possible outcomes:
Even if Eisenkot cannot immediately form a coalition, a parliamentary majority opposed to Netanyahu could try to elect a new Knesset speaker, establish a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 attacks, and advance legislation on ultra-Orthodox military service.
Netanyahu would try to do everything he can to prevent such an outcome. His Likud party's billboards are already promoting a scenario in which the party could claim that the election was stolen, a move that could lead to chaos in the days after the vote.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot currently supports the establishment of a Palestinian state in the foreseeable future. Their most significant differences concern democratic institutions, the occupied West Bank and Israel's relationship with the world.
Netanyahu has governed with ultra-Orthodox and far right parties that support settlement expansion in the West Bank and a weaker supreme court. His far-right partners have pushed for annexation of the West Bank and expulsion of Palestinians, drawing sanctions from the U.K. and Europe.
Eisenkot presents himself as a more institutional and pragmatic alternative. He has also taken a tougher position against violence by Israeli settlers and says he would act against settlement outposts that are illegal even under Israeli law.
Eisenkot has opposed settlement construction in E1, a strategically sensitive area just east of Jerusalem. Critics of the settlement plan say Israeli construction there would further divide the West Bank and make the creation of a territorially contiguous Palestinian state much more difficult.
The choice facing Israeli voters is therefore not a straightforward contest between left and right. It is also a contest over Netanyahu's leadership, accountability for Oct. 7, the role of religion in the state, the independence of Israel's institutions and what kind of alliances the country will pursue at home and abroad.
NPR's Daniel Estrin contributed to this story.

title: UCC-UTAG demands clearer boundaries for GTEC’s regulatory role
body: The University of Cape Coast (UCC) Chapter of the University Teachers Association of Ghana (UTAG) has admonished the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) to refrain from interfering in university affairs and focus on its core mandates. It noted that GTEC has been a useful ally in the education space but has often overstepped its boundaries, undermining academic freedom and disrupting other university activities. The Association made the call at the UTAG Experts’ Forum 2026, held on the theme: “Rethinking Autonomy, Power and Oversight: GTEC’s Regulatory Authority and the Politics of Academic Freedom in Ghanaian Universities.” Professor Philip Ebow Bondzi-Simpson, a Senior Member of the Faculty of Law, UCC, noted that beyond being a regulator, the GTEC was, by law, an advisor, coordinator, and accreditor, a mandate he said the Commission had failed to execute effectively and efficiently. Prof Bondzi-Simpson noted that by executing its core mandates, including regulation, the GTEC would have less time to veer into matters outside its remit, stressing that the GTEC’s Director-General and staff were legally required to operate within their defined mandates and implement decisions of the Commission’s governing council. He argued that any exercise of authority must be grounded in a clear mandate, warning that actions outside that scope would be unlawful. “So, a Chief Executive whose mandate is set out by law does not go hovering around all manner of tertiary institutions to see what they are doing right or wrong. Any such thing should be in furtherance,” he said. “The mandate must always precede the assertion of authority, and if that is not done, the exercise by the director general or a deputy director general or any director or staff on his behalf is ultra vires,” he added. On other concerns, Prof Bondzi-Simpson objected to the GTEC’s membership of University Councils, arguing it contravened the law. He said: “Nowhere in the GTEC law does it require membership on a university council. It is not in the letter of the law, nor does it conform to the spirit of the law. Because a regulator cannot be sitting on council; council is a governing council that makes decisions about the university, participating in the process while wearing one hat. “Then in the next hat, it will go and negate or undermine those decisions. If you are part of it, you are bound by the decision. A referee or regulator cannot employ you, your staff, determine the policy.” “A referee cannot choose the coach and the players and the captain or the general captain and then come and referee the game. So the letter of the law does not allow it. The spirit of the law does not allow it,” he stressed. It was also the case of Prof Bondzi-Simpson that the Commission’s “policeman” posturing stemmed from its frequent description as a regulator in public discourse, adding that emphasising its roles as an adviser, coordinator and accreditor could help change their approach. He called for stronger collaboration between tertiary institutions and GTEC. Sharing similar concerns, Prof Denis Worlanyo Aheto, the Vice Chancellor of UCC, reiterated the call for GTEC to respect universities’ autonomy. He called for a regulatory framework that strengthens accountability and academic standards without the Commission unnecessarily interfering in legitimate academic decisions. Turning to the institutions, he challenged universities to embrace accountability, stressing that academic freedom must be exercised responsibly with strict adherence to sound governance, ethical conduct and institutional integrity. “Our goal should not be to weaken GTEC or diminish the authority of universities. Rather, we should build a relationship of constructive engagement in which regulatory authorities and universities understand their respective mandates and work collaboratively towards excellence in higher education,” the Vice Chancellor stressed. For her part, Dr Cynthia Sena Kpeglo-Freiku, the Executive Secretary of the Vice Chancellors Ghana (VCG), among other disquiet, expressed concern about regulatory directives affecting staff appointments, internal organisational structures, retirement arrangements and academic programme development. She said excessive interference delayed recruitment, created teaching gaps, increased administrative costs and disrupted academic delivery. She called for a review of overlapping legal mandates, meaningful consultation with affected institutions, transparent regulatory procedures and a permanent mechanism for dialogue and dispute resolution. “Strong universities require effective regulation. Effective regulation requires institutional trust, and institutional trust requires accountability on both sides,” Dr Kpeglo-Freiku stated. Prof Kwadwo Appiagyei-Atua, the Regional Director of the African Coalition for Academic Freedom, suggested that GTEC’s regulatory powers must be checked against the Constitution. He called for legislative instruments jointly developed by government, academic unions, and students through broad stakeholder consultations to prevent arbitrary directives and protect university autonomy. Prof Appiagyei-Atua further argued that GTEC’s Board composition must be reviewed to ensure balanced representation, calling for the inclusion of academic unions and student representatives to limit excessive executive influence and promote democratic decision-making in university regulation. “My recommendation is that it should not be done by the Minister alone. It should involve academic unions like UTAG, CETAG, and student representatives so that we all sit around the table, consult among ourselves, and agree on the details of the law,” he said. Professor Jerry Opoku Ansah, the UCC UTAG President, explained that the forum, organised over the years, provided a platform to discuss local, national, and global matters objectively, offer informed policy alternatives, and contribute to development at all levels. Speaking to the theme of this year’s forum, he emphasised that universities had a responsibility to maintain academic standards freely and produce well-trained graduates, but acknowledged the need for regulation to safeguard quality and public confidence. He, therefore, called for a more collaborative relationship between tertiary institutions and GTEC.

title: No plans to lift Russian gas ban even if Ukraine peace deal reached — EU official
body:
BUDAPEST, October 26. /TASS/. The European Union will not lift its full ban on Russian gas imports, scheduled to take effect in November 2027, even if a peace agreement on Ukraine is reached, European Commissioner for Energy Dan Jorgensen told Hungary’s 444.hu media outlet.
Commenting on Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s remark that EU countries could resume Russian gas purchases after the Ukraine conflict ends, Jorgensen said that it would be a mistake for the bloc to start buying Russian gas again.
Earlier, the EU approved a full ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports under long-term contracts starting January 1, 2027. Imports under short-term contracts were banned in April 2026. Pipeline gas supplies are expected to cease by September 30, 2027 but could continue until November 1 in countries failing to fill their gas storage facilities.

title: Two Sydney Greek Restaurants Earn Good Food Guide Hats
body: From a neighbourhood gyros shop in Marrickville to a modern Greek taverna in Redfern, Sydney’s Greek food scene earns recognition in the 2026 Good Food Guide. Two Sydney restaurants serving Greek cuisine feature among the venues recognised in the 2026 Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide, highlighting the diversity of Greek dining across the city. Olympic Meats in Marrickville appears among the new one-hat restaurants, while Olympus Dining in Redfern retains its place in the one-hat category. The recognition comes as the guide broadens its focus beyond high-end dining, celebrating restaurants that deliver quality food and memorable experiences across different styles and budgets. Olympic Meats brings Peloponnese flavours to Marrickville Olympic Meats has quickly established itself as a destination for Greek grilled meats, gyros and traditional dishes in Sydney’s Inner West. Chef and owner Timothy Cassimatis named the restaurant after his grandmother Olympia. Its menu draws on the food traditions of the Peloponnese in southern Greece, where his family comes from. The restaurant centres on charcoal-grilled meats prepared in the Greek kontosouvli style, alongside house-made sourdough pita, meze and traditional Greek pastries. Its approach is deliberately straightforward, focusing on quality ingredients and cooking methods rooted in Greek food culture rather than formal fine dining. Located in Marrickville, an area long associated with Sydney’s Greek community, Olympic Meats offers a contemporary expression of the neighbourhood’s culinary heritage. Olympus Dining celebrates the Greek taverna Olympus Dining, located in Redfern’s Wunderlich Lane precinct, brings a more elaborate take on the traditional Greek taverna. The restaurant features a menu built around sharing, with Greek meze, grilled seafood, souvlaki, spanakopita and slow-cooked meats. Its dining room is centred around a large bougainvillea beneath a glass roof, creating a setting inspired by communal Greek dining. A Taste of Mount Olympus Descends Upon Sydney’s Redfern Owned by Jonathan Barthelmess, whose hospitality ventures include The Apollo, Olympus aims to recreate the atmosphere of an Athenian taverna, where friends and families gather over generous plates of food. Its inclusion among the guide’s one-hat restaurants recognises its place in Sydney’s competitive dining scene. A broader definition of great dining The 42nd annual Good Food Guide awards assessed more than 500 restaurants across New South Wales and the ACT, with anonymous reviewers evaluating food, hospitality, setting and value. Restaurants are scored out of 20 points. Venues scoring 15 points or more receive one hat, while those earning 16 or 17 points receive two hats. Three hats are reserved for restaurants scoring between 18 and 20. This year, co-editor David Matthews said reviewers were encouraged to judge each venue according to the dining experience it aims to deliver, rather than comparing every restaurant against an imagined standard of luxury. That approach creates room for a range of dining experiences, from neighbourhood grills and casual eateries to destination restaurants. Visit the restaurants Olympic Meats, Marrickville Address: 12 Dudley Street, Marrickville, NSW 2204 Phone: 0435 949 759 Website: https://www.olympicmeats.shop/ Olympus Dining, Redfern Address: Wunderlich Lane, 2 Baptist Street, Redfern, NSW 2016 Phone: (02) 8354 0649 Email: info@olympusdining.com.au Website: https://olympusdining.com.au/ 10 Sydney Restaurants to Know in 2026 From acclaimed fine dining to Greek food rooted in tradition, these 10 restaurants stand out in Sydney’s 2026 Good Food Guide. Saint Peter, Paddington Three hats. Chef Josh Niland’s celebrated seafood restaurant is known for its innovative approach to Australian seafood. Sixpenny, Stanmore Three hats. An intimate dining destination recognised for its carefully crafted tasting menus and seasonal ingredients. Bennelong, Sydney Opera House Two hats. Modern Australian dining in one of the country’s most recognisable architectural settings. Firedoor, Surry Hills Two hats. A destination for wood-fired cooking, with fire playing a central role in the kitchen. Ester, Chippendale Two hats. A neighbourhood favourite known for inventive dishes and wood-fired cooking. Aria, Circular Quay Two hats. Contemporary Australian dining overlooking Sydney Harbour. Olympic Meats, Marrickville One hat. A Greek grill house celebrating flavours inspired by the Peloponnese, with charcoal-cooked meats, gyros and house-made pita. Olympus Dining, Redfern One hat. A contemporary Greek taverna serving share plates, grilled seafood and traditional Greek-inspired dishes. Corner 75, Randwick One hat. A neighbourhood restaurant recognised for its Hungarian-inspired cooking and distinctive approach to familiar flavours. Catalina, Rose Bay One hat. A long-established waterfront restaurant known for seafood and views across the harbour. The selection spans different cuisines, neighbourhoods and dining styles, while highlighting the breadth of Sydney’s restaurant scene. For Greek food lovers, Olympic Meats and Olympus Dining are two names worth adding to the list. Sources: The Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide 2026; Broadsheet; official Olympus Dining website.
