"We did a little ceasefire, which I never liked very much. I considered it sort of a waste of time," he said at a Republican campaign event in Mississippi. "We did a little ceasefire, so we let some ships get in. You know, we want to be nice, but it was just a waste of time, as far as I'm concerned," Trump added.
Speaking about the outbreak of the conflict, Trump claimed that the United States had no choice. "This should have been done by other presidents a long time ago," he said, adding: "It'll be over soon."
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding envisaging an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including Lebanon. However, early on July 8, the United States resumed massive airstrikes on Iran, accusing Tehran of violating their previous agreements regarding the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Zelensky Outlines 3 Security Options as US Pushes for November Talks With Russia
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Washington was willing to discuss security guarantees that could include an American military response to renewed Russian aggression, but insisted that any agreement must spell out exactly what US forces would do and receive congressional approval.
In an extensive interview with TSN’s Alla Mazur, Zelensky said Ukraine was considering several postwar security arrangements, including NATO membership, direct US guarantees and a European-led coalition backed by Washington.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
He stressed that the terms could not be dictated by Moscow and that Ukraine would not accept neutrality or restrictions on its armed forces.
“What are the US prepared to do? In what numbers? Aviation or ground operations, if Ukraine needs to be defended quickly?” Zelensky asked.
He said the current US administration was prepared to discuss such arrangements, but the details had to be written into a binding agreement rather than left to political promises between presidents.
Zelensky said a bilateral security agreement must survive changes in political leadership in Washington and Kyiv.
“Congress must vote for the security guarantees,” he said, rejecting another arrangement resembling the Budapest Memorandum, which failed to prevent Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.
The president outlined three possible security frameworks: Ukrainian membership in NATO, bilateral US guarantees, or a European-led Coalition of the Willing involving more than 30 countries with American support.
NATO membership remained his preferred option, but he acknowledged that direct US guarantees without formal accession could provide a compromise.
However, he said key questions remained unanswered, including whether American forces or military installations could be stationed in Ukraine and how Washington would respond if Russia invaded again.
Zelensky said the same uncertainty applied to a European military presence, which Moscow has repeatedly opposed.
The president rejected suggestions that Ukraine had agreed to trade territory for security guarantees as Washington prepared for renewed negotiations with Russia.
“We are not exchanging anything for anything. We are ready for discussions,” Zelensky said.
He insisted that territorial questions could be addressed only by national leaders, while technical delegations could negotiate other aspects of a settlement.
Zelensky said US negotiators had presented several proposals following talks in Oslo on Oct. 20, which American envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently took to Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
He emphasized that the document was not a completed peace plan submitted to Putin for approval.
“Russia does not decide,” Zelensky said, explaining that the proposals were intended for discussion among the parties involved in ending the war.
He added that Russian demands could not determine Ukraine’s security arrangements.
“The limitation of our army and Ukraine’s neutrality are not up for discussion,” he said.
Zelensky said the size of Ukraine’s postwar armed forces would remain an internal decision, dependent on financing and the security arrangements eventually agreed upon.
“If I have enough money, I want to maintain an army of 800,000,” he said.
He stressed that he would not negotiate the size of Ukraine’s military with Russia or, for that matter, with the US.
The president said NATO membership could change Ukraine’s military requirements, but the decision would depend on the alliance’s readiness to help finance and equip Ukrainian forces.
Without NATO membership, Ukraine would require other credible guarantees alongside a large, well-funded army equipped with modern weapons and technology.
He said Washington’s proposals also covered economic questions, reconstruction and territorial matters, although he declined to reveal all details because of understandings with American negotiators.
Zelensky said the Oslo negotiations had also helped reopen a diplomatic channel with Moscow.
According to the Ukrainian president, US officials traveled to St. Petersburg after the meeting and subsequently informed Kyiv that Putin had agreed in principle to trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US in November.
Abu Dhabi was among the locations discussed, although Zelensky said the talks could also take place elsewhere in the Middle East or Europe.
Kyiv wants European representatives involved and hopes technical negotiations can lead to a meeting between national leaders.
Zelensky said such a meeting could address territorial disputes, while other discussions could explore an energy ceasefire, a maritime ceasefire to protect Ukrainian exports and imports, and further prisoner exchanges.
He welcomed the return of 270 Ukrainian prisoners but said a comprehensive all-for-all exchange would require negotiations at the leaders’ level.
The president said Russia was also seeking security guarantees in discussions with Washington. He acknowledged that he did not know the full details of Putin’s conversations with American envoys, including whether economic issues influenced Moscow’s position.
Zelensky described the Oct. 20 Oslo meeting as productive, saying it helped resolve two of Ukraine’s three immediate disputes with Washington.
He identified the problems as limited US intelligence sharing on Russian ballistic missile launches, restrictions affecting Starlink and Starshield satellite capabilities, and shortages of air defense systems.
According to Zelensky, intelligence sharing on ballistic threats had been fully restored, while satellite capabilities returned to the speeds required by Ukrainian forces.
He said that during overnight checks with defense officials, the satellite service had resumed operations at speeds corresponding to 420 kilometers (261 miles) per hour, following earlier restrictions.
Ukraine’s military welcomed the restoration, he said.
The president thanked American officials and Ukraine’s negotiating team for resolving both issues, adding that public attention may also have helped.
However, the shortage of air defense weapons remained unresolved.
Zelensky said the Oslo meeting had produced tangible results but warned that the situation could change, particularly amid US domestic political developments.
Zelensky also disclosed that he had invited US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to visit Bucha during their earlier trip to Kyiv, but they did not go.
The president said he had taken them to St. Sophia Cathedral to show them Ukraine’s historical heritage and the reality of life in a country resisting Russia’s invasion.
He wanted the American delegation to experience Ukraine firsthand rather than rely on narratives emerging from its contacts with Moscow.
Zelensky said he had also hoped to show the envoys Bucha, the Kyiv suburb where Russian atrocities occurred in 2022.
“We offered,” Zelensky said when asked whether the Americans had been invited.
He said he wanted them to see both the consequences of Russian occupation and how communities were rebuilding.
“They did not find the time, but they found time for many other things,” he said.
The president acknowledged that the reasons for not visiting Bucha could have varied.
Nevertheless, he said showing the envoys Kyiv’s historic sites and the resilience of its residents had helped create an emotional connection with Ukraine.
He noted that St. Sophia Cathedral predates Moscow itself, underscoring Ukraine’s long history and independent identity.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Ebola: How much have Nigerian states allocated to emergency preparedness?
body:
Nigeria’s first confirmed case of Ebola in more than a decade has raised questions about how prepared state governments are to detect and contain the virus before it spreads through their communities.
The World Health Organisation said on 20 October that Nigeria had recorded an imported case of Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus. The patient is the wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja. She arrived in Nigeria on 3 October after travelling from Uganda and developed symptoms a few days later. The patient and her spouse were later evacuated to Switzerland on Monday while health authorities identified 53 contacts and began monitoring them.
The confirmation followed weeks of warnings from the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) about the risk of the virus entering Nigeria from an outbreak that began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Health authorities are identifying people who may have been exposed, tracing their movements, testing suspected cases, protecting healthcare workers and preventing further transmission. Much of this work depends on coordination across states, local government areas and health facilities, where people live and seek treatment.
A PREMIUM TIMES review of states’ 2026 approved budgets shows differences in allocations for disease surveillance, infection control, emergency operations and infectious disease facilities.
Some states made substantial provisions for health emergencies, while others allocated smaller sums to specific disease-control activities. Some budgets provide for preparedness under general health emergency headings, while others identify particular diseases, facilities or surveillance programmes.
The allocations do not establish how much money is available for an immediate Ebola response or whether the systems funded are operational. They show what state governments have provided for in their 2026 budgets, offering a basis for examining their stated priorities for public health preparedness.
The NCDC (Establishment) Act 2018 provides the statutory foundation for the agency’s work in preventing, detecting and controlling diseases of public health importance. The agency coordinates disease surveillance, provides technical support to subnational authorities and supports responses to public health emergencies.
The International Health Regulations (2005) , a legally binding international framework, also requires countries to develop and maintain the capacity to detect, assess, notify and respond to public health risks.
The National Health Act 2014 provides another part of the framework. Section 11 establishes the Basic Health Care Provision Fund to support essential health services, particularly at the primary healthcare level. Although the fund is not a substitute for state emergency-response budgets, primary healthcare facilities play an important role in early detection, referral and disease reporting.
These frameworks do not prescribe a uniform amount that every state must earmark specifically for Ebola. They nevertheless underscore the need for functional public health systems capable of identifying and responding to infectious disease threats.
In May, the NCDC warned that the risk of Ebola being imported into Nigeria was high. It cited international travel, population movements and the difficulty of distinguishing early Ebola symptoms from common illnesses such as malaria. The agency urged states and the Federal Capital Territory to strengthen their preparedness and ensure they could detect and contain suspected cases promptly.
The subsequent confirmation of an imported case has made those preparations more urgent.
On Monday, the World Health Organisation said Nigeria currently has no active Ebola case after the country evacuated its index patient to Switzerland. The WHO Regional Director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, said this in a post on X, shortly after Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, confirmed the patient’s evacuation from Nigeria.
Among the largest provisions identified in the 2026 approved state budgets are Delta’s N37.28 billion for emergency operations centres, Zamfara’s N20 billion for a health emergency response fund and Lagos’s combined N17.79 billion for two infectious disease research facilities.
Delta’s 2026 budget also provides N590 million for integrating national disease surveillance, N100 million for the control and management of infectious diseases and N50 million for communicable diseases.
Zamfara’s N20 billion allocation for a health emergency response fund could provide substantial funding for public health crises. Its effectiveness will depend on how the money is released and deployed.
Lagos’s combined N17.79 billion allocation comprises N15.27 billion for a public health epidemics and infectious disease research institute and N2.52 billion for an infectious disease research institute at Mainland Hospital, Yaba. The facilities could strengthen the state’s capacity to respond to outbreaks such as Ebola, although their contribution will depend on their completion, staffing, diagnostic capabilities and recurrent funding.
Meanwhile, Ogun provides N2.5 billion for a medical emergency preparedness and response project and N4.8 billion for national disease surveillance. Akwa Ibom allocated N1 billion for upgrading statewide emergency health interventions and N100 million for upgrading its health emergency operations centre.
These allocations show the amounts the states have provided for emergency preparedness in their 2026 budgets. They do not, on their own, establish how much funding has been released or which systems are ready for immediate use.
An operational emergency operations centre with trained staff, reliable communications and established response procedures may be more useful in the early hours of an outbreak than a facility still under construction. Similarly, a functioning surveillance system may detect a suspected case before a large emergency allocation translates into operational capacity.
The 2026 approved budgets show different approaches to health security, ranging from hospital rehabilitation and emergency equipment to disease surveillance and community-level prevention.
Cross River allocated N350 million to upgrade the abandoned tuberculosis hospital in Obubra into an infectious disease hospital, N300 million for a disease-control and partners complex, and N20 million for communicable disease prevention and control. The combined allocation is N670 million for infrastructure and disease-control activities.
Enugu’s 2026 budget includes N129.33 million for communicable diseases, N100 million for medical equipment intended to strengthen health security, N20 million for furniture and information technology equipment for a health sector command centre or public health emergency operations centre, and N10 million for fencing an infectious disease hospital. The four provisions total N259.33 million.
Kaduna allocated N179.69 million for monitoring and tracking public health emergencies and N620.68 million for the Kaduna State Centre for Disease Control. Together, the two provisions amount to N800.37 million.
Kebbi allocated N410.37 million for disease surveillance tools, equipment and essential emergency drugs for its emergency operations centre. Kwara set aside N301.5 million for integrated national disease surveillance, while Plateau provided N25.7 million for the same general purpose.
Kogi allocated N500 million for health security involving emergency preparedness, response and disease control, alongside N3.02 million for controlling emerging public health diseases. Benue provided N19.38 million for infection control and community awareness.
Other states made provisions for surveillance vehicles, emergency response systems and outbreak management. Taraba allocated N107 million for disease surveillance and response vehicles, in addition to N27.37 million for establishing and maintaining a responsive public health emergency system.
Adamawa’s 2026 budget includes N10 million for communicable diseases, N2 million for emergency response to rural outbreaks and N27.8 million for chemicals used in fumigation and decontamination.
In the North-east, Bauchi allocated N500 million for surveillance and disease outbreak prevention, N100 million for medical equipment for communicable diseases, N100 million for rehabilitating the infectious disease hospital at Bayara and N300 million for renovating another infectious disease hospital.
Gombe provided N35 million for disease surveillance under its public health emergency system, N10 million for emergency operations centres and N3 million for communicable diseases. Yobe allocated N1.09 billion for health emergency services, while Borno earmarked N35 million for research on communicable diseases.
In the North-west, Jigawa allocated N135 million for renovating its infectious disease hospital in Dutse. Kano’s 2026 budget includes N92.7 million for integrated disease surveillance, N115 million for coordinating communicable disease activities in primary healthcare, N20 million for coordinating public health emergencies at local government level and N54.67 million for strengthening its communicable disease prevention task force.
Katsina provided N50 million for an infectious disease fund and another N50 million for communicable disease control. Sokoto allocated N500 million as counterpart funding for health emergencies, N73 million in recurrent funding for the Infectious Disease Hospital in Amanawa and N75 million for an ambulance for the hospital. The budgets also contain provisions for equipment and community-level prevention.
In the South-east, Abia allocated N4.5 million for research on vaccine hesitancy and disease burden, N4.5 million for an electronic surveillance system for communicable diseases and N10 million for distributing buckets with taps to 903 primary healthcare centres.
Anambra provided N90 million for a disease control and surveillance centre, N10 million for controlling emerging communicable diseases and N15 million for surveillance and epidemic response equipment.
Ebonyi allocated N15 million for equipment for emergency response to epidemic disease control. Imo’s N500 million provision is specifically for operational funding for its COVID-19 emergency operations centre. The existing centre could potentially support an Ebola response, depending on its capacity and readiness.
In the South-west, Ondo’s appropriation includes N95 million for disease outbreak monitoring, response and free health commodities, N60 million for emergency preparedness and disease surveillance, and N13.6 million for procuring 10,000 personal protective equipment items. Osun allocated N119.7 million for communicable diseases, while Oyo provided N38 million for a responsive public health emergency preparedness system.
Bayelsa budgeted N30 million for research and development into early warning systems and integrated national disease surveillance. Niger State’s 2026 budget includes N860 million for a USAID grant-related consortium programme focused on universal health coverage, malaria and other communicable diseases.
Nasarawa allocated N590 million for vehicles, an ambulance, isolation ward equipment, oxygen and medical air plants, and other infrastructure at the state’s Infectious Diseases, Diagnosis and Research Centre in Lafia. The budget also includes N4 million for communicable diseases and N7 million for disease surveillance, prevention and control.
This review did not identify a relevant emergency allocation in Ekiti’s approved 2026 budget. The state may have provisions for health emergencies under other headings, but the review could not identify an allocation for that purpose. The 2026 approved budgets for Rivers State and the Federal Capital Territory were not publicly available for this review.
The NCDC’s preparedness guidance identifies several requirements for responding to Ebola, including early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, risk communication, and protection for health workers.
These activities require more than construction projects. They depend on trained surveillance officers, functioning reporting systems, reliable transport, protective equipment, access to testing and facilities capable of safely managing suspected cases.
Nigeria’s experience in 2014 illustrates the importance of these systems. After an infected traveller arrived in Lagos, cases were subsequently recorded in Port Harcourt. Nigeria recorded 20 cases and eight deaths before transmission was interrupted.
The outbreak demonstrated the importance of quickly identifying exposed people, tracing their contacts, isolating cases and coordinating public health action across jurisdictions.
The recent Ebola case has not been reported to have spread across Nigeria. Preparedness measures are designed to prevent an imported infection from developing into sustained community transmission.
Koko Udo, a director of Bestway Initiative for Health, Education and Self Sufficiency, who holds a PhD in virology, said the immediate question for state governments was whether the systems provided for in their budgets were operational and accessible when needed.
“A state may have a designated infectious disease hospital, but do they have trained staff, suitable isolation arrangements, adequate protective equipment and the ability to refer patients safely?” he said.
Mr Udo said an emergency operations centre should be assessed on its staffing, communications, surveillance links and capacity to coordinate a response, rather than its mere inclusion in a budget.
“There is need for states to learn from the 2014 Ebola and Covid-19 outbreak. The state governments need to release money for these preparations immediately,” he said.
Mr Udo said surveillance funding should translate into health workers who could recognise suspected cases, report them promptly and receive support to investigate alerts. He also called for clear procedures for releasing emergency funds to prevent avoidable administrative delays in procurement and deployment.
He urged the NCDC and federal health authorities to publish state-by-state preparedness assessments identifying gaps and the support needed to address them. Such assessments, he said, would help the public distinguish states with functioning emergency systems from those whose provisions existed only on paper.
The legal and policy frameworks provide a basis for coordinated disease surveillance and response. The 2026 approved budgets show how state governments have chosen to fund parts of that responsibility. Neither the frameworks nor the allocations establish that the systems are working.
As Nigeria responds to its latest Ebola threat, the test is not simply which governor has announced the largest allocation or which state has budgeted for the most expensive infectious disease facility.
It is whether a health worker who encounters a patient with symptoms consistent with Ebola knows what to do, whether the alert reaches the relevant authorities promptly, whether a response team can arrive without delay, and whether the state can isolate and refer the patient safely while protecting other patients and health workers.
This is because while Nigerians need to know what their governments budgeted for health emergencies, they also have to know what those funds have made possible.

title: [Vantage Point] Tubig Pilipinas’ backdoor listing move opens into another suspension
body: Tubig Pilipinas Holdings Inc. (TPHI, listed as TUBIG) has completed one of the local bourse’s most literal corporate metamorphoses: a dormant coal shell has been refashioned into a piped-water holding enterprise. TPHI and Tubig Pilipinas Group Inc. (TPGI) are distinct corporate entities. TPHI is the publicly listed parent company whose shares trade on the exchange, while TPGI is the unlisted operating arm that develops, manages, and operates the underlying water distribution utilities. With TPHI acquiring 100% of TPGI through a share swap, the investing public now holds its economic interest in the water assets indirectly through the listed shell. Yet for ordinary minority shareholders watching from the sidelines, the initial dividend of this transformation is neither a buoyant commercial pipeline nor an invigorated business. It is a stock certificate they are legally barred from trading. The Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) lifted the company’s extended suspension on October 14 after classifying the transaction as a backdoor listing. The reprieve proved ephemeral. Just five trading sessions later, the bourse slapped TUBIG with another trading freeze because the share swap diluted the public float from 28.31% to 10.64%, well below the mandated 20% threshold. Under the exchange’s amended rules, the company has a strict six-month cure period. Failure to restore the float within that compressed window triggers automatic delisting. That timetable creates an immediate strategic disconnect. In its disclosures, TUBIG indicated plans to execute a follow-on public offering within a year of completing the swap. The exchange’s trading suspension sends a sharp counter-signal: the market will not wait that long. The asset transaction was massive relative to the legacy corporate chassis. To acquire full control of operating subsidiary TPGI — owned equally by Pure Water Corporation and Quadwater Corporation — TPHI issued 66.46 billion new common shares at a par value of P0.10 each. That pegged the acquisition value at P6.646 billion. The transaction handed the vendors a dominant 62.43% equity slice, ballooning total outstanding shares from 40 billion to 106.46 billion. The resulting registry consolidates control into a few hands. Following the swap, Pure Water and Quadwater emerged with matching 37.65% stakes. Affiliate Pure Energy Holdings Corp. preserved a 4.69% toehold, while Dutch investment vehicle CEF2 A09 B.V. took 9.36%. Together, this controlling bloc locks up 89.35% of the company. The legacy public float, stranded at an unchanged 11.33 billion shares, was relegated to a residual 10.64% corner. The underlying arithmetic shows the sheer scale of the balance-sheet surgery required to cure the deficit. If the controlling shareholders execute a secondary placement, they must unload roughly 9.97 billion shares to the public. If management opts for a primary offering, TUBIG would need to issue approximately 12.46 billion fresh shares, as the enlarged capital base demands higher share volume to reach 20%. Even at par, a primary issuance implies raising P1.25 billion in fresh equity—an ambitious capital call whose clearing price will test market appetite. Rely on faith Consequently, that equity offering is no administrative footnote. It represents the solitary bridge between an engineered private arrangement and an active public market. More critically, its clearing price will deliver the first authentic, arm’s-length market test of the P6.646-billion valuation ascribed to TPGI. For now, minority investors are asked to rely on faith. Filings indicate that Isla Lipana & Co. prepared an independent fairness opinion and valuation report dated January 29 using income and market approaches. Yet published disclosures omit the substantive quantitative machinery: there are no disclosed discount rates, cash-flow projections, terminal growth assumptions, peer matrices, or sensitivity ranges. The complete valuation report was visibly missing from the public bundle. This opacity is difficult to reconcile with TPGI’s audited financial position. The water business recorded 2025 revenue of P270.77 million, an operating loss of P27.53 million, and a net loss of P31.34 million. Total equity stood at P818.18 million against P1.93 billion in long-term loans. Current liabilities of P1.87 billion eclipsed current assets of P1.15 billion, leaving a working capital deficit of roughly P719 million. To be clear, the business is not a hollow shell. TPGI generated P193.01 million in operating cash flow in 2025 while absorbing P750.78 million in capital outlays. It operates 12 water distribution facilities, manages five projects under development, and projects P1.93 billion in capital expenditures through 2031. It is an authentic, capital-intensive infrastructure play undergoing buildout. Yet an acquisition price of P6.646 billion represents 8.1 times book equity and 24.5 times trailing revenue for an unprofitable asset. While long-gestation utility concessions can justify premiums on future cash flows, those multiples make the underlying math essential reading for public investors whose holdings were diluted. I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com Below are some Vantage Point pieces you might have missed: [Vantage Point] High barriers, high stakes: The SEC’s liquidity gambit [Vantage Point] JAZA’s painful question: Why aren’t we winning? Click here for other Vantage Point articles.

title: Abdul El-Sayed’s election race is one of America’s most consequential in recent years
body: The US Senate race in Michigan state between the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, and his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, is this year’s most important election in America. It’s significant, on a number of levels, not the least of which is that Mr El-Sayed is an Arab-American Muslim of Egyptian descent. Prior to this, the country had four Arab Americans elected to the US Senate – former majority leader George Mitchell, James Abourezk, James Abdnor and John Sununu – none of them Muslim. If elected, Mr El-Sayed would be the first Muslim in the Senate. This is a breakthrough that hasn’t been lost on Republicans and President Donald Trump, who have made a determined effort to exploit it at every turn. They’ve done TV ads alleging that Mr El-Sayed’s mother was affiliated to the Muslim Brotherhood in the 1970s. The problem with this charge is that Mr El-Sayed’s parents separated when he was three; she moved back to Egypt, and he grew up with his father in Michigan. But when using slanderous attacks to tarnish a candidate is the goal, facts don’t seem to matter. And so, the Republican Party has persisted in spreading the Muslim Brotherhood accusation on social media. Hecklers at a few of Mr El-Sayed’s campaign events have pestered him with questions like: “Will you denounce the Muslim Brotherhood?” A recent exchange of this sort backfired on one of the instigators. At a town hall when a young man asked whether Mr El-Sayed would denounce the group, Mr El-Sayed shot back, “Yes, absolutely”, and then pivoted by asking the questioner, “Why are you asking me this?” wanting to know whether it was because of his name and how he prayed. He then made clear that the document to which he would take an oath was the US Constitution and smartly compared the attacks against his religion with those levelled against late president John F Kennedy in the early 1960s – that Mr Kennedy would be more loyal to the Catholic Pope than to the Constitution. Mr El-Sayed concluded noting that he wasn’t running to be a Muslim senator, but a senator who happened to be a Muslim. An El-Sayed victory will succeed in advancing a progressive agenda That exchange went viral on social media, drawing more than 50 million viewers on the first night. The next day, it was revealed that the heckler was a former staffer for a conservative anti-Muslim senator. He had been hired by a group that had received a very substantial contract to recruit hecklers to disrupt Mr El-Sayed’s events. This brings into focus another reason why this election is so important: the role of dark money in American politics. Dark money refers to money raised by “super Pacs” and independent expenditure funds that are not required to report donors before elections. This has allowed billionaires and special interest groups to amass large sums and spend them to defame candidates who oppose their agendas. Increasingly, these dark money sources are raising and spending more on campaigns than the candidates raise for themselves. In the primary, Mr El-Sayed was confronted by dark money expenditures of $70 million ($31 million from pro-Israel groups), much of it on negative attacks against him. Despite being outspent by a margin of 11 to 1, Mr El-Sayed won. In the general election, it is estimated that another $100 million in dark money will be spent against him. If he wins, it will demonstrate the limits of dark money and help advance the argument that it should be banned because of its corrosive role in American democracy. From the beginning of his campaign, Mr El-Sayed has been a clear and consistent critic of US support for the Israeli war in Gaza. This appears to be the main reason why so much pro-Israel super-Pac money was spent to defeat him. His Democratic primary opponent made support for Israel central to her campaign, at one point emotionally noting how much she loved and would always stand by Israel. Pro-Israel Jewish organisations denounced Mr El-Sayed and did their best to tarnish him, labelling him anti-Semitic. This succeeded in costing Mr El-Sayed some support from Jewish-American Democratic voters. He won the primary, with one pre-election survey saying he had nevertheless retained the support of a bloc of progressive Jewish voters. Now in the general election, Mr El-Sayed is still being confronted by the same attacks and an organised effort among these same pro-Israel groups that are pledging to vote for his opponent. Mr El-Sayed has made it clear that instead of spending billions to buy bombs to kill Palestinians, America’s wealth ought to go to build better schools, provide health care, and provide for people’s needs here at home. While this was once a taboo topic, it has resonated with Democrats and independent voters. This, in itself, is a breakthrough. Finally, an El-Sayed victory will succeed in advancing a progressive agenda . Despite being attacked as a socialist, he maintains that he is a supporter of capitalism who wants to see it work to meet the needs of people. He makes this point with a mantra he uses to begin his rallies: “Money out of politics, money in your pockets, Medicare for all.” His arguments are simple. It shouldn’t be easier for a billionaire to make another billion than it is for a family to be lifted out of poverty. Health care should be seen as a human right for all, not a privilege that can only be afforded by some. And instead of spending billions for wars, the US government needs to invest in schools and the quality of life at home. These are the challenges Mr El-Sayed presents to US politics. If he wins, he will have succeeded in shattering taboos and raising issues that will have a lasting impact. And even if he loses, American politics will never be the same. On so many levels, this is a historic, transformative campaign.

title: UK envoy warns that state hostage-taking on the rise
body: The UK's newly appointed hostage envoy wants to build international alliances to prevent state hostage-taking. Alistair Burt, who became the UK’s first special envoy for complex consular affairs last month, warned that state hostage-taking was on the rise, but that countries could work together to prevent it. He said he had met with counterparts among the Five Eyes Group and the Gulf states in the hope of strengthening the network of countries affected by state hostage-taking. “I want to advance the international process. Actually preventing this, persuading the states that do it, this is not the way that will bring them any success,” he said on Monday. “The rise in state hostage-taking has been noticed. That is what has increased international interest in this and how things can be tackled collectively. I’m building that up,” he told MPs of the Foreign Affairs Committee, which scrutinises the government’s foreign policy. The UK hopes to host the “core group” of hostage envoys from the Five Eyes alliance in the UK next year. “It would give (the meeting) greater prominence. We would want high-level representation at such a meeting. It would add to the visibility of the UK being extremely concerned about such a practice,” he said. Mr Burt served as the Tories' Minister for the Middle East from 2017 to 2019, a crucial period during which the UK was seeking the release of British nationals detained in Iran, including Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe and Anoosheh Ashoori. The position of special envoy for hostages was created last month after growing demand from families and their MPs. The American diplomat Roger Carstens, who served as US presidential envoy for hostage affairs, is widely seen as the precursor to the role that was created in the UK. Mr Burt said the role would consist of providing more support for the families of people who have been arbitrarily detained or face cruel treatment in prison. He would also be advising the government on alternative solutions to secure the detained person’s release. One high-profile case was that of Craig and Lindsay Foreman, who are being held in an Iranian prison after being given 10-year sentences for espionage. The couple and the UK government have rejected the accusations, insisting that they were innocent tourists. The couple's family – who met with Mr Burt last month – have repeatedly accused the government of failing to act quickly enough to secure their release. The case is complicated by the US-Iran war, and repeated alleged Iran-backed attacks on British soil that have strained relations. Mr Burt said he could not speak publicly about individual cases without the family's consent. But he warned that the role must not replace the work of the government’s consular services, who already deal with other states directly on these matters. “Every case is handled by a competent consular team who are already doing everything they can in every circumstance. What would be wrong would be to give an impression that the engagement of the envoy materially changes that,” he said. That concern had previously been voiced by Ms Zaghari Ratcliffe, who was detained for six years in Iran’s Evin prison. Ms Zaghari-Ratcliffe welcomed Mr Burt’s appointment last month but said she feared the role could quickly become an “excuse” for government inaction. “We don't want to see that the government is hiding behind the fact that now we have got this team, we have got Alistair, we've got this kind of entity which is looking after the families of hostages, but then pretending that that's it, and we can’t do anything else,” she said in September. Mr Burt acknowledged that the families of hostages faced impossible and frustrating situations when dealing with the British government on securing the release of their loved ones. “At the end of all this, there is only one measure of success for the families: they want someone back,” he said. “It’s the one thing that is outside the gift and the control of the UK. We are not detaining people – others are.”

title: Ballon d’Or 2026: Harry Kane beats Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal to claim top prize
body: Harry Kane completed his long quest for football's highest individual honour on Monday, with the Bayern Munich and England striker winning the Ballon d'Or after a record-breaking season that cemented his status as one of the game's greatest goalscorers. Kane is the first Englishman to win the prestigious award in 25 years, since Michael Owen claimed it in 2001. Kylian Mbappe of France and Real Madrid finished second and Spain's Barcelona wonderkid Lamine Yamal was third. Rodri was fourth and Lionel Messi fifth. “Wow, wow, wow!” Kane said after taking the stage. “I am almost speechless. Being here in London has made it extra special. It's a good omen for me tonight. Thank you to everyone who voted for me. I can imagine it was tough this year. “Some world-class players are in the room tonight. Congratulations to all the winners and nominees. It's an impressive showing of what determination and hard work can achieve.” Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for the third time. Kane's move to Bayern in 2023 brought him the team trophies that had long eluded him. In 2025-26, he coupled that success with goalscoring numbers that made him the leading Ballon d'Or candidate. The England captain produced his most prolific campaign, scoring 61 goals in 51 games for Bayern across all competitions as the German side completed a domestic league and cup double. By the end of the season, Kane had established himself as Europe's leading goalscorer. His influence stretched far beyond club football. HARRY KANE IS THE 2026 BALLON D'OR! #ballondor pic.twitter.com/k3CUlwLF1E — Ballon d'Or (@ballondor) October 26, 2026 He scored six goals at the World Cup and led England to the semi-finals, combining his clinical finishing with the leadership and composure that have defined his international career. The award represents the culmination of a remarkable journey. Few players have experienced a career arc quite like Kane's. In his emotional speech, he thanked all his career coaches, as well as Tottenham Hotspur and his wife, Kate. Having struggled to establish himself at Spurs as a youngster and been sent out on numerous loan spells, he developed into one of the most complete centre-forwards of his generation, capable of scoring every type of goal while also functioning as a playmaker. “It's about the journey,” Kane said. “Anything is possible. Work hard when nobody is watching. “For any young boy or girl wanting to achieve their dreams, anything is possible. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs. I had to find my way to become the very best.” Kane's consistency shines through The Ballon d'Or has often rewarded players whose success was built on flair and spectacle, but Kane's triumph is a tribute to consistency, intelligence and productivity on an exceptional scale. Week after week, he delivered. Match after match, he decided contests. There were no prolonged slumps and few quiet nights. His numbers were almost impossible to ignore. Kane finished the campaign with 73 goals for club and country, a total rarely seen in the modern era. More importantly, those goals arrived in moments of genuine significance, helping Bayern collect trophies and driving England deep into the biggest tournament in the sport. The competition for this year's award was fierce. Mbappe broke World Cup scoring records, while Yamal helped Spain to World Cup glory. Yet voters ultimately chose Kane, whose excellence lasted throughout the season. Thank you Alexia & Harry! A very first night to remember in London for the Ballon d'Or ceremony! We'll see you soon... #ballondo pic.twitter.com/JAFjTRrMu0 — Ballon d'Or (@ballondor) October 27, 2026 At 33, Kane has finally claimed the game's highest individual honour, adding a Ballon d'Or to a legacy that already places him among football's greatest strikers. He is also England's all-time leading goalscorer and their record World Cup scorer. Putellas was presented with the women's award after winning the treble with Barcelona in the 2025-26 campaign, in addition to the Spanish Super Cup. She moved to Women's Super League side London City Lionesses in July after 14 years at Barca. Spain and Barcelona players won the young talent awards, with Lamine picking up his third trophy and Vicky Lopez taking home the women's award for the second successive year. Spain coach Luis de la Fuente was named men's coach of the year, while Barcelona's Pere Romeu won the women's coaching award. The men's goalkeeper award went to Unai Simon of Spain and Athletic Bilbao, while Cata Coll of Spain and Barcelona won the women's award. Paris Saint-Germain won the men's club of the year award, while Barcelona picked up the women's honour. Kane won the men's striker of the year prize, while Charlyn Corral was named top women's striker. Arsenal and England winger Bukayo Saka was presented with the Socrates Award for humanitarian work.

title: Where to stay in the Maldives, from secluded luxury escapes to family resorts
body: With its white-sand beaches, turquoise waters and luxurious overwater villas, the Maldives is one of the world's most sought-after holiday destinations. But with hundreds of island resorts to choose from, deciding where to stay can be overwhelming. From secluded luxury retreats and romantic honeymoon hideaways to family-friendly resorts and more affordable all-inclusive escapes, there's something for every type of traveller. To help narrow down the options, here are some standout hotels in the Maldives, tried and tested by The National . Four Seasons Resort Maldives at Kuda Huraa Distance from Male airport: 20km (25 minutes by speedboat) Unique selling point: Traditional Maldivian village charm and a spa on its own private island The Four Seasons Resort Maldives at Kuda Huraa has been welcoming guests for almost 30 years. Designed in the style of a traditional Maldivian village, the resort has 96 villas with thatched roofs, natural timber interiors and private pools, surrounded by lush tropical greenery and white-sand beaches. Its compact size makes it easy to explore, while calm, shallow waters, a children's club and watersport facilities cater to younger guests. Couples will appreciate the private beach pavilions, excellent dining and secluded spa experience, while marine enthusiasts can take part in coral restoration and turtle conservation activities. Read our full review from October 2026 here . The Westin Maldives Miriandhoo Resort Distance from Male airport: 112km (30 minutes by seaplane or a 25-minute domestic flight to Dharavandhoo Airport followed by a 20-minute speedboat trip) Unique selling point: Wellness-focused luxury in a Unesco Biosphere Reserve Located on a small coral island in the Baa Atoll – a Unesco Biosphere Reserve – The Westin Maldives Miriandhoo Resort offers a peaceful escape surrounded by turquoise waters and a thriving house reef. The 70-villa resort combines understated luxury with a focus on wellness, incorporating Japanese-inspired design, lush tropical greenery and spacious accommodation, all with private pools. The resort is particularly well-suited to families with young children who want a quieter Maldivian holiday without sacrificing comfort. Couples seeking privacy, wellness and a laid-back island experience will also appreciate its unhurried pace. Read our full review from October 2026 here . JA Manafaru Distance from Male airport: 316km (70–90 minutes by seaplane or a 55-minute domestic flight to Hoarafushi Airport followed by a 10-minute speedboat) Unique selling point: Remote, secluded luxury in the Maldives' northern-most atoll In the remote Haa Alif Atoll in the far north of the Maldives, JA Manafaru offers a secluded luxury escape that makes the most of the country's natural beauty. The resort has 84 villas and residences, ranging from beachfront hideaways to spacious overwater villas and a three-bedroom residence, each with a private pool. Its remote location makes JA Manafaru particularly appealing to couples, honeymooners and travellers seeking privacy away from busier resort islands. However, the lengthy transfer makes it better suited to a longer stay than a quick getaway. Read our full review from July 2026 here . Huvafen Fushi Distance from Male airport: 26km (30 minutes by speedboat) Unique selling point: An underwater spa with treatment rooms beneath the Indian Ocean A quick speedboat from Male's international airport, Huvafen Fushi offers a secluded private-island experience where the emphasis is on space, tranquility and understated luxury. Set in the North Male Atoll, the five-star resort’s luxurious pavilions feature private pools, generous living areas and uninterrupted ocean views, with some offering glass floor panels through which guests can watch fish swimming below. One of its standout attractions is its underwater spa, where guests can enjoy treatments in submerged rooms as marine life glides past. Personalised butler service, stargazing and the opportunity to spend uninterrupted time enjoying the island's natural beauty are among its biggest draws. Larger pavilions also make it an option for groups of friends or families seeking a private luxury retreat. Read our full review from July 2026 here . Anantara Kihavah Maldives Villas Distance from Male airport: 125km (30 minutes by seaplane or a 25-minute domestic flight to Dharavandhoo Airport followed by a 30-minute speedboat ride) Unique selling point: Underwater dining and an overwater stargazing observatory Set in the Baa Atoll's Unesco Biosphere Reserve, Anantara Kihavah Maldives Villas combines spectacular marine life with five-star luxury. The resort is home to 80 villas and residences, each with a private pool, including recently refreshed overwater villas with expansive sundecks, outdoor showers and glass-bottomed bathtubs. One of its biggest attractions is the exceptional house reef, where snorkellers and divers can encounter turtles, reef sharks, rays and hundreds of species of fish. Other highlights include its underwater dining experiences, overwater observatory for stargazing and an impressive swimming pool. Although the Maldives is traditionally associated with honeymooners, Anantara Kihavah is particularly well suited to families who want to experience the luxury of an overwater villa with children. Thoughtful amenities, personalised villa hosts, babysitting services and the Thiththi Boli Kids Club, catering to children aged four to 12, make family stays easier. Read our full review from October 2025 here . Centara Grand Lagoon Maldives Distance from Male airport: 24km (30–40 minutes by speedboat) Unique selling point: Access to two neighbouring resorts, combining tranquility with family-friendly attractions Part of The Atollia, a multi-island resort development in the Maldives, Centara Grand Lagoon combines Thai hospitality with the natural beauty of the Indian Ocean. Opened in April 2025, the resort offers contemporary beachfront and overwater accommodation, including villas with private plunge pools and direct lagoon access. Guests can enjoy a choice of swimming pools, including a quieter adults' serenity pool, as well as a spa, fitness facilities and varied dining options, from authentic Thai cuisine at Suan Bua to Mediterranean dishes at Bluefin beach club. Its location alongside sister property Centara Mirage Lagoon means guests can enjoy additional facilities, including a lazy river and more family-focused entertainment, before returning to the quieter atmosphere of the Grand. Read our full review from September 2025 here . Niyama Private Islands Maldives Distance from Male airport: 180km (45 minutes by seaplane or a 35-minute domestic flight to Dhaalu Airport followed by a 7-minute speedboat) Unique selling point: Two distinct islands called Play and Chill and world-class surfing Spread across two islands named Play and Chill, Niyama Private Islands offers an unusually varied Maldivian escape, combining beachside relaxation with adventure and family entertainment. Located in the Dhaalu Atoll, the resort has spacious beach and overwater villas, including family accommodation, with private temperature-controlled pools and tropical outdoor bathrooms. Its attractions range from surfing and snorkelling to spa treatments, cycling trails and marine conservation experiences. The sheltered Blue Hole snorkelling spot offers opportunities to discover marine life, while the island's surf breaks have made it increasingly popular with wave riders. Read our full review from December 2024 here . The Ritz-Carlton Maldives, Fari Islands Distance from Male airport: 45km (45 minutes by speedboat) Unique selling point: Striking circular architecture and access to Fari Marina Village Set across three interconnected islands in the North Male Atoll, The Ritz-Carlton Maldives, Fari Islands offers a contemporary take on traditional Maldivian luxury. The resort stands out for its striking circular architecture, minimalist interiors and 100 private pool villas, with both beachfront and overwater options. Dining is a particular highlight, with five restaurants serving everything from Cantonese cuisine to Japanese teppanyaki, while the distinctive overwater spa, snorkelling excursions and personalised butler service add to the experience. Guests can also visit neighbouring Patina Maldives and Fari Marina Village for additional dining options. The Ritz-Carlton is well suited to luxury travellers, food lovers and couples seeking a sophisticated island escape. With a transfer of as little as 15 minutes by seaplane or 45 minutes by speedboat from Male, it is also an appealing option for those wanting to maximise their time on the island. Read our full review from September 2024 here . Nova Maldives Distance from Male airport: 97km (25 minutes by seaplane) Unique selling point: Access to whale shark and manta ray encounters in South Ari Atoll Located in the South Ari Atoll, Nova Maldives is a small, contemporary resort that places the natural beauty of its surroundings at the heart of the experience. The island has just 76 villas, including 25 overwater options, with minimalist interiors, ocean views and direct access to the turquoise waters. Its biggest attraction is its location in one of the Maldives' most celebrated marine environments, with more than 30 manta ray and whale shark spotting sites, shipwrecks and dive locations within 40 minutes. Guests can also enjoy snorkelling, watersports, spa treatments and a choice of three restaurants. Its compact size means everything is within walking distance. The hotel is only accessible by seaplane and does not currently offer a speedboat service from its nearest domestic airport, Villa International Airport Maamigili. Read our full review from July 2024 here . Oblu Xperience Ailafushi Distance from Male airport: 13km (15 minutes by speedboat) Unique selling point: Affordable all-inclusive island living with an underwater restaurant Just 15 minutes by speedboat from Male's international airport, Oblu Xperience Ailafushi offers a more accessible take on the traditional Maldivian island holiday. The four-star, all-inclusive resort combines white-sand beaches and turquoise waters with a lively atmosphere and accommodation ranging from ocean-view rooms and family suites with bunk beds to beach and overwater villas. Highlights include a large swimming pool, watersports centre, dolphin-spotting excursions and the opportunity to dine at Only Blu, an underwater restaurant where marine life swims past the windows. Oblu Xperience Ailafushi is particularly well suited to families and budget-conscious travellers who want the Maldives experience without the expense associated with many of the country's five-star resorts. Its all-inclusive Fushi Plan makes holiday spending easier to manage, while the children's club offers a shallow pool, karaoke room, cinema and gaming facilities for different age groups. Read our full review from October 2023 here . All reviews have been conducted at the invitation of the hotels and reflect standards at the time. Seaplanes operate during daylight hours and are weather-permitting.

title: Sheikh Khaled arrives in Ottawa to begin official visit to Canada
body: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed , Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, has arrived in Ottawa for the start of an official visit to Canada in which he is to hold talks with Prime Minister Mark Carney aimed at bolstering long-standing ties. Sheikh Khaled was greeted at Ottawa Macdonald-Cartier International Airport by Anita Anand, Canada's Minister of Foreign Affairs, state news agency Wam reported early on Tuesday. Sheikh Khaled and Mr Carney are expected to explore ways to advance the strategic partnership between the countries. Talks will focus on expanding co-operation across priority sectors, with both sides seeking to build on shared interests and aspirations for long-term growth and prosperity. No specific sectors were named before the visit. Sheikh Khaled is accompanied by a high-level delegation that includes Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology; Reem Al Hashimy, Minister of State for International Co-operation; Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi, Minister of Foreign Trade; and Mohamed Alsuwaidi, Minister of Investment. Boosting ties Sheikh Khaled's visit comes only weeks after President Sheikh Mohamed spoke by phone with Mr Carney to explore efforts to deepen partnerships, with a focus on the economy, investment and advanced technology. In July, the UAE finalised a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement ( Cepa ) with Canada which will seek to reduce trade barriers to goods, services and investment. The key deal followed a $50 billion investment commitment made by the UAE government as part of Mr Carney's visit to the country. The Cepa gives Canadian companies better access to the UAE, which remains the largest market for Canada's exports to the Middle East, and could help attract capital into energy, mining, artificial intelligence and ports. Overseas engagements Sheikh Khaled's trip to Canada comes only days after he completed an official visit to Greece, during which he met Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis . The two countries strengthened growing relations during the visit, with the UAE agreeing to invest a further €15 billion ($16.8 billion) into Greece as part of a joint initiative between the nations. Sheikh Khaled has also this year represented the UAE at the Brics Summit in India last month and met Xi Jinping, President of China, during an official visit to the country in April.

title: Tehran meeting shows regional push for endogenous security
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 27 (MNA) – A senior Iranian security official said the quadripartite meeting in Tehran involving Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan was the product of Iran's resistance, and reflected a regional turn toward endogenous security.
Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy for international affairs of the Supreme National Security Council, said the quadripartite meeting of Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iran held in Tehran on Monday was the fruit of the Iranian people's resistance and the armed forces' bravery.
Bagheri said the meeting followed important and strategic developments in the region over the past months, centered on the brutal aggression of the Zionist regime and the terrorist US government. He described the meeting as a notable event.
Bagheri said two key points emerged. First, the Islamic Republic of Iran stood up to two blatant aggressions at two different times by two regimes, relying on its national and internal capabilities, and succeeded in both stages. Second, Iran's capabilities in confronting these aggressions came from domestic capacities: its equipment and weapons are the product of the minds and thinking of the country's young scientists as well as the efforts of its artisans and technologists, and these capabilities proved themselves on the battlefield.
He said the Americans and Western countries have sanctioned Iran in strategic areas for decades, and those sanctions have now taken other forms, with their horrific and brutal realities becoming clearer to the world. He said they did not allow advanced equipment and facilities to reach Iran, especially in the military field, but advances made by Iranian youth in the armed forces proved their effectiveness in practice.
Bagheri said reliance on internal capabilities is the way forward. Some regional countries thought that linking themselves to a major power like the United States would protect them from any threat, but in practice they saw that this assumption did not match reality. Regional countries have therefore concluded that there is no way but to rely on regional interaction and to establish security based on cooperation and synergy among regional countries.
Bagheri said what was evident in the remarks of all four parties was an emphasis on self-reliance and endogenous power.
He said the second point evident at the Tehran meeting was that the Zionist regime is the source of insecurity, instability, crisis and tension in the region. All four parties sought to create a path for cooperation, he said.
Bagheri noted that the three countries, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, had earlier held a meeting in Pakistan and were very keen for Iran to attend, but conditions for Iranian participation were not ready. Later they held another meeting in Turkey and again expressed a desire for Iran to attend, but this time they themselves initiated the idea of traveling to Iran and holding the meeting in Tehran.
Bagheri said all three countries raised the point that these four countries, if they cooperate, can be very influential both in the Islamic world and at the regional level.

title: New report tracks how Russia helps China build better drones
body:
Russia's defense cooperation with China extends far beyond imports of dual-use goods, with evidence pointing to sharing drone design technology, providing testing services, and joint research, according to a new report from U.S. think tank C4ADS.
The report adds to earlier findings by the Kyiv Independent regarding China's military collaboration with Russia throughout the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit that investigates security threats, released a report in October that maps lesser-known layers of cooperation between the two countries' defense industries, drawing on Russian trade records, corporate filings, leaked documents, and academic papers.
The investigation found that Russian designs for rocket-launched drones likely helped shape weapons China unveiled in 2025 and that Russian wind tunnels kept testing aircraft models for China's top arms maker after the invasion of Ukraine.
The report also documents how researchers from the two countries are jointly developing algorithms that could underpin combat drone swarms. Moreover, it shows that some suppliers to Russia's defense industry are moving production to China.
Beyond China’s well-documented supplies of components , raw materials and machine tools to the Russian defense industry, and Russia's recently revealed sales of airborne combat vehicles and munitions to China, the two industries increasingly work together further upstream, sharing designs, testing services and research.
A notable example involves the Science and Production Association SPLAV, Russia's leading maker of multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS). SPLAV is subject to multiple international sanctions and export controls.
Trade records show SPLAV sent Chinese arms giant Norinco technical documents for a "reconnaissance rocket" in 2014–2015, and apparently again in April 2022, less than two months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The rocket is most likely SPLAV's 9M534, which releases a reconnaissance drone in mid-flight.
In March 2025, China unveiled the Feilong 60A, a loitering drone launched from Norinco's SR-5 rocket system and reportedly capable of operating in swarms. Three months later, Norinco tested Sky Eye, a drone fired from a cannon. Both drones are similar to the Russian 9M534.
C4ADS believes the Russian technical documents helped speed up Norinco's work on both systems, though it notes that this conclusion rests mainly on how closely the Chinese and Russian systems resemble each other.
Russia's aerospace testing base is also working for Norinco, which now faces U.S. sanctions and Japanese and Taiwanese export controls.
The Russian state-owned Central Aerohydrodynamic Institute (TsAGI), which is under multiple Western sanctions, tested Chinese scale aircraft models in its wind tunnels and returned them to Norinco with the test data at least nine times between 2022 and 2024. The work comes as Norinco has been expanding into military drones over the past decade.
The cooperation also extends to universities and research institutes. Drones have become a growing focus of joint research by Chinese and Russian scientists, according to C4ADS.
Researchers from the two countries co-authored 86 academic papers on drones and other unmanned systems between 2022 and 2026, an average of about 17 a year. In the dozen years from 2009 to 2021, they produced only 36 such papers, or about three a year.
Evgeny Neretin, a department head at the Moscow Aviation Institute, has co-authored multiple papers with researchers tied to Chinese defense laboratories — labs that also funded the work. The papers deal with algorithms for autonomous drone combat and, more recently, for keeping several drones in formation while they track targets, a likely building block for drone swarms.
In June 2025, the Chinese government approved the creation of a joint educational institute between the Moscow Aviation Institute (sanctioned by the U.S. and EU), and China's military-linked Northwestern Polytechnical University (subject to U.S. and Japanese export controls).
The C4ADS report also indicates that some Russian makers of machine tools and chips are moving production to China.
Stankomashstroy, a sanctioned Russian machine-tool maker, plans to move production of advanced five-axis machine tools to an industrial park in China's Shaanxi province.
In 2025, the company sold equipment to the Votkinsk Plant , which builds ballistic missiles , and to Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol, a producer of air defense systems and long-range attack drones.
Illustrating Moscow's reliance on Beijing for chips, Russia's sanctioned state-owned chipmaker Element set up at least four subsidiaries in China in 2025 and began assembling chipsets there. In 2026, Element also bought power electronics intellectual property from the Chinese defense contractor Shijiazhuang Tonhe Electronics.
According to C4ADS, these moves would likely help Element produce military-grade microelectronics despite Western sanctions and export controls. They also fit a recent Kremlin initiative to build up Russia's chip industry.
The C4ADS report adds fresh details to previous findings by the Kyiv Independent regarding China and Russia's military partnership.
While China officially claims neutrality in Russia's war against Ukraine, Beijing remains Moscow's key trading partner, economic supporter, oil buyer, and provider of dual-use equipment.
According to leaked Rostec documents, China bought Russian airborne combat vehicles, ammunition, and parachute systems after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Dozens of Chinese officers and arms industry staff visited Russia during the war to negotiate the deals.
Separate Kyiv Independent investigations found that Chinese suppliers have helped keep Russia's missile and drone production pipelines running.
Machine tools shipped mostly from China fueled the expansion of the Votkinsk Plant , which makes ballistic missiles — including intercontinental ones.
Chinese and Hong Kong companies also supplied parts to the maker of Russia's Lancet attack drones and remain the main channel for Western chips used in Russian weapons.

title: CDABI president launches two books on digital asset regulation
body: President of the Chamber of Digital Assets and Blockchain Innovations (CDABI), Ghana Chapter, Dr Caleb Kwaku Afaglo, has launched two books on digital asset regulation to inform policy decisions and industry development in Ghana and West Africa. The books were soft-launched in Accra on Thursday, October 22, 2026, on the opening day of MOBEX Africa 2026. They are “Global Digital Asset Regulation Read from Accra: A Reference Report for Ghana and West Africa” and “Rules for a New Money: Building Digital Asset Regulation from Accra”. The main launch is scheduled for Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 0930 hours at the Africa Stablecoin Summit in Cape Town, South Africa. CDABI, in partnership with Vessel & Light Publishing, published the reference report, the first volume in a new CDABI reference series. It examines digital asset regulatory frameworks across Europe, China, Hong Kong, Singapore, Russia, South Africa, East Africa, West Africa, and the Gulf. The 176-page report compares regulatory approaches to retail access, transaction monitoring, tax reporting, banking participation and central bank digital currencies. It also presents 13 policy findings and outlines six decisions Ghana could consider without introducing new legislation. The report draws on 313 sources and reflects legal and market developments as of September 30, 2026. Dr Afaglo said Ghana enacted its virtual asset law, Act 1154, in December 2025, with the Bank of Ghana Virtual Assets Department (VAD) supervising the sector. He said decisions on regulating digital assets would determine whether Ghana became an active participant in emerging payment systems or remained an endpoint. He said the report provided regulators, banks, and industry players with a common evidence base for considering policy options. “Rules for a New Money”, authored by Dr Afaglo and published by Vessel & Light Publishing, describes how Ghana’s virtual asset regulatory framework developed. The book examines the policy trade-offs, discussions between regulators and industry players, and outstanding decisions concerning the sector’s regulation. Dr Afaglo said the book documented the reasoning behind Ghana’s regulatory choices, which he said the final regulations would not necessarily explain. He said Cape Town was an appropriate venue for the main launch because South Africa had developed a regulatory framework for crypto assets that other African jurisdictions frequently studied. CDABI offers print copies of the reference report, while Vessel & Light Publishing offers “Rules for a New Money”. Amazon is expected to list paperback and Kindle editions of both books after the Cape Town launch.

title: Macklemore vows to fight until 'last breath' at opening of 'Free Palestine' tour
body: American rapper Macklemore vowed to continue to speak out loudly against Israel's war in Gaza at the opening of his "Free Palestine" concert tour, organized after he was dropped as the opening act for Ed Sheeran over pro-Palestinian remarks.The Grammy-winning rapper received a deafening ovation in Dublin, where fans in the overwhelmingly pro-Palestinian country came draped in Palestinian flags, black, red and green football jerseys and keffiyeh scarves being sold by vendors outside."I am proud to stand here on stage in solidarity with the Palestinian people. We will continue to fight for collective liberation until our last breath," Macklemore said on stage, where he waved a Palestinian flag for much of his set."Six weeks ago, two words is all that it took," he said, referring to the rallying cry of "Free Palestine" and his criticism of the Israeli government's actions in Gaza and the West Bank at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium that led to his removal from Sheeran's US tour."Those two words are so threatening to some people that we'd rather silence those two words than confront what they actually mean... Somehow those words have become more controversial than the suffering that made them necessary."The crowd, who snapped up the 13,000 tickets for Dublin's 3Arena within minutes, chanted "Free Free Palestine" throughout.Macklemore a 'speaker for our time,' concert attendee says"We need a speaker for our time. It has to be somebody like that who can reach out to people. He made it feel so alive, and I've come out feeling I want to be part of something," said Siobhan Lyons from Dublin, who attended the concert with her daughter.Irish artists who have spoken out against Israel's actions played in support on Monday, including "Take Me to Church" singer Hozier, rap group Kneecap and Beoga, one of the acts who quit Sheeran's tour in solidarity with Macklemore.Palestinian singer Lina Makhoul and Palestinian American DJ Habibeats also performed, and pro-Palestine activists such as Game of Thrones actor Liam Cunningham spoke between sets.Sheeran, one of the world's top-selling recording artists, said stadium owners on the remaining dates threatened to bar any further shows with Macklemore on the bill.Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 ​people have been killed in Israel's assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people ​in southern Israel on October 7, 2023. Israeli officials deny their actions in Gaza amount to genocide.The "Free Palestine" tour will continue in Paris and London this week, with US dates due to be announced later, Macklemore has said.

title: At Economic Summit, Tinubu Says the Nigerian Story is Being Rewritten
body: • Oyedele unveils policy framework to ring-fence economic policies against reversals •Abubakar Bagudu: Tinubu won’t reverse economic reforms • Chukwuma Soludo: lack of local patronage costs Nigeria 10 million jobs, says 12% annual growth needed to achieve $1 trillion economy, 8% acceleration to address poverty Deji Elumoye and James Emejo in Abuja President Bola Tinubu yesterday said his government was rewriting Nigeria’s decades-long story of economic underperformance through far-reaching reforms designed to dismantle structural barriers, unlock the nation’s enormous potential, and deliver jobs, productivity, and shared prosperity. Tinubu said rewriting the story of a nation that had performed below its potential for far too long was what the administration came into office to achieve: The president spoke in Abuja while formally declaring open the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit (NES#32), with the theme, “Growth that Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity.” At the summit, Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele, presented the Nigerian Economic Policy Framework, which he described as a national economic doctrine establishing how Nigeria made economic decisions and measured real progress. Oyedele said the blueprint aimed at curbing arbitrary policy changes. Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Senator Abubakar Bagudu, ruled out a return to petrol subsidy, insisting that the Tinubu administration will sustain its economic reforms, despite mounting pressure on households and businesses. Bagudu told the conference that reversing reforms would undermine efforts to address longstanding distortions. Governor of Anambra State, Professor Chukwuma Charles Soludo, said lack of local patronage of Made-in-Nigeria products had robbed the country of 10 million potential jobs, adding that everyone has a role to play in boosting growth. Soludo said the economy needed between seven and nine per cent annual growth rate to address multidimensional poverty. Tinubu, who was represented at NES#32 by Vice President Kashim Shettima, stated that his government began on a difficult note because there was no shortcut to economic growth. He stated, “Distinguished ladies and gentlemen, we came to rewrite the story of a nation that has performed below its potential for far too long. But there is no shortcut to economic growth. This is why we began with a difficult reset. For us, rescuing the economy means rescuing livelihoods and transforming the fortunes of young jobseekers, farmers, manufacturers, entrepreneurs and innovators. “We cannot harness the immense opportunities offered by our growing population without first stabilising the economy. We must also create the conditions for the public and private sectors to invest, expand and generate productive employment.” Tinubu observed that the summit’s theme, “Growth That Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity,” built on the ambition of the previous edition of the annual event to achieve a prosperous and inclusive Nigeria by 2030. He stated that his administration had “since set in motion a series of reforms to dismantle the structural barriers that have prevented our abundant human and natural resources from yielding prosperity”. The president said, “These reforms are restoring confidence, strengthening our economic foundations and laying the groundwork for sustainable growth.” He added that the administration was encouraged by what it had accomplished so far. Acknowledging that creating jobs was only half the task, the president stressed the need to “improve the quality of work, reduce underemployment and harness the potential” of the country’s underutilised workforce. He stated, “Our pursuit of prosperity demands greater productivity from every worker, enterprise and investment. We must judge infrastructure by the economic activity it generates and education by the skills and productivity it delivers. “We must judge industrial policy by the competitiveness of our firms and investment incentives by the capital, technology, exports and jobs they attract.” Tinubu outlined the achievements of his administration’s reforms, saying they have been well documented. He cited figures from the National Bureau of Statistics indicating that Nigeria’s inflation-adjusted GDP grew by 3.89 per cent in the first quarter of 2026, compared with 3.13 per cent a year earlier. On economic diversification, he stated that “non-oil activities accounted for 96.08 per cent of GDP, while manufacturing grew by 3.29 per cent and the oil sector by 2.57 per cent”. He emphasised that the gains had reinforced his administration’s confidence in the path of recovery and diversification. The president stated, however, that his administration’s ambition must go beyond favourable statistics, even as the development narrative was changing and investor confidence was returning. Outlining the administration’s gains so far, he said, “In the first quarter of 2026, our capital importation reached $10.37 billion, an increase of 83.83 per cent over the corresponding period in 2025. This comprised both portfolio and foreign direct investment. We will, therefore, continue to ease regulatory burdens, strengthen transparency and policy predictability, and expand access to finance. “Our tax reforms seek to build a modern, equitable system that finances development and gives businesses certainty. This discipline must guide our investments in all sectors of the economy, including energy, agriculture and solid minerals. We are reforming the electricity market to improve supply and attract investment in generation, transmission, distribution and alternative energy.” On agriculture, Tinubu said the administration was connecting farms to storage facilities, processing centres, and markets, while expanding irrigation, mechanisation, finance, and rural infrastructure. He added that the government was also seeking “to move beyond extraction into domestic processing, industrial production and exports” in the solid minerals sector. The president, however, stated that despite the gains of his administration’s economic reforms, the task remained far from finished, even as young Nigerians had demonstrated their capacity to compete globally in technology, financial services, and the creative industries.
