Oyedele unveils framework to guard against policy reversals Oyedele, at the summit, presented the Nigerian Economic Policy Framework, saying it is a national economic doctrine that establishes how Nigeria makes economic decisions and measures progress. He said the plan aimed to curb arbitrary policy reversals, reduce uncertainty for businesses, and ensure economic reforms delivered measurable improvements in jobs, household incomes, and productivity. He said the economic doctrine was intended to outlive successive administrations. The minister stated that Nigeria’s persistent development challenges stemmed not from a shortage of economic plans but from inconsistent policymaking, weak implementation, and the tendency of successive governments to reverse or undermine previous reforms. According to him, policy uncertainty imposes an invisible cost on businesses, discourages investment, raises the cost of capital and prevents potential employment opportunities from materialising. Oyedele said, “Governments will come. Governments will go. But Nigeria’s economic horizon must outlive every electoral calendar.” The proposed framework is intended to establish enduring principles for economic decision-making, rather than serve as another development plan, catalogue of government projects, or manifesto of an administration. Oyedele said the document was being released for public consultation and had not yet received government approval. The consultation, which runs until November 27, 2026, will seek public input on 17 core questions through the Ministry of Finance’s website. Following validation, the framework will be presented to the Federal Executive Council (FEC) for approval and the National Economic Council (NEC) for endorsement. A central feature of the proposal is a mandatory policy impact assessment for major economic interventions, including tax adjustments, tariff changes, regulatory restrictions and incentives. Under the proposed arrangement, policymakers would be required to establish the problem a measure seeks to address, provide supporting evidence, identify its beneficiaries and those bearing its costs, and specify the conditions under which it would expire. The framework also proposes an annual National Economic Scorecard, to be published on or before October 1, to track whether real wages are rising, productive employment is expanding, and poverty is declining. Oyedele maintained that headline economic growth and investment announcements alone were insufficient measures of success, stating that economic performance must translate into tangible improvements in living standards. He outlined seven interconnected priorities for the framework: stability, productivity, enterprise, capital, people, markets and institutions. The minister identified private enterprise as the principal engine of economic growth, with government responsible for providing public goods, maintaining the rule of law, correcting market failures, and protecting vulnerable citizens. He also advocated competitive markets, warning against using industrial policies and tariffs to shield inefficient businesses indefinitely from competition. On coordination, Oyedele said government institutions must assess the cumulative burden of their policies on businesses instead of pursuing isolated departmental The minister invited members of the Nigerian Economic Summit Group (NESG) and private sector experts to make valuable contributions to the development of the framework by rigorously critiquing the draft proposal with facts and figures. He said the principles underpinning the framework included enterprise, open but fair markets, and whole-of-government coherence. Bagudu Rules Out Return to Petrol Subsidy, Says Tinubu Won’t Reverse Reforms Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Senator Abubakar Bagudu, ruled out a return to petrol subsidy, insisting that the Tinubu administration will sustain its economic reforms, despite mounting pressure on households and businesses. Bagudu, at NES#32, said reversing the reforms would undermine efforts to address longstanding economic distortions and stabilise the economy. “For those of us serving under the president and vice president, the instruction has been clear: we must stay the course,” he said. His position came amid opposition calls, including from the African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, for the restoration of petrol subsidy to ease the rising cost of living. Bagudu, however, acknowledged that sustaining the reforms would require improved implementation, responsive policy adjustments, and targeted interventions to cushion vulnerable Nigerians. He said the government was focused on translating economic gains into jobs, higher productivity, and improved living standards, while strengthening domestic production and attracting investment. The minister stated that increased revenue accruing to federal, state and local governments presented an opportunity to expand infrastructure and improve public services, stressing the need for stronger coordination among the three tiers of government. He also reiterated Nigeria’s ambition to build a $1 trillion economy by 2030, saying this would require higher productivity, expanded industrial capacity, stronger private-sector participation, and a more competitive business environment. Bagudu identified agriculture, manufacturing, digital technology, and human capital development as key drivers of the administration’s growth strategy. He said the Renewed Hope Ward Development Plan would unlock productive opportunities across Nigeria’s 8,809 wards through targeted interventions based on local economic strengths, including agriculture, fishing, livestock, and textiles. On agriculture, Bagudu highlighted the need for improved access to financing, mechanisation, irrigation, processing, storage and markets to boost production, reduce post-harvest losses, and improve food affordability. He also cited the Nigeria Industrial Policy 2025 and Nigeria First Policy as initiatives aimed at strengthening local manufacturing and supply chains. Bagudu highlighted a proposed 90,000-kilometre fibre-optic infrastructure initiative, being pursued with the European Union and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, to expand broadband connectivity. He called for improved access to finance for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, including through a proposed credit guarantee framework, while urging public- and private-sector stakeholders to mobilise investment to close Nigeria’s development financing gap. Soludo: Poor Patronage of Local Products Costs Nigeria 10m Jobs Soludo said limited local patronage of Made-in-Nigeria products was costing the country about 10 million potential jobs. The former CBN governor said while the current stability must not be take for granted, the country should not be carried away by the euphoria of massive huge currency appreciation. He said the current growth was not sufficient to eliminate poverty, adding that the economy needs to grow between seven and nine per cent per annual to address poverty. Among other things, he said growth needed to average 12 per cent annually to achieve the proposed $1 trillion economy by 2030. According to him, the average Nigerian still lives on less than $1 per day, urging coordination and collaboration between federal and states governments to rein in inflation and attract investments into the country. Rabiu Seeks 100 More Major Industrial Firms, Cites FX Reforms Rabiu commended the economic reforms of the Tinubu administration, saying they have begun to address longstanding challenges confronting Nigerian businesses. He acknowledged the difficulties experienced by ordinary Nigerians but stated that improvements in access to foreign exchange had created a more predictable environment for businesses. He called for policy consistency, affordable long-term financing and improved infrastructure to accelerate industrialisation, warning that uncertainty in the business environment can undermine investments requiring decades to deliver returns. He stressed that the success of Nigeria’s economic reforms would depend on the government’s ability to create conditions that enable businesses to expand production, create jobs, and compete effectively. “We cannot expect businesses to make 20-year investments if they cannot plan with confidence beyond the next few years,” he said. The industrialist identified high borrowing costs and limited access to long-term capital as major constraints preventing small businesses from evolving into large-scale manufacturing concerns. He explained that industrial investments typically required substantial upfront spending on land, factories, equipment, workforce development, and production, often years before businesses begin to realise significant returns. “You cannot build a strong industrial economy primarily with expensive short-term finances,” he said. Rabiu said the next phase of reform must focus on expanding productive capacity and building more big Nigerian businesses capable of competing internationally. He said foreign-exchange reforms had eased a major constraint for industrialists, who previously had to lobby the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) for dollar allocations even when they had the naira to pay for imports. Businesses can now obtain foreign exchange through the market, he said, describing the change as a significant improvement for companies seeking machinery and industrial inputs. The BUA chairman cited the cement industry’s transition from heavy dependence on imports to domestic self-sufficiency and net exports as evidence of what sustained investment and local production could achieve. He challenged Nigeria to develop 100 more major industrial companies across critical sectors, like manufacturing, agriculture, mining, technology and other sectors, stating that such businesses would generate jobs, support local suppliers and increase exports. However, he identified expensive financing as a major obstacle, saying industrial projects often require 10 to 20 years to mature and could not be sustainably financed with costly, short-term loans. He called on pension funds, insurance companies, banks, development finance institutions, and capital markets to channel more long-term funds into productive investment. Rabiu also urged the government and private sector to agree on a new economic accord anchored on policy consistency, infrastructure, human-capital development, and shared prosperity. He said, “For many years, one of the greatest challenges facing businesses was access to foreign exchange. You could have all the naira but be unable to obtain the foreign exchange needed to buy raw materials and machinery.” Amina Mohammed Urges Consolidation of Economic Reforms United Nations Deputy Secretary-General, Dr. Amina Mohammed, assessed the reforms implemented under the Tinubu administration, acknowledging the gains, while urging their urgent consolidation and stabilisation, as well as the effective management of expectations among citizens and other stakeholders. Mohammed applauded the African Development Bank (AfDB) for its new financial architecture for development across the continent, particularly its prioritisation of financing programmes that targeted impactful development. Dercon: Nigeria Must End Business Protection, Boost Non-Oil Exports to Drive Sustainable Development In his keynote, Professor of Economic Policy at the University of Oxford/former Chief Economist for the UK’s Department for International Development, Stefan Dercon, said macroeconomic stabilisation must be followed by a credible growth strategy capable of raising incomes and expanding economic opportunities. Dercon stated that Nigeria’s income per capita remained around its 2010 level, stressing that the country needs a broader development bargain linking government, businesses, and citizens around measurable economic objectives. He advocated stronger non-oil exports, lower trade barriers, and time-bound incentives that reward firms for becoming competitive rather than protecting them indefinitely. He said Nigeria should aim to at least double non-oil exports by the end of the next administration, while warning that import tariffs could also raise costs for exporters who depend on imported inputs. Dercon urged the federal government to double the non-oil exports by the end of the next administration, warning that economic stabilisation alone cannot deliver sustainable growth, jobs and poverty reduction. He commended the Tinubu administration for unifying the exchange rate, curbing monetary financing of the budget and implementing tax reforms. However, he said Nigeria must move beyond stabilisation to fundamentally restructure its economy, which he said remained constrained by an elite bargain centred on sharing oil revenues rather than creating broad-based prosperity. He stated that income per capita had barely improved since 2010, despite previous reform efforts, while oil output per capita had declined by about 60 per cent since 2000. According to him, Nigeria needs a new development compact that prioritises productivity, competitiveness and job creation over the distribution of economic rents. Flour Mills MD Seeks Incentives to Boost Private Sector Exports Group Managing Director/Chief Executive, Flour Mills of Nigeria Plc, Mr. Omoboyede Olusanya, promised significant investment by the private sector to drive exports if government provided the needed incentives. Olusanya said infrastructure remained a major challenge for businesses in the country. He stressed the need to deal with supply chain challenges, tackle the inflationary environment, and cut interest rate. NESG Chairman Urges Shift from Policy Consensus to Practical Solutions Earlier, in his welcome address, Chairman of NESG, Mr. Olaniyi Yusuf, said participation at the 32nd summit reflected stakeholders’ commitment to contributing to inclusive and impactful growth, while acknowledging the federal government’s efforts to improve the ease of doing business in the country. Yusuf said although the reforms of the Tinubu administration might have introduced significant changes to Nigeria’s economic structures, the task before economic experts at the summit and beyond was to ensure stabilisation rather than seek a reversal of the policies. He added that the 32nd edition of the summit must help Nigeria move from policy consensus to a framework that resolved practical issues, stating that deliberations would be guided by proposals for job creation, improved productivity, and shared prosperity. ADC Campaign Replies Shettima Over Atiku’s Education Meanwhile, African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Campaign Council criticised Vice President Kashim Shettima for mocking former Vice President Atiku Abubakar’s educational background, challenging Shettima to explain alleged discrepancies in President Bola Tinubu’s academic records. The council, in a statement yesterday by its Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, accused Shettima of diverting attention from the country’s cost-of-living crisis by questioning Atiku’s attendance at the Kano School of Hygiene. The reaction followed Shettima’s remarks at the opening of the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja, where he reportedly questioned Atiku’s qualifications and suggested that he lacked the skill set required to govern a modern Nigeria. Countering the vice president’s criticism, the ADC campaign council stated that Atiku’s educational journey was not a legitimate basis for ridicule, particularly at a time when Nigerians were grappling with rising living costs. “What, exactly, is shameful about Atiku’s education?” Shaibu asked. He added, “He completed secondary school, pursued further training and built a life through work. Millions of Nigerians have travelled the same road.” Shaibu stated, “Their parents sacrificed to get them into the schools they could afford; they studied, worked and rose. Shettima looked at that struggle and saw something to laugh at.” The campaign council subsequently turned its attention to Tinubu’s academic history, citing what it described as an inconsistency in documents associated with his education at Chicago State University in the United States. “If Shettima wants to examine school records, he should begin with the man he serves,” Shaibu said. He alleged that a document in Tinubu’s Chicago State University records listed him as having graduated from Government College Lagos in 1970, although the school was established in 1974. “Shettima should explain how a man graduates from a school before it exists, instead of mocking Atiku for attending a school whose doors were open,” the statement said. The council also raised questions about the name on a National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) certificate Tinubu submitted to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), alleging that it bore the name “Tinubu Bola Adekunle”. According to Shaibu, Atiku had challenged the discrepancy in court. “Shettima cannot ridicule Atiku’s documented schooling while refusing to address questions about the name on his principal’s certificate,” Shaibu added. The campaign council maintained that Tinubu’s Chicago State University documents remained the subject of litigation in the United States, stating that questions surrounding documents submitted in connection with his election should be addressed on their merits. It also referenced the documented 1993 forfeiture involving Tinubu in Chicago, which arose from a narcotics investigation, saying the issue continued to attract public attention. The allegations and interpretations in the statement were advanced by the ADC campaign council as part of its political response to Shettima’s remarks. ADC Says Economic Hardship Deserves Priority Over Political Attacks Beyond the controversy over academic qualifications, the council stated that the exchange had diverted attention from the economic difficulties confronting households and businesses. Shaibu cited World Bank estimates, as presented in the statement, that nearly seven in 10 Nigerians would live below its lower-middle-income poverty line in 2026, while 35 million people faced acute food insecurity. “Shettima says Atiku wants Nigerians to ‘backslide into penury’. Back from where?” he asked. Shaibu said, “Poverty is not a future threat to these families. It is the life they are struggling through today.” He added that Nigerians forced to choose between transport costs and feeding their families did not need lectures about poverty from government officials. “A parent choosing between transport to work and food for the children does not need Shettima to explain penury,” Shaibu said, accusing the administration of being disconnected from the daily realities of ordinary Nigerians. The statement also challenged the federal government to respond to Atiku’s proposal for a targeted, capped and independently audited subsidy tied to petrol refined in Nigeria. “If Shettima thinks it cannot be funded, he should show his figures and offer a better way to lower prices,” Shaibu said. “Insulting Atiku will not fill a cooking pot, pay a bus fare or put fuel in a tank.” The council maintained that Atiku had no reason to be ashamed of his educational background, stating that his experience reflected the circumstances of many Nigerians who had pursued education through the opportunities available to them. It accused Shettima of choosing personal attacks over an explanation of the administration’s economic policies and their effects on citizens. Looking ahead to the 2027 general election, the campaign council said Nigerians would have an opportunity to express their views on the administration’s performance at the ballot box. “Nigerians will answer the Vice-President’s mockery and his boss’s record with their votes,” Shaibu said. The statement concluded with a direct political challenge to the president and his deputy, asserting that voters would hold the administration accountable for its policies and record.

title: NUPRC: Domestic Refiners Got 127 Million Barrels in 9 Months Amid Improved Supply
body: • FG assures Nigeria’s four refineries won’t be left stranded •NMDPRA expands gas supply access with new network code • Targets 9 fuel laboratories nationwide by 2027 •Authority, NNPC to pilot national strategic fuel reserve Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja and Peter Uzoho in Lagos The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) has disclosed that domestic refineries received more than 127 million barrels of Nigerian crude oil and condensate between January and September 2026, reflecting improvements in the implementation of the Domestic Crude Supply Obligation (DCSO). Also, the federal government has said it is pursuing a more rigorous, commercially sustainable approach to rehabilitate and reposition the four national refineries in Port Harcourt, Warri and Kaduna to prevent them from becoming stranded assets. In the same vein, the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority, (NMDPRA) has signed and unveiled Revision II of the Nigerian Gas Transportation Network Code (NGTNC), aimed at expanding gas supply access to power, fertiliser plants, shippers and investors. The NURPC Chief Executive, Mrs. Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, who spoke yesterday in her speech at the OTL Africa Downstream Energy Week 2026 in Lagos, restated that the commission was also consulting producers, refiners and other stakeholders on a domestic crude swap framework. Speaking on the theme: ‘’Secure Energy, Shared Prosperity’’, the NUPRC boss, who was represented by the Assistant Director, Operations, Mr. Prosper Omonedo, said the commission’s intervention had improved crude oil deliveries after commercial disagreements between producers and refiners affected supplies in the first quarter. “We engaged producers and refiners, and in the second and third quarters, 53.7 and 45.1 million barrels of crude oil and condensate were supplied to domestic refineries, an overall performance of 97.4 and 76.2 per cent, respectively. “From Q1–Q3 of 2026, more than 127 million barrels of Nigerian crude went to Nigerian refineries,” she said. Under Section 109 of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) 2021, the NUPRC allocates crude oil to domestic refineries before export. The NUPRC chief executive said the NUPRC was also consulting producers, refiners and other stakeholders on a domestic crude swap framework. “Under it, a refiner could receive crude from the nearest suitable production or export point instead of moving an allocated grade over long distances, which could take an estimated three to four dollars off the cost of every barrel,” he added. On production, Eyesan said Nigeria recorded an average of 1.717 million barrels per day of crude oil and condensate in September, a 2.34 per cent increase over August. Crude oil production alone averaged 1.53 million barrels per day, marking the fifth consecutive month the industry met or exceeded its quota. She attributed the improvement to better asset integrity, enhanced security of evacuation infrastructure, stronger collaboration with operators and sustained regulatory efforts to restore shut-in production. On the 2026 Licensing Round, she said the 40 blocks on offer would be subjected to a transparent evaluation process, with published criteria and mandatory disclosure of beneficial ownership. The NUPRC boss added that the commission was enforcing the drill-or-drop principle to discourage speculative holding of licences, noting that 22 recent awardees were expected to contribute at least 250,000 barrels per day within five years. She reaffirmed the commission’s commitment to meeting the Domestic Gas Delivery Obligation and working with the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) to align refinery demand with crude supply planning, ensuring that upstream gains translate into tangible benefits for households, industries and power generation. At the event, the federal government said that it was pursuing a more rigorous, commercially sustainable approach to rehabilitate and reposition the four national refineries in Port Harcourt, Warri and Kaduna to prevent them from becoming stranded assets. Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Petroleum Resources, Mrs Patience Oyekunle, in her remarks, said the government remained committed to ensuring existing national refining assets run by the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) were not lost, supported by technical assessment, stronger partnerships and improved operational discipline. “At the same time, the government remains committed to ensuring that existing national refining assets are not allowed to become stranded investments. We are pursuing a more rigorous, commercially sustainable approach to the rehabilitation and repositioning of our refineries, supported by technical assessment, stronger partnerships and improved operational discipline,” she said. She said the 20th anniversary of OTL was a testament to resilience and relevance, commending the platform for bringing government, investors, operators and regulators together. The government noted that Nigeria is transforming from import dependence to domestic refining, private investment and regional competitiveness under the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA). “Today, we are beginning to see the results. Nigeria’s crude oil production has been strengthened significantly,” she explained. She said Nigeria has maintained its compliance with the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) quota for the fourth consecutive month, owing to the rise in the nation’s crude oil production as shown by October output which surpassed 1.7 million barrels per day including condensates. She said increasing production was only one part, with greater emphasis on value addition at home through refining, petrochemicals, gas processing and manufacturing. “The emergence of large-scale private refining capacity represents an important turning point. The Dangote Refinery has reached its 650,000 barrels-per-day nameplate capacity, strengthening Nigeria’s prospects of becoming a net exporter of refined petroleum products,” the government said. On gas, the federal government said Nigeria with over 215 trillion cubic feet of proven reserves must move from resource-rich to value-creating economy, citing the Gas Master Plan 2026 targeting 10 billion standard cubic feet per day by 2027 and 12BCF/d by 2030. “Gas will power industries, support electricity generation, expand CNG and LPG utilisation, strengthen LNG exports and provide feedstock for petrochemicals,” she said. She warned that the era of extracting value without building value was changing, with expectations on local content, technology and host-community development. On its part, the NMDPRA said the new Network Code will deepen domestic gas utilisation and guarantee open, fair access Authority Chief Executive, Rabiu Umar, who signed and unveiled the code with partners comprising power generation plants, fertiliser plants, shippers and investors at the OTL opening, said the code is the rulebook for shared pipelines. “The Network Code basically is the rulebook for gas transportation. As we know, there’s one pipeline that different producers put their gas into. And for there to be equity, there needs to be a code, or if you like, rules of engagement on how you put your gas inside, how the gas is measured, and how you nominate gas,” Umar said. “The pipelines deliver their full value only when access to them is open and fair. It is therefore a pleasure to announce that the Authority has officially launched revision 2 of the Nigerian Gas Transportation Network Code,” he explained. Umar said about three-fifths of gas processed in September went to power plants, factories, NLNG and West African Gas Pipeline, while cooking gas demand outstrips supply. He said the Obe-Obiafu-Obrikon (OB3), the Escravos-Lagos Pipeline System (ELPS) midline compressor and the Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano (AKK) pipeline at over 80 per cent completion will double transport capacity from 2.2 to 4.4 BCF/d, linking the south to north. “Since Revision I, more shippers have come onto the network, and the imbalance on the Western network has fallen by about 30 per cent Revision II builds on these gains,” he said, noting clearer provisions on Shrinkage Factor and initial rules for Trans-Saharan and Trans-African pipelines. On downstream stability, Umar said three in four litres of petrol last month were refined domestically compared to over half imported a year ago, showing energy security built at home. Although, he noted that much supply still came from one large refinery (Dangote Refinery) above nameplate in September, requiring diversity via modular and state refineries and competitive imports on merit-based licences. Umar disclosed that NMDPRA is in advanced talks with NNPC to pilot strategic stock at National Pipeline and Storage Company Limited (NPSC) depots in Ibadan, Enugu and Suleja to cushion against external shocks, after eight months of Gulf war pushing crude to $100. He announced the first of nine fuel laboratories launched recently in Port Harcourt, two more by year-end, all nine by second half 2027, in partnership with Bureau Veritas and Ace Energy and Power Solutions towards a National Reference Laboratory. Chairman of OTL Africa Advisory Board, Mr Adetunji Oyebanji, in his welcome address, said 20 years of OTL mirrors Africa’s downstream evolution from securing imports and managing administered prices to shaping own supply arrangements, with private refining changing possibilities. “When OTL began in 2007, much of Africa’s downstream discussion centred on securing imports. Those concerns have not disappeared. But the continent’s capacity to shape its own supply arrangements has strengthened,” Oyebanji said, citing Ghana’s 2015 price liberalisation, Dangote refinery, Kenya’s Mombasa-Nairobi pipeline, Egypt’s Mostorod upgrade, South Africa’s Lesedi terminal and Angola’s Cabinda refinery. He warned of Middle East conflict, shipping route insecurity and Russian supply disruptions still pressuring diesel availability and freight costs, requiring dependable feedstock, efficient operations and clear rules to sustain confidence.

title: Alleged N582m Fraud: Judge Threatens Arrest of NNPC Coop Society’s Ex-President, Ogunbayo over Absence in Court
body: Alex Enumah in Abuja A High Court of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, has threatened to order the arrest of a former President of the Nigeria National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Staff Multi-Purpose Cooperative Society, Olalekan Ogunbayo, over his failure to appear in court and take his plea in an alleged N582 million fraud charge. Justice Lesley Wike issued the threat on Monday following complaints by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) that Monday’s proceedings was the third time Ogunbayo refused to appear in court for arraignment on the alleged financial misappropriation of the society’s funds. When the matter was called, prosecution counsel, R. U. Adagba informed the judge that only the 2nd defendant, Abolade Nurudeen was in court. The lawyer complained that Ogunbayo was granted administrative bail but jumped the bail and that all efforts to locate him for service of the charge have been unsuccessful. The EFCC stated that Ogunbayo had stalled the arraignment twice due to absence in court and applied that bench warrant be issued against him to facilitate his arrest and production in court. Adagba cited Sections 35, 113, 114 of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act (ACJA) 2015, arguing that the court has the power to order arrest of the defendant. However, counsel to the defendants, Innocent Adoo, opposed the arrest warrant application, arguing that arraignment in a criminal trial could not proceed without proper service of the charge on the defendant. He submitted that a defendant must be informed of the allegations against him and given adequate opportunity to prepare his defence, adding that service could not be waived by any party. Adoo told the court that Ogunbayo was still on administrative bail and was unaware of the scheduled arraignment. He explained the defence had used the information available to it to communicate with Ogunbayo who was said to be in Warri and unable to secure a flight to Abuja for today’s proceedings. The defence counsel consequently urged the court to adjourn the matter to enable both defendants to appear and take their pleas in the interest of justice. Reacting, Justice Wike held that in the interest of justice, the matter be adjourned to enable the first defendant made himself available for arraignment. The judge, however, warned the court would take the necessary steps if Ogunbayo fails to appear on the next adjourned date. She subsequently adjourned until November 23 for arraignment. The anti-graft agency had filed an eight-count criminal charge bordering on alleged criminal misappropriation, abuse of office, corrupt practices and obtaining money by false pretence over the sale of the cooperative society’s property at Plot 50, Karsana North, Abuja. The prosecution alleged that Ogunbayo, the society’s president, and Nurudeen, who operates under the name and style of Abolade Nurudeen & Co., conspired in January 2024 to misappropriate proceeds from the transaction. In one of the counts, the defendants were accused of dishonestly misappropriating N582 million realised from the sale of the property. Ogunbayo was also accused of allegedly receiving N100 million, N10 million and N50 million through different bank accounts in connection with the transaction. The prosecution further alleged that Nurudeen received N180 million into an account belonging to his firm after representing that the property had been sold for N1 billion. Both defendants were also accused of involvement in an alleged N160 million corrupt transactions.

title: Oborevwori, Dafinone, Guwor Mourn Okonjo-Iweala’s Mother, Prof Kamene, 96
body: Sylvester Idowu in Warri Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori, Senator Ede Dafinone, and Speaker of Delta State House of Assembly, Hon. Emomotimi Guwor, have mourned the death of Professor Kamene Okonjo, mother of Director-General of World Trade Organisation (WTO), Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala. They described the deceased as an accomplished scholar, revered matriarch, and community builder. Kamene, who died on Friday at the age of 96, was the wife of the late Professor Chukwuka Okonjo, a former traditional ruler of Ogwashi-Uku Kingdom in Aniocha South Local Government Area of Delta State, and mother of the kingdom’s current monarch, Obi Ifechukwude Okonjo II. Oborevwori, in a condolence message by his Chief Press Secretary, Sir Festus Ahon, described the late professor as a distinguished scholar whose contributions to the academia, women’s empowerment, and society would remain indelible. The governor said Kamene’s remarkable achievements in scholarship and advocacy for women’s rights had earned her recognition beyond Nigeria, while her humility, compassion, and commitment to service distinguished her as a woman of exceptional character. He also acknowledged her invaluable contributions to her family and society, stating that her legacy as a mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother would continue to inspire generations. Dafinone also extended his condolences to Okonjo-Iweala and the Okonjo family of Ogwashi-Uku Kingdom over the death of their matriarch, Kamene. Dafinone described Kamene as a woman who lived a remarkable life of purpose and impact, distinguished by her contributions to scholarship, women’s empowerment, and service to humanity. He stated that Kamene’s legacy of excellence, compassion, and devotion to family would continue to inspire generations, adding that her passing is a profound loss to her family and society. The senator particularly sympathised with Okonjo-Iweala, His Royal Majesty, Obi Ifechukwude Okonjo II, and other members of the Okonjo family over the loss. According to him, although the family would deeply feel Kamene’s absence, there is comfort in the knowledge that she lived a fulfilled life and left enduring footprints in society. Guwor, for his part, described the late nonagenarian as a distinguished matriarch whose life was defined by intellectual accomplishment, service, and an enduring commitment to her family and community. In a statement by his Chief Press Secretary, Mr. Nkem Nwaeke, the speaker said Kamene’s death was a painful loss not only to the Okonjo family and Ogwashi-Uku Kingdom but also to Delta State and Nigeria. He stated that Okonjo was more than the mother of a globally recognised figure, describing her as an accomplished academic, a revered traditional queen, and a community builder whose influence extended beyond her immediate family. Guwor said the deceased had made lasting contributions as a scholar, served her community with dignity, and raised children whose achievements had brought pride to Delta State, Nigeria and Africa.

title: NDC Discloses N8.5bn Income, N2.4bn Spending in Seven Months
body: • Cleopas: Members deserve to know how party funds are managed •Party unveils campaign council, commissions national secretariat •Umeh seeks greater funding for state chapters as chairman pledges reconciliation Sunday Aborisade in Abuja and Sunday Ehigiator in Lagos The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) on Monday disclosed that it generated N8.529 billion from nomination forms, membership dues, levies and contributions within its first seven months of operation, while spending N2.402 billion on primaries, publicity, staff salaries and other activities. The party presented the financial figures at its National Executive Committee (NEC) meeting in Abuja, where its National Chairman, Senator Moses Cleopas, said the disclosure was intended to promote transparency and accountability in the management of the party’s resources ahead of its first anniversary. The NEC Meeting was attended by the National Leader of the party, Senator Henry Seriake Dickson; the Presidential Candidate of the party, Mr. Peter Obi; his Vice, Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso; serving and former members of the National Assembly and other notable leaders of the party, among others. Cleopas said the party decided to account for its finances before the statutory deadline for submitting its audited accounts to the relevant government institutions, insisting that members had a right to know how funds entrusted to their leaders were being managed. He said the decision was not prompted by allegations or criticisms on social media but reflected the party’s commitment to accountability and responsible leadership. According to him, the party’s leadership considered it necessary to provide members with an early account of its financial position, even though the NDC had yet to complete its first year of operation. He said, “One of the critical instruments that destroys leadership or communal living, as I have been taught, is the management of public funds. When you have a responsibility to sit over a public forum, you also owe the people who entrusted you with that privilege an obligation to be open to them. “They must know what you are doing from time to time. Any attempt to foreclose that will lead to suspicion and give room for people to say what is not true. “When you find yourself in a leadership position, accountability must be your sense of duty, especially when it has to do with common wealth. “That is what Nigeria is suffering from. Nigeria is so blessed. We cannot say that we do not have resources in this country. The question we are asking is: where are our resources? What are our resources being used for that will bring relief or blessings to Nigerian citizens?” The national chairman said the NDC would submit its properly audited financial statement to the constitutionally authorised institutions when the appropriate reporting period ended. He explained that the party’s financial management process involved a committee comprising the national chairman, national secretary, financial secretary, treasurer and auditor, with the party’s legal adviser co-opted when necessary. The National Treasurer, Dr Peter Onigah, presented the financial statement at the meeting, outlining the funds received and expenditure incurred during the period under review. The disclosure comes as the NDC intensifies preparations for the 2027 general election, with the party also inaugurating its presidential campaign council, present certificates of return to its candidates and commission its national secretariat at the Jabi Area of Abuja. Cleopas said the activities were part of efforts to strengthen the party’s structures and demonstrate its readiness for the forthcoming elections. He said the inauguration of the presidential campaign council followed consultations aimed at identifying people willing to commit their time and resources to the party’s electoral project. “It is not a matter of rushing to announce a campaign council. It is a matter of getting people who are committed, people who are ready to serve this nation in that capacity,” he said. The chairman also cautioned party members against interpreting the initial list of campaign council appointments as a complete representation of all those who would eventually be involved. “Some are calling to ask, ‘Why is my name not there? Why is my name not there?’ We are not finished. Let them wait for us,” he said. Cleopas said the party presented certificates of return to its candidates to prevent individuals who did not win its primaries from parading themselves as candidates and misleading voters. He described the NDC as a party intended to outlive its founding leaders, urging young Nigerians to identify with it and prepare for future leadership responsibilities. Cleopas said, “This party is intended to be a generational party for as long as we remain on earth. This party is intended to outlive us. And if that is the vision we have, there is a particular set of people we must target. “We have the youth to target in this country. The reason is that they must be prepared for leadership. So, this is a party of mentorship,” he said. Umeh Seeks Funding for State Chapters At the meeting, Senator Victor Umeh, representing Anambra Central, commended the party’s leadership for making its financial position available to members, describing the disclosure as an important step towards building public confidence. Umeh said providing financial information would help members understand the party’s operations rather than rely on speculation. He, however, called on the national leadership to ensure that state chapters received an appropriate share of the funds generated through their activities. Responding, Cleopas said the issue of funding for state chapters was already under consideration, assuring members that the party would address the matter in line with its constitution and organisational objectives. The chairman also disclosed that the party’s reconciliation committee had visited the six geopolitical zones to engage aggrieved aspirants and other members dissatisfied with the outcomes of its primaries. He said the national secretariat was holding regular meetings to resolve outstanding disagreements and prevent internal disputes from undermining the party’s preparations for the elections. Cleopas urged candidates, party leaders and supporters to put aside their differences and work collectively for the success of all NDC candidates. He said the party could not afford to allow personal disagreements to weaken its electoral prospects, particularly when its presidential and vice-presidential candidates would require the support of lawmakers and other elected representatives to implement their programmes if elected. The chairman argued that supporting only the party’s presidential candidate while abandoning its candidates for governorship and legislative seats could undermine the party’s ability to govern effectively. He said, “Don’t you also know that they need a majority, if not all, in the National Assembly from our party? If you don’t know so, how will they get the president they want? How will they get the Senate president or the speaker of their choice? “You may not like the face of the candidates, but they are your party’s candidates. We must work together so that we can have the Nigeria of our dreams.” NDC Insists on Candidate Compliance, Vote Protection The NEC meeting also heard updates from party officials on preparations for the 2027 elections, including efforts to resolve disputes involving candidates and strengthen the party’s grassroots structures. The National Vice-Chairman for the North-east, Dr Dallamiya Nzukumbe, said preparations were progressing, although the party had encountered some disagreements between candidates and party leaders in certain areas. He said the leadership was working to resolve the disputes and ensure that the party’s structures remained focused on the elections. Nzukumbe also urged Nigerians to reject the notion that their votes would not count, calling on voters to remain at polling units after casting their ballots to ensure that votes were counted and results properly documented. “We will vote, we will wait, and we will escort,” he said, stressing that the party wanted an electoral process in which votes cast at polling units were accurately reflected in the final results. He said voters in the North were particularly concerned about insecurity, the disruption of farming activities and attacks on schools, adding that residents wanted to return to their farms, travel safely and send their children to school without fear. “The children in the North must go to school,” he said. Another party official, speaking on preparations in the southern part of the country, said the party was working to resolve outstanding disputes arising from its primaries and restore harmony among members. He said the NDC was intensifying voter education and sensitisation on electoral responsibilities, particularly the need for voters and party agents to protect their votes after voting. According to him, the party was documenting its agents and working with candidates at different levels to ensure adequate representation at polling units and collation centres. He urged voters not to leave polling units immediately after casting their ballots but to remain until the votes were counted and the results properly recorded. Cleopas, in his closing remarks, also addressed concerns over the omission of some candidates’ names from the relevant electoral processes. He said the party was pursuing both administrative and legal avenues to address the matter and expressed confidence that candidates who had fulfilled the requirements of the law would be able to contest the elections. “The party is not folding its hands. The party is interfacing on administrative fronts and legal fronts,” he said. He added that the leadership was conscious of its responsibility to candidates who had completed the required processes and would continue to pursue the matter. The NDC chairman urged members to remain united as the party moved from internal preparations to the next phase of its electoral activities. He said the party’s immediate priorities included commissioning its national secretariat, inaugurating the presidential campaign council, presenting certificates to its candidates and resolving outstanding grievances before the 2027 general election.

title: Court Orders el-Rufai to Enter Defence on Alleged Wiretapping Trial
body: Alex Enumah in Abuja Justice Joyce Abdulmalik of a Federal High Court, Abuja, on Monday ordered the immediate past governor of Kaduna State, Nasir El-rufai to enter his defence if he so desires in his ongoing trial on bugging the telephone communications of the National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu. Justice Abdulmalik made the order shortly after dismissing the no-case submission filed by El-rufai, in response to the prosecution’s case. In her ruling on the no-case submission, the judge held there is sufficient evidence by the prosecution to warrant the court to call on the defendant to enter his defence if he so desires. She subsequently adjourned till November 25 for the former governor to open his defence. The African Democratic Congress (ADC) chieftain is standing trial on a five-count criminal charge brought against him by the Department of State Services (DSS). At the no-case submission hearing on September 22, the prosecution, represented by Oluwole Aladedoye (SAN), objected to the submission and urged the court to dismiss it and order the defendant to enter his defence. According to Aladedoye, the defendant failed to address Exhibit “B”, which the prosecution claimed contains El-rufai’s admission in relation to the tapping of Ribadu’s phone. He contended that since the prosecution has effectively established a prima facie case against El-rufai, through its two witnesses, the defendant is required by law to enter a defence. Defence lawyer, Akinyemi Aremu, while adopting his client’s no-case submission, argued that the prosecution failed to establish a prima facie case against the ex-governor to require him to be called upon to enter a defence. Aremu urged the court to uphold the no-case submission and discharge his client. El-rufai opted for a no-case submission after the prosecution closed its case upon calling two witnesses – an operative of the DSS and a lawyer, Deji Adeyanju. Adeyanju, who testified as a subpoenaed witness, told the court that the ex-governor admitted during a television interview that he wiretapped the NSA’s phone lines.

title: Atiku’s Aide Demands Answers over Seven SUVs Displayed by APC Youth Leader
body: Chuks Okocha in Abuja Paul Ibe, media adviser to former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, has demanded an explanation from the All Progressives Congress over seven 2026 Toyota Prado SUVs reportedly displayed by the party’s National Youth Leader, Dayo Israel. Ibe, in a statement on Monday, questioned the source of funding for the vehicles and whether public resources were involved in their purchase or distribution. He said Israel had displayed the vehicles, thanked First Lady Remi Tinubu for her support and later deleted the post. However, Ibe argued that removing the pictures did not resolve questions about the vehicles’ ownership, funding and intended beneficiaries. “Deleting the pictures does not erase the questions,” he said. Ibe criticised the development against the backdrop of rising living costs, unemployment and poverty, arguing that the reported distribution of luxury vehicles to party operatives contrasted with the economic difficulties facing many Nigerians. He also questioned the call for Nigerians to make sacrifices amid reports of luxury vehicles being made available for political activities. “Is sacrifice only for the poor?” he asked. The former vice-president’s aide called on the First Lady, Israel and the APC to disclose the total cost of the seven vehicles, identify their purchasers and explain the sources of the funds used to acquire them. He also demanded the identities of the donors and beneficiaries, evidence of payment and details of the purpose for which the vehicles were provided. Ibe further asked the party to clarify whether any funds or assets belonging to the Federal Government, the Office of the First Lady or government agencies were used in the transaction. He called on the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission and the Independent National Electoral Commission to examine the funding arrangements and determine whether public resources were used for partisan activities or whether applicable campaign-finance rules were breached. “The Nigerian treasury is not the APC’s campaign purse, and the Presidency must not become the ruling party’s election-financing machinery,” Ibe said. He maintained that deleting the social media post should not end scrutiny of the reported vehicle distribution. “Deleting the post cannot delete the demand for accountability,” he added. The statement did not provide independent evidence that public funds were used to acquire the vehicles or establish the circumstances surrounding their purchase.

title: N76bn Fraud Trial: EFCC Witness Calls Arik Air Receivership Scam
body: • Insists airline owes Union Bank nothing, court admits AMCON board resolutions Wale Igbintade Director of the Lagos Zonal Directorate 2 of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Bawa Usman Kaltungo, yesterday described the receivership of Arik Air as fraudulent, insisting that the airline is not indebted to Union Bank of Nigeria Plc. Kaltungo, the fourth prosecution witness in the ongoing trial of former Managing Director of Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON), Ahmed Kuru, and others over an alleged N76 billion ($31.5 million) fraud, told the Special Offences Court in Ikeja that the purported bad debt that formed the basis for the receivership did not exist. The witness, who testified before Justice Mojisola Dada, said his investigation into a petition concerning the airline revealed that the basis for appointing a receiver-manager over Arik Air was faulty. In a significant development, however, the court admitted AMCON board resolutions tendered by Kuru’s counsel, Uyi Giwa-Osagie, to challenge the prosecution witness’ assertion that the former managing director had unilaterally approved the receivership. The documents were admitted despite the prosecution’s objection to their relevance. The court held that they emanated from AMCON’s board as a corporate body and had been duly certified in accordance with Section 104 of the Evidence Act. During cross-examination by Giwa-Osagie, counsel to the second defendant, Kaltungo, said he headed the EFCC team that investigated the petition concerning Arik Air. He told the court that he had informed AMCON’s top management at a meeting that the airline was not indebted to Union Bank and that the appointment of a receiver-manager to take control of the company was defective. The witness said, “The foundation for the appointment of a receivership over Arik Air was fraudulent and faulty. There was no bad debt; it does not exist.” The testimony came amid allegations surrounding the handling of Arik Air’s loan obligations, its takeover by AMCON, and transactions involving the airline’s assets. During the cross-examination, Kaltungo maintained that Kuru, in his capacity as AMCON’s Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, had extensive powers and had unilaterally sanctioned the appointment of a receiver-manager over Arik Air. Giwa-Osagie challenged the account by tendering AMCON board resolutions intended to demonstrate that the receivership decision was taken at the corporate level rather than solely by Kuru. The prosecution objected to the admissibility of the documents, arguing that they were too remote to the issues before the court. However, Giwa-Osagie argued that the documents were relevant to determining his client’s culpability in the alleged offences. He submitted that Kuru was not standing trial over the propriety of AMCON’s powers to appoint a receiver-manager but over the specific allegations contained in the charge sheet. The defence counsel maintained that the board resolutions were necessary to establish the circumstances surrounding the decision and challenge the witness’s account of Kuru’s role. He further argued that the documents were public records that could properly be tendered from the Bar. In her ruling, Dada upheld the relevance and admissibility of the documents, holding that they emanated from AMCON’s board as a corporate body and had been duly certified in accordance with Section 104 of the Evidence Act. The admission of the resolutions provides the defence with documentary evidence to challenge the prosecution witness’s assertion that Kuru acted unilaterally in approving the receivership. However, their admission does not, in itself, determine the legality of the receivership or resolve the allegations against the defendants. EFCC instituted the case following a petition by human rights activist and lawyer, Femi Falana, SAN, on behalf of Arik Air’s promoters and shareholders over the airline’s receivership and related transactions. The defendants are Kuru; Kamilu Alaba Omokide, a former receiver-manager of Arik Air; Captain Roy Ilegbodu, the airline’s chief executive officer; Union Bank of Nigeria Plc; and Super Bravo Limited. They are facing a six-count charge bordering on conspiracy, stealing and abuse of office. The prosecution’s case includes allegations concerning the handling of Arik Air’s loan obligations, the transfer of its debt exposure to AMCON and the alleged conversion of N4.9 billion belonging to the airline for the benefit of NG Eagle Limited. The dispute also raises questions about the exercise of AMCON’s statutory powers and the responsibilities of a receiver-manager appointed to take control of a distressed company. Section 553(2) of the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 requires a receiver-manager to act in the company’s best interests, including preserving its assets and furthering its business objectives. The defendants were arraigned on January 20, 2025, and they pleaded not guilty to all the charges. One of the counts reads, “That you, Union Bank of Nigeria Plc, sometime in 2011 or thereabouts, in Lagos, within the jurisdiction of this Honourable Court, with the intention of causing and/or inducing the unwarranted sale of Arik Air loans and bank guarantees with Union Bank, made false statements to the Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON) regarding Arik Air Limited’s performing loans, following which you transferred a bogus figure of N71,000,000,000.00 (Seventy-One Billion Naira) to AMCON.” Another count reads, “That you, Ahmed Lawal Kuru, Kamilu Alaba Omokide (as Receiver-Manager of Arik Air Limited), and Captain Roy Ilegbodu (Chief Executive Officer of Arik Air Limited in Receivership), sometime in 2022 or thereabouts, in Lagos, within the jurisdiction of this Honourable Court, fraudulently converted to the use of NG Eagle Limited the total sum of N4,900,000,000.00 (Four Billion, Nine Hundred Million Naira only), property of Arik Air Limited.”

title: LCCI Seeks Stable Business Climate to Unlock Investment in Small-scale LNG, CNG Distribution
body: Dike Onwuamaeze and Oluchi Chibuzor The Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) has called on the government to create predictable regulatory and commercial environment to attract private investments into small-scale Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) and Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) distribution. The LCCI stated that this would bridge the gap between the country’s abundant gas resources and the energy requirements of productive enterprises. It also called for the establishment of dedicated clean energy financing windows for Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) to address high upfront cost of solar systems, battery storage, gas conversion equipment and energy-efficient machinery. These calls were made yesterday by the President of LCCI, Mr. Leye Kupoluyi, during the chamber’s Liquefied Pressure Gas (LPG) and Downstream Natural Gas Sectoral Group’s, “LCCI Eko Gas Scheme 3.0,” event with the theme “Empowering SMEs Through Affordable Clean Energy.” Kupoluyi said: “Nigeria must bridge the gap between its abundant gas resources and the energy requirements of productive enterprises. “This requires investment in gas gathering and processing facilities, transportation infrastructure, distribution networks, storage and appropriate safety systems. “We encourage the government to create a predictable regulatory and commercial environment that attracts private investment into small-scale LNG, CNG distribution and gas-based industrial energy solutions.” He also made a case for strengthened regulatory coordination and policy consistency, saying investors required clarity regarding energy pricing, licencing, market access, technical standards, and the responsibilities of the different regulatory authorities. “The government should ensure effective coordination among relevant federal and state institutions, including energy regulators, gas-sector authorities, and agencies responsible for investment promotion and environmental compliance. “It should provide targeted fiscal incentives for clean energy adoption by considering appropriate tax incentives, accelerated capital allowances, and reduced import-related costs for qualifying clean energy equipment, battery storage systems, energy-efficient machinery, and essential components that are not competitively available locally,” Kupoluyi added. He said unlocking the potential of natural gas and other clean energy solutions would offer opportunities for industrial development, particularly where it could replace more expensive and less efficient fuels. “With appropriate infrastructure and commercially viable delivery systems, LNG, CNG), and other gas-based solutions can support industrial clusters, manufacturing enterprises, and businesses in areas with inadequate grid electricity,” Kupoluyi said. According to him, the ultimate objective was not simply to promote a particular energy source, but to reduce the total cost of energy while improving reliability and reducing harmful emissions. He pointed out that unreliable electricity supply was compelling businesses to depend on petrol and diesel generators, which expose them to volatile fuel prices, high maintenance costs, equipment breakdowns and disruptions to production. Kupoluyi said Nigeria could not rely exclusively on expanding the national grid to meet the immediate energy needs of all SMEs. According to him, embedded generation, renewable energy mini-grids, industrial micro-grids and shared energy facilities offer additional pathways to reliable electricity. The Chairperson, LPG and Downstream Natural Gas Sectoral Group, LCCI, Mrs. Jacqueline Addy, said energy remains a critical driver of productivity, business growth, and economic development. Addy noted that the rising cost of energy was directly affecting operating expenses and profit margins of SMEs and their ability to grow and create jobs. She said: “Access to affordable and reliable energy is, therefore, essential to their sustainability and competitiveness. “Wider access to LPG can help businesses improve efficiency, manage energy costs, and operate more sustainably. “However, we recognise that the transition to cleaner energy must be supported by affordability, accessibility, awareness, and, above all, safety.”

title: Market Capitalisation of Dangote Cement Crosses N20trn Mark on NGX
body: Kayode Tokede The market capitalisation of Dangote Cement Plc on the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX), yesterday crossed the N20 trillion mark, making it the second most capitalised listed company on the bourse. The milestone N20.62 trillion market capitalization as of October 26, 2026 is on the backdrop of a 10 per cent gain in its stock price to N1,222.10 per share from N1,111.00 per share it opened for trading this week. At N1,222.10 per share, Dangote Cement stock hit a 52 week high amid the ongoing Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals’s Initial Public Offering (IPO). The stock price of Dangote Cement that opened for trading this year at N609 per share has gained 100.67per cent to close at N1,222.10 per share as of October 26, 2026. Capital market analysts stated that surge demand for Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals by retail and institutional investors spread to Dangote Cement stock on the NGX. The landmark IPO Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals enters its final days, with investors accelerating participation ahead of the closing date of October 27, 2026. The company said, “This is the final deadline, and no further extension will be granted. Investors wishing to participate must complete their subscriptions before the offer closes.” The surge in demand follows the refinery’s recently released nine-month financial results, which showed exceptional growth in revenue, profitability, and cash generation, reinforcing investor confidence in the company’s long-term prospects. Dangote Cement yet to announce nine months ended September 30, 2026 revealed that its Group revenue increased by 21.4 per cent to N2.514 trillion in the half year (H1) ended June 30, 2026, while Group EBITDA rose by 25.8 per cent to N1.188 trillion, reflecting a margin of 47.3 per cent. Earnings per share advanced by 24.3 per cent to N38.22, as the company closed the period with a strong net cash position of N215.2 billion. Overall Group volumes grew by 11.8 per cent to 14.9 million tonnes, supported by resilient demand in key markets. Nigeria continued to anchor earnings, with EBITDA from the domestic market rising by 28.4 per cent to N1.086 trillion and margins improving to 60.1 per cent. Operational efficiency remained a key focus, with the company reporting a strong reduction in Nigeria cash costs, supported by a more favourable energy mix. It also commissioned the Okpella mobile refuelling unit and added 300 compressed natural gas trucks in Tanzania as part of efforts to improve logistics efficiency and reduce operating costs. Speaking on the results, chief executive officer, Dangote Cement, Mr Arvind Pathak, in a statement said the first-half performance reflected the strong momentum the company had built since the start of the year, supported by disciplined execution, higher sales volumes and sustained demand across key markets. “Our performance in the first half of 2026 reflects the strong momentum we have continued to build since the start of the year. The business delivered another solid set of results, supported by higher sales volumes, disciplined execution, and sustained demand across our key markets,” Pathak said. He noted that revenue growth, stronger EBITDA and the N215.2 billion net cash balance underscored the resilience of Dangote Cement’s business model and its capacity to invest in future growth while maintaining disciplined capital allocation.

title: Tinubu Felicitates Friend And Brazilian President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, on Re-Election For Record Fourth Term
body: • Reiterates Nigeria-Brazil multilateral cooperation and historical ties Deji Elumoye in Abuja President Bola Tinubu has felicitated his friend and President of Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, on his re-election for a record fourth term. Tinubu also reiterated Nigeria-Brazil multilateral cooperation and historical ties. Tinubu, in a six-paragraph release issued on Monday stated, “I congratulate my friend, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, on his re-election for a record fourth term. “Your renewed mandate offers an opportunity to strengthen the longstanding friendship and historical ties between Nigeria and Brazil. “As two leading nations of the Global South, we can promote economic integration and advance our shared interests in a rapidly changing global order. “I look forward to expanding cooperation in trade and investment, agriculture and food security, energy, oil and gas, manufacturing, science and technology, education, aviation, and cultural exchange. “I affirm Nigeria’s continued commitment to working with Brazil to strengthen multilateral cooperation and advance shared priorities in Africa, South America, and across the Global South. “On behalf of the people of Nigeria, I wish you a successful new term in office.” Natasha Woos European Investors to Kogi, Renews Call for Ajaokuta Revival Sunday Aborisade in Abuja The senator representing Kogi Central, Natasha Akpoti-Uduaghan, has wooed European investors to Kogi State, hosting ambassadors from Belgium, Denmark, Italy and Spain on a tour designed to showcase the state’s investment opportunities, cultural heritage and indigenous industries. The visit, which featured engagements with local communities, artisans and cultural groups, provided an opportunity to explore potential economic and humanitarian partnerships while highlighting the commercial prospects of Kogi Central beyond its tourism attractions. The diplomats visited historical landmarks in Lokoja, including Lord Lugard’s Rest House on Mount Patti and the confluence of the Niger and Benue rivers, before proceeding to Kogi Central for cultural activities and interactions with residents. The Ambassador of Italy to Nigeria, Roberto Mengoni, expressed optimism about the prospects for collaboration, describing Kogi as a state with considerable potential. “Kogi is very rich, and we look forward to partnership,” Mengoni said, while thanking Akpoti-Uduaghan for facilitating the visit. The engagement also offered the European diplomats an opportunity to experience the traditions, hospitality and entrepreneurial activities of the Ebira people, with particular emphasis on the potential of locally produced goods to attract investment and access wider markets. Belgium’s Ambassador to Nigeria, Pieter Leenknegt, expressed satisfaction with the experience, particularly the hiking expedition around the historic hills of Ihima, commending the opportunity to explore the area’s landscape, culture and cuisine. The programme, according to a statement by the senator’s media office on Monday, included a visit to Obeiba Hill, where the diplomats sampled traditional delicacies, including akara, apapa and akamu. They also witnessed indigenous production processes, including shea butter and palm kernel oil extraction, black soap making, pottery and traditional Ebira cloth weaving. The statement added that the masquerade performance further exposed the visitors to the cultural identity and artistic traditions of the community. Denmark’s Ambassador to Nigeria, Jens Ole Bach Hansen, praised the ingenuity of local artisans, particularly women engaged in pottery, traditional clothing and other indigenous crafts. He said the products demonstrated the creativity and determination of the artisans, noting that their skills and enterprise could provide opportunities for economic growth, business development and access to larger markets. Akpoti-Uduaghan said the visit was intended to demonstrate the economic potential of Kogi Central and draw international attention to the skills, industries and entrepreneurial capacity of its people. According to her, the district’s development prospects extend beyond tourism to include indigenous manufacturing, traditional crafts and other productive activities capable of generating employment and improving livelihoods. “To attract investment, we must give people the chance to see our strengths for themselves: our skills, our enterprise, our culture and our people,” the senator said. She disclosed that discussions with the diplomats covered investment and humanitarian opportunities, expressing hope that the engagement would produce practical partnerships with lasting benefits for residents. The senator said such partnerships could create opportunities for women, young people, artisans and tourism operators while strengthening local enterprises and improving the commercial prospects of indigenous products. However, the statement added, the delegation’s planned visit to the Ajaokuta Steel Company Limited could not take place because access to the facility was not approved despite a written request. The diplomats could only view the complex from outside its gates. The development disappointed Akpoti-Uduaghan, who renewed her call for the revival of the steel plant, describing it as critical to Nigeria’s industrial development ambitions. “Ajaokuta remains central to the industrial future we want for our people, and I will continue to advocate for its revival,” she said. The senator’s renewed appeal comes amid longstanding concerns over the continued non-operation of the steel complex, which has remained a focal point of national discussions on industrialisation, manufacturing capacity and economic diversification. The revival of Ajaokuta has been widely regarded as an opportunity to stimulate domestic manufacturing, create jobs, develop supporting industries and strengthen local supply chains. For Kogi State, the facility’s successful rehabilitation could also provide a significant boost to economic activities, with potential benefits for businesses and communities within and beyond the state. Akpoti-Uduaghan’s decision to include the steel complex in the programme, the statement explained, underscored her effort to connect Kogi’s cultural and entrepreneurial strengths with broader opportunities for industrial investment. The senator thanked community leaders, residents and artisans for welcoming the delegation and helping to showcase the cultural heritage of the Ebira people to an international audience. She also acknowledged the ambassadors of Belgium, Denmark, Italy and Spain—Leenknegt, Bach Hansen, Mengoni and Félix Costales Artieda, respectively—for accepting the invitation and engaging with local communities. The visit provided a platform for promoting Kogi Central’s tourism assets, indigenous industries and cultural attractions, with the senator expressing optimism that the engagement would translate into concrete investment commitments, expanded market access and sustainable economic opportunities for the district.

title: Tinubu Seeks Stronger African Defence Partnership, Local Capacity over Insecurity
body: • Northern senators urge better security in Taraba after Binari killings, death toll rises to 58, govt provides relief Sunday Aborisade in Abuja and Wole Ayodele in Jalingo President Bola Tinubu has called for stronger defence partnerships among African countries, insisting that military cooperation must go beyond equipment supplies to the development of local expertise, strengthening of indigenous industries, and improvement of the continent’s capacity to sustain its security operations. Tinubu spoke at the opening ceremony of Africa International Defence Exhibition (AFRIDEX) 2026 in Lagos, where he was represented by President of the Senate, Godswill Akpabio. In a related development, Northern Senators’ Forum called on security agencies to intensify operations in Taraba State following the killing of worshippers, vigilantes, women, and children in an attack on Binari community in Karim-Lamido Local Government Area. The legislators demanded urgent measures to prevent further bloodshed. They urged the police, Department of State Services (DSS), and Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) to launch a comprehensive security surge across Karim-Lamido and the River Benue corridor, including the establishment of a Forward Operating Base and intelligence-led patrols along the Kompany-Asusar route. Taraba State Police Command confirmed the death of additional 15 people, who died when the boat in which they were fleeing their assailants capsized, bringing the death toll from Friday’s attack on Binnari community to 58. Tinubu’s address at AFRIDEX 2026 outlined a broader continental approach to tackling the evolving security challenges confronting African countries. The president said threats ranging from terrorism and insurgency to banditry, piracy, and emerging cyber risks required stronger cooperation among African nations. “From the Gulf of Guinea to the Sahel, from our territorial borders to cyberspace and outer space, the threats confronting us are becoming more complex and interconnected,” Tinubu said. He added that the threats were claiming lives, displacing communities, disrupting trade and undermining development. “Africa’s security must, therefore, command our collective attention, because there can be no enduring prosperity where fear governs daily life,” he said. Tinubu said Nigeria had experienced the devastating consequences of insecurity, including deaths, displacement, disrupted livelihoods, and lost economic opportunities. He commended the armed forces for confronting terrorism, insurgency, banditry, piracy, and other transnational threats, while acknowledging the sacrifices made by personnel in the line of duty. The president said, “Our armed forces have confronted terrorism, insurgency, banditry, piracy and other transnational threats with courage and sacrifice. We honour their service and remember those who have paid the supreme price.” He added that the sacrifices of military personnel placed an obligation on political leaders to provide the equipment, training, resources, and institutional support required to improve operational effectiveness. He stressed that lasting security depended not only on military action but also on strong institutions, public trust, reliable partnerships, and the domestic industrial capacity to sustain defence operations. According to him, African countries must ensure that defence agreements produce long-term benefits beyond the immediate delivery of military hardware. Tinubu stated, “Our defence partnerships must, therefore, deliver value long after equipment has been supplied. Every major acquisition should help develop skills, transfer knowledge, strengthen local industry, and deepen our capacity to maintain what we operate. “The measure of a successful partnership is the capability it leaves behind. African engineers must gain expertise; African enterprises must grow; African institutions must become stronger.” Tinubu also called for more predictable funding, adequate equipment, rigorous training, and sustained institutional support for African-led peace operations. He stated that the effectiveness of peacekeeping missions depended on ensuring that personnel deployed to conflict zones had the resources and capabilities needed to carry out their assignments. He said, “The courage to respond to crises must be matched by predictable resources, adequate equipment, rigorous training and sustained institutional support. “Those we send to keep the peace must have the means to keep the peace.” The president also called for stronger maritime cooperation among African countries, particularly in the Gulf of Guinea, which he described as vital to trade, energy security, and shared prosperity. He urged African governments to strengthen cooperation against criminal networks operating in maritime spaces and protect legitimate commercial activities. Tinubu also highlighted the growing influence of cyber capabilities, space technologies, artificial intelligence, and autonomous systems on modern warfare, urging African countries to invest in the knowledge and institutions required to understand and deploy such technologies responsibly. He described AFRIDEX 2026 as an opportunity to translate Africa’s potential into practical defence capabilities through cooperation, knowledge exchange, and industrial development. Northern Senators Urge Better Security in Taraba After Binari Killings Northern Senators’ Forum, in a condolence message through their chairman, Senator Abdulaziz Musa Yar’Adua, expressed sympathy with the Taraba State governor, residents of the state, and families affected by the attack on Binari on Friday, October 23. Gunmen had attacked Binnari community in Karim-Lamido Local Government Area of Taraba State last Friday while the community market was in full spring and killed scores of people while property worth millions of naira were destroyed. The senators’ forum said it received with shock reports that innocent worshippers, vigilantes, women, and children were killed shortly after Juma’at prayers.
