title: Jordan says 20 ISIS militants killed in air strikes on Syria
body: Jordan said on Tuesday that its armed forces killed at least 20 ISIS members in strikes on Syria launched in “retaliation” for a deadly church attack in the kingdom last week. Syrian authorities said at least seven people, including three children, a woman and an elderly man, were killed in the strikes, which occurred late on Monday. At least one of the strikes hit an area in Deraa governorate, near Mismiyah, about 30km south of Damascus, residents told The National on Tuesday. The strikes present a major test in the relationship between Amman and Damascus. The Syrian government has been improving its ties with Jordan and other Arab countries since militant forces led by President Ahmad Al Shara ousted Bashar Al Assad's regime in December 2024. Mismiyah is in the northern part of Al Lajat, also known as the "black desert", a plateau covered with volcanic rock that stretches between Syria, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. The rugged, 50,000-square-kilometre area is at the centre of the Captagon trade , as well as becoming a refuge for militant groups. Jordanian government spokesman Mohammad Al Momani said the attacks killed 20 members of ISIS. But he did not disclose where the attacks occurred in Syria. "Jordan's patience has ran out as far as the movements of these terrorist organisations and their targeting of national security," Mr Al Momani said, adding that the strikes were "based on field information" and aimed at "neutralising sure threats and terrorists operations against Jordan". The kingdom regretted "the fall of civilian victims" in the strikes, he added. Mr Al Momani said the attacks were co-ordinated with Syria, without giving details on who was contacted on the other side. Dozens of people on Tuesday attended a funeral ear Mismiyah for the three children, the woman and one of the men killed. Footage recorded by The National showed a destroyed building and collapsed corrugated iron among the rubble, which residents said was hit from the air. The woman was the wife of Massed Al Salem, 67, and the three children were his grandchildren. They were living in a tent in an unfinished part of the building. "We had erected a tent [to live in] until we have money to [continue] building," he said. "Money did not come to us and this disaster occurred." Damascus denied any co-ordination with Jordan and said it had launched an investigation. Syria informed Jordan ​of its "complete ⁠reservation" over the strikes, the ‌Foreign Ministry said. The Syrian government expressed its solidarity with the families affected by the attacks. Damascus and Amman have been co-operating to establish transport routes through both countries as an alternative for trade, amid disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Syria closed the Nassib border with Jordan shortly after the strikes. Jordan's armed forces said they hit the hideouts of militants responsible for the attack on a church in Karak on Friday that killed nine Christians. "The operation was conducted in retaliation for the martyrs of last Friday’s Hamoud church attack in Karak," the military said. The Information Ministry said those who carried out the church attack were linked to terrorist organisations in Syria. It added that the strikes resulted in the “killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”. On Monday, Jordanian authorities said they had arrested three suspects, all Jordanians from the same family, after a three-day manhunt. The church attack was the largest against the Christian minority in the kingdom since the 1950s. Christians number about 250,000 out of Jordan's population of 11 million. The nine killed were all men and mostly belonged to the Halasah clan, one of the most prominent families in Jordan. Jordan has been supportive of the Syrian government led by Mr Al Shara since it came to power. Jordan's King Abdullah II and Mr Al Shara have agreed to strengthen co-operation, particularly on border security. Previous Jordanian strikes have typically hit suspected drug trafficking sites.

title: In Marawi, therapy helps mothers find new ways to connect with their children
body: October 27 is marked as World Occupational Therapy Day to raise awareness about how therapists help people of all ages gain or regain everyday life and working skills When Sania Naga calls her son, Amal, for help, he answers, “Yes, Mama.” It is an ordinary exchange, but one Naga could not always have with her firstborn. For many years, Amal was non-verbal. At three, Amal was not saying “Mama” or “Papa.” When he wanted milk, he handed Naga his bottle. When the television would turn off in a power outage, he pointed to it and cried. Naga noticed that other children Amal’s age were already discovering words and sounds and becoming talkative. They could follow simple instructions from their parents. Others assured Naga that some children develop later than others, but she still worried. Neither she nor her husband knew what to do. “What will happen to my child when he gets older? What will happen to him when his father and I are no longer around?” Naga recalled thinking. An opportunity to seek help came when Amal fell ill. During a visit to a pediatrician, Naga raised her concerns about his development. The doctor referred them to a specialist in Cagayan de Oro, roughly three hours from their home in Marawi City. Distance, time, and then the pandemic became hurdles to getting treatment. When they tried to set an appointment, a year had passed before Amal was seen by a doctor. Amal was initially diagnosed with cognitive development delay, a condition where there is a lag in thinking, learning, and reasoning skills. Naga asked whether medicine could help. The recommendation was therapy. Getting it meant traveling to the nearest therapy center in Iligan, about 45 minutes away, every week. Amal had an hour of occupational therapy and another of speech therapy. Naga arranged Saturday appointments around her job, her husband’s work, and caring for their two other children. “During the first six months, I felt like giving up,” she said. Then the therapist began noticing Amal’s progress. His behavior, once marked by hyperactivity, became more manageable. He became calmer as he learned to express himself more. At home, Amal began making eye contact and responding when she greeted him good morning. Gaps at every stage of care Naga’s experience underscores the care and treatment gaps facing children with disabilities. The gaps span all touch points that starts from having their needs recognized, reaching someone who can assess them and link them to care, and sustaining treatment and support. Data from the government’s January 2026 National Education Plan estimates that there are about 4.7 million to 5.1 million children with disabilities. Statistics from the previous year indicate that there are about 391,000 identified learners with disabilities in public schools during the 2024-2025 school year. Roughly 6 in 10 lacked a formal diagnosis. In addition, a shortage of specialists and therapists complicates getting therapy and care even when assessed. In Naga’s case, occupational therapy was one of the interventions recommended for Amal to help him develop skills for everyday activities such as eating, dressing and participating in school. LEARNING. Regular therapy helps children with intellectual and developmental delays. Photo courtesy of REACH Foundation The World Health Organization listed fewer than 6,000 registered occupational therapists nationwide in 2025, with services concentrated in urban areas. In Marawi, where Naga and her family live, accessibility is also a geographic problem. In 2024, there were reportedly only two developmental pediatricians in Northern Mindanao. Families from Marawi seek care in Iligan and Cagayan de Oro. Appointment waits can reportedly reach three and a half years. Jalil Usman, a social worker for Community and Family Services International (CSFI) in Marawi, said that intensified mental health outreach around 2019 as part of the recovery efforts after the Marawi siege brought them to parents needing support for their children with intellectual and developmental delays. “There were gaps in understanding and, in some families, shame about showing others that a child had a disability. As families learned about available help and shared their experiences, others approached us,” said Usman. “Some parents had assumed their children could never learn certain everyday skills, but it turned out they could,” Usman added. CFSI secured funding to partner with the Medbay Therapy and Learning Center in Iligan to provide 21 children through 10 sessions each of occupational therapy. Getting children to therapy became somewhat of a field trip. CFSI staff picked up some families from their homes and drove them to Iligan in an office vehicle. In the clinic, the parents would wait for their turn for their therapy session. However, funding was not enough to cover the recommended 72 sessions. When the CFSI funded sessions ended in 2023, Naga paid for the treatment costs out of pocket. “Sometimes, when we did not have enough money, we would miss sessions,” she said. Teletherapy to bridge access CFSI partnered with the Rehabilitation and Empowerment of Adults and Children with Handicap Foundation (REACH) , a non-profit organization in Manila that provides free occupational and speech therapy to undersupported children and adults with disabilities. Together, they developed and conducted teletherapy sessions adapted to the children’s needs. Through sessions conducted online or by phone or through other messaging platforms, therapists work with family members to develop home-based interventions using everyday or improvised materials. “We often use toys, books, school materials, kitchen items, and other familiar household objects to make learning part of the child’s daily life,” said Archie David, founder and president of REACH Foundation. A simple clothespin, for example, can help strengthen fine motor skills, while everyday activities such as preparing meals, sorting laundry, or playing games can become opportunities for learning and development. ONLINE. Teletherapy sessions adapt to every child’s needs. Photo courtesy of REACH Foundation Amal’s occupational therapy program focused on visual perceptual skills, which are important for handwriting, copying from the board, organizing written work, and other classroom tasks. Another child, Shoraim, had a hearing impairment that made spoken conversations difficult to follow in school. His mother, Sohairah Batabor, used gestures and written words to communicate with him. Through occupational therapy and guidance at home, Shoraim developed everyday skills, including dressing, bathing, and preparing simple meals like his favorite noodles and fried egg. His daily morning routine is comprised of reading the Quran and praying. “The most meaningful changes are not always reflected in assessments. Sometimes it is a parent noticing that their child is joining family activities more often, participating in class, communicating a need, or trying something independently for the first time. These moments may seem ordinary to others, but for families, they can be life-changing,” said David. “As a child’s confidence grows, so do his opportunities to build relationships, independence, and a stronger sense of belonging at home, in school, and in the community,” David added. Amal, who is now 12 years old, is attending a mainstream school as a Grade 3 student. He can eat, manage his hygiene on his own, and communicate with his parents. Naga recalled the advice of the therapist to call Amal even when she needed nothing from him. “Amal, come here. Mama wants to talk to you,” she would say. Before, Amal could not answer. Now he does by saying, “Yes, Mama.” – Rappler.com Disclosure: The writer and Abelardo David Jr. are both Senior Fellows of the Equity Initiative–CMB Foundation.

title: ‘The single most important thing’ is accurate passenger data – Prof Amuasi on Ebola preparedness
body: Ghana must prioritise accurate passenger information to strengthen its Ebola preparedness, Prof John Amuasi, KCCR’s Global Health Lead, said. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, he warned that airport temperature checks and hand rubs offer reassurance but have limited value in detecting infected travellers. “So for me, the single most important thing is being able to collect as accurate data as possible on every single person who comes off the plane in this country, making sure that the phone numbers they submit are accurate and finding a way of verifying it.” His call comes as Ebola cases in Nigeria and Kenya put cross-border surveillance under scrutiny. Nigeria confirmed an imported case on October 20. The patient developed symptoms four days after arriving from Uganda. That gap between arrival and illness highlights the importance of tracing passengers after they leave the airport. Kenya had recorded nine confirmed cases and two deaths as of October 25. All cases were linked to its first imported infection. Uganda also recorded cases during the wider outbreak, although its outbreak has ended. Prof Amuasi said relying on visible signs of illness at arrival leaves a major gap. “The point I was making is that nobody is going to be coming off an aeroplane or even jumping on an aeroplane when they are visibly sick with signs and symptoms of Ebola, and therefore your ability to catch it when someone is coming off a plane is really limited.” He said testing every arriving passenger was not practical. “We can’t be doing PCR tests for everyone coming in.” Instead, authorities should verify passengers’ contact details and ensure they can be located when necessary. Travellers must also know where to seek help if symptoms develop. “Making sure that we have a way of being able to geolocate them if necessary, and also making sure that they are able to report to designated facilities or via the phone lines or the contact means if they come down with any of the symptoms.” For him, education must target people entering the country. It must be backed by detailed information that allows authorities to follow up. He stressed that temperature checks and hand rubs should not create misplaced confidence. “They help people to be more confident and comfortable. But at this stage right now, they don’t count very much.”

title: Your past prescriptions haven’t helped developing countries – TOR MD tells IMF
body: Mr Edmond Kombat, the Managing Director of the Tema Oil Refinery Limited (TOR), has challenged the International Monetary Fund (IMF) over its long-standing prescriptions for state-owned enterprises. He noted that the Fund appears to be revising its literature because its past advice “hasn’t helped” developing countries. Mr Kombat was responding to a question on the reason for the recent visit by a delegation from the IMF to the state-owned Oil Refinery, at the Government Accountability Series Press Conference held at the Presidency in Accra. Mr Kombat said the Fund had written extensively about Ghana’s energy sector, including TOR. He traced the country’s history with IMF-backed programmes—from the Economic Recovery Programme to the Financial Sector Recovery Programme and the Divestiture of State Enterprises—and observed that the Fund had traditionally promoted private business and “usually they don’t like state entities running businesses.” “But it looks like they are changing their literature, because most of those prescriptions that they give actually haven’t helped the developing countries,” he said. He said in Ghana, state-owned enterprises were beginning to show that state institutions could work and work very well. “And we were happy to receive them and show them that under His Excellency President John Dramani Mahama, state entities are working, and are working profitably, and are not the lost making entities,” Mr Kombat added. He noted that the IMF delegation seemed impressed, reiterated that “but we also remain guarded.”

title: Yellow Card wins top Diamond honour at 2026 Money Awards
body: Yellow Card has won Gold in the Diamond category at the 2026 Money Awards, securing its second consecutive recognition at the global fintech awards following its Grand Prix victory in the Payments category last year. The award was presented on Sunday, October 18, in Las Vegas during Money20/20 USA. According to the company, the Diamond category is the programme’s highest honour, recognising transformative achievements in the global financial technology industry. Yellow Card Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder Chris Maurice said the recognition reflected the company’s growth from its early ambitions in emerging markets to expanding its operations globally and working with major corporate and financial institutions. “This year, we made bold decisions to take what we’d built in emerging markets and expand our vision globally,” he said, adding that the award was particularly meaningful at the current stage of the company’s development. The award follows a year of significant developments for the stablecoin infrastructure provider. In June, Yellow Card was named on Fortune’s inaugural Crypto Innovators list. It also secured $40 million in strategic funding, expanded into Latin America, Asia-Pacific and North America, and obtained anti-money laundering regulatory affiliation in Switzerland. The company also launched Global Accounts, a service that allows businesses to open named US dollar, pound sterling and euro accounts and access local payment systems in more than 190 countries through a single application programming interface or its Treasury Portal. Chief Technology Officer and Co-Founder Justin Poiroux said the recognition highlighted the work of the team in developing technology to simplify cross-border payments and support businesses operating across different markets. He said receiving the honour for a second consecutive year was a proud moment for the company, as it continues to build stablecoin infrastructure connecting businesses and financial institutions around the world.

title: The real reason why A24 movies take so long to reach cinemas outside the US
body: If you live outside the United States, by the time an A24 film reaches your local cinema, you may already know far more about it than you wanted to. Often, reviews have been out for months, memes are circulating on social media and American fans are posting long TikToks and reels discussing an ending you are still trying to avoid. That is the situation facing many prospective fans of You Can See Everything , Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. It has earned an estimated $45.1 million in North America in two weeks, but has not yet been released anywhere else. Australian, New Zealand and British audiences will wait until November, but much of the rest of the world, including the UAE, is yet to receive a release date. If a film is attracting that much attention, why is it taking so long to reach audiences elsewhere? The answer begins with how movies reach cinemas to begin with: through distributors. An A24 release can involve different distribution companies in different countries, each with its own costs, campaign and opening date. The company’s American success can help persuade overseas buyers to take a chance, but bringing a film to their cinemas requires a separate commercial calculation. Who decides whether an A24 film comes here? In many overseas markets, A24 sells distribution rights to another company, which then arranges the local release and promotion. That gives A24 income from the film while placing the cost of releasing it with the buyer. Recent Middle East deals show how much the partners can vary. Front Row acquired regional rights to The Smashing Machine . Sony bought international rights which cover the region to Materialists and Bring Her Back , having previously acquired Middle East rights to Beau Is Afraid . Vox Cinemas has also worked with A24 for direct distribution. Box Office Mojo lists it as the UAE distributor of Marty Supreme and Backrooms, without a separate distributor logo listed on marketing materials. And while it's more famous now for being a production company, sometimes A24 is itself solely a distributor. The Australian horror hit Talk to Me was sold internationally by Bankside Films, which struck separate deals with A24 for North America and Front Row for the Middle East. An A24 logo on a trailer therefore tells you less about a film’s international release than you might expect. Why can’t the films open everywhere at the same time? They sometimes do. Kane Parsons’ horror film Backrooms opened in the UAE in May, a day before its US release. The Smashing Machine also reached UAE cinemas alongside its American opening last year. There are agreements covering several films, too. In February last year, Nordisk Film announced a partnership covering six A24 titles in Denmark, Sweden, Norway and Finland, including Warfare , Eddington and Marty Supreme . A24 handles some releases itself in markets including Britain and Australia. But securing the rights and getting a film into cinemas are separate stages. Distributors need time to prepare campaigns and find a place in schedules crowded with competing releases. In its examination of You Can See Everything , Variety identified the short turnaround following the documentary’s surprise unveiling as one possible explanation for the staggered release. A24 declined to provide comment to the publication on its strategy. Delays can also reflect a distributor’s judgment about when a film has the best chance of finding an audience, and how big of an audience it may have. A horror film like Backrooms , which had a built-in global fandom thanks to its YouTube presence, is perhaps an easier sell than a documentary that is building buzz through word of mouth. Surely there are enough A24 fans to make it worthwhile? A devoted following helps, but it does not make every film a safe bet. TheWrap reported that 70 per cent of You Can See Everything ’s US opening-weekend audience was under 35. An audience poll supplied by A24 also found that 70 per cent of respondents named Fielder as a major reason for buying a ticket. His following is clearly part of this film’s appeal; another A24 title may draw a different audience. A distributor has to estimate how that interest will translate into revenue in its own market, weighed against the rights fee and release costs. The Smashing Machine , starring Dwayne Johnson as mixed martial artist Mark Kerr, illustrates the risk. Director Benny Safdie put its production budget at $49 million in an interview with Filmmaker . It earned about $21.1 million worldwide, according to Box Office Mojo. Those are gross ticket sales, of which cinemas retain a share. Variety reported last October that A24 had reduced its exposure by selling foreign rights. Rival executives estimated that overseas partners would bear most of the losses, although individual distributors’ accounts were not disclosed. “They may not want to come back to the well again,” one unnamed rival independent-film executive said. There are successes, too. Celine Song’s Materialists earned more than $100 million worldwide, with roughly two-thirds coming from outside North America, including about $1.2 million in the UAE. A24’s films can find substantial international audiences, but the results vary enough to make each acquisition a separate bet. Doesn’t waiting risk losing the audience? That concern has been raised by distributors themselves. Everything Everywhere All at Once reached French cinemas in August 2022, more than five months after its US opening. Speaking to Le Parisien the following year, Tristan Dulaz, founder of French co-distributor Originals Factory, said piracy had cost the film potential admissions. The newspaper described A24 as a tough negotiator in overseas sales. “The more time passes in negotiations, the longer the film takes to come out,” Dulaz said, in comments translated from French. “But with A24, there is now progress.” Local choices also contributed to the wait. France Inter reported that Originals Factory selected a late-summer opening in the hope of finding a better slot. American digital releases can further complicate the timing. Variety reported that British previews of Oppenheim’s Primetime , starring Robert Pattinson, would begin on October 28, only days before its US video-on-demand release. Viewers in one country can be preparing to watch a film at home while those elsewhere are still waiting for it to reach cinemas. Will You Can See Everything come to the UAE? Sony Pictures Worldwide Acquisitions has bought rights covering the Middle East, according to Deadline . It has also acquired regional rights to Primetime . Neither film has an announced UAE cinema date. Recent releases show how widely the wait can vary, even with the same local distributor. Vox’s UAE release of Marty Supreme came in March, months after its American debut, while Backrooms arrived alongside its US launch. Sony’s acquisition gives both You Can See Everything and Primetime a route to the region. The next step for UAE audiences is a local release announcement confirming when and where they can watch them.

title: After 30 years in the Gulf, Abu Dhabi head teacher of BSAK to leave UAE
body: After three decades in the region and 12 years leading The British School Al Khubairat, Abu Dhabi head teacher Mark Leppard will leave the UAE next August. He will take up a new role as chief executive of Singapore’s Tanglin Trust School, founded in 1925. Mr Leppard, 57, will be succeeded at BSAK by Robin Macpherson, currently head of college at Robert Gordon’s College in Aberdeen, Scotland, who has previously worked at Repton School Dubai. “I’ve been here for 12 years, in the region for 30 years,” Mr Leppard told The National . “I consider this as home for me. My children have grown up here. I’ve had a fantastic life. “It wasn’t an easy decision, leaving the UAE , but an opportunity to test myself in another environment [arose].” Mr Leppard began his teaching career in the Gulf region in 1996, when he joined Doha College in Qatar. He worked as a physical education teacher and head of year, before becoming assistant principal, and then, for the last nine years, principal. Similar to BSAK, Doha College is a non-profit institution. The Gulf region, and the UAE in particular, have always been “very ambitious for education ”, Mr Leppard said. “It’s really changed, but for the positive,” he said. “There’s more focus on education. There’s more focus on AI, there’s more focus on physical literacy.” He expects artificial intelligence to have a far greater impact on education in the coming year. He also noted the flurry of well-known British schools opening branches in the UAE. These schools were “providing very good service”, Mr Leppard said, adding that the sector was well regulated and offered quality education,. However, not-for-profit schools such as BSAK have a “unique selling point” because they reinvest “every single dirham” in the school. This includes investments in staff training. “We retain quality staff, and they want to come here and stay here,” he said, adding that the school’s staff retention rate, between 92 and 96 per cent, was “incredible”. BSAK has also expanded during his tenure, growing from about 1,600 pupils when he arrived to around 2,030 pupils today. The school caters to children aged 3 to 18. “We’ve worked hard on academic results, which have improved year-on-year,” he said. In addition to strong academic outcomes, Mr Leppard said BSAK was “a community school” and had as many as 100 co-curricular or extra-curricular activities a week. His contribution to education was recognised in 2015, when he was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE). BSAK, established in 1968, was founded on land donated by the UAE’s Founding Father, the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan. Mr Leppard said he hoped to contribute positively to the school’s history. “I generally think I’m just a cog, hopefully a positive cog, in its history,” he said. His move to Singapore reflects a desire to experience a different culture and challenge himself in a new environment. “If you’re in an institution for a period of time, you need a fresh challenge,” he said. “I’ve been challenged every day at BSAK. It would be good to stretch myself and try it in a different context.” Mr Macpherson will take over as BSAK head teacher in August, shortly before the start of the 2027-28 academic year. He has led Robert Gordon’s College as head of college since 2020. The independent school has more than 1,400 pupils aged three to 18. He previously worked at Repton School Dubai between 2008 and 2011, giving him experience of the UAE’s education landscape. In a statement, BSAK said Mr Macpherson “brings valuable regional experience and an understanding of the cultural context and relationships that underpin a thriving international school community”. Mr Macpherson has written books on educational theory and practice, including co-authoring The Teaching Life: Professional Learning and Career Progression . He has also written history textbooks. Faisal Raja, chairman of BSAK’s board of governors, said the board was particularly impressed by Mr Macpherson’s educational vision, values-led leadership and commitment to academic excellence, inclusion and community. “His belief in creating an environment where pupils and staff are supported, challenged and inspired to thrive aligns closely with BSAK’s ethos,” he said.

title: How OpenAI turned its coding tools into dots, an always-on personal assistant
body:
The always-on AI personal assistant, which keeps working in the background even when you aren’t asking it to, is this year’s answer to the question of how people will actually use deep learning models. The startup Instinct became an overnight sensation, and Meta put the full force of its marketing behind its assistant, Muse.
OpenAI wasn’t going to be left out. The company released dots , its assistant offering, at its developer day in late September. Alexander Embiricos, who leads OpenAI’s enterprise product team, joined us at TechCrunch Disrupt this month to explain where the product came from — starting with the question of why so many companies seem to be turning to cutesy mascots as avatars for their trillion-parameter matrix multiplication machines.
“There’s kind of this convergent evolution happening,” Embiricos said of the efforts to build AI assistants. “As we were working on the product, we realized if we could frame this as, it’s an entity and it’s a single conversation, not many different conversations….it starts to become intuitive.”
The assistant is available in the ChatGPT desktop and mobile apps to subscribers on the Pro tier or higher, with plans starting at $100 a month. Once it is connected to your calendar, email, computer and other tools, the agent tries to help you get your work done.
Embiricos points out that you could achieve much of dots’ functionality with Open AI’s Codex app, its coding tool, released at the beginning of this year. But that requires more work and hand-holding. He recalled celebrating when his wife started leaving her computer on all night so that her agents could keep working.
“On the product team, what I think about is, how do we make this intuitive and useful to people?” he told Disrupt attendees. “A lot of that isn’t building some new piece of tech into the product; it’s how you frame it to the user and how it feels.”
Making the technology feel intuitive meant repackaging the functionality of the company’s models into something more accessible, a path it was already on as it spun ChatGPT Work out of the agentic coding tools it had built for software engineers. Even the name — a play on the negative space inside of OpenAI’s logo — is intended “to feel like just something that could eventually be ubiquitous.” (Asked when he learned that rival AI entrepreneur Elon Musk owns the dot.com URL, Embiricos said, “I found out very late.”)
The idea of a persistent agent is that it doesn’t need prompting. For OpenAI, that means more token usage, and for users, a more pro-active assistant “that’s sort of thinking about you and thinking how to help you,” as Embiricos put it.
In our testing, the assistant’s ability to think ahead is apparent and often useful, but it isn’t quite there yet. It will flag calendar conflicts and upcoming deadlines, but not necessarily in the most timely fashion.
“The first time it told me about one of those [conflicts] — this is like early in development — it told me three minutes before the thing,” Embiricos says of his dot. “It’s like, ‘Hey, this thing is coming up. You might want to do something about it.’ I only have three minutes!”
Embiricos expects the timing to improve over time, but the proactive approach is key to the product. “I was hearing about an engineer at a drone delivery startup, and they were saying, ‘We had this outage, and by the time I noticed that the outage was going on, my dot had already noticed the outage was happening, had already analyzed the outage, and had come to me with useful information for how we could resolve the outage.’”
As with most AI agent use cases, there’s a tension between the personal information an AI model needs to be useful and exactly how much personal data you are exposing to a software company. Muse has been criticized for the profiles it builds of your family and friends, which the software uses to know, say, what kind of restaurant you might want to go to with a specific pal, but could also add incredible value to Meta’s advertising business. Does dots collect similar data?
“Yes, we have a thing that we built into dots, which we call proactive research,” Embiricos said. “On a cadence, it will think about what it knows about you, what is the conversation that it’s had, and then what have you given it access to that it can think about, and then it will go and research, ‘What could I do to be more helpful to you?’ And then, basically, it will propose that.”
It’s difficult to separate the data needs of the agent from that of its parent corporation. Hark, a startup developing its own AI personal assistant, is explicit in pointing out that it doesn’t collect data to fuel an advertising business the way that OpenAI and Meta do.
With dots, OpenAI says that the agent has the same privacy controls as ChatGPT itself: Users can turn off model training (stopping OpenAI from using their conversations to improve its AI), and control which resources it accesses within your computer and how. Still, those controls aren’t granular and the app can be pushy. For example, it refuses to accept read-only access to cloud drives.
“What I think we need to do is basically build out super, super, super granular controls,” Embiricos said, but he pointed to the model’s intelligence and discretion as the other side of this coin.
“This is actually something we kind of got some flack about when we launched,” Embiricos said. “We had really conservative defaults over what the agent would do, and it would ask for permission a lot. I remember knowing that we were going to see that feedback, but thinking, ‘This is okay, we can tune that over time.’”
The other big question about AI agents is whether they can scale. They’re fun when only a few people have them, and stories of agents snagging hard-to-get reservations abound. But businesses don’t necessarily like dealing with agents and might not be equipped to. People certainly don’t like dealing with them (note: stop having your AI agents pitch me), and Embiricos is among those people. He also has a human assistant because OpenAI’s corporate partners want to interact with a person, he said, adding, “I personally never intend to have a meeting with someone else’s agent.”
If the AI industry is right that agents are our future, can we get there without overwhelming the infrastructure that our world currently runs on, from businesses and websites to payment networks?
“At OpenAI…we’re not always moving the fastest in terms of shipping the next ability for the agent to work with the world,” he said. “When we do, we’re doing it really closely in collaboration with the rest of the ecosystem. I probably can’t say too much here, but we’re deep in lots of conversations with payment processors.”
Letting an AI assistant spend money through partnerships with payment companies would be a potentially lucrative first for OpenAI, but also a big ask for consumers. Giving an assistant access to my email inbox already feels like a big ask, but my bank account is off limits. For now.

title: NDC and the battle within
body: By Hussein Yahaya, Abuja; Sani Ibrahim Paki & Salim Umar Ibrahim, Kano With 81 days to the January 16, 2027 presidential elections, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) is enmeshed in a fresh crisis over the composition of its presidential campaign council. The NDC on Sunday unveiled its national campaign council, appointing Ibrahim Abdulkarim as its Director-General and the NDC National Secretary, Ikenna Enekweizu, as the council’s secretary. Under the structure, the NDC National Leader, Senator Seriake Dickson, will serve as the chairman of the council; the presidential candidate, Peter Obi, will serve as co-chairman; Senator Cleopas Moses Zuwoghe (NDC National Chairman) is the vice-chairman, while Rabiu Kwankwaso, the party’s vice-presidential candidate, is the co-vice chairman. The council also features prominent figures including former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Babachir Lawal, heading the National Advisory Council, former Deputy Senate President Senator Ovie Omo-Agege, Pat Utomi, and Buba Galadima. Daily Trust reports that no sooner had the NDC unveiled its council than the OK (Obi-Kwankwaso) Movement launched an attack on the party, saying the list casts serious doubt on the party’s readiness for the upcoming general elections. Analyst say for the NDC to get its acts right ahead of the elections, it must clearly define the extent of how the diehard supporters of their presidential and vice presidential candidates could influence decisions. In a statement issued in Abuja, Director-General of the OK Movement, John Ughulu, criticised the NDC leadership for dragging its feet in mobilising its electoral machinery, warning that political ambition without ground-level coordination portends defeat. “With less than three months until the general elections, they are only just announcing their Presidential Campaign Council,” Ughulu said. “What exactly have they been doing all this time? Where is the structure? Where is the strategy? Where is the machinery required to prosecute a serious national election?” Taking a jab at the composition of the campaign list, Ughulu boasted that the OK Movement had already completed the heavy lifting required for victory, predicting that the party elite would soon seek assistance. The fresh wave of criticism underlines a widening rift between the NDC leadership and the OK Movement over control and campaign strategy for Obi and his running mate, Kwankwaso. The OK Movement had, in September, unveiled a 59-member Presidential Campaign Council comprising zonal and state coordinators, as well as directors overseeing various aspects of the campaign, but the party dissociated itself from the list, saying a support group did not have the right to constitute a campaign council for the party. The resultant friction in the internal workings of the party is yet to abate, with the movement objecting to the naming of a national campaign council by the party on Monday. Names of prominent members of the movement were omitted from the council, including that of Ughulu and the OK Movement’s network of state, local government and ward coordinators. National leader of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Henry Seriake Dickson (4th left); NDC presidential candidate, Peter Obi (middle); his running mate, Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso (4th right); members of the National Working Committee (NWC) and party leaders during the opening ceremony of the party’s new national secretariat and campaign office in Jabi, Abuja yesterday Why the rift persists The fresh wave of criticism, party members say, exposes a widening chasm between the NDC leadership and the OK Movement. The exclusion of the OK Movement leadership from the council is linked to the bitter dispute over the movement’s decision to establish its own independent presidential campaign council. The move was previously dismissed by the leader of the party, Dickson, as “unheard of” and “nonsensical,” with the party insisting that support groups must complement official party structures rather than run parallel operations. Despite the friction, Ughulu remained defiant, asserting that the party’s official machinery cannot bypass the grassroots networks built by the movement. “The funny part of this list is that 90 per cent of the people on it will still come knocking on the doors of the OK Movement to beg for the very structure they have failed to build themselves!” He added. Reinforcing the group’s independence, Ughulu asserted that the OK Movement would never settle for being a ceremonial support outfit. He emphasized that the movement’s true strength rests in its formidable organisational capacity and unwavering commitment to the Obi-Kwankwaso presidential mandate. “Leadership is not about who makes the loudest noise. Leadership is about who prepares, organises, builds, and delivers when it matters most,” Ughulu declared. “The OK Movement is ready. The question is: are they? Nigeria will be OK.” Dickson had maintained that the NDC would work with support groups but expected them to function within their proper roles. Ughulu, however, insisted that the OK Movement is an independent political organisation, not merely a conventional support group, and would not surrender its national, state, local government and ward structures to the NDC or any other organisation. The OK Movement director-general argued that elections are won through sustained grassroots mobilisation, strategic planning and effective coordination rather than prominent names on campaign councils. “Elections are not won by titles, press releases, political noise, or the number of big names on a campaign council. Elections are won through grassroots mobilisation, effective coordination, strategic planning, committed people, and a well-established structure that reaches every polling unit,” he said. The politician maintained that the movement had recognised the importance of grassroots organisation long before the electioneering season and was better prepared to mobilise voters. With the appointment of Babachir Lawal to the campaign council, there are fears that it may escalate the growing friction in the Adamawa chapter of the NDC following his rejection by the governorship candidate of the party, Aisha Binani and other party candidates over his appointment as the party’s North-East leader last month. Though the party promised to call the two for a reconciliation meeting, it is not clear at press time how far it has gone in this regard. Ossai Director, the party’s Publicity Secretary, did not respond to calls put across to him on the latest stand of the OK Movement. However, a chieftain of the party told our correspondent that the movement went too far by setting up a presidential campaign council even before the political party. “A support party must not go that far, but the party leadership should have also included some of the leaders of the movement in the NDC campaign council in the spirit of reconciliation. “This, the party failed to do and it shouldn’t be so,’’ he said. The OK Movement was formally unveiled in Abuja on April 20, 2026, by supporters of Obi and Kwankwaso ahead of the 2027 general elections. Its emergence followed growing uncertainty within the opposition coalition, particularly over the choice of a presidential candidate capable of challenging President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. The organisers described it as a coalition bringing together supporters of the Obidient Movement, Kwankwasiyya, the NNPP and the African Democratic Congress (ADC). Justin Ijeh was named its National Publicity Secretary, while the group announced plans to establish structures across Nigeria’s 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. The initial idea was to build a common political platform capable of combining Obi’s reform-oriented appeal with Kwankwaso’s grassroots political machinery. Prof Ochefu rejects NDC appointment Professor of Economic History and Strategic Studies at Rev. Fr. Moses Orshio Adasu University, Makurdi, Prof. Yakubu Ochefu, has rejected his purported appointment to the National Campaign Council of the NDC, clarifying that he is not a member of the political party. Ochefu, in a statement, said he was neither consulted before the inclusion of his name in the campaign list circulating on social media nor did he grant consent for the appointment. The academic—who serves as National Chairman of the Association of Nigerian Universities Alumni (ANUA) and President-General of Ochetoha K’Idoma—emphasised that his leadership roles require strict non-partisanship, given that the memberships of both organisations span diverse political affiliations. He said, “My attention has been drawn to a list circulating on social media, titled ‘Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) National Campaign Council’, which names me as a member of its National Campaign Caucus. “I wish to inform the public that I am not a member of the NDC and have never been. I was not consulted before my name was included, nor did I give consent. I have written to the Chairman of the Council to decline the appointment and to request that my name be withdrawn and a revised list published. “As National Chairman of the Association of Nigerian Universities Alumni, ANUA, and President-General of Ochetoha K’Idoma, I lead organisations whose members cut across all political parties. These offices require me to remain non-partisan, and I intend to honour that obligation. “I thank all who reached out for clarification, and ask that you disregard the list insofar as it concerns me.” A cross section of voters in the past election ‘Campaign council crisis may affect election coordination’ A political analyst and lecturer at the Kano State College of Arts, Science and Remedial Studies, Dr Kabiru Sa’idu Sufi, warned that the crisis over the composition of the NDC Presidential Campaign Council could undermine coordination and effectiveness of the party’s campaign ahead of the 2027 elections. He said the disagreement between the party leadership and the presidential camp could result in parallel campaign structures operating without proper coordination. According to him, there is a likelihood that both the presidential team and the party would run separate campaign coordination mechanisms. “If you look at the composition of the campaign itself, there is a possibility that we will have parallel coordination. While the presidential team is having its own coordination, the party may also be having its own coordination,” he said. He said the absence of synergy between the two camps could affect the organisation of campaigns. “For now, the party has rejected the composition of their own candidates, and the presidential team has also rejected the composition of the party’s campaign council. “So, I think there may be no synergy, there may be no coordination, and as such, it may affect the organisation of the campaign,” he added. The analyst described the disagreement as a reflection of the party’s inability to fully unite after the emergence of its presidential candidate. He said the development was not entirely surprising, arguing that similar disputes had occurred in previous political platforms associated with Obi, the Labour Party. “I think it shows that the party has not been able to close ranks since the emergence of the presidential flag bearer. It is not something entirely new and we have seen similar situations in the past,” he said. Sufi noted that the NDC should have learned from previous experiences and addressed internal differences before the campaign season. “But it seems no lesson was learned, and what we are seeing now is a repeat of some of the issues that affected campaign coordination in previous elections,” he said. On whether reconciliation between the party and the OK Movement was still possible, the analyst expressed optimism, saying dialogue remained the best option. “If they can come together and sort out their differences, it will be better for them and they may be able to achieve something positive,” he said. He, however, cautioned that failure to resolve the dispute could continue to hamper effective coordination of campaign activities. Sufi dismissed suggestions that external forces might be influencing the crisis, insisting that the problem stemmed largely from internal misunderstanding. “I don’t think there is any external influence. It does not seem as if either of the sides is being controlled from outside. I think it is simply a matter of lack of synergy and cooperation, and the issue is continuing along that line,” he said. NDC declares N8.53bn revenue Meanwhile, the party has revealed that it generated approximately N8.53 billion in total inflows, expended about N2.40 billion, and retained a balance of approximately N6.13 billion to fund its ongoing political operations. Presenting the report, the NDC National Treasurer, Dr. Peter Onigah, stated that the leadership had exercised strict financial discipline to safeguard resources entrusted to the party. Onigah explained that the party’s financial operations were guided by experienced party officials, advice from national leaders, and the National Working Committee (NWC). Onigah appealed to party members and the general public for sustained financial backing, noting that the NDC is still constructing its organisational structures and has not secured power at any government level. “As a new party, we don’t have people in government yet. All of us are outside the government. So we need to contribute and ensure that our party will prevail and achieve the desired objectives,” he added. Reacting to the presentation, Senator Victor Umeh commended the party’s leadership for transparency and for maintaining a N6.13 billion balance. Who is NDC DG, Ibrahim Hussain Abdulkarim? With the release of the NDC campaign list ahead of the 2027 general elections, all eyes are on Alhaji Ibrahim Hussain Abdulkarim, who was appointed as the Director-General of the party’s presidential campaign council. Abdulkarim is described as a businessman, public-sector advisor and political strategist, representing a modern, data-driven approach to political mobilisation in Nigeria. Born on October 14, 1976, in Sokoto State to the family of Alhaji Hussain Abdulkarim, he earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Geography at Bayero University, Kano (BUK). He later specialised in Geographic Information Systems (GIS), spatial data management, and technology-driven development solutions. He serves as the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of EasyGIS Nigeria Limited, a pioneering technology firm specializing in Geographic Information Systems, data management, information systems architecture, and business process improvement. Between 2019 and 2021, he served as the Chairman of the Advisory Committee on Efficient Land Administration, Urban Planning and Development, and Improving Revenue Generation and Collection in the Nasarawa State Ministry of Land and Urban Development.

title: Ebola scientists to probe Nigeria case origin, Africa CDC says
body: A team of ​leading Ebola scientists will travel to Nigeria to help investigate how the country’s first patient in more than ‌a decade got infected, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya said. Their task will involve trying to work out how the female patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, caught the Bundibugyo species of Ebola. Her travel documents show she had not visited the outbreak epicentre in Democratic Republic ​of Congo, Kaseya said in an interview with Reuters in London. Keep up with the latest medical breakthroughs and healthcare trends with the award-winning Reuters Health Rounds newsletter. Sign up here. Finding out how she became ill matters to ensure ​that the deadly Bundibugyo outbreak, already the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record, is not spreading silently ⁠in as-yet undiscovered locations, and to help trace and isolate all contacts. ‘MANY UNKNOWNS’ “We have so many unknowns,” said Kaseya. “I’m bringing a ​group of scientists in Abuja because… we need to be led by science.” One theory the scientists will investigate is a potential link between the patient in Nigeria and the first case in Kenya, reported earlier this month in a man who had travelled from Congo. On Friday, genomic sequencing showed that the viruses that infected the two patients were closely related. The patient in Nigeria had been on holiday in Uganda and ​travelled through Entebbe Airport on October 3. The patient in Kenya, who has since died, was likely in the airport at ​the same time, as their flights were around 40 minutes apart, although they did not depart from the same gate and it is not ‌clear ⁠whether they had any contact, Kaseya said. Kaseya said while genomic sequencing had shown that the viruses were similar, it did not mean that one of the patients had directly infected the other and the patient in Abuja, whose condition is improving, has said she does not remember meeting the Kenya patient. However, he said they were not excluding any options, including that there may have been indirect ​contact through another person, for ​example. Ebola spreads through close ⁠contact with the infected bodily fluids of a person with symptoms, according to the World Health Organization. INVESTIGATION ONGOING Kaseya said all countries involved were now willing to collaborate in the investigation, after what ​he described as tension last week when Uganda’s government insisted the patient in Abuja had been to ​Congo, while Nigerian ⁠authorities suggested she had not and was infected in Uganda, which has been Ebola-free since August. Kaseya said the team, which will be led by the co-discoverer of Ebola, Congolese expert Jean-Jacques Muyembe, would also look at more sequencing data to work out where the Kenyan ⁠patient was ​infected. The Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in Congo has now caused almost 10,000 cases and ​more than 4,600 deaths in Congo, and spread to three other countries in Africa – Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe ​cases, internal and external bleeding. There is currently no approved vaccine or treatment for Ebola Bundibugyo.

title: Russia pushes stronger media ties with Africa, proposes awards for cross-continental reporting
body: By Nkiruka Nnorom Russia has proposed stronger media ties with Africa, including the establishment of a journalism award to promote cross-continental reporting. Director of the Department of State Policy in the Field of Mass Media, Ministry of Telecom and Mass Communications, Larina Ekaterina, made the proposal at the Russia-Africa media forum in Moscow and invited the continent to join the alliance for global fact-checking initiative to combat disinformation. Ekaterina said the award would recognise African journalists who report on issues connected with Russia, as well as Russian journalists who actively cover issues relating to African countries. She said the award would help strengthen direct relationships between African and Russian media organisations and encourage journalist exchanges and training. “There is an excellent non-material way to strengthen cooperation and motivate participants through competitions. “We propose that our hosts today, together with all of you, consider establishing a journalism award for media professionals who cover issues relating to Russia and Africa,” she said. On combating disinformation, Ekaterina said fact-checking was another major area of cooperation. “Another major area in which we have work to do and experience to share is fact-checking and combating disinformation,” she said. She also disclosed that three weeks ago in Moscow, the Alliance for the Protection of Children in Aggressive Environments was established. According to her, the Central African Republic was among the countries that signed the agreement, while Tanzania expressed support, with several non-governmental organisations from Africa and Asia also joining. “I hope that this area will also become one of the important topics and focal points of our cooperation,” she said. Sergey Kuzovnikov, Director of Strategy, Russian News Agency, TASS, said the importance of the Russia-Africa media forum lies in giving Africa its own voice, allowing African countries to tell their own stories through direct sources rather than second-hand interpretations. He noted that direct engagement would help Russia and Africa learn about each other’s countries through media cooperation and exchanges. “Most importantly, I believe the significance of this forum lies in the fact that it allows us to speak directly rather than speaking on behalf of others. It allows Africa to tell its own story,” Kuzovnikov said. “In my view, this is one of the most important aspects of the media forum because it provides direct access between you and our audience, as well as access in the opposite direction,” he said. Kuzovnikov said TASS, which has maintained presence in Africa since Soviet times and currently has six foreign bureaus in countries including Egypt, Tunisia, Kenya and South Africa, plans to increase its representatives across the continent. He said during the Soviet era, TASS had presence in practically every African country, adding that information about Africa must now reach Russian audiences through direct sources. “Information about Africa must reach our audiences through direct sources rather than through second-hand accounts or other people’s interpretations. By communicating directly and getting to know one another, we can avoid many mistakes and distortions,” he said. He said over 300 African media organisations currently provide news feeds in Arabic and French to TASS, enabling direct flow of information, while also accessing information about developments in Russia and the world. On learning through exchanges, Kuzovnikov cited the TASS international press tour known as “TASS Africa”, saying journalists from 10 African countries participated in the tour organised in November last year. “As you have rightly observed, exchanging media content helps people gain a more personal understanding of other countries. There is a significant difference between hearing someone talk about a place and seeing it with your own eyes,” he said. He said such opportunities were particularly valuable for people studying Russian language and said that TASS is working to organise more similar programmes. “I believe that we can continue this work in the future, enabling you to learn more about Russia and our country’s current situation,” he said. Kuzovnikov said with 122 years of history, TASS is ready to share its knowledge through educational programmes covering artificial intelligence, fact-checking and data management. The Managing Director and CEO, News Agency of Nigeria (NAN), Ali Muhammad Ali, commended the evolving collaboration between Russia and African media, stressing that the trend would strengthen the integrity of news delivery, especially amid the rise of fake news and Artificial Intelligence. He noted that direct media exchanges would eliminate the practice of relying on third parties for news reports, while also improving the accuracy and authenticity of reports. “In the past, we in Africa relied on global media hegemons to get stories about Russia. But that is now eliminated. We are dealing directly with the gatekeepers and hunters of news,” he said. He noted that while questions remained about propaganda and authenticity, Nigerian media are scaling skills, vigilance and gatekeeping, adding that though digital media offers alternative feeds, it has weakened traditional gatekeeping with the spread of unverified news. The post Russia pushes stronger media ties with Africa, proposes awards for cross-continental reporting appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Oxi Day: Why Greeks Mark 28 October 1940 Every Year
body: Each 28 October, Greeks around the world remember the morning their country said “No” to Mussolini. Here is the story behind Oxi Day , what came after it, and how the day is marked today, from Thessaloniki to Sydney. Contents What is Oxi Day? The ultimatum of 28 October 1940 The Greco-Italian War and the push into Albania The German invasion of April 1941 and the occupation Why Oxi Day mattered in the Second World War How Oxi Day is celebrated in Greece and Cyprus How the Greek diaspora marks Oxi Day Oxi Day FAQ What is Oxi Day? Oxi Day (also written Ochi or Ohi ; in Greek, Epeteios tou Ochi , “the Anniversary of the No”) falls on 28 October. It is a national holiday in Greece and Cyprus, and Greek communities everywhere observe it. The day remembers how Greece rejected an ultimatum from Fascist Italy in the early hours of 28 October 1940, and the war of resistance that followed. The word oxi means “no”. For Greeks it is a shorthand for a whole generation’s refusal to give in: soldiers who fought in the freezing mountains of Epirus and Albania, civilians who went hungry under occupation, and resistance fighters who kept going until liberation in 1944. The ultimatum of 28 October 1940 A tense summer Greece was neutral when the war began, but by 1940 it was under real pressure. Italy had occupied neighbouring Albania in April 1939. Then, on 15 August 1940, the feast of the Dormition, a submarine sank the Greek light cruiser Elli while she lay at anchor in Tinos harbour. The submarine was later confirmed as the Italian Delfino . Mussolini was also annoyed that Hitler had sent German troops into Romania in October 1940 without warning him, and he wanted a quick victory of his own. A knock at the door in Kifisia Shortly after 3am on 28 October 1940, the Italian ambassador in Athens, Emanuele Grazzi, arrived at the Kifisia home of Prime Minister Ioannis Metaxas. Grazzi handed him an ultimatum. Italy demanded that its troops be allowed to enter Greece and occupy unnamed “strategic points”. Greece had until 6am to agree. The reply Popular memory says Metaxas answered with one word: Oxi . By most accounts, though, he actually spoke in French, then the language of diplomacy: “Alors, c’est la guerre” , meaning “Well then, it is war.” Either way the answer was a refusal. Italian forces based in Albania crossed the Greek border at about 5:30am, before the ultimatum had even run out. Metaxas had ruled Greece as a dictator since 4 August 1936, and his legacy is still debated. But his refusal that morning matched the mood of the country. As news spread, crowds filled the streets of Athens and other cities, and people from across the political spectrum rallied to defend Greece. The word “OXI” first appeared as a newspaper headline on 30 October 1940, in the Athens paper Ellinikon Mellon (“Hellenic Future”), over an article by Nikos P. Efstratiou. The Greco-Italian War and the push into Albania Holding the line in Epirus and the Pindus Italy expected an easy campaign. What it got was hard fighting over a narrow front of rugged mountains with very few roads. In Epirus, Greek forces built their defence around the Kalpaki position and the marshy Kalamas river. To the north-east, in the Pindus mountains, a small Greek detachment under Colonel Konstantinos Davakis met the elite Italian Julia Alpine Division. Greek reinforcements arrived, and by mid-November the Italian advance had been stopped and pushed back. Davakis was badly wounded in the fighting. The counteroffensive Under commander-in-chief General Alexandros Papagos, the Greek army counterattacked on 14 November 1940. Within days the Italians had been driven off Greek soil. On 22 November Greek troops entered Korçë (Koritsa), the first major town they took in Albania. Over the following weeks they captured Gjirokastër (Argyrokastro) on 8 December, along with Sarandë (Agioi Saranta) and Himara. In this region, known to Greeks as Northern Epirus, many residents were ethnic Greeks. Winter and stalemate Fighting in the Albanian mountains through the winter of 1940–41 was brutal. Many soldiers suffered frostbite, and Greek supply lines were stretched to breaking point. Greek forces took the strategic Klisura Pass in January 1941. Metaxas died in Athens on 29 January 1941. In March, Mussolini travelled to Albania to watch a major Italian spring offensive, which failed to break the Greek lines. Greece’s counteroffensive of November 1940 was one of the first significant Allied land victories over an Axis power, and it won admiration across the free world. Britain, Greece’s ally, sent air units and later ground forces, including Australian and New Zealand troops. The German invasion of April 1941 and the occupation Hitler had come to see the Balkans as a threat on his southern flank, especially once British forces were in Greece. On 6 April 1941 Germany invaded Greece and Yugoslavia at the same time (Operation Marita), attacking through Bulgaria. Greek forts on the Metaxas Line put up stubborn resistance, but German armour soon broke through via Yugoslavia. Most of the Greek army was still committed in Albania. The Greek Army of Epirus surrendered later in April, Commonwealth forces fell back towards Thermopylae and then evacuated, and German troops entered Athens on 27 April 1941. The Battle of Crete followed in May 1941. German paratroopers landed on the island, and Greek, British, Australian and New Zealand troops and Cretan civilians resisted fiercely before the island fell at the start of June. Greece was then split into German, Italian and Bulgarian occupation zones. The years that followed were among the darkest in modern Greek history. Famine struck in the winter of 1941–42, killing huge numbers of people, especially in Athens and Piraeus. Villages were destroyed in reprisals, and most of Greece’s Jewish communities were deported and murdered in the Holocaust. Resistance started early. On the night of 30–31 May 1941, two young men, Manolis Glezos and Apostolos Santas, tore down the swastika flag from the Acropolis. Armed resistance movements grew in the mountains. Athens was liberated on 12 October 1944. Why Oxi Day mattered in the Second World War When Greece entered the war in late 1940, Britain and its Commonwealth were the only other powers still fighting the Axis in Europe. France had fallen, and neither the Soviet Union nor the United States had entered the war. Greece’s victories over a much larger Italian force lifted Allied morale. They also showed that the Axis could be beaten in the field. People often say the Greek campaign delayed Hitler’s invasion of the Soviet Union, Operation Barbarossa. That invasion began on 22 June 1941, weeks later than the mid-May date in early German planning. Hitler himself later blamed Mussolini’s Greek adventure for the delay. Anthony Eden, Britain’s foreign secretary, also made the argument. Historians remain divided, however. Many, including Ian Kershaw and Antony Beevor, argue that an unusually wet spring, logistics and Germany’s own planning problems were more important to the timing. They also argue that the Balkan campaign made little difference to how Barbarossa turned out. Others still argue it had some effect. What no one disputes is the courage of the stand Greece made, and its symbolic weight at a moment when much of Europe had fallen. A famous saying has come down from that winter: “Hence we will not say that Greeks fight like heroes, but that heroes fight like Greeks.” It is often credited to Winston Churchill, but researchers have found no record of him saying it. The earliest known version appears in a Greek diplomat’s article in The Manchester Guardian in April 1941, presented as a saying already in circulation. How Oxi Day is celebrated in Greece and Cyprus In Greece, 28 October is a public holiday. Government offices, schools and most businesses close. Blue-and-white flags hang from balconies and public buildings in the days before, and churches hold doxologies (services of thanksgiving) and memorial services for the fallen. The main military parade is held in Thessaloniki. The city also celebrates its patron saint, Agios Dimitrios, on 26 October, and the anniversary of its 1912 liberation, so the last week of October is a festive one there. Across the rest of the country, from big cities to island villages, the day centres on school parades . Students in uniform march behind the Greek flag past local officials and veterans’ groups, while families line the footpaths. Schools usually hold ceremonies the day before, with poems, songs and re-enactments of the events of 1940. Wreaths are laid at war memorials, and many towns organise local events, concerts and exhibitions. In Cyprus, 28 October is also a national holiday. It is marked with school and student parades, church services and wreath-laying ceremonies honouring the Greek Cypriots who served in the war. How the Greek diaspora marks Oxi Day For Greek communities abroad, Oxi Day is one of the key dates on the calendar, alongside Greek Independence Day on 25 March. The OXI Day ceremony at the ANZAC Memorial in Hyde Park, Sydney. Photo: Nick Bourdaniotis/GreekCityTimes In Australia , home to one of the world’s largest Greek diasporas, community organisations, churches, Greek schools and consular offices hold commemorations each year in Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, Brisbane, Perth and Canberra. These typically include wreath-laying ceremonies at war memorials and cenotaphs, church services, and marches or gatherings. Greek-school students take part, often in traditional dress, and so do veterans’ and community groups. Oxi Day has special meaning for Australians, too. Australian soldiers fought beside Greeks in mainland Greece and on Crete in 1941, and many Cretan and Greek families sheltered Allied soldiers during the occupation. So many Oxi Day services in Australia also honour the Anzacs. In the United States , Greek Orthodox parishes, Hellenic societies and Greek-language schools hold doxologies, school programs and community events in late October. Organisations also work to tell American audiences about Greece’s role in the Second World War. Elsewhere, in Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, South Africa and beyond, Greek communities mark the day in the same spirit. They gather around the flag, remember the fallen, and pass the story of 1940 on to children and grandchildren who may never have lived in Greece. Oxi Day FAQ What is Oxi Day? Oxi Day is a Greek and Cypriot national holiday held on 28 October. It commemorates Greece’s rejection of Mussolini’s ultimatum on 28 October 1940 and the resistance that followed during the Second World War. What does “Oxi” mean? Oxi (όχι, also spelt Ochi or Ohi ) is Greek for “no”. It is the answer Greece is remembered as giving to Italy’s demand to occupy Greek territory. What did Metaxas actually say to the Italian ambassador? By most accounts, Prime Minister Ioannis Metaxas replied in French, “Alors, c’est la guerre” (“Well then, it is war”). The single word “Oxi” became the popular symbol of his refusal. Is Oxi Day a public holiday? Yes. 28 October is a public holiday in Greece and Cyprus, marked by military and school parades, church services and flag displays. In Australia and other countries it is not a public holiday, but Greek communities hold their own commemorations. How is Oxi Day celebrated in Australia? Greek-Australian communities hold wreath-laying ceremonies, church services, marches and school events in capital cities including Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide and Canberra. Many of them also honour the Australian and New Zealand soldiers who fought in Greece and Crete in 1941.
