For Nigerian businesses, the bank’s entry could provide additional access to international financing networks and specialised financial services, particularly for companies seeking to fund large-scale projects, raise capital or expand into foreign markets. The proposed institution could also strengthen financial relationships between Nigerian businesses and international investors by connecting local companies with JPMorgan’s global corporate and institutional banking network. What it means for Nigeria’s financial sector The proposed expansion comes as Nigeria pursues financial sector reforms aimed at strengthening banking stability, improving investor confidence and attracting foreign capital. JPMorgan’s presence as a locally licensed merchant bank could increase competition in corporate and investment banking while broadening the range of services available to major businesses and institutional clients. On its website, J.P. Morgan describes itself as a global leader in financial services, offering solutions to the world’s most important corporations, governments and institutions in more than 100 countries. For the US banking giant, Nigeria offers access to a large economy with substantial financing needs. For local businesses, its entry could mean more options for capital raising, financial advisory services and international transactions. However, the entry has been generating mixed reactions among economists and financial analysts. Some said the excitement and interest generated by the planned entry of the bank into Nigeria could be as a result of the recent Nigeria-US agreement on mining. It would be recalled that Nigeria and the United States recently signed a framework aimed at unlocking investment in Nigeria’s estimated $700 billion mineral resources and deepening bilateral cooperation in the critical minerals sector. …Entry may be driven by US interests – Okeke Economist and former banker, Dr. Marcel Okeke in a chat with our correspondent questioned the timing of JPMorgan’s planned entry into Nigeria’s merchant banking sector, suggesting that broader American commercial and strategic interests may be behind the move. Okeke said the decision should be examined against the background of Nigeria’s economic and diplomatic relations with the United States, including a recently signed agreement relating to mineral resources. According to him, JPMorgan’s proposed operation could provide a trusted financial channel for American businesses and investors seeking to pursue opportunities in Nigeria. He argued that the bank’s decision to establish a merchant banking operation, rather than a conventional retail banking business, raises questions about the specific interests it intends to serve. “When you see something that nobody expects to happen, you know that there is a lot behind it,” Okeke said. He added that the broader relationship between Nigeria and the United States could provide important context for understanding the bank’s proposed entry. “You remember recently there was some kind of mineral agreement signed between Nigeria and the US. I don’t have the details of that agreement, but because it involves a lot of money, you have to consider the financial institutions that will be trusted to handle such transactions,” he said. Okeke said JPMorgan’s reputation within the American financial system could make it a preferred institution for facilitating transactions involving American commercial interests in Nigeria. He also questioned why the bank was seeking to establish a merchant bank at a time when security concerns had prompted several countries to issue travel advisories relating to Nigeria. “Why is JPMorgan coming into Nigeria at this particular time, when many countries are issuing travel advisories to their citizens about security concerns in different parts of the country?” he asked. But other analysts see it as a reflection of the ongoing reforms in Nigeria which have brought about renewed investor’s confidence in the Nigeria’s financial system. Ayokunle Olubunmi, a financial analyst said the entry of global financial services giant JPMorgan into Nigeria’s merchant banking sector could improve access to finance, bring international expertise and strengthen support for local businesses. Olubunmi said the bank’s experience across different markets could help introduce Nigerian businesses to financial solutions and transactions that had been successfully deployed elsewhere. He noted that an international financial institution operating across multiple markets could draw on its global expertise to support businesses in Nigeria, while potentially providing access to additional capital. “When a company that is exposed to various markets comes into your country, it brings the experience it has gained in those markets. Some transactions that you may never have thought of have already been carried out elsewhere, and that experience can help,” he said. According to him, JPMorgan’s global reach could also create opportunities for Nigerian businesses to benefit from the bank’s financing capabilities and international networks.

title: No more policy changes without impact assessment – FG
body: The minister of finance and coordinating minister of the economy, Taiwo Oyedele says the federal government is proposing mandatory impact assessments before major economic policy changes to reduce uncertainty for businesses and investors. He made the disclosure on Monday at the ongoing 32nd Nigerian economic summit (NES) in Abuja, while presenting the proposed Nigeria economic policy framework for public consultation. He said the framework would require policymakers to explain the problems a proposed intervention seeks to solve, the evidence supporting it, who would benefit, who would bear the cost, and the conditions under which the policy would end. The framework, which he said is still a consultation draft, is intended to establish enduring principles for economic policymaking across successive administrations rather than serve as a development plan or the manifesto of a particular government. “Our challenge has never been a shortage of ambition or good ideas. It has been the absence of an enduring economic philosophy, consistent policy making, and disciplined implementation,” Oyedele said. He said frequent policy reversals, inadequate impact assessments and limited consultation with businesses had undermined investment and economic growth. “Policy uncertainty is an invisible tax on enterprise, and unlike most taxes, it generates no revenue for the government. It only destroys value and discourages investment,” he said. According to Oyedele, the proposed framework would organise Nigeria’s economic priorities around seven interconnected areas: stability, productivity, enterprise, capital, people, markets and institutions. He said the framework would also introduce an annual national economic scorecard, to be published on or before October 1, to track indicators such as real wages, productive employment, and poverty. “GDP growth matters, but per capita income matters even more,” he said, adding that economic progress should be measured by improvements in household incomes, employment, and business productivity rather than aggregate figures alone. Oyedele said the framework would be guided by three principles: enterprise as the engine of growth, open but fair markets, and coordination across government institutions. He said the government would support private enterprise by providing public goods, maintaining the rule of law, addressing market failures and protecting vulnerable groups. On trade policy, he said tariffs should support the development of local industries rather than shield inefficient businesses from competition indefinitely. “A tariff must serve as a runway for local industry to take off, never a permanent shelter from competition,” he said. Oyedele said the framework will be open for public consultation from November 27, 2026, with Nigerians invited to respond to 17 questions through the federal ministry of finance’s website. He said the draft would proceed to the federal executive council for approval and the national economic council for endorsement after the consultation and validation process. Also speaking, the Chairman of NESG, Niyi Yusuf noted that transformation cannot be delivered by any single institution, as it requires collaborative effort. “Government must sustain stability, and deepen reforms that lower production costs, strengthen infrastructure, secure lives and improve shared prosperity. State Governments must improve their investment climates and develop their productive advantages. “Governments should do more to privatise public assets that can benefit from private sector management, expertise, know-how and capital to unlock investments. Businesses must invest, innovate, develop skills and create decent jobs. “Development partners, civil society and the media must support evidence and accountability. Our priority is to strengthen the transmission from stability to investment, from investment to productivity, from productivity to jobs, and from jobs to rising incomes and shared prosperity,” he explained.

title: Dangote Refinery targets $60m saving with new AI technology
body: Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals is set to become the first industrial facility to deploy Honeywell Technologies’ newly launched artificial intelligence platform, with the technology projected to generate more than $60 million in annual gross operational benefits at full refining capacity. The platform, known as Forge Plant Cognition, combines Honeywell’s process engineering expertise with NVIDIA’s artificial intelligence capabilities and Dell Technologies’ computing infrastructure to improve refining efficiency, maximise output and strengthen operational reliability. Honeywell said the platform would make its global debut at the Lekki-based refinery, one of the world’s largest, as the company seeks to demonstrate how artificial intelligence can improve the performance of complex industrial facilities. Preliminary assessments indicate that the technology could deliver operational benefits exceeding 29 cents per barrel processed. At full-capacity throughput, this could translate into more than $60 million in annual gross benefits, although actual results will depend on operating conditions. Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals, David Bird, said the decision to adopt the technology reflected the company’s commitment to innovation, operational excellence and the development of Nigerian engineering talent. “We chose Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition because the platform can deliver unrivaled industrial expertise combined with differentiated AI capabilities to help us optimize performance, unlock greater value from our operations and evolve how we operate our assets,” Bird said. He added that the investment would support the refinery’s ambition to develop Nigerian professionals capable of operating complex industrial facilities to international standards. Unlike conventional monitoring systems that analyse operating data and generate recommendations, Forge Plant Cognition integrates real-time plant information with engineering knowledge, advanced calculations and physics-based models to identify constraints and support faster operational decisions. The technology is designed to help engineers detect potential equipment failures before they escalate, identify production bottlenecks and recommend corrective actions to improve throughput, product yields and overall performance. Honeywell said the platform would focus on improving refining margins, reducing unplanned downtime and making specialised engineering expertise more accessible to plant personnel. By embedding technical knowledge in artificial intelligence-powered tools, the system is expected to help Nigerian engineers and operators solve complex problems more efficiently while strengthening their industrial skills. The initiative aligns with Dangote Refinery’s objective of building a workforce comprising more than 70 per cent Nigerians, reducing dependence on external expertise while expanding local technical capacity. President of Honeywell Technologies UOP, Rajesh Gattupalli, described the collaboration as an example of how artificial intelligence could transform large-scale industrial operations. “Industrial plants are among the most complex operating environments in the world, with enormous potential to realise greater performance and value using digital technologies and connected solutions,” he said. Gattupalli said the deployment would demonstrate how AI could drive higher productivity, reliability and profitability across industrial facilities. The project marks another stage in the refinery’s development, shifting attention from construction and commissioning towards advanced digital systems designed to maximise productivity, strengthen competitiveness and support future expansion.

title: After 14 years, P1.49-billion Ifugao irrigation project finally opens
body: BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – A ₱1.49-billion irrigation project that took more than 14 years to complete was inaugurated by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Alfonso Lista, Ifugao, on Monday, October 26, promising a more reliable water supply to 1,315 farmers who have long depended on rainfall for their crops. The Alfonso Lista Pump Irrigation System (ALPIS), which draws water from the Magat Reservoir, is designed to irrigate 2,300 hectares of farmland across four barangays. According to National Irrigation Administration (NIA) records, construction began on May 22, 2012, and was completed on October 7, 2026. The project was originally scheduled for completion in 2017, but limited annual funding releases pushed construction years beyond that target, according to a NIA source familiar with its implementation. The source said the project also encountered damage from several typhoons, right-of-way problems, delays involving the transportation of explosives needed for tunnel construction, and a lengthy process of securing approval for its electrical connection. Construction-material prices increased during the extended implementation period. Pending clearance from the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) also prompted an agreement to suspend construction activities in 2019. The source, however, said the higher material costs and NCIP-related suspension had minimal or no effect on the overall delay. More water, bigger harvests Marcos said the completed facility would expand irrigation coverage from 275 hectares to 2,300 hectares and could increase palay production from 900 metric tons to 26,000 metric tons once fully utilized. He also projected farmers’ earnings to increase from ₱16 million to ₱159 million, although the period covered by these estimates and whether they represent gross or net income were not specified. “Alam po naman natin na ang pinakamahalaga sa pagsasaka ay ang patubig. Malaki ang pagbabago kapag ang non-irrigated areas ay magawan na ng paraan na mapatubigan,” Marcos said. (We all know that the most important element in farming is irrigation. There will be big changes if we find a way to irrigate non-irrigated areas.) The irrigation system will serve Sto. Domingo, Namnama, Namillangan, and Calupaan, farming communities in eastern Ifugao near the boundary with Isabela. Its facilities include five pumping units, an electrical substation, a water intake facility, a transbasin tunnel, nearly 32 kilometers of main and lateral canals, and more than 14 kilometers of access and service roads. NIA said the system is operational and will remain under the agency’s operation and maintenance. Rodolfo Manglallan, president of the Sto. Domingo Irrigators’ Association, said farmers previously relied on rainfall, leaving their rice fields vulnerable to prolonged dry spells. “Of course, magbabago yung ating sistema ng pagsasaka at nawawala yung pangamba namin na yung palayan namin ay matuyuan,” he told the Presidential News Desk. (Of course, our farming system will change and our fear that our rice farms will dry up is disappearing.) Preparing for El Niño The inauguration comes as the government prepares for potentially severe El Niño conditions that could bring prolonged dry spells and threaten agricultural production. NIA Administrator Eduardo Guillen said reliable irrigation would give farmers better opportunities to increase their harvests and improve their livelihoods. He urged beneficiaries to conserve water and help maintain the new facilities, particularly as the government prepares for possible water shortages. Guillen also noted that the inauguration came a day before the 44th anniversary of the inauguration of Magat Dam on October 27, 1982, during the administration of former President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. More than four decades later, the reservoir continues to support agriculture, with the Alfonso Lista project extending its irrigation benefits to additional farming communities. The severity and duration of the anticipated El Niño remain subject to continuing climate monitoring. Ifugao seeks more projects Ifugao Governor Jerry Dalipog welcomed the inauguration but also used the President’s visit to seek additional national government assistance. He requested improvements to farm-to-market roads to help farmers transport their produce and improve access to schools, healthcare facilities, and markets. Dalipog also sought support for completing the Ifugao Sports Complex and proposed a commemorative garden honoring Marcos Sr. in Lamut, Ifugao. No funding commitments for these proposals were specified in the governor’s prepared remarks. Marcos, meanwhile, unveiled the irrigation project’s marker, inspected its control rooms and pump house, and viewed agricultural produce displayed by farmer-beneficiaries. NIA records show that as of September 30, Ifugao had developed 19,997 hectares, or 77.42% of its estimated irrigable land, leaving another 5,833 hectares for irrigation development. The newly completed system is expected to help farmers cultivate previously rain-dependent fields more consistently and potentially increase their cropping cycles. After more than 14 years of construction, its projected benefits will now depend on reliable water delivery, regular maintenance, and the harvests of the 1,315 farmers it was built to serve. – Rappler.com Must Read El Niño ‘wrecking ball’ could cause record Pacific temperature rise, UN says

title: Trump surrogates discuss Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government with Israeli officials - report
body: Surrogates for US President Donald Trump spoke with Israeli officials about the possibility of a unity government that includes both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yishai party, The Washington Post reported on Monday.The report cited a Likud official who said, "Eisenkot has shown he lacks the backbone and the determination that Netanyahu has, and I think Trump understands that.""What Trump wants is a stable and reliable Israeli government that can be formed as soon as possible after the election," the official added.According to the report, officials within the Trump administration are divided on the issue of a unity government.Sources: Netanyahu believes Eisenkot would be best partner if Iran war resumesSources told The Washington Post that Netanyahu told US officials that he believes Eisenkot would be the best partner if hostilities resume between Israel and Iran.The report noted that Netanyahu told US and European officials that he would push for a more moderate coalition if he partnered with Eisenkot.Ben-Gvir claims Likud is working against himOtzma Yehudit chairman Itamar Ben-Gvir attacked Netanyahu and Likud on Monday, claiming the party is working to weaken Otzma Yehudit ahead of the elections.Ben-Gvir alleged that the Prime Minister's Office has pledged to European countries that the next government will be a unity government without Ben-Gvir. "Instead of bringing votes from Eisenkot, they are trying to lower me below the threshold," he said. He added that Netanyahu announced that he would not be reappointed Minister of National Security, and accused Likud of trying to form a unity government without him.

title: STL Capital, COPE expand free breast cancer screening
body: STL Capital Group and the Care Organisation Public Enlightenment (COPE) have renewed efforts to promote breast cancer awareness and early detection through an 8km awareness walk and free screening exercise. The initiative, which marks the fourth consecutive year of partnership between the organisations, featured public enlightenment, distribution of educational materials and advocacy to encourage Nigerians to seek timely medical attention. Speaking during the exercise, Group Managing Director of STL Capital Group, Funmi Ekundayo, said the organisation had expanded its support following its transition from STL Trustees into a capital market holding company comprising three businesses. She said the initiative was designed to reach more people through sustained awareness campaigns, stressing that breast cancer education should involve both men and women. “Breast cancer is not gender-sensitive. We have been distributing flyers to both male and female participants, making public announcements and intensifying advocacy to create awareness,” Ekundayo said. She urged members of the public to take advantage of available screening opportunities, noting that early detection could improve treatment outcomes. “We believe people should take advantage of these opportunities to get screened, as early detection saves lives. We are passionate about supporting COPE and are delighted to continue partnering with them to raise breast cancer awareness,” she said. Ekundayo reaffirmed the group’s commitment to supporting public health initiatives through corporate social responsibility, adding that STL Capital would continue working with COPE and other organisations with similar objectives. Also speaking, Executive Director of STL Capital Group, Akin Oni, called on corporate organisations to increase their contributions to public health campaigns, particularly those promoting early diagnosis and treatment. He observed that fear and inadequate awareness often discouraged people from seeking medical attention, emphasising the need for education to encourage individuals to understand their health status. Oni urged businesses to take corporate social responsibility seriously, noting that their contributions could support interventions beyond breast cancer, including polio prevention and other public health programmes. “My message to other corporate organisations is to take corporate social responsibility seriously. It may not necessarily be in the area of cancer; it could be polio or any other public health issue,” he said. He added that timely medical assessment was essential to improving treatment options and outcomes. The Managing Director of COPE thanked STL Capital Group for sustaining its partnership with the organisation, saying the support had helped maintain its free breast cancer screening programme. She explained that COPE conducts free breast ultrasound screening on the third Saturday of every month, with assistance from corporate organisations and other partners, including STL Capital Group. According to her, the programme provides women with an opportunity to access screening without financial barriers. She advised women to seek medical attention if they notice unusual breast changes, including lumps, changes in size or shape, nipple inversion, unusual discharge or skin puckering. She also cautioned against allowing fear of a possible diagnosis to prevent women from seeking screening, stressing that early medical assessment could improve treatment options. Through the annual awareness walk, public enlightenment and free screening programme, the partnership seeks to strengthen awareness, encourage early detection and improve access to breast health services.

title: Ukraine Confirms Honoring US-Brokered Truce in Russian-Occupied Oleshky
body:
Ukraine confirmed that a US-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky took effect early Tuesday, Oct. 27, to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations, although uncertainty remains over monitoring and whether residents can safely leave the devastated southern Ukrainian city.
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said the localized truce began at 3 a.m. Kyiv time (4 a.m. Moscow time), following negotiations mediated and coordinated by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments,” Lubinets wrote on X .
He said the arrangements were agreed with Yana Lantratova, who headed the Russian negotiating delegation.
Lubinets pledged to continue updating the public, emphasizing that the safety of civilians in Oleshky and compliance with the agreement remained Ukraine’s priorities.
Neither Kyiv, Moscow, nor Washington has publicly identified an independent monitoring mechanism or disclosed detailed arrangements for the humanitarian operation.
The truce is intended to facilitate aid deliveries and prepare for the evacuation of civilians from Oleshky, where an estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain under Russian occupation, many of them elderly.
While Ukraine has confirmed its compliance, officials have not yet reported that humanitarian convoys have entered the city or that evacuations have begun.
Questions also remain over the operation’s duration, safe passage for residents, and whether both sides will maintain the ceasefire in an area devastated by years of fighting, flooding, and severe shortages of food and medicine.
In a Telegram statement , Ukraine’s General Staff said the ceasefire would apply exclusively to designated areas involved in the humanitarian operation, including aid deliveries and preparations for civilian departures.
The military urged the public to rely on official information and refrain from circulating unverified details about evacuation routes, convoy movements, or the timing and location of humanitarian operations.
Ukrainian forces were taking all possible measures to assist residents and protect civilians, the General Staff said.
Ukraine’s military has previously used drones to deliver food and medicine to residents stranded in Oleshky and surrounding settlements.
The Russian military has said it would facilitate the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy, including engineering reconnaissance of the route, according to AFP.
However, Ukrainian officials have not yet announced when humanitarian supplies will reach residents or when the first evacuations will take place.
Lubinets said the arrangements followed direct negotiations with Russia’s representative, Yana Lantratova, coordinated through the US first lady’s humanitarian initiative.
The agreement covers several stages, including a localized cessation of hostilities, the de-mining of routes, humanitarian aid deliveries, and the voluntary departure of civilians.
“We have recorded all the agreements and signed an agreement,” Lubinets said in an earlier Telegram statement .
He warned that implementing the arrangements would be difficult and would require a gradual approach.
His latest confirmation that Ukraine is honoring the ceasefire marks a new stage in the operation, though the success of aid deliveries and evacuations has yet to be established.
Ukrainian authorities have emphasized that residents must be free to choose whether and where they evacuate.
It remains unclear how their preferred destinations will be verified or whether international humanitarian organizations will participate directly in the operation.
Announcing the agreement Friday, Oct. 23, Melania Trump said Ukrainian and Russian civilian officials would visit residents in their homes to assess their humanitarian needs.
Those wishing to leave would receive transportation and support to reach their preferred destinations, she said.
“I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said in a White House statement .
The White House originally announced Thursday, Oct. 29 as the start date, but Ukrainian and Russian authorities subsequently agreed on Tuesday, Oct. 27.
Melania Trump also said an American media organization would accompany the humanitarian mission to document conditions and the treatment of civilians.
US television network Newsmax said it had secured exclusive access to accompany observers entering Oleshky on Thursday.
However, neither side has publicly explained who would independently monitor compliance with the ceasefire or oversee the evacuation process.
Oleshky, situated across the Dnipro River from Ukrainian-held Kherson, has been under Russian occupation since the opening stages of Moscow’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
The city’s prewar population of approximately 24,000 has fallen to an estimated 1,700 to 2,000, including around 50 children, according to Ukrainian and US estimates.
Conditions deteriorated further following the destruction of the Kakhovka dam in June 2023, which caused widespread flooding along the lower Dnipro River and severely damaged local infrastructure.
Former residents told AFP that people still living in Oleshky were surviving on garden produce or hunting pigeons as food supplies dwindled.
“They’ve forgotten what bread is. You need flour for bread, and there’s not even flour left,” Olga, who remained in contact with two families in the city, told AFP.
Residents have also faced severe shortages of medicine, drinking water and reliable electricity.
Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly reported that Russian occupation forces prevented civilians from leaving Oleshky, restricting evacuation routes and leaving residents stranded amid worsening humanitarian conditions.
Russian representative Lantratova claimed on Monday that most residents wishing to leave had already done so voluntarily.
However, Ukrainian officials and volunteers have warned that remaining residents face significant obstacles to evacuation through Russian-controlled territory.
Despite confirmation that the ceasefire has taken effect, the humanitarian mission faces considerable challenges because Oleshky remains under Russian military control and lies close to the active front line.
Years of fighting have left roads and surrounding areas damaged or potentially mined, complicating the safe movement of humanitarian convoys and civilians.
Ukrainian Pravda reported on Monday that the initial stages of the operation were expected to include de-mining routes and delivering essential supplies before evacuations could begin.
Lubinets said Ukrainian officials intended to monitor implementation of the agreement and verify conditions inside the city.
However, neither Ukraine nor Russia has announced how long the ceasefire will last or provided a public timetable for completing the humanitarian mission.
The localized truce comes as broader US-mediated negotiations between Ukraine and Russia are expected to resume in November after months without substantive progress.
For residents still stranded in Oleshky, the ceasefire offers a potential opportunity to receive desperately needed supplies and leave the occupied city, but its humanitarian impact remains uncertain.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Sask. First Nations leaders raise land rights, policing concerns at historic Ottawa meeting
body:
First Nations leaders from Saskatchewan who attended a long-awaited first ministers meeting say they raised several concerns affecting their people.
Speaking to reporters afterward, Lac La Ronge Indian Band Chief Tammy Cook-Searson said she was given three minutes to speak. She used them to advocate for a proposed change to the Indian Act that would allow any person with at least one status parent to inherit federal Indian status.
“We have children, grandchildren, members of our communities that are not part of our nation because of this discriminatory policy of the federal government,” Cook-Searson told reporters Monday.
Cook-Searson, acting as Saskatchewan’s regional representative, said she did not hear any commitments from the federal government on the issue but will “continue to push forward.” The bill, known as S-2, has passed the Senate and awaits action from the House of Commons Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs.
She also asked Ottawa to consider adding survivors of the Timber Bay Children’s Home, near Lac La Ronge, Sask., to the residential school settlement agreement.
She says she has pushed for this since she first became chief more than two decades ago. At one point, Ottawa was at the table, but the province was not.
Now, Cook-Searson says Premier Scott Moe has “given us his word” that Saskatchewan will return to the negotiations.
“Now we need the feds to come back to the table, so if we can get the two together, the province and the feds. Then we will be able to settle this injustice with the Timber Bay Children’s Home survivors and their families.”
Premier Scott Moe was among the premiers at the meeting but did not make himself available for media comment Monday.
Cook-Searson was joined by several other chiefs represented by the Prince Albert Grand Council, who each raised their top concerns in hopes Ottawa would take note.
For Chief Kirby Constant of James Smith Cree Nation, policing remains top of mind four years after a mass stabbing attack that killed 11 people and wounded 17 others on the First Nation. He wants to see support for First Nations policing to improve public safety in the region.
“Without First Nation Policing, we’re feeling that the RCMP is not fulfilling their requirements to keep our community safe,” Constant told reporters, adding that the service would allow people with similar cultural backgrounds and traditional knowledge to serve their communities.
As the meeting was underway, members of the Onion Lake Cree Nation, located approximately 50 kilometres north of Lloydminster, Sask., took to the streets of Ottawa to protest the event.
“No organization or government has the authority to speak for Onion Lake Cree Nation, negotiate our rights, or make commitments on our behalf without our consent,” Onion Lake Cree Nation Chief Pete Chief told Global News in an interview Monday.
Onion Lake formally withdrew from the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) three years ago, after an internal referendum ended its membership.
Chief said his First Nation has no problem with Prime Minister Mark Carney’s development agenda but wants meaningful consultation that goes beyond a closed-door meeting where not everyone is present.
“Come to our lands, come and develop that relationship with us and so that we also can be a part of the development, a part of whatever the project may be,” he said.
Carry the Kettle First Nation also opposed the meeting. In a letter posted on social media, the nation said it has not consented to being represented by the Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations (FSIN) or the AFN.
“In the absence of our consent and any rights at law, we request that FSIN and AFN expressly exclude our Nation from any representation today at the Prime Minister and First Ministers,” wrote Carry the Kettle Chief Dwayne (Cliff) Thomson.
Before the meeting, the AFN said regional representatives would attend. FSIN Chief Bobby Cameron is Saskatchewan’s regional representative, but it is unclear whether he was there, since Cook-Searson presented herself as his proxy.
Global News has asked the FSIN to confirm Cameron’s attendance and has not yet heard back.
Earlier this month, the FSIN announced it would take the federal government to court after Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) served it a final repayment notice for $12.4 million, following a forensic audit in the fall of 2025. ISC later said it would file a statement of claim to recover the money.
The last time Indigenous leaders met with the premiers and the prime minister of Canada was during the Kelowna Accord talks in 2005, which were centred on socioeconomic gaps in Indigenous communities and were led by then-prime minister Paul Martin.
Carney said Monday it’s “sobering” to consider that this is the first meeting to bring together federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in two decades.
“Our task is twofold. First is to work together to create opportunities for all our peoples, while building a country that is stronger, more sovereign and more independent,” he said.
The meeting may not be the last. Cook-Searson said representatives received “a commitment” from some premiers to meet annually.
Representatives of Saskatchewan’s Métis people were also absent, but the president of Métis Nation-Saskatchewan says talks with the federal government are ongoing.
“We just did our lobbying not very long ago last week and it went very well with the speaker and the speaker’s lounge and got to meet all parties and begin this conversation in regards to the importance of having the Metis be involved,” he said.

title: Mahama must demand Sammy Gyamfi’s retraction on galamsey – Prof. Appiagyei-Atua
body: President John Dramani Mahama has been urged to publicly clarify his administration’s position on illegal mining and ask the Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), Sammy Gyamfi, to retract his controversial remarks on the practice. A lecturer in International Law and Human Rights at the University of Ghana School of Law, Professor Kwadwo Appiagyei-Atua, said the President needed to intervene to prevent the comments from being interpreted as reflecting the government’s official position on the fight against illegal small-scale mining, popularly known as galamsey. He argued that failure to publicly disavow the remarks could create the impression that the government accepted or supported them. Speaking to Bernard Avle on Channel One TV on Monday, Prof. Appiagyei-Atua said the President was best placed to address the controversy because Mr Gyamfi was a senior government appointee whose comments could be associated with the administration. “The responsibility lies with the President to be able to make sure that what Mr Gyamfi said, he said it in the name of the government. So who else is better placed to respond to this question? Because if you don’t condemn, then you are deemed to be condoning. And I think the President is the one who, as we say, hires and fires,” he said. Calls for retraction Prof. Appiagyei-Atua said the President should ensure the GoldBod CEO publicly clarifies his comments and, if necessary, apologises to remove any ambiguity about the government’s stance on illegal mining. He said such a clarification would help prevent illegal miners from interpreting the remarks as a signal that the government was softening its position on galamsey. “He should probably ask the GoldBod CEO to come out clearly and state that, ‘Here, you got it wrong. So please, let us not create the impression that we are supporting illegal mining.’ So just come out, retract the statement and then, even if you have to apologise, make the message very clear to the illegal miners that you are not endorsing this practice,” he said. The professor maintained that the issue went beyond an individual public official’s comments, touching on the government’s responsibility to communicate a consistent position on illegal mining. Galamsey remains a major environmental and public policy concern in Ghana, with illegal mining contributing to forest degradation, water pollution, and damage to agricultural land. Efforts to tackle the practice have involved law enforcement, regulation of mining activities and calls for stronger accountability. ‘The law has not changed’ Prof. Appiagyei-Atua also stressed that the GoldBod CEO’s comments could not alter the legal framework governing mining in the country. He said any change to existing laws would have to follow the proper constitutional and legislative processes, rather than be inferred from public statements by government officials. “The law has not changed. The CEO cannot change the law,” he stated. His comments underscored the distinction between public statements by government appointees and the laws that regulate mining activities. The professor said the President should make the administration’s position explicit to avoid confusion over whether the government remained committed to combating illegal mining. “The President should come out clearly to let us know the position of the government on the galamsey fight and not to endorse the statement made by Mr Gyamfi,” he said. Government’s position under scrutiny Prof. Appiagyei-Atua further argued that the remarks needed to be condemned because, in his assessment, they amounted to an endorsement of illegal mining. His intervention adds to scrutiny of public comments by government officials on galamsey, an issue that has generated sustained public concern because of its environmental, economic and social consequences. The controversy also raises questions about public officeholders’ responsibility to ensure their statements align with government policy and the legal obligations governing their institutions. While the professor called on President Mahama to intervene, the substance of the controversy and the government’s position would need to be assessed against the full context of Mr Gyamfi’s original remarks and any subsequent clarification from GoldBod or the Presidency.

title: Alvin Tedjo wins Mississauga mayoral race, defeats Parrish and Crombie
body:
One-term Mississauga city councillor Alvin Tedjo will become mayor after a race against the incumbent and her predecessor.
Unofficial results posted by the city show Tedjo leading the race with 74,479 votes as of 11:30 p.m. Monday. With about all polls reporting, incumbent Carolyn Parrish received 51,853 votes, while former Mississauga mayor and Ontario Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie garnered 43,191 votes.
“Mississauga has voted for change,” Tedjo said in his victory speech. “Today, the City of Mississauga has made a clear and historic choice to demand a change at city hall.”
Tedjo’s victory comes after weeks of campaigning that saw the rookie councillor pick up steam as it went on.
Parrish told supporters it wasn’t the result they wanted, “but sometimes the world changes.”
“I am very confident that my two-and-a-half years or however long it was, I did a really good job,” she said. “This wasn’t a normal election. We haven’t had a normal two-and-a-half years. These are tough times that we’re living in.”
She went on to say her campaign team should have “simplified our message,” adding she had anticipated this result for the past day or two and was “at peace.”
“(Tedjo)’s going to have a tough job ahead of him and he can pick up the phone anytime and I’ll tell him what not to do,” she said.
Speaking to supporters Monday, Crombie said she had called Tedjo to congratulate him on his victory.
“Alvin, your energy, your enthusiasm and the joy you bring to politics matter,” Crombie said in her concession speech. “You’ve inspired people to get involved and to believe that they can help shape the city’s future. That is something to be proud of.”
She added that a “new generation” was taking the reins and would cheer for the city to succeed under Tedjo’s leadership.
Only a few days before election day, Tedjo was shown by a Liaison Strategies poll on Oct. 22 with 31 per cent support, just behind Crombie.
Tedjo has sought the mayor’s position before, having run for it during the 2024 byelection. He came in second with 25 per cent, behind Parrish’s 31 per cent.
Crombie and Parrish sparred at a debate earlier this month with the incumbent saying staff was “terrified that the blonde bombshell is coming back.” Crombie appeared to criticize how Parrish governed, saying “sometimes you have to leave your office, go meet people” and convince investors to come to Mississauga.
During his time on council, Tedjo served on multiple committees and on the Region of Peel Council.
The mayor-elect said it was a “tremendous responsibility” and said he would begin the work of “making our plan a reality.”
He thanked Crombie and Parrish and all candidates for running, speaking of the years of service the two former mayors put into the city.
Tedjo also thanked his family, team and volunteers for the work they put into the campaign.
“I look forward to starting the hard work of putting our plan into action, to build that better future for every single resident in Mississauga,” Tedjo concluded.

title: Winnipegger raises money for CancerCare Manitoba with giant jack-o’-lanterns
body:
Chris Okell carves out over 1,000-pound pumpkins displayed in his driveway in honour of his mom who loved Halloween.
Chris’ mom, Marietta Okell, passed away in 2010 from pancreatic cancer, and asked Chris to promise her that he will keep carving pumpkins for the kids. It’s a promise he’s upheld every year while trying to raise money in hopes to find a cure for cancer.
“I’m going to keep going for as long as I can and continue to raise money for anybody who needs this, because I lost three people this year alone,” said Okell. “Is there a cure? I hope so, and if there is, let it free. Let people stop suffering.”
People can donate online through CancerCare Manitoba or in person at 39 Baisinger Dr.
Watch the video above for the full story.

title: More than 40 sets of World War II remains exhumed in Mlyniv, Rivne region
body:
Oleksii Zlatohorskyi, director of the specialized institution “Volyn Antiquities” and an archaeologist, told Ukrinform about this.
“During search operations in July of this year, 15 coffins containing remains were discovered on the grounds of the Memorial of Glory in the center of the village. The Soviet monument itself bears the names of 347 people who are supposedly reburied there. These are not local residents, but Soviet soldiers who died during World War II, who were originally buried on the outskirts of the village and later reburied in the center of Mlyniv. However, this figure has not been confirmed. “Preliminarily, during the exhumation, we discovered 47–48 sets of remains. The final figure will be known after a more detailed examination,” the archaeologist said.
Zlatohorskyi is a member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. While on leave, together with his fellow archaeologists Artur Alyoshin, Nazariy Romanyuk, and Dmytro Demianchuk, he conducted the exhumation of this burial site at the request of the Mlyniv community leadership.
As the search team discovered, based on the accompanying documentation, it can be concluded that most of the remains belong to military personnel. In particular, the remains of six women were found among them. The remains of two children were also discovered.
"I suspect that, perhaps, while excavating World War II-era graves near the local cemetery, they unearthed remains from a civilian burial site. That is why children were found buried at the memorial. As for the women, according to the accompanying materials found, they were military personnel,” Zlatohorskyi said.
Along with the remains, archaeologists found spoons engraved with their owners’ initials. They say this usually indicated military status. They also found pieces of leather belts, boots, fragments of eyeglasses, and a razor. Materials that may be important for identification will be transferred to the Rivne Regional Museum of Local History after processing and cleaning. Samples were also collected during the examination of the remains for DNA analysis.
According to Zlatohorskyi, working during the exhumation in Mlyniv was difficult because, during the reburial, the remains of 10–15 people had simply been dumped into a coffin, covered with clay, and placed in brick-lined crypts.
“For the Soviet authorities, the ideological significance of this memorial was more important than respect for the people they supposedly wanted to honor,” the archaeologist added.
The remains exhumed in Mlyniv were reburied at the local cemetery.
Previously, the memorial in Mlyniv was included in the list of 100 monuments to be dismantled as part of the decommunization process by the “Decolonization. Ukraine” project.
Suspilne. Rivne reported that, in order to dismantle the sculpture of a Soviet soldier and renovate the complex, the village council appealed to the Ministry of Culture to have the memorial’s status as a historical monument revoked. Subsequently, in coordination with the Ministry of Culture, search operations were conducted to locate the remains of World War II victims for their subsequent reburial. After obtaining all necessary permits and completing the exhumation and reburial of the Soviet soldiers, the plan is to transfer portraits of soldiers from the Mlyniv community who died in the Russian-Ukrainian war to the memorial grounds.
As reported by Ukrinform, a Ukrainian expedition completed search operations in Laskowo , Poland, where the remains of more than 40 people were discovered.

title: Ukraine reportedly strikes Russian ammunition depot in occupied Luhansk Oblast
body:
Ukrainian forces attacked an ammunition depot in occupied Luhansk Oblast, setting off explosions at the site overnight on Oct. 27, monitoring channels reported.
Ukraine used strike drones in an attack that took several hours near the city of Khrustalnyi, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova Plus.
Khrustalnyi has been occupied by Russian forces and their proxies since 2014 and is located about 65 kilometers (40 miles) southwest of the city of Luhansk .
Ukrainian forces regularly strike military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Ukraine struck several targets, including a petrochemical plant and a warehouse in Siberia around 2,500 kilometers away from the border on Oct. 24, monitoring channels reported.
A fire first broke out at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Omsk, according to Exilenova Plus.
Later, a warehouse belonging to major Russian online retailer Ozon was also hit in the Ukrainian drone attack, the channel reported.
On Oct. 26, a chemical plant producing dual-use goods in the southwestern Russian city of Voronezh was likely hit in a Ukrainian drone attack, independent Russian media outlet Astra reported.
A drone reportedly also struck a business center in Voronezh , as explosions and fires were reported across the city amid an ongoing drone attack, the outlet wrote.

title: Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again
body:
Former FBI Director James Comey speaks during a Senate Intelligence Committee hearing on Capitol Hill, Thursday, June 8, 2017, in Washington. Alex Brandon/AP hide caption
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director's lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment.
The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents an unmistakable escalation in the administration's targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year. The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week's midterm elections.
"Well, they're back — again," Comey said in a video statement Monday. "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me; I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary."
The Justice Department said it had filed what's known as a "criminal information" to extend the statute of limitations for when they can permissibly bring an indictment.
"Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," a department spokesperson said.
An information can be filed without the approval of a judge or a grand jury's finding of probable cause to a court. Comey's lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid and barred by a 10-year statute of limitations.
"For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence," his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement.
The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.
Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI's conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey's attorneys said in a recent court filing.
In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney's office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name "Tropical Vortex." But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an "Information" against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit," Fitzgerald said.
Prosecutors in a newly unsealed filing said investigators found evidence that Comey "sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before" that New York Times story was published, directed his staff to speak to a journalist at the newspaper related to accuracy concerns "and thereby illegally transferred classified information."
The criminal information was filed under seal on Oct. 6, 2016, 10 years after the story was published. "But," Comey's lawyers said, "the applicable statute of limitations explicitly demands an indictment within 10 years of the offense; an information does not suffice."
They have asked a judge to dismiss the information, a request that is still pending.
The first criminal case against Comey, filed in federal court in Virginia, accused him of having lied to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47," a case he has sought to dismiss and some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.
The cases are part of a Trump retribution campaign that has even extended to Comey's daughter, Maurene, who was fired from her job as a Justice Department prosecutor in New York last year in a termination that a federal judge on Monday ruled was illegal.
Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush's Republican administration.
But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.
Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump's campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.
The two men have been bitterly at odds ever since Comey's firing. Comey in 2018 published a memoir, "A Higher Loyalty," that painted Trump in deeply unflattering ways, likening him to a mafia don and characterizing him "untethered to truth." Trump, for his part, has repeatedly claimed that Comey should face charges for "treason" — an accusation Comey dismissed as "dumb lies" — and called him an "untruthful slime ball."

title: Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident
body:
Stories about how and why companies use Go
How Go can help keep you secure by default
A complete introduction to building software with Go
Reference documentation for Go's standard library
Tips for writing clear, performant, and idiomatic Go code
Learn and network with Go developers from around the world
Roland Shoemaker, on behalf of the Go Security team 26 October 2026
On October 19, the Go team initiated an expedited security release to protect Go users and their applications from a critical public key infrastructure (PKI) compromise involving certificates issued by eMudhra.
Within approximately seven and a half hours of being notified, we shipped a targeted patch, which was included in our first-ever URGENT track security release.
Here is the context behind the incident, why Go stepped in at the runtime level to protect our users and how our incident response unfolded.
On October 17, Mozilla added eight intermediate certificates (six used for TLS, and two used for code signing) issued by a root certificate controlled by eMudhra to OneCRL, effectively blocking their usage in Firefox. Soon after, a number of security researchers noticed this and began investigating what might’ve caused this.
On October 19, the Go Security team was made aware of these investigations and their conclusions, which showed that the keys associated with these intermediates were trivially weak, allowing recovery of the private keys in microseconds.
Due to the fact that the eMudhra root certificate was present in most trusted root programs, recovering the private keys would allow any attacker to sign arbitrary TLS certificates for any domain name, without the usual requirement to show proof of control of said domain name. This would allow an attacker to man-in-the-middle (MITM) TLS connections and present a valid certificate for a domain name they did not control, effectively allowing them to impersonate any TLS server the targeted machine attempted to connect to.
Go ships a TLS certificate verifier in the standard library. When users use net/http or crypto/tls to connect to a TLS service, the verifier is called to check if the certificates the other side of the connection presents are valid. On Windows and macOS we delegate these checks to the platform APIs, and on Linux, which lacks platform APIs, we use our own verifier implementation.
Since Linux does not have a uniform built-in mechanism to handle revocation checking, and in order to provide a timely fix for users on other platforms that might not receive platform updates, we decided the best way to protect Go users was to do an URGENT track security release which similarly removed trust.
A typical Go security release follows a multi-day process, with advanced pre-announcements in order to allow those who rely on Go to prepare. In this case, because we believed that private key exposure was imminent, our team chose to use the URGENT track for the first time in order to ship protections before active public exploitation could begin.
Our Security team was alerted by an independent external researcher, citing unreported actions by Mozilla and other organizations to remove trust in eight eMudhra intermediates. It became clear quickly that this was due to weak private keys they used.
Mozilla independently reported the issue to our Security team, confirming the issue, and asking that we not immediately disclose the issue, but encouraging us to release a fix as soon as possible.
We finalized a patch which blocked the usage of certificates which chained to the compromised intermediates, and thanks to the researcher who initially alerted us to the issue, had a set of certificates signed using the recovered keys to test against.
We began the process to release minor Go versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 containing our patch. Due to the urgent nature of this issue and its exploitability, and with the belief that the private keys would likely become publicly known within hours, we decided an immediate release was the most prudent option.
We finalized the release and announced it publicly. At this time the underlying issue was still not widely known. In an effort to give other defenders a chance to protect as many users as possible without revealing to attackers how the issue could be exploited, our patch and communications were somewhat opaque, warning users that we were “blocking trust in a small set of intermediate certificates due to specific security concerns around their operation” and urging users to immediately upgrade to this release.
In under seven and a half hours from initial notification, patched Go releases were live worldwide, giving users everything they needed to secure their deployments before the keys became public.
By the morning of October 20, numerous independent researchers had publicly disclosed the weak keys.
This was our first ever URGENT track security release, and during the release process we ran into a number of issues which caused the release to take longer than expected.
While we are happy we were able to get a release out the same day we were notified of the issue, in the modern security environment we feel that we should be able to provide releases in a more compressed timeline. The issues we ran into caused our release process to take just under four and a quarter hours from start to finish.
These issues had previously not been problematic, since the typical release process is split up over a number of days.
We’ve subsequently made a number of changes to improve our release efficiency, which should significantly reduce the time it takes us to push out a release, enhancing our ability to quickly respond to urgent security threats.
PRIVATE track security fixes are pre-announced three to seven days before their release. URGENT track fixes happen on a shorter time schedule, but we could have pre-announced the upcoming release when we began the release process, giving users at least a few hours to prepare.
While on Windows and macOS we rely on the revocation mechanisms the platform APIs provide, on Linux we don’t currently have a similar mechanism. The lack of this support was one of our major drivers to issue an expedited security release, as we did not want to leave Linux users exposed to this issue longer than was necessary.
Hence we are planning on prioritizing work to bring parity to revocation support on Linux, to help mitigate this class of issues in the future. Part of this work will involve investigating adding support for the upki project, which aims to “provide reliable, privacy-preserving and efficient certificate revocation” for Linux (see issue #82402 ).
If you run Go binaries which interact with network services using TLS (such as directly via net/http or crypto/tls or via a dependency such as gRPC), ensure you are running on the latest minor releases. Binaries rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 will automatically reject certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates.
You can verify your current toolchain version using go version and you can check the version of Go a binary was built with using go version -m <path_to_your_binary> .
The govulncheck tool can also be used to determine if a binary is affected by this issue:
For us, securing Go and its users extends beyond fixing direct security vulnerabilities in the runtime and libraries we ship. In order to keep the ecosystem secure, we believe we also need to provide users with the right tools to write secure software, look towards the future of cryptographic algorithms and protocols, and proactively respond to ecosystem wide issues when we can.
We are grateful to the independent security researchers and the Mozilla security team for this rapid notification and coordination during this incident.
