title: THE OGUN STATE ABORTION LAW
body: JOSHUA NWACHUKWU contends that the safe termination of pregnancy law raises constitutional questions On the 24 of September 2026, the Ogun State House of Assembly passed the Ogun State Safe Termination of Pregnancy Bill, 2026 and forwarded it to the Governor for assent. A critical look at Part III of the Bill, particularly Section 9 of the Law, makes one conclude that the law simply seeks to legalise abortion in Ogun State. Section 9 establishes several grounds upon which abortion can be sought, depending on the stage of gestation and the circumstances of the pregnancy. In summary, the Law provides as follows: First, within the first 12 weeks of gestation, a woman may obtain an abortion after counselling, without need to establish any specific medical or other justification. Second, between 12 and 24 weeks of gestation, abortion may be gotten where the pregnancy poses a risk to the woman’s physical or mental health, where there is a risk of foetal abnormality, and, within 18 weeks from conception, if the pregnancy is as a result of rape, incest or other criminal sexual offences. Third, beyond these periods and at any stage of gestation, the Law permits abortion including where the pregnancy endangers the woman’s life, where the foetus has a condition incompatible with life, or where the pregnancy poses significant mental health risk or poses a risk of mother-to-child transmission of any life-threatening condition. Taken together, these provisions create a framework under which abortion may be permitted for a broad range of reasons, beyond saving a woman’s life. At this point, it is important to note that the law allows women from age 10 to have an abortion. Although girls under 18 are required, under section 12(2) to have parental, guardian or in loco parentis consent, while adults obviously can consent for themselves. With regard to married adults, one is forced to question, what is the interest, right or duty of a husband if the wife wants to abort a child and he doesn’t consent, or he wants an abortion and she refuses? These questions are important, but the more fundamental constitutional difficulty lies elsewhere: the conflict between this and the existing criminal law governing abortion in Southern Nigeria. Ogun State is in Southern Nigeria, where the Criminal Code framework applies. The relevant provisions of the Criminal Code, particularly Sections 228–230, criminalise various acts associated with procuring a miscarriage. Section 228 criminalises the unlawful procurement of a miscarriage, including conduct undertaken by a woman herself. Section 229 addresses the supply or procurement of substances or instruments for the purpose of unlawfully procuring a miscarriage, while Section 230 deals with certain acts performed by medical practitioners and other persons. The statutory framework therefore criminalises not only the procurement of a miscarriage but also various forms of assistance in procuring one. The precise liability and applicable penalty depend on the provision and circumstances involved. The law provides an exception under Section 297 of the Criminal Code, which protects certain surgical operations performed in good faith and with reasonable care and skill for the benefit of a person, subject to the statutory requirements. This exception does not amount to a general authorisation of abortion on demand as envisaged by the Ogun State Law. Furthermore, Section 309 provides that, “when a child dies in consequence of an act done or omitted to be done by any person before or during its birth, the person who did or omitted to do such acts is deemed to have killed the child.” Section 328 provides that “any person who, when a woman is about to be delivered of a child, prevents the child from being born alive by any act or omission of such a nature that, if the child had been born alive and had then died, she would be deemed to have unlawfully killed the child, is guilty of a felony, and is liable to imprisonment for life. These sections of the Criminal Code Act are exactly the same in the Criminal Code Law of Ogun State. That means in Ogun State, abortion is currently illegal and section 20 of the Ogun State Safe Termination of Pregnancy Bill, which seeks to invalidate any law that contravenes the bill is also not a cure, based on the Supreme Court Judgment in Udeogu v FRN. In Udeogu and FRN, the Supreme Court frowns at legislations, using phrases like “any other law”, or “any other law to the contrary”, when the law which the new bill seeks to override is not even defined. With regard to the status of abortion in Nigeria, several judicial and professional disciplinary proceedings have definitely stated what it is. In the article “Is Abortion Criminalized in Nigeria? A Critical Examination of the Nigerian Legal Framework,” Abdulqayum Kehinde Yunu discussed authorities that addressed the criminal consequences of unlawful abortion and the interpretation of the relevant criminal code provisions. In Medical and Dental Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal v. Dr. F.A., the tribunal removed a doctor from practice for performing abortions outside life-saving exceptions, defining abortion as “unlawful termination of pregnancy via medical or surgical means,” culpable under S.228 regardless of consent. In State v. Ifeanyichukwu, the court held that herbal concoctions resulting in fetal death constituted miscarriage under S.228, sentencing the defendant to 10 years’ imprisonment, thereby including traditional methods alongside clinical procedures such as D&C. The Supreme Court in A.G. Lagos v. Egun, clarified that abortion means “any deliberate interference with normal pregnancy processes to end fetal life,” unlawful without S.297 good faith, rejecting therapeutic expansions absent statutory amendment This is the law in Nigeria and a state cannot, declare a procedure lawful where a federal law has made that procedure illegal and when such happens, Section 4 (5) of the Constitution will apply Section 4(5) provides that, “If any Law enacted by the House of Assembly of a State is inconsistent with any law validly made by the National Assembly, the law made by the National Assembly shall prevail, and that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.” The provision establishes a clear constitutional rule: where a valid federal law and a state law conflict, the federal law prevails to the extent of the inconsistency. This is normally referred to as the Doctrine of Covering the Field. In Attorney-General of Ogun State v. Attorney-General of the Federation, the Supreme Court clarified that where both the National Assembly and a State Assembly make laws on the same matter (especially under the Concurrent List), and the federal law is valid and comprehensive, the state law becomes void if it conflicts. Fatayi-Williams, JSC stated; “If both federal and state laws exist on the same issue, the state law must give way if the federal law has fully covered the area.” and Kayode Eso, JSC, provided a concise definition as follows: “Covering the field” simply means once the federal law legislates fully on a matter, any conflicting state law is of no effect.” Based on the above it is not in doubt that the Ogun State Safe Termination of Pregnancy Law, 2026, raises a serious constitutional question. The issue is not simply whether abortion should be legalised as a matter of public policy. It is whether the Ogun State House of Assembly possesses the constitutional authority to create exceptions to the applicable criminal law in the manner contemplated by the Law. In my humble opinion, they don’t. One is forced to wonder if the Ogun State House of Assembly sought the view of the Attorney General of the State, Oluwasina Ogungbade SAN. If they did, surely the learned silk would have highlighted the unconstitutionality and futility of their action. Nwachukwu writes from Lagos

title: THE RIGHTS OF AWAITING TRIAL INMATES
body: Extended pre-trial detention is a violation of human rights Recent figures from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) and other stakeholders of awaiting trial inmates in the country underscore the need to review the correctional system. The facilities that are supposedly meant to reform convicted offenders are populated largely by people who have not been found guilty of any offence. Between 64 and 68 per cent of the inmates are reportedly awaiting trial. “These figures represent people – mothers (including nursing mothers), fathers, daughters, sons, members of the community – many of which have committed minor offences,” according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) in a recent report. In a judgment delivered in May this year, the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Court of Justice ruled that prolonged detention of awaiting-trial inmates and overcrowding in the facilities of the Nigeria Correctional Service (NCS) violates the liberty, dignity, fair hearing, presumption of innocence and trial within a reasonable time for the inmates. The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has similarly continued to identify extended pre-trial detention, arbitrary arrest, torture, denial of access to lawyers and poor detention conditions as persistent human rights concerns. What the huge gulf between the number of convicted persons and those awaiting trial clearly reveals is that the machinery of justice dispensation is faulty. Indeed, there are stories that in many of the stinking, tiny prisons across the country, some inmates have spent between 10 and 20 years in detention without trial. Prisoners and detainees, majority of whom had never been tried in court, have also reportedly been subjected to extrajudicial execution, torture, food and water shortages, and infrastructure deficiencies. Given the current situation, it is not unlikely that many of those unfortunate Nigerians may have spent longer than the period for which they would have been jailed if their cases had been promptly disposed of. But the main concern is that there is no sign that anything would change or that efforts are being made to address this problem that has festered for decades. While we do not advocate for a wholesale release of these detainees, it is unconscionable to keep people perpetually detained without being convicted of any crime. There is therefore an urgent need for some intervention measures which should include access to justice programme for the inmates, better endowment for prisoner education, vocational training and rehabilitation programmes. Authorities in the justice sector should also conduct prison inspections on a regular basis while there must always be a swift response to complaints. Above all, the federal government must work with the states on how to decongest the correctional centres, especially by releasing those who ordinarily should not be there. It is noteworthy that many of the so-called correctional facilities were built during the colonial era, hence the decayed infrastructure are unable to cater for the increasing population of inmates. It is therefore no surprise that whereas the prison systems in most countries are meant to reform the inmates, our custodial centres actually harden them. Efforts at decongesting them or ameliorating the plight of awaiting trial inmates would come to naught without adequate judicial reform aimed at a complete overhauling of the country’s criminal justice system. That is the only way we can ensure that our prisons are not populated by innocent people while the real criminals roam the streets. We reiterate our earlier call for the Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN), Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, to institute the necessary reforms that will address the problem.

title: EPIDEMIC OF COUNTERFEIT BEVERAGES
body: COSMAS ODOEMENA argues for life imprisonment for counterfeiters It is tempting to demand the ultimate punishment for those who manufacture counterfeit alcohol in Nigeria. The scale of the crime warrants our deepest fury. Recent regulatory crackdowns have exposed a terrifying reality: in open markets from Aba to Lagos, unscrupulous syndicates are bottling slow-acting poison camouflaged as premium spirits, killing innocent citizens and shattering families. In response, prominent voices within NAFDAC and the presidency have called for a drastic escalation in legal retribution, advocating the death penalty for fake product dealers. While the moral outrage driving this demand is entirely justified, channelling it into state-sanctioned executions is a dangerous, short-sighted misdirection. Capital punishment will not deter these syndicates. Only systematic, uncorruptible institutional reform can dismantle them. To understand why this crisis evokes such anger, we must look at the horrific physical and emotional devastation these counterfeiters inflict. This is not a victimless economic crime or a simple trademark dispute; it is premeditated mass poisoning. When a criminal syndicate introduces industrial chemicals like methanol into bootleg gin or whisky to cut costs, they pour a lethal toxin directly into human bodies. Every sip launches a silent assault on internal anatomy, destroying the liver and burning through the kidneys. The physical results are catastrophic: sudden, permanent blindness, acute organ failure, and agonizingly painful deaths. The damage, however, extends far beyond physical health. The psychological trauma rippling through our communities is immense. Families are subjected to the sudden, shocking grief of losing healthy loved ones to a casual, everyday drink. Survivors who escape with their lives but lose their sight face a devastating psychological battle against severe depression and anxiety as they adjust to a dark, dependent reality. On a larger scale, this epidemic breeds a pervasive paranoia. It destroys our collective peace of mind and erodes the basic everyday trust required to live and do business together. Why does this trade thrive so flagrantly across our commercial hubs? The answers lie at the intersection of economic desperation, regulatory blind spots, and civic silence. Counterfeiters exploit the current inflationary climate, offering deep discounts to retailers or bleeding fake batches into legitimate inventories to pad profit margins. Furthermore, community enforcement remains highly reactive. In many instances, illegal packaging operations function for years in crowded neighbourhoods while residents look the other way. This civic complicity gives these syndicates the breathing room they need to thrive. Yet, we must look past the immediate symptoms of this crisis to fix the root cause. The call for the death penalty is an emotional response to a broken system. We see the cycle play out constantly in the national media: a grand spectacle is made where a parade of bootleggers and counterfeiters are displayed on television, handcuffed alongside rows of seized, toxic products. It satisfies our immediate thirst for justice. Yet, in no time at all, these very same individuals are quietly back on the streets, free to return to their deadly activities. Even when regulatory agencies claim that suspects are out on bail, the reality on the ground reveals a revolving-door justice system. Wealthy syndicates routinely exploit legal loopholes, slow courts, and institutional corruption to buy their freedom and resume their trade. This frustrating cycle proves a total fallacy: the belief that the cruelty of a punishment automatically deters a crime. The truth is that criminals are not deterred by how harsh a sentence is, but by how likely they are to get caught and convicted. The calculated greed driving these counterfeit kingpins operates on a simple risk-versus-reward matrix. If a producer knows that a media parade is the highest hurdle they have to clear, and that a loophole or a well-placed bribe will shield them thereafter, the threat of the gallows means absolutely nothing. They operate under the comfortable assumption that they can always buy their way out of trouble—just like the bandits, terrorists, and kidnappers who continue to exploit the same structural fractures in our nation. Furthermore, introducing the death penalty carries immense, irreversible risk within a judicial framework that battles deep systemic vulnerabilities. An execution leaves absolutely no room for human error. Given the institutional challenges within police investigations, the lack of reliable tracking, and the susceptibility of lower courts to influence, the risk of wrongful convictions is dangerously high. Nigeria risks a scenario where desperate, low-level warehouse labourers or small-time distributors are sent to the gallows to satisfy public anger, while the wealthy, politically connected kingpins who finance these syndicates use their immense resources to buy immunity. Instead of pursuing sensationalist legislative changes, Nigeria must focus on hitting counterfeiters where it hurts most: their pockets and their freedom. The National Assembly should look toward mandating life imprisonment with hard labour rather than executions. When a syndicate leader knows that being caught means spending the rest of their days facing grueling physical work behind bars, alongside the immediate, permanent seizure of every home, luxury vehicle, bank account, and legitimate business tied to their enterprise, the economic incentive vanishes completely. While NAFDAC deserves immense praise for its intensified daily enforcement raids, public health cannot be protected by reactive regulatory measures alone. Legislative machinery must move with greater urgency. The National Assembly must review penal codes to ensure the legal framework treats beverage counterfeiting not as a minor regulatory infraction, but as a severe felony akin to manslaughter. When a merchant knowingly bottles industrial chemicals for human consumption, they are committing slow-motion homicide, and the judiciary must sentence them to the maximum weight of the law. Ultimately, institutional and civic transparency remain the primary prescription to heal this broken supply chain. Hospitality stakeholders—nightclubs, hotels, lounges, and event planners—must enforce ironclad, auditable procurement chains, completely banning the purchase of alcohol from unverified, third-party vans or grey-market distributors. Simultaneously, legitimate international and local spirit manufacturers must step up by aggressively deploying un-clonable, scannable QR verification seals on all packaging to empower the end consumer at the point of pour. We can no longer afford to laugh off “fake drinks” as a humorous, expected hazard of the Lagos nightlife experience. It is a lethal healthcare crisis draining our medical infrastructure, cutting short the potential of our youth, and filling hospital wards with preventable chronic illnesses. The next time a cork is popped and a glass is raised, remember that in a compromised market, the price of entry is paid in cash, but the final bill is settled in tissue, blood, and years cut short from a human life. We must sanitize our supply chains today, or continue to watch our tomorrow get poured down the drain. Dr Odoemena is a Consultant Family Physician in Lagos

title: Man lying on sidewalk succumbs to injuries after he was run over: Calgary police
body:
Calgary police investigators are still trying to figure out why a man was lying on a sidewalk before he was run over in the northeast community of Martindale early Monday morning.
Police were called to Dashmesh Cultural Centre in the 100 block of Martindale Boulevard around 5:40 a.m. where they say the man was lying in front of the parking lot entrance.
Staff Sgt. Andy Woodward with the Calgary Police Traffic Unit says at the same time a driver was attempting to turn in to the parking lot.
“(The driver) didn’t see the victim because it was dark and the victim was in dark clothing,” says Woodward. “The driver drove over him and then the gate was locked or shut, so he reversed back over him thinking it was just a traffic calming and not a person.”
The victim was initially transported in serious condition to a nearby hospital but was declared dead not long after.
Police say the driver of the vehicle involved, a man in his 50s, remained at the scene.
In a statement to Global News, the Dashmesh Cultural Centre said that it is “deeply saddened by the incident, and our thoughts and prayers are with the pedestrian involved and their loved ones.”
The man’s death marks the ninth Calgary pedestrian to be killed in vehicle incident this year and the 32nd traffic fatality in 2026.
The investigation into what happened is ongoing and police are asking anyone who may have witnessed what happened or has dashcam footage to contact the non-emergency line at (403)266-1234 or Crime Stoppers.

title: Canada receives first two F-35s as full purchase remains under review
body: Canada has received its first two Lockheed Martin F-35A fighters, beginning the replacement of its aging CF-18 fleet while the government continues to review how many of the next-generation aircraft it will buy. The Royal Canadian Air Force received the jets at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona on October 22, 2026, and announced their arrival the following day. Designated CF-35As in Canadian service, the aircraft will remain in the United States to support pilot training. The delivery comes nearly four years after Canada announced an agreement to acquire 88 F-35As. Prime Minister Mark Carney subsequently ordered a review of the purchase amid deteriorating relations with Washington, leaving the eventual size of the fleet unresolved even as the first aircraft begin to arrive. Ottawa has been considering alternatives that could include a mixed fleet of F-35s and Saab Gripens, but no decision has been announced. Under Canada’s published procurement plan, the first eight fighters will be based at Luke’s F-35 pilot training center while facilities are prepared for the aircraft in Canada. The first arrivals on Canadian soil are scheduled for 2028. The RCAF has not provided a pilot training start date for the F-35s. Canada selected the F-35 following a competition in which the Lockheed Martin fighter and Saab’s Gripen remained the final eligible contenders. The government entered negotiations for the F-35 in March 2022 and announced the acquisition agreement in January 2023. The purchase also includes weapons, training, software support and infrastructure needed to operate the fleet. Canada is preparing fighter facilities at Cold Lake, Alberta, and Bagotville, Quebec, as part of the transition. The new fighters are intended to replace the CF-18 Hornets that have served as the backbone of Canada’s fighter force for many years. Their duties will include defending Canadian airspace and supporting the country’s NORAD and NATO commitments. The government’s published schedule calls for initial operational capability in 2029-2030 and full operational capability in 2032-2034. It expects the fleet to remain in service beyond 2060. The post Canada receives first two F-35s as full purchase remains under review appeared first on AeroTime .

title: ALTERNATIVE ENERGY IS REVIVING SMALL BUSINESSES
body: Across Nigeria, alternative energy is breathing new life into small businesses, reducing operating costs, creating employment opportunities and opening new pathways for economic growth. From roadside phone-charging outlets and barbershops using rechargeable clippers to solar-powered viewing centres, hotels, restaurants, offices and farms, entrepreneurs are increasingly finding ways to overcome persistent electricity challenges. For many business owners, access to alternative power has become more than a convenience; it is a lifeline. Rechargeable lights, portable power stations, solar panels, inverters and battery storage are enabling businesses to operate for longer hours, serve customers more efficiently and reduce their dependence on expensive petrol and diesel generators. For years, unreliable electricity and rising fuel costs have constrained Nigeria’s micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs). Many entrepreneurs have struggled with shrinking profit margins, interrupted operations and the high cost of generator maintenance. Alternative energy is helping to ease these pressures, allowing businesses to redirect some of their savings towards expansion, improved services and better staff welfare. One significant but often overlooked benefit is the potential to improve employees’ earnings. When businesses spend less on fuel and electricity, the savings can create room for owners to increase staff salaries, provide incentives, improve working conditions or employ additional workers. Although such improvements depend on actual savings and business performance, lower energy costs can give entrepreneurs greater flexibility to reward employees and retain valuable staff. The impact extends across several sectors. Solar-powered irrigation systems enable farmers to pump water for cultivation, particularly during dry seasons, while solar refrigeration helps traders preserve food, fish and other perishable goods. Viewing centres can screen football matches with fewer interruptions, while hotels, restaurants, retail outlets and cybercafés can maintain essential services more reliably. Beyond supporting existing businesses, the renewable energy sector is generating new opportunities for solar installers, technicians, equipment distributors and maintenance providers. It is creating demand for technical skills, encouraging youth entrepreneurship and contributing to the development of a growing green economy. The Federal Government deserves recognition for initiatives aimed at encouraging investment in cleaner energy. Financing interventions through the Bank of Industry (BOI) and programmes supporting solar adoption demonstrate the role development finance can play in expanding access to renewable energy. Applicable customs duty concessions on eligible equipment can also help reduce costs and encourage wider adoption. Nevertheless, the high initial cost of solar installations, battery replacement and quality equipment remains a major obstacle for many small businesses. Expanding affordable financing, strengthening product quality standards and providing technical support would help more entrepreneurs benefit from these solutions. Nigeria’s energy transition should therefore be viewed not merely as an environmental objective but as a practical economic development strategy. Reliable and affordable power improves productivity, protects livelihoods and strengthens business competitiveness. Ultimately, every solar-powered shop, rechargeable barber’s clipper, illuminated roadside stall and irrigated farm represents an opportunity to build a more resilient economy. With sustained government support and greater private-sector investment, alternative energy can help Nigerian businesses move beyond survival towards sustainable growth—while creating jobs, improving staff welfare and giving business owners greater capacity to reward the people who contribute to their success. Kenechukwu Aguolu, kenerek1@gmail.com

title: THE REVENGE OF BAND A
body: Many “victims” of the so-called Band A electricity tariff are turning to solar energy, writes PAUL C NWABUIKWU Many Nigerians celebrated the failure of former minister of power Bayo Adelabu, the Band A Minister, to clinch the APC governorship nomination in Oyo State with the glee of children screaming “up NEPA!” after months of sweaty darkness. A friend remarked that it was the best news to come out of the country’s endless and underachieving power reform programme in years. The comment was a bit harsh but also understandable given the context. Like food rotting in the fridge during power blackouts, decades of epileptic power supply have soured the minds of many Nigerians against public officials who promised much and delivered little. Things had looked much brighter for Adelabu when he decided to seek greener political pastures after almost three years in office. The pudgy, gregarious scion of the Penkelemesi political dynasty had left for Ibadan with fanfare after resigning as minister. He had departed in a blaze of glory, heralded by supporters and sycophants, to seek his party’s nomination to serve the good people of Oyo State as governor after two unsuccessful previous attempts. His success seemed like a foregone conclusion. Many believed he would be third time lucky. He was a largely unknown quantity outside Oyo during his first two efforts. But this time he was more prepared, more visible, more confident. With federal might on his side, the backing of many big wigs and the intimidating profile and resources conferred on him by “Abuja”, the governorship was in the bag. But the forecasts turned out to be too optimistic. Adelabu’s prospects before the primaries turned out to be wildly overstated. His loss was described as “crushing” by more than one commentator. Senator Sharafadeen Alli got 578,143 of the votes cast. Senator Abdulfatai Omotayo Buhari was a distant second with 32,265 votes. Only 19,193 delegates entrusted their votes to Adelabu who lost to Alli by a staggering 558,950 votes. It was, electorally speaking, the equivalent of massacring one person. Many explanations have been offered for Adelabu’s abysmal performance. But perhaps the best summary is that Alli had done the hard work and captured the party structure while Adelabu was being hailed as “Incoming governor” and “Your Excellency” by contractors and sycophants in Abuja. He is not the first candidate to learn the hard lesson that Abuja money and profile cannot do the necessary magic if a home boy with deep pockets has already secured the support of critical party operatives and charmed the hearts of the locals who have enjoyed many bowls of Amala with him. There is a simply psychological explanation for this. People tend to trust people they know, not those who parachute in with promises at the last minute. Beyond money, this factor also explains the success of charismatic corrupt and incompetent local politicians over better qualified fresh politicians with “plenty grammar”. The theory that Adelabu’s political progress was halted by the curses of Nigerians is a rather dubious one. If curses were that effective, we would have cursed our way to a better country. But to the helpless victims of an uncaring system, the idea that their anger is more powerful than the National Grid which collapsed about two dozen times while Adelabu was power minister is understandably an attractive one. The rejoicing over the former minister’s loss, in all honesty, was a bit unfair. Adelabu did not invent Nigeria’s power problems. Power cuts have been a depressing constant for many decades, crippling the productivity of businesses and making life a misery for families. From available evidence, Adelabu was determined to make a difference when he arrived. And he made many promises to show he was serious about turning things around. He declared that within six months, Nigerians would start seeing significant improvement in power supply. He assured that under his watch, the collapse of the grid would gradually become a thing of the past. He pledged to electrify industrial clusters and agricultural hubs. But his biggest promise was that supply would hit 6,000 megawatts, a feat that he later claimed that he achieved in his resignation letter but which Daily Trust said in a special investigation did not happen. According to the paper: “While generation approached the 6,000MW mark, it did not surpass it based on verified industry records…. Average generation capacity rose to 4,922MW in Q4 2023 shortly after Adelabu assumed office from 4211.44MW in Q3, 2023. It dropped to 4,249MW in Q1 2024, recovered to around 5,296MW by Q4 2024 and then about 5,430MW in Q3 2025 before declining to approximately 4,089MW by March 2026.” In other words, nearly cannot kill a bird. But the legacy that will haunt Adelabu and define his tenure is the multi-band payment policy which many Nigerians consider a wickedly designed initiative that has worsened the crisis of public trust in government and left consumers with bigger bills and less than the advertised value. The plan sounded like a great idea: move energy pricing from blanket subsidy pricing to a new structure, a hierarchical model (bands A to E) in which big men and big women consumers (and rich firms and factories) will be rewarded with extra hours and charged a higher price per unit for the privilege. According to the official communication, the objective was “to increase revenue for Discos, enable them to strengthen their networks, provide more power to high-paying customers, and ultimately improve power reliability nationwide.” The road to hell – and frustration – is paved with good (official) intentions. Incentives that were supposed to sweeten the deal for higher paying customers have largely not materialized. For instance, DISCOs have largely ignored the requirement that they cannot charge Band A customers in Abuja, Lagos and other cities N209.50 per unit if they don’t meet 20 hours per day target. The policy also states that “if a DISCo misses the committed service level for a Band A feeder (distribution line) for seven consecutive days, the feeder is automatically downgraded.” That requirement, to a quote a popular pidgin expression, “don enter voice mail”. Those in charge of the system have not kept their end of the bargain and the Band A customers, the only customers paying non-subsidized bills have suffered the most. I should know. I’m a victim. But unlike Adelabu’s gubernatorial aspirations, there is a light at the end of the tunnel for Band A victims. And the light is powered by solar energy which has become the new refuge for unhappy high net-worth consumers who can afford to squeeze out a few extra millions to purchase any of the numerous solar packages peddled across the country. The number of Nigerians who are frantically reducing their dependence on the grid is increasing daily and the trickle may soon become a flood. It’s the ultimate vote of no confidence on the system left behind by Adelabu and his predecessors. There was an interesting social media story recently about a customer in Lagos who was penalized by the local DISCO for the crime of sabotaging the DISCO’s revenue projections by investing in solar energy! Embarrassed by the report, the DISCO quickly apologized and promised to make amends. But the incident is more evidence that the future is solar and Band A victims are the warriors who are fighting hardest to achieve that future. Adelabu will deserve a huge part of the credit when it happens – even if that wasn’t his intention. Nwabuikwu is a member of THISDAY Editorial Board

title: Diri unveils AI robotic tutors in Bayelsa medical university
body:
Governor Douye Diri of Bayelsa State has unveiled Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered robotic tutors and other digital learning innovations at the Bayelsa Medical University (BMU), Yenagoa.
The News Agency of Nigeria reports that the initiative is part of the government’s efforts to advance medical education, research and technological development in Bayelsa.
The innovations were unveiled alongside the university’s 2025–2029 Strategic Plan on Monday in Yenagoa.
Mr Diri described the initiative as a significant step towards modernising medical education, saying that the digital tools must complement human instruction and make learning more interactive.
He urged the institution to deploy technology to improve teaching, learning and research without replacing physical classroom interactions and the mentorship role of lecturers.
He also challenged the university’s management to translate its strategic plan into measurable improvements in academic standards, research, infrastructure and the quality of graduates.
The governor reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to supporting BMU’s ASPIRE Agenda, which focuses on academic excellence, sustainability, partnerships and engagement, innovation and technology, as well as research excellence among others.
He commended the Vice-Chancellor, Dimie Ogoina, and the university management for developing a roadmap for institutional growth, charging them to collaborate with the state’s Ministries of Education and Health to achieve its objectives.
Mr Diri said his administration was strengthening science, technical and vocational education to equip young people with practical skills for employment, entrepreneurship and self-reliance.
He expressed confidence that the science-oriented schools being established across the state would provide qualified candidates for BMU and other tertiary institutions.
According to him, this will help the state to produce more doctors, nurses, pharmacists, radiologists, engineers and other professionals.
The governor acknowledged the late governor Diepreye Alamieyeseigha, who initiated the development of the former 500-bed hospital where the university is located, and his successor, Seriake Dickson, who revived the project and transformed it into the medical university.
He disclosed that the university’s campus at Sampou was nearing completion and would provide additional space for its expansion.
Mr Diri also inspected facilities at the newly established Bayelsa Medical University Teaching Hospital and expressed confidence in the institution’s capacity to provide advanced diagnostic services.
He said the teaching hospital was equipped to conduct x-rays and advanced scans, including Computed Tomography (CT) scans, which use x-ray technology and computer processing to produce detailed images of internal body structures.
The governor said the availability of such facilities would improve access to specialised diagnostic services and reduce the need for Bayelsans to travel outside the state for certain medical procedures.
Mr Diri also undertook a tour of facilities at the Bayelsa Emergency Medical Services and Ambulance System.
Earlier, the Vice-Chancellor, Mr Ogoina, said his vision was to transform the school into a globally recognised institution for medical education, research and innovation, driven by technology and sustainability.
He explained that the ASPIRE Agenda was being implemented through institutional teams and initiatives designed to improve academic quality, accountability, innovation and student welfare.
The vice-chancellor disclosed that the university had secured accreditation for nine academic programmes while its nursing science students recorded a 96 per cent pass rate in their professional examinations.
He also revealed that the university’s College of Medicine had attained full membership of the Consortium of Medical Schools of Africa while BMU was selected as one of 18 medical schools in Nigeria for a high-impact intervention programme.
On digital innovation, Mr Ogoina said the university had established a virtual reality, artificial intelligence and mixed-reality studio, expanded digital connectivity and introduced a “Talk to the VC” application to enable students and staff communicate directly and confidentially with the university leadership.
He added that the institution was strengthening simulation-based learning through its clinical skills laboratory and pursuing plans to develop a smart campus, improve internet connectivity and increase internally generated revenue.
“The BMU is developing a Centre of Excellence for Digital Health and Biomedical Innovation, alongside the Niger Delta Centre of Excellence for Health, Environment and Development to address regional health and environmental challenges,” he said.

title: Greece Records €7.55 Billion Primary Surplus in First Nine Months
body: Greece recorded a primary budget surplus of €7.554 billion in the January-September 2026 period, exceeding the government’s target of €5.129 billion, as stronger-than-expected tax revenues, particularly from value-added tax (VAT) and income tax, boosted public finances, according to final execution data released by the Ministry of National Economy and Finance. However, after adjusting for delayed payments and special receipts, the primary surplus exceeded the target by a more modest €305 million. Regular tax revenues, excluding special receipts, surpassed the target by €1.426 billion, or 2.6%. The primary surplus for the same period in 2025 stood at €9.449 billion. State Budget Records Overall Surplus Greece’s state budget recorded an overall surplus of €127 million in the first nine months of 2026, compared with a targeted deficit of €1.897 billion. The budget had recorded a surplus of €2.401 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. The adjusted primary surplus reflects several timing differences and exceptional receipts. These included €695 million in delayed payments under the Public Investment Programme, €385 million in delayed defence procurement payments and €905 million in delayed transfers to General Government entities. The calculation also excludes €135 million from the second instalment of the concession fee for the operating licence of a casino at Ellinikon. The ministry noted that payment timing differences do not affect the General Government result under national accounting rules. The casino receipt had been expected at the end of 2025, although fiscal accounting records the revenue over the concession period. Net Revenue Exceeds Target by €2.5 Billion Net state budget revenue reached €57.811 billion during the nine-month period, exceeding the budget target by €2.501 billion. The comparison reflects the timing of payments from the Recovery and Resilience Facility. The budget had projected a €1.258 billion receipt in June. The government received €884 million earlier, in April, while it expects to collect the remaining €374 million before the end of 2026. Excluding the Recovery and Resilience Facility amount, net revenue exceeded the target by €2.876 billion. Tax revenue totalled €55.967 billion, including €306 million from the Egnatia Odos concession agreement and €135 million from the Ellinikon casino licence. Excluding these two special receipts, tax revenue reached €55.526 billion, surpassing the target by €1.426 billion, or 2.6%. VAT and Income Tax Drive Revenue Growth VAT generated the largest positive deviation from the budget target. Revenue reached €23.062 billion, exceeding the target by €1.093 billion after excluding the €306 million associated with the Egnatia Odos concession. Income tax revenue totalled €20.171 billion, beating the target by €360 million. Personal income tax receipts exceeded expectations by €408 million, while corporate income tax revenue fell €58 million short of the target. Other income taxes contributed a further €10 million above target. Excise duty revenue reached €5.326 billion, falling €239 million below the target. Property tax receipts totalled €2.1 billion, exceeding expectations by €63 million. The results point to stronger consumption-tax receipts amid higher prices, alongside increased income-tax revenue associated with rising incomes. Other Revenue Categories Social contribution revenue reached €40 million, falling €5 million short of the target. Transfer revenue totalled €4.764 billion, exceeding the target by €79 million. Public Investment Programme receipts within this category were €72 million above target. Revenue from sales of goods and services reached €1.465 billion. Excluding €306 million from the Egnatia Odos concession, the total stood at €1.159 billion, exceeding the target by €274 million. Other current revenue reached €2.3 billion, beating the target by €518 million. This included €319 million from the Public Investment Programme, €206 million above the corresponding target. Revenue refunds totalled €6.727 billion, exceeding the budgeted €6.206 billion by €520 million. The ministry attributed much of the difference to a €306 million VAT refund linked to the Egnatia Odos concession agreement. September Revenue Results In September alone, net state budget revenue reached €6.460 billion, exceeding the monthly target by €170 million. Tax revenue totalled €6.486 billion, beating the target by €74 million, or 1.1%. VAT receipts reached €2.518 billion, exceeding expectations by €188 million. Income tax revenue stood at €2.490 billion, falling €79 million below target. Personal income tax receipts missed the target by €25 million, corporate income tax by €49 million and other income taxes by €5 million. Excise duty revenue reached €665 million, €8 million below target, while property tax receipts totalled €123 million, broadly in line with expectations. Social contributions generated €4 million, €1 million below target. Transfer revenue reached €271 million, exceeding expectations by €146 million, although Public Investment Programme receipts within this category fell €26 million short of target. Revenue from sales of goods and services reached €61 million, broadly in line with the target, while other current revenue totalled €264 million, exceeding expectations by €31 million. Revenue refunds reached €626 million, €79 million above the target of €548 million. Total Public Investment Programme revenue stood at €94 million, €26 million below target. State Spending Rises by €5.4 Billion Year on Year State budget expenditure reached €57.683 billion in the first nine months of 2026, exceeding the target of €57.206 billion by €477 million. Spending also increased by €5.423 billion compared with the corresponding period of 2025. Regular budget payments came in €1.094 billion below target. By contrast, investment expenditure reached €10.395 billion, exceeding the target by €1.571 billion as the government accelerated projects funded through the Recovery and Resilience Facility. Investment spending also rose by €2.209 billion year on year. Major transfers and payments included €1.544 billion for the National Organisation for Healthcare Services Provision (EOPYY) and €1.994 billion for the Organisation of Welfare Benefits and Social Solidarity (OPEKA). The government also allocated €131 million to Information Society S.A. for Fuel Pass payments, €136 million for diesel fuel subsidies and €232 million in extraordinary financial support for families with children. Further expenditure included €917 million for the National Central Health Procurement Authority to purchase medicines, products and healthcare services for public hospitals, as well as €1.032 billion in transfers to hospitals and primary healthcare services. Subsidies to public transport operators OASA, OASTH and OSE totalled €327 million. Ministry Clarifies Scope of Budget Figures The Ministry of National Economy and Finance stressed that the figures cover the primary balance of Central Government on a modified cash basis, rather than the entire General Government sector. The cash-based result differs from the fiscal result. General Government includes Central Government, legal entities, local government organisations and social security organisations. title: England striker Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or award
body:
LONDON, October 27. /TASS/. Bayern Munich and England striker Harry Kane has won the 2026 Ballon d’Or award, presented by the French magazine France Football to the world’s best player.
The award ceremony took place in London.
Kane scored 61 goals for Bayern Munich last season, and the club won the Bundesliga title and the German Cup.
Kane also won the European Golden Shoe award as the top goalscorer from a Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) member country.
At the 2026 FIFA World Cup, he won a bronze medal with England.

title: Thermal Blueprint: USER INTERFACE 2026 Resurfaces with Technology-Driven Climate Innovation
body: As urbanization accelerates, the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect intensifies, creating challenges in contemporary cities that increase energy demand, threaten public health, and heighten climate vulnerability. In response to this, the Civil Engineering Executive Organization (CEO), a duly recognized academic organization from the College of Engineering and Agro-Industrial Technology of the University of the Philippines Los Baños, presents USER INTERFACE, a national seminar dedicated to technological innovation in building information modeling and infrastructure. USER INTERFACE is an annual undergraduate seminar focusing on the intersection of technology and engineering to promote safer, smarter, and more sustainable solutions by delivering the latest advancements, including engineering software, innovative research, and design projects. This is organized as part of the celebration of the organization’s 26th anniversary, representing its mission of fostering professional, social, and academic proficiency among future engineers. For this year’s theme, distinguished presenters and industry experts will share their expertise and insights regarding urban sustainability and heat mitigation initiatives, including technology-based platforms. With this, engineering students, software developers, engineers, and associates from all institutions, universities, and businesses nationwide are all welcome and encouraged to participate, as the event is free for the general public. This will be an opportunity to interact with top professionals and companies to gain valuable perspectives. In keeping with the CEO’s commitment to giving back to the community, teachers, and students, the proceeds of this event will support the organization’s 26th Anniversary Celebration initiatives, which consist of an exhibit, thanksgiving mass, Fiestambayan, and an outreach program. With this, we invite you to be a part of USER INTERFACE 2026—Thermal Blueprint: Engineering Urban Sustainability and Heat Mitigation through Technology-Based Climate Innovation this coming October 24, 2026, at 1:00 PM via Zoom and Facebook Live. Registration can be done through this link: https://tinyurl.com/UIPH2026 For more information and inquiries, you may contact our Registration Head, Ms. Karen Faye Catcatan.
