The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter . Alexander Dunayev

title: CBD COP17: Global biodiversity fund receives $60 million in new pledges
body:
The United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity said national and sub-national governments have pledged $60 million to the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund (GBFF) to strengthen biodiversity conservation and restoration worldwide.
The pledges were announced during a finance day session at the ongoing CBD COP17 in Yerevan, Armenia, on Monday.
The UN said new commitments are expected to support countries and communities working to conserve and restore wild species and ecosystems, while promoting their long-term sustainability.
At the same session, Spain and Uzbekistan announced contributions of €50 million and $4.5 million, respectively, to the ninth replenishment of the Global Environment Facility Trust Fund (GEF-9).
The United Kingdom also reaffirmed its £330 million contribution, bringing total pledges to GEF-9 close to $4.4 billion for the July 2026 to June 2030 funding period.
Representatives of Armenia, which holds the COP17 presidency, joined officials from Germany, Iceland and Monaco, as well as representatives of the Canadian province of Québec and the city of Berlin, in announcing new contributions during the pledging session.
The session brought together representatives of developing countries receiving support from the fund, Indigenous Peoples and local communities, implementing agency partners, philanthropic organisations and the private sector.
Speaking at the event, Diego Mesa Puyo, Chief Executive Officer and Chairperson of the Global Environment Facility (GEF), said the pledges demonstrated a commitment to translating biodiversity ambitions into practical action.
“Today’s pledges send a powerful signal: our partnership is ready to move from ambition to action for nature,” Mr Mesa Puyo said.
He said the contributions would help integrate environmental action with development priorities, attract additional funding and private investment, and accelerate the delivery of conservation projects.
Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, described the GBFF as an important mechanism for mobilising resources to implement the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
She said the new pledges, including multi-year commitments and the fund’s first contribution from a city, indicated growing support for biodiversity financing.
“These new pledges, including multiannual commitments and the fund’s first contribution from a city, are encouraging signs of growing support for biodiversity finance,” Ms Schomaker said.
She added that the contributions showed that efforts to protect nature were gaining momentum.
COP17 President and Armenia’s Minister of Environment, Hambardzum Matevosyan, said the financial commitments demonstrated the potential of multilateral cooperation to advance biodiversity conservation.
He said Armenia had begun preliminary internal discussions on a possible contribution to support the implementation of global biodiversity commitments.
Since its launch in August 2023, the GBFF has received $446 million in commitments from 14 sovereign governments and two sub-national governments.
Within three years, the fund has programmed $362.1 million for 82 projects across 87 countries, including 47 Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries.
The fund supports countries in strengthening biodiversity management, policies, governance and resource mobilisation. It also promotes blended financing mechanisms designed to attract private-sector investment into conservation efforts.
According to the fund’s figures, 32 per cent of its programmed resources have been allocated to support actions by Indigenous Peoples and local communities, while 39 per cent has been directed to Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries.
Another 30 per cent has been channelled through international financial institutions.
These allocations exceed the fund’s respective targets for supporting Indigenous Peoples and local communities, vulnerable countries and international financial institutions.
Established at the request of parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, the GBFF is designed to accelerate implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
The framework sets global targets for halting and reversing biodiversity loss, including the conservation of at least 30 per cent of the world’s land and inland waters, and of marine and coastal areas, by 2030.
The fund has streamlined procedures and expanded governance arrangements to improve support for developing countries. It can receive contributions from public, private and philanthropic sources.
The UN said new pledges to GEF-9 have brought total commitments close to $4.4 billion for 2026–2030.
About 70 per cent of the replenishment resources will support objectives under the Convention on Biological Diversity.
Spain’s €50 million contribution represents a 60 per cent increase over its contribution to the previous replenishment, GEF-8.
Maria Rodriguez de Sancho, Spain’s Director-General for Biodiversity, Forests and Desertification, said the commitment reaffirmed the country’s support for multilateral action to halt and reverse biodiversity loss.
Uzbekistan’s $4.5 million pledge marks the country’s entry as a GEF donor.
Aziz Abdukhakimov, an adviser to Uzbekistan’s president on environmental issues and chairman of the National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, said the country intended to contribute to global nature protection and create opportunities for communities.
Germany also announced plans to contribute another €50 million to the GBFF before the end of 2026.
Carsten Schneider, Germany’s Federal Minister for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety, said the fund was already delivering results by supporting vulnerable countries and enabling the participation of Indigenous Peoples and the scientific community.
He urged other governments, private-sector organisations and non-profit institutions to contribute to the fund.
The GEF, which serves as a financial mechanism for six multilateral environmental conventions, approved $4.64 billion for 649 projects across 144 countries during the GEF-8 period, from July 2022 to June 2026.
The projects supported implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, alongside broader efforts to address environmental degradation, climate change and pollution.
The new pledges come as delegates at COP17 continue negotiations on financing and implementing the global biodiversity framework, with countries under pressure to translate agreed conservation targets into measurable action before 2030.

title: Seven families to press charges against Obuasi SHTS headmaster amid threats and blackmail
body: Seven families of girls allegedly sexually abused by the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High and Technical School (SHTS) are preparing to press charges against him, amid reported threats, intimidation and attempts to blackmail those seeking justice. The decision follows engagements between the families, the victims and officials from the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection during an official visit to Obuasi to support the victims and advance efforts to secure justice. During the engagement, the affected families and girls recounted their alleged ordeal to the government officials, detailing their experiences. However, the pursuit of justice is reportedly being complicated by threats against some of the families, with concerns that intimidation is discouraging others from openly participating in the case. Gender Minister, Dr. Agnes Lartey, disclosed that her ministry is working with National Security to identify and deal with individuals allegedly threatening or blackmailing the victims and their families. She said authorities were also taking steps to remove audio and video recordings circulating on social media that expose the identities of the girls, particularly content mentioning their full names. “We are working with National Security to pull down those audios and videos, if possible, the ones that mention their full names so that the families will feel safe and protected,” she said. The Minister indicated that the process had already commenced but declined to provide further details, citing concerns that the threats were connected to the ongoing efforts to pursue accountability. “I don’t want to give details because their threats are centred around that, and it is not just political. Threats are coming from families and other influential persons,” she stated. She added that efforts were underway to trace those allegedly making threatening and blackmailing calls, with the aim of bringing them before the law. “We are finding a way to track those who are calling to blackmail and threaten them so that we bring them to book as offenders of the law,” she said. The Minister further revealed that more than seven people have been identified as willing to support the case, although fear of possible repercussions was forcing some to remain behind the scenes. According to her, at least one person had indicated a willingness to support the legal process privately but was reluctant to appear publicly or formally report the matter because of threats and pressure from family members. “We are having more than seven people now. One of them felt them it’s beyond him so he said he and the family can support from behind but because of the threats from family. How the issue has escalated overwhelms some of them, so they want to support the case in running but not to show up to report. “But because of the threats from family, and how the issue has escalated, it overwhelms some of them. They want to support the case in running, but not to show up to report,” she said. The disclosure highlights the challenges confronting efforts to secure justice for the alleged victims, as concerns over intimidation and exposure continue to weigh on families deciding whether to participate in the case.

title: Pizza Fan Case: First Five Defendants Released Under Restrictive Conditions
body: The first five of 10 defendants in the Pizza Fan case have been released under restrictive conditions after appearing before an investigating magistrate, with the proceedings continuing as five more defendants prepare to give their statements. Following the hearings, the magistrate and prosecutor jointly imposed conditions on the defendants, depending on each case. These include reporting to a local police station and paying bail of €5,000. The five defendants include three accountants, a software developer and the owner of a Pizza Fan franchise in Nea Ionia. Their lawyer, Miltiadis Zisidis, said his client had been released after a lengthy hearing. “After a lengthy and exhausting statement, we highlighted all the critical legal and substantive gaps in the case file, in our view, as well as technical shortcomings, because the algorithm operated differently from the way it was presented,” he said. “With the agreement of the investigating magistrate and prosecutor, my client was released.” Tax authority investigates possible information leaks Meanwhile, Greece’s Independent Authority for Public Revenue (AADE) is investigating whether any of its employees may have been involved in allegedly leaking information ahead of a tax inspection at Pizza Fan. The inquiry follows revelations concerning the alleged illegal activities of the business owner and associates. On Monday, October 26, at the instruction of AADE Governor Giorgos Pitsilis, the authority’s Internal Affairs Directorate formally asked the relevant Greek Police departments whether their investigations or evidence in their possession indicated that specific AADE employees may have been involved in the alleged leaks. The authorities are examining claims that people connected to the restaurant business, which faces allegations of tax evasion, received advance warning of an impending tax inspection. The request stems from references in recorded conversations between people involved in the case. According to the allegations contained in those conversations, the business’s representatives had learned about the planned inspection before it took place. The investigation into the possible leak remains ongoing. title: Vucic swept aside in Serbian elections. Can Belgrade break free from Russia’s orbit?
body:
The Student List's election victory ends more than a decade of Aleksandar Vucic's rule, hinting at a new chapter in Serbia's relations with the EU, Russia, and China.
Supporters of the Student List opposition movement walk on a portrait of former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic following his concession of defeat on Oct. 25, 2026 in Belgrade, Serbia. (Pierre Crom/Getty Images)
Belgrade erupted in celebration on Sunday night as Serbia's Gen Z-led protest movement transformed nearly two years of anti-corruption demonstrations into an electoral victory over the political establishment of former President Aleksandar Vucic, who had held power for 14 years.
Among the crowds was Dijana Hrka, whose 27-year-old son Stefan was one of 16 people killed when a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad on Nov. 1, 2024.
Hrka, who had been demanding accountability for the tragedy and had previously gone on hunger strike, broke down in tears after Vucic conceded defeat.
"I have been waiting for this moment for almost two years," she told N1 television, struggling to speak through her emotions. "This is the victory of all of us, the victory of our children."
Protests in Serbia erupted following the Novi Sad disaster but soon evolved into a nationwide challenge to the government, mobilizing students, academics, workers, and citizens who had never before engaged in political activism.
By Sunday night, the movement had achieved what years of fragmented opposition efforts had failed to accomplish — a decisive electoral victory over Vucic's political camp. The Student List
The Student List — an electoral alliance formed by Serbia's anti-corruption protesters , bringing together 250 academics, professionals, and public figures — won almost 53% of the vote.
The coalition led by Aleksandar Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party secured less than 39%, according to preliminary results published on Oct. 26.
"The feeling is almost surreal," Dr. Mario Reljanovic, who ran on the Student List ballot, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The overwhelming support received by the Student List is a sign that we have managed to give the people of Serbia hope that a different society is possible, (a society) based on justice, the rule of law, solidarity, and the removal of party influence from the public sector," Dr. Reljanovic added.
The turnout, at almost 69%, was the highest since the fall of the Serbian strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000. The students are projected to secure around 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, giving them a majority to form a government without needing coalition partners.
"The election result marks the end of a government that displayed authoritarian tendencies," Serbian political scientist Aleksandar Ivkovic told the Kyiv Independent.
"It ended much the same way as the regimes of Viktor Orban in Hungary (2026), Milo Djukanovic in Montenegro (2023), and Nikola Gruevski in North Macedonia (2022), which were similarly authoritarian, and were deeply entrenched in corruption and organized crime."
The result marks a potential turning point not only for Serbia's domestic politics but also for its relations with the European Union, Ukraine, Russia, and China.
The Student List has pledged to pursue EU-oriented reforms and keep Serbia on a European path, a commitment that could reshape the country's relations with Brussels and redefine its place in Europe.
The Student List's electoral success was built on an unusually broad mobilization. Long marches from towns across Serbia culminated in a mass rally in Belgrade shortly before the vote. Queues formed outside polling stations on election day, while Serbian citizens abroad also turned out in large numbers.
Formally known as the "Students Are Winning" activist group, the opposition electoral list was formed over the past few months to turn the student protest movement into an electoral alternative without becoming a conventional political party.
"The Student List is a phenomenon that will be studied for decades to come," said Ivkovic. "It is a movement, not a political party designed to last."
The students avoided presenting a single dominant leader and instead emphasized civic participation, professional expertise, and accountability. The campaign was deliberately collective. Rather than putting forward a familiar party leader, the student movement assembled a list of 250 candidates from different professional backgrounds, including academics, doctors, lawyers, farmers, athletes, and cultural figures.
The first on the list is Ilija Srdanovic, a cardiologist and professor at the University of Novi Sad's Faculty of Medicine.
Srdanovic, who could become the new prime minister, became widely recognized in 2025 after publicly supporting student protests and university blockades, including demonstrations over the past two years. The candidates earned voters' trust primarily through their professional achievements rather than previous political experience. Around 170 people on the list hold doctoral degrees.
"While many come from academia, the list also includes farmers, lawyers, journalists, teachers, and cultural workers, reflecting the movement's emphasis on expertise and diversity of backgrounds," says Dr. Reljanovic, who holds a PhD in Law.
He expects that the same principle is expected to guide ministerial appointments.
"Given that ministerial portfolios have until now been treated and distributed as political party spoils, this represents a different approach to forming a government, one in which professionals with relevant expertise will predominate."
The Student List's program centers on restoring the rule of law, freeing the judiciary and media from political influence, investigating corruption, reviewing public contracts, and improving education and healthcare. It has also promised to direct money recovered from illegal enrichment towards economic development and public services.
"The purpose of the Student List will be fulfilled once it achieves the student movement's key demands — freeing institutions from political influence, holding those responsible for the Novi Sad canopy collapse and similar scandals to account, and improving media freedom and electoral conditions," Ivkovic added.
Ivkovic believes that once the goals set by the Student List are met, Serbia's political landscape is likely to reorganize.
"Many established parties may not survive in their current form, but Serbia will quickly return to a system where old and new parties will compete in a conventional, multiparty system."
The immediate task for the Student List is to form a government and begin implementing its 11-point program of institutional transition, which will require decisions on the judiciary, public administration, media regulation, and the security sector.
The movement will also have to decide how to approach Serbia's relationship with the European Union. Its victory has been welcomed by European leaders, who have signaled that the EU is prepared to support democratic reforms and Serbia's European future.
"I do not expect radical foreign-policy shifts, but I expect a significant change in relations between Serbia and the European Union," Marko Todorovic, senior researcher at Belgrade-based think tank Center for European Policy (CEP), told Kyiv Independent.
"Above all, I expect an end to anti-European rhetoric and the creation of space for more objective information for citizens about the EU and the benefits of European integration," he added.
Serbia, an EU candidate country since 2012, has faced mounting criticism from Brussels over stalled reforms and remains one of the few European countries that has refused to join Western sanctions against Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"I do not expect sudden breaks in relations with either Russia or China, but I expect both countries to lose their current symbolic significance in Serbia's foreign policy," Todorovic added.
Over the last 14 years, Serbia remained an EU candidate country while preserving close relations with Russia, particularly in energy, and deepening economic ties with China. Belgrade condemned violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity at the United Nations but refused to join Western sanctions against Moscow.
Serbia also remains one of Europe's few remaining buyers of Russian natural gas, underscoring a dependence that leaves Moscow supplying about 80% of its total gas imports. Therefore, the question of sanctions against Russia is likely to remain one of the most sensitive tests for the new government.
As he conceded, Vucic suggested that a change of government could lead to sanctions being introduced against Moscow by March or April. However, Todorovic cautions against treating that possibility as an imminent policy shift.
"For now, there are no indications that sanctions against Russia will be introduced within such a short period. On the contrary, the student movement stated during the campaign that it opposed their introduction," he added.
A more democratic Serbia could offer Ukraine a more predictable partner.
"Serbia will certainly remain consistent in supporting Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, with the expectation that humanitarian aid and other forms of bilateral cooperation with Ukraine will continue," Todorovic added.
Vucic's defeat marks the end of an era in which Serbia's president sought to maintain close ties with both Brussels and Moscow while consolidating political power at home.
His Serbian Progressive Party came to power in 2012, and Vucic served as prime minister from 2014 to 2017 before becoming president .
During that period, the government promoted infrastructure projects, attracted foreign investment, and presided over economic growth. At the same time, critics accused it of weakening democratic institutions, exerting pressure on independent media, and allowing political influence to permeate state institutions.
Several controversies came to define the period, while the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station canopy became the most consequential crisis of Vucic's rule. Protesters argued that the tragedy exposed systemic failures in public oversight and government responsibility. The authorities rejected many of their political accusations, while investigations and legal proceedings continued.
The Student List has promised to investigate corruption, strengthen independent institutions, and redirect public resources towards citizens. Delivering on those promises will require not only political will but also the ability to govern a diverse coalition and overcome resistance within the existing state apparatus.
"There is enormous excitement at the prospect of having the opportunity to implement a concrete and detailed program to rebuild institutions, the economy, culture, and science, all of which have been undermined," Dr. Reljanovic said.
"We must use the mandate we receive to lay the foundations for a different way of running the country, so that politics is no longer synonymous with crime and corruption, and so that a cult of personality and a subservient relationship between citizens and those in power can never exist again."
Jovana Georgievski is a freelance journalist with a particular focus on Russia-related stories and their impact across Europe. She has reported and produced long-form and current affairs programs and worked on award-winning BBC documentaries, including projects for Eye Investigations.

title: Ukraine to implement ceasefire in Oleshky area from midnight on October 27
body:
This was reported by the press service of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine , according to Ukrinform.
“Oleshky: Ceasefire and Assistance to Civilians. We remind you that starting at 3:00 a.m. on October 27, Kyiv time, Ukraine is implementing a ceasefire in a designated area to conduct a humanitarian operation in the temporarily occupied town of Oleshky in the Kherson region,” the statement reads.
It is noted that the ceasefire is being established exclusively for the humanitarian operation: to deliver aid to residents currently in the city and to prepare for the free movement of the civilian population out of Oleshky .
“We urge everyone during this period to be especially cautious regarding the information you receive and share,” the General Staff emphasized.
Citizens were urged to rely on official sources of information and not to trust unverified reports, as well as to refrain from spreading rumors regarding the routes, times, and locations of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys.
“The Ukrainian Defense Forces are doing everything possible to help the residents of Oleshky and will ensure that the necessary decisions are implemented to guarantee the safety and rescue of our fellow citizens,” the General Staff assured.
As previously reported, U.S. First Lady Melania Trump stated that she had brokered a local ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, which applies only to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in the Kherson region.
According to the White House press office, the parties agreed to temporarily suspend all hostilities in Oleshky to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and prepare for the evacuation of civilians via an agreed-upon safe corridor.

title: Greek Student Rocket Team Wins Two European Awards
body: A student team from the National Technical University of Athens (NTUA) successfully launched a research rocket in Portugal, secured two major awards and finished sixth overall at the European Rocketry Challenge (EuRoC) 2026. The interdisciplinary team, White Noise NTUA, designed and built its solid-propellant research rocket, Aurora, which stands approximately three metres tall and aims to reach an altitude of 3,000 metres. The students also developed their own flight electronics and telemetry systems, alongside an active aerodynamic braking system that allows them to control the rocket’s maximum altitude. According to the team, Aurora’s most distinctive feature is its innovative recovery system. Four movable carbon-fibre fairings open at the rocket’s maximum altitude, allowing its parachutes to deploy. The successful launch in Portugal marked the culmination of months of work by team members, who handled every stage of the rocket’s development, from design and construction to testing and flight. Research payload investigates airborne microplastics Alongside Aurora, White Noise NTUA designed and built a research payload to study airborne particles, with a particular focus on detecting and characterising microplastics. The experimental system combines environmental sensors with Digital Holographic Microscopy (DHM) technology, which enables researchers to optically record microscopic particles. The team also incorporated machine-learning algorithms into the experimental design to identify and classify the particles. During the flight, the payload collected data on environmental conditions and airborne particle concentrations, providing useful information for further research. Two awards and sixth place overall White Noise NTUA finished sixth in the overall EuRoC 2026 rankings and received two awards: Rookie of the Year: Recognising the best first-time participating team. Payload Award: Recognising the team’s research experiment. Founded in 2017, White Noise NTUA develops aerospace systems through collaboration among undergraduate students from different academic disciplines. The team combines theoretical knowledge with practical experience and creative engineering to deliver complex technical projects. The team also acknowledged the significant support it received from NTUA’s School of Mechanical Engineering and the Machine Elements Laboratory, directed by Professor Vasileios Spitas, during the rocket’s construction. title: Hebron business demolitions carried out without prior hearing, state tells High Court
body: Parts of two business premises near the site of Friday's deadly shooting terrorist attack in Hebron were demolished without a prior hearing, the state acknowledged in a response to the High Court of Justice on Sunday, saying the military commander considered the work urgently necessary.The state also said it had not posted a demolition notice at the site because of an error. In connection with the affected site, business owners, who deny any involvement in the attack, petitioned the court to stop the demolitions, arguing they amounted to collective punishment.The petition concerns two commercial compounds near Hebron's northern entrance. It is separate from the broader evacuation of Palestinian residents and restrictions imposed across the city following the October 23 attack in which two IDF soldiers were killed.In her initial decision on Friday, Justice Gila Canfy Steinitz directed the state to respond and said she expected it to refrain from changing the existing situation pending a further decision.The state subsequently said the demolition work described in its response had taken place before the petition and the court's decision reached the authorities, and that work stopped immediately upon their receipt.Mustafa and Sufian Qawasmeh and the Al-Quds ceramics and sanitary ware company filed the petition through attorney Muhammad Dahleh. It concerns approximately 17 dunams of commercial property containing offices, display areas, and merchandise.IDF soldiers operated without written order, explanation, petition claimsAccording to the petition, soldiers instructed the owners to remove goods ahead of demolition without providing a written order or explaining how they could challenge the decision.The petitioners said the business was closed on Friday apart from a guard, and that the gunmen had climbed over a locked gate. They denied assisting the attackers, knowing about the attack in advance, or being connected to the ploy in any way.The state's response presented a different account of the grounds for demolition. It said the terrorists had used a factory at one of the premises as cover and fired from behind a corrugated fence and equipment.According to the response, the military assessed that construction near the checkpoint posed an immediate security risk. The work included removing fencing at the premises used by the attackers and demolishing a fence and an office container at the compound opposite it.The state also cited a demolition order issued in August 2012 for the fence and office at the second compound, but did not explain the intervening enforcement history.Those grounds differ from the punitive-demolition allegations presented in the petition. The owners' charge of collective punishment remains disputed.Regarding the matter of the absence of a hearing, the state reiterated that military officials considered the demolition urgently and immediately necessary. It said officials had orally explained the intended work to the owners and allowed them an opportunity to remove merchandise.The response added that no further demolition was immediately planned at either compound and that any subsequent enforcement against unlawful construction would follow the applicable procedures.These proceedings come amid a wider dispute over the military's actions in Hebron following the attack.In a separate legal letter to the military, the Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) demanded that displaced residents be allowed to return, movement restrictions be lifted, and demolitions carried out as punishment be halted. It also requested the orders authorizing the measures already taken.ACRI: Approximately 1,500 Palestinians forced from their homesACRI said approximately 1,500 Palestinians had been forced from their homes, citing Palestinian authorities. It argued that public statements by ministers indicated a punitive purpose, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's description of demolitions as serving as deterrence and as exacting a price for the attack.“No attack, however grave, gives the military license to punish an entire city,” ACRI executive director Noa Sattath said.The IDF, in information provided to reporters, described civilians' departure differently, saying residents who wished to leave temporarily were permitted to do so through designated checkpoints.It estimated that approximately 2,000 people lived in the area and were part of the Jaba'a clan, which the military described as associated with Hamas and as the clan from which the attackers came.The military said forces had searched approximately 200 sites and arrested 10 suspects. It described demolition near the attack site as enforcement against unlawful construction and the removal of potential security risks.Beyond that briefing, The Jerusalem Post repeatedly requested clarification from relevant IDF officials about how a mass evacuation could be legal absent evidence that the vast majority of the evacuees had taken illegal action and were not ideologically pro-Hamas.Additionally, several media reports confirmed that IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir insisted on withdrawing troops from the area, but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insisted on them staying and maintaining the evacuation of the Palestinians – without specifically articulating a security necessity.

title: Brazil’s Bolsonaro drops plans of challenging presidential election outcome
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, October 26. /TASS/. Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost in Sunday’s runoff presidential election in Brazil, has abandoned his plans to seek the annulment of the second-round results under the pressure from his allies, the Folha de S.Paulo newspaper reported.
According to the newspaper, Bolsonaro was dissuaded from seeking to challenge the voting legitimacy by his lawyers and key allies, including prominent senators and Sao Paulo State Governor Tarcisio de Freitas. They cited the lack of concrete legal arguments and the unfavorable balance of power for the senator in the courts and warned of new political risks. They called on Bolsonaro to consider the election "a closed chapter."
The second round of Brazil’s presidential election took place on October 25. According to the electoral commission, after 100% of ballots had been counted, Lula da Silva was reelected president with 51.79% of the vote. His fourth term as head of state will begin on January 5, 2027.

title: Supreme Court to hear case on division of retirement, disability pay in military divorces
body: The U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to consider a case that challenges whether divorce settlements are enforceable if they agree to protect a former spouse’s share of military retirement pay and the amount is later affected by disability compensation. Under federal law, former spouses may receive up to half a service member’s time-based military retirement pay. But medical-based military retirement pay and any Veterans Affairs disability pay is protected and not divisible. In Marschner v. Marschner, which was accepted by the high court earlier this month, Roxane Marschner, who married North Dakota Army National Guard soldier Richard Marschner, is seeking to enforce a clause in her divorce settlement in which Richard agreed to pay her the equivalent of her portion of military retirement pay if any of it was offset by disability compensation. The couple married in 1994 and divorced 22 years later. In their settlement, Roxane was to receive a percentage of Richard’s military and federal civilian benefits when he retired. But Richard later was medically retired as a result of service-connected injuries and received medical retirement pay and VA disability compensation — neither of which is divisible under the Uniformed Services Former Spouses Protection Act. Roxane then took Richard to court, arguing that he had agreed to pay her if she did not receive her share of benefits. The lower court ruled in her favor. Richard then petitioned the North Dakota Supreme Court, which said the provision was unenforceable. Roxane Marschner then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to consider the case, saying that the law and a previous Supreme Court ruling only limited courts from instating provisions that divided disability compensation and did not apply to private agreements negotiated by spouses. She also argued that other states, including Virginia, Illinois, Nevada and Alaska, have allowed enforcement of such agreements, known as indemnification provisions, in divorce settlements, and a decision by the U.S. Supreme Court was necessary to ensure equity across the legal system. Richard Marschner’s attorneys have said the state courts don’t have the authority to divide federally protected benefits and the North Dakota district courts order to Richard to pay Roxane is invalid as a result. Marschner’s attorney, Johanna Clyborne of Minnesota-based Brekke, Clyborne and Ribich, told Military Times that divorce agreements such as the Marschners’ happen “more than people realize” because veterans — and attorneys — often don’t understand federal protections of disability benefits and medical retirement payments. “Congress has spoken on this issue, right, and it is non-divisible. There’s going to be different sorts of interpretations, but Congress thought that the veterans were entitled to disability benefits and basically prioritized, and to allow them to be stripped by a state court in very narrow circumstances is not what was intended,” Clyborne said in an interview. Several previous cases have addressed the division of retirement pay and disability benefits in military divorces. In Howell v. Howell, the Supreme Court ruled in 2017 that state courts cannot require a veteran to compensate his spouse half his retirement pay when he waived a portion of it to receive non-taxable VA disability compensation. The Court has not scheduled a date for Marschner v. Marschner, although the case could be heard as early as January. Clyborne said the case has the potential to affect divorce agreements for veterans who receive Combat-Related Specialty Compensation, Concurrent Retirement Disability Pay and other benefits. “Hopefully it will settle a lot of questions folks have been wrestling with,” Clyborne said.

title: Beyond the Headlines: Three small stories, one important message - opinion
body: The following are three special messages I received this week that I'd like to share here. Each is beautiful and moving in its own right, but together they reminded me of our strength and unity, and of something we may have lost sight of amid the election campaigning.The first message came from Sderot. A group of tenth-grade girls from the city's Be'eri Ulpana recently took a trip to Kiryat Shmona. They encountered a city coming back to life, with new families moving in, but they also saw the enormous challenges it still faces. So they decided to return this week, this time with a different purpose."We're heading to Kiryat Shmona, all the way from Sderot, for three days of volunteering and community service. Every donation we receive by next week will help us bring light to Kiryat Shmona."Then they sent me a detailed document titled "Partnership Proposal." With youthful enthusiasm, but also an impressive sense of responsibility, they outlined exactly how they intend to spend the NIS 50,000 they are raising."Precisely because we know what it means to be resilient, to be evacuated from our homes, to miss home, and to cope with hardship, we want to come and help, from the south to the north."Their proposal includes an itemized budget, from board games that will remain in the city's schools, to shopping at local businesses, to a project in which they will interview 20 longtime residents, hear their stories, and publish a special newsletter honoring them.'Nice to Meet You'The second message came from an initiative called "Nice to Meet You," a project that was first featured right here in this column.Dr. Eliezer Be'eri, director of the Rehabilitation and Respiratory Care Department at ALYN Hospital for children, suffered a cardiac arrest while playing squash. His wife, Shira, was shocked to discover that he had been rushed to the hospital and admitted as an "unidentified patient" because no one had recognized him.She chose a lovely photograph of her husband, wrote a short account of his life, and hung it beside his hospital bed. The first nurse who saw the poster told Shira how inspiring and motivating it was. When Dr. Be'eri recovered, thank God, the two of them began promoting the idea.Their goal is to help medical staff in hospital departments see the patient as a whole person, rather than simply as a medical file. Volunteers create personalized posters that are displayed beside patients' beds, allowing everyone to get to know them a little better and bring a greater sense of humanity to the medical experience.The volunteers visit hospital departments, sit with patients or their families, and get to know the person behind the diagnosis. To date, they have created some 3,000 posters.Remembering those who fell in Kfar AzaThen came the third message. Rabbi Moshe Shachor of the Ein Yehudit organization from Sderot sent me moving photographs from the Keshet School in the Sha'ar HaNegev Regional Council.Another public, nonreligious school is helping to write a Torah scroll. This happens quite often, but this week there was a particularly poignant moment of coming full circle, a special connection between religious and secular Jews, and between this world and the next."A few years ago," Rabbi Shachor told me, "my friend Ofir Libstein, of blessed memory, from Kibbutz Kfar Aza called me and our mutual friend, Rabbi Yehuda Alon of the Sulamot organization. He wanted to commission a Torah scroll for the children of Sha'ar HaNegev. We began working on the project."On October 7, Ofir, who was head of the Sha'ar HaNegev Regional Council, was among the first people murdered. We remembered his request, which had now become his final wish."Precisely on October 7, three years later, we held a ceremony as part of the Otiot Shel Ahavah (Letters of Love) organization, which brings Torah scrolls to Jewish communities around the world. After Jews from around the world had written letters in the scroll, the schoolchildren also wrote letters in the new Sefer Torah, in memory of Ofir and all those from Kfar Aza who fell on October 7."The new head of the Regional Council, Uri Epstein, came to offer his blessings. Uri is Ofir's brother-in-law. Uri's son, Neta, was also killed that day, as was his mother, Bilha Epstein."It's hard to describe the emotion and the extraordinary intensity of that moment, as we watched the sacred letters being written into the Torah scroll that will be brought to Kibbutz Kfar Aza."Something shifted within all of us, especially the children, who have all been through so many challenges and upheavals. We saw the light in the eyes of the next generation. We felt that we had fulfilled the mission Ofir had entrusted to us."ChoicesThese words are being written before the elections in Israel, but they will be published after the elections. A great deal of energy has gone into deciding which ballot to place in the ballot box. That is important, of course, but let's take the word elections, which in Hebrew also means choices, and apply it to other areas of our lives. Let's think about the other decisions we make. Even without multimillion-shekel campaigns trying to influence our opinions, we should remember that we have the right to choose, and not only in the political sense.This is a good time to recall the words of Maimonides: “Every person should regard himself throughout the year as though he is half meritorious and half guilty. And the entire world, too, is half meritorious and half guilty. If he commits a single sin, he tips the balance for himself and the entire world toward guilt, bringing about destruction. If he performs a single mitzvah, he tips the balance for himself and the entire world toward merit, bringing salvation and deliverance to himself and to them.”Our freedom to choose does not end at the ballot box. It continues every moment of our lives.In these weeks, as we read the weekly Torah portions, Avraham Avinu and Sarah Imeinu step onto the stage of history. Verse after verse, they choose goodness, faith, justice, and integrity. The Torah describes the good and righteous choices they make in their relationships with their family, their neighbors, and even their enemies.Generation after generation, we continue to choose to follow in their footsteps.Want to read more by Sivan Rahav Meir? Google The Daily Thought or visit sivanrahavmeir.com

Monday’s display unfolded before astonished residents, with the F-16’s engines roaring overhead and the frigate Kimon lying silently in the port below. The scene evoked a simulated combat scenario, bringing together two of the Greek Armed Forces’ principal military assets: the Hellenic Air Force’s fighter aircraft and the Hellenic Navy’s modern frigate. Their joint presence offered a dramatic demonstration of Greece’s air and naval capabilities. title: Op-Ed: The US Navy CAN Fix the Fleet with Distributed Manufacturing
body: It’s easy to be a critic of U.S. Navy programs. Bureaucratic friction, backlogged shipyards and workforce bottlenecks have made skepticism the default position. But as the Founding Father of the modern U.S. Navy Teddy Roosevelt said: It’s not the critic who counts but the man who is actually in the arena. By George Whittier, CEO of Fairbanks Morse Defense Contrary to skeptics, the challenges facing the fleet are not insurmountable. America can rebuild naval power. But it will require a transformation, not just at the policy level, but a practical shift in the way we design, build and acquire ships. Modular assemblies, distributed manufacturing and commonality of parts across ship classes are all critical, interconnected elements of how industry can adapt to fix the fleet at speed and scale. The Navy’s 2026 Shipbuilding Plan takes an important step in recognizing the need for change. It demands an increase in distributed shipbuilding from 10% today to 50% in the long term. This call comes amid multi-year, multibillion-dollar backlogs at U.S. shipyards and labor shortages have stifled throughput and maintenance at key ports. Rather than pushing more work to backlogged shipyards, distributed manufacturing leans into a geographically diverse supplier base. It relies on domestic and allied original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and suppliers to deliver complete assemblies for final assembly in the shipyard. Contrary to legitimate concerns about domestic sourcing, a distributed approach does not conflict with national sovereignty. It reinforces a broader trend of localized production to regional talent and manufacturing resources to meet the demand we’re seeing from global navies. A Geographic Solution Many of the delays plaguing surface vessels and submarine fleets stem from an overreliance on a small number of capacity-constrained shipyards. Instead of centralizing production around a few drydocks, the industry should be looking beyond the ports to broaden and strengthen the existing supplier base. Right now, a large portion of maritime industrial capacity is chronically underutilized. In its annual survey of companies, the Amphibious Warship Industrial Base Coalition ( AWIBC ) found only 8% of suppliers were operating at full capacity. Across the industry, up to 90% of U.S. suppliers report excess capacity that is ready to be mobilized. Fairbanks Morse Defense’s naval handling facility in Peterborough, Ontario. The facility became FMD’s official Canadian headquarters in July 2026. (Credit: FMD) Similarly, shipyards are reckoning with massive labor shortfalls. The U.S. Navy has estimated industry will need to hire 250,000 new workers over the next decade to meet fleet goals. At the same time, young workers are facing disproportionate job displacement due to artificial intelligence and market uncertainty. The answer to this challenge is not to relocate thousands of new workers to already-crowded coastal hubs. The demand for skilled labor is too great not to take advantage of the geographic distribution of talent. Changing the approach will not only relieve pressure on shipyards, it will expand the talent pool and create the high-paying jobs that help rebuild local communities and economies. The Flipside of the Same Coin The irony is that there is nothing new about distributed manufacturing. It’s how world-class shipbuilders in Japan and South Korea produce tens of millions of tons of ships per year, compared to the tens of thousands of tons produced by the United States. The American automotive sector has used distributed manufacturing for decades, building one of the most prolific manufacturing industries in the world. These principles can and must be applied to American shipbuilding. There is a caveat, however. For the shift to be successful, it will not only require changing where maritime systems are built, but what is being built. Commonality and standardization of parts and designs answer the question of what and serve as the flipside of the distributed manufacturing coin. While there are valid reasons for customization and some degree of “boutique” design, commonality and interchangeability form the fundamental building blocks of an efficient, scalable maritime defense industry. Design commonality helps suppliers achieve economies of scale and benefit from large-volume orders across ship classes across allied fleets. Without it, production will remain limited to low-volume, high-cost customization. The newly established Davit Manufacturing Center of Excellence launched in Redzikowo, Poland under Vestdavit, a Fairbanks Morse Defense company, with the support of the Pomeranian Regional Development Agency and Polish Investment Zone. (Credit: FMD) One of the reasons the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer (DDG-51) has the longest continuous production run of any surface combatant in the U.S. Navy is because of the high degree of commonality across flights. The hull, propulsion and other core structural systems have remained constant for decades, while upgrading sensors, software and combat capabilities. Stable, standardized designs are precisely what the supply chain needs to achieve accelerated demand. They provide a repeatable manufacturing baseline that drives down unit costs, improves speed, production maturity and builds workforce competency. The advantages of modular production extend beyond industrial efficiency or workforce retention and beyond a single nation’s shipyards or supplier base. Applying a distributed approach to what and where ships are being built becomes a force multiplier. Production can be localized to domestic or allied suppliers, relying on a broader, more geographically diverse base to meet global demand and support maintenance, repair and overhaul. This is not at the expense of national sovereignty and does not mean producing identical hulls. Instead, it relies on shared standards and common designs that allow suppliers to plug into a more predictable, long-term national and multinational demand signal. Across North America and Europe, nations are committing large portions of their defense budgets to modernize and rebuild the industrial base. The U.S. shipbuilding budget for FY2027 is $65.8 billion , with $8.6 billion dedicated to the maritime industrial base. European members of NATO are expected to spend roughly $639 billion on defense. Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the United Kingdom are aggressively increasing naval spending. These commitments give industry an opportunity to build capacity that lasts. The challenge for shipbuilders, suppliers and policymakers is transforming historic government investments into more ships, faster repairs and a stronger fleet. Success will depend on the production model used. We must give manufacturers stable designs and predictable orders, qualify more suppliers to produce complete assemblies, put available capacity to work across the country, then bring those assemblies together at the shipyard. Restoring naval power is not an abstract concept. It depends on us stepping into the arena and implementing practical changes. Together, these can fundamentally alter the pace at which the Navy builds and sustains its fleet. title: B.C. First Nations chief warns ripping up DRIPA is a ‘declaration of war’
body:
The newly-elected B.C. Conservative government says B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act must be repealed.
However, the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs warns against ripping up the agreement and instead urges using it as a framework for reconciliation.
On the campaign trail, the BC Conservatives have repeatedly said that repealing B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA) was a top priority.
Now that they are forming a majority government , First Nations are warning that it can’t happen.
“We’re not going to stand idly by while the government-elect does, in fact, rip it up,” Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, president of the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs said.
The day after winning the election, Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said his party is committed to repealing DRIPA, which was unanimously passed in the legislature in 2019.
Doerkson said on Sunday that since then, DRIPA has only caused more problems.
“The reality is it hasn’t solved anything,” Doerkson said.
“We are in court all over British Columbia with respect to docks at Pender Harbour, mining opportunities in the province. It hasn’t solved anything. And what we need to do is work together for the betterment of all people in British Columbia.”
Phillip calls DRIPA the solution, describing it as the roadmap to reconciliation.
He said he expects the new government to work meaningfully with First Nations to recognize their inherent title and rights, describing it as a historical crossroads.
“Is British Columbia going to become a war zone, or are we going to continue the challenging work of reconciliation?” he said.
“We face off with Colonel Doerkson and his crew. We’ll see where we end up, but we’re not about to roll over.”
Doerkson said his party is contemplating a shortened fall session, meaning the contentious issue of DRIPA likely will not be on the table until the spring.
However, First Nations groups are making it clear where they stand and the possible consequences.

title: Judge rules Trump DOJ 'unlawfully' fired Maurene Comey
body:
Judge Jesse Furman said Comey’s termination violated civil service rules.
A federal judge in New York on Monday ruled against President Donald Trump and the Justice Department over the firing of Maurene Comey , daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from the Manhattan U.S. attorney's office.
Judge Jesse Furman said Comey's termination violated civil service rules.
"Yes, the Attorney General is authorized by law to remove an AUSA. But the Attorney General (and anyone to whom the Attorney General delegates that authority) is also limited by law, namely the CSRA, to do so only in a particular manner and only for certain reasons," the judge wrote.
Furman ordered Maurene Comey, who most recently led the prosecution of Sean "Diddy" Combs , reinstated with back pay.
In addition to calling her termination unlawful, Furman decided Trump and the DOJ violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and Maurene Comey's due process rights.
"The Department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course," a DOJ spokesperson told ABC News.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York declined to comment.
ABC News has reached out to Maurene Comey for comment.
Furman's ruling outlines that Maurene Comey's reinstatement applies from the date of her termination in July of 2025 until December, when she effectively resigned from her role by accepting a new job in the private sector.
In ordering Maurene Comey's reinstatement, Furman rejected what he described as the Trump administration's "sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority."
The Trump administration had argued that not only was Maurene Comey's firing lawful under federal statute, but that the laws protecting civil servants were also an unconstitutional intrusion into Trump's authority.
"The question at the heart of this case is whether these limitations on the removal of Assistant United States Attorneys are consistent with Article II and the constitutional separation of powers," Judge Furman wrote.
To make its argument, the DOJ pointed to the Supreme Court's decision in Trump v. Slaughter -- where the justices effectively supercharged presidential power by greenlighting the firing of the leaders of independent federal agencies -- and the Trump v. United States immunity case
"On their view, AUSAs who represent the United States in criminal cases in court exercise prosecutorial and investigatory functions that fall squarely within the President's 'conclusive and preclusive' powers," Furman wrote. "Accordingly, they argue, the President -- and, by extension, the heads of departments appointed by the President -- must have the power to remove such AUSAs for any reason or no reason at all."
But Furman rejected the DOJ's interpretation of the legal precedent, pointing to decades of other cases which affirm the legal protections for line prosecutors. He also noted that neither case cited by the DOJ applies to inferior officers or "supports their sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority."
"Defendants' argument is contrary to an unbroken line of Supreme Court decisions dating back almost two centuries, and the Supreme Court itself has not formally overruled any of those decisions. That is sufficient, in itself, to reject the argument," wrote Judge Furman.
To accept the DOJ's argument, Furman wrote, would "unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system."
Maurene Comey was an assistant U.S. attorney who successfully prosecuted Ghislaine Maxwell , the former associate of sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and multiple gang members before the split verdict last year in the trial of Combs, who was convicted of a prostitution-related charge but acquitted of more serious charges.
She was also involved in the office's case against Epstein, who died by suicide in 2019 at New York City's Metropolitan Correctional Center while he was awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.
Trump fired James Comey during his first term in office after Comey announced publicly that Trump's 2016 campaign was being investigated over potential ties to Russia.
Prior to Maurene Comey's firing, Trump privately vented about having a Comey work in his administration, sources previously told ABC News.
Earlier this year, Furman blocked the Justice Department's attempt to move Maurene Comey's lawsuit over her firing as a federal prosecutor out of court.
The Justice Department argued at the time that her case belongs before the Merit Systems Protection Board and not in federal district court.
Furman decided the case belongs with him because Maurene Comey was fired pursuant to the president's executive authority and not the usual procedures for civil servants.
"Maurene Comey was, by all accounts, an exemplary Assistant United States Attorney. In her nearly ten years working at the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York, she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases, and she consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike," the judge's opinion in April said.
The DOJ, in court filings, has characterized Comey's case as routine.
"A federal employee's claims that removal from federal service was arbitrary and capricious or conducted in a manner that did not provide the process to which they contend they were due is not a novel issue," government attorneys previously said.
Following her termination last year, Maurene Comey told colleagues in a farewell email that she was fired as a federal prosecutor without being told a reason but urged them not to succumb to the "fear" she said her firing could cause.
"If a career prosecutor can be fired without reason, fear may seep into the decision of those who remain," Comey said in her email, a copy of which was obtained by ABC News. "Do not let that happen."

title: European Shipowners Seek €33 Billion to Fund Green Transition
body: European shipowners are calling for a threefold increase in emissions allowances to support shipping’s green transition, arguing that the European Commission’s proposed funding will not cover the high cost of cleaner fuels and technologies. A new study by the European Community Shipowners’ Associations (ECSA) estimates that the sector needs at least €33 billion between 2028 and 2040, three times the approximately €11 billion available under the Commission’s proposal. The estimate assumes a carbon emissions allowance price of €100 per tonne of CO₂. ECSA notes that alternative marine fuels currently cost an average of four times as much as conventional fuels. How the proposed funding mechanism would work The proposal centres on the European Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism, which aims to help shipping companies adopt cleaner fuels and technologies. Under the scheme, companies would receive carbon emissions allowances with financial value to offset part of the additional cost of the green transition. The European Commission proposes allocating 110 million allowances for 2028–2040. ECSA argues that the sector needs at least 330 million allowances, three times the proposed allocation. High costs of alternative fuels The substantial price gap between conventional and alternative fuels remains one of the biggest obstacles to shipping’s transition to cleaner energy. ECSA says sustainable marine fuels cost an average of four times more than conventional alternatives. The Commission’s proposal would allow the SMAP mechanism to cover 55% of the remaining cost difference for biogas and advanced biofuels, 80% for low-carbon hydrogen and comparable fuels, and up to 90% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin. The scheme would also cover 90% of the additional costs of eligible technologies. However, ECSA warns that companies cannot count on receiving these maximum support rates. If applications exceed the available funding, the mechanism would reduce support proportionally across applicants. The association therefore considers the total number of available allowances crucial to helping shipping companies plan future investments with greater certainty. Shipping contributes around €9 billion annually to the EU emissions market The study also highlights shipping’s financial contribution to the European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). Although shipping accounts for approximately 10% of emissions covered by the EU ETS, the sector purchases around 90 million allowances annually. This represents nearly 20% of the allowances auctioned under the system. At an illustrative price of €100 per allowance, the sector faces an annual cost of approximately €9 billion. Unlike other European industries, including steelmaking, cement production and aviation, shipping has not received free emissions allowances. From the 2026 emissions year, shipping companies must cover 100% of the emissions falling under the European system. ECSA estimates that, if emissions remain at current levels, shipping’s total obligation for 2028–2040 would amount to approximately 1.17 billion allowances, worth €117 billion at the assumed price of €100 each. Even if the Commission adopted ECSA’s proposal for 330 million allowances, the funding directed towards the green transition would cover only around 28% of that total cost. Under the Commission’s current proposal, the share would stand at approximately 9%. European shipowners lead orders for alternative-fuel vessels The study also highlights European shipowners’ role in ordering vessels capable of using sustainable fuels. According to figures cited by ECSA, European owners account for 44% of the global capacity of vessels on order that can use sustainable fuels. However, building new ships alone will not deliver the necessary emissions reductions. The sector also needs sufficient supplies of alternative fuels at competitive prices, alongside the infrastructure and technologies required to use them. ECSA is therefore calling for energy-efficiency projects to qualify for support. Such investments could reduce ships’ fuel consumption and emissions directly. SMAP could cut annual emissions by up to nine million tonnes The proposed mechanism could deliver environmental benefits beyond financial support for shipping companies. According to the European Commission’s impact assessment, cited by ECSA, SMAP could reduce annual greenhouse gas emissions by between 1.7 million and nine million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent by 2035, depending on the level of available funding. ECSA argues that developing a viable market for alternative fuels could accelerate shipping’s energy transition and help the sector meet the targets of the EU’s FuelEU Maritime Regulation. The study nevertheless acknowledges significant uncertainties in its projections. Future fuel prices, production capacity and the development of new technologies remain difficult to predict. title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push
body:
Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom at its experience level of 70 or below.
Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter. The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people.
Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies. Capital expenditures for the September quarter should exceed $50 billion, Microsoft said in July. In the same quarter a year ago, capital spending and finance leases came to $34.9 billion.
That's put a strain on Microsoft's finances. In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for. Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees .
"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees . "This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program."
Microsoft is in the midst of a business model transformation , increasingly trying to charge clients based on how much AI they actually use. It has armed programmers , sellers and supply chain workers with AI tools and observed noticeable results . At the same time, the 51-year-old maker of Windows and Office wants to ensure that it has the right talent to go after its most compelling new growth opportunities.
The idea is to make the shift without weakening Microsoft's financial profile. In the second quarter, cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year.
Some marketing, sales and engineering teams have decided not to participate in the new buyout, the person said. Employees must decide whether to take the offer in early December, and those participating will leave on Dec. 31, the person added.
More than 30% of those who could join the voluntary retirement program went ahead with it, Microsoft said in July . But that was open to those at the senior director level of 67 and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan. The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around.
On Wednesday, Microsoft is scheduled to report third-quarter results.

title: Scam ads in Yahoo Mail hid a fake Microsoft support alert
body: Sponsored messages in the AT&T edition of Yahoo Mail led some readers to a fake Microsoft security alert. The alert told them to call a support number. Our visits from a data center or a phone got a dating or personal finance article instead. William Vincent, a whack.sh customer, noticed something off about the ads and asked Tuxxin to dig further. We traced two scam operations through the same ad slot on October 7 and 8, 2026. One of them had also used a Taboola ad on September 24. The scam kit behind the first ad appears in 747 public scans from July 12 to October 10, the 90 days our search could reach. Those scans cover 536 cloud hostnames and 160 phone numbers. The technical writeup on whack.sh traces both ad chains hop by hop and lists every indicator. The ad looked like a new message The ad sat in the inbox list like an email. Its sender line read "CHECKOUTERS" and its subject read "(1) New Message". A small "Ad" label marked it as sponsored. The ad row in AT&T Yahoo Mail, October 2026. Screenshot by William Vincent, cropped to the ad, with personal details removed. Taboola sells the native ads across Yahoo's sites under a 30-year agreement . Yahoo's ad space opened to Taboola advertisers worldwide in October 2023. When it announced the deal in 2022, Taboola said Yahoo reached nearly 900 million monthly users worldwide. A click on the ad passed through Taboola's click tracker under the publisher ID "yahoo-mail-att". That is the AT&T edition of Yahoo Mail, which serves att.net, sbcglobal.net, bellsouth.net and other AT&T addresses. In our scans, only Windows desktops on home broadband got the scam whack.sh , Tuxxin's URL scanner, opens one link from several networks at once and compares what each receives. It scanned the original ad click links that William Vincent sent us. Windows desktops on home broadband lines at Comcast, Charter and Cox got the scam. One Comcast visit got the scam and the next got the plain article. An Android phone on T-Mobile got a dating article, and a visit from a data center in France got a personal loan article. The same ad link from a data center and from home broadband. whack.sh scan, October 8, 2026. The phone numbers are stamped FAKE. The scam only appeared on visits that arrived through a fresh ad click. We opened the first ad's landing page directly eight times. Every visit returned the dating article. Two operations used the same ad slot The first ad led to a dating article site that covered itself with a full-screen frame from Microsoft Azure. The frame showed the fake alert while the address bar kept showing the dating site. The second ad passed through a Branch deep link and a filtering server (TDS) that sorted visitors by network. Our home broadband visit went to a scam page on Azure with a live chat window. The same chat account appeared on another scam page on September 24, reached through a Taboola ad. The scam kit runs on hundreds of cloud hostnames The first operation's scam page comes from a kit, a set of files reused on every host. Public scans recorded it on 536 hostnames between July 12 and October 10, 2026, most of them on Microsoft Azure Container Apps. A second review by Kirk of ohey.ca added 31 of those hostnames. The pages listed 160 phone numbers, 126 of them US toll-free numbers. The kit sends each visitor to a version for their operating system: Windows, macOS, Android or iOS. The Windows version adds a fake locked screen with a Microsoft account sign-in box. Its fields are read-only, and the box points the visitor to the phone number. When we re-checked the hostnames on October 11, nine still served the kit. How many people saw the ads Taboola holds the impression and click counts for both ads. We reported both ad chains to Taboola on October 11, 2026 and requested those counts. No exposure counts have been supplied. The first ad's tracking link listed a cost of 0.25 per click, with no currency. Victims reported $1.46 billion in tech support fraud losses in 2024 to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center. People aged 60 and over reported $982 million of that total. What we reported The scammers used services from each company below. We sent each one the evidence for its part on October 11, 2026, and filed reports with the FTC and the FBI. Recipient What we sent Response as of October 11 Taboola Both ad chains, with a request for impression and click counts Case opened Yahoo Screenshots and a short alert offering the full report and indicator list. Its form could not take the full report. Case opened Microsoft Azure abuse portal The Azure-hosted scam pages. Only the side-by-side capture above could be attached, so the hostname lists were left out. Submitted, no case number given Microsoft Report Fraud The Microsoft impersonation and tech support scam "Your request has been submitted." Branch The two deep link apps in the ad chains "Thank you for your feedback!" Tawk.to The live chat account on the scam pages "Report received." apiip.net The API key the scam pages used for location lookups No reply Vultr The filtering server (TDS) address and the ad redirect chain No reply Namecheap The filtering server (TDS) domain and the ad redirect chain Case opened Cloudflare Registrar The ad landing domain, checkouters[.]app Case opened Cloudflare Trust and Safety checkouters[.]app, then further context and a list of 13 Cloudflare Workers and Pages hosts running the kit Said it could not detect abusive or malicious content and asked for more specific information. No reply yet to our follow-ups. Laravel Forge 34 on-forge[.]com hosts running the kit Laravel Security said it disabled "the domain in question" and notified the responsible party. The reply did not name the host, and we have not checked the result. REG.RU The tracker domain and how the scam pages used it Request opened Stellar Group The tracker's server No reply FTC The scheme and the callback numbers Report filed FBI IC3 The ad chains, callback numbers and technical evidence Complaint filed On the evening of October 11, Microsoft Edge showed a phishing warning for checkouters[.]app. When the warning first appeared, and what triggered it, is unknown. If you saw this alert Microsoft states that genuine Microsoft error messages never include a phone number to call. Close the browser tab. If the page blocks closing, end the browser in Task Manager on Windows or with Force Quit on a Mac. If you called the number, uninstall any remote access tool the caller asked you to install. title: I held a séance with dead programming languages — meet seance 👻
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built seance is a small Python CLI that lets you ask a question and get an answer from the ghost of a long-dead programming language — COBOL (1959), FORTRAN (1957), BASIC (1964), or ALGOL (1958). Each spirit answers in its own voice: COBOL in formal ALL-CAPS divisions, FORTRAN in terse numerics and GOTOs, BASIC in friendly numbered lines, ALGOL in precise begin/end blocks. It takes the Week 4 theme two ways at once: it is spooky (a séance, on Halloween week), and it honors the past (the languages that built computing, remembered in their own words, in the spirit of Día de los Muertos). Repo: https://github.com/sonawaneutkarsh/seance Demo Real runs, offline mode, no model needed: $ python3 -m seance "Will my code outlive me?" --spirit cobol --offline The spirit of COBOL ( 1959 ) speaks : PROCEDURE DIVISION . I HAVE READ YOUR QUERY , AND I HAVE FILED IT . Your question — "Will my code outlive me?" — echoes in the machine room. The dead answer in formal , procedural , ALL-CAPS divisions . END PROGRAM . I return to the mainframe now . It never sleeps . [source: offline fallback (deterministic)] $ python3 -m seance "Why did you disappear?" --spirit basic --offline The spirit of BASIC (1964) speaks: 30 REM I HAVE BEEN WAITING SINCE 1984. ASK AWAY. Your question — "Why did you disappear?" — echoes in the machine room. The dead answer in friendly, numbered lines, eager to help. GOTO 10. The loop closes. The loop always closes. [source: offline fallback (deterministic)] Code seance/spirits.py — the four spirits and the deterministic fallback seance/ollama_client.py — minimal stdlib Ollama client seance/__main__.py — the CLI: summon, list spirits, offline mode tests/test_seance.py — 9 tests, all passing (Ollama mocked) How I Built It The question goes to Gemma, running locally through Ollama , prompted to answer in the chosen spirit's voice. No accounts, no API keys, no question leaves your machine. And because a séance should work with the lights off, there is an honest offline fallback: when no model is reachable, lines are picked by hashing (spirit, question), so the same question always summons the same answer — and the reply always labels its source, so a fallback is never passed off as AI. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? The whole project only works because the pieces are open. Gemma is an open-weight model I can run on my own laptop, so communing with the past does not mean uploading my questions to someone else's server — and the dead languages themselves are the original open inheritance: ALGOL's ideas live on in nearly every language used today precisely because they were shared, not locked away. A closed model behind an API could vanish tomorrow and take the séance with it; a local open-weight model and a stdlib-only codebase will still answer in ten years. The past, kept open, stays reachable. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma — Gemma (via local Ollama) powers the AI séances. Tags: #devchallenge #hf26challenge
