title: Canada-U.S. trade talks ‘moving quickly’ at political level ahead of midterms: sources
body:
The once-stalled trade talks between the U.S. and Canada are now “moving quickly” at the political level, multiple sources with direct knowledge of the negotiations have told Global News.
But despite talks moving forward after almost two months of stalemate, the sources expressed skepticism that a deal can get done before the American midterm elections on Nov. 3. Others noted that U.S. President Donald Trump routinely says deals have been struck, only to blow them up again — such as during the last round of U.S. trade talks in August.
The most recent discussions have stayed at the political level,with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic Leblanc leading the Canadian side, the sources said. More formal negotiations between trade representatives have not yet taken place, according to comments from Canada’s lead negotiator Janice Charette last week.
Sources told Global News that the Canadian side views this as a window to reach a deal with Trump’s administration ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Meanwhile Reuters, citing four Canadian and two U.S. sources, said the two countries are working on a deal to ease Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel and autos ahead of those elections.
“Canada is ready to sign an agreement that is in the interest of Canadians, all Canadians. We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August,” said Prime Minister Mark Carney in a press conference Monday.
“To the extent to which the U.S. is moving towards accepting those aspects, then there’s a greater prospect of a deal. But if there is (a deal offered), we’ll judge it as a whole.”
Asked how he knows that Trump will sign the next agreement “in pen” — meaning standing by whatever agreement is reached by the two countries — Carney responded simply “I don’t.”
Trump’s tariff war has become a political issue for Republicans, particularly in key Senate races in Michigan and Maine, as the GOP braces for what looks like a drubbing in the midterms.
Global News granted the sources anonymity to speak openly about the politically sensitive negotiations.
If a deal were to be struck over the coming week, two sources said the Americans would need to make multiple concessions on issues that led to talks breaking down on Aug. 21. Those issues included Canada’s freedom to strike trade deals with other countries, and what U.S. tariffs on auto, steel and aluminum would apply to under a new deal.
Whether all the various players in the Trump administration would agree to those concessions is an open question.
Last week, Carney signaled the Trump administration has already shown some flexibility on their previous demands.
“They’ve already moved on several (of Canada’s red lines), by the way, since we rightly walked away from a deal that wasn’t in Canada’s interest,” Carney said on the Real Talk with Ryan Jespersen podcast.
Trump, for his part, told supporters on Sunday that he expects his trade war with Canada to end “pretty soon.”
As the sources noted, there’s no indication Canada will take the U.S. president at his word on that. During the same speech to supporters, in Port Huron, Michigan, Trump launched into his usual invective against Canada, suggesting the country has been “ripping off” the U.S. for years. But as the midterms approach, it suggests that Canada-U.S. trade is rattling around somewhere in Trump’s mind.
Trade talks between the two counties have been off since Canada walked away from negotiations in late August. After the talks collapsed, Carney said the U.S. made a last-minute push for language that would limit Canada’s ability to enter into trade deals with other countries, water down French language requirements, and hurt the country’s struggling auto industry.
The Trump administration responded with additional tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of Canadian goods, and Ottawa responded in kind with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs.
On Friday, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins — in a tough fight to hold her seat in Maine — revealed that Trump agreed to lift tariffs on Canadian corrugated paper, plastic boxes and several types of agricultural machinery important to her state.
“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said in a statement.
But while Trump lifted some tariffs, he imposed new ones on Canadian goods like cocoa powder, paints and varnishes, shampoos, vinyl flooring, archery equipment and carpets. The Americans will now apply 50 per cent tariffs on sewage sludge and some types of municipal waste.
The trash issue appeared to seemed to strike a chord with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who appeared at the Port Huron rally with Trump.
“Those Canadians send truck after truck loaded with their trash into our state,” Rogers, in a competitive race with Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, said to boos from the crowd.
“The president, just this week, announced he’s going to tariff those trash trucks.”
With files from the Canadian Press and Reuters.

title: AWS Transit Gateway and Cloud WAN Introduce 1:1 NAT for Seamless Network Interconnection
body:
Posted on Oct 26 • Originally published at pklavc.com • AI-assisted
AWS announced on 2026-10-23 that AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN now support managed one-to-one (1:1) Network Address Translation (NAT) directly on their attachments. The capability integrates with Regional Private NAT Gateway and is available in all AWS commercial regions where Transit Gateway and Cloud WAN operate.
1:1 NAT enables private networks with overlapping Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) blocks to communicate without renumbering either network, deploying a separate NAT appliance, or writing explicit return-traffic rules.
Customers define address-translation rules on a Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN attachment, specifying the private IP range each source CIDR translates to.
Translation applies automatically in both directions across Amazon VPC, AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Direct Connect, and SD-WAN appliances connected through Transit Gateway Connect.
AWS operates, scales, and manages the NAT capability as part of the attachment; no separate NAT appliance is deployed by the customer.
Configuration is supported via the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), AWS SDKs, and AWS CloudFormation.
Translated traffic can be monitored through Amazon CloudWatch metrics and Amazon EventBridge events.
Pricing follows the Amazon VPC pricing model; the announcement directs users to the VPC pricing page for details.
Documentation references include the AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN product pages and their respective developer guides.
The introduction of managed 1:1 NAT on Transit Gateway and Cloud WAN attachments addresses a long-standing architectural constraint in enterprise cloud networking: the inability to interconnect private networks that share overlapping RFC 1918 address space. Historically, this scenario forced organizations into one of three undesirable paths — manual IP renumbering (high risk, high effort), deployment and maintenance of third-party NAT appliances (operational overhead, scaling limits), or complex policy-based routing with asymmetric return-path handling (fragile, difficult to audit). By embedding 1:1 NAT directly into the attachment plane, AWS eliminates the need for any of these workarounds for the supported attachment types.
From an operational perspective, the feature shifts NAT state management from customer-run instances or virtual appliances to a fully managed, regionally scoped service. The announcement confirms that translation is applied automatically in both directions with no separate return-traffic rule, which implies symmetric NAT behavior handled by the control plane. This design reduces the surface area for misconfiguration — a common source of connectivity failures in hybrid and multi-cloud environments — because the same attachment configuration governs both ingress and egress translation.
The integration with Regional Private NAT Gateway suggests that the underlying data plane leverages the same managed NAT infrastructure used for outbound internet connectivity, but repurposed for inter-attachment translation. This has practical consequences for throughput and availability: customers inherit the horizontal scaling and zonal resilience characteristics of the Regional Private NAT Gateway without provisioning capacity explicitly. However, the announcement does not disclose per-attachment throughput limits, latency overhead, or whether translation occurs at the network layer (L3) or includes port-level mapping (L4). These parameters would affect capacity planning for high-throughput workloads such as data replication or real-time analytics across merged VPCs.

title: Presigned Uploads for Large E-commerce Images (and the Trade-offs)
body: To use presigned URLs for uploading AI-generated images, let your backend authorize a short-lived upload and let the client send the bytes directly to object storage. Large product images never pass through your application server, and the browser or worker never receives a permanent access key. That is the short answer to using presigned URLs for AI-generated images in Node.js: generate a URL for one bucket and object key, preserve the headers used to sign it, then make an HTTP PUT with the image bytes. The hard part is not the PUT . It is choosing a key scheme, making retries harmless, and accepting the storage features your workload actually needs. How do I use presigned URLs for uploading AI-generated images? A presigned URL is a temporary capability. Your backend authenticates the caller and asks the storage service to create a URL scoped to a particular object. The uploader gets permission to perform that operation without getting the bucket credentials. That is the boundary. The scope matters. For a product-image pipeline, the key should carry tenant and job identity, such as tenant-42/products/job-781/hero.webp . The worker that creates the image can receive permission for that object; it should not receive permission to list every tenant's objects. Signing does not make an image private after upload. It also does not solve every concurrency problem. A retry can overwrite the same key unless the application chooses a new key or coordinates writes. There is no If-Match conditional write in the described storage surface, so strict mutual exclusion belongs in a queue or database. Headers are part of the contract. If the presigned request was generated with Content-Type: image/webp , send that same header on the upload. A mismatch can invalidate the signature or leave downstream consumers with misleading metadata. This is the sort of small edge case that tends to appear only after the first batch of generated images is already in production. How should the upload flow handle large files? For a large-file workload, keep the control plane and the data plane separate: The tenant-authenticated backend validates the requested object key and image type. It generates a presigned URL for that exact bucket and key. The Node.js worker uploads the generated bytes directly with PUT . The backend records the object key, tenant, generation job, content type, and upload result in its own database. The presign operation is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key} . The subsequent upload goes to the returned URL, not to your application endpoint. Keep the presigning endpoint behind the normal tenant authorization boundary; a signed URL is powerful precisely because it can be used by whoever obtains it until it expires. Here is a small control-plane example. It requests a presigned URL from Infrai, using the same HTTP behavior a Node.js worker would implement with Axios or the built-in https module. The URL and headers must come from the presign response; they are deliberately not reconstructed in the client. import json import os import time from pathlib import Path from urllib.error import HTTPError from urllib.request import Request , urlopen def request_presign ( bucket : str , key : str ) -> dict : endpoint = f " { os . environ [ ' INFRAI_BASE_URL ' ]. rstrip ( ' / ' ) } /storage/object/presign/ { bucket } / { key } " request = Request ( endpoint , data = b " {} " , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' INFRAI_API_KEY ' ] } " , " Content-Type " : " application/json " , " Idempotency-Key " : f " image-presign: { bucket } : { key } " , }, method = " POST " , ) for attempt in range ( 4 ): try : with urlopen ( request ) as response : if response . status < 200 or response . status >= 300 : raise RuntimeError ( f " presign failed with HTTP { response . status } " ) return json . load ( response ) except HTTPError as error : if error . code != 429 or attempt == 3 : detail = error . read (). decode ( " utf-8 " , errors = " replace " ) raise RuntimeError ( f " presign failed with HTTP { error . code } : { detail } " ) from error retry_after = error . headers . get ( " Retry-After " ) time . sleep ( float ( retry_after ) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt ) raise RuntimeError ( " presign failed after retries " ) def upload_image ( presigned_url : str , image_path : str , content_type : str ) -> None : image_bytes = Path ( image_path ). read_bytes () request = Request ( presigned_url , data = image_bytes , headers = { " Content-Type " : content_type }, method = " PUT " , ) with urlopen ( request ) as response : if response . status < 200 or response . status >= 300 : raise RuntimeError ( f " upload failed with HTTP { response . status } " ) presign = request_presign ( " catalog-images " , " tenant-42/products/job-781/hero.webp " ) upload_image ( presign [ " url " ], " hero.webp " , " image/webp " ) For very large objects, reading the whole file into memory is a poor worker design even though the request shape is correct. Stream the file in the Node.js implementation, cap concurrent uploads, and make the job retry policy explicit. If the image generator can produce a 300 MB asset, measure memory and socket pressure at that size instead of assuming that a small thumbnail test represents production. Which storage option fits the constraint? The main comparison is not a feature-count contest. It is about where large-file throughput, tenant isolation, and operational ownership sit in the system. Option Where it fits Important boundary Amazon S3 A broad default when the team wants mature object-storage controls, ecosystem integrations, and multipart workflows More service configuration and credential policy become part of the platform team's job Cloudflare R2 Useful when an existing Cloudflare deployment and its S3-compatible workflow are a strong fit Check the exact data-access, replication, and operational features required by the workload rather than assuming S3 parity MinIO A sensible choice for self-hosted or controlled infrastructure where the team owns capacity and operations The team owns upgrades, disks, availability, and the consequences of a bad capacity forecast Infrai storage A reasonable option when a backend already benefits from one REST API, one key, and one bill across services, and direct presigned uploads are enough It is not a fit for public-read image hosting, object versioning or WORM retention, self-service browser CORS configuration, cross-region replication, or GCS/B2 vendor coverage The last row needs a sober reading. A single credential and billing surface can reduce dashboard and invoice sprawl, and the same workflow gets a consistent REST boundary. That convenience does not replace an object-storage policy review. In particular, the available storage behavior has no public or public-read ACL outcome, no object versioning or object lock, and no independently exposed set_cors route for browser-direct configuration. For a tenant-scoped export, private objects plus an application-controlled download path may be exactly right. For a static catalog that must serve permanent public URLs, it is the wrong tool. For regulated records that must be immutable, lack of WORM semantics is a decision blocker, not a footnote. Keep the export private. What failure cases should the worker own? Presigned URLs do not remove failure handling; they move the bytes away from your web process. Treat a response outside the 2xx range as a failed upload and preserve the response body in structured job logs. A timeout is ambiguous: the server may have received the object even if the client did not receive the response. The retry decision deserves more room than the happy path. A 429 should honor Retry-After when it is present, then back off instead of hammering the presign endpoint. A network timeout after the PUT needs a reconciliation step because the object may exist. Query the job database first, and only issue another write when the key policy says an overwrite is safe; otherwise create a new generation key and record it as the authoritative pointer. At 300 MB, that distinction is operationally more important than shaving a round trip from the presign request. Use a deterministic object key for a generation job only when overwrite is acceptable. Otherwise, put a unique generation identifier in the key and make the database record the authoritative pointer. This is safer than retrying a write blindly when conditional writes are unavailable. The lifecycle details also matter for throughput planning. The shortest lifecycle expiration is one day, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule. If the design later switches from one-shot uploads to multipart uploads for very large images, add an explicit abort and cleanup process. Do not assume abandoned parts will disappear on their own. Browser uploads add another boundary: CORS. The browser must be allowed to send the signed request and its required headers, but the storage surface described here does not expose an independent route for setting CORS rules. A server-side worker avoids that browser configuration issue. If direct browser upload is a requirement, verify the bucket configuration and test the actual origin and headers before committing to the architecture. A measured rollout for tenant exports Start with one tenant, private keys, and a modest concurrency limit. Record object key, content type, byte count, generation ID, and the final upload status beside the export job. Compare end-to-end throughput against the application-proxy design; the useful metric is completed image bytes per worker hour, not the presign call count. Then test the awkward cases: a retry after a client timeout, two workers targeting one key, an expired URL, an incorrect Content-Type , and an interrupted large upload. Add cleanup for failed jobs before increasing concurrency. I initially treated presigning as an authentication detail. It is really a write-coordination boundary, and that distinction is what keeps a tenant export from quietly publishing the wrong image. The decision rule is compact. Choose presigned uploads when the goal is private, tenant-scoped object writes without exposing access keys and the system can coordinate keys and retries. The limitation is equally clear: choose a different storage path, or add external controls, when the product requires permanent public links, WORM retention, conditional mutual exclusion, browser-managed CORS, or cross-region replication. Sources Infrai storage documentation, available through its official documentation site Amazon S3 presigned URLs Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs MinIO presigned operations MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

title: A Privacy Policy is a promise. Zero-knowledge is a property.
body: Why we built a team workspace around one question: what does a fully compromised server learn? Most “private” workspace tools protect your data with a promise. The promise lives in a privacy policy: we will not look, we will not sell, we will not share. It may be sincere. But a promise is only as strong as the people keeping it, the staff who can reach the database, and the next attacker who gets in. lockORG takes a different approach. It is a workspace app (notes, kanban boards, tags, todos and a journal) for small teams and individuals, and everything in it is encrypted on your device before it is sent. The server stores it, syncs it, and never reads it. Nor can it. That is the difference between a promise and a property. A promise can be broken. A property is how the system is built. The one question asked of every change Every change to lockORG is judged against a single question: What does a fully compromised server learn? The answer must not grow. Here is what it is today. Imagine someone has the whole database, the image files, the logs and the server configuration. Look at the left column carefully. It is not empty, and we do not pretend it is. More on that below. Why a weak password does not sink you Most encrypted products have a quiet weakness: if your key comes only from your password, a stolen database can be attacked offline, guessing passwords as fast as hardware allows. lockORG ’s vault key is derived from two things: your password and a 128-bit account secret key. That secret key is generated on your device at sign-up, printed once in a recovery kit, and kept on your devices. The server never stores it. So even with a weak password, offline brute force against a stolen database is hopeless. Your password is never sent to the server either. Signing in uses a separate value derived through a different path, so a leaked login credential says nothing about the key that opens your data. Private means private, even from your admin In a team workspace, the natural question is: can my admin read everything? Shared material (notes, boards, tags) is encrypted under a workspace key that every verified member holds. But your todo list and your journal are encrypted under your personal key. Other members, admins included, hold no key for them. The server will not even address another member’s personal rows. What we do not claim Honesty about limits is part of the design, so here is the list we would rather say before anyone else does: Not “military-grade”, “bank-level”, “unhackable” or “100% secure”. Those phrases do not describe anything checkable. Not anonymous. The server knows your email, who is in which workspace, when you write and how much. Not protected against a malicious operator shipping malicious JavaScript to your browser. This is the known limit of any web client. Native clients with pinned cryptography are the long-term answer. Not recoverable without you. Lose your password and your recovery kit and your data is gone. Nobody, operator included, can bring it back. (An optional recovery key gives you a second way in, if you create one.) No two-factor sign-in at launch. It is planned, not shipped. No real-time co-editing. That is deliberate: it would mean either a server that sees content or a far more complex protocol. Every claim is a test A security page is easy to write. What makes lockORG ’s claims worth something is that each one is backed by a test that fails when the property breaks: published cryptographic test vectors, an authorisation test covering every API route, generated tests that try to reach across workspaces through every endpoint, tests that search browser storage for secrets after sign-in, and mutation testing on the security-critical code. The security model, the threat model and the protocol will all be published. The threat model lists, item by item, the risks that are accepted and cannot be fixed. lockORG will also be open source once a solid foundation is in place and the basic functionality has been brutally tested with early users. Opening the code is not a substitute for good engineering; it is a way to make the engineering inspectable. You will be able to read what the application does, verify the claims against the implementation, and hold us to the promises we make. When the time is right, we would rather be checked than trusted.

title: The campaign ends with Iran, and the question of trust - analysis
body: In the end, it is all about Iran.At least narrowly. More broadly, as Israelis go to the polls on Tuesday, it is about trust.Do they trust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who presents himself as the one leader capable of preventing an Iranian-inflicted second Holocaust?Or do they accept the change bloc's argument that Netanyahu can no longer be trusted, including to distinguish between what the country needs for security and what he needs for his own political survival?Do they trust the military leadership reportedly questioning his judgment? Do they trust the media reporting those questions?October 7 hovering over Israel's electionsAnd hovering over all of this is October 7, which makes each question considerably more complicated.It seems fitting that Iran should be the campaign's closing issue. The Iranian threat, and Netanyahu's claim to have the experience, determination, and international standing to confront it, have framed his reelection case. As the campaign ends, that same issue is being used to argue against giving him yet another term.For Netanyahu, Iran is the reason he must remain. For his opponents, the way he is handling Iran embodies the reason he must go.That divide came into sharp focus on Sunday when the prime minister shared an AI-generated image of a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, accompanied by a warning suggesting that his defeat could expose Israel to a second Holocaust.The message went well beyond the familiar argument that one party's security policies are better than another's. It linked the country's very survival to the continued tenure of one man.That is an enormous claim. It asks voters to believe that the institutions, capabilities, and alliances Israel has built over decades cannot adequately protect it without Netanyahu at the helm.For supporters who believe Netanyahu identified the Iranian danger early and showed a willingness to act against it, the message may reinforce an existing conviction: this is not the time to change leaders.His opponents see a prime minister turning a real national threat into a claim that he is indispensable.Iran is dangerous. It does not automatically follow that replacing Netanyahu increases that danger. Yet his campaign is asking voters to make that leap.Sunday night's N12 News site report about a confrontation between Netanyahu and IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir gave his rivals an opportunity to challenge that leap.Zamir reportedly avoided Iran war-triggering actionAccording to the report, Zamir resisted an instruction for an undisclosed military operation that defense officials feared could trigger a confrontation with Iran. He reportedly sought further deliberations and signed documentation concerning its legal authorization.Netanyahu denied any such confrontation or tension with the military's top brass over Iran.The political significance was clear. Netanyahu wants voters to ask whether they can entrust Iran policy to his rivals. The report invited them to ask whether even the military's leadership trusts his judgment.But before voters get to that question, they must ask another: Do they believe the report?For some, N12's account will be evidence that military professionals are trying to restrain a prime minister whose political considerations are shaping his security decisions.For others, it will look like another anonymously sourced story – like the subsequently contradicted report that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel visited Israel shortly before October 7 to warn of an attack – appearing at precisely the moment it could do the most electoral damage.Anonymous sources are essential to security reporting. They can expose disagreements the public has a legitimate interest in knowing about.But sources can also be motivated by institutional interests, personal grievances, and political preferences. Anonymity does not make their information false. Neither does it shield their motives or the timing of their disclosures from scrutiny.Likewise, suspecting a media agenda does not make an uncomfortable report untrue.The details matter. Zamir's request for written authorization does not, by itself, establish that an operation is unlawful. Nor does a disagreement between Netanyahu and the chief of staff establish that the prime minister is acting for electoral reasons.But in a deeply polarized country, people often consider the messenger before the message. Those who distrust Netanyahu may readily credit the account. Those who distrust the broadcaster may dismiss it just as readily.Regardless, the political significance is clear.Then October 7 enters the picture.The instinct to view the military's leadership as a professional counterweight to political calculation is understandable. But assuming military judgment deserves automatic deference – which the change bloc seems to be doing in this instance – is much harder to sustain after that catastrophic day.The military and intelligence establishments failed disastrously in their assessments and preparations, and in protecting the communities overrun by Hamas.For voters who remember those failures, a report that military officials oppose a prime minister's proposed action may prompt a blunt response: Why should we trust their judgment now?That is a legitimate question. This does not mean Zamir's judgment is wrong. It does mean that just because the military says one thing, we should automatically treat it as settled.But the question runs both ways.Netanyahu was prime minister on October 7 and bore ultimate political responsibility for the country's security. If the military's failure undermines its claim to unquestioned trust, the political leadership cannot emerge from the same disaster with its own claim intact.October 7 damaged confidence in both the political leadership and the security establishment. That is what makes this election's trust question so difficult: voters are being asked to choose whom to believe among leaders and institutions whose credibility has been badly shaken.And there is no simple formula.Military leaders can be wrong. Political leaders can correctly overrule them. Yet the decisions of elected officials – especially just days before an election – can be clouded by those electoral considerations.The Iran controversy has brought all this into focus.Netanyahu is asking voters to trust his experience. The change bloc is asking them to trust that different leaders can manage the same threats more responsibly. Both are making their case against the backdrop of October 7, which exposed the limits of experience and expertise.When Israelis go to the polls on Tuesday, they will choose a party and help determine the coalition and government that will have to address many issues beyond Iran.But the competing closing arguments about Iran sharpen the choice: whose judgment do they trust, whose warnings do they credit, and whose motives do they trust?Netanyahu says the danger is too great to replace him. His opponents say it is too great to leave him in place.On Tuesday, Israelis will decide which warning they believe.

title: Former Referee Ilias Koromilas Jailed as Two Others Face House Arrest
body: Former Greek basketball referee Ilias Koromilas has been remanded in custody following his testimony before an investigating magistrate in the BasketGate case involving alleged match-fixing and bribery. Fellow referees Vaso Tsaroucha and Tasos Pil oidis, meanwhile, will remain under house arrest with electronic monitoring bracelets, following a joint decision by the investigating magistrate and prosecutor. The court also barred Tsaroucha and Pil oidis from any involvement in basketball. They are the only defendants in the case to receive this form of pre-trial restriction, according to the report. During his testimony, Koromilas denied having any authority over referee appointments and said he could not influence the selection process. “I was never a member of the Central Refereeing Committee (KED), nor did I have any authority or involvement in the selection, appointment or replacement of referees for matches,” he reportedly told the magistrate. “Those decisions belong exclusively to the competent refereeing bodies. Consequently, I had no authority over referee appointments or replacements, nor could my position and duties have given me decisive influence over the selection and appointment process,” he added. Koromilas Denies Allegations of Bribery Koromilas also denied involvement in nine alleged acts of bribery involving referees and club officials. “I had no involvement whatsoever in the acts attributed to me, which I categorically deny in their entirety,” he reportedly said. He argued that the accusations against him relied primarily on testimony from just two people and lacked specific objective evidence establishing his personal involvement in the alleged activities. The case also includes allegations that a referee accepted bribes in connection with 13 matches he officiated, allegedly influencing their outcomes in exchange for payment. The accused referee denied any connection with paid match-fixing. During his testimony, the former referee described the allegations made against him by a prosecution witness as fabrications. He also cited a complaint he had filed against the witness for allegedly giving false testimony. Panagiotis Giannakis Incident Also Under Scrutiny Koromilas also addressed an incident involving Panagiotis Giannakis in 2018, when Giannakis coached Aris Thessaloniki. The incident concerned Giannakis’ ejection after receiving two technical fouls during a match that investigators are examining. Reports allege that the decision served as a “gift” to a person implicated in the case. Koromilas reportedly rejected that account. “Panagiotis Giannakis is a legend of Greek basketball. I would never do anything to harm him,” he said. Giannakis intends to join the proceedings in support of the prosecution. title: Six weeks from notice to KEV: the disclosure timeline behind the Plex RCE chain
body: Six weeks from notice to KEV: the disclosure timeline behind the Plex RCE chain Plex published a security notice on 1 September 2026 without naming a single CVE. By 20 October, CISA had added four identifiers to its exploited catalog and the vendor was telling owners of exposed servers to assume compromise. The gap between those two statements is the part worth studying. 1 September: a release note with no identifiers Plex announced Plex Media Server 1.43.3 and Plex Desktop 1.115.0, stating that the release addressed a number of security issues and recommending that all server owners update. The notice said CVEs had been requested and would be added to the thread once published. It also listed update instructions per platform and warned that not all app stores would carry the build immediately. That is an ordinary disclosure pattern for a vendor that wants patched binaries in place before exploit detail becomes public. For defenders it also means a version number alone was the signal available in September. 23 September: four records appear NVD published CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656 on the same day. Their scores from a secondary CVSS source are 4.3, 6.5, 4.3 and 7.2. Each record describes a distinct mechanism: an unauthenticated SSRF in /player/timeline that accepts any X-Plex-Token value; incorrect neutralization of URL values in searchOne ; an address request through the transcode path parameter; and an arbitrary file write through the TranscoderH264Options preference into a Codecs directory whose .so files are loaded without signature checks. All four name the same affected range: before 1.43.3.10861. Nothing in the four records states that they chain. That conclusion comes from the vendor. 16 October: a public proof of concept Plex reports that a public proof of concept for the chain appeared on 2026-10-16. That date matters for two reasons. It marks the point where the exploit stopped being private, and it precedes CISA's catalog entry by four days. 19 October: the vendor confirms exploitation Plex updated the same thread with the CVE table and a blunt assessment. Chained together, the issues let an unauthenticated remote attacker run code with the privileges of the Plex Media Server process. Servers on 1.43.3.10861 or later are not affected. The update also records what attackers did with the access: cryptocurrency miners and proxy software that routes other people's traffic through the victim's connection. It names process examples, myawesomeproxy , mylovelyminer and x12345 , tells operators to look for unfamiliar .so or .dll files in the Codecs folder and for outbound connections to proxystream.st , and advises anyone running an older build behind the internet to assume compromise. That last sentence is the strongest statement in the whole timeline, because it converts a patching task into an incident response task for a population of unknown size. 20 October: CISA adds all four The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog entry dated 2026-10-20 lists the four identifiers with Plex and Media Server as vendor and product. The required action points to vendor mitigations and to BOD 26-04 guidance. The deadlines split the chain: 2026-10-23 for CVE-2026-96656 and CVE-2026-96654, and 2026-11-03 for CVE-2026-96652 and CVE-2026-96655. CVE-2026-96656 also carries a forensic triage requirement. The catalog describes all four as chainable with each other, matching the vendor's account. What the timeline says about preparation Three observations follow from the dates rather than from the exploit detail. First, the release preceded the identifiers by three weeks. An organisation that tracks only CVE feeds learned nothing on 1 September, while one that tracks vendor release notes could have staged the update. Second, the exploitation report came from the vendor, not from a third-party research publication. Reading the advisory thread itself, not only its first post, was the way to learn that the flaw had moved from theoretical to active. Third, the KEV deadline for two of the four CVEs was three days after the listing. That is not enough time for a change board to approve work across a large fleet, which argues for pre-authorising updates to internet-facing media servers. What to do with a host today Check the version in Plex Web under Settings, then General, and compare the full build string against 1.43.3.10861. Turn off remote access that nobody uses, and avoid forwarding port 32400 directly. For a server that was exposed on an older build, work through the compromise checks and prefer a rebuild from a clean installation to cleaning a host in place. Sign out all devices, change the Plex password, and treat mounted shares and stored credentials reachable from the service account as exposed. Exposure context A ZoomEye query for app="Plex Media Server" returned 507,974 matching assets when this article was prepared, while vul.cve="CVE-2026-96654" returned 0. The product figure counts reachable installations at a point in time, not hosts that were unpatched during the window this timeline describes. References Plex security notice and 19 October update: https://forums.plex.tv/t/important-security-update-for-plex-media-server-v1-43-2-and-earlier/942319 CVE-2026-96652 record: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-96652 CVE-2026-96654 record: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-96654 CVE-2026-96655 record: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-96655 CVE-2026-96656 record: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-96656 CISA KEV catalog: https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog?field_cve=CVE-2026-96654

title: DiffScribe: The Commit Message Writes Itself (Locally)
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine The most lied-to text box in software Every developer knows the moment. The work is done, the tests pass, and then you face the emptiest, most judgmental input field in all of software: the commit message box. So you type what we all type: fix stuff updates final version (2) Git keeps perfect records of what changed. The why and the what it means live in commit messages and changelogs — the two texts written last, fastest, and worst. git log archaeology is a running joke precisely because the record we leave behind is so much worse than the work it describes. The fashionable fix is to paste your diff into a cloud AI and let it write the message. That works, and it also means shipping your unreleased code — every secret you forgot to gitignore, every internal hostname — to someone else's server, per commit, forever. I wanted the drafting help without the disclosure. So for this week's challenge I built DiffScribe : a small command-line tool that reads a git diff and drafts a conventional-commit message and a changelog entry, running entirely on my own machine. The AI at its core is an open-weight model small enough to run on a laptop CPU. The interesting part isn't that it works — it's how little of the output the model is trusted with . What DiffScribe does Stage some changes, run one command: python3 -m diffscribe draft It parses the diff, builds a compact digest (files, exact +/- counts, and a few "signal" lines like new function definitions), and asks a local model — Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Apache 2.0), served by llama.cpp (MIT) — for two small wordings: a commit subject, and a handful of changelog bullets. Then deterministic code takes over again: it validates both texts, generates the per-file stats body itself, and assembles the final draft with labels showing exactly which words came from the model and which came from rules. The governing rule of the whole design: the model words things; code counts things. A language model — especially a half-billion-parameter one — will happily write "+47 −13" whether or not those numbers are true. So it is never given the chance. Every number in DiffScribe's output was counted by parsing the diff. The demo — read it like a skeptic ./scripts/demo.sh drafts for a real staged diff: a README usage section, a new test file, and a new count_sentences function added to a toy text-statistics project. Recorded verbatim: COMMIT MESSAGE: feat: add docstring for textstat/count.py Files changed: 3 (+20 -1) - README.md: +5 -1 (modified) - tests/test_count.py: +9 -0 (added) - textstat/count.py: +6 -0 (modified) CHANGELOG ENTRY (Unreleased): - Updated README for easy navigation - Added new installation steps - Updated tests with new code - Improved textstat count functionality Now the honest reading, because this output is good and imperfect in instructive ways. The subject is well-formed, correctly typed, and points at the right file — but the diff adds a function , not a docstring. The bullets are reasonable paraphrases, except "Added new installation steps": the README gained a usage section, not install steps. Nothing here is malformed, and nothing is quite fabricated — it's the confident near-miss of a very small model. That is exactly the failure profile I designed for. DiffScribe cannot make a 0.5B model wise. What it can do is bound the blast radius: validate the shape (conventional-commit format, length caps, bullet counts), validate the grounding (more on that below), generate every fact-shaped part itself, and label whatever the model did write so a human editor — you, before you commit — knows what they're reviewing. A drafter, supervised. Not an oracle. How it works Parse. The unified diff becomes structured per-file changes: path, kind (added/modified/deleted/renamed), binary flag, exact added/deleted counts, and up to three signal lines per file (added lines that open a definition — def , class , export function …). One subtlety the tests cover: a content line can look like a diff header ( ---deleted text inside a removed string), so parsing keys off the diff --git file boundaries, not vibes. Digest. The parsed change is rendered to a text digest capped at 1,400 characters. Per-file entries truncate before whole files are dropped, and the exact totals line always survives — the model sees a faithful summary even for a huge diff, while the stats in the final output still cover every file. Draft. Two separate model calls (subject, then bullets), each with a one-shot format example, greedy decoding — temperature 0, so the demo above reproduces byte-for-byte. Validate, per text, independently. The subject must match the conventional-commit shape, fit 100 characters, and — the check I'm proudest of — its scope must be grounded : if the subject claims feat(auth): , the string "auth" must appear in a changed file's path or signal lines. Bullets must be 1–6 lines, each ≤ 140 characters. Either text can fail on its own and be replaced by a labeled rule-based draft (type inferred from the change shape, exact stats included) without discarding the other. Assemble. Stats body from code, wordings from wherever they legitimately came from, everything labeled. There is also a --no-llm mode that skips the model entirely and emits the pure deterministic draft — vaguer, and never wrong about the facts. The full recorded transcript of both modes is demo-output.txt in the repo. The run where my model lied with a straight face The grounding check exists because of a specific, embarrassing run early in development. My first one-shot example — meant only to teach the output format — used an auth-flavored sample: a digest about auth/login.py , subject fix(auth): reject expired tokens during login . I then fed DiffScribe the text-statistics diff, and the model returned, confidently and in perfect conventional-commit format: feat(auth): reject expired tokens during login There is no auth code in that diff. There is no login. The model hadn't read my diff at all; it had copied my example and changed one word. Every format check passed. This is the tiny-model failure mode that matters: not gibberish — gibberish is easy to catch — but fluent, well-formed, entirely wrong. Two fixes. The example is now deliberately bland and topically distant (a README edit), because an example a model might parrot should be one whose parroting is obvious. And the deterministic grounding check: a scoped subject whose scope appears nowhere in the diff is rejected and replaced by the fallback, no matter how pretty it is. There's a regression test named after the incident ( test_assemble_rejects_leaked_example_subject ). The subject in the demo — slightly wrong about "docstring", but genuinely about this diff — is what the model produces under those constraints. A second, quieter reuse bug deserves a sentence: I copied last week's download script for llama.cpp, and it kept failing with a polite "Not Found" before a bash -x trace showed why — the asset name in the URL had a doubled letter ( llama-bb11580… ), a latent typo that had been sitting in the old script all along. Inherited code inherits bugs. It also inherits the ability to find them, because the script was mine to read. Hold that thought for the next section. Why open innovation matters This is the third week I've built on the same openly licensed stack — open weights, an MIT inference engine, a standard-library-only program — and DiffScribe is the week the compounding became visible. Reuse is real when the licenses let it be. The llama.cpp wrapper, the greedy-decoding discipline, the labeled-fallback pattern, even the download scripts came straight from my Week 2 and Week 3 entries. Nothing had to be re-negotiated, re-purchased, or re-permissioned; the licenses (Apache 2.0, MIT) were the whole conversation. And when part of what I reused turned out to be buggy, openness was the debugging tool: the script was a file on my disk, readable to the last character, fixable in one line. Open weights change who gets to build. DiffScribe's model is a ~490 MB file I downloaded once. No account, no API key, no per-commit bill, no terms-of-service roulette about whether my use case is allowed this month. A student on a metered connection in Ahmedabad and a staff engineer at a Fortune 500 company get the same artifact — and, because it's just a file, the same ability to inspect what it is and pin exactly which version produced an output. My demo reproduces byte-for-byte because the weights, the engine version, and the decoding settings are all fixed and named in the repo. That reproducibility is an open-artifact property; a hosted model that silently changes under you cannot offer it. Openness is also a quality strategy. The most important line in this project is a test that encodes a failure. Small open models fail in public, cheaply, on your own machine, where you can watch them do it and engineer around it — validation, grounding, fallbacks. That loop (watch it fail → bound the failure → write the test) is the actual craft of building with AI right now, and open tooling makes the loop tight enough to run in an afternoon. On this week's theme — Ghost in the Machine — DiffScribe fits on the honouring-the-past side of the brief, and I want to be plain about the limits of that fit: this is not a ghost-story generator, and it is not an ofrenda builder. What it is, is a keeper of a project's past. Every commit is a trace of work already done, and when those traces are written as "fix stuff", that past is effectively lost — the story of why a change was made fades, just as surely as an unrecorded memory does. DiffScribe tries to keep that history legible, drafting the commit message and changelog entry that let a future reader reconstruct what happened and why, from the diff itself. And there is a literal ghost in this machine, too: a half-billion-parameter open-weight model that lives entirely on my laptop, offline, drafting words in the dark with no server and no internet — a small, local presence that remembers how to phrase the past, and forgets nothing it was never sent. Honest limitations Validation checks shape and grounding, not truth. The demo subject says "docstring" where the diff adds a function; a bullet says "installation steps" where the README adds usage docs. Plausible near-misses survive every check I have. Read the draft before you commit — the tool assumes a human editor, which is why its outputs are labeled by origin. Scope grounding is a substring heuristic. It catches wholesale example leakage (its actual job), not subtle irrelevance; a scope of auth would also match a path containing author . Huge diffs are digested, not read. Past the digest cap, later files are summarized by counts alone; the model's wording may skew toward the early files. The stats body remains exact and complete. Fallback drafting is deliberately vague ( chore: update code (3 files, +20 -1) ) — correct about every fact it states, useless as prose. It is a safety net, not a writer. No partner or hosted technology is used — by design, not omission. The project's entire premise is that this job can be done locally, offline, with openly licensed parts. Prize Categories None entered — no partner technology is used, by design (see Honest limitations above). This submission is entered for the overall prize only. Try it Repo: https://github.com/swarnnim/diffscribe git clone https://github.com/swarnnim/diffscribe && cd diffscribe ./scripts/download-llamacpp.sh && ./scripts/download-model.sh ./scripts/demo.sh # recorded demo, both modes python3 -m unittest discover -s tests # 50 tests git add -A && python3 -m diffscribe draft # draft for your own change Standard library only; the downloads are the single network touch, and after that DiffScribe will happily draft commit messages on a plane, in a tunnel, or wherever your git log has been embarrassing you. DiffScribe was built in the open, from open parts, for the most open-source month of the year. Week 1 taught me to ship small, Week 2 to keep data local, Week 3 to build the guardrails first. Week 4's lesson: trust the model with the wording, never with the facts — and write the test for the day it confuses the two.

title: Moscow, Minsk should maintain joint defense mechanisms — Russian ambassador
body:
MINSK, October 26. /TASS/. Moscow and Minsk need to maintain the existing joint defense mechanisms and ensure constant coordination, Russian Ambassador to Belarus Boris Gryzlov said.
"First and foremost, we must maintain the readiness of existing joint defense mechanisms and ensure permanent coordination. We have many-years’ experience of cooperation between defense agencies and operational coordination within joint exercises. Operational data is exchanged in real time," he said in an interview with the National Defense magazine.
According to the diplomat, the agenda is not reduced to purely military matters. It includes cooperation in combating terrorism, extremism, organized crime, drug trafficking, and illegal migration, including with partners within the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). Another area of cooperation is countering illegal restrictive economic and financial measures. "Since security issues are under the personal supervision of the presidents, I can assure you that everything necessary is being done to protect the borders of the Union State (of Russia and Belarus - TASS)," Gryzlov emphasized.

title: How to Run AI Models Locally & Offline in 2026
body: How to Run AI Models Locally & Offline in 2026 Most people use AI through a website. You type a question, it goes to a faraway server, and the answer comes back. This is easy, but it has a cost. You pay every month, you need the internet, and your words travel to a company you do not control. There is another way. You can run AI right on your own computer. It works without the internet. Your data stays with you. And in 2026, it is easier than it has ever been. This guide explains everything in simple words. You will learn what local AI is, what you need, which tools to use, and how to start today. What Does "Running AI Locally" Mean? Running AI locally means the AI model lives on your own computer. When you ask a question, your computer does all the work. Nothing is sent to the cloud. Think of it like this. Cloud AI is like eating at a restaurant. Someone else cooks, and you pay each time. Local AI is like cooking at home. You buy the tools once, and then you can cook whenever you want. "Offline" means it works with no internet at all. You download the model once. After that, you can turn off your Wi-Fi and it still works. Why Run AI on Your Own Computer? Here are the main reasons people are moving to local AI. 1. Privacy. Your chats, files, and ideas never leave your computer. This matters for work documents, school projects, health questions, or anything personal. 2. No monthly fees. Many cloud AI tools charge every month. Some also limit how much you can use. Local AI has no usage limits. Use it as much as you like. 3. It works offline. You can use AI on a plane, on a train, or in a place with weak internet. 4. No sudden changes. Cloud tools can change their prices, rules, or models at any time. With a local model, you keep the exact version you downloaded. 5. Freedom to experiment. You can try many different models, change settings, and learn how AI really works. Is Local AI as Good as Cloud AI? This is the most common question, and the answer is a big yes. Local AI can do almost everything cloud AI can do. It can write, explain, summarize, translate, help with code, answer questions, and even make images and videos. Local models have improved a lot, and new ones keep getting better. The main difference is speed, and speed depends on your PC. A strong computer with a good GPU and plenty of RAM can run big models and give fast answers. A simple laptop can run the same kind of tasks too. It may just take a little more time to reply. And local AI wins in many other ways. It is private, it is free to use after setup, it has no limits, and it works offline. So you are not giving anything up. You are just getting more control. What Do You Need to Run AI Locally? You do not need a super computer. But your hardware does decide which models you can run. Here are the parts that matter. 1. RAM (Memory) RAM is very important. The model has to fit in memory while it runs. 8 GB of RAM: you can run small models. 16 GB of RAM: you can run medium models comfortably. 32 GB of RAM or more: you can run bigger and smarter models. 2. GPU (Graphics Card) A GPU makes AI much faster. The most important number is VRAM, which is the memory on the graphics card. No GPU: AI still works on the CPU, just slower. 6 GB to 8 GB of VRAM: good for small and medium models. 12 GB to 24 GB of VRAM: good for large models and image or video work. 3. CPU Any modern CPU can run small models. A faster CPU with more cores will give faster answers. If you have no GPU, a good CPU matters even more. 4. Storage Models are big files. A small model can be 2 GB to 5 GB. Larger ones can be 20 GB or more. Image and video models can be even bigger. An SSD is best, and you should keep at least 50 GB free. A Simple Rule of Thumb A model with 7 billion to 8 billion parameters, shrunk to 4 bit, needs about 5 GB to 6 GB of memory. A model with 13 billion parameters needs about 8 GB to 10 GB. Bigger models need more. If a model is too big for your memory, it will run very slowly or not at all. Understanding Model Sizes and Quantization You will see two things again and again when you look for models. Parameters. This is the size of the model. You will see names like 3B, 7B, 14B, or 70B. The "B" means billions. More parameters usually means a smarter model, but it also needs more memory. Quantization. This is a way to shrink a model so it fits on normal computers. A full model might use 16 bits for each number. A quantized model uses fewer bits, like 8 bit or 4 bit. The file becomes much smaller, and the quality drops only a little. For most people, a 4 bit version (often named Q4) is the best balance. It is small, fast, and still smart. The Main Ways to Run AI Locally There are many tools. Here are the most popular ones, from easiest to most technical. Option 1: Desktop Apps With a Simple Interface These tools give you a window with buttons. You pick a model, click download, and start chatting. No coding needed. LM Studio lets you search for models, download them, and chat in one app. Jan is a simple open source chat app that runs models on your device. GPT4All is another easy app made for regular computers, including ones without a GPU. This is the best place to start if you are new. Option 2: Command Line Tools These tools are small and fast, but you use them by typing commands. Ollama is very popular. You type one command to download a model and one command to run it. It also works as a background service that other apps can connect to. llama.cpp is the engine behind many local AI tools. It is very efficient and runs on almost any hardware. Option 3: Web Interfaces You can add a nice chat page on top of tools like Ollama. Open WebUI gives you a chat page in your browser that looks like popular cloud chat tools, but it runs on your own computer. Option 4: Image and Video Tools Chat is only one part of AI. You can also make images and videos locally. ComfyUI and Stable Diffusion based tools let you create images on your own PC. They are powerful but can feel complex at first. Open video models can make short clips locally, but they need a strong GPU and a lot of patience. How to Run Your First Local AI Model Here is a simple path for beginners. It takes about 15 minutes, plus download time. Step 1: Check your computer. Look at how much RAM you have. If you have 8 GB, pick a small model. If you have 16 GB or more, you have more choices. Step 2: Install a tool. Download and install LM Studio, Jan, or Ollama from their official websites. Always use the official site to stay safe. Step 3: Pick a model. Search for a small, popular model. Good families to look at include Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, and Phi. Start with a model around 3B to 8B in size, in a 4 bit version. Step 4: Download it. This needs the internet once. The file may take a few minutes. Step 5: Start chatting. Type a question. Your computer will think and answer. The first reply may be a little slow while the model loads. Step 6: Go offline. Turn off your internet and ask another question. It still works. That is local AI. Which Models Should You Try? New models come out all the time, so think in terms of tasks. For everyday chat and writing: pick a general model from the Llama, Qwen, Gemma, or Mistral families. For coding: pick a model made for code. Many families have a coding version. For reasoning and math: look for models trained to think step by step. For low power computers: pick very small models, around 1B to 4B. They are fast, even on a laptop. For images: use Stable Diffusion based models or other open image models. Read the model page before you download. It tells you the size, the license, and what the model is good at. Also check the license if you plan to use the output for business. How to Make Local AI Faster If your model feels slow, try these tips. Use a smaller model. A 3B model is much faster than a 14B model. Use a more compressed version. A 4 bit model is faster than an 8 bit model. Use your GPU. Make sure your tool is using it. Update your graphics drivers. Close other heavy apps. Browsers with many tabs and games use a lot of memory. Use a shorter chat. Very long chats need more memory and time. Start a new chat when you can. Keep models on an SSD. Loading is much quicker. What Can You Do With Local AI? Once it is running, there is a lot you can do. Write and edit emails, blog posts, and reports. Summarize long documents without uploading them anywhere. Get help with homework or learning a new topic. Write, explain, and fix code. Translate text. Brainstorm ideas, names, and plans. Create images and short videos. Build your own small tools by connecting a local model to other apps. Common Problems and Simple Fixes The model is very slow. It is probably too big for your computer. Try a smaller or more compressed version. The computer freezes or runs out of memory. Close other apps and pick a smaller model. The answers are poor. Small models have limits. Try a larger model, or write a clearer, more detailed question. The model makes things up. All AI models can do this, local or cloud. Check important facts yourself. The download is huge. That is normal. Models are big. Plan your storage before you download many of them. Safety Tips Download tools and models only from official or well known sources. Check the license before using a model for business. Remember that offline does not mean perfect. Keep your own backups. If you connect a local model to tools that can edit files or run commands, be careful about what you allow it to do. The Problem With Using Many Separate Tools Here is something you may notice after a while. To do everything locally, you often need many different tools. One for chat. Another for images. Another for video. Another for coding. Each has its own setup, its own settings, and its own problems. That is fine for people who enjoy tinkering. But if you just want things to work, it can feel like a lot. A Simpler Way: HDQGen If you want local AI without the setup headache, you can try HDQGen . It is an all in one AI studio for your desktop. It gives you chat, image generation, video generation, music, and a coding agent in one place. Everything runs privately on your own device, with no cloud needed. It works on both CPU and GPU, so you do not need an expensive graphics card. On Windows, it runs on Windows 7 or later, 64 bit. There is no subscription and no credits. You pay once and use it forever. You can learn more or download it at www.hdqgen.com . Final Thoughts Running AI locally is no longer only for experts. With a normal computer and a free tool, you can have a private AI that works offline and costs nothing each month. Start small. Install an easy app, download a small model, and ask it a few questions. Once you see how it works, you can go deeper with bigger models, image tools, and more. AI does not have to live only in the cloud. In 2026, you can keep it on your own computer.

title: JetBlue stock surges as company outlook calms investors
body:
JetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but shares surged as the carrier's upbeat forecast that it will return to profitability appeared to calm investors after a Monday rout.
JetBlue stock rose 18% in trading Tuesday after hitting a new low a day earlier as investors fretted about the company's financial future.
The Monday drop came after the Wall Street Journal reported Friday that a group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners .
"We have no intention, no plans to file for bankruptcy. We are not engaged with any restructuring company," CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC on Tuesday. "We are focused on delivering to our shareholders what we laid out for at the beginning of our turnaround plan."
She said there is a "fundamental disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results actually demonstrate."
The New York airline late Monday reported that its revenue per available seat mile, a key metric measuring how much operating revenue a carrier generates for every seat flown one mile, would be up as much as 22% in the fourth quarter, bringing the annual increase to an expected 13.5% to 14.5%
"We're not seeing any meaningful pushback," Geraghty said in the interview.
JetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million.
The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.
JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday.
"Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."
Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:
JetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.
Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares .
JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.
The airline has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals.
It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines , which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines .
The carrier expects to grow capacity no more than 4% in the current quarter. One bright spot, executives said, has been expanding at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport, the former home hub of Spirit, which collapsed in May.
