title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to up to 60,000 staff
body: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to up to 60,000 employees across the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and India. Chief People Officer Amy Coleman says the program gives staff financial support and career planning resources as the company trims its workforce without a new round of layoffs. The move follows a broader effort to curb costs and re‑engineer Microsoft’s workforce, according to TechCrunch. Key takeaways Scope: Up to 60,000 employees in the US, UK, Canada and India are eligible. Leadership message: Amy Coleman frames the offer as financial support and career planning assistance. Cost‑cutting aim: The buyouts are part of Microsoft’s latest effort to reduce expenses, per TechCrunch. No new layoffs: The voluntary exits are meant to avoid another round of involuntary layoffs. Eligible groups: Staff in AI experiences, Copilot, CoreAI, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance and HR can apply. What happened Microsoft announced a voluntary exit program that targets up to 60,000 workers across four major markets. The offer applies to employees in a wide range of divisions, including its AI experiences, the Copilot and CoreAI teams, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance and human resources. In an internal memo, Amy Coleman wrote that the program provides “the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources.” Sources familiar with the situation told The Verge that the buyout offers are open to staff across the company, not limited to any single business unit. The company frames the initiative as a way to “trim staff without another round of layoffs,” signaling a preference for voluntary departures over forced cuts. While the exact financial terms of the buyouts were not disclosed, the messaging emphasizes support for those who choose to transition out. TechCrunch notes that the buyouts mark Microsoft’s latest effort to cut costs and rework its workforce. The announcement comes after a period of hiring freezes and earlier rounds of layoffs, suggesting the firm is now turning to voluntary exits to meet its financial targets. By offering a structured exit pathway, Microsoft hopes to reduce headcount while preserving morale among remaining staff. Why it matters A voluntary buyout program of this scale signals a strategic shift in how large tech firms manage workforce reductions. Rather than issuing blanket layoffs, Microsoft is providing an option that includes financial assistance and career‑planning help, potentially easing the impact on affected employees. The move also reflects broader industry pressure to control operating expenses amid slowing growth in cloud and AI services. For employees, the program offers a clear exit route with resources that might otherwise be unavailable after an involuntary layoff. For investors, the voluntary nature could be seen as a less disruptive way to achieve cost savings, preserving productivity and reducing the risk of negative publicity associated with mass layoffs. Geographically, the inclusion of the United Kingdom, Canada and India shows Microsoft’s intent to address global headcount, not just its U.S. workforce. This aligns with the company’s multinational operations and suggests the cost‑cutting measures are being applied uniformly across its major markets. The reaction Public reaction has been muted so far, with most commentary focused on the size of the offer rather than specific employee experiences. Industry analysts have pointed out that voluntary buyouts can be an effective tool when a company wants to avoid the morale damage of layoffs, but they also warn that the success of such programs depends on the attractiveness of the financial terms. Internal sources, as reported by The Verge, indicate that employees in the AI and Copilot divisions are among those eligible, raising questions about how the exits might affect Microsoft’s ongoing AI initiatives. No official statements from employee unions or advocacy groups have been recorded in the sources. The broader tech community is watching to see whether Microsoft’s approach will set a precedent for other large firms facing similar cost pressures. If the buyout program meets its target, it could become a template for balancing fiscal discipline with employee goodwill. What comes next Microsoft has not disclosed a deadline for the buyout applications, but internal communications suggest the program will run for several months to allow employees to evaluate the offer. The company will likely monitor uptake closely, adjusting the scale if the response falls short of the 60,000 target. Future reporting may reveal the financial impact of the buyouts on Microsoft’s operating expenses, as well as any shifts in project timelines for the divisions most affected. Stakeholders will also be interested in whether the voluntary exits translate into measurable cost savings without compromising product development. If the program succeeds, Microsoft may continue to rely on voluntary exits as a primary tool for workforce management, reducing the need for future involuntary layoffs. Conversely, a low participation rate could force the company to revisit other cost‑cutting measures. The takeaway For workers at Microsoft, the buyout program offers a structured exit with financial and career support, potentially easing the transition for those ready to leave. For investors and industry observers, the initiative demonstrates a shift toward voluntary reductions as a way to meet cost targets while preserving morale. The ultimate impact will hinge on employee uptake and how the exits affect Microsoft’s AI and cloud ambitions. Sources The Verge: https://www.theverge.com/tech/1018666/microsoft-expands-buyouts-60000-employees-eligible TechCrunch: https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/26/microsoft-offers-buyouts-to-around-60000-employees-reports-say/ This article was originally published at codekhabar.com . For more tech news, visit codekhabar.com .

title: Obuasi SHTS scandal: Plan International Ghana demands independent probe, nationwide safeguarding reforms
body: Plan International Ghana has called for independent investigations and comprehensive child protection reforms following allegations of sexual abuse involving female students of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS) and the school’s headmaster. The organisation says the allegations raise serious concerns about students’ safety, the abuse of positions of trust and weaknesses in safeguarding systems within Ghanaian schools. In a statement, Plan International Ghana stressed that educational institutions must provide safe environments where children can learn without fear of exploitation, intimidation or abuse. “A school must be a place of safety, learning and opportunity – not fear, exploitation or abuse. Every child has the right to learn in a safe environment and to be treated with dignity,” the statement said. While welcoming investigations into the allegations, the organisation insisted that the response must extend beyond the possible dismissal or punishment of an individual to address potential institutional failures. “Dismissal alone cannot heal affected students, address institutional failures or guarantee that other children will be safe,” it emphasised. Plan International Ghana called for thorough, impartial and child-sensitive investigations, including an examination of how previous complaints were handled, while ensuring that anyone found responsible is held accountable in accordance with the law and due process. It also urged authorities to provide affected students with confidential, trauma-informed psychosocial care, healthcare, legal assistance and continued educational support, while protecting their identities and preventing victim-blaming, intimidation and retaliation. The organisation further demanded investigations into whether school management or education officials ignored, mishandled or suppressed complaints, stressing that institutional safeguarding failures must attract appropriate consequences regardless of an individual’s position or influence. Additionally, it called for confidential reporting channels for students and staff, stronger protections for whistle-blowers and mandatory safeguarding and professional-boundaries training for teachers and school leaders. Plan International Ghana also proposed a nationwide review of how sexual abuse complaints are reported, investigated and resolved in schools, alongside a time-bound action plan to address gaps in existing policies and laws. “This must not become another scandal that fades from public attention without justice or meaningful reform,” the organisation warned. It urged the media and the public to respect the privacy and dignity of affected students by avoiding the circulation of identifying information or sensationalised accounts of their experiences. “No child should suffer in silence to protect an institution’s reputation. No teacher should face retaliation for speaking up for a child. And no complaint concerning the safety of a child should be ignored,” the statement added. Plan International Ghana reaffirmed its commitment to collaborating with the government, Ministry of Education, Ghana Education Service and other relevant institutions to strengthen safeguarding systems and ensure safer, more inclusive learning environments across the country.

title: Bomfa installs new chief after 8-year chieftaincy dispute
body: The kingmakers of Bomfa in the Juaben Traditional Area of the Ashanti Region have enstooled 62-year-old Nana Kwame Agyemang Opambuor as the community’s new chief, ending an eight-year period of chieftaincy disputes and uncertainty. The new chief, known in private life as Kwame Agyemang, succeeds Nana Opoku Acheampong, who was destooled over issues relating to accountability to the people he served. Nana Opambuor swore an oath of allegiance to his people in the presence of the Juabenhene, Daasebre Otuo Sereboe II, pledging to uphold the dignity of the Bomfa Stool, the Juaben Traditional Council and the Asante Kingdom. Addressing the gathering, the Juabenhene cautioned the new chief against arrogance and urged him to govern with humility, integrity and inclusiveness. “The stool gives you power and honour. You should not do anything contrary to the stool’s bidding. I do not want to see you in an arrogant or proud manner. Work with truth and accuracy, remain calm and rule with dignity, bringing all those who matter in decision-making on board,” Nana Otuo Sereboe II advised. He also urged the kingmakers and residents to rally behind the new chief to consolidate peace and accelerate development in the community. Nana Kwame Agyemang Opambuor commended the Juabenhene for helping resolve the chieftaincy disputes, paving the way for the installation of a new traditional leader. He said the resolution of the protracted dispute would restore hope and provide a unified platform for cultural preservation, local governance, social cohesion and community development. The new chief pledged to work with his kinsmen and other stakeholders to attract major development projects to Bomfa. His priorities include the establishment of a police station and a senior high school, upgrading the existing health centre and constructing a modern palace. To make education more attractive to children, Nana Opambuor also proposed the establishment of an amusement centre equipped with educational materials to combine recreation with learning. He further urged the youth to embrace responsible behaviour and contribute meaningfully to the development of the community. He cautioned against drug abuse, thuggery and robbery, warning that such activities could derail the aspirations of young people and undermine their future.

title: php2shell on a dead distro: rebuilding patched PHP for Debian 9 and 8
body:
On 21 October 2026 the PHP project fixed two critical bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , quickly nicknamed php2shell . Both can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. In the first, an out-of-memory error can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized; request parsing is the easiest way to get there, but not the only one. In the second, request-owned state survives in a persistent worker after its memory has been freed. Full RCE was demonstrated on Apache mod_php; on PHP-FPM the exposure is more limited and depends on the configuration, but "limited" is not "safe". The fixed releases were 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, and the PHP project published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. Anything older depends on distributions and LTS providers. AWS saw a first exploitation attempt against its honeypots on 17 October, four days before disclosure ( AWS ). If you run PHP from deb.sury.org on Debian 9 stretch or Debian 8 jessie , there is no patched package for you. Upgrading the operating system is the real fix, but it is weeks of work, and a hole like this one needs to be closed in days. This post shows how to do that: find a patched source, rebuild it for a distribution its maintainer no longer supports, avoid the traps along the way, rehearse the installation on a copy of a production server, and roll it out while checking that the pages you serve do not change. The examples use php7.2 7.2.34-66 ; other branches need their own compatibility checks. Step 0: read what you actually run Before choosing anything, read every host, read-only: grep PRETTY_NAME /etc/os-release ; uname -r php -v | head -1 ; php7.2 -v | head -1 # `php` may point to another branch dpkg-query -W -f = '${Package} ${Version}\n' 'php7.2*' 'libicu*' 'libsodium*' php-common php-fpm7.2 -i | grep -E '^(session.upload_progress.enabled|memory_limit)' # FPM defaults, before pool overrides ls /var/cache/apt/archives | grep php7.2 # rollback material cat /etc/apt/sources.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ * .list php-fpm7.2 -i does not show what a pool or the web server overrides ( php_admin_value , PHP_VALUE ): read the pool configuration too. Three questions decide everything else: Is there a package to install? As of 26 October 2026, sury's repository answers 404 for stretch and buster. The patched builds exist only for Debian 11, 12 and 13: Debian 7.2 8.2 8.3 8.4 9 stretch, 10 buster 404 404 404 404 11, 12, 13 7.2.34-66 8.2.35 8.3.36 8.4.27 Does apt still work? On an old host, sources.list often still points at Debian mirrors that stopped serving stretch long ago, so any apt-get -f install fails. Whatever you install has to bring its dependencies with it. Is the apt cache still there? Some hosts keep the exact .deb files of every PHP package they run. That is your rollback, if it is there: check files, versions and architecture rather than assuming. Two cheap mitigations can go in right away: session.upload_progress.enabled = Off in php.ini or in the pool configuration (not with ini_set : it must apply before the request is parsed), then restart the workers. One of the documented exploitation paths of the second CVE goes through it. On 23 October PHP also recommended keeping it off until the next release because of a further, unlikely vector, CVE-2026-115560 . If a virtual host only ever needs to answer GET and HEAD requests, make the web server refuse other methods and cap request bodies before PHP sees them: client_max_body_size 1k ; if ( $request_method !~ ^(GET|HEAD) $ ) { return 405 ; } This limits bodies to 1 KB, it does not reject them. Add OPTIONS only if that virtual host needs it (for example for CORS preflight), and check your access logs first, to be sure nobody legitimately sends anything else. These reduce exposure; they do not fix anything. The advisories list further temporary measures and their limits. The options Mitigations only. Necessary, not sufficient: they do not close every path to either CVE. Paid extended support. Freexian publishes patched PHP for old Debian releases, from Debian 9 up; jessie is not on their list ( Freexian PHP LTS ). A perfectly good option, if it covers your exact combination and fits your budget. Containers on the old hosts. The newest Docker CE in Docker's stretch archive is 19.03.15. With the old Docker we tried, the default seccomp profile broke thread creation ( clone3 ) in images based on recent glibc. Test your exact runtime and image before betting on it. Jump to PHP 8.x on stretch, compiled from source. stretch's libraries meet PHP 8.3's basic build requirements (8.4 needs libcurl ≥ 7.61; stretch has 7.52), but every extension you use has its own. And your application may need changes, or may not run on PHP 8 at all: that is a project, not a patch. Rebuild sury's patched package for your old Debian. On 21 October sury published php7.2 7.2.34-66 with a backport of the fix, and the source package is public. If it builds on stretch, it installs over your current 7.2 with the same package names, the same /etc/php/7.2 and the same php7.2-fpm service: no application change. That is the route described here. What is inside sury's source package dpkg-source -x php7.2_7.2.34-66+0~20261021.122+debian12~1.gbpe0bcd4.dsc php7.2-src wc -l php7.2-src/debian/patches/series # 159 Do not add --no-check : it also disables the checksum checks. And a download over HTTPS is not authentication. This .dsc carries no signature of its own, so authenticate the files through the repository's signed metadata: the InRelease file (verified with sury's archive key), then the Sources index it lists, then the checksums of the source files. Keep that metadata next to the files. PHP 7.2.34 plus 159 patches : six years of security backports and packaging changes. The last one is the fix: 0159-Avoid-state-corruption-via-bailout.patch Minimal mitigation for EOL version. Fix GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w (CVE-2026-109618) Fix GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp (CVE-2026-109619) Backported from the PHP 7.4 version It touches 16 files in Zend/ , main/rfc1867.c , main/SAPI.c and ext/session/session.c . Before building anything, check the two things most likely to make the idea fail, in a throwaway debian:stretch container: do all patches apply, and do the build dependencies resolve on stretch? dpkg-source -x php7.2_ * .dsc php7.2-src # applies all patches cd php7.2-src mk-build-deps -i -r -t 'apt-get -y --no-install-recommends' debian/control dpkg-checkbuilddeps && echo "BUILD-DEPS OK" Both pass (stretch's debhelper 10 is new enough). Ten minutes to know the plan is viable. The backport is not upstream's fix "Minimal mitigation for EOL version" means what it says. Read the patch before shipping it: when a request hits memory_limit (and on a few other allocation failures), the patched allocator prints the fatal error to stderr and ends the process with _exit(1) : no normal request shutdown, no shutdown handlers, no session write, and the message does not go through PHP's error log. Under FPM the worker dies and the master replaces it; enable catch_workers_output in the pool if you want to see those messages; the session upload progress callback returns unconditionally ( || 1 ), so that feature is off even if php.ini says On . Ordinary file uploads are a different thing and keep working. A comparison of ordinary pages does not exercise either change. Test uploads, error handling and FPM recovery on the replica. The telemetry patch Patch 0144 is a surprise: "Add minimal privacy-preserving secure DNS telemetry to check current version" , added on 12 February 2026. It adds main/secure_dns_telemetry.h and hooks it into the FPM and mod_php startup: at every start it builds v1|
|
|
, encrypts it with a public key, and sends it as a DNS query (UDP 53) to the configured host; a reply may carry an advisory, which is only logged if it says "high", "critical" or "emergency" (and both the FPM and the mod_php hooks define the logging macro as empty); nothing received is executed. The next day's changelog entry says "The secure DNS telemetry is disabled at the compile-time" , and debian/rules says "not enabled in build by default" . The hostname is not in the patch: the startup call is compiled in only when TELEMETRY_HOST is defined, and debian/rules picks it up, if present, from /usr/lib/php/php-common.mk , shipped by the php-common installed where the package is built (it is a build dependency). In Debian's own php-common that file is empty. In the one published on packages.sury.org it contains (checked on 26 October 2026): -DTELEMETRY_HOST = '"telemetry.sury.org"' \ -DTELEMETRY_PORT = '"53"' \ -DTELEMETRY_PK = '"…"' So packages built against sury's php-common have the call compiled in, and Debian's own builds do not. We found telemetry.sury.org in an official php-fpm8.1 binary from sury's repository. Check your own binaries ( strings /usr/sbin/php-fpm7.2 | grep telemetry ). A project that lives on donations has good reasons to want to know how many installations exist, and the code is careful. We dropped the patch from our build anyway: it is not a security fix, builds from before February 2026 never had it, and even with the call disabled the header is included and FPM is linked against libsodium, which breaks the build on stretch (it needs libsodium ≥ 1.0.14; stretch has 1.0.11). No later patch touches its files, so removing it is clean. Building for stretch, and the ICU trap The builder is a Dockerfile on debian:stretch , with the archived repositories. This is the core of it, not the complete build (the ICU part follows): FROM --platform=linux/amd64 debian:stretch RUN printf '%s\n' \ 'deb http://archive.debian.org/debian stretch main contrib non-free' \ 'deb http://archive.debian.org/debian-security stretch/updates main contrib non-free' \ > /etc/apt/sources.list && \ echo 'Acquire::Check-Valid-Until "false";' > /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/10no-check-valid-until && \ apt-get update && \ apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates curl dpkg-dev devscripts \ equivs fakeroot quilt xz-utils ARG SURY_VERSION=7.2.34-66+0~20261021.122+debian12~1.gbpe0bcd4 ARG SURY_POOL=https://packages.sury.org/php/pool/main/p/php7.2 WORKDIR /build RUN curl -fsSO " $SURY_POOL /php7.2_ ${ SURY_VERSION } .dsc" && \ curl -fsSO " $SURY_POOL /php7.2_7.2.34.orig.tar.xz" && \ curl -fsSO " $SURY_POOL /php7.2_ ${ SURY_VERSION } .debian.tar.xz" && \ dpkg-source --skip-patches -x "php7.2_ ${ SURY_VERSION } .dsc" php7.2-src && \ cd php7.2-src && \ sed -i '/^0144-Add-minimal-privacy-preserving-secure-DNS-telemetry-.patch$/d' debian/patches/series && \ QUILT_PATCHES = debian/patches quilt push -a --fuzz = 0 RUN cd php7.2-src && apt-get update && \ mk-build-deps -i -r -t 'apt-get -y -q --no-install-recommends' debian/control Check-Valid-Until "false" only accepts the archive's expired release dates; signatures are still checked. If you authenticated the source files elsewhere (see above), copy them in instead of downloading them here. The build itself gives the packages a local revision, so they are recognizable on the servers and sort above the old ones (check with dpkg --compare-versions against what the hosts run, and never reuse a revision for different contents): dch -b -v "7.2.34-66+stretch2" -D stretch "Rebuilt for Debian 9 stretch, without the DNS telemetry patch (0144), intl against ICU 64." DEB_BUILD_OPTIONS = "nocheck parallel= $( nproc ) " dpkg-buildpackage -b -uc -us nocheck skips PHP's own test suite: a package that compiles is not a tested package, so the checks later in this post are not optional. Our first package built, installed cleanly and served pages. One page was different: Italian dates had turned from 7 ott 2026, 17:12 into 07 ott 2026, 17:12 . The PHP being replaced had not been linked against stretch's ICU 57. sury's 2019 builds for stretch used a backported ICU 64 , together with backported pcre, libsodium, libargon2, libgd and libtidy. ICU 57 carries older locale data (CLDR), which formats Italian medium dates differently. The same library drives localized dates and number formats, and the Transliterator that many applications use to generate URL slugs, so this is not cosmetic: a slug generated with the new build could differ from the one the old build generated for the same title. Check which ICU your current intl.so declares before you build ( objdump -p … | grep NEEDED ), and record what PHP reports at runtime too. We could not find ICU 64 development packages for stretch in any repository or archive we checked, not even in sury's pool. What worked: Install the libicu64 runtime package your servers already have in the builder (copy it from a host's apt cache). Build ICU 64.1 from upstream only for its headers and pkg-config files. Check the tarball's GPG signature against unicode-org's KEYS file (it is signed by ICU's release manager) and pin its SHA-512 in the Dockerfile. Replace the libraries of that ICU build with links to the packaged ones, so anything linking "ICU 64" links the library the servers already have. Point PKG_CONFIG_PATH at it, because PHP's configure asks pkg-config first. COPY prod-debs/libicu64_*.deb /tmp/ RUN dpkg -i /tmp/libicu64_ * .deb RUN curl -fsSL -o /tmp/icu.tgz " $ICU_URL " && echo " $ICU_SHA512 /tmp/icu.tgz" | sha512sum -c - && \ tar -xzf /tmp/icu.tgz -C /tmp && cd /tmp/icu/source && \ ./configure --prefix = /opt/icu64 --disable-samples --disable-tests && make -j " $( nproc ) " && make install && \ for lib in /opt/icu64/lib/libicu * .so * ; do rm " $lib " ; done && \ for lib in /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libicu * .so.64 ; do \ name = $( basename " $lib " .64 ) ; ln -s " $lib " "/opt/icu64/lib/ $name " ; ln -s " $lib " "/opt/icu64/lib/ $name .64" ; \ done ENV PKG_CONFIG_PATH=/opt/icu64/lib/pkgconfig configure duly reported checking for location of ICU headers and libraries... found 64.1 . The package still declared Depends: libicu57 . Most likely, the linker had resolved -licuuc through the development symlinks of libicu-dev 57 ( /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libicuuc.so → .so.57 ), which come before our directory on its search path: headers from 64, library from 57. Either way, that package was unusable. A post-build check that only reads Depends would not catch the cases where the two disagree; this one does: mkdir /x && dpkg-deb -x php7.2-intl_ * .deb /x objdump -p /x/usr/lib/php/20170718/intl.so | grep NEEDED | grep icu # must say .so.64 dpkg-deb -f php7.2-intl_ * .deb Depends # must say libicu64 Make the build script fail if either says 57, then check on the replica that the module loads and formats as expected. Our first version of that check also had a bug: it called dpkg-deb on the Mac, where it does not exist, and fell back to a Docker command that passed the * unexpanded. Test your tests. Retargeting those development symlinks to 64 and moving the ICU 57 headers away fixes the link, and breaks the next build: libxml2's own headers include
, so ext/libxml stops compiling. The final fix points /usr/include/unicode at the ICU 64 headers instead of removing it. At runtime libxml2 keeps using ICU 57 and intl uses ICU 64, both loaded in the same process, exactly as with the old build: these ICU builds export their symbols with a version suffix ( ucol_open_64 ), so the two did not clash. Check your own binaries rather than assuming every ICU build does the same. Each build took about 50 minutes under amd64 emulation (Rosetta) on an 8-core Apple Silicon laptop, and three of ours failed: telemetry and libsodium, ICU linked to 57, libxml2 headers. Put everything that can fail fast at the beginning of the Dockerfile, and give each rebuild a new revision ( +stretch1 , +stretch2 ) so a bad package can never be mistaken for a good one. A production replica to rehearse on Before touching a server, build a debian:stretch container that is one of your servers, as far as PHP is concerned: the exact production .deb files, copied (read-only) from a server's apt cache: PHP packages, pecl extensions and backported libraries, with their checksums; the production /etc/php , copied the same way, with only the changes needed to keep the replica away from production: sessions, databases, queues, mail, and any other outbound connection; the same web server version as production, with development virtual hosts. ssh your-server "cd /var/cache/apt/archives && tar -cf - php7.2-* php-apcu_* …" \ | tar -xf - -C prod-debs Mount the application code and point it at a development database, and the replica serves real pages. A container shares the host's kernel and usually does not run systemd: use it for packages and application behavior, and check service start, reload and log rotation on a real host. Then compare. Capture a list of representative pages (home, a few dynamic pages, login, an error page, pages with localized dates), flush the application cache, capture again. Measure the noise before comparing anything. Two captures with the same PHP will differ in things like debug toolbars, CSP nonces, CSRF tokens, last-modified metadata, timestamps embedded in HTML or JavaScript, and lists whose content varies on its own. Normalize only those fields, keep the raw captures, and compare the rest byte by byte: normalize () { sed -E \ -e 's/nonce="[^"]*"/nonce=""/g' \ -e 's/(name="csrf_token" value=")[^"]*/\1/g' \ " $1 " } normalize before/page.html > before/page.norm.html normalize after/page.html > after/page.norm.html cmp before/page.norm.html after/page.norm.html Adapt the patterns to your pages, do not squeeze whitespace (it can matter), look at the raw diff too, and check that tokens still work rather than just hiding them. With the right ICU, every page we sampled was identical after normalization, Italian dates included. That is a bounded regression check, not a proof that nothing else changed. Six bugs the rehearsal found in our own install script The rehearsal is not only about the package. Running the exact installation procedure on the replica found six bugs in ours before it ever touched production: apt-get install debs/x.deb (relative path) is read as a package name. apt wants ./debs/x.deb or an absolute path. macOS tar adds Apple extended attributes that GNU tar on the server warns about: --no-xattrs --no-mac-metadata . Missing rollback packages produced a warning and the procedure carried on. Now it stops. install ran even after a failed preflight . Now preflight leaves a token that install requires and consumes, tied to the host and to the exact package set. preflight rewrote the "state to roll back to" every time it ran: after one install and one more preflight, a rollback would have "rolled back" to the new version. Now the original state is written once. The rollback looped over dpkg-query output, which also lists virtual names such as php7.2-apcu (provided by php-apcu ) with an empty version, and stopped on the first one. And one difference between a replica and production that matters: official Debian Docker images delete downloaded packages after every apt run ( /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/docker-clean ). A rollback that relies on the apt cache can work on real servers and silently have nothing to work with in the container. Remove that file in the replica, and on production keep an explicit rollback bundle instead of trusting the cache. Installing without breaking things The first, naive installation attempt on the replica used dpkg -i . A dependency was missing ( libargon2-0 , which stretch has but the host did not), and dpkg did what dpkg does: it unpacked everything and left the packages unconfigured. The PHP CLI broke immediately: php: error while loading shared libraries: libargon2.so.0: cannot open shared object file Anything that runs the PHP CLI, such as cron jobs and queue workers, would be down, and package scripts can restart PHP-FPM too. So the installation goes through apt, with apt allowed to see only the local .deb files and the installed packages : APT_LOCAL =( -o Dir::Etc::SourceList = /dev/null -o Dir::Etc::SourceParts = /dev/null -o Dir::State::Lists = /tmp/apt-empty-lists -o Dpkg::Options:: = --force-confold ) apt-get install -s --no-install-recommends --no-remove " ${ APT_LOCAL [@] } " " ${ debs [@] } " # simulation apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends --no-remove " ${ APT_LOCAL [@] } " " ${ debs [@] } " If a dependency is missing, apt refuses during the solver phase, before unpacking anything; --no-remove makes it refuse instead of removing packages. That does not make the installation atomic: a full disk or a failing maintainer script can still stop it halfway. Compute the list of packages per host: the new version of every php7.2-* package installed there, nothing more, plus the runtime libraries that travel with them. preflight preflight must succeed before install agrees to run. It: backs up /etc/php/7.2 ; records the state: package versions, the modules loaded by the CLI and by FPM, and the output of a few intl calls that would expose an ICU change: $d = new DateTime ( "2026-10-07 17:12:00" , new DateTimeZone ( "Europe/Rome" )); foreach ([ IntlDateFormatter :: SHORT , IntlDateFormatter :: MEDIUM , IntlDateFormatter :: LONG , IntlDateFormatter :: FULL ] as $s ) echo ( new IntlDateFormatter ( "it_IT" , $s , IntlDateFormatter :: SHORT , "Europe/Rome" )) -> format ( $d ), PHP_EOL ; echo ( new NumberFormatter ( "it_IT" , NumberFormatter :: CURRENCY )) -> formatCurrency ( 1234.5 , "EUR" ), PHP_EOL ; echo Transliterator :: create ( "Any-Latin; Latin-ASCII; Lower()" ) -> transliterate ( "Perché l’università è così?" ), PHP_EOL ; writes the rollback target once, and checks that every package needed to go back is available (copying it from your own set when the host lacks it); checks free disk space; simulates the installation and stops on any planned downgrade or removal . After install , the recorded state must differ only in what you expect: version numbers, and the behavior changes of the backport described above. Anything else is a reason to roll back. What real hosts can still teach you A newer library than yours. A host may already have sury's 2019 libargon2-0 , newer than the stretch one you ship. apt refuses the downgrade, with Packages were downgraded and -y was used without --allow-downgrades , and touches nothing. Install dependencies only when missing or older, and run the downgrade check in preflight . (Our first version of that check died silently: a dpkg --compare-versions … && echo returning 1 inside a while loop under set -e -o pipefail . It failed closed, which is the right way to fail.) A missing rollback package. Some hosts have nothing in their apt cache, or have packages installed that your rollback set does not cover, such as a -dbgsym debug package. preflight should stop; add the missing package to the rollback set, taken from another host's cache. A full disk. Check free space before installing, not halfway through. php-fpm.conf gets replaced where it is still the stock file (dpkg updates untouched conffiles), while customized php.ini files are kept by ucf, with the new version saved as php.ini.ucf-dist . --force-confold does not govern ucf. Diff /etc/php against the backup after the first host, not after the last. A new syslog line : the new systemd unit runs ExecStartPost=-/usr/lib/php/php-fpm-socket-helper , which an older php-common does not ship. The leading - makes systemd ignore the failure, but the socket alias that helper creates does not exist. Harmless only if nothing uses it. Rolling it out Start with a single host. Capture pages twice before installing (the two captures must be identical after normalization), install, capture again. Then compare the patched host with an unpatched one at the same moment , on pages generated per request ( Cache-Control: no-cache, private ), including pages with localized dates. Make sure every request really reached PHP on the host you think it did, past any cache. Then one host at a time. Take it out of the load balancer, wait until its connections drop to zero, capture, preflight , install , check that the old workers are gone and the new binary is serving, capture again, compare, put it back, and listen for a few minutes: connections, load, PHP-FPM state, web server errors by type , not by count. Two things worth knowing: Health checks can lag. If your health check is a PHP script toggled by a flag in its source, OPcache may keep serving the old version for up to opcache.revalidate_freq seconds (when opcache.validate_timestamps is on). A flag read from a file or a cache has its own rules. Retry for a while before declaring the host back. Load goes up for a few minutes after each FPM restart , because OPcache and APCu start empty. Expect it, and check it settles without new errors. Some special cases: Hosts you cannot drain. Reduce what PHP is exposed to first (the request-method rule above), plan for a short interruption, then install in place and compare on real requests, body and significant headers. Old packages that no longer exist. If the exact packages a host runs are gone everywhere, you have no exact rollback. Pick a recovery target you can install with the same configuration, test that it works, and remember it is just as vulnerable as the original. CLI-only hosts. Patch them too if they run the same application: with a different PHP and ICU, their jobs would generate slugs and dates that differ from the website's. Running processes keep the old binary and extensions in memory until they exit: restart long-running workers, and watch jobs that start during the installation itself. Debian 8 jessie The same source builds for jessie, with more surgery: remove the tidy and zip extensions if your application does not need them (jessie's libtidy and libzip are older than required): delete their debian/rules.d/ext-*.mk files, and debian/control is regenerated without them; disable Argon2 password hashing (jessie has no libargon2), after checking that no stored password hash uses it; take debhelper and libsodium-dev from jessie-backports , and nothing else , so the packages depend on libraries the server actually has; remove one compiler flag: jessie's gcc 4.9 does not know -Wno-error=incompatible-pointer-types , and with it configure cannot compile anything; jessie's dpkg-buildpackage writes no .buildinfo file: adjust whatever copies the results. jessie's apt (1.0) cannot install local .deb files. A tiny local repository solves it: dpkg-scanpackages . /dev/null > Packages # in the builder, next to the .deb files echo 'deb [trusted=yes] file:/path/to/debs ./' > local.list apt-get -o Dir::Etc::SourceList = local.list -o Dir::Etc::SourceParts = /dev/null \ -o Dir::State::Lists = lists -o Dir::Cache = cache update apt-get … install -s php7.2-common php7.2-cli php7.2-fpm … # simulation, then the real one [trusted=yes] skips apt's signature check for that directory: fine for files you already verified and keep in a protected place, never for a repository on the network. If the host runs an older minor version, such as 7.1, PHP 7.2 can go in next to it: different package names, separate FPM services, separate sockets. That is still an application upgrade, so test it, and check what happens to the php CLI alternative too. Nothing changes for visitors until you point the web server's virtual host from php7.1-fpm.sock to php7.2-fpm.sock and reload. To be sure requests really go to the new PHP, check the new pool's status page or access log; the I/O counters of the two FPM pools around a few requests are a quick extra signal (the new one goes up, the old one does not move). Rolling back is the same line and another reload; once you are confident, remove the old version, which is still vulnerable. A difference we almost reported as a bug After the upgrade, php-fpm.conf contained: ; pid = / var / run / php / php @ PHP_MAJOR_VERSION @.@ PHP_MINOR_VERSION @- fpm . pid Commented out, placeholders unsubstituted, while the 2019 package wrote pid = /run/php/php7.2-fpm.pid and Debian's own packages (8.2 on bookworm, 8.4 on trixie) still do. We traced it to the packaging (a sed that only rewrites an uncommented pid line) and drafted a bug report with a one-line fix. Then we looked for the project's tracker. The GitHub repository is archived; the tracker moved to Codeberg, and there the change had already been discussed ( issue #113 ). It is deliberate: the changelog calls it "Do not create obsolete PID file", in the same May 2026 release that hardened the systemd unit. Without a pid file, systemd does not care ( Type=notify , reload via $MAINPID ), and log reopening was rewritten to use systemctl kill ( issue #117 ). Only the old init.d scripts need it, and the maintainer said he would rather drop them than patch them. No report needed. The same release hardened the systemd unit ( ProtectSystem=full , PrivateDevices=true , RestrictNamespaces=true and more; debian/NEWS lists them and warns that less standard FPM setups may need changes). ProtectSystem=full makes /usr , /boot and /etc read-only for PHP-FPM, so an application that writes there will break, and an older systemd ignores the options it does not know, with a warning in the journal. Test start, restart, reload and log rotation on the target. Takeaways An end-of-life OS turns a five-minute apt upgrade into a project. Budget the migration before the next CVE does it for you. Read what you run, pools included. php-fpm -i and the pool configuration, not just grep php.ini . Read the backport, not just its title. A minimal mitigation can change behavior. Measure the noise before you compare. Normalize only what you proved is noise, then compare byte by byte. Check what a binary actually loads ( NEEDED ), not only what its package declares. Rehearse the installation procedure, not only the package , on a replica built from the production packages and configuration. Ours found six bugs. Install through apt with local files only , simulate first, refuse downgrades and removals, keep the rollback packages next to you. Read the patches you ship. One of them may phone home. Check the upstream tracker, and where it lives now, before filing. It may be a decision, not a bug. None of this replaces upgrading the operating system: it buys you time. But it can close a critical hole in days, with the pages you checked unchanged.

title: U.S. Army practices nighttime Patriot reloads to sustain air and missile defense operations
body: Crews used a modified M985 heavy tactical truck equipped with a crane to remove and replace canisters on a Patriot M903 launching station. Headlamps lit their work areas, but soldiers still had to monitor the movements of personnel and equipment as they lifted, positioned and secured each canister. “It’s not enough to get a Patriot system into position. Our Soldiers must be able to keep it operational,” said Capt. Grace Ko, Delta Battery’s commander. “Training these reloads at night gives our crews experience working through challenges they could face during a real mission. We need to be ready to sustain the fight.” Junior leaders and crews were responsible for carrying out the drill. First Sgt. Pattrick Harris said battery leaders set standards and provided resources, then allowed the teams to execute. “We set the standard, give them the resources and let them execute,” Harris said. “That’s how they build confidence, and that’s how we find out what our crews are capable of.” Sgt. Kobly Bagley served as the reload crew’s signal person, helping coordinate equipment movements. He said the experience reinforced the need to trust the soldiers working around him. “One of the biggest things I took away from this reload was learning to trust my safety more,” Bagley said. “You have to trust the people around you to do their jobs.” The reload training was part of a mission readiness exercise that began October 19. The exercise evaluates how firing batteries, headquarters and support personnel establish, operate and sustain Patriot air defense systems in the field.

title: Western borders of Russia-Belarus Union State under growing threat — ambassador
body:
MINSK, October 26. /TASS/. Threats to the western borders of the Union State are growing, Russian Ambassador to Belarus Boris Gryzlov told the Natsionalnaya Oborona (National Defense) magazine in an interview.
"Threats to our shared western borders are increasing. We can see the consequences of the policy course pursued by the United States and its allies for decades - NATO’s eastward expansion, the military buildup near our borders, and the violation of agreements on arms control," the diplomat said.
Given the West’s provocative policy course toward Russia and Belarus, additional measures have been taken to strengthen the shared defense and security space at the Union State, based on the Union State’s military doctrine, its security concept and the bilateral agreement on security guarantees as part of the Union State, Gryzlov continued. "Our defense capabilities include a regional battlegroup, joint patrols of the Union State’s air borders, a unified regional air defense system and a number of other components," he maintained.

title: NBA Embraces the CFTC on Prediction Markets as the NFL Fights It in Court
body:
The NBA has struck a deal with the top U.S. derivatives regulator to help police prediction markets, becoming the latest major sports league to formalize an integrity partnership as betting on games moves onto federally regulated platforms.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission said Monday it signed a memorandum of understanding with the basketball league to protect the integrity of professional basketball in prediction markets.
Under the agreement, the two will share information and communicate regularly on integrity matters while working to keep the markets fair and transparent.
“The NBA joins the MLB and NHL in taking a responsible step toward protecting sports integrity and market participants from abuses in prediction markets like insider trading and fraud,” CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said in a statement, thanking Commissioner Adam Silver for prioritizing “the integrity of professional basketball and America’s financial markets.”
The pact reflects how quickly sports-outcome betting has migrated to CFTC-regulated venues like Kalshi and Polymarket, which let users trade “event contracts” on real-world outcomes, including who wins a given game.
That shift has raised integrity concerns familiar to the gambling world, chiefly the risk that insiders could trade on nonpublic information. The league-regulator MOUs are meant to build a channel for flagging suspicious activity, following the NHL’s move to become the first major league to license its trademarks to a prediction market and MLB’s integrity agreement tied to a Polymarket deal.
The NBA is a pointed addition, given the league is still reeling from one of the biggest betting scandals in recent memory. An October 2025 FBI operation led to the arrest of Miami Heat guard Terry Rozier and a coach over alleged involvement in gambling schemes, including one centered on manipulating game outcomes to influence bets. The case put a spotlight on exactly the kind of insider misconduct these partnerships are meant to catch, making the NBA’s cooperation with the CFTC especially resonant.
The partnership also lands amid a fierce jurisdictional fight over whether these markets fall under federal or state authority.
The CFTC recently moved to define event contracts as “swaps” squarely within its remit while excluding casino-style gambling, and a court battle pitting the NFL against Kalshi has drawn the Supreme Court’s attention. Notably, the NFL has so far balked at signing on, making the NBA’s cooperation a contrast among the major leagues.
The stakes are only growing. Analysts at Bernstein have projected prediction markets could generate billions in revenue by the end of the decade, and new entrants keep arriving, with Blockchain.com among the latest to seek CFTC approval to offer event contracts.

title: EchoVault: I Built an Open-Source AI That Helps Forgotten Memories Live On
body: EchoVault: I Built an Open-Source AI That Helps Forgotten Memories Live On Some of the most valuable things we own aren't expensive devices or files stored in the cloud. They're the stories we hear from our grandparents. The recordings we make during family gatherings. The letters we keep but rarely revisit. The little details that seem ordinary today but become priceless years later. And yet, these memories are surprisingly easy to lose. Recordings remain buried in folders. Audio files are difficult to search. Handwritten notes get separated from their context. Eventually, the people who remember these stories might no longer be around to tell them. For Hacktoberfest Week 4, I wanted to explore a different interpretation of Ghost in the Machine . What if AI could help preserve the voices, stories and memories that time might otherwise erase? That idea became EchoVault. What I Built EchoVault is an AI-powered memory archive designed to help people preserve, organize and rediscover personal stories. Instead of treating old recordings and written memories as files that simply sit on a device, EchoVault helps turn them into a searchable collection of stories. The workflow is simple: Upload an audio recording or written memory. Transcribe supported audio recordings. Generate a concise summary and extract useful details. Save the original material alongside its transcript and metadata. Search the archive and ask questions about the saved stories. Create a remembrance page that brings the material together in a readable format. The goal isn't to make AI replace the people behind these memories. It's to make their stories easier to preserve, revisit and share. EchoVault is about helping memories survive, not pretending that AI can bring someone back. Demo In the demonstration, I'll upload a sample recording, show how EchoVault transcribes and summarizes it, and retrieve a detail from the saved story. I'll also demonstrate how the original recording and its generated content remain connected, so users can verify the archive entry against its source. Code The repository contains the application source code, setup instructions, model configuration, dependencies and documentation for running EchoVault. The goal is to make the project reproducible so other developers can experiment with the models, improve the archive workflow or adapt it to their own use cases. How I Built It I built EchoVault around Python, Streamlit and open-source AI tools. The architecture separates transcription, language-model processing, storage and retrieval so that each component can be tested independently. 1. Transcription For supported audio recordings, EchoVault uses OpenAI Whisper running locally to convert speech into text. The transcript makes a recording searchable and gives the next stage a text representation to work with. Transcription accuracy still depends on recording quality, accents, background noise and the languages supported by the selected model. 2. Memory extraction An open-weight Gemma model processes the transcript and generates structured metadata such as a title, summary, key events and people mentioned. I designed this stage to distinguish the original story from AI-generated interpretations. The original transcript remains available for verification. 3. Searchable archive EchoVault stores the original files and associated metadata, making it possible to revisit individual memories rather than repeatedly processing every recording. 4. Grounded question answering The question-answering feature retrieves relevant material from the archive and uses it to formulate an answer. Rather than treating the model as an unrestricted storyteller, the application is designed to ground responses in the saved records. If a question cannot be answered from the available material, the system should say so instead of inventing a memory. 5. A human-centered interface I used Streamlit to create an interface for uploading recordings, reviewing transcripts, exploring archived stories and generating remembrance pages. I wanted the experience to feel more like a digital archive than a generic chatbot. This part of the project taught me that building a useful AI application involves more than prompting a model. Data handling, validation, retrieval and the way users verify generated content all matter. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? For a project dealing with personal memories, the choice of AI infrastructure matters as much as the interface. Privacy and control Family recordings and personal stories can contain sensitive information. Running transcription and language models locally can reduce the need to send this material to external AI services. In a fully local configuration, recordings and generated content can remain on the user's device. This is an architectural goal, not an automatic guarantee: the complete application must be checked for external network calls, telemetry, cloud storage and other data transfers before claiming that it is fully offline. Freedom to experiment Open-weight models give developers more flexibility to choose models, change prompts, compare performance and adapt the application to their requirements. For EchoVault, this means being able to experiment with different transcription and language models without designing the entire product around a single proprietary AI API. Preservation beyond a single service An archive should not become inaccessible simply because a hosted service changes its pricing, API or availability. Keeping original recordings, transcripts and metadata in portable formats makes the collection easier to back up and migrate independently of a particular model provider. Making the technology accessible A local-first approach can reduce dependence on recurring hosted inference charges, although users still need compatible hardware, storage and electricity. The larger point is that useful AI tools should be adaptable and understandable, rather than locked into an infrastructure that their users cannot control. My Agent Session I used python to implement and test EchoVault. The session documents the decisions, experiments and debugging steps that shaped the final application. The Spirit of It The theme Ghost in the Machine made me think about how technology interacts with memory. A recording is only a collection of bits until someone listens to it. A transcript is only text until someone recognizes the person, place or moment behind it. AI cannot replace the human experience of remembering someone. It can, however, help make the material we leave behind easier to preserve and understand. I want EchoVault to make it easier for someone to rediscover a story they had almost forgotten, find a detail in an old recording, or bring together memories that would otherwise remain scattered across devices. The most meaningful result isn't an AI-generated story that sounds convincing. It's helping someone find a real story worth remembering. What's Next? I'd like to explore better multilingual transcription, additional document formats, richer search, exportable remembrance pages and tools for organizing large collections of recordings. I also want to improve source attribution so users can move directly from a generated summary or answer to the original passage that supports it. EchoVault began with a simple question: what if we could use open-source AI to help preserve the stories that matter to us? My answer is a small step toward making personal archives more accessible, searchable and useful. Because sometimes the most valuable thing an AI can do isn't generate something new. It's help us hold on to something we already have. devchallenge #hf26challenge

title: Russian strike on Kharkiv kills and injures civilians
body:
Mayor Ihor Terekhov reported this on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
According to him, the enemy attack damaged apartment buildings, private homes, and cars.
In a previous post, the mayor noted that a major fire broke out at one of the locations following the invaders’ strike.
Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, clarified on Facebook that those injured as a result of the Russian Federation’s missile attack on the Novobavarskyi district include two men aged 61 and 77, a 60-year-old woman, and a 17-year-old girl.
