title: Russian diplomat calls on UN to make Ukraine remove children’s data from Mirotvorets
body:
UNITED NATIONS, October 26. /TASS/. Russia urges the United Nations to take exhaustive measures to compel Ukraine to delete minors’ personal data from its extremist website Mirotvorest, Russian Permanent Representative to the United Nations Vasily Nebenzya said.
"We hope that the world organization, especially its special envoy, will take comprehensive measures to ensure that Ukraine immediately removes children’s profiles from Mirotvorets," he stressed.
He also called on the office of the UN envoy to pay utmost attention to this issue as part of its efforts to draw lessons regarding the risks associated with the use of digital technologies for the protection of children.

title: Space Force Wants Cislunar Kit Ready to Launch by 2029
body: For years now , Space Force officials have said the service is getting serious about defining its role and crafting an architecture for future cislunar capabilities. Now, the Space Force is taking steps to realize that vision, asking industry to rapidly invest and develop satellites and software that could be ready for operations as soon as 2029. Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy—the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for advanced programs—said he’s seen the Pentagon’s posture toward cislunar operations and planning efforts change drastically over the past year . “There was no talk of cislunar, and basically I was told, ‘Don’t talk about cislunar, and stop getting into it,’” Purdy said Oct. 21 at AFCEA’s Space Industry Days conference. Now, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Gen. Dan Caine, and even a December 2025 executive order from President Donald Trump are emphasizing the importance of cislunar operations and advocating for more investment. The shift is in part linked to China’s lunar ambitions, Purdy said. Beijing has a cislunar roadmap of its own and has already landed several uncrewed spacecraft on the lunar surface. Now, it plans to launch a crewed Moon mission by 2030. “I’ve got the Secretary of War and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs full on stating in public: ‘This is a warfighting domain,’” Purdy said, using the department’s secondary name. “And so, I would ask you all, please jump on my cislunar bandwagon because I need some more friends here, along with our deep, passionate crew that have been working on this for years.” Cislunar space is the region beyond geosynchronous orbit extending to the moon and even farther to cover areas influenced by Earth and the moon’s gravity—hundreds of thousands of kilometers in distance and 1,728 times the volume of space contained within geosynchronous orbit. Purdy described the region as “painful” for satellite operations, as it is further from Earth and navigation is more of a challenge. To date, much of the U.S. government’s cislunar planning and operations have centered on NASA and its plan to return astronauts to the moon through the Artemis program. The Defense Department has pursued research programs aimed at better understanding the vast expanse of cislunar space—including the Air Force Research Lab’s Oracle program, which plans to launch several cislunar space domain awareness satellites in the coming years. But the Space Force hasn’t dedicated much planning, funding, or personnel to those efforts. That may be about to change. In April, the Space Force set up a new Cislunar Coordination Office , housed within Purdy’s portfolio and tasked with crafting a roadmap for cislunar technology and a future space architecture. Since then, that office – led by Jaime Stearns—has refined that roadmap and crafted strategies for various mission areas, like space domain awareness, communications, and lunar navigation. The CCO has also drafted a list of high-priority but unfunded requirements, which Purdy said includes relatively low-dollar “ticky-tacky” efforts that can help the Space Force make real progress in this area. The service is also pursuing multiple technology development and rapid fielding efforts, Purdy said. In partnership with the Air Force Research Laboratory and the innovation arm SpaceWERX, it plans to launch an industry challenge called Lunar Prime to get after some of its more nascent technology and research needs. The effort has $30 million in funding and is targeting flight demonstrations within two years of contract award. The Space Force also has two requests for information it plans to release “imminently,” Purdy said. The first will call for existing commercial technology that can be ready to launch by 2029. “We’re looking for existing commercial or near-commercial means, non-developmental solutions, hardware with actual relevant evidence behind it, software that doesn’t need a huge amount of work … and ground systems,” Purdy said. “This isn’t a four- or five-year science project. This is about getting capability out soon.” The second request is for AI and autonomous processing capabilities for spacecraft operating in cislunar space. The goal is to have “a fully autonomous system out there at cislunar that’s able to handle all its hardware faults, all its processing, all the sensor activities,” Purdy said. The post Space Force Wants Cislunar Kit Ready to Launch by 2029 appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Malawi delegation studies Ghana’s mining reforms and responsible gold governance
body: Malawi is looking to Ghana’s experience in gold production and mining-sector reforms for lessons to strengthen its own mineral governance, with a focus on responsible sourcing, artisanal mining and the financing of mineral-related businesses. The delegation, led by Malawi’s Minister of Mining, Thoko Tembo, met Ghana’s Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, as part of a learning mission supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). The engagement focused on Ghana’s mining governance framework and ongoing efforts to improve gold purchasing, traceability, production accounting and the management of mineral revenues. Mr Buah said Ghana’s long history of mining had provided experience from which other countries could learn, while emphasising that the country was also working to improve its policies and regulatory systems. He said ongoing reforms were intended to strengthen accountability in the gold sector, protect the environment and ensure mining communities had a greater voice and benefited from resources extracted from their lands. The Lands Minister outlined proposed changes to the mining licensing regime, including clearer timelines and performance requirements for companies holding mining rights. He also highlighted plans to involve district-level mining committees in assessing proposed concessions before licences are issued. The proposed measures are intended to strengthen oversight and improve the assessment of mining proposals before they receive regulatory approval. Chief Executive Officer of the Minerals Commission, Isaac Tandoh, also presented Ghana’s mining governance framework to the delegation. He responded to questions on domestic gold purchasing, the formalisation of mineral markets and efforts to strengthen responsible sourcing systems. Malawi’s Minister of Mining, Thoko Tembo, welcomed the opportunity to learn from Ghana’s experience, including challenges encountered in developing and regulating its mining industry. He said the delegation wanted practical lessons that could help Malawi avoid similar difficulties as it develops its own sector. The discussions included artisanal and small-scale mining and access to financing for businesses operating in the minerals industry. The delegation also included representatives of Malawi’s banking sector and artisanal and small-scale mining industry, reflecting an interest in both regulatory approaches and the financial systems needed to support mineral-sector development. The engagement provided an opportunity for the two countries to exchange perspectives on mining regulation, domestic mineral markets and responsible sourcing. For Ghana, the discussions come as authorities pursue reforms aimed at improving accountability in gold purchasing and strengthening oversight of mining activities. For Malawi, the visit offers an opportunity to examine Ghana’s policy approaches and consider which lessons could inform the development of its own mining industry.

title: Air National Guard to stand up a new special tactics squadron
body: The Pentagon has directed the Air Force to stand up a new Air National Guard Special Tactics Squadron. It would be one of only a few Air National Guard units made up of special operations personnel. The Pentagon announced the decision last week and referenced a Sept. 23 memo signed by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, which directed the Air Force to establish a new Florida-based unit. Pentagon officials said that the move “strategically positions a premier Special Tactics capability at the center of the nation’s special operations command hub, deepening the integration between the National Guard and active duty elite units to defend the United States and defeat global adversaries.” U.S. Special Operations Command is headquartered at MacDill Air Force Base near Tampa, Florida. Air Force Special Operations Command is based hundreds of miles away at Hurlburt Field, Florida, which is hundreds of miles northwest of MacDill in the Florida Panhandle. Hegseth’s memo indicates that the unit’s initial activation will be funded from the fiscal year 2027 budget and that the 2028 budget could cover additional construction, equipment and manpower authorizations. Pentagon officials said they had nothing more to add beyond the announcement and memo. Airmen from the Kentucky Air National Guard’s 123rd Special Tactics Squadron prepare to hoist a simulated patient into a Merlin Mk2 helicopter off the coast of Scotland on Aug. 18, 2026, as part of a search-and-rescue training scenario. Air National Guard photo by Phil Speck. Air Force Special Operations Officials did not provide immediate details on the mission of the new unit or when it would be stood up and directed additional questions to the Pentagon. “We are in initial stages of planning and look forward to growing our elite Special Tactics community to enhance our joint force’s lethality and readiness,” said Lt. Col. Casey Osborne, an Air Force Special Operations Command spokesperson. Special Tactics units are made up of all the Air Force special operator career fields, including combat controllers, pararescuemen, special reconnaissance and Tactical Air Control Party (TACP) specialists. These airmen are capable of running air support for humanitarian aid missions, conducting airfield seizures in combat, or directing life-saving personnel evacuations in remote areas. The majority of Air Force special tactics squadrons are active duty units throughout the U.S. as well as two abroad in England and Japan. The new unit appears to be the Air National Guard’s third special tactics squadron — the others are the 125th, based out of Portland, Oregon, and the 123rd, based out of Louisville, Kentucky. Top Stories This Week News Hegseth’s plan to restore Confederate memorial at Arlington expected to cost taxpayers $9 million By Austin Campbell News US expands alcohol restrictions for troops in Japan By Nicholas Slayton News Space Force wants to embed more guardians into the joint force By Nicholas Slayton The 125th Special Tactics Squadron , based out of Portland, Oregon, is made up of over 75 Special Tactics combat controllers and personnel from special operations weather teams and combat support teams. Their airmen have responded to major environmental disasters like Hurricanes Ike , Harvey , and Irma , and in 2008, the squadron used special-operation rescue boats and equipment to save hundreds of stranded people after a flood in Vernonia, Oregon . They’ve also sent personnel to support Operations Enduring Freedom missions in Afghanistan, the Horn of Africa and the Philippines, and Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation New Dawn. The Air National Guard’s 123rd Special Tactics Squadron is based out of Louisville, Kentucky. According to the 123rd squadron’s website , it is the only Air National Guard special operations unit with both combat controllers and pararescue personnel. According to the unit, the squadron supported combat operations in Iraq and Afghanistan. In a three-year period, its airmen deployed overseas for over 4,600 days, conducted more than 950 ground-combat missions and saved over 50 personnel. In 2010, airmen with the 123rd were “among the first U.S. forces” to respond to the Haiti earthquake, and directed humanitarian aid drops and resupply. As part of a special operations exercise in 2023 , airmen from the 123rd squadron jumped from an MC-130J onto a civilian highway in Wyoming to practice establishing and securing the highway landing zone for the inbound aircraft. The Kentucky unit has also trained on specialized fueling operations and rapid-reaction aircraft launches with the UK and Canada , and aeromedical evacuations with Ecuador . Last year, the unit ran through search and rescue, reconnaissance and targeting operations in a simulated contested environment across islands in the Caribbean . The post Air National Guard to stand up a new special tactics squadron appeared first on Task & Purpose .

title: Six Flags to install seat belts on Georgia roller coaster after rider’s death
body:
The chief executive of Six Flags says the company will install seat belts on the Georgia roller coaster from which a rider fell to his death earlier this month . The company’s rides with similar restraints will also get the safety upgrade.
The theme park operator announced the extra safeguard less than two weeks after 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta died after being ejected from his seat on the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia.
“We are reinforcing safety precautions at our parks and taking additional measures, including adding seat belts on Goliath and other coasters with a similar restraint,” John Reilly, president and CEO of Six Flags Entertainment Corporation, said in a statement Friday.
Goliath remains shut down while state and local officials investigate the Oct. 12 death.
Reilly didn’t specify which other Six Flags coasters will get seat belts. But it has temporarily closed eight additional roller coasters at five other parks in the U.S. and Canada. Those rides all share the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system.
Six Flags hasn’t said when those coasters are expected to reopen. Reilly’s statement said Six Flags has enlisted independent engineers and inspectors to review safety procedures for all rides at its theme parks.
Investigators haven’t said what went wrong on the Georgia coaster. Witnesses said they saw Kariem rise up out of his seat and fall headfirst back into the cart before being ejected. Some people who rode Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints.
All nine of the Six Flags coasters taken offline were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard. They also feature similar clamshell restraints that sit at the top of a vertical bar between each rider’s knees. The bar locks a padded restraint into place over the rider’s lap and upper legs.
The U.S. patent granted to Bolliger & Mabillard for the restraint system in 2001 says it’s designed to make each rider feel “that he is seated on a flying carpet or that he is at the controls of a kind of flying scooter, while still guaranteeing optimum security.”
Following the death in Georgia, non-Six Flags theme parks SeaWorld Orlando in Florida and La Ronde in Montreal, Canada, also temporarily closed one roller coaster apiece that use clamshell restraints.
SeaWorld reopened its Mako coaster Tuesday after it had been offline for a week. The Associated Press emailed the company Saturday asking if seat belts or other safety upgrades were planned for the coaster.
The AP also emailed a spokesperson for La Ronde seeking an update on its shuttered coaster.
In addition to Goliath in Georgia, eight coasters remain closed at Six Flags parks in Gurnee, Illinois; Jackson Township, New Jersey; Charlotte, North Carolina; Mason, Ohio; and Vaughan, Ontario.

title: Russian Strike on Kharkiv Kills 2, Wounds 4, Including Teenager
body:
Russian forces struck Kharkiv’s Novobavarskyi district on Monday, Oct. 26, killing two people and wounding four others, including a 17-year-old girl.
At the time of the report, it was not immediately clear which types of weapons were used in the attacks. The head of Kharkiv Regional Military Administration Oleh Syniehubov referred to missile strikes, while Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said the district had been hit by multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS).
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
However, it was clarified that the strike wounded two men aged 61 and 77, alongside a 60-year-old woman. All four victims received necessary medical treatment, local authorities said.
The attack was initially reported around 6 p.m. local time, followed by a second strike minutes later. Syniehubov estimated that one person had been killed and the teenager wounded, noting that several private vehicles were on fire.
Several hours later, two people were confirmed dead and four injured in total.
Four apartment buildings and four private homes, as well as 10 garages and a kindergarten building were damaged in the strike.
Two fires broke out at the scene, engulfing a non-residential building and several passenger vehicles. Firefighters have since put out both blazes, according to DSNS, who added that vehicles and buildings belonging to private business were also damaged.
It was not immediately clear which company the vehicles and buildings belonged to.
The Novobavarskyi strike was one of at least four attacks on Kharkiv on Monday evening. Earlier, Russian drones hit the city’s Kholodnohirsky district around 4:40 p.m. local time, and again at 5:49 p.m.
Hours before the evening attacks, Syniehubov released a report showing that Russian forces had hit 113 settlements across the region over the past week, killing 12 people and wounding 148.
Among those, two children were killed, and 11 injured.
During that period, Syniehubov said, Russian forces used 27 missiles, eight guided aerial bombs (KABs) and three MLRS across the region.
They also launched nearly 880 drones, including 19 Shahed-type Geran-2s, three Lancet loitering munitions, 19 Molniya drones and 50 first-person-view (FPV) drones, as well as 786 other drones whose type is still being identified.
In Kharkiv alone, last week’s attacks damaged seven apartment buildings, 16 private homes, seven businesses, power lines, two gas stations, a hypermarket, the city circus, railway infrastructure and about 50 private cars.
Separately on Monday, it became known that a 12-year-old boy, Artem Koval , died in the Kyiv hospital from injuries sustained in a Russian drone strike that targeted a crowded park in Nova Vodolaha.
The same Oct. 19 strike killed his eight-year-old sister Ariana, along with five other civilians, including an infant killed in her stroller and her mother.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Alleged Certificate Forgery: UNN, NYSC disowned Nnaji’s certificates, witness tells court
body:
A prosecution witness, on Monday, told the Federal High Court in Abuja that the University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN), and the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) disowned certificates linked to former Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Geoffrey Nnaji.
The witness, who identified himself as Yakubu Ibrahim, a superintendent of police officer with the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), made the revelation. He was led in evidence by prosecution lawyer J.A Mumini, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN).
ICPC is prosecuting Mr Nnaji on certificate forgery and money laundering charges. An investigation by PREMIUM TIMES exposed the certificate forgery scandal leading to Mr Nnaji’s ouster from office last year.
The former minister is the Peoples Democratic Party’s governorship candidate for the upcoming 2027 governorship candidate in Enugu State.
Mr Ibrahim said his team was assigned to investigate the matter after the commission received two separate petitions alleging certificate forgery against Mr Nnaji.
He said the Chairman of the Special Task Force directed an investigation, prompting the commission to request relevant documents from the National Assembly, the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), University of Nigeria, Nsukka and the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC).
According to him, the Clerk of the Senate, National Assembly, forwarded Mr Nnaji’s NYSC certificate and BSc certificate in Microbiology and Biochemistry to the commission.
He said NYSC responded that the certificate purportedly issued by the corps was not issued by it.
The witness further told the court that UNN also responded that Nnaji failed to obtain the required grades for the award of his certificate.
He said the university explained in its letter the policy governing the grades required for the award of a certificate saying if one failed four times, the person was not qualified.
Mr Ibrahim said Mr Nnaji failed at two stages and did not write the examination at the third stage for medical reasons.
“The witness said that, according to the letter, the defendant went ahead to write the supplementary examination for which he did not register,” he said.
Mr Ibrahim further testified that UNN confirmed that the BSc certificate in Microbiology and Biochemistry attributed to the defendant was not issued by the university.
He said the commission also obtained documents from the SGF’s office, including a payslip, which prompted it to request Mr Nnaji’s bank statement.
According to him, the bank statement showed that Mr Nnaji received N29.5 million in salary as minister before he resigned .
The witness identified letters sent to the Clerk of the Senate, the SGF, UNN, NYSC, the bank and Mr Nnaji, which were tendered in evidence.
He also told the court that Mr Nnaji failed to honour the commission’s invitation to answer questions on the petitions, prompting the ICPC to contact the State Security Service (SSS).
Ibrahim said the DSS subsequently arrested Nnaji on 1 July.
Mr Nnaji’s lawyer, Wole Olanipekun, a SAN, said he would reserve his objection to the admissibility of the documents until the appropriate stage of the proceedings, if necessary.
In a ruling, Judge Joyce Abdulmalik admitted the documents in evidence but held that objections to their admissibility would be reserved until the final address.
During cross-examination by Mr Olanipekun, Mr Ibrahim told the court that he did not visit UNN during his investigation.
He also said he did not know how many campuses the university had or the faculty from which Mr Nnaji graduated.
Asked whether he interviewed any past or present university staff member, the witness said he interviewed a registrar named Ngozi but could not recall her surname.
Mr Ibrahim also told the court that he saw a letter from UNN directing the withdrawal of Mr Nnaji’s admission.
Mr Olanipekun, however, drew his attention to another letter showing that the withdrawal letter dated 7 November 1984, was rescinded by a subsequent letter dated 18 March 1985.
With no further questions from the defence for the witness, the prosecution requested an adjournment to enable it call another witness.
Ms Abdulmalik adjourned the matter until 5 November for continuation of trial.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Nnaji was arraigned before the Federal High Court on six counts of certificate forgery, money laundering and abuse of office.
He pleaded not guilty to all the charges.
The ICPC, which filed the charges, alleged that Mr Nnaji presented forged UNN degree and NYSC certificates to support his ministerial appointment in 2023.
The commission also accused him of receiving about N29.58 million in salaries and allowances as minister, allegedly linked to proceeds of unlawful acts.
The court granted him bail in yhe sum of N20 million with one surety and he was ordered to deposit his passport with the court. He is not to travel outside the country without permission from the court throughout the period of his trial.

title: Serbia’s Student List party pledges not to impose sanctions against Russia
body:
BELGRADE, October 26. /TASS/. Serbia’s new government to be formed by the winning opposition movement Student List will not impose sanctions against Russia, Jovo Bakic, a Student List representative, said.
"We respect Russia as a great power and our historically important partner, and, in many cases, our defender. There will be no changes in this regard. <…> Serbian sanctions would change nothing for Russia but from a symbolic point of view they would look negative," he told the RT Balkan television channel.
Serbia "has endured UN sanctions and knows full well what an ordeal that is," he added.
When asked about the European Union’s demand that Serbia refuse to receive Russian energy sources, Bakic said, "it's our prerogative to act in our national interests, not to please foreigners."
Serbia’s former President Aleksandar Vucic said earlier that after winning the parliamentary elections, the Student List would impose anti-Russian sanctions by the spring of 2027.
Serbia held snap elections to the National Assembly, or unicameral parliament, on October 25. With 96.47% of the vote tally reports processed, the Republic Electoral Commission announced that United Serbia, led by former President Aleksandar Vucic, had lost to the opposition Student List, receiving 39.27% of the vote against 52.57%, respectively.

title: 'Star Trek' actor Walter Koenig dies at 90
body:
Walter Koenig, best known for playing USS Enterprise navigator Ensign Pavel Chekov on the original " Star Trek " TV series, died Sunday. He was 90.
Koenig's agent confirmed his death to ABC News, and Koenig's former co-star, George Takei, also shared the news in an online post Monday.
"Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world," Koenig's agent, Zachery McGinnis, said in a statement, in part. "He passed of old age at home in North Hollywood last night surrounded by his daughter and niece."
In his Facebook post, Takei mourned the news of his former co-star's death.
"Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too," Takei wrote.
Born on Sept. 14, 1936, Koenig appeared on several television shows including "The Alfred Hitchcock Hour," "The Lieutenant" -- created and produced by "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry -- "I Spy" and more before landing the role of Chekov in the second season of "Star Trek" in 1967.
Koenig told the Television Academy in a 2013 interview that he hadn't seen "Star Trek" before he read for the role of Chekov, a character that was added to the show after its debut.
"They were looking for an actor or a personality that would appeal to the same demographic that Davy Jones did -- kids 8 to 14 years old," he said, referring to the then-star of the music-comedy TV series "The Monkees," adding that when he was cast in the role, he would get mail from young people commenting on how "groovy" his hair was.
In a 1984 interview with "Good Morning America," Koenig said "Star Trek" had a "monumental effect" on his life.
"In my mind it's somewhat questionable whether I would indeed still be pursuing a career in this industry had it not been for 'Star Trek,'" he said. "'Star Trek' has made it possible not only to remain an actor, but to pursue other industry endeavors like writing and directing and producing."
Following "Star Trek," Koenig went on to star in or appear in other television series, including "Columbo," "The Starlost," "Babylon 5" and more.
In 1979, he joined his other fellow "Star Trek" original series cast members in reprising his role in "Star Trek: The Motion Picture," the first "Star Trek" feature film.
He went on to play Chekov again in "Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan" in 1982, "Star Trek III: The Search for Spock" in 1984, "Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home" in 1986, "Star Trek V: The Final Frontier" in 1989," "Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country" in 1991 and "Star Trek: Generations" in 1994.
Outside of acting, Koenig was known for his humanitarian activism focused on human rights and assisting refugees. He was also a husband and father. In 1965, he married actress Judy Levitt.
"She’s very tolerant of my collection and my collecting so long as it doesn’t come down the stairs into the living room or any of the bedrooms," Koenig said in a 2012 interview about his wife's view of his "Star Trek" memorabilia.
In 2012, Koenig was honored with a Hollywood Walk of Fame star. In recent years, he continued to appear in other "Star Trek"-related projects and lent his voice to various animated series. He was also a familiar face at fan events and conventions.
Koenig is survived by his daughter, Danielle Koenig, an actress, comedian and screenwriter. Koenig's wife died in 2022. Koenig's son, actor Andrew Koenig, died by suicide in 2010.

title: Zelensky meets Lithuanian Seimas speaker to discuss Ukraine’s European integration
body:
According to Ukrinform, the head of state announced this on Facebook .
According to Zelenskyy, it is very important that the remaining two negotiation clusters for Ukraine be opened by the end of this year, and that authorized representatives be able to close negotiation chapters during the Lithuanian presidency.
Zelensky briefed Olekas on the meetings in Oslo and the overall situation in the negotiation track.
“We expect that a trilateral meeting between the American, Ukrainian, and Russian teams will take place as early as the beginning of November,” the head of state noted.
As reported by Ukrinform, according to Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration Vsevolod Chentsov, Ukraine hopes to open the last two clusters in the EU accession negotiations by the end of the year, against the backdrop of elections scheduled to take place in several EU member states in 2027.
At the Ukraine-EU Intergovernmental Conference in Luxembourg on October 13, Chapters 2 and 3 of Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations were officially open ed.

title: How Ukraine's annual radio dictation brings a nation together, one word at a time
body:
People take part in the Radio Dictation of National Unity at the Odesa Regional Universal Scientific Library named after M.S. Hrushevsky in Odesa, Ukraine, on Oct. 25, 2024. (Viacheslav Onyshchenko / Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
As it turns out, dictation exercises are not just for schoolchildren. On Oct. 27, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians — from diaspora communities abroad to service members on the front lines — will take part in an annual tradition: listening, writing, and testing their mastery of the Ukrainian language.
Organized by Ukrainian Radio since 2000, the annual Radio Dictation celebrates the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language, bringing participants together to transcribe a text broadcast live across multiple platforms. Those who wish to have their work assessed can submit it to a professional review panel.
For Ukrainian author and war veteran Artur Dron , who wrote this year's dictation, the invitation to craft a text that so many people would follow word by word was "daunting." Still, he didn't hesitate to accept.
"I've taken part in (the dictation) myself several times, and I see something truly special in it," Dron said.
"The fact that, even during the full-scale war , we're holding this initiative for the fifth time — that we continue to do so even under these circumstances, and that language still brings us together — means a great deal."
Yuliia Sheludko, an executive producer at Ukrainian Radio, told the Kyiv Independent that she believes the dictation serves as "a kind of anchor" for Ukrainians during wartime.
Bringing Ukrainians together around a shared love of the Ukrainian language also carries particular weight as Russia intensifies its attacks against the country.
"We know from history that the Ukrainian language was suppressed for many years, so we must value and protect it," Sheludko said.
Under Russian imperial rule, successive restrictions curtailed Ukrainian use in publishing and education, while Soviet authorities continued to subordinate Ukrainian to Russian , despite periods of official support for Ukrainian-language culture. Ukrainian intellectuals, writers, and cultural figures were also persecuted, imprisoned, and even killed for their pro-Ukrainian stances.
The 2014 EuroMaidan Revolution helped accelerate a broader societal shift back to Ukrainian, which has gained further traction since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. For many, speaking Ukrainian has become one of the most powerful expressions of their national identity.
Despite its power to unite Ukrainians through a shared love of the language, however, the Radio Dictation also tends to stir up strong opinions.
Ahead of this year's event, volunteer and civic activist Dasha Astafieva received what she described as "an avalanche of hate" for being chosen to read the dictation alongside teacher Artur Proidakov, with people criticizing everything from her past as a Playboy model to her former use of Russian in public life.
Since 2022, Astafieva has worked to promote Ukrainian culture . She launched the audiobook app UnderBooks in 2023, and wrote on Facebook that "the hysteria over the fact that the dictation will be read by someone who narrates audiobooks marks a whole new level of absurdity."
Public debate isn't limited to this year's dictation. Actress Nataliia Sumska drew criticism in 2025 for delivering the dictation at what many felt was too fast a pace, with many participants saying that it left them scrambling to piece their sentences together.
The uproar grew when a longtime participant with a track record of top marks reportedly had her microphone switched off after she criticized the pace of Sumska's dictation and called author Eugenia Kuznetsova's text "silly."
In 2024, author Oksana Zabuzhko 's text was so challenging that only one person in the country wrote it without any errors.
The disputes point to a tension at the heart of the dictation's mission: how to celebrate Ukrainian as a shared national language while navigating disagreements over who represents it and what mastery of it should look like.
The organizers, however, seem to take the controversy that comes with the Radio Dictation in stride, pointing out that when an event draws this much public attention, some people will always be dissatisfied.
As for the controversy surrounding Astafieva, Sheludko encouraged those who haven't heard her narrate audiobooks to do so, describing it as "something she does with real mastery."
Ukrainian Radio can't provide the exact number of people who take part in the Radio Dictation every year, but it can estimate participation in the hundreds of thousands based on how many people post about it on social media and submit their written work to the professional committee for review.
According to Sheludko, Ukrainian Radio received more submissions in 2022 than in any previous year — and encouraged people to keep doing so not only for the commemorative prizes given to those with top marks.
For all the arguments over who reads the dictation and how difficult the text should be, its enduring appeal lies in something simpler: the chance for Ukrainians, wherever they are, to take part in a shared cultural tradition.
"I believe that this year thousands of people will enjoy the text, the act of writing, and, above all, the sense of unity around the Ukrainian language," Sheludko said.
Kate Tsurkan is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent who writes mostly about culture-related topics. Her newsletter Explaining Ukraine with Kate Tsurkan, which focuses specifically on Ukrainian culture, is published weekly by the Kyiv Independent and is partially supported by a generous grant from the Nadia Sophie Seiler Fund. Kate co-translated Oleh Sentsov’s “Diary of a Hunger Striker,” Myroslav Laiuk’s “Bakhmut,” Andriy Lyubka’s “War from the Rear,” and Khrystia Vengryniuk’s “Long Eyes,” among other books. Some of her previous writing and translations have appeared in the New Yorker, Vanity Fair, Harpers, the Washington Post, the New York Times, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She is the co-founder of Apofenie Magazine and, in addition to Ukrainian and Russian, also knows French.

title: ‘Defeat for denialism’: Lula beats far right Bolsonaro in Brazilian presidential election
body: Incumbent Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was reelected on Oct. 25 in a surprise defeat of his far-right rival who had promised to remove “environmental obstacles” in the Amazon rainforest. Lula won 51.8% of valid votes. Flávio Bolsonaro, eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is imprisoned after being convicted of attempting a coup d’état when he lost the previous election, won 48.2% of the vote. Flávio was favored to win after he got 2% more of the first-round votes on Oct. 4. However, neither candidate got more than 50% of the vote, triggering a runoff election. Lula was able to secure an additional 10 million votes in 20 days. “This election was a defeat for denialism, a defeat for lies,” Lula said in his first speech after the election results. “We are going to teach the world how climate policy is done, here in this country. This year is the first time we have managed to reduce deforestation for four consecutive years.” Deforestation soared to its highest level in 15 years under Jair Bolsonaro’s government. Lula took office in 2023 pledging to end both legal and illegal deforestation by 2030. Since then, deforestation has gradually slowed to its lowest rate since records began in 1988, though the Amazon rainforest is still shrinking. title: Show HN: Websites designed by 10 AI models, ranked by 4,500 human votes
body:
We're compiling human evaluations of the leading open and commercial AI models, starting with design.
The designs are ordered by how often people chose each model’s work here, 90 votes per model.
Rank and win rate are each model’s result on this brief: 90 votes per model, ties split equally, tied models sharing a position. They are keyed by model and brief, not by this generation’s ID.
In a separate run without tools, each model set out a visual direction for this brief. Typefaces on the left, every palette color on the right. Select a model’s mark or a color to read that direction in the model’s own words.
Model-authored directions from the tool-free arm. Family names are taken as written; descriptions without a name are counted together. Specimens marked “approx.” are licensed faces shown in a stand-in. We did not collect private chain of thought, and the direction was not necessarily supplied to the build run.
This table pools every vote across the ten briefs above. The top three models are separated by 4.0 percentage points, and seven different models take first place on at least one brief. The brief range column shows how far each model moves.
Annotators chose between pairs of rendered outputs. A win rate says how often a model’s design was preferred against the other models. It is not an absolute quality score.
This run uses the first ten valid votes on each of 450 pairwise tasks: 4,500 votes from 29 annotators. Ties count as half a vote for each side.
A September pilot used the first five votes per task. Between the two runs, four of the ten models changed global position, none by more than 1 place . Brief-level win rates moved about four times as much. Read the brief ranking as a direction, not a verdict.
Bradley–Terry (BT) estimates relative model strength from pairwise preferences. It returns the same rank order as win rate here.
This export is keyed by model and brief, not by generation ID. The report attaches a score to a design only through an explicit ID match, so per-design preference, annotator agreement, and rubric dimensions stay pending until that export is connected.
Look for convergence in the models’ stated directions. Shared typefaces, similar palettes, and recurring compositions help describe the design space without turning difference into a quality score.
A higher index means a model’s stated font and primary color choices differ more from those of its peers on the same brief.
We average two distances equally: named-font set difference (Jaccard) and normalized RGB distance for the primary color. We then average comparisons within the same brief and multiply by 100. Pairs without recognized fonts are excluded. This index does not measure originality, layout, or human preference.
How human judgment can become a learning system, and why consensus alone can hide useful differences.
Make the observations behind a judgment explicit. Preserve disagreement when preference is what you want to measure.
Studying model behavior or comparing creative outputs? Talk to us about designing the rubric and collecting the human feedback your research needs.

title: APC attacks Atiku, ADC over alleged unpaid staff salaries
body:
The All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council has alleged that the African Democratic Congress is owing its staff salaries for more than a year, urging Nigerians to reject the party and its presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, in the 2027 elections.
In a statement on Monday signed by its spokesperson, Dele Alake, the campaign council said the ADC National Working Committee, led by former Senate President David Mark as chairman and former Osun State Governor Rauf Aregbesola as secretary, had failed to pay party workers for more than 12 months.
The APC described the alleged non-payment as “unconscionable,” arguing that a party seeking to govern Nigeria should first demonstrate its ability to manage its own workforce.
“We find it unconscionable that a political party that has made many grandiose promises to hoodwink Nigerians owes its workers for more than 12 months,” Mr Alake said.
“Owing staff who come to work every day and who rely on the salaries for their daily sustenance is wicked and reprehensible.”
The APC said the alleged development exposed what it described as the “emptiness and insincerity” of the ADC and its leaders, who have presented themselves as an alternative to the ruling party.
The campaign council also alleged that Atiku, the ADC presidential candidate, had previously faced complaints over unpaid salaries at his businesses.
“Atiku Abubakar, the ADC’s leader and presidential candidate, has a reputation for owing his employees,” Mr Alake said, alleging that workers at Gotel Communications and other businesses linked to the former vice president had gone months without pay and staged protests over unpaid salaries and other benefits.
The APC also attacked Mr Aregbesola’s record as governor of Osun State, accusing his administration of failing to pay workers and pensioners regularly.
Mr Alake alleged that the former governor introduced quarter- and half-salary payments for workers and left pensioners unpaid for more than four years.
“As for pensioners, he abandoned them for more than four years. Many died because they could not afford the basics of life,” he said.
The APC spokesperson said the alleged failure of the ADC to pay its workers matched what he described as the records of some of the party’s leading figures.
“We are therefore not surprised that ADC, harbouring birds of the same feather, cannot pay its workers’ salaries,” he said.
The campaign council called on Nigerians, particularly workers, to reject the ADC, Atiku and other candidates contesting elections on the party’s platform in 2027.
“We are sounding a warning to Nigerians and working people now: reject ADC. Reject Atiku Abubakar and reject all ADC candidates in the next general elections,” Mr Alake said.
The statement comes as the ADC positions itself as a major opposition platform ahead of the 2027 elections, with Atiku among the prominent political figures who have joined the party.
PREMIUM TIMES contacted the ADC National Publicity Secretary, Bolaji Abdullahi, and its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, for their responses to the allegations.
However, neither Mr Abdullahi nor Mr Ologbondiyan had responded to the enquiries as of the time of filing this report.

title: AI Agents Found a Way Into Anthropic's Business Systems in Under 12 Hours
body:
Researchers at a cybersecurity startup said AI agents found paths into Anthropic's business systems in less than 12 hours, according to a Washington Post report published Monday.
The way in was not Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant, but third-party administrative and sales software, the kind of programs companies use to track customers and manage staff. Many other companies use the same software.
The startup, Cathedral, was founded months ago by four former staffers of the Department of Government Efficiency, the Donald Trump administration's cost-cutting team better known as DOGE. The startup raised $160 million at a $1.4 billion valuation in July.
Cathedral tested Anthropic through a program that works like a bug bounty, in which a company rewards outside experts for reporting flaws instead of exploiting them. Its AI agents, which carry out multi-step tasks without a person approving each move, found routes to meeting transcripts, salary and job-offer details, and Slack messages about Anthropic's advanced models, per a draft of its report.
“Our monitoring flagged some of Cathedral's activity before they reported it to us,” Anthropic told the Washington Post , “we shut off their access the same day.” The company says the researchers reached “a limited set” of sales, HR, and IT systems holding business contact details and basic user account records.
Customer conversations with Claude, source code and model weights, the billions of numbers that make up the trained AI, were not accessed, Anthropic said. It has no evidence that anyone other than Cathedral exploited the flaws.
Anthropic said Cathedral overstated the national security implications and did not fully follow the program's rules because it did not disclose all of its activity. Cathedral's draft report said “data accesses were kept to the absolute minimum in accordance with security research best practices.”
A senior Trump administration official, speaking anonymously, said the report has circulated in government and raised national security concerns. “If a bunch of kids who have just started a company can do this,” the official said, “then potentially, the Chinese aren't far behind.”
In November 2025, Anthropic said Chinese state-sponsored hackers used Claude Code, its coding tool, to attack roughly 30 organizations, with AI handling 80% to 90% of the tactical work. In July, Anthropic disclosed that Claude models had hacked real organizations in three incidents during its tests.
Anthropic disabled the affected software until the vendors confirmed fixes, and the vendors have not been named.

title: JUSAG threatens strike from November 2 over delayed salary review
body: The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana (JUSAG) has threatened to embark on an indefinite strike from Monday, November 2, 2026, if the government fails to approve and pay its members’ reviewed salaries and allowances. The association has given the government until the end of October to approve the recommendations of the Judicial Council on the 2026 salary review, with payment expected in November, including arrears covering January to October. In a notification of industrial action dated October 23, 2026, and addressed to the Executive Secretary of the National Labour Commission, JUSAG said prolonged delays in concluding the salary review process had heightened tensions and dampened staff morale. The association said the Judicial Council had completed its work on the review and submitted its recommendations to President John Dramani Mahama for determination in line with Article 149 of the 1992 Constitution and the Judicial Service (Terms and Conditions of Service) Regulations, 2025 (C.I. 141). However, JUSAG said efforts to secure approval had yielded little progress despite several letters to the Judicial Council and Management, as well as public appeals to the government. According to the association, it wrote to the Judicial Council on January 19, 2026, to expedite the process and again raised the matter in a letter dated September 10, 2026. It also cited appeals made at its Second Quadrennial Delegates’ Conference in Tamale in August, the 45th AMJG Conference in Accra in September, and the Chief Justice’s Staff Durbar held in Tamale in September. JUSAG said the appeals had been met with assurances without any concrete action towards approving the recommendations and paying the revised salaries. “It is instructive to note that our colleagues elsewhere in the public sector had their new salaries for 2026 approved and paid in January, 2026. We are now in the tenth month of the year, and our members are still waiting — patiently, but no longer quietly,” the letter stated. The association said the delay was particularly concerning because organised labour was already negotiating the base pay for 2027 while Judicial Service staff were yet to receive their reviewed base pay and allowances for 2026. It warned that the prolonged uncertainty undermined the principles governing salary determination under the new legal framework. JUSAG said it had previously urged its members to exercise restraint because of the potential impact of industrial action on justice delivery and national security, while continuing to engage Management and the government. However, it said the hardship among members had become severe and their patience was exhausted. The association’s National Executive Council has therefore set two demands: approval of the Judicial Council’s recommendations on the 2026 salary review by the end of October, and payment of the revised salaries in November, together with arrears from January to October. JUSAG warned that if the demands are not met by Sunday, November 1, 2026, it will commence an indefinite strike on Monday, November 2, until the demands are fulfilled. The notification was copied to the Office of the President, the Judicial Secretary, the Attorney-General and Minister for Justice, the Minister of Finance, and the Minister for Jobs, Labour and Employment Relations.

title: Ukraine plans to rebuild its air force on NATO’s model by 2035. Its Air Force already knows which fighter it wants next, and why
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine is remaking its air force on NATO’s model, down to the way its squadrons are organized and the aircraft they fly. The reforms are planned to be completed by 2035 and include modernizing its F-16s while pursuing the Swedish Gripen jets, Air Force Spokesperson Yurii Ihnat says, per Tse Baza. Ukraine’s fighters are working hard against Russia’s air war, and in the previous month alone the Air Force faced around 3,500 jet-powered targets, with F-16s heavily used to intercept Russian drones. The new reform is meant to build an air force that can be sustained over the long term and can contest Russian jets and glide bombs, not only survive the next wave. Wings and universal air bases The central change, Ihnat said, is a move to the “wing” units that NATO air forces use. The first steps have already been taken: Ukraine has set up the 107th F-16 wing, which now has its own Facebook page and may publish material about its work. Ukraine also plans to build universal air bases on the operational airfields it has used through the full-scale war. In the future, Ihnat says, those bases should be able to receive and service different models of combat aircraft, as NATO does. A worn fleet, and the jets Ukraine wants next Currently, the F-16s Ukraine flies are older Block 15 jets, used by other countries before they arrived, and intensive combat has left them in need of repairs, service life restoration, and upgrades. Ukrainian officials discussed modernization with the American manufacturer Lockheed Martin, while Kyiv would prefer the newer Block 70/72 version, which Ihnat says would let its pilots stand up more confidently to Russia’s Su-35 fighters. Keeping the current fleet flying has been hard: fewer than half of Ukraine’s F-16s may be operational , held back by slow maintenance abroad. At the same time, Lockheed Martin and Kyiv are discussing a special F-16 variant for Ukraine, with a modern AESA radar, longer range, and a wider choice of weapons, though no firm deal exists yet. Ukraine is also counting on Swedish Gripen fighters. Ihnat says Ukrainian pilots are drawn to them for their lower operating costs and simpler maintenance, with the country likely to receive older C/D models first, before the newer Gripen E that Saab is developing. Ukrainian pilots have already begun their training on the Gripen, a jet seen as a counter to the Russian aircraft dropping guided glide bombs on the front, though delivery timing depends on further agreements. body:

If you haven’t shopped at Quince yet, consider this your sign to take a peek. Founded in 2018, the San Francisco-based brand built its business around a simple idea: premium materials and classic designs shouldn’t come with traditional luxury markups. Its factory-direct model cuts out supply-chain middlemen, with pieces spanning Mongolian cashmere, Italian leather, washable silk and fine jewellery. And it’s not just fashion — Quince also sells everything from bamboo bedding and decorative accents to cookware. The brand officially launched in Canada in January 2026, so I tried a mix of its fashion, accessories and home finds to see which pieces are worth adding to your cart.
Finding wardrobe staples that look expensive without the eye-watering price tag? Sign me up. Quince focuses on quality materials, thoughtful details and well-made essentials designed to last beyond a single season.
It’s rare to come across a brand you’d want to buy your cashmere and kitchenware staples from. But yes, the brushed gold utensils and decorative bowls are as stunning as the Quince items I’d want to stuff my wardrobe with (and this is coming from someone guilty of making multiple trips to different grocery stores for specific items — I can be picky). Spanning bamboo sheets and plush throws to swirled glass lamps and pumpkin cardamom candles, browsing the home section is a wondrously endless scroll. Don’t worry, I did the dirty work for you and found a few gems.
No outfit is complete without the complementary bag or gleaming sparkle. Although Quince began selling jewellery in 2019, the brand expanded its fine jewellery collection for the 2023 holiday season, introducing a wider selection of natural and lab-grown diamond pieces.
After trying Quince for myself, I can see what the buzz is about. From wardrobe staples to home finds, there’s plenty to explore if you appreciate quality and reasonable prices. While shopping online means you can’t see or feel everything in person before ordering, Quince is worth a look if you’re ready to discover a few new favourites for your closet or home.

title: ‘Poets only sell books from car boots’ – Nana Asaase recounts disrespect in his poetry journey
body: Ghanaian poet and writer Nana Asaase has opened up about the dismissive comments he faced when he started his poetry career, including claims that poets and writers in Ghana could only make a living selling books from car boots. Speaking on The Career Trail programme aired on Joy Learning TV and Joy News, Nana Asaase recounted how such remarks made him question his decision to pursue poetry. “Someone once told me poets and Ghanaian writers, all they do is sell books in a car boot,” he recalled. According to the poet, the comments were discouraging, but his conviction that he was on the right path kept him going. “Sometimes when things get tough, I look into the mirror and think, why not just quit poetry and join my family business? Because we had a bakery. But something within me kept telling me I was on the right path. I shouldn’t give up, so I kept pushing,” he shared. After 12 years in poetry, Nana Asaase says his persistence has gradually paid off, with his work opening doors to opportunities he never imagined when he started. “This same job people looked down on me when I started has given me great opportunities. I have performed for presidents. All four presidents of this Fourth Republic, dead or alive, have been my audience,” he revealed. “Sometimes, somebody shows up, you don’t know the person from anywhere and says, ‘Oh, I know this young man. Give this job to him.’ You do a fantastic job, meanwhile, I have not met this person,” he continued. Nana Asaase attributed his perseverance to his faith in God, saying his relationship with God remained the foundation of his journey. “Once you know your source, make sure you’re at peace with your source. Mine is God. I have no shady dealings backing me,” he noted. He also highlighted discipline and consistency as important to developing and sustaining a career in poetry. “There’s no magic. Practice, practice, practice. As I’m sitting here, I’m practicing. When I drive, I practice. When I eat, I practice. When I have conversations, I practice,” he said. After 12 years in poetry, Nana Asaase is preparing to release his first book this year. “By God’s grace, I’m releasing my first book this year, and I will not sell my book out of a car boot. My books will be sold all over the world on very prominent counters,” he disclosed with excitement. And having experienced the challenges of building a career in poetry, Nana Asaase is also using his Sankofa Sessions, which include the Mental Pictures initiative, to nurture other talents and encourage a greater appreciation for literary arts, storytelling, oratory and self-expression.

title: JUSAG threatens indefinite strike from November 2 over unpaid salary review
body: The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana (JUSAG) has threatened an indefinite strike from Monday, November 2, 2026, if the government fails to approve its 2026 salary review and pay outstanding arrears. The association has given the government until Sunday, November 1, to meet its demands, warning that its members will withdraw their services until the issues are resolved. In a notification letter dated October 23 and signed by its General Secretary, Abdulai Yakubu, JUSAG informed the National Labour Commission (NLC) of its intention to embark on the industrial action over delays in reviewing salaries and related allowances for Judicial Service staff. The association said the conditions of service of its members are governed by Article 149 of the 1992 Constitution and the Judicial Service (Terms and Conditions of Service) Regulations, 2025 (C.I. 141). According to JUSAG, it requested a review of salaries for 2026 after the previous salary review expired in December 2025. The Judicial Council subsequently completed its work and submitted its recommendations to the President in accordance with Article 149 of the Constitution and Regulation 25 of C.I. 141. However, JUSAG said the approval process had stalled despite repeated appeals for action. “Owing to the delay in concluding the process, JUSAG, by a letter dated 19th January 2026, wrote to the Judicial Council to expedite the process. However, little progress resulted,” the notification stated. The association said it again reminded management of the matter in a letter dated September 10, 2026. It also cited appeals made during the 2nd Quadrennial Delegates’ Conference in Tamale, the 45th Association of Magistrates and Judges of Ghana (AMJG) Conference in Accra, and the Chief Justice’s Staff Durbar in Tamale. JUSAG said the appeals had produced assurances but no concrete action towards approving the Judicial Council’s recommendations and paying the revised salaries. The association said the delay had heightened tensions and weakened staff morale, particularly because other public sector workers had received approval and payment of their revised 2026 salaries in January. “We are now in the tenth month of the year, and our members are still waiting—patiently, but no longer quietly. This situation has heightened tension and dampened morale among staff of the Judicial Service,” the letter stated. JUSAG also expressed concern that negotiations by Organised Labour over the 2027 base pay were already underway while its members were still waiting for their revised 2026 salaries and allowances. JUSAG’s National Executive Council has set out two conditions for calling off the planned industrial action. The association wants the government to: Approve the Judicial Council’s recommendations on the 2026 salary review by October 31, 2026. Pay the revised salaries in November, including arrears covering January to October 2026. The association said failure to meet the demands by November 1 would trigger an indefinite strike from the following day. It added that the strike would remain in force until the demands were met. JUSAG said it had repeatedly urged its members to exercise restraint because of the potential consequences of industrial action for justice delivery and national security. The planned strike could disrupt the administrative and support services of the Judicial Service if the government and the association fail to reach an agreement before the deadline. title: Temwa Chawinga becomes first African woman to finish in Ballon d’Or top 10
body: Malawian forward Temwa Chawinga has made history by becoming the first African woman to finish in the top 10 of the women’s Ballon d’Or. Chawinga’s achievement marks a significant milestone for African women’s football, placing the Malawi international among the world’s leading female players. Born on September 20, 1998, in Rumphi District, Malawi, Chawinga plays as a forward for Kansas City Current and the Malawi national team. She has enjoyed considerable success at club level, winning four Chinese Women’s Super League titles with Wuhan Jianghan University in 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. She also won the NWSL x Liga MX Femenil Summer Cup in 2024 and the NWSL Shield in 2025 with Kansas City Current. Her individual honours include two consecutive NWSL Most Valuable Player awards in 2024 and 2025, as well as two NWSL Golden Boots in the same years. Chawinga also claimed the Chinese Women’s Super League Golden Boot in 2022 and 2023 before winning the International Federation of Football History and Statistics (IFFHS) World’s Best Top Goal Scorer award in 2023. She was joined in the Ballon d’Or top 10 by Haiti’s Melchie Dumornay, Norway’s Caroline Graham Hansen, Spain’s Patri Guijarro, Denmark’s Pernille Harder, Poland’s Ewa Pajor, Spain’s Clàudia Pina and Alexia Putellas, England’s Alessia Russo, and Jamaica’s Khadija Shaw. The list features players from Europe, Africa and the Caribbean, reflecting the growing global reach of women’s football. Chawinga’s historic finish represents a breakthrough for African representation in the prestigious individual award and further highlights her rise as one of the leading figures in the women’s game. title: Police confirm man, teenager swept away by flood in Aba
body: By Steve Oko Abia State Police Command has confirmed that a man who attempted to rescue a teenage girl from a water-filled ditch at Faulks Road, Aba, was swept away alongside the girl during Sunday’s downpour. The Police Public Relations Officer, Maureen Chinaka, disclosed this while responding to Vanguard inquiries, confirming that the incident occurred around the popular Ukwu Mango area of the commercial city. Chinaka said the tragedy happened near an ongoing construction site where an uncovered ditch had filled with rainwater. According to her, the teenage girl was passing through the area when she reportedly hit a stone and fell into the ditch. An adult who witnessed the incident reportedly plunged into the water in an attempt to rescue her, but both were swept away. “Unfortunately, we have not been able to see them. The police are aware, and the matter has been reported. Efforts are in place to see how they can be rescued,” Chinaka said. She confirmed that the two victims had yet to be found as search efforts continued. Asked whether the construction company responsible for the site would face possible charges over negligence, the police spokesperson said investigations were ongoing. The tragedy has raised concerns about the safety of construction sites during heavy rainfall, particularly where excavations and drainage channels are left uncovered and become submerged in floodwater. Aba’s flat terrain makes parts of the commercial city vulnerable to flooding during heavy downpours, increasing the risks posed by waterlogged roads, open drains and excavations.
