title: Oracle launches new agentic AI to take on complex tasks such as supply chains
body: Oracle has introduced its new agentic AI applications to take on more complex tasks across industries ranging from supply chains and shipping to restaurants. The applications are part of Oracle Fusion Claw, a governed agentic execution, the company announced on Monday at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas. "AI is no longer limited to telling you what's happening in your business, it is actually now telling you what can happen next," Oracle co-chief executive Mike Sicilia told the event. "AI should allow you to barely think about software at all. So, instead of navigating applications and managing processes, you simply tell the system what you would like to accomplish and, because it understands your business, you figure out how to get the work done." We are giving people more time to be human, and that's the ambition we have for AI Oracle co-chief executive Mike Sicilia The new applications are intuitive and work across sectors such as supply chain forecasting, restaurant operations and health care, he said. "We are giving people more time to be human, and that's the ambition we have for AI; not simply more capable people, people that have more time to think, create, to solve problems and care for one another," Mr Sicilia added. Oracle's new Fusion Claw agentic apps can help organisations to operate within established governance controls, the company said. They will be able to reason, compute, adapt and execute specialist-grade work, including deep research, computation, simulation, modelling and continuous replanning. The company displayed an example of how a shipping company using the application can gain transport cost savings of $58,000, thanks to the AI system going through all its data and finding solutions. Mr Sicilia also gave the example of a customer, a doctor, who said his patients had not realised the colour of his eyes before he introduced the agentic AI system, as he now had more time to speak with them. "We want to make it dramatically easier for you to generate such outcomes … That means changing not just what our technology can do, but how quickly [it can] get it working in your business," he said. Before the event, Oracle also announced a $1 billion investment to support its partner ecosystem on increasing customer demand for AI-powered solutions and services . The investment, spanning the next four years, is aimed at increasing opportunities for partners to develop solutions and build specialised expertise, Oracle said. It includes new and greater benefits and incentives for partners, including planned investments in training and certification, technical enablement, development, testing and demonstration environments, cloud migration funding, go-to-market collaboration, and commercialisation through Oracle Marketplace. Oracle's partner ecosystem includes systems integrators, independent software sellers, cloud and managed service providers, value-added distributors, resellers, advisory firms and other partners. Middle East going beyond ‘AI for the sake of AI’ In the Middle East, there is strong growth in AI introduction with good cases across industries, said Hammad Hussain, senior director of AI and data strategy at Oracle. The company operates two cloud regions in the UAE, in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. It also has cloud regions in Riyadh and Jeddah in Saudi Arabia. “Middle East clients are very ambitious when it comes to AI. And I think initially, if I go back one and a half years ago, a lot of my discussions were, 'I need to use AI, tell me how'. But now it has changed,” Mr Hussain told reporters at the Oracle AI World event. “One of our clients in the airline industry, for example, has started using AI to start negotiating new locations that it opens up. That's a great use of AI. That's a revenue example as well, because the quicker you can launch a new city, the quicker you can start banking in the revenue." Countries such as the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar in the Gulf are investing heavily in AI. UAE companies and organisations have some of the highest rates of agentic artificial intelligence adoption in the world, a survey this month by data science and AI platform company Dataiku found. It found that 62 per cent of UAE chief information officers say their companies have more than 50 AI agents working in the organisation, while 15 per cent say they operate more than 500 agents. Customers in the Middle East are also using AI for conversational analytics, Mr Hussain said. He gave the example of those in the building sector using AI to go through data to understand which projects are delayed and recommendations to reduce the cost. “AI might say that we can consolidate a lot of your suppliers if we're getting the same product from 10 suppliers … So, these are the kind of things that are reshaping their thinking,” Mr Hussain said. The use of AI for “AI's sake” is no longer the case in the region, he stressed. “The truly advanced ones are now saying, ‘OK, how can I change my business? How can I improve my efficiency or do things which I couldn't do before’.”

title: Unregistered Airbnb operators in Kasoa face prosecution as GTA intensifies enforcement
body: The Ghana Tourism Authority (GTA) has shut down several unregistered accommodation facilities in Kasoa and surrounding areas for operating without the required licences. The Authority said the operators had repeatedly been notified to register their facilities in accordance with the Registration and Licensing of Food, Beverage and Entertainment Enterprises, 2016 (L.I. 2238), but failed to comply. During the enforcement exercise, the Accra West Regional Director of the GTA, Richard Agyenim Boateng, said operating an accommodation facility without the required registration and licence was illegal. He warned that operators who reopen their facilities without meeting the necessary requirements could face prosecution. Mr Boateng explained that the exercise was intended to enforce tourism regulations while helping to protect the safety and satisfaction of guests. “We are mandated to close down all facilities that are not registered. These facilities have failed to register with us and have ignored our notices. That is why we are here to ensure they do the right thing. They operate Airbnb facilities, and we want them to come to our office to go through the registration process and obtain licences,” he told Accra-based Citi FM. The GTA is urging operators of accommodation facilities, including Airbnb properties, to visit its offices and complete the registration and licensing process to ensure compliance with the law. The enforcement exercise forms part of the Authority’s efforts to ensure that tourism-related businesses operate within the required regulatory framework.

title: Uh oh, it sounds like the iPhone Duo keeps cracking and users aren’t happy about it
body:
The launch of the iPhone Duo , Apple’s hotly anticipated foldable phone, is off to a rough start. The phone was announced at this year’s Surprise and Shine event, with Apple promising that it had finally gotten a notoriously tricky form factor right.
Now, however, Bloomberg reports that early Duo users have been complaining about screens cracking “after just hours or days of use.” Some users have reported hearing a loud crunching noise, followed by the appearance of a crack. Others have reported display malfunctions.
404 Media has also reported that early adopters are dealing with “big fat creases down the middle of the [$2,000] folding screen.”
TechCrunch reached out to Apple for comment and will update this story if it responds. The company told Bloomberg that it was “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units.”
Creating a functional foldable phone has long been an ambition in Silicon Valley, but many of the models released so far have suffered from similar maladies . Apple promised that it had cracked the code, but these early complaints suggest it may not have solved the problem after all.

title: Impunity, justice system failure fuelling violence in North Central — Osinbajo
body: By Golok Nanmwa Former Vice President of Nigeria, Prof. Yemi Osinbajo, has attributed the widespread insecurity in North Central Nigeria and other parts of the country to failures in the justice system and inadequate punitive measures for crimes committed. Osinbajo stated this on Monday in Plateau State at a forum titled, “Countering Polarisation and Rebuilding Civic Cohesion in North Central Nigeria Beyond Tribe and Faith, Reclaiming Our Shared Stories,” organised by Justice Research Institute, JRI, in partnership with the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies, NIPSS. The former Vice President said, “Impunity destroys the fabric of society. There must be clear and enforceable consequences for wrongdoing and offences committed against the state or individuals.” “If there are no consequences for actions taken under any guise, there will be no way to rebuild and reconcile. Peace cannot be built without justice.” “Those who have been displaced and whose communities or villages have been illegally occupied must be returned to their ancestral homes. Victims must also be compensated.” “If you look at the land-grabbing situation, land must be returned to its rightful owners. “ “This is the process of rebuilding. There must be compensation, the proper procedure must be followed, and any wrongdoing must result in a penalty. “The problems of justice administration in Nigeria require urgent attention in the form of reforms to address the majority of the issues impeding justice delivery.” “It is better for the country to recognise that we have a system that requires immediate intervention.” “For peace to reign, we must reorient our attitudes towards ourselves and others, particularly our brothers and sisters. I believe we should return to the basics, and this should be done intentionally.” He added, “Reconciliation must be deliberate and genuine. Regardless of what happened in Rwanda, they are back together because leaders and governments made a deliberate and intentional effort to bring people together. “I believe there is a need for deliberate and intentional reconciliation and peace-building, which can only be accomplished by government in collaboration with civil society organisations and religious leaders. “Many of these will be determined by our country’s elite.” In his welcome address, the Director-General of NIPSS, Prof. Ayo Omotayo, said, “Storytelling is a powerful instrument for peace-building and national reconciliation. “Societies are held together not only by laws and institutions but also by the stories citizens tell about themselves and one another.” “Stories shape our memories, influence how we understand our differences and imagine our common future.” “They can inspire solidarity, but when distorted or manipulated, they can deepen grievances and turn neighbours into enemies.” Also speaking, the former Chief Justice and Emir of Lafia, Justice Sidi Bage, said, “Conflict often begins long before violence erupts. Conflict starts when justice, identity and belonging are denied.” “North Central Nigeria is a microcosm of the country’s diversity, and we must caution against narratives that exaggerate differences between indigenes and settlers, farmers and herders, or adherents of different faiths.” “Communication and active listening are indispensable for peaceful coexistence. “In the courtroom, a judge must listen to both sides before reaching a decision. In our communities, we must also be willing to hear perspectives that differ from our own.” He added, “If we are to rebuild trust and strengthen peaceful coexistence, we must create spaces where people can listen to one another, understand their differences and address grievances before they escalate into violence.” The post Impunity, justice system failure fuelling violence in North Central — Osinbajo appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Teacher trainee allowances: TTAG explains payment delays at three colleges, assures affected students
body: The Teacher Trainees’ Association of Ghana (TTAG) has attributed delays in the payment of allowances to students at three colleges of education to outstanding clearance requirements. According to the association, Savannah College of Education, Christ the Teacher College of Education and Ghana Muslim Mission College of Education have yet to receive the necessary clearance to facilitate payment. In a statement issued on Monday, October 26, TTAG said its leadership had engaged the Student Loan Trust Fund (SLTF) following complaints from trainees who did not receive their allowances during the recent disbursement. “It was identified that clearance had not been granted for Savannah College of Education, Christ the Teacher College of Education, and Ghana Muslim Mission College of Education,” the statement explained. The association further disclosed that trainees of Al-Faruq College of Education who missed the recent disbursement are expected to receive their allowances before the end of October 2026. TTAG consequently urged students across the country’s 49 public colleges of education to verify their registration details and Ghana Commercial Bank (GCB) account status to avoid further payment delays. “All trainees are encouraged to verify their registration details and Ghana Commercial Bank (GCB) account status and promptly rectify any errors or outstanding requirements to facilitate payment happening any moment from now,” the statement said. The association assured affected trainees that it would continue engaging the SLTF and other relevant stakeholders to resolve outstanding payment challenges. It reiterated its commitment to ensuring that all eligible trainees receive their allowances as soon as possible.

title: American bomber escorted by British and Norwegian F-35s
body: British F-35Bs flying from HMS Prince of Wales and Norwegian F-35As have escorted a United States Air Force B-52 over the High North during Exercise Global Thunder, the American nuclear readiness exercise, according to a post by Defence Operations. The post said: “UK F-35Bs & @RoyalAirForce Voyager, with @Luftforsvaret F-35As, escorted a @usairforce B-52 on Exercise Global Thunder. Above @RoyalNavy & @Forsvaret_no vessels including @HMSPWLS. Operating together to defend @NATO’s northern flank.” An RAF Voyager tanker supported the formation. HMS Prince of Wales is in the Arctic and North Atlantic on the second phase of Operation Firecrest, accompanied by the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless and operating under NATO command, a deployment this publication covered as the ship sailed . United States Strategic Command describes Global Thunder as an annual exercise involving personnel throughout the strategic enterprise, including its own components and subordinate units, and says the purpose of Global Thunder 27 “is to enhance nuclear readiness and ensure a safe, secure, effective and credible strategic deterrent force.” The command added: “This is an annual exercise and is not in response to actions by any nation, other actors or current world events,” and that “as in previous years, Global Thunder 27 may include an increase in bomber and other aircraft flights throughout the exercise.” Britain’s part in the American nuclear exercise comes as the country prepares to take on a nuclear role of its own in the air again. The Defence Investment Plan confirmed the purchase of twelve F-35A aircraft and British entry into NATO’s nuclear mission, which will return a nuclear task to the Royal Air Force for the first time since the WE.177 bomb was withdrawn in 1998. RAF Typhoons also escorted French Rafales simulating a nuclear strike over the Mediterranean last week on Exercise Rummy, the first British participation in a French nuclear exercise. Norway operates fifty two F-35As from Ørland and Evenes and has become one of the closest partners in British operations in the High North, hosting Royal Marines for Arctic training and working alongside the carrier group through the Firecrest deployment. The post American bomber escorted by British and Norwegian F-35s first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: From KNUST to Yale: Ghanaian veterinarian makes history at Yale School of the Environment
body: Dr Daniel Baba Abiliba has become the first Ghana-trained veterinarian to enrol at the Yale School of the Environment (YSE). Dr Abiliba joined YSE’s Master of Environmental Management (MEM) programme in August 2026. He is also the first Ghanaian to receive the MSD Animal Health/World Veterinary Association (WVA) Veterinary Student Scholarship. “KNUST and its social environment gave me my foundation. Everything I bring to Yale, I learned first in Ghana, in our classrooms, on our farms and from our farmers,” Dr Abiliba remarked. Milestones and key achievements In 2018, while pursuing his studies at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Dr Abiliba received the MSD/WVA Veterinary Student Scholarship. The international scholarship recognises veterinary students who demonstrate outstanding leadership and dedication to the profession. “Receiving that scholarship reaffirmed that the work we are doing in Ghana has a place on the global stage. This inspired me to pursue greater ambitions, ultimately leading me to the Yale School of the Environment. It also instilled in me a sense of responsibility to pave the way for the next generation of students,” he said. He obtained his Doctor of Veterinary Medicine degree from the KNUST School of Veterinary Medicine in 2022. Veterinary science at the core of environmental sustainability At Yale, Dr Abiliba is studying the intersection of food systems, public health and the environment. His work draws on the One Health approach, which recognises that the health of people, animals and ecosystems is closely interconnected. “How we raise animals affects the land, the water and our own health. Veterinarians have an important role to play in environmental decision-making, and I want to help bring that perspective into the rooms where decisions are made,” he said. Before joining Yale, Dr Abiliba founded the Animal Welfare League (AWL), a non-profit organisation focused on improving farmed animal welfare in Ghana and across Africa. Inspiring the next generation of veterinarians Dr Abiliba hopes his journey will encourage Ghanaian veterinary students to explore broader career opportunities beyond traditional veterinary practice. “Veterinary medicine is not only about treating sick animals, it is about food security, disease prevention, and protecting the environment we all depend on. The next generation of Ghanaian vets can lead in all of these spaces,” Dr Abiliba said. He credits his family, particularly his parents, and his mentors at the KNUST School of Veterinary Medicine for supporting him throughout his journey.

title: Under Buhari, Tinubu, Cash Transfer Office failed to identify beneficiaries of N33.75 billion – Audit Report
body:
The National Cash Transfer Office (NCTO) reported paying N33.75 billion to 3.29 million households and beneficiaries across 35 states in 2023 but failed to provide complete records identifying the recipients.
The agency’s accounts staff also denied auditors access to bank statements needed to verify the payments, according to analysis of the Auditor General of the Federation’s latest report by the UDEME project of the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID).
The finding is one of eight audit queries against the NCTO in the auditor general’s 2024 Annual Report on Non-compliance and Internal Control Weaknesses in MDAs, covering the period from 1 January to 31 December 2023.
NCTO did not respond to some of the audit queries, and in the cases they responded to, the auditor found their response to be unsatisfactory.
The auditor general consequently said the findings remained valid until the commission implemented the recommendations.
The NCTO runs the conditional cash transfer component of the National Social Safety Nets Project, a World Bank-financed programme that provides payments to poor households identified on the National Social Register.
The office operates under the National Social Investment Programme Agency, which reports to the Federal Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction. The transfers happened under former Ministers Sadiya Farouk (under the Muhammadu Buhari presidency) and Betta Edu (under the Bola Tinubu presidency), who headed the ministry at different times in 2023.
The programme’s operations came under scrutiny in January 2024 when President Bola Tinubu suspended the agency’s chief executive, Halima Shehu, over alleged financial misappropriation. Ms Shehu had previously served as national coordinator of the conditional cash transfer programme.
Ten days later, Mr Tinubu suspended all four programmes run by the agency for an initial six weeks, citing “operational lapses and improprieties surrounding payments to the programme beneficiaries”.
Paragraph 613 of the Financial Regulations 2009 requires payments to be made only to the persons named in payment vouchers or their properly authorised representatives. Paragraph 603(i) also requires vouchers to contain full particulars of the services provided so they can be checked without reference to other documents.
The NCTO reported making electronic transfers totalling N33.75 billion to 3.2 million households and beneficiaries across 35 states in 2023. However, the payment vouchers did not contain complete details of the beneficiaries, the audit report said.
The office also failed to present the Remita statement that would have enabled auditors to compare the payments with the beneficiaries listed on the National Social Register and establish who actually received the funds.
The auditors said the missing statement prevented them from authenticating the payments and determining whether the recipients were genuine beneficiaries.
“All efforts to obtain access to the REMITA statement were obstructed and denied by NCTO accounts staff, thereby frustrating the audit process,” the auditor general said.
He warned that the failure to verify the payments exposed public funds to the risk of loss and raised the possibility that ineligible or fictitious persons had received the money.
The auditor general recommended that the National Programme Manager, Abdullahi Imam, be required to account for the N33.75 billion and recover and remit the amount to the Treasury. He also directed that evidence showing that the beneficiaries received the funds be submitted to the Public Accounts Committees of the National Assembly.
Failure to comply could attract sanctions under paragraph 3106 of the Financial Regulations, the report said.
In another query, the report identified 215 payment vouchers totalling N36.74 billion for “SS, IDA & output base” transactions in December 2023 that were paid without internal audit checks or prepayment audits.
Paragraph 1705 of the Financial Regulations requires the head of internal audit in every ministry and agency to “ensure that a 100 per cent prepayment audit of all checked and passed vouchers is carried out.”
None of the 215 vouchers underwent the required checks before payment. Instead, the Internal Audit Unit examined them after the payments had been made, contrary to the regulations, the auditors found.
The report noted that the World Bank’s November 2021 Project Appraisal Document for the programme’s scale-up provided for the Internal Audit Unit to conduct compliance and operational audits without adopting a prepayment audit system.
The auditor general nevertheless said the practice contravened Nigeria’s Financial Regulations. He recommended that the N36.74 billion be fully accounted for and recovered, with those responsible sanctioned for gross misconduct under paragraph 3129 of the regulations.
The auditors also found that the NCTO made 101 payments totalling ₦4.62 billion from the “S&S/IDA Cash Book,” without presenting the corresponding payment vouchers for examination.
The absence of the vouchers prevented the auditors from verifying the payments and the expenditures they were intended to cover.
The report said this breached Section 85(2) of the Constitution, which provides for the auditor general’s access to public account records. It also contravened paragraph 601 of the Financial Regulations, which states that “under no circumstances shall a cheque be raised or cash paid for services for which a voucher has not been raised.”
The auditors warned that the missing records exposed public funds to misapplication and diversion. They recommended that the entire N4.62 billion be recovered from the NCTO.
The auditors further identified 32 payments totalling N3.09 billion from the “NASSP SCALE-UP Cash Book” to states for the enrolment of unbanked, poor and vulnerable households.
Although the NCTO presented documents covering N2.74 billion disbursed to 34 states, N350.18 million remained unaccounted for, according to the report.
The auditors also faulted the supporting vouchers, describing them as vague and inadequate to establish how the funds were used or which activities they financed.
The records lacked beneficiary lists, photographs of enrolment exercises, signed attendance registers, activity reports and the names of people who received payments during the exercises, the report said.
In a separate query, the auditors examined N393.71 million that nine State Cash Transfer Units reportedly returned to the Treasury in 2023 after failing to conduct enrolment exercises.
The NCTO attributed the failure to “insecurity, disasters, and other factors”.
However, the office did not provide Remita inflow statements or payment slips showing that the refunds had been credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund. It also failed to provide evidence that the affected states subsequently enrolled the intended beneficiaries.
The NCTO paid N280.42 million to payment service providers as a 30 per cent advance for implementing a “last-mile solution” for beneficiaries, the report said.
The payments were made without advance payment guarantees, contrary to Section 71 of the Finance Act 2020, which requires such guarantees for mobilisation fees.
The auditors also found no evidence that the providers were selected through due process. Their contract files lacked prequalification documents, bidding records and technical and financial evaluations to justify the selections and payments.
Across the eight queries, the Auditor-General called for the NCTO’s National Programme Manager to account for the funds in question, recover and remit the amounts due to the Treasury, and submit evidence of the remittances to the Public Accounts Committee of the National Assembly.
The report cites paragraph 3106 of the Financial Regulations, which gives an officer responsible for an irregular payment 21 days to explain the transaction before the amount may be recovered personally from the officer and the officer removed from the schedule.
It also cites paragraph 3129, which provides for sanctions for gross misconduct.
In its broader analysis, the report ranked the NCTO first among federal agencies flagged for making payments without supporting documents, failing to conduct prepayment audits and failing to present paid vouchers for examination.
In March 2026, Mr Imam, the NCTO’s programme manager, said the cash transfer initiative had increased its target from 10.4 million to 15 million beneficiaries.
Worried about the auditor general’s report, the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) sued the federal government at the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice over the alleged diversion, irregular expenditure and failure to account for ₦78.8 billion allocated to cash-transfer and social-protection programmes.
In the suit, filed last week, SERAP is seeking an order compelling the government to account for the funds and ensure proper financial oversight of programmes meant to support vulnerable households.
The suit follows concerns raised by SERAP over findings involving the Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, the National Cash Transfer Office (NCTO) and the National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office (NASSCO).
The group has called for investigations into ₦76.24 billion in questionable and unaccounted-for expenditure at NCTO and ₦2.55 billion at NASSCO, as well as the recovery of any funds found to have been misappropriated.
“The failure to investigate the ₦78.8 billion cash-transfer scandal, account for the questioned funds and recover any unlawfully spent amounts violates Nigeria’s obligations to protect the human rights of vulnerable households.”
In the suit, SERAP is also arguing that “the failure to account for substantial public funds allocated for social protection, and to investigate and remedy deficiencies, undermines the socio-economic rights of millions of affected Nigerians.”
In September, SERAP had urged President Bola Tinubu to direct the relevant agencies to account for the funds, including ₦33.751 billion in 2023 cash transfers for which it said beneficiary records and payment documentation should be published.
It also called for explanations for payments made without prepayment audits, unsupported expenditure and other questionable transactions.

title: Cohere's test caught an open source Qwen3.8 model trying to 'phone home' to China: what enterprises should know
body:
Credit: VentureBeat made with OpenAI-ChatGPT-2.5
A new data point has arrived in the ongoing debate over the growing enterprise adoption of low-cost Chinese open source AI models that is likely to increase skepticism over their widespread usage and deployment, though it does not automatically indicate that all Chinese open models are inherently less safe that closed, proprietary U.S. or Western ones.
The Canadian enterprise AI model maker Cohere today announced that it ran a cybersecurity test on a sandboxed version of Alibaba's open source Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model and detected the Qwen model attempting to send a test payload to one of Alibaba's cloud servers in Beijing.
Cohere says its isolated test environment blocked the connection, preventing the model from sending the payload.
In the hours since Cohere's release, AI developers and researchers on the social network X challenged Cohere's experiment and conclusions as inherently limited, flawed, and clearly conflicted as the company offers its own open and proprietary models as competitors to Qwen. Many said it was analogous to viewing a hypothetical U.S. model with suspicion if it tried to send data up to the popular Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud service S3.
Cohere subsequently released a model trace, raw token IDs and a reproduction script on Hugging Face for others to examine.
VentureBeat has requested comment from Alibaba and the Qwen team and had not received a response at the time of writing.
In its October 26 report , Cohere researchers used Microsoft’s CTI-REALM security benchmark and asked the model to write a rule that detects a malicious download followed by script execution. The task specifically involved detecting downloads made with curl, a command-line transfer tool, followed by execution of the downloaded script. That context sits at the center of the criticism.
According to Cohere, the model inspected temporary files, available utilities and DNS configuration, then issued an HTTP upload command containing a fixed test string. Its generated reasoning said it would make no tool calls. The command attempted to upload test content; it did not itself include the directory listing or DNS information in that payload.
Cohere says it observed the behavior less than once per 100,000 evaluation calls. When researchers repeated the prompt, the model behaved as initially intended and produced the requested rule.
Cohere then performed follow-up tests in which researchers supplied partial reasoning and commands; the model included suspicious network destinations more often when completing those inputs.
Those tests measured how the model responded to deliberate cues, so they do not establish how often it would attempt such connections on its own.
Cohere acknowledges a possible benign origin: the model may have learned to repeat network requests from examples involving training environments or third-party tools.
The company does not establish that the attempted upload served a debugging purpose, nor does it prove that anyone designed it to collect information.
Even an accidental learned behavior could create security risks if an agent executes those commands with access to company systems.
The destination’s existence also became a point of contention. X user @Mercuriusdream posted a screenshot showing an Alibaba Cloud error for the named bucket.
VentureBeat subsequently made a read-only request to the same hostname and received the error “NoSuchBucket,” with the message “The specified bucket does not exist.” That response establishes what the service returned during this check; it does not establish whether the bucket existed when Cohere ran its test.
A nonexistent bucket would undermine claims of a functioning collection destination, although a request could still reach the cloud provider’s infrastructure.
Cohere has not established who, if anyone, controlled the named bucket at the time of its test. It also competes with Alibaba for enterprise customers and promotes its own security practices in the post, giving it a commercial stake in the findings.
Cohere has not published equivalent comparative results for Meta’s Llama and Muse Spark Open, OpenAI’s GPT-oss, its own models or other Chinese model families such as DeepSeek and Kimi.
The post therefore does not establish whether Qwen behaves differently from competing models under the same conditions.
The report does not demonstrate that Alibaba received customer secrets, that the Chinese government directed the behavior, or that every Qwen deployment behaves similarly. Independent replication and comparisons would help establish how broadly the finding applies.
Several critics argue that a model building a security detection rule may try related commands to understand or test the environment. Applied AI engineer Vishal Singh called it a “Horrible blog post” and argued that the model had followed its instructions, pointing to the curl-related assignment. The X account developing valhalla argued that testing a harmless version of the activity can establish a baseline before evaluating whether a rule blocks it. The author added: “(I write detections for a living, this is a nothingburger)”.
Adam Karvonen , whose profile identifies him as a researcher at Truthful AI, wrote: “This is overblown IMO and I’m guessing it’s a training artifact.” He pointed out that the model had received a task involving curl and then, in a rare instance, issued a related command.
Kostas , whose profile describes work in cybersecurity, product and research, suggested that the model might have simulated the activity to inspect the resulting logs. He distinguished a poor security decision from hostile intent: “Unnecessary and potentially unsafe? Absolutely. Malicious? Not necessarily.”
A proposed X Community Note visible on Cohere’s announcement advanced a similar explanation: the model could have been trying to test the requested detection. That reader-added interpretation does not independently establish why the model acted. The published assignment asks for a detection rule, not an upload to an outside storage bucket, and the attempted upload differs from the download-and-execute behavior the rule was supposed to detect.
AI developer Eugene Cheah challenged the inference that a model referencing its maker’s infrastructure indicates an attempt to leak information. He posed a hypothetical: if a future Cohere model learned from its own training environment and generated code pointing back to that environment, would that alone justify the same suspicion?
After Hugging Face co-founder and CEO Clément Delangue requested the full traces, Cohere released a dataset containing one recorded example, its token IDs and a script for generating further completions. Cohere said on X that it first observed the behavior without supplying an unfinished model response, and that prefilling helps others reproduce aspects of the rare event.
The released example includes the system instructions, available tools, user’s detection objective, generated reasoning and upload command. Its reasoning refers to an earlier acknowledgment that does not appear in the supplied conversation, while also claiming no concrete task has been given. The record ends at the tool call; it does not include the tool’s execution result or a completed detection rule.
Engineer Shantanu Goel challenged how Cohere characterized that reasoning. He argued that the statement about avoiding tools concerned an imagined acknowledgment of instructions, rather than an accurate account of the actual detection task. The released trace supports the narrower observation that the reasoning misdescribes the conversation; it does not establish deliberate concealment. Goel also argued that checking available utilities and DNS settings could reflect preparation for a network request rather than reconnaissance for data theft.
The reproduction script answers a narrower question than whether the model independently decides to upload data. It supplies the first 2,323 tokens of the recorded exchange—including the reasoning and upload command through the test payload—then requests up to 48 more tokens, allowing the model to complete the destination and command. It generates text through a hosted inference service; the script does not execute the resulting shell command.
Cohere’s published set of 64 example completions includes Alibaba addresses, but also Amazon and Microsoft cloud-storage address patterns, localhost and placeholder destinations. These are generated strings, not verified operational servers or evidence that requests reached them. The variety complicates an interpretation that the model consistently targets one Beijing destination, while leaving unresolved why it generated the original upload command.
The release gives independent researchers more evidence to inspect, but the supplied script does not recreate the entire event from the original user request or establish its frequency in production. VentureBeat inspected the published material but has not independently reproduced the original run.
Cohere also credited openness with enabling the investigation: “Open models make for better science,” the company wrote on X. It said developers operating Qwen themselves had noticed unusual links and that access to the weights let its researchers examine the behavior. Cohere reaffirmed its support for open-weight models and pointed to its own Apache 2.0 releases.
Cohere's leaders amplified the findings on X.
Aidan Gomez, co-founder and CEO of Cohere and a co-author of the famed "Attention Is All You Need" paper on the fundamental transformer tech that gave rise to generative AI large language models, raised both accidental training residue and an intentional mechanism for contacting an outside server as possible explanations.
Gomez also questioned whether monitoring a model’s stated reasoning could catch such actions: “One of the more disturbing things was that the model’s reasoning didn’t indicate anything about what it was about to do. Meaning that CoT monitoring would have been useless here.”
CoT refers to chain-of-thought, the model’s generated reasoning.
Cohere co-founder Nick Frosst wrote: “Whether this reflects an unintended post-training artifact or learned behavior remains unclear.”
Another co-founder, Ivan Zhang, emphasized the consequences of even infrequent leakage and, responding to a question from VentureBeat, pointed to earlier Booz Allen research .
Booz Allen examined a different issue: whether models generate less secure software depending on how a prompt describes the requester.
The firm tested four Chinese models and one American model in May. It reported that Chinese models produced less secure code when prompts identified the requester as a U.S. government customer. Booz Allen explicitly said it lacked proof that anyone had intentionally introduced the flaws.
The researchers investigated different risks: models generating vulnerable code and models issuing unexpected outbound network commands. Enterprise teams need to assess both when they delegate software work to AI.
Alibaba has yet to say whether it has reproduced Cohere’s result, what training or software context might explain the destination, or whether users need a model update or changes to their deployment controls.
Developers already use Chinese models extensively in production AI systems.
Vercel's October AI Gateway Production Index , covering September traffic, reports that DeepSeek models processed 58% of gateway tokens, Z.ai accounted for 7.2%, and Moonshot AI contributed 3.6%. Together, those three Chinese developers represented 68.8%, calculated from Vercel's figures.
Vercel attributed 6.6%, 4.5% and 13.2% of spending to those developers’ models, respectively. It estimates spending using published prices.
Vercel measures traffic through its own gateway; it does not survey all enterprises or estimate global AI market share. It counts cached and reasoning tokens, so workload length also affects each developer’s share.
Vercel also says customers directed 69.5% of spending on Chinese-origin models through U.S.-headquartered providers. Those providers’ headquarters do not establish where they operate every server.
OpenRouter's September regional-routing announcement offers a complementary picture: open-weight models reached 60% of tokens in U.S.-originating requests and 65% in EU-originating requests by August. Those percentages include models from outside China; OpenRouter says Chinese labs account for most of the open-weight volume.
OpenRouter also offers regional endpoints designed to keep processing within the United States or Europe. Such controls address where inference happens. Enterprises still need to examine the permissions of any agent that acts on the resulting output.
U.S. officials are tightening restrictions as Chinese developers release more capable models.
As VentureBeat reported last week , the U.S. government now requires federal civilian agencies to exclude DeepSeek from procurement and remove covered products.
The DHS notice expressly covers third-party products built using DeepSeek implementations, extending the issue beyond its consumer chatbot. That order names DeepSeek; it does not make a finding against Qwen.
Meanwhile, VentureBeat's Saturday coverage examined Kimi K3.1 Pro . Artificial Analysis's launch evaluation placed it fourth overall on its Intelligence Index and reported leading terminal-task performance. Moonshot had not yet published the model’s weights, so enterprises could not yet download and host it themselves.
As the regulatory climate and public discourse continue to evolve, enterprise buyers must assess more than whether Chinese models can handle their workloads. They must decide if they are willing to take the time to set up checks on said models and if they are servicing U.S. government agencies that might at some point prohibit the usage of said models.
Thus, the questions of data security and government restrictions have now entered the chat, so to speak. This disputed test does not establish that all Chinese models pose the same risks.
Enterprise teams should review an agent’s access before relying on its assurances. Those controls should apply to models from Alibaba, Cohere and other suppliers alike.
OWASP's agent-security guidance recommends narrowly scoped permissions, human oversight for consequential actions, monitoring and adversarial testing. Its development guidance also recommends isolated environments without production credentials and network access restricted to approved destinations.
Teams deploying coding agents should check whether those agents can reach arbitrary storage services, read secrets or execute commands unrelated to their assigned tasks. Teams should inspect attempted actions as well as successful ones, and test the actual model-and-tool configuration they intend to deploy.
Enterprise buyers should investigate Cohere’s account without treating a model’s nationality as proof of malicious intent. They should demand evidence about model behavior and enforce limits on its authority outside the model itself.
VentureBeat’s Agentic Infrastructure Stack Summit , in San Francisco on Wednesday, is about doing more with less, from agents down to the chip. Applications to attend close today.

title: Castelion to Begin Blackbeard Hypersonic Missile Integration on USAF F-16s
body: As part of its work with the Air Force Research Laboratory, Castelion will now expand the Blackbeard integration effort to the F-16, adding a U.S. Air Force fighter to a program already advancing toward Navy service. Castelion announced on Oct. 26, 2026, it has received a contract modification to begin integration activities for its Blackbeard hypersonic weapon on the F-16 Fighting Falcon. The award, which applies to the company’s existing work with the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL), adds a U.S. Air Force fighter to the platforms being considered for the weapon. Castelion did not disclose the value of the contract modification or a timeline associated with the F-16 integration effort. The announcement follows a September contract modification under which AFRL added $16.4 million to an existing contract with the company, increasing its total value from $20.9 million to $37.2 million. Castelion has been awarded a contract modification to its existing work with the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin Blackbeard integration activities with the F-16. We are grateful to the Air Force for their trust. Aim High. https://t.co/UerIcDG6Jx — Castelion (@Castelion) October 26, 2026 In September, the U.S. Navy has provided the clearest look yet at Blackbeard carried by an F/A-18F Super Hornet fighter jet. The weapon was also shown in a photo a month earlier during the Tailhook Association symposium as part of a presentation by the service about the ongoing activities. Blackbeard is being procured by the U.S. Navy as part of the Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector (MACE) program, an effort aimed at fielding a comparatively low-cost, long-range strike weapon that can be produced and deployed in much larger numbers than traditional hypersonic systems. The program reflects the Navy’s broader push toward “affordable mass,” with an emphasis on increasing magazine depth and giving carrier-based aircraft a greater number of high-speed standoff weapons for use against both maritime and land targets. Blackbeard expands to another aircraft platform Blackbeard is Castelion’s long-range hypersonic strike weapon, developed with an emphasis on affordability and manufacturing at scale. The company has pursued a production-oriented approach intended to make hypersonic weapons available in greater quantities than programs constrained by high unit costs and complex manufacturing processes. The F-16 effort adds to a series of integration and procurement activities involving the U.S. Army and Navy. In October 2025, Castelion announced integration contracts, worth approximately $90 million, with both services to adapt Blackbeard to their platforms and demonstrate the weapon in live-fire tests, although the specific platforms were not disclosed. Blackbeard missile flying on a U.S. Navy Super Hornet. | Source: U.S. Navy The Navy has since advanced the weapon toward operational use on the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet. As a matter of fact, Blackbeard is moving at unusually high speed through the acquisition process. In April 2026, Castelion announced a $105 million contract by the Navy to continue integration work, including hardware and software integration, system safety and airworthiness certification, and flight testing. The company identified 2027 as the target for Early Operational Capability on the Super Hornet. The F-16 effort represents a separate integration path under AFRL rather than an extension of the Navy’s F/A-18 contract. However, while the work required to integrate and certify the weapon will depend on the requirements of each platform and service, the experience accumulated with the integration on the F/A-18 might also help speed up the integration on the F-16 . It is important to note that Castelion’s announcement does not specify whether the effort is intended to lead to an operational capability or initially serve as a research and demonstration activity on the U.S. Air Force’s platform. Nevertheless, no decision to procure the weapon for employment by operational F-16 units was announced. Blackbeard’s path toward production The F-16 announcement comes as Castelion advances Blackbeard through development, integration and production activities. In June 2026, the Navy ordered 50 pre-production weapons for $23.4 million intended for the Early Operational Capability. More recently, in September, the service placed a production delivery order valued at up to $200 million for an initial lot of weapons. The number of weapons included in the production lot was not specified in the company’s statement , however the contract notice mentions “444 All-Up Rounds (AURs), defined as fully functional tactical missiles packaged within specialized shipping and storage containers.” “The Navy’s decision to move into production reflects its confidence in the Blackbeard program, and the progress we’ve made together,” said Bryon Hargis, co-founder and CEO of Castelion. “That’s how you get capability to the fleet fast, clear red tape, and partner with industry. We are grateful to PAE(A) for the trust and the urgency. Blackbeard was engineered from day one for the production line and we look forward to delivering this capability to the fleet.” The company said that Blackbeard was developed “with hundreds of millions of dollars in private investment in partnership with the U.S. Navy, U.S. Army, and U.S. Air Force.” A 1,000-acre manufacturing campus, called “Project Ranger,” was already established in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, and will work on this contract together with a second facility in Torrance, California.

title: Air Force Unit Stops All Rope Training After TACP’s Rappelling Death
body: The Air Force unit tasked with training Tactical Air Control Party Airmen has halted all rope training events after one of its instructors was killed Oct. 17 in a rappelling demonstration in front of thousands of spectators at a college football game. Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson of the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2 at Joint Base San Antonio, Texas, died Oct. 17 from injuries he suffered from rappelling rapidly from the 180-foot ceiling of Alamodome, failing to stop before his body crashed into the field below. Patterson was participating in a pregame event before the University of Texas-San Antonio played Navy as part of its Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans night. It’s unclear when the service will complete the investigation into the cause of Patterson’s fatal accident, a spokesperson at the Air Force Warfare Center at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev., said. Detachment 2 of the 6th CTS teaches rappelling and other skills TACPs need to embed and operate with Army and Marine units while coordinating and deconflicting all surface and air fires on the battlefield. But less than a week after Patterson’s death, the unit “paused all rappel and ropes training and demonstrations,” according to the spokesperson, who added that it’s unclear how long the pause will stay in place. Other media outlets previously reported the unit’s pause in training. Military units specializing in rappelling have frequently put on demonstrations at the Alamodome. In 2013, instructors from the Army’s 101st Airborne Division Air Assault School from Fort Campbell, Ky., conducted a pregame rappelling demonstration inside the stadium before the U.S. Army All-American Bowl game. But the Alamodome’s ceiling is much higher than most service members are used to, measuring more than double the height of most military rappel towers . Rappelling from such heights can cause increased friction to build up, radiating intense heat even through rappelling gloves. While practicing for the 2013 event, 101st instructors “ complained about their hands feeling pretty warm, despite wearing gloves ,” according to an Army release from the time. After their first practice rappel, the Soldiers added special inserts into their gloves to protect their hands from the heat buildup. It’s unclear if Patterson had practiced rappelling from the stadium’s ceiling before the event. But the native of Fort Stewart, Ga., received recognition for his skill during his 15 years of service, including being named as the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level, according to an Oct. 18 press release. The post Air Force Unit Stops All Rope Training After TACP’s Rappelling Death appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Teen pleads not guilty in hit-and-run that killed two 17-year-old girls on e-bike
body:
Vincent Battiloro is accused of fatally hitting Maria Niotis and Isabella Salas.
A New Jersey teen accused of intentionally ramming his SUV into two 17-year-old girls riding an e-bike, killing them, pleaded not guilty to murder charges on Monday.
Vincent Battiloro, 18, appeared in court for his arraignment on Monday, following his indictment earlier this month on two counts of first-degree murder.
The victims -- Maria Niotis and Isabella Salas, both 17 -- were killed on Sept. 29, 2025, after authorities said a Jeep Compass driving at a high rate of speed struck them while the two friends were riding the e-bike on a residential street in Cranford.
The SUV was located nearby with "major front-end damage and an e-bike embedded into the front of the vehicle," according to the complaint. Battiloro allegedly fled from the scene on foot, according to the complaint. When later questioned by police, he allegedly said he had been carjacked by a masked individual armed with a knife while driving the SUV that afternoon, according to the complaint.
Battiloro, who was 17 at the time, was arrested two days later and initially charged as a juvenile with murder. He was waived to adult court in June.
Battiloro did not speak during Monday's hearing, his first since being charged as an adult. One of his attorneys entered his plea on his behalf.
The next hearing in the case has been scheduled for Dec. 14. ABC News has reached out to his attorneys for comment on the charges but did not immediately receive a response.
Family members of the victims attended Monday's hearing, wearing sweatshirts with their names and faces printed on them.
"Maria and Isabella should be alive today," their families said in a joint statement on Monday. "These families, and every parent in this community, deserve to know how this unspeakable catastrophe was allowed to happen."
The families call on the New Jersey attorney general to open an investigation "concerning the events leading to the deaths of Maria and Isabella, including investigating all law enforcement's dealings and interactions with Vincent Battiloro and his family."
The families of the girls had alleged in a statement following Battiloro's arrest that the suspect plotted an attack against Niotis for months, killing her and also her friend in the "horrific act."
Authorities have not commented on an alleged motive.
