title: Why I now focus more on singing than dancing — Paul P-Square
body:
Nigerian singer Paul Okoye, popularly known as Rudeboy, reaffirmed his identity as a singer and songwriter, saying he has become more deliberate about dancing as he grows older and wants to conserve energy for live performances.
The former P-Square member made the remarks in an interview with Luna Lifestyle TV in Zambia, where he performed in Ndola over the weekend.
When asked whether he considered himself a better dancer or singer, Rudeboy said he excelled more at singing and songwriting, while acknowledging his background in dance.
“I’m a very good singer and songwriter. I’m everything music. Dance, first of all, I dance, but I think when I was young, that was the energy that was there,” he said.
The singer explained that his approach to performing had changed with age, noting that dancing could take up energy he needed for singing on stage.
“As I get older and I start singing, I realise dancing can take your energy, which might not make you perform well. No, I don’t need that, so you pace yourself,” he added.
Rudeboy also recalled joining a dance group formed by his elder brother, Jude Okoye, explaining that dancing was part of his musical journey before he became widely known for his vocals and songwriting.
He recounted how the group’s choreography helped shape P-Square’s stage performances, particularly after he and his brother Peter Okoye, known as Mr P, recognised the importance of dancers in delivering more engaging live shows.
Beyond the family dispute, Rudeboy used the Luna Today interview to reflect on the evolution of African music and the role his generation played in securing greater recognition for Nigerian artistes.
He argued that African musicians who embraced their languages and cultural identities helped create a distinctive sound that gained international recognition.
Reflecting on P-Square’s contribution, he said the group helped challenge the perception that African performers should occupy supporting slots when international artistes visited the continent.
“We’re the one that kicked that door,” he said, referring to the efforts of his generation to improve the treatment and visibility of African performers.
Rudeboy also recalled the importance the group placed on music videos, saying production quality was central to their efforts to compete internationally.
He explained that producing videos to match international standards came at a significant cost, particularly when the group began shooting in South Africa using expensive film equipment.
The singer also criticised the pressure on musicians to stay constantly visible on social media, arguing that it has reduced the privacy artistes once enjoyed.
“Social media, I think I call it Nigerian language, call it ‘see finish’. You know what ‘see finish’ means? Like, it finishes you, like you are too exposed,” he said.
He argued that artistes used to maintain some distance from fans, who mostly encountered them through music videos and public appearances.
According to him, social media has changed that relationship by giving audiences access to musicians’ everyday activities, leaving less room for privacy.
Rudeboy also expressed concern about artificial intelligence in music production, questioning whether technology could undermine originality and threaten the livelihoods of creative professionals.
“Where is the content? Where’s the originality?” he asked, discussing the growing use of AI tools to generate songs.
He argued that the technology could reduce demand for songwriters, producers, graphic designers, and video professionals by letting users create content with minimal input.
“You see how people are losing their jobs. You don’t need a producer, you don’t need a songwriter, you don’t need a graphic designer. Okay, you don’t even need a video anymore,” he said.
The singer further argued that the ease of generating music with AI tools could contribute to the production of songs that struggle to endure over time.
“That is why music nowadays doesn’t last,” he said, contrasting the speed of AI-assisted production with the personal experiences and emotions that often inform songwriting.
His comments also come months after his brother, Mr P, was accused of using artificial intelligence in his June 2026 comeback single, I Can’t Look Away. Shortly after the song’s release in June 2026, social media users, music producers, and commentators online alleged that the track used generative AI or Suno-style vocal and melodic patterns.
The comments come amid renewed public attention on the brothers’ strained relationship and longstanding disagreements over their respective contributions to P-Square.
In a 2024 interview with City FM, Rudeboy addressed claims that he had reduced Peter’s role in the group to dancing while presenting himself as the singer.
“I was being accused of saying that he [Peter] was the dancer and I’m the singer. I know whenever we go to the airport, people ask, ‘Are you a singer or a dancer?’ I didn’t know it was touching him,” he said.
The singer added that the brothers had previously discussed how to respond to such distinctions, saying he had encouraged Peter to take pride in his contribution to the group.
The issue resurfaced in January 2026 when Rudeboy reportedly declined a fan’s request to dance more in his videos, saying he was a singer and was too old for the activity. Fans criticised the remarks, remembering P-Square for combining vocals with elaborate choreography.
Rudeboy and Peter rose to prominence as P-Square in the 2000s, building a successful music career around catchy songs, coordinated dance routines and elaborate music videos. Their catalogue includes hits such as Do Me, Busy Body and Temptation.
The duo first split in 2017 after disagreements over family relationships, creative differences, and management. They reunited in 2021 but separated again by 2024, and their disagreements later played out in public.
Their dispute intensified in 2026 after Peter alleged financial misconduct against Jude, who managed the group. The allegations included claims concerning royalties, business arrangements and access to financial records. Jude has denied wrongdoing, and the matters remain subject to legal proceedings. The brothers have also exchanged public criticisms over their relationship and musical contributions.

title: Former senior Tax Authority officials among 11 suspects in NIS 80 million fraud probe
body: Lahav 433, the Israel Police's elite investigations unit, recently wrapped up a complex investigation by its National Fraud Investigation Unit and the Tax Assessor's Office. The probe examined suspected bribery, fraud, breach of trust, and money laundering and targeted 11 suspects, including former senior officials at the Israel Tax Authority.During the investigation, conducted both undercover and in the open, the unit found evidence that a deputy tax assessor and a former senior Tax Authority coordinator took bribes for several years from a certified public accountant (CPA) who represented taxpayers. Together, they allegedly defrauded the state of more than NIS 80 million (nearly USD 30 million).Prosecutors specializing in tax and economic crimes oversaw the case from the start. On Monday, they transferred the case, along with the investigators' recommendations, to the State Attorney's Office to decide whether to file indictments.MK May Golan questioned for 10 hours over allegations of stealing thousands from charitiesDuring a different incident on Thursday, MK May Golan was questioned by police for 10 hours on Thursday over allegations that she pocketed donations intended for a nonprofit she founded.During questioning at Lahav 433, Israel Police's national crime investigation unit, Golan denied the allegations and said she had documents showing where the money had gone. When investigators cited evidence provided by employees in her ministry, she asked to hear the recordings herself.One part of the investigation focuses on whether Golan used funds from the nonprofit she founded and managed for personal expenses. Investigators told her they had a witness who alleged she took about $22,000 in donations for herself.Nationwide wave of arrests executed in crackdown on multi-million-shekel military machinery schemeAuthorities have been operating against fraud cases during the last week, with one of the latest cases being the one where 21 suspects were arrested, including soldiers, in a multi-million-dollar fraud crackdown on October 20.An investigation, conducted by the National Economic Crime Unit (YALAK) of Lahav 433 in cooperation with the Military Police, as well as the Tax Authority, uncovered a scheme in which heavy machine contractors teamed up with IDF soldiers to inflate reports, forge hours, and report fictitious activity for heavy machinery operation in the Gaza Strip throughout the Swords of Iron campaign.The investigation culminated in a nationwide wave of arrests, with individuals being detained on suspicion of obtaining goods by deceit, bribery, and money laundering. In the course of the operations, it is suspected that fraud on the scale of millions of shekels was committed.Hodaya Ran and Jonah Davidov contributed to this report.

title: Ukraine Extends Martial Law and Mobilization Until Jan. 29
body:
Ukraine has extended martial law and general mobilization for another 90 days, until Jan. 29, 2027, as Russia’s full-scale invasion continues in its fifth year.
Since February 2022, both measures have been renewed every three months. On Monday, Oct. 26, President Volodymyr Zelensky signed laws No. 5029-IX on martial law and No. 5030-IX on mobilization after they were approved by the parliament on the same day.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Both laws take effect on Oct. 31, when the current extension expires, Ukrinform reported .
The laws Zelensky signed approve two presidential decrees; No. 1060/2026 on extending martial law and No. 1061/2026 on extending general mobilization, which required parliament’s consent to take effect.
The martial law decree points to Russia’s continuing large-scale armed aggression against Ukraine as the reason for the extensions.
It was issued on a proposal from the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC), under Article 106 of Ukraine’s Constitution and the law on the legal regime of martial law. The decree amends Article 1 of Decree No. 64/2022 of Feb. 24, 2022, which first introduced martial law nationwide.
According to Ukrinform , lawmakers approved both measures earlier on Monday, after parliament’s committee on national security, defense and intelligence had endorsed them.
Bill No. 16182, approving the martial law decree, received 293 votes, while Bill No. 16183, covering mobilization, passed with 281 in favor.
Speaking in parliament ahead of the vote, NSDC Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine Ihor Klymenko said the extension would help Ukraine take “adequate measures to counter armed aggression.” The move would also safeguard the country’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, he argued.
According to Klymenko, the extension also keeps in force the special powers held by state authorities, the military command, military administrations and local governments, which they need to repel the invasion.
The extension comes days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretsky’s government finalized an overhaul of Ukraine’s worker deferment system on Oct. 23, effectively ending automatic exemptions from mobilization for defense and energy companies.
Unless they qualify for a deferment due to health-related issues or work, Ukrainian law requires men aged 25 to 60 to serve in the military. Under the previous rules, most critical companies could defer up to 50% of their draft-age employees, while defense and energy firms have been allowed to defer up to 100%.
The latest overhaul ends automatic 100% protection and aims to create fair rules for those working away from the front, and, above all, for soldiers who have been fighting for nearly five years and need a realistic chance to return home.
“Unconditional full deferment is unfair to those who serve and opens the door to misuse,” Koretskyi said earlier, adding that some companies had been set up purely to obtain deferments and that “it became a business.”
The new approach makes full protection conditional – companies can keep their entire workforce only in case they contribute to the military on a rotating basis.
“The ultimate goal is that no one has to search for anyone on the streets,” Koretskyi said, in an apparent reference to recruiters forcibly detaining men in public.
Defense manufacturers have already lobbied against the new measures, noting that lowering the quota, even to 85%, could halt production lines, delay weapons deliveries and expose companies to penalties for missing state contract lines.
Speaking at the Kyiv International Economic Forum on Monday, Koretskyi reiterated that Russia could mobilize another 300,000 to 500,000 people. Without planning ahead, he argued, Kyiv could again be forced into unpopular emergency decisions.
On Sept. 28, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree No. 700 , increasing the size of Russia’s armed forces to 2.4 million, including 1.5 million active-duty military personnel, marking the fourth time such a decree was signed in 2026 alone.
Around the same time, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia had already begun additional mobilization , including the expansion of foreign troops, with over 8,000 already in Russia and up to 50,000 more planned.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Tanker Disabled in Strait of Hormuz Attack, Another Vessel Reported on Fire in Persian Gulf
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, July 31, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer
Two new maritime security warnings issued Monday point to continued dangers for commercial shipping in the Middle East, with one tanker confirmed disabled by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and another vessel reportedly on fire in the northern Persian Gulf.
UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said it received a verified, time-late report of a tanker struck by an unknown projectile while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz on October 23 at 0839 UTC.
The impact disabled the vessel, although all crew members were reported safe. UKMTO did not identify the tanker or provide details about the extent of the damage. No assessment of possible environmental impacts was available.
The incident was disclosed three days after it occurred, highlighting the continuing delays in reporting attacks against commercial vessels in the region.
In a separate warning issued Monday , UKMTO said it had received multiple third-party reports of a vessel on fire approximately 63 nautical miles southeast of Al-Faw, Iraq, in the northern Persian Gulf.
The vessel’s identity, crew status, extent of damage and potential environmental impact were unknown.
UKMTO classified the report as suspicious activity rather than a confirmed attack. The cause of the fire remains unclear, and authorities are investigating.
The two reports come amid continued attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, with violence increasingly extending into the wider Persian Gulf.
In its latest advisory, issued October 25 , the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) maintained its SEVERE threat assessment for the Strait of Hormuz, warning that further deliberate attacks were highly likely.
The assessment also kept the threat level across the wider Persian Gulf at SUBSTANTIAL , citing five attacks inside the Gulf since October 7, including incidents near anchorages and ship-to-ship transfer areas.
JMIC reported 156 confirmed maritime security incidents across the region since March 1. That figure was published before UKMTO disclosed the latest verified tanker attack.
The advisory highlighted another recent incident involving an LPG tanker struck by an unidentified projectile on October 22, approximately seven nautical miles northeast of Limah, Oman. That vessel subsequently reached an anchorage off Khor Fakkan.
According to JMIC, Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps activity continues to include attacks, attempted attacks, drone overflights, surveillance and radio communications directing commercial vessels toward Iranian-controlled routes.
The latest incidents also underscore the growing risks beyond the Strait itself, particularly in the Persian Gulf, where ships waiting at anchor or conducting cargo transfers remain exposed.
Despite efforts by the United States to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, commercial traffic remains well below historical levels.
JMIC reported 101 U.S.-facilitated vessel transits between October 22 and 24, compared with a historical average of approximately 138 vessels per day in 2025. The figures use different reporting methodologies, with the U.S. tally covering assisted transits rather than all commercial movements.
Separate tracking data showed only single-digit daily transits outside the U.S.-facilitated system.
Congestion also remains severe. As of October 25, JMIC estimated approximately 492 vessels were waiting outside the Strait of Hormuz, with large concentrations near Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and other regional anchorages.
The continuing disruption comes as U.S. forces enforce a naval blockade of Iranian ports while attempting to maintain safe passage for other commercial shipping.
JMIC warned that vessels using the Strait face persistent threats from projectile attacks, possible renewed mining activity and electronic navigation interference.
UKMTO has advised vessels operating in the affected areas to exercise caution and report suspicious activity while investigations continue.

title: Why Prediction Markets Got the Brazilian Election So Wrong
body:
Prediction markets got the results of Brazil's presidential election wildly wrong, with Polymarket putting Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's chances at just 20% before election day, when he ultimately won out.
Experts say the whiff is the result of Brazil banning prediction markets in the country and a wave of retail investors diluting the expertise of the money on the line.
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, commonly referred to as Lula, beat right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro in the Brazilian presidential election on Sunday. Bolsonaro came out ahead after the first round of voting at the start of October, but hadn't reached a majority, and a second round of votes was required. That second round is what Lula won , with a majority this time, and he will serve his fourth term as president.
Going into election day, Lula hovered around a 20% chance of victory with Bolsonaro sitting at 80%, per Polymarket . Even once polls and results started to roll out, one Polymarket whale told Decrypt that the market was slow to push up the odds.
"Sharps [a term for professional, high-stakes predictors] knew the market was mispriced, probably closer to 30-40% on [event] day. Mispricing was most evident during live trading, Lula was nearly a lock by 6:15 pm ET when Lula ‘Yes’ was 60c," pseudonymous Polymarket whale FhantomBets said. "Retail traders were so against Lula that you could get unlimited size at 60-80c when Lula had [essentially] already won."
Prediction markets settle at $1, with prices below that—such as $0.60 on a “yes” bet for Lula in Brazil’s election—providing implied odds of that event occurring.
The Polymarket trader added that many whales, including himself, were selling off long-term positions to get liquid capital so they could add more size to the Brazil market. Essentially, FhantomBets is claiming that retail traders with less prediction market experience inflated Bolsonaro's chances right until the very end.
Luke Nolan, senior researcher at CoinShares, pushed back on this notion and said Polymarket results reacted as polling results were released throughout the night.
"I don’t think more users are inherently a problem. They can bring liquidity and different perspectives, including local knowledge. What matters is whether participation brings different information, and whether traders can act on it," Nolan told Decrypt . "I would be wary of explaining the result simply as professionals being right and retail being wrong."
Instead, Nolan suggested Brazil’s ban on prediction markets is likely a bigger reason why the market was so harshly mispriced. Einar Knobel, CEO and co-founder of sportsbook and prediction market firm TxODDS, agreed.
"The price was set mostly by people outside the country," Knobel told Decrypt . "They were trading the first-round result, poll headlines, and the story built around them."
Brazil issued a sweeping ban against prediction market platforms in April, citing investor protection concerns and the rise of gambling addiction in the nation. Finance Minister Dario Durigan said the platforms violated betting regulations and lacked proper regulatory oversight.
Knobel added that liquidity was also relatively thin, with the market attracting just 4.5% of the volume that the 2024 U.S. presidential election garnered. "With fewer participants and almost no local knowledge in the book, little was there to correct the price," Knobel said.
Nolan believes predictors put too much weight on Bolsonaro's first-round performance, underestimated the increase in voter turnout for the second round, and assumed how voters would transfer based on the eliminated candidates.
"That said, Lula was priced at around 20% before the vote," Nolan said. "That is still some form of meaningful chance of winning. I think there are good reasons to question whether the market underestimated him. Ultimately, something that has an 80% chance of happening does not happen 20% of the time."
The mispricing of the Brazilian election was a significant upset, but Nolan cautioned against seeing it as a massive failure. He said prediction markets continue to price things better than traditional betting platforms—pointing to Betfair giving Hillary Clinton an 83% chance the day before the 2016 U.S. election.
"Across enough events, outcomes given a 20% chance should happen roughly 20% of the time. We should also compare their performance with other forecasts available at the same time," Nolan told Decrypt . "The concern would be a persistent pattern of overconfidence or a failure to incorporate relevant information, rather than an individual upset."

title: A faster way to compute signed 64-bit floor division by constants
body:
What is signed integer floor division? Signed integer floor division is where you do a/b and get a result that rounds towards â â , whereas standard ( âtruncatedâ ) signed division rounds towards 0 . As stated in Hacker's Delight: â[I suspect that] floor division more often gives the result you wantâ .
This article is about full-range floor division where the divisor is known at compile time .
Despite the usefulness of this function, the world of integer floor division is in shambles:
This blog post aims to not only shine light on the fast algorithms, but will also introduce a new fast approach which, with ideal compilation:
The benchmark section has a detailed overview showing per-divisor results over many platforms, for throughput and latency.
It works in all bit-widths, and may find use on some 32-bit or SIMD applications, but the biggest benefit is in 64-bit. It also can be used for faster positive-modulus, and faster "Euclidean" division (differs to floor division for negative divisors) .
Floor division can be much faster than you probably realise. Below is a snapshot throughput benchmark for division by 86400 (the number of seconds in one day) , the kind of performance you can expect using most languages' built-in methods, vs fast alternatives outlined in this blog.
Floor Div 86400 throughput - ARM64 Chips As tested on MacBook Pro M4 Pro and Snapdragon X1-26-100
Floor Div 86400 throughput - X86 Chips As tested on AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D and Intel Core i7 (MacBook Pro 2016)
*Rust provides "div_euclid", which matches floor-div for positive divisors. See the benchmark section for a deeper comparison across over 40 divisors.
Since some people visiting this page will be just looking to copy/paste code, I'll start with this function builder on the right:
For the avoidance of doubt, the license only applies if you copy/paste the comment and code verbatim. No license is required if you re-write the same logic in your code.
Testing A set of 65535 divisors from -32768 to 32767 for 64-bit can be generated into a single self-contained C++ file. It includes a boundary test in the same file. See the comment at the top of the download for how to build and run it.
Using this form, you can choose any bit-width and any divisor to get a copy/paste function ready to go.
There is also reference algorithm (a reusable C++ template with additional microarchitectural performance tweaks) .
As you can see, the technique is so simple that I'd expect that somebody has done this before, but I've looked around and not found it documented anywhere. If it turns out to have been done before, at least this page will make it discoverable.
For the rest of us, I'll cover a narrative about floor division, which matches my process of discovery... And if you want to create a fast library or compiler/language implementation, this will be your one-stop shop.
If you want to skip the history lesson, you can jump straight to the new stuff .
Let's suppose you want to convert a Unix timestamp measured in seconds, to rata-die (a day count). And let's also suppose you forgot how to do this properly, and you use standard ("truncated") division.
We need to divide by 86400 (60Ã60Ã24) . We'll use a 64-bit timestamp, since a 32-bit timestamp can only hold about Â±68 years.
You'll be very happy with this implementation on the right until somebody hands you a timestamp before 1970!
The above function returns incorrect results for most negative values.
Of course, you should be using floor division , the type of division that's useful for tracking repeating patterns like timestamps, angle rotations, tile positions etc. This is the type of division where the associated "%" operation is a proper positive modulus , not that fake modulus that " % " provides in C++, JavaScript etc.
Nonetheless, it's useful to understand what is going on under the hood when doing standard division like this. The pseudocode below shows what the compiled assembly is actually doing. It's essentially a mulâshift and bump-by-1 for negatives.
If you haven't bit twiddled much, the step u64(ts) >> 63 might seem odd. This is just moving the highest-bit down to the bottom. Since the top bit is the sign-bit on 2's complement computers, this leaves a 1 for negative numbers and a 0 for positive numbers.
Btw, if you're new to all this, you might think: "Great! I now understand how signed division works at the compiler level!" Sorry to burst the bubble, but here's what the same thing looks like for 64-bit division by 100:
You should notice we now have some extra junk in there: ((wide >> 64) + x) >> 6 . This is required because the magic multiplier for 100 happens to require all 64-bits for M . This causes the top bit to be 1 , making M a negative number, and as computed, the value of M ends up 2^64 lower than it should be. Since we compute x * M , the value of wide is thus 2^64 * x lower than it should be. By adding x to the upper-register of the wide double-register result, we correct for it perfectly. Divisors that require these corrections are referred to by some authors as uncooperative divisors .
The main takeaway here is that regular division is usually the cost of around 1 multiplication + 2-3 cycles.
Okay, back to div 86400 ; you get bitten by the bug, and decide to patch it. It's pretty clear that the bug can occur when x < 0 , but not always. If it's negative and divisible by 86400, it still works. So therefore, it needs adjusting when rem < 0 , like so:
But you think to yourself, surely there must be a faster way? Computing the modulus is almost as expensive as the division itself, and it gets thrown away after the bump in our theoretical use-case.
The 2nd example below is perhaps the first simplification that may come to mind, but it's actually slower! You can visit the Godbolt link to see that it produces more assembly lines...
Okay, screw this unintuitive nonsense, let's Google "fast floor division in c++" , and get an AI summary like this (cached PDF export) .
This AI summary is very misleading , as it falsely claims "Here are the fastest, branchless methods for each scenario." , before presenting a constant floor division routine that is no better than our attempt here, despite faster ways being known for 30 years+ (although it handles negative divisors at least) .
In any case, the code to the right is what it suggests.
At least now we can have a flexible utility function, and it seems GCC and Clang can compile this into the same assembly as our previous version when the divisor is hard-coded ( see on Godbolt ) .
This is basically the same function used by Java Math.floorDiv , Python's numpy , Zig , Ruby and many other libraries.
Hacker's Delight, 2nd Edition, has a section listed in the table of contents: "10â12 Applicability to Modulus and Floor Division" . That sounds promising!
It comes immediately after dozens of awesome pages with fancy tricks for other types of division (signed, unsigned etc.).
Normally, it might be copyright infringement to duplicate an entire section from a book, but in this case it's so short I think I'm covered by fair use.
Although Warren doesn't offer any solutions, the section highlighted in yellow perfectly predicts the new approach I'll introduce later.
At this point, you would be forgiven in thinking this can't be optimised any further; maybe it can't for runtime divisors (I have not investigated, since I've focused mainly on compile-time). Looking further, the first Google Search result: the archaeological remains of the once bustling Stack Overflow. The title looks promising: Fast floor of a signed integer division in C / C++ .
The post is from 2017, and has 6 answers. The OP and the top five up-voted results all use variations of the above technique.
Finally, if you scroll to the bottom, you see after seven years, user ufoguy finally posts an answer that is notably faster for compile-time divisors: "[Not] sure why this one wasn't mentioned; just one division, no modulo, branch-less:"
By my benchmarks this gives a neat improvement, it runs around 50% greater throughput on most devices.
What does ufoguy get for adding this? No thanks, no up-vote, just a comment pointing out that this does not account for negative divisors. A fair caveat. If we're going to make a fast general purpose lib, it might as well be flexible.
Luckily, the general case was solved at least as far back as the 90s. It is documented clearly on page 6 of Division by Invariant Integers using Multiplication - Granlund, Montgomery, 1994 .
Using the technique from that paper, we can create a simple flexible template function (non-zero divisor known at compile time). I've prepared an example using that technique which can be called like this in C++: floor_div<int64_t(86400)>(timestamp); .
Note that the paper demonstrates a fully branchless version, but I prefer the one above for division by constants, as it's just blindly clear what's going on, and also given the branch is compile-time, it's guaranteed to simplify. Compilers readily recognise the repeated comparison eg. (x < 0) and reuse the result. However see a Godbolt comparison of the fully branchless version to see how MSVC struggles to simplify it.
Seems like floor-div is solved right? We're only just getting started...
Code highlighted in green is compile-time only and has no runtime impact.
The division in the previous section was, at best, a mul-shift plus 5-6 cycles. Why so many?
Luckily for us, Granlund and Montgomery have another trick up their sleeve, but it's only specified for positive divisors:
The diagram to the right is my attempt at visualising this. It's a bit crazy!
The operation x ^ s moves negative inputs to the non-negative domain, specifically negative values become -1 - x ; (now >= 0 ) .
This is the same as reflection around -0.5 , hence the pivot point of the arcs all lie along this vertical dashed line.
The big saving here comes from the fact that a is not only unsigned, but also only has a range of 0..2^63-1 (half of the usual range). This means that a mul-shift will work in all cases, even for uncooperative divisors .
I've found one library in the wild that uses this technique, PyPy , but it falls back to div/mod algorithm for negative divisors.
If you're counting along, this looks like a mul-shift plus 3 cycles , a clear improvement. On ARM it could theoretically be a mul-shift plus 2 cycles, as the right-shifts can fuse with the XORs, but in practice on the machines I've tested, these fused operations don't result in the speed gain that raw cycle-counting would suggest.
The next really great paper on floor division seems to be: N-Bit Unsigned Division Via N-Bit Multiply-Add , 2005, by Arch D. Robison . The paper is primarily about unsigned division, but Section 4.3 covers floor division.
The idea presented in the paper is amazing, it almost seems like a magic bullet. There's no branch or ternary, it's a simple mul-add-shift in many cases.
You can use the form to the right to configure any division you like. Below is an example of the simplicity of it in the best of cases:
Note that in that example above, I'm using an additive value of 0x28F50000 , which is different to the paper, which uses A/2 . This is the same hex-value with the bottom 2-bytes zeroed out, which makes for more compact ARM assembly. Not all divisors can have this optimisation applied, it must be made carefully.
For the avoidance of doubt, the license only applies if you copy/paste the comment and code verbatim. No license is required if you re-write the same logic in your code.
Testing A set of 65535 divisors from -32768 to 32767 for 32-bit can be generated into a single self-contained C++ file. It includes a simple exhaustive test in the same file. See the comment at the top of the download for how to build and run it.
On ARM devices, this compiles to a single fused "multiply-accumulate" operation, followed by right-shift. Even on ARM32, it can use the smlal operation to multiply, add the constant, and obtain the upper 32-bit result, without ever needing any 64-bit emulation.
Of course, x86-64 devices can run this fine: mul, add, shift. 32-bit x86 is where it becomes less clean (but not terrible). On this platform, the addition is performed on the lower 32-bit result, followed by adc to the upper 32-bit result (adds the "carry flag", which holds a 1 or 0 depending on whether the lower register overflowed or not).
So, what's the problem with this formula? Well, there's two problems ...
Problem #1: It often requires a wider multiply. To the right is how things change for division by 101 . There's a big difference here, see if you can spot it...
Notice that A is no longer i32 but i64 ? This is an instance of this formula's uncooperative divisor; a case where the number of bits required in the multiplier is just one-too-many.
Problem #2: Wider multiplication gets clunky at 64-bit In the previous examples we talked of using wider types. This doesn't really work in 64-bit, you can use a type of "128-bit" in code, but it will be "emulated" using pairs of 64-bit registers. The below is how the Robison formula works out for our usecase 86400 :
You can visit the Godbolt link to see that this compiles fairly reasonably on x86, the main hindrance is the "add back": it's only a couple of operations on x86 ( adc ), but on ARM64 it's a double-whammy: there's two multiplication operations ( mul and smulh ). This is because ARM64 requires a separate multiplication for each high and low 64-bit half-result.
The "add back" is needed for the same reason as noted in the âAside on Uncooperative Divisorsâ earlier.
These "issues" aren't terrible, this is still a really fast floor division function. It just leaves more left on the table to optimise.
Note: in case you haven't realised yet, problem #1 and #2 are really the same.
There's a second way to write the same math, which spells out the carry by hand instead of leaving it to a 128-bit addition. An example is in the code block below.
In theory the compiler should emit equivalent assembly for either form; in practice the two forms don't always compile the same, so it's useful to know both and swap in whichever your compiler handles better. The ideal output for the carry form is an add followed by a carry-consuming instruction ( adc on x86, cmp + cinc on ARM64) ; the failure mode is a longer dependent chain on the critical path.
You can see the assembly for each approach on Godbolt here . GCC and Clang each produce tighter assembly for a different variant. Since compilers treat these differently, both of them are included in the benchmarks for a more thorough comparison.
There's one more compiler quirk worth knowing about: when the multiplier A is a compile-time constant, clang will rewrite smulh(x, A) into umulh(x, A) + (x >> 63) * A , adding two instructions to every divide. A one-line inline-asm barrier that holds A in a register but hides its value from the optimiser is enough to shut this down â the constant still gets materialised once and hoisted out of the loop.
Nonetheless, where widening is possible, Robison's approach is great. This includes 32-bit floor division on ARM (even SIMD in this case). It's ideal in all 8-bit scenarios, as all mainstream chips seem to require doubling width anyway for 8-bit multiplication. It can also lead to some really cool special cases, such as: fast_i8_floordiv_51 => (x * 5 + 2) >> 8 That function above can compile to just 2 assembly operations on x86! ( LEA + arithmetic right-shift).
Let's try to go down to bare metal, and see what we get if we do a plain mul-shift for division by 3. No corrections, no nothing.
We choose 3 , because it's the first non-trivial divisor (power-of-2 divisors are solved with a simple arithmetic right-shift).
The round-up multiplier gives a perfect sequence of sets-of-3 in the positive direction, and just one discontinuity in the negative direction with a set of -1 and -2 (everything negative is shifted right) .
Note: visualising this makes clear why standard truncated division is implemented for cooperative divisors like this with a simple mul shift, with a +1 bump for negatives, that gives five values of zero centred around the origin.
But, we are not here for truncated division... â forget about that chart below!
Anyway, if we use the round-down multiplier:
...we get the opposite result: the negative direction has a perfect sequence, and the positive direction has a broken quadruple set at 0-3 (everything positive is shifted right) :
It turns out that 3 is a very flexible divisor, and for now you'll just need to take my word for it that in 64-bit, the neat half of each continues over the entire signed-64 bit range. So the answer here is simple, we can just use a different multiplier for positives and negatives:
This is the ideal scenario, as the value M + (x >> 63) can be computed very cleanly. It involves no extra constant materialisation, no flag-to-register conversion, and on ARM64 chips it can be computed with a single shift-add assembly operation ( add x0, x1, x2, asr #63 ).
GCC compiles this well, however in my benchmark loops Clang seems to bungle it a little. One can force better compilation on Clang in C++ by writing asm("" : "+r"(m)); after the 2nd line, which stops the compiler from proving that m >= 0 , which fixes the bungled optimisation. Note: similar asm-hacks were required in the benchmark to get the best out of the Robison algorithm.
However, it's not the only way we can implement it. Two other options are available in the case of floor division by 3:
In the first case, we don't want to bump x = -1 because that will give an incorrect result of y = 0 . In the second case, we don't want to bump x = MAX_INT64 because that will overflow. The reason we don't need to bump x = MAX_INT64 (x = 2^63-1) , is because (2^63-1) FLOOR_DIV d = (2^63) FLOOR_DIV d for any divisor d that is not a powerâofâ2. These would only differ if 2^63 was divisible d , but it's clearly not since the prime factors of 2^63 are all just 2 . That identity is about exact division though, and the round-down multiplier is only approximate. If d divided 2^63-1 , then skipping the bump would leave INT_MAX an exact multiple nudged slightly downward, and the result would be one too low. Those divisors are safe to ignore here only because the INT_MIN check (see Implementation) already rules them out at register-sized shifts. This is the same reason a saturating increment is used in fast unsigned division of certain divisors (see ridiculousfish / libdivide) .
It is fortunate that the two bounds for the latter approach can be implemented with a sign cast and single comparison. Both constants of -1 and 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF can also materialise in a single ARM assembly operation due to their repeating bit-patterns. In a tight loop, such constants would typically be materialised once outside of the loop.
Anyway, why talk about all this when the case of 3 was already solved? Well it turns out that not all divisors are as flexible as 3 .
All non-power-of-2 integer divisors come in two overlapping sets:
Divisors that can use both, are eligible for the Sign-Selected-Multiplier version.
Below you can see the first 100 divisors, and what method is selected. The pattern is quite chaotic, but easily computed at compile-time:
The number under this denotes the shift-size, highlighted when it's a clean register-sized shift.
Whoops, the above widget lets you select "Negative" divisors, but I haven't talked about those yet...
Everything we have gone through works the same with negative divisors. We just have to be careful with signs, comparisons etc. I'll refer to "round down" multipliers as those that round towards zero, and "round up" multipliers as those that round away from zero.
The divisor -3 happens to not be flexible, it requires "round down", but -5 works both ways with bit-shift of 65:
Below are the two alternative approaches for -5 :
Note: This variant works with a clean 64-bit shift
The term (1 << 63) can alternatively be written 0x8000000000000000 .
Floor modulus flows naturally from floor-division, and is a "positive modulus" function for positive divisors:
For certain divisors of the form 2 N â 2 K , I have a faster alternative that uses an add-shift-mask:
See the day-of-week article and time-of-day article for more details about this identity.
Euclidean division is the same as floor division for positive divisors. For divisors less than -1 , we can use the following identity which results in just one extra cycle for the subsequent negation (the first negation for the floor_div call is performed at compile-time). The second runtime negation can in some cases be absorbed for "free" in subsequent operations, such as in obtaining Euclidean modulus:
The simplicity of these functions above comes with extra compile-time complexity to solve the constants and variant, but it builds fast.
Basically it boils down to iteratively testing the worst-case scenario for both the round-up and round-down versions, starting with an ideal register-sized shift W . A solution is valid if it passes the worst-case numerator. Eg:
One detail matters here: the worst case for round-down is INT_MIN , and its product must not land exactly on an integer, or the result comes out one too high. That happens exactly when D divides 2 W â 1 â 1 (in 64-bit: 7, 49, 73, 127, 337, 511, â¦) . For these divisors, writing r = 2 S mod D , r = 2 S â ( W â 1 ) at every register-sized shift, so round-down never passes and they are forced to round-up . (For negative divisors it's the other way around: round-up is the one that can land on an integer, for |D| dividing 2 W â 1 + 1 , in 64-bit: 3, 9, 19, 27, 43, 57, â¦)
If solutions are found for both, then the sign-selected variant will also work, at a shift equal to the greater of the two solutions found.
My benchmarking (in 64-bit) suggests it is fastest to choose sign-selected when possible, except for some rare cases:
On x86, round-up loses to sign-selected because its bias is a signed compare (x < -1) . The result of a signed compare isn't left in the carry flag, so the compiler needs cmp â setl â add , one more instruction than round-down's cmp â adc , and that extra cycle cancels the saving from skipping the extra shift. On an Intel Mac I got equal performance between them, but on an AMD processor I saw the sign-selected version run faster. As such, my benchmarks and the reference implementation alter the choice here for x86.
These exceptions noted above (register-sized shifts) are somewhat common for small divisors, eg 5 , 6 , 9 , 14 etc., however, over the full set of possible 64-bit divisors, it is a vanishingly small set. The Venn diagram below shows the distribution of divisors, and this tiny set is noted in the lower right.
The problem of finding out which variant works for a given divisor boils down to the same problem as finding an unsigned divisor in a bit-width one-size smaller than usual, i.e.: 63 , 31 , 15 , or 7 ; and others have written at length about this, hence I'd like to keep this section brief. The more important thing is the proof that the negative side works given the positive side is well studied (see Annexure A - Proof ).
Well, by all means feel free to, but make sure to test it thoroughly, otherwise you might end up with a bug like in Google's TensorFlow.
If you're interested, you can view the source to try to figure out yourself what was wrong with it.
The source uses templates, but I've written a simpler 64-bit pseudocode version to the right.
There's two reasons this implementation is not great for division by constants known at compile-time. One is a bug, one is a performance issue.
The buggy implementation of this floordiv function was present in the 1.0 release in Feb 2017. This bug then remained in place for over 4 years until it was fixed in May 2021 .
No shade to the author, this is fiddly to get right. The main reason I wanted to highlight this was to show how easy it is to get wrong, even in a mature, heavily-reviewed codebase. This is all the more reason for languages and standard libraries to provide this function outright.
A fix to avoid the overflow could be to do what CPython does , by using unsigned integers, and factoring out the abs_y term. This might still cause issues at INT_MIN though.
This mostly solves the bug, but given you've read this far you probably know a few faster ways to do it by now.
Tests used for validating the functions in this article can be found in the testcase code: https://github.com/benjoffe/fastdiv .
The same repository is used for benchmarking, and you can run them yourself like this:
The benchmarks run for all non-power-of-2 divisors between -2^4 and 2^5 , as well as a handful of cherry-picked larger positive divisors (100, 360, 86400, 10 5 , 10 7 , 86400000, 10 8 ). The reason is detailed in the x86 section below.
In the charts, the x-axis represents these various divisors, and the y-axis is the nanoseconds-per-division (lower = faster).
All results were obtained by running the benchmark with -repeat=10 and recording the median results. The -batch=8 command runs each divisor 8 times before loading the next entry from memory. This ensures that the processor is not bottlenecked by memory access. Latency results use the same command but replace the batch flag with -latency . This mode feeds the result of each computation into the next division, so there is no parallelisation.
To avoid making this page huge, I have grouped the benchmarks by chip type (ARM, x86) and benchmark type (throughput, latency).
On Clang, the New algorithm has highest throughput for all divisors, and occasionally tied with gm-v2 . The fastest alternatives are gm-v2 for positive divisors and Robison for negatives. MSVC appears to produce sub-optimal assembly for negative divisors for a few of the algorithms.
Device and Compiler: MacBook Pro M4 Pro - macOS 15.6.1 - Apple Clang 17.0.0
Device and Compiler: Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 (Windows 11 25H2) - Snapdragon X1-26-100 @ 2.956 GHz - Clang 23.1.3
Device and Compiler: Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 (Windows 11 25H2) - Snapdragon X1-26-100 @ 2.956 GHz - MSVC 19.51.36260
We get similar results for latency, with the New algorithm performing best, or tied-best.
Device and Compiler: MacBook Pro M4 Pro - macOS 15.6.1 - Apple Clang 17.0.0
Device and Compiler: Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 (Windows 11 25H2) - Snapdragon X1-26-100 @ 2.956 GHz - Clang 23.1.3
Device and Compiler: Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 (Windows 11 25H2) - Snapdragon X1-26-100 @ 2.956 GHz - MSVC 19.51.36260
x86 processors are where we have more of a mixed bag. For throughput, the fastest algorithm seems to fluctuate between Robison and the New algorithm. Sometimes gm-v2 comes out tied as fastest (eg. divisors 6 and 9 ). You can see now why some larger divisors were cherry-picked: they demonstrate that some useful divisors perform well in the New algorithm.
The cases where the New algorithm does not win follow a clear pattern:
Device and Compiler: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D - Ubuntu 24.04.1 - Clang 18.1.3
Device and Compiler: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D - Ubuntu 24.04.1 - GCC 13.3.0
Device and Compiler: 2016 MacBook Pro - macOS 12.7.6 - Apple Clang 14.0.0
Latency benchmarks are where we start to see a clearer winner on x86. While there was a lot of fluctuation before, now Robison wins for nearly all divisors. Rarely, the New algorithm seems to win on both throughput and latency, as seen for 14, -7, -14 (round-down with 64-bit shift) .
Device and Compiler: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D - Ubuntu 24.04.1 - Clang 18.1.3
Device and Compiler: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D - Ubuntu 24.04.1 - GCC 13.3.0
Device and Compiler: 2016 MacBook Pro - macOS 12.7.6 - Apple Clang 14.0.0
Finally, I note that if you need the modulus, the gap between "traditional" and the faster algorithms will close, but they still remain faster. I would like to actually finish this blog post one day so I'll skip these benchmarks.
The points below may be worth considering for anyone looking to make a fast floor division library or language/compiler feature:
The New algorithm presented in this blog post has been adopted by the following open source projects:
If you found this interesting, you might also like to see the below two recent blog posts. They both discuss a new trick for faster positive-modulus for divisors of the form 2^A - 2^B (eg. 12, 24, 60 etc.) , which might be worth including in any library that does both floor division and positive-modulus.
You should follow me on X to get notified when I publish more optimisation articles.
Positive divisor, non-negative x . For x â¥ 0 , x is just an unsigned ( W â 1 ) -bit number, so the unsigned results (GranlundâMontgomery, ridiculousfish) apply directly with N = W â 1 . Either the round-up multiplier M works directly, or the round-down multiplier M â² works with an increment. At least one of the two always does, using an N -bit multiplier, at a shift no larger than:
Writing q = â n / D â for an unsigned N -bit input n , both variants land strictly between q and q + 1 whenever n > 0 :
These inequalities are strict (not â¤ ), and this is a requirement rather than a free fact. That D isn't a power of 2 only tells us neither multiplier is exactly 2 S / D . For round-up the strictness then follows from the bound. For round-down, the product at n + 1 = 2 N lands exactly on q when D â£ 2 N â 1 , since for those divisors 2 S = 2 N â r at every register-sized shift. The solver rejects round-down for them, which forces them to round-up.
In simple terms, these mul-shifts slowly "drift" away from the true ratio. Apart from at x = 0 , the non-rounded terms are never an integer (the check above ensures this) . The reason to point this out is that we will use the below identity which relies on that fact:
â â y â = â 1 â â y â for non-integer y .
Negative x . Let u := â¼ x = â 1 â x . Bitwise NOT maps the negatives one-to-one onto 0 â¤ u â¤ 2 N â 1 â exactly the range n ranges over above â and also satisfies:
Combined with the standard floor/negation fact ( â â y â = â 1 â â y â for non-integer y ), each case of the bump follows:
So whichever rounding works for unsigned ( W â 1 ) -bit division also works across the whole signed W -bit range, with the same multiplier and shift.
Sign-selected. This uses round-up's unbumped half and round-down's unbumped half, so it works at any shift where both roundings work. A rounding that works at some shift keeps working at larger shifts, so it's enough that each works somewhere within the N -bit multiplier limit.
So this is the positive-divisor problem applied to â x . The one difference is the range: â x runs from â ( 2 W â 1 â 1 ) up to 2 W â 1 . The non-negative side holds one value more than W â 1 bits allow (the image of INT_MIN), and the negative side holds one value less. That extra value is where round-up can land on an integer, which it does for | D | â£ 2 N + 1 , so those divisors can't use round-up. The missing value on the other side is the one that ruled out round-down for D â£ 2 N â 1 , so for negative divisors that exclusion goes away. That's why the reference implementation adjusts the bounds based on the divisor's sign.

title: Greece Leads Six Nations Against Turkish-Libyan Maritime Deal
body: Greece, the European Union, Cyprus, Egypt, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates have jointly rejected the 2019 Turkish-Libyan maritime memorandum, declaring it invalid under international law despite its ratification by Libya’s House of Representatives. Greece Leads Six Nations Against Turkish-Libyan Maritime Deal Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis delivered the joint statement at the United Nations, warning that the agreement raises serious concerns about regional stability and the international legal order. The statement follows the Libyan parliament’s decision on October 20, 2026, to ratify the memorandum signed by Turkey and Libya’s Tripoli-based Government of National Accord in 2019. The agreement seeks to delimit maritime jurisdictional areas in the Mediterranean, drawing objections from Greece and other countries over its implications for maritime boundaries and the rights of neighbouring coastal states. Six Parties Reject the Memorandum Speaking on behalf of the six parties, Gerapetritis argued that bilateral agreements cannot override established principles of international law or undermine the maritime rights of third countries. He specifically referred to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which provides the international legal framework for maritime zones and the delimitation of maritime boundaries. The joint statement declared that the Turkish-Libyan memorandum disregards geographical realities and the rights of coastal states, including the maritime entitlements of islands under international law. It also stressed that Libya’s parliamentary ratification does not alter the agreement’s legal status in the eyes of the six parties. “The memorandum remains invalid, contrary to international law and cannot constitute a legal basis for the delimitation of maritime zones nor produce legal effects for third states,” the statement said. Gerapetritis warned that accepting bilateral agreements that disregard international legal principles would establish a dangerous precedent and undermine efforts to resolve disputes peacefully. Greece Signals Willingness to Continue Talks With Libya Despite its opposition to the memorandum, Greece reaffirmed its commitment to resolving maritime disputes through dialogue and negotiations based on international law. Gerapetritis said Athens had conducted bilateral discussions with Libya over the delimitation of maritime zones in good faith and remained prepared to continue those efforts. He also emphasised the importance of Libya’s institutional reunification and the establishment of a stable, prosperous state capable of contributing to regional cooperation. “A stable Libya, actively participating in regional cooperation, is essential for peace and security throughout the Mediterranean,” the statement said. Greece maintains that respect for international law and good neighbourly relations must guide Libya’s political transition and its relations with neighbouring countries. European Union Reaffirms Its Position Following the joint statement, European Union Ambassador to the United Nations Stavros Lambrinidis reiterated the bloc’s longstanding opposition to the Turkish-Libyan memorandum. Lambrinidis said the EU regretted Libya’s parliamentary ratification of the agreement and reaffirmed that the bloc considers it incompatible with the law of the sea. He referred to the European Council’s December 2019 conclusions and its subsequent reaffirmation of the EU position in June 2025. According to Lambrinidis, the memorandum infringes on the sovereign rights of third countries and cannot produce legal effects for them. The EU also called on all countries to respect the sovereign rights of its member states in accordance with European and international law, including UNCLOS. Brussels has consistently maintained that the agreement cannot determine maritime boundaries in a way that disregards the rights of other states. Strategic Implications for the Eastern Mediterranean The dispute over the Turkish-Libyan memorandum remains a significant point of tension in the Eastern Mediterranean, where overlapping maritime claims affect territorial rights, energy exploration and regional cooperation. Greece argues that the agreement fails to account adequately for the maritime entitlements of Greek islands, including Crete, while Turkey has defended the memorandum and rejected objections raised by Greece and the European Union. Libya’s parliamentary ratification has added a new dimension to the dispute, prompting renewed diplomatic efforts by Athens and its partners to reinforce their legal position at the United Nations. The latest joint statement demonstrates a coordinated diplomatic response involving European, Mediterranean and Gulf partners. However, the dispute remains unresolved, with Greece continuing to advocate negotiations with Libya under international law while rejecting the 2019 memorandum as a valid basis for maritime delimitation. title: Amazon fires trap Manaus in smoke as authorities target arsonists
body: MANAUS, Brazil — Midway through the conversation with Mongabay, Otacílio Farias, a 75-year-old farmer, stops to read a message on his phone: “Right now, there’s a fire near a friend’s house.” Farias has lived his entire life near the Autaz Mirim River, near Manaus, Brazil’s largest city in the Amazon. Forest fires have affected the area for more than 30 days. “Nearby, Lake Miriti was shrouded in haze at dawn, but it wasn’t morning mist: It was smoke,” he said. Farias says the nearby municipalities of Autazes and Careiro da Várzea are experiencing the worst fire crisis of his lifetime. “My throat and nose are in terrible shape,” he said. Farias’ community WhatsApp groups are packed with pleas to save crops and reports of elderly residents rescued as flames approached. Farias was at home on Oct. 1 when friends of his 18-year-old son, Fabrício, arrived on motorcycles, calling for help against fires approaching homes. Around 100 community members joined the effort. It wasn’t until Oct. 10, however, that the Amazonas state government declared an emergency in 36 municipalities, paving the way for federal assistance. Between Oct. 1 and 19, Brazil’s space agency, INPE, recorded 1,921 fire hotspots in Amazonas, up 202% from the same period in 2025. The daily average also rose 51.5% compared with late September 2026. Of these, 584 (30.4%) were in the Manaus metropolitan area: 197 in Autazes, 134 in Itacoatiara and seven in Manaus. Hotspots also spiked after the first round of Brazil’s presidential election: INPE…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: 2027: INEC puts preliminary voters’ register online, publishes final document Dec. 15
body: By Omeiza Ajayi The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has made the Preliminary Register of Voters for the 2027 General Election available on its online platform, following concerns raised by some stakeholders and in preparation for the certification and publication of the Final Register of Voters on December 15. The register can now be accessed at https://display.inecnigeria.org. It is the same list that was earlier displayed at Registration Areas nationwide. National Commissioner and Chairman, Information and Voter Education Committee at INEC, Mohammed Kudu Haruna, said in a statement on Monday that the Commission “has taken note of the concerns expressed by Nigerians and other stakeholders regarding the desirability of making the Register accessible through its online platform in addition to the physical display already conducted.” “Accordingly, and in furtherance of its commitment to transparency, accessibility and public confidence in the electoral process, the Commission has decided to make available on its online platform https://display.inecnigeria.org the same Preliminary Register of Voters earlier displayed at the Registration Areas,” he said. Haruna recalled that the physical display was held in accordance with Section 19 of the Electoral Act, 2026, from 9th to 15th October, 2026. According to him, the exercise provided “registered voters the opportunity to inspect their particulars and submit claims and objections as prescribed by law.” He said the online publication does not replace the exercise already carried out. “This additional measure complements the physical display already undertaken and is intended to facilitate wider public access to the Register,” he said. The Commission said it is still processing the claims and objections that arose from the display. “Meanwhile, the Commission continues to process claims and objections arising from the exercise in accordance with the Electoral Act, 2026, preparatory to the certification and publication of the Final Register of Voters on 15th December 2026. “The Commission appreciates the continued interest and constructive engagement of Nigerians and stakeholders and reiterates its commitment to transparency, accountability and the faithful implementation of the Electoral Act, 2026 in delivering credible elections,” he said. The post 2027: INEC puts preliminary voters’ register online, publishes final document Dec. 15 appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Space cybersecurity market to swell to $8.59 billion by 2031, study projects
body:
DELRAY BEACH, Fla. The global space cybersecurity market is projected to grow from $5.52 billion in 2026 to $8.59 billion by 2031, at a CAGR of 9.2% during the forecast period, according to a recent study by MarketsandMarkets, "Space Cybersecurity Market -- Global Forecast to 2031."
According to the study authors, the space cybersecurity market is growing as government and defense organizations, commercial satellite operators, and space agencies seek more robust protection for satellite networks, ground infrastructure, communication links, and mission-critical systems. Advances in encryption, identity and access management, threat detection, security analytics, cloud security, and secure satellite communications are enabling space systems to operate more securely against evolving cyber threats.
In addition, investments in cybersecurity are also supporting wider adoption of integrated security solutions across satellite communications, Earth observation, navigation and PNT, mission planning and control, data processing, and launch operations.
The largest market share in 2026 is coming from the defense segment, the study authors estimate, with the Asia-Pacific segment expected to exhibit the highest CAGR of 12.0% between 2026 and 2031.
For additional information visit the MarketsandMarkets website .

title: Economy Ministry begins developing Ukraine's industrial strategy through 2030, plans to present it in three months
body:
The Ministry of Economy and Environment has begun developing Ukraine's industrial strategy through 2030 and plans to present a draft for discussion with the professional community over the course of three months, Deputy Minister Vitaliy Kindrativ said.
According to him, the Federation of Employers of Ukraine (FEU), the Institute of Economic Modeling, relevant industry associations, and experts are involved in drafting the document.
"Our priority today is, on the one hand, to support the domestic manufacturing industry, and on the other hand, to help it enter foreign markets," the deputy minister emphasized during the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) titled "People. Business. Economy. What's Next?" on Monday in Kyiv, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
Kindrativ said the strategy will focus on sectors with high added value and the potential to enter foreign markets, particularly in mechanical engineering, the manufacturing sector, and agricultural processing.
He said that once work on the document is completed, it will be discussed with relevant business associations, whose input will form the basis for its final approval by the government. Furthermore, in his view, a clear definition of priority sectors and government support programs will serve as an important signal for attracting foreign investment and capital into the Ukrainian economy.
For his part, CEO of the Federation of Ukrainian Industries (FUI) Ruslan Illichov said the document must be based on the real needs of domestic businesses.
"This strategy must be built, first and foremost, on an understanding of the perspectives of the industries operating in Ukraine. We must take our most competitive existing industries and ask what they need to scale up," the FRU head said.
Illichov added that key components of the document should also include maximizing localization in large government and infrastructure projects and coordinating a common industrial policy with European partners to integrate Ukraine into EU markets.

title: Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phone
body:
Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, hit store shelves on Friday to considerable lines and long wait times for preorders.
But some customers who were lucky enough to get the $1,999-and-up phone on its first weekend have been reporting a pretty big problem: The inner screen of the phone can break, showing horizontal bright lines emanating from the phone's hinge.
Apple on Monday said that it was aware of the issue, which it said affected a "small number" of phones, and that it would replace the devices under its AppleCare warranty.
"We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," an Apple representative told CNBC. "If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."
Apple says on its website that an inner-screen repair will be $999 for iPhone Duos that are out of warranty.
Most of the reports are from anonymous customers on online forums such as Reddit and X , and there are fake images online as well. But well-respected device repair firm iFixit weighed in on Sunday, after tearing down the new device and testing its resistance to dust, and theorized the issues may have to do with Apple's hinge design.
"Many of these damage reports describe folding or unfolding the phone, hearing a crunch, and pushing past it," said iFixit technician Shahram Mokhtari in its teardown video . "Right where the damage is happening, the hinge is shaped a little differently."
"The hinge is actually dozens of parts, with ludicrous precision," iFixit CEO Kyle Wiens posted on X. "A manufacturing variance or grain of sand can kill the fragile display panel it protects."
Breaking screens have been an issue with foldable phones going back to 2019, and have been seen as one of the major roadblocks to the technology's widespread adoption. That year, Samsung released one of its first folding devices, and reviewers quickly found that its inner screen cracked during normal use.
Early reviewers praised the experience of using the iPhone Duo when unfolded, especially for multitasking or media, but said that many apps had not been updated to take full advantage of the phone's larger and wider screens.
Apple said Monday that apps were already being updated for the new foldable device.
"The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor," an Apple representative said in a statement.

title: Ukrainian forces evacuate 2 severely wounded soldiers from battlefield using drone, video shows
body:
Ukraine's 475th Separate Assault Regiment Code 9.2 evacuated two severely wounded soldiers from the battlefield using a domestically developed aerial evacuation drone, StarGate, the unit reported on Oct. 26.
The two soldiers, 25-year-old Yevhen, call sign " Izium ," and 24-year-old Artem, call sign "Kolobok," had suffered severe limb injuries and were stranded in a contested area about five kilometers (three miles) from the Russian border.
Ground evacuation was impossible due to difficult terrain, water obstacles, and the threat of Russian first-person-view (FPV) drones, the regiment said .
The two evacuation missions were carried out over the course of a week in cooperation with SkyFall, the Ukrainian company that developed and manufactures StarGate.
The operations required coordination between several units and fire support from heavy Vampire attack drones to suppress Russian positions.
During one mission, StarGate flew nearly 30 kilometers (20 miles) to reach a wounded soldier and approximately the same distance back with him aboard.
Russian electronic warfare systems attempted to jam satellite navigation signals in the area, but the drone completed the evacuation using its AI-based navigation system and the pilots' skills, according to the regiment.
Oleksandr Nastenko, commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, said the unit plans to use the experience to train additional crews and make aerial evacuations a regular practice.
The operations come a week after Ukrainian forces reported what they described as a first-of-its-kind aerial evacuation of a severely wounded soldier who had spent nearly 500 days at a front-line position, using a drone.

title: Prof. Ochefu rejects appointment to NDC National Campaign Council
body: By Peter Duru, Makurdi Professor of Economic History and Strategic Studies at Rev. Fr. Moses Orshio Adasu University, Makurdi, Prof. Yakubu Ochefu, has rejected his purported appointment to the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) National Campaign Council, insisting that he is not a member of the party. Ochefu said he was neither consulted before his name was included in the list of members of the campaign council circulating on social media nor did he give his consent to the appointment. The university don, who is also the National Chairman of the Association of Nigerian Universities Alumni (ANUA) and President-General of Ochetoha K’Idoma, said his leadership positions required him to remain non-partisan, as the memberships of both organisations cut across political parties. In a statement he personally signed, Prof. Ochefu said, “My attention has been drawn to a list circulating on social media, titled ‘Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) National Campaign Council’, which names me as a member of its National Campaign Caucus. “I wish to inform the public that I am not a member of the NDC and have never been. “I was not consulted before my name was included, nor did I give consent. “I have written to the Chairman of the Council to decline the appointment and to request that my name be withdrawn and a revised list published. “As National Chairman of the Association of Nigerian Universities Alumni, ANUA, and President-General of Ochetoha K’Idoma, I lead organisations whose members cut across all political parties. These offices require me to remain non-partisan, and I intend to honour that obligation. “I thank all who reached out for clarification, and ask that you disregard the list insofar as it concerns me.” The post Prof. Ochefu rejects appointment to NDC National Campaign Council appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: AI company Anthropic announces IPO, expected as early as November
body:
The artificial intelligence company disclosed more than $16 billion in revenue and an $80 billion net loss for the first half of 2026.
Anthropic announced that it had filed S-1 registration with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for an initial public offering on Nasdaq, marking a significant step for artificial intelligence companies.
A Monday S-1 filing with the SEC suggested that Anthropic could be aiming for a mid-November IPO, listing its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ANT. title: Trump administration pushes for food assistance card upgrade to fight fraud
body:
A SNAP recipient checks her balance left after purchasing food supplies with a California EBT card in Los Angeles on Oct. 31, 2025. Damian Dovarganes/AP hide caption
In a major step to combat a form of fraud that has robbed food stamp recipients of millions of dollars , the Trump administration is proposing a requirement for states to bolster the security features on their food assistance cards.
In recent years, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, has been the repeated target of card skimming, when thieves extract personal information from payment terminals and drain money from accounts. Most SNAP cards rely on a magnetic stripe for swipe payment – which tends to be vulnerable to skimming because it does a poor job of securing the data stored on cards.
Many banks in the U.S. took action against this issue over a decade ago by upgrading their cards to include microchips and tap-to-pay, which are considered more secure. But states have lagged in making such a transition for Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) cards, which are what SNAP recipients use to access food aid. Currently, fewer than a third of states have made the switch or are in process of doing so, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).
Now, under the proposed rule released by the USDA last week, all states would have to adopt chip-enabled EBT cards. It also requires retailers that accept SNAP benefits to have payment terminals that support tap-pay. The USDA's Food and Nutrition Administration, which administers SNAP, attributed card skimming as a reason behind the proposal.
"These proposed changes will protect SNAP benefits from thieves and ensure benefits are accessible by approved households," the Food and Nutrition Administration said in its summary of the rule.
Back in January, the USDA Office of Inspector General projected that SNAP theft could climb to $233 million between 2025 and 2026 — largely as a result of skimming. A recent ProPublica investigation found that last year, $470 million was stolen electronically from SNAP recipients. The total was calculated using data from Propel, an app that helps SNAP recipients check their food benefits.
In most states, stolen benefits are not replaced — leaving recipients to make difficult choices, such as skipping meals or borrowing money in order to pay for groceries, according to Propel .
Earlier this month, NPR reported that food assistance card modernization had widespread support from state officials and federal watchdogs, as well as Republicans and Democrats in Congress. But money has been a major barrier for states to make the switch. According to the Government Accountability Office, chip-enabled cards are about 10 times more expensive to produce than their magnetic strip counterparts.
The federal push for stronger card security features comes as state SNAP agencies are facing new budget pressures triggered by President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The proposed regulation recognized the financial barrier, adding that the USDA is interested in hearing from state agencies about the cost burden.
"As stewards of taxpayer dollars, the Department considers these administrative costs as a necessary investment to deter the loss of Federally-funded SNAP benefits," the proposed rule said.
The public has 60 days to submit comments on the proposal before the USDA publishes a final rule. The department is considering giving states a two-year deadline from that publication date to implement the rule, but it also welcomed input on whether that's enough time.
When asked if the department would consider providing funding to help states upgrade their card technology, the USDA said that "For years, States had access to administrative funds to stop this egregious abuse of taxpayer resources. Yet few acted."
The USDA added that the proposed rule has been in the works for nearly four years. It estimates that the changes will reduce stolen benefits by at least $1.5 billion over the next decade.
SNAP has been one of the focus areas in the Trump administration's war on fraud. Last week, the Justice Department announced that its fraud division helped uncover nearly $42 million in schemes targeting food benefits. The investigations ranged from identity theft to retailers illegally exchanging cash for food benefits.
