title: Pope Leo meets with AJC delegation, reaffirms condemnation of antisemitism
body: American Jewish Committee (AJC) leaders met with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on Thursday, marking the first lay leadership delegation to visit the pontiff since the beginning of his papacy.During their visit to Rome, the AJC delegation also held discussions with senior Vatican officials, including Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin and Vatican Secretary for Relations with States Archbishop Paul Gallagher. They also met with diplomatic figures and representatives from the Italian Jewish community.In a historic meeting at the Vatican, @AJCCEO Ted Deutch and AJC leaders met with Pope Leo XIV, who reaffirmed his commitment to combating antisemitism and strengthening Jewish-Catholic relations. As antisemitism and anti-Israel hatred rise around the world, AJC will continue working with Catholic leaders to turn this shared commitment into meaningful action and strengthen the bonds between our communities. https://t.co/d3nkA3nPWV— American Jewish Committee (@AJCGlobal) October 25, 2026The ties between AJC and the Catholic Church stretch back more than a century to at least 1915, with the Holy See and the advocacy group maintaining a decades-long partnership that included a pivotal role in the formulation of Nostra Aetate, the landmark 1965 Vatican declaration that transformed Catholic-Jewish relations by rejecting antisemitism, affirming Judaism's eternal covenant with God, and building new bridges of understanding. Vatican continues to uphold cooperation with Jewish communityAlthough recent disagreements and divergent viewpoints regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict have occasionally created friction, AJC noted that the Vatican continues to uphold the core principles of the historic document. This enduring commitment was highlighted in a letter sent to Rabbi Noam Marans in May 2025, where Pope Leo pledged “to continue and strengthen the church's dialogue and cooperation with the Jewish people in the spirit of the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate.”The delegation was led by AJC Chief Executive Ted Deutch, President Bobby Lapin, and Director of Inter-religious Affairs Rabbi Noam Marans, alongside AJC Chair of Inter-religious Affairs Dr. Joyce Silberstang, AJC Associate Director of Inter-religious Affairs Rabbi Allyson Zacharoff, AJC Representative in Italy and Liaison to the Holy See Lisa Palmieri-Billig, and dozens of other AJC leaders.During the audience, the delegation presented the Pope with a piece of commissioned artwork titled Honoring a Sacred Relationship. Created by Rabbi Matthew Berkowitz, Izzy Pludwinski, and Yair Medina in Jerusalem, the piece displays key passages from Nostra Aetate, written in both the original Latin and an official Hebrew translation. Encircling these texts is a decorative border inspired by an 1822 illuminated Jewish marriage contract from Ferrara, Italy, with the ketubah design purposefully chosen to symbolize the enduring covenant and lasting bond between the Church and the Jewish people.During the papal audience, Pope Leo addressed the delegation about the longstanding relationship between the Church and the organization, stating, “It is a pleasure to welcome you to the Vatican on this day when the Church remembers in a special way my beloved predecessor, Saint John Paul II, whose efforts contributed so greatly to fostering the friendship between Jews and Catholics.”Pope's commitment to combat antisemitismThe Pope also recalled remarks made to the committee's board of governors in 1995, noting that his predecessor observed that “dialogue between Christians and Jews must find eloquent expression in the life of both of our communities.”“These words remain relevant today, as reflected in your organization's longstanding commitment to dialogue and to cooperation with the Catholic Church,” Pope Leo said. “I, therefore, welcome this opportunity to express gratitude to all who continue to build relationships, grounded in sincerity and mutual respect, between our respective communities.”We are deeply moved that Pope Leo XIV, so early in his papacy, has reaffirmed his commitment to Catholic-Jewish relations. In a letter to AJC's Director of Interreligious Affairs, Rabbi Noam Marans, he pledged to continue to strengthen dialogue with the Jewish people in the spirit of Nostra Aetate. As we approach the 60th anniversary of this landmark declaration, we look forward to working together to deepen understanding and cooperation.— American Jewish Committee (@AJCGlobal) May 12, 2025Reaffirming the stance of the Church, the pontiff added, “In this regard, on the occasion of the 60th anniversary of the Declaration Nostra Aetate from the Second Vatican Council, I affirmed that 'the Church does not tolerate antisemitism and fights against it, on the basis of the Gospel itself.'”Deutch highlighted the importance of the meeting during a time when inter-religious dialogue faces ongoing challenges.“When Pope Leo XIV reached out to AJC on the very first day of his papacy, he reaffirmed the enduring importance of the relationship between the Catholic Church and the Jewish people,” Deutch said. “At a time when dialogue across faiths is more important than ever, this gift celebrates a relationship sustained by decades of trust, dialogue, and shared values, rooted in the historic breakthrough of Nostra Aetate. We thank His Holiness for his partnership, generosity, and unwavering support for Jews across the world.”Lapin stated, “It is a great honor to represent AJC as we met Pope Leo.”He added, “We are proud of AJC's long history of leadership in Catholic-Jewish relations, and are grateful for Pope Leo's commitment to this relationship and leadership in combating antisemitism.”Marans noted, “It is particularly poignant that we are able to reaffirm our joint commitment to Catholic-Jewish relations in person not only with Vatican officials, but with Pope Leo himself, who on the occasion of his inauguration, reached out directly to AJC and the Jewish community.The rabbi added: “AJC is deeply moved that this group of Jewish leaders was welcomed to a papal audience while His Holiness continues to recover, and is among the first to meet him as he resumed his schedule of public meetings – a clear demonstration of the value he places on maintaining and fostering the enduring relationship between the Church and the Jewish people.”

title: Atiku not qualified to preside over modern economy – Shettima
body: Vice-President Kashim Shettima has taken a swipe at the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, saying he lacks the skill set to govern a modern economy. Shettima also criticised the former vice-president’s proposal to restore petrol subsidy if elected president in 2027. He made the disclosure on Monday at the ongoing 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja, where he described Atiku’s proposal as a move to take Nigeria backwards for political convenience. “One of the leading presidential candidates (Atiku) is advocating a return to the subsidy scheme. He wants us to backslide into primitivity for political convenience,” Shettima said. ‎FACT CHECK: How Tinubu’s Image on Bread Was Edited to Depict Obi 2027: Outrage over Donation Of Luxury SUVs To APC Youth Leaders “I dare to put forward that his skill set… he was trained in sanitation at the Kano School of Hygiene. So he doesn’t have the skill set to govern a modern economy. That’s a painful truth. “So it’s for you, as Nigerians, to make informed decisions. Even that certificate in sanitation, I know he will find it difficult to distinguish the difference between flu and COVID, that are airborne diseases, and Ebola that is human contact ailment. Nigerians would have to decide.” Shettima said. He defended Tinubu’s decision to remove petrol subsidy, saying the president took the difficult decision because he understood the economic realities. “The president took those painful decisions because he understands the dynamics,” he said.

title: Most of Anthropic’s Q3 revenue came from models that barely existed six months ago
body: Anthropic’s long-awaited S-1 , filed Monday ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut under the ticker ANT, shows how quickly customers are spending on its newest models. According to the filing, models released in the six months leading up to September 30 accounted for more than 80% of the company’s third-quarter revenue. Anthropic released eight widely available Claude models between April and September 2026, plus three restricted-access Mythos models. The filing doesn’t say how much revenue each generated; models launched in late September had only days to contribute to the quarter. But that raises an interesting question for developers: Are newer models delivering better results for developers’ tasks, and what do those results cost? Are newer models delivering better results for developers’ tasks, and what do those results cost? How new models compound The filing suggests there’s a reason newer models account for so much of Anthropic’s revenue. The company says customer spending is closely tied to how often it releases new models and what those models can do. Each improvement naturally gives customers more reasons to use Claude, while more capable models attract new customers and encourage existing ones to use Claude more and spend more in the process. That spending helps fund the next round of development. Anthropic says in the filing that the company relies on growing revenue to pay for the research, computing power, and technical talent needed to build more capable models. Those improvements can then attract more customers and drive additional spending, creating a cycle in which each generation of Claude helps fund the next. Improvements can then attract more customers and drive additional spending, creating a cycle in which each generation of Claude helps fund the next. Did demand drive releases? The filing shows how important newer models are to Anthropic’s revenue, but it doesn’t establish whether customer demand has influenced the company’s faster release schedule in 2026. While the two may be connected, Anthropic doesn’t say that increased spending is what drove it to release models more frequently. Revenue, not customer migration The 80% figure also doesn’t tell us how many customers switched to newer models. A relatively small group of customers spending heavily on the latest releases could account for much of that revenue. The filing offers some context for how much spending can vary. Anthropic’s heaviest Claude Code enterprise users spend roughly 20 times more than other enterprise users . That doesn’t tell us which models they’re using, but it shows why revenue alone can’t tell us how many customers have made the switch. Choosing the newest model Developers building coding agents, retrieval pipelines and automation tools may default to the most powerful model without first checking whether a smaller or cheaper alternative could handle the job. That spending adds up. Reuters reported — citing attendees at Anthropic’s October 14 investor meeting — that the company generated $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue. Anthropic reportedly generated $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue. Whether developers actually need the latest models or simply prefer them, Anthropic benefits from the spending. With models released since April accounting for more than 80% of its third-quarter revenue, Anthropic has a strong financial incentive to keep improving Claude. Anthropic has also called for pacing frontier AI development so safety work can keep up with growing model capabilities. The filing does not show whether commercial demand has affected that approach . title: EU Council mobilizes EUR 4.9 bln for Ukraine through European Peace Facility
body:
The Council of the European Union has decided to mobilize EUR 4.9 billion for Ukraine through the European Peace Facility.
According to a press release issued on Monday, a package of eight decisions was adopted for this purpose, enabling the use of funds for Ukraine under the European Peace Facility (EPF). "These decisions allow for the partial reimbursement, through the EPF, of military aid already delivered by member states, amounting to a total amount of €4.7 billion. They also provide additional financing for the EU Military Assistance Mission in Support of Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine), amounting to a total of €230 million," the EU Council said.
The statement notes that these decisions "mark a major step towards implementing the political agreement reached by EU member states on 25 September 2026 to mobilise €6.6 billion for Ukraine under the EPF." "The agreement included the provision of €1 billion in new military aid to Ukraine and further reinforcement of EUMAM Ukraine in 2027," the EU Council said.
Thus, thanks to today's decisions, the total amount of support the EU is providing to Ukraine through the European Peace Fund has reached EUR 10.8 billion. This amount includes EUR 9.9 billion to reimburse the cost of military aid provided by member states and EUR 950 million for military training within the framework of the EUMAM mission.
"Today's decisions confirm the EU's continued firm and unwavering support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders in the face of Russia's war of aggression," the EU Council said.

title: Algeria Initiates Major Foreign Personnel Deployment to Support Niger Security
body: Algeria’s parliament has approved the deployment of ground forces to neighbouring Niger, marking a major departure from the country’s longstanding policy of avoiding overseas ground deployments. The move would be Algeria’s first deployment of ground forces abroad since it sent troops to support Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli War. The deployment follows the landmark arrival of Algerian Air Force Su-30MKA fighter aircraft to Niger in late August, following a failed coup attempt in the country. This represented a major landmark in defence ties between Algiers, and Central African states that recent extracted themselves from the European sphere of influence. The Algerian Defence Ministry announced that the deployment of two fighter squadrons had been made at the request of Niger's military authorities, highlighting the long range of the aircraft and the country’s ability to provide logistical support for unexpected foreign operations. By placing advanced combat aircraft at Niamey's principal military airfield, Algeria in August signalled its willingness to support Niger's existing government against further attempts at destabilisation. This followed multiple attacks by jihadist insurgents which Niger and its neighbours have repeatedly alleged are being supported by Western Bloc countries, most prominently France, to undermine stability and facilitate a return of Western control. The proposed mission for the Algerian Army expected to focus on protecting energy infrastructure in northern Niger, near the Libyan border, although the number of personnel involved and the deployment timetable have not been announced. The deployment was authorised through votes in both chambers of Algeria’s parliament on October 25. The upper house, the Council of the Nation, approved the proposal unanimously, with all 148 senators participating in the vote backing the measure, before the lower house also endorsed it. The Algerian Army is widely considered the most capable in Africa and the Arab world by a considerable margin. Its mission is expected to focus on protecting energy facilities and investments associated with Algeria’s state-owned energy company, Sonatrach. The company is involved in oil exploration in Niger’s Kafra region and in plans for the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline, which would transport natural gas from Nigeria through Niger to Algeria for export to international markets, particularly Europe. Algerian senator Belkacem Boulghiti said the deployment was intended to secure economic infrastructure rather than wage war in Niger. Algeria and Niger signed a military cooperation protocol during Nigerien Defence Minister Salifou Modi’s visit to Algiers in October. Western assessments of the growing defence ties between the two African states have widely interpreted Niger’s reliance on Algerian support as a result of the shortcomings of Russian contractor forces in combating jihadist insurgents in the country.

title: B.C. election sets record for lowest voter turnout
body:
The 2026 B.C. election is over, but the results mark a historic low, w ith fewer than half of eligible voters casting a ballot.
According to Elections BC, preliminary figures show just 48 per cent of eligible voters participated, down about 10 percentage points from the 2024 provincial election.
For Stewart Prest, a political science lecturer at UBC, the record-low turnout reflects a campaign that failed to motivate many voters, particularly those who had previously supported the NDP.
“This is Mr. Eby’s low-turnout election to own, and this is going to be part of his legacy,” Prest said.
The NDP saw more than 270,000 fewer votes than it did in the 2024 election, a significant drop that suggests many of its previous supporters didn’t show up at the polls. By comparison, the Conservatives received about 49,000 fewer votes.
Prest says the party’s decision to call an election just two years after its previous majority appeared politically opportunistic to some voters. That, combined with a polarizing campaign, may have further alienated its own supporters. Some voters questioned why they were being asked to return to the polls before the government had delivered on key issues. He says the party’s failure to present a positive vision, particularly on issues such as housing affordability and jobs, may have further discouraged its own supporters.
Prest says the Conservatives’ victory was also shaped by voters frustrated with the NDP’s record and looking for a change in government.
For some Conservative voters, the early election call may have reinforced that frustration. After being asked to return to the polls just two years after the last election, some saw the vote as unnecessary and were motivated to send a message to the governing party, Prest says.
Prest says voters are more likely to participate when they believe their vote matters — and when governments deliver on issues such as housing affordability and jobs.
With turnout at a record low, the election raises questions about how political parties can reconnect with voters who no longer feel motivated to show up.

title: Two rescued in foiled kidnap attempt on Benue road
body: Troops of the Joint Task Force, Operation Whirl Stroke (OPWS), have rescued two victims from suspected kidnappers who attempted to abduct motorists and other road users along the Naka–Ahume Road in Benue State. The rescue followed a firefight between the troops and the suspected kidnappers during a fighting patrol on October 24, 2026, forcing the assailants to abandon their captives and flee. A statement issued on Monday by the Acting Media Information Officer, Headquarters of the Joint Task Force, Lieutenant Ahmad Zubairu, said the troops encountered the armed suspects while they were attempting to abduct motorists and other road users. The statement said the troops engaged the suspects in a firefight, forcing them to abandon their victims before fleeing the scene. Hardship: Wike backed PDP knocks Tinubu, APC Man remanded for allegedly impersonating Kwankwasiyya praise singer It added that the troops pursued the fleeing suspects but made no further contact with them. One of the rescued victims, Mrs Mngunengen Ihom, 36, from Ahume, sustained machete wounds during the incident and was evacuated to Naka General Hospital for medical attention. The Force Commander of OPWS and General Officer Commanding, 5 Division, Nigerian Army, Major General Moses Gara, has directed troops to sustain aggressive, intelligence-led operations against armed groups threatening the safety of residents in the joint operations area. Gara also urged personnel to strengthen intelligence gathering, particularly through human sources, to improve early warning and response to security threats. He reassured residents of the task force’s commitment to restoring peace and security, while urging members of the public to provide credible and timely information to security agencies to support ongoing operations.

title: US Army practices digging temporary battlefield graves
body: The Army is preparing for the grim possibility of burying fallen soldiers on the battlefield, testing how fast it can dig temporary graves while preserving remains for eventual identification and return to families after the end of a conflict. During an exercise in North Carolina, engineers, preventative medicine teams, chaplains and fatality management specialists prepared for mass temporary interment not used on a large scale since the Korean War, the Army announced in a release last week. For more than twenty years during wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, U.S. air superiority allowed the quick evacuation of remains back to the United States through mortuary affairs channels. Future conflicts — especially those with large-scale combat operations, or LSCO — may not have the same capabilities. Phase II of Operation Dragon Covenant challenged troops to test and validate temporary burial operations and remains preservation at a large scale. Engineer soldiers involved had to use their equipment to excavate and then fill burial trenches without damaging mock remains, made of skeletal models and water containers, so that hypothetical future forensic teams could unearth and repatriate them after the end of a conflict. Chaplain Maj. Warwick Fuller, 20th Engineer Brigade, XVIII Airborne Corps, leads a prayer to consecrate a designated battlefield temporary interment site, Oct., 20, 2026, Fayetteville, North Carolina. (Sgt. 1st Class Ange Desinor/U.S. Army) “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management leader for 3rd Corps Sustainment Command (CSC), in the release. “If we went to war tomorrow, we would be making this up as we went along. What we are doing here is taking a scientific, field-tested approach so that we can maintain positive control and respectfully care for our fallen.” The U.S. requires the evacuation of human remains when operations in wartime situations permit, but U.S. joint service guidance authorizes temporary graves during mass casualty incidents in war, where decedents cannot be safely moved due to safety, lack of transportation, or if the deaths are a result of chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapons. Soldiers, civilians or enemy combatants buried in temporary graves must be treated with dignity and their information — if available — preserved, the military dictates. The Geneva Conventions require that even the bodies of enemy forces be recorded and that identifying information be collected. Cremation is rarely authorized, save for hygiene or religious grounds. Army doctrine prescribes that temporary interment plots consist of five parallel trenches to hold 100 bodies, with ten bodies lining each side of the trenches. In previous trials, units using standard backhoes could excavate only one trench — and thus ten remains — per three hours. According to the service’s release, operators during the most recent exercise used D6 bulldozers to excavate a trench large enough for 20 remains in an average of one hour and 15 minutes. Based on that, commanders can plan for an engineer company with the requisite equipment to dig and cover trenches for up to 2,400 bodies every 24 hours, if operating nonstop. Operators also learned that published instructions on trench standards did not reflect current Army equipment. The service said that doctrine called for seven feet between rows, which the team found too narrow to drive a dozer without disrupting the burial trenches. This discovery, and any others, will be reflected in future Army doctrine. Beyond the physical trenches, the exercise also gave religious specialists and chaplains an opportunity to prepare for LSCOs by developing sensitive protocols. “In a high-intensity, contested combat environment, fatality management teams cannot stop a 24-hour interment operation for individualized religious gravesite services,” Lt. Col. Ruska, chaplain for the 3rd CSC, said in the release. The team, he added, also may be unable to determine an individual’s faith after death. “We consulted with Chaplains from various low density faith groups for advisement,” he said. “The consensus was that by consecrating the site before remains are placed in the ground reassures families that their loved ones are treated with reverence, dignity and honor despite the inability to provide a memorial ceremony in a contested combat environment.” The exercise will continue, the Army said, with Phase III of Dragon Covenant in Spring 2027, integrating security, medical facilities and a mortuary affairs collection point.

What we are doing here is taking a scientific, field-tested approach so that we can maintain positive control and respectfully care for our fallen.” The U.S. requires the evacuation of human remains when operations in wartime situations permit, but U.S. joint service guidance authorizes temporary graves during mass casualty incidents in war, where decedents cannot be safely moved due to safety, lack of transportation, or if the deaths are a result of chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapons. Soldiers, civilians or enemy combatants buried in temporary graves must be treated with dignity and their information — if available — preserved, the military dictates. The Geneva Conventions require that even the bodies of enemy forces be recorded and that identifying information be collected. Cremation is rarely authorized, save for hygiene or religious grounds. Army doctrine prescribes that temporary interment plots consist of five parallel trenches to hold 100 bodies, with ten bodies lining each side of the trenches. In previous trials, units using standard backhoes could excavate only one trench — and thus ten remains — per three hours. According to the service’s release, operators during the most recent exercise used D6 bulldozers to excavate a trench large enough for 20 remains in an average of one hour and 15 minutes. Based on that, commanders can plan for an engineer company with the requisite equipment to dig and cover trenches for up to 2,400 bodies every 24 hours, if operating nonstop. Operators also learned that published instructions on trench standards did not reflect current Army equipment. The service said that doctrine called for seven feet between rows, which the team found too narrow to drive a dozer without disrupting the burial trenches. This discovery, and any others, will be reflected in future Army doctrine. Beyond the physical trenches, the exercise also gave religious specialists and chaplains an opportunity to prepare for LSCOs by developing sensitive protocols. “In a high-intensity, contested combat environment, fatality management teams cannot stop a 24-hour interment operation for individualized religious gravesite services,” Lt. Col. Ruska, chaplain for the 3rd CSC, said in the release. The team, he added, also may be unable to determine an individual’s faith after death. “We consulted with Chaplains from various low density faith groups for advisement,” he said. “The consensus was that by consecrating the site before remains are placed in the ground reassures families that their loved ones are treated with reverence, dignity and honor despite the inability to provide a memorial ceremony in a contested combat environment.” The exercise will continue, the Army said, with Phase III of Dragon Covenant in Spring 2027, integrating security, medical facilities and a mortuary affairs collection point.

title: PREMIUM TIMES journalist nominated for PSHAN health investigation award
body:
Mariam Ileyemi, a journalist with PREMIUM TIMES, has been nominated for the Outstanding Health Investigation Award ahead of the 2026 Private Sector Health Alliance of Nigeria (PSHAN) Annual Awards.
The nomination was announced on Monday in the Media and Innovative Health Communication category, with Ms Ileyemi listed among the top three nominees.
Ms Ileyemi was nominated for her open-source investigation, “Social media, anonymous websites drive Nigeria’s poorly regulated weight-loss injection market,” which examined how weight-loss injections are being marketed and sold without prescriptions. The investigation also uncovered a network of anonymous websites promoting weight-loss injections, including retatrutide, an investigational drug still undergoing clinical trials.
PSHAN says the Outstanding Health Investigation Award recognises investigations that uncover systemic healthcare issues. Ms Ileyemi is nominated alongside Sadeeq Atanda of the Foundation for Investigative Journalism and Yemisi Adegoke, Chigozie Nwonwu and Lina Shaikhouni of BBC/BBC Eye.
PSHAN said an expert panel of judges will select the winner of each award and announce the results at its Annual Awards and Gala Night on 20 November 2026.
Other awards include the Health Influencer of the Year, which recognises digital creators promoting credible health content, and the Health Journalism Excellence Award.
The top three nominees for Health Influencer of the Year are Olawale Ogunlana, Olufunke Arowolo and Chinonso Egemba, popularly known as Aproko Doctor.
For the Health Journalism Excellence Award, the nominees are Racheal Abujah of the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN), Ojoma Akor of Health & Science Africa, and Bilkis Abdulraheem-Lawal of Radio Nigeria/Grassroots Broadcast.
Ms Ileyemi is a journalist on the Health and Development Desk at PREMIUM TIMES, where she reports on health, gender and development issues. She was named PREMIUM TIMES Reporter of the Year 2025 at the newspaper’s Annual Editorial Awards.
She is a fellow of the 2025 Africa Health Communications Fellowship by Fraycollege, South Africa, and a beneficiary of the 2023 Media-EIS Fellowship, among other fellowships.
She is also a recipient of the Mamman Marshall Scholarship for Women in Journalism and was nominated for the 2024 Nigeria Healthcare Excellence Award in the Prevent Epidemics category.
Ms Ileyemi holds a degree in Mass Communication from the Lagos State University (LASU).

title: Hardship: Wike-backed PDP knocks Tinubu, APC
body: The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) faction backed by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike has criticised President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) for saying the prevailing hardship in the country is caused by the opposition. Speaking at the APC presidential campaign flag-off at the Kaduna Township Stadium on Saturday, President Tinubu said his government was working to eradicate the hardship caused by the opposition. Reacting to the comment, Jungudo Haruna Mohammed, National Publicity Secretary of the PDP, said the opposition, especially the PDP, is not responsible for the hardship in the country, asking the APC to own up to its responsibility. The PDP said it considered the statements as “attempts to evade responsibility and divert public attention from the pressing challenges facing the country under the APC-led administration.” Kano Assembly screens six commissioner nominees FACT CHECK: Video of Tinubu Shaking Dignitaries With Left Hand Is fake The PDP spokesman argued that rather than engaging in political blame games, the APC should explain what it intends to do to make “food affordable, support farmers, strengthen local food production, create jobs, improve security, fight corruption, improve electricity supply, reduce transportation costs, and restore the purchasing power of ordinary Nigerians, among other pressing concerns.” “We firmly reject any attempt to use the PDP’s sixteen years in government as a blanket justification for the shortcomings of the present administration.” “After more than APC’s 10years in office, Nigerians deserve answers, not excuses. The APC must tell Nigerians what it has achieved, outline the concrete measures it is taking to address the country’s present day challenges, and demonstrate its commitment to improving the welfare of citizens rather than continually dragging the PDP into its own shortcomings. “The PDP maintains that the economic challenges confronting Nigeria cannot be resolved by repeatedly blaming previous PDP-led administrations. While historical circumstances may provide context, they cannot serve as a permanent shield against accountability. “Every administration must be judged by its policies, decisions, achievements, and, most importantly, the living conditions of the people it governs.” the statement said. PDP said Nigerians were demanding practical solutions, affordable food, economic stability, and improved security, not endless political arguments and blame shifting, adding that they remain confident that Nigerians will judge political parties by their records, policies, and commitment to the welfare of the people. “We believe that the growing desire among Nigerians for a return to PDP leadership reflects their yearning for better governance, improved living conditions, and a more secure and prosperous country. “Our message to the APC is simple: stop the blame game and start taking responsibility. Nigerians deserve solutions, not excuses. The government in power must address the country’s challenges through concrete, measurable, and sustainable actions that will bring meaningful relief to citizens. “The PDP is not responsible for the hunger Nigerians are experiencing today. The APC must own its record, address the nation’s challenges, and deliver on its promises to Nigerians. The government in power must answer for its stewardship and present a credible path towards economic recovery, food security, and a better standard of living for all Nigerians.” PDP said.

title: From emergency repairs to resilience in the housing sector: How Transitional Development Assistance contributes to Ukraine's social recovery
body:
Representatives of the six housing pilot cities of the Strengthening of Urban Resilience in the Areas of Supply Infrastructure and Housing (SUR) project visit a construction site during a housing conference in Zhytomyr, Ukraine, on May 6, 2026. (SUR)
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Iryna Simakina was in Enerhodar, a city in southern Ukraine, home to Europe's largest nuclear power plant.
As Russian forces advanced on the city , staying became increasingly dangerous. Simakina, who uses a wheelchair because of a disability, eventually left her home behind, uncertain whether she would ever return.
Simakina found refuge in Zhytomyr, northwestern Ukraine , in 2023, where she initially stayed with a friend. In December 2025, she received a call that changed her life.
"I didn't believe it and didn't dare to hope. And I received a call: 'Come pick up the keys,'" she said.
Simakina was one of 15 new residents to receive an inclusive apartment for use through a partnership between the Zhytomyr authorities and the Strengthening of Urban Resilience in the Areas of Supply Infrastructure and Housing (SUR) project, implemented by Deutsche Gesellschaft fur Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH.
SUR is part of Germany's Transitional Development Assistance (TDA), a flexible crisis-response instrument of the Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) that bridges the gap between short-term humanitarian relief and long-term development cooperation. TDA operates in line with the U.N. 2030 Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, while aligning its work with EU priorities on local resilience, crisis prevention, and the Humanitarian–Development–Peace (HDP) Nexus. About 10.8 million people in Ukraine need humanitarian assistance, 6.4 million needing water and sanitation services, 5.6 million needing shelter, and 4.5 million needing health care, according to the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, nearly 4.7 million people have been registered as internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Ukraine, according to the Social Policy, Family and Ukraine's Unity Ministry . The actual number remains difficult to determine, while Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets has warned that the figure has not been updated for nearly two years, with a flawed system for identifying and counting IDPs.
The scale of displacement, even if difficult to measure precisely, places enormous demands on the state to provide housing and to help people settle into new communities.
The pressure is compounded by continued Russian attacks on civilian and critical infrastructure, particularly the power grid . The impact is especially severe in winter, when hours-long blackouts, disrupted water supply , and homes without heating threaten Ukrainians nationwide.
"If there is anything I would describe very much in the spirit of TDA, as our truly fundamental principle, it is the commitment to be guided by the most urgent needs of our Ukrainian partners," Erik Schweikhardt, the SUR project director, told the Kyiv Independent.
The broader aim of SUR is to help Ukrainian cities withstand the impacts of Russia's war and prepare for future challenges, while supporting the most vulnerable groups, including internally displaced people and returnees. Operating in more than 100 cities, primarily in eastern and central Ukraine, the project helps war-affected municipalities maintain and restore essential services, including electricity, heating, water supply, and housing, while strengthening local disaster risk management.
In wartime, decisions often need to be made quickly. At the same time, communities need long-term solutions that can be adapted to similar ongoing and future challenges. This approach helps communities stabilize during emergencies, strengthen their resilience, and better prepare for future shocks.
“Reconstruction should go beyond restoring what was lost and be embedded in long-term urban planning and development.”
"Within the framework of TDA, reconstruction should go beyond restoring what was lost and be embedded in long-term urban planning and development, guided by these principles," Schweikhardt said.
In this way, the project addresses urgent needs while helping people maintain their daily lives. Access to clean water is one example. Mykolaiv, a city in southern Ukraine with roughly 460,000 residents , has been without a centralized drinking water supply since Russian forces destroyed a key water pipeline in 2022. To address this ongoing challenge, the project is supporting a decentralized network of public drinking-water points, helping ensure that residents have access to clean, safe water.
At the same time, the project is investing in the long-term resilience of urban water infrastructure. It supports risk assessments in the water sector and helps cities develop resilience plans for their local water utilities. These efforts aim to establish more sustainable and reliable water services that can better withstand current and future threats.
Supporting municipal energy systems is another key area of SUR's work. The project helps municipalities maintain electricity and heat supplies by providing essential equipment, including cogeneration units, mobile boiler houses, battery storage systems, and hybrid generators. This support is particularly critical during the harsh winter months, when attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure threaten essential municipal services.
"Housing should be viewed as part of the city's overall development."
To help municipalities maintain reliable electricity and heating supplies, more than 450 energy units have been supplied and commissioned, including 118 combined heat and power plants. The equipment has benefited more than 4.5 million people. The support was provided in part through the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ)'s "Winter Aid 2024/2025" initiative and in cooperation with other GIZ projects.
In addition to providing decentralized heat and energy to help mitigate outages caused by damage to centralized municipal systems, SUR supports cities in modernizing their heating infrastructure. These systems remain vulnerable to external shocks, including large-scale destruction, and are heavily reliant on carbon-intensive energy sources.
In Kryvyi Rih, a city located roughly 70 kilometers (nearly 40 miles) from the front line and frequently targeted by devastating Russian attacks, the project is supporting the development of a district heating strategy that integrates urban resilience and disaster risk reduction while aligning with the EU's long-term decarbonization goals.
SUR has also supported municipal hospitals in Kryvyi Rih by upgrading their heating networks. Hospitals are particularly vulnerable to energy disruptions, as life-saving equipment and medical procedures depend on a reliable power supply. To strengthen their energy resilience, the project has developed plans for three municipal hospitals to establish a stable, decentralized energy supply that can operate independently of the grid. These plans also integrate project-provided boiler houses into the hospitals' energy systems.
In nearly three years of operations in Ukraine, SUR has supported the restoration of municipal supply and waste management infrastructure in war-affected regions, benefiting more than 2 million people.
In the housing sector, SUR has so far contributed to restoring more than 800 homes since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, enabling Ukrainian families to remain in their communities rather than face displacement. The project focuses on rehabilitating war-damaged private homes, developing and piloting rehabilitation approaches for damaged multifamily residential buildings in cooperation with local authorities, and helping homeowners' associations access funding for repairs.
"At the same time, it would be misleading to describe the project as simply something that acts quickly and locally," Schweikhardt said. "In line with TDA, its interventions are also designed to build structures and capacities that remain valuable beyond the immediate crisis."
The shortage of affordable housing, compounded by the precarious living conditions many internally displaced people continue to face, underscores the need for effective, long-term municipal housing strategies.
In cooperation with the Housing Initiative for Eastern Europe (IWO) e.V., SUR is supporting six pilot cities — Zhytomyr, Poltava, Kremenchuk, Bila Tserkva, Mykolaiv, and Kalush — in conducting a diagnostic analysis of the housing sector, including an assessment of local housing needs. Based on the findings, concepts for municipal housing strategies aligned with Ukraine's national housing strategy and the requirements of Reform 7 under the Ukraine Facility, "Ensuring Access to Housing for People in Need," are being developed.
"Ukraine's housing policies have long addressed the consequences of deeper structural issues rather than their root causes," Yuliia Popova, project director at the Housing Initiative for Eastern Europe (IWO) e.V., told the Kyiv Independent.
“Ukraine's housing policies have long addressed the consequences of deeper structural issues rather than their root causes."
At the heart of the problem is an incomplete privatization model. Mass privatization transferred individual apartments to residents but left buildings without the legal, financial, or institutional mechanisms needed to manage and maintain them as shared property. The state also failed to deliver on its promise to finance the first round of major repairs, leaving a growing backlog of renovations.
Meanwhile, housing policy largely ignored the rental market, leaving it poorly regulated, while privatization steadily depleted the municipal housing stock.
As demand for rental housing grows, most of Ukraine's rental market remains informal, operating outside the formal housing system. IDPs, who make up a significant share of renters, face not only high housing costs but also legal uncertainty because of informal rental agreements. War-related destruction has deepened these challenges, compounding longstanding structural problems. Addressing both the immediate consequences of the war and the housing sector's deeper flaws requires fundamental changes in how housing is provided and managed. Reform is no longer optional, but a structural necessity.
Municipalities must balance three competing priorities: meeting the immediate housing needs of displaced and vulnerable residents, repairing and renovating existing homes before they deteriorate beyond repair, and rebuilding housing destroyed by the war.
All three demand the same limited municipal resources, staff capacity, and political attention. At the same time, cities must align their efforts with national reforms and seek funding from a fragmented donor landscape.
"The local housing strategies we are developing with the pilot cities within the SUR project take a bottom-up approach to build a comprehensive picture of local housing conditions. They bring into municipal planning perspectives that have often been overlooked: housing market monitoring, assessments of existing housing stock, analysis of needs across population groups, including IDPs, and structural problems in housing stock management," Popova said.
The diagnostic process and subsequent recommendations for housing strategies translate competing needs and priorities into a structured, evidence-based plan of action. They provide a basis for inclusive local debate and help bring fragmented resources and capacities together around shared goals. Zhytomyr, Kremenchuk, and other cities participating in the SUR project are demonstrating that this is possible even under current conditions.
Kremenchuk has been cooperating with GIZ for several years, Maletskyi said, with housing policy now among its main priorities. The issue is particularly urgent given that more than 31,000 IDPs are currently registered in the city. At the same time, Maletskyi said the development of municipal housing should also benefit families who cannot afford to buy a home.
Svitlana Olshanska, deputy mayor of Zhytomyr, said housing remains an urgent issue for the city as well, and that Germany's approach offers a model Ukraine could learn from.
"When the full-scale war began, Ukraine found it difficult to respond to the challenges of providing housing," Olshanska told the Kyiv Independent. "At the same time, many Ukrainians who relocated to Germany saw similar situations addressed."
"We cannot provide affordable housing even to those who need it because we do not have a housing stock for crisis situations," she added.
Like Kremenchuk and other pilot cities, Zhytomyr , together with GIZ, is developing strategies to address the housing crisis. Olshanska said a long-term strategy is important not only for residents, who need a clear understanding of how their city will develop, but also for partners, donors, and potential lenders.
Maletskyi also stressed that affordable housing and broader development strategies should be centered on the needs of the local community, which should benefit from such initiatives and play a role in the city's future.
"One of the key takeaways for us is that housing should be viewed as part of the city's overall development. If a person has a job but cannot find decent, affordable housing, it will be difficult to keep that person in the community," Maletskyi told the Kyiv Independent.
Affordable housing, including municipal housing, is in high demand among large families, people with disabilities, older people, orphans, and low-income households. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, however, IDPs are one of the largest groups in need of housing, with their numbers continuing to grow as Russian forces continue their assault.
For people like Simakina, who was forced to leave her hometown and move to another city, securing accessible housing can be life-changing, providing the stability to remain in Ukraine, support her community, and build a new life away from home. At the same time, her dream remains unchanged.
"My plans are to go back home (to Enerhodar)," Simakina said. "I really want the war to end soon so I can go back home as soon as possible."
Ukraine is gradually updating its housing policies at both the national and local levels. Yet, governing during wartime comes with significant constraints — from the legal and time limits imposed by martial law to supply-chain disruptions , permitting delays, data security challenges, relentless Russian attacks, and corruption risks. Mariia Kostenko, GIZ project adviser for housing and urban planning, said that a shortage of staff is one of the key bottlenecks in some communities. Employees often juggle multiple roles, leaving them with limited capacity to focus on longer-term strategic and conceptual goals. Another challenge is the sheer volume of urgent tasks, risks, and threats competing for their attention due to constant attacks on the Ukrainian cities.
"Sometimes we can make plans and agree on things, and then we get a call saying, 'We've been attacked.' For the next few days, local authorities are completely focused on dealing with the aftermath," Kostenko told the Kyiv Independent.
Despite these challenges, Schweikhardt said municipalities continue to move the work forward.
"I'm continually struck by the dedication and resilience of our Ukrainian partners," Schweikhardt said. "Even under tight constraints, we continue to work together constructively and proactively." "The project is not operating in isolation; it is part of German-Ukrainian cooperation and Germany's broader civil and development support to Ukraine," he said. "We have established communication channels and, perhaps most importantly, a level of trust. For me, this is one of the project's major achievements and a very strong basis for continued cooperation."
Deeper cooperation between Ukrainian and European municipalities could open up new opportunities for peer learning and collaboration. At the same time, work on initiatives already underway — including resilience strategies and universal reconstruction mechanisms — should continue. "The demand is still enormous," the project director said.
Kateryna Hodunova is a News Editor at the Kyiv Independent. She previously worked as a sports journalist in several Ukrainian outlets and was the deputy chief editor at Suspilne Sport. Kateryna covered the 2022 Olympics in Beijing and was included in the Special Mentions list at the AIPS Sport Media Awards. She holds a bachelor's degree in political journalism from Taras Shevchenko University and a master's degree in political science from the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.

title: Pentagon cautions personnel against betting using insider information
body: The Pentagon instructed personnel that they are prohibited from engaging in financial transactions while using nonpublic information, arguing it impacts operational security and staff judgment. All Department of Defense personnel are forbidden from such financial transactions either directly or through a third party when using insider information, according to a memo signed last week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. “The lives of our service members often depend on the enemy not knowing what is coming,” Hegseth wrote in the memo. “The men and women who carry our flag into harm’s way deserve a Force that protects them — not one that exposes them to the enemy for personal gain.” The memo comes six months after a U.S. soldier involved with the capture of ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro was charged with using insider information to win $400,000 by betting on his removal through the prediction market Polymarket . The soldier, a master sergeant with U.S. Army Special Forces, later pleaded not guilty , and his criminal trial is slated for early December. The same month, individuals across the globe used Polymarket to place bets on the rescue mission of Dude 44 Bravo, one of the airmen who ejected from a U.S. Air Force F-15E Strike Eagle that was shot down over Iran by enemy fire during Operation Epic Fury. Polymarket later took down the wagers, saying it didn’t meet the site’s integrity standards, but other war-related markets users can bet on were created before and after the Iran war began, causing concern over national security among lawmakers and experts. Another instance of an individual betting on military operations involved an anonymous Polymarket account making $550,000 off of trades on the first day of strikes in Operation Epic Fury, wagering on the U.S. strikes against Iran and the removal of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed by Israeli air strikes on the war’s first day. The recent memo, which was shared with senior Pentagon leadership, combatant commanders, defense agencies and field activity directors, reinforces federal law that prohibits government employees from using nonpublic information from their work for personal financial gains. The ban extends to all financial platforms, including betting platforms and prediction markets, with the directive pointing to Polymarket and Kalshi as specific examples. The memo first publicly circulated on the unofficial Facebook page Air Force amn/nco/snco . A Defense Department official shared a copy of the memo with Military Times, confirming the authenticity of the one circulating on social media. The directive asserts that signals are generated when personnel engage in a financial transaction on a military outcome. The signal can then be watched by adversaries in these markets and exploited by hostile foreign intelligence services to anticipate American movements, targets and timing. “The memorandum from the Secretary of War regarding predictive markets is a reminder that engaging in financial transactions using nonpublic information, and using nonpublic information to further private interests, is prohibited and may result in punitive action,” the Pentagon official told Military Times. “The Department takes this misconduct seriously and will take appropriate action, to include coordinating with the Department of Justice, to ensure anyone who engages in this misconduct is held accountable,” the official concluded. Violations can result in administrative, disciplinary or criminal action under the Uniform Code of Military Justice or applicable federal law, the memo says. Alongside operational security unease, Hegseth argues in the memo that financial stakes can negatively impact judgment and weaken the “warrior ethos” as personnel become invested in certain outcomes. “We are restoring lethality, discipline, and singular focus on fighting and winning our Nation’s wars, and nothing should distract us from that sacred mission,” Hegseth writes. “Not entertainment. Not a payout.”

The same month, individuals across the globe used Polymarket to place bets on the rescue mission of Dude 44 Bravo, one of the airmen who ejected from a U.S. Air Force F-15E Strike Eagle that was shot down over Iran by enemy fire during Operation Epic Fury. Polymarket later took down the wagers, saying it didn’t meet the site’s integrity standards, but other war-related markets users can bet on were created before and after the Iran war began, causing concern over national security among lawmakers and experts. Another instance of an individual betting on military operations involved an anonymous Polymarket account making $550,000 off of trades on the first day of strikes in Operation Epic Fury, wagering on the U.S. strikes against Iran and the removal of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed by Israeli air strikes on the war’s first day. The recent memo, which was shared with senior Pentagon leadership, combatant commanders, defense agencies and field activity directors, reinforces federal law that prohibits government employees from using nonpublic information from their work for personal financial gains. The ban extends to all financial platforms, including betting platforms and prediction markets, with the directive pointing to Polymarket and Kalshi as specific examples. The memo first publicly circulated on the unofficial Facebook page Air Force amn/nco/snco . A Defense Department official shared a copy of the memo with Military Times, confirming the authenticity of the one circulating on social media. The directive asserts that signals are generated when personnel engage in a financial transaction on a military outcome. The signal can then be watched by adversaries in these markets and exploited by hostile foreign intelligence services to anticipate American movements, targets and timing. “The memorandum from the Secretary of War regarding predictive markets is a reminder that engaging in financial transactions using nonpublic information, and using nonpublic information to further private interests, is prohibited and may result in punitive action,” the Pentagon official told Military Times. “The Department takes this misconduct seriously and will take appropriate action, to include coordinating with the Department of Justice, to ensure anyone who engages in this misconduct is held accountable,” the official concluded. Violations can result in administrative, disciplinary or criminal action under the Uniform Code of Military Justice or applicable federal law, the memo says. Alongside operational security unease, Hegseth argues in the memo that financial stakes can negatively impact judgment and weaken the “warrior ethos” as personnel become invested in certain outcomes. “We are restoring lethality, discipline, and singular focus on fighting and winning our Nation’s wars, and nothing should distract us from that sacred mission,” Hegseth writes. “Not entertainment. Not a payout.”

title: USS Colorado to be First Sub for Submarine Rotational Force – West
body: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence Richard Marles, and UK Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting are pleased to announce the designation of the USS Colorado (SSN 788) as the first U.S. Navy Virginia-class fast-attack submarine assigned to Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-West) beginning in late 2027. This announcement comes ahead of the upcoming United States Submarine Maintenance Period, which begins later this week and will further demonstrate Australia’s growing ability to sustain U.S. and UK nuclear-powered fast-attack submarines. SRF-West is projected to host up to four U.S. fast-attack submarines and one UK fast-attack submarine on a rotational basis at HMAS Stirling, a Royal Australian Navy base in Western Australia. SRF-West will accelerate Australia’s readiness to own, operate, maintain, and regulate a sovereign, conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarine capability, as well as support submarine deployments by expanding maintenance options and sustainment infrastructure in the region for AUKUS partners. SRF-West, established at Australia’s invitation and as mutually determined, will operate in accordance with relevant international agreements between and among the United States, Australia, and the UK, including the United States – Australia Force Posture Agreement. AUKUS activities associated with SRF-West will be conducted consistent with the AUKUS partners’ respective international obligations, including those under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, and Australia’s obligations under the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty (Treaty of Rarotonga). As President Trump has stated, and Prime Minister Albanese and Prime Minister Burnham have reaffirmed, AUKUS is moving “full steam ahead.” The selection of USS Colorado (SSN 788) as the first submarine assigned to SRF-West in 2027 marks a significant milestone for AUKUS Pillar I and is a decisive step in strengthening collective deterrence in the Pacific. title: Singapore Yards Chase Profit From Europe’s Offshore Wind Push
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Photo courtesy U.S. Department of Energy
(Bloomberg) — At a shipyard in northern Singapore, a yellow platform towers over a maze of scaffolding and cranes. Resembling a 15-story building, the piece will be shipped halfway around the world to Europe to be installed into an offshore wind farm.
The 30,000-ton platform, known as a high-voltage direct current converter, is scheduled to leave Seatrium Ltd.’s yard for the North Sea in 2028, where it will sit 60 kilometers offshore and help transmit electricity generated by wind turbines back to land. It’s the latest effort by Singapore to tap into Europe’s green push.
Singapore is repurposing expertise built over decades serving the largest offshore oil and gas companies for the energy transition. One of the biggest opportunities is exporting these enormous converters — known as HVDC platforms — to Europe, where the technology is widely used to transmit offshore wind power over long distances.
The specialized technology is one bright spot in an otherwise battered offshore wind industry. Investment plummeted 72% year-on-year globally to about $12 billion in the first half of 2026, according to BloombergNEF. Yet few yards have the expertise and capacity to build the platforms, threatening a supply bottleneck as the European Union pushes ahead with plans to expand capacity.
Seatrium’s platforms, each designed to handle about 2 gigawatts of electricity, are the largest of their kind in the world. It takes five years to construct one platform, which will operate for 40 years. GE Vernova Inc. supplies the HVDC technology in the platforms.
The city-state and nearby islands now account for up to 20% of global capacity outside of China for the platforms, according to Ember analyst Lam Pham, up from a negligible share just a few years ago. Demand is poised to rise as Europe builds wind farms further out to sea, giving the region’s shipyards an opportunity to capture more of the business.
“The country has invested, the company has invested — and this is a showcase of what is possible,” said Chris Ong, chief executive officer of Seatrium.
Seatrium, which is partly owned by Singapore state investor Temasek Holdings Pte, was tapped by European grid operator TenneT Holding BV to build four platforms for North Sea clusters. About 7,000 workers will build the structures at yards in Singapore and Batam, an Indonesian island that’s 50 minutes away by ferry. Each platform, along with connecting infrastructure, costs as much as €5 billion ($5.6 billion) each, according to TenneT.
Such platforms will be critical to unlocking growth in the global offshore wind industry, which faces challenges including high costs, supply chain shortages and regulatory hurdles.
Despite these hurdles, Europe is still pressing ahead with a massive expansion of offshore wind to meet ambitious green energy goals. The UK awarded a record 8.2 gigawatts of capacity in its latest subsidy auction, while Germany and the Netherlands are implementing new revenue-protection mechanisms. With enough state support, BNEF expects installations to double by the end of the decade, led by China, UK and Germany.
Singapore is now trying to position itself as the top choice for European developers. Rival yards in the Middle East are upended by the regional conflict; China and South Korea are mostly meeting domestic demand; and Europe’s shipyards are being taken up for building defence-related vessels.
“Singapore would make it cheaper, even including the higher shipping costs, because the industry is very labor-intensive and labor costs in Europe are super high,” said Ember’s Lam.
While wind turbines generate alternating current electricity, offshore developers use HVDC platforms to convert that power to direct current, allowing it to travel longer distances with less energy loss along the way. This will become a growing trend as wind farms move further from crowded shores.
Ong – who was CEO of oil rig-builder Keppel Offshore & Marine before it was merged with Sembcorp Marine to form Seatrium in 2023 – is hoping to capitalize on offshore wind demand over the next two years. The company was chasing S$9 billion ($7 billion) worth of HVDC and HVAC projects across Europe and Asia Pacific as of July. Clean energy-related contracts currently make up about 40% of the company’s order book.
In the yard in Singapore, the future of offshore wind power is slowly taking shape, with welders hunched over steel panels, piecing together the massive yellow structure one module at a time. For Ong, the demand for this infrastructure is not only being driven by the energy transition — it is part of Europe’s effort to secure future power supply.
“The scale and the massive need for offshore wind is a big security drive,” he said. “It has to happen.”

From the bright minds that brought you FTX Arena and NBA Top Shot NFT maketplace (where sales last month dropped to $762,781, which is a 99.66 percent decrease compared to the February 2021 peak of $226,350,843), the NBA announced Monday that it has new “preferred” prediction market deals for Kalshi and Polymarket, as well as a memorandum of understanding with the US CFTC about how to manage the relationships. It also announced an expansion of its DraftKings deal to include prediction markets, and says that more expansions will be announced with others soon.
The NBA is already facing scandals after Jontay Porter pleaded guilty to conspiracy over a gambling and manipulation scheme in 2024, Malik Beasley is reportedly in negotiations over a plea deal on similar charges, while former player Terry Rozier and coach Chauncey Billups are under indictment on charges of allegedly rigging prop bets and participating in rigged poker games, respectively.
NBA Head of Media Distribution & Partnerships Scott Kaufman-Ross proclaims that “Protecting the integrity of the game is our top priority,” as it establishes its integrity framework for the Kalshi and Polymarket deal. Under the new arrangements, prediction markets will be able to use official league data and IP, while promising limitations on “permissible markets” and information-sharing on suspicious trades and investigations.
That last bit will probably be important, as prediction markets have already drawn insider trading activity for everything from US military activity in Venezuela to Trump’s teleprompter . Currently, New York attorney general Letitia James is just one of many state AGs suing Kalshi and the others as senators investigate reports pointing out how DraftKings and others use AI to target the gamblers who are more likely to lose , while restricting bets from those who win .

title: Lockheed Martin’s subsidiary PZL Mielec to produce F-35 wiring harnesses in Poland
body: The F-35 programme covers 287 harness types using conventional electrical connections and fibre-optic technology. At the target annual output, production will require the assembly of more than 90,000 connectors and thousands of assembly, inspection and testing operations. “Including PZL Mielec in the global F-35 programme marks an important milestone in our history and reflects Lockheed Martin’s continued investment in the Polish aviation industry,” said Janusz Zakręcki, president and general director of PZL Mielec. “The F-35 is the most advanced multirole aircraft in the world, and locating production of its components in Mielec is a significant achievement for our company and our employees.” The harnesses distribute power and transmit signals between the aircraft’s onboard systems. Their manufacture will require fibre-optic production and testing technologies, high-speed data transmission solutions and measures to protect transmitted information. The work is subject to stringent quality, configuration and traceability requirements because of its use in a modern military aircraft. Preparations include expanding production infrastructure, investing in equipment and developing the skills of manufacturing and quality teams. Poland’s Industrial Development Agency has granted PZL Mielec a support decision allowing an income tax exemption worth up to approximately PLN 17 million. The decision, issued under the Polish Investment Zone framework, will help the company prepare for both new programmes. PZL Mielec said the investment would diversify its production and create jobs, without specifying an employment figure. The F-35 harness programme is scheduled to enter its production phase during 2027–2029.

title: From Nigeria to Multiple Markets Across Borders: How SharpPunter Is Changing the Way Punters Analyse Sports
body: A typical Saturday slip in Nigeria is put together from several places at once: a booking code a tipster posted in a WhatsApp group with no explanation behind it, a few games a friend swore were safe, and, for many fans, their own club, added out of loyalty before anyone has checked its form. If the code was shared from a bookmaker the punter does not use, he first has to rebuild it on his own bookmaker by hand, one match at a time, and once it is placed, a single one of its twelve games going the wrong way is enough to take down the slip and every version of it shared around the group, a pattern that repeats with codes passed around in Accra, Nairobi and Douala. SharpPunter, a sports analysis platform built in Nigeria, was set up to give those punters a clearer look at what they are betting on before they place the slip. Six months after its launch in April 2026, it has users across West, East and Southern Africa, works with booking codes from 37 bookmakers and has just released V2, a rebuilt version of its app. Built in Nigeria, for the way Nigerians bet “I built SharpPunter because I was tired of seeing people stake their money on tips they had not checked by themselves, and I wanted something that would help punters truly understand which games were worth backing,” said Oluwatobi Abobade, who founded SharpPunter. “Over time, the way people use the product has shaped how we built V2. Users kept tagging our X bot with codes from friends, so checking a code is now one of the two things you see when you open the app. We also saw how closely people follow their own clubs and how often that turns their picks into emotional ones, so V2 lets you follow your club, get updates on its live matches and see the stats, alongside unbiased picks you can use.” Where slips go wrong, and what SharpPunter does about it The first problem is the tip itself, since most codes that circulate in group chats arrive with no rationale, and give punters no way to judge whether the picks are valid. Every SharpPunter pick shows the reasoning behind it, such as a team’s recent form or its record against that opponent, and carries a rating of Strong, Fair or Slim, and the Optimizer reads any code a user pastes in and rates each match SharpPunter covers. The second is the single weak game that usually sinks a whole accumulator, often across every variation of the slip a punter has placed. In V2, the Optimizer flags the weakest selections on a code and suggests swaps before the bet goes in, while the Shuffle tool deals the matches from several codes into balanced slips so that one bad pick cannot take all of them down. The third is the code that only works on one bookmaker, which leaves punters rebuilding a friend’s slip by hand, one match at a time. SharpPunter’s converter rebuilds the same matches on the punter’s own bookmaker, and it now supports conversions across 37 bookmakers. On top of these, many fans let loyalty make the call and back their own club out of habit. SharpPunter’s model has no favourite team, so its picks show how a game rates on the numbers whichever team a fan supports, and in V2 users can also follow a club to get updates on its matches as they happen, with club pages showing its recent results, its next fixture and the league table. V2 also adds a Live tab that lets users monitor games in real time, with the score, goalscorers, possession, shots, expected goals and corners updating during the match, and a rebuilt SharpSlips that puts together a slip based on how many picks a user wants and how adventurous they want it to be. Hot on X and the new Community tab The newest part of V2 is a Community tab, built around the booking codes people already share. Its Hot on X feed gathers codes posted by popular accounts on X into one place, so a user does not have to scroll through timelines to find them. Codes can be filtered by bookmaker and sorted by what is hot, newest, most viewed, or starting soon, and each one shows the number of picks, the total odds, the kick-off time, and how many SharpPunter users have checked it. From the feed, a user can copy a code to their own bookmaker or run it through the Optimizer to see how SharpPunter rates each selection before deciding whether to play it. The tab also has a Trending feed, which shows the matches most looked at on SharpPunter over the last 24 hours and which way the crowd is leaning on each one, and a Following feed, where users can keep up with the codes checked and converted by the people they follow. Weekly tasks in the tab, such as checking a code or booking a slip, earn credits for the booking code tools. Demand from outside Nigeria came within weeks SharpPunter’s first users were in Nigeria and Ghana, and the early product followed the way they already played, with accumulators, booking codes and slips passed around on X, Telegram and WhatsApp. SharpSlips, the platform’s slip builder, put together accumulators from the day’s strongest picks, while the Shuffle tool and an X bot, @SharpPunterAI, which reviewed any booking code a user tagged it in, gave users ways to work with the slips they already had. SharpPunter was designed with West Africa in mind, but within weeks of launch, sign-ups were coming in from Kenya, South Africa and other parts of East and Southern Africa, as well as from Africans living abroad. The platform now sells its plans in local currency in Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, South Africa, Zambia, Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda, and in CFA francs for users in francophone West and Central Africa, including Cameroon, Senegal and Côte d’Ivoire, with prices also listed in US dollars. “We built SharpPunter in Nigeria, but the slip that dies on one bad game looks the same in Accra, Nairobi and Johannesburg,” Abobade said. “If we can show a punter which game is carrying the risk before they play, we have done our job, and sometimes that means telling them the slip is not worth playing at all.” One converter for 37 bookmakers SharpPunter’s booking code converter takes a code, reads the selections directly from the bookmaker it came from, and rebuilds the same matches as a new code on the user’s own bookmaker, naming any selection the new bookmaker does not offer so that nothing goes missing without the user knowing. The supported bookmakers include SportyBet, Bet9ja, Football.com, MSport, Betika, 1xBet, 22Bet, BetWinner, Melbet, PariPesa and Helabet, and a user can paste any code to see every match on it for free before deciding whether to convert it. What comes next SharpPunter’s rebuilt app is free to start on iOS, Android and sharppunter.com , and first-time users get full access to its premium features for a limited period, so they can try everything before choosing a plan. After that, users can subscribe to unlock every prediction, or buy credits if they only want the booking code tools. None of it changes what happens on the pitch, but a punter who checks SharpPunter before placing a slip can now see the reasoning behind each game, which selections are weakest, and how every match rates on the numbers, including the ones involving the team they support. About SharpPunter SharpPunter is an AI-assisted sports analysis platform covering football (soccer), basketball and tennis, with volleyball and American football planned next. Launched in Nigeria in April 2026, it publishes daily predictions with the reasoning behind each pick, settles every pick publicly against the final result, and offers tools to check, optimise, convert, merge and shuffle booking codes across 37 bookmakers. Sports fans across West, East and Southern Africa can sign up at sharppunter.com or on iOS and Android and pay for a plan in their own local currency. SharpPunter provides sports analysis and predictions for information only. It is not a bookmaker and does not accept or settle bets. No prediction is guaranteed, and past results do not promise future outcomes. Betting is for people aged 18 and over. Only stake what you can afford to lose, and seek support from a responsible gambling organisation if betting stops being fun.
