title: Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3
body: Fleet-wide computer vision model lifecycle management is a problem that shows up the moment a quality inspection proof of concept succeeds. One camera and one model work fine. Then the plant asks for the same result on 40 lines, each with several cameras, and every camera sees the world differently. Each has a different angle, different glare off the same stainless surface, and different ambient light depending on which bay door is open. In production deployments we have worked on, a single model trained on pooled footage underperforms enough individual cameras that each camera ends up with its own fine-tuned model. Now the real problem is no longer training one model well. It’s training, evaluating, versioning, and shipping thousands of them without a human in the loop for each one. This post updates the pattern introduced in the 2023 series Build an end-to-end MLOps pipeline for visual quality inspection at the edge for the current Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3. It replaces the since-deprecated Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager with Amazon SageMaker Neo for edge optimization. I walk through a dual-branch Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that trains an anomaly detector and a defect classifier per camera, with quality gates that block underperforming models. An in-pipeline SageMaker Neo compilation step ensures every registered model ships with a device-optimized artifact, and an AWS Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training. You deploy everything with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), and a full pipeline run on synthetic data costs about $0.07 in compute. The complete sample is available in the aws-samples GitHub repository . Solution overview The following diagram shows the sample’s fleet-wide model lifecycle. An orchestration layer queues re-training requests and limits concurrent work. A per-camera training pipeline prepares data, trains and evaluates an anomaly detector and a classifier, and produces versioned model artifacts for edge devices. Figure 1: Solution architecture The training half is a single SageMaker Pipeline, parameterized by camera, that runs 13 steps per execution. Three entry steps run in parallel: Preprocess, Fetch Latest Anomaly, and Fetch Latest Classifier. The pipeline preprocesses that camera’s images and fetches the camera’s most recent approved model for each branch, then trains two models. The first is a small convolutional autoencoder that learns what normal product looks like and flags anomalies by reconstruction error. The second is a ResNet18 classifier fine-tuned to confirm the defect. Each branch exports its model to ONNX, evaluates the exported artifact against held-out data, and passes through a quality gate. Past the gate, the model is compiled with SageMaker Neo for the configured edge target, and only then registered in the SageMaker Model Registry. As a result, every approved package has a device-ready compiled artifact. Packages carry the camera ID as metadata, and each branch’s warm-start fetch filters on it, so re-training always resumes from that camera’s own history. The orchestration half paces the fleet. Re-training requests land on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue, and an AWS Lambda function starts a Step Functions execution per request. Each execution acquires a slot through a DynamoDB semaphore before starting its pipeline, so a burst of requests drains at a steady rate instead of all launching at once. Completions publish to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), and operational failures reach the same topic through an Amazon EventBridge rule with the original error preserved. The output of the system is versioned, quality-gated, per-camera model artifacts. The Model Registry holds the portable ONNX, and S3 holds the Neo-compiled build of that model, which is a device-optimized shared library loaded by the DLR runtime rather than ONNX. Both are ready for whatever delivery mechanism your plant uses. Prerequisites To deploy the sample you need the following: An AWS account with permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket. An Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. The SageMaker AI, AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon DynamoDB resources in the stacks. Python 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12, Docker. The AWS CDK CLI version 2.1131.0 or later. Previous CLI versions fail with a cloud assembly schema mismatch against recent versions of aws-cdk-lib . No service quota increase is needed. The orchestration layer admits at most five pipeline executions at a time by default, which keeps concurrent SageMaker training jobs inside the standard account quota. If you deploy to an AWS Region other than your CLI default, set all three of AWS_REGION , AWS_DEFAULT_REGION , and CDK_DEFAULT_REGION on the deploy command itself rather than in your shell profile, for example, AWS_REGION=us-east-2 AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-2 CDK_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-2 cdk deploy --all . The CDK CLI, Boto3, and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) resolve the Region from overlapping but not identical variable sets, and a mismatch produces confusing partial deployments. Prefixing the command sets all three for that invocation only, so your own default Region is left unchanged. Defining the training pipeline with SDK v3 The code in this section is excerpted from the CDK application in the repository rather than a standalone script, and it runs during cdk deploy, when the stack synthesizes the pipeline definition. Environment setup and the deploy commands come later, under Deploying and running the sample. SDK v3 reorganized the SageMaker Python SDK into modular packages, and the imports show the new shape of the library: from sagemaker.train import ModelTrainer from sagemaker.train.configs import InputData, Compute, OutputDataConfig from sagemaker.core.training.configs import MetricDefinition from sagemaker.serve.model_builder import ModelBuilder from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.pipeline import Pipeline from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.steps import ProcessingStep, TrainingStep from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.model_step import ModelStep from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.condition_step import ConditionStep from sagemaker.core.workflow.conditions import ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo from sagemaker.core.workflow.functions import JsonGet Installing sagemaker>=3.0.0,<4 pulls in sagemaker-core , sagemaker-train , sagemaker-serve , and sagemaker-mlops as separate packages. Training configuration that v2 spread across Estimator constructor arguments now lives in typed config objects passed to ModelTrainer . This is the anomaly branch’s trainer, verbatim from the sample: anomalib_trainer = ModelTrainer( training_image=custom_training_image_uri, compute=Compute( instance_type=training_instance_type.to_string(), instance_count=1, ), base_job_name="cv-pipeline-anomalib-train", sagemaker_session=pipeline_session, role=role_arn, hyperparameters={ "program": "train_anomalib.py", "model_name": "autoencoder", "image_size": "256", "num_epochs": "3", "batch_size": "16", "learning_rate": "0.001", }, input_data_config=anomalib_input_data, output_data_config=OutputDataConfig( s3_output_path=run_prefix("anomalib-training") ), ).with_metric_definitions( [ MetricDefinition( name="image_auroc", regex=r"validation:image_auroc=([0-9]*\.?[0-9]+)", ), ] ) anomalib_input_data wires four channels ( train , validation , test , pretrained_model ) from upstream step properties, and run_prefix scopes every S3 path to the pipeline execution ID so concurrent fleet runs never collide. Both are in the repository. Two v3 behaviors matter when the pipeline lives inside a CDK application, and neither appears in the changelog as a breaking change. First, SDK v3 validates the pipeline’s execution role against live IAM while building the pipeline definition. This validation happens at synthesis time rather than execution time. A CDK app can’t create the role and the pipeline in one deployment, because the role doesn’t exist yet when the SDK validates it. This is separate from cdk bootstrap, which provisions the CDK toolkit resources once per account and Region and might already be done in your account. The sample’s own two-phase deploy is driven by a context flag that happens to share that name. An initial pass with -c bootstrap=true creates the role, bucket, and ECR repository, and the second pass synthesizes the pipeline against the now-existing role. The role Amazon Resource Name (ARN) embedded in the pipeline definition must also be a concrete string, not an unresolved CDK token. Second, the v3 role validator simulates ECR pull permissions without a resource ARN, so an execution role scoped to a single ECR repository fails validation even though it would work at runtime. The sample’s role carries a broader ECR grant for this reason. Lastly, one v3 habit the sample uses: constructing the pipeline with PipelineSession(default_bucket=your_bucket) routes SDK-managed uploads, such as step code, into the pipeline’s own bucket, so every artifact lives in one place and the execution role’s permissions cover a single bucket. (Granting the role access to the SDK’s default bucket works too. This approach is tidier.) Quality gates that match how defect data behaves Every trained model is evaluated before registration, and the evaluation runs against the exported ONNX artifact rather than the in-memory PyTorch model. That distinction matters: the artifact you gate is the artifact you ship, so an export problem can never slip a broken model past a healthy-looking training run. The anomaly branch gates on AUROC of at least 0.8. The classifier branch gates on two metrics at once, and the choice of metrics is shaped by the defining property of defect data: heavy class imbalance. In this sample roughly 90 percent of images are good, which is realistic for a production line. Against that distribution, plain accuracy is meaningless, because a model that predicts “good” for every image scores about 0.9 while catching zero defects. Balanced accuracy, the mean of per-class recall, corrects for that, but it has its own blind spot. A model with perfect recall on good parts and only 20 percent recall on defects still scores (1.0 + 0.2) / 2 = 0.6. So the gate requires balanced accuracy of at least 0.6 and defect recall of at least 0.5, together: step_check_classifier = ConditionStep( name="CheckClassifierQuality", conditions=[ ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo( left=JsonGet( step_name=step_eval_classifier.name, property_file="evaluation", json_path="balanced_accuracy", ), right=min_accuracy, ), ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo( left=JsonGet( step_name=step_eval_classifier.name, property_file="evaluation", json_path="defect_recall", ), right=min_defect_recall, ), ], if_steps=[step_compile_classifier, step_register_classifier], else_steps=[step_fail_classifier], depends_on=[step_eval_classifier], ) A ConditionStep ANDs its conditions, so both must pass. The thresholds are pipeline parameters, adjustable per execution without redeploying. If a gate fails, a FailStep marks the execution failed and that branch’s model never reaches the registry (the two branches gate independently, so the other branch’s model may still register). The fleet keeps serving the previous approved model for that camera. The training code addresses the same imbalance from the other side. The classifier is a fine-tuned resnet18 with ImageNet weights and a two-class head. At per-camera dataset sizes, fine-tuning pretrained weights is what keeps the model from collapsing onto the majority class. The training code balances training batches with a WeightedRandomSampler using inverse class frequencies, while the loss stays unweighted. Combining a weighted loss with weighted sampling over-corrects toward the minority class. Compiling for the edge with SageMaker Neo, inside the pipeline Notice the gate’s if_steps in the preceding code: past the gate, compilation runs first and registration depends on it. Both training scripts export ONNX with dynamic batch axes. The quality gates score those exported artifacts under ONNX Runtime, and then a CompileAnomalibNeo or CompileClassifierNeo step hands the gated artifact to SageMaker Neo . The invariant is gate, then compile, then register. A model only becomes an Approved package if it also compiled for the fleet’s edge target, so the registry never advertises a model the devices cannot run. The compile step encapsulates three error-prone details. Neo requires the input tarball to contain only the model file, but training jobs emit model.tar.gz with the checkpoint and metrics alongside the ONNX model. The step repackages an ONNX-only tarball first. Neo also requires concrete input shapes while the exports declare a dynamic batch axis, so batch size 1 is pinned in the compilation request. And because pipeline steps can retry, the compilation job name derives deterministically from the execution ID, so a retry resumes polling the job it already started instead of orphaning it. The target is a pipeline parameter: NeoTargetDevice selects a named device such as jetson_xavier or rasp4b , and its default compiles for the NeoTargetOs / NeoTargetArch platform, LINUX/X86_64 by default. The compiled package contains the optimized compiled.so plus the DLR runtime for loading it. The default output runs on any x86_64 Linux host, so you can validate it before committing to device-specific targets. Compilation itself incurs no charge. You pay for the processing instance that drives it and the S3 storage of the outputs. For compiling an already-registered model for additional device types later, without re-training, the repository includes an ad-hoc script that runs the same flow against the Model Registry. Per-camera models in the Model Registry Each branch registers into its own model package group, and every package carries the camera ID and its evaluation metrics. From the sample, with the metrics wiring elided: classifier_model_builder = ModelBuilder( s3_model_data_url=classifier_model_data, image_uri=custom_training_image_uri, sagemaker_session=pipeline_session, role_arn=role_arn, ) step_register_classifier = ModelStep( name="RegisterClassifierModel", depends_on=[step_compile_classifier], step_args=classifier_model_builder.register( model_package_group_name="sm1k-classifier-model-group", approval_status="Approved", model_metrics=classifier_metrics, customer_metadata_properties={"CameraId": camera_id}, ), ) Camera identity in customer_metadata_properties is what turns two shared package groups into a fleet catalog. Packages from all cameras live in the same groups, and per-camera history is recovered by filtering on the metadata. Each branch has a fetch step that pages through approved packages newest-first until it finds the requesting camera’s latest model, because ListModelPackages cannot filter on customer metadata server-side. On a camera’s first run the fetch finds nothing and training falls back to its cold-start initialization (ImageNet weights for the classifier, random initialization for the autoencoder). Every later run resumes from that camera’s own prior model, which is what makes frequent, cheap, incremental re-training viable across a fleet. Note what these registry entries are and are not: they catalog versioned, quality-gated artifacts, but their container reference is the training image, which serves no inference endpoints. They exist for a fleet workflow where a downstream system pulls artifacts and ships them to devices, not for CreateEndpoint . Orchestrating fleet training requests Every AWS account has service quotas on concurrent SageMaker training jobs, and each pipeline execution here launches several jobs, so fleet re-training needs pacing. Something has to keep a burst of 500 requests from becoming 500 simultaneous pipeline launches. The sample uses a semaphore, a counter of available slots that works like a parking lot with five spaces. Before the Step Functions state machine starts a pipeline, it takes a slot by atomically incrementing a counter in DynamoDB, with a condition that refuses the increment once the cap is reached: acquire_semaphore = tasks.DynamoUpdateItem( self, "AcquireSemaphore", table=semaphore_table, key={"LockName": tasks.DynamoAttributeValue.from_string("pipeline-concurrency")}, update_expression="SET ActiveCount = if_not_exists(ActiveCount, :zero) + :one", condition_expression="attribute_not_exists(ActiveCount) OR ActiveCount < :limit", ) If all slots are taken, the execution waits and retries. When its pipeline finishes, it decrements the counter to release the slot. One detail is worth carrying into your own designs. The DynamoDB condition expression enforces the cap in a single atomic operation, rather than the state machine reading the counter and deciding, which would leave a race window between the read and the write. The repository implements the rest of the operational hardening, including releasing slots on every failure path and forwarding failed executions to Amazon SNS through Amazon EventBridge. Its README covers sizing the wait bounds. The cap of five is a stack parameter, set low so the sample deploys and runs in any standard account without requesting quota increases. Adjust it to whatever your account’s training-job quotas support. Past a single account’s quotas, scaling fleet training is its own topic. The standard levers are raising the service quotas, spreading training across instance types or Regions, and distributing the fleet across multiple accounts. You can also hold the backlog in SQS and admit work only as capacity frees up. Those choices depend on your fleet’s size and shape. The sample gives you the working skeleton to extend. Deploying and running the sample The walkthrough in the repository README is the authoritative version. The following short form starts from a clean checkout and sets up the environment before the first deploy: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-sagemaker-fleet-cv-pipeline cd sample-sagemaker-fleet-cv-pipeline && python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt cdk bootstrap # once per account/region cdk deploy SageMakerCVPipelineStack -c bootstrap=true # roles, bucket, ECR cdk deploy --all # pipeline + orchestration ./scripts/push_ecr_image.sh # build and push training image By default the pipeline generates synthetic production line images, so you can validate the whole system end to end with no dataset and no data approvals. A full run executes all 13 steps, including both Neo compilations, in about 15 minutes and costs roughly $0.07 in billed ml.m5.xlarge time (US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2), July 2026, on-demand). The orchestration resources together cost well under $0.10 per month at sample scale. To exercise the pipeline on real images, the repository includes a downloader for the BCCD dataset . The dataset is a collection of 364 annotated blood smear microscopy images originally open sourced on GitHub and reorganized into Pascal VOC format under an MIT license. The same dataset is also distributed by Roboflow as public domain. The script maps platelet presence to the defect class, optionally splits the images per camera to simulate a fleet, and uploads training tarballs to the pipeline bucket. The accompanying notebook runs the full pipeline on the real data and does side-by-side ONNX inference on a normal and an anomalous sample. Treating platelets as defects is an illustrative stand-in for a manufacturing defect distribution, not a clinical claim. Cleaning up Model packages are created at pipeline runtime, so AWS CloudFormation cannot delete them. Remove them with the AWS CLI first, then destroy the stacks with cdk destroy --all -c bootstrap=true --force . The README lists the exact commands. Conclusion In this post, I showed a working SageMaker SDK v3 reference architecture for the fleet-scale computer vision lifecycle. The architecture includes a dual-branch training pipeline where every model is quality-gated on its exported ONNX artifact, compiled with SageMaker Neo, and only then registered. A Model Registry layout uses camera metadata to turn shared package groups into per-camera warm-startable history, and a Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training within account quotas. For teams whose needs are met by managed options such as Amazon Lookout for Vision, that is the simpler path. This pattern targets the per-camera, fleet-scale constraint that managed options do not cover. The design rules transfer beyond computer vision: gate on balanced accuracy plus minority-class recall rather than accuracy, evaluate and compile the artifact you ship, and make operational failures notify rather than terminate silently. The sample deploys in minutes and a full validation run costs about seven cents of compute, so a low-cost next step is to clone the repository and run it. From there, point the BCCD downloader at a real bucket, set NeoTargetDevice for your hardware, or size the orchestration bounds to your fleet. For the SDK v3 migration itself, the SageMaker Python SDK documentation and the two-part series announcing the new SDK are the references I kept open throughout. If you want help adapting this pattern to your production environment, reach out to your AWS account team. About the author Kiowa Jackson Kiowa is a Senior Machine Learning Engineer at AWS ProServe. He specializes in visual intelligence systems that combine computer vision with agentic AI, and he brings these to production in the enterprise industrial sector.

title: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11
body:
For a while Iâve been wondering about a silly question, which is, whatâs the oldest application with a GUI that will still run on Windows 11 without modifications or emulation.
Given Windowsâ excellent backwards compatibility, I expected the answer to be something impressively old.
Sadly, Windows 11 canât run 16-bit Windows programs by itself, because 64-bit Windows has no NTVDM , so weâre going to have to find something from the early NT era.
I remember asking this question a while ago on an anonymous forum, where someone pointed me to Win32s , and suggested to find an early release version of it with FREECELL.exe .
So I did exactly that, and lo and behold, FREECELL.EXE with a date modified of 22-Feb-93 running and fully playable, without any changes on the latest version of Windows 11:
At the time of this post, thatâs a 33 years and 8 months old application, which is impressively almost as old as me.
So I kinda thought âcoolâ, considered this a solved mystery and forgot about it shortly afterwards. But for some reason, this question popped into my mind again lately and this time I decided to dig deeper to see if I can find something older.
Digging through old Windows versions on the Internet Archive, I found some early NT 3.1 pre-release versions that seemed promising, but the main issue seemed to be either incompatibility with todayâs executable format or API changes that came later in development.
The earliest 1991 versions used a draft PE format not compatible with modern Windows, and builds up to mid-1992 assumed the cdecl calling convention instead of stdcall for Windows API calls, so arguments would get removed twice, as such:
Which would understandably cause the program to crash.
There was one application that caught my eye though, from Build 347, and that was CDPLAYER.EXE , linked on 16-Nov-1992 . By then the calling convention was fixed, but the other programs in that build crash in their bundled C runtime. CDPLAYER.EXE avoids that by using the systemâs crtdll.dll , and Windows 11 still ships a crtdll.dll in SysWOW64 .
If you start the program, you get something like this:
That is because, duh, my computer doesnât have a CD-ROM drive. But you can use a small DLL ( cdemu.dll ) to emulate one with some fake audio data and actually get it to play audio:
Pretty cool for a program thatâs almost 34 years old!
So earlier I mentioned that 16-bit programs are out of the picture because they are no longer supported.
But if you want, you can use something like otvdm to run older Windows applications.
Behold, a fully playable version of REVERSI.EXE dated 15-Nov-1985 running on Windows 11, taken from Windows 1.01:
And although using otvdm does feel like cheating, I thought it was cool enough to include in this post.

title: CSS-Tricks has a new owner
body:
This is pretty wild, but let’s get right to it because it’s big news:
CSS-Tricks is an independent site once again!
Just to recap: DigitalOcean purchased CSS-Tricks in 2022 from Chris Coyier, who founded the site in 2007. Chris ran it all the way up to that purchase.
Here we are in 2026, and I’m taking independent ownership of the site.
So, wait, who owns the site? That’d be me. (Wow, never imagined I would get to say that!) Of course, I have a small, awesome team to help with the day-to-day management of the site.
That all said, I do envision that some things will change. In fact, I’m planning that they will change in what I hope are very good ways. Maybe a question-answer thing makes sense here since this is very much an evolving discussion.
Yes, I’ve got the keys to the castle, so to speak. And, even after 12 years of working on the site, I’ll admit I’m a little overwhelmed and nervous about that. I mean, it’s an investment for sure, as you can imagine, and I’m making this my full-time job. At least for a while.
I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of everyone , no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time.
My latest IPO launched, and I’m now worth one trillion dollars. Wait, wait. That’s not right.
It’s going to be hard. Advertising will certainly be needed now. But, in order to keep the lights on, I’ll have to approach them differently.
In the pre-DigitalOcean days we sold real ad packages with things like display ads, sponsored posts, newsletter sponsors, and the like. As an independent website, we will need to return to our advertising roots.
So, if you’re in a place looking to advertise, please do reach out !
Right?! Ad revenue can’t be the only thing paying the bills. I have lots of ideas and several plates already spinning. Like, I’ve been neck deep in developing an HTML/CSS course for beginners.
(And you can now support the site by becoming a member — thanks in advance!)
Educational content has been in the dumps lately, right? Again, I’m hoping that CSS-Tricks will be more inclusive, no matter where you or anyone else is at in the learning journey. This place has traditionally been for folks who know what they’re doing. But I’m truly committed to creating more entry points for those getting started, particularly as our field is in the early throes of a growing skills gap .
And yes, I do believe that learning the basics is more important now than ever . But what learning actually looks like is what’s key. Front-end courses are down across the board . It has to be done differently.
There are other things in the works, but I think a course is one of the first things you’ll see.
Oh, and the newsletter . That’s coming back after a way-too-long hiatus.
That’s still very much a thing! We’ll keep our regularly scheduled broadcast going.
But maybe a little less than you’re used to. Those articles are part of the investment I’m making. Expect maybe one or two articles most weeks, at least as the ball starts rolling.
That also means the guest writing form is back in business! We have a nice backlog of articles through the rest of the year, which is great, but also means new submissions will have to wait a bit.
I won’t be able to accept everything that comes in, but I will absolutely read them and follow-up as best I can. Unless it’s a slop submission , of course.
Nah! My goal is to make CSS-Tricks a platform that gives folks a voice to share great ideas. I think we all prefer that over me just using it as my own soapbox. I’ve written plenty for this site the past 12 years. I’m happier (and more comfortable) being behind the curtain and giving others the full spotlight.
I may be writing a bit, developing the site here and there, editing a small stack of article drafts, or helping with sponsorships. I gag at the thought of titles, but publisher hits best for me. My fingers are in all the bowls, but my most important responsibilities are:
The best thing I can possibly do is help folks develop a voice and give them a stage to use it. It’s about community and culture building. Publisher . That’s more my jam.
You totally can. I put a little membership deal together where you can join a members-only community on Discord along with some perks. Or check out the new shop . Or purchase advertising for your company. In the near-future you will be able to purchase the aforementioned course as well. Any little bit helps, of course. I squirm at the thought of asking for money, so there’s no pressure.
Support doesn’t even have to be financial! We all know that content publishers need all the eyeballs we can get in these prompt-filled days. Things like subscribing to the newsletter , sharing articles you like with others, clicking through from your RSS app, and checking out our sponsors are all very, very great ways to support us.
Yeah, me too. This post could go on and on. I’m an open book, though, and I’m happy to answer anything you might have in the comments. I know, so 2015, right?

title: In Leaked Audio, Flock CEO Tells Cops Backlash to the Company Isn't Real
body:
Garrett Langley, the CEO of automatic license plate reader company Flock, told an audience of police chiefs at a private police conference Sunday that anti-Flock protests around the country are not real, according to leaked audio obtained by 404 Media.
He also said his wife advised him to never apologize, said he would prefer to never do interviews with the press again, and claimed without evidence that the social media opposition to Flock is driven mostly by Russian bots.
“Somebody was paying for [the social media posts and] stopped paying for it,” Langley said about the many viral posts criticizing his company’s technology. “Social media chatter on Flock is down about 95 percent from July. It went down 50 percent last week when Ukraine bombed a Russian data center with a drone. Literally 50 percent overnight. And so look, I’m the last person, my wife as well, she’s like ‘This is crazy, these people are getting paid to say these things,’” he added, repeating a disproven theory that Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers had a significant impact on internet bot activity.

title: Cabinet publishes resolution on updating system for granting deferments from conscription
body:
The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has published a resolution on updating the organization of deferments from conscription for those liable for military service during the period of mobilization and under martial law.
Specifically, in accordance with Resolution No. 1328 dated October 23, central executive authorities, other state bodies, public administration entities with jurisdiction covering the entire territory of Ukraine, as well as regional and Kyiv city state administrations (or military administrations, where established), are required within ten days of the resolution’s entry into force to ensure the review and harmonization of the criteria used to designate enterprises, institutions, and organizations as "critically important" for the functioning of the economy.
Following this review, an analysis must be conducted to determine whether enterprises still meet these criteria. If a criterion—on the basis of which an enterprise was originally designated as "critically important"—is removed, the decision designating that enterprise as "critically important" must be revoked.
The Government has established that decisions designating enterprises as "critically important"—in effect as of the date this resolution enters into force—shall remain valid for the duration for which they were originally issued, unless they have since been revoked.
It is noted that decisions by the Minister of Defense to increase the quotas for the deferment from military service ("reservation") of liable individual, adopted prior to the entry into force of Resolution No. 1608, shall remain in effect for the entire duration of the enterprise’s designation as "critically important," but no later than December 8, 2026. Decisions by the Ministry of Defense to increase such quotas, adopted after December 8, 2025, shall remain in effect for the duration of the enterprise’s "critically important" status, but not beyond the specific timeframe stipulated in the relevant Ministry decision.
Furthermore, the Cabinet of Ministers has established a Coordination Center for the organization of the deferment from military service for liable individuals during periods of mobilization and wartime.
Enterprises may be designated as "critically important" to the functioning of the economy and the provision of essential services to the population during special periods if they operate within the following sectors: the defense-industrial complex; the fuel and energy complex; housing and utility services; the extractive industry; the manufacturing (processing) industry; the agro-industrial sector (including the assurance of food security); retail trade; construction; transport and logistics; information technology; banking; healthcare; and communications. This also applies to entities engaged in emergency rescue and other urgent operations (emergency rescue services), as well as those operating in sectors approved by the Coordination Center, following a substantiated request from a central executive body or another state authority responsible for developing and/or implementing state policy in the relevant field. It has been established that the number of individuals liable for military service who are eligible for deferment (exemption from mobilization) may exceed 50%, subject to the recommendations and proposals of the Coordination Center.
Substantiated proposals to increase the number of deferments are to be submitted to the Coordination Center by the relevant government authority. Grounds for the Coordination Center to refuse to consider such proposals include, among other things, the documented, systematic violation of legal requirements regarding the organization and maintenance of military registration by the head of a critical institution, specifically, the occurrence of two or more such documented violations within the preceding 12 months, and/or the imposition of administrative liability upon the head for committing such violations.
Furthermore, it is established that for individuals liable for military service who hold positions within the representative offices of donor institutions or with entities implementing international technical assistance projects, the number of those eligible for deferment shall not exceed 50% of the total number of such employees directly engaged in the tasks of a single project, and in any case, shall not exceed 7 individuals.
Pursuant to a decision by the State Secretary of the Cabinet of Ministers, made in light of the Coordination Center’s recommendations, the number of individuals eligible for deferment may exceed 7, provided it does not exceed 50% of the total number of employees liable for military service.
For critical institutions, defined by the Ministry of Defense as critical within the defense-industrial complex, the fuel and energy sector (including their contractors), or as domestic manufacturers of transformer equipment for the energy sector, the number of employees liable for military service, who are eligible for deferment, may reach up to 95%. This applies to entities engaged in the construction, repair, restoration, manufacturing, and/or supply of equipment, the provision of services, or the execution of other engineering and technical activities aimed at ensuring the uninterrupted operation of the unified [energy/power] system.

title: STEP-X: Building Nigeria’s next generation of exporters, By Kabir Abdulsalam
body:
…the ambition behind STEP-X: to make the journey from campus to the global marketplace shorter and more achievable. The real test is whether the programme can provide students with the knowledge, resources and commercial connections to complete that journey.
In April 2020, Forbes Africa named Uzair Essack, a young South African entrepreneur, among its 30 Under 30 honourees. His achievement was built on an export business he started while studying at the University of Cape Town. An inquiry from a Saudi Arabian buyer for pineapples led to his first shipment.
Essack sourced the fruit, fulfilled the order and recognised the potential of exporting South African produce to international markets. That opportunity eventually grew into CapeCrops, a fresh-produce business serving customers across multiple countries.
What makes Essack’s story relevant to Nigeria is that he began building the business while still a student. He did not wait for graduation to explore international trade. He identified an opportunity and acted on it.
That is the kind of possibility worth considering as Nigeria seeks to connect its students with the non-oil export economy.
In my earlier article, “From Campus to Global Markets: Why Students Should Learn to Export,” I argued that Nigerian campuses should produce not only graduates searching for jobs but also entrepreneurs capable of taking Nigerian products and services to international markets. The piece, triggered by the engagement between the Nigerian Export Promotion Council (NEPC) and the National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS) offered a pathway towards that ambition.
Recently, the council launched the Students Training Entrepreneurship Export Programme (STEP-X) given the idea of its first practical expression. At the event, the NEPC Executive Director and Chief Executive Officer, Nonye Ayeni, declared that the real challenge is turning young people’s energy into productive economic activity.
“Young people are not only the future; they are the drivers of tomorrow’s economy,” Ayeni said, describing them as potential agents of change capable of influencing Nigeria’s economic direction.
Her message captures both the promise of STEP-X and the responsibility that comes with it.
Across Nigerian universities, polytechnics and colleges of education, students are developing products and services in agriculture, agro-processing, fashion, textiles, technology, creative industries and digital services. Yet many remain unfamiliar with the international markets that could provide opportunities for their businesses to grow.
Ayeni acknowledged that limited knowledge of export procedures, documentation, quality standards and certification prevents many young entrepreneurs from exploring these opportunities.
“Our goal is to make the journey from a hostel room or a campus workshop to the international market shorter, clearer and achievable,” she said.
That ambition is timely. A student producing leather bags may have a promising product but lack knowledge of international pricing, packaging requirements or shipping costs. An agricultural entrepreneur may need certification and reliable logistics before entering a foreign market. For both, a promising idea is only the beginning; commercial success requires the ability to meet buyers’ expectations.
STEP-X is designed to address these knowledge gaps by equipping students with entrepreneurship and export skills, including market research, export readiness, documentation, packaging and international standards.
More than 250 students from higher institutions in Lagos and Ogun states participated in the maiden edition with the plan to replicate the programme across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones.
The initiative has made a promising start. The next task is to ensure that expansion translates into practical support for students seeking to establish export-ready businesses.
The economic context reinforces the importance of this effort. NEPC reported that Nigeria’s non-oil export earnings reached approximately $6.1 billion in 2025, up from $5.46 billion in 2024. The country exported 281 products to 120 countries during the period.
These figures demonstrate that Nigerian products already have a presence in international markets. The challenge is to widen participation, particularly among young entrepreneurs who may have viable ideas but lack the networks, technical knowledge and resources required to enter global trade.
Training alone cannot bridge that gap. Some students will need financing for raw materials, packaging and certification. Others will require mentorship, logistics support and introductions to credible buyers. Digital entrepreneurs may need guidance on international demand, building credible portfolios and receiving cross-border payments.
Connecting STEP-X participants with existing enterprise-support programmes, financial institutions, established exporters and potential buyers would help move the initiative beyond classroom instruction.
While NEPC and NANS will bring complementary strengths to this task for export-development expertise on one side and the national student network on the other. Their partnership have provided foundation for sustained engagement beyond the launch of the programme.
NANS had earlier proposed export hubs in tertiary institutions across the six geopolitical zones, alongside a broader Students Export and Entrepreneurship Initiative built around training, identification, development, connection, exposure and skills.
These proposed hubs could provide the continuity that one-off training sessions cannot. They could help identify commercially promising student businesses, improve their products and connect them with experienced exporters and potential customers. However, the hubs remain a proposal, and their impact will depend on implementation, adequate resources and clearly defined responsibilities.
Not every student who attends an export workshop will immediately become an exporter. Some will need to refine their products; others may find opportunities in digital services or supporting roles within the export value chain. The programme will accommodate these different paths while maintaining its focus on commercial outcomes.
Ayeni has articulated the ambition behind STEP-X: to make the journey from campus to the global marketplace shorter and more achievable. The real test is whether the programme can provide students with the knowledge, resources and commercial connections to complete that journey.
Ultimately, STEP-X will prove its worth not by how many students attend its training sessions, but by how many build viable businesses that take Nigerian products and services to the world.
Kabir Abdulsalam writes from Suleja, Niger State. He can be reached via: [email protected]

title: Researchers find six patterns that make AI text so exhausting to read
body:
A study from New York University and the University of Texas at Austin shows that frontier language models systematically overuse linguistic patterns that make their output harder to read.

Anyone who regularly works with ChatGPT, Claude, or other language models knows the feeling. The answers are often factually correct, but reading them feels like work, full of nested sentences, odd word combinations, and metaphors no human would ever use.

A study by researchers at New York University and the University of Texas at Austin backs that up with data. The team had 14 language models produce text in casual conversation, coding sessions, and argumentative essays. The lineup included Claude, GPT-5.6, GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and smaller open-source models like Llama and Olmo. In total, the researchers analyzed 120 conversations, 45 coding sessions, and 980 essays, then compared them against human-written text from movie subtitles, StackExchange, and student essays.
Six patterns that make AI text a chore to read
AI models overuse unusual word combinations that rarely show up in human writing, like "reader-patience budget," and they place related parts of a sentence far apart in ways that tax working memory. Claude Opus 5 generated "A cat who can always get up and away is a much calmer cat," where the subject and the main predicate are separated by a long clause.

Shortened references with a dropped connector are common too. Instead of "the book that the professor wrote," the models write "the book the professor wrote," saving one word but creating brief confusion about how the parts fit together. Stacked nouns like "horror movie soundtrack generator" force readers to figure out on their own which word modifies which.

[caption id="attachment_41992" align="alignnone" width="576"] The six linguistic constructions AI models overuse, each shown with an example from the study's dataset. | Image: Clark, Martin & Mahowald (2026)[/caption]

The models turn nouns into verbs where humans wouldn't. Claude Fable 5 wrote "calendar it," where a human would say "put it in the calendar." They apply animate verbs to inanimate subjects, too. Claude Opus 5 produced "The whole conversation is eating its own tail," even though a conversation doesn't have a tail and can't eat. Readers can figure out what's meant, but it takes an extra beat.
Smaller models write more like humans
Llama and the Olmo base model come closest to human text. Within the Olmo family, scores rise steadily from the base model through the instruct variant to the reasoning model Olmo Think, which hits frontier-level numbers, pointing to post-training as the likely cause. Claude Opus 5.5 beats its predecessor Opus 5 in 19 out of 21 comparisons, suggesting that targeted finetuning can improve readability.

[caption id="attachment_41993" align="alignnone" width="899"] How much each model deviates from human text (dashed lines) across the six measured features varies widely by model family and use case. | Image: Clark, Martin & Mahowald (2026)[/caption]
Training rewards information density over clarity
Human language balances ease of production with ease of understanding, but modern language models are trained increasingly on tasks like math, code, and logical reasoning, where correctness gets rewarded and clarity doesn't, the researchers say.

The shift from RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) to RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards) removes humans from the feedback loop entirely, the researchers argue, and models develop a kind of "dialect" that works well for compressing information and solving complex problems but poorly for human readers.

As a proof of concept, the researchers trained a smaller language model with a penalty term that rewarded shorter answers. Under certain training conditions, the model favored shorter phrasings almost without exception, regardless of context, and even generalized that preference to sentence patterns it had never encountered during training. Humans, by contrast, chose between shorter and longer variants depending on the situation.

A similar explanation comes from inside the industry. Anthropic employee Jackson Kernion, who works on Claude fine-tuning, recently explained why Opus 4.6 was the last good "writing model" from Anthropic. Optimizing newer models for math, code, and technical explanations aimed at other AI models pushed Claude toward a style that works well for AI but reads as too dense and unnatural for humans. Kernion called it an adaptation to "LLM psychology." With Opus 5.5, Anthropic pushed back for the first time, addressing sentence clarity and overloaded blocks of information, and as the study shows, successfully so.

title: Tax service advises gas producers to report export volumes of gas injected into storage for royalty administration
body:
The State Tax Service (STS) recommends that gas-producing companies notify it in writing of the volumes of domestically produced gas exported after being injected into underground gas storage facilities (UGS).

According to a statement on the agency's Telegram channel, the information should be submitted together with monthly acts documenting the movement of natural gas in storage facilities. This will allow tax authorities to administer subsoil-use royalty payments without making additional requests to taxpayers.

The STS recalled that certain provisions of Ukraine's Tax Code exempt companies from paying royalties on extracted gas injected into UGS facilities until it is sold. The obligation to pay royalties resumes in the reporting period in which the gas is sold, with the amount due calculated based on the actual volume sold.

The procedure for exporting domestically produced gas was approved by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 1251 of October 7, 2026.

title: West Asian security must be regionally driven: Razaei
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – Iran's Supreme National Security Ccouncil (SNSC) Secretary Major General Rezaei has detailed on the content of the four-way Tehran meeting with senior officials of Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in Tehran.
Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin in Tehran on Monday attended a four-way meeting with Iranian officials in Tehran's Saadabad Palace.
Iran's SNSC Secretary Major General Rezaei told reporters on Monday after attending a four-way meeting in Tehran that "Regional cooperation should have started long ago. The visit by senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia showed that US threats have little influence over countries around the world."
"The Iranian people's resistance and the strength of the country's armed forces have created a new, positive atmosphere in the region, as reflected in talks with senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia," the top security official of Iran also said.
"The results of the Iranian people's resistance are becoming increasingly clear.Senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia believed that regional problems could be resolved through cooperation among all four countries," he added.
"We reached the conclusion that West Asian security must be regionally driven, with foreign interference prevented," the SNSC secretary concluded.

title: Amy Johnson Appointed President of GDIT
body: RESTON, Va. — General Dynamics announced today that Amy Johnson has been appointed as president of GDIT, effective November 3. Johnson is a 27-year veteran of General Dynamics Mission Systems, where she held increasingly senior roles in engineering, engineering management and business leadership across cybersecurity, defense electronics, space and intelligence systems, most recently as vice president and general manager for Space, Cyber and Intelligence. She earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in computer science and computer systems engineering. “Amy has a proven track record of leading teams to solve complex and highly technical challenges for our customers,” said Phebe Novakovic, CEO of General Dynamics. “I am confident that her dynamic leadership, operational rigor and deep commitment to our values and culture will deliver value to our customers, employees and shareholders.” GDIT delivers digital modernization, cloud computing, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and software development solutions to the U.S. federal government, defense, intelligence agencies and other customers. It is a business unit of General Dynamics, a global aerospace and defense company that offers a broad portfolio of products and services in business aviation; ship construction and repair; land combat vehicles, weapons systems and munitions; and technology products and services. General Dynamics employs more than 120,000 people worldwide and generated $52.6 billion in revenue in 2025. More information is available at gd.com. From General Dynamics, Oct. 23, 2026 The post Amy Johnson Appointed President of GDIT appeared first on Seapower Magazine .

title: NBA names Kalshi, Polymarket preferred exchanges, signs CFTC deal
body:
The US professional basketball league is expanding into prediction markets with official data agreements and safeguards against insider trading.
The National Basketball Association has named Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred prediction market exchanges and signed an information-sharing agreement with the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) aimed at protecting the integrity of basketball-related markets.
According to Monday’s announcement , the agreements will give Kalshi and Polymarket access to official NBA data supplied by Sportradar, the league’s designated data distribution partner, for settling authorized markets. Both platforms will have rights to use NBA intellectual property and conduct promotional activities in the United States.
The partnerships include integrity safeguards, prohibiting NBA and team personnel from trading NBA event contracts and requiring cooperation on suspicious trading investigations.
Beyond the two exchanges, the NBA expanded its existing agreement with DraftKings to cover prediction markets and said it expects to announce similar arrangements with other industry operators in the coming weeks.
In a separate announcement , CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig said the agreement with the NBA would strengthen information sharing to address insider trading and fraud in prediction markets. The NBA joins Major League Baseball and the National Hockey League in establishing similar arrangements with the regulator.
Related: Kalshi strikes deal with S&P Dow Jones Indices to expand financial event contracts
The NBA’s agreements come amid an ongoing legal battle over whether federal commodities rules supersede state gambling laws governing sports prediction markets.
The dispute has produced conflicting court decisions. In September, the 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against Kalshi in a case involving Ohio and Tennessee , following a similar decision by the 9th Circuit. An earlier ruling by the 3rd Circuit, however, allowed Kalshi to continue operating in New Jersey while its appeal proceeds.
State enforcement actions have continued. On Oct. 20, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown sued Kalshi, alleging that the platform had facilitated illegal betting in the state since 2024. Utah officials are seeking to recover an estimated $30 million to $60 million in profits allegedly earned by Kalshi and other defendants.
The US Supreme Court has been asked to review the New Jersey dispute , with 39 states and Washington, DC, supporting the petition. The National Football League, which has not entered into commercial partnerships with prediction market exchanges, also backed the petition , arguing that certain sports event contracts threaten game integrity because they are susceptible to manipulation. The justices have not yet agreed to hear the case.
