title: Marketability of poetry hasn’t been explored enough – Nana Asaase
body: Ghanaian Poet, literary coach, and writer Philip Boakye Dua Oyinka, popularly known as Nana Asaase, has urged young creatives to explore the commercial potential of poetry, saying the art form offers opportunities beyond stage performances. He believes poetry can be applied in various fields, including public relations, sales, marketing, music and academia, but many practitioners have yet to fully explore its marketability. He made these comments in an interview on The Career Trail programme aired on Joy Learning TV and Joy News. “Poetry or whatever craft you choose to get involved in pays you in so many ways. Of course, there is a pecuniary interest where there is fiscal cash. But it will usher you into spaces which other things otherwise couldn’t have taken you into,” he said. Drawing on his own experience, he explained that poetry had given him access to influential spaces, sensitive conversations and opportunities he might not otherwise have encountered. “Poetry or whatever craft you choose to get involved in pays you in so many ways. Of course, there is a pecuniary interest where there is fiscal cash. But it will usher you into spaces which other things otherwise couldn’t have taken you into. Take me for instance, I have walked into rooms I wonder which academic qualification could have opened for me. I have been privy to sensitive and important conversations and entrusted with documents from reputable organisations and individuals,” he shared. He advised aspiring poets to prioritise developing their skills rather than making money their primary motivation, stressing that excellence in their craft could create opportunities for growth and recognition. “If you want to do this and you’re looking for money, it is good, but money should not lead. Hone the craft. Build it,” he emphasised. He observed that some emerging poets expected quick financial returns and recognition, without giving themselves enough time to develop their skills, establish professional relationships and learn from experienced practitioners. “Patience is a lot of strength. Patience is a weapon. Patience is a virtue,” he said. He further cautioned young creatives against relying on social media engagement as the sole measure of their progress, urging them to accept constructive criticism and remain open to learning. According to him, the ability to perform well when given an opportunity is crucial, as the quality of a creative’s work can influence whether further opportunities come their way. Beyond performance, Nana Asaase believes poetry has untapped commercial applications that could provide practitioners with additional income streams. He cited songwriting for musicians, the development of content for public relations and marketing campaigns, sales promotion and teaching as areas where poetic skills could be put to use. He also highlighted the cultural value of traditional appellations used to hail chiefs before they speak, describing the practice as an example of poetry that could be presented to wider audiences. Nana Asaase encouraged poets to take advantage of opportunities in churches, schools, communities, weddings and other social gatherings to practise their craft, build confidence and connect with potential audiences. He said recognising the wider applications of poetry, alongside a commitment to improving one’s skills, could help practitioners move beyond the limited perception of poetry as an art reserved mainly for school programmes and special occasions.

title: Dutch Foreign Ministry receives diplomatic note from Russia over defence minister’s remarks
body:
The Dutch Foreign Ministry confirmed to a Ukrinform correspondent in The Hague, in response to an inquiry, that it had received a diplomatic note from the Russian side.
Meanwhile, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen said, in response to questions from members of parliament on the issue during a debate, that the statement did not signal a change in the country’s policy towards Russia. According to him, the Netherlands’ approach remains unchanged, regardless of whether Russia is described as an aggressor or an enemy.
“Our policy has not changed. Whether we call Russia agressor or enemy, that does not have an impact on our policy. Both the EU and NATO have been clear and outspoken on the fact that Russia poses the greatest threat to our security. We are not at war with Russia, but we do see increasingly hostile behavior from Russia. It is in that context that the Minister of Defence made this statement. The Netherlands continues to work on strengthening our security and resilience, takes measures where it is necessary, and continue support for Ukraine”, he emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, Dutch Defense Minister Dilan Yeşilgöz-Zegerius said that Russia is no longer merely an aggressor, but an enemy.

title: Groundhog Day for AI agents: Prompt caching patterns for using OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock
body: Every time you spin off your agent, it has to re-read its whole life story before performing an action. Here’s how to make it remember without having to feed it the same context again. In the movie Groundhog Day , Bill Murray’s character re-lives the same February 2 every day. He wakes up to the same song playing on the radio, in the same inn, and the same small town, again and again for what some movie fans estimate to be 34 years. Nothing he accomplished the day before carries over unless he works it out again from scratch. AI agents live in a version of Groundhog Day. Every time an agent takes a step (calls a tool, reads the result, decides what to do next), it has to send the model its entire story so far to maintain continuity: the tool definitions, the instructions, every previous tool call, and every result. The model only predicts the next token based on the input you provide. It has no internal memory between requests, so it must read all of it again. By turn 20 of a coding session, the model re-reads turns 1–19, and it’s you who pays for every one of those tokens, again and again. Prompt caching breaks the cycle. The service stores your input prompt (instructions, tools, and content) and reuses it on the next request, at a fraction of the input price. In this post, I walk you through an agent’s life, from its first turn to when it gets new tools and spawns helpers. Along the way, I show you how prompt caching keeps costs down and keeps agents responsive and consistent. What an agent sends to its LLM Before talking about caching, it helps to look at what a typical agent’s first invocation to the large language model (LLM) contains: Tool list – The definitions of every function the agent can call. Changes when you ship a new release. Instructions – The developer prompt: rules, persona, policies, examples. Also changes per release. History – Everything that happened in this session so far: the task, the model’s tool calls, and the tool results (which grows every turn). New turn – The latest tool result or user message (which might be different every time). What an agent sends to the model, turn after turn if you don’t set up caching: Figure 1: What an agent sends to the model on every turn How prompt caching works under the hood When a model reads a prompt, it first does a write called prefill . During prefill, it processes every input token and builds its key and value vectors (also known as key-value, or KV), which form the model’s working state. This happens before the model writes its first token. Prompt caching saves that state, which contains the system prompt, tools, content, history, and so on. When a later request starts with the same input tokens (that is, the same text), the prompt caching service loads the saved state instead of computing it again. It then processes only what is new in the next payload to the model. Prompt caching can be implicit, where Amazon Bedrock selects where the reusable prefix ends, or explicit, where your code marks that endpoint using prompt_cache_breakpoint . You can use both approaches together, and we recommend doing so. Turn 1 compared to turn 2 Figure 2: Turn 1 saves the prompt prefix up to the breakpoint, and turn 2 reuses it and pays full price only for the new question Implicit or explicit, and why do we need both? For agentic workloads, implicit caching lets Bedrock choose what to cache as the conversation grows. With explicit caching, you can mark shared content, such as tools and instructions, for reuse across sessions and when spinning up helper agents. You don’t always need both forms of caching, but combining them gives you a reusable starting point while Bedrock manages the growing conversation automatically. New sessions can also reuse that shared starting point while each conversation builds on its own cached history. In this post, we start with the first turn, then show how to carry cached content through later turns, new tools, and across subagents. Hello cached world The first win is to cache the static part of the prompt: the tools and instructions that stay the same across requests. These examples use your existing Amazon Bedrock client, TOOLS , and task . Replace the shortened INSTRUCTIONS string with your real policies and examples. The reusable prefix must reach 1,024 tokens to qualify. When caching static content, use explicit mode: choose where the saved prefix ends. KEY = "support-agent:v7:gpt-6-astra" INSTRUCTIONS = "Your full support policies and examples..." # Rendered context: [provider context][TOOLS][INSTRUCTIONS] | [task] # Cache starts at the beginning; the marker below chooses its end. resp = client.responses.create( model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra", store=False, # Response storage; prompt caching still works. include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"], prompt_cache_key=KEY, prompt_cache_options={"mode": "explicit", "ttl": "30m"}, tools=TOOLS, # Rendered before instructions; keep order stable. input=[ { "role": "developer", "content": [{ "type": "input_text", "text": INSTRUCTIONS, # Save through this whole block, including TOOLS. "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}, }], }, # User message is processed but not cached. {"role": "user", "content": task}, ], ) The prompt_cache_key tells the service which requests are meant to share a cache. We come back to how to use it when we get to reading the cache in new sessions. In one of our tests using explicit caching, the roughly 4,000-token tools-and-instructions prefix wrote 4,120 tokens on the first request and read those 4,120 tokens on later requests. The task (or user request) comes after the cache boundary, so this doesn’t trigger a write to the cache. Keep in mind that prompt caching works only when you pass exactly the same text. Make sure that the agent’s instructions and tool lists are serialized the same way every time. Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and other forms of tool delivery need to be indexed to make sure they stay consistent. Keep anything that varies, such as the date, the user’s name, or a request ID, after the cached instructions. As the content grows and varies (different tools and content), use implicit mode to let the service follow the conversation. Here, the first request has no explicit marker. Its latest eligible message is the user’s task, so the automatic breakpoint comes after that task and covers the tools, instructions, and task together. The mode is shown explicitly in the following example for clarity, even though implicit is the default. Setting store=False leaves conversation history in your application. It doesn’t disable caching. def ask_with_implicit_cache(history): return client.responses.create( model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra", store=False, include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"], prompt_cache_key=KEY, prompt_cache_options={"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "30m"}, tools=TOOLS, input=history, # Everything gets cached ) history = [ {"role": "developer", "content": INSTRUCTIONS}, {"role": "user", "content": task}, ] # Automatic endpoint: the end of the user message. resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history) This is useful when the next turn continues the same task. A different task doesn’t match the prefix through the old task, and the implicit write doesn’t necessarily create a separate entry for only the tools and instructions. Use an explicit marker there when you need that shorter shared prefix to be reusable across tasks. Use both when the agent needs a shared starting point and a growing history. Start with the marked developer block in the following code example and call the function ask_with_implicit_cache . The request-level mode stays implicit. The block-level marker adds an explicit save point after the instructions. The service can also save through the latest eligible message. This keeps the shared prefix available while the conversation grows. history = [ { "role": "developer", "content": [{ "type": "input_text", "text": INSTRUCTIONS, "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}, }], }, {"role": "user", "content": task}, ] # Still implicit mode, now with an explicit startup save point in the history. resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history) Caching conversation history and tool results The model requests tools by name and supplies their arguments. Your application must execute them. execute_function is a helper you build to route those requests to the matching Python functions and return their results. The following loop uses this helper to run each requested tool. It appends the model’s output and all tool results to the history list, then sends that list again until the model returns a final answer. In implicit mode, Amazon Bedrock can reuse the unchanged prefix and cache the added content through the last tool result. Keep earlier messages and the initial TOOLS unchanged. import json # Map tool names to their Python implementations. TOOL_HANDLERS = { "get_owner": get_owner, # Register your other initial tools here. } def execute_function(name, arguments): """Run the requested tool and return its result.""" handler = TOOL_HANDLERS.get(name) if handler is None: return {"error": f"Unknown tool: {name}"} return handler(**arguments) while True: # Preserve all output items, including encrypted reasoning. history.extend(resp.output) calls = [x for x in resp.output if x.type == "function_call"] if not calls: break for call in calls: result = execute_function(call.name, json.loads(call.arguments)) history.append({ "type": "function_call_output", "call_id": call.call_id, "output": json.dumps(result), }) # The last result in this group supplies the automatic endpoint. resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history) For follow-ups, append a new user message and call the helper again. Keep earlier messages unchanged so their cached endpoints remain available. Rolling breakpoints: Each turn reads everything before it Figure 3: Rolling breakpoints, where each turn reads everything before it and writes only its own tool result For a separate explicit-only run, recreate the two-message history from the combined Hello cached world example. This loop wraps tool results in input_text blocks and marks the final result in each batch. Earlier markers stay in history . See the current lookup rules for long conversations. import json while True: resp = client.responses.create( model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra", store=False, include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"], tools=TOOLS, prompt_cache_key=KEY, input=history, prompt_cache_options={"mode": "explicit", "ttl": "30m"}, ) d = resp.usage.input_tokens_details print("read", d.cached_tokens, "write", d.cache_write_tokens) history.extend(resp.output) # Includes encrypted reasoning. calls = [x for x in resp.output if x.type == "function_call"] if not calls: break batch = [] for call in calls: result = execute_function(call.name, json.loads(call.arguments)) batch.append({ "type": "function_call_output", "call_id": call.call_id, "output": [{"type": "input_text", "text": json.dumps(result)}], }) # Add the newest boundary; retain every earlier marker. batch[-1]["output"][-1]["prompt_cache_breakpoint"] = {"mode": "explicit"} history.extend(batch) GPT-6 Astra tied for the best implicit result in this six-turn workload: about 62 percent lower input cost than running without caching. Explicit rolling breakpoints saved about 61 percent on the same model. Both reused more history as the conversation grew. These are workload results. Measure your own agent’s savings. Figure 4: Input cost of every caching setup on GPT-6 Astra, relative to no caching Watch out for: Only a static breakpoint in explicit-only mode – The tools and instructions are cached, but the growing history is processed again on every turn (0.61). This limitation doesn’t apply to the combined example, which also saves through eligible conversation endings. Moving a single breakpoint can prevent cache reuse and cause repeated writes in explicit-only mode. Keep the previous turn’s breakpoint too. Only an implicit write through a changing task – A new task might share the tools and instructions but not the previously saved endpoint. Add an explicit marker after the shared instructions if different tasks need to reuse that shorter prefix. When tools change Sometimes an agent’s tool list changes, or new tools get added. Keep the initial list stable: adding, removing, or reordering definitions can invalidate the cached prefix. Choose the approach that fits how the tool becomes available. When known tools are invoked in different steps of the agent’s flow: Send the same sorted TOOLS and use allowed_tools to limit what the model can call. With allowed_tools , "mode": "auto" lets the model decide whether to call an allowed tool, and "mode": "required" requires at least one allowed tool call. Pass this as tool_choice . The restriction doesn’t change the cached catalog: tool_choice={"type": "allowed_tools", "mode": "auto", "tools": [{"type": "function", "name": "get_owner"}]} New tools during a session. Both Amazon Bedrock Runtime and Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoints accept an input item type called additional_tools for GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-5.6 Luna. For model availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . Register the new tool get_due_date in the helper function execute_function , then append its schema to the completed history from the agent loop. Keep the initial TOOLS unchanged: TOOL_HANDLERS["get_due_date"] = get_due_date NEW_TOOL = { "type": "function", "name": "get_due_date", "description": "Return the due date for a support case.", "strict": True, "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": {"case_id": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["case_id"], "additionalProperties": False, }, } history.append({ "type": "additional_tools", "role": "developer", "tools": [NEW_TOOL], }) history.append({ "role": "user", "content": "Find the due date for case C-123.", }) # Implicit mode saves through this new user message, including NEW_TOOL. resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history) d = resp.usage.input_tokens_details print("old prefix read", d.cached_tokens, "new write", d.cache_write_tokens) # Example output: # old prefix read 2048 new write 256 A new tool arrives mid-session Figure 5: Appending a tool keeps the earlier prefix reusable, with example counts from GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock Runtime Continue the tool-execution loop with the new response. The loop adds the model’s output to history , runs any requested tools, and appends their results. Keep the additional_tools item in later requests so the new tool remains available. In implicit mode, Amazon Bedrock can cache through the new user message, including the tool definitions that precede it. In explicit-only mode, retain earlier breakpoints and add one to an input_text block in that user message. The additional_tools item itself can’t hold a breakpoint. Different roles, different catalogs. When different agent roles need different tools, choose a stable tool profile, such as support or billing, at the start of each session. Each profile gets its own cached prefix. Mark the shared instructions so later tasks with that profile can reuse them, then use either mode as the conversation grows. Cached tool profiles Figure 6: Each tool profile has its own cached prefix, reusable by matching sessions Subagents and side calls Delegating shouldn’t make every helper reread the same background. Share the prefix, then add each helper’s task at the end. Be aware that when you use caching with AI agents, tools and system prompts can be leaked or exploited. Establish responsible AI practices that include your prompt caching implementation as part of that governance. Warm once, then fan out. Send an ordinary request first and wait for it to finish before launching helpers. Mark the shared context explicitly in every request, even when the mode is implicit: shared = {"role": "developer", "content": [{ "type": "input_text", "text": INSTRUCTIONS, "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}, }]} warm = client.responses.create( model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra", store=False, tools=TOOLS, prompt_cache_key=KEY, prompt_cache_options={"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "30m"}, max_output_tokens=16, input=[shared, {"role": "user", "content": "Reply READY."}], ) d = warm.usage.input_tokens_details if not (d.cache_write_tokens or d.cached_tokens): raise RuntimeError("Shared prefix was not cached.") from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor # helper_tasks contains the task text for each helper. helper_inputs = [ [shared, {"role": "user", "content": task}] for task in helper_tasks ] with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool: helpers = list(pool.map(ask_with_implicit_cache, helper_inputs)) The helpers use the same TOOLS , model, and KEY as the warm-up. A warm-up that ends at the output cap can still populate the cache. The usage check confirms cache activity before the helpers start. Subagents: Warm the shared prefix once, then fan out Figure 7: Warm the shared prefix before launching helpers, and each helper then adds its own task Give side calls the same beginning. The agent loop builds history by appending every resp.output and its matching tool results, including encrypted reasoning. After the parent finishes, copy that complete list for a summarizer or judge. The same helper keeps the tools, model, and key unchanged: from copy import deepcopy # history is the completed history built by the agent loop above. # Copy it so the helper can add instructions without changing the parent. helper_history = deepcopy(history) helper_history.append({ "role": "developer", "content": "Summarize this conversation in one sentence. Do not call tools.", }) summary = ask_with_implicit_cache(helper_history) d = summary.usage.input_tokens_details print("history read", d.cached_tokens, "write", d.cache_write_tokens) print(summary.output_text) # Example output (assumed values and conversation): # history read 4096 write 32 # Case C-123 is due on October 31, 2026. The helper can reuse the cached portion of history , but the appended developer message doesn’t automatically extend the cache to include the summary instruction. If later requests reuse the same history and instruction, place the instruction in an input_text block with prompt_cache_breakpoint . For a one-time summary, no additional marker is needed. Pauses, restarts, and the cache key Pauses. Cached prefixes have a minimum 30-minute time to live (TTL), refreshed by successful reuse, and might remain longer. If a session resumes soon, an ordinary warm-up can refresh the prefix before it expires. Compare that request’s cost with letting the cache expire. For the TTL rules, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation. New sessions. Keep prompt_cache_key stable for requests that are meant to share a prefix. A session-specific key isolates sessions even when their prompts match. In the following example, switching to a shared key let sessions reuse the prefix. New sessions reuse the cache only if they share the key Figure 8: A session-specific key separates cache entries, and a shared key lets matching sessions reuse them Reuse of existing cache content requires the same model, AWS account, and Region, and an available matching prefix. The following example combines an explicit startup marker with implicit mode. Each session starts with the same instructions and its own task. Both use the same computed key: import hashlib def cache_key(app, model, prompt_version, instructions): digest = hashlib.sha256(instructions.encode()).hexdigest()[:12] return f"{app}:{prompt_version}:{model}:{digest}" KEY = cache_key("support-agent", "us.openai.gpt-6-astra", "v7", INSTRUCTIONS) prefix = {"role": "developer", "content": [{ "type": "input_text", "text": INSTRUCTIONS, "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}, }]} for label, question in [ ("session A", "Explain the refund policy without calling tools."), ("session B", "Explain the escalation policy without calling tools."), ]: # A fresh conversation for each session; the startup prefix matches. session_history = [prefix, {"role": "user", "content": question}] result = ask_with_implicit_cache(session_history) d = result.usage.input_tokens_details print(label, "read", d.cached_tokens, "write", d.cache_write_tokens) On a cold start, session 1 writes the shared prefix. Session 2 can read it even though its task can be different. Each task can also be cached implicitly. Check the usage counters: matching keys and markers make reuse possible, but a cache entry still has to be available. What prompt caching delivers Cost. For a GPT-6 Astra powered agent with an 8,000-token startup prefix and six turns adding 2,000 tokens each, one-time static caching reduced cost to $0.50, and rolling breakpoints reduced modeled input cost by 64 percent: from $0.87 to $0.32 per session. Figure 9: Cumulative input cost per session for the support-agent example, using Amazon Bedrock on-demand prices for GPT-6 Astra How to tell caching is working Start with response usage. cached_tokens reports input read from the cache, and cache_write_tokens reports input written to it. As the conversation grows, check that later turns reuse earlier history and that new writes reflect the content being added. For production monitoring on the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint, use the CacheReadInputTokenCount and CacheWriteInputTokenCount metrics in Amazon CloudWatch. Enable model invocation logging when you need individual request records, then query them with Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights. For the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint, record the response usage fields in your application logs. Its Amazon CloudWatch namespace currently has no separate cache counters. To check costs, filter AWS Cost Explorer to Amazon Bedrock and group by Usage type . Cache reads, cache writes, and uncached input appear as separate entries per model. Exclude output-token entries when calculating their shares of input cost. A short checklist Keep the reusable prefix stable. Put shared tools and instructions first, then append conversation history and new turns. Changing a timestamp, message, or tool definition prevents reuse beyond that change. A shorter prefix can still be reused if it has its own saved endpoint. Choose boundaries around content you want to reuse. Use implicit caching for growing history, explicit markers for shared prefixes, or both. Explicit-only mode avoids writing disposable suffixes. When extending an explicit-only conversation, retain earlier markers so later requests can find the saved prefixes. Keep the initial tool catalog unchanged. Use allowed_tools to restrict which tools are callable. Append known definitions with additional_tools , or discover them through namespaced client-side tool_search . Choose a stable tool profile when different agent roles need different catalogs. Check prefix size and lifetime. A cacheable prefix must contain at least 1,024 tokens. Cached prefixes remain eligible for reuse for at least 30 minutes after their latest write or successful reuse. Warm shared content before launching helpers. Mark the shared prefix in both the warm-up and helper requests, including when using implicit mode. Finish the warm-up request before starting parallel calls. Keep cache keys stable within each sharing group. Requests intended to reuse a prefix must use the same key. Separate keys can keep cache accounting distinct between customers or users. Measure savings across the workflow. Cache writes cost 1.25 times the normal input rate. Read prices depend on the model. Track write costs alongside read savings, using response usage during development and monitoring and billing data in production. Waking up on February 3rd Bill Murray only escapes Groundhog Day once he stops repeating the same mistakes and starts carrying what he learned from one day to the next. Agents get there in a similar, if less romantic, way: by keeping the start of their prompt byte-for-byte stable and using automatic or explicit cache boundaries as the history grows. In this post, we covered how to cache shared tools and instructions, grow the cache across agent turns, and preserve reuse when adding tools, launching helpers, or starting new sessions. Keep the shared prefix stable and append new information as the workflow progresses. Use implicit caching for growing conversations and explicit breakpoints for shared content. Combine them when you need both, or choose explicit-only mode when a changing suffix is unlikely to be reused. Compare cache reads, writes, total input cost, and latency to find what works best for your agent. To apply these patterns, follow the Amazon Bedrock prompt caching documentation for OpenAI models and check model availability by AWS Region and endpoint . Start with one workflow and measure the savings as your conversations grow. About the author Claudio Mazzoni Claudio is a Sr Specialist Solutions Architect on the Amazon Bedrock GTM team. Claudio excels at guiding customers through their Gen AI journey. Outside of work, Claudio enjoys spending time with family and working in his home garden.

title: Man swept away by flood while trying to rescue drowning teenager in Abia
body: . Rescue team in desperate search for duo By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — In a heartbreaking twist of fate, a good Samaritan who risked his life to save a teenage girl from a flooded gutter in Aba, Abia State, was swept away by the same rushing water alongside the girl he tried to rescue. The tragedy occurred on Sunday evening at Ukwu Mango, Faulks Road, during a downpour, leaving residents and sympathisers scrambling desperately to find the two missing persons. The Samaritan reportedly slipped into the gutter while attempting to rescue the girl, only for the surging floodwater to sweep both of them away. Residents immediately launched a frantic search, hoping to find the pair alive, but their efforts yielded no result, fuelling fears that the victims might have been carried into the Aba River. The desperate search entered a new phase on Monday as the Abia State Fire Service and other government officials joined residents in combing the drainage channels for the missing duo. Police personnel also arrived at the scene to control the crowd and maintain order as the rescue operation continued. However, as of the time of filing this report, the victims remained missing, leaving their families and the community in agonising uncertainty over their fate. When Vanguard contacted the Police Public Relations Officer, PPRO Maureen Chinaka, she promised to revert but had yet to do so at the time of filing this report. Aba’s flat terrain makes the commercial city prone to flooding, particularly during heavy rainfall. The post Man swept away by flood while trying to rescue drowning teenager in Abia appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Canada’s Stablecoin Draft Allows Usage Rewards, Bars Issuers Paying Yield via Third Parties
body: Canada’s Department of Finance has published draft Stablecoin Regulations that spell out where a permitted reward ends and a banned yield begins: payments linked to using a stablecoin would be allowed, while arrangements that pay people for holding one, including through third parties, would not. The proposal appeared in the Canada Gazette on Oct. 24 , starting a 60-day comment period that runs to Dec. 23. The regulations are needed to bring the Stablecoin Act into force. That law received royal assent in March 2026 and already contains a ban on issuers paying interest or yield on held coins. Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter . Where Rewards End and Yield Begins Under the draft, a payment or reward linked to a stablecoin transaction, and not to holding the coin, would not count as interest or yield. A reward “tied to only the use and not the holding of a stablecoin” is allowed “to encourage adoption of the stablecoin,” the department wrote in its analysis of the rules. The draft also reaches beyond the issuer itself. A deal between an issuer and any other party, holder or not, would count as indirect yield if it lets that party earn a return from holding the issuer’s coin, income sharing included, or if it prompts that party to pay holders a return. Finance said in the Gazette notice that it wants to keep stablecoins apart from products that “compete directly with bank deposits or other interest-bearing instruments,” and to stop issuers from passing reserve income, such as interest on short-term government debt, to holders. Fintechs and financial institutions both called yield an important part of the framework, according to the department, which said it reached its position after several rounds of consultation. Redemption and Reserves Holders could redeem at par with no minimum amount. Issuers would have three business days to complete a redemption, with fees capped at 1% of the amount redeemed, though they could limit daily redemptions if a liquidity shortfall in the markets for their reserve assets left them unable to meet every request. Finance said it settled on 1% even though redemption fees in today’s market run to roughly 0.1%, arguing a ceiling set at current levels would be too tight for newer and smaller issuers. Reserves would have to match at least the value of outstanding coins at the close of each day, held in cash and demand deposits, government debt maturing within three months, overnight reverse repos, or money market funds holding only those assets. Custodians would have to be financial institutions incorporated in Canada. Issuers could keep returns earned on reserves as long as backing stays at least one-to-one. Next Steps Finance intends the rules to take effect in fall 2027 , alongside the act. The Bank of Canada , which will register and supervise issuers, plans to put out guidelines for consultation once the final rules are published. Issuers already operating would get 30 days after the act takes effect to apply for registration or stop issuing. Finance’s cost analysis assumes five issuers would fall under the act. The current players it cites include Stablecorp’s QCAD , Loon Technology’s CADC and Circle’s USDC , and it expects others to enter once the framework is in place. Penalties could reach C$10 million for a very serious violation. title: Trump told DOJ to sue to block Alaska Senate results if Republican narrowly loses
body:
The lawsuit cites name confusion around Sen. Dan Sullivan and another candidate.
President Donald Trump said Friday that he had directed the Justice Department to preemptively file a lawsuit to try to block the certification of the crucial Alaska Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, citing name confusion among the candidates.
Republicans have alleged that candidate Dan J. Sullivan is running a sham campaign to purposefully confuse voters and draw votes away from incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan based on their names being similar .
Asked Friday about the lawsuit, which the Justice Department filed on Thursday, Trump said, "Well, I'm one that said, 'Do it.'"
"They have two guys run named Dan Sullivan running. So the Democrats put up a guy never -- I don't think he ever voted before," Trump said of Dan J. Sullivan, who appears on the ballot with no party affiliation and told The New York Times that he has in the past voted for both Democrats and Republicans.
"All of a sudden he decides to run for the Senate, and his name is Dan Sullivan. One is Daniel S., one is Daniel J. The Daniel J. is the fake," Trump said.
"Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan ... the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election," the number-three ranking official at the Department of Justice, Stanley Woodward, wrote in Thursday's filing.
An earlier legal challenge to Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy was rejected by Alaska's supreme court, which ordered that he be included on the ballot.
In bringing the case, the Justice Department says it's guarding against the possibility that Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses in a manner that suggests he would have won were it not for votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan. The incumbent senator is facing Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, as well as Dan J. Sullivan.
"To guard against this danger, it is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion. An election result may be impacted by voter confusion if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska's rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election," Woodward wrote.
A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement, "Alaska's Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot. Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters."
A spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan said, "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course. Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska." A statement from Peltola's campaign called the suit "a despicable political threat to overturn an election."
The Alaska Secretary of State's office and a campaign spokesperson for Dan J. Sullivan did not respond to a request for comment from ABC News.
On Wednesday, President Trump posted on social media that he was looking at "powerful legal options" to remove Dan J. Sullivan from the ballot.
Over the summer, Alaska's election office said that Dan J. Sullivan would be removed from the ballot because the office determined his candidacy was not in good faith, but was meant, per an official, "to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality."
Dan. J. Sullivan then sued the state over the decision, and a state judge ruled that he was eligible to be on Alaska's Senate primary ballot. The Alaska Supreme Court upheld the ruling, after which the DOJ began investigating.
Fielding questions from reporters just hours before the lawsuit was filed, Attorney General Todd Blanche wouldn't rule out the DOJ intervening in a state's election process, but suggested only a "doomsday scenario" would warrant such action.
"I mean, is there any scenario? Yes, of course. There's scenarios that we could all come up with hypothetically, you know, some doomsday scenario, for example, right?" Blanche said. "It is not DOJ's intention to, and it's never our intention to improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process."
ABC News' Devin Dwyer contributed to this report.

If you want a decent pair of noise-canceling earbuds without spending a fortune, Nothing’s Ear 3A are worth considering. The wireless earbuds offer a lot of features for the price, and they’re an even better value now that all four colors are on sale at Amazon , Walmart , and Best Buy for $79 ($20 off), matching their all-time low price.
The Ear 3A deliver great performance for the price, with extensive EQ options that let you fine-tune the sound to your liking. My colleague John Higgins found the default sound a little too bass-heavy, but appreciated how easy it was to adjust — which is great, since that level of customization is unusual for earbuds at this price. While they won’t completely drown out chatter of your local coffee shop, the ANC does a good job of quieting low drones, including air conditioners and airplane cabin noise. We did encounter some bugs in testing, however, including abrupt changes in noise cancellation levels when using adaptive ANC, as well as occasional issues with voice calls in noisy environments.
Still, they’re relatively minor drawbacks given what you get for the price. The Ear 3A also come in some fun colors — including a striking pink shade — and each pair includes extra-small ear tips for a more comfortable fit.
