title: Zelenskyy signs decree on updating Ukraine’s National Security Strategy
body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has signed a decree enacting a decision by the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) of Ukraine, dated October 5, 2026, regarding the updating of Ukraine’s National Security Strategy.

The corresponding decree, No. 1066/2026, was published on the website of the Office of the President of Ukraine on Monday.

"In accordance with Article 107 of the Constitution of Ukraine, I hereby decree: to enact the decision of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine dated October 5, 2026, 'On updating the national security strategy of Ukraine' (attached)," the decree states.

According to the document, the Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine is tasked with overseeing the implementation of the NSDC’s decision.

title: APC accuses ADC of owing staff salaries, urges Nigerians to reject Atiku
body: The All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council has accused the African Democratic Congress (ADC) of owing its workers more than 12 months’ salaries, urging Nigerians to reject the party, its presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, and its candidates in the next general elections. The council’s spokesperson, Dele Alake, made the call in a statement, accusing the ADC National Working Committee, led by Senator David Mark as chairman and Rauf Aregbesola as secretary, of neglecting party workers despite their reliance on salaries for their daily needs. Alake described the alleged failure to pay the workers as “wicked and reprehensible”, questioning the party’s capacity to manage the country’s affairs if it could not meet its obligations to its own employees. “We find it unconscionable that a political party that has made many grandiose promises to hoodwink Nigerians owes its workers for more than 12 months,” he said. “Owing staff who come to work every day and who rely on the salaries for their daily sustenance is wicked and reprehensible.” The APC PCC spokesperson said the allegation exposed what he described as the insincerity of the ADC leadership, adding that Nigerians should reject the party at the polls. “We have clearly stated that ADC leaders and their presidential candidate, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, do not mean well and can do nothing for our country,” Alake said. He further alleged that Atiku had a history of failing to pay workers, claiming that employees of Gotel Communication and other businesses linked to the former vice-president had previously gone months without salaries and staged protests over unpaid wages and other benefits. Alake also criticised Aregbesola’s record as governor of Osun State, alleging that his administration struggled to pay workers and pensioners during his eight-year tenure. He said the state government had introduced quarter-salary and, at times, half-salary payments, while pensioners allegedly went unpaid for more than four years. “We are therefore not surprised that ADC, harbouring birds of the same feather, cannot pay its workers’ salaries,” he said. Alake urged Nigerians and workers to reject the ADC, Atiku and all candidates running on the party’s platform in the next general elections. “We are sounding a warning to Nigerians and working people now: reject ADC. Reject Atiku Abubakar and reject all ADC candidates in the next general elections,” he said. He argued that a party seeking to govern Nigeria should be able to demonstrate responsible management of its own affairs and the welfare of its workforce. The post APC accuses ADC of owing staff salaries, urges Nigerians to reject Atiku appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Two killed, four injured in Kharkiv
body:
The number of people killed and injured following a series of strikes on Novobavarsky district of Kharkiv is rising, city mayor Ihor Terekhov reported.

"As a result of the strikes on Novobavarsky district, there are now two dead and four injured. Apartment buildings, private homes, and vehicles have been damaged," Terekhov wrote on his Telegram channel.

Earlier, it was reported that one person had been killed and two others injured.

title: Wontumi is a critical culprit in Tano Nimiri illegal mining case – Police investigator
body: A police investigator in the case involving former Ashanti Regional Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), Bernard Antwi-Boasiako, popularly known as Chairman Wontumi, has described him as a “critical culprit” in the alleged illegal mining activities in the Tano Nimiri Forest. Chief Inspector Eugene Akpo Glover, the fourth prosecution witness, made the assertion during cross-examination by Wontumi’s lawyer, Samuel Atta Akyea, at the High Court on Monday, October 26. Asked who he had identified as a critical culprit in the investigation, Chief Inspector Glover told the court that “A2 (Wontumi) is a critical culprit in the ongoing investigation.” The investigator, however, admitted that Wontumi had not personally operated any mining equipment in the forest, but insisted that his agents had used mining equipment in the area. He identified the first and second prosecution witnesses, PW1 and PW2, as among those who had used the equipment. When Mr Atta Akyea questioned whether the agents could have acted contrary to their employer’s instructions, Chief Inspector Glover maintained that the agents had acted in the interests of A1 (Akonta Mining) and Chairman Wontumi and for their benefit. He also told the court that Wontumi had instructed his agents to mount barriers and signposts in the forest, insisting that the alleged instructions were captured in the evidence before the court. The defence lawyer challenged the investigator’s account, suggesting that his understanding of the case was based largely on hearsay. But Chief Inspector Glover rejected the suggestion, explaining that his conclusions were based on several investigative methods, including witness interviews, site inspections, drone surveillance and a review of documents. He further cited Wontumi’s caution statement in 2021 and a letter allegedly written by PW1 to the Western Regional Security Council seeking assistance to drive away illegal miners from the concession. A copy of the letter, he said, was personally handed to the police during interrogation. Mr Atta Akyea argued that the letter demonstrated Wontumi’s opposition to illegal mining, but the investigator disagreed. Chief Inspector Glover also told the court that between August and September 2022, security personnel from Akonta Mining took control of the forest and restricted forest guards and other security personnel from entering the area. According to him, persons seeking to conduct lawful activities in the forest were required to obtain permission from Akonta Mining management and surrender their phones before being allowed entry. He said the situation was documented in a police report submitted to the Commissioner of Police and the Inspector-General of Police. When the defence lawyer demanded evidence that A1 and A2 were engaged in illegal mining, the investigator maintained that he had gathered what he described as “clear and convincing evidence” linking them to the activities. He said the evidence had been captured in exhibits tendered before the court. Chief Inspector Glover also defended the credibility of the prosecution’s evidence, insisting that the materials presented in court had been verified and authenticated. However, he acknowledged that the alleged head of security who was said to have prevented officials from entering the forest had not been arrested and was currently at large. He told the court that video evidence corroborating the allegation had been tendered in evidence. The case was adjourned to Tuesday, October 27, at 9:30 a.m. by Justice Rugby Aryeetey for continuation

title: Global LNG exports may grow by 50% above 2025 year level — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Global liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports may reach 650 mln cubic meters in 5-10 years, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters.
"The LNG market is developing proactively. According to estimates, its global exports may reach 650 mln cubic meters during the next 5-10 years, exceeding the 2025 level by almost 50%," he said.
The African nations account for almost a half of seats in the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) and OPEC, Ushakov noted.
Russia assumed when preparing the summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) that its countries promote natural gas as a practical kind of fuel, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters.
"The participants agree upon the measures to promote natural gas in global energy markets as a rather affordable, reliable, versatile and practical kind of fuel as part of the forum. Proceeding from this understanding, Russia made the initiative to hold the eighth GECF summit here, in Moscow," Ushakov said. The forum brings together key producers and suppliers of gas and fuel, he added.

title: Bandits Shoot Resident, Rustle 28 Cattle in Sokoto
body: Bandits have attacked Gidan Sarki, a community near Usmanu Danfodiyo University, Sokoto (UDUS), shooting a resident in the leg and rustling 28 cattle. The attack occurred around 9pm on Sunday in the community located behind the university’s Jummat Mosque, triggering panic among residents. The Sokoto State Police Command confirmed the incident, saying the attackers shot the owner of the livestock before escaping with the animals. A senior police officer told our correspondent that the attack appeared to have targeted the victim’s household because of the large number of livestock kept there. FACT CHECK: Video of Tinubu Shaking Dignitaries With Left Hand Is fake Alleged wire-tapping: Court dismisses El-Rufai’s ‘no-case’ submission “The attackers invaded a house in Gidan Sarki and shot the owner, identified as Malam Shehu Muhammad, in the leg. He is responding to treatment. “They also rustled 28 cows belonging to him and his son, Mustapha Shehu,” the officer said. He added that the police received information about the attack and directed the divisional police officer in charge of Wamakko Local Government Area to mobilise personnel to the community. The police spokesperson, Ahmed Rufa’i, also confirmed that one person was shot and 28 cattle were stolen during the incident. Residents said the attackers had threatened members of the community and demanded that students living in the area be brought out. “They threatened us to bring out the students living in this community, but thank God it was during the holiday,” a resident said. Hussaini, another resident who visited the community on Monday morning, said the victim survived the shooting and had been taken to hospital for treatment. Another resident, Jameel Muhammad, confirmed that the gunmen escaped with more than 20 cows after shooting the owner in the leg. The attack occurred while the university was on break, although some newly admitted students were reportedly around for registration. They were not residing on the main campus, according to a university staff member who spoke on condition of anonymity. The staff member confirmed that the affected community was near the university but stressed that the attack did not occur within the institution’s main campus. Efforts to obtain an official comment from the university were unsuccessful, as its spokesperson, Isma’il Muhammad Yauri, declined to comment, saying the institution was not involved in the incident. Background The latest incident comes amid previous security incidents involving communities around the university, although authorities have distinguished attacks outside the campus from incidents within its premises. On November 18, 2023, the university management refuted a report published by one of the national dailies (not daily Trust) alleging that gunmen had attacked its main campus, killing one person and injuring others. In a statement, the university’s spokesperson, Isma’il Muhammad Yauri, said the incident occurred in Dundayen Bakin Gulbi, a village about two kilometres from the institution, and not within the university. The management described the report as false and unfounded, adding that the university maintained security arrangements through collaboration with state security agencies and its internal security network. Earlier, on October 3, 2023, the police confirmed an armed robbery at the university’s mini-market. The then police spokesperson, ASP Ahmad Rufa’i, said about six hoodlums attacked shops, injured two shop owners and stole items, including beverages and food products. He said security personnel responded to the incident and deployed two patrol teams within the university. The university’s Dean of Student Affairs, Professor Umar Aliyu, also described the incident as armed robbery rather than a bandit attack, explaining that the assailants fired shots into the air to scare people away before looting shops. He said the attackers did not enter student hostels or staff residences and that normalcy was restored following the deployment of security personnel.

title: The Shadow In The Twilight: An Ode to Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti (1926–2026)
body: By Marindoti Oludare There are men whose lives are measured in years, others whose lives are measured in accomplishments, and a rare few whose lives are measured by the generations they have inspired. Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti belonged to that rare breed of men whose very existence became a moral compass for society. He lived for a century, but the measure of his life was never in the number of years he lived. It was in the principles he upheld, the lives he touched, the institutions he built, and the causes for which he never ceased to fight. For as long as I can remember, Baba Fasoranti has been one of the men I looked up to. He represented everything I believed public service ought to be: integrity without compromise, leadership without arrogance, political conviction without blind loyalty, and an abiding belief that the welfare of the people must always be the supreme purpose of government. It was this admiration that, in the lead-up to the 2023 presidential election, made his endorsement of Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu one of the most consequential influences on my decision to join the campaign for his presidency. I believed that a man who had spent his life advocating true federalism, restructuring, state police, and public accountability would not lend his moral authority lightly. If Baba believed that Tinubu could advance these causes, I believed there was good reason to join that effort. Today, as we mourn his passing, I find myself reflecting not only on the extraordinary life he lived but also on the promises we owe his memory, some of which remain painfully unfulfilled. Baba was born on May 11, 1926, into a Nigeria still under British colonial rule, long before independence, long before the First Republic, and before many of the political institutions we now take for granted had been conceived. To say that he participated in Nigerian politics for almost as long as modern Nigerian politics has existed is hardly an exaggeration. His life traversed colonialism, nationalism, independence, civilian administrations, military dictatorships, and the return to democracy. Yet his journey began not in the corridors of power but in the humble pursuit of knowledge. As a young man, he dreamed of becoming a medical doctor. But the educational limitations of his time stood between him and that ambition. At Ondo Boys’ High School, where he received his secondary education, the absence of adequate science teaching denied him the opportunity to pursue the subjects needed for medicine. For many young men, such a disappointment might have ended in bitterness or resignation. For Baba, it became the foundation of a lifelong mission. He would dedicate himself to ensuring that the generations coming after him did not have their ambitions determined by the limitations of the schools they attended. He went on to study at Yaba Higher College and University College, Ibadan, before pursuing advanced studies in education in Britain and Australia. He became a teacher, an administrator, and subsequently a principal. In 1957, he became the founding principal of Anglican Grammar School, Iju-Itaogbolu, which began with only 30 students. He would later help establish Omolere Nursery and Primary School, Akure High School, and St. Frances’ Academy, named in memory of his beloved wife. The young man who could not study medicine because his school could not adequately teach the sciences devoted his life to building schools where other people’s children could pursue their dreams. What greater testimony to selfless leadership could there be? Baba’s political life was equally remarkable. He was an admirer and disciple of Chief Obafemi Awolowo, whose philosophy of progressive governance, education, social welfare, and federalism resonated deeply with his own convictions. But Baba was no political sycophant. His loyalty was to principles, not personalities. Perhaps no episode demonstrates this better than his extraordinary encounter with the political establishment of the Action Group in Akure. When Awolowo’s political machinery supported a candidate for the chairmanship of the Akure Local Council whom Baba and his associates believed did not represent the wishes of their people, he refused to surrender his convictions to party authority. Instead, he and his supporters established the Alarm Clock Party, challenged the established political order, and defeated the Action Group candidate at the polls. Imagine the audacity of that young man! A committed disciple of Awolowo, standing against the candidate preferred by the very political leader he revered, not out of personal animosity but because he believed that the people of Akure deserved the right to determine who represented them. And perhaps even more remarkable was what followed. Having made his point and secured the mandate of his people, Baba returned to the Action Group. He had not abandoned his political philosophy; he had merely refused to abandon the people for the sake of party convenience. There lies a lesson for today’s political class: loyalty to a political party must never become disloyalty to the people. A party is merely the vehicle through which the people exercise their democratic rights. It must never become an instrument for suppressing those rights. The story of Baba’s service in the Akure Local Council also provides an enduring lesson in public morality. While serving as council chairman and simultaneously working as a school principal, he refused to draw two salaries. He considered his income as a principal sufficient and chose to offer his political service without collecting remuneration from the council. At a time when public office has become, for too many, an invitation to personal enrichment, such a disposition almost sounds unbelievable. But Baba belonged to a generation that regarded leadership as a duty to be discharged, not a privilege to be exploited. His years in local government are also remembered in Akure’s history of early public infrastructure, including local recollections of pioneering road development around Arakale. For him, the measure of political authority was not the prestige of occupying an office but the visible improvement in the lives of those who elected him. This philosophy followed him into the Second Republic when he served as Commissioner for Finance under the administration of Chief Michael Adekunle Ajasin between 1979 and 1983. Together, Ajasin and Fasoranti represented a tradition of public probity that has become distressingly scarce in contemporary Nigerian politics. The resources of the state were held in trust for the people, and public officials were expected to account for their stewardship. Their reputation for integrity was tested when the military overthrew the civilian government in December 1983. The succeeding military administration subjected members of that government to imprisonment, investigation, and prosecution. Chief Ajasin was famously tried twice and acquitted twice, yet remained in detention. Baba Fasoranti also endured imprisonment and prosecution in the aftermath of the coup. It was an era in which allegations against the political class became a convenient justification for military intervention, and men who had devoted their lives to public service could find themselves deprived of liberty by those who claimed to be rescuing the nation. Baba emerged from these ordeals without abandoning his principles. He would go on to participate in the struggle against military dictatorship, lending his voice to the campaign for the restoration of democratic government. The same man who had challenged his own party over the wishes of the Akure electorate would later stand against military rule in defence of the sovereignty of the Nigerian people. His was not a convenient democracy that mattered only when his preferred candidates won. It was a conviction that the people’s mandate must remain sacred. And so I wonder what Baba would make of the political developments in our country today, where party nominations are sometimes determined not by the wishes of the electorate but by the influence of powerful individuals far removed from the communities whose futures they seek to control. What would he say to political imposition, the manipulation of electoral processes, and the growing belief that power belongs to those who can control the machinery of a party rather than those who can win the confidence of its members? I believe his life has already answered these questions. A man who once challenged Awolowo’s preferred candidate to defend the democratic rights of Akure people would hardly have wanted future generations to surrender those same rights without resistance. Baba’s life was not without profound personal tragedy. He lost his beloved wife, Frances, in 1991. He endured the death of a daughter while he was in military detention. Then, in July 2019, another daughter, Funke Olakunrin, was brutally murdered by gunmen along the Benin-Ore highway. For any father, the loss of a child is an unbearable burden. To lose a daughter to the same insecurity against which one has spent years warning one’s country is a cruelty beyond words. Yet Baba did not allow his personal grief to diminish his concern for the suffering of others. If anything, the tragedy reinforced the urgency of his lifelong advocacy for the protection of lives and property. This brings me to one of the most poignant images of Baba’s final years: the frail, elderly statesman, confined to a wheelchair, who nevertheless found the strength to travel to Abuja and appeal directly to President Tinubu for the restructuring of Nigeria and the establishment of state police. Dr. Marindoti Oludare, Pa Reuben Fasoranti, and Marindoti’s dad, Dr Patrick Oludare, at the home of Papa in Akure, on July 6, 2023 On April 17, 2024, Baba led an Afenifere delegation to the Presidential Villa. At an age when most men would have withdrawn completely from the affairs of the world, he was still pleading for a country where its citizens could live without fear. He was not asking for a contract. He was not seeking a political appointment. He was not requesting a favour for his children or grandchildren. He was asking for a safer Nigeria. There is something profoundly moving about a man nearing a hundred years of age, who has already lost a daughter to violence, continuing to spend what little strength remains in his body demanding the security of other people’s children. That, to me, is the essence of Baba Fasoranti. And it is here that my admiration must coexist with my disappointment. President Tinubu has taken steps toward the establishment of state police, including supporting constitutional changes and legislative proposals. These developments deserve acknowledgment. But I remain deeply saddened that the reform did not become a functioning reality while Baba was alive to witness it. Indeed, the irony of history could hardly be more painful. On October 23, 2026, just three days after Baba’s death, the Presidency announced that the proposed constitutional amendment to establish state police had secured the support of 24 state Houses of Assembly, crossing the constitutional threshold necessary for the reform to advance. Three days after he departed. Baba had lived a hundred years. He had waited through colonialism, military dictatorship, and successive civilian administrations for the emergence of a truly federal Nigeria. Yet he departed before seeing one of his most enduring aspirations become reality. I wish President Tinubu had moved with greater urgency, not merely for Baba’s sake but for the countless Nigerians whose lives remain vulnerable to insecurity. Baba deserved to witness more than promises and proposals. He deserved to see the machinery of a restructured security system take shape in his lifetime. Nevertheless, this disappointment must not become an excuse to abandon the struggle. Rather, it must strengthen our resolve to complete it. We who remain must now take up the mantle. We must insist on state policing that is genuinely accountable to the communities it serves, with proper safeguards against political abuse, independent oversight, and a firm commitment to protecting every Nigerian, regardless of ethnicity, religion, political affiliation, or social standing. We must continue the struggle against corruption, that malignant disease which robs our schools of classrooms, our hospitals of medicines, our roads of durability, and our security institutions of the resources required to protect the people. We must resist the manipulation of elections and the imposition of candidates, for a society that permits its people’s votes to be stolen cannot credibly claim to honour the memory of a man who once defied his own political leader to defend the right of his people to choose. We must remember that political leadership is not measured by the number of convoys surrounding an officeholder, the size of the allowances he collects, or the fortunes accumulated by his associates. It is measured by the opportunities created for the next generation and by the dignity with which the ordinary citizen is treated. Above all, we must restore integrity to public life. For me, Baba Fasoranti will remain a North Star, a constant moral reference by which to judge not only those who seek to govern us but also our own conduct as citizens. At a hundred years of age, he had nothing more to prove. He could have spent his final years in the comfort of his family, receiving tributes and enjoying the gratitude of a society he had already served beyond measure. Instead, he continued to concern himself with the unfinished business of Nigeria. Therein lies the final lesson of his remarkable existence: a life of service never truly retires, and a conviction worth holding is a conviction worth defending until one’s final breath. Now Baba has entered the twilight of eternity. The sun that illuminated a century of Nigerian history has finally dipped below the horizon. The voice that once rose in defence of the people of Akure, that challenged political imposition, that upheld probity in the management of public resources, that resisted military tyranny, and that pleaded for the security of our country has fallen silent. But there is something about the twilight that we must remember. As the sun descends, the shadows of great things stretch farther across the earth. And so it shall be with Baba Fasoranti. Though he has sailed beyond the horizon into the quiet embrace of the night, his shadow remains cast upon our nation. It will stretch across our political institutions, across the schools he founded, across the roads of Akure, and across the conscience of every Nigerian who still believes that public office should be an instrument of service rather than self-enrichment. His body may have surrendered to the passage of time, but his ideals have not. His voice may have fallen silent, but his example still speaks. His eyes may have closed to the troubles of our nation, but the light of his convictions must continue to illuminate our path. And when the darkness of corruption, electoral manipulation, insecurity, and political expediency threatens to overwhelm our country, may we look toward the North Star of his example and find the courage to do what is right. Let us not merely mourn Baba. Let us become worthy of him. Let us complete the work he could not finish. Let us build the Nigeria he believed in. For Baba Fasoranti may have departed into the twilight, but his shadow will remain with us long after the night has fallen. And so long as we keep his ideals alive, the darkness shall never claim his light. Rest peacefully, Baba. Your struggle is now ours. Your mantle has fallen into our hands. And we must not let it fall to the ground. Dr. Oludare, a US-based, Nigerian-born medic, is Convener, Social Rehabilitation Gruppe (SRG). He writes from Texas.

title: Reddit's r/opensource bans all AI-related projects, sparking backlash and a rival subreddit
body:
The Reddit forum r/opensource has banned all posts about projects that use AI, were built with AI, or are designed for AI. Open source means a piece of software's source code is public, and depending on the license, anyone can use, modify, and share it. Developers use the forum to showcase their projects and get feedback.
The moderators published the new rules on Saturday evening, writing that AI in its current form doesn't fit the open-source community. Beyond the AI ban, projects must also be at least a year old, actively maintained, and have multiple contributors. Posts from people who don't speak English will no longer be accepted either, since the moderators say they can't tell whether a text was written by AI or just translated.
Critics call the rules too broad and too vague, pointing out that even the Linux kernel now contains AI-generated code. Moderator Wolvereness named some exceptions, like auto-generated subtitles. In response, the rival forum r/TrueOpenSource popped up, which doesn't exclude AI, The Verge reports . Ad Ad

title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK
body:
This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated. It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question , and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen. Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works. In August 2024, Build an end-to-end RAG solution using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock and the AWS CDK deployed the single-shot design as a CDK application: an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) corpus, an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection and index, a knowledge base, and a data source, provisioned as CDK stacks whose order you sequenced by hand. Three things have changed since it was published. Amazon Bedrock now offers a managed knowledge base (Type: MANAGED), which owns the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval itself. The OpenSearch Serverless collection and index that post provisions are no longer something you need to create, scale, or pay for with OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the agentic half , a Gateway that exposes each knowledge base as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool, a Runtime that hosts the reasoning agent, and AgenticRetrieveStream, which reranks internally and returns a synthesized, cited answer. Agentic retrieval is available only on the Managed Knowledge Base. The observability and evaluation story is now something you can provision , not something you bolt on. This solution ships two Amazon CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation, on-demand and continuous, from the same deployment. This post builds that system: an agent that routes across two knowledge bases, retrieves through the Gateway, and returns a grounded, cited answer, with every layer of its behavior instrumented, as a single AWS CDK application in Python. One command deploys all of it, and CDK derives the order. If you read the 2024 post , the path from an Amazon S3 bucket to the knowledge base will look familiar, and everything after it is new: the vector store is gone, the retrieval is agentic, and roughly half of what the app provisions exists to tell you what the agent did. If you didn’t, this post stands on its own. The services at play and the path one question takes through them: the agent decides whether to retrieve and which knowledge base to consult, the Gateway exposes each knowledge base as a tool it can call, the Managed Knowledge Bases search and cite, and the loop repeats as many times as the question needs. Everything the agent does along the way lands in Amazon CloudWatch. Figure 1: The services involved and the path a single question takes through them Background Before the walkthrough, it helps to establish three things: what makes retrieval agentic, why the Managed Knowledge Base is the right foundation for it, and why observability and evaluation belong in the design rather than bolted on later. From RAG to enterprise agentic retrieval Classic Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) does one retrieval and one generation. Enterprise agentic retrieval puts a reasoning agent in the loop: it decides whether and what to retrieve, can retrieve several times to refine, chooses which knowledge base is relevant (semantic routing), and only then composes a grounded answer with citations. With the Managed Knowledge Base, this is a first-class service capability, the AgenticRetrieveStream API performs the multi-turn planning, executes the retrieval, and returns a cited answer, rather than an orchestration layer you build and maintain over a raw vector search. That produces better answers on complex questions, but it also produces a more complex system to operate, which is exactly why observability and evaluation are built in from the start. Managed compared to do-it-yourself Knowledge Bases Amazon Bedrock now offers a Managed Knowledge Base (Type: MANAGED): Amazon Bedrock manages the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you, including embedding and reranking with service-managed models by default, so there is no vector database to provision, scale, or patch . This differs from a Customer-managed (DIY) Knowledge Base, where you choose and operate the vector store (for example, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless) yourself. Two differences matter most for this solution: Capability Amazon Bedrock managed Customer-managed (DIY) Agentic retrieval (AgenticRetrieveStream) Supported Not supported AgentCore Gateway integration Supported Not supported Data store Auto scaling, fully managed by Amazon Bedrock You provision, scale, and maintain it Embedding + reranking Built-in managed models, no extra cost You configure them Infrastructure to manage None Vector DB + more Because agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector are available only on the managed knowledge base, it is the natural foundation for enterprise agentic retrieval. It also means Amazon Bedrock manages the storage and indexing for you, so there is no OpenSearch Serverless collection or OCU capacity to provision in this design. The customer-managed option remains the right choice when you want to select and operate your own vector store, for example to reuse an existing OpenSearch Serverless collection or to meet specific data-residency, tuning, or compliance requirements. For enterprise agentic retrieval, the managed knowledge base is what makes the capability possible. Why observability and evaluation An agentic system that returns an answer isn’t enough for production. You need to see how it behaves (latency, call volume, token usage), how good the retrieval and answers are, and you need those signals continuously. This solution ships two CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation (on-demand and continuous), all provisioned by the same CDK application. The grounding, citations, and evaluation layers also support responsible use. Cited answers trace back to their source passages so responses stay auditable, and the faithfulness and correctness scores let you catch answers drifting from their sources rather than finding out in production. Why CDK for this particular solution Any infrastructure-as-code tool can create these resources. CDK earns its place here for a reason specific to this architecture: the four stacks are densely cross-referenced . The Gateway needs both knowledge base ids. The agent needs the URL and ARN for the Gateway. The dashboards need the KB ids, the Gateway ARN, and the agent runtime id, seven values crossing stack boundaries, each one a dimension on a metric or a target on a connector. Written as raw templates, that is a set of stack exports and cross-stack lookups kept in agreement by hand, plus a script that deploys in the right order and threads outputs forward, and both drift the moment anything is renamed. In CDK you pass the construct, and the export and the dependency edge are derived from that one act of passing it. The 2024 solution had three stacks and a mostly linear dependency chain. At four stacks with seven values crossing between them, the difference stops being stylistic. Solution overview Here is the path a single question takes through the system, end to end. It’s worth a slow look, because the rest of the post walks through it left to right. The following diagram traces the end-to-end agentic retrieval workflow. A user’s question enters the agent on the AgentCore Runtime, which routes it through the AgentCore Gateway to one of two AgenticRetrieveStream tools, one per managed knowledge base, financial and weather, each ingested from Amazon S3. The selected tool returns a grounded, cited answer, and every step streams to Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray. The numbered badges map to the following walkthrough. Figure 2: End-to-end agentic retrieval workflow for a single question The numbered steps in the diagram map to the workflow, which is as follows. Step 0 — one-time, at deploy. Before any question is asked, each corpus in Amazon S3 is ingested into its own Managed Knowledge Base: Amazon Bedrock parses, chunks, embeds, and indexes it automatically. This happens once when the stacks deploy, it isn’t part of the per-question path, so it is drawn as a dashed arrow and marked step 0. Every question then follows steps 1–6: A user sends a question to the agent hosted on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The Runtime auto-instruments the whole reason-and-act loop with OpenTelemetry (OTEL) spans, so the system is observable from the very first call. The agent’s reasoning model plans and routes across knowledge bases. Because each knowledge base is exposed as its own retrieval tool, the agent selects the tool whose topic matches the question, financial or weather, rather than searching one blended index. The selected tool call is brokered by the AgentCore Gateway over MCP , authorized by the agent’s IAM task role and signed with SigV4, which invokes that knowledge base’s AgenticRetrieveStream API on the Managed Knowledge Base. AgenticRetrieveStream does the within-knowledge-base work: it decomposes the question into sub-queries, retrieves iteratively from the data store that Amazon Bedrock manages (ingested from the corpora in Amazon S3), and synthesizes a grounded, cited answer that streams back through the Gateway. The agent checks whether the returned context is sufficient. If not, it loops, routing and retrieving again, before composing its final answer. If so, it returns the cited answer to the user. Throughout, the Runtime emits spans, token counts, and metrics to Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray, populating the seven observability layers and feeding both the on-demand and continuous evaluation scores. Internally, that workflow is one CDK app, app.py , that declares four stacks. You don’t choose the order, CDK derives it from the construct references you pass: kb_stack = KnowledgeBasesStack(app, f"{project}-kb", env=env) gateway_stack = AgenticGatewayStack( app, f"{project}-gateway", env=env, financial_kb=kb_stack.financial_kb, # ← the reference creates the dependency weather_kb=kb_stack.weather_kb, ) agent_stack = AgentRuntimeStack( app, f"{project}-agent", env=env, gateway=gateway_stack.gateway, ) DashboardsStack( app, f"{project}-dashboards", env=env, financial_kb=kb_stack.financial_kb, weather_kb=kb_stack.weather_kb, gateway=gateway_stack.gateway, agent_runtime=agent_stack.agent_runtime, ) That is the whole wiring. Those four constructor calls are what replace the export/import bookkeeping and the deploy script. # Stack What it creates Note 1 -kb S3 bucket, corpora upload, two Type: MANAGED KBs, data sources, IAM, ingestion KBs reach ACTIVE, corpora ingested 2 -gateway Gateway (AWS_IAM / MCP), per-KB AgenticRetrieveStream targets no Cognito needed 3 -agent ECR, CodeBuild, instrumented Strands agent on Runtime, vended logs/traces, online eval ~8–10 min (image build) 4 -dashboards agentic-observability + kb-observability dashboards empty until you drive traffic The agent runs a reason-and-act loop: it thinks (a large language model (LLM) call), decides which KB tool to call, reads what came back through the Gateway, and often retrieves again before composing its final, cited answer. Every step is auto-instrumented by the Runtime, so the seven observability layers fill from real traffic. The seven layers. L1 KB-native metrics, L2 ingestion, L3 agentic retrieval quality, L4 Gateway/MCP metrics, L5 OTEL span tree , L6 token usage, and L7 evaluation scores. Layers 1, 4, and 5 are emitted automatically. Layers 3, 6, and 7 are published as custom metrics by the driver notebook. Everything tunable lives in one file, config.py : Setting Meaning Default EnvSettings.PROJECT_NAME Name prefix for every stack and resource bmkb-obs-cdk EnvSettings.ACCOUNT_REGION AWS Region to deploy into us-west-2 (or your profile’s) KbConfig.EMBEDDING_MODEL_TYPE MANAGED (bundled) or CUSTOM (bring your own ARN) MANAGED AgentConfig.MODEL_ID The agent’s reasoning model, the Layer 6 spend Claude Haiku 4.5 EvalConfig.SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE Online-evaluation sampling rate, see the disclaimer 100 Changing PROJECT_NAME gives you an independently-named copy of the whole solution, so two deployments can coexist in one account. The driver notebook reads the same constant, so it follows the rename automatically, there are no stack names to keep in sync by hand. Describe the dataset The solution ships with two small corpora, bundled in the repository under data/: Financial — A synthetic Octank Financial 10-K (octank_financial_10K.pdf, ~198 KB). Weather — A real, publicly available U.S. Congressional Research Service report on tornadoes ( IF12695 , tornadoes_report.pdf, ~560 KB). About the data: The financial corpus is synthetic . Octank is a fictional company and the 10-K is model-generated sample data (CC0-licensed). It is n’t real financial data. The weather corpus is a real, public-domain U.S. Government work and is a Congressional Research Service report, publicly available at sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/IF12695.pdf (works of the U.S. Government aren’t subject to copyright). To use your own data, drop files under data/ and adjust the prefixes in config.py , no other change is required. The two corpora are intentionally distinct, so the agent must route each question to the right knowledge base, the semantic-routing story. Because these are Managed Knowledge Bases, we don’t configure chunking, embedding, or an index: on ingestion, Amazon Bedrock parses each PDF, chunks it, embeds it with its managed model, and indexes it automatically. We use two separate knowledge bases, each exposed through the Gateway as its own retrieval tool, rather than one knowledge base holding both corpora and that choice is deliberate. Giving the agent two named tools makes routing an explicit act of reasoning it can be observed making: the span tree shows which tool it chose for a given question, and the retrieval-quality metrics in Layer 3 stay separable per knowledge base, so financial and weather precision never blur into a single number. A single tool spanning both corpora would collapse that distinction, the routing decision would move inside one index’s ranking, out of view, and every quality signal would be an average across two unrelated domains. Keeping the corpora and their tools separate is what makes the agent’s behavior legible, which is the whole point of the exercise. In CDK, getting the corpora into S3 is a BucketDeployment: s3deploy.BucketDeployment( self, "FinancialCorpus", sources=[s3deploy.Source.asset(str(ROOT / "data" / "financial"))], destination_bucket=self.source_bucket, destination_key_prefix=KbConfig.FINANCIAL_PREFIX, ) BucketDeployment is worth knowing about precisely because the alternative is so tempting: without it, the custom resource that triggers ingestion tends to grow an upload step, and now one resource owns two unrelated jobs. Here it only has to ingest . Managed ingestion scans, chunks, embeds, and indexes each document automatically: one document indexed per knowledge base, zero failures. Figure 3: Managed ingestion results, one document indexed per knowledge base with zero failures Deploy the solution This section walks through deploying the whole solution with one command. After the prerequisites are met, cdk deploy --all provisions all four stacks in CDK’s derived dependency order and threads every cross-stack value through automatically. Prerequisites An AWS account with permissions for Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore (Runtime + Gateway), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) , CloudWatch, AWS X-Ray , Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) , AWS CodeBuild , Amazon S3, AWS Lambda , and AWS CloudFormation . The agent’s model available in the account (default us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0 ). CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled, so OTEL spans land in aws/spans for Layers 5–7. Node.js 18+ and the CDK CLI ( npm install -g aws-cdk ), plus Python 3.13+. The account and region bootstrapped for CDK (cdk bootstrap), once per account/region. No local Docker, the agent image is built by CodeBuild (ARM64). One command To deploy the solution, clone the repository, create a virtual environment, install the dependencies, and run cdk deploy --all . Run the following commands from your terminal: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/amazon-bedrock-samples.git cd rag/managed-knowledge-bases/07-IaaC/managed-kb-observability-cdk/ python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt cdk bootstrap # once per account/region cdk deploy --all The first two commands clone the sample and move into the project directory. The next two create and activate a Python virtual environment and install the CDK app’s dependencies. cdk bootstrap prepares the account and region for CDK (you only need it once per account/region), and cdk deploy --all provisions all four stacks. Account and region come from your AWS profile (CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT / CDK_DEFAULT_REGION), so the app deploys with no edits. Region availability: The managed knowledge base, agentic retrieval (AgenticRetrieveStream), and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime and Gateway) aren’t available in every AWS Region. Before you deploy, confirm that all of these are offered in your target Region, and set ACCOUNT_REGION in config.py accordingly. The default is us-west-2. For current availability, see the Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and the AWS Regional Services List . There is no deploy script in this version, and that is the point: cdk deploy --all walks the dependency graph it derived from app.py , deploys the four stacks in order, and passes every cross-stack value automatically. The terminal reports each stack as it completes, bmkb-obs-cdk-kb [1/4] (the default PROJECT_NAME), then gateway [2/4], then agent [3/4], then dashboards [4/4] and that order is derived, not declared: it falls out of the construct references between the stacks, so adding a fifth stack that consumes an existing output reorders the deploy on its own. Stack -agent builds the agent container with CodeBuild, so allow roughly 8–10 minutes for that stage. The other three are quick. Each stack prints its outputs on completion, which is where you pick up the knowledge base ids, the Gateway URL, the runtime ARN, and both dashboard URLs. When the deploy finishes, all four stacks are complete. The following screenshot shows the AWS CloudFormation console after a successful cdk deploy --all . Figure 4: AWS CloudFormation console after a successful deploy, with all four stacks CREATE_COMPLETE On the console, all four stacks, kb, gateway, agent, and dashboards, report CREATE_COMPLETE, each with its [n/4] position in the derived dependency order shown in its description. A note on long-running resources Two things in this solution take far longer than the 15-minute ceiling of an AWS Lambda function allows for naive polling: the KB ingestion sync and the CodeBuild image build. The AWS CDK Provider framework handles this with an on_event / is_complete split, where one handler starts the work and a second is polled until it reports done. cr.Provider( self, "IngestSyncProvider", on_event_handler=on_event, # StartIngestionJob, return the job id is_complete_handler=is_complete, # GetIngestionJob, report IsComplete query_interval=Duration.seconds(30), total_timeout=Duration.minutes(30), ) Nothing blocks, the response protocol back to CloudFormation is owned by the framework rather than hand-written into each handler, and the 30-minute budget is a property rather than something to engineer around. Launch and test Open notebooks/01-drive-and-observe.ipynb and run it top to bottom ( pip install -r requirements-notebook.txt first). It reads the stack outputs, then sends topic-specific prompts to the deployed agent, one session per KB , so you can see both the answers and the semantic routing in one place: financial questions are answered from the Octank 10-K and weather questions from the tornadoes report, each routed to the matching AgenticRetrieveStream tool automatically. The notebook discovers everything from the stack outputs, so there is nothing to paste in by hand: # Stack names are derived from the same PROJECT_NAME the CDK app uses, so renaming the # project in config.py cannot leave this notebook pointing at stale stacks. from config import EnvSettings PROJECT = EnvSettings.PROJECT_NAME STACKS = {suffix: f'{PROJECT}-{suffix}' for suffix in ('kb', 'gateway', 'agent', 'dashboards')} def outputs(stack_name): s = cfn.describe_stacks(StackName=stack_name)['Stacks'][0] return {o['OutputKey']: o['OutputValue'] for o in s.get('Outputs', [])} The notebook imports the same config.py the app does, so the two can never disagree about what the stacks are called. The driver sends per-KB prompts through the deployed agent. Financial questions route to the financial KB and weather questions to the weather KB, each with a grounded, cited answer. Figure 5: Per-KB prompts routed to the matching knowledge base, each returning a grounded, cited answer The notebook also computes the reference-free Layer 3 retrieval-quality signals from what the agent actually retrieved and cited, no ground truth, no extra judge, and publishes them to CloudWatch. Figure 6: Reference-free Layer 3 retrieval-quality signals per knowledge base Observe: The seven-layer dashboards The two dashboards are where the seven layers become visible. The stack creates both dashboards, and driving traffic populates them. The following screenshot shows the two dashboards as they appear in the CloudWatch console. Figure 7: The two dashboards in the CloudWatch console, end-to-end agentic observability and per-KB observability Both dashboards appear in the CloudWatch console: one for end-to-end agentic observability and one for per-KB observability (BMKB, Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base). The rest of this section walks through what each layer shows. In this version the dashboards are built from typed objects rather than a JSON string. A metric is a Metric, a widget is a GraphWidget, and the layout is a list of Rows: cw.GraphWidget( title="L4 — Gateway metrics (MCP)", width=12, height=6, period=PERIOD, statistic="Sum", left=[ self._gateway_metric("Invocations", gateway_arn, "tools/call Invocations"), self._gateway_metric("SystemErrors", gateway_arn, "SystemErrors"), self._gateway_metric("UserErrors", gateway_arn, "UserErrors"), self._gateway_metric("Throttles", gateway_arn, "Throttles"), ], ) The practical benefit isn’t fewer lines, dashboards_stack.py runs to 400 lines, more than the equivalent DashboardBody JSON would. It is that a misspelled property or an invalid widget combination fails at cdk synth , on your laptop, in about a second. The same mistake inside a DashboardBody string deploys successfully and renders as a broken widget on the AWS Management Console, where you find it by looking at it. Because a Row accepts any widget, the documentation is part of the layout rather than a wiki page that drifts. Each dashboard interleaves TextWidgets with the graphs: [cw.TextWidget(width=24, height=7, markdown=self._l3_explainer())], [ self._quality_widget("L3 · Financial KB — agentic quality (reference-free, 0–1)", fin_id), self._quality_widget("L3 · Weather KB — agentic quality (reference-free, 0–1)", wx_id), ], _l3_explainer() returns a markdown table defining each ratio and how to read it, so the widget that explains grounded_coverage ships in the same commit as the widget that plots it, and a reader who opens the dashboard cold doesn’t need to guess what a reference-free metric is. Dashboard A — agentic observability (end to end). The board opens with an explainer of how each layer counts a different thing (for N queries you’ll see ~ N agent invocations, ~2 N retrievals, ~3 N LLM calls, and ~5 N Gateway MCP operations, the agentic loop made visible), then shows KB metrics (L1), Gateway metrics and latency (L4), token usage (L6), and because the agent uses AgenticRetrieveStream, which returns a synthesized, cited answer rather than per-chunk scores, the reference-free Layer 3 quality signals, defined inline and plotted per KB. On Dashboard A, the Layer 3 reference-free quality signals are plotted per knowledge base. First, the financial KB. The following chart plots its retrieval_utilization, grounded_coverage, and duplicate_rate. Figure 8: Financial KB Layer 3 quality, plotting retrieval utilization, grounded coverage, and duplicate rate The weather KB shows the same three signals, tracked separately so the two domains never blur into one number. Figure 9: Weather KB Layer 3 quality, tracked separately from the financial KB The two charts plot retrieval_utilization, grounded_coverage, and duplicate_rate for the financial KB (left) and the weather KB (right), so each knowledge base’s retrieval quality stays separable rather than averaged into one number. Dashboard B — per-KB (BMKB) observability. The operational signals that also determine spend, per KB: index size (from S3 source bytes), retrieve volume, agentic tool-calls, session token usage, and generation token usage by model, each with an inline explanation. The following screenshots show Dashboard B’s four metric widgets, populated after a run. The first widget reports index size, derived from S3 source bytes, per knowledge base. Figure 10: Dashboard B index size per knowledge base, derived from Amazon S3 source bytes The second widget counts retrieve calls per knowledge base. Figure 11: Dashboard B retrieve-call count per knowledge base The third widget counts agentic tool-calls through the Gateway. This one is shared across both KBs rather than split. Figure 12: Dashboard B agentic tool-call count through the AgentCore Gateway, shared across both knowledge bases The fourth widget reports session token usage per knowledge base. Figure 13: Dashboard B session token usage per knowledge base The four widgets show index size (from S3 source bytes), retrieve-call volume, agentic tool-calls through the Gateway, and session token usage. Each is broken out per knowledge base except the Gateway tool-call count, which is shared across both. One dimension detail is worth calling out, because the typed API won’t catch it for you: the AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases namespace expects a prefixed id, knowledge-base/
, while the solution’s own BMKB/* namespaces use the bare id. Both are only strings as far as CDK is concerned. # L1 — AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases wants the prefixed form. dimensions_map={"Operation": "Retrieve", "KnowledgeBaseId": f"knowledge-base/{kb_id}"} # BMKB/* — our own namespaces use the bare id. dimensions_map={"KnowledgeBaseId": kb_id} Layer 5: The span tree Layer 5 is the raw OTEL span tree in aws/spans, and it is the layer that shows you the agentic loop directly. It is worth reading carefully, because the nesting isn’t obvious: one LLM call produces three spans. The Strands invoke_agent span wraps the turn, an internal chat span wraps the model call, and a chat
span of kind CLIENT is the actual call, and all three repeat the same gen_ai.usage.* token attributes. The following screenshot shows the span tree in aws/spans, with the three-span nesting visible in the top rows. Figure 14: Layer 5 span tree in aws/spans, showing the three-span nesting of a single LLM call Reading the top three rows: an invoke_agent Strands Agents aggregate, then an internal chat span, then a CLIENT chat span, all reporting an identical 7,299 input and 268 output tokens. That is the same LLM call appearing at three levels of the tree, which is why aggregation needs care. That structure matters the moment you aggregate. To count each LLM call once, filter to the CLIENT leaf: fields attributes.gen_ai.request.model as model, attributes.gen_ai.usage.input_tokens as in_tok, attributes.gen_ai.usage.output_tokens as out_tok | filter ispresent(in_tok) and kind = 'CLIENT' and name like /^chat / | stats sum(in_tok) as input_tokens, sum(out_tok) as output_tokens, count(*) as llm_calls by model Without that filter the same query reports three times the tokens and three times the calls. Applying that CLIENT-leaf filter, the following screenshot shows generation token usage by model with each LLM call counted once. Figure 15: Generation token usage by model, with each LLM call counted once With the filter in place, the run shows 14 LLM calls totaling 60,472 input and 2,709 output tokens. Without it, the same query would report three times the calls and three times the tokens. Evaluate: On-demand and continuous Quality is measured two ways, and both are provisioned by the app. On-demand: The driver notebook calls AgentCore There is no deploy script in this version, and that is the point: (LLM-as-judge) over each session’s spans for built-in evaluators, Correctness, Faithfulness, Tool-Selection Accuracy and publishes the scores to CloudWatch, where they appear as Layer 7 on Dashboard A. The following screenshot shows Layer 7 on Dashboard A: on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, with the Layer 5 OTEL span table on the same dashboard. Figure 16: Layer 7 on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, beside the Layer 5 span table Layer 7 shows the on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, with the Layer 5 OTEL span table alongside, so the scores and the spans that produced them read together on one board. Continuous (online): The agent stack also provisions an AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OnlineEvaluationConfig that samples live sessions and scores them automatically, no notebook run required. The configuration itself is visible in the Bedrock AgentCore console under Assess → Evaluations → Evaluation configurations . Results land in the log group /aws/bedrock-agentcore/evaluations/results/
, and every score is also published as a CloudWatch metric in the Bedrock-AgentCore/Evaluations namespace, keyed by evaluator name and configuration id, so you can graph the scores or alarm on them without parsing logs. The following screenshot shows the online evaluation configuration in the AgentCore console, under Assess, then Evaluations, then Evaluation configurations. Figure 17: The online evaluation configuration in the AgentCore console, with four built-in evaluators at 100 percent sampling The configuration lists four built-in evaluators, Tool-Selection Accuracy, Faithfulness, Correctness, and Response Relevance, set to 100 percent sampling and shown as ACTIVE and enabled. Because the scores are ordinary CloudWatch metrics, they graph like anything else, no log parsing, and the same widget could carry an alarm. The following screenshot shows those four evaluator scores graphed as ordinary CloudWatch metrics. Figure 18: The four continuous evaluator scores graphed as ordinary CloudWatch metrics The four evaluator scores appear as metrics in the Bedrock-AgentCore/Evaluations namespace, each keyed to the evaluation configuration id and the agent’s service name, so you can graph them or alarm on them without parsing logs. Online results only arrive after a session closes . Scoring runs on the completed session, so the results log group stays empty for roughly the session idle timeout (~30 minutes) after you drive traffic. An empty group right after a run is expected, not a misconfiguration. Each result event carries session.id , so it joins to every other layer. The on-demand path in the notebook has no such wait, which is why both are here. Across the four built-in evaluators on this run, the continuous path scored 1.00 on Correctness, Faithfulness, Response Relevance, and Tool-Selection Accuracy, five scored traces per evaluator, each result carrying a written explanation. Sampling and cost. This app sets SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE = 100 purely for the blog experiment , so every session is scored and the results are immediately visible. This isn’t a production recommendation. Online evaluation invokes an LLM-as-judge per sampled session, so cost scales with the sampling rate and traffic volume. For a real deployment, choose a sampling percentage that fits your quality-monitoring needs and budget, and align the configuration with your organization’s own policies and cost-governance requirements before enabling it. The rate is a single constant, EvalConfig.SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE , in config.py . Clean up When you’re finished, remove the solution so it stops incurring charges, since stored KB data, the agent image in ECR, and the still-active online evaluation all cost money while the stacks sit idle. One command tears everything down: cdk destroy --all CDK deletes the stacks in reverse dependency order on its own, dashboards, then agent, then gateway, then kb: the same graph it derived for the deploy, walked backward. There is no teardown script to keep in agreement with the deploy script, which is one of the more quietly valuable properties of modelling the dependencies once. Two removal behaviors are worth knowing, because both replace hand-written cleanup code: self.source_bucket = s3.Bucket( self, "SourceBucket", removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.DESTROY, auto_delete_objects=True, # replaces a list_object_versions delete loop ) self.repository = ecr.Repository( self, "AgentImageRepo", removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.DESTROY, empty_on_delete=True, # replaces an image-delete loop ) Both are set for sample hygiene, for anything you care about, switch the bucket to RemovalPolicy.RETAIN . The CDK bootstrap stack ( CDKToolkit ) and its staging bucket aren’t removed. They are shared account-wide infrastructure that other CDK apps may depend on. What changed since the single-shot solution Both this post and the 2024 solution are CDK applications in Python, deployed with cdk deploy . The authoring tool is the constant here, what changed is the architecture underneath it, and most of the change is subtraction: Concern 2024: Single-shot RAG This solution Vector store An OpenSearch Serverless collection and index you provision, scale, and pay OCU for None. Type: MANAGED, Amazon Bedrock owns storage and indexing Index lifecycle A custom resource creates the index and waits for it to become searchable Nothing to create Embedding model You select it and grant model access Service-managed by default Stacks 3: KB role → OpenSearch infra → KB + data source 4: kb → gateway → agent → dashboards Retrieval One Retrieve, top-k chunks by vector similarity AgenticRetrieveStream, reranked internally, returns a synthesized cited answer Choosing a knowledge base Not applicable, there is one index The agent routes semantically across two Second look at the corpus Not possible in one shot The agent retrieves again before answering Telemetry None provisioned Seven layers, two dashboards Evaluation Manual: sync, pick a model, ask questions On-demand and continuous, both provisioned Cost floor when idle OCU charges accrue whether or not you query Storage only The trade is real in both directions. A single index answering single-shot questions is cheaper per query, simpler to reason about, and entirely sufficient when one corpus holds the answer. Reach for this design when it doesn’t. The CDK constructs doing the work Four constructs carry most of the weight in this app, and they are worth naming because each replaces something people otherwise hand-write: Provider – For custom resources that outlive the 15-minute ceiling of an AWS Lambda function. The on_event / is_complete split means nothing sleeps in a poll loop, and the response protocol back to CloudFormation is the framework’s job rather than a vendored urllib callback in every handler. BucketDeployment – Uploads the corpora, so the ingestion custom resource only ingests. auto_delete_objects=True and empty_on_delete=True , replace the hand-written list_object_versions and image-delete loops that a stack otherwise needs to be destroyable at all. repository.grant_pull_push(project) – One line for the eight ecr:* actions CodeBuild needs, spelled correctly by construction. And typed dashboards, from the Observe section: Metric / GraphWidget / Row objects instead of a DashboardBody JSON string, which moves an invalid widget combination from “renders broken on the console” to “fails at cdk synth .” Two things CDK doesn’t change, and both are worth knowing before you start: Free-form JSON stays camelCase . connector_parameters and parameter_values are passed through verbatim, so the AWS CDK snake_case to PascalCase conversion does not apply inside them. Keys like bucketName and inclusionPrefixes must be spelled exactly as the API expects, and nothing will tell you otherwise until the resource fails. String-typed values are still strings. The knowledge-base/
versus bare
dimension difference from the Observe section is invisible to the type system. Typed constructs check structure , not semantics . Neither is a reason to prefer one tool over the other. They are the boundary of what “typed” buys you, and knowing where that boundary sits is most of what makes CDK pleasant instead of surprising. Conclusion We built a complete enterprise agentic retrieval solution on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base and AgentCore: multi-KB semantic routing, a reasoning agent, seven layers of observability, and both on-demand and continuous evaluation, and deployed all of it as a single AWS CDK application. Two things are worth taking away. The managed knowledge base removed infrastructure rather than adding it: no vector store to provision, no index to create and wait on, no OCU line item accruing while the system sits idle. It is also the knowledge base type that supports agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector, as described in the Amazon Bedrock documentation . And once retrieval became agentic, observability stopped being optional. Roughly half of what this app provisions exists to answer what the agent actually did and whether the answer was any good, which isn’t overhead on an agentic system. It’s the part that makes one operable. The CDK authoring model earned its place on the seams. Seven values cross stack boundaries in this architecture, and every one of them is a construct reference rather than an expor

title: Sixteen Ukrainian doctors who work near fighting went through three Western trauma programs in one week. American surgeons led drills
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine has held its first international course in military surgery and resuscitation, under instructors from the American College of Surgeons and other Western trauma bodies, the Defense Ministry says . “Tryzub”, or Trident, has been conducted for front-line surgeons and anesthesiologists. The week-long drills put 16 doctors, eight surgeons, and eight anesthesiologists through three standard Western trauma programs: Advanced Trauma Life Support, Definitive Surgical Trauma Care, and Advanced Surgical Skills for Exposure in Trauma. All of them work at stabilization points close to the fighting. The course has been run with the International Association for Trauma Surgery and Intensive Care and the Global Medical Knowledge Alliance, a non-profit that helps rebuild Ukraine’s healthcare, with support from Razom4Ukraine and Expertise France. The wounds have changed The course answers a battlefield that has grown deadlier. Ukrainian combat medics say modern combat trauma has fundamentally changed : drones and shrapnel now cause most of the complex wounds, often tearing through several parts of the body at once. Bleeding has become the main cause of death on the battlefield, and the window to stop it is measured in minutes. That is the gap a well-drilled surgical team near the line is meant to close. “People who will do everything to save his life” Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara has framed the course as a promise to troops at the front. “When a soldier goes into battle, he must know that if he is wounded, there will be people beside him who will do everything they can to save his life,” Khmara says. Experience, he added, is a kind of trust that matters enormously at the front. “That is why we want our medics to have the best knowledge and skills, and to be able to act as one team," he states. Ukrainian front-line medicine already draws international notice: one Azov brigade medic was named Europe’s best military medic of the year, and off-duty Ukrainian medics recently saved a man’s life at a London crash scene. Read also Russia tries to drag a village north of Kupiansk into no-man’s-land after its losses in Ukraine’s underground operation A 4-watt video link passed Ukraine’s state tests, its maker says, and could stretch STING interceptors’ radius from 20 km to 30 km UN commission finds Russia’s grid strikes are crimes against humanity, citing last winter at minus 21°C. Now they’re intensifying

title: Lockheed Martin Completes $3.5 Billion Deal For Ultra Maritime

title: Nurse killed in attack while responding to Ebola alert in DR Congo
body: A nurse has been killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack as they were responding to an Ebola alert in north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The two were targeted by local youths who accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the Ebola virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi. The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack. In an attempt to prevent the virus spreading, neighbouring Uganda has banned all non-essential travel to and from DR Congo and says its citizens returning from there will be quarantined for 21 days. More than 4,800 people have died and nearly 10,000 been infected in DR Congo since this outbreak began in May. Reacting to the attack in DR Congo, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said health workers “must be able to carry out their duties in safety and dignity”, adding that healthcare personnel should always be protected. The UN agency also extended its condolences to the family and colleagues of the nurse who was killed and wished the injured worker a swift recovery. The BBC has contacted the Ebola response team for comment on the circumstances surrounding the attack in DR Congo. This is not the first time such an attack has happened in DR Congo. Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents during the first 100 days after the outbreak was declared. Earlier this month, two countries – Kenya and Nigeria – reported their first cases of Ebola linked to the current outbreak. The patient in Nigeria was on Monday flown from Abuja to Switzerland for further treatment. She is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya. She was evacuated alongside her husband, who has shown no symptoms. Nigeria’s health ministry said she was stable, conscious and able to communicate. Authorities are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus. The new restrictions announced in Uganda come after questions were raised over her case and that of a Kenyan businessman. Both tested positive for Ebola after travelling through Uganda, even though no cases have been reported there since August. The Kenyan had arrived from DR Congo where he had business interests. Only essential travellers, including aid workers, truck drivers and security personnel, will be allowed to cross the border from DR Congo to Uganda, subject to strict health screening, the health ministry announced. In addition, all travellers entering Uganda, regardless of their country of origin, will be required to complete locator forms to facilitate contact tracing where necessary. It said returning Ugandans would “undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost”. About 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan patient have all been discharged, it added. In Kenya , the first group of 20 contacts of the first case have gone home, after spending 21 days in quarantine, the health ministry announced on Monday. Another 98 are still being supervised, while seven people who have tested positive for Ebola were stable it said. The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi. A second woman, related to the businessman, died over the weekend. “All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola,” Uganda’s Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC’s Newsday programme. Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August. The two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda’s Entebbe airport on the same day. Diana Atwine, the health ministry’s permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients. Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure. The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to “remain vigilant”. “We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties,” Baryomunsi said. The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment – though trials are under way.

title: Bitmine’s Holdings Value Dips to $15 Billion Despite 10,452 ETH Buy
body: Bitmine Immersion Technologies bought 10,452 ETH in the week through Oct. 25, lifting its holdings to 6,051,933 ETH , while a lower ether price contributed to a drop in the value of its combined crypto, cash and stakes to about $15 billion , the company announced on Monday.
