title: Agriculture is key area of cooperation between Russia, Africa — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Agriculture is one of the mainline areas in cooperation between Russia and Africa, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said.
"Speaking about specific cooperation [between Russia and Africa], then, certainly, agriculture is one of main areas. Our country is a stable supplier of food, fertilizer and other critical agribusiness sector products [to countries of the continent]," he said.
Russian mineral fertilizer supplies climbed above 2.2 mln metric tons in 2026, Ushakov told reporters.
"Russian deliveries of mineral fertilizers stood at 1.5 mln tons last year and surpassed 2.2 mln [tons] this year," Ushakov said.

title: Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing
body:
Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions.
At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported. Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass:
It pays to be an Amodei
Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Admittedly, it is at the lower end of the Big Tech scale, but it is still a tidy sum.
And that’s not all. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055.
The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission.
Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors
Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong. Anthropic’s is no exception. But alongside standard warnings about competition, regulation, and market shifts, there are some less conventional risks too.
For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges. There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company.
It’s hungry for compute
It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering. The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years.
Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US.
It has a really weird corporate structure
Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation. But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public. Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters. Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development.
Anthropic names only two rivals
There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google. Condolences to SpaceX, Meta, and the rest of the AI world.

title: Zelenskyy signs laws extending martial law and mobilization
body:
The President of Ukraine has signed laws extending martial law and general mobilization for another 90 days, effective from October 31, 2026, and has also signed the corresponding decrees.
As reported on the Verkhovna Rada website, the law on extending martial law in Ukraine (No. 5029-IX; draft law No. 16182) and the law on extending the period of general mobilization (No. 5030-IX; draft law No. 16183) have been returned bearing the signature of the President of Ukraine.
The respective draft laws were submitted to the Ukrainian parliament by the President, approved by the relevant committee on national security, defense, and intelligence, and subsequently supported by members of parliament earlier on Monday.
Additionally, on Monday, Zelenskyy signed decrees No. 1060/2026, "On the extension of martial law in Ukraine," and No. 1061/2026, "On the extension of general mobilization."
"In connection with the ongoing large-scale armed aggression by the Russian Federation against Ukraine, based on a proposal by the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine, and in accordance with Paragraph 20 of Part 1 of Article 106 of the Constitution of Ukraine and the Law of Ukraine 'On the legal regime of martial law,' I hereby decree: in order to partially amend Article 1 of the Decree of the President of Ukraine dated February 24, 2022, No. 64/2022 'On the imposition of martial law in Ukraine', which was approved by the law of Ukraine dated February 24, 2022, No. 2102-IX—the period of martial law in Ukraine shall be extended for 90 days, effective from 05:30 on October 31, 2026," states the text of Decree No. 1060/2026, published on the Head of State’s official website.

title: DStv unveils four new subscription packages with prices from GH¢50 to GH¢570
body: MultiChoice Ghana has announced four new DStv subscription packages, with monthly prices ranging from GH¢50 to GH¢570, as part of efforts to provide subscribers with more affordable and flexible viewing options. The packages, which take effect on November 5, 2026, were unveiled at a joint press briefing organised by the Ministry of Communications, Digital Technology and Innovation and MultiChoice Ghana on Monday, October 26. Speaking at the briefing, the Country Chief Executive Officer of MultiChoice Ghana, Alex Okyere, explained that the new packages offer different channel selections, sports coverage and entertainment content to suit subscribers’ budgets and viewing preferences. Under the new arrangement, the Starter Pack, priced at GH¢50 per month, provides access to 90 television channels, making it the most affordable option. The Select Pack, which costs GH¢100 monthly, offers 123 channels, providing subscribers with a broader range of entertainment and television programmes. For sports enthusiasts, the Sports Pack, priced at GH¢250 per month, provides football coverage alongside channels available under the Starter and Select packages. The Ultimate Pack, costing GH¢570 monthly, is the highest-priced option, combining premium sports coverage with a wider selection of entertainment content. MultiChoice Ghana explained that the revised subscription structure is intended to give customers greater flexibility in choosing packages that meet their entertainment needs and financial circumstances. The new pricing arrangement will officially come into effect on November 5, allowing subscribers to select from the four packages based on their preferred content and monthly budgets.

title: Defense Forces strikes communications hub, command posts, supply depots belonging to Russian troops – AFU
body:
On Sunday and into Monday night, units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a communications hub, command posts, a drone control center, a UAV workshop, and warehouses containing logistical supplies belonging to Russian troops in the temporarily occupied territories of Zaporizhia, Donetsk, and Luhansk regions.
According to a Telegram post by the press service of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), a communications hub belonging to a Russian unit was struck near Melitopol in Zaporizhia region, and the occupiers' command posts were struck in the vicinity of Myrnohrad in Donetsk region and the village of Chervonohirka in Zaporizhia region.
In addition, an enemy drone command post was struck near the town of Vyshneve, and a UAV workshop was struck near Melitopol.
The Defense Forces also struck Russian army logistics depots near the settlements of Komisarivka and Katerynivka in Luhansk region.
As noted by the General Staff, striking a communications hub disrupts the enemy's communications and command and control, while destroying command posts complicates the coordination of its units on the battlefield. The destruction of the command post and the UAV workshop reduces the Russian troops' ability to attack the Defense Forces' positions and frontline communities with drones, while the destruction of the supply depots hinders the resupply of Russian units.

title: Russia considers important to support reliable gas supplies — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russia considers important to provide for reliable and stable gas supplies, taking into account growing needs across the globe, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said.
"Considering growing gas needs, we consider important to ensure stability and reliability of supplies and guarantee further confident development of countries," he said.
"This is particularly so that Russia, being a responsible player on the global gas market, ranks first globally in terms of natural gas reserves and second in its production," the presidential aide noted.

title: PM Koretskyi: We expect Ukraine and Moldova to join EU together
body:
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi made the statement at a joint briefing with Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“We appreciate and respect the progress Moldova has made toward reforms and the implementation of legislation. Ukraine is taking many significant steps along this path. We therefore expect both countries to be able to meet all the requirements at the same time and move toward joining the European Union together,” Koretskyi said.
He stressed that the accession of both countries to the EU is important for the security of Ukraine and Moldova, as well as the entire region. Synchronized integration also has an economic dimension, as the two countries are closely connected by transport corridors and have strong trade ties.
“Moving toward EU membership together will help develop cross-border trade, attract investment and integrate our economies into the EU market,” Koretskyi added.
He also thanked his Moldovan counterpart for Moldova’s consistent support for Ukraine and for constructive dialogue.
As reported, Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan arrived in Kyiv on Monday, October 26, for a working visit.

title: Trade turnover between Russia, African countries above $27 bln in 2025 — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The trade turnover between Russia and African nations was above $27 bln in 2025 and increased by 1.5 times since 2023, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters.
"The Russian trade turnover with African countries exceeded $27 bln last year. It means this indicator increased by 1.5 times from our previous summit in St. Petersburg, which was held in 2023. Dynamics is good but actions could have been even more efficient," Ushakov said.
Russia has 22 bilateral intergovernmental commissions with African countries, the diplomat noted. "This is quite a lot," Ushakov added.
Russia sent more than 18 mln metric tons of grain to Africa last year and 13 mln metric tons more were shipped during the nine months of this year, he said.
"In 2025, we shipped over 18 mln tons of grain to Africa, and 13 mln [tons] more during the first nine months of this year," Ushakov said.

title: UBA launches Group-Wide Climate Action Week to advance green finance and sustainability across Africa
body:
Africa’s Global Bank, United Bank for Africa (UBA) Plc, has launched a Group-wide Climate Action Week to deepen climate awareness, promote responsible environmental practices and advance sustainable finance across its African and international operations.
The five-day campaign, running from 26 to 30 October 2026, is themed “Banking on Africa’s Climate Future” and reflects the Bank’s commitment to integrating environmental responsibility into its operations, customer engagement and financing solutions.
The initiative commenced with the deployment of waste segregation bins across UBA offices and measures to reduce the use of single-use plastics at the Bank’s head offices. These activities underscore UBA’s commitment to translating sustainability principles into practical actions within its workplace and across its wider ecosystem.
Throughout the week, UBA will disseminate educational content across its media and digital platforms to highlight the causes and consequences of climate change, including its impact on food prices, energy consumption and urban flooding. The campaign will also promote responsible plastic disposal, recycling and the critical role of financial institutions in financing clean energy, sustainable agriculture and other environmentally responsible businesses.
As part of the campaign’s community engagement component, UBA staff volunteers will participate in a Group-wide clean-up exercise on Saturday, 7 November in major cities across its markets. In Nigeria, the exercise will take place in Lagos, Kano and Port Harcourt, mobilising employees to contribute directly to cleaner and healthier communities.
UBA’s Group Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer, Oliver Alawuba, emphasised the importance of collective responsibility in addressing the growing impact of climate change.
“Climate change is no longer a distant environmental concern; it is increasingly shaping everyday life across Africa. We see its effects in rising food costs, increased energy demand and flooding that disrupts homes, businesses and livelihoods.
“At UBA, we believe that building a sustainable future requires collective action, beginning with the choices we make at work, at home and in our communities. Through this Climate Action Week, we are encouraging every member of the UBA Tribe, alongside our customers and other stakeholders, to embrace practical, sustainable habits and inspire others to do the same,” Alawuba said.
As part of its stakeholder engagement activities, UBA will sponsor Climate Convergence Week in Lagos on Friday, 30 October where the Bank will deliver a speaking session and participate in a panel discussion. The engagement will provide an opportunity to showcase UBA Green Finance, highlight the Bank’s sustainability initiatives and explore how financial institutions can support Africa’s transition to a more sustainable and climate-resilient economy.
Alawuba, noted that climate considerations were increasingly important to business resilience, risk management and long-term economic growth.
“Climate change presents significant risks to businesses, communities and economies. These risks can affect business continuity, operating costs and financial performance, making sustainability an increasingly important consideration for both businesses and the financial institutions that support them.
“Through UBA Green Finance, we seek to support eligible businesses investing in cleaner technologies and more sustainable operations. By helping customers explore financing solutions aligned with their needs, we can contribute to a more resilient private sector while unlocking opportunities for sustainable economic growth across Africa,” Alawuba further said.
In a step towards further strengthening its sustainability capabilities, UBA is set to join the Sustainability Professionals Institute of Nigeria (SPIN). The move is expected to deepen the Bank’s environmental, social and governance (ESG) expertise and support the continued professional development of its employees in sustainability-related disciplines.
The Climate Action Week forms part of UBA’s broader sustainability strategy, which integrates environmental responsibility into its Customer First philosophy through responsible business practices, employee engagement, community initiatives and green finance. By combining awareness, practical action and financing solutions, the Bank aims to encourage more sustainable choices while supporting businesses and communities in navigating the challenges and opportunities of climate change.
United Bank for Africa is one of Africa’s leading financial institutions and one of the largest employers in the continent’s financial sector, with approximately 25,000 employees and over 45 million customers globally. Operating in 20 African countries, as well as the United Kingdom, the United States of America, France and the United Arab Emirates, UBA provides retail, commercial and institutional banking services, advancing financial inclusion and leveraging technology to deliver innovative financial solutions.

title: Shoga: City Boy Movt’s Efforts Contributed To Success Of APC’s Kaduna Rally
body: .Says inauguration of Abuja–Kaduna highway opens economic platform for N’West Folalumi Alaran in Abuja Director-General of the City Boy Movement (CBM), Hon. Oluwatosin Shoga, has attributed the large turnout of youth at Saturday’s flag-off of the All Progressives Congress (APC) re-election campaign of President Bola Tinubu in Kaduna as an affirmation of the Movement’s sustained grassroots enlightenment and mobilisation efforts in support of the President. According to him, the impressive youth participation at the rally demonstrated growing interest among young Nigerians in the Tinubu’s development programme and their determination to participate actively in determining Nigeria’s political and economic future. In a reflection titled, “Beyond the Road: Unlocking Opportunities, Empowering Young Nigerians, and Building a Prosperous Future,” released in Abuja, the CBM boss attributed the enthusiasm witnessed at the Kaduna rally partly to sustained grassroots engagements, including the Movement’s mobilisation activities and street walk in Kano. His words: “The City Boy Movement was proudly on the ground, engaging with young Nigerians and grassroots supporters who came out to demonstrate their commitment to the future of our country. “The enthusiasm witnessed in Kaduna, alongside our grassroots engagement and street walk in Kano, reinforces our conviction that young Nigerians want to be part of a national conversation about development, opportunity, and a more prosperous Nigeria.” Shoga stressed that the Movement’s activities extended beyond mobilising electoral support for Tinubu, adding that its central mission was to educate and empower young people to understand government policies and take advantage of emerging economic opportunities. He referenced the inauguration of an 81-kilometre section of the Abuja–Kaduna highway during the campaign flag-off, describing the development as a demonstration of the Tinubu administration’s commitment to improving infrastructure and stimulating economic activities in the North-West. According to him, the strategic road corridor linking Abuja, Kaduna, Zaria and Kano offers opportunities for agricultural transformation, industrial expansion, regional trade, private investment and employment generation. He noted that improved connectivity could benefit farmers, traders, transport operators and young entrepreneurs by facilitating access to markets, reducing transportation difficulties and encouraging investments in logistics, manufacturing, food processing and related businesses. “The objective is not simply to build infrastructure. It is to create the conditions in which people can build businesses, earn sustainable incomes, create jobs, and improve their standard of living”. Shoga, however, emphasised that infrastructure development must be complemented by sustained security operations, effective intelligence gathering, reliable electricity and investment-friendly policies to unlock the region’s full economic potential. “A good road connects destinations. A secure road connects people to opportunity. Together, infrastructure and security can help unlock the economic potential of an entire region”, he further said.

title: Natural gas demand to grow by 28% by 2055 — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The natural gas demand is predicted to grow by 28% to 5.4 trillion cubic meters by 2055, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters.
"The requirement for the [Gas Exporting Countries] Forum as a traditional mechanism is rather significant. In view of the growing demand for the natural gas globally, it will grow, according to forecasts, from 4.2 trillion cubic meters at present to 5.4 trillion cubic meters, meaning an increase by about 28%," Ushakov said.
The GECF members are Russia, Algeria, Venezuela, Egypt, Iran, Qatar, Libya, Nigeria, Trinidad and Tobago, Equatorial Guinea and the United Arab Emirates. Eight observer countries are Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru, and Senegal.

title: Wazirin Tinubu: The influence and burden of Ibrahim Masari, By Umar Farouk Bala
body:
As a young Nigerian involved in TMS, the political culture I want to see is one grounded in evidence, respectful dialogue, accountability and measurable performance. If Masari’s political philosophy truly rests on results over rhetoric and honest engagement over inflated claims, then those principles deserve attention.
When the Tinubu Movement for Sustainable Governance Foundation, widely known as Tinubu Must Stay (TMS), inaugurated its national leadership in Abuja, I accepted the responsibility of serving as its National Youth Leader. For me, it was more than an appointment. It raised a larger question about the political culture into which young Nigerians are being invited.
The Foundation’s structure includes a Board of Trustees, National Coordinators and six directorates focused on citizen engagement and evidence-based communication. It is chaired by Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, director-general of NITDA, while Dr Benjamin Obi Nwoye serves as national coordinator (South). Former Obidient coordinator, Marcel Ngogbehei, was appointed director-general, with Engineer Ibrahim Uba overseeing mobilisation and data management.
At its inauguration, Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi emphasised simplifying government reforms, connecting data to everyday realities and confronting misinformation through technology-driven outreach, town halls and grassroots engagement. Benjamin Obi Nwoye similarly argued that many government interventions remain inadequately communicated.
Since then, one question has stayed with me: What values should define the politics young Nigerians inherit?
For me, that conversation leads naturally to Ibrahim Kabir Masari, special adviser to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu on political affairs and an increasingly influential figure in the president’s northern political engagement.
At the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council in Abuja on 14 October, Masari reportedly challenged party leaders to abandon inflated claims about votes and focus instead on measurable results at state, ward and polling unit levels. His instruction was strikingly simple: “Stop talking to yourselves and start talking to the people.” He also urged campaigners to explain the administration’s work in areas such as education, healthcare, economic reform and infrastructure; to acknowledge outstanding challenges; and avoid misinformation and hate speech.
That message matters because young Nigerians increasingly demand more than slogans. We want evidence. We want to be listened to. We want claims that can be measured against our own experiences.
Masari’s political journey also offers context for understanding his approach. His background includes service as national welfare secretary of the All Progressives Congress. In 2022, his name was submitted to INEC as Tinubu’s temporary running mate before Kashim Shettima emerged as the substantive vice presidential candidate. Masari stepped aside, saying the decision would give Tinubu greater flexibility to accommodate wider interests. Following the 2023 election, he was appointed senior special assistant on political affairs and was later elevated to special adviser on political affairs.
But perhaps the most symbolic indication of his growing political profile is the title increasingly associated with him: “Wazirin Tinubu.”
President Tinubu has publicly addressed Masari as “My Waziri.” In northern Nigerian usage, the traditional title carries connotations of counsel, responsibility and proximity to leadership. In this context, it is better understood as an expression of presidential trust than as a constitutional office.
Yet this is precisely where admiration should give way to scrutiny.
The significance of being Wazirin Tinubu cannot ultimately be measured by access to the president, titles or public recognition. It must be measured by what that access produces.
A trusted political adviser occupies one of the most sensitive spaces in government. He must understand the president’s priorities while remaining alert to the concerns of party members, elected representatives and citizens. He must know when to speak and when to listen, when to intervene and when restraint is more useful. Such a position demands discretion, political maturity and the capacity to reconcile competing interests. That are exactly what he does in promoting and protecting the reputation of President Tinubu.
For Masari, therefore, presidential confidence is both an advantage and a burden. Influence creates access, but access creates responsibility.
Recent reports have portrayed him as a significant convener in northern politics and one of the Ppresident’s closest political figures in the region. Such influence will naturally attract scrutiny, and it should. The closer any political adviser stands to presidential power, the more legitimate the public interest becomes in how that access is exercised.
This is why I find his emphasis on measurable performance important. If political leaders insist that campaign organisers should abandon exaggerated claims, communicate honestly and speak directly to citizens, then those principles should also become the standards against which their own influence is judged.
For those of us trying to encourage greater youth participation in public affairs, this distinction is crucial. Young Nigerians should not be introduced to a political culture in which proximity to power is itself an achievement. We should be introduced to one in which access creates an obligation to solve problems, listen to inconvenient truths and help government understand citizens beyond the atmosphere of political praise.
Nor should evidence-based politics mean communicating only achievements. Credibility also requires acknowledging shortcomings. A genuine conversation about government must have room for what worked, what did not work and what still needs correction. Otherwise, “evidence-based communication” risks becoming another sophisticated name for political marketing.
This is perhaps the heavier meaning behind the Waziri symbolism. Counsel is valuable when it tells power what it needs to hear, not merely what it wants to hear.
Ibrahim Kabir Masari today occupies a position from which political relationships can be built and disagreements mediated. His emergence as one of Tinubu’s prominent northern political interlocutors makes his choices consequential.
The ultimate question, therefore, is not how close Masari is to the president. It is what that closeness achieves for governance and political engagement.
As a young Nigerian involved in TMS, the political culture I want to see is one grounded in evidence, respectful dialogue, accountability and measurable performance. If Masari’s political philosophy truly rests on results over rhetoric and honest engagement over inflated claims, then those principles deserve attention.
But they also deserve consistent application. Because the greater the influence, the heavier the responsibility. And for Wazirin Tinubu, that may ultimately be the real burden of presidential trust which he has so far performed exceedingly well.
Umar Farouk Bala is national youth leader of Tinubu Must Stay (TMS).

title: Egyptian parliament approves military aid to Saudi Arabia — TV
body:
CAIRO, October 26. /TASS/. Egypt’s House of Representatives, the lower house of parliament, has approved military aid to Saudi Arabia, according to state television channel Al-Qahera Al-Ekhbariya.
It said this concerns "support in defense-related matters." No other details were provided.
According to Article 152 of the Egyptian constitution, the declaring of war and sending the army on foreign missions is discussed by the country’s National Defense Council and the House of Representatives.
The Egyptian National Defense Council approved aid to Saudi Arabia on October 18.

title: Filmmaker Paweł Pawlikowski grew up in a world where the Cold War made everything seem clear. Today’s world, he says, feels like science fiction.
body: After festival premieres in Cannes, Telluride, Toronto, New York, and London and its selection as Poland’s Oscar entry, Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland” is opening in theaters worldwide. The film follows German writer Thomas Mann’s journey through postwar Germany. One of the season’s standout films and a deserving winner of the best director prize at Cannes, it has prompted critics to draw comparisons between Europe in the 1940s and Europe today. Anton Dolin spoke with Pawlikowski about the similarities and differences. — Would you say “Fatherland” completes a trilogy that began with “Ida” (2013) and “ Cold War ” (2018)? — I wish my ideas came together as neatly and logically as film critics imagine! “I think I’ll make a trilogy about postwar Europe, and I’ll shoot it in black and white.” Back then, “Ida” grew out of a period of confusion and searching, out of my exhaustion with trying to make “normal movies.” Everything irritated me; I wanted to change something. With “Ida,” I felt as though I’d gone back to cinema’s starting point: black-and-white images, static shots, a small budget, minimalism. Those constraints worked beautifully. I found the work easier and more interesting. That was also when I met Łukasz Żal, who’s now my cinematographer. We immediately knew we were a good fit. That’s how I’ve shot films ever since: I compose every shot like a photograph, don’t show too much, and don’t move the camera unless it’s absolutely necessary. The story and the relationships between the main characters are all that drives the action. It’s a challenge! So is the somewhat contradictory task of making a meticulously composed film in a documentary style. Documentary footage is inherently spontaneous and doesn’t offer the control over framing that I’m after. “Ida,” 2013 “Ida,” 2013 “Ida,” 2013 “Ida,” 2013 — Your new film resembles the previous two in its visual style and period setting, but it’s also different. For the first time, it centers on real people — Thomas Mann and his family — and events that actually happened. — That came about through a series of coincidences. It started when my German producers sent me a biography of Mann. It was an incredibly absorbing read, but there was no way to turn it into a film — it covered far too much, too many stages of his life and too many events. Biopics don’t interest me, and I don’t dare take on a TV series. One episode caught my attention: the writer’s trip to Germany in 1949. I started looking for other sources and reading everything I could about it. Thomas’s own diaries and letters, his driver’s memoirs — because on that trip he was actually accompanied by his driver, rather than his daughter Erika . But Erika’s writings proved useful too: there was another trip a year later, this time with her. They went to Weimar for an anniversary celebration in Schiller’s honor. The research took quite a while. I was drawn to the lives of the Mann family — Erika’s dilemmas, Klaus’s personal drama. And suddenly I decided to try to distill it all into a single road movie, fitting the events that interested me into five days and adding a few important supporting characters from the Manns’ lives. “Fatherland,” 2026 — Why Thomas Mann in particular? — During the war, he became a kind of respected institution in his own right. He managed to maintain an impeccable reputation throughout those years. You can’t say that about the early years of Nazism — Mann certainly had things to reproach himself for then. The situation felt far too familiar to ignore. A system collapses, and aggressive narratives rush to fill the void — each doing everything it can to draw you into its orbit. Analogies are never exact! Back then, there weren’t any “digital bubbles” with their simplistic agendas, but there were other, rather similar bubbles. Thomas Mann tried to overcome them, to burst them open with universal human values: culture, literature, and the humanist tradition. He was the “good German,” the ideal embodiment of a view from the other side, someone who could offer common ground… Of course, it didn’t work. “Fatherland,” 2026 But Mann’s story also shows what happens when you have a public mission and something in your personal life that doesn’t quite fit with it (the suicide of his son Klaus — Meduza) . The reasons were, let’s say, historical: Klaus wasn’t just a drug addict but a lost soul — a German without a Germany, a writer without a language he could write and publish in. None of his attempts to write in English succeeded, and he didn’t know whom he was writing his books for. Unlike his father, Klaus was neither an institution nor a Nobel laureate. Still, you can’t explain it all through external circumstances: there was a tangled web of relationships within the family. Almost a love triangle, with Erika at its center: she loves both her brother and her father, both are very fragile and weak, and she wants to help them both but doesn’t know how. It turned into something like a Greek tragedy against the tragic backdrop of postwar Europe, divided between two visions of the future, neither of which seemed entirely satisfactory. — The Cold War seems to be the period that interests you most. Is that only because of the parallels with the present? — It resonates, of course. There’s no denying that. But what exactly resonates? The world today is too complicated; we can’t fully understand what’s happening around us. I certainly can’t. If only I could read an intelligent book about what’s going on in the world now, written, say, 20 years from now… We’ve ended up in what feels like a science-fiction story. But I grew up during the Cold War, and it shaped my parents in Soviet-controlled Poland. It’s easier for me to identify with that generation and the political world of my childhood, with “analog people,” with an era of relative clarity. Back then, the West symbolized freedom and liberal values for us, and the Soviet Union meant subjugation. That was clear! I certainly feel some nostalgia for that world, where things were simpler. “Cold War,” 2018 “Cold War,” 2018 “Cold War,” 2018 — Which particular similarities between that era and today might have influenced the making of “Fatherland”? — None of it influenced me consciously. It was more a vague feeling that there were already far too many similarities. Klaus’s opening monologue is very close to how I feel: What can you believe in, what can you hold on to, when you feel as though you’re sinking into quicksand? It’s very personal. So is Thomas’s situation. For instance, I wasn’t thinking about Putin’s Russia, although Russians keep telling me how interesting and relatable they find the film. Emigrants in particular. But I’m an emigrant myself. I left Poland at 14, lived in Britain, Germany, and France, and spent years not knowing what language to write and make films in, or what audience to address! I went through a Russian phase, too — I was deeply fascinated by the country. That’s passed now, though, for obvious reasons… — Aren’t you worried that historians and experts will criticize you for inaccuracies and altered facts? — I don’t pretend that “Fatherland” follows what actually happened step by step. Quite the opposite: the facts are just a framework for my screenplay, and I allow myself as much invention as the plot requires. This film isn’t a reconstruction or a biopic. My conscience is clear. I still felt uneasy at times, and I consoled myself with the thought that I was trying to capture the emotional truth. For instance, when Klaus killed himself, his father, Thomas, was in Stockholm, not Germany. But he’d gone there to give a lecture on Goethe, and he didn’t change his plans to attend his son’s funeral on the French Riviera. He shut out his emotions, he was angry with Klaus… Erika didn’t go either; she felt paralyzed. I think I portrayed all her dilemmas and inner torment truthfully. I certainly imagined and invented a lot, but I always started from the truth — except, perhaps, for one thing: No German ever saw Thomas Mann cry. “Fatherland,” 2026 — What about Mann’s speeches on Goethe? At times they sound almost like parodies in your film, although the texts are authentic. — There’s a simple reason for that effect: Context matters too. I don’t think Mann’s speeches were ill-timed or foolish at all. He just had no chance of being heard and understood. He was certainly right to invoke “Faust” and utopian ideas about building a new society when addressing East Germany’s pro-Soviet authorities. In Mann’s view, utopia is unattainable because the flaws and risks are already built into the ideal, before anyone even tries to put it into practice. Still, I think Mann felt more warmly toward his East German readers and listeners. At least they were trying, in their own way, to rid themselves of Nazism and start building a new, fairer society. The West was mired in confusion and chaos; people there weren’t even setting themselves those goals. Don’t forget, Stalinist repression wasn’t common knowledge in Europe at the time. And here’s another historical fact, though the circumstances were a little different. Mann really was asked to mention the persecution of dissenters in East Germany in his speech, and he decided not to because he thought his mission was something else, something “more significant.” — How did you end up shooting a film about Germany in Poland? — We spent a long time choosing locations very carefully and traveled all over Germany. The screenplay was complicated, the budget wasn’t huge, but we needed a certain level of accuracy. We concluded that it would be easier to find the ruins we needed in Poland. Many of them are sets we built ourselves. I’d say the landscape isn’t all that different. We didn’t want to cut archival footage into what we were shooting, and it took work to recreate an authentic setting in front of the camera. And then… casting, finding extras in the towns and villages where we filmed. That took an especially long time. I didn’t want anyone on screen who looked like someone from today. We needed people from a very, very wide range of social backgrounds, so we put a huge amount of time and money into it. But I believe it worked and really shaped the film’s look and feel. Łukasz Żal is a true painter; he’s extremely exacting, and I’m happy with the result. Paweł Pawlikowski and cinematographer Łukasz Żal — Thomas Mann is an immensely interesting character for a drama — or a comedy. What about as a writer? — He’s become increasingly important to me over the years. I can’t say I love his work all that much. I have a complicated relationship with the novels. Five years ago, I finally slogged through “The Magic Mountain.” It all depends on what you value in literature, whether you can enjoy meticulous, elegant, detailed descriptions of human feelings. When I was young, that irritated me; it seemed mannered. But this time I was able to finish it and enjoy it. Still, I rate the novellas more highly — “Tonio Kröger,” “Death in Venice.” At any rate, I respect Mann as a writer. That just wasn’t what prompted me to make this film. It’s as a central character that he interests me. The language he created for himself in his books became his identity. He hid in a castle of words, and he didn’t deny it. Hiding the truth about himself, including his sexuality , he sublimated it in literature. — And what’s your relationship with Goethe and Bach — the film’s other points of reference? — Like Thomas Mann, Goethe lived a very long life and went through many different phases, from the Romantic Sturm und Drang movement and the wave of suicides he inspired to classicism. What Mann revered in him, and tried in his own way to emulate, was that ability to synthesize, to bring different elements together — rather than revel narcissistically in his own development as an artist. To try to understand humanity rather than one particular person, to bring people together rather than divide them: That was his overarching ambition. Thomas Mann thought he could try applying that approach to postwar Germany, drawing on the poet’s wisdom to overcome the weaknesses of different ideologies. Bach, of course, is also a cornerstone of art, with all his work rooted in his faith and his devotion to the Luther Bible. Art often confronts us with unbearable questions: Whose side are you on — Stalin’s or Mickey Mouse’s? I understand that those questions are legitimate, but I feel I’d betray myself as an artist if I made that choice and gave up a fuller picture of how the world works. But sometimes that very loyalty to broad truths is a betrayal of yourself, because it can make you lose sight of individual people and their pain. title: Ex-GitHub CEO launches a GitHub rival that reinvents the pull request
body: Entire, the startup founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke , on Monday launched its GitHub alternative that replaces the traditional pull request model with a new agentic code review system called Trails. The company has been launching parts of its platform since it announced a $60 million seed round in February. Early on, Dohmke occasionally noted he wasn’t planning to compete with GitHub. But with Monday’s launch, Entire is launching a full GitHub alternative, with its own twist on what a modern GitHub for the agentic era should look like. At launch, Entire supports native hosting for private repositories. Public repositories and self-hosted Git nodes are still on the roadmap. Slide from Thomas Dohmke’s keynote last week at AGNTcon+MCPcon. (Credit: The New Stack ) “It’s the moment we’ve been waiting for,” Dohmke told The New Stack last week during an interview at the Linux Foundation’s AGNTCon + MCPcon in San Jose, California. “It’s exciting for us because what we set out to do a year ago is landing now — and bringing the Git hosting and the infrastructure layer together, with sites around the world, […] and the idea of continuous integration, continuous delivery, continuous memory, and then with Trails, our reinvention of the pull request.” “It’s exciting for us because what we set out to do a year ago is landing now.” Entire, like other devtools startups, argues that the new bottleneck for developers isn’t writing the code — agents take care of that — but code review. Unlike some other startups in this space, the company isn’t solely focused on that. Instead, the Entire is betting that solving the code review bottleneck requires an entirely new platform. In his keynote at AGNTCon + MCPcon, Dohmke described a review queue growing in two directions: agents producing more changes, and those changes containing more code. “I open a pull request, and I realize I have no idea what all that code does,” he says of his previous experience using coding agents. Right now, that platform consists of Entire’s Git-compatible server, the continuous memory feature for agents that the company originally launched with, and Trails. Entire Trails. (Credit: Entire) From pull requests to Trails Trails is Entire’s take on the pull request model , but instead of developers reviewing code changes manually, Trails gives them a dashboard with customizable evals scored by agents. That system may assess how risky a code change is, for example, or how much intent drift has occurred over a long LLM-driven development session. Entire says those evals run on every push, with findings available through both its web interface and its open-source CLI. Coding agents can then use that feedback to address problems and push another revision, while the developer validates the progress. In the end, the original request, the agent’s session history, and the resulting code all become part of the review. GitHub already offers agentic code review through Copilot . Entire’s pitch goes beyond adding an AI reviewer to a pull request: It makes the intent behind a change and the agent’s work part of the review process alongside the code. For Entire, the idea here is that if the evals come back green, it’s ok to merge the code without a detailed human review (though few human code reviews are probably as detailed as they should be). By default, Entire provides preset review agents, but developers can also define their own configurations in a JSON file and choose among supported Claude and OpenAI models. “We’re redefining how the developer lifecycle works, and it’s really cool. I’ve been at home in the evenings, sitting on my couch, and texting my agents — all the while getting links from my team to their Trails on Slack and opening them.” “We’re redefining how the developer lifecycle works, and it’s really cool,” Dohmke says. “I’ve been at home in the evenings, sitting on my couch, and texting my agents — all the while getting links from my team to their Trails on Slack and opening them. And because the user interface is designed for seeing — we’re calling it the head-up display for the pilots– so I look at my head-up display, and I see the ‘stop cop,’ one of the evals that we have internally, and if that’s green and the confidence is high, then we’re merging it.” Entire is also partnering with Buildkite and Depot for CI. Developers can convert their existing GitHub Actions workflows using Buildkite’s bk pipeline or Depot CI, then connect the repository in Entire. A faster, distributed Git forge While Trails is the headline news here, Entire’s core is its Git-compatible distributed source control server, which debuted earlier this summer. Entire says it can push up to 89x faster than GitHub and 6x faster than Cursor’s Origin. But while a distributed system with mirrors across geographic regions helps, the key feature for many corporate users may be that Entire was built from the outset to offer private repositories in specific regions, too. Given today’s data governance landscape, that’s an increasingly important feature. The available regions include the U.S., Europe, India, and Australia. Dohmke says customers choose a primary region and can add mirrors elsewhere, with Entire handling synchronization between them. Memory for agents Continuous Memory is Entire’s third pillar. It syncs AI agent sessions into a project’s repository and makes that available to the agents for future use. For Dohmke, those sessions also preserve the approaches a developer rejected and the moments when they told an agent that working code still wasn’t what they wanted. The company says the system combines a codebase graph that helps agents find relevant code with an “agentic brain” that turns previous sessions and prompts into memories they can query. That lets agents retrieve earlier decisions and the context behind them when they start another task. Dohmke expects agent run costs to become the next bottleneck, with teams paying closer attention to token efficiency alongside engineering productivity. He argues that developers may find it’s cheaper to use an existing open-source project or a service like Entire than to spend tokens generating their own replacement. The platform is free; however, Dohmke says customers pay only for the tokens the review agents consume. But because these review agents run on LLMs, they still cost money. Right now, Dohmke says, Entire is giving all its users a $100 starter credit. Once users have run out of these credits, they will pay market rates for the model of their choosing. The arbitrage between the discounts it can get and that market rate seems to be Entire’s current business model. GitHub has always had very generous plans for open-source projects, and its maintainers and Dohmke hinted that the company may offer help there as well, noting that Entire is already working with some partners, including model vendors, on ideas. “More to come,” he says. Also of note: Entire’s announcements on Monday come two days before the 2026 edition of GitHub Universe, the company’s flagship developer event in San Francisco. What timing. The post Ex-GitHub CEO launches a GitHub rival that reinvents the pull request appeared first on The New Stack .

Kazakhstan had reason to cheer after receiving a commitment from the International Finance Corporation to help develop infrastructure projects worth $3 billion. But that happy foreign investment news was offset by an international arbitration court’s decision to throw out $12 billion in Kazakh claims against Western oil giants in a dispute over the development of the Kashagan oil field.
The IFC, the World Bank’s private-sector wing, will get involved in projects covering the 2026-31 period, focusing on fostering public-private partnerships (PPPs), the Kazakh State Agency for Strategic Planning and Reform announced October 21. The IFC will provide advisory services via Kazakhstan’s Joint Economic Research Program. Projects will aim to expand transport infrastructure and achieve efficiencies in the management of water resources.
The involvement of PPPs “not only facilitates private investment but also enhances the quality of infrastructure design, construction, and operation throughout the entire lifecycle of the assets,” according to an agency statement.
The same day Astana announced the IFC investment, Kazakh officials received the unwelcome news that the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague had excluded $12 billion in Kashagan-related claims, Bloomberg reported . The court asserted that Kazakhstan’s claims covering the $12 billion, costs allegedly incurred between 2011-15, were filed after the statute of limitations had run out. The court let stand another $8 billion in claims, however.
Kazakhstan is seeking compensation from a consortium of oil companies dominated by Western oil majors, including ExxonMobil, Shell and TotalEnergies, for what Astana claims were delays and cost overruns in the development of the Kashagan field, which sits just offshore in the Caspian Sea, near the Kazakh city of Atyrau. The field’s development posed an engineering challenge given the sea’s shallow depth and variable weather conditions, ranging from high heat in summer to frigid winter temperatures.
Kashagan is estimated to hold upwards of 13 billion barrels of recoverable reserves, according to the US Energy Information Agency (USEIA).
Citing Kashagan’s “adverse operating environment and complexity,” USEIA in a background report noted that Kashagan began pumping oil in 2016 after years of delays and “significant cost overruns.”
“[Kashagan’s] reservoir contains high levels of hydrogen sulfide, which is both highly toxic and highly corrosive and has been blamed for pipeline leaks,” the USEIA report stated. “In addition, conventional drilling and production technologies such as fixed or floating platforms cannot be used because of the shallow water and cold climate. Instead, offshore facilities are installed on artificial islands (drilling and hub islands) that house drilling and processing equipment.”
In addition to seeking compensation for Kashagan delays and overruns, Kazakh officials are pursuing separate claims of over $130 billion in lost revenue relating to production delays. ExxonMobil maintains that further development of Kashagan cannot proceed until the arbitration cases are settled.
Kazakhstan’s oil production for the first eight months of 2026 stood at 61.7 million tons, representing an 8.4 percent decline compared to the same period in 2025. Kazakh officials in August downwardly revised estimates for annual production in 2026 to 96 million tons: the country pumped just under 100 million tons last year. Russia-Ukraine war-related disruption to Kazakhstan’s main oil export route, the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, is a major factor in hampering the country’s oil production.

title: Everything old is new again with the Fitbit Edge
body:
Last week, I sank into my living room couch and watched a bedraggled, nihilistic Matthew McConaughey take a drag of a cigarette in season 1 of True Detective. “You know, someone once told me time is a flat circle. Everything we’ve done, or will do, we’re gonna do over and over and over again.” I assume most people aren’t thinking about fitness trackers or gadgets while watching that scene. But in that moment, I couldn’t help but think about the Fitbit Edge on my wrist.
The $179.99 Edge is a modernized version of the 2014-to-2020 era of fitness bands — your Charges, your Altas, your Inspires. If you’ve ever owned one, you already know the vast majority of what the Edge is like. It’s lightweight. You swipe on a small display that shows you basic health and fitness metrics. It lasts for about a week on a charge — though that shrunk down to about a day and a half with the always-on display enabled. It’s a device that isn’t trying to be much more than what it is.
[Product: Fitbit Edge | https://www.amazon.com/Google-Fitbit-Edge-glanceable-quick-charging/dp/B0HG61DKC8/?tag=theverge02-20, https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/101881227/type/dlg/https://store.google.com/product/google_fitbit_edge?hl=en-US, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fgoogle-fitbit-edge-advanced-fitness-health-tracker-with-colored-display-works-with-android-and-ios-obsidian-2026%2FJ39TC826ZP%2Fsku%2F6689374]
The difference is that the Edge feels more refined on the wrist. Where the Fitbit Charge 6’s display felt boxy, the Edge is fully rounded, giving it a softer vibe. The straps are interchangeable, but with an easier button-release system. The metal link bracelet gives it a more jewelry-like feel, though it costs almost as much as the Edge itself at $150. I’m partial to the $60 magnetic strap, which mimics leather despite being made of silicone. The widgets borrow heavily from the Pixel Watch’s Material 3 Expressive redesign. Though to be clear, this is a proprietary Fitbit OS, not Wear OS. Some of the new watchfaces are elegant, though others highlight the Edge’s big black bezels. (Some things truly never change.)
Functionally, it’s also a step above the Fitbit Air. There’s built-in GPS for tracking walks and runs without your phone. You can have alarms, view notifications, and control music. You can’t take calls on the wrist — there are no microphones or speakers. Contactless payments are also a no-go. Andy Abramson, head of product at Google Health, says that’s because “less than one percent [of Charge 6 owners] used the feature” and that Google instead prioritized a “sleek design, altimeter, and weeklong battery.” That walks back some of the advancements that have come to the Charge lineup over the years, but if you want to put a silver lining on that, it narrows the Edge’s focus. This is a fitness tracker. There’s some glanceable information, but there’s absolutely no smartwatch creep here.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268783_Fitbit_edge_AKrales_0077.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268783_Fitbit_edge_AKrales_0052.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268783_Fitbit_edge_AKrales_0126.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The big software change is the demise of the Fitbit app as we knew it. It’s Google Health now, with an AI coach if you pony up for the yearly subscription. (You get three months free with purchase; otherwise it’s $10 monthly.) I’ve written about the overall experience in my Fitbit Air review. The broad strokes are the same, though in the months since, Google has spent a lot of time tinkering with and iterating on it. Most notably, the company has beefed up automatic activity tracking.
To test this, I tracked a handful of runs on the Edge without officially starting an activity. I then compared that to one tracked by an Apple Watch Ultra 4 and my iPhone’s Runna app. I was surprised, but noticed limitations. For example, on a 2.4-mile run with a five-minute warmup walk and cooldown, the Edge correctly identified the exact moment my warmup transitioned into a legit run and then back into a walk. The estimated distance was also pretty decent at 2.55 miles. It wasn’t quite as good at gauging my running speed. It logged me as running a 10’49” mile pace, whereas my actual pace according to the Apple Watch and my phone was 11’38”. This pattern was fairly typical across my testing, so it’s more that this is a nifty way to still “get credit” if you forget to track an activity.
Otherwise, the AI coach is still a Chatty Cathy and requires some weekly hand-holding to get the most out of it. I’ll say it again: The Google Health app can feel cluttered, and I get tripped up looking for information that used to be easy to find, like past workouts. However, if you’re new to fitness and want guidance in creating and sticking to a custom AI-generated routine, this is still the best experience I’ve had so far. The bar is in hell, though, and beware what you initially share with the coach. I regret ever telling it I used to have shin splints, as it remains convinced my perfectly fine shins are in danger of disintegrating with every run.
[Image: It’s still such a Chatty Cathy. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268783_Fitbit_edge_AKrales_0137.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
I wish I could tell you about the Health Guardian features, which should let Fitbit Edge users see noninvasive insulin resistance and blood pressure trends. Alas, the way my testing schedule worked out, I have to wait until November 1st to get my initial results.
All in all, I enjoyed the Fitbit Edge as a low-key tracker. This will appeal to folks who just want the basics, but aren’t willing to commit to the screenless life. I’m thinking of the Vergecast listeners who occasionally write in, wondering what happened to simple fitness bands, tired of the smartwatch agenda that took over the past few years. The only gripe I really have is $179.99 feels a tad expensive for what you’re getting. Especially since the Fitbit Air is only $99, and for iPhone users, the Apple Watch SE 3 starts at $249. Brands like Xiaomi and Amazfit also offer much cheaper trackers with displays, even if they’re not quite as sleek on the wrist.
You have to admit: It’s kind of funny that in 2026 we’ve gone full circle and come back to this particular form factor. For the past two weeks of testing, I felt like I’d been blasted back to what I thought was a bygone era in my career. My bet is still on smartwatches being the dominant wrist-based wearable in the years to come. However, this renewed yearning for simpler trackers feels significant at a time when AI health and fitness coaches demand more data in increasingly invasive ways. There’s a growing weariness that can’t be ignored — and yet for many of us, it’s not fully practical to truly log off with a screenless device. So if that’s you, the Edge is here because hey — time truly is a flat circle.
---
Agree to Continue: Google Fitbit Edge
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
To use the Google Fitbit Edge, you must pair it with an iPhone or Android smartphone. That includes the phone’s Terms of Service, privacy policy, and any other permissions you grant. The same goes for any third-party health integrations with other services. For example, if you choose to upload your medical records, you’re agreeing to use CLEAR for identity verification — meaning you’d be agreeing to CLEAR’s terms of service and privacy policies too. There are several optional permissions for things such as location, Bluetooth, camera, background app refresh, notifications, and cellular data.
By setting up the Fitbit Edge, you’re agreeing to:
* Fitbit Terms of Service
* Google Health Additional Terms of Service
* Google Health Data and Privacy Policy (formerly Fitbit)
If you’re concerned about your health data being used to train Google’s AI, that option is turned off by default and must be opted in to. Similarly, the terms and conditions for Google’s acquisition of Fitbit require that your health data be stored separately and not used for Google’s targeted ad business.
Final Tally: three mandatory agreements, several optional permissions
---

title: Israel elections: Netanyahu, Trump, and the battle for Israeli democracy - opinion
body: One day before Election Day, most people in Israel are on edge since, more than ever, the future of the state appears to be at stake, and a clear-cut decision by the voters does not appear to be at hand.At present, there are two alternatives. The first is that Israel will continue to deteriorate into becoming an authoritarian state, under yet another all-right religious government, in which its center-left and Arab populations will be subject to progressively growing oppressive measures and physical attacks by unruly right-wing bullies.As in the current government, the new government's leader will again be Benjamin Netanyahu, who was and still is bent on a continuous bleeding war, irrespective of its cost or consequences.It will be a coalition of parties who seek the unilateral application of Israeli sovereignty in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, and turning Israel into a more religious state than it is today.The second alternative is that Israel will continue to exist as a more or less liberal state, which tries to remain both Jewish (in terms of its serving as the national home of all sections of the Jewish people) and democratic (in terms of being tolerant to all its citizens, whether Jewish or Arab, religious, secular, or everything in between), and attentive to the rules of international law to the maximal extent, without endangering Israel's survival.At this stage, in the existing circumstances, I do not believe that a well-functioning national unity government – which is what Israel most urgently requires – is an option, as long as Netanyahu is still the leader of the Likud.Unfortunately, also the prospects of a stable government in which one of the sides has a clear majority are close to nil, especially if predictions that the Arab population will turn out to vote in large numbers and thus increase the number of Arab MKs to as many as 16 will materialize.When US President Donald J. Trump announced his “complete and total endorsement” for Netanyahu on October 18, nine days before polling day in Israel, his accompanying words undoubtedly warmed the hearts of all those in Israel who support another Netanyahu-led government, while disgusting and angering its opponents, both Jewish and Arab, who happen to constitute a majority of the Israeli electorate.This majority disagrees with Trump's statement that “Netanyahu has been a great warrior prime minister, and an even greater partner for peace in combating the Islamic Republic of Iran.”Most of this majority sees Netanyahu as the man who bears most of the responsibility for the greatest catastrophe to have befallen the Jewish people since the Holocaust – the massacre of October 7, 2023 – but who, over three years after its occurrence, still refuses to accept any responsibility for it, or to appoint a national commission of inquiry to examine the events that preceded it.It also believes that despite some brilliant military operations in the last three years, Netanyahu has, time and again, promised a total victory over Iran and its proxies but has failed to bring about even a single victory, while managing to isolate the State of Israel in the international arena and turn himself into a person wanted for trial by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.Trump's endorsement statement also rejected all the other potential candidates to head Israel's next government, even though the Israeli elections are not about electing a prime minister but about electing parties to the Knesset, which may become part of a coalition government.At the moment, it doesn't look like Netanyahu, even with Trump's endorsement, will manage to muster sufficient parties, with sufficient Knesset seats, to form such a government.Trump ended his endorsement by stating to the Israeli voters that “Bibi Netanyahu will never let you down!” Time and again, Netanyahu has let a majority of Israel's citizens down – not least of all over the return of all the Israeli hostages – both alive and dead.In fact, it is Trump himself who was responsible for bringing them all back home – not Netanyahu, who kept sabotaging efforts to reach an agreement with Hamas over the release of the hostages, when more of them could have been brought back alive. There were allegedly strategic considerations for this enervating action of his.Apparently, we must also thank Trump for dissuading Netanyahu from attacking Iran two weeks ago and thus sabotaging tomorrow's elections. Nevertheless, Trump remains guilty of unwarranted intervention in the Israeli elections.Incidentally, though it is generally assumed that international law categorically rejects intervention by states in the elections of other states, in fact, so far, no treaty-based solutions to the problem of foreign election interference have been formulated.What does exist is an International Court of Justice ruling from 1986 that the principle of nonintervention is a pillar of customary international law.In addition, traditional international law prohibits actions that are coercive by nature – i.e., intervention that compels a target state to act against its will.Finally, there are several UN General Assembly resolutions that explicitly condemn direct or indirect interference, foreign financing of political groups, or attempts to sway domestic electoral processes.Strictly speaking, what Trump has done is not illegal under international law but is certainly enervating and objectionable to those who believe that Netanyahu's continued premiership is dangerous to Israel's continued existence as a liberal democratic state. Some even believe that it endangers Israel's existence altogether.Final words A few words should be mentioned about the ugly and libelous campaign by the Likud and its non-haredi partners against Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is one of the current promising candidates for the premiership of the opposition parties, and has been unjustifiably belittled and mocked.The worst manifestation of this was the disgusting referral to him, by Channel 14 moderator and close associate of Netanyahu, Yinon Magal, as “an oriental-Moroccan monkey, who is backed by the Ashkenazi elites that manage him.”It doesn't matter whether Magal used the word “monkey” in the physical sense, or – as he later explained – as the word used in the Israeli underworld to mean a front man, puppet, or straw man. In both senses, the meaning of the word “monkey” is disgusting, demeaning, and meant to belittle and insult.Hopefully, tomorrow will go by peacefully – both in verbal and physical terms.And just one final word to Netanyahu personally. The way to deal with threats of international economic sanctions against Israel, which you mentioned several days ago, is not by moving over to crypto or turning Israel into a super-Sparta, but by changing your policies that have led to the threats of sanctions against our state.The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.

title: Iran monitors situation following reports Ukraine deploys UAVs near its borders
body:
TEHRAN, October 26. /TASS/. Iran is closely monitoring developments along its borders following reports Ukraine has been deploying unmanned aerial vehicles in neighboring areas and stands ready to counter any associated threats, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei has said.
Earlier, Iranian news agency Tasnim, citing various sources, reported that Ukraine was actively deploying thousands of drones in countries bordering Iran, including Iraq’s Kurdistan region. One source told the agency that Tehran views Kiev’s actions as part of a hostile strategy pursued by NATO and the European Union and is assessing possible countermeasures.
"Those responsible for maintaining readiness to act whenever necessary to defend the country, repel hostile actions, and neutralize threats are doing exactly that. Wherever we have identified a threat to the country, our armed forces have responded resolutely to defend it, and they will continue to do so," Baghaei said at a news briefing.

title: LAWMA begins expansion works at Olusosun dumpsite to boost waste evacuation
body: By Olasunkanmi Akoni The Lagos Waste Management Authority, LAWMA, has initiated critical stabilisation and expansion works on tipping platforms E1 and E2 at the Olusosun dumpsite in Ojota. ​The upgrade, executed in partnership with Zoomlion Nigeria Limited, aims to expand platform capacity, allow more waste collection trucks to discharge simultaneously, and significantly enhance operational safety and speed. ​Speaking at the agency’s headquarters in Ijora-Olopa on Monday, LAWMA Executive Director of Finance, Mr. Kunle Adebiyi, disclosed that construction on the site is progressing according to schedule. ​Adebiyi noted that the Olusosun upgrade is part of a broader infrastructure plan that includes ongoing improvements at other major dumping facilities, such as Solus III and Epe. “Together, these upgrades are expected to strengthen the state’s overall waste evacuation network, dramatically reduce truck turnaround times, and improve service delivery across Lagos,” he stated. ​To minimise disruption during the construction phase, Adebiyi appealed for cooperation from Private Sector Participation, PSP operators, waste truck drivers, and other key industry stakeholders. ​The agency therefore reaffirmed its commitment to upgrading waste management infrastructure and maintaining a cleaner, healthier environment for all residents of Lagos State. The post LAWMA begins expansion works at Olusosun dumpsite to boost waste evacuation appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Joe Mettle to headline Ɔdadeɛ bonfire night as PRESEC celebrates 9th NSMQ title
body: Gospel musician Joe Mettle will headline the 2026 Ɔdadeɛ Torch & Bonfire Night as former students of Presbyterian Boys’ Secondary School (PRESEC), Legon, celebrate the school’s ninth National Science and Maths Quiz (NSMQ) title. Dubbed the “ADO9 Edition”, the event will take place at the PRESEC School Park, Legon, on Friday, October 30, at 6pm. Team Eternity Ghana and Daughters of Glorious Jesus will also perform at the celebration, which will combine gospel music, thanksgiving and the school’s torchlight and bonfire traditions. Joe Mettle, whose songs include Bo Noo Ni , My Everything and Yesu Mo , will lead a line-up centred on praise and worship. The annual gathering brings together generations of PRESEC old boys, known as Ɔdadeɛ, for fellowship and performances. Its signature activities include a torchlight procession and a bonfire lighting. According to organisers, this year’s edition draws inspiration from PRESEC’s ninth NSMQ championship, with thanksgiving at the centre of the programme. The event returned in 2023, while its 2024 edition featured dancehall musician Stonebwoy. Organisers are inviting old students, year groups and friends of the school to celebrate the quiz champions and reconnect with fellow alumni.

title: Strategy’s Weekly STRC Buyback Climbs to $205 Million While Its Bitcoin Stack Stays Put
body: Strategy spent $204.9 million repurchasing 2,068,459 shares of its STRC preferred stock between Oct. 19 and Oct. 25 and bought no bitcoin over those seven days, the company disclosed in a Form 8-K on Monday. It was the first full week since the board lifted the cap on its preferred buyback program to $3 billion from $2 billion. Strategy had repurchased $193.1 million of STRC the week before and $192.4 million the week before that. The company’s holdings stayed at 848,517 BTC , acquired for a combined $64.02 billion at an average of about $75,446 each, fees included. Strategy also skipped stock sales under its ATM program this time, a week after selling MSTR shares to fund most of a 267 BTC purchase. Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter . Paid From USD Cash All of the STRC repurchases were funded from what Strategy calls USD Cash , a balance management keeps for general purposes that can include buying bitcoin. It fell to $242.4 million as of Oct. 25, from $447.3 million on Oct. 18. The separate USD Reserve, which the company says is meant to support preferred dividends and debt interest, held at $4.83 billion . Executive Chairman Michael Saylor put Strategy’s total dollar holdings at $5.1 billion in a post on X on Monday. He added in a follow-up post on X that “USD Duration is 3.4 yrs and STRC’s BTC Credit is 54 bps assuming 10% BTC ARR, 40% BTC Vol, and a BTC price of $81,200.” Room Left to Repurchase After the latest week, $956.8 million remains available under the digital credit securities repurchase program, down from $1.16 billion as of Oct. 18. STRC was the only security Strategy bought back. It repurchased none of its STRF, STRK or STRD preferred shares and no MSTR common stock, which has $1.0 billion still available under a separate program. The board had already doubled the preferred program to $2 billion in September before last week’s increase. On Oct. 28, common shareholders vote on switching STRC and Strategy’s three other U.S.-listed preferreds to daily dividend payments.
