title: How is the Muslim world reporting on Israel’s election?
body: The upcoming election is drawing attention across the Arab world, with regional media examining the political contest, its implications for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's future, and what a change in government could mean for the future of Palestinian statehood and the two-state solution.Beyond speculation about Netanyahu's political future, several Arab media outlets have focused on the potential influence of Arab voters and Arab-led parties on the election outcome, particularly the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad, and Mansour Abbas's Ra'am party. With neither major political bloc guaranteed a parliamentary majority, many Arab outlets have focused on the parties' electoral performance's significance in determining the next government.Egypt's Alghad TV reported on remarks made by Hadash politician Shadi Shweiri on Sunday, highlighting the influence of the Arab vote and what he described as a unique opportunity for Arab citizens of Israel to advance their national demands through the electoral process. The report referred to Arab citizens of Israel as “Palestinians in the country” and emphasized that Arab parties should not support just any candidate seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but one willing to halt Israel's military operations in the region and improve economic opportunities for Arab citizens.Shweiri accused the current government of racism and of committing crimes against Palestinians in Gaza. He also argued that Arab citizens' right to vote should not be viewed as evidence of goodwill on Israel's part, but as a right secured through international pressure.Shweiri: Choice for Israel's Arabs 'between the bad and the worse'“Our situation is that we are being asked to choose between the bad and the worse, rather than between the good and the better,” Shweiri said. “I want to emphasize something for our brothers and sisters in the Arab world who hear and see Israel described as a democratic state that gives equal voting rights to Jewish and Arab citizens. This was not an act of goodwill by the Zionist movement or the Israeli government. It was a fundamental condition for Israel's acceptance as a member of the United Nations in 1948 and as part of the international community.“They cannot take this right away from us, although, as Netanyahu does, they can act outside the bounds of legitimacy.”Meanwhile, Iranian officials have downplayed the significance of Israel's election, which is taking place amid continued tensions between the two countries following years of confrontations and conflict involving Iran-backed groups.Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said at a press conference on Monday that the outcome of Tuesday's election “makes no difference to us.”“I do not agree with elections in the occupied territories at all; there is competition between different gangs to commit more evil,” Baghaei said. “Their most important slogan is that 'I can commit more crimes than you.' It makes no difference to us in such an environment who becomes the helm of a regime that has achieved nothing but killing and genocide.”Despite Baghaei's assertion that the candidates' identities make no difference to Tehran, Iranian state-affiliated media, including the Tasnim News Agency, have reported on multiple polls examining Likud's chances of winning the election.The London-based Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, owned by Qatar's Fadaat Media, reported on Monday on fears of a potential “political stalemate” that could leave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu leading a caretaker government.In an analysis by Qatar-based Palestinian journalist Beirut Hammoud, the outlet framed the election as taking place after three years of what it described as “genocide” and “ethnic cleansing” across the Palestinian territories, including east Jerusalem.After examining polls measuring Netanyahu's chances of electoral success, Hammoud highlighted what she described as declining international support for Israel. She argued that even opposition politicians differed little from the prime minister, whom she accused of leading a “government of ruin.”“They differ from him only in their methods of managing the conflict,” she claimed.Pro-Hezbollah outlet accuses Netanyahu of portraying Arab vote as liabilityMeanwhile, the Lebanon-based, pro-Hezbollah media outlet Al-Khanadeq published an analysis on Monday alleging that Netanyahu had manipulated the political landscape by portraying the Arab vote as a liability.The article pointed to AI-generated campaign material associated with Netanyahu's camp depicting political figures, including Gadi Eisenkot, alongside Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas.“Portraying Eisenkot as a hostage of Arab politicians specifically targets the 'soft right,' which might distance itself from Likud. Thus, the campaign's impact extends beyond weakening the Arab vote; it also reaches Jewish voters who want Netanyahu gone but are hesitant about a government based on Arab partnership,” the author argued. “The incitement works in two directions: it redistributes seats and raises the cost of utilizing them after the election.”The analysis also cited efforts by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify Arab-majority parties and alleged attempts to deter Arab citizens from voting through the deployment of 2,000 activists. The author presented these developments as evidence of what they characterized as Netanyahu's attempts to evade the consequences of the electoral process.The Palestinian news site Al Quds, based in east Jerusalem, paid special attention to the timing of Israel's elections around the United States' midterms, noting that the result of both could reshape the region.Written by Dr. Ahmed Youseff, a former senior adviser to assassinated Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh, the article argued that Eisenkot's victory could reopen the door for Israel's international diplomacy efforts and for accountability for Israel's security failures, but it would necessarily “dismantle established political systems or guarantee a shift in positions.”“The hopes are clear: that Netanyahu and his allies will lose, that Israeli society will have an opportunity to reassess its policies of war and extremism, that the language of threats and incitement will subside, and that those responsible for failures and violations will be held accountable,” he wrote. “The American vote should also curb Trump's drive toward confrontation and empower Congress to hold the administration accountable and push for a political path that spares the region a wider war.“However, a realistic assessment requires us not to confuse hopes with certain outcomes…the true value of these elections will be measured by the opportunities they offer for accountability, pressure, and policy change, and by whether the voters' voices translate into concrete steps that curb war and extremism and restore respect for rights and justice.”

title: Media Excellence Awards honour outstanding work
body:
MUSCAT, OCT 26 The winners of the 2026 Media Excellence Awards were honoured at a ceremony organised by the Ministry of Information at its theatre on Monday, under the auspices of Dr Madeeha bint Ahmed al Shaibani, Minister of Education, and in the presence of Dr Abdullah bin Nasser al Harrasi, Minister of Information. The competition received 433 entries across journalism, radio, television and digital media, highlighting the diversity of media production and the importance of professional standards in the Sultanate of Oman. The awards comprise three main fields — journalism, radio and television, and digital media — divided into 21 categories covering various media formats and specialisations. The competition targets media institutions, individuals and media students, with winners in each category receiving RO 1,500, a trophy and a certificate of appreciation. Of the total entries, 235 met the participation requirements and were referred to four independent judging committees comprising 20 academics, experts and specialists. The submissions included 115 entries in journalism, 85 in radio, 100 in television and 132 in digital media. The committees assessed the entries against established professional criteria, using independent evaluations and confidential procedures, with final results calculated based on the average scores awarded by the judges.

The competition targets media institutions, individuals and media students, with winners in each category receiving RO 1,500, a trophy and a certificate of appreciation.
Of the total entries, 235 met the participation requirements and were referred to four independent judging committees comprising 20 academics, experts and specialists. The submissions included 115 entries in journalism, 85 in radio, 100 in television and 132 in digital media. The committees assessed the entries against established professional criteria, using independent evaluations and confidential procedures, with final results calculated based on the average scores awarded by the judges.
The main judging committee included Dr Moza al Rawahi, Dr Mohammed al Araimi and Dr Sabah al Hajri. The journalism committee comprised Awad Baqweir, Dr Hosni Nasr, Zainab al Nasiri and Masoud al Hamdani. The radio committee included Mohammed al Ghamari, Awad al Midailawi, Sultan al Eisari and Dawood al Qasimi. The television committee comprised Said al Malki, Dr Maiya al Habsi and Said al Hatmi, while the digital media committee included Dr Khamis al Busaidi, Dr Suad al Ishaqi, Dr Al Mutasim al Maamari and Safiya al Farsi. In his address, Mohammed bin Said al Balushi, Under-Secretary of the Ministry of Information and Chairman of the Main Committee, said the awards reflected the ministry’s commitment to empowering media professionals, improving institutional performance and fostering competition to strengthen skills and develop content across different platforms. He emphasised that media has a responsibility to reinforce national identity, deepen public understanding of national issues and present accurate information within its proper context. He added that responsible media contributes to public trust, counters rumours and misinformation, promotes dialogue and social cohesion, and strengthens national belonging. Al Balushi stressed that media excellence extends beyond winning an award, describing it as a continuous professional commitment demonstrated through daily work, dedication, adherence to professional standards and responsibility towards audiences.

The ceremony also featured an artistic performance depicting the journey of perseverance and creativity through a character named “Fikra” (Idea), who confronts challenges and transforms obstacles into opportunities for success. Omani actors Saleh Zaal and Fakhriya Khamis participated in the performance, celebrating the country's artistic legacy and the continuity of creativity across generations. A musical segment entitled “Oman Media” celebrated the country's print, audio and visual media sectors, with lyrics by poet Hisham al Saqri, music by Asaad al Raisi, performance by the Cortage group and arrangements by Raed al Farsi. The programme also revisited memorable opening themes from Omani television dramas, programmes and quiz shows, bringing together nostalgia and a celebration of the country's media heritage. Prepared and written by Mohammed Bait Said and directed by Mohammed al Dhabouni, the performance combined drama, music and stage presentation to highlight milestones in Oman's media journey. Launched in 2004 as the Media Creativity Awards, the competition adopted its current name in 2011, while digital media was added as a category in 2019. The 2026 edition introduced further organisational and digital improvements, including dedicated guidelines for participation and judging, with registration, review and evaluation conducted through an integrated electronic system. The awards continue to support media creativity, promote professional quality and encourage competition among institutions and individuals, in line with the evolving media landscape in Oman.

title: Global gas sector needs forum for depoliticized dialogue — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The world gas industry needs a floor for the depoliticized dialogue and the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) fits this role, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters.
"I would like to note that the global gas industry has found itself in a challenging situation in the environment of dramatic aggravation of the situation in the Middle East, in one of global gas production centers, after terrorist acts against Russian Nord Stream gas pipelines, introduction of illegitimate Western restrictions on procurement of gas, relevant equipment and technologies," the presidential aide said.
"A platform is objectively needed in this situation, which offers an opportunity to hold professional depoliticized dialogue. The Gas Exporting Countries Forum is exactly such platform," Ushakov added.

title: Israel to Supply Cyprus with an Offshore Patrol Vessel Equipped with Advanced Naval Systems
body: On October 26, 2026, the Israeli Ministry of Defense (IMOD) and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Cyprus signed an agreement for the acquisition of a new Offshore Patrol Vessel (OPV). Israeli MoD press release The ceremony was held in Cyprus. The deal was led by the IMOD’s International Defense Cooperation Directorate (SIBAT) and the CyMOD’s Armaments & Defence Capabilities Development Directorate. Under the agreement, signed by IMOD Director General Maj. Gen. (Res.) Amir Baram, and his Cypriot counterpart, Mr. Stelios Kountouris, Acting Permanent Secretary of the Cyprus Ministry of Defence, Israel will supply Cyprus with a new patrol vessel built by Israel Shipyards and fitted with a range of Rafael naval systems. In parallel, the systems aboard Cyprus’s existing Israel Shipyards-built patrol vessel will be upgraded. Commodore Andreas Ioannides – P61 (Credit: Cyprus MoD). The systems aboard Cyprus’s existing Israel Shipyards-built patrol vessel will be upgraded. The agreement was signed in the presence of Head of SIBAT Brig. Gen. (Res.) Yair Kulas. Also attending the ceremony were Israel’s Ambassador to Cyprus, Shuli Davidovich; Israel Shipyards CEO, Eitan Zucker; Head of Rafael’s Naval Warfare Systems Directorate, Ran Tavor; and other senior officials. This agreement marks another important step in strengthening the operational capabilities of the Cyprus Naval Command and enhancing its capacity to respond to maritime security challenges. The new OPV, alongside the upgraded OPV IOANNIDES, will support expanded patrol, surveillance, and search-and-rescue missions. By strengthening their capabilities and deepening their partnership, the two countries reaffirm their commitment to regional stability. – End – The post Israel to Supply Cyprus with an Offshore Patrol Vessel Equipped with Advanced Naval Systems appeared first on Naval News .

title: EXPLAINED: Can Oleshky Be Evacuated, Razed to Eliminate Russian Strategic Lookout?
body:
A ceasefire is due to take effect along the front line near Oleshky, a city close to Kherson, on Oct. 27 to allow a humanitarian evacuation operation.
It will involve delivering humanitarian aid to the city and evacuating civilians who wish to leave.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
However, the idea has not been welcomed by everyone, despite support from Pope Leo XIV and US First Lady Melania Trump .
The idea that partial ceasefires and humanitarian initiatives can gradually de-escalate the Russian-Ukrainian war is not new. But in Ukraine, it is met with skepticism, particularly by people living in Kherson , a major regional center located directly across the river from Oleshky.
Oleshky is a district-level city in southern Ukraine, on the left bank of the Dnipro River — Ukraine’s equivalent of the Mississippi — directly opposite Kherson, a regional capital with a population of 300,000 on the right bank. Before 2022, Oleshky had a population of more than 20,000.
During the fighting in 2022, both Oleshky and Kherson were occupied by Russian forces. The Russians were driven out of Kherson in the fall of 2022. However, Ukrainian forces were unable to cross the major water obstacle and dislodge Russian troops from Oleshky. Since then, the city has remained under Russian occupation, with the Dnipro serving as a de facto line of separation. Both Oleshky and Kherson found themselves on the front line .
Kherson and Oleshky on the Deepstate OSINT map. Green-colored – zone of Ukrainian military control; Red-colored – Russian occupied and controlled territory (Screenshot from Deepstate map)
Kherson and Oleshky on the Deepstate OSINT map. Green-colored – zone of Ukrainian military control; Red-colored – Russian occupied and controlled territory (Screenshot from Deepstate map)
Over time, Oleshky became a staging ground from which Russian artillerists, drone technicians and operators launched attacks on Kherson .
“They are simply very close. A drone just has to cross the Dnipro — and that matters for fiber-optic drones. The shorter the distance, the better. And then there is Kherson,” a military service member who spent a long time fighting on the Kherson front told Kyiv Post.
As a result, the Ukrainian forces began actively targeting Oleshky, disrupting Russian logistics.
Civilians became hostages to the fighting. Oleshky’s population has fallen to one tenth its peak during the war.
According to local Proposal, the city’s current population does not exceed approximately 2,000.
Residents face shortages of food and fresh, potable drinking water — a problem that became recurring afte the Russian military blew up the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant in the summer of 2023, flooding large areas with contaminated reservoir water.
Fresh produce was last delivered to the city several months ago. Sometimes, the Ukrainian Armed Forces help locals by delivering food by drones, but its impossible to deliver enough food for thousands.
“It would be wrong to say that only ‘waiters’ — that is, pro-Russian people — remain in Oleshky.
Often, these are simply people who have nowhere to go and no money to leave: poor people, pensioners without relatives, and so on.
Russia uses them as cover, setting up positions directly inside their residential buildings, including private homes,” said Serhiy Nikitenko, a journalist from Kherson.
According to one service member, Ukrainian artillery crews and drone operators already know “every house in Oleshky where Russians are stationed, but they do not attack because there are civilians there.”
This is the first reason for the skepticism. Few people believe the Russians will allow civilians to evacuate from a key staging ground for attacks on Kherson.
“Once civilians leave Oleshky and the Russians no longer have a human shield in this open, steppe city, the Ukrainian military will tear them apart,” a volunteer from Kherson told Kyiv Post.
Several hundred people are expected to leave the city. However, it is unlikely that the Russians will allow everyone to evacuate.
The second reason for concern is that previous attempts to establish “humanitarian corridors” to deliver supplies to various locations have generally ended with the Russian side blatantly violating the agreements and delivering … additional weapons and ammunition to the settlements instead of food and water.
“People in Kherson expect things to get even worse because, in previous cases, the Russians brought in new drone operators to replace those eliminated by Ukrainian drone crews, fuel for generators powering military equipment, ammunition, and other supplies. Everyone expects that after this ‘delivery,’ Kherson will be hit by everything that can fly, and the destruction will be even greater,” said Oleksandr Vlasov, a Kherson businessman and lifelong resident of the city.
Serhiy Nikitenko shares this view. He notes that Russian drone attacks on Kherson have become somewhat less frequent over the past month, thanks to Ukrainian drone operators who have prevented reinforcements and additional equipment from reaching Oleshky.
Meanwhile, residents are actively discussing in Kherson social media groups whether anyone will be able to monitor what exactly — and how much — the Russians bring into Oleshky through the humanitarian corridor. Their conclusion is bleak: no one will.
“The saddest thing is that the only ones who will benefit from this kind of ‘humanitarian initiative’ are the Russian military and perhaps a few dozen people who want to evacuate. For the most part, nothing will improve for Oleshky’s residents, while things will only get worse for people in Kherson,” an administrator of a Kherson social media group told Kyiv Post.
For now, sources in the city say there are no visible signs of preparations for tomorrow’s operation in Kherson itself.
However, that does not necessarily mean nothing is happening behind the scenes.
“Many Kherson residents plan to rush to their houses or apartments in the dangerous zone near the Dnipro if the ceasefire takes effect, hoping to retrieve valuables. Normally, they simply cannot access homes closer to the river,” Vlasov said.
A local activist also said he had hired a car so that, if the ceasefire comes into effect, he could “take out the household appliances” from his apartment. He has not visited it for more than two years because of the risk of drone strikes: it is too close to the Dnipro, and going outside in the area is dangerous.
However, according to locals, there are still no visible signs in Kherson of tomorrow’s operation.
Several days ago, a Russian drone struck a passenger bus in the city, killing and injuring people.
Meanwhile, residents of neighborhoods farther from the river continue to move around while constantly scanning the sky.

title: LEAP India Q2: Profit Zooms 62% YoY To ₹18 Cr, Revenue Up 18%
body: Logistics company LEAP India reported a net profit of ₹17.8 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), up 62% from nearly ₹11 Cr in the year-ago period. Sequentially, the company’s profit dipped 28% from ₹24.7 Cr in Q1 FY27 . Meanwhile, revenue from operations jumped 18.2% to ₹211.2 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹178.7 Cr in Q2 FY26. On a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) basis, the company’s top line remained largely flat and rose 3.8% from ₹203.4 Cr in Q1 FY27. Including other income of ₹4.7 Cr, total income for the period stood at ₹215.9 Cr in the quarter under review. Meanwhile, expenses rose 14.7% to ₹185.2 Cr in Q2 FY27 as against ₹161.5 Cr in the quarter ended September 2025. LEAP India also incurred an additional ₹6 Cr in tax expenses during the quarter. Founded in 2013 by Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions spanning equipment pooling, inventory management, transportation, and repair and maintenance. It serves customers across sectors such as FMCG, beverages, ecommerce, automotive and retail. (This story will be updated soon) The post LEAP India Q2: Profit Zooms 62% YoY To ₹18 Cr, Revenue Up 18% appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Putin to meet with Zimbabwe, Madagascar, Sudan, and Namibia leaders, Kremlin aide says
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet on October 29 with the presidents of Madagascar Michael Randrianirina, of Zimbabwe Emmerson Mnangagwa, of Namibia Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, as well as with Chairman of the Sovereign Council of Sudan Abdel Fattah al·Burhan, Aide to the Russian leader Yury Ushakov said.
Meetings are planned "with the president of the Republic of Namibia, with the president of the Republic of Madagascar, and the Republic of Zimbabwe," Ushakov said, also noting that a meeting with the leader of Sudan will take place on that day.
A series of bilateral meetings will begin after two plenary sessions of the Russia-Africa summit.

title: Zelenskyy enacts NSDC decision on creating engineering barriers for all-around defense of cities – decree
body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has enacted a decision by the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) of Ukraine regarding the creation of a belt of engineering barriers to ensure an adequate level of city defense, as well as the mechanisms for their implementation.

Corresponding decree, No. 1067/2026, was published on the website of the Office of the President of Ukraine on Monday.

According to the document, the decree enacts the NSDC decision of September 25, 2026, "On measures to create a belt of engineering barriers to ensure an adequate level of city defense and the mechanisms for their implementation (all-around defense of cities)."

title: For the third time this year, Ukrainian drones hit Russia’s rocket-fuel rubber plant in Samara Oblast. This time they reach the raw-material shop feeding it
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukrainian drones damaged a process pipeline, two butyl-rubber units, and a rectification (distillation) unit at Russia’s Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant on 24 October, Ukraine’s General Staff said on 26 October. The damage hits the production chain of solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles, it added. The strike was part of a string of Ukrainian hits on Russian plants over four days, most of which the General Staff links to missile production. Ukraine hit an electronics plant in Oryol on 23 October and struck a battery plant in Yelets on 25 October or the following night. The General Staff ties both to missiles: Oryol makes components for missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities, and Yelets makes batteries for Iskander-M systems. Then, overnight on 26 October, drones also went after Voronezhsintezkauchuk, another Russian synthetic-rubber plant. For Tolyattikauchuk, this is the third time this year that strikes have reached its butyl-rubber shops. What Kyiv and Russian officials say The General Staff first confirmed the strike on 24 October with a report of an explosion and fire near the plant. It said the plant makes synthetic rubbers, monomers, fractions, and high-octane gasoline additives, and that its synthetic rubbers are used in solid rocket fuel. Meanwhile, Russian officials have not named the plant in their statements. However, Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh claimed that industrial facilities were damaged and, citing preliminary data, that no one was killed or injured, Russian outlet Expert reported . What OSINT channels report Drones hit at least two production facilities, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ said. One is the shop where isobutane is turned into isobutylene, a raw material for synthetic rubbers. The other is outdoor unit No. 2 in shop BK-4, which produces and purifies high-purity isobutylene for butyl rubber. Aftermath of the attack on the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant. Analysis by Exilenova+, satellite image by Vantor. The damage could delay rubber output and the supply of feedstock for other processes, including solid rocket fuel. Tolyattikauchuk can make about 260,000 metric tons of synthetic rubber a year, OSINT-Varta data show. Hit again and again Tolyattikauchuk had come under fire before. Overnight on 4 April, about 10 drones reached the plant by various accounts. Footage showed fires at storage shops D-12 and D-1 and at the BK-2, BK-3, and BK-4 units, though more sites may have been hit, the analysts added. Ukrainian forces struck the plant again on 12 June, the General Staff confirmed. Then, on 12 September, a strike set fires at the BK-2, BK-3, and BK-4 shops, an OSINT community Absolutely Reliable Source reported . Without those shops running steadily, the line that makes MTBE, a key high-octane gasoline additive, is cut, the channel noted. title: Israel heads to polls at pivotal moment for Middle East
body: Israel goes to the polls on Tuesday in one of the most momentous elections in its history as voters deliver their verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's wartime leadership. Mr Netanyahu is seeking re-election after a four-year term defined by the catastrophic security failure of the October 7, 2023 attacks, Israel's destructive war in Gaza and its subsequent campaigns in Lebanon, Iran and across the region. Polls suggest a close race that could result in long coalition talks just as Middle East countries try to restore stability. Forecasters give Gadi Eisenkot, a former top general, the best chance of unseating Mr Netanyahu from a range of opposition candidates . Voters from the country's Arab minority could play a key role. Political sources have told The National their turnout is expected to be “astronomical”. Senior opposition officials have also said there is a possibility of a coalition or agreement for a minority government with the Arab parties. “After what they have witnessed over the past three years, they have understood the difference between bad and worse,” said an Israeli political observer, referring to the hard-right parties that have shaped Mr Netanyahu's government. Voting centres close at 10pm Israeli time, when exit polls will give a first indication of the results. Preliminary results will emerge as votes are counted overnight. Opposition supporters used the campaign's final days to call for a call for a formal inquiry into the October 7 attacks, something Mr Netanyahu has resisted. He has countered with steps to underline his hardline security stance, from warning of a "second Holocaust" if Iran is allowed to rearm, to ordering an operation of questionable military value in the occupied West Bank. In the final hours before Tuesday, the opposition also rallied behind Israel's military chief of staff, amid reports that Mr Netanyahu plans to fire him if he regains power, after the pair were said to have fallen out over the Prime Minister's efforts to restart fighting with Iran for political reasons. "Chief of Staff Zamir will conclude his role only in accordance with the date stipulated by law," Mr Eisenkot wrote in a post on X on Monday evening. "Tomorrow the people of Israel will elect a prime minister whose considerations will always be for the good of Israel, who will never act out of political interests at the expense of Israel's security and the fighters of the [Israel military]." Mr Netanyahu called the reports "another piece of fake news". "I have no intention of firing the Chief of Staff, and we will continue working together for Israel's security. I do intend to permanently remove the Iranian nuclear threat. I will do so together with my friend President Trump, and we will also sign peace agreements with additional countries." With Israel's standing abroad badly damaged, notably by its devastating campaign in Gaza and settlement expansion in the West Bank, Mr Netanyahu has quoted support from US President Donald Trump as a key sellling point. Mr Trump sent a late message of endorsement, hailing "a great relationship in winning together". Mr Eisenkot has kept his policies vague, running on a brand of down-to-earth honesty. But most of the main candidates hold belligerent views towards Iran and few are enthusiastic about the idea of a Palestinian state, although some have offered hints of conciliation. An alliance of former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid has declined in the polls. Gazans have expressed little optimism about the vote. Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim said he did not believe the situation would change significantly whether Mr Netanyahu wins or loses. Many Gazans are nonetheless hoping he loses, holding him responsible for mass destruction of the territory during a war that has killed more than 70,000 people. About 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote for the 120-member Knesset. There are 36 parties running, although most are not expected to win enough votes to enter parliament. Israel has a history of political deadlock. Between 2019 and 2022, the country held five elections as parties repeatedly struggled to form stable governments. Mr Netanyahu – who has led Israel for all but 18 months since 2009 – would remain as a caretaker prime minister during a period of coalition talks. Some believe he might use such a deadlock to his advantage, possibly by initiating a new round of fighting with Iran. “If Benjamin Netanyahu wins again, I’m genuinely scared for this country. I don’t think I have a future here,” Romy Schlegel-Cohen, 17, told The National in Tel Aviv's Hostage Square. Reports claim Mr Netanyahu had been pushing for a joint US-Israeli strike on Iran before the election, which Mr Trump did not approve. Mr Eisenkot said he had “full trust” in the military.

title: Vučić Out, Students In: Still, No Sanctions Against Russia
body:
Serbia’s Student List won the Oct. 25 parliamentary election, ending 14 years of what many described as Serbian leader Aleksandar Vučić’s dictatorship.
Tens of thousands of people in Serbia and abroad rallied behind the list, made up of students, professors and doctors, hoping to free the country from corruption and political pressure on its institutions. The country secured a historic win in its highest turnout of 70%, the biggest Serbia has seen in nearly three decades.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Yet even as the result brings Serbia a step closer to the European Union, the list has said it will not impose sanctions on Russia, despite Vučić’s claims that it would do so within months.
Speaking to RT Balkan, a Serbian-language broadcaster run by the Russian state-owned network RT (formerly Russia Today), Professor Jovo Bakić of the Student List claimed that Belgrade respects Russia, “both as a great power and as our historically important partner, and in many cases even our protector,” adding that “there will be no changes.”
He claimed that sanctions from such a small country would essentially change nothing for Moscow, since even the entire EU had failed to harm it.
However, the move would damage bilateral relations, he said, adding that Serbia knows what “kind of misery that [sanctions] is,” having lived through UN sanctions during the 1990s.
“I said this during the election campaign, and I’m saying it after the elections,” Bakić said, echoing the Student List’s earlier position.
“The Republic of Serbia will retain its principled stance on not introducing restrictive measures toward the Russian Federation,” the list previously said in a statement on Sept. 30.
With the list holding an absolute majority of nearly 140 seats, the next step is a presidential election, which Serbia’s constitution requires by Dec. 26. Until then, Ana Brnabić of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), closely linked to Vučić, is serving as acting president.
Vučić conceded defeat, saying his coalition, United Serbia, won 105 seats.
The name of his coalition closely echoes United Russia, which won the Sept. 18-20 State Duma elections, held in Russia and occupied territories of Ukraine, without the main election-monitoring body of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE).
The same Duma elections that the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) deemed illegitimate earlier this month.
Vučić’s concession, however, quickly proved to be anything but a surrender. He claimed that “you will see, in six months, no one will be happy and joyful anymore,” adding that “from tonight, we start preparing. We are going to defeat them.”
He also blamed foreign forces for his defeat, echoing Russia’s similar rhetoric towards the West.
“What brought us down is this verified revolution, which they carried out with direct support from various European countries, and the deep American state, the one against [US] President [Donald] Trump,” Vučić said .
“I congratulate them, even though they are just executors of work. Executors of dirty work, which someone else designed to bring down a sovereign country. For a moment you have succeeded. For how long, we shall see,” he continued, as if years of intense public frustration with corruption had not been enough to produce such a result.
The Student List grew out of the Nov. 1, 2024, collapse of the railway station canopy in Novi Sad, north of Belgrade, which killed 16 people.
Four children were killed as well, with the youngest victim aged 5.
The tragedy sparked mass protests across Serbia, which escalated over Vučić’s refusal to accept responsibility and the use of a sound cannon against the students, a high-frequency weapon that causes disorientation, nausea and panic.
The movement eventually formed its own list, led by Novi Sad cardiologist Ilija Srdanović.
Its program , the “Student Plan,” has 11 points in three sections, aiming not just to change the people that hold power, but to dismantle decades of systemic corruption.
“Serbia or the Mafia” pledges an independent anti-corruption police unit, a purge of Interior Ministry officers tied to organized crime or the protest crackdowns, confiscation of illegally acquired assets, audits of opaque state projects and an end to political control over the media regulator and public broadcaster RTS.
“Knowledge Is Power” promises merit-based public hiring, free textbooks for all primary and secondary students and support for startups, entrepreneurs and farmers to move Serbia beyond a cheap-labor economy.
“Serbia Grows With Us” would cap fixed-term employment at 12 months instead of 24, curb the import lobby’s grip on food prices, offer affordable housing to young families and essential workers, lower medicine prices and reopen rural clinics.
Vučić, first elected president in 2017 and re-elected in 2022, signed his resignation live on television on Sept. 26, cutting his final term short by eight months.
Following months of what could be described as world’s biggest anti-government protests, he stepped down to campaign “as an ordinary citizen,” planning to become prime minister if SNS won.
On the same day of his resignation, Vučić held a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, during which he emphasized Serbia’s energy partnership with Moscow, while also boasting their 14 year long friendship.
In a video address posted on social media, Vučić said that he secured a “good and low gas price” of €318 (roughly $361) per 1,000 cubic meters (264.172 gallons), far below the market rate of €868 ($987) at the time.
Currently, Serbia remains one of the few European countries that have not joined EU sanctions on Russia, and it continues to import discounted Russian gas and oil.
Vučić has long insisted no sanctions would be introduced while he was in power. On election night, he claimed the students would impose them by March or April, something the list had ruled out a month earlier.
Around the same time of Vučić’s resignation, Russian-state-owned media TASS reported that while analysts expected no major foreign policy shift, a student win could move Serbia closer to Western positions.
Polina Sokolova, a research fellow at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, said a Serbian turn against Russia under Western pressure “cannot be excluded.”
According to TASS, this is because European countries, “which have been Ukraine’s main sponsors, do not demonstrate any intention to enter substantive negotiations.” However, EU leaders consistently urge Russia to enter meaningful negotiations and agree to an immediate ceasefire. Ukraine itself has agreed to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire in March 2025.
The argument mirrors Vučić’s own claim about “dirty work” designed abroad.
However, despite Vučić’s decades-long ties to Moscow, Serbia has backed Ukraine on several main issues, including territorial integrity on Crimea and Donbas. Belgrade has also provided Kyiv with non-military assistance throughout the war, which has drawn sharp criticism from Russia.
Similarly, Vučić showed support to Kyiv by attending the Carpathian Eight (C8) initiative, launched by President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept. 18 in Bukovel, western Ukraine.
“We have much to offer - from railway lines and roads to more open borders,” Vučić said, signaling openness to future cooperation with Ukraine across several sectors.
Several European leaders welcomed the result.
“This is clearly a new chapter in the history of the country and its people,” Zelensky said , adding that Ukraine is ready to continue expanding cooperation with Belgrade.
In a telephone call with the Student List, Hungary’s Prime Minister Péter Magyar compared Serbia’s elections to its own, held earlier in the year. “I assured them of Hungary’s support,” he said . “I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle.”
Meanwhile, President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen said that Europe stands “ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union.”
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos reiterated that Europe is ready to support the new government in progressing on its EU path, citing “their [Serbia’s] demands for the rule of law, the fight against corruption and free media.”
While cheap gas could keep Serbia close for now, should the EU membership ever demand a choice, the country may have to take a stronger stance towards Russia.
The question now is how the students, who campaigned for democracy and freedom, will steer Serbia toward European standards while still nurturing its friendship with Moscow and avoiding sanctions.
The Kremlin urged Serbia’s incoming leaders to maintain ties with Russia , claiming that cooperation “is in Serbia’s interests.”
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
body:
Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working. More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year.
“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday , reads.
As of September 30, Anthropic recorded more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000; more than 1,900 customers spending upward of $1 million; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more annually.
Anthropic attributes customer momentum to a “significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations,” which drove net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter.
Throwing shade at the entire legacy SaaS industry, Anthropic pitches Claude as not a “static product that serves a single use case,” but rather “frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities” spanning the models, the developer platform, and the applications users interact with directly.
“An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps.
The playbook is familiar. Uber began by selling rides but has expanded into food delivery and freight. With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave. Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers and then Cowork to their broader workforce.
Those app users become far more valuable. In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20x as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing. The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.
Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams. An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward-deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude.
Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.”
Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.”
The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.
“Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers … could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

title: Diplomatic efforts canbring security, stability
body:
Sayyid Badr bin Hamad al Busaidi, Foreign Minister, affirmed that the Sultanate of Oman continues its diplomatic efforts to enhance security and stability in the Gulf region. This is pursued by facilitating dialogue between parties, working towards the resolution of conflicts, building trust, and advocating for the establishment of a comprehensive regional security framework that includes all states bordering the Gulf. This came during a lecture delivered on Monday by Sayyid Badr at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom, titled 'Comprehensive Security in the Gulf,' which was attended by diplomats, experts, and academics specialising in foreign policy. The minister said that the Sultanate of Oman — which maintains peaceful relations with all its neighbours — bases its policy on the recognition that its own security is contingent upon the security of its regional environment. This understanding drives Oman to persist in its outreach to countries in the region, aiming to settle disputes, preserve peace, and expand its reach. Sayyid Badr also highlighted Oman’s role in facilitating negotiations between the United States and Iran over the past two years, which sought to reach a settlement regarding Iran’s nuclear file and end decades of hostility between the two nations. He noted that, in Oman’s view, the negotiations had achieved significant progress and that reaching an agreement had been within the grasp of both parties. title: Leader outlines roadmap for an ‘ever-stronger Iran’
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 26 (MNA) – Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei has outlined a comprehensive roadmap for an “ever-stronger Iran,” calling on the elite community to break scientific boundaries.
In a message issued on Monday, coinciding with the martyrdom anniversary of Lady Fatimah Zahra (peace be upon her), the Leader addressed Iran’s scientific and sports medalists.
Accoridng to Press TV, Ayatollah Khamenei congratulated the Iranian people on the recent successes in various scientific Olympiads—including astronomy, mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, artificial intelligence, and humanities—as well as their triumphs in international sports arenas.
“The motivation and hope of our elites to bring about changes in the country is a bright flame I have witnessed, both from near and afar, over the course of many years and decades.”
The Leader specifically praised the hardworking athletes for showcasing to the world Iran’s vitality and strength, highlighting the role of female athletes who “make the honorable symbol of the Iranian women’s attire shine before the world.”
Defining the true nature of an elite, the Leader said, “The distinguished elite aren’t people who, merely by virtue of possessing a notable amount of talent and intelligence, regard themselves as somehow set apart from others and who only think of their own fleeting, personal desires.”
“An elite is someone who is deeply concerned with developing their abilities, sees themselves as an effective member of society, and uses their talent and potential for the advancement of themselves and their society alike.”
Ayatollah Khamenei pointed to the tangible impact of Iranian elites in solving real-world problems. “The Iranian elites have demonstrated that knowledge and talent can be turned into tools for addressing the real problems facing the people and the country.”
“From stem cell research, nanotechnology, and biotechnology to advanced aerospace technologies and technologies in industry, mining, medicine, agriculture, nuclear energy, and infrastructure, they have consistently sought to put their knowledge, scientific expertise, and abilities to practical use.”
“We’re all seeing the tangible effects and manifestations of this progressive movement in our daily lives.”
The Leader cited electricity generated by Iranian turbines, knowledge-based desalination plants, agricultural drones, advanced technologies at the Royan Institute, as well as radiopharmaceuticals, remote-sensing satellites, and groundbreaking advancements in the defense and military sectors.
“A strong Iran depends on scientific and technological power, and this core pillar is one of the most important factors for shaping Iran’s role in the emerging global equations and the new world order.”
The Leader pointed to the hostility of Iran’s enemies, noting that their crimes are a testament to the pivotal role the elites play in maintaining Iran’s power.
“The same enemy that has assassinated our society’s prominent scientists and the influential elite during the Second and Third Imposed Wars – and of course, in academic settings and in their everyday lives years prior to that – cannot bear to see Iran advance and grow stronger.”

title: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
body:
SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday . In a statement, SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing” .
Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing.
SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.
The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services.
Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.”
The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.
The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business . SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.
Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s October 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.
The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits.
While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals.
Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads.
“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X . “Some will make it through, but not many.”

title: Nace AI Releases Drex for Search for AI Agents: 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus With 12.6 Search Calls
body: Nace AI has released Drex for Search , which brings its Drex decision models to document search. Drex for Search is a retrieval layer that helps people and agents find evidence. Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode call it through CLI, SDKs, MCP or REST. In Nace’s evaluation, it scores 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus with GPT-5, using 12.6 search calls per question. TL;DR Size: a hosted search system built to search over 1M+ files. It pairs with an answering model such as GPT-5, Gemini 3.5 Flash or Qwen 27B. Runs on: Nace’s managed cloud, a dedicated cloud, your own AWS or Azure account, or on-prem and air-gapped. Performance: ranked #1 or #2 on 3 of 4 public leaderboards, per Nace. Best: 77.5% R@1 on VisDocAgentBench, 10 points above Claude Opus 5 (67.5%). What did Nace AI release? Nace AI frames search as a series of decisions. Drex for Search applies its Drex models to those decisions. Drex scores given options with a calibrated probability each, in 1 forward pass. That makes it cheap enough for every agent step. The release targets classic RAG, which Nace sums up as chunk, embed, top-k, hope. The pipeline breaks in 3 cases: the answer sits in a table on page 23 the answer needs 2 hops across files the answer is inside a scanned PDF How does Drex for Search work inside an agent? Nace describes 3 steps: Classify: Before any search runs, Drex decides if the question needs a quick lookup or an agent. The agent route reads documents and queries tables. Squeeze: Drex walks the workspace level by level: folder, file, section, page. Inside a sheet, it narrows to table and column. Each level keeps only what can hold the answer. Answer: Only the kept pages and tables reach the LLM. The answer cites the file and page. Depth is fixed, so Nace says a million files take as many steps as a thousand. How much does it help coding agents? Nace AI tested 9 agent and model pairs on OfficeQA Pro , a 133-question benchmark over U.S. Treasury Bulletins. Key highlights: 6% more answers right, 62% fewer steps, 56% fewer tokens, and 2.3x faster. Files: PDFs and scans, xlsx, csv and Parquet, mp3 and mp4, docx, pptx, md, json and txt. Citations: every answer names the file and the page, row or minute it came from. Workspaces: isolated, with their own index and knowledge graph, and shareable with invited members. Storage: upload files or folders, or keep workspaces in your own S3 bucket or Azure Blob container. Zero retention: available with your own storage. Domains: Tax, M&A, SEC 10-K, Contracts, or your own. How does it perform on BrowseComp-Plus? BrowseComp-Plus asks a deep-research agent 830 multi-hop questions over about 100K fixed web documents. With GPT-5, Nace AI reports: 92.05% accuracy , #2 of 86 entries on the leaderboard . 12.61 search calls per question, 16.6x fewer than the only entry ahead (209.27 calls). 87.32% in a single pass with 8.93 search calls, the best of any entry under 10 calls. +20.4 points over the Qwen3-Embed-8B baseline, with the same GPT-5 model. window.addEventListener("message",function(e){if(e.data&&e.data.mtpEmbed==="mtp-drexsearch-a2"){var f=document.getElementById("mtp-drexsearch-a2-frame");if(f)f.style.height=e.data.h+"px";}}); How does it score on document benchmarks? On VisDocAgentBench , an agent finds 1 target page among 2,375 arXiv pages. Drex for Search scores 77.5% R@1 with an open-weight Qwen 27B planner. The best published agent, Claude Opus 5, scores 67.5%. R@1 is 97.5% on direct questions, 77.5% on one bridge, and 57.5% on two. On MADQA , agents answer over 800 PDFs and cite pages. Nace reports 94.7% accuracy with Gemini 3.5 Flash and a page-attribution F1 of 88.2. Its effort calibration (Kuiper) is 6.66. Nace ranks it #1, based on the leaderboard as read on October 20. With open-weight Qwen 27B, Nace reports 93.4%. On EnterpriseRAG-Bench , with 500,000+ internal company documents, Nace reports an overall score of 88.22, which it ranks #3. title: Mutilated body of motorcyclist found as similar mystery killings rise
body:
The mutilated body of a motorcycle rider has been found along Longvel Road in Shendam Local Government Area of Plateau State , with his motorcycle reportedly stolen.
The killing, reported on Monday, bears similarities to previous attacks on motorcycle riders in other parts of the state and adds to a series of violent incidents involving farmers, travellers, vigilantes and traditional leaders in recent weeks.
The identity of the latest victim and the circumstances surrounding his death remained unclear as of Monday.
Henry Homsuk, a community resident, said residents woke up to the disturbing news.
“Sadly, someone would be killed and his motorcycle taken away,” Mr Homsuk said.
He said the incident had been reported to security operatives and urged them to investigate the killing, recover the stolen motorcycle and arrest those responsible.
Mr Homsuk also called for increased security along Longvel Road and other vulnerable areas in Shendam, saying residents should be able to carry out their lawful activities without fear.
Efforts to reach security operatives to confirm the incident were unsuccessful at the time of reporting.
The Shendam incident bears similarities to several reported killings of motorcycle riders in Plateau, where victims were allegedly attacked and their motorcycles stolen.
On 23 September, an unidentified person was killed along the Maikatako–Foloh Road in Butura District, Bokkos Local Government Area, in an incident suspected to have involved armed robbers who stole the victim’s motorcycle.
According to a report by security-focused publication Zagazola Makama, troops of Operation Enduring Peace responded to the incident at about 3:50 p.m. and found the victim’s body after the suspected assailants had fled.
The body was subsequently handed over to the police in Bokkos for further action, while security forces began efforts to track down the perpetrators.
Earlier, on 25 August, gunmen reportedly killed Danladi Idi Dakum while he was riding his motorcycle along the Matelem–Ndung Road in Tangur District, also in Bokkos.
A report by Zagazola Makama said troops deployed in the area responded to information about the attack and found Mr Dakum dead at the scene. Preliminary information suggested that the attackers might have been motorcycle snatchers.
In another incident, an unidentified motorcyclist was killed along the Nyong–Bodel Road in Bokkos on 4 September.
According to Zagazola Makama, troops responding to the attack found the victim’s body beside his motorcycle. The attackers had fled before the troops arrived.
The incidents have raised concerns about the safety of motorcycle riders and other road users, particularly on routes linking rural communities where residents depend on motorcycles for transportation and commercial activities.
However, there is no evidence that the killings are connected or that the same perpetrators were responsible.
The Shendam killing also recalls the discovery of a mutilated body behind Monday Market in Pankshin Local Government Area earlier in October.
Residents discovered the unidentified man’s body on 6 October and alerted security operatives.
A community source, Panshak Rogo, told journalists that some parts of the body, including the ears and nose, had been cut off.
The remains were evacuated to General Hospital, Pankshin, as residents urged anyone with information about missing relatives or the deceased’s identity to contact the police.
The discovery came two days after separate attacks in Jos South, Mangu and Riyom local government areas reportedly left at least 13 people dead.
In one of the attacks, nine passengers travelling towards Jos were killed when gunmen opened fire on their vehicle at Dungus in Jos South.
Two people were also reportedly killed in an attack on Vodni community in Pushit District, Mangu, while two others died in a separate attack at Tahoos in Riyom.
The killings heightened concerns about the security situation in the state, where communities have continued to report attacks on residents and travellers.
Violence has also affected traditional institutions and local security groups in Plateau.
On 12 October, gunmen attacked Jatau Samkwar, the Mishkaham Bokkos, at his residence in Daffo, Bokkos Local Government Area. He later died after receiving medical attention.
The Mwaghavul Traditional Council, Bokkos branch, announced his death, while community peace observers expressed concern over recurring attacks in the area.
Earlier in October, four vigilantes were reportedly killed when gunmen attacked Shurum village in Dorowa Babuje District of Barkin Ladi Local Government Area.
Community sources said the victims were on duty protecting residents when the attackers struck.
On 24 October, a woman was reportedly killed and two other people injured while harvesting groundnuts at Gwom-Ajang in Foron District, Barkin Ladi.
The attack prompted community representatives to renew calls for improved security and protection for farmers.
The incidents have affected farmers, travellers, vigilantes, traditional leaders, and commercial transport operators, highlighting the risks residents face across several local government areas.
In Shendam, residents are urging security agencies to investigate the circumstances surrounding the rider’s death, recover the stolen motorcycle and bring the perpetrators to justice.
As of Monday, security operatives had not publicly confirmed the incident or announced any arrests.

title: BC Tory landslide raises mining hopes, rights fears
body: The Conservatives’ landslide election victory in British Columbia has raised mining industry hopes for faster permits and stronger exploration incentives, while setting up a clash over plans to repeal the province’s Indigenous-rights law. Lorne Doerkson’s party led in 63 of 93 ridings, against 28 for the governing New Democratic Party (NDP) and two for the Greens, according to Elections BC’s preliminary count updated Sunday. The Conservatives had 48% of the vote. Final counting is scheduled for Nov. 6. Outgoing Premier David Eby said he would resign as NDP leader after Saturday’s defeat. “British Columbians have elected a government that has made mining a priority and our members are ready to help deliver on that,” Association for Mineral Exploration (AME) president and CEO Todd Stone said in a statement on Sunday. For explorers and developers, the test is whether the new government can turn campaign promises into predictable approvals without deepening disputes over land and consultation. Red Cloud Securities called the result positive for permitting and investor sentiment but warned that repeal could shift uncertainty from the legislature to the courts. Permit pledges The Conservatives’ platform promises legislated approval timelines, a single review for each project and quarterly progress reports. Exploration permits would face deadlines matching or beating competing Canadian jurisdictions. The party pledged to expand the provincial Mining Exploration Tax Credit and press Ottawa to extend flow-through eligibility to engineering and feasibility work. For operating mines and smelters, it promised competitive electricity and carbon costs, alongside fixed timelines for operating permits and mine-life extensions. Roads, rail and ports serving mineral districts would be treated as “provincially significant” infrastructure. AME welcomed the permitting and tax commitments, while calling for reliable land access built on early partnerships with First Nations. Ahead of the election, the association sought amendments to the Indigenous-rights law and the Interpretation Act, rather than repeal. The Mining Association of British Columbia (MABC) congratulated Doerkson and the Conservatives on their majority, saying the incoming government could help increase mining investment, government revenue and jobs. It looked forward to working with the government on responsible resource development, the association said in a LinkedIn post . New projects MABC’s policy priorities include faster permits, more funding for First Nations to participate in reviews, skills training and expanded electricity and transport infrastructure. The association identifies permitting delays as the province’s biggest barrier to mining development. Its May economic assessment identified 31 proposed new mines and expansions across B.C., including 20 critical mineral projects. The association says the existing industry supports more than 56,000 jobs. The Greater Vancouver Board of Trade urged the incoming government to reduce regulatory barriers to investment in resource and other major projects. It also sought permanent cancellation of the proposed provincial sales tax expansion to professional services and removal of the tax on machinery and equipment. Shorter, fixed permit timelines could benefit developers such as Seabridge Gold (TSX: SEA; NYSE: SA) at KSM and Spanish Mountain Gold (TSXV: SPA) at its namesake project, Red Cloud said in a note on Monday. Tax incentives and clearer land access would matter more for earlier-stage explorers, it added. “The change in tone is real and will lift sentiment quickly, especially among investors who have avoided B.C. over permitting and title,” Red Cloud said. “But that money leaves as fast as it comes.” Rights dispute The Conservatives pledged to repeal the 2019 Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, known as DRIPA, and section 8.1 of the Interpretation Act. Their platform also commits to respecting constitutional rights and the duty to consult and accommodate First Nations where required. DRIPA requires B.C. to align its laws with the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, while section 8.1 requires them to be interpreted consistently with it; AME says this has pushed even small exploration permits toward seeking First Nations consent, increasing delays and uncertainty. The First Nations Leadership Council urged the incoming government to retain the Declaration Act, saying it offers a framework for reconciliation and certainty. The council represents the political executives of the BC Assembly of First Nations, First Nations Summit and Union of BC Indian Chiefs. “We are at a historical crossroads: Battleground B.C. or reconciliation through the principles and road map of the Declaration Act,” Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, president of the Union of BC Indian Chiefs, said in the council’s post-election statement . Duty to consult Repeal would not remove the constitutional duty to consult, Red Cloud cautioned. Since March 26 last year, B.C. has required consultation before new mineral claims are registered, responding to a 2023 court ruling against the previous automatic registration system. That process is distinct from obtaining permission to drill or build a mine. The legal dispute remains before the courts. The Supreme Court of Canada agreed on May 21 to hear B.C.’s appeal of a December ruling that its mineral claims system was inconsistent with the UN declaration, which the appeal court found DRIPA had incorporated into provincial law. Investors should watch the first budget for the size of the exploration-credit increase and the legislature for permitting deadlines and any replacement consultation process, Red Cloud said. “Whether this works out well for B.C. mining depends less on repealing DRIPA than on whether the new government can get permits out on time with First Nations on side,” its analysts wrote.

title: Strive’s Bitcoin Treasury Reaches 43,000 BTC as It Files a $1 Billion SATS ATM
body: Strive bought 6,182 bitcoin between Oct. 17 and Oct. 23 at an average price of about $82,732 each, including fees, lifting its holdings to 43,000 BTC , the Nasdaq-listed company disclosed in a filing on Oct. 26. CEO Matt Cole put the cost of the week’s buying at $511.4 million in a post on X . On the same day, Strive filed a prospectus supplement for an at-the-market program that lets it sell up to $1 billion of its 15.00% Series A Perpetual SATS Preferred Stock over time. A week earlier, Strive held 36,818 BTC , and its 7 million-share SATS IPO had not yet closed. It closed on Oct. 20. Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter . How the SATS Program Works Cantor Fitzgerald and Barclays are among the seven sales agents, alongside Clear Street, StoneX, B. Riley Securities, Maxim Group and H.C. Wainwright. They can earn a commission of up to 2% of gross proceeds, and the filing says “none of the Agents are required to sell any specific amount.” Shares can be sold on Nasdaq or through other channels at prevailing market prices. SATS pays a cumulative 15% annual dividend on a $100 stated amount, which is also its floor liquidation preference. The stock last traded at $94.88 on Oct. 23, according to the prospectus. If Strive sold the full $1 billion at $100 a share, 17 million SATS shares would be outstanding, up from 7 million now. Strive said in the prospectus that it intends to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, including “the acquisition of bitcoin and bitcoin-related products,” working capital, income-generating assets, buybacks of its Class A common stock or SATA preferred, and preferred dividends. It set no amount for any single use. The board has declared a first SATS dividend of $0.8710 a share, payable Nov. 9 to holders of record on Nov. 6. Cash and Cost Basis Cash and cash equivalents rose to $504.4 million as of Oct. 23 from $317.5 million a week earlier, the 8-K shows. Strive also holds 505,000 shares of Strategy’s STRC preferred, worth $50.2 million. Together they make up the $554.6 million in cash and marketable securities Cole cited, an increase of $187.7 million on the week. Class A shares outstanding grew by about 3.27 million to 118.1 million over the same period. The prospectus puts the total cost of Strive’s 43,000 BTC at $3.8 billion , or an average of $87,785 a coin with fees, against a fair value of $3.5 billion as of Oct. 23.
