title: The Sony WH-1000XM4C bring back a beloved headphone design
body:
When Sony announced the WH-1000XM4C headphones, I was perplexed. A product revamp usually includes at least one or two significant improvements. Or if it’s a nostalgia play, it’s from a decades-old product and not one that came out in 2020. Beyond a few minor tweaks, though, the XM4C are remarkably similar to their six-year-old namesake, the beloved WH-1000XM4. They even use the same processor for active noise cancellation (ANC).
And while I went into this review questioning the XM4C’s existence, after spending some time with them, I get it. The Sony XM4C aren’t the cutting edge of headphone technology, but they are great headphones that I love using. They still sound great, the design is classic, and they get you pretty close to the performance of Sony’s current-gen flagship, the WH-1000XM6, for a lot less money.
[Product: Sony WH-1000XM4C headphones | https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HFB8N519?tag=theverge02-20, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fsony-wh-1000xm4c-wireless-noise-cancelling-headphones-m4-2nd-gen-black%2FJ7XSRH5447%2Fsku%2F6689199, https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/101881227/type/dlg/https://electronics.sony.com/audio/headphones/headband/p/wh1000xm4c-v]
What I, and many others, loved about the original XM4 is still at the heart of the XM4C. They fold up into a compact size and come with a hard-shell zippered case (which now has its loop on the zipper instead of the edge) that’s easy for travel. The faux-leather ear cups are squishy and comfortable — I wore them for hours at a time during testing without issue. Codec support is also the same as the XM4, with SBC, AAC, and LDAC for high-res wireless audio with supported devices.
The similarities continue with the XM4C’s 40mm driver and, by extension, their sound. Bass is on the heavier side as it is with the XM4, but it isn’t overpowering and instead supports everything above it. Kick drum and tom hits have good oomph and definition. Low-end loving tracks like “bad guy” by Billie Eilish really drive forward. The midrange — like the attack of the acoustic guitar in Tracy Chapman’s “Fast Car” or the bite of Robert Plant’s vocals — can sound slightly covered or muted. It’s not something I hear on my original XM4s, although the difference isn’t drastic. There’s a 10-band EQ in the Sony Sound Connect app (up from five bands on the original XM4) and after boosting the frequencies between 1kHz and 4kHz, the midrange opened up. But even without that small EQ change, the XM4C sound great.
In a world that’s continuing to move away from 3.5mm connections, the XM4C still have one, which works in both powered mode (to use the ANC) or with the headphones off if the battery is low. Like the XM4 (and the XM5 and even last year’s XM6), the XM4C only support wired listening over 3.5mm, though, and not USB-C. The XM4C headphones also only include a 3.5mm cable. You’ll need to provide your own USB-C cable for charging.
[Image: The XM4C (in white) are remarkably similar to the original XM4 (in black), and that’s not a bad thing. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/sony-wh-1000xm4c-headphones-comparison.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
As with the XM4, the XM4C use four mics with Sony’s older QN1 chip for noise canceling, and because of that the ANC performance is basically the same. Going back and forth between the two, the XM4C blocks out a little more of the low end from air conditioners and big trucks driving by outside. But that difference could come from the XM4C’s ear pads, which are six years newer than the worn ones on my XM4.
Not that the XM4C’s ANC is bad, but it’s where their six-year-old tech shows the most. ANC has improved a lot over the past few years, and there are headphones that offer comparable performance for half the price, like the Anker Soundcore Space 2. And it doesn’t compare to the more expensive headphones in Sony’s XM series. Both the XM5 (which also has the QN1 chip, although with eight mics) and XM6 (12 total mics with the more advanced QN3) are better at isolation across the frequency range, especially at the lower end. The slightly more expensive second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones block lower frequencies a bit better than the XM4C, too. Still, the performance is solid, and I never felt distracted by outside noise when it was active.
[Image: While recent headphones have been eschewing the 3.5mm jack, the XM4C include one for wired listening. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268823_Sony_XM4C_JHiggins_0004.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
It’s the same with call quality. The XM4C block ambient sound on calls well, and my voice is clear and understandable, but sometimes louder noises break through or cause my voice to sound a bit compressed. They get the job done; they’re just not top tier like the XM6 (which cost $160 more).
One of the selling points of the XM4C is their replaceable battery — required by upcoming EU regulations for Sony to sell them in Europe. The replacement battery is not for sale in North America, and there’s no indication from Sony when (or if) it might be available here. At the moment, there also aren’t any instructions on how to do the replacement yourself. The ear cups are definitely easier to remove than before — I was able to pop them off and on with my hands instead of prying them up with an extra tool. But once they’re off, there’s no easy way to figure out which screws to remove to get to the battery. (Removing just the four visibly obvious silver screws with arrows pointing to them doesn’t do it.) Now, this isn’t a huge deal on brand-new headphones with batteries that should last you a few years, but it’s also not encouraging for American customers expecting the extra longevity that a user-replaceable battery provides.
The change to a removable battery has also slightly affected battery life on the XM4C, down to 27 hours with ANC on from the 30 hours with the XM4. It’s still more than enough to get through a few days, though.
One disappointing omission is Bluetooth LE, and therefore Auracast support. With the move to Bluetooth 6.0, and the fact the XM5 and XM6 both support it, I was hoping these would, too. It doesn’t mean they might not eventually get Auracast through a firmware update. (That’s what happened with the XM5.) It’s just a shame they don’t have it at release.
[Image: The XM4C can fold into a compact size. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268823_Sony_XM4C_JHiggins_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The XM4C also keep the capacitive touch controls apart from the power and ANC buttons, like in the XM series. A sensor on the right ear cup allows for track and volume controls. Holding your palm over it activates transparency mode until you move it away for quick moments when you need to hear someone. The controls work decently, but I’ve always preferred physical buttons.
The release of the XM4C was a surprise, but it’s a welcome one. Even with only minor improvements on a six-year-old design, the XM4C are still great headphones. I enjoy how they sound, the ANC works well, and they’re incredibly comfortable. Is $300 a bit more than I’d expect for headphones based on a model from 2020? Yeah, a little. But those looking for an XM4 replacement will be incredibly happy with them. The Sony XM4C prove that even though a design is old, it doesn’t mean it should be forgotten.
Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

title: Putin to take part in Gas Exporting Countries Forum’s summit — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will participate in the summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters.
"The forum kicks off tomorrow, on October 27. President of the Russian Federation Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin will take part in it," Ushakov said.
The GECF members are Russia, Algeria, Venezuela, Egypt, Iran, Qatar, Libya, Nigeria, Trinidad and Tobago, Equatorial Guinea and the United Arab Emirates. Eight observer countries are Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru, and Senegal.

title: Houthi online propaganda campaign ties Saudi Arabia leadership to Jeffrey Epstein - report
body: The Iranian-backed Houthis are waging a propaganda war against Saudi Arabia by tying its leadership to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, The New York Times reported on Friday.Mahdi al-Mashat, head of the Houthis' Supreme Political Council, condemned the Saudis for having allegedly given Epstein tapestries that had draped over the building that is the spiritual center of Islam, the Ka'ba.“Those who gave Epstein the Ka'ba's cover are the ones targeting Mecca,” Mashat claimed on the Houthis' official news media.After Mashat's initial statement, numerous social media accounts repeated the condemnation across the internet.Houthis 'obsessed' with Epstein, 'very plugged in,' analyst says“They are very plugged in,” Mohammed al-Basha, founder of the risk advisory firm Basha Report and a Yemen analyst in Washington, told NYT.According to Basha, the Houthis' communication operation includes television channels, websites, radio, newspapers, email campaigns, official and unofficial social media accounts, and cultural influencers, all of which promote and amplify content for the group.Basha added that the Houthis, as well as all the groups in Iran's "axis of resistance," were "obsessed" with Epstein, using him as a shorthand for US and Israeli corruption.

title: Standard Chartered Nigeria wins International Banking Excellence Award at 2026 BAFI Awards
body:
Standard Chartered Bank Nigeria Limited has won the International Banking Excellence Award at the 2026 Banking and Other Financial Institutions (BAFI) Awards, organised by BusinessDay.
The award comes as Standard Chartered continues to draw on its international network and local market expertise to connect clients in Nigeria to opportunities across global markets.
Commenting on the recognition, Ayodeji Adelagun, Chief Executive Officer, Standard Chartered Bank Nigeria Limited, said:
“We are honoured to receive the International Banking Excellence Award. The recognition reflects the strength of our franchise, the commitment of our colleagues and the trust our clients continue to place in us.
Nigeria remains an important market for Standard Chartered. By combining deep local expertise with the breadth of our international network, we are able to connect clients to capital and opportunities across markets. We remain focused on supporting their ambitions, delivering innovative solutions and contributing to Nigeria’s economic growth.”
The recognition comes against the backdrop of Standard Chartered’s continued role in significant transactions supporting investment, trade and economic activity in Nigeria and across Africa.
In September 2026, Standard Chartered acted as Financial Adviser, Global Coordinator, Lead Arranger and Bookrunner for the US$1.1 billion financing supporting the IMA Gas Development Project, a joint venture between TotalEnergies and Amni International. The financing supports a major gas development project in Nigeria and demonstrates the Bank’s ability to combine international capital, structuring expertise and local market knowledge to support strategic infrastructure.
Earlier in the year, Standard Chartered and the International Finance Corporation announced a US$300 million risk-sharing facility aimed at strengthening supply chains and supporting business growth across eight African markets, including Nigeria. The facility supports companies in sectors including agriculture, healthcare and manufacturing, with Standard Chartered acting as originator and provider of supply chain and trade finance.
Standard Chartered NIgeria also received recognition in 2026 for its digital and transaction banking capabilities, including Best Data Analytics Initiative – Africa, Best API Initiative of the Year – Nigeria, Best Virtual Account Initiative – West Africa, and Outstanding Payments Solution for Corporates.
The International Banking Excellence Award adds to these recognitions and comes as Standard Chartered continues to combine its international network, local expertise and product capabilities to support clients in Nigeria and across its markets.

title: Putin to highlight gas sector problems at GECF summit
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will deliver a speech at the summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), where he will highlight challenges faced by the global gas industry, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters.
"Naturally, Vladimir Putin will speak first and will note in his speech the value of the natural gas as an energy source supporting economic growth, mention problems, including of geopolitical nature, the gas industry faces, and highlight areas of work that are priority, from our point of view, to solve existing problems," Ushakov said.
The summit’s program will begin on October 27, the high-ranking official said.

title: Canada Nickel, Swiss Steel plan transatlantic partnership
body: Canada Nickel (TSXV: CNC) says it will explore a long-term strategic partnership with Swiss Steel for the supply of steel products from Canada. The stock surged. The companies signed an agreement outlining the potential collaboration. Under this framework, Canada Nickel would provide Swiss Steel with access to about one million tonnes of semi-finished steel products per year starting in 2030. “This intended partnership supports an important element of our strategy: focusing our own industrial footprint while securing flexible access to competitive, low-carbon pre-material,” said Frank Koch, Swiss Steels’ CEO. Shares in Canada Nickel rose 7.61% to 99¢ apiece Monday morning in Toronto. European markets The news comes as Canada Nickel advances its Crawford Nickel project in Timmins, Ont. Through its subsidiary, NetZero Metals, the company says it wants to transform the nickel-chromium magnetite concentrate produced by the mine into stainless- and specialty-steel products for Canadian and European markets. “As Canada prepares to host the European Union later this week, this partnership demonstrates how we can translate our shared economic and industrial priorities into tangible commercial opportunities,” said Mark Selby, Canada Nickel’s CEO. “Canada’s mineral resources and competitive, low carbon energy advantages, combined with Swiss Steel’s manufacturing expertise and European market access, create an opportunity to build secure, low-carbon supply chains that benefit both economies.” George Pirie, Ontario’s minister of northern economic development and growth, called the collaboration a “perfect example” of how Northern Ontario products can “benefit the world.” He said, “Initiatives like this reinforce Northern Ontario’s role in building secure supply chains, driving long-term economic growth and strengthening Canada’s position in global markets.” An initial supply concept has been developed and validated for the American, Canadian, German, Swiss and French facilities.

title: Arik Receivership: Court admits AMCON board resolutions
body: By Henry Ojelu The Lagos State Special Offences Court, Ikeja, on Monday admitted certified board resolutions of the Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON) as evidence in the ongoing criminal trial of its former Managing Director, Ahmed Kuru, and others over the receivership of Arik Air Limited. Justice Mojisola Dada admitted the documents in a bench ruling, holding that they were relevant to the proceedings and duly certified in line with Section 104 of the Evidence Act, 2011. The documents were tendered by counsel to the second defendant, Mr Uyi Giwa-Osagie, to counter the claim by the fourth prosecution witness, Bawa Usman Kaltungo, that Kuru had unilaterally authorised the receivership. Kaltungo, head of the AMCON desk at the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, and leader of its investigating team, had maintained during cross-examination that Kuru, as AMCON’s managing director and chief executive officer, had unfettered powers and personally sanctioned the receivership. However, Giwa-Osagie tendered the certified board resolutions to establish that the decision was approved by AMCON’s board as a corporate body. The prosecution counsel, Dr Wahab Shittu, SAN, objected to the admissibility of the documents, arguing that they were too remote and irrelevant to the charges. But Giwa-Osagie argued that his client was not standing trial over the propriety of appointing a receiver but over other allegations contained in the charge sheet. He maintained that the documents went to the root of the case and were capable of establishing his client’s innocence. He also argued that they were public documents duly certified and tendered from the Bar. In her ruling, Justice Dada upheld their admissibility, noting that the resolutions emanated from AMCON’s board as a corporate body and had been certified in accordance with the law. The EFCC had arraigned Kuru; Kamilu Omokide, former receiver-manager of Arik Air; Captain Roy Ilegbodu, the airline’s chief executive officer; Union Bank Limited; and Super Bravo Limited over allegations arising from the airline’s receivership. The prosecution followed a petition by Mr Femi Falana, SAN, on behalf of Arik Air’s promoters and shareholders. The court adjourned the case until October 27, 2026, for continuation of trial. The post Arik Receivership: Court admits AMCON board resolutions appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: At Yerevan’s COP17 biodiversity summit, a steep climb ahead for ‘30 by 30’ target
body: GAYE TOWN, Liberia – Deep in the Liberian bush, there’s a dispute about what to do with a big swath of rainforest. The conservation group Wild Chimpanzee Foundation (WCF) and Liberia’s Forestry Development Authority (FDA), backed by the EU, are looking to establish a new 172,000-hectare (425,000-acre) national park. However, advocacy NGOs say they’re bypassing the land rights of nearby communities. It’s an argument with potentially serious repercussions for biodiversity in Liberia. The proposed Kwa National Park would be one of just a handful of strictly protected habitats for chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), forest elephants (Loxodonta cyclotis) and pygmy hippos (Choeropsis liberiensis). The land it would protect is under real threat — commercial cocoa farming is destroying forests in the region at an accelerating pace. Some people from the surrounding villages have sent migrant workers inside Kwa’s proposed boundaries to build new cocoa farms. They now want the Liberian government to excise these areas from the park. “We want the [Forestry Development Authority] to push the boundary line back small,” said Tommy Yarkpawolo, an elder from the tree-ringed village of Gaye Town. He has a 600-hectare (1,482-acre) farm with 30 workers inside Kwa that just earned him more than $400 — enough to start building a new mud-brick house, he said. Cacao saplings underneath burned trees in the proposed Kwa National Park. Photo by Ashoka Mukpo / Mongabay. Many of his neighbors oppose the idea of moving the boundary back. title: Japan air base imposes junior enlisted alcohol ban, curfew after local murder
body: American junior enlisted personnel at a U.S. air base in Japan are banned from consuming alcohol and must adhere to a curfew following the recent arrest of a U.S. Marine for allegedly robbing and murdering a local woman. Kadena Air Base on Okinawa implemented the new restrictions for all personnel in grades E-1 to E-4 beginning late last week, according to a memo signed by 18th Wing Commander Brig. Gen. John Gallemore. “The 18th Wing continually assesses measures to reinforce good order and discipline and maintain positive relationships with our host community,” a base spokesperson told Military Times. In early October, Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force headquartered at Camp Courtney on Okinawa, was arrested under suspicion of killing Anna Yagi, a 39-year-old Naha resident, at a hotel in the city. The police report stated that he also stole her wallet, among other belongings. The murder and subsequent arrest reawakened concerns over the large American troop presence on the island, with the Japanese government lodging what Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described as a “strong protest” against the U.S. while demanding full cooperation with local authorities in the investigation. Shortly after Ballard’s arrest, U.S. officials directed all military personnel on Okinawa to cease operations for 48 hours to allow leaders to conduct standards training. Commanders and senior enlisted leaders trained all service members on standards, discipline and troops’ responsibilities as members of the local community. After the training period, personnel transitioned to a 30-day Period of Reflection, during which there are restrictions on liberty to remind personnel it is a responsibility and privilege to maintain. The new restrictions for Kadena junior enlisted personnel are in effect through the rest of the Period of Reflection, which will end on Nov. 8, the memo reads. “As part of the ongoing 30-day period of reflection on Okinawa, Japan, Brig. Gen. John B. Gallemore, 18th Wing commander, determined that additional preventive measures were appropriate to reinforce expectations for responsible conduct among service members,” the base spokesperson said. The undated memo first circulated on social media on the unofficial Air Force amn/nco/snco Facebook page. A base spokesperson would not confirm or deny the authenticity of the memo to Military Times. Alongside the alcohol consumption ban, off-base liberty is restricted from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. for junior enlisted airmen. Possession of alcohol is forbidden in dormitories and common areas within the base, per the memo, and commanders at all levels are authorized to conduct unannounced Health and Welfare inspections of dorms assigned to personnel to ensure compliance. “These inspections must be administrative in nature and conducted uniformly across the unit or randomly based on objective criteria,” the memo states. “This policy does not authorize warrantless, targeted criminal searches of specific individuals without probable cause and properly executed command search authorization.” Some establishments on Okinawa have been found serving alcohol to military personnel during curfew hours and allowing them to stay past the curfew, in violation of the 30-day Period of Reflection order, according to a Kadena Emergency Off-Limits Order . The order, issued last week, declared a bar in Okinawa off-limits to all Kadena personnel. The mandate is temporary and is slated to be discussed at the next meeting of the Armed Forces Disciplinary Control Board to decide when the ban will cease. “Military members who continue to patronize establishments past curfew hours often engage in high-risk behavior due to overconsumption of alcohol, leading to physical altercations, hospitalizations, and incidents arising from driving under the influence of alcohol,” the order reads. “The demonstration of this establishment to allow members to openly violate the 30-Day Period of Reflection endangers the already strained relationship between the people of Okinawa and U.S. military personnel.”

title: ‘We will protest until the end’: Tbilisi locals protest planned development at Expo Georgia
body: Residents of Tbilisi’s Didube district gathered on Thursday and Sunday to protest plans to build high-rise residential buildings and commercial space on the grounds of Expo Georgia, arguing that the development threatens one of the area’s few recreational spaces. The protest was the second demonstration against the proposed project. Residents said they would continue opposing the plans, citing concerns about traffic congestion, air pollution, and the loss of green space for local families. The development is planned for the Expo Georgia site at 118 Akaki Tsereteli Avenue. Cityzen announced that apartment pre-sales would begin on 22 October, although the project had not yet received a construction permit and no approved detailed development plan could be found in official public sources. The plans envisage buildings ranging from 12 to 32 storeys, with most of the complex intended for residential use and part for commercial purposes. Maia Jojua, a resident of Tsereteli Avenue, said the development would add to the area’s existing traffic and air pollution problems. ‘The traffic is already terrible. People will move into these buildings with their cars, and if even more cars are added, it will become impossible to move along the avenue’, Jojua told OC Media . Protesters hold placards reading ‘Save Expo!’ Photo: Lana Kokaia/OC Media. She said pollution was already preventing her from opening the windows facing the avenue, and expressed concern about the additional impact of the planned construction. Cityzen has not yet responded to OC Media’s request for comment. Jojua also described Expo Georgia as a green oasis in Didube, where she had taken her children for years to play and spend time outdoors. ‘My children grew up here. I brought them here every day for years so they could get some fresh air, especially in the summer’, she said. ‘We must not let them do this’. Khatia Gvenetadze, a resident of Didube, said the Expo Georgia grounds were one of the few places in the district where residents could walk, take their children outdoors, and exercise. ‘We categorically oppose the construction of 16-, 20-, or 30-storey buildings here. We will protest until the end, because this is the only such spot in Didube, on Tsereteli Avenue’, Gvenetadze said. Architect Levan Kalandarishvili also opposed the plans, arguing that the new buildings would destroy the park and undermine the character of the site. Kalandarishvili said the area held personal and architectural significance, recalling that he had spent much of his youth there when the Cosmos cinema operated on the grounds. He also questioned the design of the proposed complex, pointing to plans for a garden on the second floor of a 32-storey building and asking how the development would accommodate the additional parking and infrastructure required by its residents. ‘There are so many problems in Didube. This will not solve them; it will solve somebody’s private interests’, Kalandarishvili told OC Media . The protest also drew people from outside Didube. Irakli Tibunashvili, a Saburtalo resident, told OC Media that the issue affected the entire city. Irakli Tibunashvili with a ‘Save Expo!’ placard. Photo: Lana Kokaia/OC Media. ‘I came to this protest because this problem concerns all of Tbilisi. I want people to be able to live comfortably in this city, without apartment blocks at every other step’, Tibunashvili said. Cityzen, the company behind the project, told OC Media that construction would take place on only 18% of the Expo Georgia site and would not affect existing recreational areas or exhibition pavilions. The company said the new buildings would be constructed along the site’s two adjacent streets, Stanislavski and Samtredia, on sections located beyond the park and pavilions, with separate entrances. It said the development would not take place in the area commonly known as Expo or the exhibition grounds. ‘Under the plans, three residential buildings and a shopping centre would be built along Samtredia Street, while a hotel and one residential building would be located on the Stanislavski Street side. The project would include 105,000 square metres of residential space, comprising approximately 1,200 apartments’, Cityzen said. The company added that the 18% allocated for development would not be used exclusively for housing. It said the site would also include a large shopping mall with facilities such as a swimming pool, fitness centre, cafés, shops, a cinema, and children's areas. ‘Our vision is to create a modern, multifunctional environment in the district, where exhibition, recreational, residential, commercial, and hotel functions complement one another’, Cityzen told. Architect and urban designer Irakli Zhvania, who addressed protesters at the demonstration, warned that the development could leave the remaining green space in shadow for much of the day, particularly in winter, when the sun is lower. He said this could affect the trees and other vegetation, while construction itself could cause further damage. Zhvania also argued that the scale of the buildings would change the architectural character of the site, where low-rise modernist pavilions currently stand. He warned that the proposed residential and commercial complex could significantly increase traffic on Tsereteli Avenue and surrounding streets. The additional vehicles, alongside deliveries and waste collection for the commercial facilities, could worsen congestion and air pollution, he said. Zhvania further warned that construction could take several years, during which dust from cement and concrete could affect people living nearby. ‘This means more time lost for you, more traffic jams, more exhaust fumes, and buses that you miss’, Zhvania told the protesters. Responding to concerns about the scale of the development, Cityzen maintained that the buildings had been designed not to cast shadows over the park. The company argued that high-rise construction would allow it to use less ground space while preserving existing infrastructure and recreational areas. Cityzen also said the project would include underground parking for up to 1,500 vehicles and several additional entrances. The company argued that the new shopping centre, cafés, and leisure facilities would reduce the need for residents to travel elsewhere for services, helping ease traffic congestion. On the project’s environmental impact, Cityzen explained that a detailed dendrological plan had been prepared following a study of the site’s green areas. The company did not specify how many trees or other plants would be removed, but said vegetation clearance would be limited to shrubs and self-seeded ailanthus trees in peripheral areas outside the park and recreational zone. It also said a team of gardeners and dendrologists would work on the project and that the company would be responsible for maintaining and developing the existing recreational areas. Cityzen said all existing exhibition pavilions would be preserved and improved. It plans to replace Pavilion No 11 with a new facility twice its size and said the park, lake, greenery, and monuments would remain in place. ‘The park will remain accessible to the public during construction, with the building site separated from recreational areas by protective barriers’, Cityzen told OC Media . The company added that it had begun meeting local residents to present the plans and gather feedback, and intended to hold further meetings with other interested groups. Tbilisi City Hall’s Urban Development Service told OC Media that the project was in its detailed development plan stage and that no construction permit had been issued. Cityzen said it was in the process of obtaining a construction permit and expected to receive it in the near future. The company said the project would be implemented across three stages, each lasting two years, with the first stage scheduled to begin in spring 2027. Expo Georgia’s history dates back to 1957, when an exhibition venue opened on Tsereteli Avenue. Today, the site covers 139,244 square metres and continues to host exhibitions.

title: Boeing subsidiary joins production of General Atomics FQ-42 Vengeance
body: General Atomics Aeronautical Systems (GA-ASI) has enlisted Boeing subsidiary Spirit Defense to help manufacture the FQ-42 Vengeance, the uncrewed combat aircraft it is producing for the US Air Force. Under the partnership, announced on October 23, 2026 , Spirit Defense will serve as a fuselage design-build partner, contributing engineering and manufacturing capabilities from design through production. Neither company disclosed the value of the agreement, the number of fuselages involved, or when deliveries will begin. The arrangement marks a departure from GA-ASI’s longstanding practice of manufacturing its aircraft in-house, including the MQ-9 Reaper and MQ-9B SkyGuardian. By bringing in an outside supplier, the company aims to expand production capacity and reduce its dependence on a single manufacturing operation as the US Air Force scales up its Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program. GA-ASI President David R. Alexander described the additional capacity as “exactly the kind of production resilience” the Air Force is seeking. Spirit Defense President and CEO Keith Schrader said the company was ready to support the program. FQ-42 Vengeance production already underway General Atomics FQ-42A Vengeance collaborative combat aircraft. (Credit: General Atomics Aeronautical Systems) GA-ASI received its initial FQ-42A production contract on June 17, 2026 , alongside rival manufacturer Anduril, whose FQ-44 Fury was also selected for production . Contract values and the allocation of aircraft between the two manufacturers have not been disclosed. The US Air Force confirmed in September 2026 that the first production increment covers 150 aircraft across both types. The service plans to field 500 combat-ready CCAs by 2032, with an eventual fleet of approximately 1,000 uncrewed combat aircraft. In September 2026, GA-ASI said it was positioned to deliver six FQ-42s per month, with additional manufacturing space available to accommodate larger orders. The company also confirmed that production was proceeding on its own investment while government funding plans continued to develop. It is unclear whether Spirit Defense’s involvement would increase that production rate. Spirit Defense was established following Boeing’s acquisition of Spirit AeroSystems on December 8, 2025 . Headquartered in Wichita, Kansas, the company operates as a non-integrated subsidiary of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, retaining independent governance and operations while supplying the wider defense industry. Boeing was among five companies initially selected to develop CCA concepts. However, in April 2024, the US Air Force chose GA-ASI and Anduril to proceed with production-representative test aircraft, leaving Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and Northrop Grumman outside that phase of the competition. The post Boeing subsidiary joins production of General Atomics FQ-42 Vengeance appeared first on AeroTime .

title: Putin to meet with president of Kenya, Kremlin aide says
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet with Kenyan President William Ruto on October 29, according to the Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov.
"A meeting with the president of the Republic of Kenya is planned," Ushakov told reporters. He added the conversation is scheduled for October 29.
A series of bilateral meetings will begin after two plenary sessions of the Russia-Africa summit.

title: How Trump’s Energy Dominance Turned Into Hubris
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
FILE PHOTO: U.S. President Donald Trump attends an event to sign executive orders in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., August 6, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein/File Photo
By Ron Bousso LONDON, Oct 24 (Reuters) – When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, “energy dominance” was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections.
Ironically, it was the US position as the world’s top oil and gas producer, perhaps more than anything else, that enabled Trump to pursue foreign policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career.
In the first two years of Trump’s second term, vast US oil and gas resources emboldened Washington abroad, strengthened its hand in trade disputes and underpinned a broader effort to restore US geopolitical dominance.
Yet the Iran war exposed the central weakness in that vision: dominating energy production does not mean controlling energy prices.
What began as a pursuit of US energy independence evolved into a doctrine of energy dominance. That is now looking like energy hubris.
The foundations of Trump’s strategy were laid long before his return to office last year. The development of cost-effective techniques to tap the country’s onshore shale basins transformed the US into the world’s largest producer of natural gas in 2009 and petroleum in 2018. By 2022, it was the leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, giving Washington unprecedented influence over global energy markets.
US crude production rose from around 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to nearly 14 million bpd today, around a fifth of global supplies, while the country also accounts for more than a quarter of global LNG exports. No single nation has ever occupied such a commanding position in the global energy system.
Trump sought to turn that advantage into a governing doctrine.
On his first day back in office, he declared a national energy emergency and ordered the government to “unleash American energy”, prioritizing oil, gas, coal and nuclear power while sidelining renewables.
Within weeks, he made “energy dominance” official US policy, establishing the National Energy Dominance Council and reviving his familiar “drill, baby, drill” slogan as the purported cure for elevated inflation and economic anxiety. In an October 2025 proclamation, Trump summed up the philosophy as “maximum production, maximum prosperity, and maximum power”.
This doctrine extended far beyond domestic energy policy.
The administration’s national security strategy, published last December, explicitly linked US influence in the Western Hemisphere to energy dominance, drawing on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to oppose European political intervention in the region.
In a little over a year, the administration wielded US oil and LNG exports in trade negotiations, promoted energy deals as part of efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war, and highlighted Greenland’s resource wealth in a push for greater influence over the Arctic territory.
The high-water mark for Trump’s energy doctrine arguably came early this year after Washington removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a swift military operation.
The US subsequently took control of Venezuelan oil exports and revenues, forced through changes to the country’s hydrocarbons legislation that displaced Chinese companies, and secured an unprecedented agreement granting it access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves.
By February, Trump’s vision of building an economy and foreign policy around abundant fossil fuel resources appeared to be taking root. The US possessed not only more energy than any rival, but also the ability to use that abundance to shape trade, diplomacy and security.
Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran in late February put that doctrine to the test.
The president initially claimed that the joint campaign with Israel against Iran would last only a few weeks. He also repeatedly indicated that vast US oil and gas resources, together with newfound access to Venezuela’s oil wealth, would shield the economy from any resulting spike in energy costs, which he also suggested would be brief.
The war launched on February 28 led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies used to flow, triggering one of the largest energy disruptions in modern history. Middle Eastern producers cut output and rerouted exports where possible, while major importers across Asia reduced consumption.
This caused oil prices to nearly double in the first two months of the conflict, with global benchmark Brent crude LCOc1 peaking at $118 a barrel in March.
That was well below the record $145 reached in 2008, when Iran-related geopolitical tensions, surging Chinese demand and a weakening US dollar drove prices higher. It was also far less than many had feared, largely thanks to reduced Chinese oil imports, ample crude stocks and the surprising adaptability of global markets. But it still represented a severe shock.
Moreover, the risk premium from the Iran war is becoming entrenched. Even though crude flows from the Middle East have mostly recovered, Brent is trading around $110.
The conflict has also spread across the Middle East, pulling in most of Washington’s Gulf allies, most notably the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, which have suffered multiple deadly attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. This has upended the market’s confidence in the security of Middle Eastern crude, unraveled longstanding supply routes and sent shipping prices skyrocketing.
Trump wanted to put his stamp on global energy markets, but this was clearly not what he had in mind.
In one respect, the 2026 energy shock has vindicated Trump’s strategy. The war cemented the US position as the world’s top supplier of crude, refined fuels and LNG, delivering enormous profits to domestic producers and exporters and allowing the US to expand its position in the global market.
Energy independence certainly offered US consumers some protection against the energy shock, particularly compared with Asian economies, where prices and demand destruction were much more extreme this year.
But that protection has been far from ironclad.
US gasoline prices at the pump climbed above $4.60 a gallon in May, the highest level since 2022, while diesel surged to a record $6.50 a gallon in September as global refining capacity was squeezed.
Those increases rapidly became a political problem for the White House as cost-of-living concerns moved to the forefront of the campaign ahead of the midterms on November 3.
The administration sought to contain the fuel-price spike by pulling almost every available lever, including easing biofuel blending mandates and, most controversially, reaching a diesel supply agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
This dynamic underscores the difference between commanding supply and controlling prices.
Oil, LNG and refined fuels are internationally traded commodities. US producers sell them at prices shaped by global supply and demand. They don’t typically reserve cheap energy for American households.
While Trump briefly floated the idea of a diesel export ban, officials ultimately rejected it. Even though a ban might have brought down domestic prices initially, it would likely have resulted in higher fuel prices over the medium term due to global market dynamics.
The administration’s assertion last October that “energy security is national security” appears more relevant than ever. The Iran war has shown that cheap and reliable energy is essential for economic growth, whether it powers heavy industry or the data centers underpinning the artificial intelligence race.
But the conflict has also changed the meaning of energy security.
For countries dependent on imports, particularly many in Asia, the shock has revealed the risks of relying heavily on distant suppliers, vulnerable shipping routes and a concentrated global refining system. Their response is likely to be broader diversification: securing more suppliers, expanding domestic fossil fuel production where possible, accelerating renewable power and shifting more transport towards electricity.
That will not kick the US off its lofty energy perch, but it will likely weaken the allure of oil and gas for many countries over the coming years.
Trump likely felt emboldened to embark on the Iran war — something his predecessors had balked at — precisely because US energy independence made a Middle East adventure seem less risky than it had when the US was heavily reliant on Gulf oil and gas.
But the conflict has, perhaps permanently, undermined Trump’s promise that energy dominance would guarantee low prices and economic security at home.
(The opinions expressed here are those of Ron Bousso , a columnist for Reuters.)

title: India’s CoinDCX Confirms $16 Million Loss Days After CEO Called It a ‘False Alarm’
body:
Indian crypto exchange CoinDCX has admitted it lost about $16 million in an attack on its wallet infrastructure, reversing its co-founder’s earlier insistence that reports of a breach were a “false alarm.”
In a blog post , the Mumbai-based exchange said 15.99 million USDT was drained and that it has absorbed the loss itself, stressing that customer funds remain safe.
The money moved on the Tron network on Oct. 21, and the company traced the incident to a failure in an internal process meant to sweep customer deposits out of wallets it had retired after a far larger hack last year .
The disclosure caps an awkward few days for the exchange. When blockchain researchers and the Arkham tracker first flagged roughly $16 million in suspicious outflows, CEO Sumit Gupta pushed back on X , writing that CoinDCX’s wallets were “not breached” and that the flagged addresses had been compromised back in July 2025, making the activity look like “a false alarm.”
On-chain investigator ZachXBT disputed that account , noting the wallet in question had still been sweeping user deposits into CoinDCX’s current hot wallet as recently as April and May, and he urged customers to withdraw their assets.
Withdraw all funds from CoinDCX if you value your assets.
Its co-founders are clowns running a circus.
They publicly and privately denied a theft of its assets occurred meaning they straight up lied or are negligently incompetent.
Later they disclosed the $16M theft and… pic.twitter.com/uEmtogPonq
The loss compounds a tumultuous stretch for one of India’s largest exchanges. CoinDCX suffered a roughly $44 million hack in July 2025 that it blamed on a server breach, prompting a bounty hunt for the stolen funds and, later, the arrest of an employee over the incident.
Together, the two episodes bring the exchange’s losses to nearly $60 million.
The retired wallets at the center of the new loss were themselves a legacy of that earlier breach, addresses the exchange had stopped using but which kept receiving residual deposits. The failure of an automated transfer system to clear them out left the funds exposed.
CoinDCX has weathered other turbulence this year. The exchange faced fraud and impersonation-scam allegations that drew a police probe, while its founder denied reports of acquisition talks with Coinbase following the 2025 hack. Coinbase has separately moved to expand across South Asia and the Middle East.
The exchange said it would share further details as its investigation continues, and reiterated that user balances are unaffected.
