title: Ghana Medical Trust Fund assures beneficiaries of free, covered treatment and safeguards
body: The Administrator of the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF), has assured beneficiaries that safeguards are in place to minimise the risk of exploitation, as patients enrolled on the Fund are not required to pay for covered services, from consultations to medications and surgeries. Madam Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku said requests for treatment underwent verification at the Fund’s secretariat before approval, while specialists were required to submit patients’ medical records to support claims. Responding to a question on the potential exploitation of beneficiaries during a stakeholders’ engagement in Bolgatanga, Madam Darko-Opoku said the involvement of specialists and the verification process made it difficult for unauthorized charges to go undetected. “When you are onboarded onto the Fund, you do not have to pay anything, from consultation to your treatment pathways, to your medication, to your surgeries and everything,” she said. She added that the likelihood of exploitation was “very minimal,” while encouraging stakeholders to report any specific instances of abuse for investigation. The Administrator further urged beneficiaries to engage with the Fund’s Patient Navigators and Regional Coordinators stationed at health facilities to ensure they received the necessary support throughout their treatment. According to her, the navigators could contact beneficiaries who missed appointments and, where necessary, visit their homes to establish the reasons for their absence and offer assistance. “They go to that extent to get very personal with you so that if you have any difficulty so far as your treatment is concerned, they will be responsible for it,” Madam Darko-Opoku said. She noted that Patient Navigators were available at 10 regional hospitals and six teaching hospitals, alongside Regional Coordinators, and urged beneficiaries to identify these officers immediately after being enrolled on the Fund. Madam Darko-Opoku further dismissed concerns that the Fund, popularly known as MahamaCares, could be politicized or discontinued by a future government because of its association with President John Dramani Mahama. She explained that MahamaCares was a popular nickname, while the institution’s official name remained the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, established by an Act of Parliament. She expressed confidence that the Fund’s relevance to healthcare delivery would ensure its continuity beyond the current administration, “It is an Act of Parliament, so it is not one that another government will come and say because Mahama’s name is on it, I have wished it away,” she said. The Administrator emphasised that access to treatment under the Fund was based on medical needs rather than political affiliation, noting that specialists enrolled and treated eligible patients without requiring them to disclose their political party membership. “When it comes to our health, politics does not play any role in there. Because if you deal with politics with your health, you will die,” she said. She described the Fund as one of the significant legacies President Mahama could leave the country, citing its support for the treatment of prostate cancer, which she said had not previously received such coverage under a national initiative of that kind. On expansion of specialist healthcare, Madam Darko-Opoku said the Fund was supporting the development of three cardiology centres, including one at the Korle Bu Teaching Hospital, which she said had performed more than 160 procedures within three months, with about 110 of them involving children. She disclosed that work on the Tamale cardiology centre, which began in February, was expected to be completed and fully equipped by December 2026, with the President expected to commission the facility. She said the centre would improve access to specialized cardiac care for residents of northern Ghana, including those in the Upper East Region, who would otherwise have to travel to Kumasi or Accra for such services. “Until we can put one here, at least it is closer than going to Komfo Anokye or Accra,” she said. She indicated that the Fund was currently financed through an allocation of 20 per cent of the National Health Insurance Levy and would account to Parliament for its performance as part of the budgetary process. She expressed optimism that the Fund’s achievements would inform future decisions on whether to maintain the existing funding arrangement or establish a direct source of funding to support its operations. Madam Darko-Opoku urged members of the public to learn about the Fund and share accurate information with their communities, churches and mosques to ensure that eligible patients benefited from the initiative

title: PM Tofan: Moldova’s airspace violated more than 100 times since war start in Ukraine
body:
Speaking from Kyiv, Prime Minister of Moldova Vasile Tofan addressed the citizens of his republic, emphasizing that supporting Ukraine is a choice in favor of Moldova’s own security.
"Dear citizens, by defending their cities, their families, and their freedom every day, Ukrainians are also contributing to the security of the Republic of Moldova. Their resistance allows us to live in peace and build our future at home. However, the war is taking place right on our borders," Tofan said during a joint briefing with Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky in Kyiv on Monday, as reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
He noted that the people of Moldova are also well aware of the threats to energy security.
The Prime Minister stated that since the beginning of the full-scale war, Moldova’s airspace has been violated more than 100 times, with drones and debris from projectiles falling onto its territory. Specifically, there were five such incidents this past Saturday alone.
"Supporting Ukraine is a choice in favor of the security, peace, and prosperity of the Republic of Moldova," Tofan emphasized.
As previously reported, on October 26, Ukraine and Moldova signed an agreement on military-technical cooperation, which paves the way for an exchange of expertise.

title: Actor Patrick Diabuah questions ‘God told me’ claims as he reflects on ‘The Ten’ role
body:
Actor Patrick Diabuah cautioned against mistaking personal ambition for divine instruction, saying people should learn to distinguish between their desires and what they believe God has told them to do.
Diabuah, who plays Pastor Matthew in Africa Magic’ s psychological thriller series, The Ten, advised while discussing the decisions that led to a church outreach trip in the series ending in the abduction of 10 members of the congregation.
When asked what he would change if given another chance, the actor identified the trip, linking the decision to Pastor Matthew’s loss of discernment.
He likened the situation to people who embark on expensive projects beyond their financial capacity because they believe God has assured them of success.
“I remember once telling somebody that it’s not the Lord that is showing you; it’s in your head. You are just forcing the Lord into it,” he said.
The actor explained that questioning such convictions doesn’t necessarily mean losing faith, noting that people shouldn’t assume every thought that crosses their minds is a message from God.
“A lot of people will see it as, ‘Oh, Pastor no longer believes in God,’ but no,” he said. “God does not have to talk to man the way we are talking like this. Sometimes it can just be those things in your mind that come to mind.”
Diabuah, with more than two decades of theatre experience, said the role offered a chance to explore the complexities of a religious leader whose personal flaws conflict with his spiritual calling.
His theatre credits include Fela and the Kalakuta Queens, Saro: The Musical and Wole Soyinka’s The Trials of Brother Jero.
Describing Pastor Matthew as a man who genuinely loves God but struggles with pride and guilt, the actor said religious leaders should be allowed to make mistakes, provided they acknowledge their shortcomings and are willing to change course.
The character’s dilemma adds to the tension in The Ten, a psychological thriller by filmmaker Lota Chukwu. The psychological thriller follows survivors of a kidnapping who reunite for a vigil led by Pastor Matthew, only for one of them to be murdered.
With a local festival leaving everyone trapped inside the church, the group finds itself in another life-threatening situation, this time with a killer among them.
The Ten airs on Thursdays and Fridays at 8:30 p.m. on Africa Magic Showcase and is also available to stream on DStv Stream.

title: Volunteer urges residents to leave Oleshky in evacuation, as town may face greater destruction
body:
The Russian-occupied town of Oleshky may face even greater destruction after civilians leave as part of a recent U.S.-negotiated ceasefire, evacuation volunteer Kseniia Arkhipova told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 26.
"When television channels around the world show that dozens of buses full of people have left Oleshky , when it is reported that the evacuation has taken place and the town is practically deserted, we are very much afraid that, after that, Oleshky will simply be wiped off the face of the earth," Arkhipova said.
"Those who remain may find themselves in even more dreadful conditions," she added.
Her warning comes after U.S. first lady Melania Trump mediated a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in and around Oleshky to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid. The ceasefire is scheduled to begin on 3:00 a.m. on October 27th, Kyiv time, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
Both Russia and Ukraine agreed to a local ceasefire during the evacuation, but the exact evacuation routes remain unclear, and the sides are still working on the arrangements.
Arkhipova urged local residents remaining in the town to consider evacuation . She acknowledged that leaving home is a difficult decision for residents who have spent their entire lives there, but staying could expose them to escalating danger, intensifying hostilities, and lacking access to help.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Located on the Russian-occupied eastern bank of the Dnipro River opposite Kherson, it has faced a deepening humanitarian crisis, with residents struggling to access food, medicine, electricity, and other basic necessities.
Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank, including Oleshky, to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Amid possible Russian escalation in the area, Arkhipova highlighted the risk that residents who remain in the town could be overlooked if reports of mass evacuations make it seem as if no civilians remain behind.
"The worst thing would be if the whole world came to believe that everyone had been evacuated from Oleshky, whilst (people) were still there. And (they) would simply be forgotten."
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help Oleshky residents leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips through Russia and Belarus. But in recent months, dangers posed by drone attacks, artillery fire, and mined roads have made evacuation by road almost impossible .
Russian forces have also prevented Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, said on Sept. 16 that more than 6,000 people may remain in Oleshky and the surrounding area, including about 200 children. His office said it had previously verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.

title: South Korean Officials Lean Toward Delaying Crypto Tax Until 2029: Report
body: South Korea’s government is leaning toward postponing its crypto income tax once more, with a January 2029 start now the most likely option, Korean news agency Newsis reported on Oct. 26, citing unnamed officials at the presidential office and elsewhere in government. An official at the presidential office, Cheong Wa Dae, reportedly told Newsis on Oct. 25 that discussions were headed toward pushing implementation back. The government plans to settle its position through inter-agency consultations starting as early as Oct. 26, the report said. The tax is scheduled to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027 . It would apply a 22% rate, including local tax, to income from disposing of or lending crypto above 2.5 million won , after necessary expenses are deducted. Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter . Waiting on the U.S. Cross-border data is the main reason. Under the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF), which lets countries automatically share crypto tax information, South Korea is among 46 countries starting exchanges next year, Newsis said. Another 29, including Canada, Switzerland, Singapore and Hong Kong, join in 2028, and the U.S. makes its first exchange only in 2029 . The presidential office official reportedly said the U.S. accounts for nearly half the crypto market and called its not providing Korea with tax information the main obstacle. A 2027 start, the official added, would leave Korean tax authorities tracing data on U.S. exchanges one by one, and the presidential office said the tax could end up falling on domestic exchange users alone, according to Newsis. A government official reportedly told the agency a final decision would likely come in late November or early December, after the National Assembly works through tax law revisions. Nothing has been decided, and no official has commented on the record. A Fourth Delay The levy was introduced through a 2020 amendment to the Income Tax Act and has been pushed back three times during National Assembly deliberations; another postponement would be the fourth. The government and lawmakers are expected to amend the law again in tax revision talks starting in November, Newsis reported. The government had originally favored starting on schedule, according to Newsis, arguing that overseas financial account reporting would let it collect tax data from abroad. At an Oct. 13 parliamentary audit, then-National Tax Service Commissioner Lim Kwang-hyun, who has since been named presidential chief of staff , told lawmakers that detailed crypto tax standards would be announced next month . Calls for a delay have since come from both the opposition and the ruling party. Democratic Party lawmaker Park Min-gyu became the first ruling party member to propose a delay , in a bill that sets the start date at Jan. 1, 2029 . From the opposition People Power Party, Song Eon-seok has proposed scrapping the tax, while Kim Sang-hoon and Jung Sung-kuk have filed bills to postpone it. title: Tinubu has no fresh ideas to tackle poverty – SDP presidential candidate
body:
The presidential candidate of the Social Democratic Party (SDP), Adewole Adebayo, has accused President Bola Tinubu of failing to address poverty and insecurity, arguing that the administration has no fresh ideas to improve Nigerians’ living conditions ahead of the 2027 election.
Mr Adebayo said the president must account for his handling of the economic hardship he inherited, the measures his administration has implemented and the plans he intends to pursue if he seeks re-election.
The SDP candidate said this on Monday while appearing on Morning Show , a programme on Arise News.
He criticised the government’s proposed 90-day plan to address economic challenges, saying it shows the All Progressives Congress (APC) administration prioritises politics over governance.
“The president is our leader in the country, and we need to give him some respect, despite our political differences,” Mr Adebayo said. “But increasingly, it is clear that the president doesn’t live in Nigeria to know the problems of the people.”
He argued that Mr Tinubu has presided over worsening poverty since assuming office on 29 May 2023 and should therefore be held accountable for his policies’ outcomes.
“Whether the poverty is inherited, imported, or falls from the sky, he has been presiding over that poverty in the last three and a half years, and he has not found a single solution to any of the indices of poverty,” he said.
Mr Adebayo also argued that the president could not blame previous administrations indefinitely, noting that none of his major opposition challengers had previously served as president.
He cited former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), as an example, arguing that the economic conditions during Atiku’s time in government differed significantly from those confronting Nigerians today.
The SDP candidate said a presidential campaign should focus on the incumbent’s record, the results of policies implemented and a clear programme for the future, rather than political alliances and references to past leaders.
“A campaign for the presidency for someone who is an incumbent has only three parts. You would account for the problems you met on the ground. Two, you would account for the efforts you have made to improve the situation. Three, you will account for what you want to do next,” he said.
“It is the solidity of your plan, not the number of poor bearers standing by your left or right, that makes a presidential campaign.”
Mr Adebayo questioned the timing and feasibility of the administration’s proposed 90-day plan, arguing that economic problems such as high prices and declining purchasing power required sustained policy interventions rather than short-term measures.
He said policies designed to influence prices, improve household incomes and reduce the cost of living required coordinated fiscal and monetary measures that could not be fully implemented within three months.
“90 days is a short-term plan, and the content of their programme, what they say they want to do, are things that are medium-term and long-term,” he said.
He accused the APC of using the proposed plan to create the impression that the government was responding to public concerns while potentially relying on temporary relief measures.
“In the medical laboratory of the APC, every problem in Nigeria, insecurity, bad roads, poor education, no healthcare, can be cured by a bag of rice,” he said.
Mr Adebayo argued that the administration should focus on structural reforms that increase food production, create jobs, and reduce the cost of essential services instead of relying on palliatives.
He also criticised the president’s economic policies, saying the government had yet to show how it intended to reverse the hardship households face.
Mr Adebayo said his party had developed a programme to address poverty and insecurity through agriculture, employment, affordable education, mass housing and lower energy costs.
He said the party’s proposed interventions would focus on increasing agricultural output, improving security, and creating employment opportunities in the economy’s productive sectors.
“We are not here to manage the status quo. We are here to change the paradigm,” he said.
Mr Adebayo said an SDP administration would also seek to improve domestic energy security by ensuring that crude oil allocated for local consumption was available to meet the country’s needs.
He questioned the management of crude oil previously earmarked for domestic use, citing the historical allocation of 445,000 barrels per day, and demanded greater accountability from the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL) and the federal government over the country’s domestic crude supply.
He argued that the government’s inability to guarantee adequate domestic crude supply, despite Nigeria’s status as an oil-producing country, raised questions about the management of the sector.
Mr Adebayo said the SDP’s economic programme was anchored on implementing Chapter II of the Nigerian Constitution, which outlines the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy, including the state’s responsibility to promote the welfare and security of citizens.
He said the party would prioritise access to food, education, healthcare and housing, alongside measures to create employment and improve household purchasing power.
The SDP candidate maintained that the 2027 election should be decided by competing policy proposals and measurable plans to improve citizens’ lives rather than political endorsements and campaign displays.

title: Kano House Of Assembly Confirms Six Commissioner Nominees
body: The Kano State House of Assembly has screened and confirmed six commissioner nominees submitted by the state executive for appointment to the State Executive Council. The Speaker, Jibril Ismail Falgore, presided over the screening during plenary. The exercise followed a motion by the Majority Leader, Lawan Hussaini, and seconded by the Minority Leader, Usman Abubakar, seeking the House’s approval to screen and confirm the nominees. Speaking during the plenary, the Majority Leader said the nominees had met the requirements for appointment as commissioners and members of the State Executive Council. He explained that the House was impressed by their level of expertise and experience, noting that several of them had previously served as commissioners, while others had held positions such as chairman of the Kano State Independent Electoral Commission (KANSIEC) and other public offices. Hussaini added that the confirmation would be communicated to the executive for the allocation of portfolios to the newly appointed commissioners. In his remarks after the screening, Air Commodore Salisu Yusha’u (retd.) noted that, as a security expert, he would work closely with relevant security agencies and local communities to strengthen security and promote peace at the grassroots. A former chairman of the Kano State Independent Electoral Commission (KANSIEC), Sani Malumfashi, emphasised the need to promote science and technology education, innovation and entrepreneurship to equip citizens with practical skills for self-reliance. Another nominee and former Commissioner for Health and Environment, Aminu Tsanyawa, pledged to work towards eradicating drug abuse in Kano State, describing it as a major challenge requiring collective efforts to protect residents, particularly young people. Other nominees who spoke after the screening included Mukhtari Ishaq, Ibrahim Namadi and Idris Garba. The post Kano House Of Assembly Confirms Six Commissioner Nominees appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Thousands of observers are to descend on polling places to monitor on Election Day
body:
Democrats and outside watchdogs are planning a massive presence at the polls on Election Day
NEW YORK -- Democrats and outside watchdogs are planning a massive presence at the polls on Election Day driven by concerns that President Donald Trump will further leverage the vast resources of the federal government to interfere with a midterm that could hobble his final two years in office.
They won't be the only ones there. A sprawling election protection effort on the left that is expected to deploy tens of thousands of monitors will be met by the largest-ever monitoring program by the Justice Department and still more observers from Republican-aligned groups. The result could be unlike anything seen at the polls in modern times.
The effort among Democratic and nonprofit groups includes training volunteers to stand watch outside polling places and report activities they consider concerning. The network includes traditional government watchdogs such as Common Cause and the American Civil Liberties Union plus a flood of volunteers assembled by state Democratic parties, congressional leaders, national activist groups and organizations focused on protecting democracy.
The Democratic National Committee's Association of State Democratic Committees created a first-of-its-kind cybersecurity unit staffed by former CIA and FBI officials to monitor and report online misinformation, including artificial intelligence deepfakes , said Jane Kleeb, vice chair of the DNC.
That's as Democratic mayors, attorneys general and secretaries of state host tabletop exercises simulating worst-case scenarios, such as a surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials at voting locations or the seizure of ballots and voting equipment .
On Capitol Hill, Democratic leaders have assembled a legal team that rivals that of any presidential campaign.
“We’ve never done this before,” Kleeb said of the party’s sweeping efforts. But “we’ve never had to deal with the president of the United States saying that he may seize ballots, put ICE agents outside polling locations and other kinds of very clear direct threats to the voting process.”
The Department of Justice has already filed lawsuits in California and Alaska that could affect ballot counting or certification .
While Trump continues to make baseless allegations of cheating in the election, administration and military officials have said they have no plans to deploy immigration agents or troops to polling sites.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis blamed “radical Democrats” for creating fears about election security by refusing to enact voter ID requirements and other Republican-backed measures.
“President Trump has done more than any other president to ensure we have free and fair elections,” Bis said.
State Democratic parties have trained an estimated 10,000 volunteers to observe polling places and report anything potentially concerning they might see from federal agents. Common Cause has trained roughly 16,000 more volunteers to stand watch at voting precincts, said Suzanne Almeida, vice president of states for the group.
She said a broader Election Protection coalition involving 300 other groups has trained tens of thousands more.
Smaller pockets of volunteers from other groups also are preparing to show up, including roughly 100 organized by Senate Democrats and hundreds more from a Democratic-allied group called Save America, which is training clergy members, veterans, teachers and other local community members. National groups such as Indivisible and MoveOn are activating their own expansive networks.
There are so many organizations working to protect the voting process — including many that cannot legally coordinate with each other — that some officials involved worry about unintentionally creating chaos outside polling locations.
Almeida said Election Day confusion is possible in some precincts but the nature of the threat requires a collective effort.
“It will actually take all of us if some of the threats we are most worried about come to pass,” she said.
Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump appointee who leads the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division , was asked on CBS’ “60 Minutes” whether the Republican administration is planning to send ICE agents to polling places.
“There is no plan to do that,” she responded.
Still, the Justice Department is planning its largest-ever election monitoring effort, with about 1,000 department staff expected to observe voting and ensure federal laws are being followed, spokesperson Kiersten Pels said. That comes after a primary season in which the department said it deployed more than 100 election monitors across hundreds of polling locations.
At least one of those placements sparked tensions with local officials. Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, said the behavior of two monitors during that state's primary was “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.” A Laramie County clerk said the Justice Department monitors arrived at the polls intending to interview voters, but her office didn’t allow it.
The department disagrees that the monitors did anything improper, Pels said. She added that the monitors are trained to comply with federal law governing conduct at polling places and won’t “interfere with the voting process.”
Democratic lawmakers and voting rights advocates have raised concerns that the Trump administration’s monitors could intimidate voters or abandon the duty they’ve had for decades to protect against civil rights violations.
The department plans to send them to every state, focusing on high-population areas, jurisdictions that have had problems in the past and districts with close elections, according to a senior department official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity under terms set by the department.
The Republican National Committee said its operation involves deploying “election integrity deputy state directors” in 22 states, among them Arizona, Michigan, Georgia and North Carolina.
Those workers are the “eyes and the ears of the RNC in the field” who recruit volunteers and organize trainings, said Ally Triolo, the RNC’s election integrity communications director. Their mission is to surface anything that seems unlawful.
At the same time, the RNC has enlisted nearly 22,000 poll workers and is recruiting poll-watching volunteers for competitive districts. The poll watchers will “observe the process and help ensure election rules are followed in accordance with the law,” Triolo said.
While federal monitors have quietly observed elections for decades, largely without incident, some election officials are taking precautions.
Chris Swope, the city clerk in Lansing, Michigan, said he preemptively contacted law enforcement and his attorney in case federal monitors violate election law, although he expects them to abide by the rules.
The Democratic Mayors Association issued guidance to local Democratic officials with detailed instructions about what to do if federal agents appear at polling locations.
It notes that federal law prohibits the presence of federal immigration agents, the FBI or other investigative personnel. It also issued a reminder that federal agents are not allowed to be armed at the polls, nor are they allowed to interact with voters or handle ballots or election equipment.
Justice Department officials have said their monitors won't be armed and will not interfere with voting. Asked about department monitors being sent to Georgia, Trump told a reporter recently: “They’re not going to do anything other than watch."
Some of the poll observations have already begun. Mary Corcoran, Save America's executive director, said her group's volunteers have been monitoring precincts during early voting in Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio to help give voters a sense of security.
“The fear is the point, and we must do something about it,” she said. “Left unanswered, fear does the work of keeping people home without a single agent setting foot at a polling place.”
___ Associated Press writers Jacqueline GaNun in Lansing, Mich., Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report.

title: Georgia's prison director resigns amid investigation into alleged inmate beating
body: Giorgi Pataridze, director general of Georgia’s Special Penitentiary Service, has resigned. The resignation came after Georgia’s Prosecutor General’s Office recommended the Justice Ministry suspend Giorgi Pataridze in connection with an investigation into the alleged beating of inmate Davit Peikrishvili. The Special Penitentiary Service confirmed to OC Media that Pataridze had been dismissed as head of the service following his resignation on Monday evening, the same day that the recommendation was reported. His departure comes amid renewed scrutiny of abuse in Georgia’s prison system, which was ignited by the case of Giorgi Davitadze who claimed that prison staff raped and humiliated him in a prison de-escalation room in December 2025. The Peikrishvili case was transferred from the Justice Ministry’s General Inspectorate to the investigative department of the Prosecutor General’s Office. The agency said that all necessary investigative and procedural measures were being carried out intensively. ‘At the same time, the Prosecutor General’s Office of Georgia has recommended that the Justice Ministry suspend Giorgi Pataridze, the head of the Special Penitentiary Service under the Justice Ministry’, the agency told OC Media earlier on Monday. The Special Penitentiary Service has categorically denied reports that Peikrishvili was physically assaulted in prison. An inmate at Georgia’s Gldani Prison, Davit Peikrishvili was hospitalised twice over a span of two days, with his lawyer alleging that fellow inmates beat him. The clinic’s director Zurab Chkhaidze told OC Media that Peikrishvili had wounds on his upper limbs. According to his lawyer, Peikrishvili said that on 16 October, a newly detained Vato Kipiani was placed in his cell and had assaulted him alongside others. Marika Pkhakadze, who legally represents Vato Kipiani, has denied the assault allegations. She told TV Formula that Kipiani did not share a cell with Peikrishvili. The Justice Ministry’s General Inspectorate launched an investigation into the alleged beating on 20 October, before the case was transferred to the Prosecutor General’s Office. Georgian inmate hospitalised twice over two days after alleged beating by other prisoners The authorities have denied the assault took place. OC Media Lana Kokaia Who is Davit Peikrishvili? Davit Peikrishvili was arrested along with his brother Giorgi this September in separate cases involving alleged group violence and extortion. In October, the Prosecutor General’s Office brought additional charges against the brothers, accusing them of laundering approximately ₾10 million ($4.9 million) in illicit funds between 2020 and 2026. If convicted, they face up to 12 years in prison. Meanwhile, Vato Kipiani, the alleged assailant, was arrested along with Avtandil ‘Katsro’ Bilanishvili, and Shota Kipiani in mid-October in connection with a fight at a restaurant. Kipiani and the Peikrishvili brothers have a long history of conflict. In 2020, Georgian authorities accused Kipiani of planning to kill the brothers, however his lawyer said he was released after nine months in detention because the court did not establish his guilt in the alleged plot. Asked by journalists whether the Prosecutor General’s Office’s move confirmed that an inmate had indeed been placed in Peikrishvili’s cell and beaten, Parliamentary Speaker Shalva Papuashvili rejected the suggestion. ‘No, of course, this does not confirm that. It confirms that the Prosecutor’s Office is conducting an investigation and may approach [the relevant authorities] to carry out whatever procedures are necessary’, Papuashvili said . The allegations come amid other reports of abuse in Georgia’s penitentiary system. In a separate case, inmate Giorgi Davitadze accused a prison escort guard of rape. One of the guards accused in the case left Georgia’s Penitentiary Service in March; the service said his departure was not in any way connected to Davidatze’s case. One guard accused in Davitadze prison rape case left Georgia’s penitentiary service in March Authorities claim the departure was unrelated to Davitadze’s claims that he was raped in December 2025. OC Media Lana Kokaia Davitadze’s family shared an audio recording on Friday, aired by opposition leaning TV Pirveli , in which another inmate, Gela Isashvili, alleged that prison staff had assaulted him after he expressed solidarity with Davitadze. The Special Penitentiary Service categorically denied Isashvili’s allegations of inhuman treatment at Prison No 6, claiming that the allegations were untrue. The service also accused Isashvili of repeatedly violating prison rules and said an investigation had been launched into an alleged assault by Isashvili against a prison employee in August 2026.

title: Physician assistants offer free health screening in Techiman
body: The Ghana Physician Assistants Association (GPAA) has begun a free community health screening exercise at four locations in Techiman as part of its 23rd Annual General Conference. The exercise, running from October 26 to 31, 2026, is taking place at the forecourt of the Bonokyempem Hall, the Regional Coordinating Council (RCC), the Techiman Central Market and the forecourt of the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) office. The initiative forms part of activities for the conference, which is being held under the theme: “From Policy to Practice: Positioning the Physician Assistant to Deliver Comprehensive Free Primary Healthcare at the Community Level.” Speaking to reporters, the GPAA Regional Secretary, Philip Yaw Bomfeh, said the exercise was intended to make health screening accessible to workers and other residents who might struggle to find time to visit health facilities. “We realised that most workers are busy and find it difficult to visit the hospital. So we decided to bring the screening to them,” he said. “Regular health screening is important as a means of knowing your condition early for early treatment,” he added. The screening also includes breast examinations and education on breast cancer awareness and early detection. Lydia Waki, a midwife in charge of the screening process at Bamiri Health Centre, urged women to seek medical attention when they notice unusual changes in their breasts and to avoid self-medication. “We are urging women to stay away from self-medication and rush to the hospital when they see any abnormal signs around their breasts,” she said. “Early detection saves lives.” Residents who participated in the exercise expressed appreciation to the association for providing the services free of charge. The GPAA is encouraging residents in and around Techiman to take advantage of the screening exercise before it ends on October 31.

title: INEC, Meta, Google, Microsoft, Rise Networks launch AI hackathon ahead of 2027 elections
body:
Rise Networks, in collaboration with the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Meta, Google, Microsoft and other partners, has launched an artificial intelligence hackathon to develop technology solutions to electoral challenges ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections.
The #AI4Elections Hackathon 2026–2027 will bring together Nigerian developers, researchers, university students, electoral experts, and civil society organisations to develop practical, responsible AI tools to support electoral processes, according to a statement the organisers shared with PREMIUM TIMES.
Participants will be competing for a total of N10 million in cash prizes across all categories. The overall winner will receive N4 million, while the second- and third-place winners will receive N2.5 million and N1.5 million, respectively.
Four additional awards of N500,000 each will recognise outstanding projects in research and policy innovation, electoral and civic inclusion, responsible AI and safety, and cybersecurity and resilience.
Applications opened on 22 October and will close on 12 November, followed by a national grand finale and innovation showcase in Lagos on 16 December, then technical support for selected projects.
Other partners in the initiative include the International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR), NITHUB at the University of Lagos, the Centre for Information Technology and Development (CITAD), CLEEN Foundation, Tap Initiative for Citizens’ Development, the International Press Centre, Legal Naija, Ahmadu Bello University and the Federal University of Technology, Akure.
The programme is supported by the MacArthur Foundation and Luminate.
In a statement announcing the initiative, the organisers said the competition would focus on addressing challenges such as misinformation, AI-generated fake images and videos, cybersecurity threats, privacy risks and access to reliable electoral information.
Rise Networks said the programme would combine the hackathon with an AI4Elections Development Hub to support the testing and refinement of promising solutions, and an Electoral Community of Practice to sustain collaboration among innovators, researchers, mentors, and other stakeholders.
The initiative builds on Run-Am, an AI-powered misinformation detection and fact-checking mobile application developed by Rise Networks for Nigeria’s 2023 general elections.
Speaking on the initiative, Rise Networks founder Toyosi Akerele-Ogunsiji said it aims to ensure AI innovation strengthens Nigeria’s electoral process rather than introducing new risks, stressing the need to protect citizens’ rights and uphold transparency, privacy, and human oversight.
Ms Akerele-Ogunsiji said Nigeria must actively use artificial intelligence to safeguard electoral integrity, improve access to reliable information, and build public confidence in democratic institutions.
“Our ambition is not to introduce technology for technology’s sake,” she said. “We are committed to promoting responsible AI innovation that respects the integrity of Nigeria’s electoral process, protects citizens’ rights, and prioritises transparency, privacy, and human oversight. Innovation must strengthen our democracy, not create new vulnerabilities for it.”
The competition will cover five areas: trustworthy electoral information; electoral data analysis and decision support; inclusive and multilingual electoral and civic technology; electoral cybersecurity and resilience; and election observation and citizen accountability. Climate resilience and environmental innovation will be an optional cross-cutting area.
“The #AI4Elections Hackathon is specifically designed as a design and development competition, and participants are expected to use Artificial Intelligence and emerging technologies to develop working solutions addressing clearly defined electoral challenges rather than submit ideas, presentations, or “mock-ups alone, ” the statement said.
The hackathon is open to Nigerians aged 18 and above, including students, researchers, software developers, data scientists, cybersecurity professionals, technology entrepreneurs and civil society practitioners. Applicants may participate individually or in teams of up to four members.
The organisers said entries must be submitted in English.
It added that projects that have previously received grants, awards or recognition in other competitions will not be accepted.
Organisers said entries will be assessed on technical functionality, innovation, relevance to electoral challenges, practical usefulness, cybersecurity, privacy protection, responsible AI practices, scalability and feasibility.
“Unauthorised testing of live electoral systems or access to institutional infrastructure is strictly prohibited, and winning the competition does not constitute approval for operational deployment. Any future institutional pilot or deployment remains subject to relevant legal, institutional, technical and security approvals,” the statement added.
“Interested applicants can find eligibility requirements and application details at ai4elections.risenetworks.org.”

title: DGI Consult, UNICEF Strengthen Primary Healthcare Management in Adamawa, Kwara, Sokoto
body: Funmi Ogundare Development Governance International (DGI) Consult, through the UNICEF-supported Enhancing Leadership, Governance and Management Capacities (ELGMC) project, has trained local government health managers and frontline health workers in Adamawa, Kwara and Sokoto States to strengthen primary healthcare delivery and improve maternal and child health outcomes. The training focused on equipping health teams with practical leadership, management and problem-solving skills to improve the implementation of Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Nutrition (RMNCAH+N) and Gender-Based Violence (GBV) programmes. Held in selected local government areas (LGAs) across the three states, the workshops addressed gaps identified through earlier facility assessments, with participants developing practical strategies to improve service organisation, resource management, accountability and decision-making. Speaking at the opening of the training in Song LGA of Adamawa State, the Executive Chairman of the Adamawa State Primary Health Care Development Agency (ADSPHCDA), Dr Sulaiman Saidu Bashir, underscored the importance of strengthening leadership and management at the local government and facility levels. He stressed the collective responsibility of health-sector stakeholders to ensure effective programme implementation and prevent avoidable deaths among women, newborns, children and adolescents. The Chief Executive Officer of DGI Consult, Dr Gafar Alawode, said the intervention was designed to strengthen the capacity of health facility and LGA teams to identify and address challenges affecting service delivery. “This is not only in Adamawa State but across health systems. The central purpose of the training is to strengthen the ability of facility and LGA teams to identify and solve problems encountered while delivering health services,” he stated. Alawode added that the intervention would not only help participating facilities develop solutions to their immediate challenges but also generate practical approaches that could contribute to wider improvements across health facilities in the states. During the workshops, participants examined challenges affecting service delivery and identified actions within their areas of responsibility to address them. They also explored how programme data and results frameworks could be used to establish priorities, monitor performance and support evidence-based decisions. Through group exercises and discussions, the health workers translated identified priorities into action plans with defined responsibilities, expected results and timelines. The workshops also introduced participants to the whole–part–rest approach to problem-solving, which encourages teams to examine challenges comprehensively, identify actions within their control, determine the support required from other stakeholders and mobilise relevant partners to implement solutions. An example of the approach was demonstrated at Primary Health Centre Yallabe in Wamakko LGA of Sokoto state, where collaboration with local health stakeholders helped address service delivery challenges. Engagement with the nutrition focal person led to the facility being designated as a distribution point for ready-to-use therapeutic food, reportedly increasing patient turnout. In addition, an official of the Sokoto State Primary Health Care Development Agency with health training from the community agreed to support the facility during busy immunisation and antenatal care sessions. Speaking during the engagement in Gwadabawa LGA of Sokoto State, the Director of Health, Alhaji Usman Aliyu Shehu, urged participants to apply the lessons from the training in their daily work and remain focused on measurable results. He said the training should be regarded as part of an ongoing improvement process rather than a stand-alone activity. Participants, he added, should routinely review progress, identify emerging challenges and take corrective action to ensure that agreed priorities translate into tangible improvements at the facility level. In Kwara State, the Director of Primary Health Care Services at the Kwara State Primary Health Care Development Agency (KWSPHCDA), Dr. Oguntoye, expressed confidence that the intervention would strengthen health workers’ capacity to deliver quality services and improve health outcomes across the state. He emphasised the importance of translating improved leadership and management into effective programme implementation, with facility teams better equipped to plan, coordinate and improve healthcare services.

title: Court Orders El-Rufai to Enter Defence on Alleged Wiretapping Trial
body: Alex Enumah in Abuja Justice Joyce Abdulmalik of a Federal High Court, Abuja, on Monday ordered a former Governor of Kaduna State, Nasir El-Rufai, to enter his defence if he so desires in his ongoing trial on bugging the telephone communications of the National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu. Justice Abdulmalik made the order shortly after dismissing the no-case submission filed by El-Rufai, in response to the prosecution’s case. In her ruling on the no-case submission, the judge held that there is sufficient evidence by the prosecution to warrant the court to call on the defendant to enter his defence if he so desires. She subsequently adjourned till November 25 for the former governor to open his defence. The African Democratic Congress (ADC) chieftain is standing trial on a five-count criminal charge brought against him by the Department of State Services (DSS). At the no-case submission hearing on September 22, the prosecution, represented by Oluwole Aladedoye (SAN), objected to the submission and urged the court to dismiss it and order the defendant to enter his defence. According to Aladedoye, the defendant failed to address Exhibit “B”, which the prosecution claimed contains El-Rufai’s admission in relation to the tapping of Ribadu’s phone. He contended that since the prosecution has effectively established a prima facie case against El-Rufai, through its two witnesses, the defendant is required by law to enter a defence. Defence lawyer, Akinyemi Aremu, while adopting his client’s no-case submission, argued that the prosecution failed to establish a prima facie case against the ex-governor to require him to be called upon to enter a defence. Aremu urged the court to uphold the no-case submission and discharge his client. El-Rufai opted for a no-case submission after the prosecution closed its case upon calling two witnesses — an operative of the DSS and a lawyer, Deji Adeyanju. Adeyanju, who testified as a subpoenaed witness, told the court that the ex-governor admitted during a television interview that he wiretapped the NSA’s phone lines.

title: Let Chaos Reign, and Then Rein In Chaos
body: Replit for Business launched today! To hear more from Amjad Masad, CEO of Replit, see his post here on the rise of the self-driving company. One thing I love about Amjad is, sometimes he really says the thing and articulates something that other people weren’t brave enough or clear enough in their thinking to express. He has one of those today, as part of Replit’s idea of an Agent Habitat as the way that more businesses are going to become self-driving companies. What Amjad says that’s so on the money is one great word: chaos . “Today, most agents live somewhere chaotic. They run in chat windows, personal accounts, and one-off scripts, holding whatever credentials and data someone handed them. Nobody decided what they could touch, and nobody can see what they did.” Chaos! It’s one of the most underrated concepts in disruptive technology adoption. One of the best tells that a technology will actually change the world is, “Does it make a chaotic entrance?” And then the most important question thereafter, as Andy Grove put it, is, who is going to let chaos reign, and then rein in the chaos? Throughout the history of computers and the internet, the most interesting, disruptive and ultimately consequential technologies are the ones that enter workplaces in a chaotic sort of way. What Replit really gets is that this joyful chaos can’t be extinguished: it has to be reined in just the right amount, so that all of the bottoms-up enthusiasm and ownership stays alive within an optimal habitat. Because the same excitement and ambition driving the initial chaos is also what’s creating deep organizational alignment, from the bottom up inside businesses, that makes these companies come alive. Agents are joining a long tradition of technologies that started as chaos and got reined in just the right amount: Computers Many people working in tech today have no memory of this, but the early wave of adoption for personal computers at work was an incredible “let chaos rein, and then rein in chaos” sort of story. Not because IT wanted it that way! But because that’s just how it happened. Like ChatGPT a few years ago, PCs mostly arrived because people brought them to work and plugged them in, allowed or not, because they helped them get things done. Once the secret was out, everyone wanted one. People lied on their procurement forms , claiming they were buying an oscilloscope, or a typewriter, or even a desk. People wanted PCs so badly that they were just necessarily going to arrive in the office in a pretty chaotic way. IT departments did not like this chaos! From a 1983 article, “Guerrillas Shift Power Balance In The Office”: With a personal computer, Keen notes, the enterprising employee can often bypass the company’s main computers to calculate profit-and-loss projections or track sales calls. More important, the personal computer can be linked to the main computer to siphon off desired information. If a corporation isn’t careful, says Keen, the proliferation of personal computers will lead to “shadow” data processing departments that perform corporate calculations hidden from top management’s view. Despite this knee-jerk reaction to regain control over these rogue PC users, smart business leaders understood how valuable this behavior was. Employees were staking a claim on new ways to work, and taking fierce ownership over them. Furthermore, this new behavior was illuminating and reinforcing the alignment inside the company that actually mattered. You can’t become an order of magnitude more productive overnight, just by adding a new tool, unless you know what to do , and have the alignment you need with the business to go out and do it. What they needed was the right habitat for people to have computers at work. Which meant a bunch of learned IT practices and workplace “harnesses,” for people to actually use PCs in a way that kept the bottom-up productivity intact without sinking the organization into chaos. Spreadsheets Meanwhile, the PC’s original killer app - the spreadsheet - was itself creating a new kind of chaos. Spreadsheets, in another sort of way, also have a claim to be the original “workplace agent.” Suddenly all kinds of people who didn’t consider themselves “programmers” could model how they felt their business should run, calculate how it was doing, and project what was possible. Spreadsheets caught on so quickly that they became the single most important reason why people wanted their own PCs. This may be difficult to imagine in 2026, but “rogue spreadsheets” back then created a very similar challenge to “rogue agents” today. You had all of these people who were now able to create real-looking business artifacts and projections, and while some of them were phenomenally valuable, you also got a lot of spreadsheets that were, essentially, hallucinations. They could be horribly documented, hard to audit, full of formula errors, and usually exactly one employee actually understood what was in them: the person who’d made it. Mitch Kapor, the original spreadsheet king, put it to Steven Levy in 1984 : “You can just randomly make formulas, all of which depend on each other. And when you look at the final results, you have no way of knowing what the rules are, unless somebody tells you.” Chaos! The answer, again, was a habitat where chaos could be reined in a little bit. Data access rules inside organizations, conventions around locking cells, version histories, standardizing formulas, and auditing output. And then inside that habitat, people continued to use that individual empowerment and autonomy that the spreadsheet gave them, and they’ve been indispensable to organizations ever since. Email Yes, even email entered the workplace more chaotically than you might’ve realized. Back before email, companies had the mailroom. It looked unimportant, but it was one of the most politically important functions in the company. The mailroom was where the company could control the flow of information inside the organization. Who could reach out to whom, and who could view, copy, or circulate what. All of it ran through the mailroom. And then email came out, and suddenly, it became really easy, at least in principle, for anyone to contact anybody inside the company. Chaos! This was, in complete seriousness, a bit of a crisis of authority and control for executive teams. And it prompted huge anxiety around secrecy and information control: what happens if employees accidentally forwarded sensitive information? What if they shared it with someone they shouldn’t? What if they did it on purpose? It was considered a reasonable idea, for a minute, to have to get managerial approval to send an email . Thankfully, again, we created habitats for company communication where employees could reap all of the benefits of instant communication and applied initiative, with the necessary permissions and access control to rein in the communication chaos just enough. So there are two lessons here from the history of computers. One is, someone has to rein in the chaos a little bit, and create the habitat for the behavior to thrive in an optimal way. The second lesson is that the chaos is an important indicator in the first place for a kind of behavior that’s really valuable: the kind that creates deep alignment inside the company, for it to do its best work. The self-driving company In all of those examples from earlier in the computing era, why was the initial chaos such a strong indicator of something important and valuable? Because people were staking a claim on something they immediately found valuable, and wanted to homestead. People felt they’d discovered something deeply aligned with their individual ability to contribute, and with the organization’s needs. Businesses are made of people who care. That was true before computers and before agents, and it will be true when companies become “self-driving,” as Amjad puts it. A successful business needs employees who are empowered and aligned with the company’s goals, and a way to turn that alignment into real artifacts at work. When disruptive technology comes along that makes people radically more productive, the first people who really come alive are the people who know what to do . There is no substitute for these people. They know what needs to be done, and now they have a tool - whether it’s the PC, the spreadsheet, or now a fleet of agents - that lets them get it done 100x more productively than they could before. I believe Replit has an example where one employee at Sumitomo Mitsui Finance and Leasing took over a development process that was supposed to take six people six months, and did it themselves in one week. That one person who knows whats going on can now just do it themselves. And, to a first order of approximation, the business succeeds based on how successfully these people are able to translate their individual alignment with the business into overall alignment on the part of the whole org, through the artifacts that they produce, and by the followers they attract. Code is the ultimate “aligning artifact” that someone can produce, because it literally is the business logic of the organization. But it’s an inherently chaotic thing to generate , if suddenly all kinds of new people are creating it from the bottom up. That chaos is an important sign that something important has happened - just like people bringing their own PCs and creating “shadow IT departments”, or people creating their own spreadsheets or sending their own emails. And it’s a good indicator that you need a habitat for that behavior to thrive. You don’t want to put it in a cage. Nor do you want to let it run completely free. But you want it free-range. To become self-driving, a company has to become aligned. And nothing creates alignment quite like expanding the opportunity set of who can contribute code. Soon, you’ll be able to measure a company’s alignment by the richness of its agent habitat. Replit and its customers already get this. Most companies don’t yet. In hindsight, it’ll be pretty obvious, once the self-driving companies have pulled ahead. title: PM of Moldova: I know what diving Shahed sounds like, and I know fear felt during ballistic missile attacks
body:
Prime Minister of Moldova Vasile Tofan shared that he lived in Ukraine for four and a half years during the full-scale invasion, and that he is familiar with the sound of a diving Shahed drone and the fear experienced during ballistic missile attacks.
"I lived and worked in Ukraine—in Kyiv—for 15 years. It was here that I raised my children and built companies. Ukraine was my second home and will always remain close to my heart. I was in Ukraine on February 24, 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale war, and I remained here for the next four and a half years, until I assumed my current position. I know the sound of a diving Shahed, the fear during ballistic missile attacks, and the incredible work of Ukraine’s heroic air defense forces. I know what it means for a million Ukrainian families to have explosions occur right next to their homes—it is their daily reality," Tofan said during a joint briefing with Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky in Kyiv on Monday, as reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
He emphasized that Moldova firmly condemns Russia’s war against Ukraine and advocates for a just and lasting peace, accountability for the aggressor, and the safe return of deported Ukrainian children.
Tofan assured his Ukrainian counterpart that Moldova will remain a reliable neighbor and partner to Ukraine.

title: Moscow prosecutors seek criminal charges against prominent human rights activist Anna Karetnikova
body: Moscow’s Lefortovsky Interdistrict Prosecutor’s Office has gathered materials to open a criminal case against human rights activist Anna Karetnikova. Prosecutors said she is suspected of “evading the obligations of a foreign agent” and “participating in the activities of an extremist organization.” According to prosecutors, Karetnikova, whom Russian authorities designated a foreign agent, distributed materials outside Russia without the required “foreign agent” disclaimer and had previously received administrative fines for it: Karetnikova, as a member of an organization that a court has ruled extremist and banned from operating in Russia, also systematically distributes materials on the organization’s behalf and takes deliberate steps to help ensure it continues operating. The prosecutor’s statement does not specify which “extremist organization” is meant, though Karetnikova has worked with the human rights group Memorial for more than 20 years. Russian authorities designated Memorial an “extremist organization” in April 2026. There have been no previous reports of criminal cases over cooperation with Memorial. Anna Karetnikova is one of Russia’s best-known human rights activists. In addition to her work with Memorial, with which she has collaborated since 2002, Karetnikova spent eight years working on Moscow’s Public Monitoring Commission (ONK). Starting in 2016, she also served as the lead analyst in the Moscow department of Russia’s Federal Penitentiary Service. Karetnikova was removed from that position in January 2023, after which she left Russia. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. title: Osinbajo, Traditional Rulers Seek End to Polarisation in N’ central
body: Yemi Kosoko in Jos Former Vice-President, Prof. Yemi Osinbajo, traditional rulers, religious leaders and policy experts have called for urgent action to counter growing polarisation and rebuild civic cohesion in North-central Nigeria, warning that injustice, impunity and divisive narratives continue to fuel conflict across the region. The leaders spoke at a national dialogue organised by the Justice Research Institute (JRI) in partnership with the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies (NIPSS) under the theme, ‘Countering Polarisation and Rebuilding Civic Cohesion in North Central Nigeria: Beyond Tribe and Faith, Reclaiming Our Shared Stories.’ Osinbajo stressed that lasting peace cannot be achieved without justice, accountability and intentional reconciliation, drawing lessons from South Africa and Rwanda. He said communities affected by violence and displacement must be helped to heal through truth-telling, restitution and institutional reforms that restore confidence in the justice system. He warned that impunity undermines social stability, insisting that justice must include restitution and restoration. “People cannot simply be told to forget. Where land has been taken unjustly, it must be returned. Where people have suffered losses, appropriate compensation and justice are necessary for healing,” he said. Speaking at the event, NIPSS Director-General, Prof. Ayo Omotayo, described storytelling as a powerful tool for national reconciliation, noting that societies are held together not only by laws and institutions but also by the stories citizens tell about one another. He warned that distorted narratives, misinformation and inherited prejudices can deepen divisions and undermine national development. Also addressing participants, the Emir of Lafia, Justice Sidi Bage (rtd), said conflict begins when justice, identity and belonging are denied. He urged Nigerians to reject collective blame, ethnic profiling and religious stereotyping, emphasizing that dialogue, active listening and mutual respect are essential for peaceful coexistence. Similarly, the Secretary-General of Jama’atu Nasril Islam (JNI), Prof. Khalid Abubakar Aliyu, warned against exploiting ethnic and religious differences for political or social gain. He called for stronger accountability, responsible communication and greater investment in youth employment, arguing that widespread poverty and joblessness remain major drivers of insecurity. Participants agreed that no community can achieve lasting peace by promoting the insecurity of another and called for inclusive governance, stronger conflict-resolution mechanisms, support for displaced persons and greater involvement of women and young people in peacebuilding efforts. The dialogue ended with a renewed commitment to promote justice, truth, responsible leadership and shared citizenship as foundations for peace, unity and development in North-central Nigeria and beyond.

title: Tunji Olowolafe Foundation, OAU Partner to Expand Digital Research, Postgraduate Access
body: The Founder of the Tunji Olowolafe Foundation (TOF), Dr. Tunji Olowolafe, has called on Nigerian universities to open research to more people, test long-held beliefs with scientific rigour and carry discoveries out of the laboratory and into the economy. Speaking at the Obafemi Awolowo University (OAU), Ile-Ife 65th anniversary celebration, on the theme, ‘Promoting Research Excellence and Innovation in Postgraduate Studies: Charting the Future,’ Dr. Olowolafe reframed research as the disciplined habit of correcting a nation’s course based on evidence. He described the postgraduate college as the intellectual engine room of a nation, where society sends its sharpest minds to challenge conventional wisdom and demand honest, data-driven answers. His first strategy called for the opening of the gates of research earlier, wider and more flexibly. He urged OAU to make its staff schools benchmarks for Africa, with science, technology and artificial intelligence at the core of the curriculum. He pointed to the Foundation’s Gbemisola Olowolafe Memorial Community Secondary School in Are Ekiti, which opened in September 2025 with 100 students and now has more than 170, alongside an ICT centre teaching artificial intelligence (AI), coding, graphic design and Mandarin, with instructors teaching live from Beijing through a Starlink connection. “The postgraduate researchers of 2040 are sitting in primary classrooms today,” he said. He also questioned whether every road to postgraduate research must run through a four-year degree, inviting universities to recognize prior learning and demonstrated expertise without lowering standards. With only about one million of the two million UTME candidates admitted in 2025, he argued that flexible, digital study must become the standard model, since a digital campus needs no physical acreage. This builds on the Foundation’s Project Digi-Teach, which is training academic staff at Ekiti State University (EKSU) for digital proficiency. His second strategy urged researchers to test what society believes. Rather than dismissing indigenous knowledge without investigation or defending it without validation, he called for rigorous testing, citing Chinese scientist Tu Youyou, whose study of a centuries-old herbal remedy produced the malaria treatment artemisinin and a Nobel Prize. He extended the same principle to national history, including sensitive chapters such as the Civil War. “She neither rejected tradition nor accepted it. She tested it,” he said. The third strategy, according to him, focused on pushing research out of the laboratory and directly into the economy. Olowolafe advocated university promotion structures that reward patents, commercial products and solved industrial problems alongside traditional journal publications. “Research is complete only when it leaves the laboratory and improves lives,” he said. Pointing to OAU’s exceptional tech pedigree, including Flutterwave and Moniepoint founded by its graduates, he challenged the global alumni community to scale up their financial, institutional and mentorship support for research tenfold. To support this vision, the Foundation will install a solar power system for the Postgraduate College, provide a virtual learning and oral defence facility and modernize the college boardroom. TOF will also fund pilot studies on a case-by-case basis and sponsor training in grant writing and donor compliance, working with OAU’s Central Office of Research and Advancement Office. “Our ambition must go beyond providing infrastructure to building institutions that can generate knowledge and attract global research funding. By strengthening the capacity of our universities, we can expand opportunities for our people and position Nigeria to compete more effectively in the global knowledge economy,” he noted. Through these ideas and commitments, the Tunji Olowolafe Foundation continues to advance its broader ambition of strengthening the institutions, skills and opportunities that support Nigeria’s long-term development. Its work across education, digital learning and research capacity reflects a sustained commitment to equipping institutions and the next generation with the tools to compete and thrive in an increasingly knowledge-driven world.

title: No Prospect of Reviving Black Sea Grain Deal, Russian Diplomat Says
body:
Russian officials remain in contact with their Turkish counterparts on issues of maritime navigation through the Black Sea, a senior Russian diplomat told the Interfax news agency on Monday, but Moscow sees no immediate prospect of renewing the Black Sea grain initiative.
“We’re considering proposals from various countries. We’re in dialogue with all countries, including Turkey,” Alexander Alimov, deputy director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s department of international organizations, was quoted as saying.
“But for now, I don’t see any prospects for reviving the ‘grain deal’,” Alimov said, referring to the Black Sea Grain Initiative, an agreement brokered by Turkey and the UN in 2022 to prevent a global food shortage.
That original deal enabled the safe transport of nearly 33 million metric tons of Ukrainian agricultural exports.
Russia backed out of the arrangement in the summer of 2023, claiming Western sanctions continued to hamper Russian food and fertilizer exports and alleging Ukraine was using the maritime corridor for military operations.
Since this summer, Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on commercial vessels and port infrastructure in the Black Sea, creating major disruptions to shipping and driving wheat prices higher on global markets.
Turkey, which has maintained good relations with both countries since the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, has for months tried to negotiate a maritime security agreement between the countries.
