title: International Space Games kick off in Moscow
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The opening ceremony of the International Space Games (ISG), an initiative designed to train specialists for key sectors of the rocket and space industry, has taken place in Moscow, a TASS correspondent reports.
The event brings together approximately 250 participants from 10 countries.
“This project is particularly important to us, as it is being implemented under the Personnel for Space federal project, which forms part of the broader Space national project,” said Irina Ganiyeva, Director of the Human Resources Department at Roscosmos. “I would like to express my sincere gratitude to our international partners who accepted our invitation and traveled to Russia. You are our strategic partners, and we greatly value that relationship. Your presence here demonstrates that space knows no borders and that Russia is ready to share its scientific and technological expertise.”
The International Space Games are large-scale engineering and educational competitions built around a simulated space mission. Young engineers participating will be tasked with sustaining a hypothetical outpost on a planet within the Solar System. They must manage its energy, food, and oxygen supplies while simultaneously carrying out a scientific research mission.
“It is a great honor to stand before you today. Through your intellect, your ability to work together, and your capacity to change the world, you will help make both the world and our country a better place. In these games, pursuing victory in the traditional sense makes little sense, because everyone is working toward a common goal. Our engineers have devoted tremendous effort to designing challenges that can only be solved through scientific and technological cooperation. This approach is intended to help you learn, through the games, how to explore space together,” said Dmitry Zemtsov, Vice-Rector of HSE University and Executive Secretary of the National Technology Olympiad (NTO) Organizing Committee.
HSE University is the organizer of the International Space Games. The event will be held across several venues, including a testing ground equipped with high-tech modular domes at the Skolkovo Innovation Center, which is supporting the project, and a dedicated Mission Control Center at Bauman Moscow State Technical University (BMSTU). The concluding events will take place at HSE University.
The opening ceremony was attended by several prominent guests, including Dmitry Peskov, the President’s Special Representative for Digital and Technological Development and head of the National Technology Initiative (NTI) Platform; Yevgeny Abakumov, Deputy Director General for Science and Strategy at Rosatom; and Natalia Kravchenko, Advisor to the Chair of the Board of the Skolkovo Foundation.
TASS is the event’s general media partner, while NEWM TASS is a media partner.

title: EFCC witness disputes Union Bank debt claim in Arik Air receivership trial
body:
An investigator with the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Bawa Kaltungo, has described Arik Air receivership as fraudulent, telling the Lagos State Special Offences Court in Ikeja that the airline was not indebted to Union Bank of Nigeria.
Mr Kaltungo, who is the Director of the EFCC Zonal Directorate 2 in Lagos, was the fourth prosecution witness in the trial of former Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON) Managing Director Ahmed Kuru and four others, said he had informed AMCON’s management that Arik Air did not owe the bank.
“The foundation for the appointment of a receivership over Arik Air was fraudulent and faulty. There was no bad debt; it does not exist,” he said on Monday.
The witness said he led the EFCC team that investigated a petition over the receivership. He maintained that Mr Kuru had extensive powers and unilaterally approved the appointment of the receiver-manager.
The defence challenged this claim by tendering AMCON board resolutions relating to the appointment.
The prosecution objected to their relevance, arguing that the documents were too remote from the issues before the court. But Mr Kuru’s lawyer, Uyi Giwa-Osagie, argued that the resolutions were relevant to determining his client’s role in the decision.
Mr Giwa-Osagie said Mr Kuru was not standing trial over AMCON’s general power to appoint a receiver-manager, but over the specific allegations. He argued that the board resolutions would help establish the circumstances surrounding the appointment.
Trial judge Mojisola Dada admitted the documents, ruling that they emanated from AMCON’s board and were certified in accordance with Section 104 of the Evidence Act.
The ruling allowed the documents to be admitted as evidence but did not determine whether the receivership was lawful or whether Mr Kuru acted without the board’s authorisation.
Mr Kuru is standing trial alongside former receiver-manager Kamilu Alaba Omokide, Arik Air Chief Executive Officer Roy Ilegbodu, Union Bank of Nigeria Plc and Super Bravo Limited. They face a six charges of conspiracy, stealing and abuse of office. All five defendants pleaded not guilty.
During an earlier sitting on 28 April, Mr Kaltungo told the court that Arik Air had paid 38 per cent of its foreign loan before AMCON took over the airline, according to an EFCC report of the proceedings.
He referred to a letter dated 4 October 2010 from Union Bank to Arik Air concerning quarterly repayments on an Airbus aircraft loan. The letter, recovered during the investigation, showed that the airline was expected to make a repayment on the facility, he said.
Mr Kaltungo said Arik Air obtained the loan from foreign lenders, including HSBC, and had serviced it until June 2010.
He argued that the document showed the facility was performing, contrary to the claim that it was a non-performing loan.
According to the witness, Union Bank converted a N51 billion guarantee into a loan and transferred the claim to AMCON without using the funds to pay the foreign creditors.
“Arik has paid 38 per cent of its loan to foreign creditors,” he said.
He alleged that the bank withheld the money meant for the creditors and still owed Arik Air in respect of the amount the airline had repaid.
Mr Kaltungo also told the court that investigators found more than N2 billion in payments in the bank records after the receivership took effect on 8 March 2016.
On the proceeds from the sale of Arik Air shares, he noted that three aircraft had been revalued at $105.718 million, equivalent to about N32 billion.
He further explained that only N9.2 billion was applied to the airline’s loan, leaving more than N28 billion unaccounted for.
During cross-examination in April, Mr Kaltungo said investigators did not trace money to the accounts of Mr Kuru and Mr Ilegbodu.
These claims have yet to be determined by the court.
The EFCC arraigned the defendants in January 2025 following a petition by Arik Air promoters and shareholders, represented by Femi Falana, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), over the airline’s receivership and related transactions.
One count accuses Union Bank of making false statements to AMCON about Arik Air’s performing loans, leading to the transfer of what the prosecution describes as a bogus N71 billion debt.
Another accuses Messrs Kuru, Omokide and Ilegbodu of fraudulently converting N4.9 billion belonging to Arik Air for the use of NG Eagle Limited in 2022.
The charge also alleges that the defendants authorised the dismantling and destruction of an Arik Air aircraft, registration number 5N-JEA and serial number 15058, valued at $31.5 million, in February 2022.

Instagram is announcing a big push into longform horizontal video, which the platform is calling “Features.”
Instagram boss Adam Mosseri has been against doing longform video on the platform “for a long time,” he says in a six-and-a-half-minute video (here’s the widescreen version ) with VP of product Tessa Lyons, saying that “one of my concerns has been, how do we make sure that we keep Instagram not just about entertainment, but about connecting with friends. If you watch a longform video, that’s “it’s a lot of Reels, photos, and carousels that you might not have sent to a friend,” meaning less likes and shares.
Now, though, the team is working on making shortform and longform video “symbiotic,” according to Mosseri, like podcasts or comedy specials that can be both long videos and broken up into shorter ones.
The announcement of this widescreen video push also follows the launch of Instagram’s TV app late last year. That app launched first as a Reels-focused experience and as a pilot for Amazon Fire TV devices in the US, but it’s since expanded to Google TVs , Samsung TVs and Apple TV , and Instagram launched new features like the ability to watch Stories earlier this year .
Mosseri also talked about the updates with creators Samir Chaudry and Colin Rosenblum, and their video includes some clips of how longform video will show up on the platform.
Today, Features are expanding to the US in a small test and is in testing with some creators in Brazil, according to Instagram spokesperson Megan Buckley. Instagram is testing a few other video-focused features as well, including clips pointing to a long video, a way for creators to create a “series” of Reels, and improvements for live video discovery.

title: UN Commission of Inquiry: Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure amount to crimes against humanity
body:
Russian authorities have committed war crimes by deliberately targeting civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts, by carrying out continuous attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine stated in its new report to the UN General Assembly.
The Commission also concluded that Russian authorities recruited men who were victims of human trafficking in various countries into their armed forces, which constitutes a violation of international human rights law.
The Commission investigated the impact of large-scale attacks by Russian armed forces on Ukraine's energy infrastructure on the civilian population, particularly during the difficult winter of 2025-2026, as well as the cumulative effects of these attacks since the fall of 2022. Over the years, systematic waves of attacks – during which hundreds of drones and missiles were deployed simultaneously – became increasingly frequent and intense, covering an ever-wider area and causing significant damage to Ukraine's energy sector.
The Commission said that last winter, when temperatures plunged to minus 21 °C, millions of people in Ukraine faced prolonged disruptions in the supply of heat, electricity, water, and gas and were forced to live in unbearable conditions.
"As a new cold season sets in, the attacks have again intensified and there is serious concern for the life and health of civilians," Commission Chair Erik Møse said.
Prolonged exposure to the cold, lack of access to basic utilities, and the constant need to find ways to survive have significantly affected the physical and mental health of the civilian population, the Commission added.
It is noted that older adults and people with limited mobility have been particularly affected. Due to the risk of getting stuck in an elevator in the event of a sudden power outage, they were unable to go down to shelters during air raid alerts and were forced to remain in unheated homes without electricity or water, lacking access to life-support equipment and basic services.
According to the Commission's assessment, the Russian commanders who ordered the attacks were aware that the heating facilities they targeted in large population centers were vital to the civilian population, especially in winter.
It is noted that Russian authorities officially declared their intention to continue the attacks and referred to plans for carrying them out. The Commission concluded that Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately targeting civilian objects.
The evidence gathered indicates that the attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure were carried out deliberately, in accordance with a state policy aimed at depriving the civilian population of electricity and other essential services dependent on energy supplies and causing them suffering. The Commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts.
The Commission relied on the testimony of 255 individuals who survived the winter under the conditions described above in Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Poltava, Zaporizhia, and Zhytomyr regions, as well as on information provided by Ukrainian authorities, doctors, and nongovernmental organizations.
The Commission also examined attacks by the Ukrainian armed forces on energy facilities in the Russian Federation and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. At the same time, the Commission was unable to investigate the consequences of these attacks in greater detail, as Russia did not grant it access to the relevant territories and did not respond to the Commission's requests for information.
Regarding the recruitment of foreign nationals into the Russian armed forces, the Commission found compelling evidence that Russian authorities engaged in human trafficking involving individuals from 29 countries. Human trafficking was carried out through deception and coercion in collaboration with agents and agencies operating in various countries around the world.
The agents and agencies that recruited men in various countries presented themselves as legitimate companies or government-backed enterprises. They arranged visas and travel documents for groups of recruits and, in some cases, accompanied them during the trip.
It is noted, however, that shortly after their arrival, they were forced to sign contracts with the Russian Ministry of Defense, drafted in Russian. The commission noted a high level of coordination between agents operating in various countries around the world and the Russian authorities.
The men were sent to the front lines in Ukraine and tasked with carrying out dangerous missions. Many of them were killed or went missing; others voluntarily surrendered or were captured by the Ukrainian armed forces and were granted prisoner-of-war status.
The Commission reiterates that international law prohibits attacks on the civilian population and civilian objects, and calls for an end to such attacks.
The Commission calls for the release from the Russian armed forces of all individuals who have been victims of human trafficking.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine is an independent body mandated by the UN Human Rights Council, in particular, to investigate all alleged human rights violations and abuses, as well as violations of international humanitarian law and related crimes, in the context of the Russian Federation's aggression against Ukraine. The Commission consists of Erik Møse (Chair), Pablo de Greiff, and Vrinda Grover.

title: Lula’s reelection in Brazil puts the brakes on Latin America’s pro-Israel shift
body: Brazilians reelected Luiz Inácio "Lula" da Silva as president, defeating the center-right senator Flavio Bolsonaro and putting the brakes on a regional shift toward closer ties with Israel.The current president, a left-wing leader of Partido dos Trabalhadores (Workers Party), obtained 51.79% of the valid votes, while Bolsonaro received 48.21%.  Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party, had pledged a close diplomatic partnership with Israel and cultivated ties with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while Lula has become a critic of Israel's military campaign in Gaza. Bolsonaro said he did not accept the election results, though it is unclear how he could challenge them.In January 2024, Lula's government endorsed South Africa's decision to bring a genocide case against Israel before the International Court of Justice (ICJ). A month later, Lula compared Palestinian suffering in Gaza to Hitler's murder of the Jews, triggering a diplomatic crisis between Brazil and Israel. Brazil's Jewish umbrella organization, CONIB, publicly condemned the comparison as a distortion that offended the memory of Holocaust victims and their descendants. The remarks were also criticized by the Holocaust Museum of Buenos Aires. Sen. Bolsonaro promised a big shift toward Israel when he spoke on June 28, 2026, in Buenos Aires in a meeting with Jewish leaders. “In 2027, Brazil will not only once again have an ambassador to Israel, but will also take the step of moving its embassy to Israel's capital, Jerusalem,” he said.Bolsonaro lauds Brazilian Jews as 'among the brightest' in multiple fieldsThat night he also lauded the 120,000 Jews in Brazil, saying, “They are men and women who rank among the brightest in Brazilian medicine, industry, science, culture and business.”After Bolsonaro finished ahead of Lula in the first round on Oct. 4, Netanyahu sent a message the following day on X/Twitter: “Congratulations @FlavioBolsonaro on yesterday's vote and good luck in the final. I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil. Best wishes for your great victory, my friend.”  Several Latin American countries strengthen Israel tiesSince 2023, several Latin American countries have strengthened ties with Israel, in some cases reversing policies adopted by their predecessors, among them: Argentine President Javier Milei, elected in 2023, who makes support for Israel central to his foreign policy and meets with families of hostages Hamas abducted in its deadly Oct. 7, 2023, raid on Israel, which launched the current war; Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz Pereira, elected in 2025, restored diplomatic relations with Israel, which his predecessor had severed; President Nasry Asfura of Honduras, elected in 2025, who immediately formally recognized Israel's new ambassador, a process his predecessor left in limbo; Chilean President José Antonio Kast, elected in 2025, who is rebuilding ties with Israel diminished by his predecessor; and Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, elected in May, who restored diplomatic ties with Israel severed by his predecessor, sent his foreign minister to inaugurate an embassy in Jerusalem and pulled out of the ICJ genocide case against Israel.

title: Musk's meddling in Ukraine's Starlink is a warning to every country relying on private tech
body:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk looks on as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House, Washington, D.C., U.S., on Sept. 29, 2026. (Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images)
Researcher at the University of Melbourne
In the midst of Donald Trump's attempt to turn Russian diesel into a political asset to help him avoid disaster in November's midterm elections, the internet went out on the front lines.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Ukrainian forces have relied on Starlink to communicate, and essentially to manage the battlefield of the 21st century. When its service was cut to Ukraine this October, there were big questions about who was responsible for pulling that particular lever.
The Wall Street Journal now reports that Elon Musk personally ordered the Starlink shutdown.
While Musk played with the levers of war and peace toward his own political benefit, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the U.S. government has no control over decisions made by private companies.
That leaves Ukraine at the mercy of a private citizen, with no formal responsibility for U.S. foreign policy, able to make a decision that immediately affected another country's ability to defend itself.
And while this matters most urgently to Ukraine right now, the very fact that modern warfare depends so heavily on technologies such as Starlink, vesting so much power in private hands, should prompt a rethink in capitals around the world, particularly those whose own security may be compromised.
One of the great paradoxes of this war is that Ukraine has redefined modern warfare while never quite gaining control over the technologies on which its own survival depends.
Elon Musk is not a neutral figure. His willingness to dictate what Ukraine can do on the battlefield is a choice defined by his own incentives.
Surrounding his Starlink decision, Musk invested $443 million to help Republican candidates in the midterm elections. While Trump has a political interest in diesel prices, Musk's interest in the election is self-preservation.
If Democrats take either chamber of Congress, he will face intense scrutiny about what his companies and his wealth have been deployed to do.
Lying on a social media platform you own is not a crime, but lying to Congress is.
The problem in this fiasco is that Ukraine's military strategy is seemingly now subject to domestic American political incentives. Most troubling is that those include private citizens who have a vested interest in the outcome of an election and influence over battlefield technology.
Ukraine is exposed to domestic American politics because it is fighting the war of the future, one powered by private technology.
The nature of this technology has changed.
For most of the 20th century, military technology could be bought, then a country was free to do as they chose with it. Once an airplane rolled off of a Boeing assembly line, it belonged to the purchaser.
The shift toward the internet-enabled battlefield is that the technology operates more like a subscription than a purchase. Military systems are reliant on software and privately maintained infrastructure. Buying a piece of technology doesn't necessarily mean getting control over how or where it's used.
For the first four years of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has met with Congress, sat with Presidents, and built relationships across the American political scene.
That was done on the assumption that the effects Ukraine would feel from the United States would come from political decisions.
Political figures can be challenged on political terms. Ukraine, even with coverage diminished in American media, remains an issue on which politicians can be judged.
But when the terms are being set by a private corporation, Ukraine has no ability to contest its decisions through the channels it has spent years cultivating. Washington tells the world that it is central to Ukraine's survival, and yet it declares itself impotent to affect the decisions of the Republican Party's most generous donor.
This has been one of the hallmarks of the second Trump Administration: the winding together of Washington and Silicon Valley.
Weeks before Starlink was closed off, Musk , alongside Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, were tapped to define the future of American military power.
All the while, Trump is leveraging American diplomatic power to demand that allies and partners make themselves dependent on American AI technology.
While the U.S. criticizes China for the deep integration of the CCP and its technology sector, the U.S. government under Trump is using its power worldwide to sell American technology to private buyers while asking Silicon Valley's leaders to make decisions about the future of American security.
And yet, when one of those companies makes a move that is politically beneficial to Republicans' political fortunes, suddenly the division between public and private sectors is sacred.
This transformation has required a far greater emphasis on private production, on companies able to innovate using their own money and then selling to governments, rather than governments specifying what they want ahead of time.
That has left Ukraine vulnerable to decisions made by the people who lead those private companies.
Ukraine continues to fight a war to prevent an invading regime from determining its future as a nation. But what does political independence mean if the ways that a country defends itself can be restricted by private interests beyond its political reach?
As American allies and partners invest more heavily in American technological infrastructure, their political relationships with Washington may no longer be sufficient to guarantee their sovereignty.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Cory Alpert is a researcher at the University of Melbourne and previously served for three years in the White House of U.S. President Joe Biden.

title: Koretsky: Ukraine counts on mutual emergency energy assistance with Moldova if needed
body:
Ukraine looks forward to developing cross-border energy ties with Moldova and providing mutual emergency assistance should the need arise, stated Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky.
"Russia uses energy as a weapon—this is nothing new. Therefore, we need to diversify our sources and routes, develop transport infrastructure, and provide mutual support, especially ahead of the heating season. I would also like to thank the Moldovan government for the 90% discount on the entry tariff for gas transit. Our gas storage facilities are also available, and Moldova is making use of them," Koretsky said during a joint briefing with Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan in Kyiv on Monday, as reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
He noted that, in the electricity sector, Ukraine is counting on the development of cross-border interconnections and mutual emergency assistance if necessary.
"Energy security was a key topic of our discussions. We need a resilient, interconnected energy system that is integrated with the European market. We want to expedite the signing of a memorandum of understanding between Moldelectrica and Ukrenergo, and also advance preparations for a second power transmission line circuit in the Dniester Delta, specifically at the Dniester Hydropower Plant. This connection could increase the capacity for electricity exchange by 500 MW. It is an important step toward strengthening the energy independence and security of both Moldova and Ukraine," the Moldovan Prime Minister stated.
Furthermore, according to him, the countries are also discussing deepening cooperation in the gas sector.

title: Brazil’s Stock Market Crashes After Lula’s Upset Victory
body:
Brazil’s stock market lost more than $200 billion in value at the open on Monday after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s runoff, a result that prediction markets had priced at roughly a one in five chance.
The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, ticker EWZ, a basket of Brazilian stocks that trades in New York like a single share, fell as much as 26% from Friday’s close of about $42.60, touching $31.40 before trimming the loss to about 23% at $32.84 by 10:38 a.m. ET.
That is memecoin-sized volatility for a fund built around Brazil’s biggest companies, and it leaves EWZ roughly where it started 2026 after a 34% gain through Friday.
The dollar rose as much as 12% against the real on Friday, while the Ibovespa, Brazil’s benchmark stock index, fell as much as 17% to about 170,000 points. For a dollar-based investor, those moves at their worst combine to a loss of about 26%, in line with the ETF’s low.
B3, the São Paulo exchange, halted trading for 30 minutes after the Ibovespa fell 10% from Friday’s close, its first circuit breaker since the COVID-19 pandemic. A circuit breaker is an automatic pause meant to slow panic selling, but the index kept sliding after trading resumed.
Investors had been positioning for the opposite result since Bolsonaro unexpectedly finished first in the Oct. 4 first round, with 47.03% of valid votes to Lula’s 45.16%. The Ibovespa jumped 7.85% the next day and EWZ gained more than 10% on bets that Bolsonaro would tighten public finances and open the way to lower interest rates. Monday’s drop erased that rally and, at its lows, left the Ibovespa about 11% below its Oct. 2 close.
But Lula didn’t just beat Bolsonaro, he also beat prediction markets.
Polymarket gave Bolsonaro an 82% chance of winning the day before the vote, and Kalshi had him near 80% on Sunday morning. Both platforms are prediction markets , where a contract that pays $1 if a candidate wins trades at 80 cents when traders see an 80% chance.
Polling pointed to a coin flip rather than a favorite, with the latest Datafolha survey tied at 50% each among valid votes and CNT/MDA showing Bolsonaro ahead 50.5% to 49.5% in mid-October. Lula won 51.79% to 48.21%, a margin of about 4.4 million votes, according to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court.
Bolsonaro said on Sunday night that he does not recognize the result and will ask the courts to annul the election, after pledging in August to respect the outcome. He objected to Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting until 7 p.m. at the request of Lula’s campaign, which he said changed the rules midgame. His own campaign had separately asked for extra voting time in parts of three states.
“It is impossible to recognize the result of the elections in the context in which these things happened,” Bolsonaro said in Portuguese outside his campaign headquarters in Brasília. “We will use our legal team, we will ask for the annulment of these elections.”

title: French FREMM frigate shoots down ballistic missile near Belgian minehunter
body: A French Navy frigate shot down a ballistic missile near the Belgian minehunter Primula in the Bab el-Mandeb strait in mid-October 2026, the Belgian Ministry of Defence confirmed to Flemish public broadcaster VRT NWS on October 26, 2026. There is no indication that the Belgian vessel was the intended target. Sources cited by De Morgen, which first reported the interception, suggested the launch may have been intended as a warning, although its purpose remains unclear. France has reportedly opened an investigation into the incident. As of October 26, 2026, no group had claimed responsibility for the launch, and neither Belgium nor France had publicly attributed it. French FREMM frigate and Aster missile likely involved Although the French warship remains unidentified, the French Armed Forces General Staff confirmed in its operational update covering October 8–15, 2026 that a FREMM multipurpose frigate was operating in the Red Sea, Bab el-Mandeb and Gulf of Aden under the European Union’s Operation Aspides. One vessel known to have been operating in the area was Languedoc, an anti-submarine warfare FREMM. On the night of October 1 to 2, 2026, the frigate used its naval gun to shoot down a drone deemed threatening while escorting the container ship CMA CGM Champs Elysées through Bab el-Mandeb, the French Armed Forces General Staff confirmed to Le Monde . French Navy FREMM frigate Languedoc escorts a convoy through the Red Sea in an image released on October 9, 2026. (Credit: Marine nationale / French Ministry of the Armed Forces) A French Navy photograph dated October 9, 2026, also shows Languedoc escorting a convoy in the Red Sea. However, there is no confirmation that Languedoc was involved in the ballistic interception. French FREMM frigates are equipped with Aster surface-to-air missiles. The longer-range Aster 30, carried by the air-defense variants and certain other FREMMs, has an anti-ballistic missile capability. The French Navy has already demonstrated this capability in combat. On March 21, 2024, the air-defense FREMM Alsace intercepted three ballistic missiles launched from Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen while protecting merchant shipping in the southern Red Sea. The engagement was carried out using Aster 30 missiles. Belgian minehunter lacks missile defenses Primula (M924) is a Tripartite-class minehunter based in Zeebrugge, Belgium. It departed on May 28, 2026 , alongside the Dutch minehunter Willemstad to join NATO’s Standing Mine Countermeasures Group 2 (SNMCMG2) in the Mediterranean. At the time, the Belgian Ministry of Defence said the deployment would allow Belgium to contribute to possible mine clearance operations in the Strait of Hormuz, subject to a political decision. Belgian Navy commander Tanguy Botman stressed that Primula lacked the necessary defenses to operate independently in a hostile environment and would need protection from other warships. Houthi ballistic missile attacks intensify across the region Bab el-Mandeb separates Yemen from Djibouti and Eritrea, linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. The strait has become a flashpoint amid renewed Houthi missile and drone attacks against shipping and Saudi Arabia. Houthi forces have repeatedly launched ballistic missiles toward Saudi Arabia in October 2026. A missile strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport (RUH) on October 10 killed 12 people and injured 309 , according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation. On October 20, 2026, the UK Ministry of Defence announced plans to deploy Royal Air Force Eurofighter Typhoons to defend Saudi cities against Houthi missiles and drones. On October 26, 2026, Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Major General Turki Al-Maliki said the coalition had intercepted another ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh. The post French FREMM frigate shoots down ballistic missile near Belgian minehunter appeared first on AeroTime .

title: Apple announces iPad Mini update and hopes are high for touchscreen MacBook
body: Apple announced on Monday that it has given the iPad Mini "its biggest upgrade ever", as anticipation builds for its “pro and tell” event. The California company said the newest iPad Mini will start at $699, with pre-orders beginning on October 28 and availability from November 6. "The larger 8.5-inch organic light-emitting diode (OLED) display, also available with a nano-texture option, delivers higher contrast and more than 2x higher peak brightness than the previous-generation iPad mini for a brilliant and immersive viewing experience," a press release from Apple reads. The newest iPad Mini will also include a 12-megapixel front camera, and something that Apple is calling an "acoustic display" for significantly improved audio. “With a remarkably thinner and lighter design, a stunning new OLED display, the incredibly powerful A20 Pro and water and dust resistance, the new iPad mini is a huge leap forward for users who love having the full iPad experience in the palm of their hand," said Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of hardware engineering. Touchscreen MacBook? Meanwhile, anticipation is building for Apple's event in Los Angeles on Wednesday, during which it is widely speculated that the company will make a significant upgrade to the MacBook line-up. Some say that the forthcoming announcement will contradict something that Steve Jobs once said. News outlets have reported that Apple plans to introduce a MacBook that uses an OLED display with a touchscreen option. It would be the first MacBook to contain a touchscreen, and the expected debut starkly contrasts with Mr Jobs ' stance on portable computer touchscreens. “We've done tonnes of user testing on this, and it turns out it doesn't work,” the late Apple chief executive said in 2010 during a product launch event, discussing why trackpads worked well with laptops and touchscreens didn't. “Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical, and it gives a great demo but after a short period of time, you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off. It doesn't work, it's ergonomically terrible.” Apple's current MacBook line-up uses mini-LED displays. But there is a lengthy list of products that have made debuts years after Apple, and even Mr Jobs, dismissed their concepts. Those products include video-capable iPods, stylus pens, larger iPhones and medium-sized iPads. “Asus, Lenovo, HP, and Dell have already helped bring OLED screens to premium notebooks, but Apple’s entry could be a turning point,” said David Naranjo, associate director for technology market analysis firm Counterpoint Research. He also pointed out that Apple's expertise in establishing dominance in supply chains could help it significantly, and even help other companies. “Not unlike smartphones, when Apple adopts OLED, it boosts manufacturing capacity, improves yields, and lowers panel costs, making OLED more affordable for a wider range of products,” he explained. Mr Naranjo said that he believed a 14-inch MacBook with an OLED display, based on the price of materials, might cost between $2,799 and $2,999. “This higher price would cover the cost of advanced tandem OLED technology, possible touchscreen features, and ongoing memory expenses,” he said. But he cautioned that although Apple's products tend to exceed expectations, new MacBooks are arriving at a time when overall PC sales are starting to slow, giving the California technology company an additional hurdle to overcome. View on Threads According to Bloomberg, Apple will also be changing the MacBook Pro's name to MacBook Ultra. As has been the case with the company's events in recent years, some are expecting new iMac and iPad models with simple upgrades consisting of faster semiconductors, improved displays and slightly tweaked designs. Regardless of what transpires at the event on Wednesday, it will cap the busiest Apple product introduction seasons in recent years. In September, the company announced the keenly awaited foldable iPhone Duo. Weeks later, it introduced a new device, HomeView , which incorporates AI, Siri and the company's iOS to allow people to interact with various products in their home. It also announced the Apple TV 4K, the first significant upgrade to the product in several years.

title: Moscow Declaration to be adopted during Gas Exporting Countries Forum — Kremlin aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The participants in the summit of the Forum of Gas Exporting Countries (GECF) will adopt the Moscow Declaration, Russian President’s Aide Yury Ushakov said.
"The meeting will conclude with the adoption of the Moscow Declaration of the eighth summit of heads of state and government of the GECF member countries," he told reporters.
Ushakov said that the document "is, so to speak, undergoing final approval at this hour within the framework of the forum’s ministerial meeting. It is expected that the document will highlight the role of the forum’s participating states as reliable suppliers of natural gas, the significant contribution of this energy resource to ensuring global energy security, and the GECF countries’ wish to develop cooperation in diversifying trade routes further, introducing modern technologies, minimizing the environmental impact, ensuring a fair price for natural gas, price predictability, and reducing the volatility of the gas market as a whole.".

title: The Anthropic S-1 Filing Is Also an AI Doomsday Primer
body:
While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race.
“Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself. (It’s the first of three times the phrase “existential risks” pops up.)
Anthropic is careful to tie that outcome, though, to a specific process: recursive self-improvement.
The idea behind RSI is strikingly simple. It describes a state in which humans hand over the research and development of AI models to other AI models. AI already plays a big role here—and at least one lab has used something close to RSI to speed up development on a model that punches above its weights—but the scenario that sparks doomsday talk is one in which humans are no longer in the loop at all.
Or, as the Anthropic filing puts it: “Risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models.”
The prospectus repeatedly makes the point that RSI could lead to AI models that develop faster than the company’s safeguards, and that the company may not even realize it has lost that race until it’s too late. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
It also gets specific about what might happen after that. “As AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the prospectus says, “there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” This is Skynet territory.
Speaking of robots, Anthropic flags concerns about those as well. “When our models direct physical equipment,” the filing says, “errors, misaligned behavior, adversarial manipulation, or misuse could result in bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances, and such consequences may be immediate and irreversible.”
You might think, given the apparently existential stakes, that serious consideration would be given to whether RSI should be pursued at all, much less embraced. In an industry as competitive as frontier AI, though, it’s become fait accompli. Here’s how Anthropic describes that same process elsewhere in the prospectus, this time in a section about the startup’s “core advantages:”
“We refer to this recursive dynamic as ‘closing the loop,’” the prospectus says, “and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI.”
Failure to “close the loop,” Anthropic later says, could result in “falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities.” In other words, the same systems that are causing all that existential concerns are the ones Anthropic sees as critical to its success.
Every AI company is dealing with this same tension. When former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral for loudly resigning, he put curbing RSI at the top of his wish list for the industry. Employees at Google DeepMind and elsewhere have had similar revelations. There are multiple bills in Congress, including one cosponsored by Bernie Sanders, that propose a ban on RSI. At the same time, these are for-profit companies, and there are trillions of dollars at stake.
It’s a tricky dynamic to navigate. Recursive self-improvement could become a runaway train that destroys humanity. But until then, just look at how fast it can go.

title: Putin to hold working meeting with heads of regional organizations on October 28
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold a traditional working meeting on Wednesday at the Grand Kremlin Palace with the leaders of major regional organizations, such as the African Union, Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov has told the media.
"On October 28, the president will hold a traditional working meeting with the leaders of major regional organizations in the St. Andrew’s Hall of the Grand Kremlin Palace," Ushakov said.
He specified that these include the African Union, the African Continental Free Trade Area, the East African Community, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, the Southern African Development Community, the Economic Community of Central African States, the Economic Community of West African States, the Arab Maghreb Union, and the African Export-Import Bank.

title: NBA enters prediction markets with Kalshi, Polymarket partnerships
body:
The NBA is embracing prediction markets for the first time by naming leading platforms Kalshi and Polymarket as its preferred exchanges.
Through the agreements, the league said there will be "significant integrity" protections for NBA markets, including limitations on which types of event contracts can be featured and information-sharing requirements regarding suspicious trades.
"Protecting the integrity of the game is our top priority," said Scott Kaufman-Ross, NBA head of media distribution and partnerships in a press release. "These partnerships represent an important step in establishing a framework that creates new opportunities to engage our fans."
As part of the announcements, the league also signed a memorandum of understanding with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal agency that asserts prediction markets are under its purview. The agreement seeks to maintain the integrity of both the NBA and event contract markets, the memo said, through exchanges of information.
The NBA is the latest league to create partnerships with the booming prediction markets industry, which has seen much of its growth over the past year come from the popularity of its sports-related offerings . The NHL in October 2025 announced partnerships with both Kalshi and Polymarket, while the MLB announced a relationship with the latter company in March .
Those same contracts, though, are under fire by states across the country, who argue that the offerings amount to sports betting and should be regulated by them . Platforms and the CFTC argue that event contracts are swaps , a type of derivative, and thus are regulated at the federal level. Courts across the country have delivered conflicting rulings on the issue, and many expect the Supreme Court will likely be needed to resolve the dispute.
"The NBA is one of the most influential sports leagues in the world, and we're excited to work together to bring fans closer to the game," said Ari Borod, president of sports business development at Polymarket, in the press release.
As preferred exchanges, Kalshi and Polymarket get rights to use NBA intellectual property along with marketing and licensing rights.
"It's an exciting time for both NBA fans and Kalshi users," Adam Barrick, head of sports partnerships at Kalshi, said in the release. "The relationship we've built together reflects a shared mindset that prioritizes fan engagement, innovation and safety."
The NBA's move on Monday now leaves the NFL as the outlier among major American sports leagues when it comes to prediction markets.
Earlier this month, the NFL in an amicus brief to the Supreme Court said that sports-related event contracts should be regulated by the states rather than the CFTC. The league added that it's not opposed to the markets, but rather thinks they should have more guardrails.
At the time, Kalshi told CNBC it had tried to work more closely with the NFL, but that the league hadn't engaged.
Adam Silver , the commissioner of the NBA, though, took a different approach on the regulation question in an interview with CNBC's Contessa Brewer in early October.
"From at least the NBA standpoint, we have roughly 40 different jurisdictions regulating us right now," he said. "So to have a consistent policy nationally, I think would be in our best interest."
— CNBC's Jessica Golden contributed reporting
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

title: Gaza ceasefire has not stopped Israeli 'genocidal acts', UN commission says
body: Israel continues to commit atrocities against Palestinians in Gaza despite a year-old ceasefire, UN investigators said on Monday, as they also accused the Israeli military of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank. The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry said Israel was “continuing to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza”. Since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025, Israeli forces have expanded their territorial control from 53 per cent of Gaza to at least 60 per cent, the commission said. Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 43 children, during that period, according to the report. “Israel’s expansion of territorial control in Gaza continues to result in the killing and harming of Palestinian civilians who approach or cross the Yellow Line,” commission chairman Srinivasan Muralidhar said. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in the year since the ceasefire, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. The yellow line marks the border between areas under Israeli military control and the rest of the Gaza Strip, under the ceasefire agreement. The report, submitted to the UN General Assembly, also accused Israeli authorities of committing crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, including extermination, persecution, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence. Investigators said Israeli military operations, reinforced by settler violence, amounted to a widespread and systematic attack on Palestinian civilians. “The targeting of Palestinian civilians across different locations in the West Bank indicates a high level of co-ordination and organised planning and is the product of state policy,” the report said. The commission found that Israeli air strikes killed 254 Palestinians in the West Bank between October 2023 and September 2026, compared with six between 2008 and October 2023. It also documented the displacement of more than 34,000 Palestinians in the West Bank, describing it as the largest displacement in the territory since 1967. The findings come amid growing international scrutiny of Israel's military operations and its conduct in the occupied Palestinian territories. The three-member commission was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021 to investigate alleged breaches of international law in Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories. Its findings could be used as evidence in future international criminal proceedings, although the commission itself has no power to prosecute alleged perpetrators. Navi Pillay , a former South African High Court judge who led the investigation until November 2025, won the Nobel Peace Prize earlier this month. Israel rejected the findings. Its mission in Geneva called for the commission to be dissolved, accusing it in a statement on social media of conducting a “misinformation campaign to demonise the state of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal.” Israel has long challenged the commission’s findings and has repeatedly denied allegations of genocide in Gaza and sexual violence by its forces.

title: Why Saudi Just Abandoned Its Core Oil Rule
body: Few could argue with U.S. President Donald Trump's key objective in launching 'Operation Epic Fury' against Iran on 28 February -- to prevent Iran from ever being able to develop a nuclear weapon. All members of his Cabinet fully backed this aim at the time, as they did the other three to effect regime change, to critically degrade Iran's ballistic missile capability, and to neutralise the ability of its proxies, especially Hamas and Hezbollah, to cause mayhem across the Middle East and the world. The degree to which these objectives have been achieved so far is a matter for debate, but what is not is that Washington's closest Arab allies now harbour deep misgivings over America's ability to shield them from the Iranian hornet's nest that U.S. attacks have provoked. This has again made them more susceptible to the soothing assurances from Beijing that it can keep them safe from the terror of Tehran over the long term. This situation, in turn, threatens Trump's 'Abraham Accords' plan that lay at the heart of his Middle East foreign policy, as fully examined in my latest book on thenew global oil market order. Several recent moves by leading Middle East power Saudi Arabia underline this threat.  The most recent was the announcement from Saudi oil and gas flagship Aramco that it and the Kingdom are seeking to partner with other countries to expand their strategic oil stockpile. Despite the perennial taking up of its crude production capabilities to boost its global profile over the years, Saudi Arabia's average oil output from 1973 to yesterday is 8.295 million barrels per day bpd, and it is currently around 8 million bpd. That said, Saudi expects oil demand to bounce when the war ends and is also working on alternative export routes to circumvent the likely ongoing Iranian threat around the Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandab Strait and Suez Canal. Perhaps the single-most strategically important component of this effort to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz remains the long-planned but now dynamically expedited IndiaMiddle EastEurope Economic Corridor IMEC. Originally launched at the 2023 G20 Summit but stalled by regional conflict, the project has been turbocharged by the Strait of Hormuz blockade, with planners now estimating it could eventually divert around 60 percent of container traffic that historically has transited the Strait of Hormuz. Its architecture is built around two integrated corridors an eastern maritime leg linking India's western ports to the Arabian Gulf, and a northern overland rail network running through Saudi Arabia and Jordan to Israel's Port of Haifa, from where shortsea shipping connects directly to Europe. Crucially, the 2026 wartime redesign anchors the eastern maritime leg in Oman rather than the UAE, allowing ships from India to unload entirely outside the Strait of Hormuz before transferring cargo onto the Arabian Peninsula rail grid. Additional 'IMEC Plus' nodes through Egypt and Syria are under discussion to create a wider lattice of landbased alternatives, while new legal frameworks -- including the IndiaEuropean Union EU free trade agreement and the U.S. Senate's 'Eastern Mediterranean Gateway Act' -- have formally designated Greece as Europe's entry hub, a very senior source inside the EU's security complex exclusively told OilPrice.com. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is eyeing the expansion of its East-West Pipeline 1,200 km long, moving crude from eastern oil fields across the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea port of Yanbu to 10 million bpd within the next two to three years.  Related 6 Million Barrels in Two Minutes Draws CFTC Scrutiny  Saudi Arabia's desire to partner with other countries to expand its strategic oil stockpile marks a seismic shift in policy. Historically, the Kingdom responded to oil demand spikes by simply pumping more crude from its domestic oilfields, drawing down from its own domestic storage, or securing barrels in the international spot and forward markets. However, this announcement signals that Saudi Arabia can no longer rely solely on its own geography and security to guarantee oil delivery. By seeking access to the strategic, government-owned stockpiles of foreign nations -- particularly in Asia -- Aramco wants to double its overseas storage capacity. That necessitates moving enormous volumes of Saudi oil out of the volatile Gulf region ahead of time and placing it directly into the backyards of its biggest customers. In other words, the Saudis are saying that the physical infrastructure inside the Middle East is too exposed to rely on exclusively, and to ensure seamless supplies in the future, they are transitioning from a model of 'we will get it when you need it' to 'we will store millions of barrels in your country so a local drone strike cannot trigger a global economic collapse.' In fact, the first such deal was quickly struck by Saudi Arabia on 26 October to store crude oil at Singapore's Jurong Rock Caverns from the second half of 2027. The caverns can store up to 1.47 million cubic metres of liquid hydrocarbons such as crude oil and condensate.  Whilst sensibly pragmatic on Saudi Arabia's part, given recent events, this general strategy is disastrous for the U.S.'s image in the Middle East. In recent years, Saudi Arabia has consistently spent tens of billions of dollars annually on American-sourced defence systems, with historical and recent baseline arms agreements valued at roughly USD75 billion a year. While Riyadh has recently allocated roughly USD83 billion per year to its total national defence budget, the U.S. remains its primary provider, accounting for nearly 80 percent of all Saudi weapons imports. However, none of this has counted for much in the face of sustained attacks from Iran. Worse still was that back in September 2019, Iran had already signalled it had no qualms about authorising its Yemen-based Houthi terrorist proxy to attack key Saudi Arabian oil targets, with drone and missile strikes against the Abqaiq and Khurais oil processing facilities. At the time, these two facilities represented around 50 percent of Saudi Arabia's oil production, or about 5 percent of the global oil supply, so the attacks caused an immediate spike of up to 20 percent in global oil prices and were considered one of the most strategically significant energy-infrastructure strikes ever recorded. Riyadh consequently increased its investment in U.S. defence technology aimed at nullifying these threats, including Terminal High Altitude Area Defense THAAD interceptors, Patriot defences, and early-warning radars. Despite this, Iranian proxy forces in Iraq and the Tehran-backed Houthis launched repeated successful drone strikes targeting the East-West Pipeline. Meanwhile, waves of Houthi ballistic missiles and explosive drones struck deep inside the Saudi homeland, with the primary targets being vital energy nodes, including an Aramco facility and the major Rabigh refinery. A similar pattern manifested itself with other U.S. allies in the region. Having bought vast amounts of American defence equipment beforehand, Iranian strikes destroyed or disabled the AN/FPS-132 early-warning radar in Qatar, multiple AN/TPY-2 THAAD radars across the region, the AN/TPS-59 radar in Bahrain, and a string of MQ-9 Reapers. This exposed the uncomfortable truth that the U.S. could not adequately defend these states, either directly with its own forces or indirectly through the systems it had sold them.  A tell-tale sign of Saudi Arabia's increasing lack of trust in being reliant on the U.S. for its security came in on 7 August when it announced the formation of the 'Makkah Defence Alliance', together with Turkey, and Pakistan. It is modelled around the core collective defence principle enshrined in NATO's Article 5 -- that is, that an armed attack on one member shall be considered an attack against them all.Saudi Arabia brings deep financing ability and a vast network of regional intelligence contacts to the grouping. Turkey -- itself a member of NATO and tied into the U.S. and its key Western allies -- has advanced military hardware, high-tech defence equipment, and a well-established production line for artillery and drones to the alliance. And Pakistan provides a huge frontline military and nuclear weapons. Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif stated that its 'full military capabilities' would be available under their defence agreements. Subsequently, it was clarified that the Alliance pact is strictly defensive and conventional -- but it still has the weapons.  So far, the Alliance has not achieved much, and its future effectiveness looks uncertain at best. What is not uncertain is that China could stop any attacks on all these Arab states with a few words to Iran such as, 'stop doing all this, or we will immediately cease buying oil and gas from you, and will stop supplying you with critical materials, equipment, and expertise that you need to keep fighting the U.S. and its allies'. Up until recently, as analysed in full in my latest book on thenew global oil market order, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Iraq -- among others -- had all heavily leaned into Beijing's sphere of global influence, and the situation looks ripe for the same to happen again.  By Simon Watkins for Oilprice.com

title: Smack Technologies lands new deal for AI prototype to enhance joint military campaigning
body: Smack Technologies will prototype its AI-powered military planning and decision support platform with U.S. Special Operations Command via a new Other Transaction agreement worth up to $7.5 million, the Texas-based startup’s Founder and CEO Andy Markoff told DefenseScoop. He discussed Smack’s “Omega” offering, which is designed to generate courses of action for joint military campaigning, ahead of the company’s official award announcement on Monday. “It accelerates and integrates command-level planning and operations: commanders can generate operational objectives, the tactics that achieve them, and the tasks that achieve those — all linked as a single plan,” Markoff said in an email. “As the fight changes and assessments come in, Omega enables commanders to repair the plan in seconds, and shows where they actually stand against their objectives.” The deal comes as SOCOM is fast-tracking frontier AI capabilities to solve real-world operational challenges and free up its leaders to focus on the most complex strategic and tactical priorities. Markoff said Omega is built on Smack’s “suite of small, domain-specific models that leverage a hybridized algorithm approach ranging from classical planning algorithms to deep reinforcement learning.” He noted that in the limited instances that a third-party large language model is applied, “its role is narrowly scoped, and its responses are grounded in Smack’s proprietary context graph.” The team designed the platform to be resilient against existing and emerging threats — like adversarial AI attacks, spoofed sensor data, or intentional data poisoning — in three primary ways, according to Markoff. “First, Omega doesn’t depend on constant cloud connectivity,” he noted. The models are small enough to run on-prem at distributed nodes. Each node works within a harness set by higher headquarters, solves locally when communications drop, and transmits data when a window opens. Second, as previously noted, the platform also pairs classical planning algorithms that are deterministic and explainable with generative ones. “Third, we prioritize offline learning,” Markoff said. “Adversaries will flood the battlespace with spoofed and poisoned data, so we validate new data before any model learns from it. Because we run many small models, we can retrain only the model that needs it, and can push a vetted update fast.” Smack was co-founded by a team of Marine Corps special operations veterans, including Markoff, a former Marine Raider. “We’ve been the end user. We know these requirements because we’ve lived them, and the commanders we work with can see that we understand their problem,” he told DefenseScoop. The startup’s OTA with SOCOM follows other prototyping contracts it was tapped for by the Marines, Air Force and Navy. Markoff said he expects Omega to move into production across multiple branches of the U.S. military in the coming months. The post Smack Technologies lands new deal for AI prototype to enhance joint military campaigning appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: Israel is not abandoned: Record-breaking numbers reveal a global movement of support - opinion
body: For months, the headlines have told us that the younger generation is turning against Israel. We have watched images of campus protests, heard the chants of hostility, and been told repeatedly that the next generation has abandoned the Jewish people.But on October 7, something extraordinary happened. Something the headlines could not ignore. Something that shattered the narrative.On the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, Friends of Zion sponsored a record-breaking 24-hour global broadcast that reached more than 250 million people across 167 countries.At a time when Israel faces relentless attacks on its legitimacy, and the Jewish people continue to endure a rising tide of antisemitism, millions of people around the world chose to watch, listen, pray, and stand with Israel.The broadcast reached more than 3.8 million people in Syria, 1.2 million in Egypt, and 1.1 million in Algeria. In Brazil, the broadcast reached more than 8.5 million people, following a public appeal by Senator Flávio Bolsonaro encouraging Brazilians to watch.Let that sink in. Millions of people in nations where public support for Israel can be politically complicated were exposed to a message of solidarity, remembrance, and hope.This was not a small gathering preaching to the choir. It was a global declaration that the Jewish people is not alone.The numbers tell a different storyPerhaps one of the most significant findings was the age of the audience. Some 59.8% of the social media audience was between the ages of 25 and 34.We have been told that young adults have turned their backs on Israel and that support for the Jewish state is destined to disappear. Yet this global initiative reached tens of millions of people through social media, with a substantial share of its audience among younger adults.We must be careful not to confuse the loudest voices with the majority, or viral outrage with the convictions of an entire generation. A protest does not speak for every student. A hashtag does not represent every young adult. And the most hostile voices on social media do not have the final word on the future of Israel.The October 7 broadcast demonstrated that a significant global audience remains willing to engage with a message of support for Israel and remembrance of the victims of terrorism.The battle for the next generation is not over. In fact, it may be one of the most important battles we face.A generation worth fighting forThe numbers from this broadcast should challenge every pastor, parent, educator, and Christian leader.We must meet the next generation where they are, communicate with clarity, tell the truth with courage, and equip them to recognize antisemitism even when it is disguised as fashionable political rhetoric.We cannot surrender the universities. We cannot abandon social media. We cannot allow the next generation to learn the history of Israel exclusively from those who deny the Jewish people's history, distort the facts, or excuse terrorism.We must offer something stronger than slogans: truth supported by history, conviction grounded in faith, and a vision of human dignity that refuses to dehumanize the Jewish people.The Friends of Zion initiative demonstrated what can happen when technology, media, faith, and a clear moral purpose converge. A message that began with a commitment to remember and stand with Israel crossed borders, reached millions, and entered conversations around the world.That is a foundation on which we must build.The future is not written by the headlinesI have spent decades working to mobilize Christians to stand with Israel. I have learned that history is not changed by those who wait for public opinion to become comfortable. History is changed by those who stand for what is right when doing so is difficult.The record-breaking reach of this October 7 broadcast should encourage us, but it should also challenge us. We cannot assume that millions of views automatically translate into millions of committed advocates. We must turn awareness into education, education into conviction, and conviction into action.We must continue building bridges between Christians and Jews, training young ambassadors, confronting antisemitism, and ensuring that the next generation understands both the historical and biblical significance of Israel.The enemies of Israel want us to believe that the world has turned away, that the younger generation is beyond reach, and that standing with the Jewish people is a losing cause.On October 7, millions across the world encountered a different message. Across 176 countries, a global broadcast brought remembrance, solidarity, and support for Israel to an audience that stretched across cultures, borders, and generations.The headlines may tell one story. The evidence tells another story.We must never surrender the next generation. We must never abandon Israel. And we must never allow the forces of hatred to have the final word.The future belongs to those willing to fight for truth and defend the innocent.The world is watching. The next generation is listening. And our response today will help determine what they believe tomorrow.The writer has written 120 books and is a #1 New York Times best-selling author and Nobel Peace Prize nominee. He is the founder of the Friends of Zion Museum in Jerusalem, the Ten Boom Museum in Holland, and Churches United with Israel, one of the largest Christian Zionist networks in America.

title: Control of Congress is up for grabs. What's the math for Democrats and Republicans?
body:
A midterm check on unified government puts congressional majorities in play.
With one week until the midterm elections, the majorities of both houses of Congress are in play as voters weigh a midterm check on unified control of government in Washington -- President Donald Trump's hold on the White House and Republican majorities in the House and Senate the past two years.
Republicans hold slim majorities in both the House and Senate and are rallying to preserve them with just days until Election Day.
Democrats on the other hand are trying to make inroads into some traditionally red areas in hopes of picking up crucial seats.
In the House, all 435 seats are on the ballot on Nov. 3 for two-year terms in the 120th Congress. Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana currently holds a historically narrow majority: 218 Republicans alongside a single independent, Rep. Kevin Kiley of California, who filed for reelection without party affiliation but continues to generally support the speaker on the floor. Democrats hold 214 seats.
There are also two vacancies in the House following the April resignations of lawmakers with ethics issues -- former Texas Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales and former Florida Democratic Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, who attempted a comeback but was rejected by voters in an August primary.
That’s a lengthy way to explain that on Election Night, Johnson effectively begins with a 220-215 edge over Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.
While Johnson and Republicans defend their legislative record amassed over the past two years -- including the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, formerly known as Trump's "One, Big Beautiful Bill" -- the closing message from the GOP has also starkly warned voters not to embrace “Mamdani madness," a reference to New York City's democratic socialist mayor and the success of some democratic socialist candidates in Democratic primaries this year.
"We are bringing down the cost of living. We are providing more jobs and opportunity for more people. The facts show it and the records show it," Johnson told CBS during a recent interview. "The success goes on and on."
Across the aisle, Jeffries, a Brooklyn Democrat, is striving to become the first Black speaker in U.S. history, campaigning largely on a plank of affordability and anticorruption that directly takes aim at Trump.
"The American people are fed up," Jeffries told reporters this month, adding his belief that Democrats are "on track" to win the House majority.
For Jeffries to get a chance to take the speaker’s gavel, Democrats must attain a net gain of three seats, pushing their numbers to at least 218 -- a simple majority.
In the Senate, 35 of the upper chamber’s 100 seats are on the ballot for six-year terms, including 13 Democratic and 22 Republican seats sprinkled across the political landscape.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Republicans currently hold a 53-45 edge over Senate Democrats, who also have two independents that caucus with them, pushing the current minority to 47 seats.
Thune could afford to have a net loss of three GOP seats and still retain the majority, given Vice President JD Vance’s constitutional power to break tie votes in the Senate.
For Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Democrats to flip the majority, however, they’ll need to amass a net gain of four seats.
Early voting is underway in many states and Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: 1 dead, 15 injured as Russia strikes university and surrounding area in Kyiv
body:
Five of the injured are students or university staff, Zelenskyy said.
LONDON -- A Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, killed at least one and injured another 15, according to Ukrainian officials.
Ballistic missiles hit crowded areas where there are no military facilities nearby, causing "extensive" damage, hitting a university campus and the South bridge amongst other urban structures, Kyiv said.
Five of the injured are students or members of the university's staff, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The number of injured climbed to 15 on Tuesday, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine said.
The strike on Monday was described by Ukraine as an attack on its civilian infrastructure, which it continues to say is threatened by delays in the delivery of defense munitions.
"The artificial and prolonged delays in the delivery of interceptor packages for Patriot and NASAMS systems, which unfortunately have occurred recently, are directly helping Russia achieve the objectives of its terrorist campaign," Zelenskyy said on Tuesday on his social media account.
Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles, two of which Ukraine shot down, Kyiv said. The attack also included at least 255 drones, according to the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said its military had targeted Ukraine overnight with a "massive" strike aimed at the Ukrainian defense industry and "transport infrastructure" in Kyiv.
The ministry said in a post on Telegram that it struck "an industrial enterprise producing and storing long- and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles" in the Ukrainian capital.
In Desnyans'kyi District, where the University stands, five of the victims are students and university staff, officials said.
One of those injured is a 20-year-old woman, who has been hospitalized, according to Kyiv’s Mayor Vitali Klitschko. The strike also damaged part of the campus, Kyoto Park, a nearby metro station and residential buildings.
Rescue operations are underway as there are reports that people may be trapped under the rubble.
There were also strikes on Ukrainian cities: Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, Kherson, and Chernivtsi, wrote Zelenskyy. Missiles targeted energy infrastructure, logistics centers, and urban facilities, Kyiv said.
"Pressure on Russia and real support for Ukraine are needed to change the situation," wrote Zelenskyy.
