title: HSL raises ticket prices and introduces a fare cap for contactless payments
body:
The Helsinki region's public transport fares will rise by an average of 1.8 percent in early 2027.
Helsinki Regional Transport (HSL) is introducing a price cap for contactless payments. The change is meant to make it easier for passengers to choose between a single ticket and a day ticket. The change takes effect on Monday, 2 November.
The cap is calculated starting from the first ticket purchase. The system then adds up the prices of all tickets bought with the same payment method.
However, HSL notes that a physical payment card and mobile payments linked to the same card are treated as different payment methods.
Once the combined total reaches the price of a day ticket, no further charges are made for additional journeys.
The fare cap depends on the zones you travel in during the 24 hours. A two-zone 24-hour ticket is €10.60.
In a press release , HSL said the cap means passengers no longer have to estimate how many trips they will make during the day.
The fare cap applies only to adult single tickets paid with contactless payment — it doesn't cover tickets bought through the HSL app or with an HSL card.
The HSL board meanwhile decided on Tuesday to raise ticket prices by an average of 1.8 percent at the beginning of 2027. In the most popular AB zone, the price of an adult single ticket will go up by 1.5 percent, from €3.30 to €3.35.
Children's single tickets and single tickets in the 50 percent discount group will stay the same in all zones.

title: Stubb, Støre hold phone call with Putin
body:
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre talked to the Russian leader on Tuesday.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb spoke by phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday, Stubb's office said .
Stubb made the call from Helsinki together with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre . Finland and Norway both share borders with Russia.
According to Stubb's office, the aim was to give Putin a direct message about upcoming negotiations to help end the war. The call was linked to peace talks to be held in Abu Dhabi, where Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators are set to meet in early November.
Stubb and Støre made the call as leaders of their respective countries, not on behalf of Europe as a whole. The call comes after the two leaders met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo last week .
At a press conference on Tuesday afternoon, President Stubb told reporters that the conversation with Putin lasted about an hour and a half, and that Ukrainian President Zelensky was briefed about the contents of the call after it ended.
"Finland never talks about Ukraine over Ukraine's head," Stubb said.
He reiterated that the aim of the conversation was to keep the peace efforts on track, noting that an end to the war "will not be achieved through silence".
"We tried to help ensure that Russia would come earnestly to the negotiating table," Stubb said.
Edit note: Article updated at 16:26 on 27.10.2026 to include the comments from President Stubb's press conference.

title: Abortion is on the ballot in Missouri again. Here's what to know about Amendment 3
body:
Amendment 3 would overturn the 2024 amendment enshrining abortion rights.
Just two years after Missouri voters approved an amendment enshrining the right to reproductive freedom in the state constitution, abortion, which was also protected by the measure, is on the ballot there again.
On Nov. 3, Missouri residents will be voting on Amendment 3, only this time it would prohibit abortion, except in cases of medical emergencies, fetal anomalies, rape or incest. If the abortion is due to rape or incest, the procedure must occur no later than 12 weeks' gestation.
Since Roe v. Wade was overruled by the Supreme Court in June 2022, 13 states have ceased nearly all abortion services while four states have a six-week ban on books, according to an ABC News tally.
Following the Supreme Court decision, Missouri enacted a trigger ban, prohibiting most abortions in the state.
However, in November 2024, Missouri became the first state to overturn a near-total abortion ban through a direct vote of the people by passing Amendment 3 -- the same name as the upcoming ballot measure -- with about 52% of the vote.
"Missourians have access to abortion care because the people made it possible," Mallory Schwarz, executive director of the nonprofit Abortion Action Missouri, told ABC News. "But not even months after our 2024 vote, politicians started plotting to overturn the will of the people and now, in a couple of weeks, voters will have to vote again to protect the right to abortion that we enshrined in the constitution previously."
Amendment 3 would repeal the 2024 amendment that granted reproductive freedom, including abortion through fetal viability, which is typically between 24 and 26 weeks' gestation.
If approved, the amendment would also permit state lawmakers to enact legislation to regulate abortions and access to care.
Examples include laws requiring physicians providing abortion care to have admitting privileges at a nearby hospital and licensing requirements for abortion facilities.
State Sen. Adam Schnelting, who sponsored the proposal that led to Amendment 3 being placed on this year's ballot, told ABC News that passing the amendment is "critical to protecting women and children and providing Missourians with a measure that is more in line with their values than the one narrowly passed two years ago."
The amendment would also prohibit gender-affirming care procedures, cross-sex hormones or puberty-blocking drugs for minors. However, gender-affirming surgeries and medical treatments for minors are already illegal in Missouri under statutory law.
Opponents of the amendment have argued that including language about gender-affirming care is an attempt to mask the parts of the amendment that would limit abortion care.
"What politicians are trying to do is mislead voters and overturn the will of the people and ban abortion again," Tori Schafer, an attorney for the ACLU of Missouri, told ABC News. "And they've shown they're willing to resort to all kinds of tricky tactics in order to do that."
Schafer said organizations supporting Amendment 3 don't use the word "abortion" in their ads campaigning for the amendment to pass "because they know, like we know, that abortion care is popular in Missouri."
Schnelting said the statutory ban on gender-affirming procedures and treatment for minors expires in 2027 and including that language in Amendment 3 would ensure such a ban is permanent.
The ACLU of Missouri said the sunset clause only pertains to hormone therapy and that surgery is currently banned in Missouri.
Possibl e cons e qu e nc e s if Am e ndm e nt 3 is pass e d
After the trigger ban was passed in Missouri in 2022, the state's last abortion clinic in St. Louis was forced to stop providing such care .
In 2023 alone, more than 12,000 Missouri women traveled to neighboring states, including Illinois and Kansas , to receive care, according to the Guttmacher Institute, a reproductive rights organization.
Additionally, in 2025, more than 3,000 Missourians obtained medication abortions through telehealth from out-of-state clinicians, nearly four times higher than two years prior, the Guttmacher Institute found.
Some abortion providers told local news outlets they were seeing patients develop complications while waiting for treatment and some patients said they'd had to flee Missouri to seek abortion care for conditions including fetal anomalies.
"Missourians have lived under an abortion ban in the past," Schwarz said. "We've seen people turned away from the emergency room when they needed emergency abortion care. We've seen women forced to wait until their complication was serious enough that they were able to access care or have to flee the state to get care in another state that they should be able to get in their own community."
Schwarz said Abortion Action Missouri's canvassers have had conversations with Missourians against Amendment 3 from all walks of life.
One such conversation was with a Catholic voter who said they did not support abortion rights but also did not support the new amendment.
"They said, 'I'm personally pro-life, but we already voted on this and I'm voting "no" this time because politicians should be listening to the people,'" Schwarz said. "'Politicians shouldn't get to overturn any vote just because they don't like it.' And so, we are hearing that [at] the doors every day, every weekend."
Schnelting said the response to Amendment 3 from his constituents has been largely positive and called the claims that it is overturning the will of the people a "specious argument."
Anti-abortion rights groups have praised the new Amendment 3, arguing that the 2024 vote was extreme and goes beyond what Missourians have historically supported.
"Despite what voters were sold before Election Day, as soon as [2024's] Amendment 3 passed, the abortion lobby brought litigation to perform late-term abortions, end parental consent and remove every safety regulation on their industry," Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, said in a statement last year. "Amendment 3 is far too extreme and dangerous."
Missouri is not the only state with abortion on the ballot on Nov. 3. Voters in three states -- Idaho, Nevada and Virginia -- will consider measures to protect abortion rights and, in some cases, reproductive freedom.
Schafer, from ACLU of Missouri, said other states can learn from Missouri about how access to abortion can be at risk even after voters vote to protect care.
"While this fight is really important to folks like me who live in Missouri and have to suffer the consequences of our legislature ignoring the will of the people, we know that this campaign will also impact folks all across the country," Schafer said. "We have friends in other states who have passed their own versions of the right to reproductive freedom, and we don't want this attempt by our legislature to embolden this opposition strategy across the country."
She went on, "So we know that a lot of eyes are on Missouri, and Missourians deeply believe in the right to make their own decisions free from political interference."

title: How election officials are working to mitigate growing distrust ahead of midterms
body:
"Our elections, in fact, are safe and secure," one expert told ABC News.
DALLAS, Ga. -- Election officials from coast to coast are facing a slew of challenges ahead of the high-stakes midterms , from the Trump administration's bid to impose itself on state-run elections to last-minute court challenges and threats faced by election workers -- all under a persistent sense of distrust in the voting process itself, some experts told ABC News.
"Usually the temperature is much higher -- and emotions run much hotter -- in a presidential election year than in a midterm election year," said Wendy Weiser, vice president of the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice at New York University School of Law. "This year, though, the temperature is staying up at a high level."
Election experts broadly lay blame for the elevated sense of distrust in elections this year at the feet of President Donald Trump , whose administration has taken unprecedented steps to question the outcome by levelling unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud.
Trump administration officials say steps they've taken in recent weeks -- including lawsuits in California and Alaska and threats to prosecute election workers -- are meant to ensure the integrity of the election.
But under the weight of those allegations , state officials say the once-collaborative rapport between the federal government and state leaders has in some cases given way to a deep sense of suspicion.
"There's no trust in that relationship," Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar told ABC News. "In order to have a working relationship, there has to be trust, and the fact that they continue to tear that trust apart and spread the misinformation and the lies that they are about our elections is wrong."
At the same time, people who oversee voting at the county level across the country are frequently fielding questions from voters who say they lack faith in the electoral process. About 6 in 10 Americans are confident the midterm elections will be conducted fairly and accurately, while nearly 4 in 10 Americans and about 3 in 10 voters are not confident , according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted using Ipsos' KnowledgePanel.
"No matter how transparent we are, people always are questioning what we're doing [and] how we're doing it," Deidre Holden, the director of elections and voter registration in Paulding County, Georgia, told ABC News. "I try to explain [that] we have nothing to hide. You're welcome to come in and watch the process."
Holden, who has been an elections official in Georgia for 25 years, said that in her early years in the role, she "used to train people on how to smile and hand out an 'I voted' sticker."
Yet over the last several years, Holden has devoted much of her time to ensuring that everyone at polling places and in the county's ballot processing facility are safe. She currently has a sheriff's deputy stationed at every polling location, and in 2024 she first showed ABC News the active shooter training her poll workers were undertaking as a precaution.
"I'm forever concerned with the security of my staff, with my poll workers, with my voters," Holden said. "You never know what someone's going to do."
Paulding County was once a solidly Republican area, but as the suburban sprawl around Atlanta has increased, the county's population has quadrupled and it is now a purple county with Democrats and Republicans living side by side. With such a partisan divide, Holden said transparency about the process is key.
"Some of our best poll workers have come from the naysayers that didn't trust us and we invited them in and now they're our best workers and our biggest advocates because they get to see behind the scenes, they get see how the sausage is made, how we do things and how we do those things with integrity," Holden said.
The official once again overseeing the election at the state level in Georgia this November is Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican who rose to national prominence in January 2021 after receiving a phone call from President Donald Trump.
"All I want to do is this: I just want to find 11,780 votes," Trump told Raffensperger at the time, claiming it was "not possible" that he lost Georgia's 2020 presidential election.
Joe Biden won the 2020 election in the Peach State and Raffensperger certified the results, despite facing criticism from some other Republicans.
"At the end of the day we did our job, we followed the law and we followed the constitution," Raffensperger told ABC News in a recent interview.
"I know I did the right thing, and I feel sorry for people that didn't do the right thing, because at some point, they're going to have to look at themselves in the mirror," he said.
Raffensperger's time in office will end in January. Early voting for the midterms is currently underway in Georgia, and Raffensperger said he is confident that residents will have an accurate idea of the projected election results by midnight after the polls close.
"Those ballots actually in effect will be counted three times just to verify the result, so at the end of the day, we know that the winner won and that's our job," Raffensperger said.
While Raffensperger was on the phone with Trump in 2021, many recent dustups between the federal government and state agencies have involved staffers going back and forth over email and video conferencing.
At the core of the growing friction is the claim by President Trump and DHS officials that the country has a "broken" election system , where they claim 278,000 people who are not U.S. citizens have registered to vote illegally.
Weiser told ABC News that the Trump administration has been attempting to "substantiate their theory that our country is plagued by widespread voter fraud."
"What they've been able to uncover is nothing," Weiser said. "Our elections, in fact, are safe and secure."
The allegations of widespread noncitizen voting have not just been made at press conferences. Over the summer, DHS employees reached out to states around the U.S., sending letters and holding meetings about "the concerning results" of what they called a "preliminary review" of potential noncitizens registered to vote.
Aguilar, the Nevada secretary of state, said members of his office ended up on a video conference call in August with DHS representatives alleging that there could be as many as 15,903 noncitizens registered to vote in Nevada.
One of the DHS officials on the call was Heather Honey, a key figure in the fight to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.
While not overtly hostile, a recording of the video conference obtained by ABC News shows palpable tension and some awkward exchanges, as Nevada officials seemed deeply skeptical of the claims made by DHS.
"So what you're saying is the 15,000 number has not been vetted?" a Nevada official asked, according to a recording of the video conference.
"I probably wouldn't use the sentence, 'It hasn't been vetted,'" a DHS representative responded, adding that each individual has not "had a full manual review."
Following the meeting, DHS officials emailed Nevada officials with a new figure -- claiming they found 185 noncitizens on the state's voter rolls during a preliminary sweep. Officials in Nevada said the DHS was wrong, replying later that, after their own review of those 185 individuals, "our records indicate that they were citizens."
In response to a request by ABC News for comment, DHS stood by their work, which they called "a service to Nevada's citizens," and accused Nevada officials of knowingly harboring illegal voters on its lists.
"Nevada knows the 185 names they keep waving around were never the full list of illegal voters," a Homeland Security spokesperson said in an email. "They were only the files [that immigration officials] had finished reviewing at the moment of the call. Since then, [immigration officials] have manually confirmed about 2,000 more aliens from the same list. The review is just beginning."
While voting in the upcoming election will conclude on Nov. 3, there is concern among some election experts that the relationship between federal leaders and their counterparts at the state and local levels might not be easily repairable.
The federal government has traditionally supported state and local officials on a slew of election-related matters, from mitigating foreign threats to cybersecurity. With the fragile state of affairs, some experts fear any Election Day complications could threaten the integrity of the vote.
"Our state and local election officials are going to have fewer resources at their disposal, less intelligence and less ability to coordinate in responding to what might be significant threats going forward because they don't trust the federal government as a partner the way they did," Weiser said.
While trust in how elections are being conducted remains top of mind for voters, election officials like Holden, Aguilar and Raffensperger are working to assure their residents that they should still have faith in the process.
"There's no reason for a voter to ever doubt their ballot," Holden said.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Hesburger's first Italian restaurant opens doors in Matera
body:
With the opening of an Italian outlet, the Finnish fast food chain now operates in 10 different countries across Europe.
Finnish fast food chain Hesburger has opened its first ever outlet in Italy.
The restaurant in the city of Matera, in the Basilicata region of southern Italy, officially began welcoming customers on Friday 23 October.
With the opening of the outlet in Matera coming in the wake of similar recent expansions into the Romanian and Polish markets, Hesburger now operates in 10 different countries across Europe.
In a press release, the firm said that the move will create 20 new jobs in the city.
The statement also noted the influential role Italian entrepreneur Venanzia Rizzi , who is originally from Matera but has lived in Finland for a long time, had in bringing the Finnish chain to Italy.
"Matera is my hometown and Finland is my second home country. That's why it's especially wonderful to connect these two important places to me through entrepreneurship," Rizzi said.
Hesburger's statement further added that its arrival in Matera — a city known for its strong food culture — has drawn both "positive and cautious reactions".
"The feedback we've received directly has been positive, and we're happy that our brand is generating interest. Above all, we want to earn the trust of local customers through quality products, friendly service, and a positive customer experience," noted Ieva Salmela , Hesburger's Director of Communications and International Marketing.
When Hesburger's plans were first revealed in September, Italian newspaper La Repubblica reported that some locals were not pleased by the arrival of another fast food chain in their city, coming just months after a similar expansion by McDonald's.
Yle News reporter Ronan Browne explains the cultural and historical context behind Hesburger's expansion into Italy.

title: Finally – Precise Uncrewed Elsight Positioning in GNSS-Denied Environments
body:
One of the keys to the novel POSITIONING solution is that Elsight built it on a patented multi-signal fusion technology, delivering highly precise geolocation. While it is also the first product of its kind with built-in active GPS spoofing detection, this compact and cost-effective technology provides reliable positioning with or without GPS. As a provider of mission-critical connectivity for uncrewed systems, Elsight recently announced its new POSITIONING capability at the Association of the US Army’s annual meeting and exposition 12-14 October in Washington DC. Elsight’s new offering delivers unprecedented accurate geolocation for autonomous platforms across air, land and sea domains – alone or in combination – in GPS-denied, jammed, or spoofed environments. Elsight Positioning The launch comes amid ongoing global GPS jamming and spoofing, as growing usage of uncrewed systems push Electronic Warfare to the centre of tactical planning. Jamming and spoofing tools once limited to specialist units are now fielded broadly by regular forces. Cellular Positioning (Graphics: Elsight) Elsight’s POSITIONING capability is built on a patented cellular-based solution that determines platform location using cellular network measurements, enabling precise geolocation when GPS is unavailable, degraded, or actively spoofed. POSITIONING is fully integrated into the company’s flagship mission enablement product, Halo. A multi-source fusion engine continuously layers in additional available inputs – including cellular Timing Advance (TA), surrounding base station signals, GPS when verified reliable, and motion and velocity vectors – to improve accuracy and resilience. Active GPS spoofing detection cross-references GPS against cellular-derived position in real time, firing an alert when the two diverge. Elsight CEO Yoav Amitai (Photo: Elsight) “While GPS remains a critical vulnerability in contested environments,” alerts Elsight CEO Yoav Amitai “…our POSITIONING product entirely removes dependency, giving uncrewed systems the ability to know exactly where they are, regardless of what is happening to the environment around them. Every alternative tells you how far you’ve moved, but Elsight tells you where you are. It is a fundamentally different approach to positioning.” POSITIONING’s benefits include: Low customer burden: requiring no additional hardware for existing customers Elsight’s Positioning application. GPS operation: functioning in darkness, at sea, and in conflict zones without internet, visual reference, or communications link. High precision geolocation: exceeding relative positioning the technology knows exactly where an uncrewed platform is, not just how far it moved. Patented cellular-based core: operating on a non-GNSS infrastructure, it is inherently resistant to GPS jamming, spoofing, and electronic interference that would compromise satellite-dependent systems, and operates on any available network. Multi-source fusion: allowing continuous combination of all available inputs, it automatically adapts as signal availability changes without a single source. title: Creepy Cat in the Hat videos reach Finland
body:
AI-generated videos featuring the children's book character the Cat in the Hat are now spreading in Finland.
Viral images that purport to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character roaming the streets after dark are sparking fear and confusion among children.
The so-called Cat in the Hat phenomenon is spreading on social media. In frightening videos, the black-and-white feline, familiar from 1950s children's books, turns up in various towns and cities.
Over the past few days, the phenomenon has also reached Finland. Police in Oulu told Yle that they have been contacted about it. They said they have searched the streets but have not found anyone sneaking around in a cat costume.
Jyrki Mikkonen , principal of Koivuhaka School in Kokkola, says he is aware that content featuring the hat-wearing feline is circulating on social media. The school learned about it from parents.
"There were posts on social media warning that the figure would show up in this area. According to messages from guardians, this is worrying kids," he says.
The phenomenon centres on videos, shared especially on TikTok, that portray the cat character as menacing and claim it has been 'spotted' in various places or is 'on its way' to a particular town or school.
Kaisa Rissanen , of Someturva, a Finnish service that helps victims of online harassment and bullying, says the pattern is familiar. About ten years ago, people dressed up as clowns sparked similar worry.
"The threat is specific to videos created with AI, not to real dangerous situations," she notes.
But even if the threat isn't real, Rissanen says children's fear is genuine.
She also points out that digital security skills are becoming increasingly important as AI-generated content on social media keeps growing.
"This is a good wake-up call that we need to address these topics more broadly," she says.

title: Jay-Z announced as Super Bowl LXI halftime show performer
body:
Jay-Z is taking the Super Bowl LXI halftime stage.
The rapper announced during Monday Night Football the he will be the Super Bowl LXI halftime show performer.
"From 'Reasonable Doubt' to standing on the Super Bowl Halftime stage, this has been a journey," Jay-Z said in a statement, referring to his debut album from 1996. "Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."
Super Bowl LXI will take place on Sunday, Feb. 14, 2027, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
Jay-Z's entertainment company Roc Nation produces the NFL's Super Bowl halftime show, leaving the "99 Problems" singer in charge of selecting the widely watched performer each year.
Roc Nation partners with the NFL and Apple Music on the annual halftime show.
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said in a statement Monday that he has been waiting for Jay-Z to take the stage himself at the Super Bowl.
"When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him," Goodell said. "I couldn’t be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring to the Super Bowl stage.”
Super Bowl LXI will be the second Super Bowl hosted at SoFi Stadium, following Super Bowl LVI in 2022.
During Super Bowl LVI, Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg, Eminem, Mary J. Blige, Kendrick Lamar, 50 Cent and Anderson .Paak headlined the halftime show and performed a medley of their greatest hits.
The artists also honored Los Angeles with a celebration of West Coast hip-hop culture and local landmarks in the stage design.
Their performance won the Primetime Emmy Award for outstanding variety special (live) and also won Emmys for outstanding production design for a variety special and outstanding music direction.
During last year's Super Bowl, Bad Bunny took the stage during halftime at Levi Stadium in Santa Clara, California, bringing his Puerto Rican culture to the stage along with a collection of his hit songs.
The 2027 Super Bowl will air on ABC and ESPN and will be streamed on the ESPN App and NFL+ on mobile.
The Walt Disney Co. is the parent company of ABC News and ESPN.

title: Jay-Z to headline 2027 Super Bowl halftime show
body: The man who has helped produce the Super Bowl halftime show is stepping into the spotlight: Jay-Z will headline the show himself.The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.The announcement included a short video of Jay-Z sitting in SoFi Stadium surrounded by goats with the caption "GOAT's out of the bag."After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his "Jay-Z 30" concerts over the weekend. The run began with three shows at Yankee Stadium in New York, continued in London and ended in Southern California.Jay-Z's Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league's entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, "If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now."Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.Since then, the headlining halftime show performers have included Shakira and Jennifer Lopez, Rihanna, Kendrick Lamar and The Weeknd, among others.Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog includes the albums "Reasonable Doubt," "The Blueprint" and "The Black Album," and hit songs such as "Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)," "99 Problems" and "Empire State of Mind," his collaboration with Alicia Keys.His 1996 debut, "Reasonable Doubt," was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame last year.Jay-Z's career has extended into music publishing, artist management and sports. He co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.Bad Bunny performed at last season's Super Bowl in February. His songs had sharp gains across streaming charts, playlists and music discovery platforms in the hours following the show.The next morning, the Puerto Rican superstar held the top six spots on Spotify's Top 50 U.S. chart, with another song coming in at No. 8. Eleven other Bad Bunny songs were ranking in Spotify's Top 50 U.S. chart at the time.

title: Appeals court declines to step in on Trump administration's California voting case
body:
The judge called the DOJ's request a "self-constructed" emergency.
A 9th Circuit Court of Appeals panel on Monday rejected a request from the Justice Department for an immediate order demanding California segregate roughly 20,000 mail-in ballots from individuals the Trump administration claims are likely non-citizens.
The 2-1 ruling from the panel said the appeals court lacks jurisdiction at this stage in the litigation, punting it back to district court, which has a hearing on the DOJ lawsuit set for Tuesday afternoon.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, and Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, a President Joe Biden appointee, ruled against the administration's request, with Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, who was appointed by Trump, dissenting.
In their ruling, Bennett and Sanchez wrote: "The United States’s claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one. At least part of the delay here is attributable to the United States’s own delay in filing suit, in realizing that existing California state law governs the issuance and processing of ballots, in recognizing that California has millions of registered voters and processes ballots on a schedule aligned with that scale, and in communicating to the court its desired relief."
Earlier this month, the DOJ filed suit against California , accusing the state of failing to review a list of alleged noncitizens that the Trump administration claimed were sent mail-in ballots for next week's midterm election.
In court papers filed earlier last week, Los Angeles officials said a preliminary analysis of 200 of the names on the 20,000-person list, included a "high percentage" of individuals who say they were born in the U.S. and many more who have no voting history at all.
Of those 200 individuals, officials said, nearly 40% "indicate that they were born in the United States, which is strong evidence of citizenship; and 71.2% of the records have no voting history," according to a filing.
In a rare Sunday emergency hearing, the Justice Department's efforts to have the appeals court quickly rule on its lawsuit faced considerable skepticism from the panel.
Bennett repeatedly questioned whether the appeals court had jurisdiction to step in at this stage in the litigation and expressed considerable constitutional concerns over the lawsuit itself.
"I don't see how we have jurisdiction," Bennett said to DOJ attorney Matthew Donnelly after pressing him over the timeline of the government's decision to seek emergency appeal when a hearing before the district judge is already set for Tuesday.
Donnelly claimed that the DOJ's decision to seek relief from the appeals court came after disclosures by California of the numbers of mail-in ballots already being processed in advance of the election -- which number in the hundreds of thousands.
Bennett's most significant concerns appeared to be the nature of the lawsuit and it appearing to directly contradict the Constitution's Elections Clause -- which mandates that states have jurisdictions over the manner their elections are run.
"How can the legislature making laws with regard to the manner of holding elections be preempted by a criminal statute passed by the Congress, especially when both the Congress and the California Legislature have made it illegal for non-citizens to vote?" he asked.
Donnelly repeatedly pointed to DOJ's position that the way California is administering its elections -- and not acting on the hard drive of potential 20,000 likely non-citizens -- infringes on the federal government's ability to enforce the federal statute barring voting by illegal immigrants.

title: Video of police being called to youth soccer game draws outrage
body: Viral video of police being called to a youth soccer game near Orlando, Florida, is drawing outrage, with some claiming the cops showed up because a 3-year-old child was too good, while the league's director says the call was made because the parents were being disruptive.No one disputes that 3-year-old Nevada, who can be seen in several videos dominating on the pitch against kids one and two years older than him, is a soccer phenom. One of the directors of the youth league Nevada was playing in told the cops when they arrived, "The kid is very good ... He's great. Really good.""He's really advanced compared to the other ones.  He's scoring a lot of goals, but he's pushing the kids and scoring," the youth league director was seen saying on police body camera video. He said he had told the kids not to push while they're playing, and that there was another incident with Nevada's parents a few weeks earlier when he swapped some of the players out, including Nevada."They don't like that," the league director said.The league director told police Nevada's parents took issue with him telling the refs not to let their son push the other kids, claiming they created "a big scene, arguing with other parents." Nevada's mom told a different story.She is seen in the body camera video saying they always stand on the opposite side of the field as the other parents to avoid causing any disruption."They're literally kicking him out of this place because he's good at soccer," she told the police. In one video of the incident taken by the family, Nevada's father is heard saying, "They called the police on a 3-year-old because he's too good."Nevada's mother told CBS News the coach told Nevada he could stay in his most recent game if he passed the ball, but about halfway through, the cops got involved. She said in the bodycam video that she saw the other parents huddle in a circle talking about him during the game.In an interview with media personality Lauren Lorosa, Nevada's mom said, "My son is already dressed. I cannot explain to my 3-year-old son that he cannot play today because he is so good." The league director said he wanted the family to leave, and he was willing to offer them a refund. Online, there's been an avalanche of support for Nevada and his family, including from YouTube star Rachel Accurso, better known as Ms. Rachel, who commented on a post about the incident, saying she'd love to have Nevada on her show.Not everybody has been supportive, with one coach writing, "These parents should be ashamed of themselves."The league, i9 Sports, wrote on Facebook that it was "aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously.""The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us," it wrote. "We are working to understand the circumstances and will not speculate or share unverified information."

title: DOJ seeking to charge Comey with conspiring to disclose national defense information
body:
The case relates to disclosures published in the New York Times in 2016.
Over the last month, a legal fight has been playing out behind closed doors about the Department of Justice’s ongoing investigation into former FBI Director James Comey over the alleged mishandling of classified information dating back more than a decade ago.
According to newly unsealed court records, prosecutors allege that Comey broke the law by directing FBI staff to leak information to a New York Times reporter for an article published on Oct. 5, 2016, titled “Yahoo Said to Have Aided U.S. Email Surveillance by Adapting Spam Filter.”
“The United States' investigation has uncovered evidence that former FBI Director, James B. Comey, sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before,” prosecutors wrote in their response to Comey’s motion to dismiss earlier this month. “Mr. Comey directed staff to speak to [the New York Times reporter] about specific accuracy concerns related to the Reuters article, and thereby illegally transferred classified information.”
The article in question centered on whether the Department of Justice sought a court order from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court to force Yahoo to search for communications between members of a foreign terrorist organization. According to court filings, Comey sought to correct claims in a Reuters story published the previous day that Yahoo “secretly built a custom software program to search all of its customers' incoming emails for specific information provided by U.S. intelligence officials.”
Prosecutors with the Department of Justice filed the charges against Comey via what's known as a “criminal information,” which does not require the approval of a grand jury. It was filed under seal on Oct. 5.
Department of Justice lawyers argue that by filing a criminal information within 10 years of the alleged crime, they stopped the clock on the statute of limitations and secured a months-long extension to secure an indictment.
“The Department filed a waiverless criminal information to toll the statute of limitations as it relates to allegations concerning former FBI Director Comey. Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further,” a Department of Justice account said on social media.
However, Comey’s lawyers argue that the statute of limitations to bring a criminal information actually expired five years ago and the rule prosecutors cited to secure an extension only applies to indictments. They also argued that the Washington, D.C., Circuit Court has not approved the practice of tolling the statute of limitations via a criminal information.
“Because the default five-year statute of limitations for federal felonies has long since elapsed on the alleged offenses, and the government's information does not meet the express statutory requirement for an extended ten-year limitations period, the information is untimely and must be dismissed,” Comey’s lawyers wrote in their motion to dismiss.
Prosecutors pushed back on that argument, claiming that the federal law in question applies to both indictments and information and arguing that “the case comes down to a syllogism" in federal law.
“Given the seriousness of espionage offenses, and given the deficiencies of the prior statute-of-limitations period in capturing treasonous conduct threatening this nation, Congress intended to lengthen the time to prosecute acts of espionage – not to split that time by instrument,” prosecutors wrote.
Comey also faces federal charges of threatening Trump after a federal grand jury indicted Comey on two charges in April after he posted a picture on his Instagram account of seashells spelling out "8647," which federal prosecutors say constituted a threat against the president's life.
Comey's lawyers are seeking to have that case thrown out. His defense lawyers argued that Trump's repeated calls for Comey's prosecution and criticism of his public statement "leave no doubt as to his genuine animus" and demonstrate that the case against him for allegedly threatening to kill Trump by posting photos of seashells on a beach is vindictive.
"The ensuing indictment is not based on a good faith application of the law to the facts; instead, it effectuates a yearslong campaign by the President to use the criminal process to punish Mr. Comey for his protected speech and because of the President's deep-seated animosity," Comey's lawyers wrote.

title: Inmate serving life sentence escapes prison
body:
Jacob Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence for first-degree murder.
Authorities have located the truck allegedly stolen by a convicted murderer who escaped prison in Tennessee, but his location remains unknown, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigations (TBI) announced on Tuesday.
The truck was found in Marion, Illinois, amid the search for the escapee, Jacob Morley, according to TBI. A local resident who had seen a news report on the escapee and stolen truck called TBI to report seeing the vehicle parked behind a business, police in Marion said.
"There was no evidence that Morley was still in the vicinity of the vehicle," the Marion Police Department said, adding that a search of the city on Tuesday "had negative results on locating Morley."
Morley, 28, who is serving a life sentence, escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville over the weekend, the Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) announced Monday.
"At approximately 11:30 p.m. on October 25, 2026, staff at NWCX confirmed Morley was unaccounted for and immediately conducted an emergency count and search of the facility," the agency said .
Security cameras "confirmed Morley breached the perimeter fence and exited the facility in his TDOC uniform," officials said.
On Monday, authorities released a photo of a truck sought in connection with the inmate. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) said newly obtained footage "shows Morley stealing a white 2008 Ford F-350, Tennessee tag 138BBQV" at approximately 1 a.m. Monday from the 400 block of Keystone Drive.
The truck was marked with Lindamood Planting Company on the side, according to TBI.
There were several sightings of the truck, including passing the Hornbeak Fire Department in West Tennessee early Monday, before it was located in Marion on Tuesday, authorities said.
TDOC said it is working with local, state and federal law enforcement to apprehend Morley.
"TDOC is committed to protecting the safety of the public and is asking the community to immediately contact law enforcement with any sightings or information," the agency said in a statement.
According to TDOC, Morley was serving a life sentence for a conviction in Carter County, Tennessee, for crimes including first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, evading arrest and vandalism.
TBI announced Monday that Morley was added to the state's Most Wanted list, and offered a reward up to $2,500 for information leading to his arrest.
Morley "should be considered dangerous," TBI said .
Authorities are asking residents in the area to review "home security and doorbell cameras, trail and hunting cameras, and other surveillance systems" for potential sightings.
TDOC said authorities have "cleared buildings and structures in the surrounding area."
The Tennessee Highway Patrol is also joining the search effort, according to TDOC, with aviation assets and state troopers helping the search.
A wanted poster from the TDOC describes Morley as 5 feet, 11 inches tall and weighing 240 pounds with green eyes and brown hair.
"If you have any information regarding the whereabouts of Jacob Morley, please contact the Tennessee Department of Correction at 1-844-832-3463 or 911," the poster read.
An updated wanted poster lists 1 (800) TBI-FIND.
Sheriff Bryan Avery of the Lake County Sheriff's Office, where the prison is located, asked the public to remain "vigilant and exercise caution."
"Anyone who encounters or believes they have spotted Morley should not approach, confront, or attempt to apprehend him," Avery said in a statement Monday. "Instead, immediately dial 911 and provide any relevant information to law enforcement."
Northwest Correctional Complex is a prison with "the operating capacity to house 1,776 male inmates with custody levels ranging from minimum to close," according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.
According to ABC News Tennessee affiliate WJHL , Morley was found guilty of murder in 2022.
Morley was sentenced to life in prison for the murder of Cody Birchfield, a previously missing man whose body was discovered buried underneath Morley's home in March 2022, according to WJHL.
The victim's sister said she is "reliving this horrible tragedy all over again."
"But this time I find myself asking the public for help to find my brother's murderer when he should be in prison locked away," Carrie Norman said in a statement.

title: Judge rules Trump DOJ 'unlawfully' fired Maurene Comey
body:
Judge Jesse Furman said Comey’s termination violated civil service rules.
A federal judge in New York on Monday ruled against President Donald Trump and the Justice Department over the firing of Maurene Comey , daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from the Manhattan U.S. attorney's office.
Judge Jesse Furman said Comey's termination violated civil service rules.
"Yes, the Attorney General is authorized by law to remove an AUSA. But the Attorney General (and anyone to whom the Attorney General delegates that authority) is also limited by law, namely the CSRA, to do so only in a particular manner and only for certain reasons," the judge wrote.
Furman ordered Maurene Comey, who most recently led the prosecution of Sean "Diddy" Combs , reinstated with back pay.
In addition to calling her termination unlawful, Furman decided Trump and the DOJ violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and Maurene Comey's due process rights.
"The Department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course," a DOJ spokesperson told ABC News.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York declined to comment.
ABC News has reached out to Maurene Comey for comment.
Furman's ruling outlines that Maurene Comey's reinstatement applies from the date of her termination in July of 2025 until December, when she effectively resigned from her role by accepting a new job in the private sector.
In ordering Maurene Comey's reinstatement, Furman rejected what he described as the Trump administration's "sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority."
The Trump administration had argued that not only was Maurene Comey's firing lawful under federal statute, but that the laws protecting civil servants were also an unconstitutional intrusion into Trump's authority.
"The question at the heart of this case is whether these limitations on the removal of Assistant United States Attorneys are consistent with Article II and the constitutional separation of powers," Judge Furman wrote.
To make its argument, the DOJ pointed to the Supreme Court's decision in Trump v. Slaughter -- where the justices effectively supercharged presidential power by greenlighting the firing of the leaders of independent federal agencies -- and the Trump v. United States immunity case
"On their view, AUSAs who represent the United States in criminal cases in court exercise prosecutorial and investigatory functions that fall squarely within the President's 'conclusive and preclusive' powers," Furman wrote. "Accordingly, they argue, the President -- and, by extension, the heads of departments appointed by the President -- must have the power to remove such AUSAs for any reason or no reason at all."
But Furman rejected the DOJ's interpretation of the legal precedent, pointing to decades of other cases which affirm the legal protections for line prosecutors. He also noted that neither case cited by the DOJ applies to inferior officers or "supports their sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority."
"Defendants' argument is contrary to an unbroken line of Supreme Court decisions dating back almost two centuries, and the Supreme Court itself has not formally overruled any of those decisions. That is sufficient, in itself, to reject the argument," wrote Judge Furman.
To accept the DOJ's argument, Furman wrote, would "unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system."
Maurene Comey was an assistant U.S. attorney who successfully prosecuted Ghislaine Maxwell , the former associate of sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and multiple gang members before the split verdict last year in the trial of Combs, who was convicted of a prostitution-related charge but acquitted of more serious charges.
She was also involved in the office's case against Epstein, who died by suicide in 2019 at New York City's Metropolitan Correctional Center while he was awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.
Trump fired James Comey during his first term in office after Comey announced publicly that Trump's 2016 campaign was being investigated over potential ties to Russia.
Prior to Maurene Comey's firing, Trump privately vented about having a Comey work in his administration, sources previously told ABC News.
Earlier this year, Furman blocked the Justice Department's attempt to move Maurene Comey's lawsuit over her firing as a federal prosecutor out of court.
The Justice Department argued at the time that her case belongs before the Merit Systems Protection Board and not in federal district court.
Furman decided the case belongs with him because Maurene Comey was fired pursuant to the president's executive authority and not the usual procedures for civil servants.
"Maurene Comey was, by all accounts, an exemplary Assistant United States Attorney. In her nearly ten years working at the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York, she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases, and she consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike," the judge's opinion in April said.
The DOJ, in court filings, has characterized Comey's case as routine.
"A federal employee's claims that removal from federal service was arbitrary and capricious or conducted in a manner that did not provide the process to which they contend they were due is not a novel issue," government attorneys previously said.
Following her termination last year, Maurene Comey told colleagues in a farewell email that she was fired as a federal prosecutor without being told a reason but urged them not to succumb to the "fear" she said her firing could cause.
"If a career prosecutor can be fired without reason, fear may seep into the decision of those who remain," Comey said in her email, a copy of which was obtained by ABC News. "Do not let that happen."

title: Trump offers $1M reward for voter fraud tips that result in conviction
body:
It is not clear where the money for this reward would come from.
President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is offering a $1 million reward for anyone who reports voter fraud -- in past elections or in the upcoming midterm elections -- that leads to a conviction.
"Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud," Trump wrote in a social media post.
Trump has repeatedly made unfounded claims that there was widespread voter fraud in past elections. It is not clear where the money for this reward that the president is offering would come from.
The White House would not provide any additional details about Trump's announcement.
Trump has pushed election reform legislation, the SAVE America Act , which he says will cut down on voter fraud. The legislation requires voter ID at the ballot box and proof of citizenship to register.
The House passed the measure earlier this year; it has failed in the Senate multiple times.
Last week, Trump announced a separate fraud whistleblower program where tipsters who successfully report and prove fraud cases will be rewarded a 1% commission of the amount of money the government is able to recover. The president said he would make the determination of whether a tipster would receive a financial reward.
ABC News' Sarah Beth Hensley contributed to this report.

title: Is the Federal Reserve likely to raise interest rates this week?
body: The Federal Reserve will announce on Wednesday whether monetary policymakers are raising interest rates for the second time this year in a bid to subdue inflation. Most economists and Wall Street analysts expect the Fed to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4%. Consumer prices have surged this year, with headline inflation across the U.S. rising at a 3.7% annual rate in September as energy costs jumped. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago amid signs inflation could be seeping into the broader economy. The Fed targets annual inflation of 2%.Gasoline prices, which have hovered above $4 a gallon for the last three months, accounted for more than half the September increase in consumer prices, according to the Labor Department."Although the latest hot inflation readings and rise in inflation expectations will concern Fed officials, they still appear broadly intent on tightening policy at a measured pace," Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at investor advisory firm Capital Economics, said in a recent research note.In September, the Fed raised the federal funds rate — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — by a quarter of a percentage point — its first hike in three years, thereby raising borrowing costs across the U.S. economy. The Fed is scheduled to announce its latest interest rate decision at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday.The meeting comes at a crucial time, as Americans head to the polls to cast their ballots in the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Many Americans have expressed frustration with the state of the economy as they contend with rising costs of gas, food, utilities and other expenses.Most economists and investors expect the Fed to raise rates one more time before year-end, likely at its last meeting of the year on Dec. 8-9.According to CME Group's Fed Watch tool, which uses 30-day Fed funds futures prices to predict rate decisions, traders see an 88% probability that the Fed will hold rates steady in October and a 71% probability the Fed will raise rates in December (no meeting scheduled for November).In quarterly projections last month, the Fed signaled that its rate-setting committee expected to raise rates later this year. At the same time, some Fed policymakers have signaled that the central bank is in no rush to lift borrowing costs. "With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information," New York Fed President John Williams said in a speech at the University at Buffalo following the Fed's rate hike in September. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will give a press conference after this week's rate decision. Until then, investors are unlikely to get any clues from Warsh, who has argued against sharing forward guidance on rate decisions.

title: 15-year-old arrested in connection with shooting near FAMU
body:
The shooting left 12 injured, including six children.
A 15-year-old was arrested in connection with a shooting near Florida A & M University over the weekend, which left 12 injured, including six children, the Tallahassee Police Department announced on Monday morning. Eleven of those who were injured had gunshot wounds.
Authorities said they made the arrest on Sunday.
The individual arrested, Anthony Rivers III, will face 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent, police said.
State attorney Jack Campbell said Monday he would be prosecuted as an adult.
According to police, "preliminary findings indicate a physical altercation occurred" before the shooting on Saturday night near Perry and Manatee streets just outside Florida A & M University's Bragg Memorial Stadium.
"Detectives believe the incident stemmed from a dispute between individuals known to one another. At this stage of the investigation, none of the victims appear to have been the intended targets," according to police.
Police added that the investigation remains "open and active" and said more arrests are possible.
"What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families,” Tallahassee Chief of Police Lawrence Revell said in a statement.
The statement continued, "While this arrest marks a significant step forward, our work is far from over. We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy."
Revell spoke with reporters during a late-night press conference after the shooting.
"We know that our youngest victim is 11 years old. At least three of our victims have sustained serious injuries and one of those is in critical condition. Eight of those are reported to be in stable condition," he said.
In a Sunday morning update, the Tallahassee Police Department said that six of the victims remain hospitalized, with one in critical condition. Five other victims have been released from the hospital, police said.
The person who was injured but not from a gunshot was "a grandmother of one of the victims," the chief said, adding that she "injured herself fleeing from the scene."
FAMU President Marva B. Johnson released a video statement Sunday afternoon, saying that while the shooting did not occur on her campus, the school is offering care and support to "members of our FAMU family who were injured in the tragic incident."

title: 'Star Trek' actor Walter Koenig dies at 90
body:
Walter Koenig, best known for playing USS Enterprise navigator Ensign Pavel Chekov on the original " Star Trek " TV series, died Sunday. He was 90.
Koenig's agent confirmed his death to ABC News, and Koenig's former co-star, George Takei, also shared the news in an online post Monday.
"Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world," Koenig's agent, Zachery McGinnis, said in a statement, in part. "He passed of old age at home in North Hollywood last night surrounded by his daughter and niece."
In his Facebook post, Takei mourned the news of his former co-star's death.
"Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too," Takei wrote.
Born on Sept. 14, 1936, Koenig appeared on several television shows including "The Alfred Hitchcock Hour," "The Lieutenant" -- created and produced by "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry -- "I Spy" and more before landing the role of Chekov in the second season of "Star Trek" in 1967.
Koenig told the Television Academy in a 2013 interview that he hadn't seen "Star Trek" before he read for the role of Chekov, a character that was added to the show after its debut.
"They were looking for an actor or a personality that would appeal to the same demographic that Davy Jones did -- kids 8 to 14 years old," he said, referring to the then-star of the music-comedy TV series "The Monkees," adding that when he was cast in the role, he would get mail from young people commenting on how "groovy" his hair was.
In a 1984 interview with "Good Morning America," Koenig said "Star Trek" had a "monumental effect" on his life.
"In my mind it's somewhat questionable whether I would indeed still be pursuing a career in this industry had it not been for 'Star Trek,'" he said. "'Star Trek' has made it possible not only to remain an actor, but to pursue other industry endeavors like writing and directing and producing."
Following "Star Trek," Koenig went on to star in or appear in other television series, including "Columbo," "The Starlost," "Babylon 5" and more.
In 1979, he joined his other fellow "Star Trek" original series cast members in reprising his role in "Star Trek: The Motion Picture," the first "Star Trek" feature film.
He went on to play Chekov again in "Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan" in 1982, "Star Trek III: The Search for Spock" in 1984, "Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home" in 1986, "Star Trek V: The Final Frontier" in 1989," "Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country" in 1991 and "Star Trek: Generations" in 1994.
Outside of acting, Koenig was known for his humanitarian activism focused on human rights and assisting refugees. He was also a husband and father. In 1965, he married actress Judy Levitt.
"She’s very tolerant of my collection and my collecting so long as it doesn’t come down the stairs into the living room or any of the bedrooms," Koenig said in a 2012 interview about his wife's view of his "Star Trek" memorabilia.
In 2012, Koenig was honored with a Hollywood Walk of Fame star. In recent years, he continued to appear in other "Star Trek"-related projects and lent his voice to various animated series. He was also a familiar face at fan events and conventions.
Koenig is survived by his daughter, Danielle Koenig, an actress, comedian and screenwriter. Koenig's wife died in 2022. Koenig's son, actor Andrew Koenig, died by suicide in 2010.

title: Teen pleads not guilty in hit-and-run that killed two 17-year-old girls on e-bike
body:
Vincent Battiloro is accused of fatally hitting Maria Niotis and Isabella Salas.
A New Jersey teen accused of intentionally ramming his SUV into two 17-year-old girls riding an e-bike, killing them, pleaded not guilty to murder charges on Monday.
Vincent Battiloro, 18, appeared in court for his arraignment on Monday, following his indictment earlier this month on two counts of first-degree murder.
The victims -- Maria Niotis and Isabella Salas, both 17 -- were killed on Sept. 29, 2025, after authorities said a Jeep Compass driving at a high rate of speed struck them while the two friends were riding the e-bike on a residential street in Cranford.
The SUV was located nearby with "major front-end damage and an e-bike embedded into the front of the vehicle," according to the complaint. Battiloro allegedly fled from the scene on foot, according to the complaint. When later questioned by police, he allegedly said he had been carjacked by a masked individual armed with a knife while driving the SUV that afternoon, according to the complaint.
Battiloro, who was 17 at the time, was arrested two days later and initially charged as a juvenile with murder. He was waived to adult court in June.
Battiloro did not speak during Monday's hearing, his first since being charged as an adult. One of his attorneys entered his plea on his behalf.
The next hearing in the case has been scheduled for Dec. 14. ABC News has reached out to his attorneys for comment on the charges but did not immediately receive a response.
Family members of the victims attended Monday's hearing, wearing sweatshirts with their names and faces printed on them.
"Maria and Isabella should be alive today," their families said in a joint statement on Monday. "These families, and every parent in this community, deserve to know how this unspeakable catastrophe was allowed to happen."
The families call on the New Jersey attorney general to open an investigation "concerning the events leading to the deaths of Maria and Isabella, including investigating all law enforcement's dealings and interactions with Vincent Battiloro and his family."
The families of the girls had alleged in a statement following Battiloro's arrest that the suspect plotted an attack against Niotis for months, killing her and also her friend in the "horrific act."
Authorities have not commented on an alleged motive.

title: Vatican confirms Pope Leo's Latin America trip after post-surgery checkup
body:
Pope Leo XIV will proceed with his planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.
VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will proceed with his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, after doctors determined there are no medical reasons preventing him from traveling three weeks after lung cancer surgery, the Vatican confirmed Monday.
The Vatican press office said the pope’s recovery continues to progress in line with favorable assessments from his medical team. It also confirmed the pope is keeping the already ambitious trip program with no announced changes.
Surgeons on Oct. 13 removed a lobe where the nodule later diagnosed as malignant was located, in the first major health event of Leo's 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma , the most common type of lung cancer.
Since returning to the Vatican, Leo has gradually resumed his activities while adjusting his schedule to prioritize recovery and periods of rest, the statement said.
The pope’s physician, Luigi Carbone, said there's no medical reason preventing Leo's trip to South America, which involves a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes.
Leo expressed gratitude for the prayers and support he has received during his recovery and said he was eager to return to a region where he spent important periods of his life.
“I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I’ve experienced so many moments of my life,” Leo said Monday. “May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy.”
The Vatican said the visit will provide an opportunity for the pope to strengthen ties with local churches, encourage the faithful and promote a message of faith, hope and peace in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

title: Trump told DOJ to sue to block Alaska Senate results if Republican narrowly loses
body:
The lawsuit cites name confusion around Sen. Dan Sullivan and another candidate.
President Donald Trump said Friday that he had directed the Justice Department to preemptively file a lawsuit to try to block the certification of the crucial Alaska Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, citing name confusion among the candidates.
Republicans have alleged that candidate Dan J. Sullivan is running a sham campaign to purposefully confuse voters and draw votes away from incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan based on their names being similar .
Asked Friday about the lawsuit, which the Justice Department filed on Thursday, Trump said, "Well, I'm one that said, 'Do it.'"
"They have two guys run named Dan Sullivan running. So the Democrats put up a guy never -- I don't think he ever voted before," Trump said of Dan J. Sullivan, who appears on the ballot with no party affiliation and told The New York Times that he has in the past voted for both Democrats and Republicans.
"All of a sudden he decides to run for the Senate, and his name is Dan Sullivan. One is Daniel S., one is Daniel J. The Daniel J. is the fake," Trump said.
"Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan ... the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election," the number-three ranking official at the Department of Justice, Stanley Woodward, wrote in Thursday's filing.
An earlier legal challenge to Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy was rejected by Alaska's supreme court, which ordered that he be included on the ballot.
In bringing the case, the Justice Department says it's guarding against the possibility that Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses in a manner that suggests he would have won were it not for votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan. The incumbent senator is facing Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, as well as Dan J. Sullivan.
"To guard against this danger, it is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion. An election result may be impacted by voter confusion if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska's rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election," Woodward wrote.
A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement, "Alaska's Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot. Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters."
A spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan said, "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course. Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska." A statement from Peltola's campaign called the suit "a despicable political threat to overturn an election."
The Alaska Secretary of State's office and a campaign spokesperson for Dan J. Sullivan did not respond to a request for comment from ABC News.
On Wednesday, President Trump posted on social media that he was looking at "powerful legal options" to remove Dan J. Sullivan from the ballot.
Over the summer, Alaska's election office said that Dan J. Sullivan would be removed from the ballot because the office determined his candidacy was not in good faith, but was meant, per an official, "to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality."
Dan. J. Sullivan then sued the state over the decision, and a state judge ruled that he was eligible to be on Alaska's Senate primary ballot. The Alaska Supreme Court upheld the ruling, after which the DOJ began investigating.
Fielding questions from reporters just hours before the lawsuit was filed, Attorney General Todd Blanche wouldn't rule out the DOJ intervening in a state's election process, but suggested only a "doomsday scenario" would warrant such action.
"I mean, is there any scenario? Yes, of course. There's scenarios that we could all come up with hypothetically, you know, some doomsday scenario, for example, right?" Blanche said. "It is not DOJ's intention to, and it's never our intention to improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process."
ABC News' Devin Dwyer contributed to this report.
